en: I go for refuge to Hari, the bestower of boons, whose abode is the elephant-mountain (Giri), the treasure-house of prosperity, the ocean of compassion, the worthy protector, and the remover of the distress of those who bow before him. 1.
I worship the Sudarśana light, which cuts through outer and inner darkness, by means of which they know the Reality whose resolve is unimpeded as the bearer of Lakṣmī. || 2 ||
Salutations to Vyāsa, who is Viṣṇu himself, who has augmented the Vedas with the great Mahābhārata and its collection of correct principles.
Salutations to that noble Rāmānuja, the supreme yogin, who extinguished the internal fever of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras.
I bow to that noble Varadarāja, the ornament of the Vatsa lineage, who, by bestowing the nectar of his commentary, brings even me back to life. (5)
I take refuge in this commentary, which has the form of the syllable Om (praṇava) and is like another stage upon which the supremacy of the Supreme Brahman is clearly perceived.

I take refuge in the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is heard of in the Upaniṣads, whose thought is cherished in the commentary, who is meditated upon in the lotus of my heart, and who is beheld in the abode of Śrīraṅgam. 7.
May the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and the knowers—being characterized by sattva—be victorious everywhere and at all times, having destroyed all misfortunes.
May the words of Rāmānuja Muni, which are not expansive yet profoundly deep, graciously reveal their own entire and firm inner meaning. (9)
At the command of the Lord of Śrīraṅga, Bhāṣyabhakti urged Vācāvijjīyana’s son, who had obtained the name Vyāsa from the Sudarśana [discus], to compose [the commentary].
The meaning heard from the gurus through words and applied by them is here set forth and elucidated, having been compiled for the ease of those desiring to know. (11)

Who knows the meaning of the entire Bhāṣya? This work is intended for the preservation of the portion that has been heard. This [work] should not be disregarded by those most learned in the Bhāṣya, even as the wealthy do not disregard a single cowrie.

If the Lord of Ascetics himself had expounded the Commentary with his words of exposition, then, due to its profundity, people of limited intellect would remain far removed from understanding those teachings.
He must be questioned as to how He is the Lord, for He is not perceived by our eyes.
May His commentary, the author of that commentary, and Hari himself be perfectly gracious toward us. (13)

For all persons whose determination of objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and who seek to acquire what is desirable and abandon what is undesirable—along with the means to those ends—in regard to that reality which consists of supramundane human goals and their means, and which is accessible through verbal testimony (*śabda*) alone; and since it has been established that even therein, the collection of syllables known as the Veda must primarily be relied upon as the authority, because it is free from the stains of the defects of human intellect; and since that [Veda] is understood to be devoted to both immediate and remote, mundane and supramundane fruits such as cattle, sons, rain, food, and heaven, as well as to the means for attaining them;

In the eastern region, and in this world situated above it—which, though capable of awakening one to the supreme human goal, is overwhelmed by hundreds of wicked words from people of various false views that act as thorns upon the path to liberation favored by the ancient teachers, and which has turned toward the evil paths shown by them and is thus utterly bewildered—I have, with the desire to revive it, cleared away those thorns and made straight the very ancient and correct path familiar to the ancient teachers who were adept at discerning the real from the unreal, in order to fulfill the aspirations of the multitude of seekers striving for the supreme human goal.

The Blessed One, the supreme compassionate commentator, who has manifested his descent through the power of destiny for the sake of people tormented by the fear of worldly existence, intends to explain the *Śārīraka-śāstra*. Since there are commentaries on these works composed by great seers (*maharṣi*), which themselves are to be explained by the seers who composed them, one must follow these very [works]. For one who is not a seer does not possess the capacity for subtle vision; only a seer can personally understand the intention of another seer, and not any other person of dull intellect.

When there is mutual contradiction among the words of the sages spoken by the same author, non-contradiction should be established through such means as the presentation of prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), the intention behind the statements, or the theory of figurative expression (*vaibhavavāda*). However, when there is a contradiction between words spoken by different authors that is difficult to resolve, one should accept that which is supported by reason; thus, there is no fault.

As for those who, despite the existence of these [authoritative texts], disregard them and take pleasure in other interpretations and alternative explanations that contradict them—their engagement in such activity itself serves as proof of their hearts being seized by dogmatic prejudice, their self-conceited claim to scholarship, and their preoccupation with displaying their own erudition.

Furthermore, the fact that other commentators have overstepped the explanations of the Sages (Ṛṣis) is made very clear in passages such as "Because of the threefold nature of meditation," "Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere," "Because of the teaching of the plenitude beyond the serene state," and "The small [ether] because of the subsequent [arguments]. However, in this case, adherence to the *Vṛtti* has been promised. Nor should one suspect that this promise is ill-conceived, for no subverting argument that cannot be avoided is perceived.

Although the Karma-mīmāṃsā has been rendered somewhat confused here and there by certain modern commentators, nevertheless, because there is no error regarding the path of ritual performance (*prayoga-mārga*), the attainment of results such as heaven—which depends solely upon the performance of rites—is independent of knowledge concerning the nature of deities, their true essence, or the doctrine of the reality of effects (*satkāryavāda*). Since the supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*) is to be accomplished through knowledge alone, any deviation from the path of knowledge results in the ruin of the self; therefore, misconceptions contrary to that knowledge must necessarily be avoided.

And in the latter part [of this work], with the intention that other points for instruction—though not explicitly stated—may be easily resolved by the very same method already demonstrated for those matters of the former part that are relevant to the respective topics at hand, the venerable author of the commentary begins to expound the Brahma-sūtras themselves.

Thus, for the sake of completing the work he has begun without obstacle and for its steady progress, he performs the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)—consisting of the worship of his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*)—as established by tradition and custom, in accordance with the Vedic injunctions, through the verse beginning with "akhila...

[etc.]: "For those who are endowed with the practice of auspicious rites, who are ever self-restrained, and who constantly engage in recitation (*japa*) and oblation (*homa*), no misfortune is found."

For it is thus recorded in tradition and taught by the respective authors of those works; furthermore, a summary of the meaning of the treatise is provided in substance for the purpose of concentrating the intellect and mind of the listener. Just as, in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the nature and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of Dharma were defined through both the literal expression and its implied meaning. Indeed, it is well known that for the ease of the listener's comprehension, the speaker’s presentation of the subject matter is preceded by a summary.

"For it is desired by the wise in this world to maintain both the concise and the detailed"—thus, both a summary of the subject matter of the treatise and a benediction have been performed. By the words "Vinatā" and "in the form of devotion," prostration is also implied, as one's bowing before Brahman is understood; for the root *ṇamu* signifies "bowing. In this way, the threefold auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) has been observed. By the first quarter of the verse, the meaning of the preceding two chapters is summarized.

But by the second [verse], the latter pair [is explained]. Just as there is a division of the six books (*ṣaṭka*) in the *Karmamīmāṃsā* due to a difference in the subject matter to be expounded, here too there is a division of the two pairs due to a difference in the subject matter to be expounded, consisting of the object (*viṣaya*) and the subject (*viṣayin*). That which is to be expounded in the scripture consists of the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*). Brahman is both the established means and the end; devotion (*bhakti*) is the means to be accomplished (*sādhya-upāya*). Among these, by means of words ending in the locative case, Brahman is described as the established means and the end. "Becoming" (*bhavati*) is *bhuvana*, meaning the category of effects (*kārya-dharma*).

By the power of conventional usage (*rūḍhi-śakti*), there is an exclusion of the potter and other such causes. For the word *bhuvana* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to a specific, vast class of effects. By the word *akhila*, all classes of eggs existing in all places and at all times are intended; thus, there is an exclusion of Brahmā and others. "Not *khila*" (fragmentary) is *akhila*; the meaning is that among effects, there is nothing whatsoever that has not become the object of Brahmā’s activities, such as creation. By this statement of distinction (*vyatireka*), the notion of mere commonality is removed.

As it is said, "There is nothing unknown to you," the term *sakalam* (all) is not used here in its positive sense (*anvayamukhena*). The term *nikhilam* (entire) is also not used for the sake of establishing the fact that the word begins with the letter *a*. For the learned have declared: "What auspiciousness is not brought about by one who employs the syllable *a*? Here, even if the intention is not to express the Lord [as a specific person], the syllable *a* is auspicious because it possesses the inherent power (*śakti*) to denote the Lord Nārāyaṇa; indeed, *a* is the primary name of the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa and denotes the Blessed One.

In the case of "aiuṇ," it is like the letter *a*. Although the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses negation, its quality as auspicious or inauspicious depends on the object being negated; therefore, just as in the expression "we worship without obstacle" (*niṣpratyūham upāsmaha*), this [negation] is even more auspicious because, by negating deficiency, it aims at completeness (*paupkalpa*). By the word "akhila" (entirety), the distinction between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is also intended. "Birth" (*janman*) refers to the forms that are eternal, occasional, and elemental (*prākṛta*); "stability" (*sthemā*) means persistence (*sthiti*).

And that [protection], being performed through various means such as the Antaryāmin, Viṣṇu’s incarnations, world-protectors (lokapālas), Manu and others, kings, mothers, fathers, and so forth, is manifold and unintended [here]. "Destruction" (bhaṅga) consists of the forms of the periodic (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and primordial (prākṛta). Although liberation (mokṣa) is included within dissolution (laya), it is not included here because the supreme purpose of the scripture is [the other three goals]; for this very reason, it should also not be included under the word "and so forth" (ādi), since, being common to all, it lacks the quality of being a clear cause for comprehension in this specific context.

For liberation has indeed been clearly specified as distinct from the former [powers]: "The creation, maintenance, destruction, and liberation from saṃsāra of the world," and likewise the Blessed Lord and the Commentator state: "The sole causes of the birth, maintenance, and destruction of the world, and of supreme bliss."

As it is stated in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*: "The sole cause of creation, sustenance, dissolution, and the cessation of *saṃsāra*"; and in the *Bhāṣya*: "The single cause of the arising, prosperity, dissolution, and supreme bliss of the entire world. By the word "to those who bow" (*vinate*) and so forth, the separate mention of the bestowal of worldly fruits such as heaven—which are included within "stability" (*sthemā*)—is unnecessary. For there is indeed a need for a separate mention only of liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the unique and ultimate purpose of the scripture.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), [actions] such as entering and governing, which are conducive to creation and so forth, are included. Furthermore, the Commentator himself will state: "The play (*līlā*) consisting of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world, as well as entering within it and governing it. Therefore, it is improper to rely on the assumption that entering within and governing are already established by the mention of birth, subsistence, and destruction alone.

Since, in the views of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and transformation (*pariṇāma*), that [sport] lacks the status of being an object, it must be stated separately according to our own view in order to exclude those positions; furthermore, when verbal expression is possible, it is improper to assume an objective reality, and because it is appropriate to intend a concise statement of the matter already explained at length, the word "līlā" (sport) is intended to signify the Lord’s perfection, having nothing dearer than Himself, and acting according to His own will. As it is said in the *Mahābhārata*: "He is immeasurable, not subject to injunctions, moving wherever He desires, and self-controlled."

"The Blessed One rejoices with beings as a child does with toys. "Immeasurability" means fullness. "Insubjection" means not being impelled by any other conscious being. By the phrase "going wherever he wishes," there is an exclusion of movements such as involuntary impulses that depend on the propulsion of wind, water, and so forth.

The meaning of the word *vaśin* (the self-controlled) is either the exclusion of activity performed according to one's own will, or the state of having play (*līlā*) as its own independent instrument. He whose entire universe is under his control is *vaśī*. The word *vaśin* is intended to exclude purposeful effort dependent on the operations of the senses; by the analogy of a child’s toy, it is meant that his play is independent of any other motive. By this, the exclusion of activities such as gambling preceded by the laying of stakes among kings is implied. Through the term "toys" (*krīḍanakaiḥ*), it is established that the greatness of the Lord is far more vast than the entire range of things to be accomplished.

[Objection: But surely *līlā* (sport) is the activity of the agent (*prayojaka*). Therefore, while it is appropriate for destruction (*bhaṅga*) to be a sport, how can birth and persistence—which consist of the activity of the object (*prayojya*)—be considered sports? [Response: It is said: for the Śruti declares, "May I become many; may I procreate. Thus, by describing the activity of the object as a sport just like the activity of the agent, its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established. Furthermore, by the word *līlā*, its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is also implied. With the words ending in "destruction, etc.," the subject matter of the first chapter has been summarized.

By the word *līlā* (sport), the objection that activity is untenable for one who has attained all desires is removed; thus, the meaning of the second definition, which serves to resolve the contradiction, is indicated. In this way, the supremacy (*paratva*) consisting of causality, as stated in the first section (*pūrvārdha*), has been summarized. For the purpose of establishing that this very Supreme Brahman is to be sought for refuge, the accessibility (*saulabhya*) characterized by being approachable and the bestower of liberation, as stated in the second section (*uttarārdha*), is now summarized.

By the words beginning with “vinate,” it is indicated that mere transcendence alone, or mere accessibility alone, is not sufficient to be resorted to—just as one would not resort to a peak of the Golden Mountain (Meru) or a clod of earth respectively; therefore, these two words are intended to exclude those two extremes. Those who are “vinatāḥ”—meaning bowed down or prostrated—are intended here to include all those established in every specific branch of knowledge consisting of the disciplines of *nyāsa* and *upāsanā*.

And their diversity—intended by way of the distinctions of divinity, humanity, caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth, as well as by birth, conduct, and qualities, which will be explained in the passages beginning with "Or even above that, on account of the possibility of becoming Brahman" and "And among those who have restrained their vital seed"—the meaning of the word *bhūta* is "having its existence obtained through the knowledge of the Lord. For the Śruti says: "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing. And for those whose essential nature has been obtained, [it is said]: "Out of compassion for them alone, I dispel the darkness born of ignorance..."

"I, abiding within their very self, destroy [their ignorance]" (Gītā 18.61); "I bestow upon them that yoga of discernment" (Gītā 10.10); "I remember my devotee" (Gītā 9.25)—in accordance with such statements, the burden of removing obstacles to direct realization and so forth rests solely upon the Blessed Lord. Thus, there is no possibility of falling away from one's true nature (*svarūpa*). The term *bhūtavrātaḥ* means a multitude of beings related to the elements; the intention is that even those related to dependents are incapable [of protecting themselves] and must therefore be protected by Him for that very reason. As it is said: "The ancestors clap their hands; the grandfathers dance."
"A Vaiṣṇava born in our family will deliver us. And: "Whether a beast, a human, or a bird, those who take refuge in Viṣṇu shall by that very act go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."

[Objection: Is it not the case that a collective term has as its scope nothing other than those [members] specified by a genitive ending, as in the expression "an assembly of Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇasamāja*)? [Response: It is not so; for in cases such as "the king’s assembly" (*rājapariṣad*), we observe something additional [to the members]. Furthermore, because the genitive occurring within a compound has as its scope mere relation (*sambandhamātra*), and because there is no grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) prescribing a restriction to nothing other than those specified by a genitive ending, when a collective term is heard, and there arises the expectation "Which are the members of this collective?", the collective residing in the denotata of the proximate words presents itself quickly.

In expressions such as "a collection of Brahmins," there is a cognition of non-difference; however, since in cases such as "the assembly of kings" one observes even something additional, it is appropriate to describe the meaning in accordance with the means of valid cognition that apprehends each respective aggregate. Thus, the meaning is exactly as stated.

This being the case, the employment of the word *brāta* would possess meaningful significance. Protection (*rakṣā*) is characterized by the attainment of the desired and the warding off of the undesired; in that regard, he is "one whose initiation is singular," meaning his initiation is primary. "Initiation" (*dīkṣā*) is a resolve (*saṅkalpa*); and the fact that the fulfillment of the resolve to protect those who have sought refuge is even more intensely desired than one's own existence constitutes its primacy. As it has been said: "I would even give up my life. And Āpastamba states: "One may indeed withhold oneself, one’s wife, or one’s son [from protection], but never a servant or a laborer."

That even for one who possesses such a memory [of his promise], the performance of the command is considered more desirable, is understood from the statement, "I would even give up my life. From the primacy of the *dīkṣā* (initiation), the primacy of protection is established as its result. By the word *dīkṣā*, it is shown that the protection of those who have taken refuge is its own purpose. For it is only the one bound by the vow (*vratī*) who experiences the results of failure or fulfillment of the vow as misfortune or prosperity; and the protection of those who have sought refuge is his very vow. As in: "I grant this vow of mine."

In this *Vinatarakṣā*, the subject matter of the third and fourth chapters has been summarized. Thus, having described [Brahman’s] being the cause of the universe and its bestowing of liberation—these two indeed constitute the unique insignia of Brahman, like the royal umbrella and the fly-whisk.

And when it is understood that being easy of access is the reason for being worthy of taking refuge—as in the passage beginning, "Those who know this become immortal," and ending, "The one God, creating heaven and earth, stretches them out with his arms and wings"—and as in, "Knowing me as the Great Lord of all worlds and the Friend of all beings, one attains peace."

In response to the expectation, "If we perceive the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the body of the object of cognition (*prameya*) will be more effectively established," he demonstrates the means of valid cognition corresponding to the object of cognition while stating the meaning of the four aphorisms that constitute the remainder of the two pairs. He says: "You are illumined by the *Śrutis*. By the term *śruti*, his intention is to express its faultlessness due to its being of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*). For this very reason, it is indicated that the principles of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, which are useful for establishing validity and so forth, serve as the basis for this [work]. By the word "head" (*śiras*), his intention is to express its exclusive focus on no other [subject].

Indeed, the Upaniṣads are those portions of the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa texts that have the supreme reality as their primary subject matter. Even in the "illuminated" earlier portion [of the Veda], it is known precisely from Upaniṣadic statements such as "That indeed is Agni, that is Āditya, that is Vāyu," etc., that Brahman alone is the object to be propounded in the form of Agni, Indra, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: "vidīpta" means especially radiant. Alternatively, while the purpose consisting of the engagement with and withdrawal from that which is of the nature of suffering—the means for attaining inferior pleasures—is radiant in the first part [of the Veda], Brahman itself, being the supreme human goal by virtue of its nature as unsurpassed bliss, is especially radiant in the subsequent part. By this, the subject matter of the *Samanvaya* section is indicated.

The meaning of the three preceding sections is also illuminated here, because [the subject] cannot be known through the Upanishads (*śrutiśirovedyatva*) in the absence of excellence in its etymological definition (*vyutpatti-lakṣaṇa-sauṣṭhava*), and because the term *śrutiśiras* excludes other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). The general term "Brahman" is intended to indicate the general terms used in the Upanishads, such as *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*. The specific term "Śrīnivāsa" is intended to indicate the specific terms, such as *Nārāyaṇa* and others.

In the injunctions "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) and "of the omentum and fat of a goat" (*chāgasya vapāyā medasaḥ*), the word "animal" (*paśu*) is determined to terminate in the specific meaning of "goat" (*chāga*) according to the principle stated in the Sūtra: "Or rather, the goat [is meant], on account of the wording of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*). Since words expressing a general category terminate their intended meaning (*tātparya*) upon encountering a word denoting a particular instance, it is indicated that general terms such as "Being" (*sat*) and "Brahman" terminate specifically in Nārāyaṇa alone.

By the etymological power (*avayava-śakti*) of the word *Śrīnivāsa*, His possession of eternal glory (*nitya-vibhūti*) is indicated; by its conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), His equality with the Trinity (*trimūrti*), His identity with them, and the subordination of Brahman to Him are negated. Furthermore, the notion that the Lord (*Īśvara*) alone is Brahman—that He is Sadāśiva distinct from the Trinity—or that even the triad beginning with Brahmā are non-lords, is refuted. Thus, the meaning of the two *adhikaraṇas*—namely, "In the Supreme" (*parasmin*) and "The bridge and measurement are superior to that" (*paramataḥ setūnmāna*)—is indicated.

By that very [means], there is an exclusion of other means of approach, because in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," that which is to be attained is designated by the word "Supreme" (*para*). Alternatively, in order to dispel the suspicion that [Brahman] possesses causality, the distinction consisting of possessing both characteristics—as established in the section beginning with "Not even on account of place does the Supreme [have parts]"—is indicated as stated in the purificatory passages. Now, he states the nature of what has been presented: "in devotion. This is a general term; "in the form of devotion" is the specific term.

Here too, the principle of "the goat [is the victim] because of the wording of the mantra" is intended. By employing the word *śemuṣī* (intellect), there is an exclusion of the view that knowledge and action are to be combined (*samuccaya*). By the term "consisting of devotion" (*bhaktirūpā*), there is an exclusion of the knowledge derived from the meaning of the scriptural texts. Furthermore, by the manner stated in such passages as "Having attained a pure state, one should carry Janārdana through devotion according to the scripture," "But by unswerving devotion," and "To know, to see, and to enter Him in His true essence," devotion—which serves as the means for attaining knowledge, vision, and entry—is also intended here.

Since it was stated without distinction that [devotion] is "of the nature of love," it is according to the manner described in such passages as "I am the abode of offenses. Having reflected upon his own self, he says "mine" and "let it be," thereby indicating that devotion alone is to be prayed for because of its supreme sweetness; or rather, to the objection that devotion is not the sweetest of all things, he replies with "mine"—meaning, mine who am free from the sins that act as obstacles. The sense is that one whose bile is pacified perceives milk as having the greatest sweetness.

By means of the locative case endings in the words from "rakṣaikadīkṣe" up to "parasmin," the perfected means (*siddhopāya*) is stated as being the very object to be attained (*upeya*). The phrase "in the form of devotion" (*bhaktirūpe*) refers to the perfected means. In this verse, the refutation of opposing views—which constitutes a portion of what is to be established by the scripture—is also indicated by implication.

By the term "origination, subsistence, and dissolution" (*janmasthemabhaṅga*), the Bhaṭṭas and Prābhākaras—who do not accept creation and the other stages as occurring simultaneously—are excluded. By the word "sport" (*līlā*), the Hiraṇyagarbhas, who maintain that the Lord is a mere witness, are set aside. By the phrase "being bowed to" (*vinata*) and so forth, those who assert the mutual difference among individual souls (*jīvas*) and their difference from Brahman—namely, the proponents of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñānavādins*)—are discarded. By the expression "the crest of the Vedas" (*śrutiśirasi*), the Cārvākas who stand outside the Veda, as well as the Buddhists and Jains, are refuted; by that same term, the proponents of an inferential Lord (*anumānikeśvaravādins*) are also excluded.

By the term "Brahman," the Sāṅkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others who maintain that the causes [of the world] are *pradhāna* (primordial matter) or atoms—which are non-Brahman in nature—are excluded. By the word "Śrīnivāsa" (Abode of Śrī), the Pāśupatas and others are excluded. By this very [term], those who propound a Brahman transcendent to Īśvara and those who propound the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) are excluded. By the word "intellect" (*śemuṣī*), those who maintain that the means [to liberation] is the combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*) are excluded; and by [the phrase] "consisting of devotion," those who maintain that the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is the means are excluded. This is how it should be understood.

To the question, "Since the means and the goal are understood through the Śruti alone, what is there for you to say?", he replies with the first verse beginning with "Parāśarya," wherein the ultimate nature of his own work is shown by way of its supreme purpose as the established form (*siddharūpa*), and the goal to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*) is indicated very briefly by the word "protection" (*rakṣā*).

Now, by the second verse, [the author] establishes: the intermediate subject matter of his own treatise; its indirect status as having Brahman as its subject matter; that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) is the immediate intermediate purpose (*avyavahitāvāntaraprayojana*) with respect to his own treatise; that liberation (*mukti*) is the ultimate purpose (*paramaprayojana*) through a traditional succession; that by stating the basis of his own subject matter in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇamūlatā*), he indicates that other [commentaries on the same] subject matter lack such a basis in valid means of knowledge; and, for the sake of distinguishing his stated meaning from other commentaries (*bhāṣya*) on the subject matter of his own treatise— [The verse: "The one who is the cause of the world, who is free from all defects, whose nature is pure bliss and consciousness, and who is the object of the supreme devotion of those who seek liberation—that Lord Viṣṇu, the Supreme Person, I shall meditate upon. [The commentary: Here, the word "world" (*jagat*) refers to the aggregate of effects consisting of the gross elements and their modifications. The term "cause" (*hetu*) denotes the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), while the phrase "free from all defects" (*sarvadoṣarahita*) denotes the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). By this, the Lord's status as the cause of the world is established. Furthermore, the phrase "whose nature is pure bliss and consciousness" (*anavadyasukhajñānasvarūpa*) serves to exclude the possibility of His being a non-sentient entity (*jaḍa*). The phrase "who is the object of the supreme devotion of those who seek liberation" (*mumukṣuvandyatama*) excludes the possibility of His being an insentient object of worship. By the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), He is distinguished from the individual soul (*jīva*). By the name "Viṣṇu," He is distinguished from the deities presiding over the Vedas. By the epithet "Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*), He is distinguished from the Pradhāna (primordial matter). The phrase "I shall meditate upon" (*dhyāye*) indicates the act of meditation (*dhyāna*) which consists of the continuous flow of mental modification (*vṛtti*) toward Him. The mention of "meditation" implies that the aforementioned qualities are not merely nominal, but are indeed real attributes. This is because it is impossible to meditate upon something that lacks reality. Thus, the Lord is shown to possess both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the attributes (*guṇa*). By the use of the first person singular pronoun "I" (*aham*), the author indicates that he himself is the one performing the meditation. By the use of the present tense suffix (*laṭ*), he indicates that the meditation is to be performed at the very moment of composing the treatise. By the use of the future tense suffix (*luṭ*), he indicates that the treatise will be composed immediately after the meditation. By the use of the word "that" (*tam*), he indicates that the meditation is directed toward a specific, previously mentioned object. By the use of the word "Lord" (*īśvara*), he indicates that the meditation is directed toward the highest object. By the use of the word "Viṣṇu," he indicates that the meditation is directed toward the most excellent object. By the use of the word "Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*), he indicates that the meditation is directed toward the most venerable object. By the use of the word "meditate" (*dhyāye*), he indicates that the meditation is directed toward the most beloved object. The term "sāmpradāyikatvam" (traditional character) and so forth refers to what is declared in the Śruti; furthermore, this auspicious practice consisting of the worship of the Guru in the form of praise is now being performed. For it is understood from such passages as "Indeed, whomsoever Madhusūdana may look upon at the time of birth," "Know that through prostration," and "I grant the yoga of wisdom," that even the approach to the Teacher has the Lord’s glance as its cause. Therefore, it is logical that the worship of the Guru occurs subsequent to the worship of the Supreme Deity.

And so says the Śruti: "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord, as he has for the Lord, so [he has] for the Guru. The ancients also acted accordingly; as was done by the venerable Vaiśampāyana: "Having bowed to Hṛṣīkeśa," and "Salutations to that Blessed Vyāsa. And likewise by the Draviḍācāryas.

"Homage to Brahmā, the sole abode of supreme qualities, who is like a jar containing the seeds of the multitude of moving and stationary beings, the protector of the world-egg; homage to Jaimini, who expanded the secrets of the Vedas hidden within their caskets; homage to those teachers whose minds are kindled by logic. And by the Westerners [it is said]: "To him whose body is pure knowledge," and "Having first saluted my gurus," and "Having prostrated before the Lord, the cause, and the sage Kaṇāda."

By the word *Pārāśarya*, the excellence of his birth is indicated, as established by the Śruti: "Vyāsa Pārāśarya said. Furthermore, it is intended to convey that he alone bears the name Bādarāyaṇa, as stated by the Great Sage himself: "O scorcher of foes, Satyavatī obtained Acyuta Bādarāyaṇa as a son from Parāśara on the island of Badarikāmiśra. Although the term Bādarāyaṇa is applied to other sages as well, the term Bādarāyaṇa referring to the author of the Sūtras refers exclusively to Pārāśarya; this has been clearly stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Knowledge, which had emerged from Nārāyaṇa and remained intact during the Kṛta Yuga, became slightly altered in the Tretā Yuga and was entirely fragmented in the Dvāpara Yuga.
When knowledge became ignorance due to the curse of the sage Gautama, the gods, led by Brahmā and Rudra, had their intellects utterly confounded.
They went for refuge to Nārāyaṇa, the source of shelter and free from all ailment; and the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, was informed of their purpose by them.
The Great Yogin, the Blessed Lord Hari himself, having descended through Parāśara upon Satyavatī, retrieved the Vedas that had been lost.
He divided them into four parts, and again into twenty-four, and likewise into a hundred, into one, and also into a thousand.
Furthermore, for the sake of understanding its meaning, Kṛṣṇa composed the Brahma-sūtras in twelve parts, which truly possess the nature of a sūtra.
Those who know the sūtras understand a sūtra to be concise, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive, unambiguous, and irreproachable.
Therefore, the *Brahmasūtra* is known by the wise as the "unqualified" (*nirviśeṣita*) sūtra, whereas they understand other sūtras to be "qualified" (*saviśeṣa*).
"The word applies to the primary [meaning] without distinction, but to others with distinction"—thus say the knowers of the Veda who understand the true nature of words.
Having composed such sūtras, the highly illustrious Vyāsa [taught them] among the gods beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, as well as among humans, ancestors, and birds.
"Having established his knowledge, the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord, sports," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase *vacassudhām*: some teachers take it to mean the "nectar of speech," referring to the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the word "speech," as in the statement "one who knows the Vedas is one who knows the scriptures," where the sentence indeed expresses the meaning of the words "Veda" and so forth. This is because of the context of the section on metaphors (*rūpaka*) and out of fear of resorting to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the word "nectar. Other teachers prefer the compound *vacaḥ-sudhā* according to the rule "that which is compared [is compounded] with tigers and the like," meaning "speech that is like nectar. By the word "nectar," the quality of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is intended. Thus, the scope of the alternative view has been stated.

To the objection, "In that case, how can Brahman be the object [of the Upaniṣads]?", he states that Brahman is the object by means of an intermediary, saying: "The Upaniṣad. For there is the statement: "It is called an *upaniṣad* because it is seated (*upaniṣaṇṇa*) in Brahman, or because it is seated in the *upaniṣad*. The commentary of Dramiḍa on this subject says: "For this knowledge is well-seated in the deep [Brahman]. Vāmana’s commentary on the Bhāṣya explains: "[It is seated] in the deep Brahman which is seated [therein]. Here, "being seated" (*upaniṣaṇṇatvam*) means the state of directly teaching the Blessed Lord.

By the word "milk" (dugdha), it is intended to convey that the Upaniṣads are more essential even than the preceding portions [of the Vedas], just as it is said, "The Āraṇyakas are from the Vedas, just as nectar is from herbs. By the word "ocean" (abdhi), the infinity and other qualities of the contemplated Upaniṣads are indicated.

By the word "middle" (*madhya*), the non-abandonment of the primary meaning of all sentences is intended; for the proximity of the middle is indeed equal with respect to all peripheral positions. By the word "extracted" (*uddhṛta*), which denotes the lifting up of what was submerged in an extremely low place, the grasping of the meaning in its entirety is indicated. The intermediate subject of one's own treatise is the Sūtra of Pārāśarya, and the intermediate subject of that [Sūtra] is the Upaniṣad.

By stating that Brahman is the object of that [knowledge]—thereby explaining that the *Bādarāyaṇa-sūtras* have the Upaniṣads as their root—it is indicated that these commentaries are undertaken with disregard for the works of the Sāṃkhya and others, since they are rooted in invalid sources (*apramāṇa*). He states the ultimate purpose arising from the scripture through this indirect means (*praṇāḍyā*) with the word "saṃsāra" (transmigration).

By the term "fire of saṃsāra," the intention is to express that saṃsāra in its entirety consists of the nature of the threefold suffering (tāpatraya), as in the verse: "Even in heaven, for one who fears falling and for that which is subject to decay, there is no cessation. By the term "flaming" (*dīpana*), which denotes constant blazing without contraction, what is intended is the impossibility of ever being prevented [from suffering] prior to the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The variety [of non-attainment] is according to its internal and other forms; and within each of those three, it is further sixfold, consisting of bodily, mental, and so forth. The *ātman* here refers to the supreme self (*paramātman*), according to the Śruti: "All these beings indeed enter into the *prāṇa* alone," and "Who indeed could breathe, who could live? By the word *gata*, its non-attainment is indicated; by the two prefixes, its beginninglessness and its manifoldness are intended. The variety of non-attainment arises from the absence of even one among the attainments of knowledge, vision, or realization.

"Saṃjīvinī" means life, or bringing back to life, which is the uprooting of *saṃsāra*. "Sā" indicates the exclusion of *kaivalya* (isolation). Now, he states its traditional authority with the word "pūrva" (ancient). By the word "ancient," there is an exclusion of recent figures such as Śaṅkara; the sense is that it is well-protected not merely by oral instruction but also in the form of a treatise (*grantha*). To the question, "If the nature of the reality has already been established through the works of ancient teachers, what is your purpose? he replies with the words "bahumati" (of many opinions).

"Many opinions" (*bahvyaḥ matayaḥ*) means either many individual opinions or the opinions of many people; because of their mutual contradictions, and because they contradict the correct meaning, he states that [the work] is difficult for people of recent times to understand by saying "situated at a distance. This does not mean merely that it was not perceived correctly, but rather that there was a misunderstanding; such is the intended sense. Since his own treatise is the subject-matter (*viṣayin*) of the intermediate topics of the Sūtras and so forth, and this was not explicitly stated previously, he says "brought near" (*ānītām*).

Thus, in the interpretation of *sudhā* (nectar), [the phrase] "by their own syllables" means by the syllables of the *gāyatrī* which constitute its parts—that is, by the syllables of nectar; for this reason, there is no mention of "my syllables. Those called *sumanasaḥ* (well-minded) are those who know how to distinguish between the essential and the non-essential; by this it is implied that the acceptance of what is unreal does not constitute a fault. Since the [meanings] of the gods and so forth are easily understood from the commentaries of Vṛttikāra, they are described as "terrestrial" (*bhaumāḥ*). "Let them drink daily": the sense is that because of its extreme relish, it does not cause satiety. Indeed, compared to other fruits, the very means to attaining the Blessed One is the most excellent of tastes.

As it has been said: "Where is the ascent to the vault of heaven, which is characterized by return; and where is the recitation of 'Vāsudeva,' the unsurpassed seed of liberation? Alternatively, the sense is that because of its profundity, it should be practiced daily.

To the objection that "in that case, one should simply read the ancient texts; what is the point of this laborious effort in composing and promulgating a new work? he says "by the Blessed One" (*bhagavat*). By the word "Blessed," it is intended to show that there is no lack of authority (*anāptatva*), as might be suspected in the case of Śaṅkara and others. By the word "Bodhāyana," the term "former teacher" (*pūrvācārya*) is also implicitly explained. By the phrase "they condensed the extensive [work]," it is indicated that commentaries (*vṛtti*) and the like are of no practical use for people living here today.

For Bādarāyaṇa composed an extremely extensive commentary (*vṛtti*); whereas the author of the Draviḍa-bhāṣya and others composed works that were exceedingly concise, disregarding the refutation of opposing views and so forth. The utility of both excessively extensive and excessively condensed works occurs only in other times and places abounding in long-lived and intelligent people; for among all men of the present day, neither a hundred-year lifespan, nor lifelong exertion in the study of texts, nor innate excellence of intellect exists.

Therefore, the meaning is that the Sūtra must be explained in a manner that is neither overly prolix—so as to refute the views of others—and yet easily grasped. One should explain the words of the Sūtra according to those [established] views, and not by means of some other view imagined by oneself. The intention is that we speak in accordance with the division of roots and suffixes of the Sūtra’s words, rather than somehow forcing the Sūtras to fit meanings imagined by ourselves. They will be explained (*vyākhyāsyante*), illuminated by the two prefixes *vi-* and *ā-*, which signify the required expansion and condensation.

Now, one might object: "That wherein the meaning of the *mūla* (root text) is described by means of sentences that imitate the *sūtras*, and wherein one's own [authorial] views are also described—that the experts in *bhāṣyas* know as a *bhāṣya*. This is indeed the definition of a *bhāṣya*. Therefore, since it lacks the nature of a commentary on the *sūtras*, the section beginning with "entirely" (*akhila*) and so forth is not included within a *bhāṣya*. If this is argued, we say no. It is indeed included within a *bhāṣya* because its purpose is to convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the *sūtras*. And that it has the purpose of conveying the intended meaning of the *sūtras* is clear from the commentary on the verses.

Furthermore, the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) is included [in this work] precisely because it is useful for the purpose of ensuring the non-interruption and completion of the treatise one intends to begin. If it is argued that the mention of salutation here is inappropriate because the authors of the *Śābara* and *Śāṅkara* commentaries did not employ such salutations, we say no; for in the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya*, one hears the salutation of both deity and teacher in the verse: "Salutation to her whose feet are the sole abode of supreme qualities. As for the *Śābara* and *Śāṅkara* [commentators], they show disregard for salutation because they do not accept the existence of Īśvara, nor do they accept a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

In this context, however, salutation is most appropriate in accordance with the established doctrine (siddhānta). Furthermore, at the beginning of Śaṅkara’s work, commentators raised the suspicion that it might be a spurious text due to the absence of a salutation and the like; they resolved this by explaining that, through the contemplation of the inner self (pratyagartha) by means of the passage beginning with "yuṣmad," an auspicious practice (maṅgalācāra) was effectively performed by implication.

Now, therefore, follows the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavijñāsā*). Desiring to explain the words [of the text] starting from the beginning, he first explains the word *atha*: "In this context, this word *atha* signifies immediate succession. For the method of exposition is defined as: "The division of words (*padaccheda*), the statement of their meanings (*padārthokti*), the analysis of compounds (*vigraha*), the construction of the sentence (*vākyayojanā*), and the resolution of objections (*ākṣepasamādhāna*)—this is the fivefold characteristic of an exposition."

Now, one might object: these two words, *atha* and *ataḥ*, need not be explained because there is no purpose for doing so; for an explanation is intended to remove ignorance and doubt. Yet, in this case, there is no ignorance regarding *ānantarya* (immediacy) and [the word] *ataḥ* signifying the cause of what has been previously mentioned, since both of these are well-known.

Nor is there doubt, because even though other meanings exist, those two [words] are well-known for their abundance of usage in the sense of the stated meaning; for indeed, in one who hears the word "cow" (*go*), no doubt arises regarding something possessing a dewlap and so forth. For this very reason, error (*viparyaya*) is also cast far away. To this we reply: since the determination that [the words] have as their purpose the sequence and the causal relationship of the preceding context depends upon the comprehension of the specific preceding context, and since the abundance of conventional usage (*prasiddhi-prācurya*) is subject to exceptions when that [context] is not understood.

Since the word *atha* is seen to be used in the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*) and so forth, and the word *etat* in the sense of what is about to be stated—as in "this is what is meant"—and since the suffix *-tas* is seen to express all case-meanings as well as meanings other than the ablative—as in "from here" (*itaḥ*)—doubt and misconception might arise; therefore, it is appropriate to provide an explanation of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* in order to dispel them. Hence, they are now explained.

In this regard, first of all, it is improper for the word *atha* (now/then) to have the sense of "introduction" (*adhikāra*). For "introduction" means a commencement; thus, the statement "the inquiry into Brahman is commenced" would be of little purpose, since the fact that something is being commenced is understood from the very act of beginning even without the expression "it is commenced. Indeed, when a person is speaking, it is understood by the person present that he is speaking—even without the words "I speak"—and not that he is not speaking. If it is argued that what is meant is "the state of being fit to be commenced," [we reply: no.

Even then, since the aphorism (*sūtra*) which establishes the system (*nyāya*) lacks the purpose of making known an instruction (*upadeśa*), the meaning would be that it is "fit for commencement" by way of reasoning; however, such fitness (*yogyatva*) is not expressed by the words [of the text]. Now, one might argue: "By means of *adhyāhāra* (supplying an ellipsis), there would be a connection; for even in the case of the word 'next' (*ataḥ*), the word 'must be performed' (*kartavya*) must indeed be supplied. This is not so, because in the view that [the word 'next'] serves the purpose of indicating the topic (*adhikāra*), there is a difficulty in connecting even a supplied word [to the rest of the sentence].

Just as when it is said "capable of being combined," it is impossible to state that the meaning is "capable of being combined with [something specific]," so too, when it is said "now, capable," it is impossible to state that the meaning is "capable of being commenced. For this very reason, it is stated in the Mahābhāṣya: "The treatise on the instruction of words is to be understood as having been commenced (*adhikṛta*)," and not "capable of being commenced. Even the term *adhikṛta* is a statement of the resultant meaning; it is not a literal verbal expression, because particles such as *ca* (and) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*).

In this context, however, it has been stated that if the purpose were merely to indicate "this is the subject matter under discussion" (*adhikṛtam*), it would be redundant. At the commencement of the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*), the status of being a subject matter was resorted to as a last resort; for there is no unique function possible for grammar—which is a subsidiary limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda—to be studied by one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) and is studying the Veda. But here, since another purposeful meaning is possible, it is improper to resort to the sense of being a subject matter. Furthermore, its status as indicating immediate sequence (*ānantarya*) and its possessiveness of a specific purpose will be explained later.

However, auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) is not the denotation of the word *atha*; rather, the word *atha*, when being uttered, brings about auspiciousness—just like the sound of a conch shell and so forth. Thus, even though it refers to another matter, auspiciousness is accomplished, just as in the case of the syllable *oṃ*. For the word *atha* is remembered as being equal to the syllable *oṃ*: "The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious."

Even if it were admitted that the words [of the sūtra] express an auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) would be praised as being itself of the nature of an auspicious rite; consequently, the sūtra would become a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) rather than a work based on logical reasoning (*nyāyanibandhana*). Furthermore, if it were not a qualification of the inquiry (*jijñāsā*), there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in the sense of "there is an auspicious rite. Moreover, it is improper for [the sūtra] to have a different meaning from the subject matter at hand; for such a thing is understood as indicating that what is about to be stated is a different matter in relation to the subject matter under discussion.

Furthermore, that [particle *tu*] is observed only when there is an intention to introduce an alternative interpretation (*kalpāntara*); however, here it is inappropriate because no alternative interpretation is being introduced. Its status as a mere question is also untenable, because of the nature of the expression, which lacks the form of a question and its answer. For instance, if it were said, "Is the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) to be undertaken?", then the answer would have to be provided by a separate sentence, such as, "It is to be undertaken."

Furthermore, no other statement in the form of a reply is perceived. If the word *atha* were intended to convey completeness (*kārtsnya*), the meaning would be that "it must be performed in its entirety. That is untenable, because there is no suspicion of it being performed only partially; for the point of doubt concerns the mere fact of whether it should be performed at all, and the Sūtra is intended to resolve that doubt. Moreover, the connection with the word *ataḥ* also precludes any other meaning such as "eligibility" (*adhikāra*) and the like.

For the word *ataḥ*, referring to the subject matter under discussion as a reason, refers to that which was presented by the word *atha* and implied by the force of the compound *brahmajijñāsā*. In that case, if it were to refer to "being the subject of the inquiry" (adhikṛtatva) as presented by the word *atha* as the reason, then [the statement] would be "because it is the subject of the inquiry, it ought to be undertaken"; thus, the reason would be indistinguishable from the probandum.

Since *maṅgala* (auspiciousness) is not the expressed meaning [of the term], it cannot be referred to by another word; even if its status as the expressed meaning were admitted, since it depends on the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) and is incomplete (*akārtsnya*), it does not serve as an antidote to the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), and thus those [factors] are not to be referred to as reasons. For the prima facie position does not arise from [the presence of] inauspiciousness, independence from the subject at hand, or incompleteness; furthermore, the Nyāya-sūtras are intended to exclude contradictory meanings, whereas the question contained within the interrogative sentence serves as the reason for that very sentence.

Since the word *kim* (what) is itself unfit for such reference while the sentence "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken" is not yet complete, how could the meaning of *kim* be referred to as a reason? Therefore, if the word *atha* is accepted as having a meaning suitable for reference by the word *ataḥ*, then its status as signifying "commencement" (*adhikāra*) and so forth is untenable.

If it were intended that the *ataḥ* (therefore) word refers back—by way of being the previously established antecedent—to that very entity favored by various commentators which is implied by the force of the term *brahmajijñāsā*, then, since that which is not useful for the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) cannot be what is implied, only a useful object can be so implied; thus, because the *ataḥ* word referring back to that [antecedent] presents a specific preceding matter as being useful for the inquiry, the word *atha* (now/then) would have its natural sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

It is not possible to accept another meaning that is forced and fruitless; therefore, like the word *ataḥ*, the force of the compound *brahmajijñāsā* itself would also exclude other meanings such as "eligibility" (*adhikāra*). Thus, by demonstrating through the context that other alternative meanings are untenable, he establishes that the word *atha* has the sense of "immediate succession."

Regarding this, the word *atha* (now/then) signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*). The proposition is: "The word *atha* [signifies] immediate succession. The three words beginning with "tadupapādakam" (the proof of that) serve as the justification for this; therein, by the word "bhavati" (it occurs/is), its natural fitness (*svārasya*) toward immediate succession is indicated. By the phrase "atrāyam i" (here this [word]...), he removes the objection that its natural fitness might be set aside by a failure to perceive a preceding topic (*pūrvavṛtta*). Here, the meaning is: in this Sūtra which marks the commencement of the Brahma-Mīmāṃsā, which consists of an inquiry into the latter portion of the Veda.

The intended meaning is that, by the force of the term *brahmajijñāsā*, a specific preceding activity in the form of an inquiry into the prior portion [of the Veda] is implied. Intending to state another reason, he says "this. This means that this word *atha* is distinct from the word *atha* found within other sūtras such as "Now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) and "Now, the instruction on yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*); thus, it is said to be preceded by the word *ataḥ*.

For this very meaning is explicitly stated in the Vedāntasāra; the intention is that by the word *etad* (this), which refers back to the subject at hand, the general nature of what has preceded is denoted. Thus, due to the natural force (*svārasya*) of both words used in conjunction, that which was stated generally and implied specifically is established as having occurred previously. Since there is no absence of the natural force—which would otherwise preclude it—consisting in the non-comprehension of a specific narrative of what preceded, the meaning of the sentence is that the word *atha* signifies immediate succession (*ānantarya*) alone.

Thus, the word *atha* belongs to the aphorism that initiates the investigation of the latter portion [of the Veda]. By those who demonstrate that the word is headed by *ataḥ* and that its natural sense is immediate succession (*ānantarya*), it follows—through the very words "this occurs here" which establish that succession—that other possible meanings, which are impossible and must be disregarded, are to be set aside in this aphorism.

Therefore, he explains the word *ataḥ* with the statement: "The word *ataḥ* [expresses] the state of being a cause for what has preceded. Here, "what has preceded" (*vṛttasya*) expresses the meaning of the base noun (*prakṛti*), and "the state of being a cause" (*hetubhāva*) expresses the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). The three words "this," "proposition" (*pratijñā*), and "is here" (*atra... bhavati*) are connected as supporting elements. By the use of the verb *bhavati*, the abundance of well-known meanings is shown through the fact that the base and the suffix refer to the meanings already stated. The meaning of "here" (*atretyasya*) is as explained previously.

By this, the specific nature of his conduct and his fitness for being a cause have been implied; that fitness will become manifest immediately thereafter. This [treatise] is preceded by the word *atha*, which by its very essence implies immediate succession (*ānantarya*); by this, the general nature of his conduct has been implied. [Objection: But surely the determination of the meaning of the word *atha* depends upon the determination of the meaning of the word *ataḥ*, and the determination of the meaning of the word *ataḥ* depends upon the determination of the meaning of the word *atha*; thus, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*). [Reply: It is not so.

Indeed, the natural sense of the word *atha* as denoting immediate succession does not depend upon the determination of the meaning of the word *ataḥ*; nor does the natural sense of the word *ataḥ* as referring to the state of being a cause for what has preceded depend upon the determination of the meaning of the word *atha*.

That the word *atha* refers to immediate succession—both by its own natural sense and by the natural sense of the other words with which it is associated—and that the word *ataḥ* also refers to the state of being a cause for what has preceded—both by its own natural sense and by the natural sense of the other words with which it is associated—is demonstrated by the two words "bhavati" and "ayam."

These are the arguments for the additional point: since the two words [of the sūtra] are established as having the aforementioned meaning solely by the force of the word *brahmajijñāsā*—which is intended here—the words *atha* and *ataḥ* have the aforementioned meanings due to the natural sense of the words *sva* and *para*, as well as the force of the word *brahmajijñāsā*; thus, there is no fault.

If it is argued that one of the two words, *atha* or *ataḥ*, is sufficient, we say no. This is because the word *atha*, which introduces the immediately following time, serves as a qualification for the upcoming inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), whereas the word *ataḥ* refers to the existence of a cause for what has preceded; thus, they are not synonyms. Furthermore, the two words have distinct purposes, functioning respectively as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). If it is asked whether "the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken" constitutes the proposition, we say no; rather, "the inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*) is the designation of the subject (*dharmin*).

The word "atha" (now/then) expresses the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); the property to be proven is not merely "obligatoriness" (*karttavyatā*) in general, but rather obligatoriness qualified by immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Thus, the distinction between the words *atha* and *ataḥ* as serving the purposes of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), respectively, is the same here as it is in the phrase "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*). For this reason, since the specific difference in meaning is not intended to be expressed, the word *ataḥ* is not employed in such cases as "Now follows the instruction on Yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*) or "Now follows the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*).

[Objection: Since the inquiry into ritual action (karmavicāra), being present in the mind as implied by the force of the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā), its status as the cause is to be understood from the word *ataḥ*; so what is the purpose of the word *atha*? [Reply: Not so.

Since the word "atha" (then) serves to indicate that the cause [of knowledge] does not depend on the intervention of hearing other treatises by way of expressing immediate succession, and since it would be impossible to accomplish [the cause] prior to hearing the Vedānta without hearing other branches [of the Veda], and because other treatises are overtaken by the lack of opportunity, it follows as a result that the exclusion of the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal and so forth—when they depend upon other treatises—is their status as having occurred previously.

[Objection: Is it not the case that not just anything past must be stated as a "prior occurrence" (*pūrvavṛtta*), for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)? Therefore, only that which is useful for what is about to occur is presented by the word *atha* as a prior occurrence; its status as a cause is also established by that very power of the thing itself—just as [the study of] other sciences is irrelevant [to the present subject]—so what is the use of this word? [Reply: It is not so.

Now, since the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) serves to dispel the suspicion that the reason implied by the preceding statement is unestablished, the reason is indeed qualified; the manner in which the Sūtra-author intends to address the suspicion of non-establishment regarding both the qualifying and the qualified portions of that reason will be demonstrated later. Thus, these two words are more purposeful.

Here, explaining the relationship between the past and the future—the former being established by the force of the term *brahmajijñāsā* as indicated by the word *atha*—and their status as cause and effect, [the author] justifies the stated sense of immediate succession with the words "having studied" (*adhīta*). By the term "knowledge of ritual action" (*karmajñāna*), the past is expressed; by the term "desire to know Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā*), that which is to follow is expressed. Through the phrases "of small and unstable fruit" and "of infinite and stable fruit," the relationship of cause and effect is shown. By the word "exclusive" (*kevala*), the exclusion of rituals preceded by the knowledge of Brahman is indicated.

How is it that the knowledge of karma alone is what precedes [the inquiry into Brahman], and how is there the immediate intuition of an infinite and stable fruit? To address this doubt, the phrase beginning with "having studied" (*adhītya*) is employed. By the term "Veda together with its head" (*saśiraska-veda*), the fact that the study of the whole is enjoined is indicated, as well as the fixed order of the subject matter (the *vyākhyeya*) which serves as the cause for the order of the commentary (*vyākhyāna-paurvāparya*), and the unity of the two parts as a single treatise. By the word "with its limbs" (*sāṅga*), the reason for producing the immediate intuition of an infinite and stable fruit is shown.

The statements such as "likewise the ancillary sciences (*aṅga*) in the dark fortnight," and "But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*," are intended here [in the phrase] "of one who has studied the Veda together with its ancillaries and the Upanishads. Thus, by means of these two genitive qualifiers—"one who has studied" and so forth—the specific qualified candidate (*adhikāri-viśeṣa*) brought forward by the words *atha* and *ataḥ*, and supported by the force of the term *brahma-jijñāsā*, is demonstrated.
For it is one who has mastered the ritual works (*karman*), who is disgusted with the fruits of worldly existence, and who desires the infinite and eternal fruit, who is entitled to this scripture.

"Anantasthiraphalabrahmajijñāsā" means the desire to know Brahman, whose nature is infinite and stable fruit. It should be understood that if "infinite and stable fruit" is a qualification of the desire to know Brahman, then the desire to know Brahman possesses that quality by way of the knowledge produced through discrimination (*viveka*) and other means arising from scripture (*āgama*). By the word "anantarabhāvinī" (occurring immediately thereafter), what is intended is the independence of this [inquiry] from other treatises, which is the implication of the words "atha" and "ataḥ."

Following the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*), the necessity of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) is established by the specific reason that actions are perceived to yield results that are both limited and impermanent. This is because the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) indicates that the preceding inquiry into action serves as the cause [for the subsequent one]; and because the inquiry into action is preceded by the perception of infinite and eternal results arising from the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*); and because through injunctions regarding repetition (*āvṛtti*) and other means, it is understood that the fruits of action are indeed limited and impermanent.

This specific reason is stated by the phrase: "because one has developed a longing for liberation through the realization that the fruits of mere ritual action are limited and unstable. Here, by the word "adhigata" (realized), the necessity of knowing ritual action *by way of its fruit* is explicitly stated; furthermore, the necessity of knowing it *in its own nature* for the purpose of its adoption is also a reason for the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-mīmāṃsā*) being a prerequisite.

It will be stated that the knowledge of the nature of the action required and the knowledge that mere actions yield results that are limited and unstable are to be understood through the *Karmamīmāṃsā*. In this regard, the cognition of the desirability [of an action] by its very nature is included within the initial cognition of the infinite and stable result; for the initial cognition of the infinite and stable result occurs precisely along with the specific means (*upāya*) and their respective procedures (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the subsequent text, as [the inquiry into the means] is included within the specific cause [of the primary inquiry].

[Objection: If the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) is an independent cause for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), then it would follow that everyone who has completed the inquiry into ritual action must inquire into Brahman; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of an absence of performance of rituals for the sake of heaven. [Reply: Not so. For those who perform [rituals] for the sake of heaven even without having studied *Mīmāṃsā*, due to the words of their preceptors and others, there is no contradiction in their performing them for the sake of heaven. Furthermore, even among those who have heard [the scriptures], there are those who seek heaven; and because of defects in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-vaiguṇya*), it is possible for them to lack the desire for liberation (*amumukṣutva*), which is rooted in hearing incorrect expositions.

If the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*) were the prerequisite for the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*), then everyone who has studied the Vedas together with their auxiliaries would necessarily engage in the inquiry into ritual action.

If it is argued that it is not always the case—since many are seen who have studied the Veda yet have not heard the *Mīmāṃsā* on ritual action (*karma*), and their failure to comprehend the investigation of ritual is due to defects in unseen factors such as place and time, rather than because the study of the Vedas with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) was not a prerequisite for them—then this is equally true here. For even when the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth are obtained, one observes many persons who have not yet comprehended the investigation of Brahman; thus, when challenged as to how the fourfold means can be the necessary cause for the investigation of Brahman, [the response follows].

Even those who maintain that [the inquiry into Brahman] occurs after that [inquiry into karma] must resolve this by saying there is no fault because of defects in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth; but this is equally applicable here as well. Their difference lies only in the presence of another objection that is difficult to avoid. Therefore, just as the potter and others [are antecedent to] the production of a jar, the inquiry into karma is necessarily prior to the inquiry into Brahman. Since a proper inquiry into karma—being free from visible and invisible obstacles—constitutes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the inquiry into Brahman, there is no defect whatsoever.
Thus, the meaning of the words *atha* and *ataḥ* has been determined.

Now, desiring to explain the meaning of the term *brahmajijñāsā*, [the author] first determines the sense of the compound, since its formation as a single word depends upon a compound (*samāsa*), by means of the passage beginning with "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). While other case-endings are prescribed for specific relations such as objecthood, instrumentality, and so forth by rules such as "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*), the sixth case is prescribed for general relations by the rule "the sixth case is used for the remainder" (*ṣaṣṭhī śeṣe*). Here, having raised the doubt that this [sixth case] refers to a general relation, it is determined to have the object as its specific scope.

In this context, since a compound in general is common to many case-endings (*vibhakti*), the author analyzes the term as "the desire to know Brahman" (*brahmaṇo jijñāsā*) with the intention of showing that other case-endings are untenable here. Although the status of being a purpose (*prayojana*) would be established if the dative case were accepted, the dative compound is not adopted because it is incompatible with the absence of a relationship between material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*).

Regarding the term "saptamī" (locative case): because of the grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) [of the rule], even if there were a compound such as *brahmaṇi jijñāsā* (desire to know Brahman), Brahman would merely be the object (*viṣayatva*), and its status as the purpose (*prayojanatva*) would not be established; thus, the locative case is not accepted here. The intention is that in a compound with the instrumental case—as in *śaṅkulayā khaṇḍaḥ* (a piece by means of a wedge)—neither the status of being the object nor the status of being the purpose can be established. Since the word *brahmaṇaḥ* is common to both the genitive and the ablative cases, and since the genitive has multiple meanings, he says "brahmaṇaḥ" in order to determine its specific sense.

To the question "Why so?", he says: "Of the agent and the object. Although the genitive case is common to both agent and object, the intention is that while the state of being the agent of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) belongs only to one who is afflicted by the threefold suffering, Brahman possesses the status of the object; thus, it is stated that "of Brahman" uses the genitive in the sense of the object. The underlying meaning is that by accepting the genitive in the sense of the object, both the fact of Brahman being the subject matter (*viṣayatva*) and its being the purpose (*prayojanatva*) are established.

[Objection: In that case, how is it appropriate for the Bhāṣya beginning with “even though” (*yadyapi*) to arise as a response to the suspicion regarding the acceptance of a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*)? [Reply: It is said: Even if a general relationship were accepted, the status of Brahman as the object (*karman*) is established by the inherent power of the word *jijñāsā*; furthermore, through a mediated connection, even related factors such as the means (*upāya*), the practitioner (*upāsaka*), and obstacles (*pratibandha*) are established as objects of inquiry; and finally, because a genitive case prescribed by specific rules (*pratipadavihitā ṣaṣṭhī*) is prohibited from forming a compound.

In this context, he raises an objection—beginning with "Even though"—in order to establish, by implication, that the genitive case has the sense of the object (*karman*), and also to establish that the attributes related to Brahman are likewise objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*).

In the phrase "the inclusion of the general relation" (*sambandhasāmānyaparigraha*), the word "pari" (all-around) indicates the establishment of the status of being an object of inquiry for those things related to Brahman as well; for by means of "comprehensive inclusion" (*parito grahaṇa*), the state of being graspable is obtained even for those situated all around. For this very reason, later on, he says "is grasped" (*gṛhyate*) and not "is comprehensively included" (*parigṛhyate*). He resolves both of these points with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

The meaning here is as follows: since the status of being an object (*karmatva*) for the primary [object], Brahman, and for the other non-primary objects is established even by implication (*ākṣepasiddha*), it is proper to accept that the status of being the primary object is denotative (*ābhidhānika*), while the status of being an object for the others is established by force of logic (*sāmarthyasiddha*) through their connection with the primary object and the power of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Therefore, the genitive case prescribed by specific rules (*pratipadavihitā ṣaṣṭhī*) should be adopted, according to the maxim: "That which is a cause of immediate cognition is stronger than that which is a cause of delayed cognition. For this genitive is used when there is a desire to express a general relation (*sambandhasāmānyavivakṣā*).

The cognition of the object (*karmatva*) would be delayed, whereas it occurs quickly when there is an intention to express the genitive case connected with a *kṛt* suffix. If it is argued that the cognition of the object is delayed because both meanings—agent (*kartṛ*) and object (*karman*)—are understood from the rule (*sūtra*), we say no. This is because for one who desires to know the agent but has already apprehended the object, the fact that the object is the primary meaning would first ascend to the mind. Anticipating the objection regarding the prohibition of compounding (*samāsa*), he refutes it with the words "and not" (*na ca*). The particle *ca* is used here to aggregate the preceding doubt.

Reversion (*pratiprasava*) is the exception to an exception; in usages such as *sarpiṣo jñānam* ("the knowledge of ghee"), there is scope for the prohibition of compounding with respect to the genitive case prescribed by rules such as *jño 'vidarthasya karaṇe*. For the meaning of that sentence is indeed "activity by means of ghee" (*sarpiṣā pravṛttiḥ*). Although the word *jñāna* ends in a *kṛt*-suffix, nevertheless the genitive in *sarpiṣaḥ* is not prescribed by the rule governing connection with a *kṛt*-suffix.

Because [the phrase] "know by means of ghee" (*sarpiṣā jānīta*) is capable of being construed with a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*), and because both the verbal root and the case-ending have as their meaning the activity and its cause respectively, this [result] is not established even when there is a connection with a *kṛt* suffix; therefore, since the counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) does not apply here, the prohibition of compounding (*samāsa-niṣedha*) retains its scope.

Objection: This genitive case should not be explained, because it is not employed [in actual usage]. For only a word that is actually employed conveys meaning in a grammatical rule (*sūtra*), not one that is unemployed; and only a word that conveys meaning should be explained. If it is argued that even though unemloyed, the case-ending is conveyed by memory and thus should be explained—no, for the meaning is understood even without the recollection of it.
