By the phrase "eight years," priority is established; for since time is subordinate to study by way of initiation (*upanayana*), and because the accusative case in the scriptural statement "one initiates the Brāhmaṇa boy" indicates that the time is subordinate to the boy, it is established that initiation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study pertaining to him. Furthermore, because initiation is prescribed by a sūtra under the category of acts not intended for the agent's own benefit (*akartrabhiprāya*), it is not established as an auxiliary to teaching. By the phrase "one should teach," it is established that [the act] consists of the recitation of words dependent on another.

The sense is as follows: since the injunctions—"One should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice for twelve days," "One should cause one desiring food to sacrifice," and "One should cause a Niṣāda chieftain to sacrifice"—establish that officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is for the purpose of acquiring wealth and is thus prompted by desire (*rāga-prāpta*), and since teaching (*adhyāpana*) is not something to be enjoined (as it is likewise prompted by desire), and because no specific qualification for the teacher is heard in the texts regarding teaching, it is stated that study (*adhyayana*) must be preceded by a teacher; thus, this is an injunction concerning the subsidiary parts (*aṅga-vidhi*) of study. To show that [study] has the observances (*vrata-niyama*) such as *upākarma* as its subsidiaries and possesses those subsidiaries, he says: "In the month of Śrāvaṇa... and so forth.

In the passage beginning with “for four and a half months,” the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) includes such statements as: “Henceforth, one should regularly recite the Vedic hymns (*chandāṃsi*) during the bright fortnights, and one should thoroughly study all the auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅgas*) during the dark fortnights. By these and similar injunctions, the time for the study of the auxiliary sciences is indicated. The term “vow” (*vrata*) refers to observances such as the *upākarma* and the *kāṇḍavrata*. It consists of regulations regarding place, time, permitted food, and so forth, as stated in passages such as: “A Śūdra is indeed a cremation ground; therefore, one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra.”

By the separate mention of "he should teach" and "by means of instructions regarding specific vows and observances," a distinction is made based on the division between Śruti and Smṛti, as well as the division between what is disputed and what is agreed upon. The sense is that just like the vows and observances such as the *upākarma*, the initiation (*upanayana*) is also an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to Vedic study; the meaning is that when there is an expectation of "what is its form? and "how is it to be performed?", the required details are enjoined by these sentences prescribing the auxiliaries.

Now, it was argued that in the passage "an eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa," it is understood that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of study; however, that is incorrect. For it is understood that initiation is a subordinate element of teaching (*adhyāpana*), which itself requires a student, through its connection with the person being initiated. This is also understood from Smṛti texts such as, "He who, having initiated a pupil... To this, it is replied:

In the statement, “The Brāhmaṇa boy is initiated,” the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) reveals that initiation has the boy as its subordinate element (*śeṣatva*). Since initiation is subordinate to the boy, and study is inherent to him, then—by the maxim of the internal and the external (*antaraṅga-bahiraṅga-nyāya*)—initiation is indeed a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of study. But one might object: in the scriptural passage, “That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call an *Ācārya*,” it is logical that initiation is a subsidiary part of teaching (*adhyāpana*), because of the direct verbal expression (*vaktṛ-śruti*).

If it is argued that "being internal" (*antaraṅgatva*) is indeed a mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the inherent capacity of the thing itself, and therefore the unexpressed word (*aśruti*) is stronger [than the expressed word], we say no. For while being internal is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the [alleged] *śruti* here resides within a Smṛti and is contained in a statement that is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). Consequently, because it resides in a Smṛti statement, it depends upon a foundational *śruti*; and because it resides in a statement that is a restatement, it depends upon another injunction (*vidhi*). Thus, there is a double delay. Indeed, among *śruti*, *liṅga*, and so forth, the cause of a delayed cognition is the reason for relative weakness. Therefore...

The hearing of the suffix *ktavatu* is not overridden by two instances of delay; furthermore, just as there is no injunction for the names "Śrotriya," "Upādhyāya," or "Guru" [to apply to one who merely initiates], this statement situated within that context must be understood as intended to enjoin the name "Ācārya" for the one who initiates and teaches. Thus, the hearing of the suffix *ktavatu* can indeed serve as the authority for the fact that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*).

Furthermore, although the *ātmanepada* ending would have applied by the rule "the root *ni* takes the *ātmanepada* when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent (*svaritañitaḥ kartrabhiprāye kriyāphale*"), the rule "the root *ni* takes the *ātmanepada* in the senses of honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowing, hiring, counting, and spending" is restated specifically for the purpose of excluding cases where the fruit does not accrue to the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*). Therefore, it is not logical that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*). For the author of the commentary on that [rule] states: "This restatement is for the purpose of [indicating] when the fruit does not accrue to the agent."

If it is argued: "Is it not the case that 'being for the benefit of the agent' (kartrabhiprāyatva) means that the fruit is intended by the agent alone? The restatement [of the rule] is for the purpose of negating that restriction; therefore, the fruit is connected to both. Consequently, since the fruit of the initiation (*upanayana*) is connected to the teacher through the medium of the student (*māṇavaka*), its status as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) to teaching (*adhyāpana*) is logical. [Response: No.

In the case of the injunction "one establishes the sacred fires" (*agnīnādadhīta*), although the ātmanepada ending is prescribed by the sūtra governing actions intended for the agent, the subsequent re-employment of that ending—since the fruit is connected to both [the agent and the recipient]—cannot serve to negate a restrictive rule; rather, its purpose is merely to exclude the condition of being intended solely for the agent. Therefore, it is not an auxiliary to teaching. If it is argued: "By the term 'intended for the agent,' what is meant is the non-connection of the fruit with a sentient being other than the agent; thus, there is no deviation in the case of 'one establishes the sacred fires. Furthermore, if the re-employment of the ending were for the sake of excluding that [non-connection], then the connection of the fruit with the teacher would be established, and consequently, it would be an auxiliary to teaching"—we say: No.

In the injunction "one should choose the officiating priests" (*ṛtvijo vṛṇīta*), although the *ātmanepada* ending is prescribed by the sūtra beginning with *svati*, we observe that the fruit [of the action] connects with a conscious being other than the agent (*kartṛ*). Since this re-enactment of the rule does not serve to negate a restrictive limitation (*niyama*), the re-enactment must instead be for the purpose of negating only that which is intended for the benefit of the agent (*kartrabhiprāya*). Therefore, initiation (*upanayana*) is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching (*adhyāpana*).

If it is argued: "Since the status of being an *ācārya* does not occur immediately after the rite of initiation (*upanayana*), and since an immediate result does not reside in the agent, the *ātmanepada* ending would not otherwise apply; yet, even though the immediate result does not benefit the agent, the *ātmanepada* is prescribed by the rule 'sammānana-' etc. Therefore, although the purpose is not for the benefit of the agent, there is no contradiction in initiation being a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of teaching, insofar as it aims at the accomplishment of the status of an *ācārya*, which occurs after an interval"—this is not so.

If it is argued that in the case of "one establishes the fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*), since the Ātmanepada is prescribed by the rule *svarita-jitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.72), we observe that the result—consisting in the attainment of the status of fire mediated by the consecration (*saṃskāra*)—is connected to the agent; therefore, the rule *saṃmānanotsañjanācāryakaraṇajñānabhṛtivigaṇanavyayeṣu niyaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.36) is intended for cases where the result does not aim at the agent, and the rule *akartari ca kārake...* (Pāṇini 1.3.14) is intended to preclude the connection of the result with the agent when the result is merely [the object], such that the fire qualified by the consecration is the result and thus the connection with the result is not mediated for the agent of the establishment (*ādhāna*). [Response: If that were so, then in the case of initiation (*upanayana*), the very accomplishment of the boy (*māṇavaka*) qualified by the rite of initiation would itself be the immediate result.

If it were the case that the *ātmanepada* ending is established by the rule regarding the agent’s intention (*kartrabhiprāya-sūtra*) alone, then the rule regarding what is not intended for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya-sūtra*) would be redundant. If, as you suggest, the mere fact of the fruit being intended for the agent—whether proximate or remote—is excluded by that rule, then the activity of the one who initiates the student (*upanetṛ*) would be untenable; for, as the saying goes, "even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose. This is not so. Even though the fruit of initiation (*upanayana*) accrues to the boy (*māṇavaka*), the activity [of the initiator] is justified by the desire for the fruit of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) obtained through another injunction, namely, "a gift should be given to the teacher."

Nor does this contradict the rule regarding actions not intended for the agent (*akartrabhiprāya*), because that sūtra concerns cases where there is no connection with a result that is unique to the agent. It is also incorrect to define "intended for the agent" as the agent’s desire for the immediate fruit of the action, and "not intended for the agent" as the lack of such desire; for this would contradict the possibility of a fruit of the action being undesired by the agent. This is because it is impossible for the refinement of the student (*māṇavaka-saṃskāra*), which serves to accomplish the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*), to be undesired by the teacher.

Therefore, initiation (*upanayana*), by way of the proximity of the boy who is about to study, is not a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the act of teaching; rather, it is exclusively a subsidiary part of the act of studying. Furthermore, it has been stated that the act of studying is not prompted by the injunction for teaching; for the injunction "one should teach" is like [the injunction] "one desiring offspring should cause [him] to sacrifice with the Dvādaśāha," and so forth.

Although, as in the case of [the injunctions] "one desiring offspring" or "one desiring food," no fruit of the activity prompted by that [injunction]—namely, study—is heard as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), nevertheless, the accomplishment of the *svādhyāya* (Vedic text) would indeed be such a qualification. This is because from the statement "one's own Veda is to be studied," it is understood that the *svādhyāya* is to be accomplished through study. Just as in the case of "one establishes the sacred fires," where the accomplishment of the fires is understood to be the qualification of the eligible person because the fires are to be accomplished through the *ādhāna* rite, so it is here.

Nor does the absence of a performer follow from the fact that the injunction for study is prompted by its own internal rule; for there are indeed awakened students. Thus says the venerable Āpastamba: "In that [matter], one should seek a teacher who is well-born, perfected in learning, composed, and a performer of the purificatory rites. If those [students] were prompted by an external injunction, such study would not be possible.

However, regarding those who are not yet awakened, knowing that the injunction for study—which is independent [of other motives]—has the boy as its object, well-wishers cause the boy to undertake study and so forth. Therefore, it is logical that study is prompted by its own injunction for both the awakened and the unawakened. If it were prompted by another injunction, the obligatory study would become prompted by an optional injunction; consequently, there would be no rule of compulsory performance.

For the teacher desires the status of an *ācārya* (teacher), since the study [of the Veda] cannot be accomplished in the absence of that desire for the status of an *ācārya*. If it is argued that this is established by the abundance of teachers, we say no; for we observe that students are even more numerous than teachers. Furthermore, although the rite of fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) is prompted by the injunctions for subsequent sacrifices, it is not prompted solely by optional injunctions, because there exist obligatory injunctions such as "One should sacrifice with the *Jyotiṣṭoma* every spring" and "One should perform the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives. Such points are to be considered in this manner.

Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. To the question, "How is the nature of the subsidiary (aṅga) and the nature of the principal (aṅgin) understood by means of the principal injunction (pradhāna-vidhi) which is endowed with the knowledge of the subsidiaries? he says: "In this way. This means that when the principal injunction has been defined together with the injunctions for the subsidiaries. By the words beginning with "satsantāna," the meaning of the statement of Āpastamba—"In that [regard], noble birth and learning..."—is summarized. "Qualities of the self" (ātmaguṇāḥ) refers to freedom from anger and so forth; by this, the meaning of the word *samāhita* is expressed. By the word *vedavit*, the meaning of the word *vidyāsamudita* is expressed.

The phrase "of one initiated by a teacher who knows the Vedas" is an attribute of the teacher intended for the sake of the student (*māṇavaka*) by means of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). The sense is that just as, when initiation is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of teaching, an attribute of the student is for the sake of the teacher, so it is here. The meaning is that even an attribute of the teacher—such as being endowed with specific vows and observances—is for the sake of the student. By the expression "repeating after the utterance of the teacher," the nature of dependent utterance is demonstrated.

The phrase "the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables" indicates that repetition is implied; for instance, in the injunction "one threshes the rice," because even a slight visible result must not be discarded, the threshing extends until the grain is husked, and thus repetition—though not explicitly stated—is established. Likewise here, repetition is established by implication, since a restrictive rule (niyama) is to be enjoined precisely without abandoning the visible purpose.

By the phrase "repeating after the utterance of the teacher" and by the phrase "of that which has been brought forward by a teacher who knows the Veda," it is stated that study—being dependent on a teacher who causes one to study—is of the nature of a dependent utterance, is impelled by its own injunction, and has initiation as its constituent part.

By the statement that "the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables is the repetition following the utterance of the teacher," the inquiry as to "what is its form? is pacified. By the phrase "of one brought by a teacher who knows the Veda and endowed with specific vows and observances," the expectation as to "how it should be performed" is fulfilled. Furthermore, by the phrase "the fruit of grasping the mass of syllables," it is also indicated that the desire to grasp the *svādhyāya* (one's own portion of the Veda) is a qualification for the entitlement to study.

Just as in the case of the injunction "one offers groats" (*saktūn juhoti*), where the offering of groats is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the person because the person partakes in the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by that offering, so too, if study were merely a refinement of the person, it would not have the acquisition of the mass of syllables as its fruit; for it would lack the purpose of establishing the *svādhyāya* (the Veda) itself, being instead intended solely for the production of *apūrva*. Consequently, since the acquisition of the mass of syllables would not be its fruit, the requirement of repetition would not be established, and study would consist merely in a single utterance. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And study... [is like] the state of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to initiation (*upanayana*).

The meaning is that this point must also be established in the same way as [the fact] that [the study of the Veda] is enjoined by its own injunction. It is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic text). The meaning is not that it is a refinement of the person, like the *saktu-homa* sacrifice, by virtue of being directed toward a transcendental result (*apūrva*). Why? To this he says: "Because of the *svādhyāya*," for from the suffix *-tavya*, the status of being an object (*karman*) is understood; indeed, it is the *svādhyāya* that is understood to be the object. For the status of being an object consists in being that which is most desired to be attained by the agent through the action; therefore, the meaning is that study is a refinement of the *svādhyāya*, and not of the person.

Regarding the question of how even that which is *nirvartya* (to be produced) and so forth can possess a commonality of being an object (*karmatva*), and why this is stated as the reason for its being a *saṃskārya* (to be refined), the mention of "the Veda" (*svādhyāyasya*) is reiterated with the intention of showing the impossibility of it being either *nirvartya* or *vikārya*. The underlying sense is that the understanding of the objecthood [of the Veda]—which is supported by the inherent capacity of the thing itself—is the reason for its being something to be refined. Furthermore, when another result is possible, it is improper to conclude that it is merely an object to be reached (*prāpya*).

Now, one might raise the objection: "Is it not the case that being an object of refinement (*saṃskāryatva*) follows merely from the fact of being an object of an action? For instance, in the cases 'he offers groats' (*saktūn juhoti*) and 'gold is to be worn' (*suvarṇaṃ bhāryam*), there is no refinement of the groats or the gold. In response to this doubt, he clarifies the nature of refinement by stating, "For refinement indeed... (*saṃskāro hi*). By the two particles *hi* and *nāma*, both well-known status and the acceptance of a counter-correlative are indicated. Furthermore, the word *api ca* may be understood as the single word *eka*, which has the same form as various indeclinables.

Although the definition of *saṃskāra* (purification) as that which serves to enhance an existing thing implies a characteristic that follows from being useful to something past or future, nevertheless—since it is impossible for the *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) to be useful to something past—the definition here is stated as being useful to something future. The sense is that, due to the impossibility of this definition of *saṃskāra*, the status of being an object (*karmatva*)—which was understood from the natural force of the suffix in such injunctions as "one should offer the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*)—is set aside. However, he says "and [there is] the state of being purified" (*saṃskāryatvaṃ ca*) because it is not similarly untenable in this case; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel doubt.

To the question "Why?", he says: "Dharma, Artha, etc. By the phrase "the four human goals and their means," it is shown that the comprehension of meaningful objects follows as a continuous sequence for the sake of unifying the previously mentioned explanations; furthermore, the state of being directed toward human goals is also continuous, for the status of being a human goal is common to Dharma and the others, since both the desired end and its means constitute human goals.

Although some objects of wealth and pleasure, as well as their means, are established in the world, nevertheless, the superior forms of wealth and pleasure—such as the sovereignty of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) or the Lord of the Gods (Indra)—and their respective means, as well as worldly things like cattle, children, and food which are established in the world yet produced by rituals such as the *citrayajña*, fall outside the scope of ordinary worldly means of knowledge (*laukikapramāṇa*). Therefore, it is logical to state that the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*) are to be known through the Veda. The meaning is that because the Veda is "that which makes known" (*avabodhaka*), it generates the knowledge necessary for their performance. He says "by recitation (*japa*) and so forth," because the quality of being a "maker known" (*arthāvabodhakatva*) is not over-extended (*avyāpta*) to sounds such as *hum* and the like.

The meaning is that even by its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), even by a single syllable being recited as a *japa*, apart from the knowledge of the meaning and the performance [of rites]. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of teaching is intended. What is meant is that knowledge conducive to performance, as well as *japa* and so forth, [are achieved] only through one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) purified by formal study (*adhyayana*). Alternatively, by the word "and" (*ca*), the status of being a means to that [knowledge] is conjoined with the status of being a means to the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) through the cognition of those goals and their means. This status of being a means is twofold: by way of *japa* and so forth, and by its own form while being maintained [in memory]. Therefore, the word "also" (*api*) refers to a conjunction of the intermediate items to be conjoined.

Thus, its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) has been established. With the intention of raising the alternative—whether the requirement that study extends until the meaning is understood is accepted on the basis of the natural force of the word "what" (*kiṃ*), or rather through the logical inconsistency of the matter—he concludes the examination of the injunction for study by refuting the natural force of the word with the words "thus" (*evam*). Regarding the phrase "like a mantra": the separate mention is intended to refer to those mantras that assist the study by being included within the observances (*vrata*).

For there is indeed the efficacy of mantras such as *śanno mitraḥ* through mere recitation even without entering into specific vows; these are the previously mentioned observances (*niyama*). Alternatively, just as the pronunciation enjoined for a child at the time of initiation (*upanayana*) and at the time of twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) is merely the recitation of syllables with observances and does not aim at producing an understanding of the meaning—since it is impossible for children to comprehend the meaning of mantras—it is the same here. This refers to the "grasping of the mass of syllables."

The primary meaning of the term "study" (adhyayana) is the recitation [of the Veda] according to its restrictive rules; thus, one who has studied some portion of the Vedas is a *brāhmaṇa*, and one who has studied a single branch (*śākhā*) is a *śrotriya*.

This is because of such usages as "one who has studied the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is an *anūcāna*," "one who has studied the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) is a *ṛṣi*," and "one who has studied the recitation of the *Kalpasūtras* is a *bhrūṇa*. Indeed, it is not possible for one who has studied only a portion of his own scripture to possess knowledge of its meaning; for since the study of the auxiliary sciences is mentioned separately, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence that knowledge of the meaning could arise even in their absence. Furthermore, the word *svādhyāya* does not denote knowledge of the meaning, but rather denotes only one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Therefore, it is proper that the object of the action is the *svādhyāya* itself, and not the knowledge of the meaning.

When there arises an expectancy for the purpose of study, since a visible result is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible one. Because the grasping of syllables (*akṣaragrahaṇa*) is proximate and because it is common to [the acquisition of] dharma and so forth, its acceptance as the goal is logical. The intention is that the knowledge of meaning is not [the goal], because it is remote and because it is not universal. To exclude the notion that the limit is merely a single utterance, it is stated that the process culminates in the grasping of syllables. By the suffix *-mātra*, the exclusion of the idea that the operation of the injunction extends up to the knowledge of meaning is established.

The sense is as follows: just as the sentence "one should establish the sacred fires" (*agnīn ādadhīta*) refers only to the act of installation itself and not to its application in subsequent sacrifices; and just as the sentence "one desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī" refers to the specific ritual action until the accomplishment of rain and not to its utility after the rain has fallen—so it is here. In this way, the view that the purpose of the word extends up to the knowledge of the meaning has been refuted on the basis of the natural force of the words.

Now, he dispels the objection regarding the lack of purpose, which is threefold: first, if the injunction were intended merely for the acquisition of the syllables, then since the Veda—already enjoined as subordinate to that acquisition—would lack any evidence for having a purposeful meaning, it would follow that its meaning is not intended to be expressed; second, because there would be no impetus for inquiry, Mīmāṃsā would be unnecessary and thus should not be commenced; and third, since the mere acquisition of a mass of syllables is a miserable state, the injunction would fail to culminate in a meaningful purpose.

By means of refuting these three doubts, [the author] demonstrates that the injunction for study extends as far as the knowledge of the meaning; he thereby dispels the doubt regarding the non-commencement of the inquiry into Brahman caused by that [lack of knowledge], and shows that the inquiries into Dharma and Brahman constitute a single treatise (*ekaśākhya*) because they are commentaries on the single continuous work known as the Veda.

Regarding the phrase "of that which has been acquired through study": here, the intended meaning is the study of the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*), referring to one who has studied the Veda along with its limbs and the *Śiras* sections. Now, it might be objected that based on the consistency between what precedes and follows—namely, the statement "from the study of the Veda with its limbs"—it is established that there is a comprehension of a purposeful meaning; for meanings such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and meditation (*upāsana*), which possess purposes such as heaven (*svarga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), are understood. By the term "purposeful meaning," any suspicion that [the Veda] should be investigated like a crow's teeth is excluded.

By the phrase "because it is seen to bring about the understanding of a purposeful meaning," it is stated that the act of knowing (*vidi*) ultimately culminates in human goals through a traditional succession. It has been stated that the immediate purpose of study is the acquisition of a mass of syllables, as indicated by the words "of what is acquired through study. This is the meaning.

Does the injunction intend for its purpose to culminate directly in the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), or indirectly? A direct culmination in the purpose is not tenable even if the injunction extends up to the knowledge of the meaning, because heaven itself is the purpose by way of performance and the unseen potency (*apūrva*). Furthermore, it is not accepted that the injunction for study culminates in heaven. If it is indirect, then this is possible even in our own position by its very nature; the meaning is that this is due to the inherent capacity of the word to convey understanding.

It is established in the world that for one who has mastered the words and their meanings, a word’s capacity to convey meaning is inherent (*svābhāvikam*). The particle *eva* (only) is intended to indicate independence from an injunction (*vidhi-nairapekṣya*); however, an application elsewhere does not obstruct the inherent orientation of a word toward its meaning. This is like the injunction for silent recitation (*japa-vidhi*): the prescriptions such as, "Having officiated at a sacrifice or having accepted a gift, one should study the Veda three times without eating," or "Or [recite] the Sāvitrī three times a night," or "One should constantly generate the Veda itself," do not prevent the Veda from being oriented toward its meaning.
To the objection that if the *svādhyāya* (one's own recitation of the Veda) is inherently capable of conveying its meaning, what is the use of *mīmāṃsā*, he says: "From what is merely grasped.

By the phrase "from what is merely grasped" (*gṛhītāt*), it is meant "from that which has been acquired through study alone"; thus, the intended meaning is its lack of the procedural details (*itikartavyatā*) known as *mīmāṃsā*. The sense is that because a superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) is susceptible to doubt and error, *mīmāṃsā* exists for the purpose of dispelling those.

By the passage beginning with "of that which has been acquired through study," it is stated that the Veda possesses the inherent nature of being a communicator of meaning; therein, the word "meaning" (*artha*) qualified by "purposeful" (*prayojanavat*) is intended to indicate that [the Veda] ultimately culminates in human goals through a traditional succession. Furthermore, it is explained that the subsequent absence of the capacity to produce an immediate comprehension (*āpātapratīti*) is due to a deficiency in auxiliary factors.

For the capacity to produce an immediate comprehension is not the inherent nature of the Veda, since its inherent nature is to produce valid knowledge (*pramiti*); thus, the absence of such immediate comprehension in one who lacks the necessary equipment known as *mīmāṃsā* does not contradict the Veda’s inherent nature of producing valid knowledge.

Just as the non-perception of color and so forth due to the absence of auxiliary conditions such as light does not undermine the inherent capacity of the eyes and other sense organs to produce the direct perception of color and so forth, likewise, the word "purposeful" (*prayojanavat*) is used again to show that even in the case of initial cognition (*āpātapratīti*), there is a cognition characterized by purposefulness. For it is the initial cognition of a purposeful object that generates an interest in its definitive determination (*nirṇaya*); indeed, the initial cognition of something useless, such as the teeth of a crow, does not generate an interest in its definitive determination.

The meaning is: "having seen [them] as they are understood at first sight. The point is that, just as in the expression "having seen the arising of a cognition in oneself," the initial apprehension of a purposeful meaning is established by one's own experience; therefore, its denial is impossible. He demonstrates the nature of the fruit of Mīmāṃsā, which is distinct from the nature of the fruits of grammar and other sciences.

Regarding the phrase *tatsvarūpa* (its own nature): "particularities of nature" refers to the primary members (*aṅgin*), while "particularities of mode" refers to the subsidiary members (*aṅga*). By the word "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), what is intended is the difference between the nature and mode of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) and the nature and mode stated in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The terms *prayojanavat* (possessing purpose), *artha* (meaningful), *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), and *vedamīmāṃsā* (investigation of the Veda) are common to both the earlier and later portions [of the Mīmāṃsā] by their very nature, and not because of an injunction; however, the two words "the person who has studied the Veda" (*adhītavedaḥ puruṣaḥ*) do establish that [obligation].

The phrase "one who has studied the Vedas" indicates that the operation of the injunction for study terminates once its portion has been performed; thus, it is shown that such a person does not have a motive to engage in Mīmāṃsā. The intention of the word "person" (puruṣa) is that, being a conscious being, he engages of his own accord through an initial comprehension of the purposeful meaning [of the Veda].

But surely, if the position is that [the study of grammar] culminates in the mere grasping of the phonemes (*akṣara*), then engagement [in it] out of inclination (*rāga*) would not be possible; for even the study of the auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*)—as enjoined in such rules as "one should recite all the Vedāṅgas during the dark fortnights," "the Veda with its six auxiliaries should be studied without [other] motive," "a twice-born man should teach the Veda," and "together with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret doctrines (*rahasya*)"—would culminate in the mere grasping of the phonemes. Consequently, since there would be no comprehension of the meaning in grammar and the rest, and because there would be no absence of superficial cognition due to the lack of knowledge regarding bases (*prakṛti*), suffixes (*pratyaya*), and so forth, [this position is untenable]. Not so.

Since grammar and the other [Vedāṅgas] are limbs of the Veda, it is impossible for something that accomplishes nothing to be a limb; and since a visible utility is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible one by abandoning that [visible utility]. Therefore, only a visible utility in the form of the comprehension of words and so forth must be accepted. Thus, because the understanding of the meaning of grammar and the others is established precisely through the impossibility of their being limbs otherwise, and because the commencement of Mīmāṃsā is justified by the establishment of an initial perception of meaningful purpose, [the study of these limbs is necessary].

By the statement, "A person who has studied the Veda proceeds of his own accord," the aphorism *athāto dharmajijñāsā* (Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma) is also explained by implication. The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that Mīmāṃsā need not be commenced, because if the act of knowing (*vidi*) consists merely in the grasping of the mass of syllables, there would be no impelling agent [for further inquiry]; and because there is no evidence that the Veda has meaning as its primary purpose. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it must be commenced, because after the study of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences, one observes that words inherently convey their meanings; thus, even in the absence of another impelling agent, engagement [in inquiry] is justified through natural inclination (*rāga*).

Now, if the inquiry into karma were obtained through mere worldly desire (*rāga*), then the Smṛti rule regarding the ritual bath upon graduation—“having studied, one should bathe”—would be its sublater; for if it were mandatory (*vaidha*), the Smṛti itself would provide scope [for the inquiry], since Śruti is more authoritative than even Smṛti.

It is not so; with what intention was this stated—that the injunction for study extends either up to the grasping of the mass of syllables or up to the knowledge of the meaning? If it extends up to the knowledge of the meaning, then there is no contradiction, because the word "study" (*adhyayana*) in the Smṛti rule "having studied, one should bathe" has that same meaning. If it extends up to the grasping of the mass of syllables, then too there is no contradiction, because the meanings are identical.

Furthermore, even when there is a contradiction, there exists direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), such as in the Chāndogya: "Having studied the Veda in the teacher’s family, and having performed the duties for the teacher according to the rules until they are completed, one should return home and [settle] in a household in a pure place," and so forth. Consequently, the Vedic injunction regarding the ceremonial bath (*snāna-śruti*), being accompanied by a Smṛti statement, is more authoritative; therefore, the discussion regarding the relative strength and weakness of Vedic and Smṛti statements is pointless. If it is argued that in this way even the Veda subverts activity prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), we say: no.

For even one who has returned home [after completing his studies] (*samāvṛtta*), listening (*śravaṇa*) is possible through passion (*rāga*). Now, an objection might be raised: if returning home occurs immediately after the study [of the Veda], then because one would be occupied with the performance of household duties (*gṛhasthakarma*) preceded by that return, no opportunity for listening would be found, and it would follow that the Mīmāṃsā inquiry could not be commenced. This is not so; for even for one who has returned home, an opportunity for listening exists, just as it does for the teacher who imparts the instruction.

If it is argued that teaching is prescribed for the teacher (ācārya) but not listening for the householder (gṛhastha), we say no; for teaching, like officiating at sacrifices or accepting gifts, arises from worldly inclination (rāga). If it is further argued that even though it arises from inclination, teaching is sanctioned by scripture—as in the injunction "one may acquire wealth through receiving gifts and so forth"—then listening is likewise sanctioned by scripture, because it is not prohibited and because it is useful for the performance of sacrifices.

If it is argued that—starting from the passage concerning Śvetaketu, "Every year, for two months each, one who is composed should dwell in the teacher’s family, desiring further learning," and continuing with "That is prohibited by the scriptures; for when the life of a householder has been established, the obligatory duties are heard [in the texts]," such as "The Agnihotra is to be performed," hearing [the Veda] is prohibited for a householder—this is not so, because dwelling in the teacher’s family for two full months is itself prohibited on the grounds that it would obstruct the performance of those very duties.

"For when one has entered into household life, the obligatory duties are heard [in the scriptures]," as it is said, "the Agnihotra and hospitality. Since even for the teacher there is no obstruction to the performance [of these duties], the Śrāvaṇa [rite] is sanctioned by scripture; therefore, the Śrāvaṇa and the Śravaṇa (listening) are equal in being subjects of permission or non-permission based on whether they cause obstruction or non-obstruction to the performance [of duties]. For this very reason, in the Mahābhārata and other texts, the listening to [the teachings of] Bhīṣma and others is established even for Yudhiṣṭhira and others who were devoted to the state of a householder.

Even though the time for hearing (*śravaṇa*) is indeed the same as the time for reciting (*śrāvaṇa*), if it is argued that this would obstruct the listener’s performance of duties such as fetching water or gathering wood, we say no. This is because activities like fetching water, which are prompted by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), cease once that [study] has been completed. Furthermore, the teacher’s act of causing [the text] to be heard is justified by his desire for other purposes such as wealth or fame, or by affection for his disciples; and since the teacher has already known the meaning, his own practical application of the knowledge is justified. If it is argued that this is not the case for the listener because he has not yet known the meaning, we say no.

Because, from the time of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) onwards, the performance [of rites] is established through the words of those who desire one's welfare; if it is asked, "In that case, would there not simply be the word of the well-wisher? What is the purpose of hearing the Mīmāṃsā?"—the answer is: for the sake of ascertaining that the well-wisher’s word is rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and for the sake of establishing it for oneself for other inquirers. If it is argued, "If performance were possible solely on the basis of the well-wisher’s word, it would follow that even Śūdras and others should perform them," we say no.

Because there exist prohibitive statements such as, "One should not give counsel to a Śūdra," "One should not teach him the Dharma," and "One should not prescribe a vow for him," it is not the case that Brahmins do not instruct Śūdras in sacrifices and the like. Nor should such prohibitive statements be restricted in scope to refer only to specific Śūdras who are devoid of service and so forth, for there is no basis for such a restriction. Furthermore, no other scriptural statement is observed that pertains to the Śūdra’s lack of eligibility for sacrifices and the like.

Furthermore, because it is stated that the entire Veda and specific mantras must be recited by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and because these are obtainable only through formal study (*adhyayana*), and because study is dependent upon initiation (*upanayana*), and because initiation is restricted to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), there is no possibility of Śūdras and others having the qualification [for such rites]. If it is argued: "The rule for initiation can be interpreted as pertaining only to the study of the three higher castes; therefore, a Śūdra’s study would be independent of initiation, and thus it is possible for him to perform the recitation of the sacrificer and so forth," we say: No.

Therefore, because the hearing of the Veda and so forth by a Śūdra is prohibited by such texts as, "Hence one should not study in the presence of a Śūdra," and, "Now, if he causes him to hear the Veda, his ears are to be filled with lead and lac; if he recites it, his tongue is to be cut out; if he retains it, his body is to be split apart," and because study is an act contingent upon the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), which has only the three higher castes as its qualified subjects, the Śūdra and others have no entitlement to it; thus, the utterance of specific mantras is logically justified [only for those who are entitled].

It does not follow that a Śūdra or others would be entitled to perform Vedic sacrifices merely because they hear the words of those seeking their welfare; thus, there is no contradiction with the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the exclusion of Śūdras). Furthermore, just as the injunction "One should perform the Agnihotra as long as one lives" provides an opportunity for activities such as the acquisition of wealth—which, though naturally prompted by desire, are necessary for one's own subsistence—according to the maxim "one's own limb [or part] is not an obstacle to itself," so too the suffix *-ktvā* signifies only the identity of the agent and the priority of time, and not immediate succession.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that immediate succession (*ānantarya*) alone is what is to be enjoined? For if it were not, the injunction would be purposeless, since the cessation of residence in the teacher’s house—which consists of suffering—is already established by its very nature. [Reply: No. Even if the injunction were intended to signify immediate succession, it would still be purposeless; and that [purposelessness] follows precisely because residing in the teacher’s house consists of suffering. Therefore, bathing (*snāna*) is indeed a specific purificatory rite accompanied by restrictive rules (*saniyama-saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), and it is this that is to be enjoined, not immediate succession. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the scriptural use of the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *adhītya* (having studied). Thus, one engages in it spontaneously.

Now, it is said: "Whoever performs a sacrifice, officiates at a sacrifice, or teaches with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity (*daivata*) are unknown, either strikes a post, falls into a pit, is carried away, or becomes worse off; his meters become exhausted. But he who knows [these] for every mantra reaches a full span of life."

The injunction for the knowledge of the meaning is established by the Śruti passage, "He becomes superior, and his meters become fresh; therefore, one should know these in every mantra," which is supplemented by the Smṛti, "He who teaches or even recites [the Veda] without knowing the seer, the meter, the deity, and the application, becomes a sinner. Thus, the requirement of knowing the meaning is proven.

If it is argued that because knowledge of the deity to be propitiated is enjoined here with respect to the mantra, then by parity of reasoning, since the word *daivata* (deity) serves to reveal the meaning of the matter to be performed as manifested by the mantra, knowledge of the meaning of the portions such as the injunctions (*vidhi*) would also necessarily be enjoined; and furthermore, because the application (*yoga*) of mantras—that is, their ritual employment—depends upon knowledge of the meaning of the Brāhmaṇa portions; [we reply: no, for this is excluded by the fact that these matters are obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*), just like the acceptance of gifts, sexual intercourse, and so forth.

For the injunction, "A Brāhmaṇa should acquire wealth through receiving gifts and so forth, and he should approach his wife during her season," does not preclude the acquisition of wealth through receiving gifts and so forth which is already prompted by natural desire (rāga).

Furthermore, since the knowledge of the meaning is enjoined by this very sentence, one need not resort to the view that the injunction for study extends up to the knowledge of the meaning; just as, because the sacrifices are established by other injunctions, the injunction for the *āghāna* (fire-consecration) is not taken to extend up to the injunctions for the subsequent sacrifices, so it is here. Moreover, this Vedic sentence does not convey that the study of the Veda must culminate in the knowledge of its meaning, nor does it enjoin the knowledge of the meaning itself, because such knowledge is already established through other means.

Furthermore, in this context, it is understood that the injunction pertains only to the knowledge of the *ṛṣi* and so forth regarding the mantra alone; consequently, while the necessity of studying the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) would be established, the necessity of knowing the meaning [of the Veda] would not, because the knowledge of the meters, deities, and so forth depends upon the *Chandas*, *Kalpa*, *Vyākaraṇa*, *Nirukta*, and other such sciences, and does not depend upon *Mīmāṃsā*.

If it is argued that there would be a need for Mīmāṃsā when a doubt arises regarding the scope of application (*viniyoga*), then, in order to dispel that doubt, one's engagement [with study] would proceed out of mere inclination (*rāga*). Furthermore, even this statement—"That which is studied but not understood is merely recited like a chant; like dry fuel in a non-fire, it never blazes"—does not indicate that the injunction for study extends as far as the comprehension of meaning.

In the passage "that which has been studied but not understood," there is a distinct mention of both study and the knowledge of the meaning; furthermore, that which is already prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*) cannot be the object of an injunction. Moreover, ritual applications (*kalpasūtra-prayoga*) such as "a Brāhmaṇa who has studied some portion of the Vedas," "a Śrotriya who has studied one branch (*śākhā*)," and "an Anūcāna who has studied the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*)," demonstrate that the knowledge of the meaning is a distinct entity from the mere act of study. Therefore, this statement beginning with "that which has been studied" is intended to encourage those who do not listen—whether due to the painful nature of hearing, laziness, or being preoccupied with other pursuits such as the acquisition of wealth.

Just as the statement, "Do not play with dice; practice agriculture; delight in wealth, considering it much," is intended for the purpose of encouraging one who is indolent—for through encouragement, activity becomes intense—it does not, by this much, destroy the fact that agriculture and the acquisition of wealth are already prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*); rather, in every such case, there is simply a mandatory injunction (*vidhi*). Similarly, this statement also does not destroy the fact that hearing [the Veda] is already prompted by natural inclination. Therefore, one engages in it solely out of natural inclination.

Thus, since engagement [with the study of Mīmāṃsā] occurs through other means, it is improper to assume that the hearing of Mīmāṃsā is something to be enjoined by overstepping the power of the words [of the Veda]. [The opponent asks: "Let there be a single treatise (*ekaśāstrya*) and let there be engagement through natural inclination (*rāga*); how then is the rule of priority (*paurvāparya-niyama*) established? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). The meaning is: since the portion concerning ritual action (*karmabhāga*) is established as the beginning of the Veda—because the form of the Veda consists of injunctions for ritual action—it follows that its exposition must occur precisely in the order in which it was studied; thus, the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) necessarily precedes [the inquiry into Brahman].

[Objection: But surely, it has not been established anywhere—in the form of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and a final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—that actions have small and unstable fruits, whereas [devotion] has infinite and stable fruits; so how is the understanding of their small and unstable fruits obtained? To this he says: "When the essential nature has been defined. The meaning is that only the essential nature of the injunction for action has been defined, and the knowledge that its fruits are small and unstable is the result of the injunction for repetition and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that only the essential nature of the injunction for action has been defined, but not the Supreme Deity who is to be worshipped.
For when [action] is performed as His worship, the attainment of infinite and stable fruits is established.

"Self-study (svādhyāya) acquired through formal study": the sense is that since formal study has the entirety of the Veda as its object, and the Upanishads are included within the term "self-study. By the word "portion" (ekadeśa), it is indicated that [the Upanishads] are parts of a single unified composition. By the word "Upanishad," he points out a specific section within the mass of words designated by the general term "Veda" that is not subordinate to anything else; by the word "Vedānta," the reason for the rule regarding the sequence of the inquiry is shown.

In the commentary expressed by the word *mīmāṃsā*, he distinguishes the specific section by means of the term *śārīraka*. The words denoting immortality (*amṛtatva*) are intended to exclude the minor and impermanent fruits mentioned as incidental [in the Karma-mīmāṃsā], such as: "He becomes possessed of food, a giver of food, great in offspring, cattle, and the splendor of Brahman. The meaning is that although the incidental fruits are minor and impermanent, there is an initial impression (*apātapratīti*) regarding the primary fruit because it possesses infinite and permanent results. Due to the fact that the mind has been refined by the Karma-mīmāṃsā, it is indeed perceived by the listener that both the incidental and the primary fruits are possible here as well.

[Objection: "Surely, because it is a fruit, one might have the thought that this too is impermanent. [Reply: Not so, because there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position. Just as the happiness of heaven and the like is recognized as distinct from earthly happiness, and even therein mutual distinctions are recognized due to differences in place, time, and essential nature, in the very same way, a happiness distinct even from that [earthly happiness] is possible; thus, its cognition would indeed generate intense passion (*rāga*). One becomes qualified (*adhikārī*); in this manner, only one who has performed the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) becomes qualified.

The intended meaning is not that one must possess the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*). Thus, the unity of the treatise (*aikashāstrya*), the sequence [of topics], and the necessity of undertaking [this inquiry] have been established. To the question of which Vedānta passages provide the initial intuition (*āpātapratīti*) conducive to the undertaking of this work, he says "And thus" (*tathā ca*); the meaning is "just as it has been explained according to the Sūtras. The word "and" (*ca*) serves either to dispel doubt or to indicate what is well-known. By the word "exclusive" (*kevala*), there is the exclusion of ritual action (*karman*) which is an auxiliary to knowledge (*jñāna*).

[Objection: Even though the perishability of the fruits of action has already been determined through the inquiry into ritual (*karmavicāra*), for what purpose are these further passages cited that produce the perception of their fruits being small and unstable? One should rather cite only those passages that produce the initial perception of infinite and stable fruits. [Reply: It is said: For a person who has mastered ritual action, by seeing a statement that accords with the determined meaning, it becomes possible to establish—on the basis of authoritative testimony (*prāmāṇikatva*)—the imperishability of the fruit of Brahman-knowledge, just as the instability of the fruit of action [was established]. Therefore, the phrase "tadyathā" (just as) is intended to stabilize one's faith. That which is seen is "loka," meaning the fruit.

By the statement, "that [merit] of his becomes merely finite," it is declared that even manifold karma of various kinds, performed over many periods of time, is perishable when devoid of knowledge. Since that statement is preceded by the passage, "O Gārgī, he who, not knowing this Imperishable, offers oblations, performs sacrifices, and practices austerities in this world for many thousands of years,"—when it is said that [the merit] is "finite," the finitude of the nature of the action itself is not something to be taught, as it is already established in the world; rather, the finitude of the *result* alone is what is established by implication.

The phrase "tadyathā" (just as) is employed at the outset to clarify this point. It is introduced to dispel the doubt that the fruits of worldly existence are unstable and that one might instead seek to achieve a permanent fruit through ritual actions alone; for it is said, "Indeed, by means of things that are impermanent, that which is permanent is not attained. To provide the justification for this, another passage is cited: "For these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts," meaning they are incapable of carrying one across to the further shore of saṃsāra because they are subject to destruction midway.

He cites the passage beginning with "Having examined the worlds" (*parīkṣya lokān*), which demonstrates—more consistently with the application of the Sūtras—that the fruits of ritual actions are meager and unstable, whereas the fruit of the meditation on Brahman is infinite and imperishable; in this passage, the approach to a teacher (*gurūpasatti*) is enjoined by way of restating a matter already established by reasoning.

Having examined—that is, having determined through the methods of Mīmāṃsā—that [the self] is accumulated by karma, gathered by karma, and produced by karma; [one sees that] the Brāhmaṇa—one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas) and the Upaniṣads (śiras)—is "uncreated," meaning eternal. Here, the person (*puruṣa*) is the subject, as indicated by the gender and because of the subsequent statement, "the imperishable person" (*akṣaraṃ puruṣam*).

One should understand that the phrase "there is no success through performed action" implies that [liberation] is not accomplished by ritual acts. He who has attained such disillusionment (nirveda) should approach a teacher specifically for the sake of knowing that [truth]. By the use of the word "specifically" (eva), it is understood as a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi). "With fuel in hand" means with hands not empty; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands."

One should approach a *śrotriya*—one who has heard the Vedāntas—who is established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*), meaning one who possesses the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. The implication is that even if one has heard the Vedāntas, if they are not established in Brahman due to a lack of inclination (*ruci*), they should not be approached. The grammatical connection is "one should approach. *Śama* consists of the restraint of the external senses; since the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has already been mentioned by the phrase "to one whose mind is tranquil," it follows by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*). By this, what is intended is the attentiveness required for hearing (*śravaṇa*), and not the complete conquest of the senses and so forth required for meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "To him, that wise one spoke. The reference "by which" (*yena*) intends *vijñāna* (realized knowledge). For it was previously introduced in general terms as "for the sake of that *vijñāna*"; alternatively, it may intend the cause [of liberation], or there may be a change of gender (*liṅgavyatyaya*). It is "imperishable" (*akṣaram*) because it is unchanging in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and "true" (*satyam*) because it is unchanging even in its qualities (*guṇataḥ*); by these two terms, the non-sentient matter (*acit*) and the individual soul (*jīva*) are excluded. "He spoke that knowledge of Brahman" (*tāṃ brahmavidyāṃ provāca*) means "he should declare it. This is explained in the *Vedāntasāra*. The use of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is according to the rule: "In the Vedic language (*chandasi*), the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and *liṭ* [may be used for all tenses]."

[Objection: Is it not the case that from the words "to one whose mind is tranquil and endowed with calmness" (*praśāntacittāya śamānvitāya*), the prior occurrence of calmness (*śama*) and so forth is understood? [Response: No, because what is intended here is merely the attentiveness suitable for hearing (*śravaṇa*). Total dispassion toward sense objects, which is an auxiliary to meditative worship (*upāsanā*), is not intended here; for that will be defined later in the passage: "He should be endowed with calmness, self-restraint, and so forth" (*śamadamādyupetaḥ syāt*).

Therefore, since these [qualities] are to be ascertained and accomplished, their status as qualifiers is untenable prior to such ascertainment; moreover, scripture shows that for a person possessing knowledge produced by the scriptures, meditation—which has tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities as its constituent parts—occurs subsequent to that [knowledge]. In the passage, "Therefore, one who knows thus, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should see the Self in the very Self," the phrase "one who knows thus" denotes the possession of knowledge produced by the scriptures, while "having become... he should see" establishes that meditation has tranquility and the rest as its constituent parts.
He cites scriptural passages concerning the supreme fruit that is exclusively stable within: "The knower of Brahman," and so forth.

In this section, because of the scriptural hearing, "from which words turn back," the attainment of an infinite and stable fruit is established. Although the Brahman to be attained is infinite and stable, he says "not again" (*na punaḥ*) in order to dispel the doubt that the attainment itself might be merely occasional. Alternatively, by "the knower of Brahman," he states the attainment of Brahman—which is the infinite and stable fruit—through knowledge; and by "not again," he states that the attainment of Brahman through knowledge is preceded by the removal of obstacles.

Because the term "death" (mṛtyu) is applied to both in such passages as, "Death is negligence (pramāda), or rather, delusion (moha); that which is considered death by the wise is indeed negligence, I declare,"—where negligence is the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the Self as it exists, and delusion is erroneous cognition, as indicated by expressions such as "delusion of direction" (diṅmoha)—it is not merely the cessation of death itself, but its effects as well that cease. Thus he says: "The seer does not see death."

Regarding this statement, it is heard [in scripture]: "Neither disease nor suffering. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "not again," etc., is for the purpose of making known that upon seeing Brahman, there is the cessation of death and so forth. In the phrase "the seer does not see death," the word "seer" (paśya) also means "one who sees Brahman," because in the immediately preceding cited passage, "he sees that One," the object has been shown. And the phrase "he becomes self-radiant" (svārāj) means that he is no longer subject to karma.

"The term *svarāṭ* (self-ruling) is to be understood as 'independent'—so say the lexicographers. By the statement "knowing Him thus," the exclusion of other means such as the worship of deities other than the knowledge of the attributeless pure consciousness is established; for it is the worship of Puruṣottama alone that is declared to be the means. Furthermore, he shows by the words "separate from himself" (*pṛthag ātmānam*) that the knowledge consisting of the worship of Him does not have identity with the Self as its object, but rather has distinctness as its object.

"Having known," that is, having understood; "then," from the knowledge of their distinctness; "favored by Him," meaning made an object of His affection and graced; "attains immortality"—this is the meaning. These Vedāntic passages are to be construed with what precedes. Someone, satisfied merely by the clearly stated passages cited, raises an objection with the words "But surely... (nanu ca). Although other objections were not explicitly mentioned in the preceding section, they are intended there because their refutations were explicitly stated; therefore, it is appropriate to include them as a conjunction with those [objections] whose sense is already established, using the word "and" (ca).

The word "alone" (*eva*) is used for the purpose of excluding anything more than that, since even one who maintains that ritual action preceded by knowledge requires the study of the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) has already accepted the necessity of such study. The meaning is as follows: because the study [of the Veda] is accompanied by its auxiliaries, and because the auxiliaries are the cause of the knowledge of the meaning, it is understood—without depending on Mīmāṃsā—that heaven and the like are the fruits of mere ritual action alone, that heaven and the like are perishable, and that the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*) yields imperishable fruit. The passage beginning with "of the meditation on Brahman" is intended as an illustration.

The particle *eva* in the phrase "it is indeed known" (*jñāyata eva*) indicates the acknowledgment of the existence of a knower; the sense is that the causal complex for knowledge (*jñānasāmagrī*) is established. To the question "What follows from this?", he says:

Regarding the word "immediately" (*anantaram*): the purpose of the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*) is indeed to establish the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) through the knowledge that the fruits of action are insignificant and unstable. However, since the desire for liberation is established by the knowledge that the fruits are insignificant and unstable even independently of that [inquiry into action], one should engage only in the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), as there is no further purpose for the inquiry into *dharma*. He refutes this with the words "In this way": "If you are satisfied merely by the cited statement, then [the answer is] 'of the whole'—the sense being that [this applies] to Brahman as well."

We have indeed cited Vedic statements (*vedāntavākya*) with clear meanings, and their meaning is understood even without depending upon *mīmāṃsā*; therefore, the meaning is that the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken for the sake of attaining knowledge of the fruit that is infinite and eternal. "True" (*satyam*) is used in the sense of partial acceptance; there is acceptance regarding the superficial appearance (*āpātapratīti*), but non-acceptance regarding independence from the inquiry into Brahman. "Superficial" (*āpāta*): superficial appearance is a cognition accompanied by doubt and error, which consists merely in the cessation of ignorance.

Furthermore, doubt and misconception may arise because the true nature of reality is difficult to ascertain through words such as *sat*, *brahman*, *ātman*, *ākāśa*, *prāṇa*, and *vaiśvānara* found in causal statements; because the impermanence of the self and so forth is perceived in passages such as "This mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them," and "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent"; and because small and unstable fruits are understood from statements such as "He becomes possessed of food, an eater of food, and great with offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge."

The meaning is as follows: since those two [doubt and error] are not removed by the mere study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga-adhyayana*), and because their exclusion is the result of sentences supported by reasoning (*nyāya*), the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) must be undertaken. This implies that you have proceeded even after considering other unquoted passages. Likewise, it means that one who recognizes that the removal of doubt and error is required here as well, should look at the unquoted passages from that very perspective.

"Indeed, the merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices becomes inexhaustible. "By means of the Full Oblation (Pūrṇāhuti), one attains all desires; the performer of the Animal Sacrifice (Paśubandha) conquers all worlds. "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal; indeed, he who piles the Nāciketa fire wins an infinite, shoreless, and inexhaustible world; his sacrifices and meritorious works (iṣṭāpūrte) are never exhausted."

For sentences such as, "He who piles the *Nāciketa* fire," are seen to be similar to those stating the fruits of the knowledge of Brahman, such as, "He attains immortality," "He enjoys all desires," and "Moving through these worlds at will, assuming forms at will. Therefore, because there is an abundance of doubt and misconception regarding these unquoted passages—just as there is with the Upaniṣadic statements—an inquiry into karma must be undertaken to dispel them; this is the meaning. Thus, the dependence on the knowledge of karma for the sake of abandoning [the world] has been shown by way of its fruit.

Now, in order to show that there is a necessary dependence on both action and knowledge for the sake of attaining one's true nature (*svarūpa*) and for the purpose of taking up [the means], he introduces the opponent’s position—characterized by the claim that action is necessarily required by one seeking liberation—with the words, "But surely... The first *eva* (only) is intended to exclude the possibility that this necessary requirement applies to anything other than what is intended; the second *eva*, however, serves to preclude the idea that something not necessarily required could have preceded [knowledge]. To the question "What of it?", he replies, "Not in dharma..."; and to the question "Why?", he says, "Having studied..."

The meaning is this: for all those who are qualified for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), [the inquiry into action] is necessarily required—that is, invariably required. However, for one who studies only the Vedāntas, there would arise therein both a superficial understanding (*apātapratīti*) and a desire to know (*bubhutsā*); because such a person lacks a superficial understanding regarding the subject matter of ritual action (*karma*), there is no necessary requirement for an inquiry into action.

Alternatively, if even for one who has studied the entire Veda, a desire for inquiry arises specifically regarding the Vedānta texts due to the force of merit from previous births, then for him there is no dependence upon an inquiry into ritual action (*karma*); in that case, the phrase "one who has studied the Vedānta" is intended to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), not to exclude connection with something else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). The meaning is that because he has studied the entire Veda, the portion consisting of the Vedānta—which was required—is necessarily already studied as well.

Thus, having refuted the necessity of knowing ritual action even for the purpose of its abandonment, he raises the objection—"karmāṅga..."—to demonstrate that it need not be known even for the purpose of its adoption, by questioning whether there is still a requirement for the inquiry into ritual action even for one who desires to know only the Vedānta. A single *sāman* has five parts, which are named *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratihāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*. These parts are designated by the term *bhakti*.

Among those five types of devotion (*bhakti*), the *prastāva* is indeed chanted preceded by the *hiṅkāra*, and the *udgītha* is chanted preceded by the *praṇava*. In that regard, the meditation on the fivefold *sāman* is enjoined in some places, such as: "One should meditate on the fivefold *sāman* in the worlds. In other places, the meditation on each individual part among the five parts of the *sāman* is enjoined; therein, the meditation on the *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*, is enjoined: "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*. These [meditations] have as their objects the *udgītha* and so forth, which are constituent parts of the ritual action, and they are based upon the constituent parts of the ritual action.

The proposition is that it is impossible for one who has not mastered the ritual action (*karman*) to perform the contemplation (*cintana*) of the *udgītha* and other such meditations. The qualifying phrase "resting upon the members of ritual action" contains the reason. If it were stated simply that "the meditations rest upon the *udgītha* and other members of ritual action," the word *udgītha* would be redundant within the reason, and it would follow that the subject (*pakṣa*) consists of meditations in general; therefore, the formulation of the statement exactly as given is appropriate.

The meaning is: "If it is argued that reflection on meditations concerning the *udgītha* and so forth is impossible before the ritual action has been mastered, and therefore the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) must be disregarded," he refutes this with reproach by saying, "One who is ignorant. Regarding the point that knowledge is what is primarily set forth in the scripture, he says, "In this [scripture]. "Difference" (*bheda*) consists of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing; "manifoldness" (*vaividhya*) is the multiplicity of its sub-divisions; thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause for perceiving such diverse differences.

The word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to avoid the fallacy of infinite regress regarding the cause of that [ignorance]. Thus, worldly suffering (*sāṃsārika-duḥkha*) consists precisely of birth, old age, death, and so forth, caused by the perception of difference created by ignorance; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of hell, dwelling in the womb, and other such states is intended. "Worldly" (*sāṃsārika*) means arising from *saṃsāra*, which is the connection with primordial nature (*prakṛti*); it is described as being of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha-rūpa*) in order to indicate that it must be eliminated. The word "ocean" (*sāgara*) refers to its boundlessness. [This refers to] "of one who is submerged."

The nature of the qualified seeker (*adhikārin*) has been stated as being the cause for the expectation of the means to the cessation of suffering. He states the purpose (*prayojana*) with the word "complete" (*nikhila*). False knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) is erroneous cognition, based on the application [in the *Yogasūtra*]: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of each preceding one. And erroneous cognition is the perception of difference.

Alternatively, "false knowledge" (*mithyājñāna*) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*) which is itself false; the word "false" (*mithyā*) is used for the purpose of indicating that it is to be sublated by knowledge. The intention is that liberation (*mokṣa*) consists precisely in the eradication of that [ignorance]. To the question of what the means to that [liberation] is, he says: "the realization of the oneness of the Self" (*ātmaikatvavijñāna*).

For it is the knowledge of the true nature of the rope that removes the delusion, not any particular action; likewise, since the perception of difference is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), the knowledge of unity alone is its remover. Thus, the meaning is that the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedānta texts lies precisely therein. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Of this [action], indeed... It is of no use anywhere; the meaning is that it is of no use either in the production of the nature of knowledge, in the production of its fruit, or in favoring the means for the production of knowledge.

It is not merely that there is a lack of utility; rather, he states [the opposite] with the words "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*), implying that such practices produce the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality. Nevertheless, since these meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth are studied in the Upaniṣads and are being investigated in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, one might argue that the meditation on the *udgītha* is required for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā*), and thus the inquiry into the *udgītha* is directly relevant. To this, he replies with the words "from the *udgītha* etc. [meaning they are not directly connected]. If that is so, how can there be study of them in the Upaniṣads and an inquiry into them in the investigation of Brahman? To this, he replies: "because there is no difference in their nature as knowledge" (*jñāna-rūpatvāviśeṣāt*).

The meaning is that [the status of being a *pūrvavṛtta*] is established because of the commonality of having the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpa*) and residing in the intellect (*buddhisthatā*), and not because of its utility for the primary subject matter. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "But that... (*sa tu*). The two occurrences of the word "but" (*tu*) serve to exclude two possible doubts. He concludes that only that which is useful for the primary subject matter to be expounded possesses the status of being a *pūrvavṛtta*. "Therefore" (*ataḥ*)—the sense is that it is something other than the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*). Connection by virtue of utility for the primary subject matter is "direct connection" (*sākṣātsaṅgati*).

Because there is some form of similarity in some respect, the presence [of the topic] in the mind constitutes a contextual connection (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, it is not logical that the inquiry into ritual action—which is required for the contemplations on the *udgītha* and so forth mentioned contextually, yet is incompatible with the primary subject matter—should be considered what has preceded [the Upaniṣads]. Rather, it is stated that it is appropriate to declare as "what has preceded" only that which is required by the knowledge of the oneness of the Self, which is the primary thing to be established.

Here the followers of Bhāskara object, saying "Certainly" (*bāḍham*). "Certainly" is used here as a partial admission. The admission concerns only this much: that whatever is the primary scripture, its prerequisite alone is the previously established subject. The proposition is "and that which is required by it. The intention of the particle *eva* (only) is that precisely what you said was not required is, in fact, what is required. To the question "Why?", he says: "from [the perspective of] combined with ritual action" (*karma-samuccitāt*). The word "combined" (*samuccita*) refers merely to concomitance (*sāhitya*), not to a logical conjunction (*samuccaya*).

In the passage, "Because [the scriptures] teach them together as 'our own knowledge' and 'knowledge of the Self,'" the phrase "by means of action and knowledge" (*karmajñānābhyām*) is not used; rather, it is specified through a qualifier-qualified relationship as "from knowledge conjoined with action" (*karmasamuccitāt jñānāt*). Therefore, the primacy of knowledge is understood; the meaning is "from knowledge that has action as its auxiliary. And the scriptural text intended here is "By sacrifice, by charity," and so forth.

The author shows the intention of the Sūtrakāra regarding the fact that ritual action (*karman*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to knowledge (*vidyā*) by stating "and he will say. The particle *ca* is used here as a conjunction to collect the supporting arguments.
