[Objection: Granted that the performance of ritual action is required as an auxiliary; however, how can its knowledge be considered prior? Why could the knowledge of ritual action not be subsequent to the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*)? To this, he replies: "And because it is required. Just like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, what is intended is that there is a requirement for an auxiliary in the form of a support for the production of the fruit at the time when the instrument (*karaṇa*), having been accomplished, is functioning.

In the fourth quarter of the third chapter, with the intention of defining the distinction between what rites are to be performed and what are not for those established in the knowledge of Brahman—whether they be those who have returned home after completing their studies, those who have not yet taken a wife, those whose wives have died, and others belonging to specific stages of life (āśrama)—it was stated: "By whom is there a combination [of action and knowledge], and by whom not? Alternatively, the meaning is that the distinction is not known as to whether there is a combination of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, but not of optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*niṣiddha*) ones.

This is the meaning: the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words. In a sentence such as "By sacrifice, by charity," since acts such as sacrifice constitute the word-meanings (*padārtha*), and because the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by the knowledge of the word-meanings, the investigation of sacrificial acts and the like must occur first. Indeed, the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence such as "One threshes rice" is not possible without the knowledge of the word-meanings such as rice; for the meaning of a sentence consists in the relation between word-meanings.

Now, an objection: since one first understands the sentence-meaning—such as the bringing of a cow—from a sentence like "Bring the cow" through the process of learning (vyutpatti), and only subsequently grasps the meanings of the individual words via the method of insertion and deletion (āvāpodvāpa), it follows that there is no rule that the knowledge of the sentence-meaning must be preceded by the knowledge of the word-meanings.

It is said: in the case of the comprehension of meaning from a word whose conventional usage is already mastered (*vyutpanna*), the cognition of the sentence-meaning is everywhere preceded by the cognition of the word-meanings. However, at the stage of learning the usage (*vyutpatti-daśā*), the understanding of the sentence-meaning may first occur through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or through another word, but not from that very same word, because it is incapable of producing cognition as long as its relationship [to the meaning] has not been grasped. Furthermore, even during the process of learning, there is no rule that the cognition of the sentence-meaning must necessarily precede [the cognition of the word-meanings].

This is because the first acquisition of meaning (*vyutpatti*) is observed for words such as "mother," "father," and "uncle" precisely when they are not yet connected with other words; furthermore, in the process of acquiring the meaning that "this word has this meaning," there is no prior existence of knowledge regarding the meaning of a sentence.

Furthermore, it is not possible to derive the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) of words such as "sacrifice" (*yajña*) within this very sentence; for since the meaning of the sentence—consisting in the accomplishment of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)—is not perceptible, linguistic usage cannot be established here, just as it is not established in cases such as "bringing a cow. Therefore, commentators have explained that the statement beginning with "Certainly" (*bāḍham*) is intended as an objection from the Siddhāntin (the proponent of the final view), based on the principle that "knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is preceded by knowledge of the meanings of its constituent words. Even in that case, the relationship between word-meaning and sentence-meaning is intended to be specified as being caused by a particular sequence.

Furthermore, the intention is this: since what is required as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) is intended to be that which is required for the sake of the primary object (*cetya*), and since ritual actions (*karman*) are auxiliaries to knowledge (*jñāna*) by virtue of being its producers, and because there is a rule of temporal sequence between the producer and the produced, it is logical that the two investigations (*vicāra*)—which are themselves auxiliary to those two subjects, namely ritual action and knowledge—must also follow that same order, given that their objects stand in a prior-posterior relationship.

For it is established by logic that a subordinate element must conform to the sequence of its principal; as for instance, in the case of the statement, "There are two Sārasvata oblations," although the two Sārasvata oblations arise simultaneously, it is determined that the performance of their constituent parts must follow that same sequence, since—according to the order of the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* mantras—it follows that the sacrifice to Sarasvatī occurs first and the sacrifice to Sarasvant occurs later.

In both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*), there is precisely a disparity in the reasons that determine the sequence of the two principal elements (*śeṣin*); for once their sequence is determined, the fact that the subordinate element (*śeṣa*) conforms to the sequence of the principal element is the same in that case as it is here.

Furthermore, since meditation (*upāsana*) alone is subordinate to inquiry (*vicāra*), one should not argue that the consideration of meditation performed in the third chapter must necessarily follow the consideration of ritual action (*karma-vicāra*). For if that were so, the entire *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* would have to follow the consideration of ritual action, because the consideration of the subject matter of knowledge (*vidyā*) and its fruits is also required by it. He concludes with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the passage beginning with "certainly" (*bāḍham*) is intended as a rebuttal by the proponent (*siddhāntin*), it is more appropriate to interpret it as referring to the view of Bhāskara.

Since this passage—"from knowledge accumulated through action, liberation is heard"—is found in Bhāskara’s commentary (*bhāṣya*), and since the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*) is accepted by him, there is no contradiction in citing the sūtra concerning that subject; furthermore, because it is recognized both verbally and semantically, and because the objection of the Siddhāntin is also included therein, the traditional interpretation is that an onlooker raises the objection beginning with "Certainly," while relying upon the positions of both Bhāskara and Yādavaprakāśa.

The construction here is as follows: in the phrase "from [knowledge] accumulated with action," an equal conjunction (*samasamuccaya*) is intended. The designation "from knowledge accumulated with action" is made by way of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), based on the widespread renown of knowledge as a means to liberation. This is supported by such scriptural passages as, "Knowledge and ignorance... In this statement, the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) denotes that karma which opposes the attainment of the goal. Yādavaprakāśa himself accepts two things to be accomplished—namely, the cessation of obstacles and the attainment of Brahman—and likewise two means to accomplish them, namely, action and knowledge respectively.

Therefore, their interpretation of the passage "Knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*) is that the first half refers to the duality of the means (*sādhana*), while the second half refers to the duality of the ends (*sādhya*). The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and he will state" (*vakṣyati ca*) serves to aggregate the objects to be established; its meaning is that he will also state [their] status as auxiliary factors (*aṅgabhāva*). For they accept that after the arising of knowledge, action functions to remove the obstacles to attaining Brahman, whereas prior to the arising of knowledge, action possesses the status of an auxiliary factor by virtue of being the producer of that knowledge.

They take up the subsequent sūtra, "sarvāpekṣā," as being concerned with the relationship between the auxiliary and the principal (aṅga-aṅgibhāva), and the sūtra "sahakāritvena ca" as establishing an equal conjunction; such indeed is their system of interpretation.

Although examples for both the state of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*) and for conjunction (*samuccaya*) should have been cited from scripture (*śruti*), sentence (*vākya*), and aphorism (*sūtra*), for the sake of brevity, scripture is cited for conjunction and the aphorism is cited for the state of being an auxiliary. By employing an aphorism concerning a sentence that establishes the state of being an auxiliary, the view of Bhāskara is also supported; thus, in both ways, the non-dependence upon ritual action is demonstrated. He asks, "What follows from this? and says: "And when it is required. This means required either as being equally primary or as an auxiliary. Everything else is as before.

Although the status of the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) as a prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*) is not accepted in the view of Yādavaprakāśa, nevertheless, since he has established that ritual action is required either through its combination [with knowledge] or as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), the critic—who stands on the sidelines and relies upon both systems—has raised the objection by way of establishing its status as a prerequisite based on that much alone; thus, there is no contradiction with the concluding section of the text.

The former teachers have provided this resolution: that the objection was raised by relying on both views, because it is natural for the word "combination" (*samuccaya*) to be construed as the primary element, because the subsequent sūtra treats it as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), and because the duality of the probandum and the duality of the means of proof will be refuted immediately thereafter.

To this, he replies: "This is not correct. For the necessity of knowing ritual actions for the purpose of their abandonment was already refuted previously, because it was stated that one who studies only the Vedānta lacks even a superficial understanding of the subject matter of rituals, and thus there is no dependence on ritual action; and furthermore, because it was stated that for one who desires to understand the Vedānta solely through the power of past merit, there is no requirement for the knowledge of rituals.

Here, wishing to refute the necessity of knowing action for the sake of appropriation (*upādāna*), [the author] first refutes the first type of appropriation—in order to establish the equality of the two types of appropriation through both equal conjunction and the status of being auxiliary members—by rejecting the duality of the means and the duality of the objects to be accomplished with the two statements beginning with "In all particulars... and so forth.

If the passage beginning with "yathā bāḍham" is intended as a refutation according to either the view of Bhāskara or the Siddhāntin's own view, then it must be interpreted as follows: wishing to reject the dependence on *karma* in every possible way conceived in the *pūrvapakṣa*, [the author] intends a dilemma—asking whether you mean a complete conjunction (*samasamuccaya*) or a state of being an auxiliary (*aṅgabhāva*)—and thus first refutes the position of complete conjunction.

"All particularities" (*sakalaviśe�sheṣāḥ*) refers to particularities in the form of exclusions and inclusions—both within themselves and with respect to similar and dissimilar classes. The sense is that [Brahman] is their "antidote," meaning it is that which causes them to cease, just as the nature of a rope is the antidote for the forms of a snake and so forth. By the term "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*), the suffix *-mātra* excludes both the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and the state of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).

Alternatively, by the term "opposed to all particularities" (sakalaviśeṣapratyanīka), it is intended that [Brahman] is opposed to the distinctions between its own kind and other kinds; by the word "mere consciousness" (cinmātra), the suffix -mātra signifies its freedom from internal differentiation; and by the word "opposed" (pratyanīka), its eternal unfitness [for such distinctions] is intended. For a fragment of mother-of-pearl can never be fit for a connection with the nature of silver; indeed, it is precisely because of this eternal unfitness that the cognition of mother-of-pearl sublates the [erroneous] cognition of silver, and it is through the knowledge of Brahman alone that ignorance is removed.

The point is that the cessation of the [illusory] state of being a snake occurs solely from the knowledge of the rope, and not through action. Thus, the duality of means has been refuted. To the objection that there exists a duality of goals (*sādhyadvitva*), he refutes the duality of goals by stating: "For liberation consists in the cessation of ignorance. Since Brahman is eternally attained, it is only the removal of the obstruction that is to be accomplished, not the attainment of Brahman itself.

The intention of the word *hi* is as follows: that very cessation of bondage which you have stated to be accomplished through action is itself known from the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras to be accomplished through knowledge, as in "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death" and "Having known God, one is released from all sins. There is an alternative reading: *pāśaiḥ* (by bonds).

"Having realized That, one is liberated from the jaws of death; and his karmas are exhausted when That, the higher and the lower, is seen. "In this very way, evil karma does not cling to one who knows thus. "The fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes in that manner. "Upon the attainment of That, there is the destruction of both subsequent and prior sins"—by such statements as these, it is stated through these two sets of passages that there is no duality of the goal and the means.

"Let liberation be simply the cessation of ignorance; what then follows regarding the independence from ritual action? To this, he says: "varṇāśrama... By this term, the previously mentioned dependence of ritual action upon distinctions is elucidated. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), prohibited acts and expiatory rites are intended. By the word "ananta" (endless), the multiplicity of castes and other categories is indicated. "Vikalpa" means distinction.

The phrase "from the cessation of ignorance, which consists in the cessation of all perceptions of difference" means that the result of the cessation of root-ignorance is indeed the cessation of the perception of difference; therefore, the meaning is that the cessation of the perception of difference is included within the cessation of ignorance. How could it be a means? Not at all—this is the sense. This is because of the rule: "For logic has no power when there is a contradiction with [authoritative] scripture."

In response to the doubt that the fact of action being disregarded—which is established by scripture—should not be sublated, [the author] shows its conformity with scripture through the aforementioned reasoning, stating "and the scriptures. The sense of the word "and" (ca) is that there is not only reasoning, but also scriptural support for it. Previously, the contradiction was stated on the basis of duality; here, however, the contradiction is shown by way of another argument, namely, the impermanence of the fruits [of action].

The phrase "by virtue of having impermanent results" means: how can action, which yields impermanent results, be the means for liberation, which has a permanent result? By the word "scriptures" (*śruti*), the author intends to show that multiple statements carry more weight than a single one. By the word "showing," he indicates that those passages with clear meaning prevail over those with obscure meaning. The point is this: if liberation were achieved through action—as in the passage "it is indeed finite"—then liberation would be impermanent; conversely, if it were permanent, action could not be its means, because action is invariably restricted to yielding finite results.

By this statement, the impermanence of actions is declared. By the phrase "that indeed," it is stated that the destruction of action occurs through its fruit. The preceding statement is for the purpose of making known the finitude of all actions performed over many periods of time; for it is heard in scripture: "Whatever one offers in this world, sacrifices, or performs austerity for many thousands of years—that becomes merely finite for him. For this very reason, the statement "The knower of Brahman attains [the Supreme]" is presented first, as a doctrine of independence from action.

The fact that knowledge is the means to liberation has been stated. To negate the distinction between the goal to be attained and the attainer, the text "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" is cited. By the words "Him alone," it is made known that the fruit of knowledge is the cessation of obstacles. Furthermore, by this, the negation of ritual action and other means—apart from knowledge—as being the path is established, for the immediately following sentence is: "There is no other path."

Thus, by citing numerous passages with clear meanings supported by sound reasoning that establish knowledge alone as the means to liberation, it is shown that the Śruti cited by the opponent—namely, "Knowledge and ignorance"—which purports to teach their equal conjunction, does not have that meaning. This is because that [particular] Śruti passage is singular, its meaning is not explicit, and it is devoid of supporting reasoning; therefore, it must be interpreted in a way that does not contradict other Śruti texts. In this manner, both scriptural authorities and logical arguments have been demonstrated to prove that knowledge alone is the means to liberation.

Now, with the words "And even though" (*yadapi ca*) and so forth, [the author] sets aside the view that the scriptural injunctions regarding sacrifice and the like are intended merely to indicate a dependence upon ritual action (*karma*). The word "even" (*api*) indicates that ritual action is accepted by all three—the Siddhāntin, Bhāskara, and Yādavaprakāśa—and thus suggests its primary status. The word "and" (*ca*) intends a conjunction, signifying that once the statement favoring conjunction has been interpreted in accordance with other scriptural passages, the scriptural injunction regarding sacrifice and the like must also be so interpreted. Alternatively, *apica* may be treated as an indivisible compound; in that case, it likewise intends conjunction in the manner described above.

As for what was stated, "Knowledge requires rituals such as sacrifice," the meaning of this formulation is that the action required by knowledge is spoken of in terms of their conjunction (*samuccaya*). There is a contradiction in reality: [rituals] produce the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality and possess impermanent fruits. This is established by examining the literal words of the scripture and determining the meaning of the suffix *san*. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates conjunction. He explains the manner in which [rituals] are useful for the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) with the words "of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*), etc. It is not [useful] for the production of the fruit, nor for the production of liberation (*mokṣa*).

For the Śruti says, "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting, the Brāhmaṇas seek to know [Brahman]," but the sense is not that they are liberated. To the question of how this is understood from a close examination of the words, he says: "Because of the hearing of the term 'seeking to know' (vividiṣanti). Thus, by examining the scriptural texts on sacrifice and so forth, the conjunction of knowledge and action is refuted; and since the word "fruit" (phala) naturally refers to liberation, the interpretation has been made in this way, rather than [referring] to the production of a [worldly] result.

Alternatively, the meaning is that by the phrase "knowledge requiring rites such as sacrifice," it is implied that the action which was previously mentioned has been set aside as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*). The sense is: "neither for the production of the fruit, nor for the production of knowledge. For, in relation to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), knowledge is the fruit; everything else is as explained before. In this interpretation, there is a natural consistency in the designation "knowledge requiring rites such as sacrifice," because this designation serves to recall the sūtra concerning the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that the action mentioned as an auxiliary (*aṅga*)—which, like the *prayāja* offerings, assists the instrument (*karaṇa*) once it has been produced at the time of the arising of the fruit—is not employed [in the production of liberation]. That is to say, it is not employed either in the arising of the fruit or in the arising of liberation; the meaning is that it is not employed by way of assisting the knowledge (*vidyā*) which serves as the instrument.

In this interpretation, there is a natural consistency in both the instruction that recalls the aphorism on the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) and the instruction regarding the arising of the fruit. Regarding the statement "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣantaḥ*), which is like saying "one who desires to conquer with a sword," there might be a doubt that sacrifices and the like could merely serve as a means for knowledge. To address the objection that it would be untenable for ritual action to be the cause for the arising of knowledge, its status as a necessary concomitant (*itikartavyatā*), or its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*), he says in the two sentences beginning with "In the case of the desire to know" (*vividiṣāyām*).

In this context, by means of the statement beginning with "in the desire to know" (*vividiṣā*), he first sets aside the status of [knowledge] as having a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) through either a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) with tranquility (*śama*) and the other qualities. By the two uses of the particle *eva*, the combination and the option of ritual action (*karman*) are excluded; for, since tranquility and the rest consist in the cessation of the activity of the senses, while sacrifices and other rituals consist in the engagement in such activity, they are mutually contradictory. With the intention that a combination is therefore not tenable, he says: "of tranquility and the rest alone."

For there is an option between two things of equal strength; however, because the realization of the Self through tranquility (*śama*) and so forth is quickly understood as being a direct means toward the vision of the Self—independently of any logical necessity—it possesses greater force.

Regarding the phrase "those who desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*): although sacrifices and other rites are naturally understood as means for achieving that desire, their status as means for attaining knowledge is established only after the natural sense [of the injunction] has been set aside. This is because it depends upon reasoning in the form of considering analogies such as "one desires to kill with a sword," whereby the fact that ritual action is a means to knowledge is apprehended only with delay. Consequently, because it is weak, there can be no option [between knowledge and action]. With this intention, he says: "The Śruti itself says... [referring to the subsequent passage].

Nevertheless, since ritual action (*karman*) is required for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), it is useful for knowledge; so why should this be abandoned while tranquility (*śama*) and the like are adopted? To address this doubt, he states the difference between ritual action and tranquility and so forth by saying, "the state of being an internal means" (*antaraṅgopāyatām*). That it is an internal means is clear from the phrase, "having become [so], one should see. For ritual action is useful prior to the desire to know, whereas tranquility and the like are useful even afterwards; with this intention, he said, "once [the desire] has arisen" (*jātāyām*).

He states that action also lacks the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) with respect to knowledge, saying "tadevam" (thus, in this way). Having raised the objection that its status as an instrument might be possible, it is refuted; however, this is not because it has been accepted [as an instrument], for the mind, when purified, is indeed the instrument, according to the scriptural text: "But with a purified mind. That [instrumentality] [is denied] due to the reasons already stated.

Since it is untenable for [the two] to constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) either by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*) or option (*vikalpa*), the term "without aiming at a result" (*anabhisaṃhitaphala*) is used to avoid the inconsistency of ritual action—which is a means to heaven and so forth—being a means to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). Furthermore, because the desire to know itself is a result insofar as it is to be accomplished by that [action], the phrase "in a specific result" is stated to exclude the possibility that this [desire to know] might also be something not aimed at. Finally, the word "in another birth" (*janmāntara*) is used to dispel the doubt that there might still be a requirement for knowledge of ritual action even now, for the sake of performing it in order to achieve the desire to know.

The word "hundred" (*śata*) is intended to dispel the doubt that [the practice] must be performed even now, based on the statement "perfected through many births" (*anekajanmasaṃsiddha*). For a cause is to be inferred from its effect; the sense is that since the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is not seen to arise at present, one must infer the performance of [such practice] over a hundred previous births. By that action, for one whose impurities (*kaṣāya*) have been rubbed away and whose sins have been destroyed—according to the Smṛti: "Actions serve to ripen the impurities, but knowledge is the supreme goal; when the impurities have been ripened by actions, then knowledge arises."*

Thus, once the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has arisen, he states the means for the production of knowledge: the sentence beginning with "Being alone" (*sadeva*) is the causal statement; the sentence "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) is the purificatory statement; the sentence beginning with "partless" (*niṣkalam*) is employed to clarify the exclusions resulting from the sentence concerning Truth, Knowledge, and so forth; and the sentence "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*) is the statement of identity.

He shows that the sentence expressing identity, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), is endowed with the sixfold marks of intentionality, such as *upakrama* (introductory context) and so forth. In this sentence, the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is heard; the statement "this self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*) is intended to make known that "the identity is heard in its entirety. Such sentences are the instrument for the arising of knowledge, not ritual action—this is the meaning. Anticipating the objection that if the knowledge produced by the sentence were to remove ignorance (*avidyā*), then the injunctions for meditation preceded by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth would be useless, he says: "of the sentence-meaning" (*vākyārtha*).

The word *ca* (and) serves to exclude doubt. He states their essential nature: "Hearing (*śravaṇa*) is that which... [referring to] those things capable of producing the realization of the meaning of the sentences. For it has been stated [that knowledge arises] "from the knowledge produced by the sentence. [Objection: Since this is opposed to the knowledge of the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva-vidyā*), how can hearing and the other means be useful for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence? To this he says: "By hearing and the rest" (*śravaṇādibhiḥ*). The meaning is that their utility consists in the removal of obstacles to the arising of the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.

"For this reason"—that is to say, for the reasons that the relationship of principal and subordinate between knowledge and action (jñāna-karma-samuccaya) is untenable. Such [knowledge], which is the commencement of the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence independent of action for the cessation of bondage—and not merely an incidental matter—is "necessarily required," meaning it is invariably required. To the question "What is required? he says: "And that. To the question "Why is this required? he says: "Without this," because the desire to know (jijñāsā) would be untenable, and thus inquiry (vicāra) would be untenable.

He establishes the impossibility [of liberation] by means of the nature of things (*arthasvabhāva*). What is this "nature of things"? It is as follows: from the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, there arises detachment from the enjoyment of the transient fruits of saṃsāra and a desire for the eternal human goal; from that, there is engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; and the perfection of tranquility (*śama*) and other qualities is conducive to that [engagement] by being the cause of one-pointedness of mind. Thus, the intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that [liberation] occurs solely from this aforementioned nature of things.

That knowledge alone is the means and that action is not required has indeed been stated previously on the basis of the nature of the matter (*arthasvabhāvāt*). Alternatively, the phrase "because without this [knowledge], the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is untenable" means "on the basis of the nature of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth. [An objection: Let it be that tranquility and so forth constitute the prior requirement; however, action might also be a prior requirement. To this he says: "precisely on the basis of the nature of the matter."

The meaning of the first *evakāra* (the particle "only") is that by whatever essential nature of the object [X] there is the state of being previously occurred for tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, by that very same essential nature of the object there is the negation of the state of being previously occurred for anything else. The second *evakāra* is for the purpose of excluding any other prior occurrence.

Here, by the term "the nature of the object" (*arthasvabhāva*), the nature of the objects such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth is stated; what is intended is the nature of the object that is knowledge (*jñāna*) and the nature of the object that is action (*karman*). Because knowledge has the nature of being a means independent of action, and because action—by virtue of its dependence on differentiation—possesses a contradictory nature, and because tranquility and the rest have the nature of cessation and are thus not opposed in nature to action which is of the nature of engagement, it is thereby stated that only the fourfold qualification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) is the prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*), and nothing else.

"It is known that this alone is the antecedent" (*idameva pūrvavṛttam iti jñāyate*): here, the words *idam* and *eva* serve to exclude non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and to exclude connection with something else (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*). For the word *idam* refers to the fourfold means (*sādhana*) as being the antecedent; the particle *eva* serves to exclude other [means]; and because of the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, there is the exclusion of non-connection with them. Therefore, due to the inherent nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*), there is the exclusion of connection with anything else.

If Brahman is devoid of all specific attributes (*sakalaviśeṣapratyanīka*), how does the activity of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) proceed? Or, how is ignorance (*avidyā*) removed by the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Saying (*vākya*) alone? By what means is the impurity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) [accounted for]? How is its purity brought about by ritual action (*karman*)? And how are these—the intrinsic natures of things that serve as the causes for excluding non-connection and excluding connection with others—possible? In response to this doubt, the author demonstrates the summarized meaning of what has been stated and dispels the doubts, beginning with the words "This has been said. Even though [Brahman] is devoid of all specific attributes, it is designated by the term "obscuring the nature of Brahman" (*brahmasvarūpācchādika*).

It has been stated that the perception of difference arises from the concealment of one's true nature (*svarūpa*). "Difference" refers to the distinction between the knower and the known, and so forth. The meaning is that it is precisely this non-ultimate perception of difference that is the root of bondage, not action (*karman*). The implication is that even action is rooted in delusion. Alternatively, the sense is that there is only the non-ultimate perception of difference; nothing at all is real. For if that were the case, there would be a dependence on action for bondage—namely, birth, old age, death, and so on.

The meaning is that bondage is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*) because it is an effect of the perception of difference rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), which itself is not ultimately real. To the question, "What follows from this regarding independence from action (*karmanairapekṣya*)?", he says: "And that [bondage]," etc. The intention of the particle *eva* ("only") is that the establishment of independence from action follows precisely from the aforementioned lack of ultimate reality; that is to say, by knowledge alone, and not by action. For the cessation of a non-ultimately real snake does not require the ritual of worshipping Vainateya (Garuḍa) apart from the knowledge of the rope.

Thus, the equal combination [of knowledge and action] has been refuted. He states that even with respect to knowledge, action is not a means [to liberation], saying: "And [it is] the remover. This means that the cognition which removes [ignorance) is produced by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For indeed, the cognition of mother-of-pearl produced by a valid means of knowledge is what removes [the misconception of] silver. Here, while tranquility (*śama*) and so forth constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the intention is that action cannot constitute the procedure because of contradiction. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). That is, of that [knowledge] which is independent of action. "Of this" (*etasya*) refers to that which has non-duality as its object.

Thus, although there is no difference between these two words in terms of denoting what is under discussion, it is appropriate that they refer to [the Self] as qualified by the distinctions of being far removed or being near. He states the reason for its having non-duality as its object: "of that which is produced by the sentence" (*vākyajanyasya*). The meaning is that because it is produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), it has non-duality as its object. Regarding liberation (*mokṣa*) as the effect: if so, where is its utility? To this he says: "in the desire to know" (*vividiṣāyām*). By the word "but" (*tu*), the status of being either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is excluded. As to how it is useful, he says:

And as for the phrase "sa ceti" (and he): by the words beginning with "pāpamūla" (root of sin), that which was stated previously—namely, "by way of the purification of the internal organ"—is explained. To the objection that the destruction of *rajas* and *tamas*, and so forth, is not heard in this sentence, he replies: "itīmam" (this [he], etc.). By the word "abhipretya" (intending), the removal of doubt is effected; "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). The meaning is: on account of reasons such as the contradiction of the actual state of things, and the impossibility of [the means] being either the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*).

"This utility" means utility consisting in the expulsion of *rajas* and *tamas* and the increase of *sattva*, that is, utility through a traditional succession. The connection of the words is as follows: "it has been stated that they 'desire to know'—this is what is meant. He concludes the subject at hand with the words, "Therefore, [there is no need] for the knowledge of ritual action. This means: therefore, because the knowledge of ritual action is not required either for the purpose of abandoning [ignorance] or for the purpose of acquiring [knowledge]. Here, the two summary verses stated by the commentators are cited: "Because of contradiction and lack of authority; because of the application [of action] to the purification of the mind; because of the scriptural statement that knowledge alone is the cause; and also because of [logical] capacity."

"Because it is traditionally taught that [knowledge] has tranquility and the other [limbs of yoga] as its constituent parts, there is no combination of knowledge and action; rather, the cognition born from the sentence, awakened by the sequence of hearing and so forth, is that which brings liberation. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the phrase "due to contradiction" (*virodhāt*), the intended contradiction consists in the fact that ritual actions have impermanent fruits and generate the latent impressions of duality; this is understood through the force of the context. Thus, the intended objective capacity (*vastusāmarthya*) is the nature of knowledge as being independent of ritual action in its capacity to remove objects of error.

He begins the final conclusion with the words, "To this it is replied. This means that the established doctrine (siddhānta) is stated in response to this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). He answers by accepting those points among those stated in the prima facie argument that are not contradictory, saying, "As for what was said": the meaning is that the cessation of ignorance is the cessation of the obstacle; the intended sense is the elimination of the duality between the goal and the means.

That which was described as the removal of obstacles achievable through action has its achievement through knowledge stated in such passages as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death," and so forth; however, the attainment of Brahman is self-established. By the two uses of the word "only" (eva), any other goal to be achieved and any other means are excluded.

Although there are two goals—the cessation of the undesirable and the attainment of the desirable—nevertheless, since the attainment of Brahman, which is the most desired object, is self-evident and does not require a separate means for its accomplishment, it is only the removal of obstacles that remains to be achieved. Once the obstacle has been removed, knowledge—which is by its very nature capable of directly perceiving everything—directly perceives all things, such as the essential nature, qualities, and majesty of Brahman.

Just as when a dam is broken, the water flows by itself and need not be led by anyone, so too—meaning that whereas the removal of a stone and the leveling of the path to reach it both require separate efforts—it is not like that here. Or rather, since non-existence is merely another state of being, the meaning is that the cessation of ignorance itself is the attainment of Brahman.

If it is granted that the duality of the probandum and the probans has been refuted, then [the opponent asks] what is the object of dispute; to this he replies with the words "ignorance" (*avidyā*), meaning that the dispute concerns the specific nature of the means of knowledge (*sādhana*). What is its form? Does it mean the knowledge described by you, which is unfit to be an auxiliary to ritual action (*karma-aṅga*), or does it mean the knowledge described by us, which is fit to be an auxiliary to ritual action? He explains what is intended by the phrase "of what form" with the words "what [is it] from the sentence," etc., stating both the opposing view and his own view, but not as an alternative within the opposing view itself.

First, the refutation of the opponent's position is undertaken, with the intention that the establishment of one's own position will follow later; thus he says, "not yet. However, the refutation is not applied to either the object of criticism or its head [the proponent]; why? To this he says, "of that" (*tasya*). The meaning is that even without a formal injunction, valid cognition is dependent on the object (*vastutantra*) and not dependent on the person (*puruṣatantra*), because it is impossible to make it, not make it, or make it otherwise; therefore, since it lacks dependence on the person, it cannot be subject to an injunction—this is what has been stated by those very [authorities].

It is from the sentence itself—specifically from sentences concerning the nature of Brahman—that there is such [understanding]. For a person possessing linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*), it is self-evident that a sentence supported by reasoning conveys its meaning; it is not dependent upon an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, it has been established that a person’s engagement in hearing such [sentences] arises solely from interest (*rāga*). Even if it were not due to interest, the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) alone would be the motivator for investigating all Vedic sentences already studied; thus, an injunction such as "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*) would be entirely redundant.

Furthermore, the fact that the knowledge of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) is a means to the highest good (*śreyas*) is not something non-worldly; therefore, it cannot be subject to an injunction in that capacity, because—just as in the case of the knowledge that sublates an error such as [the perception of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—it is accepted that the knowledge which sublates bondage has a perceptible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Consequently, an injunction would be redundant.

Therefore, [the author] stated, "even without its being enjoined," in order to demonstrate the contradiction with numerous Śrutis: namely, those Śrutis which teach that devotion takes the form of repeated realization and must be practiced as long as one lives—such as "Before I am released, I shall then attain [Brahman]"; those which teach that liberation occurs immediately after the fall of the body; and those which describe the path by speaking of the departure through a specific channel. Otherwise, these many Śrutis would result in being rendered purposeless.

Now, he demonstrates the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) by means of the phrase "by that much alone" (*tāvanmātreṇa*). Since that same portion exists even in what is more than that, the words "by that much alone" are stated for the purpose of excluding that [excess]. By stating these two refutations—namely, contradiction with many scriptures and contradiction with direct perception—the venerable Āpastamba also rejected the notion that the mere knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences is the means to liberation: "Just as the attainment of security once the intellect has awakened is contradicted by the scriptures; for if the attainment of security occurs when the intellect has awakened, then there is no suffering here [in this very life]."

"One should understand the other [cases] by this same explanation. By the use of the plural "scriptures" (*śāstraiḥ*), the contradiction with the many scriptural passages cited previously is intended. "Contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) refers to a negation by that which possesses greater force, and not a negation by that which is of equal force as in the case of *prakaraṇasama* (the counter-argument based on equal strength). It is stated as "contradictory" (*vipratiṣiddham*) with the intention of the maxim, "The majority shall be stronger," since the contradiction with many scriptures is more powerful.

Having restated the two-fold response given by others to this objection, he refutes it with the words "na ca vācyam" (nor should it be said). He states that there is no way to maintain the position that the sentence "na ca vācyam" does not produce the arising of knowledge at this time; thus he says "bhedeti. If it is argued that the arising of knowledge is indeed observed at this time, he says "avidyānivarttakam" (it is that which removes ignorance) as a rebuttal to that.

If it is argued that even later on, a clear knowledge capable of removing ignorance arises from the statement alone, then why does it not produce it right now? To this he replies with the words "in the latent impression of difference" (*bhedavāsanāyām*). The absence of obstacles is also included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*); therefore, because of a deficiency in the causal complex, the knowledge has not arisen. The meaning is that the injunctions for meditation and so forth serve as means for the removal of obstacles.

By this, the contradictions with scripture (*śāstra*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*) are resolved. To the objection that it is untenable for knowledge to arise even in Sanaka and others—who are renowned in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* as possessing superior knowledge—the author states another solution: "Even when [the body] has been born," etc. Because ignorance (*avidyā*) is one, and because the appearance of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-pratibhāsa*) is of the nature of a dream belonging to the single Brahman, it is said "of all. It does not lead to a fault; that is, its non-removability does not constitute a defect.

He provides an illustration for the case where delusion does not cease even upon the arising of knowledge with the words "in the case of the oneness of the moon. He says "even though it has not ceased" because, if the perception of difference were to persist, it would continue to be a cause of bondage. [The phrase] "with its root cut" means that its root, called ignorance (*avidyā*), has been severed, and thus it is incapable of producing effects.

The sense is as follows: just as a burnt cloth, although still perceived with its former configuration, becomes unfit for functions such as covering and gradually perishes; or just as a potter’s wheel, once the operator has ceased his exertion, continues to spin by itself for some time due to prior momentum and then gradually comes to rest—such is the case here. The word "here" (atra) is to be construed with the phrase "is not to be stated" (na vācyam).

First, he refutes the arising of knowledge with the words "satyām" (when it exists). The meaning is that a sentence supported by logic (*nyāya*) alone is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*); if it is argued that there exists a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of non-difference which acts as an obstacle, he replies with the words "satyām api" (even when it exists), meaning that the latent impression to be removed does not become an obstacle to the arising of the remover.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the sense faculty (*indriya*) is included. For example, in a cave long permeated by darkness, no contrary perception arises; yet once a lamp is lit, the darkness is destroyed instantly. Or, for instance, a person who has wandered for a long time thinking there is a snake in a certain place comes to know through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) that there is no snake there. Or, for example, having heard that a forest was not burned, one who has been wandering for a long time later goes there and, upon seeing signs such as embers, the knowledge arises that it was indeed burned. And likewise, after a long time...

The statement, "because the arising of subverting knowledge is observed through authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*), inferential marks (*liṅga*), and so forth," is made with the intention that just as when an object has been conceptually determined (*vāsita*) as a snake, the cognition of it as a rope arises suddenly through the operation of the senses immediately after one has approached it, so too is it here. For the Vedāntic sentence is the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*); therefore, authoritative instruction is mentioned first. Then, having restated the second [factor] which sustains the analogy, he refutes it with the words "even though" (*satyapi*). The word *mātrayā* means "to a small degree" (*alpa*).

The intended meaning is: "by you, who propound the falsity of everything other than Brahman. He explains the point indicated by the word "bhavatā" (by you) with the words "bhedeti" (regarding difference). The sense is that since even latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are equally false, it must necessarily be accepted that they too are sublated by knowledge.

Placing two doubts in his heart—namely, whether it is being said that even upon the arising of knowledge the latent impression (*vāsanā*) does not cease, or whether, even upon its cessation, the perception of difference occurs without a cause—he refutes the first [doubt] with the words "even upon the arising of knowledge. Since everything other than Brahman is false, the latent impression also ceases solely through the cessation of [false] knowledge; otherwise, for the reason that there is no distinction in their both being [objects of] knowledge, [the perception of difference] would not cease by any other means of reasoning. If it is argued that the latent impression perishes of its own accord, that is incorrect.

If by "by itself" one intends independence from subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), then it would follow that even a latent impression (*vāsanā*) which is perishable must be real. If, however, "perishes by itself" is intended to mean that it causes its own destruction by itself, this leads to a logical contradiction (*vadhāpāta*). Furthermore, even if [the impression] were perishable through the destruction of its final cause or the fruit, the consequence of its reality remains unavoidable; for the Vaiśeṣikas have described it as such in the case of karma, sound, and so forth, and they regard these as ultimately real.

Furthermore, just as in the case of one's own dreams and so forth, if the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is false, then its arising and its persistence are also false; consequently, its destruction too would be false. Therefore, the delusion regarding that destruction would persist once more, and thus there could be no cessation of delusion without remainder. Now, he dispels the second doubt: "the latent impression" means "having its root cut," that is, having its root known as the latent impression severed. "The talk of fools" means the consequence of the arising of an effect without a cause.

The point is this: if the perception of difference were causeless, then liberation would likewise be independent of knowledge; there would be comprehension of the meaning of the Vedic sentences even without hearing them and so forth; the delusion of the world would occur even without ignorance; and ignorance itself would produce its effects even without a substratum. Now, one might ask: "In that case, why does the perception of two moons not cease even when the subverting knowledge is present? To this he says, "dvicandra... (regarding the double moon). The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction from the intended meaning [of the previous argument].

The sense is that even when a sublater (*bādhaka*) is present, and even when the knowledge of that [sublater] is present, the defect such as *timira* (ophthalmia) remains ultimately real because it is not sublated by that knowledge. That ultimate reality of the defect must be admitted by the opponent even in a conventional sense (*vyāvahārikatayā*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that after the instruction of a reliable person, the conventional usage of the "rope-snake" would cease once the defect is gone, and similarly, after the statement "it is false," the conventional usage of the "double moon" and so forth would cease due to the removal of the defect. Therefore, because the defect continues to exist, the delusion of difference possesses a basis (*sabhūlatvam*).

By this, two objections—the existence of the sublated object in the presence of the sublator, and the production of an effect from a non-existent cause—are refuted in the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). However, in the view of the opponent (*paramata*), those two objections remain; therefore, he says "prabala" (powerful) to address the objection that [teachings such as] "this is a snake" would be useless. In relation to a person who has the delusion that a rope is a snake, the cessation of effects such as fear is stated to be the result.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [actions such as] driving away [the cause] and so forth are included. Furthermore, in the case of the cognition of two moons, the cessation of the awareness that one's own sense organs are unimpaired and the application of medicines and the like are the results. In cases such as the illusions of a magician, although there is in reality a state of error due to the predominance of the cause of error, there might be an obstruction to the ascertainment that the object is unreal; therefore, the term "stronger means of knowledge" (*prabala-pramāṇa*) is used for the purpose of excluding that [obstruction]. Thus, even while the appearance persists, it functions by way of the ascertainment that the object lacks reality.

The meaning is that authoritative instruction (āptopadeśa) is the cause for the cessation of fear and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is the cause for the cessation of fear and so forth by means of the direct perception of the true nature of reality through its correct engagement. The word "tu" (but/however) serves to exclude doubt. Since the position that knowledge does not arise [from scripture] is widely favored, he refutes it by looking back like a lion (siṃhāvalokitakena), beginning with "apica" (furthermore): for the negation of difference occurs through a perceptible means, as in the case of [knowing] "this is a rope, not a snake"; if it were by way of an imperceptible means, it would entail the consequence that difference is real.

Therefore, the meaning is that the removal of a vast latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality by a very slight latent impression of non-duality is untenable. Now, one might object: if [the impression] is to be removed through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), then it is not undesirable for the object to be removed to be real; for we admit the reality of a latent impression during the state of worldly transaction, just as a snake [is admitted as real] until it is removed by meditation. But once knowledge has arisen, its arising, its persistence, and its destruction would be sublated. This is not so.

If it were argued that, just as a snake removed by meditation is merely non-existent and never established as something sublated, so too would there be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the latent impression (vāsanā) removed by unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) must likewise be real; [we reply: if meditative contemplation (nididhyāsana), consisting of the cultivation of identity, were the remover of the obstacle, then the aforementioned fault would indeed apply. However, that is not for the sake of removing the obstacle, but rather serves as a cooperative factor (sahakārī) for the arising of the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha-jñāna).

It is not so; for since meditation (*nididhyāsana*) in the form of recollection (*smṛti*) depends upon experience (*anubhava*), it cannot serve as an auxiliary cause for the production of knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. Now, one might object: even if meditation is of no assistance to indirect experience (*parokṣānubhava*), nevertheless, the sentence, when conjoined with meditation, may become the cause of immediate intuition (*aparokṣadhī*).

It is not so; for even if it were assisted by *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), it could not be the cause of immediate intuition (*aparokṣadhī*) simply because it is verbal in nature, just like the sentence concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. Thus, due to the contradiction between the scripture and direct perception, and because it is impossible to resolve that contradiction [if the former were taken literally], the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence cannot be the means of cessation [of bondage]. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), he states "Therefore" (*ataḥ*), implying that what is intended to be enjoined is a knowledge of the means to liberation that is distinct from the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. It is not merely the method of elimination; he says "And likewise" (*tathā ca*) to show that there are also scriptural passages (*śruti*) that support this.

In the two sentences beginning with *vijñāya*, the word used is a general term for knowledge (*jñāna*). The inclusion of these two sentences is intended to demonstrate that even though there is a difference in prefixes, and despite the presence or absence of an injunctive suffix, there is no difference in meaning. *Dhyāyatha* is a specific term. By *nicāyya*, the meditative state’s resemblance to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is shown; for the verbal root is *cāyṛ* in the sense of "seeing. Through the word *upāsīta*, it is established that knowledge is denoted by the term "meditation" (*upāsana*).

The statement "it is to be sought" (*anveṣṭavya*) refers to hearing (*śravaṇa*) preceded by reflection (*manana*). By including the terms "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) and "it is to be desired to be known" (*vijijñāsitavya*), it is shown that even though these forms contain the desiderative suffix (*san*), the sentences refer to the knowledge that is being sought. The inclusion of both desiderative forms is due to their status as general and specific terms, respectively. In the phrase "and so forth" (*ity-evam-ādyāḥ*), the word *iti* refers merely to the form of the scriptural passages cited, while the word *evaṃ* refers to the various modes such as the presence of the desiderative suffix, the presence of a prescriptive suffix, the absence thereof, and the distinction between prefixes (*upasarga*).

In order to dispel the doubt that—in the cited statements—the specific content required by words denoting knowledge in general might culminate in the nature of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning itself, he says: "here" (atra). The syntactical connection is as follows: "here," meaning in the sentences set forth, meditation is enjoined by such [words] as these.

By the phrase "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) and so forth, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) intends to include other statements expressing specific types of knowledge free from doubt. Furthermore, there is a single intended meaning (*aikārthya*) due to the principle of "the cognition of all Vedic branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), which results in the acceptance of what is unspoken yet required. In that regard, according to the principle of "the goat [is understood] from the wording of the mantra," words expressing generalities must ultimately resolve into specific meanings.

Regarding the inquiry: "In the passages 'having understood, he discerns' (*anuvidya vijānāti*) and 'having discerned, one should cultivate wisdom' (*vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta*), by which word is the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence restated (*anūdyate*), and by which is meditation (*dhyāna*) enjoined?", [the author] says: "'Having understood' and 'having discerned' are the restatements. To the question, "What is the purpose of this restatement?", he says: "Because they are conducive to meditation. The result of employing these two sentences—"one should cultivate wisdom" and "he discerns"—is precisely what was stated previously. Thus, even in the *Smṛtis*, a general term is seen to terminate in a specific meaning when there is a factor that brings that specific meaning to mind.
Eating forbidden food, excessive greed of the tongue, speaking false words with pride, and tasting the mouth of a woman in her menses are equal to the drinking of liquor.
In this context, it is understood that the general act of eating what is generally prohibited is the cause of loss of caste (pātitya):
"Having intentionally eaten mushrooms, a village-pig, garlic, a village-cock, onions, and leeks, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]."

In this context, the specific consumption of a particular prohibited substance is seen to be the cause of loss of caste (*pātitya*). Here, the preceding text culminates in the meaning of the final text. Let it be that a general term culminates in a specific sense; however, regarding the point that the word "to be heard" (*śrotavya*), which denotes knowledge in general, should culminate here in the specific knowledge consisting of hearing, he says: "And [it is] 'to be heard'. The particle *ca* (and) serves either to dispel a doubt or as a conjunction; the meaning is that this is a restatement (*anuvāda*), similar to the expression "having understood, one should follow" (*vijñāyānuvidyet*).

He establishes that point in brief with the words "of the study" (*svādhyāyasya*). Through superficial comprehension (*āpātapratīti*), the hearing (*śravaṇa*) would be obtained by itself; however, since reflection (*manana*) lacks such a cause, [the opponent suggests] that its culmination should lie there. To this he replies: "because it is for the sake of establishing the hearing. The word "and" (*ca*) is as before. Therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed the practice (*vyāna*) itself, and not the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*).

One might object: could the injunction "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) not be intended to exclude activities such as looking at books? This is not so; for the exclusion of looking at books and the like regarding the Vedānta texts is already established by the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). Furthermore, writing and reading [the Brahmasūtras] are not prohibited. Moreover, the word "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) does not have its primary meaning in the context of approaching a teacher (*gurūpasatti*), and even if that [approaching] were not enjoined here, it is established by another scriptural passage: "One should approach a guru alone" (*gurumevābhigacchet*).

If it is argued that "listening" (*śravaṇa*)—the hearing of specific meanings accessible only through direct instruction, which cannot be understood from mere sentences endowed with reasoning—is what is enjoined by the injunction "one should listen," we say no; for this listening, occurring prior to reflection (*manana*), is understood to consist of knowledge produced by sentences supported by reasoning, and because this is the natural sense of the word itself.

Nor should it be said that "it is to be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) is an injunction for reflection (*manana*) consisting in the cultivation of the object of meditation; for the word "to be heard" (*śravaṇa*) is well-known to denote knowledge derived from sentences supported by reasoning, while the word "to be reflected upon" is most commonly known to denote the establishment of that [knowledge], and there is no exception to this. Furthermore, if both words were to convey two previously unestablished meanings, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Moreover, when another way is possible, it is improper to resort to an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vidhāna*), for an injunction, having its power exhausted in one place among the meanings understood from the words, acts for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*).

In other cases, [the text], requiring a restatement (*anuvāda*) by its own nature due to the absence of a means of attainment (*prāpaka*), possesses its purport (*tātparya*) regarding a qualified [object]. However, here, because a restatement is possible, it is not proper to assume that the subject matter is a qualified [entity]; therefore, it is a restatement. Consequently, this term *śravaṇa*—being common to both the stages of the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*)—will be explained later along with another sentence of clear meaning that serves as a restrictive regulator.

[Objection: But surely there is no commonality [between the two], because from the suffix *tavya* in "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), it is understood that the act of seeing is what is enjoined, whereas a result is not something that can be enjoined. [Reply: It is said in response: Since enjoining the act of seeing would lead to a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—just as in the case of enjoining meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)—and because the certainty of its being an injunction is obstructed by its hearing in association with reflection (*manana*) and recollection (*anu-vāda*) which are already established, and because it is impossible to resort to a qualified injunction when no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is found for the object, which consists in the vision of that which is to be meditated upon (*upāsya*), [the text says]: "He rejoices, beholding with the mind these desires which... and so forth.

Furthermore, since the validity of such vision at the stage of fruition is established by such passages as, "In the world of Brahman, one beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high," it is proper to suspect that the word *draṣṭavya* (to be seen) serves to present the fruit—disregarding its status as an object of injunction like the word *śrotavya* (to be heard). Therefore, [the nature of] what follows must be explained hereafter.

Now, in order to strengthen the fact that meditation (*upāsana*) is intended to be enjoined, the author shows the intention of the Sūtra-kāra by stating "and he will say. He cites the Sūtra beginning with "repetition" (*āvṛtti*) to exclude the possibility that such a Sūtra might not exist. Since the word "meditation" is not explicitly heard in the Sūtra, its purport is not immediately clear; therefore, he states its meaning: "that very knowledge" (*tad idam vedanam*). To exclude the notion of repetition occurring only twice or thrice, the word "repeatedly" (*asakṛt*) is used in the Sūtra. In response to the question "Of what is there repetition?", he says: "of that very knowledge."

This very point was introduced at the conclusion of the third chapter with the sūtra: "Thus there is no restriction regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state remains constant"; the meaning is that the fruit of liberation is knowledge (*jñāna*). Alternatively, it refers to meditation (*upāsana*) in the form of repeated practice of "knowing" (*vedana*), as expressed by general terms such as "one should cultivate wisdom" (*prajñāṃ kurvīta*).

By the words ending with "is understood," the portion of the Sūtra stating "repetition is not [once]" has been explained; he now explains the term "from instruction" (upadeśāt) and cites three instances: "mind," "speech," and "the year. The sentence "Mind is Brahman" is like the injunction "one should approach the nights"; just as in the passage "Verily, those who undertake these nights find a firm foundation," the phrase "those who undertake these nights" is a reference back to the Satra for the sake of the result, so too the phrase "he who knows thus" is a reference back to the previously enjoined meditation for the sake of its fruit.

There is a distinction between *kīrti* and *yaśas* due to differences in their causes, such as crossing over [difficulties] and valor. In passages such as "One should meditate upon the mind as Brahman" and in the passage beginning with "He who knows that," there is a wide separation between the words denoting "knowing" (*veda*) and "meditating" (*upāsīta*). Therefore, the word "here" (*atra*) is used to indicate the unity of the context. [The phrase] "instruct me in her"—referring to the deity you meditate upon—means "teach me concerning this deity. The root *śās* preceded by the prefix *anu* has the sense of making known after having analyzed; the meaning is, "make it known after having analyzed it."

By the rule *vyavahitāśca*, the separation of prepositions [from their verbs] is permitted in the Vedic language (*chandas*). In the phrase *na sa veda*, the word *atra* is not employed due to its proximity [to the verb]. Regarding the phrase *na sa veda*: "Now... [the commentary continues].

Because the sentence "He who worships another deity... precedes this, the word *upāsana* (worship) occurs in the opening and the conclusion, while the word *veda* (he knows) occurs in the middle; this is what is intended by the statement that this is seen from the opening and conclusion in the preceding passage. The meaning is: "He who knows that"—Raikva, the knower of that Brahman—"and what he knows"—the Brahman which is the object known by Raikva—"both that knower, Raikva, and that object known, [are] to be imparted to you."

By the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), it has already been demonstrated by the Commentator himself that words denoting knowledge in general mentioned in one context ultimately refer to a specific type of knowledge mentioned in another context. However, in the commentary on the Sūtras, the observation of the correspondence between the opening and the conclusion within each individual section was stated as the meaning of the term "instruction" (*upadeśāt*). Although both [general and specific] should be stated as the reason in both cases, only one is mentioned in each for the sake of brevity.

For this very reason, both will be stated as causes in the fourth chapter. This [passage beginning with] "tad idam" is the commentary on the sūtra. Otherwise, that which is intended to be enjoined as the means to liberation would not be called "knowledge" (vedana), but rather would be called "meditation" (dhyāna) or "worship" (upāsana); for otherwise, it would be inconsistent with the context of the preceding discussion.

Furthermore, since meditation (*dhyāna*) is described by the previously mentioned term "meditation" as being of the nature of an uninterrupted stream of mindfulness—like a continuous flow of oil—if it were intended in the preceding text that meditation is of the nature of worship (*upāsanā*), then in the subsequent passage, worship would be designated by the word "worship" as being of the nature of an uninterrupted stream of mindfulness.

Thus, once the meaning of the present sūtra has been determined, [the author] establishes that the previously mentioned [term] possesses the nature of *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant recollection). The intention of the Sūtrakāra, who states "and meditation" (*dhyānaṃ ca*) with the repetition of the word *veṇa*, is as follows: just as it is established that words expressing knowledge in general have as their ultimate referent knowledge consisting of repeated practice because they terminate in a specific instance, so too, when other specific terms are present, it is logical that a term terminates in that specific instance.

Therefore, after the author of the Sūtras has established through repeated statements that knowledge consists in the form of repetition, he states "and meditation" (*dhyāna*) to indicate another specific feature intended by him which is suggested by other scriptural passages. By this passage, in order to dispel the doubt that repetition might be interrupted, it is stated that there must be no intervention by any heterogeneous cognition.

In this context, if the term *dhyāna* (meditation) is intended to apply commonly to both interrupted and uninterrupted streams of memory, then by the words "and meditation" (*dhyānaṃ ca*) and so forth, it is stated that the term culminates in a specific distinction; whereas if the term *dhyāna* is not common to interrupted streams of memory, then the word *dhyāna* is explained [in its primary sense]. Regarding the state of being an uninterrupted stream of memory, he states the defining characteristic with the word "steadfast" (*dhruva*). The steadfastness of memory consists in its being a continuous stream unintercepted by other heterogeneous cognitions, since individual instances of memory are momentary.

Because it is heard [in scripture] that [this knowledge] is the means to liberation (*apavarga*), the repeated practice of that knowledge which serves as the means to liberation has been stated there. Here too, because the recognition of its being a means [to liberation] is present, the intended meaning is that it must consist of an uninterrupted continuity. Its nature as "vision" (*darśana*) is expressed by the words "and that" (*sā ca*); the sense of the word "form" (*ākāra*) is that there is similarity not only due to the identity of the object, but also due to its being immediate (*aparokṣya*). The "knots of the heart"—that is, of the mind—are attachment (*rāga*) and so forth.

Alternatively, just as in the expression "the beds cry out," the word *hṛdaya* refers to the living being residing therein—either by that usage or from the etymology "that which moves (*mayati*) within the heart" (*hṛt*). Its "knot" (*granthi*) is its connection with *prakṛti*; or else, the body, indicated by the word *hṛdaya*, is the knot. The word "doubt" (*saṃśaya*) is intended to indicate error (*viparyaya*) as well; the meaning is that ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of such things as the conceit of identifying the body with the self. "Actions" (*karmāṇi*) are those of the nature of merit and demerit.

The meaning is: "by means of meditation whose form is identical to the vision [of Brahman], which brings about the cessation of the connection with *prakṛti* produced by karma accumulated through ignorance. And the phrase "this being so" (*evaṃ ca sati*) means: "given that it has been established by other clear scriptural passages that knowledge takes the form of vision during the stage of the means (*upāyadaśā*). The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to dispel the suspicion that the word "seer" (*draṣṭavya*) refers to the stage of the fruit (*phaladaśā*).

Although the word *darśana* can possibly refer to cognition in general, because hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other stages are mentioned separately in such passages as "It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," and "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, reflected upon, and realized, all this is known," the term "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) refers to the state of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*). The word *dṛṣṭa* has a meaning equivalent to that [intuition], yet it refers to the stage of the means (*upāyadaśā*), since it is stated: "When That is seen, the knot of the heart is severed."

Because the fruit has been specified in the preceding and following passages—such as "by which I might become immortal," "there is no hope for immortality through wealth," and "this much alone, O dear one, is immortality"—and because the state of direct realization mentioned in other contexts must also be stated here, the injunction of what is required is stronger than the injunction of what is not required.

An objection may be raised: "Is it not improper to enjoin that the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) itself has the nature of vision (*darśana*), since constant recollection and vision are taught in different contexts? For, like the meditations on the *dahara* and *śāṇḍilya*, they are understood to be independent means to the goal. This is not so; for they are enjoined by a single sentence: "He is to be seen, He is to be meditated upon with intense reflection" (*draṣṭavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*).

Furthermore, even in that case, it is not possible to enjoin two separate meditations (*vidyā*), because there is no difference in their form; for precisely on that account, since the unity of the sentence is possible, it is improper to resort to a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). Moreover, this would entail the undesirable consequence of those two meditations being optional alternatives (*vikalpa*), just like other distinct meditations. If it is argued that an option is acceptable for one who maintains that the two are independent means, we say no; for it is improper to accept such an option—which is tainted by eight defects—when another way out exists. Indeed, such [an option] is seen in the case of the scriptural injunctions regarding rice and barley.

[The ritual action] is vitiated by six defects. In the case of performing [the sacrifice] with rice (*vrīhi*), there is the abandonment of the authority of the *yava* (barley) scripture, and the postulation of its non-authority where none exists; in the case of performing it with barley, there is the acceptance of that [scripture] whose authority was previously abandoned, and the abandonment of the non-authority that had been accepted—thus there are four defects in the *yava* scripture. Furthermore, at the very time of the first performance when using barley, there is the abandonment of the authority of the rice scripture that was previously accepted, and the postulation of its non-authority; and when rice is being taken up in the third performance, [there is the abandonment of the authority of the barley scripture accepted in the second performance, and the postulation of its non-authority].

In the case of the *vrīhi* scripture, there are four defects: the acceptance [of the scripture], the abandonment of its authority, the abandonment of that which has been accepted as authoritative, and the acceptance of what has been abandoned. Here too, these defects apply as far as possible. Alternatively, since each "head" (each type of sublation) possesses four defects—namely, sublation of comprehension (*pratipatti-bādha*), sublation of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-bādha*), sublation of the unseen potency (*apūrva-bādha*), and sublation of the fruit (*phala-bādha*)—it is corrupted by eight defects in total.

Therefore, since there is no other alternative and because conceptualization is incompatible [with the object], constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) and direct vision (*darśana*) do not constitute separate means, nor do they constitute a combination (*samuccaya*). This is because the word "and" (*ca*) is not heard [in the text], and because there is no mention of them as a dual compound (*dvandva*), as in the case of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
