Furthermore, because the Supreme Self is beyond the senses, its direct perception cannot be enjoined upon one engaged in yoga—as it would be impossible to do so—just as it is impossible to perceive sound with the eye. Thus, a combination is untenable, similar to the combination of memory and visual cognition regarding the objects of sound and form respectively.

[Objection: But surely, since the Supreme Self is to be grasped by a mind purified through yoga, the vision of It is not equivalent to the verbal knowledge [of It] obtained through the eyes; therefore, because it is logical that the activity which serves as the means to such vision should be enjoined, the combination [of meditation and ritual action] is possible. [Reply: True;

What is the means for seeing Him? If it is argued that it is meditation (*dhyāna*) alone, based on the scriptural text, "But then, meditating upon Him, one sees Him who is partless," then there would be a tautology between the two terms *draṣṭavya* (to be seen) and *nididhyāsitavya* (to be meditated upon), since both would be indistinguishably intent on enjoining meditation as the means of seeing. When the means of seeing is enjoined by the word *draṣṭavya*, the question arises: "What is the means? and in response to this expectation, *nididhyāsana* is enjoined.

If it is argued that there is no tautology because the status of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) as a means to that [vision] is not known in the absence of the word "to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), and thus its purpose is to make that known—this is not so. For even upon hearing the word "to be seen," it is not perceived that vision is to be accomplished by meditation; indeed, the desire for vision is not what is heard [in scripture]. If that were the case, then meditation would have a visible instrumental efficacy toward vision, just as sacrifice has toward heaven; therefore, since the relationship of means and end between the two would not be understood through any other means of knowledge, [the scriptural injunction] would be redundant.

Furthermore, if realization were to be accomplished by meditation, then a conjunction of meditation and realization would be impossible; for if there were a conjunction with respect to realization, it would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), wherein realization would be the means for realizing itself.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of a combination (*samuccaya*) regarding liberation, because meditation—which is separated from liberation by its own result, namely [theoretical] vision—cannot have an immediate auxiliary effect toward liberation alongside that vision. Indeed, there is no combination with the final unseen potency (*apūrva*) for acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) or threshing (*avaghāta*), which are intended for the accomplishment of a sacrifice. If it is argued that another kind of knowledge, having a form identical to [theoretical] vision, must be enjoined so that meditation may have an immediate auxiliary effect toward direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), that is incorrect.

Otherwise, there would arise the undesirable consequence of violating the natural sense of the understanding that *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is an independent means toward its goal—just as the vow of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice is an independent means toward heaven; for it is not understood from the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" that the Jyotiṣṭoma’s status as a means to heaven depends upon another action.

Nor is there a word "ca" (and) here, nor is there a copulative compound (*dvandvasamāsa*); therefore, when the expectancy arises as to what the qualifier "having a form identical to [the object of] vision" qualifies, no other substantive is perceived. Since *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection) is proximate, it is logical to accept that this very practice is intended to be enjoined as having a form identical to vision; consequently, there would be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), and the natural force of the understanding that *nididhyāsana* is an independent means would not be sublated.

Now, one might object: "If recourse is indeed taken to an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), why could there not be an injunction for intensive contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)—which consists of hearing the meaning accessible solely through instruction, reflecting upon it, and meditating upon it as a virtuous support? It is not so; for although the assumption of intentionality (*tātparya*) applies to all four stages, the assumption of it for only two of them is more parsimonious (*laghu*).

Furthermore, since it is impossible to resort to a heavy alternative when a light one is available, one should not suspect that the practice of reflecting upon the support for attaining the directly taught meaning is unestablished because there is no injunction in this specific sentence; for this is already established by another scriptural passage which states: "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should remain in a state of childlike simplicity; and having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he then becomes a sage."

For that will indeed be examined under the sūtra, "The injunction for another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantaravidhi*). Therefore, there is an injunction for *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) characterized by the quality of having a form identical to [the object of] vision. [Objection: Even so, it is not established that all forms of worship (*upāsanā*) consist of *nididhyāsana* whose form is identical to vision, because the statement "He is to be seen, He is to be meditated upon" occurs in the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa; therefore, in that case, only the specific form of worship being propounded would have to be established as having such a nature.

It is not so, because by that very passage—“Indeed, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known”—it is understood that all meditations (*upāsanā*) concerning the cause of the world consist of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) whose form is identical to direct perception (*darśana*). This sentence does not enjoin a specific type of knowledge (*vidyā*), for its purpose is the declaration that through the knowledge of the Cause, everything becomes known; indeed, the Cause alone is the object of meditation for all forms of knowledge, as shown by the text beginning with “And who is to be meditated upon? and concluding with “But the Cause is to be meditated upon. Thus, it is the Cause itself [that is the object].

Because meditation is enjoined as the object of contemplation, it is understood here that the worship directed toward the Cause consists of *nididhyāsana* (intense meditative reflection) which takes the form of a vision-like perception (*darśanasamānākāra*). For in this passage, the word "vijñāta" (known) refers specifically to *nididhyāsana*, based on the evidence of its position [in the sequence]: "It is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (*draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), and "when it is seen, heard, reflected upon, and known" (*dṛṣṭe śrute mate vijñāte*).

Therefore, since this sentence concerns only the common cause for all forms of knowledge, if the worship of the Cause of the world is undertaken, it is understood to consist of *nididhyāsana* in the form of a vision-like perception.

Furthermore, since the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of various types of knowledge will be discussed later, and because the distinction between great and small effort would result in the futility of the scriptures concerning the domain of the Guru’s tradition, and because the inherent power of the reality (*vastu-sāmarthya*) is more forceful than the context, the forms consisting of constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*), the form of vision (*darśana*), and the form of devotion (*bhakti*) to be discussed later must be common characteristics shared by all forms of knowledge.

Now, one might object: "Directness (*aparokṣatva*) belongs indeed to an experience born of the senses; how then can it belong to memory? To this he says, "And it occurs... The meaning is as follows: the latent impression of cultivation (*bhāvanāvāsanā*) consists in having a form identical to that of perception—that is, a form similar to perception—as seen in such cases as "I see [it] in every tree," where memory is observed to have a form similar to perception. Moreover, this consists in having a very clear manifestation (*viśadatarāvabhāsa*), and this is not unique to direct experience, because its existence in memory is also established by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

If it is objected that the prescription of having a form identical to the vision (*darśana*) is improper—since, according to the logicians, the rule "in an injunction, the word does not have its secondary meaning" renders it non-primary for a word denoting vision to bring about the presentation of something identical in form to it—[we reply]: by those very [logicians], in the case of the sentence "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* are accepted as names of rituals through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and in the sentences concerning the Śyena and others, the words *śyena* and so forth are accepted as names of rituals through metaphorical usage (*gauṇī vṛtti*). [Furthermore,] "He should measure half within the altar and half... [is cited].

Furthermore, since even in the case of the phrase "outside the altar" (*bahirvedi*), the indication of the central region (*madhyadeśa*) is accepted, one might object: "How can there be an injunction for that which is not dependent on a person (*apuruṣatantra*), given that extreme clarity is the nature of the fruit? If this is raised, we say no; for an injunction is possible here just as it is in the case of the "inspection of the clarified butter" (*ājyāvekṣaṇa*). If it is argued that in that case the injunction concerns the mental activity directed toward the operation that causes the direct perception of the butter, then here too it is logically consistent that the injunction concerns the mental activity directed toward the continuous stream of memory that brings about extreme clarity.

Now, he shows this statement according to the intention of the author of the Sūtras by means of the author of the Vākya (the Bhāṣyakāra). "All this" means that which was explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras and that which was intended; "expounded" means stated in the form of prima facie arguments and final conclusions. He explains each individual sentence of the fourfold set beginning with "The expansion [of the universe] is not meditation" (*prapañcaṃ na vedanam upāsanaṃ syāt*). "In all the Upaniṣads" means not only in the Chāndogya.

The term "knowledge" (*vedana*) is specified as being enjoined as a means to liberation (*mokṣa*), thereby excluding knowledge of objects such as jars. The word "enjoined" (*vihitam*) excludes [the mere] hearing and so forth that are merely restated (*anūdita*). To clarify this point by way of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), and to avoid the suspicion that the sentence "one should perform the cognition once" (*sakṛt pratyayaṃ kuryāt*)—by virtue of hearing the injunction—might mean that "knowledge" (*vedana*) is actually "meditation" (*upāsana*), he explains the passage beginning with "once" (*sakṛt*). Thus, it is the very sentence beginning with "once" that represents the prima facie view, and not [the term "knowledge"].

The sense is that the statement "the meditation [should be] on the Veda" establishes its nature as meditation immediately thereafter. He shows that it has been established in this way with the words "But it is established"; the meaning is "but the established conclusion (siddhānta) is," or alternatively, "it is established that the Veda is meditation."

He explains this [point] regarding the word *upāsana* (meditation): that it is knowledge repeated many times. He shows that its nature consists in an uninterrupted stream of memory, which is intended by the author of the Sūtras and explicitly stated by the author of the Vākya, by means of the observation "it should be meditation" (*upāsanaṃ syāt*) and from the etymological definition in the scriptural passage. The phrase "of that very [knowledge]" means of that which is prescribed as the means to liberation. The phrase "of the form of meditation" contains a reason: because it has the form of meditation, that is, because it is denoted by the word *upāsana*, it means that it is repeated many times.
For knowledge that has been repeated many times is indeed meditation; thus, its nature as an uninterrupted continuity of memory has been established.

The intention of the author of the *Vākya* (Brahmanandin), who states that the form of repeated practice is explicitly taught by the author of the *Sūtra* and that it constitutes "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*), is as follows: by the same logic, when there is a statement that does not introduce any specific qualification, words such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and so forth should terminate in that [repetition]. Therefore, intending to show that the previously mentioned state of having a form identical to direct perception (*darśana-samānākāratva*) is also intended by the author of the *Vākya*, he says: "This [is that]. This means that it consists of repeated practice and takes the form of constant remembrance.

Anticipating the objection that the word *darśana*—given its usage in such expressions as "one who sees the object" (*arthadarśī*) or "one who sees reality" (*tattvadarśī*)—is common to both indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*aparokṣa* [perception]), he says: "And the nature of seeing is the attainment of directness. This means the attainment of a form identical to that of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The meaning is that [the distinction is established] because of separate mention even in the earlier sūtras concerning indirect knowledge through hearing and so forth, such as: "Verily, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this is known," and "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, thought, and meditated upon. When the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Vākya (Brahmā) state certain specific points, their intention is that these should culminate in the presentation of other specific points; therefore, he says "In this way" to indicate that there exists another specific point established by other scriptural passages.

By this, since hearing and so forth are denied as means to liberation, the doubt that meditative worship (*upāsana*) might be a means to liberation is also dispelled. In the manner thus described, the meaning is "attained to direct perception" according to the logic of the general and the particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*). By the phrase "become a means to liberation," the exclusion of symbolic worship (*pratīka-upāsana*) is intended.

In the phrase "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), the term *pravacana* indicates *manana* (reflection), because the teaching is the fruit of reflection, or because reflection is the fruit of the teacher's instruction; or alternatively, by the instrumental derivation "that by which it is taught," *pravacana* is reflection. *Medhā* is *nididhyāsana* (contemplation), by process of elimination. In this passage, while hearing and the other [stages] are perceived as not being the means, nothing is established as a qualification of "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*).

Therefore, he explains that [the scripture] "teaches by means of this"—meaning by means of mere hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) devoid of the specific qualifications to be mentioned hereafter. The sense is as follows: just as in the injunction "The fire-altar is not to be piled on the earth," the piling of the altar on the earth is prohibited when it is devoid of a gold plate (*hiraṇya-upadhāna*), but not on the earth per se; so it is in this case.

Desiring to show the intended specific meaning by determining the purport of the sentence, he demonstrates the syntactical connection of the sentence, stating: "It has been said that [the Self] is to be obtained only by whomsoever this Self chooses. To the doubt—"Let it be that He is obtained by the one who is chosen; how then is there a specification of the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*)?"—he states the worldly-established perception in order to demonstrate that: "For from Him alone [comes] what is dear," and so forth.

The state of being chosen does not belong to every object of affection; rather, it belongs only to one who is accepted when he has presented himself spontaneously. Therefore, to exclude such cases, the phrase "who loves Him" (priyamataḥ) is stated. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Of whom. For that very worshiper for whom this Supreme Self is the object of unsurpassed love, He alone becomes the object of unsurpassed love for that Supreme Self. Since both possess consciousness, the state of being chosen by the Lord belongs only to one who possesses unsurpassed love for the Lord.

Alternatively, self-love and being desirable as a bridegroom belong only to one who loves himself; the Lord’s love for sacred fields and the like is for the sake of choosing a person who loves Himself, while His love for leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth is based on their connection to Him. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "He alone," there is the exclusion of those who possess only hearing and other such [means] without [devotion].

In response to the inquiry, "How is it known that only one who possesses supreme love for the Blessed One becomes an object of the Blessed One’s love? the author demonstrates a scriptural statement from the *Smṛti* as the authority for this, while also explaining the manner of selection, beginning with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). This person is one who possesses unsurpassed love for the Blessed One; the meaning is that by being one who loves [the Lord], he becomes an object of the Blessed One’s unsurpassed love.

It has been stated that the Lord Himself exerts effort with the desire to explain the meaning of the words "I give that yoga of wisdom"; by this, the manner of selection (*varaṇa*) is shown. By the emphatic particle *eva* in the phrase "spoken by the Lord alone," the excellence of the Lord's attainment is indicated. Regarding the phrase "to those who are ever-devoted" (*satatayuktānām*), the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent according to the rule "the suffix *kta* is used like a present participle when expressing a wish" (*āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacceti*); thus the construction is "I give with love" (*prītipūrvakaṃ dadāmi*). By this, the mutual affection between the object of worship and the worshiper is demonstrated.

He says, "For he is dear," in order to make clear the meaning of the term *satatayukta* (constantly engaged). "Exceedingly" (*atyartha*) means that which transcends what can be expressed; the meaning is that his dearness is beyond the range of words. It was stated previously that this qualifies *dhruvānusmṛti* (constant remembrance). Here, since it is said that the Blessed One is full of affection for that devotee who possesses affection for the Blessed One, one might ask: how is this a qualification of *dhruvānusmṛti*? To this he says, "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: because the matter thus stated is established by both worldly experience and traditional scripture.

Alternatively, the meaning is: because of the mention of the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*), because of the mention of its being something to be chosen (*varaṇīya*), and because of the mention that the object to be chosen possesses unsurpassed love for the Blessed One. By the phrase "recollection in the form of direct perception," it is shown that this [recollection] possesses a further distinction while being characterized by the previously mentioned forms. The sense is that, since the object being recollected is exceedingly dear, the recollection itself is also exceedingly dear; for the distinction between cognitions lies solely in their objects, as they themselves are devoid of form (*nirākāra*).

This designation, "one who is herself dear to the object," is figurative—just as one speaks of "experience" even when that which is being experienced is the experience itself; the meaning is that she consists of extreme love. Alternatively, "atyarthapriyā" means having an extremely favorable form; for since the remembered object, the Blessed Lord, is infinitely and unconditionally favorable, the remembrance directed toward Him is likewise unsurpassedly favorable.

Alternatively, because it is extremely favorable by its very nature, the constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is linked even during states of non-concentration through knowledge in the form of affection; thus, it is called "the beloved. For this very reason, it is sought after in such passages as, "That love which belongs to those lacking discrimination," and so forth. Since it has been stated that constant recollection in the form of affection is the means to liberation (*apavarga*), while elsewhere devotion (*bhakti*) is seen to be the means, one might ask how these two can have the same meaning. To this, he says: "of such a form."

Alternatively, since it was previously stated that "wisdom (*śemuṣī*) consists in the form of devotion (*bhakti*)," thus establishing that knowledge in the form of devotion is the means [to liberation], one might ask: "How is it now established that constant recollection (*dhruvānusmṛti*) in the form of love is the means? To this he says: "of such a nature. The meaning is that constant recollection itself—extending from the state of direct perception to the state of being in the form of love—is what is denoted by the word "devotion" (*bhakti*). Why is this so? To this he says: "because it is a synonym for *upāsana* (meditative worship)."

What is intended here is that words such as *upāsanā* and the word *bhakti* function with the same meaning (*ekārthavṛttitva*), but not that they are synonyms (*paryāyatva*) in the manner of the words *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*. This functional identity of meaning is understood precisely from the lexicographical statement: "Service (*sevā*) is worship (*upāsti*) in the form of devotion (*bhakti*). Furthermore, one should reflect upon such passages as: "Devotion (*bhakti*) is defined as meditation preceded by affection; this verbal root *bhaja* is proclaimed to signify service (*sevā*); therefore, service is extensively designated by the word 'devotion' by the wise."

Although it might follow that statements concerning the nature of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), the nature of devotion (*bhakti*), and so forth—which, despite being contained within specific contexts (*prakaraṇa*) dealing with particular forms of knowledge (*vidyā*)—are nevertheless common to all meditations (*upāsana*) because it is illogical to assume an alternative between easy and difficult efforts, nevertheless, in the case of *prapadana* (seeking refuge), the logical argument regarding the impossibility of an alternative between easy and difficult efforts is set aside by the force of the scriptural statement itself.

Indeed, logic has no power where there is a contradiction with scripture; its application occurs only when there is no contradiction with scripture. For the purpose of establishing the unity of meaning among those Vedic passages in the Upaniṣads that are devoted to meditation (*upāsana*), it was stated that meditation alone—when it has reached the stage of devotion (*bhakti*)—is the means of knowing the path to liberation. Furthermore, the citation of Smṛti passages was made to clarify the meaning of the Śruti. Now, however, by means of the unity of meaning between Śruti and Smṛti, it is demonstrated that the means of knowing the path to liberation is indeed meditation in the form of devotion; this is why [the author says] "for this very reason."

Therefore, the meaning is: precisely because the knowledge of the means to liberation (*apavarga*) consists of worship in the form of devotion (*bhakti*). The statement "Only by knowing Him... is heard in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*. Since the word "Śiva" is employed there in the phrase "Therefore, Śiva is omnipresent," some of dull intellect might fall into the error of thinking that its subject matter is Śiva as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). To dispel that [error], [the text continues]: "I know this Great Puruṣa," and "The Great Lord is indeed the Puruṣa; He is the impeller of existence."

Thus, in order to demonstrate that this Upaniṣad—whose subject matter is determined by its opening and conclusion—is devoted solely to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) and shares the same purport as the *Puruṣasūkta*, the sentence "One who knows Him thus" (*tamevaṃ vidvān*) has been cited. By the sentence "One who knows Him thus," the prohibition of any means other than the knowledge of the Supreme Person is established through the words "There is no other path" (*nānyah panthā*). Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Not by the Vedas" (*nāhaṃ vedaiḥ*), the prohibition of any means other than devotion to Him is stated. This is because both of these statements—the explanatory supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) and the text to be supplemented (*upabṛṃhaṇīya*)—possess the status of the highest authority (*pramāṇatama*).

The sense is that the identity of meaning for all non-contradictory terms—such as "knowledge" (*veda*), "vision" (*darśana*), and "attainment" (*prāpti*)—is established when they culminate in devotion (*bhakti*). The statement "I am not [attained] by the Vedas" (*nāhaṃ vedaiḥ*) has been cited because it explicitly negates other means and explicitly states that knowledge, vision, and attainment are accomplished through devotion.

An objection may be raised: "Surely, from the statements 'He comes to know Me through devotion' and 'Then, having known Me in truth, he enters [Me] immediately thereafter,' it is understood that knowledge produced by devotion alone is the immediate means, and not devotion itself. This doubt is resolved by the verse beginning with "Not by the Vedas. For here, just as with knowledge and vision, it is understood that attainment is also accomplished through devotion; thus the syntactical connection is: "And it is possible to enter [Me] through devotion."

Even in the statement "by devotion unto Me," it is understood that devotion alone is the means of attainment, as it is devotion—referred to by the word "from that" (*tataḥ*)—that is entered; for if "from that" were a mere semblance of a reference to devotion, there would be the consequence of redundancy with the phrase "immediately thereafter. Therefore, devotion alone is the immediate means. Furthermore, in the verse "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha," the fact that He is attained through devotion is understood by its own inherent force (*svarasataḥ*) as devotion being the instrument of attainment.

By this, it is indicated that just as there is identity between the reality taught in the *Puruṣasūkta*—which is recognized through the recurring word "Person" (*puruṣa*)—so too is the identity of the means taught therein logically established. [An objection is raised: "Granted that the realization [of Brahman] is thus established as being of the nature of devotion (*bhakti*) and worship (*upāsanā*), what follows for the subject at hand—the requirement of ritual action (*karman*)? To this, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). The sense is that the specific stages of knowledge which are the means to liberation—intended by the author of the *Vākya-kāra* and the author of the *Sūtra*, and explicitly stated by them—are accomplished through ritual action, specifically in the form of such [realization] characterized by the attributes of immediacy and love.

The meaning is as follows: the phrase "the means for the recollection of the Imperishable" (*dhruvānusmṛteḥ sādhanāni*) implies that, just as in the expression "he wishes to kill with a sword" (*asinā jighāṃsati*), the sword is the instrument for killing and not the instrument for the desire [to kill], so too in the passage "they desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), it is stated that sacrifices are the instruments for knowledge (*vidyā*) itself, and not the instruments for the desire for that [knowledge]; for it is improper to enjoin sacrifice and the like as instruments for the desire to know.

For indeed, the activity of all persons toward intermediate means for achieving a goal is not possible without a desire for the ultimate goal, just as activity toward the acquisition of wealth—which serves as a means for travel and so forth—is not possible without a desire for the unseen merit (*apūrva*) or other results achieved through travel and the like; likewise, the performance of practice for the sake of fulfilling that desire is not possible without a desire for the knowledge produced by that desire.

Therefore, once a desire for sensation has arisen, there would be the performance of an action intended to achieve that desire which serves as the means to sensation; and once that [desire] has arisen, the performance of such an action would be unnecessary, rendering the injunction for its performance purposeless.

Furthermore, if non-establishment depends upon its own establishment, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Alternatively, if one performs ritual action for the sake of establishing desire through the desire for knowledge, and the establishment of the desire for knowledge results from that performance of ritual action for the sake of establishing desire, there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, it is not logical that ritual actions are the means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). [Objection: If the performance of ritual action for the sake of establishing desire were beset by such fallacies as self-dependence, then desire would never be possible at all, because the performance of ritual action—which is the cause of desire—would be impossible.

Nor is desire dependent merely upon the cognition of the distinctness of an object, for we observe that even when there is such a cognition, desire does not arise in some individuals. Therefore, since desire arises in someone, you must resort to the view that it is causeless, and that is untenable for you. This is because the arising of desire is logically explained as resulting from the cognition of the distinctness of an object, accompanied by the awakening of prior latent impressions (vāsanā) stimulated by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of experience. Nor should it be argued that the desire for knowledge is established through sacrifices and the like, based on the force of unknown past merits—just as one might have a taste for dharma—as is the case with Dharmaruci.

Since sacrifices and the like—which must be accomplished through great expenditure of wealth and effort—cannot possibly exist in the form of unknown merit, the meaning of the statement "they desire to know by means of sacrifice" must be considered; therefore, the performance of sacrifices and so forth is necessarily preceded by conscious intent. In that case, if there is no desire to know the means to liberation, such actions accomplished through great wealth and effort are invariably preceded by an intention for some other fruit, and thus do not accomplish the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). However, sacrifices and the like, when devoid of any intention for other fruits, [accomplish it] even without the desire to know.

This is not tenable, because the activity of a discerning person cannot occur without aiming at a purpose, and because it is impossible for one who lacks desire for a preeminent purpose and its means to abandon a minor purpose; therefore, since performance for the sake of achieving an intermediate goal is not possible without the desire to know the ultimate goal, there would certainly be defects such as self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because the performance of an action for its own accomplishment depends upon that very accomplishment—this will be explained, and we shall demonstrate it therein. This is the meaning.

Having accepted that there is no fault such as *ātmāśraya* (self-dependence) regarding sacrifices and other means for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), he says "even though" (*yadyapi*). "Of that very [desire]" refers to that which has become the object of the desire. By saying "of the nature of meditation" (*dhyānarūpasya*), the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences is excluded. To exclude the notion that meditation need only be performed for a single day, he says "day after day" (*aharahar*). He states the fruit of performing it day after day with the words "through practice" (*abhyāsa*). Even regarding performance day after day, he says "until death" (*āprayāṇāt*) in order to preclude the idea that it should have a limit such as a month, a season, or a year.

Although [the practice] continues until death, it is stated that "performed day after day" is for the purpose of excluding those instances interrupted by one, two, or three days; even there, it is stated that it is "of the nature of meditation" (dhyāna) in order to preclude the interruption of the recollection (smṛti). For the sake of its arising—that is, for the arising of the desire to know (vividiṣā)—the word "that" (tat), although "knowledge" (vedana) is the immediate subject matter, refers to the desire to know by the force of the context, for it is spoken while accepting that [meditation] is a means to the desire to know.

Regarding the question of what authority there is for the continuation of meditation day after day until death (*āprayāṇāt*) and for the disregard of ritual action (*karman*) for as long as one lives (*yāvajjīvam*), he says: "And he will state [it]. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel doubt. With the intention that by showing the Sūtra, the scriptural passage (*śrutivākya*) which is its subject matter is also shown, the Sūtra concerned with the continuation of meditation, namely *āprayāṇāt*, is presented; the corresponding Śruti is: "He, indeed, living thus for as long as life lasts... (*sa khalvevaṃ vartayan yāvadāyuṣam*).

Because the word "as long as" (yāvat) signifies totality, the performance [of rites] day after day is established; and with respect to the requirement for such actions, he says "the Agnihotra," etc. Although the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) are subordinate to the stage of life itself, he says "and as auxiliary factors" (sahakāritvena ca) to indicate that they also serve as limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga). The meaning is that he will explain this matter in these and subsequent sūtras.

Having raised the objection that the statement regarding action being a subsidiary part of knowledge (*vidyā*) is untenable because it contradicts the fact that meditation (*upāsana*) has tranquility (*śama*) and so forth as its subsidiaries, the author—desiring to resolve this contradiction and wishing to demonstrate the authoritative basis for his position by citing scriptural passages on the subject—says "by the sentence" (*vākyena*). The sense is that even those who know the intention of the Sūtra-author have stated this very thing. In the phrase "the attainment of that" (*tallabdhiḥ*), the word "that" (*tat*) is explained by the term "constant recollection" (*dhruvānusmṛti*). The meaning is that [knowledge is attained] from discernment (*viveka*) and the other means alone, and not through mere ritual action (*karman*) or mere tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.

The *Vākyakāra* (author of the *Vākyakāra-bhāṣya*) cites [this] as "attaining that" (*tallabdhi*). For it is the subject under discussion that "meditation is constant recollection" (*upāsanaṃ syād dhruvānusmṛtiḥ*); therefore, the meaning is "attaining constant recollection. The compound *viveka-vimoka-abhyāsa-kriyā-kalyāṇa-anavasāda-anuddharṣebhyaḥ* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound. This is used in the sense of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), because it would be difficult to attain [the goal] through any one of these alone, and because their combination is possible here. Thus, the author of the *Vākyakāra* indicates the intent of the sentences prescribing *viveka* and the others to be taken in combination by employing a *dvandva* in the sense of mutual conjunction.

But is it not the case that *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) is a distinct category from *samuccaya* (aggregation)? How, then, can *samuccaya* be obtained through a *dvandva* compound of mutual conjunction? It is said in reply: *samuccaya* as read together with *anvācaya* (subordinate inclusion) is a distinct category from *samuccaya* as the correlate of *vikalpa* (option). *Anvācaya* as read together [with *samuccaya*] refers to the connection of several means, each independent of the others, toward a single effect.

However, there is no contradiction in the case of a conjunction expressed through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is the connection of mutually dependent factors toward a single effect; that itself is "mutual conjunction" (*itaretarayoga*). If it is argued that there can be no conjunction because of the opposition between cessation in the form of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, and engagement in the form of sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth, we say no. This is because there is no opposition due to their having different objects. For tranquility and the other [virtues] have as their object those things that are neither enjoined nor prohibited, but are merely desired (*kāmya*). This is because such a combination is possible and logical, and because of the explicit scriptural statement (*nirvacana*); that is to say, on account of both authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*) and logical consistency (*upapatti*).

"What is the nature of discrimination (*viveka*) and the others, and how is there no contradiction with the practice of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth? To this he says: "And he states the essential nature of discrimination and the rest. The meaning is that the author of the *Vākya* (Brahmānanda Sarasvatī) has stated not merely their enumeration, but also their essential nature. First, he cites the passage concerning the nature of discrimination: "Based on birth, substratum," and so on.

The term *viveka* (discrimination) is intended here to mean the discrimination between food and its objects; that is, the discrimination between unwholesome food and *sāttvika* foods. Foods that are defective by nature (*jāti-duṣṭa*) include the *kalañja*, *gañjana*, and so forth. The "source" (*āśraya*) refers to the person who owns the substance; food belonging to one who is accused of a crime, an outcaste, a *caṇḍāla*, or similar persons is "defective by source" (*āśraya-duṣṭa*). Food defiled by remnants, hair, and the like is "defective by cause" (*nimitta-duṣṭa*). The word *viveka* is used figuratively for the purity of the body, which is the fruit resulting from the discrimination of food free from these three types of defects.

Alternatively, *viveka* (discrimination) is the separation of one’s own body from a body nourished by *rājasa* and *tāmasa* foods through the practice of consuming pure (*vivikta*) food. For purification is indeed the separation [of the self] from impurities; the word *iti* belongs to the author of the Bhāṣya. Here, the phrase *nirvacanam* is also a passage from the Bhāṣya. *Nirvacanam* means "extracted speech" (*niṣkṛṣṭavacanam*). The meaning is: speech that has been extracted from non-authoritative sources and has become authoritative (*pramāṇabhūta*).

The phrase beginning with "In the purity of food" (*āhāra-śuddhau*) is an etymological explanation. "Liberation" (*vimokaḥ*) refers to non-attachment to desires. That modification by which one is unable to remain without having experienced an object is "attachment" (*abhiṣvaṅga*); from such statements as "From desire, anger is born," the absence of anger and other such states is here implied as the result. In the etymological explanation "One should meditate being tranquil" (*śānta upāsīta*), the word "tranquil" (*śānta*) intends the absence of passion, hatred, and so forth.

The "beginning" (*ārambhaṇa*) is the support (*ālambana*), the auspicious basis; its repeated practice (*saṃśīlana*) is the means for this end. How so? For it is not this [practice] that is to be accomplished; rather, what is to be accomplished is the "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) denoted by the word "yoga," which is to be practiced according to the specific places and times mentioned in the passage beginning with "having established [the image] in a pure place. This, however, is the constant practice that assists the meditation to be performed during the time of yoga; for he will say later, "always permeated by that state. Indeed, in the absence of constant remembrance of the Lord, what was practiced at other times [would not suffice] during the times of yoga.

The object [of meditation] would then reside within the intellect; therefore, the practice of *ārambhaṇa* is not identical to the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, by the fact that the commentator has cited a definition from the *Smṛti*, it is understood that the definitions previously mentioned are also those stated in the *Dramiḍa-bhāṣya*.

The etymological derivation from the Śruti is "atha muniḥ," but since that requires the presentation of logical reasoning (*nyāya*) and must therefore be explained in the section concerning "the injunction of another auxiliary" (*sahakāryantaravidhi*), and because the Smṛti derivation has a clear meaning, the Smṛti derivation is cited here. The collection of statements ending with "Therefore, at all times, remember Me" is intended here. Regarding the phrase "the five great sacrifices" (*pañcamahāyajña*), it is said "according to one's ability," for scripture does not enjoin what is impossible. The statement "this person is a performer of action" (*kriyāvān eṣaḥ*) is devoid of the suffix *san*.

The most excellent among the knowers of Brahman—indeed, the best among those who know Brahman, for it has been stated that he is not merely among those who desire to know Brahman. To clarify the meaning of the words regarding his actions, he says: "This very one... Truthfulness is that which is beneficial to beings as they truly are. Straightforwardness is the uniformity of mind, speech, and body. Compassion is the inability to endure the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest. Non-violence is the cessation of harming others even by means of the three instruments [mind, speech, and body]. Generosity is the absence of greed.

Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the notion of ownership regarding what belongs to another, or fruitless brooding, or brooding over the insults committed by others; non-covetousness (*anabhidhyā*) is the absence of these. By the word "by truth" (*satyena*), the author of the *Vākya* includes a collection of statements that establish straightforwardness (*ārjava*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "despair and elation" (*avasādoddharṣau*), since despair and elation are themselves the opposites of [the virtues] beginning with contentment (*anavasāda*) and lack of elation (*anudgharṣa*), the author of the *Vākya* has stated merely their definitions; the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which consists in their opposites, is established by implication—this is the intention of the author of the *Vākya*.

The "object of sorrow" (*śokavastu*) is the object that serves as the cause of sorrow, such as the death of a son in the past; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the cause of fear regarding the future is intended. For sorrow has the past as its domain, while fear has the future as its domain. "Lack of luster" (*abhāsvaratva*) is an explanation of the term "dejection" (*dainya*); it means dejection is defined as the state of being incapable of engaging in desired activities. Alternatively, "contrary to luster" is an adjective qualifying dejection; the particle *ca* (and) is displaced in order, meaning "and that which arises from it," i.e., dejection born of dejection.

Even when the misery of one's kinsmen is seen, there arises a state of wretchedness (*dainya*). This wretchedness is caused by the unfavorable conditions of place and time, as well as the recollection of objects of grief and the like; it consists in the mind’s lack of luminosity or its opposition to luminosity. Furthermore, "the wretchedness born of wretchedness" means the despondency of the mind. Alternatively, the passage may be construed as two separate sentences: the despondency of the mind, characterized by a lack of luminosity, is produced by the recollection of objects of grief and the unfavorable conditions of place and time. To the question, "What is being said here?", he replies: "The wretchedness born thereof."

That "luminosity" (*ābhāsvaratva*) and "dejection born from that" (*tajja-dainya*), which arises from the causes already mentioned—these two constitute a pair of sentences in the form of an explanation and that which is to be explained. The commentary passage beginning with "the opposite of that" (*tadviparyaya*) [clarifies this]. "By one who is weak" means by one who is deficient in mental strength. "Born from the opposite of that" means born from the lack of excellence regarding place, time, and the suitability of things such as the object of meditation, as well as from the lack of recollection. The sentence consists of only these words: "Contentment is elation" (*tuṣṭir uddharṣaḥ*); thus, "the opposite of that is non-elation" (*anuddharṣaḥ*) is established by implication.

Regarding the question of how there can be a requirement to abandon that which was prescribed in the words, "One whose self is restrained [should practice] study, purity, contentment, and austerity," he says here: "The meaning is that excessive contentment (*atisaṃtoṣa*) is also an obstacle. The sense is that not only is discontentment an obstacle, but excessive contentment is as well. Just as one's activity might otherwise be directed toward other objects, so too is contentment that becomes excessive; it is this that is said to be abandoned.

The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the etymological explanation also" (*nirvacanam api*) serves to include all [other] etymological explanations. Thus, the meanings of the words have been explained. Regarding the sentence beginning with "the attainment of that" (*tallabdhi*), he states the meaning of the sentence as follows: "Thus. By the separate mention of "one who is thus endowed with self-restraint" (*evam niyamayuktasya*) and "by the performance of duties prescribed for the stages of life" (*āśramavihitakarmanuṣṭhānena*), the division between the two alternatives consisting of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) is shown. By these two terms, mere tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, as well as mere ritual action (*karman*), are excluded. The meaning is that both tranquility and so forth, and ritual action, are to be practiced in combination as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).

The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that the accomplishment of knowledge occurs by that very means which you stated to be the instrument for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). The phrase "this is what is meant" signifies that such is the meaning of the sentence. To refute the interpretations favored by Śaṅkara and Yādavaprakāśa regarding the scripture, "Knowledge and ignorance," he takes up [that verse] with the words "And thus," intending to explain it. By this, both the necessity of ritual action and another scriptural passage devoid of the suffix *san* (denoting desire) are demonstrated.

Furthermore, the intention of the author who employs both the words *tathā* (thus) and *antara* (other/different) is that another Śruti passage—which was otherwise explained by you—is actually in accordance with the meaning we have stated. By the word *antara*, he intends to indicate the distinction of this sentence from those concerning sacrifices (*yajña*) and so forth, because it is endowed with [the quality of] being beneficial (*satrahita*). To the objection that no word denoting ritual action (*karman*) is heard in this sentence, he replies: "In this [sentence]."

In this scriptural passage—"But that which is the notion of the Self in what is not the Self," and so forth—the term *avidyā* (ignorance) may refer to the action (*karman*) prescribed for the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). To the question, "What is thereby stated?", he explains the meaning of the sentence by elucidating the other words as well, beginning with "by ignorance" (*avidyayā*). [The phrase] "by ignorance-action" (*avidyākarmaṇā*), and in the phrase "by knowledge-ignorance" (*vidyayājñānena*), the words "action" (*karman*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refer to the following: "Actions are the ripening of impurities; knowledge, however, is the supreme goal. (Gītā 4.37)

The Smṛti text, "When the *kaṣāya* has been ripened by actions, knowledge then arises," is thus recalled as being based on its own source. Actions are the ripening of *kaṣāya*; they are the causes for the ripening of *kaṣāya*. The word *kaṣāya* here refers to sin, because it has the same meaning as the phrase, "By dharma one casts off sin. Although the word *kaṣāya* can also refer to passion (*rāga*) and so forth, its status as a cause for ripening occurs through the removal of sin. Knowledge is the supreme goal, meaning it is the means to the supreme goal. In both cases, there is a metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause. The meaning is: "When the *kaṣāya* has been ripened, knowledge then proceeds," that is, it spreads forth.

In this context, it is clear that the function of action (*karman*) is to remove what is opposed to the means (*upāya*). For it has not been said that "liberation proceeds" or "the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) proceeds," but rather it has been stated simply that "knowledge (*jñāna*) proceeds. Relying on the meaning of this statement, [the author] says: "[Karma is] opposed to the arising of the knowledge of death. However, the meaning is that it is not opposed to the attainment of Brahman, nor is it opposed to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). That actions opposed to the goal (*upeya*) are to be dispelled by knowledge is established by hundreds of *śruti* and *smṛti* texts.

As it is said: "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8); likewise, "In this way, evil karma does not cling to the knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23); "And his actions are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8); "Having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 3.15); "By knowing the God, one is liberated from all sins" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.7); and "Just so, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes" (Gītā 4.37).

Thus, since it is heard that [ignorance] which is opposed to the goal (*upeya*) is to be removed by knowledge, and because the phrase "there is no other path" naturally excludes other means in order to eliminate what is opposed to the goal through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), there arises the undesirable consequence of restricting the scope of the word "other"—which refers to everything apart from the Veda—by including ritual action (*karman*) as a means under the view of equal combination (*samasamuccaya*). Furthermore, this is supported by the direct statement that ritual action is a cause for the means in the passage, "They desire to know by sacrifice," and by the harmony with the Smṛti text: "When the impurity has been cooked away by rituals, then knowledge arises. Thus, [the exclusion applies] in a general sense.

Even though [the word] *mṛtyu* is understood [in its general sense], it culminates in a specific form—namely, action that is opposed to the means [of liberation] and is to be discarded. Likewise, since the status of [sacrifices and so forth] as means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has already been refuted by arguments such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), and because by process of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) the meaning of the root and suffix in the word *vividiṣanti* (they desire to know) is perceived as the means for both knowledge and the desire for it without distinction, yet—in accordance with Smṛti texts such as "From that, knowledge proceeds"—there is a predominance of the desired object, which is the meaning of the verbal root.

Furthermore, because this has been determined by those learned in political ethics (*nīti*), it is established that [the word "death"] functions as a means for the realization of the primary sense [of the Self]. Therefore, the intention is that here it is precisely action (*karman*)—which is opposed to the means [of knowledge] and is to be removed by ignorance—that is denoted by the term "death. Since knowledge in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*) or renunciation (*nyāsa*) removes that which is opposed to the goal and would thus remove both subsequent and prior sins, the word "prior" (*prācīna*) was used to exclude that [knowledge].

The meaning is that the action which dispels what is opposed to skillful means pacifies only prior demerit (*pāpa*), but not subsequent evil; he explains the word "having crossed" (*tīrtvā*) by saying "having removed" (*apohya*), the sense being that it expresses attainment, as in the phrase "having crossed this bridge" (*na tvenaṃ setuṃ tīrtvā*).

By the explanation of the two words "having crossed over through ignorance" (*avidyayā tīrtvā*), the interpretation according to the system of Śaṅkara is excluded; for his interpretation is that one remains having reached transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) by means of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Furthermore, in his view, ignorance is to be known as something to be abandoned (*heya*). Alternatively, the interpretation favored by Śaṅkara might be that the word "ignorance" refers to ritual action (*karman*) which obstructs the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); or the interpretation favored by Yādavaprakāśa is that the word "ignorance" refers to ritual action which obstructs the attainment of the goal (*upeya*); [or it may mean] that which is opposed to the arising of knowledge.

The exclusion of both [karma and ignorance] is achieved by the explanation of the word "death" (*mṛtyu*). One might ask: "Why could this word 'ignorance' (*avidyā*) not refer to the lack of knowledge that is the cause of *saṃsāra*, and how could it have the meaning of 'action'? To this, he says: "crossing over death. The intended meaning is that the root *tṛ* (to cross) naturally signifies "crossing over," whereas if it were taken to mean "attaining," its natural sense would be violated.

The word *avidyā* denotes action; the intention is that it means "that which is other than knowledge" (*vidyetarat*), where the negative particle (*nañ*) has the sense of "other than that. By the restrictive particle (*eva*) in the phrase "only prescribed action," ignorance (*ajñāna*) and un-prescribed action are excluded. Here, the two words "and" (*ca*) in the verse "knowledge and ignorance" (*vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca*) signify a conjunction of items not explicitly mentioned.

That which is connected with action (*karmānubandhi*) is victory; that which is not explicitly mentioned must be understood as being conjoined by the word "and" (*ca*). That which is connected with knowledge (*vidyānubandhi*) consists of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth; that which is connected with action consists of the absence of desire for fruits and the absence of the conceit of agency, and both of these are to be conjoined by the word "and. Alternatively, just as in the verse, "In dharma, in artha, in kāma, and in mokṣa, O bull among the Bharatas," the word "and" conjoins items, here too the two instances of "and" may serve to conjoin things that are contrary to what has been stated.

By means of the two "ca" (and) particles, that which is opposed to knowledge (*vidyā*) and that which is opposed to action (*karman*) are conjoined as things to be known for the purpose of abandonment. *Vidyā* refers to the knowledge of Brahman; its opposites are the cognitions of objects other than that [Brahman] and attachment, aversion, and so forth toward those objects. *Avidyā* refers to action that is an auxiliary to knowledge; its opposite is action accompanied by the desire for fruits and so forth, which is the cause of transmigratory existence, as well as sin (*pāpa*). The intention of the two "ca" particles is that both of these are to be known for the purpose of abandonment.

Alternatively, the two words *ca* may serve to indicate each individual term (*pratipadadyotaka*), just as in the expression "in dharma, in artha, and in kāma," where the function of indicating the conjunction of what is denoted by each term is called "indicating each term. That same function would apply here as well; furthermore, in this sentence, he shows a corroborative statement (*upabṛṃhaṇavacana*) for the purpose of establishing that the words "crossing over ignorance" (*avidyātaraṇa*) refer to the meaning already stated, saying "as it has been said. "Taking refuge in knowledge" (*jñānavyapāśrayaḥ*) means by virtue of the knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*).

"Having taken recourse to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā)" means having adopted meditative knowledge (*upāsanā-ātmaka-jñāna*) as the goal to be accomplished. When there is a desire to understand the difference in meaning between the words *jñāna* and *vidyā*, it is indeed appropriate to interpret them as referring to those two types of knowledge produced by discrimination (*viveka*) and other means arising from scripture (*āgama*), since they are the subject under discussion.

By the phrase "to cross over death" (*tartuṃ mṛtyum*), the suspicion that the root *tṛ* (to cross) signifies "attaining" is dispelled; for Keśidhvaja, the king who was a knower of Brahman, did not perform sacrifices and other rites in order to attain saṃsāra. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the word "death" (*mṛtyu*) refers to those actions that obstruct the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), because by the phrase "having taken refuge in knowledge" (*jñānavyapāśrayaḥ*), possession of the knowledge produced by the scriptures is expressed, and because it is said "having established himself in the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyām adhiṣṭhāya*); for it is certainly not said "having established himself in the desire for the knowledge of Brahman."

In response to the doubt—namely, how it is that "ancient karma" is said to be opposed to the arising of knowledge when the word *karman* (karma) is used in a general sense common to both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*), whereas the Śruti states, "By dharma one casts off evil," thus declaring that only a specific type of karma consisting of demerit is to be cast off—the author says, "and because it is opposed to knowledge," in order to demonstrate that even in that context the word "evil" refers to both merit and demerit, and to establish that both of these are denotable by the term "evil" (*pāpa*) by showing that both are obstacles to the arising of knowledge.

Furthermore, if both merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*) are equally opposed to knowledge upon the cessation of doubt, how is it that scripture declares one—the demerit—to be something to be discarded, while the other—the merit—is that which discards [demerit]? To this he says: "Of both as well. The intended meaning is that what is meant to be removed is both of these two, whereas the remover is specifically another form of dharma that is free from attachment to fruits and the like.

How is it that both [the Veda and the killing of a Brahmin] are denoted by the word "pāpa" (evil)? To this he says: "Upon the arising of the knowledge of Brahman... The phrase "by way of having an undesirable result" indicates the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*). The intended meaning is that *pāpatva* (the state of being evil) consists in being a unique cause of an undesirable result while being something non-worldly (*alaukika*). For this very reason, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to weapons and the like, nor to the Lord (*Īśvara*), as it is said: "O Maitreya, for one whose mind is fixed on Vāsudeva during recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth, even the status of Indra and other such fruits are obstacles."

By such passages as, "These indeed, O dear one, are hells for the abode of the Supreme Self," it is established that even merit yields undesirable results for one who seeks liberation. Furthermore, the Śruti, concluding its discussion by referring to previously mentioned merit (*sukṛta*) with the term "evil" (*pāpman*), states: "Neither day nor night cross this bridge; neither old age, nor death, nor sorrow, nor merit, nor evil—indeed, all evils turn back from here."

Furthermore, the word *pāpa* does not have as its object other unspecified evils; for since the word *duṣkṛta* is commonly understood to apply to all sins collectively, it is impossible for it to refer to other unspecified evils. Even if such were possible, the word *pāpman* does not have as its object only those other unspecified evils, because in the immediately following sentence—"This world of Brahman is indeed free from evil (*apahatapāpmā*)"—which is employed in agreement with the cessation of all things to be abandoned that were previously mentioned, we see that the word *pāpman* refers to all things to be abandoned.

For the statement of the cessation of only a few unspecified evils does not establish the correspondence with the cessation of all things to be abandoned (*heya*). Even though the word *pāpa* (evil) is used figuratively in the case of grief and so forth, its primary sense must not be discarded here, because the possibility of engaging in good deeds (*sukṛta*) and turning away from evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*) exists; for there is no rule that what is used figuratively in one instance must be used figuratively everywhere. Therefore, in the phrase "all evils," the term refers to those characterized by sin through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), according to the maxim of the "parasol-bearer" (*chatrinyāya*); however, in the phrase "by dharma [one overcomes] evil," it retains its primary sense alone.

How is it that evil (*pāpa*) is opposed to knowledge? To address the doubt that this is understood [to be the case] only for *rajas* and *tamas*, he states that there is no contradiction because of the relationship between the door and the one who uses the door (*dvāradvāribhāva*). Once it is established by authoritative means (*prāmāṇika*) that both evil and *rajas-tamas* are opposed to knowledge, the relationship of door and door-keeper is postulated; thus he says, "And of evil... Now, might this scriptural passage not rather concern the desire to lead downward (*nirayaninīṣā*), since leading downward is the opposite of leading upward? We reply: what is intended here is that [evil] is a cause for leading upward, in the form of bringing about meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

Nor should it be suspected that "leading upwards" (*unnayana*) means leading to heaven and the like; for the "leading upwards from all these worlds," as understood from the passage "him he leads up from these worlds," consists in the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*). If it is argued that, in that case, "leading downwards" (*avanayana*) would mean leading to the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—consisting of conception, birth, old age, death, and so forth—and thus there would be no contradiction with meditative worship (*upāsana*), we say no. This is because it is understood that "leading upwards" functions by way of generating knowledge, as seen in the introductory statement: "Worship me, whom you consider the most beneficial for man."

For it is understood that the meditation intended to be performed is the immediate means [to liberation]; other scriptural passages such as "There is no other path" also convey this. That [immediacy] would be contradicted if actions were an immediate means toward liberation; therefore, since there is no contradiction with the introductory statements (*upakrama*) and other criteria, it is determined that good actions serve as a means toward liberation only by way of meditation. Consequently, the status of actions as causes for elevation consists in their producing meditation.

It is very clearly understood that the opposite of that—downward leading—is of the nature of an obstacle to meditation. Furthermore, although upward and downward leading consist in causing one to reach heaven or hell respectively, nevertheless, it is established that unwholesome actions are antagonistic to knowledge. For, if the two dispositions of desiring to lead up and desiring to lead down were causeless, it would follow that the Supreme Self is partial and cruel; therefore, those two dispositions must have as their object the conduct of sentient beings.

It is understood that [the Lord] has as His object those who perform extremely abundant merit and demerit, which serve as the causes for the desire to lead [beings] to the two destinies. And in that regard, the Lord’s role as the instigator of the successive good and evil actions sufficient to bring about those two destinies does not occur independently of the intellect of the individual soul (*jīva*), as is the case with possession by spirits (*bhūtāveśa*) and the like. For if that were so, due to the absence of knowledge, volition, and other such factors, transmigrating beings would lack subjection to the scriptures—just like grass blown by wind or water—and the experience of the fruits of their actions would be impossible.

Thus, the two statements beginning with "He alone" (*eṣa eva*)—which are supported by the reasoning that the transmigrating souls' status as enjoyers of the fruits of their actions would otherwise be inexplicable—are understood to concern the Lord's role as the causal agent (*kārayitṛtva*) through the medium of bestowing knowledge; this being so, it also accords with the Smṛti: "The gods do not protect [people] by taking up a staff like herdsmen. Whomsoever they wish to protect, they endow with intelligence; but for whomsoever the gods ordain defeat... (*Mahābhārata*, Śāntiparvan 178.32–33).

For it is said: "The intellect of one who has been drawn away perishes once it is led astray. Likewise: "Virtue, when practiced again and again, increases wisdom; but a man whose wisdom is lost constantly undertakes only evil. In this context, the intended meaning is the production of a cognition contrary to reality preceded by the loss of right knowledge—expressed as "they draw away the intellect" and "they destroy wisdom"—because otherwise, the commencement of another action would be impossible.

Although this collection of statements pertains generally to all deities, nevertheless, because the knowledge of the Blessed One is not outside the scope of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), it is established that unwholesome action is its opposite. Furthermore, it is stated specifically: "I bestow upon them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me; but the deluded ones, having entered demonic wombs birth after birth, fail to reach Me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state."

Thus, by this scripture, which is reinforced by logic and tradition, it is established that evil actions are indeed obstacles to knowledge. This interpretation is more appropriate than the previous one, as it accords with the context. In this way, the evidence for the fact that sin is an obstacle to knowledge has been shown. Now, he demonstrates the evidence for the fact that rajas and tamas are obstacles to knowledge, and that sattva is the cause of knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "of rajas and tamas," [the author] asks: "What follows from that for the subject at hand, which is the requirement of action? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataśca*). "Therefore" means because of the statement that sin is an obstacle to knowledge. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And its removal" (*tannirasanañca*). Fearing the objection that—since both merit and demerence, denoted by the term "sin," are equally to be removed—it would be impossible to perform an action that removes only demerit, he states: "by that which has no intended fruit. By this, actions that yield fruits such as heaven are excluded.

The sense is that [liberation occurs] through practice, and not by mere knowledge alone. To the question "What is the authority for this?", he says: "And so says the Śruti. Now, regarding the meaning of this sentence which has been cited as authoritative evidence for the specific refuter, the meaning of the word expressing the object to be refuted within this sentence has already been explained; the meaning of the word expressing the refuter has been stated immediately thereafter.

Now, one might ask: why should this word *dharma* not refer exclusively to duties in the form of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*? On what basis is it determined that its subject matter is *dharma* whose fruit is not intentionally sought? It is said [in response]: "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting"; "peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn, and patient"; "when the impurity has been cooked away by actions, then knowledge arises"; "sacrifice, charity, and austerity—action is not to be abandoned; it must indeed be performed"; "sacrifice, charity, and austerity are indeed purifiers."

Since sacrifices, gifts, austerity, tranquility (*śama*), and so forth—stated in Vedic and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) such as "tranquility, self-control, austerity, and purity" as requirements for one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*)—are heard here; and since this section has as its subject matter the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), as seen in passages such as "from realization comes bliss, the source of Brahman," it is understood that the word "dharma" refers here to those duties whose fruits are not intended (*anabhisaṃhita-phala*) and which are required by one desiring liberation.

In this context, within the sequence of sacrifices, gifts, and so forth, the mention of worldly fruits—such as in the passage, "By giving, enemies become friends"—should be understood as referring to incidental results that are conducive to the knowledge of Brahman, similar to the statement, "He becomes possessed of food and an eater of food. This is because the primary fruit is heard in the text: "O wise one, you shall not go to death again."

Furthermore, although this statement is not intended solely for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), it cannot be intended solely for those not seeking liberation either, because the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are common to both. For "the state of being a source of desired results" is not the meaning of the word *dharma*; rather, the meaning would be: "one should dispel the uncommon cause of undesirable [results] by means of the uncommon means for achieving the uncommonly desired [result] that is beyond worldly experience. Consequently, with respect to one seeking liberation, since optional action (*kāmyakarman*) results in undesirable fruits, it is unfit to be denoted by the word *dharma* and is, in fact, included within what is denoted by the word *pāpa* (sin).

It would have been stated that, by the force of the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), both merit and demerit are to be removed by means of dharma whose fruit is not intentionally sought. He concludes that knowledge is dependent upon action with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*). This is because of the statements of the Śruti, the Smṛti, the logical arguments supporting them, and the authors of the Sūtras and Vākyas. Having kept in mind that it will be explained later how all those belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama*) possess the qualification for meditation (*upāsanā*)—which has as its constituent parts the specific duties of their respective stages—in order to remove obstacles to the means [of liberation], he stated that [knowledge] is dependent on the actions of all stages of life.

Then, in response to the inquiry, "What, then, is the status of the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) as a prerequisite for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*)?", he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Because the performance of rituals depends upon knowledge, and because knowledge is dependent upon Mīmāṃsā, the inquiry into that [ritual] is a prerequisite. He explains: "Therefore," because the knowledge of Brahman depends upon the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) performed without desire for rewards; for knowledge is either for the purpose of abandoning or for the purpose of acquiring. Here, however, it is for both purposes, as he says: "dependent. Abandoning occurs by way of the result [of the object], while acquiring occurs in its own nature.

Since the term *mīmāṃsā* applies to both the earlier and later [parts], it was stated that [the truth] is to be understood through *karmamīmāṃsā*; the meaning is that "that very same [system] which was rejected by you as contradictory" is what is being referred to. Furthermore, with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth, that which was stated by the opponent to be unnecessary is said to be necessary, while that which was stated by the opponent to be necessary is said to be unnecessary.

The phrase "and [the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities]"—the word *ca* (and) has the sense of *pratyuta* (on the contrary), meaning that without hearing the Mīmāṃsā, that is, without hearing the Mīmāṃsā of Karma and Brahman—they will not be accomplished. By the expression "will not be accomplished," their posteriority is stated. To the question "Why?", he says "Phala... etc. "Phalaviśeṣaḥ" means the specific fruit consisting of enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). "Karaṇaviśeṣaḥ" means the specific instruments such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and meditation (*upāsanā*). "Itikartavyatāviśeṣaḥ" means the specific procedures such as the *prayāja* offerings, as well as the sevenfold means (*sādhanasaptaka*).

The specific types of qualified practitioners (*adhikāriviśe�ṣa*) are those who desire worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*). Apart from their respective certainties, the nature of action (*karmasvarūpa*) consists of that which is of the nature of sacrifice (*yajñātmaka*) along with its auxiliary limbs, and that which is of the nature of meditation (*upāsanātmaka*). The Commentator (Śaṅkara) will indeed state that action is both of the nature of sacrifice and of the nature of meditation; for instance, he will cite the sūtra, "And there is illumination in action through practice," and his commentary on it: "In action consisting of meditation."

The status of meditation (*upāsana*) as an action (*karman*) arises because, being of the nature of a continuous stream of recollection (*smṛti-santati*), it is accomplished through effort. To this effect, Manu has stated: "Through verbal defects of action one attains the state of birds and wild animals; through mental ones, the state of the lowest castes; and through bodily defects of action, a man goes to the state of stationary beings. Thus he spoke of "mental defects of action," and the fruit is twofold—both worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*)—depending on whether those qualities such as stability, instability, permanence, and so forth, are permanent or impermanent.

By the word "etc. (ādi), it is intended to include such qualities as the nature of knowledge and bliss, as well as the fact that the selves consist of liberation (*nirvāṇamaya*), as previously stated. If it is argued that here the reason (*hetu*) appears to be non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*), we say: not so. In Mīmāṃsā, the conclusion reached for each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) through its respective logical principles regarding the fruit, the instrument, the procedure, and so forth, constitutes the reason. Thus, the probandum is the valid cognition (*pramiti*) concerning the means and the end, which is produced by a collection of scriptural statements supported by the logical principles of those various topical sections.

The meaning is that the ascertainment of the meaning of the great sentence, which consists of the collection of those [meanings], is to be accomplished through the ascertainment of the meanings of each respective subordinate sentence. This is not like the case where it is said that the ascertainment of the sentence-meaning results from the ascertainment of the word-meanings, for [in that case] there would be no distinction between the means and the end to be accomplished.

For this very reason, after the means (*karaṇa*), the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), and so forth were previously explained separately by their respective terms, they are subsequently mentioned by the term "the nature of action" (*karma-svarūpa*). It would be improper to claim that the *bhāṣya* passage beginning with "the fruit and the means" pertains exclusively to the *Karma-mīmāṃsā*, because it is inappropriate to speak of the permanence or impermanence of the fruits of those actions, as well as the eternality of the Self and other such matters. Furthermore, since the word "Mīmāṃsā" without qualification is used in the *bhāṣya*—in passages such as "the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra"—to refer to both parts [of the system], the meaning is exactly as stated: therefore, [this inquiry] occurs subsequent to the investigations into both action (*karman*) and Brahman.

The discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, followed by dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*), and the perfection of the means such as tranquility and self-restraint (*śama*, *dama*, etc.)—for the nature of these means, beginning with tranquility and self-restraint, is indeed defined in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā by the rule, "One should be endowed with tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. If this quartet were already established, then the inquiry into Brahman would follow; yet if the inquiry into Brahman were required for their establishment, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). Therefore, it is untenable for that which occurs later to be a prerequisite.

If it is argued that the mere superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) arising from the study and recitation of the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) constitutes the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*), that is incorrect; for such a superficial understanding is not the cause of dispassion toward the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, nor of the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*), since it is [in fact] a perception of the eternal and the non-eternal in a state of inversion.
