Furthermore, while initial intuition is common to both parts [of the inquiry], it is more appropriate to engage first in the inquiry into action (*karma*), because the desire to know remains in both cases and there is no reason to bypass the first. Moreover, the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*) and so forth cannot be established even by another scripture; for, due to the force of the injunction to study one's own Veda (*adhyayanavidhi*), a person has no opportunity for other scriptures at the very outset.

Furthermore, in other treatises, many doctrines contrary to the Vedānta are found, such as the view that atoms are the cause, that the Pradhāna (primordial matter) consisting of Brahman is the cause, that space and so forth are eternal, and that the Lord is merely the efficient cause. Therefore, the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities produced by other treatises—being in contradiction with the Vedānta—cannot have preceded the inquiry into the Vedānta.

Furthermore, since other treatises establish that the knowledge of six categories, sixteen categories, and so forth, is a means to liberation, and because they render the hearing of Vedānta unnecessary, it is not logical to claim that the discrimination (*viveka*) arising from those [treatises] must have occurred previously; for it is stated here and there: "Dharma is that which results in the attainment of prosperity and the highest good (*abhyudaya-niḥśreyasa*)," and "The attainment of the highest good comes from the knowledge of the true nature of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)."

Furthermore, the Śruti itself—in the passage, "Therefore, one who knows thus, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, should see the Self in the very Self"—refers to knowledge produced by the scripture by the word "one who knows thus," and teaches tranquility (śama) and the other qualities as auxiliary members (aṅga) to the meditation (upāsana) undertaken through the injunction "he should see. Therefore, the position that tranquility and the rest must precede hearing (śravaṇa) is contrary to the Śruti; as for the Śruti passage beginning with "to those of peaceful mind," it has been stated that its purpose is to bring about the concentration necessary for hearing.

If it is argued that the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*) arises from hearing the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, then, since the nature of Brahman would be understood from those very sources, the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*) would be unnecessary to begin. If it is countered that because there is an abundance of doubt and error even in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, the inquiry into Brahman is required to dispel them, [we reply: for that very reason of the abundance of doubt and error, the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal is also difficult to achieve therein; thus, it is not logical that the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) should have preceded [the inquiry].

Regarding the statement that "those which abide in the eternal and the non-eternal are the eternal and non-eternal entities (nityānityavastūni)," i.e., their properties (taddharmāḥ), Vācaspati has explained: the eternity and reality of the eternal substratum (dharmin) follow from that very fact, and for that reason alone it is to be accepted (upādeya); the non-eternity and unreality of the non-eternal substratum follow from that very fact, and for that reason alone it is to be rejected (heya). Thus, the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal substrata and their respective properties is what constitutes "discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal entities" (nityānityavastuviveka).

To this we reply: first, the unreality of the impermanent should be understood as having been refuted by the method to be explained [later]. Furthermore, both [the claims] that "whatever is permanent is to be accepted" and "whatever is impermanent is to be rejected" are untenable. This is because we observe the cognition of acceptability only in the case of pleasure, the cessation of suffering, the means to those, and what is conducive to them; and we observe the cognition of non-acceptability only for that which is distinct from these. Even if something were permanent, if it were of the nature of suffering or a cause of suffering, it would be perceived simply as something to be rejected; it is not [to be rejected] if it is neither of these two.

If it is argued that if something were neglected, and if even an impermanent thing were of the nature of happiness or a cause of happiness, it would be accepted; whereas for one who investigates, it is to be rejected—this is not so. For when there is no perception of another superior happiness, no realization that it is achieved through extreme suffering, and no realization that it results in future suffering, even for the investigator, the notion of its acceptability is observed. A grain of rice is discarded upon obtaining a meal of milk-rice; food mixed with poison is discarded out of fear of death; but garlands, sandalwood, and the like are [retained] over those [other things].

Even that which is limited is accepted because it brings about the attainment of excellent pleasure and because it lacks the accompaniment of intense suffering at its beginning and end; therefore, the fact that the impermanent is to be rejected is not caused by its mere impermanence. If it were argued that the permanent is to be accepted because it consists of pleasure unmixed with suffering, while the impermanent is to be rejected because such [pleasure] is impossible, [that would be incorrect].

It is asked: Is the nature of the eternal as consisting of pleasure unmixed with suffering understood through logical pervasion (*vyāpti*), or from scripture (*śāstra*)? Not the first, because we do not observe that time and other such eternal things possess the nature of pleasure, nor do we observe that the eternal self possesses the nature of pleasure unmixed with suffering; for suffering is indeed experienced by the self in the form, "I am suffering."

If it is from scripture (*śāstra*), does that mean it is knowledge derived from the Veda? And is that [knowledge] merely superficial (*āpātajñāna*), or is it of the nature of valid cognition (*pramiti*)? In the first case, since it would be common to both the *karma* and *brahma* sections, it would be illogical for it to be a prerequisite for the inquiry into Brahman by bypassing the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*). If it were of the nature of certainty, it would constitute the fruit of both parts of Mīmāṃsā; furthermore, if its source were another tradition (*āgama*), it would be useless due to contradiction, and because it would be independent of this [Vedic] system, it could not be a prerequisite. To this, it is said: "That which is eternal is to be adopted."

The understanding is not as follows—that eternal happiness is to be accepted if it is possible, while that which is impermanent is to be rejected when such [eternal] happiness exists—but rather, it must be stated that the knowledge of the possibility of eternal happiness is useful for the inquiry into Brahman by way of generating the desire to obtain that eternal fruit. Since there is no obstacle to the possibility of an eternal fruit in other scriptures and in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) of the Veda, those too would have to be commenced immediately after the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal; for in them, an eternal fruit is indeed perceived.

If it is argued that [the Vedas] are non-existent, that non-existence would have to arise either from a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) or from being intended for something else (*anyaparatva*). Since neither of these two can be established without the *Mīmāṃsā*, its status as a prerequisite must be accepted. If it is argued that the first aphorism is intended to indicate that [status], we say no; for that aphorism is concerned with the subject matter and purpose pertaining to the commencement of its own system, and thus lacks the intent to establish the lack of authority of other systems.

If it is argued that its lack of authority and so forth are intended because they are useful for one's own purpose, then it follows that the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*) and the section on reasoning (*tarkapāda*) must precede it, since those are required to establish the basis upon which this [present work] depends. For the lack of authority of other scriptures is to be understood from the first section of the *Karmamīmāṃsā* through contradictions with other passages and the like; the determination that the eternal fruits are not intended to be expressed depends on the principles found therein; and the defects in the subject matter of other scriptures will be demonstrated in the *Tarkapāda*.

Furthermore, if the understanding that other systems lack an eternal fruit is derived from the very first sūtra itself, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the engagement in the inquiry into Brahman depends on the understanding that other systems lack an eternal fruit, while that understanding depends on the engagement in the inquiry into Brahman.

This being the case, one should not suspect a circular argument even regarding the *dharmajijñāsā* sūtra; for it is possible for a person who has completed the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*)—prompted by the injunctions of his father and others—to engage in the inquiry simply through the initial apprehension of a purposeful meaning. A circular argument would apply only to those for whom the investigation of Dharma is mandatory (*vaidha*), wherein there would be the cycle: "from the knowledge of its mandatory nature comes the inquiry, and from the inquiry comes the knowledge of its mandatory nature."

Furthermore, it must be explained how the knowledge that fruits are impermanent and subject to abandonment serves the inquiry into Brahman by way of generating a desire to renounce fruits such as heaven; for how is it understood that the fruit of heaven and the like is impermanent and intermingled with suffering? If it is understood through another scripture, then since the attainment of the eternal human goal would be accomplished therein, there would be no further need (nairākāṅkṣya), and thus the commencement of the inquiry into Brahman would be impossible; consequently, its status as a prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*) is untenable.

If [you argue that] "whatever is happiness is impermanent" based merely on your own speculative reasoning, then the inquiry into Brahman would be obstructed by that very [reasoning], since it would preclude the possibility of a permanent human goal (*puruṣārtha*). [Objection: It is not impossible for there to be a permanent human goal, because the cessation of suffering lacks an end, and because innate happiness, being an eternal entity from beginningless time, logically possesses the quality of being endless. [Reply: This is not so. If it is the cessation of suffering, then it is necessarily accompanied by suffering, because it is a cessation of suffering, like anything currently accepted as such. If it is happiness, then [it must be impermanent] precisely because it is happiness.

Because it is difficult for those who rely solely on logic to establish the possibility of the eternal human goal through the mere fabrication of fallacious reasoning such as "it is created," one might argue that the determination of pervasion (*vyāpti*) concerns both the eternal and its opposite as established by scripture. If this is claimed, it is not so; for there would arise the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the determination of pervasion would be preceded by the hearing of the Vedānta, and the hearing of the Vedānta would be preceded by that determination of pervasion. Therefore, regarding the inquiry into Brahman, for the sake of employing the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal attributes, [the following is stated] in the division of the eternal and the non-eternal:

Since perception does not apply [to this matter], since reasoning is over-extensive, since other scriptures result in a lack of expectancy for the inquiry into Brahman, and since they are useless as they contradict that [Veda], the Veda alone must be accepted as the authority. Furthermore, because the superficial understanding (*āpātapratīti*) therein is common to both parts [of the Veda], and because the determination of the eternal and the non-eternal is the fruit of the two-fold Mīmāṃsā, the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is insurmountable; therefore, it is incorrect to say that "the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities" consists in the knowledge of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding the eternal and the non-eternal.

As for the objection raised—that since there is no prohibitor of the possibility of eternal results in other scriptures, it would follow that one who possesses the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānitya-viveka*) and so forth might still engage in those [other systems]—that is incorrect. For the first Sūtra serves as a prohibitor of other scriptures, and thus the meaning of the Sūtra is that Brahman alone is to be investigated, not *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. This is untenable;

for this meaning is not accepted by those who maintain that the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) must precede [the inquiry]. This meaning was stated by those who maintain that the knowledge of the "three-fold affliction" (*tāpatraya*) must precede it, yet this meaning is not logically consistent.

For it must be stated that this matter is neither taught nor commanded by the author of the Sūtras, but rather established; for the Sūtras are based on reasoning (*nyāya*). And does this establishment consist in the weakness of other systems, or in the strength of one's own system, or in both combined? It cannot be the first, because if one's own system were weak, even Brahman would not be an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). Nor can it be the second, because if another system were stronger, the very status of Brahman as an object of inquiry would not be established.

Regarding the third [point], the Sūtra would be redundant, because both [the authoritativeness of the Veda and its capacity to denote Brahman] are established by the *codanāsūtra* and others within the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* itself; furthermore, it would follow that [the *Brahmasūtra*] is merely a continuation of that [previous system], since it is necessarily dependent upon it. If it is argued: "Even though the mere authoritativeness of the Veda is established, the authoritativeness regarding Brahman is not established by that alone," then those reasons by which the doubt arises regarding the impossibility of the Veda's authoritativeness concerning Brahman must be refuted—and these are the arguments such as the impossibility of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) with respect to an already established entity (*siddha*). Therefore, by refuting those [arguments], [authoritativeness] regarding Brahman...

If [the *Sāṅkhya*] were intent upon establishing the authority of the Vedānta, our own position would have been adopted; for that very reason, the claim that the knowledge of the affliction by the threefold suffering is a prerequisite has also been refuted. To explain: is the knowledge of suffering in this world the prerequisite? Or is it the knowledge of suffering in hell? Or is it the knowledge that even heaven and the like are included within the threefold suffering due to their being meager and unstable? Not the first, because the means for its removal are understood through Āyurveda and other sciences, making inquiry into the Vedānta unnecessary.

The second [alternative] is not tenable, because there is an abundance of scriptures that enjoin vows and observances which remove the sins that are the causes of the suffering of hell, and thus they are independent of the Vedānta. As for the third, there would indeed be a dependence on the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*); for one who is already subject to the injunction to study [the Veda] from the very beginning lacks any opportunity to understand other scriptures. Even if such an opportunity were present, since the means to liberation is understood through those very same scriptures—which indicate that heaven and the like are limited and impermanent—there is independence from the Vedānta. This is so even regarding those [scriptures] that propound meanings contrary to the Vedānta.

Since it is impossible for the comprehension of those [qualities] to be preceded by the knowledge of Vedānta, and since ordinary perception (*āpātapratīti*)—as well as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—is a cause for the opposite cognition of what is small and transient versus what is infinite and eternal, the fixed order [of the means] was stated based on their nature as things to be explained first. Now, its establishment is also stated based on their nature as things to be explained [in this work]: "Of these" means of these [means] such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth. "The state of being a means" (*sādhanatvam*), with the particle *ca* used in a conjunctive sense, is to be understood from their application (*viniyoga*). Application is the making known of their status as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*).

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And its application. To the further question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that is [discussed] in the third [chapter]. This means it is stated in the third chapter. This has been stated for the sake of illustration, because the inquiry into Brahman (brahmavicāra) depends upon all the logical principles stated in the inquiry into ritual action (karmavicāra). For these are indeed the subject matters (prameya) of the chapters of the Mīmāṃsā of Action: in the first chapter, the definition of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa) was treated.

In the second chapter, the distinction between scriptures or the distinction between ritual acts is established, along with the grounds for such distinction: difference of words, repetition, number, quality, context, and name. In the third chapter, the nature of subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) is defined, as well as the means of proof that indicate subsidiarity: direct assertion (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*). In the fourth chapter, by defining the distinction between what subserves the sacrifice and what subserves the person, the application of elements subserving the sacrifice through those subserving the person is determined.

In the fifth [book], the order [of performance] is treated; the authorities for that order are *śruti*, *artha*, *pāṭha*, *pravṛtti*, *mukhya*, and *kāṇḍa*. In the sixth, the determination of the qualified performer (*adhikārin*) is set forth. In the seventh, general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*) is defined. In the eighth, specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*). In the ninth, modification (*ūha*). In the tenth, sublation (*bādha*). In the eleventh and twelfth, the principles of the archetypal sacrifice (*tantra*) and incidental application (*prasaṅga*) are discussed. As it has been said: "The inquiry into Dharma [is conducted] through the distinctions of the subject matter, the means of knowledge, the divisions, the subsidiary elements, the application, the order, and the ritual acts, along with extension, specificity, modification, sublation, the archetypal sacrifice, and incidental application."

This dependence upon the *Nyāya-sūtras* and this dependence upon the *Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa* are to be observed here and there within the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*). Therefore, it was stated [in the previous section] for the purpose of demonstrating that [the *Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa*] belongs to the third [section of the Vedas]. Now, as a supplementary argument regarding the dependence on the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), the subsequent author states the connection by way of a contextual transition (*prasaṅga*) with the words "the Udgītha, etc."; however, in this [present] case, the direct connection is established by the words "even those intended for the success of ritual action."

The statement of the author of the *Vākya* (Bodhāyana), "For the sake of the prosperity of ritual action, that is its purpose, because of the etymological derivation," has been recalled [in the sense that] "they have the form of the vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭirūpāṇi*). The "vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭi*) is the vision of Brahmanhood in what is not Brahman; the meaning is that, because they have the form of the vision of Brahman, they depend upon the knowledge of Brahman. The particle *iti* indicates a reason: these are to be considered here [in this inquiry into Brahman] and not in the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*). The phrase "those rituals as well" means those meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth which are for the sake of the prosperity of those rituals.

The phrase "having results not intended" means that, because their results are not intended, they give rise to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). The word "iti" here indicates a reason. "The excellence of producing that [result]" refers to the excellence of bringing about [the conditions for] that [knowledge], namely, the quality of bestowing the fruit quickly even when powerful obstacles are present. Thus, the meaning is that they swiftly accomplish the knowledge of Brahman by producing that excellence.

These meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth are therefore even more appropriately connected here; for while their presence in the mind arises from similarity and the like due to their lack of utility for the primary subject, "connection" (*saṅgati*) consists in dependence on one or both [of the two topics], which constitutes direct connection. In this case, however, it has been established that both are required, as these meditations take the form of viewing [the *udgītha*, etc. as Brahman; thus, the dependence of the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth upon the knowledge of Brahman is stated.

The phrase "which produce the knowledge of Brahman" indicates that the inquiry into the knowledge of Brahman is stated to depend upon meditations such as the *udgītha*; with this intention, the word "sutarām" (all the more) is used. The meaning is that because these [meditations] exist here [in the Vedānta] in relation to both [the knowledge of Brahman and ritual action], the connection is all the more appropriate here, and not in the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*).

Now, one might ask: how is it that the inquiry into the *udgītha* and so forth has a particularly close connection (*saṅgati*) with the inquiry into Brahman alone? It has an equally close connection even with the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*), for a connection common to both is indeed a "particularly close" connection. This is because the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth depend upon the constituent parts of ritual action; thus, the inquiry into them requires the inquiry into ritual action. Furthermore, rituals themselves require the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth for their own successful fulfillment. Since this mutual dependence exists, [the inquiry into the *udgītha* connects with both].

It is said: the requirement for meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth for the sake of the perfection of ritual action (*karmasamṛddhi*) is equal for both mere rituals and rituals that are auxiliary members of knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, the reason "being for the sake of the perfection of ritual action" is a common one. The reason "having as its basis the constituent parts of ritual action" is the uncommon reason for the connection with the inquiry into the first part [of the Veda]. The reason "dependence upon the knowledge of Brahman" is the uncommon reason for the connection with the inquiry into the second part [of the Veda].

Thus, although there is equality in possessing both common and uncommon causes, meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—consisting of the "vision of Brahman" (*brahmadṛṣṭi*)—are dependent upon the knowledge of Brahman; without that, such contemplation is impossible. For in the investigation of the first part [of the Vedas], an inquiry into Brahman is not possible prior to the inquiry into ritual action (*karma*), because those two are characterized by the specific relationship previously mentioned. However, in the second part [of the Vedas], since the knowledge of Brahman is easily accessible, it is possible to contemplate meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth even for one who has not yet performed an inquiry into ritual action.

For this very reason, because they are possible, the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth are enjoined in the Upaniṣadic portion [of the Veda] and are likewise investigated in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*. Thus, since the requirement for both [the Upaniṣads and the *Mīmāṃsā*], which is distinguished by these three differences—being enjoined in the Vedānta portion, being investigated in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, and being possible—exists only in the latter portion [of the Veda], it follows that the connection based upon that exists even more strongly there alone; with this intention, it was said: "They are connected here all the more."

And this is an additional reason: since even a subordinate subject matter is directly connected [to the inquiry], an investigation of karma is necessarily required for it as well; thus, the "primary reason"—consisting in the fact that what is primarily set forth must necessarily be expected—has already been stated. To the question, "What then follows from this regarding the immediate sequence of the present topic? he says: "Or rather, of those... (teṣāṃ vā).

Regarding those meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, there is universal agreement that they are directly connected [to the ritual action]; for when the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is to be considered, its dependence upon ritual action and knowledge is undisputed by all. As for the claim that one who has studied the Vedānta has no need for the acquisition of ritual knowledge; [that is not the case].

That is incorrect; for even in the Vedānta, there would be the undesirable consequence that a person who studies only those passages concerning the means [to liberation] and liberation itself would have to hear only the third and fourth chapters during the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), since the third and fourth chapters depend upon the principles (*nyāya*) stated in the first and second. If it is argued that this is so because the entire inquiry into Brahman depends on the principles of the inquiry into ritual action (*karmavicāra*), and therefore that alone must be the prerequisite (*pūrvavṛtta*), [we reply: if it is argued that for someone—due to specific merits from other births—there is a dependence on the inquiry into Brahman alone, then for such a person...

Why should there not be a dependence on the third and fourth [limbs] due to a specific excellence of merit? Or rather, why should there not be independence from the entire investigation of Brahman due to the preeminence of one's merit? Furthermore, you yourself must admit that studying merely those portions of the Vedāntas that deal with means and fruits would be unscriptural; this applies equally to the study of the Vedāntas alone, since the study of the entire Veda is what is prescribed. Therefore, it is inconsistent to claim that whatever is required by those who transgress the injunctions constitutes the "previously occurred" (pūrvavṛtta).

Regarding the requirement for occasional hearing even by one who has studied the entire [Veda] due to the force of past merit (*sukṛta*), the answer has already been given. The objections summarized in the text beginning with "because of contradiction" and "because of lack of authority" have been refuted here by the Siddhānta-bhāṣya beginning with the words "it is said in response to this."

For instance, the contradiction [of ritual actions] due to their having impermanent results is removed by the fact that their results are not intended; however, the contradiction with the knowledge of unity—arising from their producing the latent impression of duality—is removed by the scriptural statement that "knowing the self as distinct" (*pṛthag ātmānam*) constitutes the means to liberation, for this is a cognition of distinction. Furthermore, this contradiction is included within the inherent power of the reality to be explained hereafter, because the nature of liberation as the cessation of all perception of difference depends upon the demonstration of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), even though the knowledge of unity is the actual means.

There is no contradiction because actions are utilized by way of the unseen principle (*adṛṣṭa*). The charge of being non-authoritative has been refuted by the observation of scriptural injunctions that employ [actions], such as: "One who performs ritual action is the best among the knowers of Brahman. As for the utility [of action] for the purification of the mind for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), this has been answered by demonstrating that it serves as a cause for the purity of the internal organ (*manas*) necessary for the arising of knowledge, and by demonstrating that even if its purpose is the desire to know, its daily performance is required. Furthermore, the claim that only knowledge is the cause [of liberation] has already been answered by the fact that we do not admit two separate means [to the goal].

What is called "capacity" (sāmarthya) is the objective capacity consisting in the fact that false bondage is removable by knowledge alone; this, however, will be refuted by the critique of the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva). Furthermore, the contradiction arising from the scriptural injunction that [knowledge] has tranquility (śama) and so forth as its auxiliary factors is resolved by the fact that there is no conflict between active rituals such as sacrifice and passive states such as tranquility, because they pertain to different objects; for it has been stated that tranquility and the rest have as their objects those things that are neither enjoined nor prohibited, as well as prohibited and desired things.

The claim that the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence alone is the means to liberation has been refuted by both direct perception and scriptural contradiction. In that regard, since there is no obstacle to the arising of the subverting [knowledge] due to the presence of the sublated latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the hearing of the scriptures (*śravaṇa*) and so forth do not require the removal of the impression of duality; thus, the attempt to avoid the charge of futility is untenable. Consequently, the view that the cognition born from the sentence—which is awakened through the sequence of hearing and so forth—is what brings about liberation is also rejected.

Regarding the fact that the fourfold means [to liberation] must have preceded [the inquiry into Brahman], the reason stated is "the force of the nature of things" (*vastusāmarthya*); however, neither of these two [conditions] has been established previously. Thus ends the *Laghusiddhānta*.

Now, he begins the demonstration of that [point]. Previously, while examining statements primarily intended as instructions on means (*upāya*), causes other than the inherent power of the thing itself (*vastusāmarthya*) were presented and refuted; for it was stated that "knowledge is what is intended to be enjoined. However, the inherent power of the thing is established by statements whose primary aim is the established reality (*siddha*). As will be stated later, "by those [statements] whose primary aim is the instruction on the nature of the thing," he therefore begins to demonstrate it by way of examining statements whose primary aim is the nature [of the thing], starting with the words, "As for what they say..."

By the word "api" (also/even), the primacy of the point about to be established is indicated; by "āhuḥ" (they say), the plurality of authors is shown, and by this, it is demonstrated that this work contains within it the entirety of the meaning expressed in various other treatises. The connection with what follows is that even that which they say—"all the Vedāntas begin [with this]"—is not to be respected. First, he asserts that Brahman alone is the sole reality, using the words "aśeṣa... (entire...).

"Entirety of objects" refers to the cognizer and so forth to be described hereafter; by the word "entirety," what is intended are all particulars—whether of a different class, of the same class, or inherent—and which, even among the inherent ones, consist of both positive concomitants and negative exclusions. "The opposite of that" means that which removes it through its own cognition, just as mother-of-pearl [removes the error] regarding silver; this is the meaning. He says "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*) to show that if it were devoid of all distinctions, it would be a mere void. By the word "consciousness" (*cit*), the exclusion of insubstantiality is indicated; for being consciousness consists in self-luminosity. By the suffix "-mātra" (only), the exclusion of being an object of knowledge is indicated.

Alternatively, even the property of being an adversary is excluded by the suffix *mātra*. Alternatively, by the suffix *mātra*, what is intended is the actual absence of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*); the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "Brahman alone" excludes the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma*). "Ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*) means the object of a means of valid cognition that reveals the truth; the sense is that sentences concerning the qualified Brahman do not have that as their primary purport, because they are intended for something else—namely, meditation—for the sake of a particular result.

How is it that Brahman alone is real? To address the doubt that "something else is also perceived," [the author] declares the falsity of the universe—both for the purpose of establishing that Brahman alone is the ultimate reality and for the purpose of showing that everything other than Him is sublated by the knowledge of Him—by the words "That" (tat).

In passages such as "Now, therefore, the instruction is: 'not this, not this,'" and regarding the subject matter of the sūtra "the finitude of what has been described," the opponents have raised the prima facie objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) that since everything is illusory, Brahman itself must also be illusory; this has been refuted. With that intention in mind, it was stated that [Brahman] is distinct from that [world]; thus it was shown that even though the negating statements such as "there is no diversity here" negate [diversity], the diversity to be negated is established as being distinct from Brahman.

"Of various kinds" (*nānāvidha*) refers to the differentiation of knowledge produced by that [ignorance], specifically the differentiation of knowledge delimited by the knower and the known; by this, the notion that the differentiation of consciousness manifested through mental modifications (*vṛtti*) is caused by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is excluded. By the word "differentiation," the internal subdivisions within each category are intended; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), birth, old age, and death—which consist of the form of suffering to be cast off—are denoted. The sense is that "all" (*sarvam*) is the meaning of the word "all" found in the Śruti passage to be cited later.

The phrase "in that" (tasmin) serves to exclude the position that error occurs without a substrate; the particle *eva* excludes the possibility of multiple substrates, for only by that being the case is it established that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is removable by the knowledge of that [substrate]. Alternatively, by the singular number in "in that," the oneness of the substrate is established. Since various superimpositions are observed to have various substrates, the particle *eva* highlights the apparent contradiction—namely, how there can be a single substrate—as well as the contradiction of a self-luminous reality serving as a substrate.

The meaning is: "that which is false" (mithyābhūtam) is that which possesses falsity, characterized by the falsity that will be explained hereafter. To the question, "What is the proof for Brahman alone being real and for anything distinct from it being false? he says: "Being alone, indeed" (*sadeva*). By "Being alone," difference consisting of dissimilar classes (*vijātīya-bheda*) is excluded; by "one alone" (*ekameva*), difference consisting of similar classes (*sajātīya-bheda*) is excluded; and by "without a second" (*advitīyam*), difference in the form of internal states or non-existences (*svagata-bhāvābhāva-rūpa-bheda*) is excluded. This sentence is cited first because it belongs to the *Sadvidyā* [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6], which is endowed with the sixfold marks of the intended purport (*tātparya-liṅga*).

Then, with the word "atha" (now), he introduces the scriptural passage concerning the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*), which explicitly contains a negation that serves as the fruit of the particle *eva*. This is a causal statement (*kāraṇavākya*) that begins by removing the defects suspected in [the cause]; for immediately after stating "the source of beings" (*bhūtayoni*), that very point is elaborated upon: "invisible, ungraspable"—not within the range of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor within the range of inference (*anumāna*), or alternatively, not within the range of the eye nor within the range of the other sense organs; "without lineage, without name"; "without color," meaning without blackness and so forth;
"without eyes, ears, hands, or feet," meaning devoid of the organs of knowledge and action; "eternal and omnipresent," meaning unlimited by time and space.

"Omnipresent" (*sarvagata*) means it has gone to, or is resorted to, by the entire world as its substratum; the meaning is that it is devoid of any limitation by material objects (*vastu*). "Extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*) refers to its invisibility not due to worthlessness or extreme distance, but rather because of its extreme subtlety—this is the intended sense. Since there is a division of sentences, the connection with multiple instances of the word *yat* (that) is justified. Now, he cites the purificatory statement (*śodhakavākya*): "The Real" (*satyam*).

This sentence has as its ultimate referent a non-differentiated reality (vastu) that is excluded from the false, the inert, and the limited; this will be explained on the grounds of its being a statement concerning the cause, its agreement with other purificatory statements, and the impossibility of accounting for its grammatical coordination otherwise. "Partless" (niṣkala) means devoid of parts (kalā), that is, without limbs. In this regard, the indicative mark is its actionlessness. "Quiescent" (śānta) means free from the six waves; hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, and old age and death are the waves.

"Blameless and stainless," meaning devoid of connection to karma and its fruits; by this, the exclusion [of all else] implied in such statements as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, is made clear. Now, with the words "of whom," he states the exclusion of being an object of knowledge, which is intended by the term "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*): "unperceived and unknown. This is a statement declaring that [Brahman] is not an object of knowledge consisting of hearing, reflection, and so on. Then, he cites a passage intended to negate the status of being a knower: "Not of sight... and so forth.

Here too, the distinction between the previously mentioned stages of knowledge is intended; for the sake of establishing this as the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*), the exclusion of non-bliss and so forth is stated in the passage, "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*). The word "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers merely to the exclusion of non-bliss and the like. For this very reason, the expression "the blissful one" (*ānandī*) is used. Thus, the collection of scriptural passages has been presented regarding Brahman’s nature as pure, undifferentiated consciousness (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*).

Now, the proof for the falsity of that which is distinct [from Brahman] is presented. First, it demonstrates that the world, being false, is superimposed upon Brahman as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in the text: "All this is what this Self is. For coordination with a substrate is observed to serve the purpose of sublation (*bādha*), as in the case of "the rope-snake."

Previously, it was asserted that everything is in That alone; by this statement, Brahman’s status as the substratum for the superimposition of all things is demonstrated. It shows the explicit verbal negation of anything distinct [from Brahman] in the words, "There is not even the slightest diversity here. By the phrase "seeing diversity," it shows that one is utterly ignorant; and by the word "death," [it indicates that such a person enters death]. Here, "death" (mṛtyu) means ignorance (avidyā), as in the passage, "He indeed goes from darkness to darkness. By the word "as it were" (iva), the unreality of diversity is shown.

If it were false, there might at some time be its cessation; to this he says, "Where indeed" (*yatra hi*). "Where" means when. The word "as if" (*iva*) is used as before. "Then" (*tadā*) means at that time. The meaning is: "one sees another by means of another. Since the question "by what? will be stated later, the word "by another" (*itareṇa*) is supplied. "But where" (*yatra tu*): "where" means when; "for him everything has become the Self alone" (*asya sarvam ātmaivābhūt*), then [there is no duality].

"By what could one see whom?"—the words "by what" and "whom" are to be supplied, since it was stated that "the other [sees]"; thus, "one should see" means "one should know," which is a statement regarding the stages of knowledge. He cites the scripture which establishes this entire world's falsity through an illustration: "Speech. A modification (*vikāra*)—such as the form of a jar and so forth—and its name are "originated from speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*), meaning they have speech as their basis; that is to say, they are merely conventional. Therefore, "it is only clay that is real."

He shows that for one who perceives multiplicity in Brahman, there is fear—the effect of ignorance denoted by the previously mentioned word "death"—in the passage beginning with "yadā hi. The particle *ud* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*), as in: "That alone is the Real, that alone they call the True; that alone is the Supreme Brahman of the seers. *Dara* means "slight" (*alpa*). Alternatively, *ut* connects with the verb *bhavati*, according to the rule "and [words] separated [by others may be construed together]. (Pāṇini 1.4.82). Thus, *ud-aram* means "even slightly."

The placement of the passage beginning with "araṃ śīghraṃ yadā hyeva" (quickly, as soon as) at the end is for the sake of ease of refutation according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); this is because the previously mentioned statements must be refuted by a single principle. The fact that Brahman is pure consciousness without attributes (*nirviśeṣacinmātratva*) and that all else is false has been shown through scripture; therein, regarding its being without attributes, the Sūtra is presented: *na sthānataḥ*. [This refers to] the "dual characteristics"—namely, having form (*sākāratva*) and being formless (*nirākāratva*). The meaning is that although Brahman exists everywhere, it is not the case that it is formless.

Regarding other forms of falsity, he cites the Sūtra: "Māyā. Why is the entire collection of dream-objects merely *māyā*? Because its nature is unmanifested, because it is difficult to define, and because it is sublated—this is the meaning. The falsity of dream-objects has been shown as an illustration for the falsity of the world. To support these two points, he presents the corroborative statements beginning with "pratyastamitabhedaṃ" (in which all difference has vanished). "Pratyastamitabhedaṃ" means devoid of distinctions between things of the same class and things of different classes.

It is mere existence (*sattāmātra*), devoid of internal differentiation, and for that very reason, beyond the reach of words. If one asks, "In that case, would it not be a mere nothingness? he says, "to be self-cognized," meaning it is self-luminous. By the phrase "designated as Brahman" (*brahmasaṃjñita*), the sense is that it possesses only the name "Brahman," but is not joined with qualities such as "Brahman-hood. When the question arises, "If it is without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), how is the manifestation of the world possible? he provides the answer: "having the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpa*). By this verse, the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) is stated.

[The text] shows that You alone are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), being absolutely pure and devoid of all distinctions, [existing] as the nature of the object and the nature of the non-insentient (*ajaḍa*). Since the multiplicity of objects is established through delusion (*bhrānti*), it demonstrates that You alone are the ultimate reality with the words "You are the ultimate reality. He explains this in two verses beginning with "That which is this... and so forth. In response to the inquiry, "If this is a delusion, for whom would it cease?", he demonstrates its cessation for some with the words "But those who know," thereby stating the truth of knowledge and the falsity of the insentient.

Now, he demonstrates the statement regarding the identity of those whose nature is the form of knowledge with the words "of that" (*tasya*). "Ekamaya" means one. He dispels even the suspicion of difference created by the designation of "self" with the words "if there were another. Here he provides an illustration with the words "as the holes of a bamboo flute. He shows the instruction on this established meaning with the words "I am he" (*so'ham*). He states that he acted according to what was instructed with the words "he abandoned it" (*tat tyāja*). Then, he demonstrates the statement regarding the identity of the selves with Brahman with the words "the producer of differentiation" (*vibhedajanaka*).

Now, he cites the statement from the *Bhagavadgītā* regarding the mutual identity of all selves with Brahman: "I am the Self" (*aham ātmā*). By the word "all beings" (*sarvabhūta*), the bodies are intended; he clarifies this with the words "and the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ ca*). By the phrase "in all fields" (*sarvakṣetreṣu*), it is made clear that the word "beings" refers to the body. In that very same passage, he shows the statement regarding the distinct falsity [of the world] with the words "that there is not" (*na tad asti*).

The meaning is that [the scriptures] are intent upon teaching the true nature of reality (*vastusvarūpa*), not intent upon means (*upāya*), and thus have no other purpose. The phrase "indeterminate pure consciousness" (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*) has the same meaning as before. The term "because of being denoted" (*abhidhānāt*) is to be construed with the previously stated proposition beginning with "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*). Now, is falsity (*mithyātva*) the appearance elsewhere of what exists elsewhere, or is it absolute non-existence (*atyantāsattva*)? In the former case, some degree of ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) would have to be admitted; in the second case, however, since there would be nothing at all to be negated, the scripture would be rendered useless.

Furthermore, absolute non-existence is untenable because [the world] is perceived. It is not possible for a self-luminous entity to be the substratum of an illusion, for superimposition (adhyāsa) is rooted in the non-manifestation of one's own true nature; such a thing is possible only for that which is insentient (jaḍa) and whose manifestation depends on something else. Therefore, regarding these two objections—that the previously asserted falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) and Brahman’s status as the substratum of illusion are illogical—the author first provides the definition of falsity to resolve the first objection, stating: "Falsity, namely..."

If it were stated simply as "the state of being removable," there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to things such as a jar, which is removed by a mallet or similar means; to exclude that, the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is used. Even with that, there would still be an over-extension to objects removable by the volitional knowledge of the powerful Lord (*Īśvara*) and others; that too is excluded because what is intended is removability by the mere knowledge of a thing exactly as it exists. Finally, the word "exactly as it exists" (*yathāvasthita*) is used to avoid an over-extension to real silver and the like, which are removable by a powerful delusive cognition.

If it were stated that "it is removable by knowledge as it actually exists" (*yathāvasthitajñānanivartyatva*), a cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would arise; in that case, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would remain intact regarding that which is removable by erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), because in that instance the nature of the cognition itself is indeed "as it actually exists," while the object alone is "untrue. Therefore, in order to exclude the suspicion of such coreferentiality, it is stated that [the thing] is "removable by the knowledge of the object as it actually exists" (*yathāvasthitavastujñānanivartyatva*).

If it is argued that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the prior absence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*), and that the phrase "preceded by being perceived" (*pratīyamānatvapūrvaka*) is intended to exclude that, [we reply: no, because a necessary rule (*niyama*) is what is intended to be expressed; for even the prior absence of knowledge is at some time preceded by being perceived, and thus [the rule] would be subverted.

Just as in the case of the statement "the relationship between word and meaning is established" (*siddhe śabdārthasambandha*), the establishment of eternality follows from the intended restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) that it is "established alone"; and just as in expressions such as "one who eats nothing but water" (*abbhakṣa*) or "one who eats nothing but air" (*vāyubhakṣa*), the restriction that he "eats" [only those things] is thereby established—so too, if it is argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because a snake [perceived] on a rope, which has ceased upon the knowledge of the ground, cannot be sublated by the knowledge of the object as it actually exists, we say: no, for even that [snake] is capable of being sublated by the knowledge of the object as it actually exists.

For this very reason, it was stated that [the object] is "that which is to be removed" (*nivartyatva*), and not "that which has already ceased" (*nivṛttatva*). Nor should it be argued that there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this definition to the case of fear—which is ultimately real—since such fear is produced by the error of mistaking a rope for a snake and is thus removable by the cognition of the rope; for fear, being momentary, ceases of its own accord and therefore lacks the quality of being removable by the cognition of the rope. Indeed, the cognition of the rope merely obstructs the arising of subsequent fear.

Therefore, the meaning is that falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being removable by mere knowledge whose object is the thing as it actually exists, preceded by the necessity of its being perceived. By this definition, the distinction from both the existent and the non-existent is established: therein, the phrase "preceded by being perceived" excludes the non-existent (*asat*), while the remainder excludes the existent (*sat*). He demonstrates that this definition of falsity applies to all things universally accepted as false, using the word "for instance" (*yathā*).

Now, although it is appropriate to extend the aforementioned definition to the subject (*pakṣa*), he states the following to resolve the second objection—that superimposition is untenable in the case of a self-luminous entity: "For that [superimposition] is imagined there due to the influence of a defect. Just as non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) is not the cause of superimposition, so too inertness (*jaḍatva*) is not; for even in the case of an inert object, superimposition is not observed when a defect is absent. Therefore, the defect alone is the universal cause of imagination. When imagination is dependent on a defect, whether the manifestation is intrinsic or extrinsic, it serves as the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for error.

Since the delusion of silver occurs when that which is present before one appears [as such], the dependence of the conceptualization in the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) upon a defect was stated in order to resolve the case of the subject of the illustration (dārṣṭāntika). Thus, by extending the two points learned from the example—that falsity consists in being sublated by the knowledge of the object as it actually exists, preceded by its being perceived in such a manner, and that the conceptualization of an unreal object arises through the force of a defect—he simultaneously dispels two doubts by implication with the word "evam" (thus).

Superimposition of several things that lack extreme dissimilarity upon a single locus is observed; for example, the superimposition of a snake, a strip of ground, or a streak of water upon a mere rope. How, then, can there be the simultaneous superimposition of an infinite world of mutually and extremely dissimilar things upon a single locus? This is the first [objection]. And how can there be superimposition upon Brahman, who is perceived in the passages beginning with "He who is all-knowing" as possessing qualities such as omniscience? This is the second [objection]. By the phrase "whose nature is pure consciousness," the previously mentioned [solution] is addressed.

He elucidates the impossibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based on self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*). By the phrase "in the supreme Brahman" (*pare brahmaṇi*), two doubts are resolved: first, that superimposition is possible because the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is of a different nature (*vilakṣaṇa*), and thus complete superimposition is justified; second, regarding this difference in nature, the intention is that while attributes such as omniscience exist in the lower Brahman (*apare brahmaṇi*), in the supreme Brahman they exist only as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and thus superimposition is justified precisely because of the connection with attributes such as omniscience.

By the word "this" (*idam*), which refers to the form of being perceived, and by the phrase "to be sublated by the realization of the true nature of Brahman as it actually exists," the previously stated definition of falsity (*mithyātva*) is restated. By the expression "imagined through defects" (*doṣaparikalpitām*), that which was stated in the passage beginning with "by the force of defects" (*doṣavaśāt*) is extended by analogy. The Lord (*deva*) demonstrates the manifold and total superimposition (*adhyāsa*). It is said to be "of a false form" (*mithyārūpam*); because it possesses the characteristics of falsity, it is declared to be false, like a snake in a rope.

What is the fault here? Is it ultimately real (*paramārtha*) or ultimately unreal (*aparamārtha*)? If it were ultimately real, it could not be sublated by knowledge. If it were ultimately unreal, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of another postulating agent, as in the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Does that [agent] postulate [the error] while Brahman is unobscured (*atirohita*), or while it is obscured (*tirohita*)? If it is unobscured, it is untenable, because—as in the case of the rope being manifest—there is a contradiction in the arising of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). If there were no such contradiction, there would be no subsequent cessation [of the error].

If [the cause] has disappeared, is that disappearance due to itself or due to something else? If it were due to itself, there would be either an impossibility of cessation or, upon cessation, the destruction of its own nature. If it were due to something else, that other factor must be explained. Furthermore, it is observed that various superimpositions have various defects as their respective causes; therefore, many defects must be admitted. To dispel these doubts, he says: "And the defect... The word "and" (ca) serves to remove the doubt. To the question "What is the defect?", the answer is "Ignorance" (avidyā).

Regarding the alternative of whether that [ignorance] is ultimately real or not ultimately real, the acceptance of its non-ultimate reality is expressed by the terms "real," "unreal," and "indefinable. The avoidance of the charge of infinite regress is addressed by the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) as a response to the alternatives of being concealed or unconcealed; this is further clarified by the phrase "non-concealment of its own nature. As for the question of whether that concealment is due to itself or to another, it is accepted as being "due to another," because a cause for concealment is specified. Furthermore, by the words "various" (*vividha*) and so forth, it is stated that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is not rooted in a single defect. *Vikṣepa* (projection) is *adhyāsa*.

It is indicated by the statement that ignorance (*avidyā*) has two states—namely, concealing ignorance (*ācchādikā-avidyā*) and distracting ignorance (*vikṣepikā-avidyā*)—because it is described as the cause of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*). Having thus proposed such an ignorance, he states the corresponding proof with the words "by untruth," and so forth. "Obstructed" (*pratyūḍhāḥ*) means led away from the opposite direction; he employs the word "of them" (*teṣām*) for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the term "obstructed."

There is no intended emphasis here on the plural number, as in the case of [the mantra] "May Aditi release the bonds. Rather, its indeterminability as either being or non-being is stated: "Neither being was there, nor non-being was there. To the question "What was there?", he says: "Darkness (tamas). If one should raise the objection that by the word *tamas* what is intended is the quality of obscuration, and that "darkness" refers to primordial matter (*prakṛti*)—as in the statement "The Imperishable dissolves into darkness"—he cites [the scripture]: "But know Māyā to be Prakṛti. He demonstrates that it is the cause of various superimpositions [in the passage]: "Indra, through his Māyās..."

He states that this [bondage] cannot be ceased without the knowledge of its identity with Him by saying "mine" (*mama*). He states its beginninglessness by saying "beginningless" (*anādi*). Here, because of the hearing of the terms "Great Lord-ship" (*maheśvaratva*), "Indra-ship," and the plural number—which depend upon something to be ruled over—it is understood that there is an association with differences consisting of extrinsic, intrinsic, and internal types; therefore, he explains [the reality] as "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*) in order to remove that [notion]. Even though qualified nature (*saguṇatva*) is perceived, the sense is that since it is consistent with the statements concerning the true nature (*svarūpa*), those passages intended to demonstrate defects do not have the purpose of establishing a perceived difference.

The sense is this: it is not that Brahman, though understood through words such as "Indra" and so forth, is the very same Brahman taught by sentences whose purport is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). By the phrase beginning with "by beginningless ignorance," he states those qualities—beginninglessness, the indeterminability of existence and non-existence, the power of concealment, and the cause of various superimpositions—which are understood from the specific sentences cited. By the term "inherent" (*svagata*), what is intended is the relationship [of the ignorance] with the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as its locus; it does not, however, refer to any internal plurality mentioned alongside similar or dissimilar categories.

Thus, the collection of words such as "Indra" and "Maheśvara," which appear in passages expressing defects, has been explained as referring to the non-dual reality by virtue of the natural force of the meaning and the superior authority of those passages whose primary purport is the essential nature [of Brahman]. Now, he shows that even through corroborative passages (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) that express defects, it is the non-dual reality itself that is said to be connected with defects, as stated in the verse beginning with *jñānasvarūpa*. Therein, it is asserted that the world is a manifestation of ignorance belonging to Brahman, which is pure consciousness alone.

"But it is not a real entity" means that it does not exist as a real entity such as the mountains, oceans, and earth which will be described hereafter. Regarding the phrase "the manifestations of consciousness," by the word *vijñāna*—derived through the instrumental analysis (*karaṇavyutpatti*) meaning "that by which various things are known"—ignorance (*avidyā*) is denoted. He establishes, by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the previously asserted fact that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is imagined by ignorance, with the words "when... [and so on]. "Pure" means devoid of ignorance. It is free from the perception of difference in its own nature, and consequently, when that cause has ceased, it is free from defects such as passion and the like.

That by which [things] are conceptualized from a single source is *saṅkalpa*, namely, ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding objects—that is, entities that constitute the substrata of properties—the "differences in substance" are differences in form. In the middle [of the text], the two verses beginning with "Is there any substance such as earth or jar-ness? establish the unreality of these differences in substance according to the manner in which the world is perceived; however, because they do not introduce any additional objects of knowledge (*prameya*), they are not included here. This will be demonstrated in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). He concludes the absence of difference between heterogeneous classes with the first half of the verse beginning with "Therefore.
Then, the second half of the verse beginning with "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) states that the plurality of selves is merely conceptual.

Having referred back to the previously mentioned oneness of the Self (*ātmaikya*) by means of the word "one" (*eka*) in the phrase "always one," [the text] negates any internal plurality and establishes that even terms such as "Supreme" (*para*) and "Other Lord" (*apareśa*) refer solely to the Reality itself, stating "knowledge" (*jñāna*). By words such as "pure" (*viśuddha*), it expresses freedom from ignorance (*avidyā*), the absence of the perception of difference caused by that ignorance, and the state of being free from grief, greed, and other passions rooted therein. "Always one" means devoid of birth, growth, and so forth; the meaning is that since there is nothing else, its nature is as described.

He states that this is not the ultimate view with the words "existence" (*sadbhāva*). Knowledge dependent on this world—that is, knowledge which rests upon the world by virtue of being its substrate—and that which exists as worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahāra*), meaning that which has become the object of universal worldly activity: even in that case, ignorance (*avidyā*) is said to be the cause. And that [ignorance] is not the ultimate view; rather, it is existence itself (*sadbhāva*) that is spoken of, in the sense of reality. Thus, through a thorough examination of the statements of the perfected ones (*siddhas*) and the supreme [scriptures], it is stated that the truth is that Brahman alone is real, while everything distinct from it is merely imagined through ignorance.

Then, in response to the doubt—namely, that the knowledge of the meaning of sentences which do not deserve to be subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the ritual action under discussion cannot be a means to liberation—the author states "of this" (*asyāḥ*) to show that even sentences whose primary purport is the means (*upāya*) have as their purport a means that is consistent with the objects established by sentences whose primary purport is the accomplished (*siddha*). The particle *ca* serves to dispel the doubt. By the phrase "of this," the intention is to convey its being qualified by attributes such as being real, unreal, or indescribable.

He shows the means of knowledge for its cessation with the words "no more. Here, "death" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); he states that its cessation arises from the knowledge of unity with the words "he sees that One. He makes known the cessation of disease and other effects of death as well with the words "the seer does not see death. The phrase "neither disease nor suffering" is a supplement to that; he shows the attainment of fearlessness immediately following the knowledge of the undifferentiated reality with the words "for when. "In the invisible" means in that which is not an object of perception and the like. "In the bodiless": *ātmya* is the pervaded body; thus, it means in that which is without a body.

"Indefinable" means that which cannot be precisely defined. "Without abode" means without a substratum. "Fearless" is for the sake of fearlessness; this is an *avyayībhāva* compound. "Firm foundation" refers to the final goal. He states that even action—which is accepted by disputants as the root cause of bondage—is brought to cessation through knowledge because it is constructed by ignorance, saying: "it is shattered. The "knot of the heart" is ignorance.

In the preceding statements, it appears as if some distinction is perceived; therefore, to exclude that and to make known that knowledge has unity as its object, he shows the result attained through unity by saying, "He who knows Brahman. For the fruit corresponds to the mode of meditation; thus, the sense is that the knowledge of unity alone is what removes bondage. To preclude other means, he cites the passage, "Him thus... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1]. To the objection that the cessation of ignorance is not perceived here because no word expressive of it is heard, he replies: "In this [passage]... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1].

In passages such as "Death runs as the fifth," the word *mṛtyu* (death) is observed to be used for Yama and others; therefore, it is stated [in the present text] in order to exclude that meaning. Here, the meaning is: "in those statements intended for the cessation of bondage. He demonstrates its usage therein with the words "as follows. From the statement "Indeed, negligence... it is understood that what was previously called "delusion is death, which is present among the wise" refers to the view of others—that delusion, which is contrary knowledge, is death—whereas for Sanatsujāta, negligence (*pramāda*) is considered death.

Negligence (*pramāda*) is non-apprehension as it truly is; for when one fails to grasp the true nature [of a thing], there arises a contrary apprehension. Therefore, negligence—which consists in a lack of attention toward the Self—is also a cause of delusion (*moha*). Thus, the intention is that ignorance (*avidyā*), being the cause of that [negligence], is what is intended by the word "negligence," and that this very [ignorance] is death. In the passages cited, it is established that knowledge removes ignorance; however, it has not yet been established that Brahman is pure consciousness devoid of distinctions, nor that the knowledge of the oneness of the Self is the remover [of ignorance]. To address this, [the text says]: "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyaṃ jñānam*).

The statement "truth, knowledge," and so forth, is cited for the purpose of demonstrating the exclusion [of Brahman] from everything else; the statement "consciousness, bliss" is cited for the purpose of making known the exclusion of suffering and the like, for the sake of the human goal. By the word "etcetera," passages such as "not gross" are included. Thus, the purificatory statements regarding the featureless nature of Brahman have been illustrated. Now, he cites the scripture for the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self, beginning with "Now, that which."

Now, the passage beginning with "He who [worships another]" is intended to eliminate the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding the distinction between the injunction for meditative worship and [the reality of] oneness. To make known that the enjoined worship has oneness as its object, he demonstrates the teaching of oneness by saying, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*). In accordance with this teaching, the meditator addresses the deity, saying, "Thou indeed [art I]. He then reflects upon the taught meaning within himself, saying, "Therefore, I am that."

To establish that this meaning is intended by the Śruti, he shows the Sūtra and states, "and he will say": "But [they] approach [it] as the Self, and [the scriptures] cause [it] to be grasped as the Self" (Brahmasūtra 4.1.3), and "One should meditate [on it] as the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). The meaning is that those seeking liberation approach it in this way, i.e., they meditate upon it; and the scriptures cause it to be grasped, i.e., they make it known. To show the statement of those who know the intention of the author of the Sūtras, he says, "and likewise. "Because of its accomplishment" means because it is superimposed there [upon Brahman].

He states "and by this" (*anena ca*) to show that there is not only scripture (*śruti*), but also reasoning (*tarka*) that supports it; the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. He says "of that which is illusory in nature" (*mithyārūpasya*) to establish that [bondage] is removable by knowledge independent of ritual action (*karman*); the status of being a cause is implied here. [Bondage is] "with its cause," meaning accompanied by the perception of the distinctions of ignorance (*avidyā*). The cessation of bondage is logical, for the point is that when an illusory snake is removed, there is no dependence on ritual action other than the cognition: "This is not a snake, this is a rope."

Now, since inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*) depend upon perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the sake of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*), perceiving the logical mark (*liṅga*), and cognizing the subject (*dharmī*), as well as for the sake of linguistic proficiency; and since inference and scripture—such as "this fire is not hot because it is a substance," or "the sacrificial post is the sun," or "the *prastara* grass-bundle is the sacrificer"—are seen to be incapable of establishing objects that contradict perception; therefore, with the intention that the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) is likewise incapable of establishing an object contradicted by perception, the proponent of difference (*bhedavādī*) raises an objection, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ceti*).

The meaning is that even when the intermediate objections within the scriptural statements have been resolved, this objection still remains: "In dreams and the like, as well as in [visions of] the earth with its oceans and so forth, the cessation of certain distinctions is observed; the word 'entire' (sakala) is used for the purpose of excluding those cases. Keeping two doubts in mind—namely, whether [the dream experience] is not sublated because it is perceptual, or whether [the waking world] is not sublatory because it is non-perceptual and based on a root [cause]—he first addresses the point that it is not sublatable due to its being perceptual.

If it is asked, "How so? and [the opponent] replies, "Because that is a pseudo-perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*)," [the author] says: No; for at the time of its cognition, it is not understood to be a pseudo-perception. If it is argued that it is known as such later through sublation by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇabādha*), then that is equally true of the perception grasping the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), since difference is sublated by scripture (*śruti*). This is what is intended here. [The opponent] then raises an objection, suggesting that because [scripture] is rooted [in perception] and is non-perceptual (*parokṣa*), it cannot be a sublater.

The word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "here, however" (*iha tu*) serves to exclude [the case of] equality. The sense is that because perception is the root, the scripture (*śāstra*) cannot be the sublater; whereas the sense is that because the scripture is indirect (*parokṣa*), it is not the sublater. If equality were the operative factor, the relationship of the sublated and the sublater could even be reversed; therefore, that [equality] is not the operative factor. Consequently, you must state another operative factor for that relationship of the sublated and the sublater, and that very thing will be our operative factor as well—with this intention, he says: "Of two equal [things]."

In order to exclude the lack of a fixed rule regarding the relationship between the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*), he raises another objection from the perspective of the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) by means of the words "of the preceding and the succeeding" (*pūrvottarayoḥ*). He states "the scripture" (*śāstra*) to show that the probans (*prayojaka*) you have stated applies equally here as well, namely, [the relationship] between the preceding and the succeeding, which are the sublated and the sublator.

In cases where the status of being "root" or "rooted-in-root" and so forth exists, it is observed that the root and the perceptual [cognition] possess sublativeness (*bādhakatva*), while the other possesses sublatedness (*bādhyatva*). Therefore, one might raise the objection: "Since the distinctions such as being root, rooted-in-root, or being non-perceptual are absent here, the presence or absence of being produced by a defective cause (*duṣṭakāraṇa*) must be the determining factors for the relationship of sublated and sublater. To this, he says: "This has been stated."

The word "equal" (*tulya*) is employed with the intention that, given equality, being produced by a defective cause and its absence are not the determining factors (*prayojaka*). Since the qualified [entity] is the cause, the qualifying portion is also a cause; thus, by means of the word "equal," a single part is taken up. What is intended is the "equality" which serves as the qualifier for both "being produced by a defective cause" and "its absence. The meaning is: when there is equality, and in the absence of causes for either superiority or inferiority, being produced by a defective cause and its absence are not the determining factors.

Dependence, independence, and the relationship between the root and the derivative are [the factors]. By the word "etcetera," the states of being indirect or direct, and being delayed or non-delayed, are intended; for it is through delay and non-delay that strength and weakness are established in the case of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth.

Alternatively, the equality mentioned as being non-conclusive (aprayojaka) is restated here by way of an illustrative example; and since there is no other difference [in the case], the two factors—being produced from a defective cause and its absence—are also intended by the word "etc. He establishes the non-conclusiveness of these points through a single example: "the flame," etc. The word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) must be supplied [to complete the sense]. The phrase "because of the impossibility of subverting perception" means because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such subversion being impossible.

For in the inference based on the distinction of flames, there is indeed a delay or lack of delay when the root and the flame are absent; since inference depends upon perception, this [argument] also refutes the claim that being produced by a defective cause or its absence is the determining factor when [the logical mark] is otherwise equal, because we observe the relationship of sublated and sublater even in the absence of such defects. To the question, "In that case, with respect to what object is perception the sublated? he says: "In that case... (tatra hi). The meaning is that the perception grasping identity is the sublated.

If so, what is the determining factor? To this he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). Since [factors] such as equality (*tulyatva*) cannot serve as the determining factor, the phrase "of two" means: of two perceptions, two inferences, two scriptures; or of perception and inference, inference and scripture, or perception and scripture. "That which has its alternative establishment suspected" (*sambhāvyamānānyathāsiddhi*) means that it is established otherwise because it has scope for another possibility (*sāvakāśatvāt*).

When it is stated that [the reason] is immediate (*anantara*), not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*), and without scope (*anavakāśa*), "having scope" (*sāvakāśatva*) refers to the possibility of finding another object or being included within the category of invalid cognition. Consequently, "being otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) means having the possibility of arising even without the validity regarding the object presented by itself; that is to say, having the possibility of arising even without being sublated by a valid cognition of a contradictory object.

"Unestablished otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddha*) means "having no occasion" (*anavakāśa*). "Being unestablished otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) refers to the state of not arising without the validity of that [specific] object; that is to say, it is the state of not arising without being sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes a contradictory object. And this [latter state] is due to having no occasion. "Having no occasion" (*anavakāśatva*) means either the non-attainment of another object or the absence of inclusion within the category of invalid cognitions (*apramāṇa*). The meaning is: the state of not arising without being sublated by a means of valid cognition that presents a contradictory object, by virtue of both the non-inclusion within the category of invalid cognitions and the non-attainment of another object.

Thus, in all cases, the meaning is that there is a contradiction between two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), whether they are of the same class or of different classes.
