One might ask: "Let this be the determining factor for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator; what does that have to do with the superiority of the treatise under discussion? To this, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). This is because the determining factor for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is precisely whether one is established otherwise (anyathāsiddhatva) or not established otherwise (ananyathāsiddhatva).

"Having a tradition that is without beginning or end and uninterrupted": because its tradition is uninterrupted, it is without beginning or end. For when there is no interruption in the tradition, the fact that the author is not remembered is the proof of its non-human (apauruṣeya) origin. "For this divine speech, consisting of the Vedas, was emitted by the Self-existent in the beginning; from it all emanations have proceeded."

Statements such as "Brahman is without beginning or end" are recalled by the term "without beginning or end. For this very reason, [the Veda] is free from defects that are impossible [in its case], for the possession of the fourfold defects—consisting of error, intent to deceive, negligence, and incapacity—is indeed caused by [the work being] of human origin. For this very reason, there is no room for doubt. The word "understanding" (*avabodha*) is construed with the word "arising from the scripture" (*śāstrajanya*). Since the acceptance of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator depends upon contradiction, he demonstrates that contradiction with the words beginning "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*), etc.; [it is] "eternal," meaning unconditioned by time.

"Pure" (*śuddha*) means devoid of ignorance; for that very reason, the word "liberated" (*mukta*) refers to the absence of birth and so forth produced by ignorance. "Awakened" (*buddha*) means appearing. The term "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśa*) is intended to exclude the dependence on another regarding the state of appearing, which was previously expressed by the word "awakened. Self-luminosity is the state of having the nature of light by itself; and this is because it is denoted by the term "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*). Indeed, self-luminosity is the essence of consciousness (*cittva*), and its nature as consciousness is established by scripture. The word "only" (*mātra*) is intended to exclude the status of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).

"By the realization of Brahman as one's own self" means by the realization of the identity between such a Brahman and oneself. "Possibly [subject to] defects" means because it is suspected of having defects; "having scope" means it has found its place among the category of non-authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). For this very reason, its "establishment through other means" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) is also implied. "Establishment through other means" refers to the possibility of arising even without subverting contrary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "perception etc.," inference and so forth are meant. "Diverse" [refers to the various types of such means].

The meaning is that bondage is precisely this manifold conceptualization of the knower, the known, and so forth—manifesting both in the form of gods and others, and in the form of one's own effects such as birth, old age, and death; [liberation] is the cessation of that. To the question, "And what is the possible defect? he says: "And when the manifold of difference... That is, the collection of differences, or alternatively, the phenomenal world (prapañca) whose nature is difference.

The term "various conceptual constructions" (*vividhavikalpa*) is a qualification of *prapañca* (phenomenal proliferation) or a qualification of "difference" (*bheda*). This difference consists of the knower, the known, and so forth; it is "various" (*vividha*) in the form of Brahmins and others, and "conceptually constructed" (*vikalpavat*) in the form of gods, humans, and so on. Some modern thinkers claim that this is a defect such as cataracts (*kāca-timira*), but that is incorrect, because such a defect is localized (*kvācitkatva*). If it is argued that, taking as an example a perception impaired by cataracts and the like, one can infer through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that the [apparent] diversity is due to a defect such as cataracts, we say no; for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that for the scripture which is said to be without beginning or end, it is indeed easy to infer a defective author by means of such reasons as "because it consists of words," and that in that case the author is excluded by the non-perception of what is otherwise suitable [to be perceived], then that is equally true here as well. Since the assumption of defects such as glass (or optical flaws) is untenable, he says "without beginning," etc., in order to exclude that possibility. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the perception of difference—which serves as the cause for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference—is intended.

The word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) regarding the relationship of cause and effect between these two; the intention is that this follows the logic of the seed and the sprout. For the perception of difference and the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of difference constitute "effect-ignorance" (*kāryāvidyā*); therefore, it is said to be "ignorance in the form of the latent impression of difference and so forth."

In statements such as "The sacrificial post (yūpa) is the sun," the non-establishment of the identity between the post and the sun is not due to contradiction with perception, but rather because the statement has another purpose; for those learned in logic hold that "the meaning of a word is that toward which the word is directed. And this having another purpose is understood from the absence of any indicative mark of intended significance (tātparya). The opponent's intention is that the sentence "The sun is the sacrificial post" is directed toward something else, as it is a subordinate part of the injunction regarding the anointing of the post.

Even regarding that which was stated to be faultless (*nirdoṣa*), there exists a contradiction in meaning (*arthavirodha*) which serves as the cause for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator; therefore, one of the two must necessarily be sublated. With the intention of asking how this can be resolved—given that the factor which would necessitate its being sublated, namely "being produced by a defective cause" (*duṣṭakāraṇajanyatva*), is absent—the author raises an objection with the word "nanu. He states that there is no cause for relative strength or weakness (*prābalyadaurbalyahetu*) by saying "anādi," where the particle *api* indicates a contradiction. He demonstrates the contradiction in meaning by saying "of those relying on difference" (*bhedāvalambinaḥ*).

By saying "it is true," he partially accepts that [the cognition] which relies on difference is sublated; however, he does not accept it when it is produced by a defective cause. It is precisely the states of being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatva*) or not being established otherwise that are the determining factors for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator; for even the previously mentioned state of being produced by a defective cause is simply a specific mode of being established otherwise.

Here too, he establishes an alternative proof for the lack of independent validity (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of different perspectives, beginning with the words "prior and posterior" (*pūrvāpara*). According to the logic of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*), the sublation of even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is equal [to that of scripture]. In that case, being rooted in a defect (*doṣamūlatva*) is an additional reason for sublation. Regarding the "annulment," the priority and posteriority of the two scriptures—prior and subsequent—is determined by the sequence in which the cognitions arise, not by the sequence of their recitation. As it is said: "The five [priests], having taken hold of one another, move forward; the *prastotṛ* takes hold of the *adhvaryu*, the *pratihartṛ* takes hold of the *prastotṛ*, and the *udgātṛ* takes hold of the *pratihartṛ*."

Regarding the interruption of the *anvārambhaṇa* (the act of holding on) prescribed for the *udgātṛ* by the *brahmán*, and for the *brahmán* by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), the expiation is stated as follows: "If the *udgātṛ* should be interrupted while they are proceeding toward the *bahiṣpavamāna*, that sacrifice is to be concluded without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*); he should sacrifice again with it, and in that [second] sacrifice he should give what he would have given in the previous one. Now, if the *pratihartr̥* should be interrupted, he should give his entire property (*sarvavedasa*)."

These two treatises constitute the subject matter. Here, when an interruption (*apaccheda*) occurs for both the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ* through different performances, each respective treatise on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies. However, when an interruption occurs simultaneously within a single performance, the expiation for the *udgātṛ* applies, because his function is primary and because it is precisely the interruption of the primary [function] that must be remedied. Alternatively, there may be an optional performance [of either]. Or, if the interruptions occur sequentially within the same [performance], the treatise on expiation pertaining to the earlier [interruption] [applies].

The weakness of the subsequent and the strength of the prior has been stated in the *Karmamīmāṃsā*: "In a sequence of priority and posteriority, the weakness of the prior prevails, as in the case of the original [archetype]. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the prior possesses strength because it arises before any contradiction has arisen, whereas the subsequent possesses weakness because it arises only in the presence of an opposing factor.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: since there is no contradicting factor at the time of its arising, the emergence of the former [cognition] is possible even without subverting it; but for the latter, because a contradicting factor exists at the time of its own arising, its emergence is impossible without subverting the former. Thus, the latter arises by having subverted the former. Because this is not otherwise established, the latter possesses superior force (*prābalya*). For the experts in logic (*nyāyavidaḥ*) hold that the emergence of the latter is indeed not established without the subversion of the former. Now, one might object: if the subsequent scripture were to arise, would it not fail to arise without subverting the former?

Could it not be that the preceding scripture is an obstacle to the arising of the subsequent one? It is not so; because the cause has already arisen, the scripture pertaining to that effect has indeed already come into being. Therefore, when the subsequent [scripture] is about to arise, its production is impossible without subverting the preceding one; thus, the preceding one is necessarily sublated.

Furthermore, since the completion of an action according to the characteristics of the act as previously described is already established by the scripture itself, that [completion] was not altered by the scripture on expiation (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*); likewise, because this is a context for altering a previously established matter, here too the former must be sublated. Thus, the investigation of action is certain. In this way, just like the subsequent scripture, the scripture on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*), being without scope [for contradiction], sublates the scripture that relies upon duality, just as the former scripture [sublates the latter]. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, [the sequence] is determined by both the order of recitation and the order of meaning; for one who investigates the reality of the Self, there is first an inclination toward ritual action because the three goals of life (*trivarga*) are its fruit, whereas the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*) follows thereafter. How, then, can one reconcile those Vedāntic passages that lack such sequential order and contain contradictions, which are devoted to the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*)? To this, he says: "Even in the Vedāntic passages... The word "even" (*api*) implies a conjunction; the meaning is that while the contradiction between the earlier and later portions has been resolved, the contradiction within the later portion is now being resolved.

How does the principle of the subsequent annulment (*apacchedanyāya*) apply here? To this he says: "because of being devoid of attributes" (*nirguṇatvāt*). By the word "supreme" (*para*), there is an exclusion of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahman*) belonging to the lower level. The meaning is that one should understand that the principle of annulment applies because we observe the realization of attributelessness, which is the fruit resulting from the application of the principle of annulment. The sense is that, since scriptural texts concerning the fruits [of meditation] such as "eating, playing, and rejoicing" may be either real or unreal, one first directs one's inclination toward the meditation on the qualified [Brahman], without yet investigating whether those fruits are real or not; for it is only after such an investigation that one becomes eligible for the knowledge of the supreme Brahman devoid of attributes. This is the intended sequence.

The sequence between the saguṇa and nirguṇa passages has been explained by way of their respective fruits for those intent on meditation (*upāsana*); however, since such a sequence does not exist between the saguṇa and nirguṇa passages that refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman], one might object: "How can there be a relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) in that case? To this, he says, "But if... (*nanu ceti*). Keeping in mind the sequence consisting of injunction and prohibition, he says, "Nirguṇa... (*nirguṇeti*). To the questions, "Which are the nirguṇa passages? and "What is their power? he says, "This has been stated" (*etaduktamiti*).

The statement beginning with "not gross" (*asthūla*) is intended to negate specific qualities (*guṇaviśeṣa*), while the statement "truth, knowledge, etc. (*satyajñānādi*) contains an implicit exclusion (*vyāvṛttigarbhatā*). The statement "without qualities" (*nirguṇam*) is intended to negate qualities in general; by the word "etc. (*ādi*), passages such as "that which is invisible" (*yattadadreśyam*) are included. [The author] clarifies the contradiction.

The word *kūṭastha* means "immutable" (*nirvikāra*) or "that which stands as the substratum of all" (*sarvādhiṣṭhāna*), for that which stands like a peak (*kūṭavat tiṣṭhati*) is indeed *kūṭastha*. By these words ending with "eternal consciousness" (*nityacaitanya*), the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman previously cited has been summarized. As for the other sentences previously mentioned, such as "He who is omniscient" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*) and so forth, the word *ca* indicates a conjunction; thus, because they refer respectively to the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the qualityless (*nirguṇa*), there is no contradiction between these two types of scriptural statements.

The meaning is: by that very same reason which was stated for the superiority of the latter [text] when there is a contradiction between the former and the latter. To the question, "Why is the statement regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*) more powerful? he replies: "Because of its posteriority due to its dependence upon qualities. For a negation arises with respect to an object of negation; indeed, there is no negation without an object. An object must first have been established as a possibility before it can be the thing to be negated. Therefore, the meaning is that a negation is "posterior" because it is dependent upon the object of negation.

With the intention that the futility of statements concerning the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇa*) is also avoided because they have meditation (*upāsanā*) as their subject matter, he says, "nothing is lost. Alternatively, with the intention that even sentences such as "He who is omniscient" are subordinate to meditation, he says, "even in the Vedānta texts," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those intent on meditation": the meaning is that even those sentences are intent on meditation for the sake of specific results, but they are not intent on [describing] reality (*tattva*). He explains the application of the principle of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*) by saying, "because of being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatvāt*); the meaning is as before.

The claim that the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) is unestablished is incorrect; for, since there is no temporal sequence between [the texts], the principle of sublation (*apaccheda-nyāya*) finds no application, as it is established that the qualities are subject to sublation. Consequently, the avoidance of the futility of the texts concerning qualities (*saguṇa-vākya*) is also untenable, because the assumption that those texts—already understood as referring to the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—are intended for meditative worship (*upāsanā*) is dependent upon the establishment of their sublation. Thus he objects with the words, "But surely... He answers with the words, "The absence of qualities... All else remains exactly as before.

Objection: One might raise an objection based on the idea that the passage beginning with "truth, knowledge," etc., which is presented alongside passages concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*), actually intends to convey the possession of qualities (*saguṇa*). [The word] *ca* in the phrase *nanu ca* serves to aggregate the objection. In the statement that qualities such as truthfulness and so forth are perceived, the words "truth" (*satya*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refer to the properties of being true (*satyatva*) and being known (*jñānatva*). This is just as in Pāṇini’s sūtra, "The dual and singular endings are used for two and one," where the words *dvi* and *eka* refer to duality and unity; otherwise, one would have had to say *dyekeṣu*.

Likewise, Śrīvatsāṅkamiśra says: "Are the qualities [the same as] truth, honor, and so forth? To clarify this statement, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is first examined; for that has been most clearly set forth by the venerable teacher [Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra] in the *Prameyamālā*. Thus, by the Blessed Patañjali, regarding the suffix *laṭ*:

In order to explain the term *sāmānādhikaraṇya* as it occurs in such sūtras as "The *tatpuruṣa* compound ending in a word denoting comparison, provided it is not in the nominative case and has a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*)," and "A *karmadhāraya* is a *tatpuruṣa* with a common substratum," the definition of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is stated: "Co-referentiality is the occurrence of words having different grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) with respect to a single referent."

The meaning of this is as follows: *pravṛttinimitta* means the cause (*nimitta*) of application (*pravṛtti*). Application (*pravṛtti*) is a preeminent function (*prakṛṣṭā vṛttiḥ*). The so-called application of a word to its object is the cognition of that object; therein, application is the function directed toward the primary object which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*). And the primacy of the substantive is established by the principle that "the cognition of qualities is indeed for the sake of the cognition of the possessor of qualities. The cause (*nimitta*) of that application is the medium (*dvāra*), as seen in usages such as "be merely the cause [of my success], O ambidextrous one" (*nimittamātraṃ bhava savyasācin*); and that is—

The qualifiers—such as genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*)—and the common single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), which serves as the locus for those qualifiers, constitute the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). By the word "one" (*eka*) in the phrase "subsisting in one object," the possibility that the word "common" (*samāna*) refers to similarity is excluded. By the force of the word "common," the word "one" signifies what is shared (*sādhāraṇa*); for the word "common" is indeed employed in the sense of being shared, as in the rule: "When two actions have the same agent, the suffix *ktvā* is used for the earlier action."

And the word *artha* refers to the primary denotatum which functions as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*); by this, the word *adhikaraṇa* is explained as being intended in the sense of a qualificand. What is meant is this: words are of three kinds. Some have the same referent in terms of both the qualifier and the qualificand, such as *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*, or *nīla* and *kṛṣṇa*. Others have different referents in both respects, such as *go* (cow) and *aśva* (horse), or *mahiṣa* (buffalo), or *nīlam* (blue) and *śuklam* (white) *paṭam* (cloth).

Furthermore, some words have distinct referents by virtue of their qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) but a single referent by virtue of the qualified (*viśeṣya*), such as "the blue lotus," "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, and red-eyed," and so forth. In this context, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words that fall into a third category—being excluded from the first two categories—is established. By the phrase "having distinct grounds for application" (*bhinnapravṛttinimitta*), it is stated that there is no coreferentiality for words like "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and "jar" (*kumbha*), which have a single referent both by virtue of their qualifiers and their qualified.

By the statement "subsistence in a single object," it is asserted that there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between words whose referents are distinct from both perspectives, such as "cow," "horse," and "buffalo. Therefore, grammatical coreferentiality exists only in cases such as "blue lotus," where the referents are distinct by virtue of their qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) but identical by virtue of their qualified substratum (*viśeṣya*).

In this context, the meaning of the two terms *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for application) and *śabda* (word) is as follows: *pravṛtti* is denotation (*abhidhāna*), and *nimitta* is the denoted object (*abhidheya*). Furthermore, the word *artha* is a synonym for the denoted object. Thus, it is stated that "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the application of words with distinct denoted objects toward a single denoted object; that is to say, co-referentiality is the culminating application of words expressing distinct qualifiers toward a single qualified substrate (*viśeṣya*).

It is understood that by the force of the distinct words (*bhinnapadasāmarthya*), the denotatum indicated by the word *nimitta* (cause) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), while by the force of the single word (*ekaśabdasāmarthya*), the denotatum indicated by the word *artha* (object) is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, it is stated by the sentence defining grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) beginning with "of those having different grounds for application" (*bhinnapravṛttinimittānām*) that coreferentiality consists in the convergence (*paryavasāna*) of words expressing multiple qualifiers upon a single qualificand, regardless of whether they function in both ways.

The previously stated [definition] is superior even to the one just mentioned: among words in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is intended to convey the connection with the qualifier, while the identical case-ending (*samānavibhakti*) is intended to convey the identity of the qualificand; by "vṛtti" (syntactic function), the communication of identity through identical case-endings is meant. Consequently, in the sentence "The king and his son are handsome," the apposition between the stems *rājan* and *tasya* is excluded; for in that case, the understanding of identity arises from the nominal stem of the word *tad*, which refers back to the subject under discussion, and not from the identical case-ending.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of "blue lotuses," the property of being a lotus (*utpalatva*) subsists even in those things that do not possess blueness (*nīlatva*); therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established there, and thus the meaning of the definition of coreferentiality is exactly as stated.

To this, the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*) say: A sentence of coreferentiality has an indivisible referent (*akhaṇḍārtha*). For instance, it is undisputed that coreferentiality aims at a single object. In that regard, one must distinguish whether the coreferential terms refer merely to qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), or to the qualifiers as qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśiṣṭa*), or to the essential nature alone (*svarūpamātra*).

First of all, these words do not have as their sole referent the qualifiers alone, because since qualifiers have multiple meanings, it is not established that they have a single meaning. Nor do they have as their referent the qualified object, because this cannot withstand analysis: do the words convey the qualified meaning sequentially or simultaneously? It cannot be sequentially. In that case, does the subsequent word establish identity with its own presented qualifier for that which was already presented as qualified by the first word?

Or is it the connection with another qualifier? In the first case, if the identity of the qualified entity is being enjoined, then just as between the two parts that constitute the qualified entity, identity would also necessarily follow between the two parts that constitute the qualifiers—namely, the genus and the quality.

Furthermore, in the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the mutual inherence (*samavāya*) of the qualifiers. For the communication of the connection with a subsequent qualifier occurs when an object, already understood as qualified by one qualifier, is subsequently made known as qualified by another qualifier. In that process, since the [subsequent] qualifier is connected as a qualifier toward the qualified object, it becomes a qualifier even for the preceding qualifier; thus, the consequence of the qualifiers being mutually related as the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is indeed unavoidable.

Furthermore, the sequential presentation of the meaning of words is unavoidable. Why? Because all sentences possess a distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). Nor can they be presented simultaneously, because that would entail the loss of the distinction between subject and predicate, and even if such simultaneous presentation were possible, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the mutual identity of the qualifiers. For instance, when nominal stems (*prātipadika*) have qualified meanings as their referents, the use of a common case-ending—which indicates the identity of the nominal stem meanings—[would be undermined].

Since it must necessarily be accepted that [the sentence] has as its purport the identity of the qualified [entity], then just like the identity of the qualified, the identity of the qualifiers would also have to be established; yet, because that is untenable, the use of a common case-ending (sāmāna-vibhakti) is not capable of establishing even the identity of the qualified. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) would not be established. Moreover, because it is the inherent nature of qualifiers to be differentiators, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the difference of the qualified following from the difference of the qualifiers is unavoidable.

For instance, the differentiator is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the differentiated is the qualified (*viśeṣya*); such is the distinction between the essential natures of the qualifier and the qualified. And the capacity of qualifiers to differentiate the qualified is observed, as in cases such as "the broken [pot]," "the shaven-headed [man]," "the jar," and "the cloth. But is it not the case that in instances such as "the blue lotus" or "Devadatta is dark and young," the identity of the qualified is observed even when there is a difference among the qualifiers?

This is not a fault; for in this case, the identity of the qualifiers with the qualified—which is established by its own nature—is set aside due to contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*). But in the case of Brahman, which is beyond the scope of perception, who can prevent the difference of the qualified resulting from the difference of the qualifiers? Therefore, a co-referential statement (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*) has as its ultimate object the thing-in-itself alone.

If it is argued that just as in sentences such as "the blue lotus," the identity of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is established in the sentence "Being and so forth" (*satyādi*) by virtue of the single number (singular) and the unity of the subject-term (*dharmipada*), we say no; for in the case of "the spotted, the hornless, the crested cow," there is a difference in the qualificands. If it is further argued that while a difference in qualifiers does not contradict the identity of the qualificand, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself is what contradicts it—and that since Brahman is beyond the reach of perception, its oneness, which is naturally obtained through the unity of the subject-term expressed in the singular, is difficult to set aside—we say no.

In sentences concerning objects that are not present to the senses, such as "The body is mottled," "He is shaven-headed," "He is horned," or "It is a cow," a difference between the qualified entities (*viśeṣya*) is perceived even though the words denoting the substratum (*dharmin*) are identical. Therefore, the identity of the words denoting the substratum is not capable of establishing the unity of the remote Brahman. Consequently, a difference in the qualified entity caused by a difference in the qualifiers is unavoidable; thus, the state of having a single referent (*ekārthatva*) is not established. Therefore, by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), it must be admitted that words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) have as their purport the denotation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone.

If that were so, the words would be synonyms, since the essential nature [of Brahman] would be apprehended by a single word alone; consequently, the employment of other words would be useless, and the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be lost due to the absence of a difference in their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). It is not so; rather, the meaningfulness of the words and their non-synonymy is established because they aim at the opposition to various factors contradictory to that single reality, thereby attaining a difference in their grounds for application, and thus the definition of coreferentiality is maintained.

For this very reason, the exclusion of the defects of unreality, insentience, and finitude—which might otherwise be suspected of the cause of the world—is accomplished by the statement "Being, Consciousness," and so forth. Nor does it follow that Brahman possesses attributes in the form of these exclusions, because the very nature of Brahman is itself the form of the exclusion of everything else. Just as the exclusion of blackness and the like from whiteness and so forth is the very nature of the thing denoted by the word [white], and not a separate attribute—since no other attribute is perceived, and because accepting such would lead to an infinite regress; so too is the case here.

Therefore, just as the words "whiteness excluded from blackness," "whiteness excluded from redness," and "whiteness" have different exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) as their objects—despite all three referring solely to the nature of whiteness itself—they do not become synonyms, nor do they lose their semantic value or their unity of meaning; and for this very reason, they possess the characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), so too there is no risk of the defect of synonymy regarding the words "Being" (*sat*) and so forth, because their respective exclusions are distinct. [Objection: But if these words thus refer to the exclusion of what is incompatible with each respective object, would that not involve figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)?

It is not so; for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurs when there is the presentation of something other than the primary denotation (*vācya*), as in the case of the word "Ganges" in the expression "A hamlet dwells on the Ganges," where the word "Ganges" presents the bank, for the bank is not the primary denotation of the word "Ganges. However, in this case, although the qualifying attributes—which constitute parts of the primary denotation of the words "Being" (*satya*) and so forth—are abandoned, there is no occasion for *lakṣaṇā*, because the essential nature of the qualified entity (*viśeṣya*), which constitutes the principal part of the primary denotation, is being communicated. If it is argued that even so, there is a violation of the natural fitness (*svārasya*) of a word denoting a qualified whole when it refers only to the qualified entity, we reply: this is not so.

There is no fault. In sentences with coreferential terms (*samānādhikaraṇa*), by virtue of their focus on a single referent, it is natural for words to intend their own essential nature alone through the abandonment of qualifiers; such is the linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). In sentences with non-coreferential terms (*vyadhikaraṇa*), however, it is natural for words to intend qualified objects. Even if metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is admitted, there is no fault; for metaphorical indication, when it conforms to the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence, is seen to be stronger than the primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) that contradicts it—as, for example, in the word *gaṅgā* [which indicates its bank], since the purport of a coreferential sentence lies precisely in identity.

[This is] agreed upon by all. [Objection: Is it not the case that metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for all words has never been observed and is illogical? For metaphorical indication of other words is appropriate only when the intended meaning (*tātparya*) has been determined through some primary mode of expression (*mukhyavṛtti*). If one accepts metaphorical indication for all words, what determines the intended meaning? [Reply: It is said: Metaphorical indication for all words is indeed observed in cases such as "Eat poison" (*viṣaṃ bhuṅkṣva*). Therein, the word "poison" indicates that which is prohibited from being eaten, and the word "eat" indicates the cessation of eating. In that context, the determination of the sentence's intended meaning occurs by virtue of semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and other factors.

In sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), the determination of the intention to convey identity is established by the force of the identical case-endings. To avoid contradicting that [intention], figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is accepted for the nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Indeed, even in the case of figurative indication within a single word, the sole cause is precisely the contradiction with the sentence's intended meaning—as seen in examples like "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā. Conversely, when there is no such contradiction, figurative indication is not observed even for a single word, as in "Fish in the Gaṅgā" or "Cows are grazing. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding contradiction with the sentence's intended meaning, figurative indication for all the words together—just as for a single one—is not a defect.

Therefore, a sentence of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*) has as its sole purport the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). To this, one objects on the grounds that it is not so, saying: "It is stated that [the qualities] such as truth, knowledge, and so forth are perceived. When this is urged, the intention of the one who says "it is stated that [they are] not so" is as follows: if by "are perceived" one intends mere superficial perception (*āpātapratīti*), then there is no purpose served by that; if, however, one intends valid cognition (*pramiti*), it is demonstrated that no such valid cognition arises.

Why is this so? To this he replies: "Because of the cognition of a single referent through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He raises an objection: "If there were multiplicity... The meaning is as follows: just as in sentences with different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇa*), where the unity of the primary sense—the action—is determined by the rule "a sentence is one because of the unity of its purpose," even though the meanings of the case-terminating words—which result in distinct referents—are not abandoned; so too, in sentences of coreferentiality, the identity of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is established even without abandoning the meanings of the words denoting the qualifying attributes (*guṇa*).

He rebukes the one who urges [this objection], calling him "ignorant of expression. This means he is ignorant of the specific distinctions between expressions consisting of words with different grammatical cases (*vyadhikaraṇa*) and those with the same case (*samānādhikaraṇa*). The term "beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priyaḥ*) means "foolish. He offers a rebuttal: "It is the state of having a single referent" (*ekārthatvam*). The meaning is that "having a single referent" refers to all the words [of a compound] culminating in a single denotable object, but not to the sentence as a whole.

Words that terminate in their respective distinct meanings possess unity of meaning (*arthaikatva*) only through their connection with a single primary meaning, which occurs precisely in a sentence with different grammatical subjects (*vyadhikaraṇa*). However, in a sentence with identical grammatical subjects (*samānādhikaraṇa*), it is stated that the words themselves terminate in a single meaning. When the question "What follows from this? arises, [the author] states the refutation—both regarding the case where words with identical subjects refer merely to qualifiers and the case where they refer to the qualified—in a single passage beginning with the word "viśiṣṭa. By the entire passage beginning with "viśiṣṭa," the refutation of the position that [words] refer to the qualified is stated.

"By the distinction of qualifiers" means by the mutual distinction of the qualifiers from one another and from the qualified (*viśeṣya*). The meaning is that there would be a multiplicity of referents (*anekārthatva*) due to the qualifiers and the qualified. Furthermore, since the word "referent" (*artha*) is intended here as referring to the qualified, this states another fault: namely, that by the distinction of the qualifiers, there would be a distinction of the qualified. Moreover, when it is stated that "by the distinction of the qualifiers there is a distinction of the qualified," it follows by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that if there were no distinction of the qualified, there would likewise be no distinction of the qualifiers.

The intention is that a case-ending in grammatical agreement, which expresses the identity of two qualified entities (*viśiṣṭaikya*), conveys not only the identity of the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) without distinction, but also the identity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Thus, the refutation of the theory of simultaneous denotation (*yugapad-abhidhāna-pakṣa*) regarding the status of the qualified entity has been stated; furthermore, the consequence of losing the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) is established by implication. If there were sequential denotation, the mutual inherence (*anyonya-samavāya*) will be discussed in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*; and as for the theory that the qualified entity is intended only as the qualifiers, the difference in meaning follows simply from the difference in the qualifiers.

A refutation has been stated: the meaning is that because there are multiple qualifiers, there is a loss of a single referent (*ekārthatva*). Thus, a difference in what is conveyed by the words has been introduced. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore, a single referent is not established. This means that the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not established. Therefore, it is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that [the sentence] refers solely to the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*); and having restated that, he raises an objection with the word "evam" (thus). That is: "If, then, it refers solely to the thing-in-itself..."

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because they denote an undifferentiated object. By this, he addresses the point that "therefore, the state of having a single meaning is not established," and states that the resulting meaning has been explained. Here, regarding the objection concerning synonymy, the intended refutation of the objection is as follows: because there is no difference in the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), there would be a loss of the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and one of the two words would be redundant; however, this is intended [only as a preliminary], since it will be refuted later. To refute these three stated objections, he says: "Having a single object... and so forth.

Listen with an attentive mind. Since the reply is to be accomplished through many sentences, one should not raise an objection in the middle; rather, the sense is that one must pay close attention because the meaning is profound. He dispels the three-fold inconsistency with the words beginning "ekatva" (oneness), etc. "Certainty regarding the purport of oneness" is established by the use of the same case-ending. "Arthavattvam" means purposefulness.

The meaning is as follows: because they produce exclusions based on distinct excluded objects, the words are not synonyms; because they acquire their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) in the form of exclusion, the establishment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is achieved; and because there is a multiplicity of exclusions, each word has its purpose (*prayojana*) in the form of that specific exclusion.

One might object: "Like sentences such as *tat tvam asi*, the definition [of Brahman] should be presented through positive concomitance (*anvaya*); what is the purpose of negative exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? Since there are many exclusions, it follows that there would be multiple meanings; and because the forms of the things to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) are infinite, it is impossible to effect that exclusion with only a few words. Furthermore, what are those entities from which Brahman is excluded? Because Brahman possesses numerous exclusions, it would follow that it has attributes (*sadharmatva*); and if one does not admit that these are attributes, the words would become synonyms. To resolve these and other such objections, he says:

This is what is meant: [it is] by way of its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), that is, by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), and not by way of an accidental characteristic (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*). By this, it is stated that this purificatory statement (*śodhaka-vākya*)—which establishes Brahman’s opposition to everything other than itself in order to exclude the defects suspected in [Brahman] due to its being the cause of the world—is rightly intended to effect exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). He avoids the contingency of having multiple meanings [resulting from] numerous exclusions by saying, "its form which is opposed to that."

The statement "it is excluded as a result" (phalato vyudasyate) refers exclusively to the essential nature [of the object]; therefore, there is a single purpose, and the exclusion is merely the resulting consequence—this is the intended meaning. He addresses the objection that because the forms of exclusion are manifold, it is impossible to exclude [the object] by means of just a few words, stating: "everything is excluded as a result by these three words. The meaning is that when exclusion is accomplished through the [object's] defining characteristic, everything is thereby excluded. To the question "What are the opposing factors?", he says: "Therein... (tatra).

By being the cause of the world, its unreality (*tucchatā*) is excluded. To the question, "For what purpose is the exclusion of the unreal (*asatya*)? it is said: "Because [the world] is a locus of modification (*vikārāspadatvena*). The term "dependent on another for its manifestation" (*anyādhīnaprakāśa*) is intended to explain the word "insentient" (*jaḍa*), which is common to things such as a pillar or ice. Although the exclusion of all [contraries] is established by each single term among "Real" (*satya*) and the others, nevertheless, because the contradictory form residing in the meaning of each term—which might still be suspected regarding Brahman—is not removed by a single term alone, the three terms together are efficacious.

He avoids the charge of having the same properties as the exclusions by saying "and not. In the Prābhākara position and in the established doctrine (siddhānta), the property is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa); however, in the Vaiśeṣika and other systems, it is of the nature of a negation (abhāvarūpa). Therefore, it is stated as "either of the nature of a positive entity or of the nature of a negation. To the question, "If exclusion is not a property, what would it be? he says "but rather" (api tu).

For in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) of an attribute is accepted because it is opposed to silver and so forth; likewise, Brahman, being opposed to everything else, is itself the exclusion—this is the meaning. Regarding the fact that the very nature [of a thing] is the exclusion, he provides an illustration with the words "just as. The exclusion of blackness and so forth from whiteness and the like is not a further attribute, because no such thing is perceived; the intention is that if it were a further attribute, there would be an infinite regress.

Anticipating the objection that the words would then be synonyms, he refutes it with the phrase "of one [thing]," intending the example statement: "whiteness excluded from blackness, excluded from yellowness, excluded from redness. The meaning is that the words possess utility through the distinction between the objects to be excluded; for that very reason, they are not synonyms. Furthermore, it is intended that the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established because the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is obtained by way of being delimited by their respective counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*).

With the intention of showing that the avoidance of the contingency of synonymity and so forth has been accomplished by means of the non-contradiction of having a single referent (*aikārthya*), it is stated that [the words] have "a single referent" (*ekārtham*); for by being intent upon the essential nature alone (*svarūpamātra*), their status as having a single referent is preserved. By the suffix *-tara* in the term *arthavattaram*, the intended identity of purpose and so forth is indicated through comparison with the example of whiteness, and because the proponent of difference [speaks of] an immeasurable number of qualities. Indeed, the example of whiteness and so forth is something directly perceived; in that case, the usage beginning with "excluded from blackness and so forth" is employed for the sake of clarity.

Since Brahman is beyond the scope of direct perception, the statement of its exclusion from everything else serves an additional purpose; thus, there is an abundance of purpose by way of illustration. Furthermore, regarding Brahman as the cause of the world, only the exclusion of suspected defects is required, and not some other quality; thus, there is an abundance of purpose compared to the position of those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*).

Thus, the reasoning (tarka) that supports the statement regarding "truth, knowledge," and so forth, has been stated. To the question of what meaning is understood from the statement supported by such reasoning, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). This means: because this statement is supported by the aforementioned logic. By the word "one" (ekam), the unity resulting from the use of the same grammatical case-ending is expressed; by the particle "eva" (only/itself), the unity in terms of essential nature is indicated, thereby excluding any partial multiplicity of meaning such as "unity in essence but difference in attributes."

He clarifies this with the phrase "devoid of all particularities" (*nirddhūtanikhilaviśeṣam*). The term "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*) is used to exclude the notion that the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) reality is a mere void. The phrase "it has been stated thus" implies "by the passage beginning with 'Truth, Knowledge,' etc. (*satyajñānādivākyena*). In this way, it has been established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," etc., has as its purport the Reality alone. Now, by means of two reasons—the identity of purport with the passages concerning the Cause and the identity of purport with the subsequent passages of purification (*śodhaka-vākya*)—the fact that it has as its purport the Reality alone is further established, starting with the words "In this manner," etc.

In this context, the "identity of meaning with the causal statements" (*kāraṇavākyaikārthya*) is first stated as the reason by the word "thus" (*evam*). The meaning is: only when there is an interpretation focused on the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣaparatva*) does the identity of meaning with the causal statements hold. Why is this identity of meaning required? Or, if such identity exists, how can there be a focus on the absence of distinctions? To address this, he says "since," and so forth. The passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*) is a defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*). Since this statement aims at providing a definition by restating causality, he cites the statement "Being alone, dear one, this was in the beginning" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*) as that which establishes causality.

The term "characteristic" (*upalakṣaṇa*) refers to that which indicates [the object] while remaining external to it, like a branch [indicating] the moon; for example, the statement "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. The meaning is: by means of this sentence. What is implied is that because this [sentence] purifies the essential nature of the causal reality, its consistency with the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*) is required.

Granted that there must be consistency with the causal statements, but since those who maintain that the cause is Brahman endowed with attributes (saguṇa) hold that this [consistency] is achieved precisely through such passages as, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," "Whose austerity consists of knowledge," "From Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food," "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords," and "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses," he says "therein" (tatra). That is, when consistency with the causal statements is required therein.

The principle of "all branches being authoritative" (*sarvaśākhāpratyayanyāya*) has as its result the acceptance of meanings not explicitly stated [in one branch]. Therefore, since it follows that what is not stated here must be accepted if it is stated in another Upaniṣad, even though the Upaniṣads intended only for the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa*) do indeed speak of the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇa*). In that regard, because the sentences concerning the unqualified Brahman are more powerful according to the principle of "the later annulling the earlier" (*apacchedanyāya*), the conclusion is that everywhere it is precisely the non-dual Brahman—excluded from all things of the same and different classes—that is established. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "The world... [and so forth].

By means of the words "the cause of the world" and so forth, [the author] restates the meaning declared by the causal sentences (*kāraṇavākya*). "The intended object of the purport" means that the purport (*tātparya*) rests solely upon the reality (*vastu*) itself. "It must be stated without contradicting that" means that this sentence must be stated without contradicting those [causal sentences], because its function is to purify the nature of Brahman as it has been apprehended through the causal sentences.

To the objection that the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) is applicable even in the sense of being without an equal or superior—as in the expression "the king is without a second"—and thus, despite having the same referent, it does not establish the status of being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), he says: "The scriptural text concerning being without a second. The intention is this: because this word "without a second" is placed in proximity with two restrictive terms—*sadeva* ("Being alone") and *ekameva* ("one alone only")—which respectively exclude what is of a different class and what is of the same class, it does not tolerate the existence of a second even in terms of qualities.

Thus, by virtue of its consistency with the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*), it has been established that the statement beginning with "Being, Consciousness" (*satyajñāna*) has as its purport the reality alone (*vastumātra*). Now, the reason based on its consistency with other purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*) is stated: "Otherwise. Otherwise—that is, if the statement "Being, Consciousness" were intended to refer to a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*); there would be a contradiction with such passages as "stainless" (*nirañjana*) and "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*). Therefore, the meaning is that in order to avoid such contradiction, this statement has as its purport the reality alone, devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣavastumātra*).

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such [scriptural passages] as "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*) and "untainted" (*nirañjana*); by this, it is established by implication that the scriptural texts concerning non-duality (*advitīyatva*) are intended to negate even a second entity in terms of its qualities. He concludes the point established by the three reasons with the words "hence" (*ataśca*). This means: hence, by the aforementioned impossibility of accounting for grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) otherwise, and by the two subsequent reasons—namely, the unity of purpose with other purificatory statements regarding the causal texts. This "definitional statement" (*lakṣaṇavākya*) is a statement concerning the essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*).

The meaning is that [the text] establishes precisely that which has an unbroken, single flavor and a nature characterized solely by being devoid of distinctions. Now, he raises the objection regarding the fault of resorting to *lakṣaṇā* (indication) by abandoning the primary sense (*mukhyārtha*), beginning with the words "But surely... and so forth. By the phrase "by the abandonment of its own meaning," the sense is: for its own meaning is the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) mediated by the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); it is by the abandonment of that [primary meaning]. Having accepted the status of *lakṣaṇā*, he declares its lack of fault: "This is not a fault. The fact that it possesses a primary sense will be explained later.

He states the reason: "even because of the function of denotation" (*abhidhānavṛtterapi*). The "function of intentionality" (*tātparyavṛtti*) is a function derived from the intentionality of the name, or one whose nature consists in being directed toward that [intention]; and here, the function of indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) is intended. The meaning is that even a primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) that contradicts the intentionality of the sentence is superseded by the function of indication which is concordant with the intentionality of the sentence. To the question, "In what sense is there this intentionality, such that indication is accepted in accordance with it? he says: "of the grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyasya*).

The meaning is that the uniform case-ending serves as the determiner of the intended sense (*tātparya*) that the purport lies precisely in identity. Indeed, this will be stated by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*. The phrase "agreed upon by all" means it is accepted both by those who maintain the identity of the qualified (*viśiṣṭaikya*) and by others. An objection is raised: "In instances such as 'A hamlet on the Gaṅgā,' no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of all the words is observed."

The intention is this: by means of a few primary functions that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*), the figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) nature of other words must be accepted in accordance with them; however, that is not possible if all the words were to possess a figurative sense. With the thought that "accepting the primary meaning of words that do not contradict the intended meaning is not inconsistent with accepting the figurative sense of words that do contradict the intended meaning," he asks: "What follows from that? (*tataḥ kim iti*).

Then, explaining what is intended by the phrase "what follows from that" (*tataḥ kim*), and having shown the opposing point by way of a counter-argument (*pratibandhi*), he presents a counter-argument containing a refutation (*bādhagarbhā pratibandhi*) for the sake of rebuttal, beginning with the words "the purport of the sentence" (*vākyatātparya*).

If the primary meaning of non-contradictory words is not incompatible with the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of contradictory words, then in the sentence "fish in the Gaṅgā," since there is no contradiction, one would not admit figurative indication; whereas in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," because there is a contradiction, figurative indication is not a fault. To this, he says "samabhivyāhṛta... (co-uttered), meaning that this is the same in the present case as well, for figurative indication of all the words is observed in expressions such as "eat poison."

The meaning is that when it is ascertained that "this is the intended purport," the indication through a case-ending in agreement [with the word to be defined] and free from exceptions serves as the determiner. The point is that for two or three words and so forth, it is precisely non-contradiction and contradiction that are the primary grounds for accepting the functions of primary sense (*mukhya-vṛtti*) and secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*), rather than the singularity, duality, and so on of the words themselves. He states "and likewise" (*tathā ca*) to show that the assumption of secondary indication for all words—not only in worldly cases such as "Eat poison," which are driven by worldly necessity—is also resorted to by other investigators.

Thus, there is no fault in the theory that all words possess secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). The sense is that this [theory] is accepted because the grounds for acceptance exist; that is, the acceptance has borne fruit. To the question, "By which investigators, or in which sentences, is recourse made to secondary signification for all words? he replies: "In sentences whose meaning is an action" (*kāryavākyārtha*). He establishes that all words in worldly sentences possess secondary signification by stating: "Only in respect to the unprecedented action" (*apūrvakārya eva*). [Objection: Let it be that the action to be accomplished (*kārya*) is secondary; how then can there be secondary signification for all words? To this he replies: "Because [words] denote what is connected" (*anvitābhidhāyitvena*). This is because words denote [their meanings] as already connected [to others].

Thus, the reasoning that supports the statement regarding the knowledge of Truth and so forth has been stated. To the question of what meaning is understood from the statement when supported by such reasoning, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This means: because this statement is supported by the logic already explained. By the word "one" (*ekam*), the unity resulting from the use of the same grammatical case is expressed; by the particle "only" (*eva*), the exclusion of any multiplicity of meaning—even in part—is indicated, such as unity in essence but difference in attributes. He clarifies this point by saying: "with all distinctions shaken off."

The term "self-luminous" (*svayaṃjyotiḥ*) is used for the purpose of excluding the insignificance (*tucchatā*) of that which is devoid of distinctions. The phrase "it has been stated thus" implies "by the sentence beginning with 'Being, Consciousness' (*satyajñāna-*) etc. In this way, the fact that the sentence beginning with "Being, Consciousness" etc. has as its purport the mere reality (*vastumātra*) has been established through the otherwise inexplicability of its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, its purport as the mere reality is further established by two reasons: its identity with the sentences concerning the Cause and its identity with other purificatory sentences (*śodhakavākya*). This is shown by the passage beginning with "In this manner," and so forth.

In this context, the "identity of meaning with the causal statements" (*kāraṇavākyaikārthya*) is first stated as the reason. "Thus" (*evam*): the meaning is that this identity of meaning with the causal statements holds only when the interpretation is established as being focused on the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*). Why is this identity of meaning with the causal statements required? Or, if there is such identity of meaning, how is the focus on the indeterminate established? To address this, he says "since," and so forth. The passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings]" (*yato vā imāni*) is the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*). Since this [defining statement] aims at providing a definition by restating [Brahman's] causality, he cites the statement that establishes that causality: "Being alone, indeed, in the beginning" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*).

The term "characteristic" (*upalakṣaṇa*) refers to an indicator that stands apart [from the object], like a branch [indicating] the moon; the meaning is that it is by means of this sentence, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. It is thereby stated that because this [sentence] purifies the essential nature of the causal reality, its consistency with the sentences concerning the cause is required.

Let it be granted that there must be a single purport for the causal statements; however, those who maintain that the cause is Brahman endowed with attributes (saguṇa-brahman) would hold that this [single purport] is established by such passages as: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," "Whose austerity consists of knowledge," "From Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food," "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords," and "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses. To this, he replies: "In that case" (*tatra*). That is to say, when a single purport for the causal statements is required.

The principle of the "corroboration by a related branch" (*savarśākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) has as its result the acceptance of a meaning not explicitly stated [in one's own branch]. Therefore, since the meaning stated in another Upaniṣad—even if not mentioned here—must be accepted, it follows that even the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman is taught in those Upaniṣads that primarily concern the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahman. In this regard, because the sentences concerning the attributeless Brahman are more authoritative according to the principle of the "successive annulment" (*apaccheda-nyāya*), the intention is that in all cases it is precisely the non-dual (*advitīya*) Brahman, excluded from all things of its own class and of other classes, that is established. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "the world," etc.

By the words "the cause of the world" and so forth, he restates the meaning expressed in the causal sentences (*kāraṇavākya*). The intended object, the ground of the purport (*tātparya*), is the mere reality (*vastumātra*) alone; this is the meaning of "the purport lies in the mere reality. It must be stated without contradicting that [reality]: because this sentence serves to purify the nature of Brahman as understood from the causal sentences, it must be stated by this sentence without contradicting them; this is the meaning.

To the objection that the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) is intelligible as meaning merely the absence of an equal or superior—as in the expression "the king is without a second"—and thus, even if it has that same referent [as Brahman], it does not establish that Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), he says: "The scriptural text concerning being without a second. The intention is this: because it is placed in proximity to two restrictive terms—*sadeva* ("Being alone") and *ekameva* ("One alone")—which respectively exclude those of a different kind and those of the same kind, this word "without a second" cannot tolerate even a second [entity] in terms of its qualities.

Thus, it has been established that the sentence beginning with "truth, knowledge," etc., has as its purport the reality alone, because it shares the same meaning as the causal statements. Now, the reason based on its sharing the same meaning with other purificatory sentences is stated: "Otherwise. Otherwise—that is, if the sentence beginning with "truth, knowledge," etc., were intended to refer to a qualified entity—there would be a contradiction with such passages as "stainless" and "devoid of qualities"; therefore, for the sake of avoiding that contradiction, the meaning is that this sentence refers to the reality alone, which is devoid of attributes.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such passages as "devoid of qualities" (nirguṇa) and "untainted" (nirañjana); by this, it is established by implication that the scriptural texts concerning non-duality (advitīyatva) intend to negate even a second entity in terms of attributes. He concludes the point established by the three reasons with the words "Therefore" (ataśca). "Therefore" means: by the aforementioned impossibility of accounting for grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) otherwise, and by the two subsequent reasons consisting in the harmony with other purificatory statements regarding the causal texts. This "definitional statement" (lakṣaṇavākya) is a statement concerning the essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa).

The meaning is that [the text] establishes precisely that which is undivided, of a single essence, and characterized by a unique nature. Now, he exposes the fault in abandoning the primary sense (mukhyārtha) and resorting to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), beginning with the words "But surely... (*nanu ca*). By the phrase "by abandoning its own meaning" (*svārthaprahāṇena*), the intended sense is: for its own meaning is the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) mediated by the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, it means by abandoning that. Having accepted the status of figurative indication, he asserts its lack of fault: "This is not a fault. The fact that it possesses a primary sense will be stated later.

He states the reason: "even because of the function of denotation" (*abhidhānavṛtter api*). The "function of intentionality" (*tātparyavṛtti*) is a function derived from the intentionality of the name, or one whose nature consists in being directed toward that [intention]. And here, the function intended is the function of indication (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*). The meaning is that even a primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) which contradicts the intentionality of the sentence is weaker than an indicative function (*lakṣaṇāvṛtti*) that is conducive to the intentionality of the sentence. To the question, "In what sense is there this intentionality, such that the adoption of indication is for its sake? he replies: "of the grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyasya*). The intentionality lies precisely in identity.

The meaning is that the case-ending agreement (*samānavibhakti*) is what determines the intended sense (*tātparya*). Indeed, this will be stated by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) in the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa*. "Accepted by all" means it is accepted by those who maintain the theory of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭaikya*) as well as by others. [The opponent] raises an objection, saying "But surely," because in examples such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of all the words has been observed.

The intention is that one must resort to a figurative (lakṣaṇika) sense for other words in accordance with the primary sense of a few key words that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*), whereas such [a determination] is not possible if all the words were taken in a figurative sense. He asks, "What follows from this? based on the principle that accepting the primary meaning of words that do not contradict the intended meaning is consistent with accepting the figurative meaning of words that do contradict the intended meaning.

Then, explaining what is intended by the question "What of it?", and having shown the refutation of the opposing view (*vipakṣabādha*) by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), he states a counter-argument containing the refutation of the opposing view in order to resolve [the objection], beginning with the words "The purport of the sentence" (*vākyatātparya*).

The intention is as follows: if the state of having the primary meaning of non-contradictory words were incompatible with the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of contradictory words, then, since one would not admit figurative indication for even a single word in cases such as "Fish dwell in the Ganges" due to the absence of contradiction, there would likewise be no figurative indication for even a single word in cases such as "A hamlet on the Ganges."

If it is argued that in the sentence "fishes in the Gaṅgā" there is no recourse to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because there is no contradiction, whereas in "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" there is metaphorical indication due to contradiction, [the author] replies that this is the same in the present case as well, stating: "samabhivyāhṛta... (co-uttered). The intention is that metaphorical indication of all the words is observed in expressions such as "eat poison. "When it is determined that this is the intended meaning (*tātparya*)"—the sense is that the mention of words in the same case-ending, free from any exception (*apavādaka*), is the determining factor.

"Of two," "of three," and so forth. The meaning is that it is precisely non-contradiction and contradiction that serve as the grounds for accepting the primary or secondary functions (*mukhya-lakṣaṇā-vṛtti*) of words, and not the singularity, duality, or other numerical properties of the words themselves. He states "And thus" (*tathā ca*) to show that the metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of all words is not only resorted to out of necessity in common worldly usage, such as "Eat poison," but is also accepted by other investigators (*parīkṣaka*). Thus, the absence of fault in the metaphorical indication of all words is admitted.

The sense is that because the reason for acceptance exists, acceptance has borne fruit. To the question of by which investigators and in which sentences the indication (lakṣaṇā) of all words is resorted to, he says: "In the view that the sentence-meaning is an action to be accomplished" (*kāryavākyārtha*). He establishes the fact that all words are indicative in ordinary worldly sentences. [To the objection] that it is only in the case of an unprecedented action (*apūrvakārya*) [that this occurs], he replies: "Connected with an action to be accomplished" (*kāryānvita*), [meaning] let the action to be accomplished be indicative; how then can there be the indication of all words? To this he says: "connected with an action to be accomplished."

Since words denote their meanings as already connected (anvitābhidhāyitva), the primary meaning of case-words—which denote an action not previously established (apūrva-kārya) as connected with that [action]—is precisely that which is so connected; therefore, the meaning is that if one abandons that connection, it is necessarily metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

If it is objected that in cases such as "a hamlet dwells on the Gaṅgā," even though the word *gaṅgā* has a secondary (metaphorical) meaning, other words expressing what is connected to it are not seen to be non-primary—[we reply: no, because in that case the bank indicated by the word *gaṅgā* does not constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). Here, however, since the word that conveys the primary intended object—the action (*kārya*)—is metaphorical, there must indeed be metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the words expressing what is connected to it. For this very reason, it was stated [by the author] that "this is said by those who maintain that the sentence-meaning is action."

If you object: "In the sentence 'The lotuses close and the night-lilies open,' even though the closing and so forth—which constitute the meaning of the sentence—are figurative (lākṣaṇika), it is not observed that the words 'lotus' and so forth, which denote those [actions] through their primary power (abhidhā), are themselves figurative," you raise this objection without understanding our intention. For it has not been established by anyone that all words have as their ultimate referent the sentence-meaning in the form of closing; thus, even when there is figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word that presents the closing, there is no consequence of the words denoting what is connected to that [closing] becoming figurative.

However, since you accept that all words possess the capacity to bring about their respective effects (*kārya*), if those words conveying the effect were to be taken figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*), then it would follow that the words expressing the meanings connected to that effect would also have to be taken figuratively. To explain: for one who maintains that the meaning of a sentence is an action to be performed (*kārya*), is the word-potency of the words determined to reside in a portion of a qualified action, or rather in a portion of a qualified, enduring action? In the first case, because there is no distinction in being a portion of a qualified action, it would follow that words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*) would have their primary denotation (*mukhyatva*) in the action to be performed (*kriyā-kārya*), just like the words denoting the factors of action (*kāraka*).

In the second [view], since the abandonment of the status of being directed toward a portion of the effect of a qualified substratum is common to all words, there would be *lakṣaṇā* (indication) on the part of the case-words, just as there is for the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others in relation to the action-effect, if they were to have as their purport only that which is connected to the action-effect.

Even though it is equal in that all words refer to a single specific part of the action to be accomplished (*kārya*), [you claim] that verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are figurative (*lākṣaṇika*) with respect to the action to be accomplished, whereas nouns denoting factors of action (*kāraka*) are primary (*mukhya*) with respect to anything merely connected to the action to be accomplished. If it is accepted that nouns denoting factors of action are primary with respect to anything merely connected to the action to be accomplished, how can verbal suffixes such as the optative be figurative with respect to the action to be accomplished?

If it is argued that because the Veda is observed to employ words in reference to a permanent effect (*sthāyikārya*), it is certain that they are prompted by the Veda, and thus it is possible for them to convey a ritual action as a task (*kriyākārya*) even through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); [we reply: since it is also observed that words denoting factors of action (*kāraka*) are employed in the Veda with reference to what is connected to a permanent effect, it is likewise possible for them to convey what is connected to a ritual action as a task through secondary indication; therefore, the presentation of what is connected to a ritual action as a task would itself be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

Now, one might object: even if the word *go* (cow) has as its primary meaning merely that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, a specific individual such as Khaṇḍa is established by other means of knowledge; however, if the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and others were to have as their primary meaning merely "action to be accomplished" (*kārya*), no specific action would be established by any other means of knowledge. Therefore, since it is impossible to postulate a single power for both [the general and the specific], and because postulating two powers would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), the optative suffixes must have as their primary meaning the "newly produced action" (*apūrva-kārya*). Consequently, the expression of the action to be accomplished [in the case of ritual injunctions] is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

If it is argued that otherwise, because the power of a word has only the "effect" (*kārya*) as its object and because [the effect] is not an object of perception or other means of knowledge, a specific effect would be without proof; [we reply: no, for there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), since the assumption of a power [of the word] occurs only if the specific effect is established by a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), and its being established by a means of valid cognition occurs only if the power is assumed.

Furthermore, if one were to postulate a power (*śakti*) there [in the verbal suffix] in order to avoid the lack of authority regarding the specific action (*kāryaviśeṣa*), then—since the connection with a specific action is not within the scope of other means of knowledge when the case-words (*kārakapada*) have as their sole purport merely that which is connected to an action, and since it would be cumbersome to postulate a power for both [the case-words and the verbal suffix]—there would be no authority for the connection with a specific action.
