To avoid that, if the primary meaning of the case-words were their connection with a specific action, then their purport being connected to an action in general (the *kriyākārya*) would have to be secondary (*lākṣaṇika*).

If it is argued that the fact that words denoting factors of action (kāraka) have as their primary purport the connection with a specific effect is established by the force of their co-occurrence with the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, then—by the force of their co-occurrence with the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*)—the optative suffix and so forth would be established as having as their primary purport a specific effect; thus, the optative suffix and so forth would [in fact] refer only to the effect in general. Therefore, since the optative suffix and so forth have their primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) specifically toward the apūrva as the effect, and since the effect consisting of an action (*kriyākārya*) is secondary (*amukhya*), one must necessarily admit that even for words denoting factors of action, their purport regarding the connection with the effect of an action is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*).

If it is argued that there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) only in the aspect of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) among the case-inflected words, and not everywhere, then it is the same in the case of a sentence with coreferential terms (*samānādhikaraṇa-vākya*): there too, the *lakṣaṇā* would reside only in the nominal stem portion (*prātipadika-aṃśa*) of the words, and not in the identical case-endings. He concludes the resolution of the objection regarding the impossibility of *lakṣaṇā* in all words with the word "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: because the justification for *lakṣaṇā* in all words has been established, and because it is accepted by both common people and investigators (*parīkṣaka*).

Beginning with the words "As for what they say," he concludes the establishment of his own intended meaning through the treatise. "Therefore, this alone" means: therefore, regarding the reality that is devoid of distinctions, its being the ultimate truth, the falsity of anything distinct from it, its being imagined through defects (*doṣa*), the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of that defect as either existent or non-existent, and its being removable by knowledge alone—all this is established by the scriptural statements accompanied by the aforementioned arguments. "This very collection of meanings" refers to the very same collection of meanings previously set forth.

But it is not [the case that] the Vedāntas are authoritative as teaching things such as an entity possessing attributes (*saguṇa*). The meaning is that since other sentences—being intent upon imaginary objects—lack the capacity to reveal reality (*tattva*), the entire collection of sentences is authoritative regarding reality only with respect to the subject matter already stated.

Previously, it was stated that when there is a conflict with perception (*pratyakṣa*), the scripture (*śāstra*) possesses greater authority, and that within the scripture, that which relies on duality is not sublated. Now, he begins to demonstrate that no such conflict with perception exists. The sense is that the connection to the meaning to be explained lies in the passage set forth to establish the superior authority of scripture over a conflict between scripture and perception; the word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction. Furthermore, since the position of non-conflict is present in the mind, the conjunction includes both that [position] and what has been stated by way of concession (*anvāruhya*).

The meaning is: "even if contradiction is admitted. Regarding the phrase "and when [it exists]," the word *ca* here functions as the particle *hi*. He asserts non-contradiction by stating that "no contradiction is actually perceived. He provides the reason with the words "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*). The term "Brahman as pure Being" (*sanmātra-brahma*) is stated for the purpose of excluding the distinction consisting of the relationship between object and subject. He raises an objection based on the contradiction of experience with the words "But surely... (*nanu ca*). He demonstrates this contradiction with the passage beginning "the pot exists," and so forth.

The meaning is that it is not merely the cognition "it exists," but rather the cognition specifically as "the jar exists" or "the cloth exists. Since there is the possibility that such a cognition might be of a mistaken nature, he states "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*) to exclude that possibility by pointing out its contradiction with empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). He answers [the objection] with "True" (*satyam*).

In such cases as "the jar exists" and "the cloth exists," because the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding existence is uniform, there is an acceptance of that much alone, while the mere appearance of difference (*bhedāvabhāsa*) is not accepted. Furthermore, it is indicated by the partial acceptance [expressed by] "it is true" (*satyam*) that the linguistic usage of difference has perception as its basis and that the appearance of difference is not accepted as being perceptual. "In the same way" (*tathaiva*): the meaning is that just as there would be perceptuality of pure Being (*sanmātra*) alone, and just as there would be the very cause for a single uniform linguistic usage, so it is.

Here, within this collection of linguistic usages concerning the nature of objects such as a jar, [the distinction] is being discerned. The meaning is that just as in the case of "this is silver," the usage "this" is rooted in perception while the usage "silver" is rooted in error, so too is the distinction discerned here. In that regard, the distinction between the two usages—the aspect of "this" and the aspect of "silver"—is made by way of their being uncontradicted and contradicted, respectively.

With the intention of asking how a distinction can be made when there is no difference between the two—namely, the non-sublation of both the essential nature and the object of the distinction—he asks, "How? With the underlying thought that there is a logical sublation (yauktika-bādha), he says, "The pot exists."

Is existence (*astitva*) and difference (*bheda*) one category (*padārtha*), or are they two? If there are two, is the empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) of both rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), or is it so for only one of them? If both are rooted in perception, does perception grasp both simultaneously or successively? Having held these alternatives in mind, [the author states]: "The identity of the nature characterized by existence and its difference is not possible, because the apprehension of difference depends upon the apprehension of the nature and the recollection of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), whereas the apprehension of pure being (*sanmātra*)..."

Intending to show that [the cognition of difference] is independent of that [external object], he says: "existence and its differentiation. Even in the unique usage "this is a jar," which is the conventional expression "it is distinct," since the jar is perceived as being excluded from the cloth, it depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*); therefore, the very usage of "jar" is said to be the usage of "difference. Furthermore, regarding duality, he says "nor for both," meaning that neither of the two usages—the usage concerning the essential nature nor the usage concerning the object of difference—has perception as its basis.

Anticipating the alternative that perception might be the basis [of these two] either simultaneously or sequentially, he refutes simultaneity with the words "Of those two" (*tayor iti*). What is intended is that there is a disparity between them consisting in the dependence on or independence from a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). He rejects the sequential position with the words "of perceptual cognition" (*pratyakṣajñānasya*); the word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense. Thus, since it is untenable for the dual usage [of "is" and "is not"] to have perception as its basis either simultaneously or sequentially, he states that one of the two is the object of perception with the words "therein" (*tatra*).

To the objection that difference (*bheda*) would then be an object of perception, he says: "In difference... (*bhede*). The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is this: the very same reason [that applies] when the identity of existence and difference is impossible, and when their respective usages are the results of cognitions occurring at different times, [applies here as well]. To the question of how the usage of difference can be possible if perception has only the thing-in-itself (*svarūpamātra*) as its object, he says: "Therefore, through delusion... (*ato bhrānti*). And thus, in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "Because simultaneity and succession are impossible for both exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and affirmation (*vidhāna*)."

"And because of the impossibility of unity, the delusion that difference is not perceived [arises]. Here, "exclusion" (*vyavaccheda*) refers to the apprehension of difference; "knowing" (*vidāna*) refers to the apprehension of the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Thus, the non-establishment of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding difference has been stated; now, he states the non-establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). By the passage beginning with "Furthermore," the absence of reasoning (*tarka*) that supports the means of knowledge is also demonstrated. He asserts its indefinability with the words "Difference, namely... The sense is that it cannot withstand conceptual analysis (*vikalpa*). The phrase "by those learned in logic" implies "not by those satisfied with superficial perception. Keeping the alternative of whether difference is the essence (*svarūpa*) or an attribute (*dharma*) in mind, he refutes the position that it is the essence with the words "Difference, first of all..."

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because [the distinction] is the very nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*). This means that, just as there would be the linguistic usage of the thing's own nature, there would follow the linguistic usage of its difference from everything else; that is to say, there would follow the linguistic usage of difference even without dependence on a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Although the apprehension of the thing's own nature does not depend on the recollection of words derived from linguistic convention (*śabdavyutpatti*), the linguistic usage "it is different" nevertheless depends upon that [recollection]; likewise, the recollection of the counter-correlative is also included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the linguistic usage of difference.

Anticipating the opponent’s view—that because there is no recollection of that [prior cognition], there is an absence of the conventional usage of difference at that very time, and not due to the non-apprehension of difference—the author says "na ca" (and not). To the question "Why?", he says "svarūpa... (of the own-form). The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that just as there is no dependence on a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) for the apprehension of the own-form, so too there is none for the conventional usage of difference. The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason. The meaning is: because, just as in the apprehension of the own-form, dependence on a counter-correlate is impossible in the case of the conventional usage of difference. To the question "Why is it impossible?", he says "svarūpa...".

In response to the objection—"Let it be that the nature of both the essence (*svarūpa*) and difference (*bheda*) is indistinguishable as 'essence'; what follows from that? It would entail the linguistic usage of difference even independently of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)"—he explains this with the words "Just as... He also states another refutation regarding the position of essence: "The hand is the arm. The sense is that if they were synonyms, their simultaneous usage would have to be abandoned. Furthermore, other refutations against the position of essence have been stated by the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādins*).

By refuting the objections already raised, those [other positions] are also answered; thus, they are not explicitly mentioned in the Bhāṣya. They are stated as follows: In the view that difference is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of things, it is not proper to employ the linguistic convention "different" (*bhinna*), for that which is "different" must be something that possesses difference. If, in order to establish this convention, another difference existing as the essential nature of the first difference is admitted, then since the convention "different" would likewise be improper with respect to that second difference, yet another difference existing as its essential nature would have to be resorted to—resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, by another word, "dharma" would have been what was stated; and in that case, the refutations directed at the position of *dharma* would follow as consequences. Moreover, is difference (*bheda*) pervasive (*anuvṛtta*), or is it excluded (*vyāvṛtta*)? If it is excluded, is it the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*)? In the first case, once the conventional usage of difference has been applied to a jar, the conventional usage of difference regarding a cloth would not occur, because [the difference] is excluded. If it is a property, then the previously mentioned defect and the refutations resulting from its being a property would apply.

If it is argued that this [existence] is pervasive and its very nature, then "pure existence" (sanmātra) would have been accepted under another name. If it is considered a property (*dharma*), the same objection as before applies. Furthermore, the root *bhid* has the meaning of "cleaving"; the so-called "division" of a single entity is its becoming two-fold, and that same process would apply to each of its parts as well. Therefore, if division is admitted in a real entity, there would be nothing but destruction through a succession of cleavings, and so forth.

Now, he refutes the position of [the opponent’s] doctrine with the words "nor even" (nāpi). To the question "Why?", he says "Because it is a property" (dharmatve). He states the undesirable consequence if there were no difference between the property and its own nature (svarūpa) with the words "otherwise" (anyathā). Let there be a difference between the property and its own nature; what follows from that? To this he says: "And if there is a difference" (bhede ca). "Of that too" means of that difference which is accepted as a property; "the difference relative to its own nature" means that the difference of that very difference, which is accepted as a property, is itself a property of that difference.

Alternatively, the distinction that is accepted as belonging to a property from its own nature—that distinction itself is also a property [of that property] from its substratum (the property-possessor). Otherwise, it would be nothing but the nature [itself]. And in that case, the refutations leveled against the position of "nature" would apply. Furthermore, that distinction is a property, and there must be a distinction of that too from its own nature; such is the meaning of the infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Having thus stated the infinite regress regarding the position of the property, he states the mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) with the words beginning with "Moreover" (*kiñca*). For the apprehension of difference occurs in three ways: when the property-possessor and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are apprehended, and when the difference is apprehended, the apprehension of the property-possessor and the counter-correlate follows.

When the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) are apprehended, there is the apprehension of their difference; when the difference is apprehended, there is the apprehension of the property and the substratum. In the case of "This is a jar," the apprehension of that which is indicated by the word "this" as qualified by belonging to the class of jars is preceded by the apprehension of its difference from things belonging to the class of cloth; otherwise, it would contradict its belonging to the class of jars. Likewise, the apprehension of the difference from cloth is preceded by the apprehension of that which is indicated by the word "this" as belonging to the class of jars; otherwise, it would follow that it is cloth.

Thus, in the apprehension of a property and its substratum—whether by way of grasping them as the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), or by way of grasping their respective generic natures (*jāti*)—a threefold mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) has been stated.

He concludes the absence of any proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: "because it is difficult to define [the relation], due to the refutations stated against the positions regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the property (*dharma*)."

Thus, the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the proof [of the self] has been stated. Furthermore, reasoning (*tarka*), which consists in the impossibility of the object of cognition (*prameya*), serves as a supplement to that; for the function of reasoning is to establish the scope of a means of valid cognition by means of an investigation into either the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) or the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the object, thereby determining its specific domain. Alternatively, he introduces a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). In that context, wishing to state an inference, he teaches the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the passage beginning "The pot exists," and so forth.

In the sūtra, "And because of dissimilarity, [the world] is not like a dream and so forth," the author of the sūtras himself will refute the inference based on being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*). Since that refutation is intended to demonstrate that all inferences for proving falsity (*mithyātva*) are to be rejected, the reason of "being excluded" (*vyāvartamānatva*) is presented in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To demonstrate its persistence (*anuvṛttatva*), it is stated: "The pot exists, the cloth exists. Keeping in mind the identity between Being (*sat*) and manifestation (*anubhūti*) which is to be explained later, he shows the persistence of manifestation through the following.

"A pot is experienced, a cloth is experienced"—this is what is said. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "here" (*atre*). This means by way of being excluded (*vyāvartamānatayā*), that is, by not existing in the objects of successive cognitions, like the rope-snake and so forth—meaning like the rope and so forth [in the case of the rope-snake], and like the snake and so forth [in the case of the snake]. He explains this with the words beginning "just as" (*yathā*). He raises an objection, showing that both reasons are fallacious due to a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), by means of their being sublated or unsublated, saying "But surely... (*nanu ca*). He states the exclusion of the probandum from the subject (*pakṣa*) through the removal of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) with the words "But here... (*atra tu*).

The intention [of the opponent] is that there is a contradiction because of the existence of contrary limiting conditions (*upādhi*). He refutes this with the words "It is said," and so forth. First, he states the point on which both parties agree: "Exclusion is observed in the case of a jar, etc. For a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is that which exists in all similar instances (*sapakṣa*) but is absent in the subject (*pakṣa*).

In this context, intending to refute the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) being "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhika*)—since it is excluded from the subject (*pakṣa*) by stating that the property asserted by the opponent as a limiting condition actually exists in the subject—he says, "What is its nature? (*sā kiṃ rūpā*), in order to demonstrate the utility of that analysis. He explains the nature of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) observed in jars and so forth, asking: "Does [the exclusion] here, in the case of 'Is there a jar? (*kiṃ ghaṭo'sti*?), result in confirmation (*saṃvāda*), or does it result in sublation (*bādha*)? Thus he speaks.

The meaning is that when there is the cognition "the jar exists," there is the absence of a cloth [in that same locus]. [Objection: "In that case, then... The point is that the absence of things such as earth-clods in a rope is indeed what constitutes sublation (*bādhitatva*). Therefore, he says "hence" (*ataḥ*), meaning that [the cognition] is precisely the result of sublation. Sublation (*bādha*) is defined as a negating cognition produced by non-defective causes; by means of this, there is an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the absence from the object present before one. Thus, he says "it" (*sā*), meaning that because it is free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhika*), its being excluded is a proof of its lack of ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*).

Because persistence, which is the fruit of non-sublation, is the determinant of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), the author shows that what persists possesses ultimate reality by saying "like a rope. Non-sublation means non-contradiction; persistence means the connection [of the object] with that [non-sublation] as its object, or the existence [of the object] in the place before one. In this way, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been taught. He says, "And there is also a formal argument (*prayoga*)," because there is not only reasoning (*tarka*), but also a supporting proof. For the Māyā-Vedāntins are proponents of the view that only consciousness is ultimately real.

To the question, "How then is the existence [of the real] established as ultimate reality? he says: "This being so" (*evaṃ sati*). The meaning is that when it is established that the properties of "being excluded" (*vyāvarttamānatva*) and "persisting" (*anuvarttamānatva*) are the respective grounds for non-ultimacy and ultimacy. Then, to the objection that there would thus be two ultimate realities, he says: "That very same [existence], being real" (*saiva satī*). Now, revealing the distinction between existence and its cognition in the form of the relationship between object and subject, he raises an objection: "But surely" (*nanu ca*). Here, "distinctness" is the probandum, and "by way of being the object" is the reason. He refutes this: "Not so" (*naivam*).

In this context, he refutes the probandum (*sādhyāṃśa*) with the words "for difference" (*bhedo hi*). The meaning is that by the very negation of the difference between objects previously mentioned, the difference between cognitions is also discarded. He refutes the probans (*hetvaṃśa*) with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). "It does not follow the path of valid cognition" means that the relationship between object and subject is established through delusion (*bhrānti*). This is conjoined with the fact that difference itself is established through delusion.

Establishing through reasoning even those matters propounded by scripture, and setting aside the doubt of nihilism (*śūnyatva*)—which arises because the relationship between object and subject has been negated and there would otherwise be no perceiver—the author establishes self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) with the words "And that... The word "and" (*ca*) serves to dispel the aforementioned doubt. In this regard, he states a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) as the reason: "because it is experience" (*anubhūtitvāt*). He demonstrates the sublation [of the reason] in the opposite case (*vipakṣe bādha*) with the words "if it were established by another" (*anyataḥ siddhau*). The pervasion (*vyāpti*) is implicit in the meaning: whatever is established by another is observed to be non-experience, just like a jar.

Having shown that this negative inference (*vyatirekin*) possesses a limiting condition (*sopādhika*)—thereby demonstrating that the counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) favored by the opponent is fallacious—he states another inference by implication through the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*), etc. Whether there is an explicit statement of another inference or an implied refutation of the counter-inference, the word "furthermore" (*kiñca*) is natural if it refers to an explicit statement of another inference; however, if it were intended as an explicit statement of a counter-inference, such a construction would be impossible to conceive. Thus, the indication [of the meaning] is natural. "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

The meaning is that not only is one's own position established, but the opponent's position is also untenable; or alternatively, it means "and another inference. Regarding "and dependence on experience": the word *ca* (and) is intended to include something other than the two items previously mentioned which are to be conjoined by the word *kiñca*. [Knowledge] cannot be postulated [as self-luminous]. The counter-inference is as follows: "Knowledge is illuminated by another, because it is an entity (*vastu*), or because it is manifest, like a jar and so forth. The meaning is that it is impossible to assert that knowledge is self-illuminating through such arguments.

To the question "Why?", he says: "By its very existence. He explains this with the words "For not... in order to dispel the suspicion that the reason—"because it is manifested by its very existence"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). The meaning is that the occasional non-manifestation during the state of existence is the probans for dependence on another for manifestation; therefore, the counter-inference is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition). It is quite clear that there is another negative inference (*vyatirekī anumāna*) based on the fact that [the self] is always manifest during the state of its existence.

As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: beginning with "If cognition were to ever remain unmanifest... and concluding with "...in that case too, manifestation must be postulated, just as in the case of a jar," this passage refutes the suspicion that the reason—"because it is manifest by its very existence"—is unestablished (*asiddha*). If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) because even pleasure and the like are always manifest when they exist, we reply no; for the intended qualification is "provided it is distinct from pleasure and the like."

According to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since pleasure and the like are also specific types of cognition, they are included within the subject (*pakṣa*); therefore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*). Another distinct inference has been stated, and it has also been shown that the counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) suspected [by the opponent] is fallacious due to its being based on a limiting condition (*sopādhika*).

Now, wishing to refute the position that [consciousness] is inferable by means of its own manifestation, he restates the opponent's view with the words, "Now, one might think," and so forth. First, he establishes the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason, "because it manifests by its very existence," with the words, "When [cognition] has arisen," and so on. The intention is that by this, the rebuttal of the fallacy of being based on a limiting condition (*sopādhika*) for the counter-inference he himself stated—namely, "because it is a real entity" (*vastutvāt*), "because it is manifest" (*bhāsamānatvāt*), and so forth—will be accomplished.

Even when experience has arisen, only the object appears; in this context, the words "this is a jar" (*ghaṭo 'yam*) must be supplied. The meaning is that only the object, "this is a jar," appears. For it will be stated later: "one who knows 'this is a jar'... As it says in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "In the cognition 'this is a jar,' only the jar is manifested, not the consciousness—this is indeed proclaimed in your assemblies. The phrase "the jar is experienced" is to be connected with what follows later.

If there were a connection with what precedes, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "only the object appears. To the objection—"How can there be the appearance of the object alone? For when one thinks 'the jar is experienced,' the experience itself also appears"—[the author] establishes that only the object appears by means of the passage beginning with "the jar is experienced. When one knows "this is a jar," one does not at that very moment know "the jar is being experienced. Why is this so? He says: "because [the experience] is not an object and lacks the nature of 'this' (anidambhāva)."

[The cognition] is distinct from the referent of the word "pot," which is not its object; it is distinct from the referent of the word "this," which is not its object. The referent of the word "pot" is a substance characterized by potness and having a shape with a broad base and a belly. The referent of the word "this" is the state of being qualified by a proximate location and the present time. Indeed, the experience is distinct from both of these. However, the meaning is that at the time of the experience "this is a pot," that [distinction] is not experienced.

The expression “not having become an object” (*aviṣayabhūtām*) is a general indication intended to include cloth and other such things as well; for this very reason, the phrase “not having become a jar” (*aghaṭabhūtām*) is not stated. Alternatively, the word “jar” (*ghaṭaḥ*) connects with the preceding [phrase] as “the jar is experienced. The particle *iti* indicates a reason (*hetau*). Since the jar alone is the object of experience (*anubhūtikarma*), and at that time experience itself does not become an object of experience, the meaning is that only the object (*viṣayamātra*) appears. This is further explained by the words “for indeed” (*na hi*).

It is observed that illuminators such as sound, inferential marks, and light possess their illuminating power only through being themselves known; therefore, if experience were not self-illuminating, it would lack the capacity to illuminate anything else. To this, he says: "Therefore, like a jar, etc. There are two kinds of illuminators: those that illuminate by their mere existence (*sattayā*) and those that illuminate by being known (*jñāyamānatayā*). In this context, the meaning is that cognition belongs to the category of those that illuminate by their mere existence. To the question, "What is the restrictive rule for this?", he says: "Therefore... [and so forth].

The meaning is that the reason—namely, "being manifest by its own existence alone"—is unestablished (*asiddha*), and because the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in the reason stated by us has been refuted. To the question, "If experience does not manifest by itself, then what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding it?", he says, "Immediately after that. The meaning is that it is known through inference: since it is occasional, it is an effect, indicated by the mark of an occasional excellence in manifestation residing in the object; and since it is an effect, it must have a cause.

If it is asked how one's own cognition is inferred by means of the mark (*liṅga*) of manifestation residing in the object, [the answer is: the inference of one's own cognition is established because it manifests for oneself. Regarding the objection that if cognition is inferred by the mark of manifestation occurring after the cognition, then it would be improper to say "the jar is being experienced" and proper instead to say "the jar was experienced," it is stated [in the text] immediately following that: "because of the excellence of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), there is the designation of its being present. This is the meaning.

By the phrase "immediately after the contact of the object with the sense organ, the jar is experienced," the doubt that there would be no occasion for inferring cognition through the mark of manifestation (*prakāṭya*) is also refuted. The meaning is that such an experience is possible due to the extreme rapidity of inference, like the piercing of many lotus petals one after another. The proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādī*), by means of what is well-known in his own system, brings about an undesirable consequence: "If that were so," [then] "insentience" (*jaḍatva*) means being distinct from cognition; that is to say, it means being devoid of consciousness (*acittva*).

And here, the conclusion reached by the counter-argument is that experience is non-inert (*ajaḍa*). To reject the undesirability of "inertness"—which is what is being entailed as the opposite—he refutes it by proposing "non-inertness" and asking: "What is this? This means: "What is this? Nothing at all"; that is to say, it is indefinable (*durnirūpa*), since there is no presentation of two alternative positions (*śirodvaya*) immediately following. The subsequent text is an elaboration of this indefinability. Alternatively, the word "what" (*kiṃ*) may be intended to introduce a dilemma (*vikalpa*).

The intended dilemma is as follows: regarding what is called "non-inertness," is it meant as a reason (*hetu*)—namely, that there is always manifestation while [the entity] exists—or is it intended as the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, that it is its own illuminator by itself? In the first case, is the intended dilemma whether non-deviation from manifestation is desired even at the time of origination, or whether non-deviation from manifestation is desired only after the moment of origination?

In that regard, considering that the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the first argument has already been stated previously, he states its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) in the second case with the words "in pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādiṣu*). He explains this with "for not" (*na hi*). He refutes the other alternative with "therefore" (*ataḥ*); the meaning is that because of these two reasons—non-establishment and inconclusiveness—the probandum (*sādhya*) is also not established. By this, it is shown that insentience (*jaḍatva*) is not undesirable. Regarding the claim that it will be proved by another inference, he says "a different matter" (*arthāntaram*).

The meaning is that, because it is self-contradictory (*vyāhata*), not even a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is capable of establishing this point. As they have said: "Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself by itself, so too knowledge, by its own part, cannot know itself. Thus, it has been shown that the reductio (*tarka*)—which consists in the undesirable consequence of insentience (*jaḍatva*)—lacks a conclusive reversal (*viparyaya-paryavasāna*), lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*), results in an undesired conclusion (*iṣṭaprasaṅga*), and is refuted by a counter-reductio (*pratitarka*) characterized by contradiction.

Thus, the word *manuṣa* connects with what precedes it as follows: Now, the proponent of self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) says, "This very [experience]," regarding one whose distinctions from experience have not been perceived. Experience, being the illuminator of everything other than itself, is "one manifestation" (*eko vibhavaḥ*) insofar as it does not depend on anything else with respect to its own nature. It is "another [manifestation]" insofar as it alone is capable of producing that linguistic usage based on manifestness (*prākaṭya*), namely, the usage "it shines forth."

Thus, one by whom the twofold majesty of experience (*anubhava-vibhava*) is not perceived is "one whose majesty of experience is unperceived"; [the phrase] refers to such a person. "The unfolding of one's own intellect" (*sva-mati-vijṛmbhita*) means that which unfolds as mere self-conjecture, independent of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). Alternatively, it is a reproach meaning "the greatness of one's own intellect. By the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), in order to lead [the opponent] to accept self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), he first rejects the mark of manifestation (*prākaṭya-liṅga*) with the words beginning with "anubhūti... and so forth.

By the phrase "distinct from experience," the exclusion of the [charge of] being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*) is effectively established. By the term "property of the object" (*viṣayadharma*), properties belonging to the self (*ātmadharma*) are excluded. Consequently, its commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) with [other objects], such as color and so forth, is established. The point is this: is the manifestation (*prakāśa*), which is a property of the object distinct from experience, perceptible or not? If it is not, then due to the absence of knowledge of a logical mark (*liṅga*), inference cannot arise. If it is perceptible, then it would be perceivable by others, just like color and so forth.

If it is argued that just as duality and so forth—produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—are perceived only by the particular person [who possesses that cognition], so too is "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*) perceived only by that same person; we say no. For numbers such as duality already exist prior [to the cognition]; they are, for instance, like all the directions [which exist] in a single location. Indeed, those directions are manifested by a relative cognition with respect to various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In the same way, duality and so forth, which are manifested by a relative cognition, shine forth only for that person in whom the manifesting agent resides.

But in this case, since it is admitted that [the cognition] is a produced property (*janyadharma*) like color and so forth, it would be perceived by everyone. If, however, it were something manifested (*abhivyaṅgya*), it would appear only to one who possesses the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*), like a treasure revealed by a magical ointment (*siddhāñjana*). A produced thing does not, however, appear only to its producer; for a jar is not perceived only by the potter. Furthermore, "like color and so forth."

The sense is this: since it is impossible for a property (*dharma*) to arise without a substratum (*āśraya*), and since manifestation (*prākaṭya*) is impossible even when past and future objects are being produced, cognition cannot be inferred through manifestation—just as with color and so forth—because manifestation is not perceived there. As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "How could manifestation be possible regarding an object that is past or future? For a property cannot possibly exist when its substratum is non-existent."

If it is argued that even for the past and the future, manifestness (*prākaṭya*) is produced just like duality (*dvitva*) and so forth, we say no; for even duality and the like cannot arise without a substratum. Furthermore, even in the absence of the production of duality and so forth in those cases, the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of duality and the like is possible because they reside in the cognition (*dhīsthatayā*), just as a jar or other objects do. As for those who do not accept duality and the like, one should not employ duality and the like as a counter-argument against them.

If it is argued that "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*) is simply the relation of object and subject, because there is no rule that a relation of object and subject must necessarily have a [separate] substrate, we say no; for since a relation cannot be cognized without its two relata, the cognition of the relata would also be perceived, and thus [manifestness] could not even be an inferable [property]. Therefore, manifestness does not serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*).

Anticipating the objection that an entity called "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*), though unperceived, must be postulated because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, [the author] shows that the postulator's argument is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) by stating, "Both... (*ubhaya*). The term "accepted by both" (*ubhayābhyupeta*) is used to dispel the doubt that by saying "by experience" (*anubhūtyā*), one might be stating a mere synonym for manifestness. The sense of the particle "only" (*eva*) is: "by that very [experience] which you yourself have asserted to be the producer of manifestness. "All worldly activity" (*aśeṣavyavahāra*) refers to activities such as avoidance, acquisition, and so forth.

Since that [manifestation] arises solely through experience (*anubhūti*), manifestation (*prākaṭya*) need not be postulated by means of it. Furthermore, the common usage "the jar is known" (*jñāto ghaṭaḥ*) or "the jar is manifest" (*prakaṭo ghaṭaḥ*) is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*), just like the usage "the jar is desired" (*iṣṭo ghaṭaḥ*) or "the jar is hated" (*dviṣṭo ghaṭaḥ*); this is the intended meaning of all such words. For desire is not inferred from the "desirability" residing in the object produced by that desire. In the expression "the jar shines forth" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*), manifestation is perceived as having the jar as its agent (*kartṛ*).

If it is argued that the experience "he experiences the jar" is perceived as having the jar as its object (*karman*) and another as its agent (*kartṛ*), and that [the status of being both object and agent] is thus postulated because the conventional usage of a single entity as both object and agent is otherwise untenable—[we reply: no, because the distinction between *kārakas* is based on the distinction between verbal roots (*dhātu*) and not on a distinction in the objective referent (*artha*). For example, when it is said, "Raising the axe, he brings it down upon the tree," and "He cuts the tree with the axe," although the axe is heard to have the status of both object and instrument (*karaṇa*), there is nevertheless no difference in the objective referent.

Although the tree is heard to function as both the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the object (*karman*), there is nevertheless no difference in meaning. This is because the distinction in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-bheda*) is based on the distinction between verbal roots (*dhātu-bheda*) and does not have a difference in meaning as its cause; thus, with the intention that linguistic usage does not necessitate the postulation of "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*), it was stated: "when all linguistic usage is accounted for. The linguistic usage "the jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ prakāśate*) is not possible without some excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in the jar; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that same usage applying to a cloth as well.

If it is argued that this excellence (*atiśaya*) is "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*), then since it is this excellence that determines [the object], why should it belong to the jar alone and not to the cloth? If it is argued that it is due to the contact with the sense organs, then let it be the cognition itself that is determined by that; what is the point of postulating another excellence? This meaning is also intended by the term "all worldly transactions" (*aśeṣavyavahāra*).

As for the claim that at the time of the experience "this is a jar," there is no experience of the experience itself—that is not so; for the non-employment of the word "is experienced" is based on a lack of desire to speak, and not on the absence of the experience itself. For when people have the desire to express the entirety of what has been experienced, they state it all; if they have the desire to express only a portion, they state that portion of what was experienced. And if there is no desire to express even a portion, they do not say anything at all.

Therefore, the non-employment of the word "is experienced" (*anubhūyate*) is not a reason for its lack of manifestation. This too is intended by the term "entirety of worldly transaction" (*aśeṣa-vyavahāra*); for even a deficient as well as a complete worldly transaction can be encompassed by the word "entirety. Thus, since worldly transaction is established otherwise, and only that which is not established otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*) can serve as a basis for postulation, the [intrinsic] manifestation cannot be postulated—this is the meaning.

He concludes the impossibility of manifestness being inferable with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: because manifestness is absent—due to both the non-occurrence of the conventional usage of non-apprehension and the fact that it could be established otherwise—cognition is not inferable from manifestness. Intending to show the impossibility of its being known through mental perception, he says: "nor is it established by another cognition. Here, the following inference stated by the opponent [is intended]: "Cognition is graspable by mental perception, because, while being momentary, it is a specific quality of the self, like pleasure, pain, effort, and so forth."

When it is stated, "because it is a specific quality of the self" (*ātmaviśeṣaguṇatvāt*), there would be an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntya*) with respect to merit (*dharma*) and so forth; therefore, to exclude those, "while being momentary" (*kṣaṇikatve sati*) is added. If it were stated, "because it is a momentary specific quality," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sound (*śabda*); if it were stated, "because it is a momentary quality of the self," there would be a deviation in the case of the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the self. To avoid these [objections], the terms "self" (*ātma-*) and "specific" (*viśeṣa-*) are used. However, this is untenable: because either momentariness or the nature of being a quality is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

Furthermore, whatever is cognizable by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is observed to be apprehended without being intended for cognition (*anubhutsitagrāhya*), as in the case of pleasure and so forth. Therefore, it must be stated that the knowledge having that [pleasure] as its object is necessarily [of this nature]. Consequently, since the knowledge whose object is the knowledge of a jar or the like would also be apprehended without being intended for cognition, it too would be cognizable by mental perception; and since the knowledge having that [second-order knowledge] as its object would likewise be so, there would be an unavoidable emergence of an infinite series of cognitions (*ananta-saṃvid-āvalī-samudaya*), leaving no room for a further subsequent knowledge (*jñānāntara*).

If it is argued that being graspable by the mind is not pervaded by being graspable by one who has no desire to know—since, for instance, inhalation and exhalation occur during sleep and so forth even though there is no apprehension of them—the answer is no; for at that time there is simply an absence of effort in the individual soul (*jīvātman*). According to the Vedāntins, the maintenance of the body and such functions at that time are dependent upon the volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This point is well-established in the section of the *Brahma-sūtra* beginning with "Like the internal collection of elements" (*antarābhūtagrāmavat*).

During sleep, the turning of the body and so forth occurs when there is extremely slight awareness due to the pain arising from the pricking of limbs and minor parts, or from the suffering caused by mosquitoes and the like. At that time, effort has cognition as its object. For this reason, because it is non-deviant, if everything graspable by the mind were graspable without being sought to be known (*abubhutsita-grāhya*), then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would certainly result. If, on the other hand, it is graspable only when sought to be known (*bubhutsita-grāhya*), then there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*): desire exists when cognition exists, and cognition exists when desire exists.

Furthermore, even if that which is known through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is to be grasped only when there is a desire to know (*bubhutsā*), since a rule of apprehension is observed in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, one must postulate a rule of desire to know for those as well. Just like that, in the case of cognition too, since the rule of desire to know would be established, apprehension would necessarily be restricted. Consequently, there would be no cessation of the succession of cognitions mediated by successive desires to know. If it is argued that cognition is to be grasped only when there is a desire to know, whereas pleasure and so forth are not, we say no; for there is no determining factor (*niyāmaka*) given that they are equally objects of mental perception.

If it is argued that there is a desire to know (*bubhutsā*) regarding pleasure and so forth, as well as regarding the first cognition of objects such as a jar, but not regarding the second cognition and subsequent ones—this is not so, because there is no restrictive rule [to the contrary]. Since there is no difference in their being apprehended by the mind (*mānasa*), who could prevent the desire to know that has already arisen? For the desire to know occurs precisely when something is apprehensible by the mind; and both pleasure and the like, as well as the first cognition of objects such as a jar, are apprehensible by the mind. If it is argued that the second cognition and subsequent ones are not cognizable through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), we say no; for even in that case, there is no restrictive rule.

Furthermore, even if [the second cognition] were a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a momentary self, if it were not graspable by the mind (*mānasagrāhya*), the reason (*hetu*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). If you argue that when it is grasped through perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is then graspable by the mind, then both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the reason must be qualified by the term "graspable by perception. Moreover, other refutations stated by others are also set forth: if this second cognition were not graspable by the mind, then that second [cognition]—lacking any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—would be non-existent.

Consequently, there would be emptiness (śūnyatā) not only of the first [cognition] but also of its objects, such as the jar and so forth. If the second and subsequent cognitions were self-established (*svataḥsiddha*), then the first cognition would likewise be so. It is with this intention that it was stated that [cognitions] are not established by another cognition. Then, he says "but rather" (*api tu*) to show that self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) is established by the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*). [He says] "all."

Otherwise, because consciousness would be void, everything dependent upon it—including its own establishment—would become void; therefore, with the intention of avoiding that consequence, one must necessarily accept self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*). With this in mind, it is stated that all [authorities] establish that experience is established by itself alone. As it says in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "For those good people who, seeing everything as void, are terrified of total nihilism, no other recourse is found except for self-luminosity."

Now, he presents the proof for self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) which is supported by reasoning (*tarka*), stating "the formal argument" (*prayogaśca*). The meaning is that self-establishedness is not merely due to the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*); rather, there is also a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*). By the words beginning with "experience" (*anubhūti*), two inferences are stated without distinction for the sake of brevity in the text.

The distinction is as follows: "Apprehension has its own properties independent of anything else, because, through its connection with itself, it is the cause of those properties in other objects; apprehension has its own linguistic usage independent of anything else, because, through its connection with itself, it is the cause of that usage in other objects. For this very reason, it will be stated later that since it is the cause of a specific usage in another, it must also be the cause of that same usage in itself. Having first accepted "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*), the first inference was stated by relying upon it.

The second [reason], however, does not depend on that [first]. The admission of *prākaṭya* (manifestness) does not contradict self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*), because it is not admitted that [manifestness] serves as an inferential mark for cognition. If the probandum were "possessing attributes" or "possessing attributes not dependent on anything else," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for attributes such as "experientiality" (*anubhūtitva*) do not depend on another cause. Indeed, the universal "experientiality" is not dependent on a cause, because it is eternal.

Even if one does not accept [the category of] "jāti" (universal), since the state of being an experience (*anubhūtitva*) does not depend on any cause other than the causal complex for experience (*anubhūti-sāmagrī*), the argument would be proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatā*). Therefore, it is stated that [the property] is "not dependent on another for its own nature" (*ananyādhīna-svadharma*). Its own property (*svadharma*) is a property related to itself by virtue of being produced by itself. The meaning is: a property in another [locus] that is absolutely similar to the property to be proven (*svasādhyadharma*). This is because the reason stated is "because it is the cause of that property in another object. Indeed, the property indicated by the term *svadharma* is the very one expressed by the word "that" (*tat*).

In another [definition], a property that is absolutely similar to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in another locus, which necessarily exists in itself, is intended as its own property (*svadharma*). For this very reason, by not attributing "possessing form" (*rūpitva*) to itself, the suspicion that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), namely "form," is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), is dispelled; and the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—as in the case of a staff, which does not bring about "being a staff-bearer" in itself without depending on another staff—is also avoided.

Furthermore, the word "other" (*anya*) refers to something else that is absolutely of the same class (*svātyantasajātīya*); otherwise, if it were independent of any cause whatsoever, the example would be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatva*). For the visibility of color (*rūpa*) depends on the eye and other factors; thus, what is intended by the term "not dependent on another" (*ananyādhīna*) is the absence of a necessary dependence on such causes. If the probandum were merely the absence of dependence on anything else, there would be the consequence of invalidation (*bādhitatva*), since the cognition of another person is observed to be inferable. Indeed, it is not the case that being beyond the scope of other cognitions is what is to be proven by this inference.

Rather, [the definition] is merely the fitness for manifestation independent of anything of its own absolute genus; and since this is possible for supreme consciousness (*parajñāna*), there is no contradiction regarding the object of the proposition. Furthermore, in the phrase "independent of another for its own linguistic usage" (*ananyādhīnasvavyavahāra*), if the probandum were simply "possessing linguistic usage," it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); therefore, the word "independent" (*ananya*) is used. Since the word "other" (*anya*) refers to that which is of an absolutely similar genus, any suspicion of contradiction based on dependence upon speech and so forth [of the same genus] is thereby removed.

In the case of the practical usage (vyavahāra) regarding the abandonment and so forth of jars and other objects, experience (*anubhūti*) is the cause that is independent of anything else of its own absolute kind. The word "self" (*sva*) is employed to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*). Furthermore, in this context, "self" refers to something other than itself that is absolutely of the same kind as the practical usage to be established by it. Being "absolutely of the same kind" as a practical usage means having an identical ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Indeed, the ground for the practical usage "it shines forth" is merely the suitability for such usage. The intention to express the absence of any restrictive dependence is intended to avoid the charge of "missing the proper time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) in the case of the practical usage of another's cognition.

He states the reason: "because of its own connection" (*svasambandhāt*). Since the reasons intended are [respectively] being the cause of a property (*dharma*) and being the cause of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*); therefore, the word *tat* (that) is used to avoid that. What is intended by the word *tat* is a property and a linguistic usage that are absolutely similar (*atyantasajātīya*) to the property and linguistic usage of itself (*svasya*).

Because a pot, due to its connection with fire, becomes the cause for the application of the term "another form" (rūpāntara) to itself—a form belonging to the same genus as its prior form—it is dependent upon fire; thus, the word *arthāntara* (another thing) was stated to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case. Furthermore, the word *arthāntara* refers to something of a different genus (*vijātīya*) from that which has been specified; by this, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*)—wherein a substance, being the cause for the application of the term "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*) to another substance, is dependent upon that other substance—is avoided. For a substance is absolutely of the same genus (*atyantasajātīya*) as a [second] substance.

Objection: Is there not an inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) in the case of a jar, which, while imparting its own state of being conjoined and so forth to a cloth, depends upon another jar for that very state? Reply: Not so; because the probandum-property—defined as the absence of a rule regarding dependence on a homogeneous entity—is present therein. For there is no such rule that a jar, in order to establish its own state of being conjoined and so forth, must depend exclusively upon a jar that is absolutely homogeneous with itself.

In the case of a son—who is the cause for the designation "son" in his father—the statement "due to its own relation" (*svasambandhāt*) is made to avoid the fallacy that [the son] would require another father in order to establish the designation "son" for himself. What is intended is an existing relation to oneself. The meaning is: because it is the cause of a designation dependent upon a property in itself that is absolutely similar to a property in another, occurring at the same time as the relation to oneself. For indeed, even when a father is exiled or dies, the sonship and the corresponding designation do not depart from the son.

For this very reason, any deviation [of the definition] with respect to a substance that causes the division of another object—while itself not undergoing a division independent of anything else—is cast far away.

[Objection: But surely this inference is also accepted by the proponent of the Siddhānta [the Vedāntin]: "The conscious being, while producing 'bodiness' (śarīratva) and the linguistic usage thereof in a body at a time identical to its own connection [with that body], does not depend on anything else for the [production of] bodiness and its usage in itself; rather, it depends upon the Supreme Self (paramātman). And since the Supreme Self is conscious, it is of the same genus (*atyantasajātīya*). Therefore, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that case. [Reply: Not so; because what is intended is the state of being the cause of a property that pervades itself (*svavyāpakadharma-hetutva*). For bodiness does not pervade consciousness.
Since even the conscious Lord lacks a body, the objection is resolved by the intended meaning of the word "own-nature" (svadharma), namely, that which is necessarily inherent to oneself.

This is what is meant: the word *dharma* may refer either to luminosity (*prakāśa*) or to mere luminosity (*dharmamātra*); and the word *anya* may refer either to mere otherness (*anyamātra*) or to something other than that which is absolutely of the same class as itself (*svātyantasajātīyānya*). In that regard, if the probandum is "luminosity independent of any cause," the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), for color (*rūpa*) is indeed luminous only in dependence upon the eye and other factors. If the probandum is "luminosity independent of anything absolutely of the same class as itself," the reason (*hetu*) contains a superfluous qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*), because the probandum is established by the mere fact of being a cause.

For no cause, such as a jar, while being a cause for something else, requires another jar for its own manifestation. If the property [of self-luminosity] were independent of a cause, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by means of [the property of] being an experience (*anubhūtitva*); furthermore, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with respect to axes and the like, because an axe, which is the cause for the splitting of wood, requires another cause for its own splitting. Moreover, if the property were independent of anything of its own absolute kind, there would again be the fallacy of proving what is already established by means of being an experience.

Furthermore, there is sublation (*bādha*) because it is observed that in the case of another cognition which illuminates an object, its illumination depends upon a logical mark (*liṅga*). Moreover, in the case of color (*rūpa*), since it lacks the causal property of possessing color within itself without depending on another color, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*). Furthermore, regarding the property of being a son residing in the father—which depends on another person (the father) as the cause for the sonhood residing in the son—there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*). Likewise, regarding the property of being conjoined residing in one substance—which depends on another substance as the cause for the conjunction in that substance—there is also inconclusiveness.

Therefore, in order to avoid such defects and the like, the argument should be formulated as follows: **Thesis (pratijñā):** Experience (*anubhūti*) does not stand in need of anything else that is absolutely similar to it, provided it possesses a property that is absolutely similar to a property produced by itself in another [subject]. **Reason (hetu):** Because it is a cause of a property at the same time as itself, which is absolutely similar to a property necessarily present in its own dissimilar class (*svavijātīya*).

Likewise, the proposition is that experience (*anubhūti*), in its capacity to be the cause of a usage (*vyavahāra*) occurring in another that is absolutely similar to a usage produced by itself, is devoid of any necessity of dependence upon something absolutely similar to itself. The reason (*hetu*) is: because it is the cause of a usage simultaneous with its own relation to something absolutely similar to the usage that is necessarily produced from what is dissimilar to itself. The "necessity" (*avaśyambhāvitva*) of the usage consists in its being based upon a property that is necessarily present.

He states the example preceded by the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "that which... He shows the properties of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) with the words "for color-form and so forth... He states the property established by the force of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the words "therefore, cognition... [and] "it is manifested as a linguistic usage. Regarding the linguistic usage "cognition is manifested," [the term] "cognition" [is used].

The meaning is: "in conventional usage. Now, an objection is raised: the status of being the cause for the conventional usage of a property in another object due to its own relation is *sopādhika* (conditioned), because the very fact of being the cause for the conventional usage of that property in another object through a specific relation is the determining factor (*prayojaka*) for the non-dependence upon anything else in the conventional usage of that property within itself. And that specific relation consists in the nature of the locus and the located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*). That [relation] exists in the case of color and so forth, but not in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*).

This is not so, because that [property] lacks the status of a *upādhi* (limiting condition) due to its absence of co-presence (*sādhyasamavyāpti*) with the probandum; for it is observed that even in the absence of a substrate-superstratum relationship, a lamp—which is the cause of the linguistic usage "it shines"—is seen to be entirely independent of anything else of its own kind even when performing that very usage within itself. Previously, by those who maintain that cognition is illuminated by another, the reason "because it is manifested by its own existence alone" was stated to be both unestablished (*asiddha*) and contradictory (*vyāhati*).

In that regard, it was stated that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because at the time of the experience "this is a jar," the word "is experienced" is not employed. This unestablishedness is refuted by stating that the deficiency or sufficiency of verbal usage is caused by a specific intention to speak, and thus has no causal efficacy regarding whether there is an experience of an object or not. Furthermore, there is no contradiction (*vyāhati*). For instance, the contradiction of a fingertip touching itself is based on empirical observation; likewise, in lamps and the like, both the state of being illuminated and the state of illuminating are observed.

Upon examination, there is no contradiction between the status of object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*). For the lamp is the dispeller and darkness is that which is to be dispelled; the lamp is the producer and knowledge is that which is produced; knowledge is the producer and worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is that which is produced. Furthermore, although the distinction [of these roles] is established by perception due to the inherent contradiction in the relation of object and agent, nevertheless, the absence of a rule regarding contradiction among indicators (*jñāpaka*) is also established by perception.

In the case of the knower and the mind, of the word "sound" and the sound itself, and of the word "word"—as well as in other such instances of different objects—non-contradiction is indeed observed. However, the rule of contradiction applies only among things that produce one another; and in those cases, there is no contradiction if they exist in different forms. Now, an objection: in the case of jars and the like, their fitness for linguistic usage is seen to be caused by a cognition distinct from themselves. If the pervasion (invariable concomitance) in the case of cognition is thus broken, then by the breaking of the pervasion that linguistic usage is preceded by cognition, it would follow that cognition itself could become the locus of linguistic usage even while remaining unknown.

It is not so; for although in the case of jars and the like, visibility to a knower distinct from the object of knowledge is observed, it is universally accepted that the knower is visible to that very same knower—thus, even the opponent must admit a breach in the pervasion regarding the contradiction between the object and the agent. Likewise, although in the case of jars and the like, visibility is through a cognition produced by an instrument distinct from themselves, this is set aside in the case of the mind, because in one's own inference, the mind itself serves as the instrument.

Likewise, although all expressible objects are denotable by words distinct from themselves, this rule fails in the case of the word "word" (*śabda*) and the term "term" (*pada*). Similarly, although jars and other things are communicable through speech distinct from themselves, this rule fails in the case of the organ of speech (*vāg-indriya*). Therefore, there is no pervasion by contradiction regarding the relationship between object and agent. Nor has the fact that linguistic usage is preceded by cognition been subverted by anyone. If it were to follow that the linguistic usage of a cognition lacks the status of being the object of that very cognition, that would not be undesirable.

Since the state of being preceded by manifestation possesses an unbroken pervasion (*avyabhicāra*), there is no contingency of its absence. Therefore, it is only knowledge that is manifesting which serves as the basis for linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, it is logical that knowledge possesses the capacity to conform to linguistic conventions regarding both its own object and the objects of others.

Now, since the refutation of the knower and the known, as well as the self-luminosity of knowledge (*jñāna-svayaṃprakāśatva*), are common even to the Buddhist position, [the author] establishes the eternality of knowledge as that which distinguishes it from them with the words "seyaṃ" (this very). The meaning is: "this [knowledge], which is identical with Pure Being (*sanmātra*) as the ultimate reality, and which is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, the meaning is: "it is well-known for possessing those attributes that serve as the grounds for its self-luminosity. It is described as "self-luminous" because self-luminosity is intended to be the ground for its eternality.

The word *ca* (and) serves either to aggregate the probandum (*sādhyasamuccaye*) or to dispel the suspicion of similarity with the Buddhists (*saugatasāmyaśaṅkānivṛtau*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvādi*). When the doubt arises as to how that [non-existence] is so, he says—with the intention that it is due to the absence of a perceiver (*grāhakābhāvāt*)—"And its absence... Desiring to establish the absence of prior non-existence and the rest through the medium of an alternative (*vikalpamukhena*), given their self-evident nature (*svataḥsiddhatvena*), he first declares the untenability of the two horns of the alternative by saying: "For not..."

Regarding the position of the proponent [of self-awareness], there is a dilemma: does experience, while existing, make its own non-existence known, or does it do so while not existing? With this alternative in mind, he refutes the position that it exists, stating "experience" [is not possible]. To the question "Why?", he says "of that" (*tasyāḥ*). The meaning is "due to the absence of an object of apprehension. In the alternative—whether experience, in the form of inference and so forth, makes its own non-existence known, or whether it does so in the form of perception—the first option is impossible because of the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so on; with this in mind, the second option is refuted due to the absence of an object of apprehension.

He refutes the position that the first alternative (vikalpa-śiras) regarding the non-existence [of the object] is untenable due to the absence of a grasper, using the word "thus" (*evam*). He refutes the position that it is one or the other of the two alternatives previously stated with the words "nor" (*na api*). [The opponent might argue: "Experience (*anubhūti*) would have no other object; what follows from that for the non-apprehension of absence? To this he replies with the words "of this" (*asyāḥ*), meaning: "Indeed, the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of something else cannot be grasped; rather, it is the absence of experience itself that must be grasped."

Therefore, its absence can only be apprehended by first making that [entity] itself an object of cognition; since it is incapable of becoming an object, its prior non-existence cannot be grasped—this is the meaning. Thus, due to the absence of prior non-existence, there is no origination, and from that, he establishes the absence of all other modifications such as transformation and so forth, with the words "therefore, of this" (*ato'syāḥ*). The meaning is: because the non-existence of both positions—that [non-existence] is either intrinsic or extrinsic—is difficult to apprehend.

If the probandum were merely the absence of transformation (*vikāra*), then the state of being unproduced (*anutpannatva*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which has an end. Therefore, the word "existent" (*bhāva*) is used to indicate that the probandum is the absence of transformation in the form of a positive entity. Alternatively, it may be understood as a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*): "the transformation of an existent. Consequently, when the probandum is the absence of all transformations consisting of both existence and non-existence, it follows that—given the condition of being an existent—the state of being unproduced is the determinant for the absence of other transformations; thus, the suspicion of deviation regarding prior non-existence is removed.
Experience is not finite, because while being an existent, it is unproduced; for whatever is finite, while being an existent, is not unproduced, such as a jar.

In order to exclude the momentariness accepted by the Buddhists and to establish permanence, its non-arising and the absence of any other transformation pervaded by that [momentariness] have been proven. Now, in order to exclude the plurality accepted by them, he eliminates difference among things of the same class by stating, "This is unarisen. This is because of the perception of something contrary to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). The meaning is: because of the perception of non-arising, which is contrary to arising—the pervader of plurality. He demonstrates this pervasion with the words, "For not... and so forth.

Regarding this text, it is not appropriate to state the meaning as "that which is unproduced is seen to be non-different," because the Māyā-Vedāntins do not admit the existence of anything other than Brahman that is both unproduced and non-different. If one were to say, "whatever is non-different is unproduced," it would not follow that by the negation of the pervader (non-origination), the negation of the pervaded (non-difference) is stated. Therefore, the meaning is this: "that which is differentiated is not seen to be unproduced."

However, by stating that "only that which possesses origination is seen," it is shown that origination pervades multiplicity. By this, it is established as a matter of course that with the cessation of origination, there is the cessation of multiplicity. Alternatively, just as when it is said, "for smoke is never seen where there is no fire," it is thereby implied that "smoke exists only where there is fire," so too here, when it is said, "the unoriginated is not seen to be manifold," it is thereby implied that "that which is manifold possesses origination"; and thus, it is stated that origination is the pervader.

Experience is not manifold, because it is unproduced. Whatever is manifold is observed to be produced, as in the case of a jar; this negative inference (*vyatireky-anumāna*) is stated by taking experience as the subject (*pakṣa*). It is difficult to allege a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space and so forth, because the Vedāntins themselves accept that those things are produced; such is the sense.

Thus, difference within the same class (*sajātīya-bheda*) has been refuted. In this context, taking both difference and another modification (*vikārāntara*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), he states a positive inference (*anvayyanumāna*) regarding "difference and so forth" (*bhedādīnām*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), production and other such qualities are intended. The meaning is: "Difference and the rest are not properties of consciousness (*anubhūti*), because they are inferable, like color and other [sensory qualities]. He further establishes that even a property in the form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-rūpa-dharma*) does not exist, stating "therefore, of consciousness" (*ato 'nubhūteḥ*). The implication is that even a property consisting of differentiation from others is absent.

Alternatively, he states a negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*)—beginning with "Therefore, of experience" (*atonubhūteḥ*)—in order to dispel the suspicion that [experience] possesses attributes such as eternality, unity, and self-luminosity (which would follow from the negation of its being subject to modification, plurality, and insentience), and also to exclude the aforementioned plurality and other such qualities. The meaning is: "even other [attributes] such as eternality. The inference is as follows: Experience does not possess attributes in the form of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), because it is of the nature of experience (*anubhavasvarūpatvāt*). Whatever possesses attributes in the form of exclusions is observed to be non-experience, such as a jar and so forth; this is the negative instance (*vyatireki*).

If, taking the property of having an excluded form (*vyāvṛttirūpadharma*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), the non-existence of the property of being an experience (*anubhūtidharmatva*) were to be proved, then "being an object of experience" (*anubhāvyatva*) would be the reason (*hetu*); for example, color and so forth would be the similar instance (*sapakṣa*). This is a positive inference (*anvayi*). Thus, internal difference has been refuted; previously, the difference between objects of knowledge was already refuted. In Vedic passages such as "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous," the eternality, self-luminosity, and other attributes of the Self (*ātman*) are established; here, however, the eternality and other attributes of consciousness (*saṃvit*) are stated.

To the question "How is that consistent?", he says "yataḥ" (since). The meaning is as follows: because all distinctions have been shaken off—by the negation of every distinction, even the distinction from heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-bheda*) is discarded—the Self is not that [dualistic] knower which consists of the falsity of heterogeneous distinction; rather, consciousness (*saṃvid*) alone, being the ultimate reality (*paramārthabhūtā*), is the Self.
