Alternatively, the meaning is that the absence of plurality—whether homogeneous, heterogeneous, or internal—which is established for the Self by the Vedāntas, is logically possible only for consciousness; therefore, that alone is the Self. [He adds] "svarūpa... (in its own nature...).

The knower is indeed that which has a substratum distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*); since such a knower does not exist—precisely because it would be other than the nature of consciousness—it is not ultimately real. Therefore, the meaning is that consciousness alone, being the ultimate reality, is the Self. That very consciousness, whose nature is self-luminous, is the Self. The meaning is that the self-luminosity of the Self established by the Vedāntas is logically consistent with consciousness; thus, consciousness alone is the Self. Alternatively, it is stated that its nature is self-luminous in order to dispel the doubt that it might be a mere non-entity (*tucchatva*).

He states that self-luminosity is the independent proof [of the Self] with the words, "and because of non-inertness" (*ajaḍatvāt*). This is expressed through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): consciousness is the Self because it is non-inert; whatever is not the Self is inert, such as a jar and the like. He explains this with the words, "in the case of being non-Self. It is pervaded by non-Selfhood. The word "pervaded" (*vyāptam*) is derived from the root *vyap* with the suffix *kta* in the active sense (*kartari*), meaning "the pervader" (*vyāpakam*), just as in the expression "one who has reached" (*prāpta*).

When the status of the self as a knower has been refuted by reasoning, [the opponent] objects that its being the object of the notion of "I" is established by the direct perception of one's own experience, stating: "But surely... (*nanu ca*). The particle *ca* is used here for the purpose of conjunction with the objection. The phrase "established by cognition" (*pratīti-siddhā*) means established by the cognition consisting of one's own experience. To this, [the author] replies: "Not so" (*naivam*). He states that such cognition is erroneous: "That [cognition] is established through delusion" (*sā bhrānti-siddhā*).

With the intention that "just as the silver-nature, previously perceived as an object of experience, becomes established as an error because it is sublated by the cognition of mother-of-pearl," he says: "like the silver-nature of the piece of mother-of-pearl. The word *śakala* (piece) is used to establish its status as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the delusion; for mother-of-pearl in its complete form cannot serve as the substrate of an error.

Alternatively, when the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is perceived, it has been stated that while the aspect of knowledge (*jñāna-aṃśa*) therein is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), the aspect of the agent (*kartṛ-aṃśa*) is not ultimately real, using the example of the silver-nature of a piece of mother-of-pearl. For in that case, the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*) is ultimately real, whereas the silver-nature alone is not ultimately real. He establishes that [the agent-aspect] is established through delusion (*bhrānti*) by saying, "because of its non-existence" (*adbhūteḥ*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says, "Therefore, [it is] a human being. He establishes the impossibility of agency by saying, "For the state of being a knower... (*jñātṛtvaṃ hi*).

Alternatively, with the intention of raising the following dilemma—namely, whether this so-called "knowership" consists in being the substratum of knowledge that constitutes the very nature of Brahman, or whether it consists in being the substratum of knowledge in the form of a function of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—the author refutes the first alternative with the words "of experience" (anubhūteḥ). The meaning is: since the ultimate reality of experience alone has been established by the arguments previously stated, its knowership would entail agency within itself; however, that is contradictory. Here, "agency" (kartṛtva) means "substratum-ship" (āśrayatva).

With the intention that the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is superimposed because it is established only through the cognition of a deluded person, he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the body's distinctness from the Self is well-established by its birth and other characteristics, it is described as "utterly external. Now, with the intention that not only is agency (*kartṛtva*) untenable from one's own perspective, but rather that agency in general—which makes no distinction between self and other—is untenable, he refutes the second position by saying "for the state of being a knower" (*jñātṛtvaṃ hi*).

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tacceti*). Because it is subject to arising and destruction, it is "of the nature of transformation" (*vikriyātmakam*); since action (*kriyā*) depends upon that [nature], its substratum is also occasional, meaning it is of the form of modification (*vikāra*). It is "insentient" (*jaḍam*) and "knowable" (*jñeyam*). For this very reason, it resides within the knot of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which is a substance subject to modification; the sense is that this is due to the commonality between the two in being insentient and of the nature of transformation. A "knot" (*granthi*) is a specific kind of binding that causes the loosening of a bond. It is called a "knot" because the ego-sense is the root of all delusions.

He states the nature of that which is contrary to this [the Self] as "unchanging" (*avikriya*). In response to the doubt that by accepting [the Self] as a witness (*sākṣitva*), one must necessarily accept it as a knower (*jñātṛtva*), he says "as a witness" (*sākṣiṇī*) with the intention that even witnesshood is consistent with having consciousness as its very nature (*jñānasvarūpatva*). The point is that witnesshood consists precisely in being the experience of ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, there is no contradiction with its being knowledge. [The term] "in the self which is pure consciousness and self-luminous" (*cinmātrātmani svayaṃprakāśe*) implies that the status of being a knower is impossible for that which is insentient (*jaḍa*), since the insentient cannot possess the quality of being a knower.

Agency and so forth are not attributes of the Self, because their establishment depends upon that which is perceived (*dṛśya*), just like color and other qualities; this is stated with reference to a positive concomitance (*anvayin*). By the phrase "because their establishment depends upon that which is perceived," he intends to include the fact that agency and so forth are objects of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) by means of the word "etc. The force of the particle *eva* ("only") is that the very same reason which establishes that difference and the rest are not attributes of consciousness (*anubhūti*) also applies here. As for the argument that the Self must be the knower because the referent of "I" is perceived as being in grammatical apposition with it, he replies: "In deep sleep, fainting, and so forth."

By relying on such scriptural passages as "Not this, not this," it has been stated that [the Self] remains even when the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) ceases. Regarding the absence of agency and the state of not being an object of the notion of "I" for the Self, he states three negative inferences (*vyatirekyanumāna*) in the form of reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), beginning with the words "kartṛtve. There are two propositions (*pratijñā*): "The Self is not an agent" and "It is not an object of the notion of 'I'"; and there are three reasons (*hetu*): "because of non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*)," "because of being the witness (*pratyaktva*)," and "because of being the Self (*ātmatva*)."

Whatever is an agent and whatever is the object of the notion of "I" is observed to be insentient, external, and non-self, such as the body. Alternatively, the Self is not an agent nor is it the object of the notion of "I," because that would entail the consequence of its being insentient and so forth, like the body. Insentience (*jaḍatva*) consists in having the nature of being perceived solely by another. Being external (*parāktva*) consists in appearing to another. Selfhood (*ātmatva*) consists in being the correlate of human goals, or pervasiveness by way of being the controller with respect to the body; the absence of that is non-selfhood (*anātmatva*).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), perishability and so forth are intended. For once it is established that the body, which is the object of the notion of "I," is not the self, it follows that the agent who is the object of the notion of "I" is also not the self; to this he says, "from that which is the object of the notion of 'I'. By the phrase "the enjoyer of the fruits of action such as heaven," its distinctness from the body is established. [This refers to] those who accept authoritative means of knowledge, other than the Cārvākas.

The doubt as to how the Self can be the enjoyer of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) if the agency belongs to the non-self ego (ahaṅkāra) is refuted by the analogy of the body. To the objection that if the Self were established as the enjoyer of heaven and so forth, it would necessarily be something known, he says: "In the same way" (tathā). For the admission of a Self distinct from the body is made on the strength of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); likewise, since the knower is also established by valid means of knowledge as being of a different nature [from the body], it must be admitted in that same way. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, it may be that the body is considered non-self because it is the object of an "I-consciousness" (ahaṃpratyaya) that lacks authoritative validity; however, one might ask how that which is the object of an "I-consciousness" possessing authoritative validity could be non-self. To this he says: "from that which is the object of the 'I-consciousness' [which is authoritative]. For it is precisely through sublation by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that the body's status as the object of an "I-consciousness" lacking authoritative validity is known.

The meaning is this: if the selfhood of the knower—who experiences the fruits of karma, possesses adventitious forms, and is subject to empirical constraints—is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the Self must be accepted as being distinct from that [knower]. Therefore, since there would be no distinction between what is established by valid means and what is not, the mere fact of being an object of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) alone is the proof of its being non-Self; this is the intended sense.

To the question, "How can there be the possibility of being a knower for one whose nature is changeless? he says, "In this way" (*evam*). Alternatively, it was previously stated that the state of being a knower resides within the knot of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). To the question, "How is the possibility of the ego being a knower established? he says, "In this way. The sense is that this status of the ego as the substratum of consciousness is due to its being a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). [Objection: Let the ego be a manifestor; but how can it be a manifestor by residing in itself? To this he says, "By residing in the Self" (*ātmasthatayā*).

By the word "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*), the sense of being the general rule (*autsargikatva*) is intended. The point is that if there is sublation by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*) in certain cases, it is not so [as a universal rule]. He shows an example with the words "mirror" (*darpaṇa*). The manifestation as residing in the self is not caused by the nature of the mirror, nor is it caused by the nature of being a reflection; rather, he uses the mention of "a piece of stone" (*khaṇḍa*) and so forth to show that it is caused solely by the capacity of being a manifestor (*abhivyañjakatvamātra*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "shaven-headed" (*muṇḍa*) and others are included.

Thus, he states "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*) to show that the appearance of being a knower belongs to consciousness (*saṃvit*) due to the relationship between the manifester and the manifested. He raises this very objection himself and then refutes it with the words "of that which is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśāyāḥ*). To the question "Why?", he replies with the example of "the rays of the sun" (*ravikara*). [The objection is as follows: It is illogical for an insentient thing to be a manifester; it is also illogical for a self-luminous entity to be a manifested object; and furthermore, it is especially illogical for that which is manifested by consciousness to be its manifester. Having raised this doubt, he refutes it by stating that [consciousness] is self-luminous. As for why this is so, he says: "like the rays of the sun."

To the question, "Where has the capacity of the palm of the hand to manifest rays been observed? he says, "In a lattice-window (*jālaka*)," and so forth. Thus, the non-ultimate nature of the state of being a knower has been stated. He establishes this very point by demonstrating the non-manifestation [of the self] at the time when the ultimately real entity shines forth, with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). By this, the previously mentioned meaning—that [the self is not perceived] even upon the disappearance of the notion of "I"—is elucidated. The phrase "since" (*yataḥ*) is an indication of the reason for the probandum, just as the presence of smoke indicates the presence of fire.

By mentioning liberation (*mukti*) together [with deep sleep], it is indicated that the disappearance of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is established by scripture even in the state of deep sleep. To the question, "How does [the self] appear then?", he says: "In that case, indeed... The scriptural passage concerning sleep is: "Indeed, at this time, one does not know oneself as 'this is I'. The Smṛti passage concerning liberation is: "Having abandoned egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness, being free from the sense of 'mine' and tranquil, one is fit for becoming Brahman."

The inclusion of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) within the field (*kṣetra*) is stated [in the verse]: "The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest. Its status as established through delusion is stated [in the verse]: "One whose self is deluded by the ego-sense thinks, 'I am the doer. The word "hi" (for/indeed) is intended to indicate its well-known status in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. He says "ata eva" (for this very reason) to show that it is not only the *Śruti* concerning deep sleep that [supports this], but there is also such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). ("And for this very reason")—the phrase "for this very reason" refers back to the probandum as the reason [for the conclusion].

How is there a reversal of the description of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)? It is as follows: that which is the probandum in the context of making known (*jñapti*) is the probans in the context of origination (*utpatti*); and that which is the probans in the context of origination is the probandum in the context of making known. Therefore, because it possesses the status of a constituent part (*aṅgin*), just like the rising of smoke, the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) is stated with reference to its being a cause in the context of origination.

To the question, "What follows from that inquiry into the previously established context?", he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By the word "therefore," he intends to state the establishment of his own view through both valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarke*), as set forth beginning with the words "even though they say 'all particularities... The phrase "with all conceptual constructions of difference dispelled" (*nirasta-samasta-bheda-vikalpa*) intends to express the manifold sub-varieties of difference, such as that between the knower and the known, by the term "conceptual construction of difference" (*bheda-vikalpa*). The term "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*) excludes internal differences such as eternity and so forth. To the question "Why?", he says: "having the single essence of pure consciousness" (*cinmātra-ekarasa*).

The meaning is "because it is pure consciousness" (*cinmātratvāt*). By this, the charge of being a mere void (*śūnyatva*) is also excluded. It is "immutable" (*kūṭastha*), meaning changeless, or rather, the substratum of all things. Regarding the phrase "eternal consciousness alone": the word *cinmātra* refers to self-luminosity, while the word *saṃvit* refers to the substantive entity; thus, there is no tautology. To the question of how difference can possibly exist in that which is pure consciousness, he says: "by delusion. The expression "it manifests through delusion" is like the description of a young elephant [emerging from its mother]. It is "pure," meaning free from ignorance (*avidyā*). It is "awakened" (*buddha*), meaning self-luminous.

"Liberated" (*muktam*) means, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), being devoid of birth and so forth arising from the perception of difference. The meaning is that all the Vedāntas are commenced for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the identity of the Self with such a Brahman. The "commencement-worthiness" of the Vedāntas consists in the commencement-worthiness of their inquiry. The phrase "all the Vedāntas are commenced," which they also say, is to be construed with what precedes.

In the inquiry as to whether the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-śāstra* is not to be commenced or is indeed to be commenced, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is established that the scripture—consisting of the investigation of Vedāntic passages which teach knowledge—is not to be commenced, because bondage is ultimately real and thus cannot be sublated by knowledge. Then, the conclusion (*siddhānta*) is taught according to the view of Brahman’s concealment by ignorance (*brahmājñāna-pakṣa*), namely: since bondage is illusory and can be sublated by knowledge alone, the scripture consisting of the investigation of Vedānta for the sake of such knowledge must indeed be commenced. This is the meaning of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*).

Therefore, since bondage is false and is removable by knowledge alone, it has been stated that the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) is not a prerequisite for the scripture whose primary focus is knowledge; thus, there is a disparity [between the two inquiries]. The triad—the means (*upāya*), which is the realization of the oneness of the Self; the goal (*upeya*), which is Brahman as non-dual pure consciousness; and that which is to be removed, which is the unreal—has been previously established in detail for the purpose of showing the independence of the inquiry into ritual action, and is here summarized in this concluding section (*nigamana*).

Now, in order to refute the capacity of those entities that contradict the status of the inquiry into karma (*karmavicāra*) as a prerequisite, he asserts—that "this very [work]"—that the means, the goal, and the things to be removed [as taught] by others are rooted in fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and fallacious reasoning (*tarka*). Furthermore, he briefly asserts that these very [points] of his own are established by valid means of knowledge and reasoning.

By the words "this very [work]," etc., he removes the suspicion that even those others who are learned in many scriptures and authors of many treatises might be prone to error; he does so by demonstrating the deficiency in the causal complex for the arising of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).

By the term "Supreme Person" (paramapuruṣa), he declares the goal (upeya); by "to be chosen" (varaṇīyatā) and so forth, the means (upāya); by "beginningless" (anādi) and so forth, that which is to be removed (nivartya); by "not previously attained" (anadhigata) and so forth, the total eradication of the opposing position; and by "supported by reasoning" (nyāyānugṛhīta) and so forth, the rootedness of his own position as well as its acceptance by many learned men. By the phrase "this very [work]," he intends the triad of the means, the goal, and the removable [obstacles] introduced in the immediately preceding sentence, as propounded by others.

By the term "the Supreme Person of the Upaniṣads," he recalls the scriptural text: "Know that Person who is taught in the Upaniṣads. By this, he indicates that the specific relationship between the means of knowledge and the object of knowledge favored by us is made manifest by the Śruti itself. By the word "Supreme" (parama), there is the exclusion of any reality other than the Lord. By the phrase "devoid of those specific qualities which are the causes for being chosen," the statement of the specific means intended in the passage, "He is to be attained by him alone whom He chooses," is established.

By this phrase, the possibility of error and the doubt regarding its logical consistency on the part of those who know many scriptures and have composed many treatises are both dispelled; for when the correct knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures arises, devotion to the Lord is also included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), since mere exertion in the study of the scriptures is an incomplete cause. As the Śruti says: "He who has supreme devotion to the God... and so forth. And the Smṛti says: "O King, you do not possess true knowledge, nor does my knowledge fail me."

"Deprived of knowledge and overwhelmed by darkness, you do not recognize Keśava. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O Gāvalgaṇa! What is that knowledge of yours regarding Janārdana, by which you recognize the Madhusūdana who appears in three ages? Sañjaya replied: "I do not resort to illusion—blessings be upon you—and I do not practice dharma in vain."

Regarding the passage: "Having attained a state of purity through devotion, one should perceive Janārdana from the scriptures," it is established here that the arising of knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures exactly as it is depends upon devotion, by the statement: "Having attained a state of purity through devotion, one perceives Janārdana from the scriptures. Furthermore: "Indeed, if Madhusūdana should behold a person at the moment of birth, he should be known as *sāttvika*; he is truly one who contemplates the goal of liberation. Or else, if Brahmā or Rudra should behold him at the moment of birth... [and so forth].

And from the statement, "His mind is overwhelmed by passion and darkness," it is understood that the knowledge of the true nature of reality (tattvārthajñāna) is dependent upon the side-long glance of the Lord, who is pleased by devotion. Now, one might object: from the question and answer, "That by which you recognize [Me]" and "I know [Him] through devotion," the identity of meaning between the words *vidyā* and *bhakti* is perceived. Furthermore, it was established previously that knowledge in the form of devotion leads to liberation.

If it be argued that there is a circular dependence—devotion being rooted in knowledge of the scriptures, and knowledge of the scriptures being rooted in devotion—the answer is not so. For at the very moment of hearing [the scriptures], when the attributes of the Supreme Self and other matters are understood as constituent parts of the meaning, they become objects of a favorable cognition; thus, the terms "knowledge" (*vidyā*) and "devotion" (*bhakti*) are used. Through this, one attains a correct determination of the meaning of the sentences. Indeed, even when such things as the Buddha's denial of the authority of the Vedas are put forward as prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), Vaidikas feel a sense of aversion toward them.

There arises an attachment of the mind toward the qualities and other attributes of the Blessed One. Nor is this devotion (bhakti)—which consists of uninterrupted meditation characterized by the conceptualization of direct realization—mutually dependent [on that realization]. Now, he states the verse beginning with "anādi" to describe that which is opposed to such devotion, which is the cause for the arising of knowledge of the true nature of the meaning of the scriptures. Alternatively, because of the absence of devotion that serves as the cause for perfect knowledge, he speaks of the persistence of sin which is opposed to perfect knowledge in the words "anādi. By the word "vāsanā," it is expressed that sin is difficult to remove due to its deeply rooted nature.

The word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), wherein impurity arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), latent impressions arise from impurity, the latent impression of impurity arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*), and ignorance arises from the latent impression of impurity. "Discernment" (*śemuṣī*) refers to the knowledge conducive to liberation. The meaning of the word "entire" (*aśeṣa*) is that the discernment regarding the entire universe—including the means, the goal, and that which is to be removed—is corrupted. By this, it is implied that the thing to be removed in our own position [of Advaita] has been stated; for it is action alone that acts as an obstacle to liberation. He states the absence of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) as the result of having a corrupted discernment with the words "not attained" (*anadhigata*).

Since the opponent has stated that scripture possesses superior authority when there is a contradiction with perception, [the author] first states the verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*) by means of the word "pada" (word), primarily because it intends to convey the qualified [Brahman] both through its individual components and as a whole. The intention behind the word "pada" is that the status of being a "word"—arising from the combination of stem and suffix—is not yet understood. The phrase "the nature of the sentence" implies that it is not yet understood that a sentence is that which expresses a specific relation between the meanings of multiple words. "The true nature of its meaning" refers to the object of its intended purport (*tātparya*).

In the phrase "perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes inference (*anumāna*). By the word "entirety" (*sakala*), the various sub-classifications of perception—such as tactile and visual—are intended; likewise, the various sub-classifications of inference—such as those based on positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—are intended.

Alternatively, the word "all" refers to the objects of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and so forth, which are favored by various disputants. "Vṛtta" means understanding; "in the form of its procedure" means that the point has not been understood—namely, that reasoning (tarka) is a corroborator of the means of valid cognition because it speaks of the sublation of those means by reasoning. For we accept reasoning precisely as a corroborator of the means of valid cognition; to this he replies: "by a sound method."

The sense is that even a reasoning (*tarka*) accepted with the intention of being beneficial is incorrect because it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the claim that only correct principles such as the *apaccheda-nyāya* were accepted, he says "of the paths of logic" (*nyāyamārgāṇām*). The sense is that the distinction between the respective scopes of application for those various principles—such as "this is the domain of the *apaccheda-nyāya*" and "this is the domain of the *sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*"—was not understood. Then, upon the question of what basis was relied upon when these treatises were composed, he says "incapable of withstanding alternative positions" (*vikalpāsaha*).

"Fallacious reasonings" (*kutarka*) are those arguments that contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and are beset by other defects such as a lack of foundation or internal contradiction. Furthermore, they do not persist for more than two or three steps; rather, they are fragile, collapsing at the very moment one must choose between their alternative horns. Thus he says, "unable to withstand analysis" (*vikalpāsaha*). The inability of reasoning to withstand analysis consists precisely in its inability to withstand the analysis of the proofs and so forth regarding its own object. [He explains this with the word] "various" (*vividha*).

If Brahman were an object of experience, it would follow that it is not consciousness (*ananubhūtitva*); yet perception grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*), and the Brahman known through the Vedānta is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge—such various mutual contradictions of fallacious arguments (*kutarka*) are intended here. Such fallacious reasoning alone is the "scum" (*kalka*), meaning the worthless dregs or the mere husk from which the Buddhists have extracted the essence. By this, it is meant that [the doctrine] has been carved out or fashioned. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).

To the question, "How can there be a determination of the invalidity of this [view] even when some possess knowledge whose object is a correct alternative meaning? he says: "by those who know the true nature of all means of valid cognition, such as perception, as assisted by logic. By this, the opposite form of what was stated previously is expressed. By the plural number, it is indicated that his own position is accepted by many authoritative teachers (*śiṣṭas*), such as the venerable Bodhāyana and others. "Unworthy of regard" means that it is not fit to be respected even for the sake of skill in presenting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) during the instruction of disciples.

The syntactical connection is as follows: whatever they have said, beginning with "pure consciousness alone, which is the opposite of all specific attributes" and ending with "all the Vedāntas begin," that too is to be disregarded.

He begins to establish the point thus briefly presented with the words "tathā hi" (for it is so). Now, an objection may be raised: first, the proponent cited specific Vedānta passages and examined everything that was to be determined therein; subsequently, he presented other means of knowledge and arguments distinct from those. Therefore, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), it would be appropriate to refute them in that same order.

How, then, is the initial determination that [Brahman] is not the object of any means of valid cognition consistent? And how, subsequently, can the Vedāntic statements be applied after first refuting the view that it is the object of perception and other means of knowledge without distinction? It is said in reply: Since the authority of scripture (*śāstra*) is accepted as prevailing over contradiction with perception, the opponent first cites the Vedāntic statements and only afterwards states everything else that needs to be said; for it is appropriate to place forward the means of knowledge that are held to be more powerful.

The proponent (siddhāntin), however, not accepting the superiority of scripture over perception when there is a contradiction with perception, explains the Vedānta passages according to their natural sense after first refuting the claim that perception and other means of knowledge have as their object a reality devoid of distinctions. In this regard, he first states the objection against the opponent’s initial thesis—that the ultimate reality is a featureless pure consciousness—by asserting that such a view is excluded from the scope of all means of valid cognition in general, beginning with the words "In the case of the featureless [reality]... (nirviśeṣe).

That is to say, the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established as being consistent with one's own position. Since it could be argued that even one's own merit is established by one's own experience, the word "this" (*idam*) is used for the purpose of excluding that. The sense is that there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that serves as a locus of agreement for others. Alternatively, the intention of the singular number is that not even a single individual instance of a means of valid cognition has the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) as its object. To the question "Why?", he says: "saviśeṣa" (with qualifiers). [Objection: But surely the qualifiers themselves are featureless (*nirviśeṣa*).

How then can a reality devoid of distinctions (nirviśeṣavastu) be considered unestablished by means of valid cognition? It is said in reply: A substrate (dharmin) is qualified by its attribute (dharma), and an attribute is qualified by its substrate. The meaning of the text is that whatever does not function as an attribute or a substrate for anything is devoid of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-śūnya). A "distinction" (viśeṣa) is that which differentiates. Furthermore, a substrate is denoted by the term "distinction" because it is that which excludes its own inherent attributes from the attributes residing in other substrates.

Furthermore, are the two words "qualified" (*viśeṣa*) and "without qualification" (*nirviśeṣa*) synonyms, or not? In the first case, their simultaneous usage would be untenable. In the second case, however, there can be no state of being "without qualification," because it is impossible for words not to be synonyms unless there is a difference in what they signify. Now, one might ask: how is it that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their object only that which possesses qualifications? For a means of cognition that apprehends smell and so forth does not necessarily inform us that the smell has a substratum. This is not so; for there is no rule that the substratum itself must be a qualification.

For consciousness itself, being the qualifier of everything, can indeed possess the qualification of all objects. Furthermore, since the perception of smell and other qualities occurs as delimited by specific factors such as time—as in the cognition "this smell is being experienced"—it is established that they have qualified objects as their domain. Such a perception will be explained later. [Objection: In that case, we do not accept the establishment of a featureless reality through any other means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa); rather, it is established by one's own self-experience. To this, he says: "But he who... and so forth.

By the word "tu" (but), qualifying the *samaya* (convention/tenet), he intends to show a discrepancy in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by his own experience, which is the root of the distinction of that convention. By saying "confined to one's own circle," he shows that it is not accepted by opponents. He shows that the experience witnessed by oneself possesses specific qualities by saying "this, I. [He says this] because its object is qualified; the qualified object is the experience itself.

This exposition is like saying "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputraka*); otherwise, it would be useless to establish the possession of specific qualities (such as form) in jars and the like, once the claim that [consciousness] is indistinguishable from its own experience has been refuted. The meaning of the subsequent passage, "even though it is being experienced, it is experience," is likewise the same; for it has the same sense as the phrase "established by one's own experience. Furthermore, the word "experience" (*anubhava*) does not refer to *anuvyavasāya* (reflective awareness). For a perception in the form of *anuvyavasāya* is not accepted [as the primary experience], since it cannot be considered perception because its object is past.

The cognition of another is one whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been lost, while one's own cognition is to be inferred; however, the other [cognition] is merely an object of memory (*smṛti-viṣaya*). And it is not the state of being an object of memory that is intended here, because the word "experience" (*anubhava*) does not have that meaning. Therefore, "being experienced" means "being manifest. By the two words "this" and "I," it is stated that experience possesses both an object and a subject. By the word "I saw," the connection with the specific quality of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) is intended. As for its pastness, however, that is not intended, because at that time [of perception], self-evident establishment (*svataḥ-siddhatva*) would be impossible.

"By some particular characteristic (*viśeṣeṇa*). The sense is that even among those [characteristics] already mentioned, at least one particular characteristic must necessarily be included in the end. Alternatively, in the phrase "I saw this" (*adarśam idam*), the particle *iti* denotes a manner; it includes, as far as possible, every particular form belonging to the same class as the subject under discussion. By this, what is intended by "by some" (*kenacit*) would be [characteristics] such as being indirect (*parokṣatva*) or being present (*vartamānatva*). Indirectness is [determined] through the medium of the object. [Objection: But surely we do not deny the cognition "I saw this."

Regarding the claim that inference, which has as its object a domain established by reasoning, is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*), he says: "Even [if] possessing features" (*saviśeṣo’pi*). Because self-contradiction will be demonstrated, he specifies "by a fallacy of reasoning" (*yuktayābhāsena*). The term "featureless" (*nirviśeṣa*) is explained as "being abstracted" (*niṣkṛṣyamāṇa*). The meaning is: when it is abstracted as "featureless," it must be abstracted in this very manner. To the question of how it should be abstracted, he says: "by those [features] that do not exceed existence (*sattā*) and are unique to itself. For if it did not exceed existence, the reason (*hetu*) would be indistinguishable from the subject (*pakṣa*).

That is incorrect; for a logical reason (*hetu*) must indeed exclude the [opposite] position. Furthermore, it is only another property (*dharma*) that distinguishes one substance from another that can possibly have the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). When the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended, that very nature—which contradicts the delusion of identity with anything else—is itself the exclusion, as in the case of "being mother-of-pearl" (*śuktitva*) and so forth.

However, because Brahman—which is a distinct reality—lacks the property of being a form that differentiates it from others, and because its own nature is susceptible to error when it appears as such, it cannot be said that its very nature constitutes its differentiation. This is stated with the intention of showing the disparity with the examples of whiteness and so forth to be mentioned later, by using the phrase "by those [properties] exceeding mere existence" (*sattātirekibhiḥ*). For if the reason were common (*sādhāraṇa*), it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and would not contradict error, just like whiteness and the like. Indeed, it is the uncommon property of being mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*) alone that contradicts the error of silver.

Therefore, it is said "by their own specific [properties]"; by the word "own" (*sva*), the fallacy of the unestablished due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) is excluded. "By specific natures" means by specific properties (*dharma*). Thus, the body of the subject matter has been stated in general terms.

Therefore, since it is unavoidable that even those reasons you yourself accept as "negative" (nirāsaka) possess the properties of "exceeding existence" (sattātirekitva) and "being unique to themselves" (svāsādhāraṇatva), the statement is repeated with the intention [of showing] that "by those which exceed existence and are unique to themselves. He says, "by some," regarding the point that whatever reasons are excluded from specific objects such as pots and so forth, and which generally establish the absence of all particulars, must by the very force of their meaning (arthasāmarthyāt) exclude their own self as well, since that self is included within the universal.

The meaning is that, therefore, one must necessarily admit both their existence (*sattā*) and their uniqueness (*asādhāraṇatva*). "By some" means by those who are unique and authoritative (*prāmāṇika*). "Of the qualified alone" implies the intention that if the proofs for featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*) are removed, featurelessness cannot be established; and if they are not removed, it follows that the entity is actually possessed of features (*saviśeṣatva*) precisely because of them. "Others" refers to...

The specific qualities (viśeṣas) such as color and so forth, which belong to those things like pots from which the reasons proving the absence of difference are excluded, are here rejected as being unauthoritative (*aprāmāṇika*) in this context; however, not all specific qualities are rejected. The meaning is that smoke, which is excluded from non-fire, indeed excludes only the state of being non-fire in the subject (*pakṣa*), but it does not exclude other forms. Regarding the phrase "nowhere": the meaning is "in one's own experience" and also "in other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception.

It is stated that because it is impossible to establish the cessation of all specific qualities through the consequence of self-contradiction (*svavyāghāta-prasaṅga*), there is no proof of a reality devoid of specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*).

Thus, having accepted the exclusion of both object and agent, [the opponent] has brought about the state of possessing distinctions. Now, [the author] says "For cognition... (*dhiyo hi*) because the very rejection of object and agent is difficult to establish. "Cognition-ness" (*dhītva*) is the illumination of an object. "Self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatā*) is the state of having an illumination that does not depend on anything else. Both of these have been presented by the opponent in the doctrine of self-luminosity as the means of proof (*sādhana*) and the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), respectively, on the grounds that cognition is perceived as having the nature of illuminating an object for a knower.

The meaning is that because [cognition] necessarily appears as the illuminator of its object with respect to its own substratum, its nature as cognition (*dhītva*) and its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) are established. "Nature as cognition" means being the instrument for the apprehension of an object; thus, since it appears in such a manner, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*). The point is that if you do not accept that self-luminosity is established by the reasoning based on the fact that it is perceived, then self-luminosity—of which that reasoning is the cause—would likewise not be established. Alternatively, "nature as cognition" refers merely to the essential form of cognition itself.

The word "hi" (for/indeed) demonstrates that this [self] is universally acknowledged through perception (*upalabdhi*). Now, an objection is raised: "Is it not the case that knowledge, as delimited by object and subject, is not the very nature of the Self? Rather, what is being established here is something entirely different—an indeterminate state experienced during conditions such as deep sleep? To this, he says: "svāpa... (deep sleep...). "Anubhava" (experience) here means the manifestation of the Self. For at that time, there is no manifestation of the attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). This was already established in its proper place when it was demonstrated that the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) alone is the Self. The sense is that this has been shown more skillfully through the very arguments advanced by the opponent.

The meaning is that [this is known] solely through the recollection of what was experienced by another, as in the statements, "I slept happily," or "I did not even know myself. Alternatively, it means more skillfully or more clearly. What is meant is this: do you assert that the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*) depends upon your own experience with respect to (1) knowledge delimited by an object and a subject, (2) knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the Self appearing as "I," or (3) that which transcends both? In the first case, there can be no absence of distinctions precisely because of the necessary delimitation by object and subject.

Regarding the second [position], it will be stated that because of its being inwardness, favorability, and so forth, its possession of distinctions (saviśeṣatva) is unavoidable. Regarding the third, it will be stated that precisely because of its emptiness (śūnyatva), it cannot be established as being without distinctions. By another approach, he states its possession of distinctions: "And those [qualities] admitted by yourselves," etc. By the word "etc.," self-luminosity, oneness, blissfulness, and so forth are intended. To the objection that "those [qualities] have been said to be mere reality (vastumātra)," he replies with "And those... He establishes this with "Reality... The Buddhists have asserted momentariness (kṣaṇikatva); however, by this [author], permanence (nityatva) is asserted.

The Vaiśeṣikas and others [assert] insentience and manifoldness; however, by this [term "Self"], self-luminosity and unity are intended, while its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is accepted by all of them. Therefore, the meaning is that it is improper to say that there is both a subject of disagreement and a subject of agreement regarding one and the same thing. By means of the demonstration following the disagreement, he shows that [the Self] is distinct from its essential nature through the words "svābhimata" (as intended by himself).

In proving the eternity of Brahman against one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvavādin*), have you established anything over and above the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the subject, or not? If you have, then it follows that [Brahman] possesses attributes (*sadharmatva*). If not, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the mere essential nature is precisely what is accepted [by the opponent]. Are the words "attribute" (*dharma*) and "subject" (*dharmin*) synonyms as they occur in the proposition "consciousness is eternal," or not? In the first case, the effort of proof is fruitless. In the second case, the implication is that one must admit an attribute distinct from the essential nature.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Because [the attributes] can be established through the proof of one's own position, they are not merely the thing-in-itself (*vastumātra*). Previously, the possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) was stated by means of reasons that negate such possession; subsequently, by means of the properties to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); and thereafter, by means of reasons that establish certain specific attributes. To the objection that these negating, proving, and establishing properties are not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*), he says "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Therefore, the meaning is that [the object] is qualified by those properties which you have stated as being some specific attributes—by way of exclusion, as the probandum (*sādhya*), and as the means of proof (*sādhana*). By the term "by those who are authoritative" (*prāmāṇikaiḥ*), a further distinction is shown from what was previously stated as "by some" (*kaiścit*). As for the phrase "qualified indeed": if there were no excess over the aforementioned existence (*sattā*) and no absence of its own unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇatva*), the destruction of error would not occur.

The point is as follows: if the property of the negator (*nirāsaka-dharma*) were not ultimately real, then—just as the reality of silver persists when the "shell-ness" is not ultimately real—the reality of the form of the object to be negated would follow as a consequence. If the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) were not ultimately real, there would be the undesirable consequence of impermanence, which is the opposite of permanence and so forth. And if the means of proof (*sādhana*) were not ultimately real, it would entail the reality of the form that is the opposite of the proven permanence and so forth.

Thus, by way of the discussion on one's own experience, the fact that even there [in perception] there is a qualified object has been established. Now, he begins to state what was first proposed: that all means of valid cognition have qualified objects as their domain. In this regard, since the opponent has asserted the superior strength of perception and because he himself maintains the excellence of [perception’s] capacity to convey a qualified object, he first states that verbal testimony has a qualified object, beginning with the words "But as for verbal testimony" (*śabdasya tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the [opponent’s] claim regarding its superior strength.

By the word "especially" (*viśeṣeṇa*), the excellence of [the scripture] in making known the entity as possessing distinctions (*saviśeṣa*) is expressed. Alternatively, having established that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have for their object an entity possessing distinctions, and having subsequently examined the self-luminous nature of the conscious reality (*cidvastu*) due to its being internal to it, [the author] states that the scripture—which is accepted by both parties as more internal than perception and other means—is concerned with an entity possessing distinctions, using the words "But of the word" (*śabdasya tu*). The term "especially" refers to the superiority [of the scripture] over other means of valid cognition regarding its having for its object an entity possessing distinctions.

By the word "tu" (but), the specific feature—that words are preceded by perception and other means of knowledge whose objects possess distinctions—is stated as being appropriate for each respective case. He states the reason for what was asserted [in the previous verse] with the words "in the form of words and sentences. To the doubt, "What follows from that regarding the fact of having distinctions as their object? he explains the operation [of words] in the form of *prakṛti* (base) and so forth. To the question, "What follows from that? he says, "of the base and the suffix. [He says], "of the word itself"; the sense is: let the sentence be set aside for now; even the word alone has as its ultimate referent that which possesses distinctions.

He explains the operation [of words] by way of sentences with the words "and the distinction of words" (*padabhedaśca*). "Distinction of words" means the mutual distinction between words. The sense is that not only is the distinction between base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) the cause of a difference in meaning, but the distinction between words (*padabheda*) is as well; otherwise, other words would be redundant—this is the underlying thought.

In response to the objection that even though a difference in words is based on a difference in meaning, the absence of distinctions [in Brahman] is established because the sentence is a single unit, he concludes that there is no evidence for a featureless [Brahman] by stating that the sentence has as its object that which possesses distinctions: "The collection of words... The meaning is this: it is precisely a specific relation among the things denoted by each respective word that is conveyed by the sentence; it is not some other meaning arrived at by discarding those respective word-meanings.

Now, does the word "without attributes" (nirviśeṣa) convey a reality that is without attributes, or one that is not conveyed at all, or does it convey a reality that possesses attributes? In the first case, since a reality without attributes has been conveyed by the word, its negation is untenable. In the second case, however, because there is no cognition of the object to be negated, the negation is untenable. In the third case, the refutation of a reality possessing attributes would have been accomplished. It is not so; for there is a distinction between erroneous cognition and valid cognition.

Indeed, it is the status of a word as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an undifferentiated reality that is negated, not its capacity to cause error. Therefore, it is logical that the error—which has as its object meanings incapable of mutual syntactic connection and is produced by words denoting the undifferentiated—is sublated by words that generate valid cognitions. For if one does not admit the restriction (*saṃkoca*) of the word for "difference" based on the locus, its specific negandum, and its counter-correlative property, then, due to the absence of a locus, the negative word itself would be syntactically unintelligible.

For a word devoid of inflection (*nirvibhaktika*), unconnected with other words, and lacking qualifiers (*nirviśeṣa*) cannot denote an object. Therefore, in the absence of a restriction [of its meaning], there is a contradiction. Even if, for some reason, the meaning of the case-ending is not intended to be expressed, nevertheless, because the word *nirviśeṣa* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the denotation of an external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is unavoidable.

Furthermore, when a *tatpuruṣa* compound is employed, the expression of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) must be understood. Therefore, if the term "devoid of distinctions" (*nirviśeṣa*) occurs within a statement that functions as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then a distinction of scope must be observed; for it lacks the capacity to establish a total absence of all particularities (*viśeṣa*). In sentences such as "What particularity is there in the city? or "None at all," the negation of particularities is seen to have a restricted scope.

Likewise, in the scriptures as well, it is said: "Therefore, they are indeed without distinction. Here, the term *aviśeṣa* (without distinction) is employed with the intention of expressing that although the elements such as earth and the rest possess qualities like smell, they lack certain specific attributes—namely, the states of being tranquil (*śānta*), passionate (*ghora*), or deluded (*mūḍha*).

Thus, the terms "self-experience" (*svānubhava*) and "word" (*śabda*) have been defined as being internal to the Self, whose nature is knowledge. Now, among the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he establishes that perception—which is the foundational one—has a qualified object (*saviśeṣaviṣayatva*), beginning with the words "of perception," etc. Furthermore, since it will be stated later that there is a synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) in determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) of an object previously experienced by indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the nature of determinate perception is first demonstrated for its utility in that regard. He now proposes that even indeterminate perception has a qualified object.

Regarding the phrase "even non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpakam api*): having kept in mind that the apprehension of a second or subsequent object among objects of the same class is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), while the apprehension of the first object is non-conceptual, he states the reason: "because it is conceptual. The term *viśiṣṭapratisandhānam* is either a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) or a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*). The meaning is: because it serves as the cause for the conceptual synthesis (*pratisandhāna*) in the conceptual [cognition] which has as its object a thing qualified by categories such as genus (*jāti*) experienced within one's own prior non-conceptual [perception].

The fact that the first individual (*piṇḍa*) is apprehended as qualified [by a universal] is obtained by implication; for it is only when the first individual is perceived as qualified by a genus (*jāti*) that the synthesis (*pratisandhāna*)—characterized by the cognition of the persistence of that genus in the second and subsequent individuals—is possible. How is this synthesis established? Anticipating the objection that the reason is unproven (*asiddhi*) on the grounds that indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) has as its object something devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), he says: "What is called indeterminate perception... He demonstrates the absence of such total lack of specific qualities with the words: "of such a [perception]..."

Having raised the alternative—whether the apprehension of that which is devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) is accepted on the basis of perception (*darśana*), or whether it is postulated through logical necessity (*anupapatti*)—he first states that it is not perception by saying "not even at any time. He rejects the possibility of postulation by saying "because of the impossibility" (*anupapatti*). The point is that the very impossibility [of perceiving such a thing] is seen to be a sublation of the cognition of a featureless entity; thus, any postulation based upon it is rejected from afar. He explains the non-perception by saying "by anyone," meaning there is no restriction to any particular mode [of perception].

The causal status of the ablative “because of the impossibility of apprehension” (*grahaṇāyogāt*) is clear. Here, the word *hi* (“for”) stands in place of the ablative. By explaining the very cognition that “this is thus,” he implicitly rejects even the conceptualization of an apprehension devoid of all particularities, stating “the triangle. He explains the lack of logical consistency by saying “because of the impossibility of apprehension. This connects with the ablative ending “because of the impossibility of apprehension” (*grahaṇāyogāt*) within the interpolated sentence expressing doubt. “Triangle” (*trikoṇa*) means “cow-faced” (*gomukha*).

The meaning is that because apprehension is impossible—since the postulation of an apprehension devoid of all specific qualities contradicts the observed pervasion (vyāpti)—such a conception is untenable. By the word "untenability" (anupapatteḥ), a reductio ad absurdum (bādhakatarka) against the counter-example is also intended: namely, that if there were an absence of having a qualified object, the very nature of cognition (pratyayatva) would be lost. The evidence supporting this reductio is perception (pratyakṣa) and the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (yogyānupalambha).

Alternatively, by the phrase "due to impossibility" (*anupapatteḥ*), the author intends to state the proof establishing that [perception] has objects possessing qualifiers: "The cognition produced by the first contact of the sense organ with its object has as its object something possessing qualifiers, because it is a cognition, like any other well-established cognition. Thus, it is established that indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is the apprehension of an object devoid of certain intended qualifiers, based on the absence of proving evidence and the presence of subverting evidence. By this, it follows that the term *nirvikalpaka* (indeterminate) possesses a restricted application.

Regarding the question of in what respect that contraction occurs, he says "ataḥ" (therefore). This means: because of the aforementioned [reasons] and the impossibility [of otherwise accounting for the experience]. In response to the doubt—"The terms 'savikalpaka' (conceptual) and 'nirvikalpaka' (non-conceptual) have not been conventionally assigned to the first and second cognitions of the object; therefore, a distinction between these two cognitions must be stated"—he demonstrates the difference in the forms of the objects of apprehension (*grāhyākāra*) with the two sentences beginning with "tatra" (therein).

By means of the two sentences beginning with "prathamapratīti" (the first cognition), [the author] demonstrates that the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the terms "conceptual" (*savikalpaka*) and "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*) consists in the cognition and non-cognition of the persistence of "cowness" (*gotva*). The "cowness" mentioned in the preceding text is qualified by the term "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*); by this it is shown that, unlike the state of being solidified butter (*dhṛtatva*) in melted ghee as conceived by opponents, there is no delay in its perceptibility due to a dependence on a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). That very same configuration is subsequently designated by the term "hump" (*sāsnādi*) in the following passage.

Thus, conceptual and non-conceptual [cognition] have been described by way of the apprehension and non-apprehension of the universal (*anuvṛtti*). Non-conceptuality does not arise from the apprehension of the universal alone; rather, it arises also from the non-apprehension of the genus (*jāti*). To address the doubt that if the universal were not apprehended, it would be the very nature of the genus itself that remains unapprehended, he says: "but not because of the non-apprehension of the form of the configuration (*saṃsthāna*)," [or rather, "the form of the genus, etc.," as the reading suggests]. Here, the word *saṃsthānarūpa* indicates the impossibility of such non-apprehension.

In response to the doubt that "cowness" (*gotva*) and other such universals are not apprehended because their commonality (*anuvṛtti*), which constitutes their specific property, is not perceived, the author explains precisely why such non-apprehension is untenable with the words: "even in the case of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, which consist of configuration (*saṃsthāna*). The term "configuration" is mentioned again to indicate that the same reason applies even to the sensory fitness (*indriyayogyatā*) that serves as the cause for apprehension.

Regarding the fact that non-conceptual cognition has a qualified object as its domain, it was previously stated that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*)—characterized by the object experienced in non-conceptual cognition—as found in conceptual cognition. Furthermore, in the absence of the non-conceptual cognition asserted by others, the non-perception of the perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) serve as the means of valid cognition; the knowledge of the reasoning that supports these two has thus been explained.

Intending the following alternative—whether the admission of the apprehension of the mere object (*vastumātra*) is due to the impossibility of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or the impossibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—he first sets aside the impossibility of the means of knowledge by stating, "because there is no difference in their being perceptible by the senses" (*aindriyikatvāviśeṣāt*). By this, the [objection regarding] smell, which is not established as separate from the earth, is excluded. [Objection: How can it be said that [inherence] is perceptible by the senses? Since inherence (*samavāya*) is not perceptible by the senses, that [claim] is incorrect. [Response: If that were so, then the apprehension of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭagrahaṇa*) in determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) would be impossible.

Therefore, since there is no impossibility of being perceived by different sense organs, there is no invalidation of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the impossibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) due to non-proximity, he refutes that by stating "by configuration" (*saṃsthānena*), because [the object] does not exist [in that way] due to its inseparable existence (*apṛthaksiddhatva*). By this, even though it is visible to the eye, there is an exclusion of things like a staff which exist separately. The meaning is that since it is grasped by a single sense organ while being inseparably existent, there is no invalidation of the means of knowledge or the object of knowledge; thus, the entity is grasped precisely together with its configuration.

Thus, the object previously indicated by the term "form of configuration" (*saṃsthānarūpa*) has been explained. It should not be suspected that there is no apprehension of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which are the forms of configuration, because of the non-apprehension of their recurrence (*anuvṛtti*); the point is that such apprehension is possible through the relation of the mode (*prakāra*) and the possessor of the mode (*prakārin*). If the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) were not apprehended at the apprehension of the first individual because of the non-apprehension of recurrence, then cowness would be difficult to apprehend even at the second individual, since recurrence is not apprehended. For recurrence consists in the concomitance (*anvaya*) across multiple individuals.

Furthermore, that [universal] is apprehended in the second and subsequent individuals only through the recognition of the persistence of the referent in previous individuals. Therefore, because the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is not apprehended in the first individual, and because there is no reflection upon its persistence, the recurrence in the form of connection with the second individual is difficult to grasp even in the second; thus, cowness remains unapprehended there as well. Likewise, due to the lack of reflection upon the connection between the first and second individuals, recurrence is not grasped in the third either, and so cowness remains unapprehended. In this way, cowness would be difficult to grasp in other individuals as well.

Therefore, it must be admitted that the apprehension of "cowness" occurs at the very first moment of grasping the individual object (*piṇḍa*). In this way, the apprehension of an entity devoid of all particularities (*viśeṣa*) is refuted. Furthermore, the position that "the universal (*jāti*) and so forth, as well as the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), are apprehended separately in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), while their apprehension as a qualified whole occurs only in determinate perception (*savikalpaka*)" is also implicitly rejected.

How is it known that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are apprehended separately? If you argue that this is because we observe in the case of a staff, an earring, and so forth, that the apprehension of the qualifier and the qualified is preceded by their separate apprehension—then, in that case, does this separate apprehension occur at the time when they are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddhi*), or at the time when they exist separately? It cannot be the first, because they are apprehended precisely as a qualified entity. As for the time when they exist separately, there is no apprehension of them as a qualified entity at all; therefore, that [separate apprehension] cannot be the cause of the cognition [of the qualified].
Therefore, since separate apprehension does not constitute a cause for apprehending a specific property, there is no contingency of separate apprehension in the case of "cowness" and so forth.

[Objection: Since the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) possesses a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the cognition of that relation requires the cognition of the nature of the counter-correlate; therefore, one must admit that the apprehension of a qualified object is preceded by the grasping of the mere nature of the categories such as genus (*jāti*). [Reply: It is said in response: What is this "requirement of the cognition of the counter-correlate"? Is it a rule that the counter-correlate must appear in the cognition of the qualified, or is it that the cognition of the counter-correlate is a cause of the cognition of the qualified? We accept the first [alternative].

And in the second case, have the categories such as "birth" (jāti) and so forth been apprehended initially as mutually excluded from one another, or not? If not, then for those things apprehended without mutual exclusion—just like preceding and succeeding flames—the cognition of their status as the counter-correlates (*pratiyogitā*) of the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) would be untenable.

If they are apprehended as distinct, then if that distinction were not present through the relation of qualifier and qualified—characterized by dependence and so forth—or by some other form suitable for it, the cognition of a reversal of the qualifier and qualified would result. If it is argued that, by the power of the object (*vastu-sāmarthya*), the qualifier-qualified relation is perceived as truly real, then this "power of the object" must consist either in the form of the qualifier-qualified relation itself or in some other form suitable for it.

If the assistance [of the qualifier] consists in the existence of the thing's own nature (*vastusvabhāva*), then since the specific cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) would be possible from the thing's own nature alone, it is incorrect to postulate the apprehension of the mere individual essence (*svarūpamātra*). If the assistance consists in being known (*jñātatā*), then because the qualifier is distinguished by that very nature, its prior cognition must exist; thus, a specific cognition would have to be admitted at the very outset. Therefore, it is better to admit that the substance itself is first cognized as qualified.

If it is argued that the nature of that [entity] is not first apprehended as being a qualifier with respect to its own qualified substrate, but rather as a mere essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*), then a reversal of the relationship between qualifier and qualified would be perceived between that qualifier and its own nature. To avoid this, if one were to admit another aspect for that real nature, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If, in order to avoid the consequence that there would be a reversal [of roles] or a priority [in cognition], it is accepted that the very intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth constitutes their status as qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*), and not some other form (*ākārāntara*), then the initial apprehension would have to occur as both a qualifier and a qualified; for if that were not apprehended, it would follow that the intrinsic nature itself remains ungrasped. And if it were apprehended in that very way, there would be a qualified cognition from the very beginning.

Since universals (*jāti*) and other categories are apprehended as both qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualificands (*viśeṣya*) within a single cognition, one must admit that the perception of the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualificand is possible from the very first moment. This being the case, if the apprehension of a qualified object were necessarily preceded by their separate apprehension, then "having as its object entities cognizable by distinct causal complexes" would constitute a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Even in the absence of anything to be excluded other than the subject (*pakṣa*), it is logical that [the property] constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because its exclusion of the subject is established by the force of the aforementioned reasoning (*tarka*). For example, when the non-existence of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) has an end because it possesses a beginning, the fact of having a beginning in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva*) serves as the limiting condition, due to the force of the reasoning that there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the re-emergence of positive entities; and just as in the inference of smoke from fire, "moist fuel" (*ārdrendhana*) is the limiting condition, due to the force of the reasoning that there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of perceiving smoke everywhere where there is fire—so it is here.

Therefore, the universal "cowness" (gotva) is apprehended at the very first perception of an individual; it must be admitted that in the second and subsequent perceptions, there is the apprehension of its persistence. Thus, the nature of indeterminate and determinate cognition is exactly as previously described.

It has been stated that the apprehension or non-apprehension of continuity (*anuvṛtti*) is the cause of conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition, respectively. To the question, "In that case, how is the apprehension of a second [object] and so forth conceptual?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This is because even at the very first apprehension, there is an apprehension of the object as possessing a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*). To the question, "How can an apprehension other than the first—which is devoid of the apprehension of continuity—be conceptual?", he says: "In the apprehensions of the second and subsequent [objects]" (*dvitīyādīti*). That is, in the apprehensions of objects such as a second individual (*piṇḍa*), by way of their being apprehended as "the second" and so forth.

By this, it is established that perception accompanied by the assistance of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), while the other is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). By this, it is further established that conceptual nature does not arise solely through the recurrence of a genus (*jāti*); rather, the apprehension of an object as qualified by the recurrence of any one among genus, quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, is also conceptual. Non-conceptual perception is precisely the apprehension devoid of such distinctions regarding the recurrence of any [of these]; for example, the cognition produced by the first contact of the sense-organ with a single individual.

But surely, even with respect to a single individual, a cognition produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) that apprehends it as qualified by the persistence of place, time, and so forth, would be conceptual (*savikalpaka*). Indeed it would be so; for there is no difference in its being produced by mental impressions or in its having persistence as its object. The statement that "the first apprehension of the lump [of clay] occurs among substances of the same class" is intended to demonstrate the persistence of the universal (*jāti*). The presentation of the examples "like the configuration" (*saṃsthānivat*) and "like that which possesses the configuration" (*saṃsthānavat*) is for the sake of clarification.

The property of being a "lump" (piṇḍadharma) is its configuration (saṃsthāna), while the property of that [configuration] is its persistence (anuvṛtti); thus, the employment of the two examples is based on the similarity consisting in the relationship between a property and its possessor (dharmadharmibhāva). In this way, it is stated that for determinate and indeterminate perception, the difference in causal equipment (sāmagrī) consists in the presence or absence of the accompaniment of mental impressions (saṃskāra), and the difference in the form of the object to be grasped (grāhyākāra) consists in the presence or absence of the persistence of "cowness" (gotva) and so forth. He concludes that both types of perception have as their object that which possesses qualifiers (saviśeṣaviṣayatva) with the word "ataḥ."

In this context, he refutes the doctrine of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) by the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). This means: precisely because it has been established that even the first apprehension of a substance (*piṇḍa*) has a qualified object as its domain. "Everywhere" (*sarvatra*) refers to the pairs of substances, universals and particulars, qualities and their possessors, actions and their agents, as well as effects and causes. To the question "How so?", he replies: "This is thus" (*idam ittham*).

Even for the proponent of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābhedavādin*), in establishing the mutual difference and non-difference of individual objects (*piṇḍa*), he maintains that "this is not that" constitutes difference, while "this is that" constitutes non-difference. Thus, in order to avoid the contradiction of a single entity simultaneously possessing the forms of existence and non-existence, he establishes difference-and-non-difference through two aspects: non-difference by way of the universal (*jāti*) and difference by way of the individual (*vyakti*).

To dispel the doubt that a single entity cannot possess a dual nature—namely, non-difference residing in the universal (*jāti*) and difference residing in the individual (*vyakti*)—the mutual difference and non-difference between the universal and the individual have been stated. To establish that, since no other form of connection is observed, cognition itself is relied upon as the sole refuge. Therefore, in order to refute that [position], he first demonstrates the contradiction with experience regarding non-difference, on the grounds that the universal and the individual are indeed perceived as distinct, by stating: "this is thus" (*idam ittham*). Here, the state of being "this" (*idambhāva*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*); the state of being "thus" (*itthambhāva*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Regarding the question "What is this 'it' aspect? and "What is this 'this' aspect?", he says "In that regard" (*tatra*). Here, there are four reasons stated by others for the difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*): (1) apprehension as non-different at the first grasping of the object; (2) the cognition permeated by a single word; (3) the employment of co-referential terms (*samānādhikaraṇa-pada*) independent of possessive suffixes (*mattvarthīya-pratyaya*); and (4) the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*). Among these, the rule of simultaneous apprehension and the co-referential cognition are the two that establish difference-and-non-difference.

The other two [reasons] are those that establish non-difference. Anticipating these four reasons, he says "for thus" (*tathā hi*). Keeping them in mind, he first sets aside the apprehension [of the object] as non-different at the initial grasping of the whole, by means of the passage beginning with "at the very first," etc. "Excluded from all others" (*sakalaitaravyāvṛtta*) means excluded from everything of a different class. To the question, "What follows from that regarding the apprehension as different? he replies: "And the exclusion," etc.

The meaning is that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is also ascertained because there is a cognition of the form "it is thus" due to its being qualified by specific configurations such as "cowness" (*gotva*). By this, the doctrine of the indivisible sentence-meaning (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*) is effectively refuted; for here, what is intended is the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with qualities such as whiteness, and that has been shown previously. [Objection: Let there be a cognition of it as qualified by cowness and so forth; nevertheless, non-difference (*abheda*), being established by its own means of valid cognition, cannot be set aside. To this, he says: "in all cases."
