The meaning is that in cases such as the universal "cowness" and its substratum, or in cases such as a staff and one who possesses a staff, the very relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*)—just as between a staff and the bearer of the staff—is what constitutes the contradiction of non-difference. Regarding the phrase "the relationship of qualifier and qualified": even when the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of the universal and the individual are not perceived, difference is grasped through another form consisting of the relationship of qualifier and qualified; for there is no rule that the apprehension of difference must occur solely through a single form. This is the intended sense.

If there were absolute difference in both cases, why would grammatical coreferentiality independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), the cognition permeated by a single term, and the rule of simultaneous perception be observed in one instance and not in the other? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). In that context—namely, in the category of "cowness" and its substrate, or "staff" and the "staff-bearer"—the state of being an occasional qualifier, which terminates in itself and is characterized by a distinct configuration (*saṃsthāna*), is the cause for the cognition of coreferentiality that depends upon a possessive suffix.

The meaning is as follows: because a category exists only as the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of a substance (*dravya*), it culminates in that [substance]; thus, its subsistence solely as a qualifier is what necessitates grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*). Furthermore, the necessity of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) and its absence are the respective causes for non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhatva*) and separability (*pṛthaksiddhatva*); it is not difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*) that are the causes. Regarding the necessity of simultaneous apprehension, since the coexistence of two things alone constitutes simultaneous apprehension, it establishes duality.

The rule [of simultaneous perception] does not apply even when two distinct things are involved; thus, because it is an uncommon inconclusive reason (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*), it does not prove either [identity]. Furthermore, it is actually contradictory (*viruddha*); for the rule of simultaneous perception that proves duality demonstrates the very restriction of duality. As for the cognition permeated by the word "one," since it is seen in cases such as "one staff-bearer" to function by excluding other staff-bearers, its purpose is the negation of another substratum (*dharmin*), and not the proof of non-difference between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum—this is the intended meaning.

If there is such a disparity between [the case of] "born" (*jāti*) and "earring" (*kuṇḍala*) and so forth, and if difference is established in both cases on the basis of the similarity in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), then—given the disparity in [other factors] such as the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*)—oneness might also follow. To this he says: "In both cases. Because of the specific nature of the relation of qualifier and qualified, the cognition of difference induced by it is unavoidable; for when the relation of qualifier and qualified exists, difference is also fully recognized.

Since identity is indeed what is contested in the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), non-difference—which would contradict the difference already admitted—cannot be postulated. The point is this: just as a specific internal discrepancy such as coldness or heat does not lead to the postulation of non-substantiality (*adravyatva*) that contradicts the common form of substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth, likewise the rule of simultaneous apprehension does not lead to the postulation of a form that contradicts difference.

Alternatively, one might argue that even for things like a staff, which exist separately and are not [inherently] qualifiers, the status of being a qualifier is merely superimposed upon them at some time due to their mere coexistence; thus, since the status of being a qualifier is absent among things that are absolutely distinct, the status of being a qualifier is not capable of proving absolute difference. To this, he says: "In both cases. The status of being a qualifier consists in being employed as that which effects exclusion (*vyāvarttaka*) within the cognition of the excluded (*vyāvṛtta*). And since this [status] is primary even in the case of a staff and so forth, it follows that absolute difference is appropriate on account of the status of being a qualifier—this is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that "oneness must be postulated for the sake of establishing the restriction that the rule of simultaneous perception applies only to the universal (gotva), its substratum, and so forth, but not elsewhere," he replies to that with the words, "But this much [is all]. The meaning is: only this much [is required], and nothing further should be postulated. If oneness were postulated for the sake of establishing the restriction regarding the rule of simultaneous perception, that would be incorrect; for it would entail the undesirable consequence of having to postulate yet another entity in order to establish the restriction that "oneness exists only there, and not elsewhere."

The sense is this: if identity were inherent there, then the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) would also be inherent; thus, one need not resort to the cumbersome assumption of a different, unperceived object that contradicts what is already established. Alternatively, just as the cognition of difference caused by the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is equal in both cases, so too the rule of simultaneous perception would apply to a staff and Devadatta and the like, or it would not apply to the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*); to this he says: "to such an extent" (*iyān*).

The meaning is that once a common form (*sādhāraṇākāra*) is accepted, internal distinctions (*avāntarabheda*) cannot be discarded. One might object that since difference (*bheda*) is the absence (*abhāva*) of a cloth in a jar, whereas non-difference (*abheda*) is its presence (*sadbhāva*) therein, there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence; and fearing this is refuted by experience according to the maxim, "Indeed, what is perceived can never be logically untenable," he says, "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: because in this way there is no perception of non-difference co-located with difference. To the question, "What then is the manner of perception? he replies, "For the manner of perception is... (*pratītiprakāro hi*).

If there were identity between the qualifier and the qualified, then only one of them would be perceived. Or, even if the perception of one occurs, there is still no identity; for example, when two men previously experienced are seen together, it does not follow that the two men are identical. If it is argued that identity consists in the very necessity of the relationship between the universal and the individual, this is not so; for the necessity of a relationship that establishes difference is itself governed by the necessity of difference. Indeed, a relationship exists only between two distinct things.

If identity were [the result of] that restriction, it would entail the collapse of the very nature of the relationship. Thus, he states "tadetad" (this very thing) to show that the refutation of difference and non-difference is the intention of the author of the Sūtras. Now, since other means of knowledge are rooted in perception, he states "ataḥ" (therefore) to show that they too have qualified objects as their domain; the meaning is that they have as their objects things such as fire, which are qualified by the relationship with smoke and so forth as perceived through perception and other means. He has thus stated the three means of knowledge according to his own view. Even if other means of knowledge are accepted, he states "pramāṇasaṅkhyā" etc., to show that they also have qualified objects as their domain.

In order to demonstrate that even at this time of the detailed exposition—that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have only qualified objects (*saviśeṣa-viṣaya*) and are thus refuted by reasoning (*tarka*)—there is no establishment of a quality-less reality (*nirviśeṣatva*), just as was previously stated in the summary and even in the *Buddhisthasvasiddhivāda*, [the author] recalls what was said before and shows the contradiction: "Even if one accepts the arguments stated by the opponent as subverting the existence of qualified objects, the possession of qualified objects remains unavoidable through the very qualifiers consisting of those arguments themselves. Thus he demonstrates the internal inconsistency.

Regarding the phrase "vastugata" (pertaining to the nature of reality): Alternatively, previously, the extraction (*niṣkarṣa*) of the distinctionless nature—which was established by one's own experience as being qualified—was refuted by means of attributes that would result in its having distinctions. The phrase "vastugata" extends (*atidiśati*) all of that [refutation] even to the extraction of the fact that the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is distinctionless.

Thus, the contradiction of the thesis that everything distinct from the ultimate reality of non-differentiated pure consciousness is non-ultimate has been shown in general by demonstrating that all means of valid cognition have as their object only that which possesses distinctions. Now, he proceeds to refute specifically the collection of proofs and arguments stated by the opponent.

The opponent, desiring the authority of scripture (*śāstra*), first adduced scripture; the proponent (*siddhāntin*), not accepting that and seeking to validate scripture regarding an object not contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), refutes the view that perception has "mere existence" (*sanmātra*) as its object. In this regard, he refutes the fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*) stated by the opponent concerning both the fact that perception has mere existence as its object and the difficulty of defining difference (*bheda*), beginning with the words "As for that which... (*yattu*).

The two passages beginning with "yat tu" (*yattvityādi*) constitute a restatement of the non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*). Regarding the word "also" (*tad api*): its sense is that not only has the establishment of [the view] that [perception] has an object possessing qualifiers been refuted, but also the impossibility of establishing that it has an object devoid of qualifiers. Alternatively, its sense is that not only has the existence of distinct objects been established, but the claim that it has "pure Being" (*sanmātra*) as its object has also been cast far aside. This refers to the phrase "of the genus and so forth alone" (*jātyādereva*).

The sense is that [the definition] is self-sufficient and independent of any other property in the form of an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), as well as independent of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). It is "cast far away" [as an objection]. Even if there were a delay caused by the recollection of a counter-correlative, the existence (or stability) of the cognition must be postulated for as long as its effect is being accomplished. Nevertheless, since universals (*jāti*) and the like—which are independent of a counter-correlative—are themselves differences (*bheda*), and since difference is easily apprehended even when perception lasts for only a single moment, the sense is that [the objection] is cast far away.

The intended meaning—that difference (*bheda*) is self- and other-establishing (*svapara-nirvāhaka*)—is demonstrated through the phrase "like consciousness" (*saṃvedanavat*) and so forth, using the very same reasoning stated by the opponent. By the expression "like consciousness and like color-form" (*saṃvedanavadrūpādivat*), both the opponent’s position and the [author’s] own concordant instance (*sapakṣa*) are treated as concordant instances. With this, he shows that the refutation stated by the opponent has been answered; for this very reason, the sense is that the removal of the objection is established by demonstrating the validity of the self- and other-establishing nature of difference at the outset. The first *ca* (and) implies that the rebuttal of the fault is accomplished through the proof of that self- and other-establishing nature.

And the second word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the two-fold refutation. If it is argued that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*)—namely, that the establishment of the avoidance of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) depends on the establishment of self-and-other-establishing capacity (*svapara-nirvāhakatva*), and the establishment of self-and-other-establishing capacity depends on the avoidance of infinite regress—it is not so; for the establishment of self-and-other-establishing capacity occurs through the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the cessation of error alone, thereby avoiding infinite regress. Even though perceptual cognition lasts for only three or four moments, he provides the solution by accepting its duration as being only a single moment, stating: "even if it lasts for a single moment."

In this regard, the following must be considered: Is the perception of difference not admitted by you? Or, even if it is admitted, is there no basis for it? Or is the basis difficult to define? Furthermore, is the object [of that perception] non-existent? Or, though existent, is it difficult to define? Among these, first, the non-admission of the perception [of difference] is untenable; for it would follow that the Vedāntas are not to be commenced, and because discourse in the form of proponent and opponent would be impossible. Moreover, the basis does exist.

Because the cause must be postulated on the basis of the body's actual functioning. For those who know the principles of logic maintain that it is indeed the perceived effect that serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the postulation of a cause; however, an effect that has been clearly ascertained does not deserve to be denied when it comes to defining its causal agent. Nor is there any difficulty in defining [the cause]; for the ease with which a cause is defined consists precisely in its conformity to the production of the effect. Since the cause’s conformity to that effect is established by the very production of the effect, it is not difficult to define. Furthermore, the object [of perception] certainly exists.

If it is not an object, then you yourself, being questioned on this point, must state whether the cognition that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated has an object or is without an object. If it has an object, then an object is indeed admitted. If not, then since there would be no sublation either, the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of the phenomenal world would follow. Therefore, an object certainly exists. Nor can it be an object that is itself sublated; for if that were the case, then even the cognition produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that sublates difference would have a false object, which would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that difference is ultimately real. To these [objections], they reply:

"If the conclusions of one's own scripture are true, then the conclusions of the world would be true; if the conclusions of one's own scripture are false, then the conclusions of the world would be true. Among the aforementioned alternatives, the first four positions are intended by the commentary beginning with the words "apica" (moreover), as will be stated; their refutation therein shall be understood from that [section].

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya—desiring primarily to reject the first and fifth positions, which hold that difference is an object of sublation—first observes that there is no sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), and thus proceeds to refute the sublation by reasoning (*yauktikabādha*). Therein, he refutes the impossibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇānupapatti*)—which consists in the untenability of the alternatives of succession or simultaneity due to the absence of another moment to be grasped, since difference is the very nature of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and thus has as its object that which is qualified by it.

Thus, since the object of cognition (*prameya*) is untenable, the consequence that there would be a linguistic usage of difference independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) under the view of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-pakṣa*) is avoided by being accepted as desirable; for the linguistic usage and the cognition consisting of rejection, acquisition, and so forth, which rely on words such as "cowness" (*gotva*), are independent of a counter-correlate. Just as in specific linguistic usages—such as *dārāḥ*, *kalatram*, and *āpaḥ*—the dependence on a counter-correlate (as in gender and number) is due to the nature of the word itself, like femininity, neuter gender, and plurality, and thus does not constitute a flaw in the object.

Since dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is observed only in the employment of words such as "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*), whereas it is absent in the cognition and linguistic usage of [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*), it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the dependence of a specific linguistic usage upon a counter-correlate is governed by the inherent nature of that specific word. Furthermore, the nature of the word consists in its being the cause for the cognition of a specific object by means of presenting an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) that delimits it, due to the commonality of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

For the word *gotva* (cowness) reveals cowness by its own nature as something unique (*asādhāraṇa*). The word *bheda* (difference), however, because its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—the state of being a cause for the cognition of exclusion—is common [to other things], reveals cowness by way of including limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of other objects such as buffaloes, which serve to delimit it. Furthermore, the consequence of the two words being synonyms (*paryāyatva*) is avoided; for even if the meaning of "distinction" is not intended, the use of the word *bhinna* is possible alongside the word *brahman* when referring to the supreme Brahman in the form of exclusion, just as the word *svarūpa* is used alongside *brahman*.

For even though there is no difference in the denotata of words that possess limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), their non-synonymy is established through the distinction of those adjuncts themselves; in this regard, the application or non-application of these terms is a matter of convention. Furthermore, the dilemma regarding whether the difference [between objects] is excluded or included is also resolved.

If one accepts that [the entity] is "excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*), then—just as in the case of the words "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) and "excluded"—the application of the word "different" (*bhinna*) can occur as a recurring usage. Furthermore, the statement "for that which is different is connected with difference" is refuted because the application of the word "different" is possible for the essential nature itself when it is qualified by differences such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. In your own view, the use of the term "different" regarding qualities such as genus is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), just like the word "excluded" applied to Brahman, which is of the nature of exclusion.

Even in the absence of a distinct attribute (*dharmāntara*), it is the cause of the cognition of exclusion from that which is associated with it. Regarding the position that it is an attribute (*dharma*), the fallacies of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*) have been avoided; for difference (*bheda*) is simply the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and because it is admitted that this very [genus] is self-explanatory as well as explaining others. Does the difference of ignorance (*avidyā*) from Brahman exist or not? If it does not, it would follow that Brahman is insentient (*jaḍa*) and so forth.

If [the difference] exists, one must observe that the refutation and its avoidance are identical whether one considers this difference to be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or a property (*dharma*). Furthermore, the refutations and their resolutions regarding the alternatives of essential nature and property apply equally to non-difference (*abheda*): if non-difference were the essential nature, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage of non-difference being independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). For in such statements as "He becomes non-different from the Supreme Self" and "Upon the destruction of the jar, the space within the jar is not different from the [great] sky," non-difference is indeed understood as having a counter-correlate.

If [Brahman] were non-dual, terms such as "Brahman" and "non-dual" would be synonyms. If it were a property (*dharma*), it would possess distinctions; and consequently, there would be a contradiction with your own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

Thus, when the position that objects are indefinable has been rejected, the opponents' only recourse is the non-acceptance of the cognition of difference; this [author] refutes that with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*), etc. First, the contradiction with experience is stated by the phrase "mere existence" (*sanmātra*); the contradiction with linguistic usage is stated by the words "If," etc.; and the contradiction with verbal testimony is stated by the words "In all," etc. [The opponent objects: "But surely all words are remembered in a single [locus], since you accept that all cognitions have 'mere existence' as their object."

It is not so; for what is intended is that once a jar is cognized, there is no possibility of applying the conventional designation "cloth" to it. In this context, the recurrence of the term *sanmātra* (pure being) in each refutation serves as a reminder that this very point is the object to be refuted. Furthermore, by the words beginning with *kiñca*, the contradiction between the specific sub-genuses of cognition is stated. Here, the term *sanmātra* is not employed because the object of refutation is already recalled by the word *kiñca*. It is stated that "due to the absence of difference" (*viśeṣābhāvāt*) in order to exclude the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), wherein a difference in time does exist.

Otherwise, there would be no distinction from memory; the meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) occurring solely through the state of being known (jñātatā). If it is argued that—as in the case of continuous streams of cognition (dhārāvāhika-buddhi)—the absence of a reflective awareness of the state of being known is logically established, we say no; for in those cases, the lack of such a synthesis (apratisandhāna) is dependent upon the absence of an immediate desire to know (bubhutsā). In the present case, however, even when the desire to know is present, the absence of a reflective awareness of the state of being known establishes nothing other than a difference in the object. This is what is meant by "at every act of perception" (pratisaṃvedanam).

The suspicion that [the opponent] might admit a distinction is intended to show that he has no other alternative. By the words "of all," etc., the undesirable consequence of the absence of a fixed order among the sense organs is stated. With the words "and not," etc., he states the distinctness of the objects in order to establish that fixed order of the organs. Herein, there is an elaboration of the contradiction regarding the cognition of the specific objects mentioned previously, as well as the refutation of the arguments that [the object] is either not a cause or has an ill-defined nature as a cause. "Inhering in the same substrate as color" means inhering in the same locus as color.

The word *samaveta* (inherently connected) refers to that whose sole nature is to be a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). A "qualifier" (*viśeṣa*) is so called because it qualifies (*viśeṣyate*). By this, it is established that [the objects of perception] have as their domain things that are distinct from pure Being (*sanmātra*) and mutually differentiated. Now, it was stated that all perception has as its object something qualified (*saviśeṣa*). However, since sound, smell, and taste are not perceived as having a substratum (*āśraya*) or as possessing other attributes (*dharmāntara*), how can the perception that grasps them have a qualified object? This is not so.

This is because even qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*), by virtue of possessing their respective configurations (*saṃsthāna*) and being qualified by time, are perceived as having distinctions. And this has been stated with reference to indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*). In determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), however, it is certainly possible for many factors such as location and so forth to function as qualifiers. He concludes the rejection of the view that the sense organs have "pure existence" (*sanmātra*) as their object—based on reasons established in common worldly experience—with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

He states that the view that perception has only pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object contradicts the positions accepted by others regarding other matters, in the verse beginning with "nirviśeṣa. The meaningfulness of the scripture (*śāstra*) arises from its having a subject matter not already established [by other means]; thus, those opponents who claim that difference (*bheda*), being established in the world, is the subject matter of the scripture, have themselves admitted this. He has already stated the contradiction with the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*); now he states the contradiction with other matters accepted by the opponents, in the phrase "of the Brahman that is pure existence. From this, he states the undesirable consequence that follows, in the word "tataḥ" (from that).

Having thus established the rejection of the view that perception grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*), [the author] leads the discussion toward his own intended conclusion—that perception has a qualified object—by means of the phrase "therefore" (*ataḥ*). In the commentary beginning with "therefore," two points have been stated: that the universal (*jāti*) is the form of the configuration of the thing (*vastu-saṃsthāna-rūpā*), and that difference (*bheda*) is indeed the universal and so forth. Therein, he first establishes that the configuration itself is the universal by means of the passage beginning with "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*).

Intending the following alternatives—whether [the universal] is perceived through direct observation or by way of logical necessity, or whether it is accepted as a genus distinct from configuration—he says "distinct from configuration" (*saṃsthānātirekiṇaḥ*) to negate the first alternative. The meaning is this: "This possesses a dewlap and so forth; this too possesses a dewlap and so forth; this has the form of a broad base and belly; this too has that form"—thus the dewlap and other such features are seen to be the objects of recurring cognition and linguistic usage. However, nothing distinct from those [features] is seen to be the object of recurring cognition and linguistic usage; therefore [there is no such genus].

Alternatively, by the phrase "of that which is cognized by a single-form cognition," he has stated the unique nature of the genus as it is accepted by others, based on its own inherent form and configuration (*saṃsthāna*). He states "to such an extent" (*tāvatā*) because even the conceptual construction (*kalpana*) [of a genus] is untenable. The point is that for words such as "cow" (*go*), just as for words like "individual," "genus," or "particular," both etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and the usage of the term across multiple instances (*anugata-prayoga*) are possible due to the influence of very similar limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). To dispel the suspicion that the genus accepted by others is being admitted under a different name, he says: "even in the theory of transcendence" (*atireka-vāde’pi*).

Others have accepted *saṃsthāna* (configuration) as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the whole (*avayavin*). What, then, is this so-called *saṃsthāna*? Is it a particular kind of conjunction of parts, or is it the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-mātra*), or is it something else entirely? In the first case, since there would be no configuration in partless selves (*ātman*), the universal (*jāti*) such as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) would not exist. In the second case, perception would not have a qualified object as its domain; there would be no consistent linguistic usage (*anugata-vyavahāra*); and the very concept of a universal (*jāti*) would be utterly destroyed.

In response to the objection that because there is no [other] state of existence in the third [category], one must accept our own position, [the author] shows that mere configuration (*saṃsthāna*)—common to both universals and non-universals—is intended for the sake of establishing the conventional usage of "universal" even in the case of partless things, by stating: "What is called configuration... The term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) is used so that the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of a jar might not be considered its configuration. "Form" (*rūpa*) is a qualifier that is inseparably established; by this, [things such as] a slave born in the house and the like are excluded.

Now, regarding the phrase "its own uncommon [property]," does the word *sva* (own/self) refer to the individual (*vyakti*)? Or does it refer to the class (*sajātīya*)? If it refers to the individual, is it intended to mean one specific individual or all individuals? In the first case, the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) would not exist in individuals other than that single one. If the word *sva* refers to all individuals, then cowness would also exist in the individual that is a buffalo. Furthermore, the term "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) would be rendered useless.

If the term "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*) refers to the genus (*jāti*), then—since the genus is a specific configuration (*saṃsthāna-viśeṣa*)—it would be stated that the configuration is the unique form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) of those things possessing a common specific configuration. Consequently, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because the determination of configuration depends upon the cognition of that [genus]. It is not so; for the word "own" (*sva*) refers to what is under discussion (*prakṛta*). And being "under discussion" consists in its presence in the intellect by virtue of being the object of current linguistic usage. If this were the case, then when a particular fragmentary cow (*khaṇḭa*) is present in the intellect, the cowness (*gotva*) would be its unique [form]; thus, cowness would not belong to a hornless cow (*muṇḍa*).

If it is argued that the "cowness" (*gotva*) of a broken cow would not be its configuration (*saṃsthāna*), because even in a hornless cow (*muṇḍa*), since cowness exists there as well, it lacks the commonality with the broken cow—[we reply: no, because for the broken cow, cowness does not exist in the form of its configuration. For the configuration of the broken cow is simply its state of being broken (*khaṇḍatva*). Is the broken cow present in your mind as merely "the broken," or as "a cow," or as "a broken cow"? In the first case, since the state of being broken alone is the unique characteristic of the broken cow, there is no consequence of the absence of cowness in the hornless cow.

For this very reason, it is not undesirable that *gotva* (cowness) lacks the nature of a configuration (*saṃsthāna*) with respect to an individual fragment. In the second case, since "the cowness of a cow is its unique property," cowness is excluded from buffaloes and the like, yet it subsists in cows; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

In the third case, just as the "lotus-ness" of a blue lotus—qualified by its blueness—is unique (asādhāraṇa), so too the "cow-ness" of a hornless cow (khaṇḍa)—qualified by its hornlessness—is unique. Thus, in the case of a shaven cow (muṇḍa), it is precisely the cow-ness qualified by hornlessness that ceases to apply, not cow-ness in general; therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. Furthermore, the "lotus-ness" qualified by blueness constitutes a single configuration (saṃsthāna), as it is the ground for the application of the term *indīvara*.

However, although there is a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified between the qualities of being a sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) and having a skin (*tvak*), there is no single configuration (*saṃsthāna*), because there is an absence of a single ground for the application of a word; thus is the distinction. Therefore, configuration is the unique form of the thing itself. What, then, is the difference between configuration as the nature of a genus and [qualities] such as whiteness? We say it is due to the absence of gradation in its own nature. For in the case of whiteness and so forth, a gradation exists, such that one is "white" and another is "whiter."

Even in the case of sound and the other objects, a gradation such as "more intense" or "less intense" is perceived, whether due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or by its own nature. A gradation in the inherent qualities of hardness, softness, and so forth is also found in touch and the rest. Even among numbers, a state of deficiency or excess is observed. And this is even more evident in the case of dimension. However, in the same way, no such gradation—such as "more cow-ness" or "most cow-ness"—is perceived in universals like "cowness. This distinction between the two cases is to be understood.

(Setting aside the position that the universal is characterized by configuration: If it is intended here that the definition of the universal consists in its form and configuration, then all individual instances that are very similar to the primary form are intended by their own respective terms. By the phrase "by the primary form," the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) is avoided, because the determination of a configuration does not depend upon the apprehension of a [prior] configuration. By the word "very similar," the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to buffaloes and the like is avoided. By the word "all," the consequence of non-existence in cases such as the "mutilated" cow is avoided, since the universal "cowness" is not absent in those [individuals].

[Objection: But how can a distinct configuration (*saṃsthāna*) produce a recurring linguistic usage (*anuvṛttavyavahāra*)? [Reply: It is said: just as the word "individual" (*vyakti*) is applied to many individuals even in the absence of a universal "individualness" (*vyaktitva*); just as the word "universal" (*jāti*) is applied to universals such as "cowness" and "horseness" even in the absence of another universal; just as the word "distinct" (*bhinna*) is applied to distinct things even in the absence of a universal "distinctness" (*bhinnatva*); just as the words "broken" (*khaṇḍa*) and so forth are applied to broken things and the like even in the absence of a universal "brokenness" (*khaṇḍatva*); and just as it is with eternal substances.

Just as for those who desire distinctions, the term "distinction" is applied to individual particulars even though the nature of being a distinction does not exist [inherently] within them, so too the linguistic usage of words such as "cow" is logically established. Furthermore, it must be examined: what exactly is this recurring linguistic usage?

Since the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) of the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga—which exist as long as space itself—cannot be established in terms of either spatial location or time, and since this sequence is dependent upon articulation (*uccāraṇa*), and articulation is perishable, the sequence itself perishes along with its correlate. Thus, how can there be persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of a word characterized by a specific sequence? If it is argued that "persistence" for words is simply their extreme similarity (*susadṛśatva*), then one must likewise accept such a form of persistence for universals (*jāti*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like, which reside in objects.

Now, what is this "perfect similarity" (*sausādṛśya*)? It is said: similarity (*sādṛśya*) is a property of the object that is the unique cause for the conventional usage of the term "similar. And like brotherhood, it is a category of entity determined by its correlative and is distinct with respect to each individual instance. Therefore, there is no difficulty regarding the dilemma of its subsistence (*vṛttivikalpa*) and so forth. "Perfect similarity" (*sausādṛśya*) is similarity due to the fullness of the specified form. By the word "fullness" (*pauṣkalya*), what is intended is the fullness of the basis for the application of the word denoting the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

It is established that the similarity of a *gavaya* to a cow is not "perfect similarity" (*sausādṛśya*). If it is objected: "In that case, then with respect to the first and subsequent individual cows, the expression 'this is very similar to a cow' would be used, but not simply 'this is a cow'," we reply: if there is a desire to express it so, then let it be used as "this is a cow" or "this is very similar to a cow," since there is no difference in meaning between these two usages. If it is asked, "Why then is [the latter] not used? we say: because of the cumbersome nature of such usage; for in the usage "cow," there is ease due to its brevity.

[Objection: In that case, would not the word for that [the self] applied to something similar to it be merely figurative, like the word "fire" applied to a young boy? [Reply: No; for figurative usage is based on the absence of the persistence of the defining characteristic of perfect similarity (*sausādṛśya*). Indeed, there is no perfect similarity between the boy and fire, but only a mere trace of similarity.

In the alternative view, however, the persistence of a definition characterized by extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*) is observed; and its status as the cause for primary application is established by the usage of the elders (*vṛddha*), just as in the case of words denoting universals (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, the repeated application [of the word] is justified. It must be accepted, according to observation, that the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of a certain word for a certain object serves as the reason for using that very same word for an object that is highly similar to it.

Even if one were to avoid the defects such as the dilemma regarding the mode of subsistence (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) by postulating an unperceived distinct entity (*arthāntara*) and relying on the force of common perception, a response to the objection based on the strength of perception regarding the very object that is actually observed is more appropriate according to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Furthermore, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti-grahaṇa*) is possible only through the persistence of a definition characterized by extreme similarity; thus, even that does not lead to the postulation of a *jāti* as you intend. Therefore, the universal (*jāti*) is not distinct from the configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

If it is argued that, because configuration (*saṃsthāna*) possesses a unique form and because the cognition of the configured object would otherwise be impossible, there could be no error such as that of silver in mother-of-pearl—since an error cannot occur when the unique form is manifest—we say: no. For an error can occur with respect to an object already perceived through some configuration, provided its object is a form that does not contradict the perceived configuration. Indeed, it is only an error whose object is a form contradictory to the perceived configuration that is impossible to arise.

In the cognition "this is white," there is no delusion regarding blackness and so forth. For whiteness is the unique (asādhāraṇa) attribute of the white substance, not of the mother-of-pearl. Therefore, both the cognition of the unique form and the delusion are logically consistent. If it is argued that such uniqueness is merely relative, then the term "unique" would be redundant; for there is no form whatsoever that does not belong uniquely to something. To this we say: no, because the word "unique" is intended to exclude [the attribution of] the generic configuration (*saṃsthāna*) to whiteness with respect to the mother-of-pearl.

Therefore, it is established that the specific configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is its own unique form, and that there is no *jāti* (universal) over and above it. Having thus demonstrated that the universal is nothing but the configuration, he now establishes—by means of the apprehension of the universal—that the previously introduced status of difference belongs to the universal itself, such as "cowness" (*gotva*), with the words "by the apprehension of the universal. In response to the objection that "the universal, such as cowness, being independent of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), cannot be the difference which is dependent upon a counter-correlative; therefore, it is more appropriate to accept that difference is a mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) distinct from the universal," it is said:

To the objection that—since a universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is independent of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), whereas difference (*bheda*) must depend upon a counter-correlative, it is therefore appropriate to admit a difference consisting of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) distinct from universals like cowness—it is said in reply: because the linguistic usage "it is different" is possible through the apprehension of the universal itself.

The meaning is this: even by one who accepts difference (*bheda*) as distinct from "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, it is admitted that in the case of the absence of an absence (*abhāvābhāva*), a positive category (*bhāva-rūpa-padārtha*) independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) possesses the nature of an absence (*abhāvatva*) which is dependent on a counter-correlate; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and because such an absence is not perceived. That being the case, the same applies here as well; for the dependence on a counter-correlate is governed by the very nature of the word whose application is based on the aspect determined by the counter-correlate, and thus it does not serve as a cause for a difference in the essential nature of the object itself. Thus, it has been stated that there is no logical inconsistency.

And he says "no" to the view that [difference] is perception, because no other category (padārtha) is perceived. He dispels the suspicion that this might be the acceptance of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) under a different name by stating "from another object" (*arthāntara*). The meaning is: even for one who maintains that there is a distinct category, difference exists in the form of mutual non-existence. Previously, it was stated that the linguistic usage of difference depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); here, it is stated that difference consists of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, independent of such a correlate.

With the intention that, in that case, even the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of difference would follow as being independent of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), he raises an objection with the words "But surely... (*nanu ceti*). The particle *ca* here refers to multiple objections directed toward a single subject matter. He replies, "True" (*satyam*). This means: there is acceptance regarding the conventional usage of the essential nature of difference when it is independent of a counter-correlate; however, there is no acceptance regarding specific conventional usages such as the word "difference" itself. The meaning of the phrase "and difference is indeed conventionally used" (*bhedaśca vyavahriyata eva*) is that it is not only perceived, but is also conventionally used independently of a counter-correlate. Thus is the sense of the conjunction *ca*.

He establishes [this] by saying, "from the conventional usage of 'cowness' (*gotva*) and so forth. To the question, "How can there be a conventional usage of difference when there is a conventional usage of cowness and so forth? he says, "cowness and so forth" (*gotvādi*). To the question, "How is cowness and so forth itself an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*)? he says, "in cowness and so forth" (*gotvādau*). What is intended here is that the particular instances (*viśeṣa*) of that [universal] are of the same class (*sajātīya*) in relation to the higher universal immediately following the previously mentioned universal. In this context, buffaloes and the like—which are of the same class in their status as non-cows—are what are to be excluded by the convention of "cow-ness. Let it be granted that exclusion is the cause for the cessation of cognitions and linguistic usages directed toward things of the same class.

To the question, "What follows from this, given that difference has been excluded? he says: "For by the very apprehension of difference, non-difference is excluded. "Exclusion of non-difference" means the exclusion of the cognition of non-difference. Thus, it has been stated that in the cognition of cowness and so forth, as well as in the practical activities of rejection and acquisition, and in the linguistic usage of words such as "cowness," there is no dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). If one then asks, "In that case, how is it that in the expression 'this is different from that' there is dependence upon a counter-correlate? he says: "This [is different] from that. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that this is not the case in the practical activity of rejection and so forth, nor even in linguistic usage in general, but rather only in a specific kind of linguistic usage, namely the verbal expression itself.

By the passage beginning with "And difference is indeed treated as such" and ending with "for it is by the very apprehension of difference that non-difference is excluded," [the author] establishes that for a certain entity, its own exclusion from another entity can consist in the very property that differentiates it from that other entity; for if there were no capacity to establish itself through something else (*paranirvāhakatvābhāve*), there could be no capacity to establish itself (*svanirvāhakatvāsambhavāt*). This applies to its own nature (*svarūpe*).

It is thus stated that when [Brahman] is manifest, there is no requirement for other properties in the form of exclusions (vyāvṛtti) that would contradict error. This being the case, since Brahman lacks the nature of a property that excludes one thing from another object, and because it does not tolerate superimposition (adhyāsa) while its own nature is being manifested, it is established that the nature itself is not the exclusion.

[Objection: Must it not ultimately be admitted that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of a substrate (*dharmin*) is its difference (*bheda*) in relation to all other attributes (*dharma*), whether positive or negative, residing therein? For if another difference were admitted, there would result the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to that [second] difference requiring yet another difference from the [first] nature. [Reply: True. However, that difference consisting of the nature itself is not opposed to superimposition (*adhyāsa*); for its cessation depends upon the connection with other attributes. Indeed, the delusion regarding the non-distinction of color from the substance of a cloth is removed by the cognition of its co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with touch.

Therefore, the difference that opposes superimposition (adhyāsa) with respect to the intrinsic properties of the substratum (*dharmin*) is the connection with other properties. Consequently, it is possible for the very nature of the substrata themselves to constitute a difference that opposes superimposition, in relation to their own locus and to other substrata possessing properties contradictory to them. Furthermore, it is logical to hold that the very nature of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vastu*) is itself qualified; it is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from another entity qualified by a property contradictory to its own, because this opposes the delusion of identity with other objects.

In this regard, with respect to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is the difference; with respect to the qualified, the very nature of the qualifier is the difference; and with respect to both, the very nature of the relation (*sambandha*) is the difference. Furthermore, with respect to one qualified entity in comparison to another qualified entity, its very nature is the difference. The designation "difference of nature" (*svarūpasya bhedaḥ*) does not have a meaning distinct from saying "the nature of the category-entity" (*padārthasvarūpam*); it refers to that nature which is expressed by its own unique, specific term.

And that term [“exclusion,” *vyāvṛtti*] is established through etymological derivation; its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is either the cognition of identity with another object intended as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), or it is the very nature [of the thing itself]. Therefore, since Brahman lacks the status of being a property of anything and lacks the state of being qualified by properties, it follows that even when its own nature is manifest, that nature cannot be an exclusion opposed to the superimposition of insentience and so forth—because it would still be susceptible to error. This is established.

Thus, the non-establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) has been refuted. Now, having restated the inference (*anumāna*) propounded by the opponent, he refutes it with the words "But as for... and so forth. The word "again" (*punaḥ*) indicates the distinction of inference from mere reasoning (*tarka*). Since the inference based on "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*) will be refuted by the authors of the Sūtras themselves, and since the refutation to be stated here is intended to demonstrate that all inferences whose object is falsity (*mithyātva*) are likewise subject to refutation, the inference based on "being excluded" (*vyāvartamānatva*) is what is refuted here.
The common refutations are: the lapse of the time [for the application of the reason] (*kālātyayāpadeśa*), the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), and contradiction (*vyāghāta*).

In that case, is the substratum (āśraya) cognized or not? If it is not, there is the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (āśrayāsiddhi). If it is cognized, and that cognition occurs through means of valid knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) as being real, then the proof of its falsity (*mithyātva*) is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhitam*). Furthermore, since being sublated within the accepted limiting condition (*pratipannopādhau bādhitatva*) is the determinant of falsity, we shall later explain that this [proof] is also "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*).

In this regard, even in cases of error concerning place, time, or object, because another entity serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and because even in those errors where subverting cognition has not yet arisen, [the reality] is sublated by the cognition of the person who points it out, the establishment of the qualified adjunct follows from the establishment of the parts consisting of the qualifier and the qualified; we shall explain this in detail.

When an alternative is made as to whether the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real, if it were ultimately real, there would be a loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), and the reason (*hetu*) of "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) would be inconclusive (*anaikāntya*), because that [reason] exists even in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). If it were not ultimately real, there would be the truth of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatā*), according to the maxim: "When the sublater (*bādhaka*) is itself sublated, there is no sublation of the nature of the sublated (*bādhyasvarūpa*). For this very reason, there is a well-known linguistic convention: "Two negatives indicate the original meaning."

One should not say, "This is the *nityasama* (eternal) fallacy, because it consists of an objection by superimposing one property onto another property"; for the *nityasama* is a refutation that results in an unauthentic succession of properties. However, the falsity of falsity (*mithyātvamithyātva*) is authentic; this is because you yourself admit the sublation of the "sublatability by cognition" asserted by the Mādhyamikas, and because we observe the sublation of the cognition of a rope in an ultimately real rope by every subsequent cognition.

If it is argued: "Even if reality exists, does reality itself possess reality or not? If it does not, the world would be unreal. If it does, then that reality must also have reality, leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā)," we say no; for we accept the principle of self-and-other-establishing capacity (*sva-para-nirvāhakatva*). If you admit that even falsity possesses this self-and-other-establishing capacity, then since falsity itself establishes its own falsity without depending on another falsity, falsity is false by itself, and consequently, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be real.

If one entertains the dilemma regarding whether the means of proof (*sādhana*) is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then if it is ultimately real, non-duality (*advaita*) is lost; if it is not ultimately real, it lacks proving power (*asādhakatva*), like mist perceived through the cognition of smoke—thus there is a contradiction. If it is argued: "Even by the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), inferences are not presented preceded by the proof of the reality of the world (*prapañca*) and the reality of the reason (*hetu*); nevertheless, those [inferences] are valid for him. Likewise, they shall be valid for me as well," we reply: No. Even if we do not prove reality, there is no contradiction with our own accepted position (*svābhyupagama*).

But for you, there is a contradiction between the acceptance of falsity and the acceptance of [the sublater] as a means of proof; thus, there is a disparity. Now, it might be argued: "The ultimate reality of the probans (sādhana-dharma) is not required. Even when the destructive hammer has perished, the jar previously destroyed is still seen as 'destroyed,' not as 'arisen. Similarly, even if the sublating cognition is false, the falsity of that which was sublated by it remains established. If this is said, we reply: no, because of the disparity between the efficient cause (kāraka) and the indicator (jñāpaka). For the destroyer is indeed an efficient cause.

Therefore, that which is to be destroyed by it must indeed be destroyed when that [sublater] is destroyed; for such is observed. Furthermore, the sublater is the indicator; when that is sublated, that which was sublated by it would indeed become real, as is seen in the case where, when someone has stated the absence of a jar in a room, the statement "it exists" sublates that [absence], and the reality of the jar is thereby perceived. Now, one might object: it is improper to claim the reality of what was previously sublated upon the sublation of the sublater.

If it is argued that even when the delusion of being a bee with respect to the stalk is sublated, the delusion of fire with respect to the *palāśa* flower—which was itself sublated by the cognition of "bee-ness"—is seen to remain unsublated, we ask: in that case, do you mean the cessation of the object or the cessation of the cognition? It cannot be the first, because the state of being a forest-fire (*dāva*) is seen to be sublated by the ultimately real stalk. If it is the cessation of the cognition, that is not dependent upon a sublating factor, since cognitions, being momentary, cease of their own accord.

The cognition of a bee, however, is an obstacle to the subsequent production of the cognition of a forest fire; and this obstructive power belongs specifically to the cognition of the bee as being real. Otherwise, one would not observe the absence of the cessation of the prior error. Consequently, according to your view, the complete cessation of all errors is never established.

Even on the position that the cessation of a cognition is produced by a sublating cognition (*bādhaka-vijñāna*), there results an infinite regress of errors, because every subverting cognition would itself depend upon a subsequent subverting cognition that is likewise of the nature of an error.

If some higher knowledge were to perish by itself, then—just as the destruction of an imaginary pot is merely imaginary—the destruction of that knowledge would also be imaginary. Consequently, the delusion consisting in the postulation of such a destruction would remain stable, and thus liberation, which consists in the cessation of all delusions, would be impossible. This results in a contradiction regarding the total cessation of ignorance and the falsity of everything. Such contradictions should be considered. Furthermore, the fact that [the opponent's position] is based on a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*) will be explained immediately hereafter.

The non-exclusive defect (*asādhāraṇa-dūṣaṇa*) regarding the two reasons—being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*) and being excluded from the locus of negation (*vyāvartamānatva*)—is their inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with respect to Brahman. That which is superimposed is known as being in grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇatā*) with its own substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), as in "this is silver. Likewise, because the substratum, which is Being (*sat*), and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—such as "the pot is Being," "the cloth is Being"—are objects of a single cognition, the reason of being an object of perception is inconclusive.

Although in the superimposition "the sky is dirty," because the sky is not an object of visual perception, the rule that the superimposed and the substratum are cognized by a single cognition is not fixed, nevertheless, it is established that the opponent accepts that pure Being (*sanmātra*) is graspable by perception; thus, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is proven. [Objection: But here, what is intended as the reason is the restriction of being an object of sight (*dṛśyatva-niyama*). That restriction of being an object of sight does not apply to Being, because Being is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*). [Reply: How so? [Objection: Because there is no difference between Being and consciousness (*anubhūti*). [Reply: No, because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*).

Once it is established that there is no difference between existence (*sat*) and experience (*anubhūti*), the pervasion of visibility by existence is not proven—since existence is self-luminous—and thus the reason of "visibility" is cleared of the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). When the inconclusiveness is removed, the absence of difference follows. If, however, the negation of difference were established by another inference, then in this case [the argument] would suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Thus, the absence of inconclusiveness has been stated by accepting the opponent's position. Furthermore, the visibility of Brahman is established by scripture, as in: "It is seen by a focused intellect" (*dṛśyate tvagryayā buddhyā*) and "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (*ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ*).

If it is argued that there is a *kālātyayāpadeśa* (the fallacy of proving what has already been refuted) when the absence of visibility (*dṛśyatvābhāva*) is sought to be established by the inference beginning with "because it is an experience," and that the scriptural statement regarding visibility is sublated by the passage "That which is invisible," we say no; for that [passage] is intended to negate visibility in general, whereas the statement "But it is seen by those who perceive the subtle, through a sharp and subtle intellect" concerns the prescription of a specific kind of visibility.

It is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other senses, but rather by the purified mind; since such passages show the negation of specific modes of being seen, and because the general negation in statements such as "it is unseen" (adṛśya) is understood to have that [specific negation] as its purport. If it is argued that Brahman is not an object of sight because of the general scriptural statement "unseen," etc., and by the inference proving the absence of visibility, we say no.

In that case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, due to the general prohibition in the Vedic scripture, "One should not harm any living beings," and by the inference based on its being an act of violence (*hiṃsā*). Therefore, "being perceptible" (*dṛśyatva*) is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason with respect to Brahman. If one wishes to avoid this inconclusiveness, one would have to admit the falsity (*mithyātva*) of Brahman. [Objection: Since "having perception as its sole nature" is intended as the reason, there is no inconclusiveness.

If it is argued that Brahman, being self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), does not have "being perceived" as its sole nature, we reply: in that case, the reason (*hetu*) would suffer from the fallacy of partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*). This is because within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which consists of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), the conscious portion—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is indeed self-luminous. Furthermore, if the unconscious portion alone were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to attributes such as eternality residing in the soul; for those attributes are known only through knowledge that has become an object (*dharmabhūtajñāna-vedya*), yet they are ultimately real (*paramārthabhūta*). Moreover, the property of "being excluded" (*vyāvartamānatva*) is also inconclusive with respect to Brahman.

Because [the self] is accepted as being distinguished from falsehood and so forth, it cannot be said that this is merely its essential nature (svarūpa), since Brahman lacks any attributes whatsoever and because [the self] is susceptible to superimposition (adhyāsa). Even if the state of being distinguished were its essential nature, it would nonetheless produce its own effect, just like consciousness (anubhūtitva). There is no restrictive rule that, although the reason is not distinct from the essential nature, it produces an effect during the stage of proof but not during the stage of refutation.

Furthermore, if both essential nature (*svarūpa*) and differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*) exist in Brahman, let it be the same in the case of jars and other objects as well. If that differentiation in Brahman is distinct from its essential nature, then it must likewise be so in the case of jars and other objects. In every respect, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is unavoidable. If Brahman’s differentiation from insentient matter (*jaḍa*) and the like were unreal (*aparamārtha*), then in reality Brahman would simply be insentient. Moreover, the term "unreal" is redundant; for even in the case of jars and the like, since their very state of being differentiated is illusory (*mithyātva*), there is no actual thing to be differentiated from.

Consequently, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntyam*) is firmly established; for you have accepted that which is non-ultimate as the reason (*hetu*), and because that [reason] exists even in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, since the negation—which culminates in the persisting pure Being (*sanmātra*)—is directed toward that [Being], [the reason is inconclusive]. Does the general property expressed in "unseen" (*adreśyam*) and so forth exist or not in relation to the excluded things such as jars? If it does exist, then for that very reason the cause of being excluded is inconclusive with respect to Brahman.

If it were not so, then the quality of being excluded (vyāvartamānatva) would apply to Brahman just as it does to jars and the like; for there is an absence of being excluded from those things that are themselves excluded. Just as silver is excluded from [the cognition of] "silver" and so forth, so too that which is not excluded from what is excluded must itself be excluded. Therefore, in either case, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) regarding Brahman. [Objection: But Brahman is indeed excluded from insentient matter and the like, and its being excluded is real; moreover, this is its very nature (svarūpa), so there is no loss of non-duality (advaita).

And because that [reality] is true, Brahman does not possess insentience and so forth; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness [of the reason]. If it is argued that the reason intended is the "state of being excluded" (vyāvarttamānatva) residing in pots and the like, which is of a non-ultimate nature, then the reason is unestablished (asiddha); for it is admitted that the mutual exclusion among pots and the like is unreal.

With the words "But that which... and so forth, he asserts that [the reason] is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition). Previously, it was argued that even sublation (*bādha*) cannot be established as a limiting condition because it is excluded from the subject (*pakṣa*); in order to refute that, he teaches the nature of sublation in order to show its absence from the subject, saying "of the two. The meaning is that the relationship between the sublated and the sublator exists only when there is a contradiction, and not merely between two cognitions such as "it is" and "it is not. Thus, exclusion belongs only to that which has been sublated.

The meaning is this: it is only the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that which is sublated within the condition of its own locus (*pratipannopādhau*) that establishes falsity; mere non-apprehension (*agṛhītatvamātra*) is not the establisher of falsity. Here, the word "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) refers to a specific kind of exclusion, whereas later on, the term "mere exclusion" (*vyāvartamānatvamātra*) appears with the suffix *mātra*, indicating a general sense. To the question, "What follows from this regarding the absence of sublation in the subject (*pakṣa*)?", he says: "In this case" (*atre*).

In order to show that there is no contradiction when there is a difference between two places and two times, [the author] shows that contradiction and sublation occur when those two are identical, using the words "yasmin" (in which). The meaning is that since there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence, one of the two must be sublated; therein, the stronger is the sublater, while the other, being sublated, ceases to exist. The word "ca" has the sense of "eva" (only). The specific exclusion intended by you belongs only to that which is sublated. Contradiction is the unfitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Sublation is the cognition of negation produced by unimpaired causes.

Sublation (*bādhakatva*) consists in being of the nature of a negation while being produced by non-defective causes. Cessation (*nivṛtti*) is either the absence of existence in what is present before one, or the non-appearance [of that object], or the absence of the appearance of reality [in it]. [The author] explains the absence of contradiction and sublation regarding a pot or similar objects in different places and times with the words "in another place" (*deśāntara*). He states with the words "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) that because there is no contradiction or sublation, there is also no cessation, which is the result thereof—namely, of that which has ceased in another place, that is, in a location free from contradiction and sublation.

"Elsewhere" means in a place free from contradiction or sublation; or alternatively, "elsewhere" refers to places and times other than its own [the object's] place and time. He explains this dissimilarity by means of an example: "in the case of the rope-snake and so forth. The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to show the difference from [the case of] jars and the like. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) useful for the refutation has been taught; now, he demonstrates the establishment of the refutation of the inference with the words "in another place and time. The word "iti" indicates the reason. Falsity (*mithyātva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

The state of being excluded (*vyāvartamānatva*) is the pervaded (*vyāpya*). By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "the mere state of being excluded," exclusion caused by contradiction or sublation is precluded. Alternatively, with the words beginning "that which again... (*yat punar...*), he declares the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the reason "the state of being excluded. To that end, he states that contradiction is the root of sublation with the words "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*). He shows its absence in the subject (*pakṣa*) with the word "here" (*atra*). He establishes the absence of contradiction with the words "in which" (*yasmin*). He states the cessation of its result with the words "elsewhere" (*anyatra*).

In the example, he demonstrates the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the words "in the case of the rope" (*rajviti*). Thus, the distinction has been shown in order to state the lack of proof (*asiddhi*). Now, he states the lack of proof with the words "in another place and time" (*iti deśakālāntareti*); this refers to the fact that [the reason] is qualified by a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*).

The meaning is this: In the statement "the cloth exists," is the absence of the pot intended to be proven, or is that same absence intended [to be proven] even in the case of "the pot exists"? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). In the second case, by the term "being excluded" (*vyāvartamānatva*), is it meant to be the state of being cognized as excluded by a cognition, intended as a reason for falsity; or is it the exclusion of that which has been sublated within its own perceived locus (*pratipannopādhau bādhitasya vyāvṛttiḥ*)? In the first case, the reason is "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhikatva*). In the second case, due to the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*), it follows that the pot and so forth are real (*satyatva*).

If it is argued that if "being subject to sublation" (*bādhārhatā*) were the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it would be indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*), and thus "being subject to sublation" itself would have to be the adjunct; furthermore, that [adjunct] does not possess co-inherence with the probandum, because a rope-snake seen on a path by one traveling alone is not sublated by anyone else—[we reply: this is not so, because there is a necessary rule of sublation by the knowledge of God (*īśvara*) and others. For those who do not accept God and the rest, even in their own position, this is indeed an adjunct.

Did you ascertain through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the falsity of that rope-snake seen on the path, or not? If not, then the non-occurrence [of the reason] in that case would not serve to establish the co-extensiveness (*sādhyasamavyāpti*) with the probandum, as it would simply be a real snake. If it was ascertained, then its sublation (*bādhitatva*) is established by that very cognition, and thus the co-extensiveness with the probandum is established. Now, one might object: is sublation within the delimited locus (*pratipannopādhau*) the necessary condition for falsity?

Or is it a case of absolute sublation (*kevalabādha*)? In the first case, since space and time are limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), an error regarding space and time lacks the status of being limited by space and time; consequently, because it does not follow all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is no co-extensive pervasion (*samavyāpti*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). Thus, in the case of a sublation occurring within a perceived limiting adjunct, that [error] would not be a limiting adjunct. In the second case, there would be the falsity of everything. To this it is replied: there is no rule that space and time alone are limiting adjuncts; rather, other things as well can be limiting adjuncts. A limiting adjunct is a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).

For this very reason, in the statement "because it is uncontradicted within the limiting conditions (upādhi) such as place, time, and so forth," the author of the Bhāṣya will later state that other entities (*vastvantara*) may also serve as limiting conditions by the use of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Therefore, in the case of an error regarding place and time, another entity serves as the limiting condition. Even though an error regarding place and time has another entity as its limiting condition, there is no circular dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) when an error regarding an entity has place and time as its limiting conditions, because the individual instances of error (*bhrama-vyakti*) are distinct.

Therefore, the sublation of that which is perceived as delimited by a particular delimiter is the cause for establishing its falsity. Alternatively, there is no fault whatsoever in the fact that time delimited by another action functions as the locus of error (bhrāntyupādhitva) without the "evening-ness" superimposed upon it or the "daytime-ness" which would remove it; the same applies to space. Thus, the establishment of the qualified locus (viśiṣṭopādhi) occurs because the two components—the qualifier and the qualified—within that qualified locus are free from the aforementioned logical inconsistencies.

Therefore, the mere fact of being excluded [from a locus] is not the reason for non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthya*). Some have argued as follows: "In the expression 'the pot exists' (*ghaṭo'sti*), are the words 'pot' (*ghaṭa*) and 'exists' (*asti*) synonyms (*paryāya*) or not? If they were synonyms, they could not be used together. If they are not, then the pot must be distinct from existence (*sad-vilakṣaṇa*). This is not so; for in such passages as "If one knows that Brahman exists" (*asti brahmeti ced veda*), if the words 'Brahman' (*brahman*) and 'exists' (*asti*) were synonyms, there would be tautology (*paunaruktya*). If they are not, then even Brahman would be distinct from existence.

In both cases, this is the resolution: a restriction is made by means of the word "exists" (asti) so as to prevent the suspicion that there might be a restatement intended to negate the very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) already established by its own term.

Now, with the words "But as for... (*yattu*), he refutes the "subsistence" (*anuvarttamānatvam*) that was stated as a proof for ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*). He presents a dilemma: is ultimate reality being proved for the nature of those individual things such as pots, which are denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*) and are fit for connection with means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or rather for some other object that subsists [in them] as their substrate? Having intended that the second horn of this dilemma suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), he states the refutation of the first horn as being a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*).

[Objection: But surely the author’s intention is that "only the existent is the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*); so how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*)? [Reply: It is said: Does this inference establish the ultimate reality of the existent, or the non-ultimate reality of something distinct from it, or both? In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established. In the second case, there is the fallacy of the reason being unestablished in the locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhatā*). In the third case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established regarding one part, and the fallacy of the reason being unestablished in the locus regarding the other part. He concludes with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Having relied upon the refutation of difference based on the non-establishment of the means and objects of knowledge by another [author], the difference between experience (*anubhūti*) and the existent (*sat*) has been discarded. Here, however, by relying on the removal of fallacious reasons for the refutation of difference, the non-difference between experience and the existent is also refuted by the words beginning with "anubhūti. In the phrase "of the particularities of experience and the existent," the word "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) indicates the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) of the reason "because of being persistent" (*anuvartamānatva*); this is because the entity denoted by the word "existent" (*sat*) is itself excluded [from being a particular], and because there is no other persisting object [to serve as its locus].

The word "existent" (sat) indeed applies to those things that are capable of being related to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since the recurring linguistic usage—"the jar exists," "the cloth exists"—is established just like the usage of mutually exclusive terms, those objects of experience that are fit for relation with a means of valid cognition and are mutually distinct are what are denoted by the word "existent."

Now, with the intention of pointing out that even regarding self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), which was accepted on the opponent’s authority, there remains a point requiring instruction, he says: "But as for [the claim] that experience... The particle *tu* indicates a difference between the two positions. He states the point that must be explained: "at the time of the manifestation of the object.
