This is because it will be stated later, "in its present state"; since that cognition, being an eternal substance, exists at all times, the phrase "in its present state" would be redundant. To dispel this doubt, he says: "at the time of the manifestation of the object."

It is understood that by the term "present state" (*vartamānadaśā*), what is intended to be expressed is the presentness of the expansion of the connection with the object; however, it does not mean [the presentness] of all [cognitions]. This is established by the phrase "of another's experience" (*parānubhavasya*). Furthermore, this is established by the phrase "not at all times" (*na sarvadā*) through the words "even of one's own experience" (*svānubhavasyāpi*). By the expression "if there were experience" (*anubhūtiśced*), the absence of the aforementioned discrepancy—namely, that [experience] occurs at the very moment of manifesting the object to its own substrate—is implicitly included.

Having thus established the possibility of experience being an object of experience, he refutes the inference stated by the opponent regarding its impossibility with the words "of experience" (*anubhūteḥ*). To the question "Why?", he says "inherent" (*svagata-*) and so forth. He states the undesirable contradiction with worldly practice that would arise if one does not accept that another's experience is inferable, with the words "another's" (*parā-*) and so forth. Then, he states the contradiction with Vedic practice with the words "of the Teacher" (*ācāryasya*) and so forth. Furthermore, the refutation of the Cārvāka is implicitly achieved by the phrase "non-acceptance of the inference of another's experience," and so on.

Because, if inference were not accepted, it would be impossible to grasp the relationship between a word and its meaning. Thus, the sublation (*bādha*) has been stated; now he refutes pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "nor is it another," etc. For the unique form [of the subject] is established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the locus (*dharmigrāhakamāna*); it does not disappear when a common form exists—this is the intention behind teaching [the opponent] the nature of experience as "experientiality" (*anubhūtitva*). Here, the word "experience" (*anubhūti*) refers to cognition in general, and not specifically to that which is distinct from memory.

When it is said that "it is being manifest," it would follow that even a jar or similar object is an experience (*anubhūti*); therefore, to exclude that, it is said to be "with respect to its own substratum" (*svāśrayam prati*). Since qualities pertaining to the self (*adhyātmadharma*), such as atomicity and eternity, are manifested by another cognition, to exclude those, it is said "by its very existence" (*svasattayaiva*). To exclude past experiences, it is said "in the present state" (*vartamānadaśāyām*). Although, because the manifestation of a past experience is impossible without another cognition, its exclusion [from being an experience] follows by implication (*arthāt*); [the explicit mention of the present state serves to clarify this].

Nevertheless, this qualification is intended to demonstrate the establishment of the past [object] by means of another cognition—a point not accepted by others. The meaning is that the connection with the object occurs during its present state. Since it would be impossible for that [connection] to exist in the case of another's experience if one were to say merely that "it is manifest by its own existence during its present state," the phrase "with respect to its own substratum" is stated in order to exclude that possibility.

This definition is accepted only by those who maintain that [consciousness] is self-luminous; thus, he states the definition agreed upon by all: "by its own existence alone. The phrase "by its own existence alone" serves as an indicator for the two preceding terms, "in the state of being present toward its own substratum. When it is said "an instrument," since things such as a staff or a wheel would also qualify as such, the term "instrument of an object" is used to exclude them.

The word *sva* (self) is used to exclude the possibility that visual cognition might establish objects other than its own [sensory] domain, since it is impossible for it to establish all objects. The phrase "by its very existence" (*svasattayaiva*) is intended to exclude the sense-faculties. The expression "in relation to its own substrate" (*svāśrayam prati*) is stated to exclude that which is impossible because of the aforementioned impossibility.

The word "own" (*sva*) is used to exclude the impossibility of [the object] establishing all objects, on the grounds that visual cognition does not establish an auditory object. The phrase "by its very existence" (*svasattayaiva*) is for the purpose of excluding the sense organs; for the sense organs and so forth are not illuminators by their mere existence alone, but rather through the mediation of the production of cognition. The phrase "in its present state" excludes past experience, while "toward its own substratum" excludes the experience of another. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And those... (*te ca*).

Since the concomitance (*vyāpti*) of "being an experience" with "being non-experiential" has not been established—because we observe the coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "experience-ness" with "experientiality," which negates the probandum-property characterized by non-experientiality—to the doubt as to how experientiality could then be seen to entail non-experience, he states that it is "conditioned" (*sopādhikatva*) by saying "but in the case of a jar, etc. Here, "non-experience-ness" means the absence of being conventionally designated by the word "experience"; thus, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*).

Alternatively, *anubhūtitva* (the nature of being an experience) consists in either one of the two previously stated definitions, but not in both combined; for they are mutually independent, and because of the use of the word "or" (*vā*). Indeed, the word "and" (*ca*) has not been employed. In that context, the meaning is that the state of being a non-experience—defined as the absence of either one of the two definitions—is conditioned (*sopādhika*), since it is occasioned by the lack of one of those two forms. Now, he states the refutation by a counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*): "Thus, of experience... (*tathānubhūteḥ*). Alternatively, [he states] that it shares the same fate as a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*).

Regarding the non-experienceability (*ananubhūtitva*) of sky-flowers and the like, [the author] suspects the existence of another limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by saying "gaganeti. He states that for the non-experienceability of jars and the like as well, there is another limiting adjunct, namely "non-opposition to ignorance" (*ajñānāvirodhitva*), by saying "evaṃ tarhi. Non-opposition to ignorance means non-opposition to the absence of the rule of manifestation (*prakāśaniyamābhāva*). Nor should it be suspected that there is an absence of co-extensiveness with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāpti*) because of its absence in pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth; for pleasure and the like, being specific types of cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*), lack the quality of non-experienceability.

In order to refute the status of "non-opposition to ignorance" as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he points out its occurrence in the subject (*pakṣa*) with the words "of experience" (*anubhūteḥ*). He states that this is equally applicable to your position as well with the words "even in the case of non-experientiality" (*ananubhāvyatve 'pi*). The meaning is that even if experience were not itself an object of experience, the aforementioned "non-opposition to ignorance" would still follow as a limiting adjunct for the reason of being "non-experience."

It has been stated that the [alleged] lack of being an experience (*ananubhūtitva*) and the non-opposition to ignorance (*ajñānāvirodhitva*), which were asserted [of consciousness] on the grounds of its being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*), would follow [absurdly] even for that which is not an object of experience, such as a sky-flower. If it is argued that the lack of being an experience and the non-opposition to ignorance in the case of a sky-flower and the like are caused by its non-existence (*asattva*) and not by its not being an object of experience, then [we reply]: if [consciousness] were not an object of experience, its non-existence would likewise follow. The non-existence of a sky-flower and the like is not caused by its merely not being an object of experience; [it is caused by its non-existence].

If it is argued that [the absence of existence] is instead caused by the lack of non-experientiality (ananubhāvyatva) while self-luminosity (svayamprakāśatva) is present—and thus that the mere fact of experience being non-experiential does not entail its non-existence—it follows that, just like [non-experientiality], the lack of self-luminosity would also entail [non-existence]. Therefore, if experience lacks self-luminosity, its non-existence, which is caused by its non-experientiality, becomes unavoidable. If it is then argued that non-existence contradicts the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends the subject (dharmin);

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that one should likewise consider that if something were an object of experience (*anubhāvya*), it would follow that it lacks the nature of being an experience (*ananubhūtitva*). Furthermore, regarding the example of a sky-flower, one should not suspect the fault of a defective locus (*āśrayavaikalya*); for opponents themselves accept that it serves as a negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) for the principle that "what is non-existent is not manifest. For they state: "A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is a manifestation devoid of a real object that follows upon verbal cognition; whereas a manifestation possessing its own intrinsic nature is a direct apprehension (*pratīti*)."

In this regard, it is logical that even that which is perceived as a mere appearance can serve as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for negation; this is also accepted by the Bhaṭṭas. Therefore, the "sky-flower" has been cited here according to the system of the opponent's school. It is "to be laughed at" (*upahāsya*), meaning it is an object of ridicule even for those standing nearby. Now, he refutes the permanence (*nityatva*) asserted by the other [school] with the words beginning "As for that which... (*yattu*). [Objection: But how is it appropriate to refute the permanence of cognition when it is accepted by those [who hold such a view]? [Reply: It is said: The Self is the substratum (*āśraya*) of cognition. And the permanent substance of cognition (*jñānadravya*), which is dependent upon that [Self] and is capable of contraction and expansion, is not admitted by the opponent.

As for that cognition which is under discussion—well-known in the world as being perceptual or non-perceptual, valid or invalid, and conforming to the positive and negative concomitance of sense-object contact and so forth—if its eternality is sought to be established, that is refuted; for the opponent has maintained the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of cognition in relation to its object, and the opponent intends eternality to be co-located with that self-luminosity, since he seeks to establish eternality on the basis of its being self-established (*svatas-siddhatā*).

Therefore, its refutation is appropriate. In that regard, although the substance of clay is established, it is logical that the substance of clay exists in an impermanent state as a pot and so forth. Likewise, although the substance called cognition is eternal, it is logical that cognition exists in an impermanent state as memory, direct experience, and so on; thus, there is no contradiction with our own position. Furthermore, even though [the self] is self-luminous, it possesses some degree of being an effect (*upādeyatva*); therefore, the word "but" (*tu*) is used for the purpose of excluding that [self-luminosity]. It is like giving a staff to a blind man born with blindness.

The meaning is that what is unestablished (*asiddha*) is established by a reason that is absolutely unestablished (*atyantāsiddha*). For in that context, the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) was stated due to the absence of both the apprehender (*grāhaka*) and the apprehended (*grāhya*); having raised that doubt, he says "of the prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāvasya*) to assert that the apprehender exists. When the alternative (*vikalpa*) has been stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), he raises the objection regarding the contradiction mentioned therein—namely, "how [can it make known]?"—in order to establish the position that it makes [the object] known only when [it itself] exists. The word "then" (*tadānīm*) is a qualifier of the non-existence, not a qualifier of the action. He refutes this with "no" (*na hi*).

With the intention of raising the dilemma as to whether the rule that [cognition] exists at the same time as its object is caused by the generality (*sāmānya*) of the object to be grasped, or rather caused by the specific instance (*viśeṣa*) of that object to be grasped, he first refutes the position that it is caused by the generality of the object to be grasped with the words: "For [it is] not experience... Alternatively, having in mind the dilemma as to whether the rule of grasping only the present is due to the nature of the experiencing subject (*grāhaka-anubhūti-svabhāva*), or due to the nature of the absence of experience of the object to be grasped (*grāhya-anubhūty-abhāva-svabhāva*), he first refutes the former with the words: "For [it is] not... The word *hi* indicates the reason.
The proposition (*pratijñā*) "not" is to be supplied.

He raises an objection in order to refute the position that the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) possesses specific characteristics: "Now, you might think... With the intention that the statement regarding the necessity of the object of apprehension existing simultaneously [with the cognition] must be preceded by observation, he asks: "But by what [means] have you...? [The phrase] "in some experience" refers to the fact that non-existence is observed as the locus for grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore, he says: "Alas, then!"—meaning that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is difficult to deny.

The meaning is that pervasion is established through the simultaneous proof of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), provided that the substratum (*dharmin*)—which consists of the antecedent non-existence of experience—is apprehended. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to subsequent destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). This refutation was stated by accepting the rule of simultaneous existence; however, he states that simultaneous existence is untenable with the words "and its antecedent non-existence" (*tatprāgabhāvaṃ ca*).

If there were no rule that experience must grasp an object existing at the same time as itself, then visual cognition would be possible even with respect to a non-existent jar; to this he replies: "of that which is born of the sense-faculties. By the word *pratyakṣa*, perceptual cognition is meant. The intention is this: the rule of grasping only what exists at the same time as itself does not apply to cognition in general, nor to valid perceptual cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) as a specific subclass thereof, nor to perception as a specific subclass of that.

Rather, [it applies] to sensory cognition (*aindriyika-jñāna*) which has the specific form of perception (*pratyakṣa-viśeṣa-rūpa*), and not to all cognitions or all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that this also applies to perception (*pratyakṣa*); this is because it accords with the explanatory text that follows. To the question "Why?", he says: "recollection, inference, etc. (*smaraṇānumāna-iti*). By the word "recollection" (*smaraṇa*), the restriction that all cognitions must have an object existing at the same time is excluded. By the words "inference" and "scripture" (*anumānāgama*), the restriction of that [simultaneity] for all means of valid knowledge is excluded.

By the phrase "yogipratyakṣādi" (yogi-perception and so forth), there is the exclusion of the restriction that perception [must be] only [of the present]. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the perception of Īśvara is included. To the question, "If the existence of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) does not exist, how can there be a distinction between valid and invalid cognitions?", he says: "For this very reason. For this very reason—because there is no rule that cognition in general must apprehend what exists at the same time as itself—the non-separation (*avinābhāva*) from the object of knowledge is established; such is the meaning.

The point is that otherwise, because a present object would not be apprehended, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between those various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their respective objects of cognition (*prameya*)—which grasp what exists at a different time—would not be established. In response to the question of how that [concomitance] is established, he explains that very invariable concomitance with the words "for there is no [relation] of the means of valid cognition... The grammatical construction is: "the relation of the means of valid cognition to the object. To the question, "In that case, what is this invariable concomitance with the object of cognition? he replies, "But rather... By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "place, time, etc.," configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is meant. It is the state of being the opposite of falsity (*mithyātva*).

*Mithyātva* (falsity) is that which is contrary to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the meaning is "the state of being that. Alternatively, it refers to an object that is contrary to falsity. The state of being such is *mithyātvapratyanīkatā* (the quality of being contrary to falsity). This constitutes the connection between valid cognition and its object—this is the grammatical construction. The meaning of the commentary beginning with "Therefore, indeed" (*ata eva*) is as follows: Precisely for this reason, because those [cognitions] universally accepted as valid are seen to apprehend objects existing at a different time, it is inferred that even in those cases there is an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) with the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

Regarding the question of how there can be an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) in that case, he says "for not" (*na hi*), and so forth. By this very instruction—consisting in the nature of the relation between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) characterized by the inseparability of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—the claim made by certain Buddhist sectarians that memory is devoid of an object (*nirviṣayatva*) is refuted. With the intention that this must be accepted, he says: "Therefore, this also... (*ata idam api*).

Thus it has been established that experience alone is capable of apprehending prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Now, [the opponent] raises the objection—“But it must be apprehended by some one among the means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*)”—suggesting that prior non-existence does not exist because there is an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to the impossibility of such an apprehension. This is introduced with the words “Now, it might be said. By the word “etcetera” (*ādi*) in the phrase “due to the absence of the mark, etcetera,” inference (*anumāna*) and verbal testimony (*śabda*) are intended. He explains this with the words beginning “For not...,” and concludes with “Therefore...”

An analogy (upamāna) is not presented [as a separate means of valid cognition] because it lacks the capacity to establish an object not yet established, since its scope is restricted to only one of the two—the similarity between an already known thing and a name, or the relationship between that name and the named object.

"He avoids [the objection] with the word 'yadi' (if). For what purpose is the word *yadi*? The word *cet* has the meaning of *yadi*. [The sense is: "Even if you have descended from your own established method into the boundaries of the treatise (*śāstra-maryādā*), even so..."—this is the meaning of *tathā cet*. He states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "by non-perception of the perceptible" (*yogyānupalabdhyā eva*). Since the opponent accepts non-existence as a means of valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), it is said "by non-perception of the perceptible" alone. Even upon examining one's own position, what is called the "non-perception of the perceptible" regarding cognition is the perception of another state that is positive in nature (*bhāva-rūpa-avasthāntara-upalabdhi*).

Indeed, the very perception of the lump [of clay] and so forth constitutes the non-apprehension of the jar under conditions of perceptibility (*yogyānupalabdhi*). Therefore, what is called the absence of knowledge delimited by past time consists either in a contraction of the mind (*jñānasaṅkoca*) or in the knowledge of another object. When one desires to know a cognition of an elephant from a previous time, the recollection of sleep or the like at that time, or the recollection of the cognition of a jar and so forth, constitutes the non-apprehension of the elephant-cognition under conditions of perceptibility. And this, by way of a logical mark (*liṅga*), brings about the ascertainment of the absence of cognition at that prior time.

As for the claim that non-existence is difficult to apprehend because consciousness (*saṃvit*) is incapable of being made an object in the form "this is [it]," that is incorrect; for if that were so, the refutation of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) would be untenable. Indeed, it is not the prior non-existence of something else, such as a jar, that is being refuted, but rather that of experience (*anubhūti*). Therefore, one must first make experience an object in the form "this is [it]" and then refute its prior non-existence. If it is argued that its prior non-existence can be refuted even in the absence of making it an object in the form "this is [it]," [then we reply:]...

Even in the absence of that [object], its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) can be established. If it has been made an object of cognition by you, then it has likewise been made an object of cognition by us; thus, its non-existence is easily proven—this is what should be understood. Indeed, this same meaning is intended in the subsequent passage beginning with "If it were eternal" (*nityañcet*).

Having thus stated that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established through the non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*), he further states "moreover" (*kiñca*) and so forth to establish it through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). It was previously stated that the impermanence of cognition is established by the non-perception of its own manifestation, which is characterized by instability; now, that same point is demonstrated by way of defining the illumination of the object. It has been stated that the apprehension of the absence of cognition is possible without distinction [between the two types of non-existence].

Now, with the intention of presenting the dilemma—whether you intend to prove the permanence of cognition *with* an object or of cognition *without* an object—he refutes the position that it has an object by means of the passage beginning with "pratyakṣa" (perception). The meaning is that at all times, even during the period when a jar exists, [the jar] is not perceived. One might argue: "Let the existence of the jar and so forth in prior and subsequent times not be perceived; what of it? To this he replies: "And the non-perception of that... Non-perception (*apratīti*) means the absence of cognition's suitability for the practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) regarding the jar.

Therefore, there is no lack of distinction from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*). The meaning is this: for perceptual cognition, which by its very nature apprehends only what exists at its own time, the fact that it does not manifest a jar even when that jar exists in the prior or subsequent moments is due solely to its own inherent absence at those times. Thus, the non-eternality of cognition has been stated on the grounds that the occasional nature of its conformity to the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding objects would otherwise be inexplicable. He states another *arthāpatti* (presumption) as well: "only with respect to objects such as jars," and so forth.

If the perceptual consciousness that exists simultaneously with its object were eternal, then objects such as a jar would also have to be eternal; therefore, the meaning is that because the non-eternality of jars and other things cannot otherwise be accounted for, consciousness itself must be non-eternal. He states another *arthāpatti* (presumption) with the words "If it were eternal": the proof of the eternality of consciousness must be performed by making this very consciousness an object of cognition, thinking "this is consciousness. However, since it is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*), it is incapable of being made an object in the sense of "this [is it]"; thus, it would have to be perceived as eternal by itself, yet it is not so perceived.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is precisely non-eternal (*anityatva*). Thus, the non-eternality of cognition has been stated on the grounds that its appearance as eternal is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*). If it is argued that [cognition] is eternal because it does not appear as non-eternal, we say no; for even though non-eternality—which depends upon the two limits of prior and posterior—exists, the non-appearance of non-eternality is established simply because those two limits are not self-luminous (*asvayaṃprakāśatva*). Alternatively, these two supporting arguments (*anugrāhakatarka*) are stated: namely, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that objects such as pots would be eternal, and the undesirable consequence that they would appear as eternal, since their occasional suitability for objective usage (*viṣayavyavahārānuguṇya*) would otherwise be inexplicable.

Now, he shows that the undesired consequence of the eternality of the objects of inference and so forth would likewise follow, by saying "in this way" (*evam*). This means: when, in this manner, the eternality of perceptual cognition entails the eternality of its objects. Why [would it be] eternal? To this he says: "because it conforms to consciousness" (*saṃvidanurūpa*). The meaning is: because it exists in such a way as consciousness manifests its own object. [Objection: Since perception is necessarily restricted to objects existing at the same time [as itself], the consequence of the eternality of the object upon the eternality of that [perception] is indeed logical.

Since cognitions such as inference can have past and future objects, how could it follow that if those cognitions were eternal, their objects would also have to be eternal? It is replied: "Pastness" and "futurity" are indeed relative. Therefore, the pastness and futurity of an object depend upon cognition. If cognition is eternal, then—given that the object's pastness and futurity are relative to that cognition—the cognition does not fail to manifest them; thus, when they are perceived as unconditioned by time, the objects would be eternal.

With the intention that the defining characteristic of eternity (*nityatva*) is precisely the state of being unconditioned by time (*kālānavacchinnatva*), it was stated that "those which are unconditioned by time are eternal. Now, an objection is raised: the pastness and futureness of an object are not in relation to consciousness (*saṃvit*); rather, they are in relation to other things such as inferential marks (*liṅga*). Therefore, since the pastness and futureness of an object are possible in relation to inferential marks and so forth, there is no contingency of its being eternal.

It is said: since the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth are objects of perceptual cognition, by virtue of its [consciousness's] eternity, there would follow the eternity of those marks and other such things that constitute its objects. Consequently, consciousness would not manifest the pastness or futureness of the object of inference in relation to them; thus, the object would be eternally unconditioned by time. The phrase "in this way" (*evam*) is stated with the intention that, depending on the aforementioned defect, there would result the contingency of the eternity of the object of inference.

Thus, in the aforementioned alternative, the permanence of experience possessing an object has been refuted; now, he refutes the position of the permanence of objectless experience with the words "na ca" (and not). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of non-apprehension" (*anupalabdheḥ*). It is not only because of the non-apprehension of consciousness devoid of an object, but also because the opponent himself establishes that consciousness possessing an object is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśatva*); therefore, even according to the manner of his own admission, there is no such thing as objectless consciousness. He states this with the words "viṣaya... (object...).

To this, he replies: "Because consciousness [is devoid] of an object" (*saṃvido viṣaya*). The meaning is that since consciousness which transcends knowledge possessing an object never has a connection with an object, its self-luminosity cannot be established; furthermore, because it would not be cognizable by another cognition, it would be a mere nothingness (*tucchatā*). Now, one might object: "If self-luminosity is established on the basis of being the illuminator of an object, then this fault would indeed apply."

If it is argued that the self-luminosity of the probandum is established by the reason "because it is an experience (*anubhūti*) even in the absence of a connection with an object," then what is this "being an experience"? Is it "self-establishedness" (*svataḥ-siddhatva*)? In that case, there would be a lack of distinction between the reason and the probandum. If, on the other hand, being an experience means "the illumination of an object," then the aforementioned fault would indeed persist. Furthermore, you must not state as a reason "the state of always appearing while existing," because this would be inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) due to pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth, which you yourself consider to be insentient (*jaḍa*).

Therefore, since self-luminosity cannot be established without relying on the illumination of objects, one does not escape the aforementioned defects. To the objection—namely, how there can be a non-establishment of consciousness as the substratum (*dharmin*) when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is self-luminosity, is absent—the author replies: "And because experience cannot be inferred by another experience. Now, it may be argued that for a single consciousness, its occasional connection with an object occurs through the medium of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).

To the objection that even upon the cessation of those [states], consciousness shines forth as self-luminous during states such as dreaming, and thus there is no consequence of its being non-existent (*tucchatā*), he says: "And not... By the word *kevala*, the lack of a substratum (*nirāśrayatva*) is expressed. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the capacity... He establishes that very point with: "Even in those... He demonstrates the logical conclusion by way of contraposition (*viparyaya*): "And that does not exist... For the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) indeed establishes the absence of the pervaded (*vyāpya*). And memory is not the pervader of experience.

Therefore, he says "nanu" (but surely), meaning that the absence of that [recollection] does not prove the absence of experience; for the point is that one who is walking on a path does not remember the grass and such things they have touched, nor objects experienced in previous births. He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "ucyate" (it is said): distraction toward other objects and so forth are merely the causes of non-recollection.

The absence of a variety of objects, the lack of intent due to a lack of purpose, another intense experience at that time, and the non-repetition of the experience are well known as the causes for mere non-recollection; hence the word "restriction" (*niyama*) [is used], because of the expression "restriction of non-recollection. Since there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even what was experienced in another life could not be recollected, the phrase "all latent impressions" (*nikhila-saṃskāra*) is stated in order to exclude that possibility.

By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*) in the phrase “separation from the body and so forth,” the sufferings of hell, the calamities of childbirth, and long intervals of time are intended. As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: “Due to death, the afflictions of hell, and even the calamities of childbirth, [experiences] from previous births, having ceased long ago, come within the range of memory. It is the inherent nature of the separation from the body and such factors to cause the obliteration of all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, due to a specific merit that serves as an exception, a certain individual possesses the recollection of their past birth (*jātismara*).

The term *prabala* (powerful) refers to predominance in comparison with other factors such as distraction (*vyāsaṅga*). In the absence of the aforementioned sublaters, recollection occurs at some time or other; thus, its absence necessarily establishes the absence of experience—this is the meaning. He says "not only" (*na kevalam*) to show that there is not merely an absence of evidence for experience, but also another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that sublates it. The word "establishment" (*siddheḥ*) is to be construed with "the absence of experience. Now, he raises the objection that the rule of non-recollection might be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*). This is expressed by "if not" (*na cet*).

"The disappearance of the ego" means the disappearance of the notion of "I. He refutes this by saying "by another object," etc.; the meaning is that the non-perception of a jar and the destruction of a cloth are not observed to be the causes for the non-remembrance of a previously perceived wall or similar object. [Objection: Since a jar or the like is not a cause for the remembrance of a wall or the like, its absence cannot be the cause of such non-remembrance; however, in the present case, the absence of the cause of remembrance is indeed the cause of non-remembrance. [Reply: This is not so.

The term "another matter" (*arthāntara*) is employed with the intention that one must, even against one's will, admit that the knower and the known are no more causes for the recollection [of an object] than a wall or other such things are for the recollection of a jar. This is the meaning: if the causality of the knower and the known toward recollection is accepted because it is observed, then by the very fact of being observed, the causality of the knower and the known toward the [original] experience must also be accepted.

If it is argued that even though the knower and the known are perceived, their status as causes of experience is not admitted, then they would likewise not be causes in the case of memory; therefore, since those [causes] are absent, there is no absence of recollection—this objection is stated while accepting the non-existence of the "I-sense" (ahamartha). However, he says "even in those cases" (*tāsvapi*) because he will demonstrate that the non-existence of the "I-sense" is also not the case; the meaning is that [the reason] does not persist and does not manifest, and thus the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

It was previously stated that a qualified experience exists during states such as dreaming; taking this as his point of reference, the opponent objects with the intent of showing contradiction, beginning with "nanu" (but...). To this, [the author] replies: "Truly, it has been said. That, however, is the experience of the Self (*ātman*); the meaning is that it is not an experience of the act of experiencing (*anubhūti*). Regarding the objection that in the absence of an experience of the act of experiencing, that Self would be devoid of qualifications (*nirviśeṣa*), he says: "And that... The meaning is that it is characterized by immediacy (*pratyaktva*) and favorability (*anukūlatva*). To the question "What is being negated here?", he says: "But here..."

He raises an objection, suspecting that our own position has been accepted under a different terminology, by saying: "If it is argued that consciousness alone is experienced as the Self. This means: "In the experience of the Self," that is, during the state of experiencing the Self alone; the consciousness which you accept as eternal in states such as deep sleep—that, due to the absence of outward diffusion and the consequent lack of limitation by objects, would at that time be "consciousness alone," i.e., devoid of distinctions, exactly as we have described. He refutes this with: "And that [is not so]. That is, the consciousness which exists as an attribute (dharma).

The meaning is that it is either devoid of objects (*viṣaya*) or else it has a substratum (*sāśraya*). Alternatively, the meaning of the passage beginning with "merely" (*kevalā*) is as follows: if it is argued that consciousness (*saṃvit*), which consists of the self’s experience—that is, the manifestation of the self—is "merely" [that], meaning it is entirely devoid of specificities such as objects and so forth, as we have stated; [the author] refutes this with the words "And that" (*sā ceti*). That consciousness, which consists of the manifestation of the substrate (*dharmin*); that will be stated to "have a substratum. For manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) is indeed an attribute (*dharma*) of that which manifests.

The meaning is as follows: just as the brilliance (*aujjvalya*) of a lamp—the substratum (*dharmin*) which is the locus of light—is a property residing in that very substratum called "lamp," so it is here. The manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of knowledge, which constitutes the essential nature of the substratum (the Self), is eternal. And that [manifestation] is its being manifest (*bhāsamānatā*), which is its suitability for empirical transaction (*vyavahārānuguṇya*). The manifestation of knowledge, however, which is a property [of the Self], arises only at the time it is connected with an object, and not at any other time. For this very reason, it was stated previously: "at the time of the illumination of the object."

And this will be explained in the passage beginning with "as in the case of masculinity and so forth. However, in states such as deep sleep, its capacity for connection with all objects is obstructed, just like the burning power of fire; therefore, there is no manifestation at that time.

Now, having concluded the incidental discussion on the experience of the self (*ātman*), he concludes the proof of the previously introduced prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: because knowledge devoid of an object lacks epistemic validity; because the permanence of knowledge delimited by space and time is refuted by the aforementioned logical inconsistency; and because the means of apprehending prior non-existence has been established. [Objection: How can consciousness, being itself existent, prove its own prior non-existence?

Thus, by the mark of non-remembrance—namely, the reflection upon the state of deep sleep in the form "for such a length of time I was not cognizant of anything"—the absence of knowledge in general is apprehended; and since the prior absence (prāgabhāva) inherent within that [general absence] is also made an object by that very [reflection], the proof of prior absence is stated according to the *svataḥ* (intrinsic) position. He states that it is also established according to the *parataḥ* (extrinsic) position with the words "anubhūteḥ" (of experience). Now, he concludes the refutation of non-arising caused by the absence of prior absence with the words "tasmāt" (therefore).

Now, with the words "Even that which... and so forth, he refutes the rejection of other modifications on the grounds of non-origination. The rejection of other modifications is untenable because the reason consisting of non-origination is unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if that [non-origination] were accepted, he states that the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) by saying "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*). He explains this with the words "For of that... (*tasya hi*). Regarding the inclusion of the word "entities" (*bhāva*), even in its absence, he censures the inclusion of the word "entities" with the intention of showing that the inconclusiveness remains the same, saying "in entities" (*bhāveṣu*). This is not, however, stated as a refutation of a different proposition (*pratijñā*).

For that is a refutation of the statement (*ukti-dūṣaṇa*), not a refutation of the meaning (*artha-dūṣaṇa*). With the words "And thus" (*tathā ca*), he demonstrates the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the nature of being (*bhāvarūpatva*); by the word "thus," the nature of being is intended, because they have established [the existence of] ignorance (*ajñāna*) as having the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). There, he anticipates the rebuttal with the words "Its modifications" (*tadvikārāḥ*). He states the pointlessness of this qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) with the words "What do you [gain]? (*kiṃ bhavataḥ*), because there is no object to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) by this qualification. The meaning is: if there is an object to be excluded, then non-duality (*advaita*) is lost; if there is none, then the qualification is redundant.

Is it being proved that there is an absence of mere modification, or an absence of ultimate (paramārtha) modification? In the first case, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntya). In the second case, it would be stated that experience is devoid of ultimate modification because it is unborn; the counter-example (vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta) must then be stated as: "whatever possesses ultimate modification has arisen, just like a jar. Since the ultimate modification of a jar is not admitted [by the opponent], the example would be excluded from the probandum (sādhyavyāvṛtta), and thus the reason would suffer from the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi); this is the intended meaning.

Now, with the words "as for what was said," he addresses the refutation of the denial of difference based on the fact of being unborn (*ajatva*). Here, is it mere difference that is intended to be refuted? Or is it difference from a different class (*vijātīyabheda*)? Or is it difference within itself (*svagatabheda*)? Even though these positions have been rejected because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), [the author], while first refuting the first and second horns [of the argument] by assuming the reason to be established, demonstrates the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in a case accepted by all schools of thought other than the Cārvākas, using the words "even of the unborn" (*ajasyaiva*).

He states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the reason precisely at the point favored by the proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādī*) with the words "of ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*). For that text reads: "Since, like darkness and light, there is no possibility of mutual non-existence between two things of contradictory natures, and since, like darkness and light, there is no possibility of mutual existence between two things of contradictory natures. Having raised the doubt that this distinction is false, he refutes it by accepting it with the words "that distinction," etc. [The term] "bound to birth" (*janmapratibaddhaḥ*) means pervaded by production (*utpatti-vyāptaḥ*).

The meaning is that if one accepts that only ultimate division (*paramārthavibhāga*) is pervaded by origination in the case of jars and the like, it would follow that the division of jars and so forth must also be ultimately real; if that [division] were not ultimately real, the qualification [in the reason] would be redundant, and thus the aforementioned fault would indeed remain. When there is a desire to refute the logical reason (*hetu*), one should consider that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavyāvṛttatva*), which implies a failure to establish the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). For the negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) is: "Whatever has originated possesses ultimate division, just as a jar."

Since it is not admitted that a jar possesses ultimate division (*paramārthavibhāga*), its exclusion from the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛttatva*) is indeed clear. He states another refutation regarding the falsity of division with the words "of ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*). Now, he excludes the absence of difference among things of the same class (*sajātīya*) with the word "unsublated" (*abādhitā*). Previously, the difference between objects of perception (*dṛśyabheda*) was established by means of refuting the inference of falsity based on the impossibility of valid means of knowledge and their objects; the meaning is that, by the same logic, the difference between perceptions (*darśanabheda*) is also established.

Anticipating the objection that the distinction resides in the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) and not in the delimited object (*avacchedya*), as in the analogy of the space within a jar or a water-pot, he says: "Because of the difference in the objects to be cut. As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "Cognitions appear directly, each distinct from the others according to each individual subject and object, like pleasure, pain, and so forth. Indeed, it is not accepted that there is no intrinsic difference in things such as conjunction or desire—which have their distinctions manifested through their correlates—nor that such difference is imperceptible."

The meaning of the first section of the text is as follows: the distinction between cognitions is immediate (*aparokṣa*) with respect to each individual subject and object. The cognition of another’s knowledge appears as something remote (*parokṣa*), whereas one’s own cognition appears as immediate. Furthermore, the mutual difference among cognitions of objects such as jars and the like is itself immediate. Therefore, the denial of this distinction is contradicted by the direct perception of one’s own experience. To the objection that "all cognition is a single unity, appearing as distinct only due to differences in the relations defined by the forms of the knower and the known," he replies with the word "relation" (*sambandhi*).

The phrase "of the difference manifested by the relata" is a restatement of the seed of the objection. Nor can the difference of cognition be considered "caused by the difference of relata" merely because it is manifested by the relata in the form of the knower and the known; for that would make it adventitious (*aupādhika*), since even conjunction and other relations would then necessarily be one, like the space delimited by a jar or a water-pot, simply because they too are manifested by their relata. For a relatum is of two kinds: that which is the cause of existence and that which is the cause of manifestation.

For that which, such as conjunction and the like, has no means of valid cognition for its own nature apart from its relata, its relatum is the cause of its existence; but for that which [does] exist [independently], such as sound or space, its appearance as distinct is conditioned by those [relata], not intrinsic. Therefore, since cognition does not attain its existence apart from the knower and the known, its difference is indeed intrinsic. Thus, the meaning is that there is no denial of difference among things of the same class. With this in mind, it was said: "because of the difference between the object to be cut and the cutter."

Now, with the words "As for that which... and so forth, [the author] refutes the arguments put forward by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*)—who, for the sake of negating distinctions such as self-nature, eternality, and unity, has taken *anubhūti* (consciousness) as the subject and stated the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) "because it is consciousness," and who has taken the perceptible (*dṛśya*) as the subject and stated the positive inference (*anvayin*) "because it is perceptible"—by showing them to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). "Inconclusive" means "unrestricted"; the meaning is that they are devoid of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Regarding the positive inference "because it is perceptible," its lack of restriction consists in its occurrence across all three categories of the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).

The phrase "because of being the seer" (*dṛśitvāt*) refers merely to the lack of invariable concomitance (*aniyatatvamātra*), characterized by the non-exclusion of the probans even when the probandum is excluded from the negative instance (*vyatirekiṇaḥ sādhyavyāvṛttāvapi sādhanāvyāvṛtti*). The structure of the inference is as follows: "Experience does not possess the attributes of the seen, because it is the seer; for whatever possesses the attributes of the seen is not the seer, just like a jar. Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "possessing the attributes of the seen" by "not being the seer" is broken in the case of experience, because experience possesses attributes such as being the seer and being eternal; this is the intended meaning.

If [the properties] such as permanence were false, it would follow that their opposite forms—such as impermanence—would result; therefore, to avoid this consequence, the author raises the objection that they are merely the essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) of the substance and refutes it with the words "And not... and so forth. Anticipating the dilemma as to whether these [properties] are of the nature of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or of the nature of negative exclusion (*vyatireka*), the first alternative—that they are the essential nature by way of positive concomitance—is refuted as being the "head" (the primary position) to be rejected; this is not, however, because it is accepted by the opponent. He states the reason for this refutation: "Because of the difference in essential nature" (*svarūpabhedāt*).

The difference from their own nature (*svarūpa*) as well as their mutual difference is intended [to be stated]. By this, what was previously stated—namely, "because of the observation of disputes regarding the difference in modes"—is explained. He states the difference in nature between the state of being consciousness (*saṃvedanatva*) and self-luminosity (*svayamprakāśatva*) by means of the two sentences beginning with "by its own existence" (*svasattayā*). "Luminosity" (*prakāśana*) is that by which something is made manifest; the meaning is that it is that which brings about suitability for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). He states the meaning of the term "luminosity" (*prakāśa*), which is common to both, with the words "and luminosity" (*prakāśaśca*).

All objects, whether conscious or unconscious, are indeed conducive to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) only when knowledge is present among the causes for their usage. In that regard, the unconscious portion is conducive to usage by possessing a knowledge that is included within its own causal complex for usage. The same applies to the conscious portion when it is an object of cognition (*vedyatva*). However, in the case of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), there is an inclusion of the self within the causal complex for its own usage, without dependence on any other knowledge.

Alternatively, they say this: conformity with empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*) means being related to empirical usage, which is to say, "manifestation" (*prakāśa*). And that [manifestation] belongs to the cognition and the cognizer intrinsically (*svataḥ*), whereas for the object of cognition (*jñeya*), it is produced by the cognition. Therefore, even for a jar or other objects situated in front [of one], that very thing is their manifestation; it is not "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*). Even if one were to admit something distinct from that [manifestation], there would be no contradiction with the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition; for since that [cognition] is established independently of it, we do not admit that manifestness serves as an inferential mark (*liṅga*) for cognition.

Alternatively, he states the unique definition of light residing in knowledge as "consciousness and non-consciousness. Light is that which resides in knowledge and is common to all objects, both conscious and unconscious, and is conducive to the practical usage of the term "conscious"; the meaning is that light is that which is conducive to the practical usage of both self and other.

Now, it is undisputed that the insentient has the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*); and that [status] consists in its being manifest (*bhāsamānatva*). If the suitability for empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*) of the insentient were located in cognition, then the common expression "the jar is manifest" would be secondary (*amukhyatva*), because the manifestation residing in cognition is only metaphorically attributed (*upacarita*) to that which is related to it. Nor is the suitability for empirical usage of the jar and so forth simply the relation to cognition; for it is impossible to define cognition as having the nature of producing suitability for empirical usage.

Since a relation resides in two terms, even the jar standing before one would, by being a cause of that [cognition], possess the quality of being conducive to the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) consisting of the relation; thus, this conduciveness to linguistic usage would be common to both the cognition and the object. It is replied: The conduciveness to linguistic usage, in the form of being the object of linguistic usage, is indeed common [to both]. For that is simply the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratisambandhitva*) of linguistic usage. That itself is what it means to be "manifest" (*bhāsamānatva*). And the linguistic usage "the jar is manifest" is primary precisely because it is based upon that [state of being the counter-correlative].

The conformity to worldly usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*), which consists in being the cause for the status of being related to worldly usage, belongs to cognition alone. In that regard, the conformity to worldly usage—consisting in being the cause for the status of being related to worldly usage with respect to one's own status as a correlate of worldly usage characterized by immediacy, favorability, and unity—belongs to cognition itself, which constitutes the nature of the knower. This applies to the substrate of the forms such as one's own nature, its inherent unity, and favorability toward externality, as well as to the relation between that [cognition] and its own object, and to the relation between that [cognition] and its object, all of which possess the status of being correlates of worldly usage.

However, the capacity for causal operation consistent with linguistic usage belongs only to knowledge as an attribute (dharma). Therefore, it is logical that the characteristic of illumination unique to knowledge is its capacity for both self-referential and other-referential linguistic usage.

Now, he states its eternity with the words "all," etc. Although the previously mentioned definition of eternity—being unconditioned by time—and the well-known definition of eternity as being existent and causeless apply here, nevertheless, because consciousness is distinct from time, the eternity of an object distinct from time is pervaded by a connection with the entirety of time. Therefore, in order to establish that [consciousness] possesses specific qualities, the definition of the eternity of an object distinct from time is stated here.

He states "of those" (*teṣām*) to show that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntyam*) even if phenomena (*dharmāṇām*) are of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpatve*). He states the refutation regarding the case where [non-existences] are not distinct from their own nature (*svarūpa*), saying "but in the case of consciousness" (*saṃvidi tu*). By the word "but" (*tu*), he intends to express the difference from the previously mentioned examples such as whiteness (*śauklya*). Because it [consciousness], as a property of something, brings about its own and others' establishment (*svaparanirvāhakatvāt*), and because it opposes error once its own nature is realized, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is indeed the very nature itself.

Since no one accepts that Brahman possesses the nature of a property (*dharma*), and because even when its own nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended, it remains susceptible to error—just like a white, shining fragment situated before one—it is not the case that the nature itself is the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). As for the words "existence" (*asti*) and such terms as "eternal," "self-luminous," and so forth applied to consciousness (*saṃvit*): do they have an additional referent (*adhikārtha*) or no additional referent? If they have an additional referent, there is the presence of distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*); otherwise, other words would be redundant, since the mere nature [of consciousness] is undisputed.
Furthermore, by means of reasons proving eternality and so forth, is mere consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) being established, or something distinct from it?

In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*); in the second, there is the presence of qualification (*saviśeṣatva*). Thus, the intended meaning is that the employment of terms in grammatical apposition is untenable, and that the reasons (*hetu*) proving eternality and so forth result in the fallacy of proving the already established (*siddhasādhana*). As it is said in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "That which was previously stated—that the object of cognition cannot be an attribute of consciousness—by that [statement] too, has something been proved regarding consciousness by you, or not? If it exists, there would be partiality [on your part]; if it does not, your labor is in vain."

If one does not admit a mutual difference between properties such as eternity and so forth, then it would suffice to establish only a single property; no other property need be established, because it would not exceed what was already established previously. For once eternity has been established, the non-limitation by time does not remain as something further to be established. Thus, both the distinction of eternity and the other properties from their own essential nature and their mutual distinction from one another are proven.

By means of establishing that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is devoid of differentiation through another [means], its status as the Self (*ātmatva*) has been affirmed. Here, by means of refuting its lack of differentiation, he begins to refute the status of consciousness as the Self with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*), and so forth. In that context, he offers a dilemma in order to establish that it possesses specific attributes: "Does consciousness exist or not?"—the meaning of which is: "Is it perceived or unperceived? He first refutes the first horn of the dilemma with the words "If it exists," and so forth.

The meaning is that it has been established previously that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have as their object only that which possesses specific qualities (*saviśeṣa*). Alternatively, an entity that is being established must possess specific qualities by virtue of being the locus of its own establishment; "establishment" (*siddhi*) means manifestation (*prakāśa*), the sense being that it must be endowed with properties conducive to practical transaction (*vyavahāra*). To avoid the faults incurred regarding the two horns of the dilemma, he raises the objection stated by the opponent: "Establishment itself... [is the object].

Since a proof (*siddhi*) does not depend on another proof, it would lack the "possession of attributes" (*saviśeṣatva*) consisting in being related to a proof, which is necessitated by being an object of valid cognition (*pramiti*). Even so, it would not be a non-entity (*tucchatva*); for the point is that a rabbit’s horn is not of the nature of a proof. To this, he states its possession of attributes: "Of what? (*kasya*). If it is a cognition (*pratīti*), it must belong to some substratum with respect to some object; therefore, both of those [the substratum and the object] must be specified—this is the meaning. He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) regarding the opposite case: "If... (*yadi*).

He explains this with the words "siddhirhi" (for accomplishment...). The object (*viṣaya*) stands in the place of the father; the substratum (*āśraya*) stands in the place of the son; and accomplishment (*siddhi*) stands in the place of sonship. For the son is indeed the substratum of sonship. Regarding the statement "of someone," he raises an objection to reject the dependence on a knower (*jñātṛ*) with the words "if it be said 'of the self' (*ātmanaḥ*). The meaning is "with reference to the self. The word "self" (*ātman*) denotes one's own [nature]. By this, the state of being the inner subject (*pratyaktva*) is established. For the self, which is the counter-correlative of accomplishment, is indeed the inner subject.

For it will be stated that "selfhood" (*pratyaktva*) consists in being manifest to oneself. With the intention that this [definition] is untenable in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), he asks: "What is this Self? The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to that which stands in a correlative relation to establishment (*siddhi*). [The question means: "What is the Self that stands in a correlative relation to establishment? The word "what" (*kim*) is used in a derogatory sense. Consciousness is not the Self that stands in a correlative relation to establishment; the meaning is that what was previously stated regarding consciousness is untenable. He raises an objection, saying "But surely," on the grounds that it is not untenable because the identity of consciousness with the Self has already been established.

He sets aside [the objection] by saying, "It has been said truly. He begins to demonstrate that the doctrine of consciousness as the self (*saṃvid-ātmatva*) is poorly stated by means of refuting that very doctrine, starting with the words "For thus" (*tathā hi*). The mention of "action" (*karman*) is for the sake of providing an illustration. By the phrase "the aggregate of objects" (*arthajāta*), the intended meaning is that the object of valid cognition (*pramiti*) is indeed a collection consisting of both attributes (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). "Of the nature of accomplishment" (*siddhirūpā*) means of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśarūpā*); therefore, it is related to both of those. The question "How? means: how can consciousness, which is an attribute of the self, be the self itself?

For what purpose is the word *siddhi* used here, given that it is common to both origination (*utpatti*) and manifestation (*jñapti*)? If illumination (*prakāśa*) is intended here, what is its nature? What is the proof for its relationship as object and agent? For while functional cognition (*vṟttijñāna*) possesses both an object and an agent, pure consciousness (*saṃvit*) is absolute. In response to the doubt as to what the result is in this mention of an object, he says: "This is what is meant. By the term "experience" (*anubhūti*), the focus on manifestation is expressed.

By the statement, "its nature is that which, with respect to its own locus, brings about suitability for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) toward some object by its very existence," its essential form (*svarūpa*) has been stated. In this way, the meaning of the word *siddhi* (accomplishment) has been explained. By the phrase, "having other names such as knowledge (*jñāna*), comprehension (*avagati*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*)," it is established that since the words *jñāna* and *saṃvit* are synonyms, there is no evidence for any distinction between the function-knowledge (*vṛtti-jñāna*) and consciousness (*saṃvit*).

By the passage beginning with "I know the jar" and ending with "is well-known through the witness of the self," it is stated that the relationship between object and agent is established by one's own experience, and that the terms *jñāna* (knowledge) and *saṃvit* (consciousness) are synonyms. Therein, its establishment through one's own experience was mentioned, and the synonymy of the words *jñāna* and *saṃvit* was demonstrated. He states the opponent's acceptance of this relationship between object and agent with the words: "by its very nature."

The point is this: by one who establishes the self-luminosity (*svayamprakāśatva*) of the self, the self-luminosity of knowledge characterized by the relationship between object and agent is also established; therefore, the position that objective knowledge is insentient (*jaḍa*), distinct from the knowledge that constitutes the self, and is of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is untenable. By the words "of this" (*asya*) and so forth, the purpose of specifying the object is demonstrated. Now, one might object: "We do not accept that consciousness (*saṃvit*) possesses agency; so how can this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) arise? It is replied:
By asserting that consciousness is the self, its character as the subject (*pratyaktva*) must necessarily be admitted.

Since inwardness belongs only to the substratum of cognition, the subjectivity of consciousness is unavoidable; and that [subjectivity] is difficult to establish—this is the meaning. Agency is the state of being a substratum; for an agent is indeed the substratum of the meaning of a verbal root.

Thus, the nature of the self as consciousness has been refuted by means of its dependence upon the states of being a dharma and a non-dharma. Now, that [nature] is further excluded by means of the difference between permanence and impermanence. The word "tathā" (thus) indicates a reason (*hetu*); by the particle "ca" (and), another reason is stated. He establishes the permanence of the agent with the words: "First, the permanence of the agent... For the permanence of jars and other objects is established because they are recognized through repeated cognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

In the same way, at the time of the recognition of a jar, because the agent is also the object of recognition—as in "it was previously experienced by me"—the permanence [of the self] is established; this is the meaning. Now, he demonstrates the arising, duration, and cessation of cognition with the words beginning with "I" (*aham*). By the expression "I know," its arising and duration are established. By "I knew," there is the perception of its pastness. To clarify this, and to indicate the reflection upon the knower as being qualified by the cognitions produced in the immediately preceding moments, the word "mine" (*mama*) is used specifically for the knower.

Regarding the phrase "origination and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes persistence and cessation. The origination of consciousness is its connection with the first moment of that [consciousness] which lasts for three or four moments; its persistence is its relation to subsequent moments. Because consciousness is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), these two [origination and persistence] are perceptible. The cessation of the cognition of a jar is the cognition of a cloth, and that too is perceptible. The particle *iti* is used in the sense of a reason. The meaning is that there is no identity between them due to their difference in nature regarding stability and instability.

Thus, the stability of the self has been established by its being the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Now, its stability is stated "in this way" by virtue of its being the substratum of recognition. In the previous case, it was said that [stability] is established through the perception of recognition; here, it is said that recognition is not possible. The intention is as follows: in cases such as a flame, where recognition occurs as its object, if there is any possibility of an alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*), then stability is not established.

In this context, although the objecthood of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) may be established otherwise, the fact that [the self] is the substratum of recognition is not so established; thus, even in the case of a recognition that is illusory in nature, the stability of its substratum remains unestablished by any other means. Therefore, the stability resulting from being the substratum of recognition is unshakable. He explains this stability through its being the substratum of recognition with the words "by another," etc.

Thus, because a stable cognizer is perceived as having both the nature of a dharma and instability, and because the impossibility of recognition (*pratisandhāna*) follows from that instability, the identity of consciousness with the self (*saṃvidātmatva*) has been refuted. Now, [the author] sets aside its being the self even by accepting its stability, stating "furthermore" (*kiñca*). The phrase "even if it were eternal" refers to the acceptance of the eternity of consciousness as a necessary consequence of accepting its identity with the self. This is the meaning.

The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that consciousness cannot logically be the self not only on the position that it is impermanent, but also on the position that it is permanent. For it is the self that performs recognition (*pratisaṃdhatte*); the meaning here is that recognition is not possible [in the case of consciousness]. He demonstrates the impossibility of that [recognition] with the words "recognition. He provides an example of it with "I am," etc. To the doubt as to what follows from this, he states that this is undesirable to the opponent with the words "for you," etc.

It is not merely that you do not accept it; rather, with the intention of showing that the experience itself being the experiencer is untenable—just as the act of going cannot be the goer—it is said: "the experience" (*anubhūti*). By the suffix *-mātra*, the status of being an experiencer is excluded. Now, as for what was stated—that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not the Self because of its being a property (*dharma*), its instability, and its lack of recollection (*apratisandhātṛtva*)—that need not be addressed, since we do not admit that the state of being an experiencer constitutes the form of the Self.

Because consciousness (*saṃvit*), being devoid of objects and substrata, lacks the status of being a quality (*guṇa*), there is no possibility of it undergoing impermanence—which would follow from its connection with those two; regarding this, he says: "Consciousness, indeed... [and so on]. Now, one might ask: how can there be an absence of knowledge that is devoid of objects and substrata? For in your own view, knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the self (*svarūpa*) is indeed devoid of objects and substrata. It is replied: This objection is quite substantial.

Do you intend to prove that for the *jñātṛ* (the knower) alone—denoted by the term "knowledge"—there exist qualities such as non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) and eternity (*nityatva*), its being devoid of object and locus, and its being the Self (*ātmatva*)? If so, that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, on the other hand, you mean [to prove these for] knowledge distinct from the knower, then we say that knowledge distinct from the knower and devoid of object and locus is empty (*śūnya*). The meaning is that knowledge apart from this triad—the knower, the known, and the nature of knowledge delimited by them—is refuted by non-apprehension (*anupalambha*).

The Buddhist partialists (bauddhaikadeśin), on the grounds of the principle of parsimony (*lāghavanyāya*)—that it is better to postulate a property (*dharma*) than to postulate a substratum possessing that property (*dharmin*)—have stated that consciousness (*saṃvit*) alone is the self (*ātman*), as this is agreed upon by both those who maintain the self is the knower (*jñātr-ātmavādin*) and those who maintain the self is knowledge (*jñāna-ātmavādin*). Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "both" (*ubhaya*). The principle of parsimony applies only to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); it does not apply to perception (*upalabdhi*). Otherwise, for the sake of extreme parsimony, one would have to abandon even knowledge itself in accordance with the Madhyamaka school. However, the principle of parsimony applies only in the realm of conceptual construction.

If it is argued that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is perceived, then the knower (*jñātṛ*) is likewise perceived. Therefore, the meaning is that because it is contradicted by perception, the identity of consciousness with the Self (*ātman*) is untenable; for consciousness is always perceived as having a substratum (*sāśraya*). To this, he replies: "It is mere experience" (*anubhūtimātra*). Alternatively, suspecting that it might have been stated that consciousness alone is the Self because it is accepted by both parties as being ultimately real, he refutes this with the word "both. [The view] is contradicted by perception. *Pratyak*...

The meaning is that the nature of the self, characterized by "thou-ness" (objectivity), is contradicted by the perception of it as being in grammatical apposition with the state of being a knower—as in "I know. It has been stated that the status of the inner self belonging to the knower alone is established by perception. Anticipating the objection that this perception might be sublated by arguments proving that the self is a featureless consciousness, he says: "It is mere experience."

The Self (*ātman*) is indeed the inward-facing object (*pratyagartha*). Its inward-facing nature (*pratyaktva*) is not established if it is taken as the object of the "I" (*ahamartha*); rather, it will be established only on the view that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the Self. Thus he raises an objection with the words, "Now, [if]... (*nanu ca*). In the cognition "I know," which is accepted by others as being the cognition of the "I" (*asmatpratyaya*), that which is the non-objective aspect (*acityadārtha*) is the Self. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it is the non-'this' part" (*anidamaṃśa*). This means the inward-facing object is distinct from the "this"-part, that is, distinct from the objective world (*parāgartha*). This statement contains a reason within itself (*hetugarbha*).

The meaning is "because it has the nature of being inward" (*pratyag-arthatvāt*). To the question "And from where does this inwardness come?", he says: "Of that which is solely light" (*prakāśaikasya*). The meaning is "because it is self-luminous" (*svayamprakāśatvāt*). The word *cit* (consciousness) is intended as a reason; the meaning is that because it is consciousness (*jñānatvāt*), it is self-luminous. Inwardness is the state of shining for itself. Self-luminosity is the state of having a manifestation that does not depend on anything else. However, the referent of "I" (*aham-artha*) is characterized by the referent of "you" (*yuṣmad-artha*). Because it is characterized by the referent of "you," the meaning is that the referent of "I" is a particular instance of the outward-referent (*parāg-artha*).

To the question, "Why is it that the nature of being the object of 'you' (yuṣmad-artha) [belongs to the ego-sense]? he says: "Because of its being illumined by that" (*tad-bala-nirbhāsitatvāt*). This means because its manifestation is dependent upon cognition (*jñāna*), and that [dependence] is due to its being distinct from pure consciousness (*cin-mātra*). In this passage of objection, three negative concomitants (*vyatireka*) regarding the self-nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-ātmatva*) and three positive concomitants (*anvaya*) regarding the non-self-nature of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha-anātmatva*) are intended. Among these, the negative example for the negative concomitants and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) for the positive concomitants are indicated by the term "the object of 'you'" (*yuṣmad-artha*). [The argument is: Experience (*anubhūti*) is the self, because it is immediate (*pratyaktvāt*).

That which is not the self (anātman) is not inward (apratyak); for example, a jar. Experience (anubhūti) is inward because it is self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśatva). That which is not inward is not self-luminous, like a jar. Experience is self-luminous because it is experience. That which is not self-luminous (established by itself) is not experience, like a jar—this constitutes the threefold negative inference (vyatirekitraya). The referent "I" (ahamartha) has its manifestation dependent upon knowledge (jñāna), because it is distinct from consciousness (cid-vyatirikta), like a jar.

"The object denoted by 'I' (ahamartha) is external because its manifestation depends upon knowledge, like a jar; the object denoted by 'I' is not the Self because it is external, like a jar"—this is the threefold positive concomitance (*anvaya*). In the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), self-luminosity (*svayamprakāśatva*) was previously stated as the direct reason for consciousness being the Self; here, however, subjectivity (*pratyaktva*) is established by that [self-luminosity], and by means of that, its status as the Self is established. He refutes this with the words "This is not so. The self-luminosity of consciousness is accepted, and the objection to be addressed has already been addressed.

Therefore, the reason proving that [the Self] is self-established results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Furthermore, it will be explained later that the reason proving that the knower is not self-established—namely, its being other than consciousness (*cit*)—is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Here, the other four inferences are refuted.

Regarding the alternatives—whether the nature of consciousness as the Self is accepted based on perception, or because the establishment of self-luminosity (pratyaktva) is otherwise untenable, or through the presumptive implication of scripture (śrutyarthāpatti), or from the natural force of the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras—the author states, "I know," pointing out the contradiction with perceptual experience in the case of the first alternative.
