Alternatively, *prasara* refers to the expanded portion; thus, the meaning is that rising and setting are the expansion and contraction of that [portion]. To the objection that if contraction and expansion were admitted, the [Self] would possess the nature of modification (*vikriyā*), he replies: "But in the case of the expansion of knowledge. The meaning is that such a nature of modification is accepted because it is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that transformation (*pariṇāma*) like that of an insentient object is not admitted. By this, the scope of the scriptural texts concerning immutability (*avikāra*) has been shown. Furthermore, he demonstrates another way of reconciling the scriptural texts concerning immutability with the phrase "And that" (*tac ca*). The meaning is that the texts concerning immutability are intended to negate natural (intrinsic) modification. To the question "What is its natural form?", he says: "Unchanging" (*avikriya*). "Own nature" (*svarūpa*) means the natural form. The meaning is that the statements regarding immutability refer to the natural form as liberated from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Regarding the claim that the agency of expansion also belongs only to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) because it is of the nature of a modification, he says: "consisting of such a modification. By the word "such" (*evaṃrūpa*), what is intended is the state of being subject to modification characterized by the agency of the expansion of knowledge, which is its own inherent attribute (*svadharma*). [The term] "whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpa*) means that for whom knowledge alone is the natural attribute; that is, one whose very essence is knowledge.

The meaning is this: the modification characterized by being the agent of the expansion of knowledge—which constitutes its own specific property (svadharma)—is possible only for the Self (ātman) which possesses that property, and not for the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), because it is insentient (jaḍatva) and thus does not possess that property. In this way, the objection that the nature of being a knower cannot be a property of the Self because it is of the nature of a modification has been refuted.

Now, he refutes the ways proposed by others for establishing the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). There are three positions: that being a knower is caused by the falling of a reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyāpatti*), caused by contact with consciousness (*citsaṃparka*), or caused by being a manifestor of consciousness (*cidabhivyañjakatva*). Among these, he first raises the doubt regarding the position of the "falling of a reflection of consciousness" with the word "insentient" (*jaḍa*). He refutes it with the question "What is this? (*keyam iti*). The meaning is: "What is this [reflection] that is so difficult to define? He analyzes the term with the question "What [is it]? (*kim iti*). The intention is to consider whether the case-ending within the compound *cicchāyā* is the genitive or the locative.

Regarding "the consciousness having fallen into the shadow of the ego" (ahaṅkāracchāyāpatti): the meaning is that the shadow of the knowerhood residing in consciousness has fallen upon the ego. Regarding "the ego having fallen into the shadow of consciousness" (saṃvicchāyāpatti): the meaning is that the shadow of the knowerhood residing in the ego has fallen upon consciousness. He refutes the first [position] with "not, for one," and he rejects the other alternative with "nor."

Having previously intended to exclude the status of the *ahaṅkāra* as a knower by means of its lack of consciousness (*acetanatva*), its being a transformation of *prakṛti*, and so forth, he says, "in the manner stated. He states another refutation with the words, "of both as well. He explains that with the words, "for not... He raises an objection to refute the contact with consciousness (*citsaṃparka*) with the word, "now (*atha*). He refutes this by means of the same alternatives as before with the words, "this is not so (*na etat*). This is a general proposition. He rejects the status of the knower in the *ahaṅkāra* due to its contact with consciousness, [stating] "in consciousness... (*saṃvidi*).

The phrase "of the ego" (*ahaṅkārasya tu*) indicates that contact with the ego vitiates the consciousness's status as a knower. The word "all the more" (*sutarām*) implies that since knowledge is non-inert, its being the substratum of knowledge is impossible according to our own view. Because the ego is inert, its actual status as the substratum of knowledge is impossible for both our own position and the opponent's; thus, the point is that the consciousness does not possess the status of a knower through contact with it. It is observed, for instance, that wood and other materials brought from a salt-lake acquire the quality of saltiness through contact with salt.

Heat is perceived in a mass of iron due to contact with fire; therefore, "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*) or its perception has been stated separately. Now, one might ask: "In the two positions mentioned previously, the reflection (*chāyāpatti*) and contact (*samparka*) of knowership were rejected. Why are the reflection and contact of cognition (*jñāna*) not likewise rejected? We reply: because they are included within the alternative position of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) which will be explained hereafter. What is called the "reflection" of cognition in the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is its manifestation as being supported by it, just as a face is manifested in a mirror.

Even in the case of contact (*saṃparka*), contact as the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not conducive to the perception of the knower; therefore, contact must be stated as being that which is superposed (*ādheya*). And that [superposition] is included within manifestation by way of residing therein (*tatsthatayā*); for this reason, it was not mentioned there [in the previous section]. Furthermore, the "falling of a reflection" (*chāyāpatti*) is refuted precisely because consciousness is not visible to the eye. Moreover, since contact must be stated in accordance with its similarity to the object of comparison, it must be stated as the relationship between an attribute and its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) in a state of non-separation (*apṛthaksiddha*); and that is not tenable.

This is because such a relationship of attribute and substratum is impossible between the insentient and the sentient; furthermore, since knowledge and the knower are never observed to exist separately—unlike a staff and Devadatta—their contact while remaining non-separate is logically untenable, as one should reflect. Now, in order to state the position of manifestation (*abhivyakti*), he demonstrates the mutual distinction of the position of manifestation from the positions of reflection (*chāyāpatti*) and contact (*samparka*) with the words "in both cases. He says "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*).

What is intended [by the author] is that [the self] is established even prior to the superimposition (adhyāsa) being produced by reflection (chāyāpatti) and so forth; it is not, however, its ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva). This is because a reflection is observed even in the case of a fire-brand wheel (alātacakra) and the like, and because heat is perceived even in water that is not hot due to contact with hot water. In the first two positions, the negation of the knowerhood [of the Self] in the other case results from the superimposition of a previously established knowerhood in one instance.

However, in the view that [consciousness] is manifested (*abhivyakti*), there is a disparity: the establishment of the self’s status as a knower occurs through the superimposition of knowledge (*jñānādhyāsa*) without depending on its prior existence. He states the view of manifestation with the words, "But the *ahaṅkāra*... He refutes it with "that is improper. When the question arises as to why this is so, he says "of the Self," etc., indicating that the Self has no need for a manifestor, nor does the *ahaṅkāra* possess the power to manifest it. To show that his own position is based on tradition and to clarify it by means of an illustration, he cites the *Ātmasiddhi* text with the words, "it has been said."

He explains the verse beginning with "śāntāṅgāra" himself. By the term "self-luminous" (*svayamprakāśa*), the absence of dependence on a manifestor is stated. By the phrase "whose establishment depends upon experience," the absence of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as a manifestor is stated. By the phrase "the insentient ego-sense," the opponent's reason—that [the Self] has its luminosity dependent on that [ego] because it is distinct from pure consciousness—is indicated. [The Self is] of a nature whose luminosity neither rises nor sets. If it were at any time non-luminous, then there would be a dependence on a manifestor.

The meaning is that, because of its absence, there is never any dependence upon a manifestor (*vyañjaka*). The sense is: "It is the cause for the accomplishment of all objects; for you yourself have established self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) by means of [the self] being the illuminator of objects. Regarding the phrase "they laugh": the meaning is that those very people of yours, standing right near you, laugh at the thought that such an ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) manifests such an experience.

The refutation was stated on the grounds that the non-acceptance [of the theory] of ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) and experience being the manifestor and the manifested leads to a fault. Now, even if it were granted that these two possess the nature of being the manifestor and the manifested, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) to show that this is not logically tenable between them. The contradiction arises from the opposition of their intrinsic natures: namely, that experience is the cause for the establishment of all objects, while this ego-consciousness, being distinct from it, has its own establishment dependent upon that very experience.

Just as, although fatherhood and sonship exist between a father and a son with respect to one another, a mutual reversal of fatherhood and sonship is not possible; so too, although the relationship of manifester and manifested may exist between those two in relation to something else, it is not possible for them to stand in such a relationship to each other—this is the meaning. He states another objection: "And because it would follow that experience itself would be non-experiential."

Regarding this point as well, he cites the *Ātmasiddhi* text with the words "as it has been said. The term *pratikūlya* (contrariety) is explained by the previously mentioned term *svabhāvavirodha* (contradiction of nature). Regarding the objection that a thing cannot be the manifestor of that which it itself manifests, he says "not so," intending to refute the example cited by the opponent. He states that the example lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) with the words "even there," and demonstrates that the same status [of being a manifestor] holds true for that case as well through an alternative proof.

The meaning is that "karatala" (the palm of the hand) is not a substance whose nature is the expansion of Brahman; therefore, it is untenable for the ego (ahaṅkāra) to be the cause of its abundance. Likewise, having proposed three alternatives regarding its manifestation by the ego, he refutes them with the words beginning with "kiñca" (furthermore). The word "kim" (what) has the sense of censure; the meaning is that [its nature] is difficult to define.

In response to the inquiry "Why [is this so]?", three alternatives are considered—namely, whether manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is (1) production (*utpatti*), (2) illumination (*prakāśana*), or (3) the assistance of the means of experience (*anubhavasādhanānugraha*)—and the position of production is first refuted with the words "Not, firstly... (*na tāvad iti*). Since the manifestation of an unproduced object such as a jar is impossible, and since even the producer—the staff, the wheel, and so forth—is a cause of manifestation only by way of producing [the jar], the alternative of production has been included among the options. Furthermore, manifestation is the production of the illumination of the manifested object (*vyaṅgyaprakāśotpādana*).

Since consciousness itself is of the nature of luminosity, the very arising of that [consciousness] is the manifestation consisting of the arising of its own luminosity; thus, the inclusion of "arising" is for the sake of the conceptual alternative. Regarding the phrase "by way of being self-established": this is because the absence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) has already been stated, or else it means "because it is beginningless. Now, he rejects the second [alternative] with the words "nor also. Luminosity is the arising of the manifestation of the object of experience.

Now he offers a reply to the third [objection] with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*). That is, precisely because manifestation would otherwise be impossible. [Objection: But then the introduction of the subsequent passage is inappropriate, since the twofold nature of the favorer (*anugrāhaka*) is useless for refuting that [position]. Furthermore, the citation of the *Ātmasiddhi* text from later on is not consistent; for since it expresses a lack of connection with the sense organs, it is of no use for establishing the twofold nature of favoring. To this it is replied:

Previously, by examining the experience of the light produced in the object to be assisted, the assistance to the means of that experience was refuted. Now, he states the refutation by examining the specific modes of that assistance, beginning with "For that [assistance]... To show the impossibility of both types [of assistance], he first states the twofold nature [of the object] with the words "Of the knowable... The statement that tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth assist the scripture is according to the view of others; for that [tranquility, etc. assists meditative cultivation (*upāsanā*). [Objection: But it is improper to say "For that [assistance] is twofold";

Since assistance (*anugraha*) exists in both categories as something infinite, [one might argue] that inference and the like also possess assistance in the form of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāptigraha*) and so forth. To this it is replied: there are only two categories, namely, assistance to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and assistance to the agent (*kartṛ*). Even the apprehension of pervasion is included within the assistance to the instrument. Alternatively, assistance is twofold: by way of the seen (*dṛṣṭamukhena*) and by way of the unseen (*adṛṣṭamukhena*). The apprehension of pervasion is also assistance by way of the seen.

Therefore, the phrase "by way of being the cause of the connection with the sense organs" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of both the assistance to the instrument and the assistance by means of a visible effect. In that context, it is stated "by way of being the cause of the connection with the sense organs" because consciousness, which is manifested by the *ahaṅkāra*, cannot possibly be an object of inference. By the phrase "by removing the impurities residing in the knower," the assistance to the agent and the assistance by means of an invisible effect (*adṛṣṭa-mukha*) are indicated. This same point is also expressed in the *Ātmasiddhi* treatise.

Thus, by showing this twofold nature, the connection is made with the implication that even though grace (*anugraha*) is divided into two types, it cannot be properly stated [as belonging to the ego-sense]. In response to the doubt as to how grace, even in its two forms, is untenable here, he cites the *Ātmasiddhi* text, saying "as has been said. By the statement, "Because the instruments (*karaṇa*) are not the ground [of experience], they cannot be the cause of that [grace]," it is shown that grace characterized as being a cause is untenable. However, the untenability of grace characterized as the removal of the impurities residing in the knower (*boddhṛ*) is not addressed in that specific passage of the text.

On this point, some teachers explain as follows: "The fact that tranquility (*śama*) and the like are supportive is established by the scriptures, whereas the fact that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is supportive is not so established; therefore, because this is obvious, it was not explicitly refuted in the text. By means of the example in the first half [of the verse], it should be understood that the second half of the verse demonstrates the impossibility of the support characterized by the removal of the impurities residing in the knower (*boddhṛ*). Thus, this second half [states]: 'Since the object of the "I" is the knower, it cannot be purified by that very same [ego-sense].'"* *This passage refers to the *Vivaraṇa* on the *Pañcapādikā*, which comments on the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*. It addresses the objection that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) might be the support for the mind's purification, similar to how tranquility (*śama*) is a support for meditation. The author argues that while tranquility is scripturally established as a support, the ego-sense is not; hence, its status as a support is not even mentioned in the text for the sake of brevity. Furthermore, since the ego-sense is itself the locus of the impurities to be removed, it cannot logically act as its own purifier. The second half of the verse thus serves to refute this possibility by showing the logical inconsistency of the knower being purified by that which constitutes its own substrate of ignorance.*

The meaning is that it is logically untenable for a single entity to be both the object to be purified (*śodhya*) and the purifier (*śodhaka*) by virtue of its own counter-correlativity (*svapratiyogitā*). This, however, is the intention of the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): Is the agency of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) in the removal of the impurities residing in the knower (*boddhṛ*) due to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), or is it through the mediation of some unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction between the object and the agent, because it is impossible for one and the same thing to be both the object to be purified and the purifier in relation to itself. In the second case, there is a lack of evidence; for there is no proof that the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) occurs through the power of the unseen merit of the internal organ itself.

Previously, a refutation was stated on the grounds that [the universal] is not admitted to be within the range of the senses; now, he states a refutation by admitting its being an object of experience, beginning with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). He teaches the nature of favor (*anugraha*) with the words "For... (*sa hi*). [Objection: Even though other modes of favor are observed in the case of a manifestation (*vyakti*), a mirror, and so forth, why is favor restricted exclusively to the form of the removal of obstructions? [Reply: It is said: because of the fixed relationship of attribute and substrate between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), the individual is the manifester (*vyañjikā*) of the genus.

In that way, there is no fixed relationship of substrate and attribute between the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the experience [of reflection]; indeed, that [notion] has already been refuted by another [author]. A mirror, being a material substance, causes the obstruction of visual rays and connects them with the face via its own material surface; however, the ego is not a material substance nor is it a cause of obstruction for anything. With the intention of showing that other modes of assistance will be untenable as will be explained later, only assistance in the form of the removal of obstacles remains as a possibility here.

He provides an illustration for such a favor with the words "just as color-form and so forth. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "And not here. He explains that [point] with the words "Not, first of all... The word "first of all" (*tāvat*) is employed with the intention of referring to the three horns of the dilemma: whether ignorance (*ajñāna*) consists of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), or whether it is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), or whether something else is being stated as the object of negation. By the passage beginning with "Not, first of all," the third alternative—that which is to be negated as something else—is refuted.

Alternatively, intending to show that both [theories]—that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is the remover of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and that ignorance is related to consciousness (*saṃvit*)—are untenable, he first refutes the idea that ignorance is removable by the ego-sense, stating "Not, firstly... He raises the objection that there indeed exists an ignorance removable by the ego-sense, saying "For it exists..."; he then refutes this, saying "No. The word "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is common to both positive entities and negative absences; the refutation, too, is common to both.

Since neither kind of ignorance lacks the quality of being removable by the realization of the "I" (ahaṅkāra), he states "for it is knowledge alone" to address what the remover is. The arising of knowledge is the remover even of antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva); furthermore, that even positive ignorance (bhāvarūpa) is removable by knowledge is accepted by the opponent as well.

Thus, it has been stated that even if ignorance were to have consciousness as its locus (*saṃvidāśrayatva*), a favor consisting in its removal would be impossible, because it could not be dispelled by the "I-maker" (*ahaṅkāra*). Now, he says "nor" (*na ca*) to show that ignorance having consciousness as its locus is also untenable. "Having consciousness as its locus" means "having a relation with consciousness. "Locus" (*āśraya*) signifies a relation. And since a relation can be of two kinds—as an object (*karman*) or as a substratum (*āśraya*)—the word "locus" here refers to both types of relation.

Because of such usages as “Brahman is the substratum (āśraya) of consciousness,” it is appropriate that the word *āśraya* also brings to mind the object (*viṣaya*). The meaning is that the relation of ignorance to consciousness—whether by way of being its substratum or by way of being its object—is untenable in either case. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of knowledge... To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "...the state of being a knower... [The phrase] "in the Witness" means that the status of being a Witness belongs only to the Seer; the intention is that even the status of being a Witness is contradicted for consciousness itself (*jñapti*).

By the statement "it ought to be so," only a mere relation—either as a substratum (*āśrayatā*) or as an object (*viṣayatā*)—is intended. By this, the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is demonstrated. He shows the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) in the absence of being the substratum of consciousness with the words "as follows" (*yathā*). For being the substratum of ignorance means either being the substratum of the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge, or being the substratum of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*). The meaning is that this [status] does not exist in things such as a jar. [The phrase] "the contingency of being the substratum of knowledge" [is used].

The sense is that it is not contradictory for the knower to be both the locus of ignorance and the locus of knowledge due to the difference in time. For the absolute absence of knowledge belongs to things such as a jar; knowledge is neither the locus of ignorance nor the object of ignorance. If one were to admit that knowledge is the locus of ignorance and its object, it would follow that it possesses the status of being a knower and the status of being an object of knowledge—this is the counter-argument (pratikūlatarka) stated. Thus, the refutation has been stated by not accepting [knowledge] as the locus of ignorance. Now, he states the refutation by accepting it: "of consciousness" (saṃvidaḥ).

Even if one accepts that delimited knowledge (*avacchinna-jñāna*) is an object of experience, one does not admit that unconditioned, essential knowledge (*anavacchinna-ātma-bhūta-jñāna*) is an object of experience; with this intention, he says: "of that which is accepted as being the Self. He states, with an illustration, that the cessation of ignorance occurs only regarding the object of knowledge: "For knowledge... The underlying intention is that if the cessation of ignorance were to occur even with respect to what is not an object [of that specific knowledge], then the delusion of a snake would be removed by the knowledge of mother-of-pearl.

Thus, it has been stated that if ignorance were the locus of knowledge, it would follow that it must be an object of knowledge. He concludes the aforementioned refutation by accepting [the opponent's position] regarding its being the locus, saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Having raised the dilemma—whether the ignorance described by you as being removable by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) entity consisting of both being and non-being, or whether it is of the nature of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge—he says "of this" (*asya*) while considering the first alternative. He addresses the second alternative with the words "prior absence of knowledge" (*jñānaprāgabhāva*).

By the word "contradictory" (*virodhin*), what is intended is the state of being an obstacle (*pratibandhakatva*), not merely non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). He concludes that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is difficult to define with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). "In any manner whatsoever" means: either as a producer (*utpādakatva*), or as an illuminator (*prakāśakatva*), or as an auxiliary to the means of experiencing it (*tadanubhavasādhanānugrāhakatva*).

Now, he refutes the manifestation [of cognition] as residing within itself by saying "na ca" (and not). He states an instance of deviation by saying "pradīpādiṣu" (in the case of lamps, etc.). He also states another reason by saying "yathāvasthita" (as it actually exists); the meaning is that "pratītiḥ" (cognition) is conformity with practical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇyam*), and this [conformity] arises from the nature of cognition and the rest which is conducive to that [usage]. He establishes that very point by saying "tacceti" (and that...).

There are four positions regarding the objects of validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*): both validity and invalidity are extrinsic (*parataḥ*), both are intrinsic (*svataḥ*), validity is extrinsic while the other is intrinsic, or validity is intrinsic while the other is extrinsic. The first [position] is untenable, because it would entail consequences such as the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). If validity and invalidity exist elsewhere and a cognition acquires their status through connection with them, then in the absence of such a connection, it is logical that the cognition possesses neither; this is like being neither hot nor cold.

In other cases, since those two [properties] do not exist, their being extrinsic (*paratastva*) is untenable; furthermore, it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress through a succession of desires to ascertain validity. Nor is intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) tenable for both; for there is a contradiction due to their having contradictory properties. Nor can the contradiction be avoided by appealing to a difference in individual instances, because there is no determining factor to distinguish which instance is the locus of validity and which is not.

The inherent nature (*svatastva*) of invalidity alone is untenable; for validity is more prevalent, whereas the other is less so. Indeed, it is logical that the more prevalent quality is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), while the rarer is adventitious (*aupādhika*). Since validity is observed even in cognitions of jars, cloths, and the like, as well as in the "this-ness" portion of cognitions such as "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell," its prevalence is established. Therefore, validity is intrinsic, while invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

In some cases, having accepted that manifestation occurs by virtue of being situated within the self, an instance of deviation was stated. Now, he says "na ca" (and not) to show that such [manifestation] does not exist even in those cases. Then, to the objection that a mirror or the like would not be employed for the purpose of seeing the face, he says "api tu" (but rather). He states "tad-doṣa" (the defect of that) because the faultiness of the reflection consists in its being the cause of erroneous cognition. To the question "What then is the manifestor there?", he says "abhivyañjakas tu" (but the manifestor is...).

He says "na ceha" (and not here) because, since the *ahaṅkāra* lacks the nature of a material, transparent, and gross substance, and since consciousness (*saṃvit*) lacks the status of being an object of knowledge and is invisible, the defect of the reflection of an object that would grasp it cannot occur within consciousness—which is not its objective domain—by means of the *ahaṅkāra*. He says "vyakteḥ" (of the individual manifestation) to show that the cognition of a genus occurs through the fixed relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmin*), and not because of being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*).

Keeping these two ways of establishing the manifestation [of consciousness] in a mirror in mind, the [opponent’s] argument that grace consists in the removal of an obstacle was previously refuted. In reality, the perception [of the reflection] occurs through the relation of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmitva*) in the case of a manifestation, whereas in a mirror it is due to the defect consisting in the form of a reflection. Thus he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*), meaning that this is not possible in the opponent's view. In reality, the cause is the relation of attribute and substrate; the defect, however, which is the cause for perceiving [the reflection] as residing therein, is the state of being a material, clear, and gross substance.

The meaning is that both [the knower and the perception] do not exist in the ego (ahaṅkāra). In reality, because of the absence of a cause, there is no state of being a knower; and because of the absence of the cause in the form of defects, it is not perceived. With this intention, he says: "There is no state of being a knower in the ego, nor is there such perception. He concludes that the Self is the knower with the word "therefore" (tasmāt). He states that it is improper for consciousness (jñapti) to be the Self, because in the absence of the sense of "I," subjectivity (pratyaktva) would be impossible: "In the disappearance of the sense of 'I'... (ahambhāva-vigame).

In the absence of an appearance conforming to the linguistic usage "I," there would be no manifestation for its own sake; therefore, the meaning is that subjectivity (*pratyaktva*) also establishes the selfhood of the referent of "I" alone.

Now, in order to establish that the "I-sense" (ahamartha) manifests even in deep sleep, [the opponent argues]: "All followers of the Vedānta must admit the manifestation of the Self in deep sleep in accordance with the scriptural teaching on its self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*). In this regard, because of the scripture stating, 'Indeed, at this time he does not know himself as "this is I"' (*nāha khalv ayam evaṃ saṃpraty ātmānaṃ jānāti ayam aham asmi*), and because of the subsequent reflection, 'I did not even know myself,' there is no experience of the "I-sense."* *Note: This passage presents the opponent's position, which maintains that the "I-sense" is absent in deep sleep based on specific scriptural texts and the nature of post-sleep recollection.*

Therefore, in response to the doubt that at that time there is only the manifestation of the experience (*anubhūti*), he asserts—supported by reasoning—that there is an indistinct manifestation of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) in the passage beginning with "darkness" (*tamaḥ*). The word "ca" (and) serves to dispel the doubt. Due to the absence of the experience of external objects, caused by the suppression of the quality of *tamas*, there is an absence of clear manifestation. "Distinct manifestation" (*viviktapratibhāsa*) means differentiated manifestation (*vyāvṛttapratibhāsa*). "Clear manifestation" (*sphuṭāvabhāsa*) means manifestation qualified by numerous attributes.

Because there is no manifestation [of the self] as qualified by external attributes such as *brāhmaṇatva* (brahminhood) which distinguish it [from others], nor as qualified by internal attributes such as cognition (*buddhi*) and pleasure (*sukha*), there is no manifestation of it as clearly distinguished from everything else. To the question "In what form does it manifest?", he says: "Because it manifests in the single form of 'I'. Here, "I" is not an imitation of the word; rather, it is an imitation of the meaning expressed by that word. The meaning is: because it manifests in the form of subjectivity (*pratyaktva*).

By the word "one" (*eka*), the non-disappearance of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) is intended. Alternatively, it means "in a single form," that is, in a form common to all selves (*sarvātman*). For [qualities] such as being the subject of immediate awareness (*pratyaktva*) are indeed common to all selves; whereas pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as divinity and so forth, are certainly not common to all selves. The sense of "I" (*ahamartha*) manifesting in the self that appears during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is what is to be proven; its manifestation in that manner is the reason (*hetu*). To the objection that the manifestation of the object "I" does not exist because there is an absence of clear appearance (*viśadāvabhāsa*), he replies: "[This would apply] even to the experience (*anubhūti*) accepted by you."

It is not only in the manifestation of the *aham-artha* (the "I-sense") that the defect of lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*) exists; you must also admit it in the manifestation of the experience (*anubhūti*). Therefore, if non-existence were to follow from the absence of a clear appearance, then even the manifestation of the self as consciousness (*jñapti-ātman*) would not occur at that time. For his own position is that "there is no distinct appearance due to the absence of contact with the knower and the known"—this is the intended meaning.

Even other disputants who are speakers of falsehood have accepted that there is an indistinct manifestation even in the waking state within non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). If they were to claim that the non-manifestation of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) is due to the absence of a distinct manifestation, even in that case, the admission of the appearance of individual objects as separate entities within non-conceptual cognition would be untenable. An indistinct manifestation of mere objects has been accepted by others in non-conceptual cognition, though it is not considered valid by them.

In this context, however, there is a distinction: following such scriptural passages as, "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous," an indistinct manifestation is accepted as being authoritative. Therefore, although the acceptance of the manifestation of the Self during deep sleep and the acceptance of an indistinct manifestation are equal, the author—desiring to show that his own position is consistent with valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) while the opponent's position is inconsistent with them—states, "For not... [and so forth].

The meaning is that it is devoid of all specific attributes such as the knower and the known, which are opposed to other objects and are distinct from the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva). The term "I" (aham) is employed here to establish its nature as immediate consciousness (pratyaktva), for it is consciousness itself that is the "I. He states "for thus" to show the consistency of this reflection with his own position. This reflection has as its object the Self experienced in the form of bliss during deep sleep. The connection with past time and the state of sleep, however, are to be inferred through non-apprehension and recognition of an object previously experienced at an earlier time.

This reflective awareness—"I slept happily"—is a specific type of recognition whose object is the "I-sense" (ahamartha), which manifests as inherently agreeable, now characterized by the sleep of the inferential time [of waking]. Thus, the difference between our own view and that of others has been stated, consisting in the presence or absence of conformity with such reflective awareness. Furthermore, the natural sense of the Śruti is in accordance with our position, because the word "person" (puruṣa) is heard in the text: "In this state, this person is self-luminous. The word "person" does not refer to pure consciousness alone.

"For this person (puruṣa) is the seer, the hearer, the taster, the smeller, the thinker, the knower, and the self consisting of consciousness"—since the scripture thus declares that the person is indeed the knower, and because the word "person" is well-known in the world as referring to the knower; furthermore, it will be stated later that the establishment of self-luminosity (pratyaktva) occurs only according to our own view. He states the meaning resulting from the aforementioned reflection with the words "by this."

In the reflective awareness, "I slept happily," the word "happily" implies that [the self] was appearing as agreeable at that time, and the word "I" implies its subjectivity, which consists in appearing to itself. The meaning is that it is just like the reflective awareness, "I walked slowly" or "I sang sweetly," by which the slowness and sweetness existing at that time are integrated along with the prior acts of walking and singing.

The term "being happy" (*sukhitva*) is stated with the intention of referring to being the counter-correlative of favorability, in the sense that it is favorable to itself by itself. The term "being a knower" (*jñātṛtva*) is stated with the intention of referring to subjectivity, in the sense of being the correlate of manifestation, insofar as it manifests to itself; however, this is not due to the flashing forth of knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*). But that [latter view] contradicts the natural drift of the *Bhāṣya*, which states: "At the time of manifesting an object, it is so for the knowing self alone; it is not so for all [selves] at all times."

Furthermore, this contradicts the natural sense of the Sūtra: "But because there is the manifestation of that which already exists, as in the case of masculinity and so forth. It also contradicts the logical justification for the rule of non-recollection. Moreover, it contradicts the natural sense of the Bhāṣya statement: "Even in the absence of mental activity during the state of transmigratory existence, knowledge has the Self as its object; and that [knowledge] is established through the door of the senses," for otherwise these words of the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya would have to be restricted in scope. And such a restriction is untenable in the absence of any grounds for limitation.

Therefore, the resultant meaning of the reflection is that at that time the self was apprehended as being proximate and agreeable. If it is asked: "Since in the cognition 'I slept happily' happiness is perceived as a qualifier of the act of sleeping, how can it be said to be a qualifier of the self?", the answer is: not so; because it is improper for the action itself to be the locus of happiness, it is logical that it qualifies the action by way of the person (the agent).

At that time, by one who asserts the self's existence as the witness of ignorance through the reflection "I was not aware of anything," the experience of the *aham-artha* (the "I-sense"), which serves as the locus of ignorance, must be admitted; just as, in the recollection "there was no elephant in the square this morning," the square—which served as the locus for the prior absence of the elephant—is necessarily kept in mind. If it is argued that, just as in the case of "I walked slowly," walking is recollected at that time, so too would sleep be recollected by the recollection "I slept," we say: no.

Just as in the case of the statement "there was no elephant at the crossroads this morning," such a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) is possible even though the prior absence of the elephant was not consciously apprehended, so too is such a reflective awareness possible regarding deep sleep—which consists in the cessation of all cognition—even though it was not consciously apprehended at that time. For in that instance, only the crossroads itself was experienced, not the absence of the elephant; rather, the absence is inferred later by the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-recollection of a perceptible object, when one who has been asked, "Was the elephant there? replies that he does not remember it. This is because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the elephant, was not remembered.

In the same way, even sleep, which consists in the cessation of all cognition, is inferred as an absence by the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-recollection of objects by those capable of such recollection. Now, an objection is raised: since there is the subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I slept happily," how can it be said that there was no experience during sleep, while at the same time there is an experience of happiness and so forth? Everything would have to be experienced, or else nothing at all. This is not so.

In the case of the cognition "I slept happily," even if the natural force of the comprehension regarding that portion for which there exists a sublater is broken, it is impossible to break the natural force of the comprehension regarding the portion that remains unsublated. Therein, the natural force of the comprehension regarding that object which cannot be experienced during the state of sleep is set aside; however, the natural force of the comprehension regarding that which is capable of being experienced at that time certainly persists.

Because sleep consists in the absence of all cognitions produced by the external and internal organs, it cannot be recollected at that time. If one were to claim that such recollection exists, then it would not be sleep at all; for there would be no cessation of all sensory cognitions. Thus, there is no inconsistency in the apprehension of pleasure and so forth, and the meaning remains exactly as stated.

Now, having restated the "otherwise-established" nature (anyathāsiddhi) of this reflective awareness (parāmarśa) as asserted by the opponent, he refutes it with the words beginning with "na ca" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because it does not have that form": having raised the dilemma—whether this meaning is accepted on the basis of the opponent’s own internal consistency (svārasya) or due to logical inconsistency—he first refutes the claim of consistency in the opponent’s cognition by stating "because there is no cognition of its not having that form," just as in the case of the statement of a reflective awareness such as, "I walked slowly" or "I sang sweetly."

For it is not possible that the slowness and sweetness [of the movement] were exactly as they are now, in the sense that "I went" and "I sang" [at that time]; rather, it is only the simultaneity of going and singing that is consistent with slowness and sweetness. Similarly, the meanings of being conscious and being happy are also simultaneous with sleep. He then removes the objection with the words beginning "na ca" (nor is there...). The inconsistency consists either in the instability of the self or in the absence of experience.

In this context, he states its stability by means of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), beginning with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Phrases such as "this was done by me" refer to reflective awareness regarding the three types of activity—mental, vocal, and physical. Now, he raises an objection concerning a specific type of reflective awareness whose object is the general negation that proves the non-experience of the referent "I" (*ahamartha*): "for all this time... He replies, "what of it? with the intention that the referent "I" is not actually the object of negation. He anticipates the opponent's intended point: "nothing [is perceived]..."; he refutes this, saying, "no."

The object of the knowable is the object appearing as the knowable. Regarding the state where everything is the object, he states the undesirable consequence with the words "not anything. One might suspect that this is not a negation of experience itself, because that [experience] persists; anticipating this, he says, "but at the time of deep sleep. The meaning is that this reflection is the opposite of your own position.

Just as a person who, having been asked about his experience of an elephant at the crossroads in the morning, later declares the absence of the elephant at the crossroads by means of the mark of not remembering it, cannot possibly declare that absence of the elephant without having had a prior experience of the crossroads—so too, one who asserts the "I-principle" (*ahamartha*) to be the locus of ignorance must admit that there was an experience of the "I-principle" during the time of sleep. Thus, the claim that the "I-principle" ceases while ignorance persists is equivalent to saying that an elephant remains present when the crossroads have ceased to exist. This is the intended meaning.

Let it be accomplished for the gods alone; for the gods consist of their forms of worship (arcā). The meaning is: "of those who do not give a reply. Alternatively, the meaning is "of those who are patient," or "in the absence of an opponent," or "spoken while looking upward."

Now, he states the reflection (*parāmarśa*) regarding the specific object of the negation with the words "mām api" ("even me"). He refutes [the objection] with the words "svānubhava" ("one's own experience"). The meaning is that there is no mutual contradiction between one's own experience and one's own statement; rather, both are contradicted by the word "negation of the persistence of the referent 'I'. Alternatively, the meaning is that there is a mutual contradiction between two parts of the experience and two parts of the statement.

And he demonstrates the contradiction with the words "I am. In the statement "I am not possessed of knowledge," the persistence of the referent "I" (ahamartha) as the witness to ignorance is established by one's own experience; furthermore, the verbal testimony is also consistent with that. Thus, the meaning is that there is a contradiction between the persistence of the referent "I"—established both by experience and by scriptural statement—and the sentence that denies it. Alternatively, the meaning is that there is a contradiction between the word denoting negation and the experience of its referent. In that context, he restates the opponent's question in order to explain the meaning of the word "me" (mām): "the word 'me'... and so forth.

Previously, stating a contradictory meaning was considered improper; however, with the intention that inquiring into the true nature of the matter is proper, he says "properly" (*sādhu*). He demonstrates the distinction between the scope of prohibition and its application by saying "that is said," and so forth. Regarding the two words "I" (*aham*) and "me" (*mām*), one might think it appropriate for both to have a qualified object, as otherwise a discrepancy in the method [of interpretation] would arise; to this he replies: "I, me. The meaning is that since there would be a contradiction if injunction and prohibition had the same object, a distinction of objects must be made to avoid that.

Anticipating the doubt that there might be a confusion regarding the distinction between objects, he shows the appropriate distinction between objects by saying "in the waking state" (*jāgarite*). That which does not manifest at that time due to the absence of its causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is precisely the object of negation; whereas that which manifests by itself independently of anything else is what persists. The meaning is that it is illogical for that which is not manifesting to persist and for that which is manifesting to be negated. Thus, he demonstrates the experience in accordance with this distinction between objects by saying "here" (*atra*).

The employment of words occurs by the force of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*): it either expresses everything present in the mind, or it expresses only a portion of it, or it expresses nothing at all. Therefore, even when the use of words is determined by intention, the experience [of the object] remains uniform. The meaning is that this experience conforms precisely to the specific division of its objects. By this, the word *ayam* (this) in the Vedic passage, "Indeed, he does not now know himself thus: 'I am this,'" has been explained.

He establishes this point according to the opponent's own view with the words beginning "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). To the question, "If the Self were accepted as being a witness (*sākṣin*), what follows?", he says: "And as for being a witness. Being a witness means being a direct knower—that is, being the substratum of knowledge in the form of immediate perception (*sākṣātkāra*). If the word "witness" is applied to one who does not possess such immediate perception, it is merely figurative. He demonstrates this with the words "For not... (*na hi*). "Of one who does not know" means "of one who is not a knower. To the question "Why?", he says: "For only a knower... (*jñātaiva hi*). He states the defining characteristic that governs the application of the term with the words "remembers" (*smarati*).

The grammatical connection is: "he remembers the word 'witness'. To the question, "What follows from that regarding the selfhood of the *aham-artha* (the 'I'-principle)? he says, "And that which... In this matter, an inference is intended to be explained in detail later; here, he states it briefly: "To the self, by itself... The statement "that which manifests to the self by itself manifests precisely as 'I'" expresses the pervasion (*vyāpti*). The waking self is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); "because it manifests to itself" is the reason (*hetu*). He concludes with "in sleep, etc."

Since an indistinct manifestation is accepted by all, and because it is consistent with the natural sense of the scriptures, consistent with the natural sense of reflective awareness (parāmarśa), and because the status of being a witness is logically established and its directness (pratyaktva) is proven, it is thereby stated that the Self shines forth as "I" during deep sleep.

Now, having restated the non-continuity of the "I-principle" (ahaṃ-artha) in liberation, he refutes it with the words beginning with *yat tu*. The particle *tu* indicates a specific weightiness of meaning. *Apeśalam* means improper or unsound. To the question "Why?", he says: *tathā sati*. The meaning is that by you—who, while refuting the destruction of one's own nature (*svarūpa-nāśa*) as being a non-goal for man (*apuruṣārtha*) in the case of the Buddhists who assert liberation to be the cessation of the stream of consciousness—you would have stated the very same destruction of one's own nature under a different name. This lack of being a goal for man is equally applicable even to the liberation asserted by the Naiyāyikas and others.

The cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness—both constitute the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). In this regard, since the non-existence of suffering—which was not previously a *puruṣārtha*—is now present, there is a connection with *puruṣārtha*; yet, because of the absence of happiness, there is also a connection with what is not a *puruṣārtha*. Thus, liberation would indeed possess a mixture of both being a *puruṣārtha* and not a *puruṣārtha*. To the objection that "the object of the 'I' (*ahamartha*) is superimposed [upon the Self], and therefore, upon its disappearance, the destruction of one's own nature (*svarūpa-nāśa*) would follow," he says: "And not so. Why? To this he says: "Because of the 'I'... That is, precisely because knowledge is perceived as a property of the object of the 'I'.

The meaning is: "precisely for the reason stated previously. By relying upon the established proof that the referent of "I" (*aham-artha*) is the Self (*ātman*), the objection regarding the loss of its essential nature (*svarūpa-hāni*) was addressed. Thus, its persistence through the cognition of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmitva*) has been demonstrated. Now, he states the presumption based on scripture (*śruty-arthāpatti*) with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*) and so forth. Previously, the presumption based on scripture was stated for the purpose of establishing the Selfhood of the referent of "I"; now, for the purpose of demonstrating its persistence even in liberation (*mukti*), he explains that same scriptural presumption in detail.

He who perceives himself as suffering is the very one who engages in the means for its cessation, and that [perceiver] is precisely the referent of "I. Even if it is argued that being a sufferer is established by delusion, he who perceives himself as erring is the very one who engages in the means for the cessation of that error, and that too is the referent of "I. For even one possessing the delusion of a double moon or similar errors requires only the cessation of their own error.

But there is no destruction of one's own [self]. Therefore, with the intention that the destruction of the *aham-artha* (the sense of "I") is not the goal of man (*apuruṣārtha*), it was stated—whether from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*) or through delusion (*bhrāntyā*)—up to the words "he connects [it]. By the phrase ending with "he connects," that which was required for the statement "I am one whose all suffering has been dispelled" has been stated. He explains the verse beginning with "dispelled" (*nirasta*) and so forth, starting with "all this is with its attributes" (*sadharmaitat*) and so on. The phrase "I would be undisturbed and established in myself" (*anākulaḥ svastho bhaveyam*) expresses the result of the statement "having warded off rebirth" (*apunarbhavamapohya*). Thus, "undisturbed" (*anākula*) is stated as the final outcome.

Agitation (*ākulatva*) is the disturbance of the mind due to the apprehension of future suffering; its absence is non-agitation (*anākulatva*). "Abiding in oneself" (*svastha*) means established in one's own nature, being intent on the experience of the self as it truly exists. "Partaking of infinite bliss" refers to the fruit. "He alone" means he who was previously afflicted by suffering; the meaning is that he alone possesses the longing for the cessation of what is undesirable and the attainment of what is desirable once they have arisen. Since it was stated previously [in the verse] "in hearing and so forth," only this much is said here: "the means for that."

With the passage beginning "This one would depart," he states the meaning resulting [from the preceding discussion] with the words "And therefore, the qualified person... The meaning is that if the scripture—which is to be accomplished through the exertion of hearing and so forth—were to culminate in something other than a human goal (apuruṣārtha), there would be no qualified person for hearing and so forth; consequently, the scripture, which depends upon hearing and so forth, would lack validity characterized by its capacity to produce valid knowledge (pramiti). He explains the phrase "Even when I am destroyed" with the words "That which is indicated by 'I'... By the term "one who acts intentionally," the word "of anyone at all" is explained.

He concludes the implication of the scriptural meaning with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). One should also consider that when the sense of "I" (*ahamartha*) disappears, the establishment of pure consciousness (*jñapti*) follows as well. He states an inference with the words "and that" (*sa ca*); the meaning of "and" is that there is also an inference. He states the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) with the words "whosoever" (*yo yaḥ*). [The phrase] "by appearing thus" means by being manifested to oneself. He shows the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) with the words "but he who" (*yaḥ punaḥ*). He states the application (*upanaya*) with the words "to oneself" (*svasmāt*). He states the conclusion (*nigamana*) with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The reason is "the state of being manifest to itself," and the probandum is "the fitness for the linguistic usage 'I'"; thus, there is no lack of distinction between the probandum and the reason. "It manifests as 'I'" means that it manifests as something fit for the linguistic usage 'I'.

He raises the objection that [the reason] is "contradictory with respect to a specific property" (*viśeṣaviruddha*) because it establishes a specific property contrary to the probandum (*sādhyaviparītaviśeṣasādhakatayā*), by saying "but not... (*na ceti*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), passion, hatred, suffering, and so forth are intended. [Objection: Surely, what is to be entailed must be a pervader (*vyāpaka*); and an effect is not a pervader of its cause. [Reply: True. However, the occasional occurrence of an effect from something belonging to the same class as the cause is indeed a pervader. Therefore, through the notion of "I," there is the entailment of non-eternality and other such qualities for the Self. He says "mokṣa... to show that the entailment of ignorance and so forth would contradict the Śruti.

"For one who sees [the Self], death is not seen, nor disease, nor even suffering"—so says the Śruti. Therefore, just as the attribution of pots and such to a mountain is precluded by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) at the very moment of seeing it, so too is there a "fallacy of the mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*); this is the meaning. He states that [the reason] is "conditioned" (*sopādhikatva*) by saying "due to ignorance, etc. (*ajñatvādīti*).

If it is argued that because the states of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*) and having the nature of the "I" (*ahamarthatva*) are observed to coexist, there would follow the consequence of being a transmigrator even in liberation (*mukti*), then [we reply]: since experience (*anubhava*) is also seen to coexist with them, the consequence of being a transmigrator would follow in your own position regarding liberation as well. If you argue that this is a case of the reason being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends liberation, or that it is "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because the state of being a transmigrator and so forth are not caused by experience, then our intention is that this is equally applicable to our own position as well.

By this [argument], it is refuted that the manifestation as "I" is not caused by being manifest to oneself, but rather caused by ignorance; thus, because the pervasion is broken by the force of scripture (*śruti*), the mere observation of concomitance is shown to be fallacious due to a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*). Having thus stated the fallacy of the lapse of time (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) and the presence of a limiting condition, he proceeds to analyze the various heads of the possible definitions of ignorance (*ajñāna*) in order to demonstrate that very presence of a limiting condition, beginning with: "What is called ignorance... and so forth.

When there is identity with the substrate (*dharmin*), knowledge that arises through the superimposition of another mode is "misconception" (*anyathājñāna*); for example, "the conch is yellow. This is the effect of *rajas*. Knowledge of one substrate as another substrate is "perverted knowledge" (*viparītajñāna*); for example, "this is silver" [when it is actually mother-of-pearl]. This is the effect of *tamas*. "O Pārtha! That intellect which perceives things incorrectly is *rājasa*. That which, enveloped by *tamas*, considers unrighteousness to be righteousness..."

"For that intellect which perceives all objects in a perverted manner, O Pārtha, is tāmasī"—so says the Smṛti. Since the nature of the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) consists in the knowledge of the Self's true form, it follows by its very opposition that the prior non-existence of that knowledge, as well as erroneous cognition and perverse cognition, have already vanished; thus he says, "only 'I'. The meaning is that the true form of the Self is simply "I," and that the true form of the Self is precisely what is fit for the conventional usage of the word "I."

By refuting the claim that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is the cause of ignorance and so forth, it is implied that the connection of ignorance with [the self] is indeed the limiting adjunct (upādhi). Alternatively, since the opponent has raised the consequence of ignorance and so forth by accepting a pervasion based on the relation of cause and effect, [the author] rejects that causal relationship in order to repudiate the pervasion, using the phrase "and because ignorance and so forth are not the cause," etc. Furthermore, he states, "How could there be transmigratory existence? to show that even the fruit of ignorance does not exist.

He states that the notion of "I" persists even in liberation through the observation that those whose ignorance has ceased still possess the cognition of the Self as "I," by saying, "by becoming the Self of Brahman. By the statement, "seeing this," which refers to the direct realization of being one with Brahman, it is understood that ignorance has been completely shaken off without remainder. He likewise describes the realization of Brahman itself as "the destroyer of all other [ignorance]"; the sense is that it is impossible for the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa), who is skilled at destroying all other poisons, to be subject to poison himself.

The phrase "possessing only the word and the notion of 'Being'" refers to the word *sat* and its corresponding notion (*pratyaya*), which serves as their object. The particle *mātra* (only) excludes the state of possessing name and form (*nāmarūpa*). By this, he indicates that even prior to the creation of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), there was the notion of "I. To clarify this notion of "I," he first cites the sentence, "May I be many. In the sentence "May I be many," the notion of "I" is established by the force of the first person singular pronoun (*asmad-yuṣmad*) used in the first person.

In the passage "I [shall create] these three," the word "I" (aham) is explicitly stated; the sense is that the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) does not possess the capacity to manifest names and forms. To indicate that this designation as "I" occurs in many Upaniṣads, he cites the text "He reflected" (sa īkṣata). The sense is that the inclusion of the word "I" is established by the use of the first-person verb "let me create" (sṛjai). He shows the Smṛti evidence with the words "tathā yasmāt" (likewise, because...). The statement "because" (yasmāt) is employed to make known the cognition of the "I"-notion in its natural form as that which transcends both the perishable and the imperishable.

For the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) does not transcend the perishable and the imperishable; therefore, even by means of the supreme person (*uttamapuruṣa*), the referent of "I" is established through the expression "I am. [The scripture] makes known the cognition of the self as the "I" by saying "I am the Self. For the ego-sense is not the inner self of the conscious and the unconscious. It shows the cognition of "I" regarding the natural, eternal form by saying "not indeed am I [the ego]. For the ego-sense is not eternal. He says "of them" to show that even that which bestows liberation—which is opposed to death—is the object of the cognition of "I. For the ego-sense does not bestow liberation.

Thus, the citation of numerous statements from the Śruti and Smṛti is for the purpose of refuting such statements intended by the opponent that [the self] is distinct [from the body]. If it is argued that pure consciousness (cinmātra) is indicated by these words "I" (ahaṃ), then the very same defect applies to the word "I" occurring in multiple sentences.

There are three statements concerning the ego (ahaṅkāra): first, the statement regarding its inclusion within the field (*kṣetra*), namely, "the great elements and the ego"; second, the statement regarding its nature as something to be abandoned, namely, "having relinquished the ego, power, pride, desire, anger, and possessiveness, one who is free from malice and tranquil is fit for becoming Brahman"; and third, another statement, namely, "the self deluded by the ego. Although these three have not been explicitly cited here, they are intended because they will be addressed later. Previously, with reference to the intent of these statements, it was said that [the ego] does not persist in deep sleep or liberation.

Taking this point as a basis, he raises an objection with the words, "How then? He provides the answer with the words, "It is said. When the opponent has objected on the grounds of the perceived non-difference between the referent of the word "I" (*ahamartha*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), [the author] demonstrates the stability of the I-notion’s status as a valid means of knowledge regarding the Self, which is the meaning of the verbal root, in order to explain the distinction between the meanings of the stem and the suffix. With the words, "In the teachings concerning the true nature [of the Self]," he shows that [the notion] is established otherwise than by its primary sense; therein, he states what is intended by the term *ahaṅkāra*: "Of the particular transformation of the unmanifest (*avyakta*). This refers to the specific modification of the unmanifest.

The meaning is, however, that this is not the case for the referent of the term "I" (*ahamartha*). Even if one accepts that the pure essential nature is designated by the word "egoity" (*ahaṅkāra*) in passages such as "Now, therefore, the instruction on egoity," there is no contradiction; for that word "egoity" refers to the cognition whose object is the referent of "I. If the inner self were also distinct from the field (the insentient) merely because it is denotable by the word "egoity," then a frog would be a lion simply because of the commonality of being denotable by the word "lion."

Therefore, the sense is that the unity of a word denoting multiple meanings does not contradict its distinct referents. As it is said in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*: "And thus, the word 'hari' is observed to denote a frog; because it is denotable by that word, is a lion merely a frog? Likewise, because it is denotable by the word 'go', would sound also possess horns? Now, he shows the manner in which the word *ahaṅkāra* denotes a specific transformation of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) with the words "But that... (*sa tu*).

The term *ahambhāva* refers to the cognition "I am. That the word *bhāva* denotes cognition is understood from its usage in the sense of intention (*abhiprāya*). Having accepted that the referent of the word "I" is uniform in all cases, he establishes—through the grammatical process of instruction—that the word *ahaṅkāra* signifies a transformation of the Unmanifest, stating: "But of this... Here, there is the elision of the entire suffix *cvipratyaya*. The suffix *dhañ* is used in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇe*). Thus, the justification for the teaching that [the ego] is included within the field (*kṣetra*) has been provided.

The instruction that "egoism (ahaṅkāra), power (bala), and pride (darpa) must be abandoned" is thus fulfilled by this very [verse]. By the word "this" (ayaṃ), the ego-sense (ahambhāva) under discussion is intended; it is not the cause for producing the ego-sense, because of the statement that it is another name for pride. For neither the Great Principle (mahat) nor the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra)—neither of which is synonymous with pride—is intended here by the word "this. Therefore, it is the ego-sense itself that is intended by the word "this. The notion of "I" regarding a praiseworthy body is the cause for the disrespect of superior persons. Ahaṅkāra is the notion of "I" (ahambuddhi).

It is appropriate that the root *kṛ*, which denotes mental activity, refers here to the intellect (*buddhi*), as in the passage: "For the wise one should again make the Lord, who consists of a single part, with his mind. For making with the mind is indeed perceiving. Therefore, *ahaṅkāra* is the cognition "I" (*ahambuddhi*). Because they contain the meaning of the suffix *cvī*, these two words—*ahaṃbhāva* and *ahaṅkāra*—refer to the state of being "I" and the cognition "I" respectively. Here, the derivation is in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*); in the previous case, it was in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Lexicographers [define] *ahaṅkāra* as "pride" (*garva*) or "self-conceit" (*abhimāna*).

[Objection: But how can the word *ahaṅkāra*, which is conventionally understood to denote that which is to be abandoned (*heya*), be employed here with reference to that which is to be accepted (*upādeya*) in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction on *ahaṅkāra*"? [Response: It is said: that word *ahaṅkāra* directly denotes the cognition whose object is the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*); it does not, however, have as its internal meaning the notion of selfhood (*ātmatva*) applied to what is not the self, nor the sense of the suffix *-tva*. He concludes the distinction between the objects of the two cognitions of "I"—one of which is to be abandoned and the other accepted—as they are conveyed by words, with the words "Therefore... He states the authoritative proof for this point with the words "As it has been said."

In that very Purāṇa, it is clearly stated that the notion of "I" and its verbal expression regarding the self are not erroneous, whereas [the same] regarding what is not the self is erroneous. As it says: "When the self stands distinct from ether, air, fire, water, and earth—who could produce a sense of 'selfhood' in the body? Yet, in this body composed of the five elements, the embodied soul, shrouded by the darkness of delusion and possessed of poor intellect, loudly forms the thought: 'This is I, this is mine.'"

In the *Ādibharata-carcā*, it is said: "For a twice-born man, this word 'I' is not a defect when applied to the Self; however, the cognition of the Self in that which is not the Self, or the word [so used], is characterized by delusion. He states "if" (*yadī*) to show that this very statement serves as a reason for the fact that the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is the Self. Regarding the phrase "in that which is not the Self": the meaning is, "How can the cognition of 'I' in what is not the Self constitute the conceit of being the Self? He concludes that the referent of "I" is the Self with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). To illustrate this point, he cites the *Ātmasiddhi* text, saying: "As it has been said... (*tad uktam*).

The logical principle (*nyāya*) consists of the cognition of the relationship between property and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*), its establishment through direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddhi*), the disparity regarding permanence and impermanence, and presumptive testimony based on scripture (*śrutyarthāpatti*). The traditional authority (*āgama*) refers to the Upaniṣadic passages cited above. The "conjunction with ignorance" (*avidyāyoga*) refers to the conjunction with the aforementioned error (*bhrānti*). Alternatively, the meaning is that if the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) were not the self, the error "I am fat" would be impossible. A corroborating text has been shown regarding the selfhood of the knower (*jñātṛ*); and regarding the non-selfhood of consciousness (*jñapti*), he cites the *Ātmasiddhi* text with the words "And thus... (*tathā ca*).

The phrase "other than the intellects" (*dhībhyo'nyaḥ*) has already been utilized here; since the word *sādhana* (means) is common to both that which produces and that which makes known, he explains it with the word "not other" (*ananya*). To dispel the doubt regarding the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the individual soul's (*jīva*) essential nature, he explains the word "pervasive" (*vyāpī*) with the words "extremely subtle" (*atisūkṣma*). Because the term "pervasiveness" (*vyāpti*) is employed in the Purāṇas, that very same term is used here in this verse. The intention is that wherever a word expressive of the soul's pervasiveness occurs, this is precisely the meaning that should be understood.

The pervasion of the individual soul (jīva) by its attribute of knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna) is stated precisely in the *Ātmasiddhi*: "Pervasion also occurs solely through consciousness alone, not through its own essential nature. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated.

Now, with the words beginning "yad uktam" (as for what was said), [the author] restates and refutes the opponent's claim regarding the superiority of scripture (*śāstra*) over direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) when there is a conflict between them. Previously, the opponent had stated: "The relationship of root and derivative, or the nature of being indirect and direct, and so forth, are not the causes for the relationship of sublated and sublator; for this is shown to be fallacious by the inference of the difference in flames. Even in cases such as 'The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is the sun,' the fact that the identity of the post and the sun is not being taught is not due to weakness [of the scripture], but rather because there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding identity, since [that statement] is a subordinate part of the injunction to smear the post with ointment. This is what was said.

In that regard, due to the inference of the difference between flames, the treatise possesses a threefold disparity not present in the inference of the difference between flames: namely, the mutual dependence arising from the lack of certainty regarding the presence of defects in the source by means of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the equality of defects between the sublated and the sublator, and the destruction of the root [of the opponent's position]. These three do not exist in the inference of the difference between flames.

For instance, it is observed in the case of a lamp that has been recently extinguished and relit that the defect known as "similarity" (sādṛśya)—which is based on its being wound from a single wick—is a cause for the cognition of identity even when identity does not exist. Since the perception of the identity of the flame by the eye is in some cases determined to be rooted in a defect, and since the possibility of being rooted in a defect exists even in other instances of perceiving identity, the direct perception of the identity of the flame would be subject to doubt for an investigator; it would not be capable of producing certainty.

If it were not observed through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the defect consisting in similarity within a flame causes the cognition of identity even when identity does not exist, there would be a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): the superiority of inference would result in the sublation of perception, and the superiority of inference would depend on that very sublation of perception. However, since the possibility of the cognition of identity being otherwise established has been observed through another means of knowledge, there is no circularity. In this case, however, the defectiveness of the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) has not been so observed by another means of knowledge.

Furthermore, in the case of a lamp, while the sublated cognition—the perception of the identity of the flame—is rooted in the defect known as similarity (*sādṛśya*), it is not observed that the sublating cognition—the inference of the difference between the flames—is itself rooted in the defect of similarity. In this case, however, both the sublated perception and the sublating scripture are equally characterized by being rooted in defects accepted by the opponent; thus, they possess equal defects (*tulyadoṣatva*).

Furthermore, in that case, the perception apprehending the substratum called "flame" during the first contact of fire with a wick-particle, the perception apprehending the pervasion between arising and destruction when the final wick-particle is destroyed, and the perception apprehending the inferential mark (liṅga)—namely, the contact with fire and the destruction of each successive wick-particle—do not have as their object something sublated by an inference for difference; rather, it is precisely the cognition of identity [that is sublated].

In this case, however, there is a threefold disparity: [the perception] that apprehends the subject (dharmin) called "word," that which apprehends the probans (liṅga) establishing its faultlessness, that which apprehends the pervasion (vyāpti) of that probans, and that which apprehends the sixfold probans of intention (tātparya)—since it is admitted that these perceptions and those probans of intention are sublated by scripture itself, their very root is destroyed. Desiring to establish these three disparities, he restates the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "by being rooted in defects" and "of the perception that relies upon all forms of difference."

The point here is this: some, such as the author of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, have asserted that defects of perception consist solely of conditions like cataracts (*kāca*) or ophthalmia (*timira*). This is not tenable, because cataracts and the like are localized (occurring only in specific instances). If, on this basis, it is inferred that other forms of perception are rooted in defects, then by the same logic—that of being a form of cognition—one might infer that the scripture (*śāstra*) is also rooted in defects simply because it is a word (*śabda*). If you argue that the presence of a defect in scripture is ruled out by the non-perception of its suitability (*yogyānupalambha*), then the same should apply to perception as well.

Furthermore, in Āyurveda, the nature of the *doṣas* (humors/defects) and the means for their removal are established. To infer that all perception is rooted in *doṣas* contradicts that [medical authority]. Moreover, he refutes [the opponent's view] with the words "What is this... and so forth, arguing that if all perception were rooted in *doṣas*, then even the perception that grasps pure existence (*sanmātra*) would be rooted in *doṣas*, and thus even pure existence itself would be false. He asks: "It must be stated what this *doṣa* is."
