The meaning is as follows: when asked "What is this defect? regarding that which was stated as the root in the form of a defect by means of this mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*), one must say "This is the defect. Alternatively, by the force of the word *yat* ("which"), the word *tatra* ("therein") is established through implication. The meaning is that when asked "What is this defect? concerning the collection of objects (the *arthajāta*) described by the phrase "by being the root of defects" and so forth, one must state [the answer]. To the question "Why must it be stated?", he says: "Because it is the root. For it is not easy to explain an alternative establishment (*anyathāsiddhi*) without first mentioning the defect.

He states the defect with the words "beginningless" (*anādi*). The particle *eva* (only) is intended to establish the essential nature [of the defect]. By the word *hi* (for), there is an acceptance of the fact that other defects are impossible; or, the word *hi* is used because of the [author's] conceit of having established the status of this as a defect according to his own system. For the status of being a defect consists in being the cause of erroneous cognition (*viparīta-jñāna*). Therefore, since pervasion by the state of being the cause of erroneous cognition has not been observed, and thus the status of being a defect is not established even though the nature of the latent impression of difference (*bhedavāsanā*) is admitted, he asks: "Of the latent impression of difference? (*bhedavāsanāyā iti*).

In the phrase "like timira, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) is intended to include similarity and so forth; for that [similarity] is the cause of the delusion of oneness regarding a flame. He raises an objection with the words "by this very [reason]," because it is difficult to state that the quality of having been previously known exists elsewhere. He refutes this with "no. Thus, by means of another proof, he has stated the disparity consisting in the occurrence of mutual dependence due to the lack of certainty regarding its being a defect. Now, he states that the sublated and the sublator possess equal defects, beginning with "furthermore" (kiñca).

Now, although the status of being rooted in defects is equal [in both cases], he raises the objection regarding "priority" (*paratva*) as the ground for sublation here. In cases such as the "simultaneous disjunctions" (*apaccheda*), and in instances like "this is silver" versus "this is not silver," a sublating cognition is observed. Therefore, the meaning is that the negating cognition is stronger because of its priority over the cognition that presents the object to be negated.

In this way, since even the treatises that establish Brahman—such as those concerning linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) and so forth—are rooted in perception and other means of knowledge, and thus presuppose them, they are "subsequent" (*para*) in relation to perception; therefore, by the same logic, the reality of the non-dual entity (*nirviśeṣavastu*) taught by them is also established. He refutes this with the words "That is not so. He demonstrates the irrelevance of "subsequent-ness" with the example of the rope-snake: because the subsequent cognition is rooted in a defect (*doṣa*), its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not certain, and thus fear does not cease.

One might object: "Granted that once error is known, the otherness [of the source] may be irrelevant; however, in this case, there is no knowledge of error. To this, he says: "And of the scripture" (*śāstrasya ca*). He establishes the fact of its being known by stating: "understood through hearing" (*śravaṇāvagata*). It is indeed universally accepted that the scripture is rooted in the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of duality. And the defectiveness of that [impression] is understood from the knowledge of the falsity of duality.

And the realization of that [world] as false follows from the realization that it is sublatable by knowledge; and the realization that it is sublatable by knowledge follows from the realization that the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self destroys all distinctions. Therefore, the meaning is that by one who performs reflection (*manana*) in the form of the practice of such sublating knowledge, the fact that the scripture has its root in defects is understood.

Thus, the disparity consisting in the fact that both the sublated and the sublator possess equal defects has been stated. Now, he speaks of the "cutting off of the root" with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). By the phrase "this scripture," there is an exclusion of the mere collection of sounds. By the phrase "whose defects are not even conceivable," there is an exclusion of the Buddhist scriptures and the like. [The opponent objects: "If by you [the defects] such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) are [admitted to be] real..."

Not by one who does not accept [this]. "Not at all," etc. [This means] that, by virtue of being self-established (*svatas-siddhatva*), it is devoid of all particularities (*nirddhūta-nikhila-viśeṣatva*). This qualification is for the purpose of demonstrating its lack of an object (*nirviṣayatva*). To the question "Why is it not cognized?", he says: "Of that [cognition]," because it is detached from all objects; that is to say, because it is without an object. For consciousness does not manifest an object without being connected to it.

In reality, although it has no object, [the Veda] makes known the superiority of its own scriptures through delusion, even though such superiority does not exist; to this he says, "And because of the absence of partiality toward its own scriptures. The meaning is that, since there is no difference between them in terms of being unrelated and non-existent, it would also make known the authority of other scriptures such as those of the Buddhists. He says "nor" to indicate that perception and the other means of knowledge do not make [this superiority] known.

Even the perception of those who enjoy [the fruits of their actions] and so forth is preceded by sensory perception, because it is an effect of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) caused by knowledge arising from scriptures rooted in sensory perception; therefore, sensory perception is mentioned first. This is because it is the root of that [other perception], meaning it is the root of the perception based on the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality. Thus, having stated the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding the subject at hand, he concludes by showing that this applies to everything according to the opponent's view, with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). There is no establishment of the object intended by oneself—that is, the intended point such as the weakness of perception and the strength of scripture.

This has been stated as an illustration for the purpose of refuting the fallacious arguments (kutarka) set forth by Khaṇḍanakāra and others. In that regard, the refutation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), pervasion (vyāpti), and so forth, is being undertaken. Here, it must be asked: regarding the point that another scripture, distinct from your own intended one, deals with non-ultimate objects, do you have a valid cognition (pramiti) of this fact, or not? If you do have such a cognition, then there is no refutation of the means of valid cognition and the rest. If you do not have it, then for that very reason there is no refutation of the means of valid cognition and the rest. Indeed, the valid cognition, its means, and so forth, do exist.

If it is argued that this [knowledge] is "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*), what is this "conventionality"? Is it ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) or non-ultimate reality (*aparamārthatva*)? If the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself non-ultimate, is it a prover (*sādhaka*) or a non-prover (*asādhaka*)? If it is a prover while being designated as non-ultimate, then the means of valid cognition accepted by others would likewise be a prover for their respective positions. On the other hand, if it is a non-prover, then the means of valid cognition and so forth accepted by other disputants would all the more be provers.

If that which you have stated—such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—is ultimately real (*paramārthabhūta*), then the dualist would be the victor. Is the distinction between one’s own position and the opponent’s position ultimately real, or is it not ultimately real? If it is ultimately real, then the falsity of difference (*bhedamithyātva*) does not hold. If it is not ultimately real, then you would have accepted the opponent’s very position; thus, you yourself would have asserted the ultimate reality of difference (*bhedapāramārthya*). The intention [of this passage] is that such contradictions should be traced everywhere.

Now, desiring to respond to the objection regarding the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing one's own position, he raises the challenge with the word "nanu" (is it not so?). He questions the nature of this [objection] with "ko 'yam" (what is this?). He shows its conventional form with "āpāta" (superficial). He refutes it with "kiṃ tena" (what is the use of that?), meaning that it does not serve the purpose of determining the probandum (*sādhya*). Why? To this he says: "by way of being a means of valid cognition. Logical sublation (*yauktika-bādha*) is sublation by reasoning; the meaning is that we observe that vapor and the like, when grasped by the cognition of smoke, do not serve as causes for the determination of the probandum. In this way, the disparity consisting in the total destruction of the root has been established.

Thus, the disparity [of the scripture] from perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been refuted by the opponent’s previous argument based on its being "other" (*paratva*). Now, [the author] raises the objection regarding the disparity of the scripture that establishes Brahman from perception, on the grounds that there is no sublater (*bādhaka*) superior to it, beginning with the words "Now, it might be said" (*athocyeta*). To state the disparity of the scripture consisting in the absence of the observation of sublation, he first states the observation of sublation regarding the object of perception, using the word "scripture" (*śāstra*). Then, he states the disparity of the object of the scripture from the object of perception, using the phrase "being the object of the scripture" (*śāstraviṣayatva*).

He refutes [the opponent's position] by accepting the observation of a subsequent sublation (*pāścātyabādhā*), stating that "that is incorrect. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of that which is unsublated (*abādhitasya*). For those who know the principles of logic maintain: "That cognition alone is incorrect for which there is a defective cause (*duṣṭaṃ kāraṇam*) and for which there is a cognition of falsity (*mithyeti pratyayaḥ*). Therefore, both a defective root-cause and a sublating cognition are individually establishers of falsity. This is contradictory: namely, that there is a determination of non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthya-niścaya*) even for that which is unsublated.

Regarding the point that "being sublated" means being determined as non-ultimate reality, he says: "This has been stated. The phrase *ajñātasvatimirasya* (of one whose own cataract is unknown) is seen in some versions; its purpose is to exclude the arising of an indirect sublation based on the knowledge of a defect. The reading *jñātasvatimirasya*, however, is the result of a scribe’s error, for it contradicts the statement that [the object] is not within the range of another person. To the question, "In the absence of a sublater, how can there be falsity? he says: "For the defect... and so forth.

The meaning is that even in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) based on the same locus as the error, the determination of falsity by means of the cognition of another person is not contradicted. Although animals lack the arising of a subverting cognition for as long as they live, their notion of the body as the self has a false object, because it is rooted in a defect consisting of [the false] association [between the body and the self]. It is precisely because an example from external illusions was intended to be clear that such an instance was not mentioned here. Now, one might object: "The delusion of the body being the self among animals is not perceptible to us."

Since the effect [of the error] is not perceived, the defect that serves as the cause of the delusion is also difficult to perceive; therefore, how can there be a determination of falsity based merely on the knowledge of a possibility that it is rooted in a defect? It is replied: prior to hearing the scripture, we and others observe the delusion of identifying the body with the self; and since those [ordinary people] lack the qualification for the scripture, it is inferred that they possess the delusion of body-and-self and the defect consisting in the contact with the body which is its root. From the certainty that it is rooted in a defect, there follows the certainty of its falsity.

In this way, for a person suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), one must seek authoritative testimony (*āptavākya*) and so forth regarding the presence of that ophthalmia; from that, the certainty of its falsity arises. Thus, with the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he concludes the point learned regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by applying it to the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*). The falsity of cognition has been stated by accepting the position of the opponent. The non-observation of subsequent sublation (*pāścātyabādhādarśana*) will be refuted later. By the words beginning with "occurring" (*bhavantīti*), he adduces an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasañjana*) if it is accepted that the scripture is rooted in ignorance (*avidyāmūla*).

It has been stated that these are called *prayogas* because they are statements that demonstrate pervasion (*vyāpti*). They are formulated in the form of a proposition (*pratijñā*), an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and a reason (*hetu*) for the purpose of making known that "even in this case, an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*) is logically appropriate. There is a distinction among them: one [reason] is simply being an object of knowledge; another is being an object of the knowledge of a corrupt person; and another is being an object of knowledge produced by a false causal complex (*sāmagrī*). The meaning of the particle "only" (*eva*) here is that the subject under consideration is the only thing that constitutes the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) in this context.

[Objection: Is it not the case that being the object of a cognition produced by a non-existent cause is unestablished for one of the two parties? Furthermore, the example "like the phenomenal world" (prapañca) is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). How, then, can such a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) be valid? [Reply: It is said: Just as in the statement, "The non-experienceability of Brahman follows [absurdly] from your own assertion," the refutation was stated by accepting the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the reductio-provoking property (*prasañjaka-dharma*) and the property to be reduced to absurdity (*prasañjanīya-dharma*) according to the opponent's own view; thus, there is no contradiction.

He restates and refutes the objection that Brahman is unreal because it is the object of a cognition produced by an unreal cause—arguing that even from the unreal, the real is seen to be reflected—in the passage beginning with "na ca" (nor...). Having in mind the dilemma of whether the impossibility lies in the unreal being a cause for the *origination* of the real or its *cognition*, he provides examples for both origination and cognition.

In this regard, although the reality of dream-objects is accepted [by some], he refutes [that view] by admitting the unreality of those objects, stating "svāpna" (dream). He establishes the reality of the cognition itself with "tatra hi" (for there). To the question "How is this determined?", he replies "teṣām eva" (of those very [objects]). He demonstrates the non-sublation of the cognition with "na hi" (for not). To the question "How does it arise?", he says "darśanam tu" (but the perception). The meaning is that a sublation pertaining to one object is not logically applicable to another.

The presentation of multiple examples here is for the purpose of making known the reality of the specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) for those respective cognitions, and that is for the sake of establishing the reality of those cognitions. The cause of a dream—the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience—is real; it is not mentioned because it is well-known. Regarding the phrase "of a magician": by the expression "arising from mantras, herbs, and so forth," the reality of the cause is stated. "Fear produced by illusion" means having a false object, or alternatively, having a diverse object. [This applies to] the word "object" and so on.

The defect of the object (*viṣayadoṣa*) consists of similarity and so forth; the defect of the sense organ (*indriyadoṣa*) consists of cataracts and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), defects pertaining to the location, such as distance, are expressed. Furthermore, the defect is real (*satya*). Regarding the phrase "it is indeed real": the proximity of the snake is a real cause; the perceiver’s cognition is also real; even in the case of the cognition of poison from suspicion, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is real; for either the bite of a non-venomous snake or the crushing of a stone or clod of earth in the dark is indeed real. Regarding the word "object" (*vastu*): water and so forth are real.

And the reflection of the visual light produced by that [mirror] is indeed real. For once the reality of cognitions has been established, it is said regarding the aforementioned examples that "from the real, there is the apprehension of the real. To this he says: "Of these" (*eṣām*). Both having an origin (*utpattimattva*) and performing a causal function (*arthakriyākāritva*) are individually proofs for reality. Indeed, silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does not have an origin, nor does it perform a causal function.

Now, one might raise the objection that since the truth of cognition is pervaded by the reality of its object, the cessation of the latter entails the cessation of the former; this is the point raised in the phrase "of the elephant and so forth. The response is "this is not so," meaning that in the absence [of such an object], there is no such state [of truth] within the perceived locus. The truth of cognition is pervaded merely by having an objective support (*sālambanatvamātra*); this is because it is uncontradicted. By the term "merely having an objective support," the restriction to having a real objective support is excluded. To the question of how something that is false can serve as an objective support, he says: "of the object. Here, "objective support" means the object (*viṣaya*).

For it is precisely the state of appearing (*pratibhāsamānatva*) that is required for something to be an objective support (*ālambana*). The meaning is that being an object (*viṣayatva*) is nothing other than the state of appearing. This is because we observe that even non-existent things, such as the past and the future, serve as objective supports when they appear, whereas even existent things lack that status when they do not appear. He states "appearing" (*pratibhāsa*) to show that this state of appearing also exists in the case [of the present object]. It is the state of being the correlate (*pratisambandhitva*) with respect to the consciousness of the appearance.

Because that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent, it is unreal in that form. Likewise, even an object that is directly manifesting would have to be a cause of cognition; for there is no distinction [between them], since both are equally manifesting as existing, just like an object whose existence is commonly accepted. To the objection that this would mean one perceives the unreal as real, he says: "due to a defect" (*doṣavaśāt*). The cause for the manifestation of the non-existent as existent is precisely the defect; it is not the non-existent object itself.

A non-existent object is not required as a cause for cognition, but only as its object; however, an existent object, appearing as such, is required both as an object and as a cause. Therefore, actual existence is the necessary condition (*upādhi*) for an object to be a cause of cognition. For causality is observed only in that which exists at a time strictly prior [to the effect]. Consequently, since that which is non-existent cannot function as a cause, it is precisely a defect (*doṣa*) that serves as the cause; thus, there is no production of the real from the unreal. This is the meaning.
To the question, "Since both are equally manifest in the morning, how can there be a determination of the unreality of the other [the dream]," he says: "But that... [referring to the waking state].

To the objection, "Why might the cognition itself not be unreal? he says: "Unsublated... The meaning is that to assert the unreality of a cognition on the grounds of the non-existence of its object is a fallacy of mistiming (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa).

Now, in the case of the cognition of objects such as those in a dream, is it mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) that is the cause for the apprehension of the auspicious and the inauspicious, or is it a specific kind of cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*)? If it is the position of mere cognition, there is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the result occurring to all cognitions]. If it is a specific kind of cognition, what is its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*)? If it is the object (*viṣaya*), is the object a delimiting factor by way of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) or by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)? If it is by way of being a qualifier, then a qualifier is indeed that which is connected with the effect along with the qualified (*viśeṣya*); therefore, since even an elephant and so forth are causes for the apprehension of the auspicious and the inauspicious, there is the apprehension of the real from the unreal (*asatyāt satyapratipatti*).

If it is argued that an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) is distinct from the object indicated (*upalakṣya*), since an indicator is indeed the means for the cognition of the object indicated, and therefore the cognition of the real arises from the unreal because the object is the cause for the attainment of knowledge—this should not be said. For one cannot claim that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because cognitions are distinguished by specific intrinsic natures characterized by their conformity to various respective conventional usages (*vyavahāra*); for if mere conformity to usage were the differentiator, the fault of over-extension would persist.

If conformity with a specific conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) serves as the differentiator, then that specific usage depends upon the object that subsumes it; thus, by virtue of delimiting conventional usage, even the untrue functions as a cause for the true.

It is said: it is precisely the cognition as a distinct exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*) that serves as the inferential mark for the auspicious, the inauspicious, and so forth. And this exclusion is [determined] by its own objective referent (*ālambana*). It has already been stated that even a non-existent thing can function as an objective referent due to the influence of defects. Even in the theory of "appearance of what is otherwise" (*anyathākhyāti*), the reality of the objective referent of all cognitions is indeed accepted; for among the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, there is some degree of reality in certain cases. The relation, which effects the establishment of the true nature of the qualifier and the qualified, does not depend on another relation for its own possession of those two.

However, that relation, appearing in the locus of error as something present before one, cannot establish its own nature as a relation in dependence upon the object present before it; therefore, in relation to the object present before it, the relation is unreal (*aparamārtha*), yet not unreal in its own essential form. Furthermore, in the case of being an objective support (*ālambana*), the quality of being "present" is not required, since even that which is not present is observed to function as an objective support.

Therefore, since they have reality as their objective support (*ālambana*), even cognitions such as those of mounting an elephant are distinguished from cognitions of the waking state because they are delimited by the dream state—which is ultimately real—and are thus delimited by objective supports consisting of real elephants and so forth. Consequently, these cognitions serve as the causes for the apprehension of auspicious or inauspicious results. Thus, there is no over-extension of the principle, nor is there the apprehension of the real from the unreal. Furthermore, in the case of inferring an original object (*bimba*) from a reflection, it is not an instance of apprehending the real from the unreal; [for the reflection itself is real].

Because the appearance of a reflection is indeed indicative of a real thing; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no distinction between the indicator (*anumāpaka*) and the indicated (*anumeya*) therein, since it is the actual object itself that is perceived as being located in the mirror due to the ocular rays being reflected back by the mirror and other such surfaces. Therefore, in some cases there is comprehension of an object through its meaning, and in others there is comprehension of various objects through their appearances; thus, what is unreal cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, is this claim that "the real is comprehended from the unreal" stated according to your own position, or according to ours?

In your position, that [valid cognition] is not established; for since even the auspicious and inauspicious are false, being unreal, there would indeed be a cognition of the unreal from the unreal. Nor is it so in our position, because we accept the theory of the manifestation of things as they truly are (*yathārthakhyāti*); thus, from what is real alone, there arises a cognition of the real. It is clear that these six examples of cognitions—such as the cognition of an elephant in a dream and others which serve as causes for the apprehension of the auspicious and inauspicious—possess a causal complex consisting of real factors such as mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the reality of cognitions has been demonstrated. Therefore, the reality of the cause is established both in respect to their production and their manifestation.

Now, by means of the argument that what is unreal is distinct from knowledge, the truthfulness of the cause is established in the attainment of the truth through the words beginning with "by the line" (*rekhayā*). Showing the unreality of the cause, he raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*); he refutes it with "Not so" (*naivam*). With the intention of setting forth the following alternatives—whether the nature of being composed of phonemes (*varṇa*) is a means for the cognition of phonemes by way of its existence (*sattayā*), or by way of its being cognized as valid (*pramitatayā*), or by way of its being perceived (*pratītatayā*)—he says "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*). The meaning of the word "non-existent" is that, because it is unreal, its status as a means by way of its existence is untenable.

The meaning is "of that which is non-existent, distinct from the existent. Because it is non-existent, its status as a means [to knowledge] by way of being an object of valid cognition (*pramita*) is untenable; this is the intended sense of the term *nirupākhya*. *Upākhyā* means valid cognition; *nirupākhyatva* (the state of being indefinable) is the state of not being an object of such cognition. As for the untenability of its status as a means by way of being an object of apprehension (*pratīti*), that will be explained later. If it is argued that even in the absence of existence and valid cognition, its status as a means exists by virtue of its nature as a phoneme (*varṇātmatā*), that is untenable due to a contradiction with the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

With the intention that conceptualization proceeds in accordance with pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says, "And [the other] is untenable. Now, even in the view that the nature of the phoneme (*varṇātmatā*)—though perceived through error—is the cause for the cognition of the phoneme, he says "Now" (*atha*) in order to show the opponent's untenability regarding the intellect (*buddhi*) being the cause. He refutes this with "If that were so, then... (*evaṃ tarhi*). To the question "Why?", he replies, "Of the intellect... (*buddheḥ*). He states another refutation with "By means of... (*upāya*). He explains that with "Of both... (*ubhayoḥ*).

The refutation of the view that the aspect of cognition (*buddhyaṃśa*) is the cause has already been stated. Now, by means of the "lion’s glance" (*siṃhāvalokita*), he states the refutation regarding the view that the aspect consisting of the phonemes (*varṇātmatāṃśa*) is the cause, beginning with the words "of the line" (*rekhāyāḥ*). The phrase "by way of being non-existent as the phoneme" (*avidyamānavarṇātmatvena*) means by way of not having the nature of a phoneme. He raises an objection with "now" (*atha*) in order to avoid the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To that too, he states the failure of his own position with "alas" (*hanta*). He explains this with "of the line" (*rekhāyāḥ*). He refutes another example with "even from a line-drawn gavaya" (*rekhāgavayād api*).

He refutes another example being stated by relying on the theory of *sphoṭa* with the words "And not for that which has a single form," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: it is also not tenable to argue that "the *sphoṭa* is a single-formed word, derived from the etymology 'that which is burst forth (*sphuṭyate*) by sounds (*nāda*)'; the various specific sounds (*nāda*) that manifest it are many; the distinctions such as *katva* (hardness) and *svatva* (shortness) reside in the manifesting sounds and are superimposed upon the word, serving as the cause for the comprehension of specific meanings; thus, there is the production of the real from the unreal. Why? To this he says: "by means of various sounds."

The specific manifestation produced by various sounds (*nāda*) endowed with particularities such as *katva* (the quality of being *ka*) and *svatva* (the quality of being *sa*) is real; the meaning is that the word, as qualified by those [particularities], is real and serves as the cause for the comprehension of the object. Even though the qualification by *katva*, *svatva*, and so forth is superimposed upon the word, nevertheless, the cognition of it is indeed real and is the cause for the comprehension of the object. Furthermore, the exclusion [of erroneous cognition] should be understood through the reality of the object of cognition itself, just as in the case of a dream-cognition.

Since it is possible for the *sphoṭa* to be the cause of the comprehension of meaning by way of a form qualified by the manifestation of [phonemes] such as *ka*, the unreal qualification by *ka*-ness and so forth has no utility for the comprehension of meaning. Thus, having accepted the unitary nature of the word (*śabda*), the objection was refuted. Now, he refutes it by not accepting that [unitary nature], stating: "the unitary nature of the word. To the question "Why?", he says: "of the letter *ga* and so forth. By the word "single" (*eka*), the word that is unitary in form is excluded; however, this does not apply to sounds such as the noise of a drum.

That [sound], however, is precisely the letter *ga* and so forth, whose specific forms have not yet been manifested. For they have explained that the letters themselves possess the capacity to convey meaning, stating: "Now, what is the word in the case of 'gauḥ'? It is the *ga*, the *au*, and the *visarjanīya*—thus says the venerable Upavarṣa. [Objection: But surely, on the authority of the scripture which states, "In each of those [subtle elements] there is only that [respective quality]; therefore, the state of being a *tanmātra* (pure element) is traditionally taught," one must accept a single, uniform sound-essence (*śabdatanmātra*). How then can that be rejected? [Reply: It is not so.

This is because the qualities of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which serve as the causes of the gross elements, cannot be perceived by the senses; for it is only the qualities of the fivefold-compounded (*pañcīkṛta*) gross elements that are perceptible to the senses. Furthermore, the state of the subtle elements is like the state of milk prior to its transformation into curds; the sound-subtle-element (*śabda-tanmātra*), which is the quality of space, does not exist after the creation of gross space.

Just as it is improper to claim that in the third great element, fire (*tejas*), there exists some "form-merely" (*rūpatanmātra*) apart from white, black, and other colors, and that these [colors] like white and black—which actually reside in the manifesting agents—are superimposed upon a single form; so too, it is improper for those who follow the scriptures propounding creation to accept the existence of a single form (*ekarūpa*) here, or that qualities such as *katva* (the property of being *ka*) and *svatva* (the property of being *sa*) residing in the manifesting agents are superimposed upon it.

In this regard, the intended meaning is as follows: Is a single, uniform sound, transcending the individual phonemes (*varṇa*), accepted because it is clearly perceived, or on the strength of conceptual construction? It cannot be the first, because nothing distinct from the phonemes such as *ga* and so forth is ever apprehended. Nor can it be the second, because there is no basis for such a construction.

Now, one might argue that since the denotative capacity of individual phonemes is untenable, and since the cognition "this is one word" and so forth is not possible with respect to the phonemes, and because of the recurring cognition "this is a word, this is a word" despite the phonemes being distinct, the existence of the *padaspota*—the word as a whole distinct from the phonemes—is established; and by that same logic, the existence of the *vākyaspota*—the sentence as a whole distinct from the collection of words—is also established. To this, he replies with the words "of the letter *ga*, etc. It is the phonemes themselves, such as *ga* and the rest, when combined, that possess the denotative capacity.

The cognition that "this is one word" or "this is one sentence" has as its object a collection of phonemes; furthermore, the recurring cognition "this is sound, this is sound" is based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being perceivable by the auditory organ. Therefore, since the grounds for postulation (*kalpaka*) are established otherwise, the meaning is that a single, unitary form of "sound" is not proven.

But surely, the assumption of a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is not established as an alternative explanation. To explain: first of all, each individual phoneme cannot be the expressive agent (*vācaka*), because that would render the other phonemes useless, and because a cow, a gavaya, an elephant, and so forth, are not cognized by the letter *ga* alone. Nor can a collection of phonemes be the expressive agent; for since phonemes uttered and heard in a sequence lack simultaneity, it is impossible for there to be a recollection of the phonemes as a collective object—just as one cannot perceive a "collection" in trees and the like [when they appear sequentially].

Nor is it logical to maintain that the final phoneme, assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the hearing of each preceding phoneme, is the signifier (*vācaka*); for the impressions generated by the experience of the phonemes serve as causes for the recollection of those experienced phonemes, and thus, lacking the capacity to cause the cognition of a different, unexperienced object, they are ineffective. Furthermore, a final phoneme devoid of such assistance cannot possibly convey meaning. Likewise, because the phonemes are distinct, the cognition "this is one word" must necessarily have an entity beyond [the individual phonemes] as its object.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the cognition of oneness to have a composite as its object—like the cognition of a forest or an army—because, unlike the case of being connected to a single location and so forth, there is no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that serves as a basis for unification. If it is argued that "being mounted upon a single memory" is the limiting adjunct, we say no; for we observe many things—such as "two words," "three words," or "many sentences"—being mounted upon a single cognition. Nor is a word a collection of phonemes delimited by a single meaning; for since it is impossible for phonemes themselves to be expressive, they lack the capacity to convey a single meaning.

Furthermore, since the recurring term "sound" (*śabda*)—as in "this is sound," "that is sound"—applies across many phonemes (*varṇa*), it is logical that this word "sound" has as its object a referent distinct from the phonemes themselves. For instance, although there is a difference between a jar, a water-pot, a room, and so forth, the word "space" (*ākāśa*), which refers to a single entity, is observed to have as its object a referent distinct from the jar, the water-pot, and the like. Nor is it reasonable to maintain that the recurrence of the word "sound" is due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being perceivable by the sense of hearing; for the sense of hearing cannot perceive itself, and even the state of being perceivable by the sense of hearing cannot be grasped by the sense of hearing through any means of knowledge (*yoga*).

If the quality of being perceivable by the auditory organ were cognized through another means of knowledge, the immediate perception of sound would be untenable. Therefore, since there is no other way to account for this (anyathāsiddhi) that serves as a basis for such a conceptualization, the word is something distinct from the phonemes; it is the sphoṭa.

To this it is replied: First of all, the existence of the *sphoṭa* is not established by the impossibility of the phonemes (*varṇa*) being expressive. Even if they were manifestors of the *sphoṭa*, the objection and its refutation would be identical [to those regarding expressiveness]; therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more reasonable to accept that the phonemes themselves are the expressive agents. For instance: first, a single phoneme cannot be the manifester of the *sphoṭa*, because the second phoneme would then be redundant, and because it would follow that the *sphoṭa* of words such as *gavaya* would be manifested by the letter *ga* alone. Nor can a collection of phonemes be the manifester; [because such a collection does not exist as a real entity].

Because phonemes heard in successive utterances lack simultaneity, their existence as a collective whole is untenable. Nor can the final phoneme, assisted by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding phoneme, be the manifestor [of the sphoṭa]; for impressions born from the experience of phonemes serve only as causes for the recollection of those experienced phonemes, and it is impossible for them to be causes for the cognition of an unexperienced sphoṭa. Consequently, the final phoneme—unaided by those impressions—cannot be its manifestor.

If it should be argued that the word is indeed perceived, and therefore a cause corresponding to that perception must be postulated—then it is logical that even mental impressions (*saṃskāras*), though occurring sequentially, can produce an effect simultaneously; for we observe the recollection "those two jars" even when two jars have been seen in succession.

Therefore, either the final phoneme accompanied by the simultaneous destruction of the preceding phonemes, or the collection of all phonemes being remembered simultaneously, is the manifestor of the *sphoṭa*. If this is so, then let it be accepted that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*)—which was already admitted as the manifestor of the *sphoṭa*—is itself the manifestor of the meaning; for the objection and its resolution are identical in both cases.

Because that which is established otherwise (anyathāsiddha) cannot lead to the postulation of another entity, and because when the denotative capacity can belong to the phonemes alone, the postulation of something additional is untenable due to the superior force of the principle of parsimony (lāghava-nyāya). Furthermore, even though the phonemes are distinct, the cognition of a single word—arising from the fact that a collection of multiple phonemes ending in a single case-suffix is present simultaneously in the intellect—does not itself lead to the postulation of another entity. Nor is there a circular argument (anyonyāśraya) such that the unity of the word follows from the unity of the meaning, and the unity of the meaning follows from the unity of the word.

Because it is certain that a collection of phonemes ending in a single case-suffix constitutes a single word; for the definition of a word is indeed "that which ends in a suffix (*sup* or *ti*). And if this [definition] possesses the intended meaning [of the opponent], there would be no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Alternatively, a word is a collection of phonemes employed for the purpose of conveying a single meaning established through a single linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Furthermore, the cognition "this is a word, this is a word" regarding many phonemes is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) as being based on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of their being perceivable by the auditory organ; thus, there is no establishment of a separate entity [such as "word-ness"].

Nor does the state of being graspable by the ear require apprehension by the ear itself, just as white, black, and yellow colors—which are visual—require the eye for the cognition of their visual nature. Furthermore, the conventional usage "this is visual" or "this is visual" is based precisely on the cognition of visual nature. The cognition that something is visual or auditory occurs because it is the object of a cognition that conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the eye, ear, and so forth, as understood through other means of knowledge. Indeed, people do not suddenly recognize [an object] as "this is sound."

First, once a sound has been determined in the form of the letter *ga* and so forth, it is understood as "sound" only through the prior recollection of the conventional linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, just as there is a delay caused by the recollection mediated by the sound itself, even the delay in the auditory inference [of the sound] is not distinguished from the rapidity produced by the proficiency of practice. Consequently, it is established that a word (*pada*) is simply a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), and a sentence (*vākya*) is simply a collection of words.

He concludes the refutation of the realization of truth from what is unreal with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). With the intention that the scripture possesses the same kind of truth as that which is found in those things regarded as true among the causes for realizing truth, he raises an objection with "nanu" (but surely). By the phrase "like a sky-flower," it was indeed stated that there is a sublation by reasoning; however, it does not mean that it is currently perceived as non-existent by ordinary people. Therefore, the meaning is that it does not possess that [kind of] unreality. He states the reason: "because it is cognizable by the intellect of the wise."

The meaning is that it is precisely the state of being "existent" (*sat*)—as that which is to be known—that is conducive to its being an effect, not [its] reality (*satyatva*). To the objection that this would then result in the destruction of the non-duality of the Existent (*sadadvaita*), he says: "having arisen. To the objection that it would then not be a means of knowledge, he says: "not then. He refutes this by saying: "it is not so. The meaning is that even at the time of the means (*upāya*), reality does not exist [in that sense]. Since knowledge is false because its object is false, and since knowledge is rooted in a defect (*doṣa*), he provides an illustration for the falsity of the object by saying: "just as..."

Previously, a refutation was stated by accepting the absence of subsequent sublation (*paścāttanabādhādarśana*). Now, he says "subsequently" (*paścāt*) to show that such [sublation] does not even exist. He establishes this with the words "empty" (*śūnyam*). He raises an objection with "that" (*tat*), suggesting that both the statement and its validity are established through delusion (*bhrānti*). He states their equality with "this too" (*etad api*). He explains that the claim that the absence of subsequent sublation is a cause for validity is a proof only for the proponent of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyavādin*); for beyond that, since there is no object to be negated, no negation can arise—thus he says "subsequent" (*pāścātya*).

The fact that validity and so forth are rooted in defects is equal for both [the proponent and the opponent]; however, the point is that the absence of subsequent sublation (*bādhā*) is an additional requirement for the Proponent of Emptiness (*śūnyavādin*). If it is argued that even for the Proponent of Universal Emptiness there is a further negation—namely, that the statement "everything exists" is indeed its negation—then, by parity of reasoning, the statement regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would also constitute a negation of the statement regarding the reality of the phenomenal world. If it is claimed that only the statement "it does not exist" constitutes a negation, then that [negation] belongs exclusively to the Proponent of Emptiness; such is the sense.

And this invalidity of the Vedas is common to both the Mṛṣāvādins (the Mīmāṃsakas) and the Saugatas (Buddhists). As they say: "The Veda is false; the scripture composed by the Buddha is false; the authority of this [Veda] and that [Buddhist scripture] is false;
the Buddha is false, and likewise the fruit of his awakening is false; thus you [Mīmāṃsakas] and the Buddhists sit together in the same assembly."

If it is argued that there is a great disparity between us because the authority of the scripture consists in the reality of its subject matter, we say no. Do you intend the reality of only some parts of the subject matter, or the reality of the subject matter in its entirety? The reality of some parts of the subject matter exists even in the Buddha’s scriptures, since such things as the self-luminosity of consciousness are admitted by both sides. However, you do not accept the reality of the entire subject matter even for the Veda. Furthermore, the reality of the subject matter is difficult to define.
This is because Brahman, which is accepted as being real, is not admitted to be an object of [empirical] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for the argument that in the statement "The sacrificial post is the sun," the identity of the post and the sun is not being taught due to the absence of indicators of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*), rather than due to the superior force of perception—it must be admitted that the absence of indicators of intention is indeed present there. Consequently, the inability to convey a meaning that is not contradicted by perception becomes unavoidable. For Vedāntins do not abandon the authority of the *arthavāda* and other such passages regarding their own literal sense simply because they are intent on something else.

Since you yourselves have established that even *mantras* and *arthavādas* possess authority regarding their own literal meaning, the claim that the identity of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun is not being propounded because [the passage] is intended as praise is a contradiction of your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). If it is asked: "How can there be no propounding of the identity of the sacrificial post and the sun if *arthavādas* do indeed possess authority regarding their own meaning?"—it is replied: Non-contradiction with other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is an indicator of the intended purport (*tātparya-liṅga*). Indeed, novelty (*apūrvatva*) in the beginning and conclusion, etc., has also been stated as an indicator of purport, according to the principle: "Repetition, novelty, and result [are indicators]."

Novelty (*apūrvatva*) consists in being beyond the scope of any means of valid cognition that could either establish or refute it, as they have said: "By the word 'not proximate' (*asannikṛṣṭa*), two things are here intended to be excluded: determination [of the object] through its identity [with what is already known], or [determination] through its opposite."

Therefore, because the indicative mark of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*)—characterized by being beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition—is absent here, there is no teaching of the identity between the sacrificial post and the sun; it is not, however, because of a lack of authority regarding its own literal meaning due to being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Thus, what is called the "absence of the indicative mark of purport" ultimately results from contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge; consequently, scripture is not capable of establishing a meaning that contradicts them. He concludes the refutation of the superiority of scripture with the word "enough" (*alam*).

Alternatively, with the words "enough" (*alam*), he concludes the refutation of the opponent's position established through the *Nyāyamukha* beginning with "that which is perception" (*yattu pratyakṣam*). Reasoning that contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is "fallacious reasoning" (*kutarka*). For this very reason, it is "unfounded. It is to be treated with derision because it employs arguments consistent with the Buddhist doctrine, which is itself self-contradictory.

By one who asserts that scripture (*śāstra*) is stronger even than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), scripture—regarded as the stronger authority—is placed first, and only subsequently is reasoning (*tarka*) set forth. In our own established position (*siddhānta*), however, we first examine the operation of worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*) which are regarded as stronger; then, having refuted the fallacious reasoning (*dustarka*) propounded by others, we reject the claim that scripture possesses superior authority when it contradicts worldly means of valid cognition.

By demonstrating the incapacity of the scripture to propound meanings that contradict worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is established in a general sense that the scripture has as its purport that which possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣa*). Furthermore, by demonstrating that the scripture has as its purport that which possesses distinctions through the specific operation of words in the form of *pada*s and *vākya*s, the fact that the scripture has as its purport that which possesses distinctions is established in a general sense.

Furthermore, regarding those specific statements cited by the opponent as being intended to establish the absence of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), he begins to demonstrate—by means of an examination of the purport of the sentences—that they are actually intended to establish the presence of attributes (*saviśeṣa*), starting with the words "As for what was said," and so forth. In that context, he restates briefly the claim of their being intended to establish the absence of attributes with the words "As for what was said. The state of being without attributes is established in the purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*) through the realization of the essence of pure consciousness; and that same state is also established in the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*).

By the term "mere object" (*vastumātra*), the absence of intent regarding anything other than the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahman*) elsewhere is indicated. When it is said "and so forth," since that [phrase] would terminate in that very Upaniṣad, the expression "and such as these" is used in order to exclude that. He refutes that, saying, "That is incorrect. To the question "Why?", he says: "By the knowledge of one [thing]. By the passage beginning with "By which the unheard becomes heard," the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one thing is proposed.

This is its meaning: by means of that which is heard, thought, and known, what has not been heard, thought, and known becomes heard, thought, and known; it does not mean that everything becomes known through the existence (*sattā*) of Brahman. This follows from the force of the illustrative example and the force of the example of clay. For an effect is not known through the existence of Brahman, nor through the existence of a lump of clay.

This is because of the scriptural statements in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known? and in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "When the Self, which is the Lord of all, has been seen, heard, reflected upon, and realized, all this becomes known. Therefore, the meaning of the proposition is exactly as stated.

Indeed, since the cognition of a cloth cannot arise from the cognition of a jar, one might suspect that "the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is impossible. To address this doubt, [the text] states, "As, my dear," showing that such a relationship is observed between cause and effect. Even there, by means of the doctrine of *asatkāryavāda* (the theory that the effect is non-existent in the cause), it dispels the suspicion regarding the impossibility of knowing everything through the knowledge of one, with the words, "A mere modification of speech. Here, the word "speech" (*vāk*)—by means of a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*)—refers to worldly activity preceded by speech. By the instrumental case in "by speech" (*vācā*), the status of being a cause is intended in the sense of being the purpose.

The word *ārambhaṇa* is derived from the root with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*); thus, *ārambhaṇam* means that which is begun or touched (*ālabhyate*). According to the rule "touching (*ālambha*) occurs in the senses of contact and injury," it is established by implication that [the clay] is touched by means of a lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍena*). "Modification" (*vikāra*) refers to states such as being a jar or being a substance. For the purpose of linguistic conventions such as naming and discarding preceded by speech, name and form are touched by means of the lump of clay; the meaning is that the lump of clay becomes possessed of name and form. He states the proof for the identity of substance between cause and effect: "Only 'clay' is real."

The meaning is that, by means of the recognition "the clay is the pot," even things such as pots made of clay are established as validly real only as the substance *mṛd* (clay). Differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth are observed among pots and the like even when there is a difference in substance; however, in cases such as "he sits," "he lies down," "I am happy," or "I am miserable," they are observed even when there is identity of substance. Therefore, these [differences] are common [to both cases].

The point here is this: just as in cases such as "I sit there" or "I lie down," the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that determines the identity of the substance is the very same one that determines the identity of the substance here as well. If it were intended here that only the clay is ultimately real while its modifications are unreal, then the word *iti* would be redundant; for in that case, one should simply have said, "the clay alone is real. Furthermore, regarding the unreality of the modification, the illustrative example would be deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because [in the example] the reality [of the clay] is already established.

If it is argued that the reality of the jar and so forth is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), then the reality of the lump of clay would likewise be merely conventional, and thus the reality of the cause is not established. If it is maintained that the cause possesses only conventional reality, then that would apply equally to the jar and other effects as well. Since the substance of the effect and the cause are one, let it be granted that the knowledge of the effect is possible through the knowledge of the cause.

Nevertheless, since one observes in the world that various classes of effects have various respective material causes, there arises the doubt that the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of One is untenable. In response to this doubt, [the scripture] declares that Brahman is the sole cause of the universe: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1). With reference to the meaning of the word *sat* (Being) occurring in the Śruti, the phrase "of that which is denoted by the word *sat*" has been stated here. With the intention that it would be difficult to offer an alternative explanation by claiming this refers to the Saguna-Brahman (Brahman with attributes), the phrase "of the Supreme Brahman" has been used. The meaning is "prior to the creation of the world."

Because creation will be discussed immediately hereafter, if one intends to exclude the diversity inherent within [Brahman] itself, as well as its difference from things of the same and different classes, then it would be improper to say "in the beginning" (*agre*). For Brahman does not possess a state of being devoid of distinctions at any particular time; furthermore, in order to avoid the charge of partiality and cruelty (*vaiṣamya-nairghṛṇya*), one must admit the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*), the stream of their karma, and the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of that stream. If it is argued that this plurality is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then since even now there is an absence of ultimate plurality, the word "in the beginning" would be redundant.

Nor is the word "supreme" (agra) intended to be devoid of meaning, because creation is mentioned immediately thereafter. Therefore, since at that time there exists difference from dissimilar things in the form of Time, difference from similar things in the form of sentient beings, and internal difference consisting of qualities such as omniscience conducive to creation, it is contradictory [to claim] that the text aims to negate the three kinds of difference—dissimilar and so forth—because it is a statement concerning the cause.

If this were not a statement regarding the cause, then because such statements are understood as negating all other possible causes, they would lack the status of being statements about a cause by virtue of their intent to exclude heterogeneous and other alternatives; consequently, Brahman’s status as the cause would be without authority. This is because we observe a rule that the particle *eva*, which expresses restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), invariably excludes what is incompatible with the meaning of the other words uttered in proximity to it, since it is itself incapable of presenting any specific thing to be excluded. Thus, the restriction "Being alone" (*sadeva*) is intended to eliminate the doctrine that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*).

For this restriction—that "this one is indeed wise"—does not exclude the state of being a Brāhmaṇa, but rather excludes only the state of being ignorant. Therefore, by the natural force of the words, that which is to be negated by the phrase "Being alone" (sadeva) is precisely unreality (asatya), and not a difference consisting of a different class (vijātīyabheda). Even though unreality is of a different class from Being, its status as something to be excluded is not by way of its being a different class, but rather by way of its being the opposite of Being. The meaning is: "It is Being alone, and never non-being."

For the word *sat* (Being) functions with reference to the Supreme Self by taking as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) existence characterized by fitness for connection with the mind. Although this word *sat* denotes the Supreme Self as the substantive, it brings to mind the Supreme Self as having Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Kāla as His body, qualified by those attributes conducive to causality, by virtue of its capacity to have the Cause as its object. By the phrase "one alone," Brahman is spoken of in His causal state, wherein name and form are undifferentiated.

In the state of being the cause, the restriction to the form of *etad* (this) refers to the unity that serves as the counter-correlative to the multiplicity of the body about to be created—as expressed in the thought, "May I be many"—and this is supported by the force of the illustration given in the passage, "By means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay [is known]. Furthermore, this is the very same meaning because it accords with the sense of another scriptural passage: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest; it became manifest through name and form. The particle *eva* (only/alone) intends the dissolution even of ether and the other elements which the Vaiśeṣikas and others describe as eternal.

Thus, because name and form were undifferentiated, Brahman’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) is established. For being the material cause consists in the connection with a prior state of that which possesses a subsequent specific state. The phrase "without a second" excludes any other instrumental cause (*nimitta*); this is because the material cause is the subject under discussion and thus the instrumental cause is what comes to mind. Furthermore, since specific dependent forms have been enjoined, and a prohibition refers to things other than those enjoined, and because the consistency with the subsequent passages requires it.

The fact that the word "one alone" (ekam eva) refers to the state of name and form being undifferentiated is understood from the phrase "may I be many. From the passage "It thought... It created fire," it is understood that the term "without a second" (advitīya) refers to the absence of any other efficient cause. That the restriction "Being alone" (sadeva) is intended to exclude the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (asatkāryavāda), because the Supreme Brahman exists at all times, is understood from the subsequent statement, "How could Being be born from Non-being? and so forth.

The passage beginning with "How [could there be] of that which is non-existent? is intended for the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika position; it is not, however, intended for the refutation of the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), nor for the refutation of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). This is because even when the refutations of momentariness and emptiness have been carried out, the knowledge of all things through a single knowledge remains dependent upon the refutation of the Vaiśeṣika position. Furthermore, it begins with the statement: "On this point, some say: 'In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. Indeed, neither momentariness nor emptiness occurs at any particular time.

Therefore, the passage beginning with "On this point, some say... is intended to refute the doctrine that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*). The meaning of the statement, "How indeed, O gentle one, could it be so? is that since what is produced from clay has clay as its essence, it would follow that what is produced from a non-entity must have a non-entity as its essence. Furthermore, the fact that production is simply a substance attaining another state—this point was already taught by the phrase "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*)—is relied upon here when it is said, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? This means: how could there be the arising of something without a substratum?

By the phrase "He thought," omniscience is expressed; by "He created," the status of being the efficient cause (nimitta); by "May I become many," the status of being the material cause (upādāna); and by "possessing all powers" and "having true resolve," qualities consistent with both of those [causal roles] are stated. Furthermore, by the words "Having entered with this living self," its state of being the innermost essence of all is declared. The phrase "with this living self" means "by me, having the individual soul as my body. This is analogous to the expression: "Having become a lion, many were eaten by me; having become a tiger, many were eaten by me."

Because it is impossible for that which possesses qualities such as omniscience to be identical with a soul whose nature is the opposite, and because of scriptural statements such as "whose body is the Self," and because of the hearing of an entry [of Brahman] into the soul—just as into the non-intelligent—in the passage "having entered into that," and because it is logical that a word denoting a body has its primary meaning in the embodied one; this alone is the correct sense. By the phrase "having the Existent as their support," the state of being the substratum of all is established, and from that very fact, the governance of all is also established.

"O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, heaven and earth stand held apart"—since it is heard that its nature as a sustainer is due to such command. Thus, through the characteristics of being the substratum of all, the ruler of all, and the innermost of all, Brahman is described as having the universe as its body. By the word "etcetera," qualities established in other Śrutis that are conducive to creation are included. By the phrase "this is its essence" (aitadātmyam), the identity of the entire universe with That is understood.

"That is Truth"—by this very fact of being of that nature (*tadātmakatva*), the world possesses its authoritative status. The meaning is that the perception of the world as being self-subsistent is an error. Therefore, He is the Self of the entire world. The designation, "All this has that as its Self; He is the Self," is made like the expression "Rāma’s younger brother Lakṣmaṇa and his elder brother," intended to emphasize their mutual relationship.

Alternatively, the meaning is that because you are the inner controller (*antar-yāmin*) of the entire universe, as in the passage, "That is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal," your Self is "He. Therefore, the words *tvam* (you), their referent, and the cognition thereof culminate in Him; this is the meaning of the phrase *tattvamasi*. He states "of such a nature" (*evambhūta*) to indicate that the word *tat* refers back to what has been previously mentioned.

In this Sadvidyā, the six marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*) are found precisely in regard to a qualified entity (*saviśeṣa-vastu*). First, regarding the introduction: in the passage, "But have you asked for that instruction (*ādeśa*)? (*uta tam ādeśam aprākṣyaḥ*), the word *ādeśa* denotes the Ruler (*praśāsitṛ*). On this point, two verses were spoken by the venerable Ācārya: "In the *Chāndogya*, some say that in the phrase 'But have you asked for that instruction,' the prefix *ā-* reveals the sense of 'teaching' (*upadeśa*); [however,] the form ending in *ghañ* does not denote one who rules over the existent. (*chāndogye kecidāhurdiśatiḥ / uta tamādeśamaprākṣya ityatrāṅpūrvastūpadeśaṃ prakaṭayati sato na praśāsti ghañantaḥ //*).

In this [system], when the agent is not expressed, the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed for the object; thus, in the teaching (*śāsti*), there would be no object. However, when that object is taught, it is to be taught by means of the term "substitute" (*ādeśa*). This is what has been stated.

To this we reply: "The Teacher (Śāstṛ) commands and speaks; he does not give instruction while facing downward. He is the one well-known as the Teacher, for there is no other here in the context of the matter intended.

It is appropriate [to use] the uncommon form with the suffix *ghañ* even when the instrument (*karaṇa*) is meant; indeed, the status of the factors of action (*kāraka*) as expressed by grammar is determined by intention (*vaivakṣikatva*), and thus there may be an intention to express the agent (*kartṛ*) by means of the instrument. Thus it is said.

By the word *ādeśa*, that which is to be taught (*upadeśya*) is expressed. The meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*) is "instruction" (*upadeśa*); the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*) is "object-ness" (*karmatva*), because the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed [by Pāṇini] in the rule "also when there is a case-role other than the agent, provided it is a name" (*akartari ca kārake saṃjñāyām*), since Brahman is appropriately the object in the act of instruction. However, in the act of ruling (*praśāsana*), Brahman is not the object, but rather the agent. For the prescription of the suffix *ghañ* applies to a case-role other than the agent. In this context, the suffix *kap* in the sense of the agent is not appropriate.

"And why? Because, due to the prohibition of *guṇa*, the verbal form [of the root] would not be established as an *ādeśa* (substitute). Nor is the addition of the suffix *ac* (as in *pac-ādi-ac*) appropriate; since the root *diś* has a *g* in its penultimate syllable (*igupadha*), the restrictive rule "after a root with a *g* in the penultimate syllable, the suffix *ka* is added" (*igupadhāt kaḥ*) applies, resulting in the suffix *ka* and thus precluding *guṇa*. Therefore, this word *ādeśa* must end in the suffix *ghañ*. Since that suffix is prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), it is more logical that it refers to the object (*karman*); thus, that which is to be taught (*upadeśya*) is precisely what is denoted by the word *ādeśa*. To this, it is replied: the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is "instruction" (*śāsana*).

Because of the abundance of established usage; otherwise, there would be a violation of the natural sense [of the words]. For the author of the Nyāsa states: "The root *diś* preceded by *ā* denotes the purpose of the one who enjoins (*niyoktṛ*), whereas preceded by *upa*, it denotes the purpose of the one who is enjoined (*niyojya*). The meaning is that it expresses the object whose purpose lies with the enjoiner. The same applies elsewhere as well. Furthermore, the state of being taught (*upadeśyatva*) is common to the worldly, the unworldly, ritual action, and the portion concerning Brahman; however, the state of being an instructor (*śāsitṛtva*) is unique to Brahman.

Because of scriptural statements such as "The Teacher has entered within the people" and "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable," it is heard that unconditioned sovereignty is unique to Brahman. If it is argued that being the object of unconditioned instruction is unique to Brahman, we say no; for that [quality] is common to the attainment of the desired, the avoidance of the undesired, and the means thereto.

Even if the attainment of immeasurable happiness, the cessation of suffering, and so forth were to be taught directly, nevertheless, the status of being an object of instruction is common to the cessation of saṃsāra, Brahman, and the meditation upon Him. Since it is logically established that whatever is to be inquired about must be an object of instruction, the mention of "being an object of instruction" is redundant.

If it is argued that, because of its syntactic unity with the statement "by which the unheard becomes heard," the quality of being the object of instruction—qualified as the cause for knowing other things through one's own knowledge—is unique [to Brahman], even so, such a status of being the object of instruction is already established by the statement of the promise (*pratijñā*) and by the mention of what is to be questioned; therefore, rather than stating this unnecessary quality of being the object of instruction, it is more logical that the required quality of being the Ruler (*praśāsitṛtva*) should be expressed. For once the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is established by the phrase "by which the unheard becomes heard," the status of being the instrumental cause (*nimittatva*) is indeed established through the quality of being the Ruler.

Since it is not possible for a single cognition to be a cognition of all things when there are distinct objective causes (nimitta), it is appropriate to explain the object intended to be communicated precisely as it is characterized by its intended, unique form.

Since the suffix *ghañ* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), such usage is justified by the maxim stated in the *Śabdakaustubha*, "The application of grammatical relations (*kārakas*) proceeds according to the speaker's intention," when one intends to express the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) in the agent (*kartṛ*) itself, independent of any other instrument. The purpose of the rule *akartari ca kārake...* is to prevent the use of such forms as agents when they lack the intended sense of being an instrument, as it would otherwise be ungrammatical.

In the case of the "instruction" (upadeśa) interpretation, there is a lack of natural fitness for the meaning of the root and a natural fitness for the suffix; whereas in the "ruling" (praśāsana) interpretation, there is a lack of natural fitness for the suffix, but a natural fitness for the meaning of the root—which is the primary element—as well as the appropriateness of the sense. Therefore, it is proper to accept that the one who rules alone is denoted by the word "ādeśa. Thus, at the outset, the connection with the attribute of unconditioned ruling has been stated. Likewise, its being the material cause of the world, its being the efficient cause, and its possession of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, which are consistent with those [attributes], have been understood.

Furthermore, in the concluding section, through the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the specific attribute consisting of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is taught. Since this very meaning is repeated many times, there is also the quality of repetition (*abhyāsa*). Thus, because qualities such as Brahman’s being the cause of the world and its being the inner self of the world are not established by any other means of knowledge, the quality of novelty (*apūrvatā*) is established.

Likewise, for the lay follower (*upāsaka*), there is indeed a fruit, because liberation is heard to occur immediately after the fall of the body in the words: "For him, it will be long only until he is released; then he shall attain [perfection]. Furthermore, since this takes the form of a reply from a father to his son, it is established as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And because it is supported by the presentation of analogies such as the lump of clay, it is also established as a logical argument (*upapatti*).

In these three illustrations as well, no illustration whatsoever is seen that is consistent with the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); rather, only those consistent with the theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*) are seen. Even in the scriptural passage concerning the subject of the illustration, it is stated, "He created fire from that," and not, "It became fire through delusion. Therefore, there is no occasion for the theory of illusory manifestation even in this scripture. In other scriptures as well, such as "He made himself his own self," it is heard; but not, "It manifested falsely. And the Sūtra says, "Because of transformation" (*pariṇāmāt*).

But it is not [the case that it arises] from an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). For in the *Smṛtis*, in passages such as, "Just as gold is held to be non-different even when appearing through distinctions such as bracelets, crowns, and earrings, so too are the atoms of the earth's surface [non-different] at the end of the wind," only the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is observed. Therefore, in accordance with the natural sense of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Sūtra*, transformation alone must be accepted. Furthermore, that transformation must necessarily be mediated by an intermediate state, because of the natural sense of numerous *Śruti* passages concerning the changelessness (*nirvikāratva*), faultlessness (*nirdoṣatva*), the entry [of the Lord into matter], and the relationship between the body and the embodied (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting those texts.

To the doubt—namely, what is the statement asserting that through one consciousness all consciousnesses [are known], and how is that established—he says "it has been explained in detail" (*prapañcita*), meaning that this is set forth at length in the *Vedārthasaṅgraha*. To the question of how the required meaning will be understood here, he says "even here" (*atrāpi*); the sense is that this section is more skillfully treated because its sole subject matter is precisely this point.

He states that the supreme knowledge (*paravidyā*) just cited refers to that which possesses attributes (*saviśeṣa*), beginning with the words "Now, the other... and ending with the phrase "...without hands or feet. He specifies the scope of these words by saying "the natural" (*prākṛtān*). "Natural" means related to *prakṛti*; by this, it is shown that the objects of negation must have some established existence somewhere, according to the principle that "negation occurs only of something that has been established somewhere. Furthermore, the defects residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) are "natural," as they are occasioned by contact with *prakṛti*.

It is invisible, ungraspable, beyond the range of direct perception, and beyond the range of inference and other means of knowledge; or rather, it is not within the range of the eye nor within the range of the other sense organs. It is without lineage (gotra) and without color (varṇa), being devoid of ordinary name and form. It is without eyes or ears; its knowledge is not dependent upon the senses. It is without hands or feet; its activity is not dependent upon the senses, according to the Vedic revelation: "Without hands or feet, yet swift and grasping; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears."

By these two lines, the negation of what is to be abandoned as pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) is established; for dependence on the senses for knowledge and dependence on them for activity are indeed attributes of the *jīva*.
