Although the textual order is "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*) and "extremely subtle" (*susūkṣma*), it has nevertheless been explained according to the logical order as "subtlety" and "all-pervasiveness. For pervasion is [achieved] through subtlety. Through eternity, there is no limitation by time. By the term "the all-pervasive Lord" (*vibhum prabhum*), sovereignty—which is the state of being a controller—is implied, resulting in the fact that He has the universe as His body.

By this, the non-limitation of substance (*vastu*) is established; through omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), there is the non-limitation of space (*deśa*). "Imperishability" (*avyayatva*) refers to the quality (*guṇa*) consisting in being the opposite of those defects indicated by the word "decay" (*vyaya*); with this intention, it is mentioned together with "auspicious qualities. Alternatively, imperishability means having a single form (*ekarūpatva*) or fullness (*pūrṇatva*). "Being the source of beings" (*bhūtayonitva*) means being the cause of the world; omniscience (*sārvajñya*) is stated by the sentence "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," which occurs in this very context.

The meaning is that the Omniscient One, the All-Knowing One, knows everything by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and knows everything by way of its specific modes (*prakāra*). The phrase "of the Supreme Brahman" has the same meaning as previously explained.

Now, regarding the purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*), he refutes the claim that the statement "Truth, Knowledge, etc. (*satyaṃ jñānam*... possesses an undivided meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*) by means of the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge... This [objection] was indeed presented by the venerable teacher for the sake of ease of comprehension. For it is as follows: the sentence beginning with "Truth" teaches Brahman as qualified precisely by attributes such as truthfulness; because in co-referential sentences (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*) such as "The lotus is blue," there is the established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) that they have a single qualified object as their purport, and because the sentence beginning with "Truth" is likewise co-referential.

Furthermore, the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has been stated by the Grammarians as "of those [words] having different grounds for application," and so forth. In this regard, it has been argued that since coreferentiality is understood to mean "having a single referent" (*ekārthya*), and since such a single referent is not established if the words refer merely to qualifiers or if they refer to qualified entities, one must accept that the words in the coreferential expression "Being" (*satya*), etc., refer to the oneness of their own essential nature (*svarūpa-mātra-ekya*). This is incorrect, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*).

It must be investigated whether the words such as "Truth" (*satya*) and so forth refer merely to the exclusion of what is incompatible with their respective objects, or whether they refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone, or whether they refer to the essential nature as delimited by the exclusion of the incompatible. First of all, they do not refer merely to the exclusion of the incompatible; for since the things being excluded are many, the status of having a single referent is not established. Indeed, because the things to be excluded are many, the exclusions themselves would necessarily be many. Nor do they refer to the essential nature alone.

If that were the case, it would follow that the words are synonyms; furthermore, because there would be no difference in their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be lost, and one or the other word would become redundant. Nor can they be intended to express the essential nature (*svarūpa*) as delimited by those [exclusions], for this cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpa*). For is the exclusion of opposites a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the essential nature by way of being a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), or by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)?

The first alternative is not tenable, because if the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is apprehended by a single defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), then other defining characteristics would be redundant. For those who know defining characteristics maintain that a defining characteristic is a property distinct from the object to be defined (*upalakṣya*) which serves as the means for the cognition of that object. This is observed in cases such as branches and the like. Furthermore, [if only one were used], there would be the redundancy of one or the other; and due to the absence of a difference in the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), there would be a loss of the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If it is asked, "How then, in your position, is it accepted that a single Brahman alone possesses many designations such as 'birth' and so forth?"—it is replied: although the substrate (*dharmin*) to be designated, namely Brahman, is one in that context, we nevertheless accept that for each designation there is a distinct property (*dharma*) of the designated object, consisting of powers of knowledge and the like, which correspond to birth, maintenance, and so on. Otherwise, the multiplicity of designations would indeed result in being purposeless even in that case.

In your position, the aforementioned defect is unavoidable because you do not admit a distinction between the various qualifiers (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*upalakṣya*). For if such a distinction were admitted, it would follow that Brahman possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). Nor is the second alternative tenable; since the exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) functioning as qualifiers are manifold, they cannot establish a single referent. A qualifier is a property included within the qualified that serves as a means for the cognition of the qualified. "Inclusion within the qualified" means inclusion within that which is to be made known.

If it is argued that even though there is a difference in the meanings functioning as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the establishment of a single referent (*aikārthya*) follows from the unity of the primary meaning functioning as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then this is equally true for one who maintains that the sentence-meaning is composite (*sakhaṇḍavākyārthavādin*). If it is asked, "What then is the distinction between our two positions?", the distinction is precisely this: in the view of the one, the words possess a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇikatva*), whereas in the position of the other, they possess a primary sense (*mukhyatva*).

As for the claim that because another qualifier is connected to an object already qualified by a different qualifier, there follows the consequence of a mutual inherence (*anyonyasamavāya*) among the qualifiers—that is incorrect, because it cannot withstand logical analysis. For a sentence conveys its meaning through the following process: "The entire collection of words, when heard, recalls their meanings as unconnected; subsequently, once they have been made manifest by the application of logical reasoning (*nyāya*), they convey the meaning of the sentence. It is by this stated procedure that a sentence brings about the cognition of its meaning.

In this regard, does the contingency of mutual inherence (samavāya) among words arise at the stage of recollecting the word-meanings (*padārtha*), or at the stage of reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*), or perhaps at the stage of the expression of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)? It cannot be the first alternative; for at the stage of recollection, since the word-meanings are recollected individually, there is no contingency of mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Nor can it be the second.

This is because, when one reflects upon a thing as it actually exists, there is the apprehension—through perception and other means—of the co-inherence (*samavāya*) of multiple non-contradictory qualifiers within that single object. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable; for at the time of denoting the meaning of a sentence, since all the words simultaneously produce a single cognition whose object is a single entity qualified by multiple qualifiers, there is no possibility of the mutual co-inherence resulting from sequential denotation.

For just as two eyes simultaneously produce a single cognition whose object is one thing qualified by numerous qualifiers such as genus and quality, so too do multiple words simultaneously produce a single cognition whose object is one thing qualified by their respective qualifiers. Even if there were denotation in succession, there would be no contingency of mutual inherence (*samavāya*); for it is only the qualificandum portion presented by one word that is further qualified by the qualifier presented by another word.

And this is because the linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) of words has as its object that which has been previously perceived; otherwise, on your view, the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified among qualifiers in the form of exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) would be unavoidable, as it would be necessitated by their sequential denotation. Therefore, the aforementioned resolution is your only refuge as well. If it is asked: "If sequential denotation is not admitted, how can the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) be established?"—it is said in reply: the distinction between the subject and the predicate is indeed the distinction between the known and the unknown.

And this [defect] does not disappear even when there is simultaneous comprehension. When a single object is connected with multiple qualifiers by means of a single sentence such that they are comprehended simultaneously, at that time, the connection with one qualifier is already known while the connection with the other qualifiers is unknown; thus, the reflection upon the distinction between the known and the unknown is indeed possible at the stage of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

As for what was also stated—that in the communication of the identity of a qualified entity, the identity of the qualifiers necessarily follows as a consequence of the identity of the qualified—this too is not sound; for the identical case-ending has as its purport the identity of the qualified alone, and this is established by linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). And linguistic usage is rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, perception apprehends only the identity of the qualified, and not the identity of the qualifiers.

Just as even when a single word such as "cow" (gauh) is employed, the singular number inherent in it does not convey the identity between the qualifier and the qualified understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), but rather conveys only the identity of the qualified object—since in that case, the cause is indeed the linguistic usage rooted in perception (*pratyakṣamūlā vyutpattiḥ*)—so too, the identical case-ending residing within a collection of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is a regulator only by virtue of its intent toward the identity of the qualified objects alone.

Otherwise, on your own position as well, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the identity of the qualifiers in the form of the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of counter-correlates such as "unreal" (*asat*). If it is argued that—even though the nominal stems (*prātipadika*) refer to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) qualified by the exclusion of their respective counter-correlates—the identity of the qualifiers does not follow because of the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti*) whereby a common case-ending (*samānavibhakti*) expresses only the identity of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), which constitutes a single part of the meaning of the nominal stem, then that is equally true in our own position. As for the distinction between us two, it has already been stated previously.

As for the statement that "the difference of qualifiers entails the difference of the qualified," that is incorrect; for the mere difference of qualifiers does not necessarily cause a difference in the qualified. This is evident from cases such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," where, despite the difference in qualifiers, the identity of the qualified is observed. If it is argued that the inherent tendency of a difference in qualifiers to produce a difference in the qualified is set aside in those instances by perception, we say no; for identity is perceived there due to the unity of the word denoting the substratum and the use of the same grammatical case-ending.

If it is argued that in the case of "the broken-horned," "the shaven-headed," "the full-horned," and "the cow," although there is identity of the word denoting the substratum (*dharmī*) and the indication of a common case-ending, a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*) is perceived despite the difference in the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), this is not so; for the capacity of those two [words] to convey the identity of the qualified, which is obtained by its own nature, is sublated therein by perception.

If it is argued that in the case of objects beyond the senses, when sentences such as "the cow is hornless," "the cow is shorn," or "the cow has full horns" are employed, a difference in the substrate is perceived despite the difference in qualifiers such as "hornlessness" and so forth—then the same analysis applies: even in the case of objects beyond the senses, when sentences such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned" or "Devadatta is young" are employed, a unity of the substrate is perceived despite the difference in qualifiers such as "darkness" and so forth. Thus, the argument is equal on both sides.

As for the question "Who is the decider?": it is observed through perception that qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of a certain class invariably have distinct substrata (*bhinnāśrayatva*); even when such qualifiers are imperceptible (*parokṣa*), they bring about a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*), as in the case of "brokenness" (*khaṇḍatva*) and so forth. However, for qualifiers of another class where no rule of having distinct substrata is observed, it is logical that they serve to specify a single qualified entity when there is identity of the word denoting the subject (*dharmivācipada*) and the use of the same grammatical case (*samānavibhaktinirdeśa*), as in the case of "blueness" (*nīlatva*) and so forth.

As for the claim that the abandonment of the qualifier occurs because it contradicts the unity understood through the use of the same case-ending (*samānavibhakti*), that too is incorrect; for it would follow that one must abandon the unity itself due to the contradiction with the connection of the qualifiers denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). To explain: if unity cannot be abandoned simply because it is understood through the connection of the same case-ending, then how can the connection with the qualifiers established by the nominal stem be abandoned—as is the case in expressions such as "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*)?

If it is argued that [the identity] is accepted there because it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then why should the cognition of identity (*aikyapratīti*) not be exactly the same in that case? If it is argued that a verbal cognition of identity is observed even in the case of something remote (*parokṣa*) when expressed with a common case-ending (*samānavibhakti*), then it is exactly so; for even in the case of a remote object in usage, a cognition of the connection of the qualifiers understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is indeed observed. Therefore, if it is claimed that the cognition of identity is verbal (*śābdī*), then the cognition of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭapratīti*) is also verbal; there is no difference other than mere dogmatic insistence (*abhiniveśa*).

Furthermore, regarding the oneness apprehended through identical case-endings—which serves as the cause for abandoning the connection with the qualifiers understood from the nominal stem—is this oneness the very nature [of the object] itself, or is it something distinct from that? In the case of it being distinct, there follows the consequence of its having attributes (saviśeṣatva). In the case of it being non-distinct, the reason is unestablished (asiddhi), because no oneness whatsoever is established by the identical case-ending apart from the nature already apprehended by the nominal stem. Indeed, the abandonment of qualifiers does not occur merely due to a contradiction with the nature itself.

Because it would follow that [the distinction between essence and attributes] must be abandoned even in sentences with different grammatical subjects (*vyadhikaraṇa-vākya*). Having first asserted that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is devoid of distinctions, if one then says "because of the understanding of identity through the common case-ending," it would effectively be saying "because of the understanding of the essential nature. Consequently, the reason—namely, the contradiction with the understanding of identity—would be unestablished (*asiddhi*). For the essential nature is not incompatible with the connection of qualifiers; indeed, it is logical that in sentences with different grammatical subjects, there is an understanding of the connection of qualifiers.

Furthermore, since it has been stated that the identity apprehended through the use of the same case-ending belongs solely to the substantive (viśeṣya), which constitutes one part of the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika), and since that identity is not incompatible with the difference of its qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), it is not logical to abandon the qualifiers on the grounds of such incompatibility. Therefore, an entity cannot be devoid of qualifiers (nirviśeṣa).

In expressions such as "whiteness excluded from blackness" or "whiteness excluded from yellowness," there is no occasion for *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication), because the difference from the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) and the specific nature of each exclusion are conveyed directly by the words themselves. This is the distinction: it is not so in sentences such as "Truth, etc. (*satyādi*). Thus, the difference between the sentence providing the example of whiteness and the sentence providing the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—namely, the sentence beginning with "Truth"—has been explained in terms of the words. The difference in terms of the meaning (*artha*) should also be understood as previously stated. If one asks how that is, it is as follows:

It is logical that a certain property such as whiteness, being a quality that differentiates its substance from other substances, does not depend on further distinct properties; however, Brahman is not like that, and thus it certainly requires distinct differentiating properties beyond its own essential nature. For if one does not admit that something is self-sufficient (paranirvāhakatva), its self-establishment (svanirvāhakatva) is impossible. Furthermore, when the essential nature of whiteness and the like is manifest, there is no possibility of the superimposition (adhyāsa) of blackness or similar qualities.

Therefore, it is logical to accept that in this case, the very nature of the thing (*svarūpa*) is its differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*). Since the superimposition of things other than Brahman is admitted upon the manifestation of Brahman’s own nature, one must necessarily admit a property in the form of the exclusion of everything else—distinct from the nature of Brahman as the substratum of all superimpositions—just as "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) is distinct from the nature of the substrate that differentiates it from silver and the like.

As for the claim that there is no indication (lakṣaṇā) because the primary portion of the denotable object is already established, that too is incorrect; for when a word culminates in the qualified object (viśeṣya) by means of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa), if the medium [the qualifier] is not denoted, the denotation of the medium itself cannot be established. Furthermore, even if it is not indicated, the abandonment of the natural tendency of a word whose essence is to denote a qualified object toward the qualified object alone must be avoided. And such abandonment is not tenable unless there is a contradiction. As for the argument that indication of all words is observed in cases such as "Eat poison," etc.:

And that [interpretation] is improper because it would require the primary sense of the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*) to be abandoned. In other cases, the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of words other than the injunctive suffix is accepted when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided the primary sense is untenable. However, since no such contradiction exists in the present case, that [figurative interpretation] is not appropriate.

The statement of the following inference—"The subject under discussion (the sentence) has an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because it is a sentence of grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇavākya*), like a well-known example"—is untenable. Is there a difference in meaning between the two words "sentence" (*vākya*) and "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārtha*) or not? If there is, then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even within the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself. If there is not, then the indivisible nature of the meaning would not even be established as the thesis. Furthermore, the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example is unavoidable, since all sentences consist of a collection of words composed of stems (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*).

If the proposition is that [the sentence] is incapable of conveying an indivisible object (*akhaṇḍārtha*) in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), then there is an inconsistency (*anaikāntya*) regarding the two co-referential terms "positive" (*bhāvarūpa*) and "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍa*), which are included within the statement of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Therefore, it is established that the sentence beginning with "Truth, etc. (*satyādivākya*) conveys Brahman as indeed qualified by truth and so forth. This is stated as follows: "Truth, knowledge, infinite," and so on. In this regard, he asserts, along with supporting arguments, the absence of a focus on a featureless (*nirviśeṣa*) reality, starting with the words "Truth, knowledge."

He explains the probans (*hetvaṃśa*) by means of words that indicate identity through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), beginning with "activity" (*pravṛtti*). In response to the inquiry "What follows from that?", he states at the point "therein" (*tatra*) that one must necessarily rely upon a distinction in the grounds for activity (*pravṛttinimitta*), whether by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). To the question "What is the specific difference there?", he replies "to this extent" (*iyān*). Regarding the necessity of such reliance, he states the refutation if those exclusions were merely the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) [of the thing], beginning with "and not" (*na ca*).

He establishes the non-establishment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "in one [entity]" (*ekasmin*). Since the fault of synonymy (*paryāyatva*) is obvious, it is not stated explicitly; for if there were a difference in qualifiers, there would be a plurality of referents. He dispels the objection that this results in the loss of the definition of coreferentiality with the words "nor [is there a problem] for one [entity]" (*na ca ekasya*). Because of the difference in qualifiedness—that is, because of the difference in the connection with each respective qualifier—such a plurality of referents is not contradictory; on the contrary, it is conducive. To the question "Why?", he says: "because their modes of application are distinct" (*bhinnapravṛtti*).

The meaning is that when there is a difference in meaning due to the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) while the qualified (*viśeṣya*) has a single meaning, there is a deficiency in the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Is a coreferential sentence intended to express the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified, or the identity of the qualified, or both? In the first case, there would be no proof for the identity of the qualified. In the second case, the connection with the qualifiers would be without proof.

"Some raise the objection: 'In the third [case], because it is impossible to convey two relations through a single sentence, there would be the contingency of a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). This is not so; for since the connection with the qualifiers is to be understood by the nominal stem itself, there is no contingency of a split in the sentence when the identity of the qualificand is established by the indication of a common case-ending. Thus, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) can be explained otherwise, the claim that sentences such as "Truth, Knowledge, etc. (*satyajñānādi-vākya*) have as their purport a reality devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*) has been refuted. Now, in order to refute their having such a purport on the grounds of their being identical in meaning with the causal texts (*kāraṇavākya*), he restates that [objection] with the words "As for what was said," and so forth."

The term *advitīya* (without a second), which is employed alongside two restrictive determinations (*avadhāraṇa*)—namely, "Being alone, one only"—which exclude both dissimilar (*vijātīya*) and similar (*sajātīya*) entities, refers by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*) to the absence of internal difference (*svagatabheda*). Thus, the meaning is that it does not tolerate even a second [entity] in terms of its qualities (*guṇa*). To the objection that there exists a unity of purport with causal statements concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa*), such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," "Whose austerity consists of knowledge," and "From Him is born this Brahman, name, form, and food," he replies: "Therefore... (ataḥ).

By the principle of "all branches being authoritative" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*), it might be argued that the quality-less nature (*nirguṇatva*) is taught in the passages concerning the quality-less cause, while the qualified nature (*saguṇatva*) is taught in the passages concerning the qualified cause. In that case, according to the principle of "subsequent annulment" (*apaccheda-nyāya*), because the quality-less passages possess greater authority, the meaning would be that all causal passages are intended to refer to the quality-less [Brahman]. To the question, "Why is it necessary for the causal passages to have a single identical meaning?", he says: "of that which is indicated as the cause. Being the cause of the world is an extrinsic definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*).

However, with the intention that this is not a definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*), it is stated "of that which is characterized" (*upalakṣitasya*). The meaning is that because it excludes defects suspected in [the status of] being the cause, it must be avoided as a single defining characteristic (*aikāthya-dharma*). Now, wishing to refute the claim that [the Upanishads] have a non-differentiated reality as their purport based on their consistency with other purificatory statements (*śodhaka-vākya*), he restates [the opponent's position] with the words "otherwise. He refutes the restated point with the words "that is untenable," and so forth. First, regarding the consistency with the causal statements, he says "the world," etc., [implying] "provided that the subject matter is qualified. "In that very way," etc.

The meaning is: "just as the term 'without a second' (advitīya) is intended solely to exclude any other presiding agent, so too [is it here]. Regarding the phrase "only the possession of diverse powers": the subsequent sentence makes known only the possession by Brahman—the material cause—of the power of being a presiding agent; it does not, however, imply its being devoid of attributes (nirguṇatva). He raises an objection with the words "without distinction" (aviśeṣeṇa): the term "without a second" is common to both the negation of everything and the negation of another efficient cause, because it is used without any qualifying adjunct.

Furthermore, since at the very beginning [of the Upaniṣad] it is stated, "Being alone, one only," thereby negating both internal (sajātīya) and external (vijātīya) distinctions, and because the promise that "by the knowledge of One, all is known" would be untenable if only internal and external distinctions were false, the term "without a second" (advitīya), in accordance with the opening statement, must intend to negate only internal distinctions; it cannot, however, be in accordance with subsequent passages, because the opening statement possesses greater authority—this is the direct objection of the opponent. [The reply is: Both being the efficient cause (nimittatva) and the material cause (upādānatva) are heard in the subsequent [text].

In this context, the objection of a bystander is that what is to be negated by the word "without a second" (advitīya) is another material cause (upādāna), and not another efficient cause (nimitta). To this, he says: "of the one desiring to create" (sisṛkṣoḥ). By this, two doubts are simultaneously dispelled. With the intention that the causal nature of this statement cannot be denied—since it was stated immediately after "That [Self] thought" (tadaikṣata)—he said "of the one desiring to create."

Furthermore, since the word "first" (agra) implies the existence of a dissimilar time when it denotes a cause, and because the scriptural teaching of the beginninglessness of souls is supported by the presumptive evidence (*arthāpatti*) of other scriptures—such as those concerning the acquisition of results not previously performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of results already performed (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*)—and because, in order to avoid the charge of partiality and cruelty, one must admit that there exists a subtle distinction between souls even during the state of dissolution; and because the restriction to oneness must be accepted by the opponent as being compatible with the subtle distinctions among souls; and because omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth are necessary for the act of creation.

Because the absence of internal differentiation—whether of a different class, of the same class, or inherent—is difficult to maintain; because the proposition that "by knowing one, all is known" must be sustained without contradicting the stated meaning; because differentiation within the dependent nature (*paratantra*) has been established; because a prohibition applies only to what is distinct from what has been established; because specific forms of independent differentiation have been prohibited by such texts as "No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen"; and because it is logical that a general prohibition culminates in that [specific instance], the term "without a second" (*advitīya*)...

The meaning is as follows: since it would follow that [the passage] is intent upon negating an independent difference, the term "one" (*eka*), which establishes the state of having undivided name and form, already proves the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*); furthermore, because another cause is present in the mind, the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) is intended to negate an independent entity in the form of another cause. He states the undesirable consequence if everything were negated with the word "all. He states that the principle of "cognition based on all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*) is contrary to the doctrine of non-difference with the words "all branches. This refers here to the doctrine of the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-vāda*).

Here, the phrase "of you" (*bhavataḥ*) implies a censure. Its result is the acceptance of qualities not mentioned [in one's own school] through the principle that all Vedic branches (śākhās) are authoritative, rather than the abandonment of qualities already mentioned; thus, the meaning is that its result is contrary to your own position. With the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he concludes that the causal statements have a single unified meaning insofar as they refer to that which possesses distinctions. The sense of the particle "also" (*api*) is that [the texts] refer to that which possesses distinctions not only because of the otherwise inexplicable nature of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), but also because of the unity of meaning with the causal statements.

Now, he refutes the argument that the purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*) have a single unified meaning as the reason for their being directed toward the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*), by saying "not so" (*na ca*). For the opponent has already resolved the contradiction between the statements concerning the attributeless and the qualified (*saguṇa*) by means of the principle of the "successive disqualification" (*apacchedanyāya*). Here, however, he states that there is no contradiction at all because they have different objects (*bhinnaviṣayatvāt*), using the words "prākṛta" and so forth. The phrase "attributeless" (*nirguṇam*) is a negation of qualities in general; "partless" (*niṣkalam*) is a negation of bodies in general; and "actionless" (*niṣkriyam*) is a negation of actions in general. Thus, the negation of qualities is not to be restricted [to specific instances].

In response to the objection that—since the absence of all qualities is understood through the force of the negation of qualities by implication (*ārthaguṇaniṣedha*), and since knowledge is not observed to be the locus of qualities such as further instances of knowledge—the Brahman's being "mere knowledge" (*jñānamātratva*) effectively results in its being "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*)—the author restates the meaning established by the scripture in order to refute this implied negation of qualities, saying: "It is mere knowledge. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Not at all... [and so forth].

In response to the inquiry "Why?", there arises a dilemma: is it being asserted that cognition lacks a substratum because it is itself cognition, or because a fixed relationship of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is impossible between two substances of the same class? To the first alternative, he replies: "Because the knower alone has the nature of cognition. The meaning of this is as follows: is the absence of cognition's being a substratum for qualities such as further cognitions stated on the basis of a universal rule (*vyāpti*), or by the force of scripture (*śruti*)?

If [it is argued] by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), since knowledge that illuminates an object is observed to be a quality (*dharma*) belonging to someone else and not itself the substratum (*āśraya*) of knowledge, let it be accepted as being a quality. If, on the other hand, it is accepted as independent on the strength of scripture (*śruti*), then by the very same strength of scripture, its being the substratum of knowledge must also be accepted. Thus, the lack of being a substratum of knowledge is caused by its being *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as a quality), and not merely by its being knowledge (*jñānatva*); therefore, there is no fallacy of a conditional adjunct (*sopādhikatva*), and consequently, no contradiction with the pervasion.

Alternatively, since an insentient object such as a jar cannot possess the status of a knower, its nature as knowledge is established by implication through its very being a knower. He addresses the second [objection] with the words "of that which has knowledge as its nature" (*jñānasvarūpasya*). The meaning is that a fixed relationship of attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) is possible between two substances of the same genus. For such an admission would only be tenable if the scripture had already established that [the Self] is the locus of knowledge; to this he replies: "For [the scripture teaches] only the state of being a knower" (*jñātṛtvameva hi*). Alternatively, the phrase "because the knower itself has knowledge as its nature" means that there is no contradiction in the knower having knowledge as its nature.

He resolves the contradiction regarding the impossibility of a fixed relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin*) in two things of the same kind by stating, "of that which has knowledge as its very nature. He resolves the [objection] that [Brahman], being knowledge, cannot be the substratum of knowledge by stating, "for it is precisely the knower... The intention here is the same as before. By the term "all," all those scriptural passages (*śrutayaḥ*) are intended which describe the attributes through which the state of being a knower bears fruit, and which explicitly mention the state of being a knower; or, by the use of the plural, many Upaniṣadic statements are intended.

By the word "only" (eva), the non-otherwise-establishment of the state of being a knower is intended. The word "hi" indicates a reason; the meaning is that because the state of being a knower is established by scripture, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

In response to the inquiry, "What, then, are these scriptural passages? [the author] shows the scriptures and demonstrates how they accomplish these three purposes: (1) to avoid the negation of the qualities of the object; (2) to establish the limitation of the *nirguṇa* (qualityless) texts; and (3) to dispel the doubt that the *saguṇa* (qualified) texts have as their object qualities produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). He begins with the words, "He who is all-knowing," and so forth. "All-knowing" (*sarvajña*) means he who knows everything in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its specific modes (*prakāra*).

By the triad beginning with "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), [the text] demonstrates that knowledge has all things as its object, its utility for both collective and individual creation, and its connection to the Self. In the verse "The eternal among eternals," the plurality of conscious beings is stated, as well as [the Lord's] capacity to grant desires. In the verse "The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant," [his] nature as a knower and his lordship (*īśvaratva*) are shown. In the verse "Him, the best of lords," [his] lordship, divinity, and fatherhood are shown; here, lordship means the state of being a controller (*niyantṛtva*).

Because one possesses the status of a controller (*niyantṛ*) only by virtue of possessing knowledge of the objects to be controlled, and because the act of controlling is itself a specific form of knowledge, the status of being a knower is established through the status of being a controller. "Deity-hood" (*devatātva*) means being the object of worship for those engaged in ritual action (*karmārādhya*). "Lordship" (*patitva*) means being the sovereign (*śeṣin*). Regarding the phrase "not of him": "effect" (*kārya*) refers to the body, and "instrument" (*karaṇa*) refers to the sense organs and so forth, as seen in the usage "in the state of being the agent of the effect and the instrument. Furthermore, the negation of equals and superiors is heard here in the scripture.

By the phrase "without a second," a general negation is made; however, according to the principle that "the goat [is the animal] because of the wording of the mantra," it is indicated that this results in the exclusion of a specific second entity, namely one of the nature of Īśvara. By the words "His [is] the supreme," the inherent nature of His powers of knowledge and so forth is stated. This constitutes the regulation of His activity. The phrase "This is the Self" provides a specific affirmation as well as a specific negation. With the intention of avoiding the negation of qualities that are implied by the sense, it is said: "of the very nature of knowledge."

The term "intrinsic" (*svābhāvika*) was stated in order to refute the notion that [the Lord's qualities] are caused by ignorance (*āvidhika*). Furthermore, by the phrase "freedom from all that is to be abandoned" (*samastaheyarahitatā*), the suspicion that they are caused by ignorance is also implicitly removed.

Moreover, by this same phrase, "freedom from all that is to be abandoned," it is established that statements regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavākya*) have a restricted scope (*saṅkucitavṛtti*) with respect to auspicious qualities such as being the knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth. For instance, the intended meaning of the phrase "auspicious qualities" is as follows: a specific injunction regarding particular qualities is not capable of subverting a general prohibition of qualities; rather, it must concern a domain distinct from those [prohibited qualities].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the injunction for a specific instance of violence—namely, "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma"—by means of the general prohibition, "One should not harm any living beings."

The meaning of the phrase "the state of being devoid of all that is to be abandoned" (*samastaheyarahitatā*) is as follows: Just as in such cases as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) or "of the omentum of a goat" (*chāgasya vapāyāḥ*), the general term—by the logic stated in the Sūtra, "Or [the animal is] the goat, because of the wording of the mantra" (*chāgo vā mantravarṇāt*)—concludes its application to a specific instance when a particular is observed; so too, the negation of qualities in general concludes in the negation of specific qualities. Furthermore, the fact that general terms conclude in specific instances is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).

Just as in such cases as "Bring the cow" or "Tie up the cow," a general term is employed by the instigating elder with a glance toward a particular [individual], for it is precisely from that [usage] that the instructed elder does not bring all individual cows, but brings only the specific individual intended to be expressed; for such is the linguistic convention (vyutpatti) in those instances.

By the phrase "thus, the auspicious qualities beginning with knowership," and by the phrase "and [the state] free from all that is to be abandoned," the principles of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) and of general and particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*) are intended. The distinction is as follows: when there is a contradiction regarding what is to be excluded apart from the specific items already mentioned, the restriction [of the general term] is the principle of general rule and exception; when there is no contradiction but the restriction is applied to avoid redundancy, it is the "ox-and-bull" principle (*govalīvardanyāya*); and when the restriction applies specifically to the subject matter of the mentioned particulars, it is the principle of general and particular.

Furthermore, in the scriptures of the inner science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), the word *guṇa* is well-known to refer to *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. For example: "Indeed, all the qualities (*guṇas*) of Him who is liberated from all qualities such as *sattva* and the rest cannot be described even by all the hosts of sages. "Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities born of *prakṛti*. "Of the one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and immeasurable... "The qualities act among the qualities. "The cause of this [bondage] is attachment to the qualities (*guṇa-saṅga*). "Devoid of qualities and yet the experiencer of the qualities. "There is no agent other than the qualities."

For instance, in such passages as: "This divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is indeed difficult to transcend"; "without the *guṇas* and other things to be abandoned"; "O Sage, he has transcended the defects of the *guṇas* and so forth"; and "of that which is eternally defiled by the *guṇas*. Thus, because the word *guṇa* alone is widely established as referring to *sattva* and the others, words such as *nirguṇa* (devoid of *guṇas*) are intended to negate *sattva* and the rest.

This distinction of subject matter is not determined by us merely because we observe the prescription of specific qualities and the prohibition of specific qualities in different Upaniṣadic passages; rather, he says "nirguṇa" (without qualities) to show that the distinction of subject matter is seen even within a single passage. By accepting the prescription of qualities in general as being equivalent to the prohibition of qualities in general, it is stated that there are both passages concerning the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) and passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*). For indeed, the prescription of qualities in general is nowhere to be seen in the Śrutis.

For indeed, only specific qualities (*guṇa*) are heard [in the texts]. However, a word for "quality" (*guṇa-śabda*) that is mentioned in conjunction with "defects" (*doṣa*) refers to those qualities that are most worthy of being adopted (*upādeyatama*). Or rather, it was stated that the statements regarding the Lord possessing qualities (*saguṇa-vākya*) are intended according to the purport of such Smṛti passages as: "His qualities cannot be [exhausted] even in tens of thousands of years," "He [described] but a ten-thousandth part of one portion of Your qualities," and "They do not reach the end of His qualities. In that context, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) denotes the opposite of defects (*doṣa-pratipakṣa*), because it is so well-known in common usage.

And because, by virtue of the context, it is logical that [the term] culminates in the specific qualities and forms of auspicious attributes—following the analogy of the goat-sacrifice animal—and because there is no contradiction with the previously stated principle, he states that the rule of sublation (*apacchedanyāya*) does not apply; thus [he says], "of the passages concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*) and the unqualified (*nirguṇa*). By the word "thus" (*iti*), all the aforementioned reasons are intended. The meaning is: [this is so] because of the principles of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), the principle of the general and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣanyāya*), and because in the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātmaśāstra*), the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is most commonly established as referring to *sattva* and the other [qualities].

Regarding the statement "of the two types of passages, those concerning the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa)": the intention here is that because there is a distinction between their respective objects, there is no contradiction; thus, the principle of the "subsequent annulment" (apacchedanyāya) does not apply. Furthermore, it should not even be suspected that one or the other has a false object. It was not said that the sublation belongs specifically to the qualified passage; rather, it was said "of either one. The meaning is that it is untenable to resort to the sublation of the unqualified passage by the qualified one, or the sublation of the qualified passage by the unqualified one.

The intention here is as follows: previously, it was resolved that there is no contradiction; now, even if a contradiction is admitted, this is not a case for the *apaccheda* (subsequent annulment) principle, but rather a case for the *virodhādhikaraṇa* (the section on contradiction) principle. For instance, the *apaccheda* principle concerns cases where the sequence of contradiction is indefinite; there is no fixed rule regarding the order of the *udgātṛ* and *pratihartr* being disqualified (*apaccheda*), and even within that, the sequence of their disqualification is itself indefinite.

For when that restriction is in place, because the entire property is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), there is a restriction due to the contradiction with the state of not having a sacrificial fee. Even when both [priests] are dismissed, since their occurrence is sequential, there is no restriction as to whether "the dismissal of the Udgātṛ occurs first and the other later," or the reverse. Therefore, the scope of the principle of dismissal (*apacchedanyāya*) concerns a contradiction occurring within the limits of a single performance. However, the contradiction between the texts concerning the qualified and the unqualified [Brahman] is based on their essential nature; furthermore, by way of being injunction and prohibition, they possess a fixed priority and posteriority.

Therefore, even if a contradiction is admitted, the principle of *apaccheda* (the rule regarding the sequence of sacrificial cuts), which concerns an indefinite order of priority and posteriority in contradiction, does not apply here; rather, it is the logic of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) that applies. For in its domain, there exists both a fixed order of priority and a fixed nature of contradiction. To illustrate: "Having touched the *audumbarī* post, one should sing" is a direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*), whereas "The entire *audumbarī* post must be wrapped" is a traditional law (*smṛti*).

In that context, *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) produces valid knowledge from the very outset, because it is an independent means of cognition (*nirapekṣapramāṇa*). *Smṛti* (tradition), however, functions with delay due to its dependence on the inference of the *śruti* upon which it is based. Therefore, the sequence [of their application] there is fixed. Furthermore, the contradiction between touching the *audumbarī* post and wrapping it [with a cloth] is certain. In that case, once the valid knowledge has already arisen through the former [the *śruti*], the latter, whose meaning is contrary to it, would be "annulled by lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

Therefore, according to the principle that "the cause of swift cognition is stronger than the cause of delayed cognition," the preceding scripture possesses greater force; thus, there is simply no arising of the subsequent scripture. Now, one might object: "But surely the subsequent scripture has already been studied here. If so, what of it? For "non-arising" refers to the non-arising of valid cognition (*pramiti*), not the non-arising of the verbal expression itself—as in the case of the statement, "The sacrificial post is the sun. One might further argue: "In that case, being a *smṛti* (tradition) and being a *śruti* (direct revelation) are the factors that determine the relationship of sublation (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*). This is not so.

Because the relationship of being based on Smṛti and being based on Śruti is caused by their respective priority and posteriority, it is established—by virtue of this same logical principle—that the very fact of priority and posteriority is the cause of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator; thus, the statements concerning the qualified [Brahman] are more powerful.

Alternatively, let it be that the logic of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) does not apply here; rather, the logic of the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*) alone operates, because there is a fixed rule regarding the priority and posteriority of contradictions. Therefore, since it is obstructed by the texts concerning the qualified (*saguṇa*), the scripture concerning the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) simply does not arise. If it is argued: "But if that which has already arisen first prevents the production of what follows later, then let the cognition 'this is silver' prevent the arising of the cognition 'this is not silver,'" we say: no.

Because there is an absolute disparity between the two indicators—one being real existence (*sattā*) and the other being being-cognized (*jñāyamānatā*). For an indicator consisting of real existence produces a cognition that is independent of any prior or subsequent reflection; it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The cognition produced therein arises precisely by subverting the preceding one, according to the principle: "The arising of the latter is established only by the non-sublation of the former. An indicator consisting of being-cognized, however, produces a valid cognition (*pramiti*) dependent upon the reflection on capacity (*yogyatā*) and other such factors.

In that case, if there is a cognition contradicted by a previous means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at the stage of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), then that [subsequent] cognition prevents the arising of the former; thus, there is an asymmetry. If it is argued that, in this case, since the cognition "this is not silver" depends upon the reflective awareness "this is silver," it follows that the cognition "this is not silver" would never arise because it is obstructed by the prior cognition—[we reply] no, because the sense organ, in generating cognitions other than recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), is independent of prior reflective awareness.

In this case as well, the subsequent valid cognition (pramiti) has "this is mother-of-pearl" as its object, specifically the property of being mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*). Furthermore, the cognition of *śuktitva* does not depend upon the apprehension of silver. Once *śuktitva* is grasped, the linguistic usage "this is not silver"—which is the result of that grasp—proceeds by depending on its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), because it is expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*). And this dependence [on a counter-correlate] is due to the inherent nature of the word. Therefore, the cognition of mother-of-pearl, arising independently of the cognition of silver, arises precisely by subverting the former [error].

Therefore, it is precisely the principle of the section on conflict (*virodhādhikaraṇa*)—or rather, the principle of the section on the beginning (*upakramādhikaraṇa*)—which applies here, as its scope concerns a fixed contradiction between what precedes and what follows; it is not the principle of the "successive disconnections" (*apacchedanaya*). If that [latter principle] were to apply in such a case, the immolation of the animal would become non-performable, because the prohibition "one should not kill," which occurs later, is more powerful. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the performance of the rite.

The rule regarding the precedence of the statements concerning the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) has been stated by the opponent himself. Therefore, since this falls under the principle of the section on contradiction (virodhādhikaraṇa), there is no room here for the principle of the subsequent annulment (apacchedanyāya); thus, the superior strength of the statements concerning the qualified is established. It is with this intention that the phrase "of the one or the other" was stated.

Because the qualities mentioned in the Śruti without reference to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are inherently established as being free from such adjuncts; because of the scriptural statement regarding their naturalness (*svābhāvikatva*); because the hearing of the lack of cause for His lordship in the passage, "No other cause exists for His ruling," establishes that the qualities conducive to that lordship are also free from adjuncts; because of the mention of "having true desires" (*satyakāmatva*) and so forth, preceded by the negation of connection with karma which serves as the limiting adjunct for the gradations of knowledge, power, and so on; because of the scriptural declaration of their reality as being like His own nature in the passage, "These are His true desires"; and [because of the passage], "Higher than this is His... [and so forth].

By means of such passages as "Power," and "Those who are a hundred," which demonstrate the unlimited nature of the qualities, there occurs the cessation of limitation—which would otherwise pervade their connection with karma.

Because the cessation of the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is established by the very nature of the facts; because the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of the attributes is established even in those scriptural passages concerning attributes that lack explicit mention of inherent nature—by the principle of the "recognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*); because there is an abundance of indicators of intent (*tātparya-liṅga*) such as "Bliss is Brahman"; because there is no contradiction due to the division of subject matter through the principles of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda-nyāya*) and the general and particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya*), since such a division of subject matter is observed within a single scriptural passage itself; and because this does not fall under the scope of the "principle of the later annulment of the earlier" (*apaccheda-nyāya*).

Even though there is a contradiction, by the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa-nyāya*), the passages concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vākya*) possess greater authority. This is because in passages such as "He who is all-knowing," which lack injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), the [Brahman's] nature is established as if it were its own form; and since it is not the object of other means of knowledge, it cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*), and thus it is impossible to negate it. Furthermore, there is the hearing of its being an object of meditation in certain places, such as: "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," "One who knows Brahman as truth, knowledge, and infinite," and "Having realized the Self and these true desires, they depart."

This summary of the points already stated and those yet to be explained—namely, that the qualities of Brahman are *nirupādhika* (unconditioned)—is presented for the sake of facilitating understanding. This is because [the objection] applies equally to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself; because in the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*), the term "quality" (*guṇa*) is most commonly used in reference to *sattva* and the other [qualities]; because there is no possibility of these [objections] applying to passages concerning the *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities); because external logical arguments are *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by the lapse of time); and because the negations of qualities—consisting of the denial of being known by speech or mind, the denial of being an object of knowledge, and the denial of having the nature of knowledge, bliss, and non-duality accompanied by two restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*)—have all been resolved.

The refutation of the presence of objective qualities established by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in the phrase "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) has already been addressed. Furthermore, at the conclusion of this section, the statement, "From which words turn back, not having attained it along with the mind," indicates the cessation of both speech and mind, which results in the realization of its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*).

In response to the doubt that the statement "Being, Consciousness, etc. (satyajñānādi-vākya) must therefore have as its purport a featureless [Brahman] because it shares the same purpose [as other texts], the author—by means of the passage beginning with "Out of fear of Him" (bhīṣāsmād)—demonstrates the consistency of this statement (which was cited by the opponent) with the aforementioned meaning, by showing that it is intended to negate qualities [only] in a figurative sense. By the phrase "Out of fear of Him," the status of being a commander is expressed. [The phrase] "having spoken of the excellence of the bliss of the Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajñānandātiśaya-muktvā).

If it were intended here to establish the state of being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*), it would have been appropriate to demonstrate the gradual diminution of qualities until one arrives at their total absence. However, in this case, having described the progressive increase of qualities, the statement regarding the cessation of speech and mind is made on account of their very infinity; such is the intention. As it is said: "The qualities and defects of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow cannot be numbered at all; due to infinity, the first category [of qualities] exists, while the latter [defects] are non-existent. Thus, beginning with human bliss, a progressive intensification has been shown.

"Excellent is the young teacher. "Excellent" means that he has mastered the tradition correctly according to the rules, being free from errors in accent, phoneme, and so forth. By the word "young" (*yuva*), freshness is intended; the meaning is that he is one who studies in such a way as to be perpetually new through non-forgetfulness. Alternatively, he is a teacher of all those of his own age; the meaning is that his knowledge exceeds theirs. "Most swift" (*āśiṣṭha*) means one whose actions are more rapid; alternatively, it means capable of eating, i.e., healthy.

Or rather, he is one who has become the object of blessings; the meaning is that he is pleasing to all, as in the expression, "they pay homage to all the gods. *Baliṣṭhaḥ* means powerful in mind; for *draḍhiṣṭhaḥ* has already been used to denote physical strength. Or else, *draḍhiṣṭhaḥ* means more firm—that is, one whose nature is not unstable. *Baliṣṭhaḥ* means possessing every kind of strength, both physical and mental. His wealth is full, because there is no deficiency in his possessions.

This is because the genitive case is permitted by the rule: *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena*. Thus, that is one human bliss. Having thus described the collection of qualities and the fullness of prosperity, the Śruti, by its own natural sense, declares that very [collection] to be bliss in the statement, "That is one human bliss. For bliss (*ānandatva*) is indeed agreeableness (*anukūlatva*). Agreeableness is a state of being desired that does not depend on the removal of the undesirable, nor on the desirability [of something else], nor on being a means to what is desired.

Because it possesses the characteristics already described, the nature of bliss (*ānandatva*) is established for both the qualities (*guṇa*) and the manifestations (*vibhūti*). Furthermore, that the cognition of those objects is also favorable is proven by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), as it is caused by the favorability of the objects themselves. This being the case, the natural sense of the scripture is also maintained; for it is said, "He is bliss," referring to the excellence of the qualities and manifestations, and not to the cognition of them.

Having described various qualities such as youthfulness and so forth, as well as His majesty (*vibhūti*), and having designated that collection by the term "bliss" (*ānanda*), the demonstration of that bliss’s state of being unsurpassed establishes that all qualities and majesty possess an infinite degree of excellence. Since the nature of bliss is simply the state of being agreeable knowledge, even though the knowledge whose objects are the qualities and majesty is itself bliss, the statement that this bliss is infinitely superior implies by necessity that the qualities and majesty themselves are also infinitely superior.

This is because that infinity is based upon the infinity of His qualities and manifestations (*guṇavibhūti*). The sense is that the concluding statement must be interpreted in accordance with the introductory statement (*upakrama*). By the phrases "of the *śrotriya* who is not overcome by desire" (*akāmahata*), it is stated that the bliss of the liberated one is identical to the bliss of the Lord; for such unsurpassed bliss is impossible in the state of transmigratory existence. A *śrotriya* is one established in Brahman. One who is "not overcome by desire" (*akāmahata*) is one whose ignorance has ceased and who is therefore unassailed by any worldly enjoyments.

By the passage ending with "that is the one bliss of Prajāpati," the excellence of the bliss of the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) has been stated. With the words "that is the one bliss of Brahman," the bliss of the Blessed Lord is expressed. For if the word "Brahman" were intended to refer to the bliss of the four-faced [Brahmā], there would be a loss of the word's natural sense (*asvārasya*); for it has been established in the Sūtras that the word "Brahman" has its primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) precisely to that [Lord], in the passages: "Jaimini [thinks it refers to the Lord] because of primacy" and "And it may belong to the One, as in the case of the word 'Brahman'."

Furthermore, this has been elaborated upon in the Bhāṣya during the occasion of explaining the word *brahman* in the first sūtra. Moreover, there would be a contradiction with the context, because the instances of the word *brahman* found within the context—such as in "The knower of Brahman attains [it]," "Infinite Brahman," "By the wise Brahman," "Brahman is the egg," "If one knows 'Brahman is non-existent'," and "If one knows 'Brahman exists'"—all refer to Brahman. Thus, the context is violated.

Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the natural sense of the word *brahman* in the genitive case—which stands as the correlate to *ānanda*—in both the preceding and subsequent passages [of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad], such as "He who knows the *brahman* of bliss. Moreover, it would be untenable to conclude the discussion of the bliss of *brahman* introduced by the words "This is the [bliss] of that" with the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā (Caturmukha). Finally, there would be a contradiction regarding the subject matter of the verse about to be cited under the heading "On this point, there is also this verse," since that verse is intended to describe the bliss of *brahman*.

Furthermore, there is no violation of the natural force of the word *prajāpati* when it appears in the singular without any qualifying adjunct in the phrase "He is one [of] Prajāpati. Nor is that a singular used for a genus (*jātyekavacana*); for this is a context where the use of the plural or singular is determined by the intention to express plurality or singularity, as it is specified thus: "of humans, of Gandharvas, of gods, of Deva-Gandharvas, of Indra, of Bṛhaspati, and of Prajāpati. Therefore, the word *prajāpati* refers to the four-faced Brahmā.

In the passage, “That one [is] of Brahman,” the word *brahman* refers to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). If it is asked how the bliss of the Blessed Lord can be limited by the statement, “Those which are a hundred [of that], this is one,” there is no such limitation. Just as in expressions such as “He glides like a discharged arrow,” where the comparison between two who travel many *yojanas* in half a moment is intended to indicate the cessation of slowness of movement rather than actual limitation, so too the designation “those which are a hundred, this is one” is intended to show the superiority of the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā (*caturmukha*), and not to imply limitation.

Alternatively, even though the specific statement "that which is yours, whether it be a hundred" or "that is one" refers to a particular numerical value, it results in the conclusion that bliss is unlimited. This is because, according to such scriptural declarations as: "There are thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands of such cosmic eggs (aṇḍas), and likewise hundreds of millions upon millions there," and "Infinite Brahmāṇḍas revolve within your pores," the cosmic eggs are infinite, and consequently, the four-faced Brahmās residing therein are also infinite.

Because the bliss of the Lord is established as being infinitely greater than the bliss of the four-faced Brahmās residing in all the cosmic eggs throughout time—being a hundred times greater than that—and because His bliss is proven to be absolutely infinite by virtue of possessing the three-quarter manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*) described in the verse: "O Sage, this entire cosmic egg is but an atom compared to Him. Regarding the phrase "the infinity of auspicious qualities": a gradual decrease in qualities has not been stated; rather, only the excellence of the qualities has been stated. Therefore, the sense is that because the excellence of the qualities is unsurpassed, there is a cessation of both speech and mind.

By the use of the suffix *ṇa* (denoting excess) in the word *atyādare*, it is stated that there is an even greater degree of reverence for its qualities than for the very nature of Brahman itself. The intention is that the Śruti says, "Knowing the bliss of Brahman," and not "Knowing Brahman as possessed of bliss. Regarding the phrase "this Śruti": the meaning is that even the Śruti passage from this context cited by you as being intended to teach the Nirguṇa [Brahman] is indeed consistent with the point we have asserted.

Thus, by means of refuting the denial of the qualities of the object (*artha*), it has been stated that the sentence beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," etc., has a qualified entity as its object, because it shares the same purport with other sentences within the context that are devoted to the infinity of qualities. Now, he establishes that it has a qualified entity as its purport even through a portion of its own constituent words, starting with "He enjoys," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the sentence which makes known the fruit": in the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," a fourfold set is mentioned—namely, Brahman, the knowledge thereof, the attainment, and the object to be attained.

The Śruti itself states that this exposition is performed by means of the mantra beginning with "satyaṃ jñānam" (Truth, Knowledge...), saying: "tadeṣābhyuktā" (Regarding that, this [verse] has been recited). This means that this Ṛg-verse was recited by the students while having that very Brahman as its object. Since it is observed that mantras function as expositions of the Brāhmaṇas, and since—unlike the subject-matter of the *Upakramādhikaraṇa*—there is no perception of an initial contradiction [between them], and because there is no difference between mantras and Brāhmaṇas regarding their being eternally faultless, the claim that the Brāhmaṇa is more authoritative than the mantra is untenable.

If it is intended that the terms "strength" (*prābalya*) and "weakness" (*daurbalya*) refer precisely to the presence or absence of the cause for clear comprehension, then there is no contradiction. The word *brahman* is explained by "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite"; the word *vid* (to know) by "He who knows [It] hidden in the cave"; "attainment" (*prāpti*) by "he enjoys in the highest heaven"; and the object to be attained by "all desires," and so forth. In that context, the phrase "of the supreme, wise Brahman" was stated in order to show that this is not a mere explanation of the meaning of the word "supreme" (*para*).

The term *vipaścit* (the wise one) is also stated to be an object of enjoyment (*bhogyaguṇa*). To explain the meaning of the sentence, he demonstrates the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the words with the phrase "by the wise one. In response to the doubt as to which word here denotes a quality (*guṇa*), he explains it through its etymological power (*avayavaśakti*) as "that which is desired," in order to exclude the desires mentioned as things to be abandoned in the passage: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are released."

Because [the world] is to be experienced by the liberated as the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, it is impossible for it to be subordinate to desires that are to be abandoned here; because even though the nature of Brahman itself can be an object of desire (*kāmyatva*), there is a mention of distinction (*vyatireka-nirdeśa*); because of the use of the plural number; because the etymological power of the word applies to its parts; and because the aforementioned quality of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) is possible in the qualities (*guṇas*). This is supported by such passages as: "He, indeed, rejoices beholding with this divine eye, the mind, these desires which are in the world of Brahman"; "Those who depart having discovered the Self here, and these true desires"; and "These... [etc.].

The meaning is that the auspicious qualities (kalyāṇaguṇāḥ) are what is denoted by the word "desires" (kāma), because this is consistent with other scriptural passages such as "His desires are true. To whom do these qualities belong? And regarding their coexistence with Brahman, is it—as in the expression "he eats rice together with his son"—by way of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), or is it—as in the expression "he eats rice together with milk"—by way of being the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*)? Anticipating and resolving this doubt, he states the meaning of the sentence: "with Brahman."

Since this statement consists of an explanation of the word "supreme" (para) as denoting that which is to be attained, and because the natural force of the immediate syntactical connection with the word "all desires"—which denotes objects of enjoyment—is expressed by the phrase "together with Brahman," the word "together" (saha) refers to the accompaniment of objects of enjoyment. Furthermore, Brahman alone, being proximate, is the substratum of the qualities. Therefore, the meaning is that one experiences Brahman as qualified by infinite attributes.

Based on the grammatical rule *saha yukte 'prādhāne* ("when joined with *saha*, [the word] denotes the subordinate"), one might suspect that Brahman is subordinate because of the word *saha*. To dispel this suspicion, he states the purpose of using the word *saha* with the words "dahara... (referring to the small ether). In the injunction "he who knows," the word *saha* indicates the predominance of the qualities (*guṇa*). For in the Dahara-vidyā, the predominance of the qualities in the meditation (*upāsana*) has been stated; likewise, here too, the word *saha* is used to express the predominance of the qualities in the meditation—this is the meaning.

Since it is heard that qualities are predominant during the state of the fruit (*phala-daśā*), one might ask how the predominance of qualities is established in the act of meditation (*upāsana*). To this, he says: "Of the fruit and the meditation. The meaning is that both the fruit and the meditation are equally endowed with qualities and possess an equal degree of qualitative predominance. By the phrase "to express the predominance of qualities," it is also established that the word "with" (*saha*) here refers to the accompaniment of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*); otherwise, it would establish the predominance of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), rather than the predominance of the qualities of the object of enjoyment.

By the use of the particle *eva* in the phrase "by scripture alone," it is intended that the aforementioned principle is explicitly stated by scripture itself, independent of any speculative construction (*utprekṣā*) based on human intellect.

Now, since it is observed that only those things possessing attributes (*saguṇa*) are objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), the negation of knowability implies the conclusion that [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). With this in mind, he cites the statement spoken by the opponent as being intended to negate knowability: "Of whom... (*yasya...*). Anticipating three possible alternatives—whether what is intended is (1) not being an object of mere cognition (*jñāna-mātra*), or (2) not being an object of cognition consisting of meditation (*upāsanā-ātmaka-jñāna*), or (3) not being an object of cognition consisting of meditation upon that which possesses attributes—he first refutes the first alternative, that it is not an object of mere cognition, with the words: "The knower of Brahman" (*brahma-vid*).

The phrase "asanneva" (only when non-existent) demonstrates the supreme emphasis placed by the Śruti upon the knowability of Brahman. Others assert that the means to liberation is not the knowledge of Brahman, but rather the knowledge of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva-jñāna*).

In such passages as "Through knowledge one attains immortality," "Likewise, the knower, liberated from name and form," "From that, knowledge proceeds," and "The fire of knowledge [consumes] all karmas," the knowledge heard of as the means to liberation has a commonality between having Brahman as its object and having the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) as its object. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This is because, in certain passages, knowledge as the means to liberation is seen to have Brahman as its object.

The meaning is that all the Śrutis—such as "By knowledge one attains immortality"—even when they do not specify a particular object, enjoin the knowledge of Brahman alone as the means to liberation, according to the principle of "the unity of the cognition across all branches" (sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya). Alternatively, the intention is that even those Śrutis which, while referring to some other subject, are devoted solely to knowledge as the means [to liberation], culminate in that very [Brahman] by virtue of the principle of "the general and the particular" (sāmānya-viśeṣa-nyāya).

Now, he refutes the position that [Brahman] is not the object of knowledge consisting of worship (*upāsanā*) with the words, "And knowledge... The scriptural passage, "Know that alone as Brahman, and not this which they worship here," is the seed for the doubt that [Brahman] is not the object of knowledge consisting of worship. The meaning is that this has been refuted by demonstrating the impossibility of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-jñāna*) being the means [to liberation]. The meaning of the phrase "not this which they worship here" is this: "That which they worship as a symbol (*pratīka*), that is not [Brahman]; you should worship that alone as the Supreme Brahman."

Now, he refutes the position that [Brahman] is the object of worship characterized by attributes (*saguṇopāsanā*) with the words "and [if it were] an object of worship. The intention is that by demonstrating that even the *sadvidyā*—which others have declared to be concerned with the attribute-less (*nirguṇa*)—actually has as its object that which possesses attributes, [the opponent's view is undermined]. Alternatively, [he says] "and knowledge consists of worship. The intention is that by the explicit statement that [Brahman] is the object of a specific kind of knowledge, the mere denial of its being knowable (*jñeyatva*) is cast far aside. Regarding "and [if it were] an object of worship": the removal of attributes (*guṇanivṛtti*), which one wishes to establish by the removal of knowability, is sublated by the scriptural injunction of attributes.

The meaning is that, therefore, by subverting unknowability, [knowability] is implied.
