To the question, "In that case, what is the meaning of the scriptural passages concerning 'unperceivedness' (*avijñātatva*) and 'not being that' (*anatattva*)?", he says: "From which speech turns back" (*yato vāco nivartante*). By the word "infinite" (*ananta*), the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*) is recalled. By the phrase "of the infinite" (*anantasya*), the infinity of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is stated; by "of the one with unlimited qualities" (*aparicchinnaguṇasya*), the infinity of its qualities (*guṇa*) is stated. Regarding this point: "Indeed, not all of its qualities can be known even by all the hosts of sages."

"He can be described as being devoid of all qualities such as existence (sattva) and the rest"; "They do not reach the end of his qualities; therefore he is called infinite (ananta)"; "Though you possess infinite qualities, only six are foremost"; "The qualities of that Great Soul—Viṣṇu, the victorious son of Vasudeva, who holds the conch, discus, and sword in his hands—cannot be fully told even by all the worlds combined over ten thousand years"; "Even if a man of pure mind with ten million mouths were to have the lifespan of four-faced Brahmā..."

"O best of gods, please be gracious; he might speak of but a ten-thousandth part of your qualities, or perhaps not at all. "Just as the jewels of the ocean are innumerable, O son, so too are the qualities of the infinite Great Soul innumerable. They cease only when the arrows are exhausted, not because the sky or the earth have ended; they cease when the intellect fails, but never from the exhaustion of Govinda’s qualities"—this and more should be observed. To the question, "If [the Lord] is known to be limited, how can the subject, Brahman, remain unknown?", he says: "Because Brahman is unlimited."

The meaning is that [Brahman], which is denoted by the word "Brahman," is unlimited both in its essential nature and in its qualities. He states "otherwise" because this meaning was explained not only to avoid contradiction with other scriptural passages, but also because otherwise there would be the consequence of contradicting one's own statement within that very same passage. "Therein" means in that very statement of one's own.

Having resolved the objection regarding the denial of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), he now addresses the denial of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) with the words beginning "As for that which... (*yattu*). He presents a dilemma: do you provide a construction by supplying the word *vyatirikta* (distinct) and taking *dṛṣṭeḥ* and *mateḥ* as ablative cases, or do you provide a construction by taking them as genitive cases without supplying the word *vyatirikta*? Intending this alternative, he first restates the position involving the supplied word: "Not from seeing" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*). He then refutes it: "That [is not so]" (*tat*).

In response to the doubt that "a prohibition applies only to what has been proposed," he demonstrates the proposal by saying, "established by fallacious reasoning" (*kutarkasiddhām*). When the question arises as to how such fallacious reasoning was presented, he briefly establishes the two reasons stated by the opponent regarding the insentience of its own nature (*svarūpajaḍatva*), namely: "by virtue of possessing the adventitious quality of consciousness" (*āgantukacaitanyaguṇayogitayā*). These are the two reasons: because of being adventitious and because of being a quality. Because it is adventitious—and thus non-eternal—knowledge cannot be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the eternal Self; and because it is a quality, it cannot be the essential nature.

Alternatively, the point is this: if that which is called consciousness—the illumination of objects—is its eternal essential nature, then it would follow that there must be illumination of objects at all times. When the nature of the Self, the agent of specific cognitions such as seeing, hearing, thinking, and meditating, is prescribed as being of the form of seeing and so forth, one should not suspect that there is any internal differentiation within the cognition that constitutes the Self's essential nature.

Since the nature of knowledge—characterized by self-luminosity—is common to all those [cognitions] whose form consists of specific types of knowledge, only that much is intended as the essential nature (*svarūpa*). This resolution applies equally to the opponent's position as well. He states the direct connection with the words "or else" (*athavā*); the meaning is that, having negated the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as the agent of seeing, hearing, thinking, and meditating, one should meditate upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Alternatively, the word "declares" (*abhidadhāti*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].

The Śruti declares: "Having negated the individual self (jīvātman), meditate upon the Supreme Self (paramātman). This is the meaning of the sentence, according to another interpretation. Alternatively, the meaning is "having negated [it] without abandoning it. Thus, the identity of the agent (samānakartṛkatva) is established.

Since it was introduced [in the Upanishad] with the words, "He who breathes in with the prāṇa, he who breathes out with the apāna—this is your Self, the innermost of all," the statement "you would not see the seer of seeing" and so forth is intended to dispel the doubt that the individual self (jīvātman), which is capable of breathing in and out by means of the prāṇa, might be the object of meditation; this is precisely the meaning. Otherwise, he states that there would be a contradiction with other scriptural passages. Furthermore, the quality of being an attribute is unestablished, because knowledge is understood from scripture to be the very nature (svarūpa) of the Self.

If it is argued that [knowledge] is adventitious (*āgantuka*), this should not be said, because it would lead to a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the Lord’s knowledge. Furthermore, the adventitious nature of the knowledge of those such as ourselves is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (contradicted by perception), based on the Vedic scripture: "There is no loss of the knower's capacity to know. Thus, both arguments are refuted. Being directed toward an object is a property belonging only to knowledge as a dharma (*dharmabhūta-jñāna*); however, the universal nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Therefore, there is no consequence of objects being manifest at all times.

Immediately after the refutation of the denial of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*), the denial of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) was refuted because it resides in the intellect. Now, following the denial of the quality of bliss (*ānanda*), that [denial] is refuted by the passage beginning with "bliss" (*ānanda*). He extends the previously stated refutation to this case with the words "that [refutation] of the substratum of knowledge. To the question, "How is this refuted by that? he says, "For knowledge itself... [is bliss]. Then, to the objection that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the terms "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) in the scriptures would otherwise be untenable, he says, "Consciousness... [is bliss].

The sense is that [the application of the term] is justified because of the difference in the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely, self-luminosity and being conducive [to liberation]. He states "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) to show that this is exactly what you yourselves have accepted. "For this very reason" means precisely because the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "bliss" (*ānanda*) have the same object. Is the non-acceptance of bliss as the locus of bliss based on scripture (*śruti*) or on logical pervasion (*vyāpti*)? If it were by pervasion, it would be a property of something [other than itself]. If you say that its independence is established by the force of scripture, then for that very reason, let it be accepted that bliss is the locus of bliss.

For it is observed that bliss which has become a property (dharmabhūta) lacks the status of being a substratum for bliss; therefore, there is no contradiction with the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*). Thus, the intended meaning is that just like independence, the state of being a substratum for qualities must also be accepted because it is established by scripture (*śruti*). Anticipating the objection that the application of logic (*nyāyasañcāra*) occurs only when there is evidence for both [the subject and the example], he states "of this" (*asya*) to show that evidence exists in the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). He then shows that it is explicitly stated even in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*).

The meaning is that the state of being blissful (*ānanditva*) is also explicitly stated, just like the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Intending to show that the scriptural mention of being a knower is also an authority for the state of being blissful, he says: "For the state of being a knower itself is the state of being blissful. The particle *eva* (only/itself) is intended to exclude a state of being blissful that is distinct from the state of being a knower. The word *hi* (for) indicates the reason for this. The meaning is that the state of being blissful consists precisely in being the substratum of favorable cognition.

The sense is that the scriptural statement regarding the knowerhood (*jñātṛtva*) is contradictory to the negation of being the substratum of knowledge and the negation of being the substratum of bliss. Now, he restates the scriptural passages cited by others as being intended to negate difference (*bheda*), in order to apply them [to his own view], beginning with "That which... (*yadidam*). By the two sentences beginning with "For where... (*yatra hi...*), the negation of difference is established. He shows the purpose for teaching difference with the words "From death... (*mṛtyoḥ...*), as in the passage: "Verily, from darkness he enters into darkness. (*tamaso vā eṣa tamaḥ praviśati*).

Regarding the question of how a difference that persists eternally can be established as an illusion, he says: "But where... In the aforementioned statements, the word "much" (*bahu*) is used with the intention of indicating the variety of rhetorical turns of expression. In the reading *bahuśaḥ*, the meaning is the repetition of the act of negation. He refutes it with the word "that" (*tat*); the word "that" is to be construed with the word "refuted" (*parihṛtam*).

Since it is contradictory for Brahman—well-known from other scriptural passages as being the opposite of everything to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīka*) and as consisting of all auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇa*)—to be one with the world which is subject to defects such as afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, which are the locus of transformation (*vikārāspada*), scripture does not teach such identity. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because the things to be abandoned are not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), we reply: even if they are not ultimately real, must these be removed or not? If not, then the scripture intended for their removal would be purposeless.

If it were something to be rejected, then the very connection with that which is to be rejected would constitute a connection with what is to be abandoned; thus, for that which is the opposite of such [rejection], being connected to it is a contradiction. Furthermore, the scripture declares a becoming manifold preceded by the resolve, "May I be many. It is impossible to maintain that for an omniscient being, the voluntary assumption of defects within oneself is inconsistent.

If [the Lord] were not omniscient, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "He sees without eyes, He hears without ears," "His power of knowledge and action is innate," and "He who is omniscient. Furthermore, even if that which is to be abandoned [by the Lord] were not ultimately real, it would be untenable for an omniscient being to produce in Himself the delusion of infinite non-ultimate goals through His own volition. One should not argue that omniscience—consisting of the delusion of becoming many—is preceded by ignorance because it is admitted to be constructed by ignorance; for this contradicts the scriptural text stating that it is "innate."

Furthermore, because of the scriptural statement, "These objects of desire are true," their reality is affirmed. If it is argued that [the Lord] does not know His own omniscience to be false because it is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), then He would not be omniscient. If, on the other hand, He does know it, then by that very knowledge His omniscience would be sublated. Consequently, the creation—which follows the karma of individual souls and is preceded by His own volition—would not be possible through a prior contemplation of the form of the world.

Therefore, it is untenable for omniscience to be characterized by ignorance (*avidyikatva*); thus, for that Omniscient One, the appropriation of what is to be abandoned within Himself is not possible. Furthermore, for Him who knows what is to be abandoned as being internal, who is omnipotent, and whose resolve is infallible, the failure to immediately eliminate what is to be abandoned within Himself is also untenable. If He were incapable, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold and innate. [Objection: There is no such contradiction;

If it is argued that non-contradiction must be accepted on the strength of scripture (*śruti*), then one must likewise accept the scriptural declarations concerning the Self and other principles, such as: "Having arisen from these very elements, [the self] perishes after them" (*vijñānaghana evaitebhyo bhūtebhyaḥ samutthāya tānyevānuvinaśyati*); "The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (*na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścit*); "Air and the intermediate space—this is immortal" (*vāyuścāntarikṣaṃ caitadamṛtam*); "From the Self, space was produced" (*ātmana ākāśaḥ sambhūtaḥ*); "There is no death, no birth, nor these two, heaven and earth" (*na jaro na mṛtyurnaiva dyāvāpṛthivī*); "That becomes finite for him" (*antavadevāsya tadbhavati*); and "His sacrifices and charitable works are never exhausted" (*nāsyeṣṭāpūrte kṣīyete*).

Since even [attributes] such as eternity and non-eternity are established by scripture, there is no contradiction, and thus both must be accepted. Consequently, if one were to accept everything exactly as it is presented [in scripture], the undertaking of Mīmāṃsā would be rendered useless. Furthermore, the postulation of a distinction between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference under discussion—on the grounds that they refer respectively to the ultimate and the non-ultimate, or to the qualified and the unqualified—is untenable; for such a postulation is intended to resolve a contradiction, and no contradiction exists here.

Consequently, the ultimate reality of difference is established; therefore, a contradiction must be admitted. Here, a contradiction is indeed perceived: the scripture declares that the apprehension of difference is the cause of transmigratory existence, stating, "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were multiplicity. On the other hand, the scripture declares that the knowledge of difference is the means to liberation, stating, "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, he becomes favored by Him and thereby attains immortality," and "When he perceives the Lord as distinct and His majesty, he is freed from sorrow."

This contradicts such Smṛti passages as "The dualists are seers of untruth," whereas [the Gītā] begins with "These two persons... and "The immutable Lord, entering... sustains... since I am beyond the perishable and superior even to the imperishable," and concludes by stating that one who knows Me thus is undeluded: "He who knows Me thus as the Supreme Person is undeluded. Since the duality established by such statements is not something already established in common worldly experience, the claim that duality is merely restated for the sake of negation is untenable.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because mere difference is established by worldly experience, the non-difference alone is what is to be known through scripture—based on the maxim that "scripture is purposeful only regarding what is not already established"—then that argument is untenable. For in cases such as "This is that Devadatta," mere non-difference is also established by worldly experience; since it is already established, scripture would have no purpose in teaching that non-difference. Indeed, the identity of Devadatta and others is established by the world, whereas the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*parameśvara*) is not.

If it is argued that, therefore, their non-difference is what is propounded by the scripture, [we reply: in that case, the difference between a jar and a cloth and so forth is indeed established by common worldly experience, but not the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). Since the difference characterized by the states of being governed and governor, supported and supporter, subordinate and principal, pervaded and pervader, and so on, is not established by worldly experience, this difference is certainly not what is propounded by the scripture. As stated by the venerable Teacher: "The words of the Upaniṣads do not propound duality, for that is already well-known; rather, let non-duality—which is not within the scope of other means of knowledge—be accepted as that which is to be known through them."

Indeed, a treatise is meaningful only when [the goal] has not been attained; therefore, this effort is in vain, since any distinction other than that which is already well-known would be like your own doctrine of non-duality (advaita).
Thus, this meaning will be stated immediately thereafter in the Bhāṣya; therefore, the resolution that it is a restatement (anuvāda) is not tenable.

If it is argued that the scriptural texts concerning difference are intended for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*) and do not have reality as their primary purport—on the grounds that such words expressive of meditation are heard in passages like "having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct" and "when he sees the other, the Lord, as the gratified one"—nevertheless, difference is indeed real; for it is stated that the knowledge of that [difference] is the means to liberation. Indeed, liberation results from the knowledge of reality. Nor should it be said that because the texts on difference serve the purpose of meditation for the sake of a specific fruit, the difference they describe is unreal.

Furthermore, because oneness would have to be unreal since it is intended for the purpose of meditation—indeed, the fact that non-duality is for the purpose of meditation is heard in scripture: "Now, he who meditates on another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know," and "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self alone. It is logical that oneness is for the purpose of meditation while difference is real; for in the meditation on Vainateya (Garuḍa), oneness is seen to be superimposed, whereas the difference between the king and Vainateya is indeed real.

If it is argued that non-difference is perceived even in those sentences that are not subordinate to injunctions (*vidhiśeṣa*), and therefore that non-difference is ultimately real (*tāttvika*), then the difference [between the two] must also necessarily be accepted as ultimately real, because it is understood from sentences that are not subordinate to injunctions, such as: "The perishable is *pradhāna*; the immortal and imperishable is *Hara*"; "The Lord of *pradhāna* and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), the Master of the qualities (*guṇa*)"; "The two, the knowing and the unknowing"; "Drinking the fruit of their deeds"; "Two birds..."; and "The eternal among the eternals."

If the ultimate reality of non-difference is asserted on the grounds that there is no difference during the state of liberation—which is the fruit of meditative worship—then the reality of difference is established by the scriptural hearing of difference during that state of liberation. Therefore, it is not tenable to resolve the scriptural texts concerning difference by claiming they have a non-ultimate subject matter merely for the sake of meditative worship.

Since difference and non-difference possess a contradiction characterized by a fixed sequence of priority and posteriority, it is not possible for them to be subject to the *apaccheda-nyāya* (the principle of the later annulling the earlier), as is the case with the qualities of having attributes (*saguṇatva*) and being without attributes (*nirguṇatva*). Therefore, according to the principle of contradiction or the principle of the opening statement (*upakrama*), there would merely be an obstruction to the arising of the negation of difference that occurs later. This has already been explained in detail previously.

Intending here what was stated in other passages—that there is an unavoidable contradiction with other scriptural texts supported by logic, and that these [other] interpretations are untenable—he shows the correct interpretation with the word "tad" (that). The word "jagataḥ" (of the world) extends up to the word "brahma-paryantaṃ" (culminating in Brahman). It is construed with the words "tasya brahma-kāryatayā" (because of its being an effect of Brahman) and "aikyāt" (because of identity). In the phrase "tad-antaryāmikatayā" (because of having Him as its inner ruler), the word "jagataḥ" is supplied by implication.

By this, the contradiction between the terms *jagat* (the world) being both an extract (*niṣkarṣaka*) and a non-extract (*aniṣkarṣaka*) when applied once is resolved. Having stated that "all this is indeed Brahman, from which it is born, into which it dissolves, and in which it breathes" (*tajjalān*), [the text] then addresses the world’s being born from and dissolving into That by way of its being an effect of Brahman. Here, the word *brahman* refers to the causal state characterized by the sentient and insentient. Having addressed its being from That, [the text] then addresses it by way of having That as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*). The pronoun *tat* (That) refers back to the substantive.

Since the qualified entity under discussion is the subject at hand, its qualificand aspect is also the subject at hand. Just as in the passage, "Having Being as their root, having Being as their abode," the word "Being" (sat) refers both to the qualified whole and to the qualificand, so it is here. That which has that Brahman as its inner ruler is "tad-antaryāmika"; the meaning is "by virtue of being such."

How is it established that He is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) by virtue of being their "life" (*anana*)? It is said: "Life" (*anana*) means existence (*sthiti*). Furthermore, Brahman’s status as the cause of the world’s existence consists in His being the sustainer through entering within and presiding over it. In the passage, "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.8.4), the two phrases "having Being as their root" and "having Being as their support" refer respectively to the origin and dissolution of things being dependent on Brahman, who is denoted by the word "Being. Dissolution culminates in final rest (*niṣṭhā*), not merely in having Being as a substratum.

Furthermore, [the term] "possessing the six bases" (*sadāyatana*) would entail redundancy; for, since the status of being a sustainer is established by the phrase "possessing the six bases"—which stands between two words expressing Brahman's causality regarding origination and dissolution—it is understood from the passage, "By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart," that the stability expressed by the verbal root *sthā* (to stand) is dependent upon being sustained by that command, as in [the verse], "He has entered within, the ruler of people."

Because it is heard that the teaching which serves as the cause of support is being performed by entering within—"Just as, my dear, the felloe is fixed on the spokes and the spokes are fixed on the nave, even so these elements (bhūtamātrās) are fixed on the elements of intelligence (prajñāmātrās), and the elements of intelligence are fixed on the vital breath (prāṇa)"—and from the Śruti and Smṛti passages, "All this is strung upon me like clusters of jewels on a thread," through the analogies of the spokes, the nave, and the thread for the clusters of jewels, we understand that [Brahman] exists within as the supporter; and because of the text, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing."

Because the entry described in that passage occurs immediately after creation and is consistent with the cited scripture, it has the purpose of [establishing] maintenance; and because the entry described in the statement, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," occurs immediately after creation and is consistent with the cited scripture, it has the purpose of [establishing] maintenance; furthermore, by the process stated in passages such as, "The seven vital breaths (prāṇas) emerge," the world that was created is, at the time of its maintenance, pervaded by Him, according to the statement, "All this is filled by that Puruṣa."

Because the Supreme Person is understood to be all-pervasive (*pūrṇatva*), and because—according to the principle that "what is taught in one branch [of scripture] applies to all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*)—the mention of any one of the functions of pervading, controlling, and supporting necessarily establishes the others; it is thus understood that His status as the sustainer and the cause of the world's maintenance consists in His entering [the world] and supporting it through His governance. Thus, based on the statement "That from which [it] is born, by which [it] lives, and into which [it] enters" (*taj-jalān*), it has been stated that the world is the effect of Brahman and has Brahman as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*). This state of being the inner controller of the Brahman who possesses both characteristics (formless and embodied) is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for Brahman’s ultimate causality of the world, and is also established by the *ghaṭaka* (complementary) scriptural texts.

The word "ca" (and) is to be construed with what follows, meaning "both by virtue of being His inner controller (*antaryāmika*) and by virtue of being identical in essence (*tadātmaka*). That which has Him as its self is "identical in essence" (*tadātmaka*). The meaning is: "by way of having Him as its inner controller and by way of being identical in essence. For the Self (*ātman*) is indeed the ruler who has entered within. Since it might be suspected that there are three reasons if one were to say "by virtue of being the body of Brahman, by virtue of being His inner controller, and by virtue of being identical in essence," the word "ca" is placed first in order to dispel that suspicion. Thus, the meaning is that both kinds of oneness have been enjoined.

Now, if identity were based on the relation of cause and effect, it would be logical for there to be an essential identity between the world in its state as an effect—qualified by its effects—and Brahman in its causal state—qualified by both the conscious and the unconscious. However, if it were based on the fact of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), there would be no identity with Brahman, but rather only the application of the number "oneness" to the qualified Brahman. Thus, there would be a difference in the meaning of the word "identity. Consequently, it would be improper to say that "the world is one with Him because it has Him as its self," since the attribute and the possessor of the attribute are distinct.

It is not so; for although there is a difference between the world and Brahman, it has been stated here that the word "world" refers to Brahman as qualified by the world. Furthermore, there is no difference in meaning for the word "identity" (*aikya*); in both cases, it refers to the identity of the qualified entity. To explain: what is called "identity" based on the relationship of cause and effect is the oneness of the single reality qualified by the sentient and insentient [factors] existing in two states; just as a jar, qualified by color, touch, and so forth, is one with the clay-substance that possesses those same qualities.

The identity between that which is qualified by the world consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness, and that which is qualified by unsurpassed greatness in both its essential nature and its attributes, is an identity of the substratum (*prakāryaikya*); it is like the identity between that which is qualified by blueness and that which is qualified by lotus-ness. Nor does the absence of identity in the qualifying portions entail a loss of the identity of the entity itself; for even in the case of clay and a jar, there is no identity between the essential nature and its color, touch, and so forth, nor between their states as effect and cause.

This is the distinction: in the case of cause and effect, there is an identity of the substratum (dharmin) based on multiple qualifiers that are mediated by states existing at different times, as in "this very person was once a youth. In other cases, there is an identity of the substratum based on multiple unmediated qualifiers related to the same time, as in "this is a Brahmin who knows the Vedas. Here, childhood and youth are states mediated by different times; whereas Vedic knowledge and the Brahmin body are unmediated qualifiers existing at the same time.

Thus, the meaning of the word "oneness" (aikya) is the oneness of the substrate (dharmin) as qualified by both kinds of qualifiers. Therefore, the designation "from the oneness of the world" (jagata aikyāt)—meaning from the oneness of the substrate denoted by the word "world"—is logically established.

Alternatively, the word "of the entire world" (*kṛtsnasya jagataḥ*) is an extractive term; the word "Brahman" (*brahma*) also refers solely to the substantive. This is because [Brahman] is the substratum with respect to the state of being an effect (*kāryāvasthā*). And this status as a substratum is primary, whether direct or indirect. Therefore, the world is an effect of Brahman. Thus, the term "having that as its inner controller" (*tadantaryāmika*) has been explained. In this way, by virtue of being an effect of Brahman and by virtue of having Brahman as its inner controller, the world has that (Brahman) as its self (*tadātmakam*).

"Being of that nature" (*tadātmakatva*) means being included within that [Brahman], because the world lacks any separate existence due to having a single essential nature consisting solely of those modes. It is unity by way of that mode, but not unity of essential nature (*svarūpaikya*). The meaning is that unity consists precisely in the inclusion of the qualified [entity] within that [Brahman]. Regarding the phrase "multiplicity opposed to that": the meaning is that multiplicity, which is the opposite of the two kinds of unity thus enjoined, is negated.

The distinction between cause and effect is an object of error rooted in fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*); the distinction inherent in things themselves is an object of error rooted in worldly perception (*laukikapratīti*). Therefore, since there is no difference in their being based on error and no difference in their being opposed to the enjoined unity, both types of distinction are referred to by the word "manifold" (*nānā*) and negated in that form; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Regarding the phrase "opposed to that": the negation of difference is supplementary to the injunction of unity; for the statement of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) serves to consolidate the meaning already stated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Furthermore, the injunction regarding unity is heard in the context of the passage, "There is no diversity here," which states, "It is to be perceived as one alone. "As one alone" (*ekadhā*) means by way of oneness—that is, as having the Supreme Self as its body, in a single manner. Likewise: "I alone existed in the beginning, I exist now, and I shall exist in the future; there is nothing else whatsoever distinct from me"; and, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, one only."

In such passages as “There is nothing else whatsoever that moves,” “But in the ultimate sense, you alone are one; there is no other, O Lord of the world,” “I am Hari, all this is Janārdana; there is no collection of causes and effects other than Him,” and “That Acyuta exists, and there is nothing else beyond Him,” the negation of difference is seen as being supplementary to the injunction of oneness. And this status of being supplementary arises through a specific function characterized by the stabilization of the enjoined oneness.

Only if the negation has as its object a difference that is opposed to the kind of identity that has been enjoined can it be established as having the purpose of stabilizing that [identity]. A negation of some other thing that is not opposed [to that identity] is not useful for that purpose. For instance, when it is said, "The clay is indeed the jar," the negation of a second jar does not assist in establishing the identity of the clay and the jar, because the existence of a second jar is not opposed to the identity of the clay and the jar.

Nor does the negation of the transformation of form and so forth when "one jar" is said to be real assist in the injunction of the identity of the property designated as "jar," because the difference in color, dimension, and so on is not incompatible with the unity of the individual jar. For only the negation of a meaning that contradicts what is to be enjoined assists an injunction. Furthermore, there is not merely an absence of assistance; rather, the intent to negate all difference is contrary to the injunction of unity, since identity is enjoined by a sentence of grammatical coordination (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) indeed consists in words expressing distinct qualifiers having a single substratum as their referent. And while there remains a difference in the modes [of being], the negation of all difference is not tenable. Therefore, since the negation of difference is supplementary to the injunction of unity, the intended meaning is that both the difference between cause and effect and the difference residing in itself are negated.

Furthermore, from such statements as, "And he has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him"; "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen"; "Who can rival that Brahman?"; and "There is none equal to you, much less any superior, O You of incomparable power throughout the three worlds," we observe a negation regarding a specific independent entity. Therefore, it is established by implication that the general negation of difference (bhedaniṣedha) culminates in that [specific entity] according to the maxim of the goat and the animal.
This is because it has been stated that "diversity is its opposite," and because that [specific entity] is explicitly mentioned in certain passages.

Now, intending to apply the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), he says "not again. The citation of scriptural passages concerning the multiplicity of Brahman in the form of its bodies is also for the purpose of demonstrating those passages concerning the multiplicity of its modes (*prakāra*).

"He, being one, moved about manifoldly"; "The one God has entered into many ways"; "You are one, having entered into many"; "He who moves within the unmanifest, whose body is death—this is the inner self of all beings, the divine, the one God Nārāyaṇa, free from sin. Thus, the multiplicity of modes and the unity of the mode-possessor are clearly heard in scripture.

Alternatively, because in the *Chāndogya* and *Taittirīya* Upaniṣads, within the context of the thought "May I be many," there is heard the statement—"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman)," "Having entered that, it became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and unconsciousness"—there is the scriptural declaration that [Brahman] assumes name and form preceded by the entry into both the conscious and the unconscious; and because it is untenable for that which possesses both characteristics (liṅga) to be the material cause (upādāna) of the world without such an intervention.

In the passage "May I be many" (*bahu syām*), it is established that Brahman’s assumption of multiple names and forms is mediated by a door; thus, with the intention that the plurality of the conscious and unconscious entities which constitute its modes is established as a matter of fact by virtue of being its body, the sentence "May I be many" is cited.

Since both the diversity of effects and the diversity of modes are thus enjoined, and since a general prohibition applies only to what is distinct from what has been enjoined, the meaning is that the scriptural texts negating difference concern either the distinction between cause and effect as established by fallacious reasoning, or the difference residing in [the Self] itself as established by worldly perception.

The objection that [the scripture] concerns the non-ultimate reality because it negates plurality is raised with the words, "nānātve... (regarding plurality). The sense is that this scripture merely restates [plurality] for the purpose of negation. He refutes this with "no," because it is impossible to make a restatement of what has not been previously established. Therefore, due to the distinction between their respective domains, it is only logical that there is no contradiction. This was stated by the venerable Teacher: "When the words of injunctions and prohibitions concerning the distinctions of qualities, bodies, modifications, actions, and so forth of Brahman, have mutually distinct domains, they do not admit even a scent of contradiction; thus, the injunctions are not sublated by the prohibitions."

Because it is impossible for that which is devoid of all things to be abandoned to be one with the form of that which is to be abandoned; because even if the thing to be abandoned is not ultimately real, its status as something to be abandoned must necessarily be accepted since it is to be discarded; because asserting identity with a thing that is the opposite of that [abandonable] contradicts its being a reality capable of connection with it; because it is impossible for the omniscient Brahman to produce, by His own volition, an error regarding Himself or concerning the objects of that abandonment; because if He were not omniscient, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts on His omniscience; and because it is impossible for the All-Powerful One not to ward off the abandonment inherent within Himself, whereas if He were powerless—

Because there would be a contradiction with the scriptures regarding [the soul's] omnipotence; and because, in the absence of such contradictions by the force of scripture, there would be no need for the application of logic anywhere—rendering Mīmāṃsā useless—since there would be no contradiction by the force of scripture between the permanence and impermanence, or the qualitylessness and possession of qualities, as established by statements such as "those very [elements] perish along with it" and "it is neither born nor does it die"; and because, since there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference, one cannot accept a distinction based on their being ultimately real or not ultimately real.

Because it is heard that the knowledge of distinctness is the means to liberation in such passages as, "Having known the Self and the Impeller as separate, being favored by Him, one then attains immortality," and "When he beholds the other, the Lord, as the favored one"; because it is recorded in the Smṛti that one who possesses the knowledge of difference is free from delusion, as in, "Since I have transcended the perishable..."; and because the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para)—characterized by the relationship of controller and controlled—is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) like the distinction between a jar and a cloth, and thus cannot be a mere restatement (anuvāda), it is impossible to negate what has been enjoined.

Because there is the contingency of resorting to [the view that] the reliance on [texts concerning] worship is for the sake of meditation—even when unity is established by such passages as "Now, he who [worships] another deity"—since unity is established by passages that are not subordinate to an injunction and because the case of difference is equal; since the rule of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*) does not apply due to the contradiction with fixed sequential order; and because, according to the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇanyāya*), the scriptural statement of difference acts as an obstacle to the arising of the subsequent negation of difference, [this applies] to the negation of difference which is subordinate to the injunction of unity.

This is because it is logical that [the scriptural texts] negate a difference that contradicts the unity already established; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the very unity understood from the co-referential (sāmānādhikaraṇya) statements which constitute their own primary subject matter. Furthermore, by the maxim of the general rule and its exception (utsargāpavāda), the negation has as its scope differences other than those specifically enjoined; and by the maxim of the goat and the animal (chāgapaśu), the negation of difference ultimately results in the negation of specific independent differences in general. Thus, the summary is: the scriptural passages negating difference are intent upon negating a plurality that is non-Brahman in nature, but they are not intent upon the negation of difference per se.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Where indeed" (*yatra hīti*) is as follows: "Where," that is, when there appears to be duality—as if there were a difference inherent in itself. The word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that this inherent difference is not ultimately real. Alternatively, the phrase "how indeed" (*katham iva*) may be a rhetorical construction whose literal sense is not intended. At that time, "one sees another by means of another. Since it will be stated later as to "by what," the word "by another" (*itareṇa*) is supplied. "Another" refers to the perceiver who is established in himself; "another" refers to the object of perception established in himself.

He sees by means of the instrument of vision established in himself. But when—[that is,] at that time—for this practitioner (*upāsaka*), everything has become the Self alone, having been directly realized through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the Supreme Self. It is not the case that what was previously non-Self now becomes the Self; therefore, the word "has become" (*abhūt*) is used with the intention of referring to direct realization, because of the expression "for him" (*asya*). At that time—[the word] "who" (*kaḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject], since the other [person] has already been mentioned.

Established in its own nature (*svaniṣṭha*), who is the seer? By what means of seeing established in its own nature could one see which object to be seen that is established in its own nature? The meaning is that among the knower, the known, and the means of knowledge, there is nothing whatsoever established in its own nature. This is because it is impossible to negate what has been definitively established; rather, only that which is established by immediate appearance (*āpātapratīti*) is subject to negation. Furthermore, since worldly perception has as its object that which is established in its own nature, it is logical that negation must occur precisely in that form.

If only the seer, the seen, and so forth were being negated, then the scriptural statement regarding the state of direct realization of the Supreme Self—"Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun'"—would be contradicted; for it records the realization of the seer-self as "I" and the realization of the objects of perception, such as Manu and the Sun.

Therefore, in ordinary worldly experience (*laukikapratīti*), because the supreme Self as the substrate (*prakārī*) is not realized, the seer, the seen, and so forth appear as self-contained (*svaniṣṭhatayā*) without being in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with It. In the state of yoga (*yogadaśā*), however, because the supreme Self as the substrate is being realized, they shine forth in apposition with the supreme Self denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃśabdavācya*). This is the distinction. One must not, however, accept that the seer, the seen, and so forth are negated;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the realization of Vāmadeva and others being mere error (*bhrānti*).

"Neither here nor manifold" (*neha nānā*): "here" refers to this phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The meaning is that there is not even the slightest thing that has become manifold through worldly perception, nor anything divided by existing in its own right (*svaniṣṭhatayā*). He states the transgression resulting from the view of things as existing in their own right with the word "from death" (*mṛtyoḥ*). This is an expression similar to [the passage]: "Verily, he enters from darkness into darkness. "As if manifold" (*nāneva*) means as if existing in its own right. The meaning is that through ignorance one attains further ignorance. The ignorance regarding objects as distinct from the body was already established; the intention is that the perception of those very objects as existing in their own right is an ignorance even more excessive than that.

Taking up the scriptural passage beginning with "For when he [sees] this," the author restates the position previously asserted by the opponent—that [the realization of Brahman] is the cause for the attainment of fear—and refutes it, saying, "That is incorrect. "That is incorrect" means that it is not the cause for the attainment of fear. To the question "Why?", he says, "Everything. The established conclusion (siddhānta) is that the contemplation of the multiplicity of the world as the body of Brahman is the cause of liberation. Now, having provisionally accepted the opponent's claim that it is the cause of peace, he speaks as follows.

To the doubt as to how there can be a perception of the contemplation of diversity therein, or how that [contemplation] can be the cause for attaining fear and how it can be contradictory [to liberation], he explains this with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*). Here, he demonstrates the perception of the contemplation of diversity by the word "of all" (*sarvasya*). For it was not said merely that "Brahman alone [is this]," but rather it was said that "all this is Brahman. And the word "all" refers to the manifold expansion of diverse distinctions. Therefore, the meaning is that the contemplation of Brahman as qualified by diversity is what is perceived.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is this: since the contemplation of non-duality is the means to liberation—consisting in the cessation of all fear—by way of being the cause of peace, the statement that the cognition of difference is the cause for the attainment of fear is contradictory to that [non-duality]. Now, one might object: why could there not be an injunction to contemplate the superimposition of everything upon Brahman within the bodies, in order to remove attachment, aversion, and so forth, just as one does with reflections appearing in jewels, swords, mirrors, and the like? It is not so.

For it has been established that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in the occurrence of words in a single referent despite a difference in their grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); furthermore, the view that it has the sense of negation (*bādha*) will be refuted by the criticisms to be stated later. Now, preceded by an objection, he states the meaning of this [passage] with the words "this is said. "Invisible" (*adṛśya*) is the exclusion of the non-conscious (*acit*). "Bodiless" (*anātmya*) is the exclusion of the bound (*baddha*), for he is pervaded by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Alternatively, *ātmya* is the body produced by karma which is to be pervaded; one who is devoid of that is "bodiless. "Indefinable" (*anirukta*) is the exclusion of the liberated (*mukta*).

For he is designated by such terms as "the gods" and so forth during his bound state (*baddhāvasthā*). The phrase "without abode" (*anilayana*) serves to exclude those who are eternally liberated (*nityamukta*), for even they have the Blessed Lord as their support. He shows the corroborative expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) regarding the subject matter stated by himself with the words "as it has been said. "Loss" (*hāni*) is the loss of what is desired. A "hole" (*chidra*) is the attainment of the undesired. "Error" (*bhrānti*) is the derangement of the mind caused thereby. "Modification" (*vikriyā*) is the improper functioning of the limbs due to being rendered powerless by that [error]. "Even when a single moment devoid of meditation has passed..."

"It is as fitting to cry out loudly as if one were being plundered by bandits: 'It is better to remain within the cage of the flames of fire than to endure the calamity of dwelling with people who have turned their backs on thoughts of Śauri. Such statements are intended by the word "etcetera" (ādi). Regarding how the word *antara*, which denotes distinction (*bheda*), can mean separation (*viccheda*), he says: "In the case of *brahmaṇi*. For uninterrupted meditation is called "without interval" (*nirantara*). Therefore, *antara* indeed means separation.

When the question arises as to whose [fear] it is, since the *pratiṣṭhā* (support) is the subject under discussion, its interruption [is implied]. Regarding the topic of the previously mentioned Brahman, as cited in the verse "And that too this," or in the subsequent verse "From fear of Him," which describes the Lord as the ruler of all sentient beings such as Vāyu and Sūrya, it is appropriate that the word *antara* signifies the interruption of meditation; it does not signify difference. Therefore, this meaning is consistent with the preceding and following passages, as well as with other scriptural texts (*śruti*), and is in harmony with the explanatory texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*);
whereas the interpretation stated by the opponent contradicts both. This is the intended sense.

Now, if in the passage "nanu yadā hyevaipa... the meaning were the severance of the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā-viccheda*), then there would have to be a feminine gender in the word "etasyām" (in this [foundation]). If it is argued that, according to the maxim "aditiḥ pāśān," the neuter gender understood from the case-ending is not intended to be expressed, even so, an inherent awkwardness (*asvārasya*) remains unavoidable. And when the natural sense is possible, such an interpretation is not tenable. Furthermore, the locative case is also awkward; for the expression "tasya vicchedaḥ" (the severance of that) is natural, whereas "tasyām vicchedaḥ" (the severance in that) is not.

Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency regarding the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) if the intent were to establish [the self] as the locus. For in the preceding sentence, the word *etasmin*—which was used with reference to Brahman in the passage, "For when he is in that which is invisible, bodiless"—is present in the mind as it recurs in the immediately following sentence. It is replied: There is no inconsistency in the gender, the locative case, or the nominal stem, because the word *etad* (this) refers back to Brahman. Moreover, the word *antara* here means "space" or "interval," as seen in the usage of *nirantaram* (without interval) and *sāntaram* (with an interval).

And "interval" (*antara*) occurs both spatially and temporally. As for the temporal interval, it is indeed a cessation (*viccheda*). Now, if one asks, "In that case, whose cessation is there?"—in response to this expectation, one might supply the word "of the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhāyāḥ*) as an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). But that is improper, because the sense can be sustained without such an ellipsis. If it is argued: "Even so, there is an awkwardness (*asvārasya*)," we reply: "That is better," because in the alternative view, many awkwardnesses would arise.

For instance, because the cause of fear is the opposite of the cause of fearlessness, the term "the supreme state that is the cause of fearlessness" cannot denote oneness; thus, the syntactical function (*vākya-vṛtti*) would be inconsistent. To ensure its consistency, if the word "state" (*pratiṣṭhā*) were taken as referring to oneness, there would be an abandonment of its primary meaning. For "state" denotes a firm connection, as in the expression "established in the kingdom. Furthermore, it is untenable to abandon the meaning of the word "state" as it was first understood.

Furthermore, there is an unnaturalness in the meaning of the verbal root *vindati* (to find), because it would have to refer to the realization of an identity with what was already established previously. Moreover, the locative case is also unnatural; for when one intends to express the relationship of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) or the limit (*avadhitva*) of a difference, the instrumental, ablative, or genitive cases alone are natural. There is also an unnaturalness in taking the root *kṛ* (to do) as meaning "realization" (*pratipatti*), since this would require supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) in the construction "he makes [it] in the mind" (*manasi kurute*). Finally, there is a contradiction with the preceding statement, "for he alone causes bliss," which establishes a state of difference.

Furthermore, immediately following this, difference is stated through the Lord’s role as a ruler in the passage, "And from fear of Him... Therefore, a negation of difference in the middle [of the text] is untenable. Moreover, since the preceding and subsequent passages—namely, "The knower of Brahman as bliss fears nothing from any quarter" and "at any time"—state that knowledge characterized by specific qualities is the cause of fearlessness, it is contradictory to claim that the negation of difference in Brahman is the cause of fearlessness.

Furthermore, because the passage begins with "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]" (*brahmavidāpnoti*), it is logical that the "establishment" (*pratiṣṭhā*) in Brahman consists precisely in the nature of knowledge, and not in the nature of identity. For it is not the case that both identity and the cognition thereof can be denoted by the word "establishment. Rather, since the word "establishment" denotes a firm connection, it is appropriate that its final meaning rests upon the relationship of the worshiper toward the object of worship, which is Brahman.
He refutes the two sūtras cited by the opponent regarding the fact that Brahman is devoid of distinctions and that all else is false, with the words "As for what was said."

Now, he establishes that the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* have as their purport that which possesses distinctions (*saviśeṣa*), beginning with the words "smṛti... and so forth. By demonstrating that the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*—that is, by establishing generally that a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its specific form, namely verbal testimony (*śabda*), have as their purport entities possessing distinctions; by establishing that a scripture is incapable of propounding an object contrary to perception; and specifically by establishing that the Vedāntic passages have as their purport that which possesses distinctions—it follows that these two (*Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*) cannot possess authority regarding an object contrary to the *Śruti*. Thus, [he concludes] regarding those two.

The fact that [the scriptures] have a qualified (saviśeṣa) purport has been established. Now, by means of a thorough examination of the preceding and following passages, it is demonstrated that even the statements from Smṛti and Purāṇas cited by the opponent likewise have a qualified purport. The intention is this: just as this Śāstra does not propound matters that contradict ordinary means of knowledge or Śruti, so too the Smṛtis and Purāṇas are incapable of propounding any matter that is contradicted by their own preceding and following sentences.

In the previous section, because all speech is equally non-authoritative (*avidyika*) and because no natural disparity among speakers was admitted—and due to the delusion that non-duality (*advaita*) is clearly established—the Purāṇic statements were presented first, followed by the citations from the Bhagavadgītā. Here, however, since a natural disparity among speakers is admitted and the possession of infinite qualities and manifestations is made explicit, the citations from the Bhagavadgītā are presented first, and the Purāṇic statements are shown afterwards.

Therefore, it was said: "from the Smṛtis and Purāṇas. First, those most explicit statements are presented which, contrary to the meaning asserted by the opponent as being conveyed by the passages he has cited, establish a different sense; this is done subsequently in order to demonstrate the meaning of the opponent's cited words in a way that does not contradict them. Regarding the verse beginning with "He who [knows] Me": here, by the word *aja* ("unborn"), there is the exclusion of the non-conscious (*acit*) and the conscious associated with it (*cetana-saṃsṛṣṭa*). By the word *anādim* ("without beginning"), there is the exclusion of the liberated (*mukta*). For its state of being "unborn" would indeed imply having a beginning (*ādimat*).

Regarding the term *lokamaheśvara* (the Great Lord of the world): this serves to exclude those who are eternally liberated (*nityamukta*). The "world" (*loka*) is that which is perceived; it refers to the threefold aggregate of sentient and insentient beings established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Here, the meaning of the second half [of the verse], "He is not deluded among mortals," is also intended to be considered. The intention is that by stating he is "not deluded" because he knows [the world] as distinct from both the sentient and the insentient, it is expressed that his distinction from everything else is ontological (*tāttvika*).

He employs the phrase "resting in Me" (*matsthāni*) to highlight the distinction [of the Self] by way of its being the sustainer and so forth, for the sake of clarity. Here, the definition of a body is indicated: all beings have their existence dependent on Me, whereas My existence is not dependent on them. He states "nor am I" (*na ca*) to show that I am not a support in the manner perceived by the world, but rather through My mere will (*saṅkalpa*). Since a negation refers to something other than what has been enjoined, this is precisely the intended meaning. "Yoga" means the divine yoga, the possession of all powers that is unique to the Lord (*īśvara*).

If it is argued that the phrase "and they do not abide in Me" is a negation of the ultimate reality of My being their sustainer, then the statement "Behold My divine yoga" would be contradictory; for in that case, one should have said, "Behold My delusion. Explaining this very point through the words "the sustainer of beings," [the Lord] clarifies the meaning as follows: "My self" means "My volition. For the word *ātman* denotes the intellect (*mati*), as in the definition: "The word *ātman* refers to effort, the sun, fire, and the intellect. Therefore, in this context, the word *ātman* signifies knowledge in the form of volition.

By the statement, "My Self is the creator of beings," the meaning of "and yet the beings do not dwell in Me" is clarified. "Creator of beings" means the one who sustains the existence of all beings. To counter the doubt that the Lord is merely a finite being possessing attributes, and in order to demonstrate the negation of any reality apart from the Cause as well as to provide His defining characteristic, He declares Himself to be the cause of the universe with the word "I. Thus, both His origin and dissolution have been stated.

Since stability is established by the statement [of the Lord] being the "sustainer," he specifies that sustaining nature with the word "in me" (*mayi*). By the phrase "pervading" (*viṣṭabhya*), His role as the controller is expressed; "pervading" means presiding over. "With one part" (*ekāṃśena*) refers to a portion of His volition, and that constitutes the characteristic of having a body. He shows the explicit statement regarding the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, which was intended in the passage beginning with "He who knows Me as unborn," etc., by the word "Supreme" (*uttama*). In the preceding statement, the terms "the Perishable" (*kṣara*) and "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*) referred to the bound and the liberated souls; "immovable" (*kūṭasthaḥ*) means changeless.

For the liberated one, there is an absence of modification in the form of the contraction of knowledge. Alternatively, the word *kūṭastha* (unchanging) may be used in a general sense; for the liberated self possesses both types of glory—as expressed in the statement "he moves at will in all worlds"—and thus possesses *kūṭasthatva*. By the phrase "designated as the Supreme Self," the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, which includes the passage "the Supreme Self is established," is recalled; and by the phrase "higher even than the Imperishable. For in that very same text, it is said: "He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Sovereign."

He is the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) because there is no decay (*kṣaraṇa*) consisting in the contraction of knowledge; he is the liberated one. He is the self-ruler (*svarāṭ*), meaning independent, not subject to karma. He is the supreme (*parama*); his supremacy (*pāramyam*) is due to the fact that there is no other state superior to this among the states attained by individual souls (*jīva*). The word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) refers to Brahmā, Śiva, and others. For in that very section, the Blessed Lord is described using terms denoting both bound and liberated souls in grammatical apposition: "He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, he is Indra, he is the Imperishable, the supreme self-ruler."

In this regard, the scriptural statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is heard: "All this, indeed, is the Puruṣa. Furthermore, the grounds for that coreferentiality are clear within that same section: "He lives upon all that," "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self," and "Nārāyaṇa stands pervading [all]. In these sets of statements, it is precisely the relationship of being supported and supporting, being controlled and controlling, being subordinate and being the principal, and being pervaded and pervading that constitutes the basis for coreferentiality, and not identity of substance (*tad-ekatva*).

This is clear. Now, the meaning of this [verse] is also stated here: by the word *āviśya* ("having entered"), the sense of the *Atharva-veda* passage "Nārāyaṇa remains pervading" is expressed. By the word *īśvara*, the sense of the passage "the Lord of the universe" is expressed; for the word *īśvara* denotes the one who is the dependent (the principal). For this very reason, in the phrase "the Lord of the universe, the Lord of the Self," the term *ātmeśvara* is used to indicate the absence of any other lord. By the word *vibharti* ("sustains"), the sense of the passage "he lives upon that entire universe" is expressed.

Likewise, it is said: "Because of pervading, because of supporting, and because of being the Lord, another [form] is declared as the fifteenth. By the words, "He who knows Me thus, undeluded," the state of being undeluded is stated for one who possesses knowledge of the complete distinction [of the Lord]. By the words, "Thus is the most secret teaching," the extreme secrecy of that subject matter is stated. Therefore, it is clear that the intended meaning lies in this sense. Furthermore, the grammatical incorrectness of the compound *puruṣottama* need not be suspected; for there is a statement in the Mahābhāṣya: "Compounds such as *nāgottama* and others are established [as valid]."

Furthermore, because the sages who provide the etymological derivation (*nirvāha*) of the term *puruṣottama* are the most authoritative, just like Pāṇini. The compound *puruṣottama* may be analyzed as a genitive-tatpuruṣa (possessive compound), for it is stated [in scripture]: "And higher even than the Imperishable. As for the rule regarding the prior placement of the first member, that applies only when co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is intended, not when it is not intended; thus, there is no occasion for the suspicion of contradicting grammatical rules.

Since the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious is established by these statements, the meaning of passages such as "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field" must be described in a way that does not contradict them. Because [the Lord] has ordained—through such statements as "He who, entering the three worlds, sustains them"—that everything is subordinate to the Blessed One, supported by Him, governed by Him, pervaded by Him, and His body, and because it is improper to deny that, the non-existence of anything other than His own nature is declared by such passages as "There is nothing that exists without Him."

Furthermore, since the term *avinābhāva* is not commonly known to mean "falsity," it must be accepted as such; this is the intended meaning. For the word *vinā* refers to the absence of a relation, because the term *avinābhāva* denotes a rule of relation (*sambandhaniyama*).

Now, the statements of the Purāṇas are presented. Therein, desiring to explain the meaning of the statement "in which all distinctions have subsided" (*pratyastamitabheda*), and wishing to show—by way of its utility—that the opening and concluding sections of that [text] are directed toward the qualified Brahman (*saviśeṣa*), he cites the opening statements beginning with "He who... (*sa sarva...*). Among those, the first passage concerns the state of being the opposite of everything to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīkatva*). "All beings" refers to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is *pradhāna*; "transformations" refers to the great principle (*mahat*) and so forth; and "faults arising from qualities" refers to defects caused by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

Those "defects" (*doṣāḥ*) are the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. "Transcended" (*vyatītaḥ*) means specifically transcended; the meaning is that by necessity, due to not being subject to them, he is unfit for connection with them. "One who has transcended all obscurations" (*atītasarvāvaraṇaḥ*): obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the connection with *prakṛti*, karmic impressions (*vāsanā*), and so on. He is one by whom all of that has been transcended—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "all obscurations" refers to the obscuration of knowledge regarding all objects. The meaning is that he has transcended the contraction of knowledge regarding all objects; or the meaning is that he has transcended the contraction of all qualities, such as the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).

He explains His being the self of all with the words "by that" (*tena*). The meaning is not, however, as in the case of "the pot has clay as its essence. The phrase "in the midst of the worlds" means within the interval between the two manifestations (*vibhūti*). Now, he states that the nature of the divine Self is solely intent upon auspiciousness (*maṅgalaikatānatva*) with the words "all" (*samasta*). If, in the expression "consisting of all auspicious qualities" (*samastakalyāṇaguṇātmaka*), one were to say merely that He possesses auspicious qualities, then the word *ātman* would have to signify "nature" (*svabhāva*). Thus, the distinction (or resolution) is that the brief statement is expanded in detail by the passage beginning with "splendor, strength, sovereignty," and so forth.

For this reason as well, it is logical that [the passage] has as its primary purport the divine nature of the Self; according to the maxim that "the injunction of what is not required is weaker than the injunction of what is required. In that case, the word *kalyāṇa* (auspicious) is one where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the predominant sense. Thus, *samastakalyāṇaguṇaḥ* means "He whose qualities and essential nature consist of all auspiciousness. This is explained in the same way that the term *dvayeka-* in the sūtra "dvayekayordvivacanaikavacane" refers to duality and unity; otherwise, it would have had to be stated as *dvayekeṣu*.

But it is not [the case] for two or one. And that [expression] was employed to indicate the grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) of a designation where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant. For this very reason, the learned have said: "The qualities are truth, knowledge, and so forth. He whose self (*ātman*), which is the substratum (*dharmin*), consists of all auspicious qualities, is "one whose nature consists of all auspicious qualities" (*samastakalyāṇaguṇātmaka*). This *bahuvrīhi* compound is figurative (*aupacārika*), like the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*). He praises the very nature of His divine self with the words "by His own power" (*svaśaktibhiḥ*).

"Having assumed the creation of beings from a mere fraction of his own parts" (svāṃśaleśāt dhṛtabhūtasargaḥ). Alternatively, *śakti* means capacity (*sāmarthya*); thus the meaning is "having assumed the multitude of beings through a small portion of his own qualities. *Bhūtasargaḥ* refers to the collection of elements (*bhūtasamūha*). Alternatively, that which is created is the *sarga*, meaning the entire range of effects (*kāryavastujāta*). Intending to describe the sixfold attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*) later according to their specific purport, he first describes his divine form with the word "desire" (*icchā*). "Desirability" (*abhimatatva*) is the state of being worthy of being desired; that is to say, its conformity to one's own [nature].

The suffix *niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle) is used in the sense of fitness (*arha*), as in "the unseen seer, the unheard hearer. For in that case, the suffix *kta* has the sense of fitness; this is because [the term] shares the same meaning with "the invisible, the ungraspable," and so forth. In the world, it is observed that what is desired may not be suitable, and what is suitable may not be desired. To exclude these two possibilities, the words "desired" (*abhimata*) and "taken by will" (*icchā-gṛhīta*) are used. The word "will" (*icchā*) without a prefix is common to both eternal will and the will produced at the time of manifestation; this is because there is no restriction [to one or the other].

Now, by way of introduction, he states the purpose of the formal composition (*vigraha*) with the words "having accomplished" (*saṃsādhitā*). Next, he describes the possession of the sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) with the word "splendor" (*tejas*). There is no intended sequence here. The words *mahā-* and *su-* are common to all the qualities. *Mahattva* (greatness) means being unlimited. As in: "Great energy, great strength, great intellect, great heroism, great power, great luster. And as in: "Exalted wisdom, incomparable strength," and so forth. By the word *su-*, their auspiciousness (*maṅgalatva*) is expressed.

Thus, he says "the Supreme" (*para*) to indicate that [Brahman] is superior in terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), its form (*vigraha*), and its qualities (*guṇa*). Regarding the phrase "defects such as the qualities," he explains the meaning of the word "defect" (*doṣa*) with the words "wherein there is not. The "afflictions and so forth" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), actions (*karman*), fruitions (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*). - The afflictions (*kleśa*) are ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the will to live (*abhiniveśa*). - Action (*karman*) consists of merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*apuṇya*). - Fruitions (*vipāka*) are birth (*jāti*), lifespan (*āyus*), and experience (*bhoga*). - Latent disposition (*āśaya*) is habitual tendency (*vāsanā*), which is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Recalling the *Yoga-sūtra*, "The Lord is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent impressions," he identifies Him as the Lord (*īśvara*). Furthermore, he states that there is a difference between the meaning of Vedānta and that of the Yoga-śāstra, beginning with the word "individual" (*vyaṣṭi*). Previously, the meaning of the scriptural texts concerning difference was explained; therefore, for the sake of reconciling the texts concerning unity, the meaning of the bridging scriptural texts is now stated, beginning with "individual. By the terms "individual" (*vyaṣṭi*) and "totality" (*samaṣṭi*), the class of conscious beings in the state of cause and effect is denoted. "Form" (*rūpa*) means the body.

One's own nature (*svarūpa*) is the body (*śarīra*), which is unique to oneself. The term "Lord of all" (*sarveśvara*) indicates the definition of the embodied one (*śarīrin*). "Lord" (*īśvara*) means a controller. By this, it is established that being controlled constitutes being a body; for a body is indeed a specific kind of object to be controlled. "All-seeing" (*sarvadṛk*) and "all-knowing" (*sarvavettā*): the meaning is that he knows everything, both in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and its specific modes (*prakārataḥ*). Alternatively, according to the method of such scriptural passages as "having eyes on all sides," the meaning is that by being all-seeing, he knows everything. Or else, [it means] he is the seer of all and the knower of all.

According to the Vedic scripture, "The eye of both gods and mortals," He is the bestower of visual knowledge. Alternatively, He is the "Knower of All" (*sarvavettā*), meaning one who finds everything, which signifies that all His desires have been attained. He possesses "all powers" (*samastaśakti*). "Power" (*śakti*) is a non-separately established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*) conducive to action. Since He has the entire universe as His body in the manner described, everything is a non-separately established attribute of Him; this is the meaning. He is called the "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*); by the word "supreme" (*parama*), His status as the peerless Lord is established (thereby excluding the existence of any other lord).

He is called *parama* (the Supreme) because [He thinks], "May no one else be superior to me. He states that knowledge regarding such a Lord alone is the means for knowing liberation (*apavarga*). Regarding the phrase "when He is known" (*sa jñāyate sati*), if the reading is *saṃjñāyate*, then "one whose faults have been destroyed" (*asta-doṣam*) and so forth are qualifiers of Brahman. By which [knowledge] produced from the scriptures He is cognized (*vijñāyate*); by which [knowledge] consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*) He is perceived (*saṃdṛśyate*); and by which [knowledge] consisting of supreme devotion (*parama-bhakti*) and direct experience (*anubhava*) He is attained—that is, experienced. As it is said: "But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, may I be known in this way."

This is because of the statement: "O scorcher of foes, [it is for the purpose] to know, to see, and to enter [Brahman] in its true essence. In the reading *sa jñāyate* ("it is known"), the phrase "free from defects" (*astadoṣam*) and so forth serves as a qualification of the knowledge of Brahman. This is because of the saying: "Indeed, the distinction among cognitions arises solely through their objects, since they themselves are formless"; thus, the quality of being free from defects and so on belongs to the knowledge by way of its object. By the term "free from defects," there is an exclusion of that knowledge which has as its object the insentient (*acid*), which is the locus of defects.

"Pure" (*śuddha*) excludes the knowledge whose object is the bound soul (*baddha-jīva*), which is impure due to being subject to karma, as stated in the passage beginning with "all those [souls] are indeed impure. "Supreme" (*para*) means stainless and absolutely stainless; by this, there is an exclusion of the knowledge whose object is the liberated soul (*mukta*), which is occasionally associated with the stain consisting in the fitness for connection with karma. "Of one form" (*ekarūpa*) excludes the knowledge whose object is the eternally liberated soul (*nitya-mukta*), which possesses multiple forms. In this manner, even though these are qualifiers of Brahman, their function as exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) is to be understood.

If it is a qualification of Brahman, it is both of a single form and a qualification useful for its function as a substratum; that is, it has a stable nature, meaning it is more firmly established in the promise of protecting those who depend upon it. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is either something other than the knowledge of the means to liberation or its opposite, according to the statement: "That is true knowledge which leads to liberation. Alternatively, ignorance is the absence of knowledge; because it lacks the quality of culminating in Brahman, its object is a thing not established in its true state. If it is a qualification of Brahman, there is a single sentence; if it is a qualification of knowledge, there are two sentences.

In the verse beginning with “pratyastamitabhedaṃ,” keeping the word *pratyastamitabheda* (in which all distinctions have subsided) in mind, statements regarding its possessing attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) have been shown. Now, with the desire to explain the phrase “beyond the range of words” (*agocaraṃ vacasām*), he shows scriptural statements concerning its being beyond the scope of speech, starting with the verse beginning “śuddha. In that regard, it was stated that in the previous verse beginning with “aśabdagocarasya,” the application of the term “Lord” (*bhagavat*) to the liberated self (*muktātman*) is figurative (*aupacārika*).

In response to the inquiry "How so?", he states "Pure" (*śuddha*) to indicate the ground for the application of the term "Lord" (*bhagavat*), which distinguishes Him from liberated souls.
