The sense is that primacy belongs only where there is a perfection of the grounds for application, and not elsewhere. Regarding "Pure": just as the word "established" (*siddha*) in the phrase "the relationship between word and meaning being established," the word "pure" contains an implication of restriction; thus, "pure" means "eternally pure."

Just as in the word *abbhakṣaḥ* (water-drinker), the word *siddha* contains an element of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), and thus the word *siddha* is explained as referring to the eternal (*nitya*); so it is here. By this quality of being eternally pure (*nitya-śuddhatva*), all sentient beings are excluded; for even the eternally perfected ones (*nitya-siddha*) possess eternal purity only by depending on the Lord’s eternal will. In the phrase "named Great Glory" (*mahāvibhūty-ākhya*), since that which has become a glory cannot itself be the Great Glory, the state of being the presiding lord over both types of glory serves to distinguish [the Lord] from all sentient beings.

By the phrase "in the supreme Brahman," the exclusion of the conscious [individual soul] is established. For the lower self is denoted by the word *brahman* alone, as in: "O twice-born, even though that Brahman is beyond the scope of words. However, later on, the supreme self will be referred to as "having become the supreme Brahman. Furthermore, in other passages, the term *parabrahman* is seen to refer exclusively to the supreme self. Therefore, in order to exclude the lower self, it is said: "in the supreme Brahman known as the Great Sovereignty (*mahāvibhūti*)."

Furthermore, the status of being the cause of all causes belongs to the Blessed Lord alone; for the liberated soul is devoid of activity regarding the world. Thus, because the grounds for its application are fully present in Him, the word "Bhagavat" is used in its primary sense only for the Lord of All, and not for anyone else—this is the meaning.

Explaining this meaning both letter by letter and as a whole, he states the meaning of the word *bhagavat* with the verse beginning "He who sustains" (*saṃbhartā*) and so forth. "Purity" (*śuddhatva*) has been explained by the phrase "without that which is to be abandoned" (*vinā heyaiḥ*). "Greatness of manifestation" (*mahāvibhūtitva*) has been demonstrated because the word *śrī* in the verse "of all sovereignty" (*aiśvaryasya samagrasya*) denotes the wealth of enjoyment (*bhogavibhūti*), while the capacity for sustaining [the world] indicates the wealth of divine play (*līlāvibhūti*). Furthermore, his being the cause of all causes will be made clear below.

For this very reason, because of His unsurpassed greatness through the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and so forth, His status as the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmatva*) is manifest. Therefore, it is appropriate that the subsequent passages constitute an exposition of the verse beginning with the word *śuddha*. The meaning is explained by dividing [the term] into *bha*, *ga*, *bhaga*, and *va*. These words take their respective forms by applying the suffix *ḍa*—according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well"—and by the elision of the *ṭi* (the final vowel and following consonant) after these verbal roots. He states the meaning of *bha* with the half-verse beginning with *sam*: "the sustainer" (*sambhartā*).

*Saṃbharaṇa* means the provision of instruments (*upakaraṇa-saṃvidhāna*). The meaning is that it renders *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and *kāla* capable of producing effects. Alternatively, the intention may be that *saṃbharaṇa* refers to the creation of the *mahat* and so forth, which is suitable for the production of the effect in the form of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). *Bhartṛ* means the master (*svāmī*). Since supporting (*dhāraṇa*) is denoted by the letter *va*, and nourishing (*poṣakatva*) is included within the sense of leading (*netṛtva*) denoted by the letter *ga*, and because an injunction regarding what is required is stronger than an injunction regarding what is not required, it is "lordship" (*svāmitva*) that is intended here.

Although the word *bharati*—when joined with a specific suffix—is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of "master," nevertheless, by the force of the previously stated reasoning supported by the verbal root itself, it is determined that the root alone denotes "lordship" (*svāmitva*). By means of the particle *iti*, the two grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), namely "sustainer" (*saṃbhartṛ*) and "supporter" (*bhartṛ*), are extracted and expressed. For this very reason, it is said that [the term] is endowed with two meanings.

In the subsequent [passage], however, although there are three grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because they are not extracted by means of the particle *iti*, the single referent (*artha*) stated is the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by all three grounds for application. He states the meaning of the word *ga* with the words "not" (*na iti*). Since the meanings made clear by the prefixes (*upasarga*) are merged into the verbal root (*dhātu*), he states the meaning of such words as "one who causes to rise" (*udgamayitṛ*) and "one who causes to join" (*saṅgamayitṛ*) with the words "not" (*na iti*). By the word "creator" (*sraṣṭṛ*), the meaning of the word "one who causes to rise" (*udgamayitṛ*) is stated; by the words "not" (*na iti*), the meaning of the word "one who causes to go" (*gamayitṛ*) is stated.

The meaning is "the one who causes [them] to abide. By the word *gamayitṛ* ("the one who causes to go"), the meaning of the word *saṅgamayitṛ* ("the one who causes to join together") is expressed, and that is dissolution (*saṃhāra*). Just as in the passage, "In which all this comes together and dissolves," the words *vyeti* and *sameti* express emanation and dissolution respectively, so it is here. Alternatively, it means "the one who causes [all things] to go to his own self as their cause"; that is, the one who effects the merging of the aggregate of effects into himself. Even though the prefixes (*upasarga*) are not explicitly used, they have been explained in this way by the venerable Parāśara because the meanings are inherently contained within the verbal root.

Now, before the explanation of the letter *va*, he states the meaning of the combination of the letters *bha* and *ga*: "Of sovereignty... (*aiśvaryasya*). The word *samagra* (complete) applies to every term. The word *samagra* is intended to exclude the limited sovereignty of [Brahmā] Caturmukha and others. *Yaśas* (fame) is the renown of possessing excellent qualities. *Śrī* (prosperity) is the abundance of objects of enjoyment. *Vairāgya* (detachment) is dispassion; the meaning is a lack of interest due to being perfectly fulfilled, as in the scriptural passage: "He who is beyond speech and beyond regard."

The possessive suffix *matup* has a well-known meaning, so it is not explained here. Now he states the meaning of the letter *va*: "they dwell" (*vasanti*). Because the suffix *ḍa*—according to the rule "it is seen in other cases as well"—has multiple meanings, its derivation applies both to the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and to the agent (*kartṛ*). [Thus, it means] "in the self of the elements" (*bhūtātmani*), that is, in the self of all beings; "in the self of the All" (*akhilātmani*), that is, in the one who has the entire universe as his body. Alternatively, by the word *bhūta*, the effect (*kārya*) is expressed; thus it means "in the self of that," or "in the self of the All," which refers to the self of the eternally liberated ones who are not included within the category of effects.

Now, he states the meaning concerning the scope of the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) with the words "jñānaśakti... (knowledge-power...). In the order of recitation, however, the verse beginning with "jñānaśaktibalaiśvarya... is read after the two verses beginning with "evameṣa...". Nevertheless, this verse beginning with "jñānaśakti... has been included here before the two verses beginning with "evameṣa... due to the logical connection of its expressing the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*). Furthermore, the verse beginning with "utpattiṃ ca pralayaṃ caiva... was not utilized in the present context; therefore, the selection was made in this manner.

The meaning is that [the qualities] denoted by the word *bhagavat* are to be understood as the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*). "In their entirety" (*aśeṣataḥ*) means not individually as grounds for application, but rather collectively. By the word "entirety," the collection of qualities such as character (*śīla*) and so forth, which consist of the subdivisions of the sixfold attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), is included. Although sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), valor (*vīrya*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) were previously mentioned explicitly, there is no tautology because the collection differs based on the insertion or omission of certain constituent members.

Nor is a collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) postulated here, by which [the word] would have as its scope only those qualities not previously mentioned. The acceptance of such a power follows from the force of the statement itself. Previously, through the explanation of the literal meaning of the syllables, the letters *bha*, *ga*, and *va* were explained; now he states the meaning of *an* with the word "without" (*vinā*). According to the maxim that "Kaśyapa is a seer," by the term *an* (which stands for *na*), "not" is expressed; and the sense is that what is to be negated is that which is to be abandoned.

Thus, because the grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) are fully present, he states that the word has its primary denotation (*mukhyavṛttatva*) in the Blessed Lord alone with the word "thus" (*evam*). It is called a "great word" (*mahāśabda*) because it contains a great meaning within it. The term "Supreme Brahman" (*paramabrahma*) is used to exclude the liberated souls (*muktātman*). To the question, "How can it have its primary denotation in Him alone, when its usage is seen elsewhere as well?", he replies with the word "there" (*tatra*). "Expression of the components of the venerable object" (*pūjyapadārthokti*) means the expression of the meanings of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*) of the venerable [word]; "convention" (*paribhāṣā*) means established usage (*rūḍhi*); it is endowed with both of these. Thus, it is distinguished by both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).

For this very reason, it is not by way of metaphor (*upacāra*). The meaning is that it occurs in its primary sense (*mukhyavṛtti*). He states that elsewhere it is non-primary. By stating that [the term] is metaphorical when applied to liberated souls (*muktātman*), it is shown by implication (*arthāt*) that it is also metaphorical in other applications; such is the intention of the word "for" (*hi*). Even though all applications within the scope of the use of the word *Bhagavat* could be established otherwise, it is not proper to postulate a difference in denotative power (*śakti*). That alone where knowledge and the other attributes are unrestrained is the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*).
Since usage is possible even through a connection with a mere fraction of those qualities, the application elsewhere is metaphorical; such is the meaning.

Now, even in the conclusion of that very section on Yoga, [the author], showing the supreme statements concerning the qualified [aspect] and stating its possession of divine weapons, says "samastā" (all). The bound soul, the liberated soul, karma, and the forms of ignorance are the powers (*śaktis*). Their establishment therein occurs through the mediation of their respective presiding deities; for the reference "wherein" (*yatra*) requires a preceding statement (*purovāda*), and such a preceding statement exists in the chapter on weapons and ornaments according to the manner already described.

The phrase "that multiformity of forms" (*tad-viśvarūpa-vairūpyam*) refers to the distinctness of its configuration (*saṃniveśa*). The word "other" (*anyat*) indicates that it is a different substance (*dravyāntara*). The term "great" (*mahat*) signifies its immeasurability. To the question of how it is possible to conceive of such a unique configuration—one which is of a different genus from everything else—he says: "of all... [etc.]. To the question "by what cause? he says: "by his own sport" (*svalīlayā*). Since sport is the purpose, the intention toward that is the cause; the meaning is that it is not by means of *karma*. To the question "what is the purpose? he says: "of the worlds" (*jagatām*).

The meaning is: "but not for the sake of enjoying the fruits of her own karma. He explains this with the words "na sā" (she is not [such]). "Pervasive" (*vyāpinī*) means devoid of spatial restriction, as in the Vedic injunctions regarding the bringing of a son and so forth. To the objection that even if she possesses the power of pervasion, an obstruction might still be possible, he says: "unimpeded in nature" (*avyāhatātmikā*). The meaning is that there is no resistance to her. Alternatively, "pervasive" means conforming to all incarnations; "unimpeded" means free from obstructions caused by space, time, or substance.

Thus, even if it is accepted that the verse beginning with "evam pratyastamite" refers to the Supreme Self, the fact that this very section has a qualified (saviśeṣa) purport is demonstrated by the opening and concluding statements, in order to refute the claim that it refers to the attributeless (nirviśeṣa) [Brahman].

Now, desiring to show that this verse has as its subject the nature of the completely purified individual soul (*jīvātman*), and that terms such as "with differences vanished" (*pratyastamitabheda*) have a limited scope [applying only to certain aspects], and wishing to demonstrate for that purpose those scriptural passages which state that the negation of difference and so forth applies only partially to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); and, in response to the doubt—"What relevance does the negation of certain differences regarding the Supreme Self have for the liberated soul?"—[the author] sets forth the qualities of the liberated one in order to establish the liberated soul's identity with the Supreme Self.

He shows the verse that extends [the attributes] to the Supreme Self with the words, "of this kind. By citing this verse, it is demonstrated that the first introductory verse of the first part, beginning with "jñānasvarūpam," which was recited in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) immediately after the verse beginning with "pratyastamitāśeṣa..."—as well as the group of four verses (*catuḥślokī*)—are all intended to establish the existence of attributes (*saviśeṣa*), even in the concluding section of the first part.

The employment of the concluding statement is made because the conclusion is present in the mind. "Of such a kind" means endowed with that manner which was described regarding the liberated self (muktātman) by such phrases as "devoid of activity" and "indefinable. In this way, the qualities of the liberated self have been attributed to the Blessed One.

The meaning is as follows: since the qualities of the liberated soul—such as being devoid of difference, being pure existence, and being beyond the reach of words—which were described [in the previous section] as "devoid of activity" and so forth, have been extended by analogy to the Lord, and since it is established by authoritative evidence that those negations apply only to certain [limited] objects regarding the Lord, it is proven that those same negations apply in that same way to the liberated self as well; thus, their application is only partial. Now, he describes the qualities of the Supreme Self as superior [to those of the liberated soul]: "pure, the adversary of impurity."

The meaning is "opposed to that which is to be abandoned along with its limiting adjuncts" (sopādhika-heyavirodhin). It is "eternal" by way of the nature of being eternally liberated; the meaning is that its state of being the adversary of impurity is eternal. It is "pervasive" by its very essence. It is "undecaying," meaning it is devoid of modification even in its attributes (dharma) by its own nature. For in the case of one who has attained liberation, there exists a modification in the form of the contraction and expansion of the mind characteristic of the prior state. Even for those who are eternally perfected, such a state was dependent on another [the Supreme]; therefore, this [Brahman] is distinguished from them. It is "devoid of all that is to be abandoned."

Previously, the state of being the opposite of that which is to be abandoned (*heya*) was stated; here, the absence of that which is to be abandoned is stated. Even for the liberated one, there is no absence of that which is to be abandoned *per se*, because that [absence] is dependent upon the grace of the Supreme Self. It is called "the abode" (*pada*) because it is reached (*padyate*). Since the term "supreme abode" (*paramapada*) is used to refer both to the divine world and to the liberated self, the phrase "named Viṣṇu" is stated in order to exclude those other meanings.

Now, even at the beginning of the first part, he demonstrates that the text is intent upon the qualified (saviśeṣa) by stating, "The highest of the high. By this, it is shown that the opening of the treatise itself is also intent upon the qualified; furthermore, it is established that the words such as "in which all difference has subsided" (pratyastamitabheda) are intended to negate only certain types of difference. Thus, there are three purposes [of this statement].

Since this collection of passages beginning with "anena paraḥparāṇām" serves as a commentary on the summary verse beginning with "avikārāya," its status as an introduction to the verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpam" is established by the sequence of meaning; thus, it is proven that this [verse] also has a qualified reality as its primary purport.

Alternatively, since the beginning and conclusion of the first section are devoted to the qualified [Brahman], it is not reasonable that the verse "jñānasvarūpam" (whose nature is knowledge), which constitutes the very commencement of that section, should contradict the natural sense of the Great Sentence; thus, its own reference to the qualified [Brahman] is established. Or else, because the verse of salutation is a supplement to the beginning of the treatise, it is established that its meaning must be described as being supplementary to that [treatise] and in accordance with it.

If it is argued that the meaning of the passage beginning with "paraḥ parāṇām" should be described in accordance with the meaning of the introductory verses of salutation (*namaskāra*), we say no; for the intention is that its meaning must also be stated in accordance with the introductory verses that describe the question, the answer, and the obtaining of the boon.

In this context, in order to establish that Brahman is the cause of the entire universe, the Vedāntas declare its infinity through such statements as, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. This infinity consists in being devoid of the three kinds of limitations. For it is never observed that objects such as jars, which are limited by space, time, and so forth, serve as the cause of everything in every respect. To be the cause of the entire aggregate of effects existing throughout the three periods of time, and to be the cause of effects located in all places, requires both spatial and temporal non-limitation.

For the establishment of its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*), the absence of limitation regarding the substance (*vastu*) is required. Indeed, a potter who is limited by his own substance cannot be the material cause, because the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the lump of clay and the potter is impossible. Therefore, desiring to explain in detail the absence of the three kinds of limitation in order to establish that [Brahman] is the cause of the whole, he first makes a summary declaration with the words "the highest of the high" (*paraḥ parāṇām*) and so forth, stating "the highest of the high" (*paramaḥ*). By this, the non-limitation by time (*kāla*) is established.

Because existing for a longer duration is what is denoted by the word *para* (supreme). By the term *paramātman*, the absence of spatial limitation is expressed. For the etymology of the word *ātman* is "that which pervades" (*āpnoti*). Being established as the self of all, it is distinguished from all things by its nature as the Self. Alternatively, because it exists as the Self and thus has all things as its body, it is "established in itself" (*svaparyavasthita*), meaning it is grounded in itself. Everything else is grounded in that [Self], since everything is a qualification [of it] by virtue of being its body.

Therefore, it is said that the state of being "unlimited in substance" (*vastvapariccheda*) means that the ultimate ground of all things is established in itself. For "unlimitedness in substance" consists in the capacity for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things; indeed, "limitation in substance" is the notion that "this is not that. Alternatively, "unlimitedness in substance" is the absence of any equal or superior in qualities other than eternity and omnipresence.

Since it is impossible for others who abide in Him to be either equal to or superior to the Supreme Self when compared to that which abides in itself, the phrase "established in the Self" establishes the non-limitation of the Reality [in space]. He explains this summarized meaning with the words beginning with "form" (*rūpa*). Therein, wishing first to express the non-limitation in time, he states "form" (*rūpa*) to show that the fivefold conceptualization existing in things limited by time does not exist in Brahman. By the word "form," the genus (*jāti*) is intended.

For those who know the principles [of logic] say: "The genus (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*) reside in the form (*rūpa*) of things that possess form. Here, the word *varṇa* refers specifically to the quality known as color (*rūpa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one intends to include smell, taste, and the like; actions such as sitting and lying down; and the possession of parts such as horns. In the reading *rūpavargādi*, the word *rūpa* refers to qualities such as blueness and yellowness, while the word *varga* refers to categories such as gods and humans; thus, it means "referring to the genus. A designation (*nirdeśa*) is a word whose basis and object is that [genus].

Those very things denoted by words are the qualifiers; [Brahman] is devoid of them. Alternatively, it is devoid of qualifiers such as form, color, and so forth, along with the words that denote them. Thus, since the quality of possessing form and so on—which is caused by karma and pervades impermanence—does not exist in Brahman, the exclusion of temporally delimited existence (kālapariccheda), which is pervaded by that [impermanence], follows from the exclusion of form and so on produced by karma. This is the meaning. Alternatively, because of the absence of form and so on produced by karma—which are pervaded by impermanence—it is impossible to infer impermanence in Brahman.
By this, the scope of the term "pratyastamitabheda" ("in which all distinctions have subsided") has been shown.

Now, since modifications are pervaded by impermanence, in order to exclude impermanence [from Brahman], he states its freedom from those modifications which pervade it, beginning with the words "decrease" (*apakṣaya*). By the word "birth" (*janman*), the two stages "is born" (*jāyate*) and "exists" (*asti*) are intended. Through the twofold application of each—namely, origination, subsistence, and destruction—the sixfold set of modifications is established for each individual entity. Because [Brahman] is devoid of these, it can be said that it "always exists. By the word "always," there is the exclusion of occasional existence.

The intention of the word "kevala" (alone) is that [the ultimate reality] is not [expressed] by words such as "it arises" and so forth. By this, the scope of the phrase "mere existence" (sattāmātra) is shown, and the scope of the phrase "beyond the range of words" (agocaraṃ vacasām) is also shown. The intended meaning of that term is that because there is an absence of grounds for application (pravṛttinimitta) such as form or color, and because there is an absence of grounds for application such as "arising" and so forth, it cannot be expressed by words that denote conceptual construction or modification.
If it is said that "beyond the range of words" means being beyond the range of all sounds, then it cannot even be said that it is "mere existence" which is beyond the range of words.

Now, he speaks of the absence of spatial limitation by way of the etymological definition [of the name], beginning with the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*). This statement is made by way of the etymological definition of the name in order to negate that Brahman is something other than the Lord (Īśvara) and to exclude any other deity. Since the *uṇādi* suffixes have multiple meanings, the derivation of the word "Vāsudeva" is stated as being both in the sense of a location (*adhikaraṇa*) and an agent (*kartṛ*). For in the Vedāntas, the Supreme Brahman is indeed described as being changeless and so forth.

To the question, "How then is that spoken of as Vāsudeva?", he says: "That is Brahman. This reference by the word "that" (*tat*) is like the statement, "For coldness is the very nature of water. For grammarians hold that pronouns bring about identity between the thing being pointed out and the thing subsequently referred to, and they take on its gender in turn. The term "eternal" (*nityam*) excludes all that is merely produced. The terms "unborn," "indestructible," and "unchanging"—meaning of a single, uniform nature—exclude the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) which is eternal only in a modified sense.

By the term "of a single nature" (*ekasvarūpa*), the absence of growth and transformation is intended. Because there is nothing to be discarded, it is "pure" (*nirmala*); this excludes the bound soul (*baddha*). By "ever-present" (*sada*), the liberated soul (*mukta*) is excluded. By "supreme" (*parama*), the eternally perfected beings (*nityasiddha*) are excluded. Alternatively, "of a single nature" excludes the bound soul, while "ever-present" and the other terms exclude the liberated soul. Thus, the meaning is that Vāsudeva alone is the Brahman described in the Upaniṣads as being distinct from all things other than Himself.

The scriptural passage expressing threefold infinity also determines the specific deity as "the Infinite" (*anantam*). The word *ananta* is both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍhi*). Therefore, it primarily denotes the Blessed Lord, who is synonymous with Nārāyaṇa and other such names, and in whom the threefold infinity inheres. In the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," the word *anantam* is masculine and ends in the accusative case; this is because it is construed with the verb "he who knows" (*yo veda*). If it were in the nominative case, it would have to be "tat yo veda" (he who knows that), which would necessitate the ellipsis of the word *tat* and result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, the meaning there is exactly as stated. Consequently, following that [text], even here, at the time of describing the lack of limitation (*apariccheda*), the specific deity has been determined. He states the non-limitation of the object (*vastu-apariccheda*) with the words "that very same" (*tadeva*). By the phrase "all this indeed," the aggregate of the manifest (*vyakta*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the person (*puruṣa*), and time (*kāla*) is expressed. The meaning is: all this, which is the very nature of the manifest, the unmanifest, the person, and time—that is Brahman. By this, the non-limitation of the object is stated; for the non-limitation of the object consists in its fitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things.

The non-limitation of the entity [of Brahman] is established because its lack of equal or superior is proven through qualities such as pervasion and sustenance, which serve as the grounds for having the sentient and insentient as its body precisely by virtue of being capable of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things. For it is impossible for anything other than Brahman to have the entire aggregate of sentient and insentient beings as its body.

Thus, at the commencement of the treatise, the reality known as Vāsudeva, which possesses both natures (liṅga), was declared as the subject to be established. And at the conclusion of the treatise, this same point is shown by the words "these two dissolve" (*līyete*). Since the term "Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) is seen to be used occasionally for the individual soul (*jīva*), the quality of being the cause of the world—which is the defining characteristic of the Supreme Self—is stated [in the phrase] "they dissolve into the Supreme Self" (*paramātmani*) in order to exclude that [individual soul]. Furthermore, the term "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*) is used to make it known that He is not distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*).

And it is stated that "Viṣṇu" is the name [of the Lord] in order to indicate that Īśvara is not some other deity. Here, by the words "the Supreme Self," "the support," and "the Supreme Lord," the definition of the Embodied One (the indwelling Self) is made clear. Thus, it has been demonstrated that in both the opening and conclusion of the scripture, as well as in the openings and conclusions of the intermediate sections, it is established that Nārāyaṇa alone—the one whose nature consists of auspicious qualities that are the opposite of all things to be abandoned—is the Supreme Brahman.

Now, since the connection with ignorance and so forth are indeed taught as belonging to Brahman itself, how can this be consistent with Brahman whose nature has been described as stated above? In response to this doubt, it is said that [the connection] is possible through the relationship of the door and the one who possesses the door (dvāra-dvāribhāva), just as in the case of the statement, "He who possesses hardness creates [the earth]. Thus, intending to explain the relationship between the Supreme Self and the individual selves (jīvas) by way of the soul-body relationship (ātma-śarīrabhāva), as well as their connection with ignorance and so forth, [the author] first demonstrates the relationship between the individual self and Brahman in the form of the soul-body relationship in two verses.

By the words "in form," etc., [he means] both the embodied and the unembodied; that is to say, the bound and the liberated. He explains this by saying, "having the nature of the perishable and the imperishable. This means possessing uncontracted knowledge, as opposed to the perishable which consists of the contraction of knowledge. And "abiding in all beings": here the suffix *kta* has the sense of fitness (*arha*). Thus, the meaning is: capable of pervading because of its extreme subtlety, and thus fit for abiding in all beings.

Alternatively, the abiding of the bound soul (*baddha*) in all beings occurs by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas for the liberated soul (*mukta*), it occurs through the medium of non-manifest knowledge (*avibhu-jñāna*) as its attribute (*dharma*). "That is the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman": that liberated essential nature is the Imperishable (*akṣara*). "All this world is the Perishable" means that the form of the bound soul is perishable (*kṣara*). He specifies the nature of this form with the words "occupying a single part" (*ekadeśa*); "power" (*śakti*) refers to an inseparable qualification that is conducive to the effect.

By the two qualifiers "situated in one place" (*ekadeśasthitasya*) and "pervasive" (*vistāriṇī*), its unmixed nature (*asaṅkīrṇasvabhāvatva*) is stated. In this verse, the phrase "the entire world" (*akhilaṃ jagat*) refers to the world consisting of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). Because the same logic applies, the status of being a power (*śaktitva*) is established for the Imperishable (*akṣara*) as well. Alternatively, the term "entire world" includes the Imperishable too; for the term "world" (*jagat*) has the same meaning as the term "world" (*loka*) used for the manifestation of the three quarters (*tripādvibhūti*), and because there is no restrictive factor for the word "entire" (*akhila*).

In the passage "All is the perishable," the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the perishable is an exception (*apavāda*); since that exception does not apply here, it is appropriate to designate even the imperishable. Because the word "this" (*idam*) refers to what has been previously mentioned, it is fitting that it denotes both the perishable and the imperishable.

[Objection: Surely, here the words *kṣara* (the perishable) and *akṣara* (the imperishable) refer to the Supreme Brahman existing in the form of effect and cause, since this allows for the primary sense of the term "Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahman*) to be established. Otherwise, there would be a discrepancy in the meaning of the various occurrences of the word "Brahman" within this single context. Furthermore, the world's being comparable to moonlight is appropriate, since light, having its constituent parts dispersed, can logically be considered an effect of fire. [Reply: It is not so; for that would entail violating the natural force of the distinct designation "the two forms of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo rūpe*).

And that [distinction] is impossible because there is no existence of cause and effect apart from Brahman. If, for the sake of the natural sense of the genitive case, "formedness" and "formlessness" were intended [as qualities], then the natural sense of the words *mūrta* and *amūrta* would be lost. If one does not intend them as having substance as their primary meaning, then there is an impossibility of grammatical coordination with the word *rūpa*. If it were argued that "Brahman has two forms, for Brahman is both formed and formless," then there would be the fault of having to supply the word *brahma* in the nominative case.

This is because it is impossible for the word *brahman*, used here in the genitive case, to be in grammatical apposition with the words *mūrta* and *amūrta*. Furthermore, the statement "and abiding in all beings" (*sarvabhūteṣu ca sthite*) would be untenable; for since the word *sarvabhūta* denotes effects, if its abiding within those effects were being asserted, it would result in the absurdity of something residing in itself. Moreover, since the cause is non-different from its effects, this would also entail the absurdity of the cause residing in itself. Nor can it be said that the "abiding in all beings" refers to the two states [of cause and effect].

This is not the meaning of the verse, because it is impossible for the words "limit of the substrate" (*dharmiparyanta*) and "perishable-imperishable" (*kṣarākṣara*) to be in grammatical apposition; furthermore, if those two were intended to refer to states (*avasthā*), their natural sense would be violated. Moreover, it is impossible for the word *jagat* ("the world"), which denotes that which possesses states, to be in apposition with the word *brahman*; and even if that [apposition] were accepted, it is impossible for the causal state to exist within the effect, and it is also impossible for the word *śakti* ("power") to denote the effect. For even by way of metaphorical usage, a term can be designated by the word *śakti* only if it qualifies something useful for the effect.

This is because being a qualification useful for the effect follows from its being a generality. For power (*śakti*) is a qualification useful for the effect that is non-different from the possessor of power (*śakta*); however, the effect is not a qualification non-different from the cause, nor is it useful for the cause; for since effect and cause are non-different, it is impossible for something to be a qualification of itself. If it is argued that "being an effect" is the qualification, that is true.

Nevertheless, since the word *jagat* (world), which denotes the substratum (*dharmin*), does not denote "being an effect," its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *śakti* (power) is untenable even by way of metaphorical usage. In our view, however, primacy would be possible [for the term *śakti*] because power is defined as an inseparable qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) that is conducive to the production of an effect. Furthermore, if the word *kṣara* were intended to refer to an effect, there would be an inconsistency with the illustrative example; for moonlight lacks disintegrated parts and thus cannot be an effect of fire.

Nor is it appropriate to interpret [the passage] as referring to the sentient and the insentient on the basis of the usage: "The mutable is *pradhāna*; the immortal and immutable is *Hara*. For this would entail the fallacy of something residing in itself (*svavṛtti*), which makes the existence of all beings within [the insentient portion] impossible. If it is argued that the abiding of both [sentient and insentient] is possible within beings that consist of an aggregate of the sentient and the insentient, we say no; for it is impossible for the two constituents of an aggregate to reside in the aggregate itself. An aggregate, indeed, resides in its constituents. Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the subsequent text.

For later on, having introduced two forms by means of the words "mūrtāmūrta" in the passage, "The form of Bhūman is both mūrta and amūrta," and having pointed out Hiraṇyagarbha and others, it is stated: "This mūrta form of Hari is endowed with the threefold bhāvanā. Indeed, an insentient entity cannot possess a connection with the bhāvanās of karma and Brahman.

In the passage, "That is the imperishable (akṣara), the supreme, the self-ruling (svarāṭ)," the word *akṣara* refers to the liberated self because it is distinct from those bound by Indra and the other gods, and because of its grammatical coordination with the word *svarāṭ*, which denotes the liberated state as in the phrase, "He becomes self-ruling. Therefore, in accordance with that, the word *akṣara* here also refers to the liberated self.

However, the discrepancy in the meaning of the word *brahman*—as seen in such scriptural passages as "By austerity, Brahman is built up" (*tapasā cīyate brahma*) and "From that, this Brahman, name, form, and food are born"—is appropriate due to the force of various supporting arguments. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. By the passage beginning with "The power of Viṣṇu," etc., he demonstrates the connection of ignorance (*avidyā*) with the individual self (*jīvātman*), which serves as the gateway for the connection of ignorance with Brahman. [The term] "all-pervading" means residing in all bodies from the four-faced Brahmā down to an ant; the singular number is used to denote the class (*jāti*).

Alternatively, [the soul] is capable of pervading everything by itself through its nature as *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute). [The phrase] "enveloped by action" means that its knowledge is contracted due to *karman*. To the objection that, if this were so, everyone would be ignorant, he says: "by that. This means that the power of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) possesses degrees of knowledge corresponding to the degrees of *karman*. Since it is well-established that knowledge is eternal for all and that it encompasses all objects in the state of liberation (*mukti*), its contraction and expansion are proven to exist in the bound state (*baddhāvasthā*).

And the gradation of that [power] has been made clear by the statements: "The person is characterized by power," and "By that power, the bound souls (paśus) are superior. Furthermore, since even universals (jātis) are denoted by the word "form" (rūpa) because they are properties inseparably established [from their substrates], he says "and the primary [matter]" (pradhānam ca) to indicate that the "form-ness" (rūpatva) under discussion is defined by the characteristic of being subject to governance (niyāmyatva), in order to exclude those [universals].

Since the fact that consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) are governed by, supported by, pervaded by, and eternal in relation to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is improper to subject them to negation because they have been so ordained. Thus, by stating their eternality, it is demonstrated that since the attributes such as being "governed" are ultimately real, and the consciousness and unconsciousness that serve as their substrates are also ultimately real, it is impossible for these two to be objects of delusion. Indeed, the reality of an attribute is not tenable without the reality of its substrate; nor is it tenable for that which is sublated to be eternal.

The meaning is: by that which has become the self of all beings, that is, by that which pervades all beings. It is by the power of Viṣṇu—that is, by the power of Viṣṇu’s governance. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement immediately following [in the text]: "That power of Viṣṇu is likewise [all-pervading]. By that [power], there is *vṛti*, meaning pervasion. Furthermore, maintenance through governance is established by scripture (*śruti*). For it is heard in the *Śruti*: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (Akṣara), heaven and earth stand held apart. Therefore, the consistency of the subsequent verse, "He sustains," is maintained.

The two possess the nature of dependence (*saṃśrayadharmin*), having the property of not existing apart from the Blessed Lord. "Separation" (*pṛthagbhāva*) is the absence of that specific relationship characterized by the status of instrument and the possessor of the instrument; it is dissolution (*saṃhāra*). For in that state, there is no instrument nor a body. "Dependence" (*saṃśraya*) is the relationship as instrument and possessor of the instrument; the meaning is "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, "dependence" is the relationship between those two, which is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). "Separation" is liberation (*mokṣa*). The meaning is that all of this is dependent upon the governance of the Blessed Lord.

Regarding this, he states an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). This is an illustration of the separation of the effect from its cause: the wind carries the droplets of water apart from it. Alternatively, it is an illustration of both the power of conjunction and the power of disjunction: the wind carries them together and apart from one another. Or else, it is an illustration of being free from even a trace of the defects inherent in *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*: for the wind carries hundreds of droplets while remaining untouched by their inherent nature.

The term *pradhānapuruṣātmanaḥ* means "of the self of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa. The object [of the verb]—namely, the entire collection of sentient and insentient entities (*samasta-cid-acid-vastu-jātam*)—must be supplied. Alternatively, the word *puruṣa* following the word *pradhāna* refers to the bound soul (*baddha*), while the word *ātman* refers to the liberated self (*muktātman*) who is free from contact with primordial matter (*prakṛti*). [The phrase] "it maintains those" refers to such a world. He states that this very world is ultimately real (*paramārtha*) by saying "this, indeed, is that. For that which is false is impermanent due to its sublation; for if it were ultimately real, its permanence would be possible.

He states the meaning of the cited passages in brief with the words "by [the phrase] beginning with... and so forth. The state of being free from all defects and the nature of possessing auspicious qualities constitute the meaning of the verses beginning with "He [is the source] of the nature of all beings" and "Possessing all auspicious [qualities]. The fact that the sport of the world's creation and so forth belongs to Him is established by the etymological derivation of the word *bhagavat*. By the word "and so forth" in the phrase "entering within, governing, and so forth," His status as the presiding overseer (*adhyakṣatva*) and the permissive supervisor (*anumantṛtva*) are expressed. By the word "beginning with" in the phrase "by [the passage] beginning with...", the statement "of a playing child" and others are intended.

The meaning of that [term] is intended by the word *līlā* (sport). This means [the sport] of one who exists in all states—whether in the state of cause and effect, or in the state of being bound or liberated. For it is possible to refer to an object within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being established through delusion for the purpose of its negation; however, since the fact of being governed by the Supreme Self and so forth is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition, it is precisely what is intended to be enjoined. With the intention that the negation of what has been enjoined is untenable, it is stated: "of that which is ultimately real" (*pāramārthikasyaiva*).

The established meaning resulting from the demonstration of the relationship between the controller and the controlled is that [the world] has the nature of being a body (*śarīratva*). This very point is expressed by the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "all this is indeed that. By the words "body-nature, essence, and parts," he states the meaning already set forth in passages such as "those two forms of that Brahman. The phrase "as it has been demonstrated" means that it has been demonstrated thus in the introductions and conclusions of the scripture as a whole, as well as in the introductions and conclusions of the intermediate sections.

By the phrase ending with "is known," the summary of the meaning of the cited statements has been provided. Through the examples given, it is established that the reality possesses specific distinctions and that the world is real.

Now, desiring to explain the verses cited by another in accordance with the meaning of the verses previously cited, [the author] first explains the verse beginning with *pratyastamitabhedaṃ*, starting with the word *pratyastamita*. [He cites: "Suffering, ignorance, and impurity are attributes of *prakṛti*, not of the Self," and "The Person is neither god, nor human, nor beast, nor tree."

In passages such as, "O King, these differences in bodily form have their origin in karma," both *prakṛti* (primordial nature) and the bodies of gods and others are perceived as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). To reconcile the meaning of these two types of statements, it is said that [the body] is a "specific transformation of the *prakṛti* of gods, humans, and so forth. The use of the term *prakṛti* in the phrase "of *prakṛti*" is intended to show that the body is itself a transformation of *prakṛti*. By the words "gods, humans, and so forth," the existence of distinct categories to be excluded within the body is demonstrated.

Now, one might object: since liberated beings cannot be objects of worship, and since the nature of a worshiper—being conjoined with the non-sentient (acit)—cannot be characterized by the disappearance of all distinctions, it is impossible to teach such a state [of oneness] for them; therefore, this verse must refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman) rather than the pure self (pariśuddhātman). To resolve this doubt, it was stated: "even though [the self] is conjoined with specific transformations of primordial matter (prakṛti), such as gods, humans, and so forth."

The intention is this: although the innate nature remains concealed even while one is transmigrating, instruction is given for the purpose of realizing its true state as it will manifest in the future. To remind us of the statement, "Though existing in his own and others' bodies," the phrase "even though associated" (*saṃsṛṣṭasyāpi*) was used. The word "even" (*api*) indicates a contradiction: just as one becomes an outcast through association with an outcast, or just as objects become salty through association with the *rumā* salt-mine, there is thus a contradiction. [The Self is distinct] by virtue of being devoid of the differences residing in those [bodies].

"Differentiation" (*bheda*) refers to form, color, and so forth. By this, the term "in which differentiation has subsided" (*pratyastamitabheda*) is explained. By the term "in which differentiation has subsided," the intended meaning is the destruction of differentiation such that it does not arise again. Consequently, there is an exclusion of the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). By the phrase "beyond the range of words such as 'Deva' which denote those [differentiations]," the expression "beyond the range of speech" (*agocaraṃ vacasām*) is explained. By the phrase "characterized solely by the existence of consciousness" (*jñānasattaikalakṣaṇam*), the word "consciousness" (*jñāna*) and the expression "mere existence" (*sattāmātra*) are explained.

In the phrase "having existence as its sole characteristic" (*sattaikalakṣaṇam*), the word "one" (*eka*) explains the meaning of the suffix *-mātra* in the term *sattāmātra*, thereby excluding modifications such as being born (*jāyate*) or existing (*asti*). When it is said that it is "existence alone," the question arises as to in what form it exists; in response to this, it is stated that it has "knowledge as its sole characteristic" (*jñānasattaikalakṣaṇam*). The meaning is that its existence is in the form of knowledge (*jñānatva*).

In order to avoid the contradiction of [the Self's] non-existence if it were beyond the scope of words, and in order to exclude the insentient nature as described by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, he states "to be self-cognized" (*svasaṃvedyam*) to explain the meaning of the term "self-cognized. Alternatively, when it has been stated by the preceding words ending with "beyond the scope of words" that [the Self] is devoid of conceptual construction and modification and is thus beyond the reach of words expressive of it, there arises the doubt: "In the absence of distinguishing attributes, how can its own differentiation be apprehended? It is in response to this doubt that he says "self-cognized."

The meaning is that appearing as direct perception (*pratyakṣatvena bhāsamānatva*) is what distinguishes [the Self] from others, for others appear as "this-ness" (*idantayā*). The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) expresses the non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) of both the attribute and the substratum without distinction. Because the knowledge that constitutes an attribute is vast, it is appropriate for the nature of the perfectly pure Self to be denoted by the word "Brahman," as in passages such as, "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman. One who is joined with yoga is one who has commenced yoga.

By the statement "pure in this manner," the nature of the liberated one is extended by analogy to the Supreme Self; thus, the liberation of the soul is understood as its equality with the Supreme Self. Furthermore, since it is clear from such statements as "free from decay and destruction" and "description of form, color, etc. that the Supreme Self is devoid of certain distinctions and the six modes of change (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*), the verse has been explained in accordance with that [equality], without excessive elaboration.

With the intention of asking how it is known that this verse concerns the liberated self (*muktātman*) and that such a self is not within the scope of the yoga under discussion, he asks, "How is this [known]? He answers with the words beginning "That is stated," etc., [arguing] that it is understood from the context itself. For this verse concerning the liberated one does not stand in isolation; rather, it belongs to the entire treatise (*prabandha*).

Therefore, with the intent to avoid the objection that "a word not grasped in its prior and subsequent context produces a different cognition," the meaning is that the sense must be described precisely through the consideration of what precedes and follows. By stating that yoga is the sole remedy for *saṃsāra*, the author intends the meaning of the verse: "There is nothing other than yoga that brings about the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśas*). Furthermore, this demonstrates the refutation of the view that the mere knowledge of the meaning of a sentence is the means to liberation (*apavarga*).

"The limbs of yoga up to withdrawal (pratyāhāra)" refers to the meaning of such statements as: "When the vital breath has been brought under control by breath-restraint (prāṇāyāma) and the senses by withdrawal, one should then fix the mind upon a virtuous object. This is the concise summary. Regarding the statement that the power (śakti) denoted by the word *śakti* belongs to the Supreme Brahman Viṣṇu: some say that in the passage "The supreme power of Viṣṇu is declared," Viṣṇu himself is the power of Brahman.

To exclude that [misconception], Vyāsa has composed the word "of Viṣṇu," based on such passages as: "the power of the Supreme Brahman," "of Vāsudeva who has become the Supreme Brahman," "therefore he is called Vāsudeva," "that eternal Supreme Brahman," "and the Supreme Self of all," "he who is named Viṣṇu in the Vedas and Vedāntas," "endowed with the power of Viṣṇu, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman," and "that power also belongs likewise to Viṣṇu. By these and other texts, it is established that Viṣṇu alone is the Supreme Brahman and that the world is his power (*śakti*).

The intention [of the author] is that [the opponent's view] is incorrect because it contradicts those various scriptural statements which establish that [Brahman] is subject to that power (*śakti*). Power is what is denoted by the word *śakti*. For power is indeed an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). And Brahman is not an attribute of anything else. Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is the power; for he is the one denoted by the word "Brahman"—this is the intended meaning.

In this regard, the following scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti) are to be considered: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman"; "At that time, Viṣṇu alone existed as Hari, partless"; "The Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self"; "No one rules over Him"; "Neither His equal nor His superior is seen"; "There is nothing else higher than whom there is another"; and "There is no one equal to You; how could there be anyone superior in the three worlds? He is described as the object of worship, possessing a divine form and being the locus of the three powers (śakti).

If Viṣṇu alone is the capable [agent], how can a portion of Viṣṇu’s body be the locus of Viṣṇu himself? For there is no body belonging to Brahman that could serve as such a locus; this is the resulting refutation. Regarding the statement that "there are two forms denoted by the word *śakti*": since these two forms, known as the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*), are later referred to by the word *śakti* in grammatical coordination with the words "higher" and "lower," the intention is that the word *śakti* does not have the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as its object, but rather refers to the form designated as "higher."

For it is said: "And that is the supreme form of Viṣṇu," and "The power of Viṣṇu is declared to be supreme. With the intent of explaining the meaning of such statements as "O King, [it is] both with form and without form," he says: "by way of the division into the formed and the formless. Regarding the meaning of the verse, "Another third power is held to be known as ignorance and karma," he says: "the third. Since it was previously stated "by way of the division into the formed and the formless," the specific designation "the division called the formed" is made by way of analysis. [He adds: "as the object of meditation for perfected yogins."

The suffix -kṛtya is not used here in the sense of "knowledge" (vidyā), but rather with the intention of expressing "possibility. This same meaning applies even in the phrase "the supreme state is to be meditated upon by yogis"; it results in the conclusion that for one who has already commenced yoga, [the goal] cannot be meditated upon because it is not naturally pure. Here, it is not stated that purity is non-intrinsic; rather, what is intended is its dependence on the grace of the Lord, due to its own inability to remove adventitious defects. Thus, the status of being a "locus of auspiciousness" is negated.

By the phrase "due to the absence of inherent purity," its auspiciousness (*śubhatva*) is negated; by the phrase "by way of having no objective support" (*anālambanatayā*), its status as a substratum (*āśrayatva*) is negated. Thus, there is a negation of both auspiciousness and being a substratum. Here, "auspiciousness" means being opposed to that which is to be abandoned (*heya*); it does not mean merely the absence of what is to be abandoned, for it has been stated: "It should be contemplated for the sake of self-purification, destroying all taints. He restates the three powers (*śaktitraya*) in order to explain their being the substratum of those three powers.

Here, the intended meaning of the statement, "And all these powers," is as follows: although the plural form "these powers" (*etāḥ śaktayaḥ*) is used, the word "all" (*samasta*) is employed to include a multitude of individual instances. "The form of the Supreme Power" (*paraśaktirūpam*) means that the Supreme Power itself is the form of the Supreme Self; or, it consists of the Supreme Power. The same applies to what follows. By the phrase "peculiar to the Lord" (*bhagavadasādhāraṇam*), there is an exclusion of the bodies of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others.

Even though [these bodies] are presided over by the Blessed Lord, they are the objects of the egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*) of those specific individual souls (*jīva-viśeṣa*). He shows that this has its root in scripture with the words "Āditya," etc. By the phrase "embodied form" (*mūrta-rūpa*), the meaning of the statement "the two embodied forms of the Blessed Lord" is expressed. To the question of what the scope of this verse is regarding the matters already mentioned, he says: "In this regard. If it is stated for the purpose of explaining the unfitness [of these bodies] to be the locus of auspiciousness (*śubhāśrayatā*), then elsewhere there would be a statement of their unfitness and a statement of the fitness of some other entity.

Regarding the phrase "it should be seen," he says "for thus" (*tathāhi*), and in this regard he cites two statements: "not that" (*na tat*) and [the following]. By the term *yogayujā* (by one engaged in yoga), he means by one who has commenced yoga. Through this passage, the state of being without an objective support (*anālambanatva*) is expressed; furthermore, the absence of intrinsic purity (*svataḥśuddhiviraha*) is intended as established by the context of the treatise. Indeed, by such passages as, "But those other supports of the mind, O tiger among men!—all those beginning with the gods—are impure and have their origin in karma," the absence of purity in all things other than the divine form of the Blessed One is stated.

The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that the statement that other forms are not worthy of Arhatship indicates the intention to show that this particular form is indeed unworthy of Arhatship. By the passage beginning with "Others, however," it is indicated through the description of impurity characterized by connection to karma that even those who are completely free from connection to karma lack intrinsic purity. To clarify that even they are to be excluded by the term "auspicious" (śubha) when referring to those established in the state of the auspicious object of focus (śubhāśraya), he says: "In the same way" (tathā).

The phrase "those who have subsequently attained awakening" has been explained by the expression "having attained their own true nature. Regarding the phrase "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass," the prefix *ā-* denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*), because of its association with the term "blade of grass" (*stamba*). For a blade of grass is subject to karma, as stated in the passage beginning with "The person is not a god" and ending with "these are the sources of action, O King. The meaning of the entire section ending with "since for them too [it comes] from another" has already been explained previously. Now, he states the meaning of the passage beginning with "therefore, that stainless Brahman... using the words "of the Supreme" (*parasya*).

The meaning of "its own uncommon" (*svāsādhāraṇam*) is as explained previously. With the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), he concludes that the verse beginning with "completely subsided" (*pratyastamita-*) does not have the purpose of negating difference (*bhedaniṣedha*).

Now, regarding the verse beginning with "jñānasvarūpam," he states that it does not intend to establish the falsity of difference by saying "jñānasvarūpamiti. The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). He demonstrates the absence of a demonstration of the total falsity [of difference] by saying "jñāna. The meaning is this: when there is an error consisting in the manifestation of that which has the nature of consciousness as having the form of an object, the non-manifestation of that objective form as being such [i.e., as an object] does not constitute an error. He establishes this very point through an illustration by saying "nahi."

He raises an objection by way of pointing out a disparity with the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the world and Brahman: "In that [example], indeed, not every instance of silver is seen to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with a fragment of mother-of-pearl; rather, it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction between the entire class of silver and the nature of mother-of-pearl; rather, the contradiction lies only with the silver that is coreferential [with the mother-of-pearl]."

In that case, due to contradiction, the silver that is coreferential (*samānādhikṛta*) with the substrate is false, whereas the silver that is not coreferential and is not contradictory is not false. Here, however, everything other than Brahman is perceived as being coreferential with Brahman. Therefore, given the contradiction between the form of cognition and the form of the object, it follows that the entire range of objects is false. He refutes this [objection] with the words: "That is incorrect."

In this regard, he first states the contradiction between the meaning of the opponent’s statement and the meaning of the entire textual passage with the words "In this [regard]... (*asmin*). Here, the connection of Brahman with ignorance and the falsity of the world are contradictory. This is because of such scriptural statements as: "The supreme state called Viṣṇu is free from all that is to be abandoned," "Then He [is called] Vāsudeva," "That Brahman is supreme and eternal," "And because there is nothing to be abandoned, It is stainless," "All those [worlds] entered into That," and "These are the manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Hari. Such is the meaning.

The statements "it exists due to erroneous perception" and "Viṣṇu, the devourer" declare that Viṣṇu, as the possessor of attributes, is the substratum of error. Therefore, [the objection] is appropriate. To dispel the doubt that the Supreme Brahman is indeed faultless, it is specified as "of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Brahman. By these two phrases—"from whom all traces of defects such as ignorance have been removed" and "whose nature consists of all auspicious qualities"—the impossibility of any connection with ignorance (avidyā) is stated.

If there were a connection with ignorance (*avidyā*), it would be impossible for [the Lord] to be free from everything that is to be abandoned and to consist of all auspicious qualities. By the phrase "of great majesty" (*mahāvibhūteḥ*), the impossibility of the world being illusory is stated. Indeed, the fact that the world is a manifestation of the Lord's majesty is not established by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that it would require a restatement for the sake of negation. Therefore, it is indeed enjoined [as a truth]. Furthermore, an injunction does not produce delusion.

That being the case, since it cannot be maintained that even the negative statement is intended merely as an error consisting of a cognition whose object is the non-existence of difference, the validity of both statements is equal. Therefore, the meaning is that the enjoined object is indeed the ultimate reality, and thus the world is not illusory.

To the objection that "if identity is perceived through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), then because of the contradiction between the form of cognition and the form of the object, one or the other must be false—just as in the case 'this shell is silver' [it is the silver that is false]"—the author says: "By way of coreferentiality. This means that while coreferentiality is possible even without the two forms being subject to sublation—that is, independently of the sublation of either one—it does not tolerate sublation; for if the two forms were not established, the very definition of coreferentiality would fail.

To the question, "How then is the contradiction between two forms in a single object resolved?", he says: "And it is not contradictory. The meaning is that even when two forms are admitted, the demonstration of oneness is not contradictory, because it is mediated by [the underlying reality]. The word "immediately" means "not in another section. The first *ca* (and) is intended to dispel doubt; the second is for conjunction (*samuccaya*). He concludes the absence of the intention to establish falsity with the words: "Therefore, this..."

Thus, the claim that the verse beginning with "evam jñānasvarūpam" has as its purport the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) has been refuted by exposing its logical inconsistency. Now, he begins to explain the verse according to his own position, starting with the words "tathā hi."

Now, for what purpose is the explanation of the verse of salutation (*praśnaśloka*) provided? It is said: In the verse beginning with "The nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpam*), it is not perceived that Viṣṇu is the substantive (*viśeṣya*) of the words ending in the accusative case; nor is the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of those words with the word "having bowed" (*praṇamya*) understood; furthermore, the fact that the verse has a qualified meaning (*viśiṣṭārtha*) cannot be comprehended without the context having a qualified purport (*viśiṣṭaparatva*). Therefore, the verses of salutation must be explained.

Since those [topics] are yet to be explained, a doubt arises as to why a salutation (*namaskāra*) is performed at the beginning of the second chapter, for it ought to have been performed right from the start. Because this treatise has descended in the form of questions and answers, a concise response to the initial questions was first provided; then, with the intention of providing a detailed exposition, the salutation was made at the commencement of the second chapter.

Otherwise, if the salutation were performed immediately after the question, the student's mind might become confused, wondering what is being said in response to our inquiry; therefore, the verses of the questions have been explained in order to demonstrate the connection of the verse of salutation by way of dispelling the aforementioned doubt.

In order to dispel the doubt that—since the opening passage beginning with "jñānasvarūpam" shows that anything distinct from the attributeless reality is established through illusion, and therefore the subsequent description must be interpreted in accordance with that—the commentary on the initial question-verse is provided both to show that the subject matter of the scripture is a specific deity endowed with manifestations (vibhūti) rather than mere consciousness alone, and to make known the intended purport of the scripture. This is done by means of the verses concerning the questions and answers and the attainment of the boon, which serve as the very prelude to the opening section.

The verses of the inquiry are now explained for the purpose of establishing that the connection with the error mentioned in the verse intended to be commented upon is mediated by a causal link, and to demonstrate—by means of the suffix *mayaṭ* in the phrase "consisting of which" (*yanmayam*)—that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based on the relationship between the body and the embodied.

In this regard, there arises the dilemma: is this question from one who has heard the Vedānta, or from one who has not heard the Vedānta? If it were the latter, a specific question would be inappropriate; if it were the former, a question would be inappropriate because there is nothing further to be heard. To address this doubt, he states that it is the question of one who has heard the Vedānta, beginning with the words "From which indeed these... By the phrase "when [it] has been deliberated upon," it is stated that the hearing of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā has been performed.

In response to the doubt as to how a question could arise for one who has already heard the Vedānta, the author shows the injunction for hearing the Itihāsas and Purāṇas by means of the verse beginning with "itihāsa. In this verse, the word "veda" refers to the Vedānta. The division is that the *pavraṃhaṇas* (expansions) consist of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, which are intended to expand upon the latter portion of the Veda (*vāda*). This will become clear in the section concerning Smṛti (*smṛtyadhikaraṇa*).

In that regard, the exposition of Brahman in the Dharmaśāstras is for the purpose of making known that ritual actions (*karma*) are of the nature of worshiping Him; the exposition of ritual action in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas is for the purpose of establishing that ritual actions are auxiliary to the meditation on Brahman. The distinction is that the Itihāsa is more venerable than the Purāṇas. Although, according to the rule *alpāctaram*, the word "Purāṇa" would have been placed first, the rule *abhyarhitaṃ pūrvaṃ prayoktavyam* dictates that the more venerable term should be used first; thus, from its being placed first, the greater venerability of the Itihāsa is understood.

He explains the first half of this verse with the words, "That which is called an *upabṛṃhaṇa*. By means of two qualifiers in the genitive case, it is stated that there exists both knowledge arising from scripture (*āgama*) and knowledge born of discernment (*viveka*). The use of the plural in the term "of the principles of reality" (*tattvārthānām*) is intended to indicate the superior authority of the *itihāsas* and other texts even over the system of Kapila. "Clarification" (*vyaktīkaraṇam*) is the extraction of the meaning one has understood for oneself, together with those specific details not yet known.

Just as there is an extraction of the meaning of the *saṃdhyopāsana* and other rites enjoined by the Veda as things to be performed, along with their specific details such as bodily purification, the methods of cleansing the teeth, and bathing, so too must the extraction of the meaning be accomplished in the Upaniṣadic portion. To the objection that since the extraction of the meaning of the Upaniṣads is established through the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*), there is no need for supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), he explains the second half of the verse with the word "sakala" (all). The second half of the verse establishes the necessity of performing supplementation for the matters enjoined in the first part [of the Veda].

"Upabṛṃhaṇa" (supplementation) means the extraction of the meaning of a studied recension together with the meanings of other unstudied recensions. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no independence from the investigation of supplementation.

Now, one might object: just as there is an inclination toward the inquiry into ritual action (*karma-vicāra*) due to the understanding of fruitful purposes through superficial cognition, and subsequently toward the inquiry into Brahman (*brahma-vicāra*) out of such inclination (*rāga*), so too—given that the infinity of the Vedas is understood from the statement found within the very branch being studied, "Infinite indeed are the Vedas"—there exists the possibility of meanings not known in the studied branch, whether they be non-contradictory or contradictory to it; and [this is supported] by sūtras such as "And because of Smṛti" and "It is also recorded in Smṛti."

Furthermore, since it is observed that the determination of the meaning of the Vedānta depends upon corroboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), it is logical that one would engage in hearing [the scriptures] out of natural inclination (*rāga*) because of this requirement for corroboration. In that case, since engagement occurs out of inclination toward the *dharmaśāstras*—which are corroborations of the earlier portion [of the Veda]—and also toward the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—which are corroborations of the Upaniṣadic portion—the injunction [to hear from a teacher] would be redundant. For a scripture has its purpose only when [the activity] is not already established [by other means]. Nor can there be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) stating "one must hear only from a teacher," because there is no word expressing such a restriction in this statement.

Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the knowledge of the meaning of this statement would lead one to engage in listening to the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, and from that engagement in listening to the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*, the knowledge of the meaning of this statement would arise. Therefore, the injunction "one should supplement" (*upabṛṃhayet*) is untenable. True; however, for the purpose of listening to specific compositions such as the *Mahābhārata*, this statement situated within them merely restates the general requirement for supplementation, which is already established by logic.

The meaning of the statement "it is understood that the supplementation (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) must be performed" is as follows: by this scriptural statement as well, the necessity of performing the supplementation—which is already established by logic—is made known. By the commentary beginning with "Supplementation is called... and so forth, it is precisely the attainment [of that necessity] through logic that is demonstrated.

Alternatively, since the established nature of reality is determined precisely by the characteristics of the reconciliation of contradictions with the concordance [of scriptures], and because contradictory forms cannot coexist in a single reality; furthermore, because it would follow that the Veda is merely the prattle of delusion if there were any possibility of another section teaching a meaning contrary to what is determined by the currently studied scriptures; and because there is no possibility of a section teaching a meaning contrary to a determined reality—then, even though specific qualities and manifestations exist in Brahman that have not yet been understood, even through thousands of corroborative texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), [it remains so].

Because it is impossible to establish its specific identity [as the Supreme], and because the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) is possible through any one of the meditations on the few specific qualities already understood, the injunction "one should supplement" is appropriate with respect to those who do not rely on the hearing of supplementary texts.

If this is so, then since there is no portion to be extracted from those matters understood through sentences supported by logic (*nyāya*) for which an *upabṛṃhaṇa* (corroborative elaboration) could be sought—and since the portion to be extracted has already been extracted by the very statements cited in the Sūtras—the injunction regarding *upabṛṃhaṇa* would have to serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). And it is not reasonable to postulate an invisible purpose when a visible one is possible. Furthermore, the text shows its visible purpose with the words: "He will deceive me. Deception of the Veda consists precisely in describing a meaning contrary to what is intended by it.

Therefore, its cessation—which is the visible result—is expressly stated by the text. When that [visible result] exists, it is improper to postulate an unseen (adṛṣṭa) result. If it is argued that the visible result is precisely that [cessation], this too is improper; for you yourself have stated that it is impossible to establish a misconception regarding reality (tattva). Furthermore, since the non-comprehension of the full majesty of Brahman and the non-comprehension of all its subordinate particulars cannot constitute a form of deception by the Veda, the cessation of those [misconceptions] cannot logically be the result.

It is said: although there can be no error in the exposition of the supreme reality and its worship, nevertheless, [it is said]: "What do the cows do among the Kīkaṭas? They do not yield the milk-mixture (āśira), nor do they heat the vessel for the Gharma."

Thinking that the specific details regarding the Supreme Self—the creation of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, their origins, and their particular modes of existence—are not intended by the scripture because they are already generally understood through common perception—just as the accounts of Pramaganda and others are understood from such sentences as "O Maghavan, bring to us the wealth of Pramaganda, the Naicāśākha, to be at our disposal"—he regards the meanings asserted by those who consider themselves learned regarding passages such as "the adulterer of Ahalyā" as being like the meanings found in the earlier portions of the Veda and the Upanishadic sections.

If one were to think that the *mantras* and *arthavādas* have a different meaning [than what they actually convey], then this person would indeed be deceiving the Veda by failing to provide the necessary corroboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) for what is not explicitly heard therein; thus, the injunction for corroboration is logically established as a remedy for that. Nor is there a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*); for just as there is no circularity in the case where the understanding of the injunction arises from the study [of the text] and the study [itself] arises from the understanding of the injunction—even though the sentence of the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*) is itself included within the "self-study" (*svādhyāya*)—so it is here as well.
