For in that case, the activity of the boy [the student] arises either from the instigation of a person who knows the injunction (*vidhi*), or from the observation of its performance. Similarly, the student's question is justified by his knowledge that the supplementary text (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) is to be accomplished—whether through the renown of the reports of learned people who know the injunction for the supplementary text, or through the word of his own teacher who knows it, or from observing another person who has engaged in the acquisition of the supplementary text. Therefore, the injunction for the supplementary text is established.

In this regard, since his own guru Parāśara was renowned for omniscience and because Maitreya had received training from him in all branches of knowledge, it is logical that he engaged in listening to the Purāṇas composed by him.

Introducing the questions while stating the distinction of this Purāṇa from other Purāṇas, he says "tatra" (therein). First, regarding this jewel among Purāṇas, which is known to all learned people in the east, north, and elsewhere, its preeminence over other Purāṇas—due to its great renown—is as undeniable as that of Mānava among the Dharmaśāstras or Pāṇinīya among the grammatical treatises.

Precisely because of its great renown, like that of the *Kūrma-purāṇa* and others, any suspicion that its original manuscript may have been lost is cast far aside. Furthermore, because it is not overly extensive, the suspicion of later interpolations does not arise. Moreover, this work exhibits an extraordinary degree of acceptance based on the testimony of others, as indicated by the phrase: "He recites the word 'Parāśara'. (He recites the word *parāśara*).

The majesty of the auspicious Agni is proclaimed in the *tāmasa* [kalpas]; and they know that the majesty of Brahmā is predominant in the *rājasa* ones. Furthermore, in the *sāttvika* kalpas, the majesty of Hari is predominant; in those very [kalpas], those perfected in the sevenfold yoga will attain the supreme goal. Whatever Purāṇa was formerly proclaimed by Brahmā in whichever kalpa, [that is the one to be followed].

However, the majesty of each [deity] is described according to its own essential nature; because this is rooted in *sattva*, which produces right knowledge, and because it lacks a root in *rajas* and *tamas*, which are the causes of ignorance and distorted knowledge respectively, one cannot even imagine that it shares the same status as other Purāṇas that possess defective causes.

It is well known from scriptural statements that *sattva* is the cause of knowledge according to reality, while *rajas* and *tamas* are the causes of non-reality and perverted knowledge, as it is said: "From *sattva* arises knowledge"; "That intellect which perceives things incorrectly, O Pārtha, is *rājasa*; and that intellect which perceives all objects perversely, O Pārtha, is *tāmasa*. Furthermore: "*Sattva* is held to be light and illuminating; *rajas* is stimulating and mobile."
It is well known from such passages as, "Darkness is indeed the choice of a teacher," and, "All those [actions] are fruitless after death, for they are remembered as being rooted in darkness."

[Objection: But surely, since the statement that Purāṇas propounding Caturmukha-Śiva and others are rooted in *rajas* and *tamas* lacks authority due to its own being rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*, the superiority of the *sāttvika* Purāṇas is not established. Furthermore, there is no evidence for this statement being rooted in *sattva*. Therefore, it is proper to declare the lack of authority of that single statement alone, and not of many Purāṇas; for the majority is more powerful. [Reply: It is said: First of all, it is not reasonable to entertain doubt regarding the authority of this statement.

Because no subverting evidence is observed, and because the intrinsic validity [of cognition] remains unsublated: "That which is indeed his *rājasa* portion is he who is Brahmā among these students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*); that which is indeed his *sāttvika* portion is he who is Viṣṇu among these students of sacred knowledge."

Furthermore, this is because the statement of the supreme [author] is consistent with the truth, being supported by such scriptural passages as, "That which is indeed his tamasic portion is this Rudra who is the religious student (brahmacārī)," and "The Great Lord is indeed the Puruṣa; He is the instigator of the sattva. For it is established in various Purāṇas that in their respective Kalpas, each specific Tattva—understood through its composition of particular Guṇas—is expounded by Brahmā, who is likewise composed of those same Guṇas.

Furthermore, in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*, which establishes the meaning of all the scriptures, it is stated: "If Madhusūdana beholds a person being born, he should be known as one of *sattva* nature; he is indeed one who contemplates the goal of liberation"—thus declaring that through the glance of the Blessed One, there arises the certainty of right knowledge rooted in the quality of *sattva*. Following this, it says: "Brahmā or Rudra beholds him as he is being born..."

Furthermore, because it is stated that "his mind was overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*," and because this demonstrates the impurity rooted in *rajas* and *tamas* through the side-glances of the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and Śiva, it is established that the literary compositions (*prabandhas*) expounding upon the Four-faced One and Śiva are themselves rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*.

Even though this statement is found in Purāṇas rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*, its lack of authority should not be suspected; for since it is impossible for a work devoted to propounding Brahmā, Śiva, and others to harbor an insistence on asserting the superiority of the Blessed Lord, it is logical that this statement is intended to convey the ultimate truth (*tattva*). Indeed, an author’s insistence can only arise regarding the deity he himself seeks to propound, and not otherwise. Therefore, there is no possibility of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*) regarding this statement.

As for the claim that because many Purāṇas lack authority, it is logical that this [single] statement alone lacks authority—on the grounds that "the majority is stronger"—that is incorrect, because there is no direct contradiction with the facts. For it is not understood from those Purāṇas themselves that the compositions (*prabandha*) which establish Viṣṇu and Śiva are rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*. Since their authority is accepted within those very compositions as being authoritative, it is contradictory for them to be rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*; thus, a contradiction results through a mediated sequence.

Regarding the statement "therein, the majority is more authoritative" and so forth: if the lack of authority of those [Purāṇas] were due solely to a contradiction with this very statement, then this fault would indeed apply. However, since it is untenable for all Purāṇas to be equally authoritative when they contradict one another, and since it is more reasonable to establish the authority of at least some of them by providing a reconciliation rather than accepting the non-authority of all, this statement—given the expectation as to which ones are unauthoritative and which are authoritative—is intended merely to provide a systematic arrangement of their respective subjects.

Therefore, since it has been made known that [the Vedic texts] have *sattva* and so forth as their root, the sublation of the series of texts with corrupt roots by means of series with non-corrupt roots occurs. Consequently, there is no sublation of those [Vedic] words by the principle of "the majority being stronger. If it is argued that the authority of the Purāṇas teaching Brahmā and Śiva follows from the abundance of Purāṇas teaching Viṣṇu, this statement is first of all unrefuted; for here the principle of "the majority being stronger" does not apply.

Thus, when it is understood through this statement—which is free from contradiction—that the Purāṇas are rooted in *sattva* (truthfulness), the abundance of Purāṇas with defective sources is not capable of subverting even a single Purāṇa that has a non-defective source. For the word of a single person who is not deluded is not subverted by the words of a thousand deluded persons. Therefore, because they teach the Blessed Lord and are thus rooted in *sattva*, there is no defect in their cause.

Likewise, no subverting cognition is observed for this [text], as is the case with other Purāṇas; for it establishes Nārāyaṇa alone as the supreme cause. Indeed, in the direct Śrutis, having declared the causality of Nārāyaṇa alone through both general and specific terms, it is stated: "There is no progenitor of him, nor is there a lord over him"; "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen"; "For there is nothing else higher than this 'Not so' (neti)"; and "Than whom there is nothing else higher. Thus, from Him who is the causal source...

Therefore, the supremacy of any other is also negated: "Neither Brahmā nor Īśāna," "Therein Brahmā, the four-faced, was born," "The three-eyed, trident-bearing Person was born," "From that [was born] the fierce Yajña, the source of strength," "To Virūpākṣa... the son of Brahmā," "Upon the navel of the Unborn, one [world] is established," "That Prajāpati alone came into being upon the lotus-leaf," and "From whose navel-lotus arose the high-souled Prajāpati"—thus [it is said] regarding both Brahmā and Śiva.

The birth [of Brahmā] from Nārāyaṇa is heard [in scripture]. However, in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*, with respect to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, there is the statement by Rudra: "You two were born from my limbs in the past, eternal ones. Since this indicates the birth of Hari and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) from Rudra, the contradiction with other Purāṇas and with the Śruti is quite evident. Even though some have accepted the equality and identity of the three deities, even in that case, this contradiction is difficult to resolve.

Even if one were to propose the production of those [entities] that are equal and unified, this is because the production of the four-faced Lord (Brahmā) and Śiva is heard [in scripture], whereas the production of Rudra and the others is not heard in any statement whatsoever; and because words such as "Śiva," which denote the cause, lack the established status of referring to Rudra and the others who are understood as effects—just like words such as "ether" (ākāśa). Furthermore: "All the Vedas consist of Viṣṇu; all qualities consist of Viṣṇu. Indeed, no other goal equal to Viṣṇu is ordained."

"In this way, the Vedas constantly sing [of Him]; there is no doubt about this. Since this is stated even in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* and other texts, it is accepted that the Vedas establish that the Blessed Lord is the supreme referent. Therefore, because of the direct Vedic scriptures which declare that Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate cause, the distinction of this [text] from other Purāṇas is clear, as it possesses a subverting cognition.

Likewise, the fact that the Dharmaśāstras, such as the Mānava and others, which establish Nārāyaṇa alone as the supreme cause, are clearly in agreement with this is evident. For through such passages as, "The waters are called *nārāḥ*," "That Puruṣa emitted by Him is designated as Brahman in the world," "One should know the Supreme Puruṣa," and "Nārāyaṇa is beyond the unmanifest (*avyakta*)," it is indeed Nārāyaṇa’s status as the cause that is declared in them. Other Purāṇas, however, are contrary to the Dharmaśāstras.

Likewise, the distinction between the speakers is established by direct Vedic revelation (śruti), as in: "He, Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, said. Here, indeed, the excellence of Vyāsa is stated by virtue of his being the son of Parāśara. Similarly, in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* as well, the distinction from Parāśara is perceived; for instance, in its second chapter: "The descent of Parāśara, of Vyāsa, and of Śuka [was for the purpose that] the destruction of the Rākṣasas was indeed accomplished by the son of Śakti."
The statement here that "this is the incarnation of Parāśara" is intended to express an excellence of degree; otherwise, one could have simply said, "the birth of Parāśara, Vyāsa, and Śuka."

Furthermore, there is a great distinction [between this Purāṇa and others] in its possession of the knowledge of the supreme divinity’s ultimate reality, which was obtained through the granting of boons by Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha. It should not be argued that there is a circular dependency—namely, that the authority of this Purāṇa depends on the granting of the boons, while the truth of obtaining those boons depends on the authority of the Purāṇa; for the statement regarding the obtaining of the boons possesses self-evident authority that remains unrefuted, as there is no subverting cognition such as "Paraśara did not obtain the boons."

In the *Liṅga Purāṇa*, it is understood that Parāśara attained knowledge of the ultimate reality of the deities; as stated there in the second chapter: "Through the grace [of his guru], he attained knowledge of the ultimate reality of the deities and the wisdom [required] for the composition of the Purāṇa, by the command of his preceptor Pulastya. And in the sixty-third chapter of that same work: "Then, through the grace of both that Pulastya and the wise Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara indeed composed the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa."

And immediately thereafter, by the verse: "Consisting of sixty thousand [verses], white in color, containing the essence of all the Vedas, and resting upon the knowledge that accomplishes all goals in six ways," the fact that this jewel among Purāṇas contains the meaning of all the Vedas is stated; for this very reason, its capacity to bring about the knowledge that accomplishes all human aims (puruṣārtha) is also declared. Therefore, the distinction of its speaker and the distinction of its composition, which are established in other Purāṇas, cannot be denied.

And this is another very significant point of distinction: that the form of the response consists of a specific answer preceded by a general question. For instance, when asked generally in such passages as, "O knower of dharma! O illustrious one! I desire to hear from you how the world came to be, and how it will come to be again; and what this world consists of, O Brahmin, and from whence this world of moving and non-moving beings arises," a response is understood that is focused on the specific detail: "It has emerged from the presence of Viṣṇu."

When a specific detail is asked about, it might be suspected that the reply—which, by favoring the specific point asked about, speaks of its excellence—is merely an incidental statement (*prasaṅgamātra*) and not intended to convey the ultimate truth (*tattvapara*). However, when a general question is asked, the reply, by the force of the context, culminates in a specific detail; thus, it must indeed be intended to convey the ultimate truth. And for this reason: "Therefore, O Sūta, foremost of the Paurāṇikas, we ask you..."

The excellence of this work over other Purāṇas—which begin with specific inquiries and provide corresponding answers such as "the meritorious Purāṇa-saṃhitā endowed with the majesty of the Liṅga"—is most clearly evident.

And this meaning of the Purāṇas is accepted here and there in the *Laiṅga* and other texts. For example, in the second chapter of the *Laiṅga*, in the summary of the contents of the Purāṇas, it says: "In all the cycles (āvartas), the birth of Viṣṇu occurs through mere sport (līlayā); and by the grace of Viṣṇu, the birth of Jiṣṇu and of Viṣṇu himself likewise occurs. And therein: "By sport alone, the destruction of his own lineage was performed by Kṛṣṇa; and the departure [of the Lord] was indeed by His own will, under the pretext of the weapon of Jarā."

For it is stated therein that the descent of the Blessed One and His departure from the world of mortals are based solely on divine play (*līlā*). Precisely for this reason, the immutability of the meaning of this Purāṇa is understood, as its substance is accepted elsewhere as well. If it is argued that, due to this commonality of purpose, those other Purāṇas should also be authoritative, we say no; because they lack complete consistency. However, it was already stated previously that the portions establishing the excellence of the Blessed One must be respected, since no insistence [on the contrary] is possible.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the fact that this jewel of a Purāṇa is rooted in non-attachment (*anāgraha*) in its entirety is understood from the very nature of the questions posed at the beginning. Therefore, even for those who are otherwise bound by dogmatic attachment (*baddhāgraha*), the fact that the subject matter taught here is worthy of respect serves as a reason for its unshakeable authority.

Furthermore, unlike other Purāṇas, this Purāṇa is not seen to propound contradictory meanings; for it conveys the excellence of the Blessed Lord alone in its entirety. In other Purāṇas, however, contradictions are perceived; for example, in the *Laiṅga*: "You two were born previously from my limbs as eternal ones. This Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, is on my right side, and Viṣṇu, the soul of the universe, born from my heart, is on my left side."

In that regard, it is stated [in the *Vāyupurāṇa*] that Hari and Viriñca were born from Śiva and chose him as their boon-granting deity after worshipping him: "Then, delighted and cheerful, the god Nārāyaṇa, having prostrated before Maheśvara—who possesses the *liṅga* yet is devoid of a *liṅga*—spoke: 'If affection has arisen [for us], and if a boon is to be granted to us both, let there be for us eternal and unwavering devotion unto you. In this context, it is further said in some places: "Rudra is born from your wrath and is enveloped by *tamas*."

By stating, “Through your grace the Sustainer of the world [Brahmā], and through your passion (rajas), the Grandfather [Brahmā] was born,” it is asserted that the four-faced one and Śiva arise from the Lord’s grace and anger; thus, there is a self-contradiction. Nor can it be argued that there is no contradiction because this is merely a description of a *līlā* (divine play) consisting of birth and worship—similar to the birth of Vasudeva and others, or the journey to Kailāsa—since in the *Bhārata*, the jewel among Purāṇas, and other texts, it is said: “He who performs the creation and destruction of the universe by his mere will—what need has he for such elaborate exertion in the destruction of his enemies?”

Nevertheless, he who follows the conduct of human beings—making peace with the powerful, waging war against the weak, employing conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and sometimes even inflicting punishment or flight—he thus conforms to the behavior of those embodied as men. This play of the Lord of the Universe proceeds according to His own will; for though He is the Great Yogi and the Master of the entire world, He acts thus.

For nowhere is there seen a passage intended to resolve such objections as: "Keśava undertakes to perform actions like a weak laborer; by means of the application of *māyā*, he deceives the worlds; those men who take refuge in him alone do not become deluded. And so forth.

In the *Bhārata* and other such texts, there is no presentation of Daśaratha, Vasudeva, and others as being superior to Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth by way of their being the cause of the world; whereas here, Rudra’s superiority to the Blessed Lord is indeed presented. Therefore, a self-contradiction is difficult to avoid [in those cases]. Furthermore, since no such self-contradiction is perceived here, this constitutes a significant distinction.

When there is a contradiction between the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa—which possesses the excellence of the characteristics already described—and other compositions that contain defects in their causes, subverting counter-evidence, or internal inconsistencies, the superiority of this jewel among Purāṇas and the weakness of the others are perfectly evident.

Thus, because it possesses a continuity of excellence established by its well-known preeminence; because for that very reason it lacks the flaw of a corrupted treasury (*naṣṭakośa*); because, not being overly prolix, it is free from the suspicion of interpolations; because it possesses an excellence in adopting the renown of the statements of others; because, being in the form of answers preceded by general questions, it is rooted in an absence of dogmatism; and for this very reason, when there is a contradiction with other treatises that lack such distinctive features and possess defects of cause, sublation, or contradictory cognition—

And because weakness is unavoidable, this glorious Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa is the most authoritative [of all]. Having kept all these reasons in mind, and demonstrating the preeminent arguments explicitly, he introduces the question by stating the distinction of this work through their very mouths, saying: "In that regard... (tatra).

Regarding the phrase "one who has obtained the knowledge of the ultimate reality of the Supreme Deity through the granting of boons by Pulastya and Vasiṣṭha," the term *devatāpāramārthya* (the ultimate reality of the Deity) excludes erroneous cognition (*viparītajñāna*), which consists of the perception of the effects of darkness (*tamaḥ*) as another substratum (*dharmyantara*) rather than [as they truly are]. By this, the expression "and the ultimate reality of the Deity" is clarified.

By the possessive suffix *matup* used in the sense of praise, the misconception (*anyathājñāna*)—which consists in perceiving the effects of passion (*rajas*) as being characterized by a different mode than their actual state—is excluded. By this, the meaning of the term "as it truly is" (*yathāvat*) is indicated. Through the word *devatā*, the intention is to express both the state of being worthy of worship through ritual action or meditative practice (*upāsana*), and the quality of being the bestower of fruits; by this, its possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) is established.

The intention is that by the statement "as it truly is" (*yathāvat*), which describes the manner [of instruction], the fact of possessing distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*) is established; thus, the mention of the obtaining of the boon serves as a proof for that possession of distinctions. By the word "Bhagavat," the possession of knowledge is expressed; from the obtaining of the boon, the excellence of that [knowledge] is established. Regarding "So 'ham" and so forth: the sense is "I am that very person who was previously instructed by you in all branches of learning. He is a knower of dharma in the sense of being one who knows the dharma expressed in such words as: "There is no distinction between a disciple and a son among the virtuous."

Or rather, O knower of dharma, [you have said] that "compassion (*ānṛśaṃsya*) is the supreme dharma. Compassion consists in being intent on protecting those who have sought refuge, according to the statement: "One is called compassionate because of [protecting] those who have sought refuge. O highly fortunate one, for the protection of others is indeed the fulfillment of all duties; the sense is that you alone are the protector, regardless of even the slightest service in return. Just as [it was asked], "from what did it arise?"—the question "from what" (*yataḥ*) is intended to ascertain which among Brahmā, Rudra, and the others is the cause.

Is causality the state of being the substratum of a transformation (*vivarta-adhiṣṭhānatva*), or is it the state of undergoing modification (*pariṇāmitva*)? Furthermore, even in that case, is it modification through an intermediary (*sadvāraka-pariṇāmitva*), or is it modification without an intermediary (*advāraka-pariṇāmitva*)? It is with the desire to know such distinctions of mode that the question "In what manner" (*yathā*) is asked. The question arises from the suspicion that there might be a discrepancy in creation due to differences between cosmic cycles (*kalpa*). For, since it is observed that a scorpion may have cow-dung as its material cause (*upādāna*), the suspicion of a difference in material causes and so forth according to different cosmic cycles is indeed plausible.

In that regard as well, the meaning of the two words "yataḥ" (from which) and "yathā" (how) is as explained previously. The apprehension that "yataḥ" and "yathā" constitute a single question is dispelled by the intervention of the other question, "yanmayam" (composed of what). This is for the purpose of making it known that just as the cause must be known, so too the manner of creation must be known separately. Furthermore, although it is something to be known, the question regarding the manner [of creation] was asked first in order to highlight its primary importance. In the word "yataḥ," the ablative case is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).

Therefore, there is a simultaneous inquiry regarding both the cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). The question "consisting of what" (*yanmaya*) concerns the nature of the Self and the body, which are employed for the sake of internal abiding and so forth. The suffix *mayaṭ* here signifies abundance (*prācurya*). By this, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indicated; for in cases such as the space within a jar, the abundance of the pervader is observed relative to the pervaded. Since pervasion occurs by way of being the Self (*ātmatayā*), and since being the Self means being the sustainer (*dhārakatva*), it follows that the question concerns "abiding" (*sthitih*), characterized by the persistence of existence (*sattānuvṛtti*) effected by the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). Thus, [the question] "consisting of what" is established.

The meaning expressed is that the world exists abundantly by means of that Inner Controller (antaryāmin) who sustains it. Indeed, it has already been clarified previously that sustaining through internal entry and governance constitutes the state of being a sustainer and the cause of its existence. By the word "and" (ca), the question implies the inquiry regarding the maintenance characterized by nourishment and so forth performed by external sustainers such as parents, as well as the maintenance characterized by the attainment of the desired and the warding off of the undesired to be effected by mothers, fathers, and others. Since the material cause is also questioned by the word "from which" (yataḥ), the suffix -mayaḥ must indeed signify abundance.

Nor should the meaning of the ablative case in the word *yataḥ* be restricted according to the maxim of the cow and the bull (*gobalīvardanyāya*), because—unlike the word "bull" (*balīvarda*) in that maxim—the suffix *-mayaṭ* lacks any other established basis for its application; thus, it cannot function as a restrictor. For scholars of logic maintain that the maxim of the cow and the bull refers to the restriction of the meaning of one word out of a desire to avoid the redundancy of another word. In this case, however, since another meaning for the suffix *-mayaṭ* is possible, it is not a restrictor. Furthermore, the word *yataḥ* is capable of signifying both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*).

The question regarding persistence (sthitipraśna) is also required; therefore, the prescription of what is not required is weaker than the prescription of what is required. Furthermore, in the scriptural passage beginning with "From which indeed these [beings arise]," since both the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna) are expressed by the word *yataḥ* alone, and because one must follow the style of the scripture, the question is [to be understood] through the principle of ellipsis (*tantra*) as "from which [cause]."

The question "consisting of what" (*yanmaya*) is raised specifically regarding the state of persistence (*sthiti*). If another meaning were accepted, there would be the fault of stating what is required and omitting what is not required. Nor is the suffix *mayaṭ* used here in its own sense (*svārthika*), for when it is possible for a suffix to have a specific meaning, it is improper to abandon that meaning. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. The questions concerning the place of dissolution (*layasthāna*) and the manner of dissolution (*layaprakāra*) are raised due to the suspicion that there might be differences in location and differences in manner among those other recensional branches (*śākhā*) not studied [by the questioner].

The fact that one deity serves as the locus of dissolution for another, as well as the distinction between being a direct door (*dvārakatva*) and being a door through an intermediary (*sad-vārakatva*), along with the specific mode characterized by the cessation of the delusion regarding the body (*kāyabhrama-nivṛtti-rūpatā*), are indeed grounds for doubt. Furthermore, the question concerning the past and the future is raised due to the suspicion that there may be a difference in the modes of the locus of dissolution according to different cosmic cycles (*kalpa*). By the word "and" (*ca*), the question regarding the agent of dissolution is also indicated; and that [question] is based on the suspicion of a difference in the agents.

Having cited the two verses concerning the inquiry into the essential nature (*svarūpa*) because they are required by the verse whose meaning is intended to be explained, the other verses of inquiry are included by means of the word "etc. In order to dispel the doubt that the verse beginning with "From Viṣṇu... might be an answer to a different inquiry, he states the meaning of those verses in brief with the words "herein" (*atra*). The term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) excludes [the topics of] manifestation (*vibhūti*) and so forth; the term "specificity of essential nature" (*svarūpaviśeṣa*) excludes [the topics of] Brahmā and others.

The "manner of the various manifestations" (*vibhūtibhedaprakāra*) refers to the specific types of divine manifestations. This is included within the inquiry concerning the celestial sphere, the structure of the universe, and so forth. Furthermore, by means of the inquiry into the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), the nature of the means for propitiating Him was asked; this is evident from the observation of the mention of specific fruits in the response.

According to the principle that "the meaning of a question is understood through the manner of its answer," the specific fruit [of devotion] is also asked about here; thus, with the intention that it is included within the previously mentioned questions, it is stated that "the specific fruits are also asked about. Since the propitiation [of the Lord] was asked about along with its purpose, it is included therein. The sense is that this very meaning is what is to be established by all the Śrutis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.

Then, in response to the expectation of what follows from the meaning of the verse under discussion, he states the meaning of the term *yanmaya* (composed of which) along with its justification, beginning with the words *brahmasvarūpa*. The phrase *sṛṣṭisthitilayakarmabhūtam* (having creation, maintenance, and dissolution as its functions) is intended to indicate that since creation and dissolution have already been mentioned, it is now necessary to speak of maintenance (*sthiti*). By the words *sthiti* and *laya*, protection (*rakṣā*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) are intended; for the world, being the object of the operations of maintenance and dissolution, cannot itself be their locus or their agent.

The meaning of the question is: what is the nature of the world—which consists of the activities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution—in order for it to endure? To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And of that... Having raised the doubt that the identity established by the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "the world" and "He" (*saḥ*) signifies a unity of essence (*svarūpa-ekya*), he refutes it with the words "And this... The meaning is: "this" refers to that which is established by grammatical coordination.

Since identity has not been observed merely through pervasion—as in the case of the sky and so forth—he explains "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) as "in the form of the inner ruler" (*antaryāmirūpeṇa*) in order to exclude that [mere pervasion]. For selfhood consists in being the controller who has entered within. Regarding the phrase "of the pervaded and the pervader": the meaning is that the world and Brahman possess the states of being pervaded and pervading, as established by scripture. He supports the proposition that this is not based on the identity of the substance itself with the words "consisting of which" (*yanmaya*). Anticipating the objection that the suffix *mayaṭ* here might imply a sense of modification (*vikāra*), he refutes it by stating "the suffix *mayaṭ*."

To the question "Why?", he says: "Separately" (*pṛthak*). If [the word *yataḥ*] had the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), then the material cause (*upādāna*) would have been asked about. But that need not be asked, because the material cause is already asked about by the word ending in the ablative case, *yataḥ*. Therefore, asking separately would be redundant. Nor does the maxim of "cattle and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*) apply here, since another meaning is possible. Furthermore, the principle is intended here that "the enjoining of what is not required is weaker than the enjoining of what is required. He refutes the view of those who advocate the doctrine of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñānavāda*), which holds that the suffix is used in its own sense (*svārthika*), with the words "Nor... (*nāpi*).

But it is not accepted that [the suffix] is admitted on the basis of either difference or non-difference; for that will be refuted later. The sense is that when a meaning is possible, it is not appropriate to resort to a lack of meaning. Indeed, it is proper to assume an unstated meaning by accepting the stated meaning, but not to abandon what has been stated. He states a unique refutation of the self-referentiality (*svārthikatva*) accepted by the proponent of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñānavādin*): "The world," etc. Under the view of self-referentiality, what would this world be said to be?

When it is asked, "What is this world?", since it is impossible for the mere form of the world—which is already known—to be the object of the question (lest the question be rendered redundant), one must admit that what is being asked is: "Is it real or is it false? In that case, the answer "It is false" ought to be given. Now, when two words are to be employed—one presenting a particular aspect and the other negating the other aspect—the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that presents both aspects simultaneously is untenable; such is the meaning.

If it is argued that "co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is for the purpose of negation," that is not so; for the sense is that the statement "co-referentiality is for the purpose of negation" is contradictory, like saying, "My mother is barren. To the question, "In that case, how could there be a reply? he says, "For then... Here, the word "Viṣṇu" is the term that presents one particular form (ākāra), while the particle "eva" is the term that negates other forms. He states the direct meaning [of the verse] with the words "therefore" (ataḥ); the meaning is: because the senses of being a suffix added without changing the meaning (*svārthika*) and being a modification (*vikāra*) are untenable.

He shows his adherence to the grammatical tradition [of Pāṇini] with the word *tat*. It is "thoroughly made" (*prakṛtam*); that is, abundant (*prabhūtam*) or copious (*pracuram*). For its examples are "a sacrifice consisting of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*) and "a journey consisting of carts" (*śakaṭamayī yātrā*). To the question of what abundance exists here, he says, "and entire" (*kṛtsnaṃ ca*). The sense is that this is established by such scriptural passages as "pervading within and without."

He concludes by stating "therefore," intending to establish that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based on the relationship between body and self. If it is argued that there is a circularity—namely, that because the word *yanmaya* has the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), the coreferentiality of "the world and he" is based on the body-self relationship, and because that coreferentiality establishes the sense of abundance for the suffix *mayaṭ* in *yanmaya* by precluding its literal meaning—[the author replies: it is not so.

This is because, once the suffix *mayaṭ* has ceased to have its own primary meaning (*svārthika*) and its status as denoting abundance (*prācurya*) has been determined, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) cannot depend on the relationship between body and self. First, the possibility of it having its own primary meaning is discarded, since when a word can be meaningful, it is improper to accept that it is meaningless; furthermore, this is also discarded by the coreferentiality expressed in "the world is That" (*jagacca saḥ*). For if it had its own primary meaning, it would be impossible for the subsequent coreferentiality to present two distinct forms.

But this is not so, because it is impossible for [the self] to be based on the notion of the body as the self. Nor does the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) depend upon the suffix *mayaṭ* abandoning its literal meaning in order to present two forms that serve as the grounds for its application; for the capacity of that [coreferentiality] to present two forms is established by its very nature, which is defined as coreferentiality. Therefore, there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*) in the claim that the suffix *mayaṭ* abandons its literal meaning because of the coreferentiality’s capacity to present two forms.

Thus, since the sense of being identical with itself (*svārthika*) has been ruled out, and since the sense of being a modification (*vikāra*) is untenable due to the redundancy of a separate question, it remains by process of elimination that *sthiti* (abiding) is what must be asked about. Consequently, because abiding is its inherent nature and in accordance with the instruction [of the scripture], it is established that the suffix *mayaṭ* refers specifically to the meaning of "abundance. Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "the world" and "He" establishes a specific basis for application consisting in the relationship of body and self; thus, there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*).

Thus, two objections have been shown: if grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) were intended to mean the identity favored by the Mṛṣāvādins, there would be the pointlessness of the suffix *-maya* and the impossibility of coreferentiality; and if it were intended to mean identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), there would be a contradiction in meaning and the impossibility of it being an answer to the question "composed of what" (*yanmaya*). He states the objection if one does not accept that it refers to the meaning he himself has stated: "Otherwise... To the question, "Otherwise, how could there be a question and an answer?", he says: "For if that were so..."

The passage beginning with "jagat" refutes the view of those who maintain that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) refers to a single substance (*ekadravyatā*) accepted by proponents of both difference and non-difference. Even under this position, if it were asked "of what is the world composed? or "what is the substance of the world?", then one must observe that the suffix *mayaṭ* would be redundant; for the question was specifically regarding the material cause (*upādāna*), indicated by the word "yataḥ. He states a further refutation with the words beginning "satya... and so forth.

It was stated that by the phrase "one whose resolve is true" (*satyasaṅkalpa*) and so forth, the defects pertaining to the individual soul (*jīva*) would attach to Brahman; and by the phrase "all inauspiciousness" (*sarvāśubha*) and so forth, the defects pertaining to primordial nature (*prakṛti*) would attach to Brahman. Alternatively, the meaning is that there would be a loss of its possession of both characteristics (the divine and the non-divine) and the acquisition of a contrary form. Regarding the objection that if a word denoting a body were to refer to the embodied one, its primary sense (*mukhyatva*) would not be maintained, he says: "the self as body" (*ātmaśarīra*). The term *sthāpyate* means "will be established. It is said "is being established" (*sthāpyate*) because it is to occur immediately thereafter.

Thus, the meaning conducive to the explanation of the present verse has been elaborated. Now, following the summary of the treatise's subject matter, at the commencement of the detailed exposition, the author introduces the seven-verse section dedicated to salutation. In order to demonstrate the connection of the verse to be explained with the other verses of salutation, he states the meaning of the six statements beginning with "To the changeless one" (*avikārāya*) by saying "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is this: because it is understood from the question and answer that the scripture has as its subject matter the Reality endowed with attributes (*saguṇa*) together with its manifestations (*savibhūtika*); and because grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) functions primarily with respect to a qualified entity. The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) connects with the phrase "and [he] pays homage to [Him] existing in the form of the individual. Alternatively, since the meaning of the scriptural statement is of such a nature, it is established that the passage beginning with "from the presence of Viṣṇu" is a summary (*saṅgraha*), while the passages beginning with "higher than the high" (*paraḥ parāṇām*) constitute the detailed expansion (*vistāra*).

In the phrase "from the presence of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇoḥ sakāśāt*), the word *sakāśāt* is intended to establish that the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) carries the sense of the fifth case (*pañcamī*). This is just as when one says "for the sake of this" (*asya kṛte*), the word *kṛte* is used to convey the sense of the fourth case (*caturthī*). Alternatively, *sakāśāt* means "from [him] possessing volition" (*sa-saṅkalpāt*). "Manifestation" (*kāśana*) refers to knowledge in the form of volition; thus, the meaning is "from him who possesses that. By this, his status as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is established. Or else, the word *sakāśa* signifies "side" (*pārśva*); by that, his body (*śarīra*) is indicated.

The phrase "from his own body" (*śarīrāt svāt*) has the same meaning as "from the body" (*śarīrāt*), as in the passage beginning "having meditated thus" (*so'bhidhyāya*). And the statement "situated therein" (*tatraiva ca sthitam*) is the answer to the question regarding the locus of dissolution. "Situated therein" (*tatra sthitam*) means having reached its final state (*niṣṭhām gatam*). By this, the permanence of the world and the transitory nature of its states are indicated. The answer to the question concerning the locus of dissolution has been stated; now he provides the answer to the question concerning the agent of dissolution and the question concerning external existence, by saying "sthitau" (in the state of persistence).

"And the world is He" is the answer to the question concerning the persistence [of the world], which was established by the phrase "consisting of that," and which is characterized by the continued existence of its reality as effected by Him in His form as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. Alternatively, it is also the answer to the question regarding the persistence established by "consisting of that," namely: "He is the agent who maintains and restrains [the world]. However, "And the world is He" is the answer to the meaning explicitly stated by the words "consisting of that. It has already been demonstrated previously that this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based upon pervasion through the nature of the Self.

If it is argued: "Is it not observed that abstracting terms such as 'whiteness' (*śauklya*) do not extend to the substratum (*dharmin*)? Since the word 'world' (*jagat*) is seen to function as an abstracting term in the expression 'that of which the world consists' (*yanmayaṃ jagat*), it lacks the capacity to denote the substratum; therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of 'the world' and 'He' (*sa*) is untenable. To this it is replied: Abstracting terms are indeed of two kinds—those that are restricted in their abstraction (*niyataniṣkarṣaka*) and those that are optional or intended (*vaivakṣikaniṣkarṣaka*). Among these, words such as 'whiteness' are restricted abstracting terms.

Words such as "human" or "white" are isolating (*niṣkarṣaka*) or non-isolating (*anīṣkarṣaka*) depending on the speaker's intention, because usage is the regulating factor. Otherwise, even the distinction between isolating and non-isolating would not be tenable. Thus, the word "world" (*jagat*) is also isolating depending on the speaker's intention. For this very reason, the answer "And that is the world," expressed in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is appropriate as a response to the question "Of what is it composed? which is expressed in grammatical subordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); for there is no difference in meaning, just as the answer "The cloth is white" is appropriate to the question "What is the substratum of the quality white?"

Thus, the connection of the verses of homage is as follows: a homage is performed in verse by way of a slight expansion of the meaning that was stated briefly and is about to be explained in great detail. The meaning is that [the Buddha] abides in his own very nature, and not as characterized by primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth.

To address the doubt that the absence of connection with anything to be abandoned (*heya*) belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone and not to Viṣṇu, [the author] states the qualification beginning with "that which has become the Supreme Brahman. This is based on the intention that, because of the scriptural statements, "He who is named Viṣṇu in the Vedas" and "The supreme state called Viṣṇu is devoid of all that is to be abandoned," it is Viṣṇu himself who is denoted by the word *brahman*, and Viṣṇu alone who is denoted by the word *Bhagavat*; therefore, a connection with things to be abandoned is logically untenable for Viṣṇu.

Regarding the term *avikāra* (unchanging): the word *vikāra* (change) refers both to the substratum (*dharmin*) and to the attribute (*dharma*), as seen in such usages as "the group of sixteen is a modification (*vikāra*). Thus, *avikāra* means that [Brahman] does not itself become a modification or an effect of anything else. By this, non-conscious effects (*kāryācit*) are excluded. Alternatively, *vikāra* refers to states (*avasthā*), such as "greatness" (*mahattva*) or "egoity" (*ahaṅkāratva*); because it is eternally devoid of connection with these, it is *avikāra*. Therefore, by the word *avikāra*, *prakṛti* (primordial nature), which possesses modifications, is excluded.

Thus, by means of the *tatpuruṣa* and *bahuvrīhi* compounds in the word "to the Unchanging" (*avikārāya*), there is the exclusion of consciousness in both its states as cause and effect. By "to the Pure" (*śuddhāya*), there is the exclusion of the bound soul (*baddha*). [The term] "eternal" (*nityāya*) means eternal by virtue of being pure; otherwise, there would be a redundancy with the word "unchanging. The word "eternal" (*nitya*) qualifies the pure reality itself as a specific attribute of the pure entity; just as in the expression "most generous" (*mahodāra*), the word "great" (*maha*), while qualifying generosity, serves as a qualifier for the donor, so it is here.

Therefore, the term *mukta* (liberated) serves to exclude [those who are not liberated]. The phrase *paramātmane* (to the Supreme Self) excludes those who are eternally liberated (*nityamukta*), for they are dependent on another and are not themselves supreme. This is because it will be stated later: "The supreme [state] of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the individual soul (*puruṣa*), the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and time (*kāla*). Some maintain that the exclusion of primordial matter, the individual soul, the unmanifest, and time is effected by the four terms beginning with *avikārāya* (to the changeless one).

Since even manifest time—consisting of states such as the blink of an eye—is excluded by the term "unchanging" (*avikāra*), and since the threefold nature of the *puruṣa* alone is established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*), it is appropriate that the aforementioned objects are excluded by the qualifying attributes, as they are capable of such exclusion. Furthermore, he declares its distinction from everything else by stating that it possesses a form that is eternally uniform (*sadaikarūparūpāya*). The first word "form" (*rūpa*) denotes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the meaning is "possessing a single, unchanging nature."

The meaning is that His nature—consisting of being the opposite of everything to be abandoned (*heya*), being the locus of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), being the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), and so forth—is unswerving in all states, such as the manifestation of the supreme array (*paravyūha*) and the state of dissolution (*vibhava*). Alternatively, "of one form" means having a nature identical to the divine self-nature; by this also, the fact of being the opposite of what is to be abandoned and so forth is established. By these words, the subject matter of the *Īkṣati*, *Ānandamaya*, and *Antarāditya* sections [of the Brahma-sūtras] is intended to be expressed.

The previously mentioned nature of being the Self (*ātmatva*) does not occur in the manner of saying "the jar has clay as its essence" (*mṛdātmako ghaṭa*); therefore, that clarity is established through the power of the individual words by means of the word *Viṣṇu* and the phrase *sarvajiṣṇavaḥ*. By these two words, there is the exclusion of [ordinary] kings and the sky. For indeed, being the embodied one (*śarīritva*) consists in being the internal controller who has entered within. Thus, the nature of being the Self is elucidated. Furthermore, because the word *Viṣṇu* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*), the determination of a specific deity is also established.

Alternatively, by the word *Viṣṇu* itself, pervasion up to the limit of control is expressed; he dispels the suspicion that He might be touched by defects residing in [the world] due to that pervasion by saying *sarvajiṣṇavaḥ* ("conquerors of all").

How can Viṣṇu be the cause, when it is understood that Hiraṇyagarbha and others are the causes of creation and so forth? To this he says *namaḥ*. The meaning is that Viṣṇu alone, assuming those respective bodies (*śarīraka*), performs creation and the rest. The word *hari*, ending in the honorific suffix *-paya* (denoting the ultimate), refers to the embodied form known as Viṣṇu, as stated in: "He assumed the state of Viṣṇu for the protection of all beings."

"The terms *Hiraṇyagarbha* and *Śaṅkara* extend up to the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān) by way of the individual soul (*jīva*)," as seen in: "Brahmā and all the gods, humans, and likewise animals, are shrouded in the blinding darkness of delusion, which is the great whirlpool of Viṣṇu’s Māyā"; and "In Hiraṇyagarbha and others, Brahman is twofold, consisting of action (*karmātmikā*)," starting from "The Blessed Lord is Hiraṇyagarbha," up to: "This embodied form of Hari consists of the threefold creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*); however, all those beginning with the gods are impure."

This is determined both by the intended meaning of the verses found in this very section beginning with "born from karma," and by the consistency with statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, such as: "These two, the best of the wise, are known to be born from [His] grace and anger; following the paths shown by Him, they are the agents of creation and destruction," and: "He who is your inner self, mine, and those of all others known as embodied beings—He is the witness of all, and cannot be grasped by anyone anywhere."

The phrase "to Vāsudeva" indicates that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with Hiraṇyagarbha and others is established by pervasion (*vyāpti*). He says "to Tāra" to show that even while situated between Brahmā and Śiva, he remains one whose essential nature is never lost. Alternatively, the meaning is that among those three, he alone is the bestower of liberation; for the Śruti states: "Now, why is he called *Tāra*? Because as soon as he is uttered, he delivers (*tārayati*) one from the great terror of the cycle of birth, old age, death, and worldly existence; therefore he is called *Tāra*."

Based on such passages as, "O Brahman! Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are the primary powers (brahma-śaktis) of Brahman," one should not suspect that Viṣṇu is the supreme reality or that he is equal to Brahmā and others. For a power (śakti) is an inseparable attribute (apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa). In that case, when the substratum (dharmin) is indicated by a word in a different case-ending, it is observed that even a word extending to the substratum refers only to the attribute, as in expressions such as "the whiteness of the cloth. Likewise, the word "Viṣṇu" here refers only to the physical form (vigraha) which serves as an attribute.

Because the subject (*dharmin*) is designated separately by the word *brahma*, which has a different case-ending; for "the powers of Brahman" (*brahma-śaktayaḥ*) means the powers belonging to Brahman. Therefore, there is a designation with a different case-ending. Alternatively, just as the Blessed One is designated by terms such as "god" or "human," He is also designated by terms such as "power" (*śakti*) or "manifestation" (*vibhūti*), because of the commonality of being a manifestation (*vibhūti-sājātyāt*). As the venerable Śrīvatsāṅka Miśra said: "But [the term] 'belonging to them' (*teṣām*) applies even to the name 'manifestation' (*vibhākhya*). Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated.

Now, in order to exclude the view that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) alone is the cause, he pays homage to the Supreme Self as qualified by primordial matter with the words "one and many" (*ekāneka*). He is one in the state of being a cause and many in the state of being an effect. Then, he describes the state of effect residing in the intellect (*dhī*) with the word "gross" (*sthūla*); likewise, he describes the causal state residing in the intellect with the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Furthermore, he states that even in those states, his essential nature remains unaltered with the phrase "the cause of liberation" (*muktihetavaḥ*).

Now, he states [the section] qualified by time, beginning with the word "sarga" (creation). Since the qualification of time is appropriate through the qualifiers to be mentioned later, and since this section is intended to convey a specific [qualification], and because it has already been established that there is a qualification by other attributes, the statement regarding the qualification by time follows by process of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*). For if that were not established, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a lack of the required injunction. Furthermore, if the text were intended solely to describe the nature of Brahman as the cause, there would be the consequence of redundancy (*paunaruktya*): because the creation within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) and so forth have already been stated, while the creation of the principles (*tattva*) outside the egg and so forth are yet to be described.

Furthermore, because this verse will be spoken of together with the manifest (vyakta), the unmanifest (avyakta), and so forth—in the detailed exposition through such passages as "of the primary matter (pradhāna), the person (puruṣa), the manifest, and time (kāla)"; "the manifest is Viṣṇu, likewise the unmanifest, the person, and time itself"; "likewise, [He] exists in the form of the person and in the form of time"; and "Brahmā, Dakṣa, and others are time"—this verse refers exclusively to time. Moreover, its reference to time is appropriate due to its immediate sequence following a verse that denotes the insentient (acid) as qualified [by the sentient].

The subsequent verse refers to the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), due to its association with the verse referring to the individual soul (*vyaṣṭijīva*). That time is the root cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction is established in such passages as: "Brahmā, Dakṣa, and others are Time," "Viṣṇu, Manu, and others are Time," and "Rudra, Kāla, Antaka, and so forth. *Jaganmaya* means abounding in the world, both by virtue of being its delimiting factor (*avacchedakatayā*) and its delimited object (*avacchedyatayā*).

Now, he pays homage to Him who exists as the collective totality of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), with the words "the substratum. He is the conscious substratum of the insentient by His very nature, according to the scriptural statements: "In this very way, these elements (bhūtamātrāḥ) are deposited in the elements of consciousness (prajñāmātrāsu)," and "O mighty-armed one! [I salute] Her who has become the individual soul (jīvabhūtā), by whom this world is supported. His subtlety (aṇīyastva) consists in being so subtle as to be capable of pervading even primordial matter (prakṛti).

Alternatively, the meaning is that, according to the manner stated as "by means of the nature of expansion and atomization," there is a state of extreme minuteness (*aṇīyastva*) due to the absence of the expansion of knowledge, just as during the state of cosmic manifestation (*sarga*). It is called *bhūta* because it exists within all beings; it abides in all the evolving principles (*tattvas*) ending with earth. Immediately thereafter, he offers salutation to the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) characterized by its particularity, beginning with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Regarding the question of which specific Supreme Self (paramātman) this verse refers to among the meanings indicated in the commentary beginning with "Hiraṇyagarbha," [the author] analyzes and demonstrates the meaning of the present verse as contained within the compound by stating "therein" (tatra). The meaning is that the connection of the Supreme Self with delusion (bhrama) occurs only through an intermediary. To the question "What follows from that?", he says "therefore" (tasmāt). By way of pointing out the inconsistency with the introduction—namely, the impossibility of describing the attainment of a boon as a response to a question if [the Self] were devoid of attributes—he states the contradiction.

Now, it is stated that [the previous argument] is not consistent with the resolution of the objections raised in the subsequent chapters, beginning with the words "yadi" (if). Alternatively, the inconsistency of the question and answer relevant to the commencement of the scripture was previously stated; now, the inconsistency of the specific details of that question and answer is being stated, beginning with "yadi. Although the association with the *guṇas* was described in the preceding chapter through such passages as "enjoying the *rajas* quality," the intention of the objector who raises the objection "of the one devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇasya*) is this: since the association with the *guṇas* is mediated by another, he himself is indeed devoid of qualities.

In the view that [Brahman] is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa-pakṣe*), terms such as "of the immeasurable" (*aprameyasya*) and so forth would be redundant, since the qualityless nature (*nirguṇatva*) is already established by the term "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇasya*) alone; furthermore, this is because qualities such as fullness (*paripūrṇatva*) and the like are not admitted. It is precisely the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other terms like "immeasurable" that establishes the restricted scope of the negation presented by the term "devoid of qualities. The phrase "it does not fit" (*na ghaṭate*) means that the objection regarding the possession of all powers—expressed in the words "the powers of being at the beginning of creation" (*sargādyā bhāvaśaktayaḥ*)—is resolved, and thus the view that [Brahman] is devoid of attributes is inconsistent with the evidence. This is the intended meaning.

To the question, "In that case, how can the objection and its refutation be established?", he says: "For if that were so... By the phrase "of Brahman devoid of attributes," the point intended is the redundancy of other words [in the scripture]. The meaning is that when the objection has been raised regarding the impossibility of agency for a Brahman without distinctions, the refutation must be stated as follows: "If agency were real, then indeed there would be such an impossibility; however, since it is not ultimately real, this very difficulty is an ornament."

To the doubt—"For what purpose are these objections and refutations, if this meaning is not being established?"—he himself states the body of those objections and refutations with the words "utpattyādi" (origination, etc.). He demonstrates, by means of the phrase "sattvādiguṇayuktā" (endowed with the qualities of *sattva*, etc.), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of agency by the opposites of the qualifiers such as "nirguṇasya" (of the one devoid of qualities), which was intended by the word "katham" (how). The opposites of the qualifiers "nirguṇatva" (qualitylessness) and so forth are, respectively: being endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and so on, being incomplete, and being subject to karma.

The opposite form of "of the stainless self" (*amalātmanaḥ*) is also established in meaning by the term "subject to karma" (*karmavaśya*). Being "stainless" (*amalātmatva*) means having a stainless nature, which is the state of being unfit for connection with karma; its opposite form is fitness for connection with karma. And that [fitness] is established in meaning by the word "subject to karma. For "subjection to karma" (*karmavaśyatva*) is indeed the effect of fitness for connection with karma. He states the meaning of the words beginning with "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇasya*) in their respective order by means of the words beginning with "devoid of the qualities such as *sattva*."

By the phrase "of one who is unfit for connection with karma," the term "of the stainless self" (*amalātmanaḥ*) is explained. Even for the liberated one, there exists freedom from the dominion of karma; however, because he was connected with karma in his previous state, he was fit for it. Therefore, being unfit for connection with karma—which excludes that [previous state]—is what constitutes the stainless nature of the self. Freedom from the dominion of karma means the absence of being a recipient of pleasure and pain produced by karma. Being of a different nature from one subject to the dominion of karma is what is meant by being unfit for connection with karma.

The objection is raised by means of an undesirable consequence (*prasañjana*) regarding a specific contradiction: that if [the Lord] were the creator of creation and so forth, it would follow that He is subject to the three *guṇas*, dependent [on others], a recipient of fruits subordinate to karma, and fit for connection with karma. This logical argument (*tarka*)—similar to the claim that "if fire were a substance, it would follow that it is not hot"—is sublated by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). Therefore, it is logical for a subject of a different class to possess properties of a different class; just as, despite possessing the nature of fire, lightning-fire cannot be extinguished by water.

Therefore, the meaning of the resolution is that the possession of all powers by Brahman—which is of a different genus from all other things—is logically consistent. Regarding the verse "The powers of all entities," this is the literal meaning of the words: "beyond the scope of inconceivable knowledge" means established through a realization that cannot be reached by logic; "creation and so forth" refers to the objects of creation and the like; "bhāva-śaktayaḥ" means the powers of entities (vastu-śaktayaḥ). The designation "the powers of the entity of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo vastu-śaktayaḥ*) is used in the same manner as the expression "identity with Brahman" (*brahma-tādātmyam*). Alternatively, [it may mean] "the powers of the being of Brahman" (*brahmaṇo bhāva-śaktayaḥ*), which are the powers of its reality.

The meaning is that these are the powers of Brahman that are inherent in its reality, connected with its existence, and unconditioned (*nirupādhika*). Alternatively, the word *bhāva* refers to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); thus, the meaning is "powers that are innate."

Now he explains the *Catuḥślokī*, beginning with the words "The ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*). Since the entirety [of the universe] culminates in Brahman and is His body, Brahman alone—whose body is the whole—is the ultimate reality; the meaning is that everything which does not culminate in Him is illusory (*mithyā*). By the phrase "O Lord of the world," space (*ākāśa*) is excluded; by the phrase "by whom [the world] is pervaded," a mere king is excluded. By this, the definition of the world as a body is demonstrated. For any one of the characteristics of being governed, being supported, or being subordinate, when accompanied by the quality of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*), serves to indicate the definition of a body.

O You whose body is the universe! If it were said that "there is nothing other than you," it would follow that only some other independent entity distinct from you—extending beyond the universe—is false, but not the universe itself which constitutes your body. Just as when it is said, "O King, there is no one other than you," the earth does not thereby become false; rather, it is only another king equal to him who is rendered false—in the same way [here]. Alternatively, the word *eka* (one) refers to preeminence (*prādhānya*). For in the rule *ekādākiniccāsahāye*, the term *asahāya* (without companion) excludes preeminence.

And the primacy of Brahman with respect to the world consists in its being the substantive (viśeṣya). At that time, by the statement "there is no other," another entity that is primary is negated, but not some other thing that is non-primary. He says "that very [thing]" (tadeva), meaning that the second half of the verse serves as a justification for the stated point by establishing its pervasion (vyāpti). Regarding that, he states the resulting meaning with the words "by which" (yena); "yena" means "because of which" (yasmāt). "Other than you" (tvadanya) means "not having your nature" (atvadātmaka).

Because everything is pervaded by you as your very self (*ātmatayā*), everything consists of you and is your body; thus, there is nothing other than you that does not consist of you. Therefore, the meaning is that you alone, whose body is the universe, are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). He states "ataḥ" (therefore) to support the aforementioned point with the phrase "this is your majesty" (*tavaiṣa mahimā*) from one part of the verse. Since majesty (*mahiman*) consists in pervasion, the statement "that which is the pervasion of all" is made; however, this is not because the primary intent lies in the act of pervasion itself. Rather, the intent lies precisely in the fact that pervasion constitutes majesty.

Alternatively, he states that the pervasion (vyāpti) serves to establish the aforementioned meaning because of its association with the word "māhima" (greatness), saying: "Therefore this is said. He demonstrates its opposition to others by saying: "Otherwise. The meaning is that if the pervaded, the pervader, and so forth were unreal, one could not say, "Your pervasion of all things is Your greatness," but rather one would have to say it is an illusion (bhrānti). Regarding the view that the entire world is ultimately unreal, he offers two further objections, beginning with: "O Lord of the world! [The term] *lakṣaṇā* refers to the definition of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-lakṣaṇā*).

In response to the objection that—since independence (*svatantratā*) is established by direct perception as being non-identical with Brahman—the scripture cannot establish its opposite, namely its culminating in Brahman, just as in the case of the statement "The sacrificial post is the sun"—the author introduces the second verse with the words "Since... (*yataḥ*), intending to convey that the cognition of dependence (*pāratantrya*), though indirect (*parokṣa*), is more powerful than the cognition of independence, even if the latter is direct (*aparokṣa*), because the former is not otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).

The realization of dependence is contingent upon the realization of the Supreme Self; since that [realization of the Supreme Self] is absent, there is an absence of its realization. Thus, the realization of independence is "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha). This means: the form consisting solely of gods, humans, and so forth—that is, the mere form of the world devoid of being the body of the Supreme Self. The point is this: just as the delusion of identifying the body with the self, though immediate, is sublated by the mediate knowledge derived from scripture, so too is the delusion of independence.

The beginning of the third verse is intended to demonstrate that for one who does not even know their own self as distinct from the body, the realization of dependence upon the Supreme Self is all the more established by logic. He explains this [verse] with the words "not merely," etc. In the world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, the term "world" (*jagat*) is intended here to signify the sentient aspect—the entire world whose nature is consciousness—as in the passage: "All this world is composed of these three states consisting of the qualities."

"Deluded, he does not recognize me as being beyond these and imperishable. Here, it is stated that the cognition of that whose true nature is consciousness as having the nature of an insentient object is an error (*bhrama*). From this, it is established that the cognition of an object's own nature as being its own nature is not an error. Furthermore, the delusion regarding the body as the self (*dehātmabhrama*) is produced by association (*saṃsarga*), like [the notion] "water is hot. Even when there is the manifestation of knowledge, which is the unique attribute of the Self, the occurrence of delusion is possible due to the lack of recognition of its uniqueness.

He explains the fourth [verse] with the words "But those who... (*ye punar iti*). Because the word *vijñāna* here signifies the Self (*ātman*), he states that they are "knowers of the Self whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpātmavidaḥ*). By the phrase "without understanding" (*abuddhayā*), he reminds us that, as the opposite of what was stated in the preceding verse, they are called "knowers of knowledge" (*jñānavidaḥ*). By the words "the wise ones" (*buddhimantaḥ*), he indicates that, as the opposite of "those who are not yogis" (*ayoginaḥ*), they are called "pure-minded" (*śuddhacetasaḥ*), meaning those whose minds are purified for the sake of yoga. Purity is the cause for being fit for yoga.

Indeed, it is heard in scripture that the accomplishment of worship, which consists in the direct realization of the Blessed Lord, occurs through a purified mind. And the purification of the mind is achieved through *karmayoga*. The meaning of "by yoga" is either "through fitness" or "through complete purification. In the previous verse, by the word "entire world," the world in the form of sentient beings was intended; in this verse, by the word "entirely born," the world in the form of insentient matter is intended.

In the view that the intended meaning is the absolute non-ultimate nature [of everything], he states—in the phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*)—the detailed refutation common to all the verses, together with the refutations not yet mentioned, which were briefly indicated in the first verse. The meaning is that there would be redundancy if there were no distinction between the delusion of independence and the delusion of identifying the body as the self. Furthermore, there would be a figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) of words such as "O Supreme Lord," "O Lord of the world," "Thy," "Greatness," and "Thou"; for the word "Thou" (*tvam*) denotes an object distinct from the "I" (*aham-artha*) directed toward oneself.

Therefore, its nature is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇikatva*). There is a contradiction with the meaning: since it is established as being uncontradicted by perception and other means of knowledge, if it were unreal, there would be a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-virodha*), and the impossibility of cessation (*nirodhānupapatti*). There is a contradiction with reasoning (*tarka-virodha*), a contradiction regarding the possession of both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva-virodha*), and a contradiction with the context (*prakaraṇa-virodha*). There is a contradiction with the praise (*stuti-virodha*); for the subject under discussion is that "the sages dwelling within the pores of the hair offer praise. If the praisers possessed non-dual knowledge, praise would be impossible; and in the absence of such knowledge, it would be even more so. There is a contradiction with the purport of the scripture (*śāstra-tātparya-virodha*), namely, a contradiction between the beginning and the conclusion, as well as the beginning and conclusion of the intermediate sections.

Now, he explains the *Ādibharata-catuḥślokī*, which is interspersed with other verses, beginning with the words "tasya" and so forth. Non-duality (*advaita*) is of two kinds as propounded by the scriptures: the non-duality of Brahman and the non-duality of the individual soul (*jīva*). Among these, the non-duality of Brahman is the non-duality of the substrate (*prakāry-advaita*), while the non-duality of the individual soul is the non-duality of the modes (*prakārā-advaita*). If it is asked what the regulating principle (*niyāmaka*) here is, it is said:

Because the non-duality of Brahman is established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the Brahma-sections of the Upanishads; because coreferentiality has as its purport the oneness of the substrate qualified by different modes; because the multiplicity of modes is explicitly stated in the passage, "Being one, he manifests himself in many ways"; because the negation of difference found in passages such as "There is no diversity here," which serves as a supplement to the injunction of oneness, must refer to a difference that contradicts the oneness thus enjoined; and because a general negation refers to things other than those specifically enjoined.

Because [the scripture] is intent on negating a plurality of modes (*prakāra*), and because of the explicit statement—"Nothing equal to Him and nothing superior to Him is seen"—which negates any other mode equal to Brahman, the non-duality of the modes (*prakāryadvaita*) alone is the non-duality of Brahman.

Since the plurality of individual selves (*jīvātman*) is established by Śruti, otherwise the distinction between the bound and the liberated would be untenable, as would the possibility of instruction and the distinction between pleasure and pain. As it is said: "The person is neither god, nor man, nor beast, nor tree"; and "This fourfold division is based upon false knowledge."

Because the negation of specific distinctions is explicitly stated in passages such as "when the distinctions of gods and so forth have been destroyed," and because of the statement regarding the equality of the liberated ones; because of the conformity with the contextual statements such as "I, you, and likewise others," "there you and I am also here," and "that mind rests in equanimity"; because the word "one" (eka) can appropriately mean "of one kind" (ekajātīya)—just as in the expression "one grain of rice" (eko vrīhiḥ); and because of the nature of the words in the verse to be cited later—the non-duality of the individual soul (jīvādvaita) is indeed non-duality of mode (prakārādvaita).

If it is argued that because the sentence, "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many," is intent upon ordaining desires, it has no intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding eternity or plurality—and if there were such an intention, it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—we say: no. Just as in the case of "The cake (*puroḍāśa*) for Agni on eight potsherds," this sentence is intent upon an injunction of a qualified entity (the cake for Agni characterized by being on eight potsherds), so too this [present] sentence is understood to be intent upon an injunction of the granting of desires as qualified by the many eternal conscious beings.

For when it is taught that one should give away many eternal things rather than a few impermanent ones—even though both grant desires—it is indeed the excellence of the gift of the eternal that is emphasized. If it is argued that since the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) is already established by common worldly experience, the scripture has no purpose there—on the principle that "scripture is meaningful only regarding what is not otherwise known"—we say no. For while the perception of plurality in the case of composite objects is established by the world, the plurality of the pure nature of the Self is not so established; it is precisely because this plurality is not established by worldly experience that the possibility for the scripture’s purport to reside therein exists.

Since the conditioned form is impermanent and the extracted essential nature is eternal, when plurality is predicated as co-locating with eternity, it is effectively stated that there is a plurality of the pure self-nature. Furthermore, instruction is not possible: if the teacher is deluded, there can be no instruction; if he is undeluded, then all the more so, because of the absence of any perception of duality. Even if duality were perceived, instruction regarding one's intended object would not be possible for one who stands before the reflection of oneself in a mirror.

The distinction between selves is established by the distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Now, what is this "distribution of pleasure and pain"? Is it the multiplicity of individual instances of pleasure and pain, or rather the multiplicity of their substrata? Since a single self is observed to experience multiple instances of pleasure and pain, the multiplicity of the *svarūpa* (essential nature) of pleasure and so forth does not contradict the unity of the self; thus, it cannot constitute a "distribution.
