If you argue that it is the difference of substrata, then the reason [you provide] is indistinguishable from the point to be proven (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*). This is not so; for the "distribution" is distinct from both of the modes you have mentioned.

The rejoinder is as follows: it is observed that there is a connection (*pratisaṃdhāna*) among pleasure, pain, and so forth when they reside in a single substratum (*ekāśraya*). However, when an obstacle is present, the absence of such a connection between pleasure, pain, and so forth is established precisely because of their having a single substratum. In the term *ekamaya*, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Alternatively, the word *eka* emphasizes the state [of oneness], meaning "oneness" (*aikya*); that which abounds in this is *ekamaya*. For it is the Self in its pure state (*śuddhāvasthā*) that possesses an abundance of oneness, not the one who is entangled in transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛṣṭa*).

For that [Self], there is an absence of predominance of unity due to internal distinctions such as intellect, pleasure, and pain, and external distinctions such as godhood and so forth. The word *eka* (one) signifies "similar" (*samāna*), as seen in such usages as: "A single grain of rice, when well-ripened, nourishes all people. By the phrase "consisting of specific modifications of the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) such as gods and humans," [it is implied]: "Suffering, ignorance, and impurity are attributes of *prakṛti*, not of the Self"; and: "The Person is neither a god, nor a human, nor an animal, nor a plant."

The identity of meaning between these two statements—“O King, these differences in bodily form have their origin in karma”—is thus demonstrated. The word *piṇḍa* (body) serves to recall the contextual statement: “Since the body, characterized by a head, hands, and so forth, is distinct from the Person (*pums*). If it is argued that by establishing oneness in the Self through the phrase “one-fold” (*ekamaya*) and thereby negating difference, what is actually being negated would be a difference in the very nature of the Self, we reply: this would indeed be the case if the oneness being enjoined were an identity of individual manifestations (*vyakti*). However, that [oneness] is rather an identity of mode (*prakāra*).

Therefore, the intended meaning is that the negation of difference is indeed the negation of heterogeneity (*vijātīyatva*). If it is asked: "Since it was stated in general that 'the dualists are seers of the unreal,' how can it be said that the duality of gods and so forth is negated?"—then why, when the negation of duality is understood in a general sense, is it specifically said to be the negation of the duality of the Self? It is not a negation of the difference between the body and the Self, because the difference between the body and the Self is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If this is argued, [we reply]: since the difference between Selves is also established by valid means of knowledge, there is no negation of that difference either.

Furthermore, the intended meaning is the negation of distinctions such as those between gods and others. If the duality residing within the Self were not prohibited, then the use of the singular number in such statements as “the Self is pure, imperishable, and tranquil” and “consciousness performs the sacrifice” would be untenable. If it were argued that the singular is used in the sense of a genus (*jāti*), then one might object that the word *deha* (body) should likewise be used in the singular; however, this doubt is resolved by the terms *deva*, *manuṣya*, and so forth. The word *vividha* (various) is used with the intention of expressing internal subdivisions among gods and others, while the word *vicitra* (multiform) is used with the intention of expressing their manifold diversity even therein.

The intention is that the singular number is used because of the identity of the self’s noble birth, while the plural number is used because of the multiplicity of intermediate castes within the individual bodies. He states the authority for this equality with the words "as it has been said. The meaning is that since plurality is enjoined and equality is established, the denial of a distinction between individual selves is untenable. He states another reason with the words "of that" (*tasya*). The meaning is that if the sense were otherwise, there would be a contradiction among the words contained in this verse. The connection is: "because it has been stated [that] the meaning is 'equal' (*samam*)."

For when a singular number is used, the resolution is that the singular refers to the genus (*jāti*); however, one might raise the doubt that since a statement intended to negate others cannot otherwise be resolved, the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikatva*) is established. To this, he states the meaning of the verse beginning with "If there were another" (*yady anyo'sti*) with the word "yadi. Since two words are employed for each single object across three locations, the objection is refuted by the fact that because the word *anya* (other) ends in the vowel *a*, it does not negate a difference between Selves. To the question of what the meaning of those two words is, he says "tatra" (therein).

The meaning is that, having referred to the substratum (dharmin) by means of the word "other," its connection with another form presented by a different word is negated. If it is asked, "How is it impossible to say 'this is I' and 'this is another,' since the properties of interiority (pratyaktva) and exteriority (parāktva) exist as distinguishing attributes?"—it is not so; for interiority and exteriority, being common to all things in relation to oneself and others respectively, lack the capacity to serve as differentiators.

Previously, with the intention that "this one is the limit [of excellence] among gods and others," King Sauvīra questioned Ādibharata out of a desire to know his specific nature. Therefore, the sense is that these words are intended to negate forms such as those of gods and so forth. When the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*) is thus established, in response to the doubt as to what is expressed by the verse as a whole, he connects it to the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), saying: "This is what has been said. He explains the meaning of the word *eṣa* (this) as "having such a form," and the meaning of the word *anya* (other) as "having a different kind of form."

The phrase "identity of form" (*ākāraikya*) is intended to mean the extreme similarity of forms; it is with this intention that it is said, "having such a form, having a different form. Otherwise, since the apprehension of the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*) would be accomplished by a single word alone, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the other word being redundant. Therefore, the meaning is that the other word refers to the "form. The conclusion regarding the opposite of this point is stated in the following verse, which has not been cited here. To explain its meaning, he says: "And not thus... (*na caivam*).

For this is the verse: "When the one Person is established within all beings, then indeed such speech as 'Who are you? or 'I am he' is futile. Here, the word *eka* (one) refers to the identity of form (*ākāra-aikya*). Attributes such as self-luminosity, eternity, and atomicity (*aṇutva*) are common to all selves. However, a distinguishing form such as that of a god (*deva*) and so forth does not exist in the self. Due to the absence of any differentiator, designation by means of a word denoting such [a distinction] is untenable.

The qualities of being perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*), being external (*parāktva*), being indirect (*parokṣatva*), being immediate (*aparokṣatva*), and so forth, are not differentiators. Therefore, the question "Who are you? intends to inquire about a form other than those [qualities]. It is not that the question "Who are you? is asking about the word *bhavat* (you); rather, the word *bhavat* refers merely to the substratum (*dharmin*). The word *kim* (what/who) refers to a differentiator such as being a god (*deva*) or the like. Consequently, since there is no form distinct from those [qualities], it is not possible to designate [the Self] by means of a word expressing those [qualities]; this is the meaning. [This is because] they are identical solely in having the single form of consciousness (*jñāna*).

The meaning is: "from what was stated previously. By means of an example illustrating the aforementioned resolution, he states the meaning of the verse cited by the opponent as being intended to establish non-duality (*advaita*) with the words "the holes of the flute" (*veṇurandhra*). The presentation of the example merely shows that things which are naturally of a single form may possess internal distinctions due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For if one were to accept complete identity in every respect, then the Self would also have to possess qualities such as having a body or being material, like space; yet that is rejected because it contradicts other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

The sense is that there is likewise another aspect found in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). When it was stated, "so too is this [aspect] of the Supreme Self," he said, "in the same way, there is a difference in the designations of the selves as 'gods' and so forth," with the intention that there should be no confusion regarding the difference in designations such as *ṣaḍja* and the rest. Although the reading is *bhedavaṣaḍjādisañjñitaḥ*, it has been explained as "the difference in designations such as *ṣaḍja* and the rest"; the sense is that the ease of perceiving the difference in forms such as *ṣaḍja*, which is otherwise difficult to grasp, depends upon the difference in designations. This is exactly the case for the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) as well.

In the example, he establishes through reasoning either the multiplicity of individual instances or the plurality of parts in response to doubt, using the verse beginning with *taijasena*. The underlying sense is that [the self] is a substance possessing touch (*sparśavat-dravyatvāt*). However, where the ether (*ākāśa*) is cited as an example, one should understand that because the ether was mentioned as an illustration for a single Self, the same applies to other Selves: "Just as the single sky appears divided by distinctions such as white and blue to those with deluded vision, so too the Self, though being one, appears separate and distinct. (Gauḍapāda Kārikā 3.12).

Just as the distinction between white, blue, and other colors in the sky occurs sequentially—belonging to that [sky] when it is in contact with clouds during the periods of autumn, the rainy season, and so forth—so too the distinction between gods and others in the case of the single Self occurs sequentially. Alternatively, even in that case, by accepting a distinction of spatial locations (*pradeśabheda*), the example of the entire space (*sarvātman*) would apply; for if one does not admit a distinction of spatial locations in space, it would follow that either the jar and such are all-pervading or that space is limited. Is there a connection of the jar and such with the entirety of space, or rather with a specific spatial location?

In the first position, it would follow that the jar and other objects are all-pervading (*vibhu*), or else that space (*ākāśa*) possesses a limited dimension. In the second position, one must admit a distinction of parts (*pradeśabheda*). For the Vedāntins, the doctrine that space is partless (*niravayava*) constitutes a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*); for in the Vedāntas, the instruction on quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) is given according to a division of parts—namely, that through one part it undergoes transformation into the state of air—and because its origin and dissolution are observed. Therefore: "Just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within the jar is not different from the [great] space."

The statement of Śaunaka, "Likewise, when the objects to be abandoned have been destroyed by Brahmā, he who is called Viṣṇu [the individual soul] [merges]," should be understood as being intended to provide an illustrative example for the absence of adventitious difference in the individual soul from the Supreme Self—due to the predominance of the non-difference between the part and the whole of the ether; for in that very same context, an illustration of equality is stated: "Just as fire cast into fire would attain identity."

Now he states the concluding verse regarding Ādibharata: "So am I" (*so'ham*). This refers to what was previously stated in the four preceding chapters. Although the word "he" (*sa*) denotes a reality qualified by the form of knowledge (*jñānākāra*), the specific mention of the qualifying attribute as "the form of knowledge of all selves" is intended to demonstrate that the purport lies in the qualifying portion itself. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the immediately following statement, "in grammatical coreferentiality with that. Thus, he concludes: "knowledge alone is the form."

Since the preceding verse immediately before the verse beginning with "so'ham" states—in its half-verse, "That which exists here as a single whole is Acyuta; there is nothing else beyond Him"—that all selves have the Blessed Lord as their body, there might arise the suspicion that the verse beginning with "so'ham" is intended to conclude by affirming the identity of the self with the Blessed Lord. But that is incorrect, because the context is devoted to the discrimination between the body and the self.

Since a conclusion (*nigamana*) is required [for this argument], and since there is no other verse following this one intended to provide such a conclusion, and because it is improper not to state what is required when something is required, the intention is that this verse is intended as a conclusion regarding the fact that the selves (*ātman*) have a single uniform form consisting solely of the knowledge that excludes the body. He states the meaning of the portion "Abandon the delusion of difference" (*tyaja bhedamoham*) as follows: "Abandon the delusion of difference among the selves caused by the non-difference of forms such as gods and so forth. The word "gods and so forth" (*devādi*) serves as an elaboration of the word "difference" (*bheda*). The difference in forms such as godhood residing in the body is the cause of the delusion of difference in the self.

The meaning is: "Abandon that delusion of difference. He states the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) if [the text] were intended to negate the entire [notion of] difference by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Nor do words such as "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*) refer to the body; for it is not the case that, having referred to the Self with that word, the identity of those bodies with that Self is taught. Nor do they refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for neither the identity of the internal organs with the Supreme Self nor their mutual identity is taught. Nor do they refer to the internal organ as qualified by the body.

For it is not taught (or established) that there is identity between internal organs qualified by bodies. Therefore, with the intention that words such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) refer to the Self as distinct from the body, the phrase "distinct from the body" is stated. Anticipating the objection that since terms such as "I-ness" and "you-ness" (*tvaṃtva*) are merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), there can be no difference in the underlying entity (*upalakṣya*) they indicate, he refutes this with the word "I. By the word "ādi" in the compound *ahantvamādi*, the word "all" (*sarva*) is intended. The expression "by the indicative" (*upalakṣyeṇa*) is a figurative designation; it means "by the word denoting the indicated object."

Regarding the phrase "all this is the very nature of the Self" (*sarvametadātmasvarūpam*): the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of all three terms—"I," "you," and "all"—with the word "the very nature of the Self" is established as the result. This inclusion of the phrase "all this is the very nature of the Self" in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is intended to make it known that the word "the very nature of the Self" is shown to be co-referential with the term "all this" (*sarvametat*), which denotes an object belonging to the same class of meaning as the referents of "I" and "you. Thus, by using any one of those three—specifically the term "all this"—it is indicated that the word "the very nature of the Self" stands in grammatical coordination with them.

In the verse, all this was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that "this entire [world] is the nature of the Self. Therefore, because words such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "Self-nature," which is intended to denote the indicated object (*upalakṣya*), it is inconsistent to claim that the meanings denoted by words such as "I-ness" function merely as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). For, in ordinary usage, one does not observe a primary coreferentiality between words denoting an indicator and words denoting the indicated object, such as in the expressions "The moon is a branch" or "The crane is a field. This is the meaning.

If it is argued that [the word "I"] exists through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the sense is that indication itself is the fault. Alternatively, the word "this" (*anena*) is a qualifier of the object indicated (*upalakṣya*). The meaning is that since all these [words] such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and "you-ness" (*tvam*) stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with this indicated object designated by the word "Self"—which is not of the nature of the Self—then their status as indicators (*upalakṣakatva*) is inconsistent. In this interpretation, it follows as a matter of fact that the reason for the designation of coreferentiality with all the words expressing meanings belonging to the same class as "I-ness" and "you-ness" is established.

If words such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and "you-ness" (*tvaṃtva*) were to extend as far as the objects they characterize, then, because the word "that" (*saḥ*)—which denotes the characterized object—is seen to be in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "the nature of the Self" (*ātmasvarūpa*) for the sake of that same meaning, the coordination of the denoters of the characteristics, namely "I-ness" and so forth, would be redundant. Furthermore, the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "I" is relative selfhood (*apekṣika-pratyaktva*); that of the word "you" is facing toward [the speaker] while being conscious (*cetana*); and that of the word "Self" (*ātman*) is the capacity for pervasion (*vyāpanakṣamatva*).

The word "sa" (he/that) refers to the form of the knowledge under discussion. Now, one might ask: in the phrase "And he is all this, the very nature of the Self," how can the pronoun *tat* (which is masculine) function as a qualifier of the "nature of the Self" (which is neuter)? It is said in reply: In passages such as "The Self is pure, imperishable, tranquil, devoid of qualities, and the maker of Prakṛti," the Self—which has been introduced as being composed of supreme knowledge—is indeed referred to by the pronoun *tat*. Therefore, there is no contradiction.

The meaning is that all this—which is perceived in the form of gods and so forth as non-conscious matter intermingled [with consciousness]—is the very nature of the Self; that Self is of the single form of knowledge alone. He explains the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "He too" (*sopi*). With the intention of asking how it is known that this section does not have the non-duality of the individual soul and Brahman as its primary purport, nor has the negation of a plurality of self-natures as its purport, but rather has the unity of mode as its purport, he asks: "From what? He provides the answer: "Because [the view that] the body is the Self... To the question "Why is even that [the case]? he says: "And that... (*tacceti*).

By establishing that the text is devoted to the discrimination between the body and the self, the claim that it is devoted to the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), as well as the claim that it is devoted to the negation of the plurality of selves, has already been answered. Now, intending to explain the meaning of the verse beginning with "the generator of difference" (*vibhedajanaka*), which occurs at the conclusion of the scripture, [the author] refutes its being devoted to any other meaning by means of the passage beginning with "vibheda... and so forth.

First, the possibility that [the passage] refers either to the identity of the nature of the self (*ātman*) or to the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is raised and then refuted. Here, because of the absence of the word "and" (*ca*), the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words *ātman* and *brahman* is possible; if that were the case, the word *brahman* would refer to the state of pure [consciousness]. In that situation, it would mean that there is no difference between the individual soul and the state of purity, and thus the identity of the nature of the soul would be stated. Therefore, he refutes the status of being a locus for doubt—that it refers to the identity of the self—by saying "ātma... (the self).

The meaning is: "by means of the aforementioned methods, such as the presumptive testimony of Śruti and Smṛti (arthāpatti), worldly presumptive testimony, and so forth. He refutes the second position with the words "jīva" and so on. "Like the body and the self" means: because of their possession of contradictory attributes. Just as there is a difference between the body and the self due to contradictory attributes such as inwardness (*pratyaktva*) and outwardness (*parāktva*), insentience (*ajaḍatva*) and sentience, eternity (*nityatva*) and mutability (*pariṇāmitva*), and so forth, even so, identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is not tenable due to contradictory attributes such as being subject to what is to be abandoned (*heyatva*) and being beyond it, possessing both sets of marks (*ubhayaliṅgatva*), being the controlled (*niyāmyatva*) and the controller (*niyantṛtva*), and so forth.

He states the proof for their possession of contradictory attributes with the words "tathāca" (and thus). The meaning is: "in this way, [there is] the state of possessing contradictory attributes. The particle "ca" has the sense of "hi" (for), indicating a reason. The fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) is used for the reasons that will be stated; this word "ca" stands in its place. "Samānam" means the tree, which is the body. "Piṣpalam" refers to the fruit of action. "Abhicākaśīti" means it shines intensely because it does not eat itself and because it causes others to eat.

Now, how can this mantra have as its purport the distinction between the individual self (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)? For this mantra has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the individual self as its purport, since it is explained accordingly in the *Paingi-rahasya-brāhmaṇa*: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit—this is the *sattva* (the internal organ). The other looks on without eating—the one who looks on without eating is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). These two are the *sattva* and the Knower of the Field."

It is understood that the commentary explains that by the passage ending with "eats the sweet" (*svādvatti*), *sattva* is described; and by the sentence ending with "shines forth" (*abhicākaśīti*), it is stated that the *kṣetrajña*—the "other who does not eat... the knower"—beholds [it]. Nor should it be said that the word *sattva* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the word *kṣetrajña* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); for the words *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* are well-known to refer respectively to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the individual soul, as in: "That is this *sattva* by which one sees the dream."

Furthermore, since it has been explained in that very same context that the terms *sattva* and *kṣetrajña* refer respectively to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), based on the statements: "Now, this embodied witness is the *kṣetrajña*; these two are *sattva* and *kṣetrajña*," and because the word *sattva* is understood as an instrument in the phrase "by which one sees"—for *sattva* is indeed the internal organ—and because the other, the *kṣetrajña*, is the individual soul due to being the seer in dreams and so forth, this mantra, "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), refers to the internal organ and the individual soul, and not to the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

It is said: First of all, it is not possible to establish that this mantra has the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman) as its subject matter. This is because the individual soul and the supreme self are understood in the subsequent mantra, "A person is immersed in the same tree," which is recognized as having the same meaning as this mantra; for this mantra shares the same sense as that one. Indeed, their identity of meaning is perceived from the phrases, "They both embrace the same tree," and "A person is immersed in the same tree."

In the mantra "On the same tree," the term *puruṣa* refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) cannot be denoted by the word *puruṣa*, and because it would otherwise result in an inconsistency with the words "the one who grieves while deluded" and "the one who sees, free from sorrow. Furthermore, the other [being] is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because He is denoted by the word *īśa* (Lord) and because His knowledge of Himself is the cause of being free from sorrow. It is not only on the basis of the consistency with the subsequent mantra that the "Two Birds" mantra is understood to refer to the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

However, it is determined from that very same passage by the hearing of both the state of being an enjoyer and the state of not being an enjoyer, namely: "He eats the sweet fruit," and "The other, not eating. Just as the eyes, ears, and so forth possess the capacities of seeing and hearing, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) likewise cannot be an enjoyer precisely because it is an instrument (karaṇa). Furthermore, for the individual soul (jīva), the state of not eating is untenable during the very condition of being embraced by the body, which is denoted by the word "tree. If so, what is the meaning of the Paiṅgi-rahasya Brāhmaṇa? It is said: *sattva* refers to the bound soul (*baddhajīva*).

This is because the *Naighaṇṭuka* lexicon states, "In the case of substances, vital breaths, and efforts, *sattva* is not feminine; however, among living beings (*jantu*), it is masculine," from which its application to living beings is understood. A "living being" (*jantu*) is a conscious entity (*cetana*), as the lexicon reads: "A *prāṇin*, a conscious one, one subject to birth, a *jantu*, a creature, and one possessing a body [are synonyms]. This is further supported by the usage: "There is no being (*sattva*) on earth, in heaven, or among the gods that is free from these three qualities born of nature," and by modern usage such as: "As if to discipline the wicked beings (*duṣṭasattvān*) of the forest."

Furthermore, the word *kṣetrajña* here refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Just as the words *ākāśa* and *prāṇa*, though well-known in other senses, are established here as referring to the Supreme Self due to the impossibility of [other] meanings, so too is the case here. This is because the term is used in the passage beginning with "The thousand names of Viṣṇu for me," followed by "the *kṣetrajña* and the Imperishable (*akṣara*)"; and because the etymological meaning of the word—“one who knows the field” (*kṣetra*)—is fully applicable only to Him. As stated in the *Mokṣadharma*: "Then, being free from the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), they directly [perceive] the Supreme Self..."

"O best of the twice-born! they enter the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), whose nature is devoid of qualities"; "Know Vāsudeva, the abode of all, to be the Knower of the Field in truth"; "With the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose, he moves alone through the Fields (kṣetra), wandering at will according to his pleasure"; and "The Fields are the bodies, and the seeds are the good and evil [karmas]; he knows them, being of the nature of Yoga, and is therefore called the Knower of the Field"—from such usage [we understand this].

This is also evident from the usage: "That which causes this self to act is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field); and that which performs the actions is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self). In the phrase "by which one sees a dream," the instrumental case (*yena*) is used in the sense of a specific state (*itthambhāve*). It means that the Supreme Self, characterized by that [instrumental factor], is said to see the dream.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction in the statement, "He who possesses hardness," because possession of hardness occurs through the medium of the earth, while the state of being the dream-witness becomes an attribute of the Supreme Self through the medium of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Moreover, the term "embodied" (*śārīra*)—as in the passage, "This very one is his embodied self"—is appropriate when applied to the Supreme Self, whose body consists of all sentient and insentient entities distinct from Himself. And the designation "the witness" (*upadraṣṭṛ*), signifying unconditioned witnessing, is fitting only for that Omniscient One.
Therefore, the mantra beginning with "Two birds... refers to the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

Regarding the verse, "The two who drink the *ṛta*": in the act of drinking, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para*) are connected by way of the relationship between the instigator (*prayojaka*) and the one being instigated (*prayojya*). The suffix *-śatṛ* in the word "pibantau" (the two drinking) refers merely to the agent in general; it does not refer to a specific agent. Therefore, both the instigator and the one being instigated are included as specific agents without distinction. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such statements as "not eating" (*anaśnan*). Alternatively, it is a case of "non-exclusive indication" (*ajahallakṣaṇā*), like the expression "those with umbrellas are going. The *ṛta* is the fruit of well-performed action (*sukṛta*).

Alternatively, the construction is "in the world of good deeds" (*sukṛtasya loke*); in that case, "good deed" (*sukṛtam*) refers to *ṛta*. Its fruit is expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), because in the passage, "thus the fragrance of meritorious action wafts from afar," the word "untruth" (*anṛta*) is used as the antonym of "merit" in the phrase, "thus one should feel aversion toward oneself for untruth. "The cave" (*guhām*) means the cave of the heart. "In the highest" (*parame*) is an adjective qualifying the world; or it may be an adjective qualifying both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), with the change of gender being Vedic (*chāndasatvāt*).

Shadow and light represent the ignorant and the omniscient, as this is consistent with the meaning of the verse: "Two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord. These are the knowers of Brahman and the knowers of the supreme self (*adhyātma*). The "five fires" and those who have thrice performed the *Nāciketa* sacrifice are those devoted to specific ritual acts (*karma*); they declare: "The Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and those people who are knowers of the supreme self—they all proclaim the Great-Souled Kṛṣṇa to be the eternal Dharma."

The connection is as follows: "He who has entered within," etc., is stated for the sake of clarifying the verse beginning with "The two drinking the *ṛta*. It is not only by the natural sense of the scripture [that this is established]; he says "in this work too" to show that it is also seen in this very treatise. By the passage beginning with "He who is in all beings," his being the opposite of everything to be rejected (*heyapratyanīkatva*) and his being a mine of auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇaguṇākaratva*) are declared. That the individual soul (*jīva*) is the locus of what is to be rejected is stated by the passage beginning with "ignorance" (*avidyā*). The phrase "as the omnipresent one" is connected with the preceding [sūtra], "because of the designation of difference"; however, it is not a direct citation of a sūtra.

This is because no subject passage (*viṣayavākya*) has been cited for this preceding sūtra, and because the Purāṇic citations quoted require the statement of their status as reasons (*hetu*). Indeed, the status of the Śruti passage as a reason is indicated by the word "and" (*ca*). The subject passage for the two sūtras beginning with "ubhaye 'pi" is "ya ātmani"; the subject passage for the sūtra beginning with "adhikaṃ tu" is "prājñena. The meaning is that the determination of the matter is made in this way through these Śruti passages within the sūtras.

Thus, the possession of contradictory attributes by the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) has been established through the *Upaniṣads*, *Purāṇas*, and *Sūtras*. Now, keeping in mind such statements as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the author raises the objection that this [difference] might be explained otherwise, beginning with the words "Nor also... He refutes that with the words "Because of being the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*)," etc. Here, "fitness for being the locus of ignorance" is meant. The word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is intended to indicate all that is to be abandoned; the word "locus" (*āśrayatva*) refers to a relationship.

The fitness for that [bondage] consists in not being the locus of the absolute non-existence of connection with the avoidable (*heya*). The unfitness for that consists in being the locus of the absolute non-existence of connection with the avoidable. By the scriptural text, "The other does not perish," the unfitness of the Supreme Self for that is established. For even when there is proximity in space and time, the lack of contact with it is due to the absence of proximity by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Indeed, unfitness is precisely the absence of proximity by way of intrinsic nature, just as the sky lacks the capacity for being moistened, burned, and so forth.

Therefore, between that which is worthy of abandonment and that which is not worthy of it, even upon the removal of what is to be abandoned, identity of essential nature is not possible. The meaning is this: for one who was previously subject to restraint and later favored, even though the state of being subject to restraint has ceased, identity with the person who performed the restraint or the favor is not possible. The sense is that there can be no identity of essential nature between one released from prison and the king who was his restrainer.

Regarding this point, he cites a Purāṇic statement with the words "as it has been said. The word *yoga* here refers to identity (*aikya*). Otherwise, the refutation—"for one substance does not become another substance"—would be untenable. If it is argued that the connection with what follows is "this is false" (*mithyaitat*), meaning that the union of the Supreme Self and the individual self is the ultimate reality, whereas the claim that "one substance becomes another substance" is false—this is not so; for the non-attainment by one thing of the nature of another substance is indeed real.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of identity between the insentient and the sentient. This is because, by the word "is accepted" (*iṣyate*), the meaning stated in the first half of the verse is indicated as being the view of another (the opponent), just as in the expression: "The sacrificial rite, which is accomplished through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, is considered [by you]. Otherwise, the word "is accepted" would be redundant.

Furthermore, since this treatise is intended to refute positions other than the one about to be stated—namely, "But the ultimate truth, O King, let it be heard in brief"—it is not logical that the second half of this verse should be devoted to establishing the unity mentioned in its first half. For by passages such as "he renounces for the sake of dharma," the status of those respective objects as the ultimate truth is indeed being rejected.

It is also improper to resort to a meaning other than what is intended, even though this word *etad* (this) naturally refers to the subject at hand; for it is illogical to abandon its inherent sense when that sense is present. Furthermore, regarding the statement "another substance does not attain the nature of that substance," the meaning at that time is simply that "this is false. If that were the case, the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *yataḥ* would be violated. For the word *yataḥ* inherently functions as a causal particle; it does not, like the word *yat*, merely refer back to the body of the subject already under discussion.

If it were argued that "the identity of the Supreme Self and the individual self, though previously separate, is the ultimate reality," this would be false; for it is because one substance does not become the substance of another that [identity] is considered false. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to supply two instances of the word "iti" (thus) in the construction: "therefore, identity is the ultimate reality. And such a supply is not justified when the passage can be explained without supplying anything. If it were further argued that "it is accepted that the identity of the Supreme Self and the individual self, which were previously distinct, is the ultimate reality," this too is false; for it is because one substance does not become the substance of another that [identity] is considered false.

Therefore, it is not the case that there was no distinction between the Supreme Self and the individual self even previously; for this would entail the necessity of supplying (adhyāhāra) the words "previously [they were] separate due to delusion," which have not been heard in the text. And such an insertion is improper when the passage can be resolved without it. Furthermore, the sentence would require completion by supplying another unspoken clause, namely, "therefore, even previously there was no distinction"; and this is improper when the meaning can be established independently of such a supplement.

Therefore, the phrase "even before there was no difference" should not be supplied [by way of ellipsis]. If it is argued that this is because the text is intended solely to refute the position that the Supreme Self and the individual self were previously distinct and later became non-different, what is the purpose of that? If it is argued that it establishes their identity even previously, we say no; for once it has been stated that the conjunction of identity between two things that were previously separate is impossible, their difference remains established even afterwards. Therefore, the meaning that is established by the natural flow of the text itself must be accepted.

Now, intending to provide an interpretation of such statements as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" that is not in conflict with numerous other scriptural passages, [the author] speaks of the attainment of equality by the liberated one, using the words "of the liberated one. Thinking that the scripture concerning equality will be shown as being contrary in meaning to the scripture concerning oneness (*aikya*), he presents a Smṛti passage that is of the same nature as the explanatory statement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) under discussion, which serves to refute the meaning favored by the opponent. He cites this [Smṛti passage] with the words "this," and includes the phrase "even in creation" in order to clarify that it refers to the liberated one.

He says, "here too," to show that the perception of difference exists for the liberated one not only in other scriptures but here as well. "Here" means at the beginning of the exposition of the summary of Yoga within this section on Yoga. For it has been said: "By means of both summary and detail—what else could be done for you? The construction is as follows: the Supreme Brahman leads this meditator to its own state, transforming him through its own power, just as a magnet transforms iron through its own power. This transformation refers to the attainment of another state.

Fire is the attractor, according to the etymology "it attracts defects. For it will be stated later on: "Just as fire with its upward-flaming crest burns dry grass when aided by the wind, so does Viṣṇu, abiding in the mind, burn away all the impurities of yogis. And in the *Śrīviṣṇudharma*: "Just as gold becomes free from defect through contact with fire, [so does Viṣṇu remove] all the impurities of yogis. And in the *Śrīviṣṇudharma*: "Just as gold becomes free from defect through contact with fire."

That fire leads the iron to its own state—that is, to its own nature, which is freedom from defects; such is the meaning. This is the correct interpretation. Alternatively, the word *ātman* signifies "self" in the sense of excluding connection with anything else. Just as fire leads iron to its own state—its own nature, a form established by itself—in that same way; such is the meaning. Or again, the attractor—the magnet—leads the iron to its own state, meaning it causes the iron to perform its own function.

He causes his own self to imitate [the devotee], just as it is said: "When he stands, she stands; when he moves, she moves. If the magnet remains still, the iron remains still; if it runs, the iron runs after it. In this way, the Supreme Self, according to such scriptural passages as "moving about at will through forms of desire" and "he becomes one who has free movement in all things," causes the worshiper to imitate His own activity; the meaning is that He makes His own activity identical to that of the worshiper. Alternatively, the word *ātman* may refer to the self (*sva*) and denote the isolated essential nature (*niṣkṛṣṭasvarūpa*).

The Supreme Self leads the devotee (upāsaka) to its own nature (ātmabhāva); that is, it leads him to purity by means of freedom from connection with material nature (prakṛti), and leads him to isolation (kevalatā). The meaning is that just as a magnet, having extracted iron sunk in wood from that wood, leads it to isolation, so it is here. Alternatively, according to the rule "the root *bhū* is used in the Ātmanepada in the sense of attainment," the word *bhāva* signifies attainment.

It leads to the attainment of the Self, meaning that it leads to its own attainment just as a magnet leads iron to itself. The expression "leads to attainment" is a locution similar to "cooks the cooking of rice. It is logical that the individual soul (*jīva*) is subject to modification through the power of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); for the soul is capable of undergoing modifications in the form of the contraction and expansion of knowledge during bondage and liberation.

In this verse, he demonstrates the absence of identification (*tādātmya*) with the words "for not" (*na hi*). The statement that "the thing being drawn attains the nature of the attractor" is applicable to all the cases mentioned. When the intention is to provide the examples of fire and gold, the word "being drawn" (*ākṛṣyamāṇa*) refers to that which undergoes transformation (*vikārya*). Regarding the phrase "common to light" (*samāno jyotiṣā*): "light" (*jyotis*) is the Supreme Brahman, according to the scriptural passages, "Having reached the highest light" (*paraṃ jyotirupasampadya*) and "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven" (*atha yadataḥ paro divo jyotirdīpyate*). Regarding "Dramiḍa": it refers to the disembodied liberated one (*aśarīra-mukta*).

Because there is an absence of a body produced by karma, "attainment" (siddhi) means direct experience. The phrase "and the Śrutis show the scriptural texts regarding the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme in liberation" indicates that the Śrutis demonstrate this. The meaning is that he "attains" the Supreme, which is to say, he experiences it. He shows the sentence that serves as a commentary on this: "He enjoys" (so 'śnute). By the words "moving along after" (anusañcaran), difference is shown. By the words "He is indeed rasa" (raso vai saḥ), it is stated that there is equality in the form of bliss. He demonstrates the cessation of dissimilarity, which is conducive to supreme equality, with the passage beginning "Just as rivers... (yathā nadyaḥ).

In the illustrative example, the conjunction [of the rivers with the ocean] is based on the abandonment of their river-nature through the relinquishing of their distinct characteristics upon reaching the ocean. For the attainment of the Supreme Self is preceded by the abandonment of ordinary name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Yet, even so, there is no cessation of difference, since the relationship between object and agent is understood from the statement, "He approaches the Person. The text shows the attainment of equality with the words, "Then... (tadā).

Is it not the case that the phrase "he attains the supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam upaiti*) denotes the attainment of identity? For the word *sama* is a synonym for the word *samāna*, and like the word *samāna*, it is employed in the sense of identity. The use of the word *sama* in the sense of identity is observed in such expressions as "existing at the same time" (*samakālavartī*). Likewise, the word *samāna*, understood as a synonym for *sama*, is also employed in the sense of identity, as in "they both embrace the same tree" (*samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte*), and in the definition: "co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence [of two words] in a single referent."

For *sāmānādhikaraṇya* (grammatical coreferentiality) is indeed *ekādhikaraṇya* (the state of having a single substratum), as it is said [to mean] "in one object. And the word *sama* is a synonym for that. Although the word *sama* is also expressive of similarity (*sādṛśya*), nevertheless, the word *sāmya* occurring in the sentences concerning liberation refers to identity (*aikya*), because it has the same meaning as other scriptural passages such as "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and because of the mention of words such as *laya* (merging) and *sāyujya* (union), and because of the hearing of analogies such as the river and the ocean, or the pot-space and the great space.

The Smṛti statement, “they have attained similarity” (sādharmyamāgatāḥ), refers to the attainment of [divine] qualities; otherwise, it would be weak due to its contradiction with direct Śruti and its contradiction with many Śruti passages concerning identity of essential nature. Therefore, by this sentence, only the attainment of identity is taught. And the supremacy of that identity consists in being devoid of the further sprouting of the delusion of difference.

To this it is replied: here the word *sāmya* denotes only similarity (*sādṛśya*), and not identity (*aikya*); for even if identity were accepted as the primary meaning, it would lack natural fitness (*svārasya*). Indeed, the word *sama* is most commonly established in the sense of similarity alone. And in the absence of any exception (*apavāda*), it is untenable to accept a non-natural meaning. Furthermore, the reasons for an exception that you have stated will be refuted immediately below. Moreover, identity is not the primary meaning of words such as *samādhi*.

When there is an intention to express oneness (*ekatva*), as in "one pot" (*eko ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth, expressions such as "equal pot" (*samo ghaṭaḥ*) do not occur; for if the word were used in its primary sense, a usage independent of a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—just like the word "one"—would necessarily follow. As for the use of words such as "equal" (*sama*) in phrases like "co-referentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyam*) or "existing at the same time" (*samakālavartī*), that is intended in the sense of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*), not in the sense of oneness. Even in the case of commonality, the usage is not primary; since the usage can be accounted for otherwise, it is illogical to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*).

For instance, *sādhāraṇya* (commonality) consists in possessing a single form of relation toward multiple correlates (*pratiyogin*). For example, wealth is common to Devadatta and Yajñadatta by virtue of being related to them as a subordinate (*śeṣa*). And between those two, there exists a similarity by virtue of their standing as the subordinates (*śeṣin*) with respect to the wealth; the wealth is related to both of them. Similarly, with respect to "blueness" and "lotus-ness," the substance is common by virtue of being related to them as the substratum (*ādhāra*). And between those two, there exists a similarity by virtue of their standing as the superstrates (*ādheya*) with respect to the substance.

The substance is related to those two. Likewise, time—which is related to both through conjunction or through the relation of the delimited and the delimiting—is common to them; thus, there is a similarity between the two insofar as they possess a connection with that same time. Time is related to both of them. Therefore, words such as *sama* (equal), *samāna* (common), and so forth, apply to substances, time, and the like by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) because of their being related to mutually similar objects; they do not apply in a primary sense.

Therefore, since there is no usage [of the term] in the sense of identity, "sameness" (*samatva*) is not the primary meaning of the word *sama*. When a primary meaning is possible, it is not tenable to accept a figurative meaning; thus, the word *sāmya* denotes only similarity (*sādṛśya*). Furthermore, the justification for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) regarding the liberated self will be stated immediately thereafter in the commentary.

What was stated—that non-difference (abheda) in liberation is expressed by the word *sāyujya*—is incorrect; for the word *sāyujya* denotes the possession of identical attributes (*samānaguṇayoga*). The word *yuk* [in *sāyujya*] means "that which is joined" (*yujyate*), and thus refers to an attribute (*guṇa*). For an attribute is indeed connected to its substratum (*dharmī*). One who possesses identical attributes is *sayuk*; the state of being such is *sāyujya*. This is the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).

Furthermore, because it is incompatible with the preparatory practice (*prayoga*), union (*sāyujya*) does not mean oneness. For the scripture declares the attainment of union with many deities for a single person: "He attains union, identity of power, and residence in the same world as these very deities. Indeed, it is impossible for a single, partless, and indivisible Self to achieve oneness with many deities.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because [the states] occur sequentially, then when one who has become one with fire attains union (*sāyujya*) with Varuṇa, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of "fire-ness" would be discarded, and thus the divinity of fire would cease to exist. If the limiting adjunct of fire-ness remains, the attainment of oneness with Varuṇa is impossible; for the attainment of oneness consists in the discarding of the difference created by limiting adjuncts, rather than the production of an oneness that did not previously exist.

If it is argued that [the soul] attains union with Varuṇa while remaining distinct from him even though it was previously situated in fire, then such a state of being distinct for that which has become one must arise from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). These adjuncts consist of the body, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth. Since the connection with these cannot be without a cause—lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—a cause must be stated.

If it is argued that karma alone is the cause, then at the stage of attaining union (*sāyujya*) with fire, has that karma perished or not? If it has perished, then because there is no further arising of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is impossible for there to be a separation from fire; and since the adjunct of "fire-ness" has not been abandoned, the attainment of union with Varuṇa—which consists in the abandonment of the previous adjunct—cannot occur even gradually. If, on the other hand, it has not perished, then because the adjunct produced by it has also not perished, the possibility of attaining identity with fire is precluded; for the difference caused by adjuncts is opposed to the attainment of identity, which consists in the abandonment of those very adjuncts.

If it is argued that even though that karma is not destroyed, it does not produce a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that causes differentiation at the time of attaining union with fire—because the bodily manifestation of karmas is restricted to specific times—even so, for the individual soul (*jīva*) embraced by those specific karmas, that very karma serves as the differentiator from the fire which is not so embraced; thus, the attainment of identity with fire is not logically tenable.

Furthermore, just as there is no possibility of the non-arising or eternity of a jar that has become one with or separate from the earth, so too there is no possibility of the non-arising or eternity of a soul that has become one with or separate from fire; therefore, liberation through union (*sāyujya*) with fire and the like is possible only while difference remains.

Furthermore, because of its association with "residing in the same world" (*samānalokatā*), "union" (*sāyujya*) does not mean identity; for it is impossible for one thing to reside in the same world as itself. Therefore, just like "residing in the same world," union is established only when difference is already proven. If it is argued that there is no contradiction between the two because the attainment of union occurs after attaining residence in the same world, rather than simultaneously—therefore they are not mutually exclusive—we say no, because in the scriptural passage, "Union, equality of status, and residence in the same world," union is mentioned first. If it is argued that the order of recitation is set aside by the order of meaning, we say no; [because...]

Because the meaning presented by the power of the individual word-components conforms to the order of recitation, and because there is no reason to assume a different meaning; for if, in order to override the order of recitation, one were to assume a conventional (*rūḍhi*) power of the word *sāyujya* referring to the sense of "attaining identity," then there would be a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the determination that *sāyujya* means attaining identity would depend upon the overriding of the order of recitation, and the overriding of the order of recitation would depend upon the determination that *sāyujya* means attaining identity.

If it is argued that the previously cited statement is set aside by the sequence [of the injunction] based on the sentence, "He attains the same world and union with these very [deities]," we say no; for since the conventional power [of the word] has not been established as referring to a contradictory meaning, no contradiction is perceived.

Furthermore, because of the greater authority of numerous statements such as, "These are indeed the names of Agni; he attains union with and residence in the same world as Agni... he attains union with and residence in the same world as Vāyu, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, and Brahmā," the sequence you have proposed must be set aside. Moreover, statements such as, "He attains residence in the same world and union with these very [deities]; he attains union with and residence in the same world as Agni," are in the nature of *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) supplementary to ritual injunctions (*karmavidhi*).

Furthermore, because it is the fruit of karma, union (*sāyujya*) with deities such as Agni and Āditya is non-eternal. Therefore, since separation from Agni and the others is inevitable once the fruits of karma have been exhausted for those who attained union with them—and since you yourself accept that the distinction between individual souls (*jīva-bheda*) persists until liberation—distinction must necessarily remain even during the state of union with Agni and the rest. If it is argued that those who have attained union with Agni and the others become separate from them again due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the answer has already been given.

Nor should it be said that the statement regarding union (*sāyujya*) with Agni and others is to be disregarded because it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*); for the Vedāntins accept that explanatory passages possess authority regarding their manifest meaning. Therefore, *sāyujya* is not identity, but rather the possession of identical attributes. Furthermore, "merging" (*laya*) does not mean identity of essential nature, because the word "merging" does not have that as its primary meaning. The determination of word-meanings must be established in accordance with actual usage. Indeed, the term "merging" is employed even in the contexts of the daily, occasional, and great cosmic dissolutions (*mahāpralaya*); yet in those cases, there is no attainment of identity of essential nature. This is certainly not the case in the daily dissolution, such as [the transition between] heaven and hell.

Nor [is it possible] according to the treatises on coming and going (*gamanāgamanasāstra*); nor even according to the occasional (*naimittika*) dissolution, because we understand that those such as Nārada who were dissolved in a previous *kalpa* are born again precisely as those possessing recognition of their prior births. It is understood from the Purāṇas that Nārada recounted here in this *kalpa* the account of his own birth and other events from the previous *kalpa*. Nor [is it possible] at the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); for, in order to avoid [the charge of] partiality and cruelty, one must admit that the individual souls (*jīva*), their plurality, and their karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*) exist at that time.

Likewise, by the venerable Parāśara himself, who stated: "The *prakṛti* which I have described, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, and the *puruṣa*—both of these dissolve into the Supreme Self"—and further: "Violence and non-violence, gentleness and cruelty, dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood..."

"Those who are permeated by that [state] attain it; therefore, that is what pleases them," "Since the powers of those to be created have indeed become the primary cause," and "Whatever actions they had undertaken prior to creation"—by such passages, the plurality of individual souls (jīvas) accompanied by their latent impressions (vāsanās) and karma at that time is demonstrated. For this very reason, the abandonment of difference is not the meaning of the word *laya* (dissolution). Nor is it appropriate to claim a discrepancy in meaning between the word *pralaya* used here and the word *pralaya* used in the context of primordial reabsorption (*prākṛta-pratisañcara*) or liberation (*mokṣa*).

For otherwise, one would be forced to accept either the postulation of a distinction in the power [of the term] or its non-primary (metaphorical) sense. Nor can it be argued that even in those cases, such as the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the word "dissolution" (*laya*) is used in a non-primary sense; for it is more appropriate to assume a non-primary sense for the word "dissolution" when applied specifically to liberation alone, rather than assuming a non-primary sense across many different referents. Therefore, a meaning consistent with all usages must be accepted. Consequently, *laya* is the conjunction with a substance—which possesses the property of being a cause—acting as the point of departure (*apādāna*) by means of abandoning a dissimilar state.

Therefore, unity is not the meaning of the word "merger" (*laya*). Furthermore, the presentation of examples such as the space within a jar is based on the absence of any difference caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); for even the principles (*tattva*) such as space possess parts. Indeed, the Vedāntins themselves accept that these possess distinct spatial divisions, as evidenced by their doctrine of the fivefold compounding (*pañcīkaraṇa*). Consequently, in the scriptural passages concerning liberation, the identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*) is nowhere perceived. The point that there is no scriptural passage whatsoever concerning the attainment of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) state will be demonstrated immediately hereafter.

Therefore, the claim that—"Because the recollection of similarity (*sādharmyasmaraṇa*) has for its object the attainment of [the Lord] with qualities (*saguṇa*), it does not have supreme liberation (*paramamokṣa*) as its object; otherwise, there would follow the weakness of the Smṛti due to its contradiction with Śruti, which has the attainment of the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) as its object"—is also poorly argued. Consequently, in the passage beginning "When the seer," the word "equality" (*sāmya*) refers to similarity. The intended meaning of the word "supreme" (*parama*) is the boundlessness of that specific form by which the equality is established. Thus, this sentence teaches supreme liberation, which consists in the attainment of the Supreme Brahman, characterized precisely by the reaching of equality with It.

Now, in response to the doubt that these scriptural passages declare the attainment of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahma*) for one who meditates on its attributes, but not the attainment of the supreme Brahman (*parabrahma*) for the knower of the supreme Brahman, he says: "In the higher knowledges" (*paravidyāsu*). This means "in the knowledges of the supreme Brahman. It further means "in all [such] knowledges—such as the *dahara-vidyā*, the *sat-vidyā*, and others—which have been described as having either the qualified or the unqualified Brahman as their object."

From the natural sense of the aphorism whose subject matter is the passage concerning higher knowledge, namely, "He whose qualities are invisibility and so forth," it is understood that this [knowledge] has the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman as its object. The aphorism, "Bliss and other [qualities belong to the Principal]," is cited to show that the object of meditation is qualified. The aphorism, "There is an option, because the fruit is not distinguished," is employed to show that the goal to be attained is qualified.

The meaning is as follows: having stated that those passages intended by the opponent to have the qualityless (nirguṇa) Brahman as their object—such as "Truth, Knowledge," and "Bliss is Brahman"—actually have as their object Brahman as qualified by attributes such as bliss, and having also stated that these attributes follow through all meditations (vidyās), it was further declared that there is an option (vikalpa) among the meditations, since even a single meditation is sufficient for the attainment of the fruit.

Therefore, since the objects intended in passages such as those concerning *sadvidyā* and *dahara-vidyā*—which are considered to have as their subject the Nirguṇa Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa*)—are both the object of worship and the fruit of attainment as possessing attributes, the attainment of the Nirguṇa is devoid of any basis in valid means of knowledge apart from the attainment of the Saguna. Consequently, it is not tenable for those who hold that the scriptures are intent on difference (*bheda*) to claim that [the texts] regarding liberation are established otherwise, because there is no disparity in what is attained.

He shows the intention of the author of the Sūtras by means of the phrase "vākya" (the statement). The phrase "yuktaṃ tadguṇakopāsanāt" (it is logical because of meditation on that which possesses those qualities) means that the object to be attained must indeed be endowed with those qualities; why? Because of meditation on that which possesses those qualities—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the option regarding the meditations (*vidyāvikalpa*) should be examined in that very same context. As for the term "saccitaḥ," it refers to one established in the knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*). To the question, "In that case, what is the meaning of the scriptural texts concerning non-difference in liberation? he says: "brahma... (Brahman...).

Regarding the statement, "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself," it will be explained later how this sentence is intended to establish that the nature of the knower under discussion manifests as culminating in Brahman. Here, however, a different meaning is stated: the scriptural passage "freed from name and form" is cited to make known the abandonment of ordinary name and form; the phrase "stainless" (nirañjana) is employed for the purpose of establishing equality.

The statement "the supreme light" (*paraṃ jyotiḥ*) serves to indicate that this very sameness is inherent. To the objection that [if this were so] it would be secondary (*amukhyatva*), he replies: "If there is identity of mode. This example is illustrative of such cases as "this is that same rice" (*so'yaṃ vrīhiḥ*). Usage such as, "Just as the various seasonal signs are seen to recur in their respective turns throughout the seasons, so too do those very same things appear at the beginnings of the Yugas," should be observed in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts.

Even when there is identity of mode in the example, the conventional usage of "that-ness" (tattā) is primary yet lacks natural plausibility (*asvārasya*); it lacks natural plausibility because, in the case of a cow previously seen, the individual aspect (*vyakti-aṃśa*) has been abandoned; whereas it is primary because the generic aspect (*jāti-aṃśa*) possesses unity characterized by extreme similarity (*sausādṛśya*).

In the case of the primary application (*dārṣṭāntika*), however, just as in the word "cowherd station on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), because there is no total abandonment of the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and because—unlike the term "Supreme Self"—there is an absence of the fullness of the ground for its application, it refers to the liberated self (*muktātman*) which possesses a portion of that ground for application; with this intention, it is said to be "primary" (*mukhya*) itself. The meaning is that it is not "entirely non-primary" (*atyantāmukhya*), unlike the word "Gaṅgā" when used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*).

For even though the liberated one possesses unlimited knowledge and bliss, he lacks both the greatness of qualities (guṇabṛhattva) conducive to being the cause of the world and the greatness of essential nature (svarūpabṛhattva). The example "this is that cow" is given because, despite identity of form, the application of the term "that-ness" (tattā) would otherwise be entirely figurative.

He says "even here" (*atrāpi*) to show that the apprehension of difference exists not only at the beginning of the section on the collection of yoga, but also in the preceding verses that follow closely thereafter. Alternatively, the meaning is that it exists not only in other sections concerning liberated beings, but also in this very section. In this verse, the phrase "in the same way" (*tathaiva*) is employed for the purpose of teaching the similarity with Brahman. The explanation of "in the same way" is "like the Supreme Brahman," and so forth. He explains the term "all mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) completely destroyed" as "the mental impression of karma."

In the reading *parabrahmavat prakṣīṇāśeṣakarmabhāvanaḥ*, the word *karman* refers generally to everything that is to be performed, including rituals such as sacrifices (*yāga*) as well as meditative worship (*upāsana*). In that case, the word *bhāva* in the verse “the threefold cultivation of dispositions” (*trividhā bhāvabhāvanā*) is explained by the word *karman*. The meaning here is this: since the knowledge of the supreme Brahman to be attained brings about its attainment, even the pure essential nature (*svarūpa*) is what is to be attained; therefore, that [pure nature] is to be contemplated.

And this is the meaning of the section [sūtra]: "The distinction [is established] because [the state of bondage] occurs when that [ignorance] is present. In that context, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the nature of the bound soul (*baddha-svarūpa*) is what should be investigated, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established that the nature of the liberated soul (*mukta-svarūpa*) is what should be investigated. To make known that this verse belongs to the same thematic section, the following verse, beginning with "the knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), is also explained.

As long as one remains in the state of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field), one is an *upāsaka* (meditator) whose instrument (*karaṇa*) is knowledge. This instrumental knowledge, having accomplished the effect that is liberation, should then cease; the meaning is that it should not cease prior to liberation. For the cessation of meditation is not something to be enjoined for one who is already liberated; therefore, the sense is that its necessity for performance lasts until liberation.

The verse beginning with *tadbhāvabhāvam* is explained for the purpose of making known the attainment of equality with Brahman through the term *tadbhāvabhāva*, and also to dispel the suspicion that there might be a word-break (*padaccheda*) as *jñāne* in the phrase *vibhedajanake'jñāne*. In the verse *tadbhāva...*, the term *tadbhāva* is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) based on a comparison. He says *tadbhāva* in order to explain the words *tat* and *bhāva* contained within the term *tadbhāva*; the word *tadbhāva* found in the commentary is not itself a *bahuvrīhi*.

However, that [compound] is a *tatpuruṣa*; for when a compound is intended to be explained, a word is taken in its specific form as a *bahuvrīhi*. Since it is the mere word "bhāva" following the word "tat" that is intended to be explained, the word is not taken in its specific form as a *bahuvrīhi*. The meaning is that by the word "tat," Brahman is denoted, and by the first word "bhāva," intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is denoted. [As the lexicon states: "The word *bhāva* [is used] in the senses of play, action, gesture, prosperity, intention, and living beings."

The lexicographers [Naighaṇṭukas] state: "In the existence of mere things, there are *ātman* and *yonisvabhāva*. Alternatively, the word *tadbhāva* found in the commentary is also qualified as a *bahuvrīhi*: "its nature" (*tadbhāva*) means the nature (*bhāva*) of Brahman, that is, its own-nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the term *tadbhāva*, the meaning is that the nature (*bhāva*) understood as being related to Brahman—which is denoted by the word *tat*—is the own-nature (*svabhāva*). Or else, even in the verse, the word *tadbhāva* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound; the second word *bhāva* denotes existence (*sattā*). He states the exclusion [of other meanings] with the words "but not... (*na tu*).

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the presence of that" (*tadbhāva*). He states another reason: "And because of the contradiction with the meaning previously stated. "Contradiction of meaning" refers to the opposition between being the opposite of what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and being worthy of abandonment. Thus, through both an examination of the words and an examination of the meaning, it has been established that the word *bhāva* denotes "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*). And he says "that which... (*yad*), referring to the state of having all mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) completely destroyed, which was mentioned in the preceding verse as denoted by the word "intrinsic nature. By the force of the pronoun "that" (*tat*), he draws in the subject from the previous verse and explains it as: "When it is thus... (*yadaivam*).

In the phrase "non-different" (*abhedī*), he analyzes the word *bheda* by separating it from the negative particle (*nañ*) in order to explain its meaning, stating that "he becomes devoid of difference. Alternatively, the sense is that "he becomes devoid of difference," meaning he does not possess identity [with those distinctions]. Otherwise, the subsequent statement, "and his difference is caused by ignorance," would not be consistent. In response to the doubt as to how there can be an absence of distinctions such as "god" and so forth, he explains the passage beginning with "and his difference... by means of the phrase "by having the single form of knowledge" (*jñānaikākāratayā*).

Because the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the subject under discussion in the phrase "he becomes non-different from the Supreme Self," and because the ablative case is intended in the expression "from the Self, [that is] Brahman," it is stated that "there is difference from that. Since the difference between Brahman and the liberated soul (*muktātman*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in another form, and since the specific kind of difference to be refuted is established by other scriptural statements, it is stated that "difference consists of the forms of the gods and so forth. By the word "form of karma" (*karmarūpa*), the word "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is explained.

The meaning is that the etymological derivation is "that which opposes knowledge. For the Śruti says, "Having crossed over death by means of ignorance (avidyā). Here too, it is recited: "Ignorance is other than what is designated as karma. In response to the doubt, "What follows from that regarding the absence of difference? the author states, "And its difference would be caused by ignorance," thereby clarifying the absence of the cause—which is established by implication—and thus demonstrating the absence of the effect. This is expressed by the words "But that... (sa tu).

He provides the authoritative proof for the fact that "differentiation" consists of forms such as gods and the like, and that the word "ignorance" (ajñāna) refers to *karman*, stating: "As it has been said. This verse occurs in the *Ādibharata-carita*. In that context, the absence of external differentiation—such as body, senses, and so forth—from the Self was previously stated by the words beginning with "white, blue, etc. In this verse, it is further stated that there is no internal differentiation either, such as intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure, pain, or desire. Regarding the phrase "of a single nature": "action-activity" (*karmavṛtti*) means that action itself is the activity. Action is twofold: external and internal.

Internal action is the cause of the soul’s inclination toward itself; external action is the cause of its inclination toward external objects. Alternatively, "external" refers to that which is non-natural (āgantuka); that alone constitutes the veil (*vṛti*). By means of that [veil], a distinction within the single essential nature is produced. The meaning is that external action, through the medium of the body, creates an internal distinction within the soul whose nature is one. When the distinctions of the bodies of gods and others—which serve as the doorways—have perished, and when the distinction within the single essential nature has perished, there is no longer any internal distinction.

Or rather, how is it that when the distinctions such as "god" and so forth have perished, there is the destruction of the internal distinctions caused by the operation of karma? To this he says: "For he is without obscuration. This means that the Self, from which the distinctions of god and so forth have ceased, is indeed free from the obscuration of karma. Alternatively, "karmic operation" refers to the body produced by karma, such as those of gods and others; the "internal distinction" is that which arises from connection with such [bodies]. When the distinctions of god and so forth have been destroyed, that [distinction] no longer exists.

To the question of how there can be no difference caused by another factor—namely, the activity generated by karma—once the distinctions such as being a god and so forth have been destroyed, he says: "For that [Self] is unobscured. The meaning is that the activity produced by karma takes the form of the various bodies of gods and others. This very point has already been stated in the sense that "the distinction of this [Self] would be caused by ignorance," in the verse beginning with "The generator of distinctions. By this verse, the meaning of the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Non-return, on account of the word" (Anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt) is expressed.

It is stated: "Who will bring about the return of the self, which has been lost from the Supreme Brahman, to its differentiation as gods and so forth? He explains the word *vibheda* as "various kinds of differentiation. To provide further evidence for the fact that this differentiation takes the form of gods and so forth, he says, "as it has been said. [The phrase] "based on false knowledge" (*mithyājñānanibandhana*) means that false knowledge is the delusive cognition regarding the Self; the meaning is that, by means of karma, that [false knowledge] is the cause of the successive differentiations as gods and so forth.

The second half of this verse is: "Likewise, O King, [the states] called gods, animals, humans, and hell-beings. He states the meaning of the sentence of the verse to be explained with the words "in the Self" (*ātmani*). The term "from the Supreme" (*parasmāt*) is used to indicate that the word *brahmaṇaḥ* ends in the ablative case. It is improper for both words to be in the genitive case in a non-co-referential (vaiyadhikaraṇya) construction, because there is no use of the conjunction *ca*; furthermore, in the immediately preceding verse, it was stated that "one becomes non-different from the Supreme Self," where the Supreme Self is mentioned as the correlate (*pratiyogitayā*).

For this very reason, it is also incorrect for [the word] to have a genitive case ending in grammatical apposition; furthermore, this would contradict the meaning previously elaborated. If it is argued that the ablative and genitive endings might be reversed, we say no; for then even the Supreme Brahman would incur the possibility of being subject to abandonment, which would entail the undesirable consequence of its being non-inherent (svābhāvika). Therefore, it is stated: "from the Supreme Brahman.
