The word *asan* is a synonym for *paramārtha* (the ultimate reality), for it has been stated in this very context: "The imperishable is the ultimate reality"; thus, the meaning here is "that which is not transitory" (*anitya*).

By this, the distinction from that which is eternal by nature is excluded. Impermanence means being occasional. Because of impermanence, the distinctions among gods and others depend upon a cause. Who will produce that? No one at all. This means that due to the absence of a cause—that is, the absence of karma as a cause—who could do so? Not only in the context of a single object is the word *ajñāna* used in the sense of *karman*, as seen in the usage of the words *ajñāna* and *karman* in the passages: "born from the activity of external karma" (*bāhyakarmavṛttiprajaḥ*) and "it would be produced by ignorance" (*ajñānakṛto bhavet*).

And in this context, he states that it is explicitly mentioned [in the scripture]: "For it has been stated right here that 'ignorance is something other than what is designated as karma. The meaning of the verse is that the distinction of the Self, which is adventitious (*aupādhika*), perishes upon the removal of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Alternatively, the meaning is: "In the absence of a limiting adjunct, who could produce a distinction that does not exist? This verse is utterly inconsistent with the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*); for in the phrase "the producer of distinction," the word *janaka* (producer) naturally refers to one who brings something into existence, rather than to a cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

The fact that the word *ajñāna* (ignorance) refers to the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) is neither established by common usage nor by scripture. Indeed, its derivation as denoting "action" has been demonstrated in this very treatise. Furthermore, the word *nāśa* (destruction) having the sense of "sublation" (*bādha*) is secondary. Moreover, the phrase "non-existent" (*asantam*) is useless, as there is nothing to be excluded from it; for we do not admit the existence of a difference within what is real. For that phrase would be meaningful only if such a difference were admitted. Finally, the word "will produce" (*kariṣyati*) is also strained, as it does not denote superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Now, he explains the statement from the *Bhagavadgītā* cited by the opponent as being intended to establish non-duality (*advaita*) with the words, "And also the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajñaṃ cāpi*). He demonstrates the internal contradiction between the preceding and following passages regarding the meaning favored by the opponent with the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*). Not only that, but because of the teaching of difference in the passage, "But the Supreme Person is another," there is an absence of intent toward identity of essential nature, as that would contradict such [teachings].

He states that the status of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*), which establishes the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is also explicitly mentioned by saying "the inner ruler. In the passage, "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings," the word *bhūta* refers to the body extending up to the self (*ātman*), as is understood from the second half of that verse, "causing all beings to wander," and also from such usages as "one should not harm any beings."

Even in the passage, "And I am seated in the heart of all," the fact that the word "all" extends up to the Self is understood from the statement, "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. The phrase "in the region of the heart" means "in the Self residing in the region of the heart"; thus, "And I am in the heart of all" is to be understood in the same way. Furthermore, regarding the statement, "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa," he explains that the word "I" has as its purport the state of being the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). Why is this so? To this he says: "For the word 'being'... The sense is that it is because of the identity of meaning with the word "all" shown previously.

With the intention that this negative indication, "There is nothing," which follows as a supplement to the positive statement that all things have the Blessed Lord as their essence, is indeed consistent with that [positive statement], he says, "Since [it is] for all. The sense is that the word *avinābhāva* denotes a necessary relation (*saṃbandhaniyama*). He states another reason with the words "the Blessed Lord," etc. Since the discourse begins with "This glory and this yoga," it is understood that the subject matter is the manifestation of His powers (*vibhūti*). Therefore, the meaning is that the conclusion is indeed consistent with the introduction.

The sense is that it is not possible to negate that very thing after having first established its nature as a manifestation (*vibhūti*). He shows that the subject matter of this section concerns manifestations with the words "whatever" (*yadyat*). "Possessing manifestations" means having things under one's control. "Prosperous" (*śrīmat*) means endowed with an abundance of objects of enjoyment. "Powerful" (*ūrjita*) means strong; it is said in the context of the undertaking of auspicious qualities. "Splendor" (*tejas*) is the capacity to overcome others, which is synonymous with authoritative command (*praśāsana*). The meaning is that [the power] arising from a portion of splendor consists of the capacity for restraint and is dependent upon the flow of the Lord’s command.

He concludes that the treatise does not have as its purport the meaning stated by others with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). "Therefore" means by the logical arguments established starting from the interpretation of the Śruti. "Error" (*bhrāntatva*) means being established through delusion. In response to the doubt that, under the view that the world and Brahman are one substance, it would follow that Brahman possesses attributes and that the world is real, he says "nor also" (*nāpi*) in order to dispel that. The notion of insentient properties in sentient beings, and the notion of independence in things that are dependent on another, is error.

However, with the intention that there is no cognition of a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*), it was stated that "there is no negation of a difference in essential nature. Alternatively, addressing the proponent of falsity (*mṛṣāvādin*) himself, he states with the words "nor" (*nāpi*) that there is no negation of a difference in essential nature between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*); the mention of the insentient material cause (*acid-upādāna*) serves as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Now, in order to refute ignorance (*avidyā*), he restates the point asserted by the opponent regarding its nature: "As for that which... He addresses the question of how error can arise in that which is devoid of distinctions with the words: "...due to defects (*doṣa*). If there were a defect distinct from Brahman, the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost; to this he replies: "And the defect... He demonstrates the scriptural and traditional arguments cited by the opponent on this point with the words: "By untruth (*anṛtena*). He establishes that [ignorance] is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent with the words: "But that..."

Because error and sublation would be impossible—meaning that being the object of error and being the object of sublation would be untenable—the meaning is that existence, non-existence, and indefinability [of the world] follow from the otherwise inexplicability of valid cognition, error, and sublation. The term "knower of reality" (tattvavit) is used to show that this is not the position of others, just as [the Lord said], "Thus has the true nature of existence been declared by Me to you."

He refutes [the opponent's position], saying "that is incorrect. Intending to refute it through the impossibility of a locus (*āśrayānupapatti*), the impossibility of concealment (*tirodhānānupapatti*), the impossibility of its own nature (*svarūpānupapatti*), the impossibility of its being indeterminable (*anirvacanīyatvānupapatti*), the impossibility of its means of proof (*pramāṇānupapatti*), and the impossibility of its cessation (*nivṛttyanupapatti*), he first states the impossibility of a locus, beginning with "For that... What does it rest upon? The meaning is: upon nothing at all. With the intention of raising the dilemma—whether it rests upon the individual soul (*jīva*) or upon Brahman—he says, "Not, first of all..."

The meaning is that there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the establishment of the individual soul (*jīva*) depends on the establishment of ignorance (*avidyā*), and the establishment of ignorance depends on the establishment of the individual soul. The refutation of the doctrine of ignorance residing in the individual soul will be explained in detail later; here, it is only a summary. Now, he refutes the position that [ignorance] resides in Brahman with the words "Nor also" (*nāpi*). To the question "How is there opposition? he says: "For she (ignorance)... Because ignorance regarding Brahman is sublated by the manifestation of That (Brahman), there is opposition.

In this context, he cites the verses spoken by Nāthamuni, beginning with "jñānarūpam" (having the nature of knowledge). What is intended here is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*). He states the reason for its being removable by knowledge (*jñānanivartyatva*) with the phrase "mṛṣātmakam" (consisting of falsehood). Having restated the position that the knowledge of the essential nature (*svarūpajñāna*) is not the opponent of ignorance (*ajñāna*), but rather only valid instrumental knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*), he refutes it with the word "jñānam. The meaning is: because, like Brahman, it is luminous, that is, its luminosity is not distinct from its own essential nature.

For even when a white, shining object has been perceived, and it has been understood hundreds of times through authoritative statements (*āptavākya*) and other means that "this is a white, shining object," the cessation of error does not occur. He states another objection with the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*). To the question "What follows from that?", he replies with the word "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). The meaning of the first verse among these verses was previously stated by the commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) in the passage ending with "that which is intended to be sublated by knowledge. He explains the second verse with the words "the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpa*).

The meaning is: "while being the manifestation of the nature of Brahman" and "while being a cognition whose object is its own nature. The phrase "due to the non-apprehension of any distinction" means "due to the absence of any difference in the object. How is there a non-apprehension of distinction? If it is argued that "there is the distinction of being produced by a means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)," what of it? For indeed, no difference in the object exists. Is there a difference in the object between the cognition that constitutes the essential nature and the cognition that effects cessation? Does such a difference exist, or not? If it exists, then there is the state of having distinctions (saviśeṣatva). If it does not, then the essential nature itself must be the cause of cessation.

Knowledge produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) might either not be a remover [of error], like the knowledge whose object is a bright thing situated in front; or, being produced by a means of valid cognition, it may lack the capacity to remove [error], because the knowledge produced by the sentence "This is a white, bright substance" lacks the power to remove [the erroneous cognition]. Therefore, the capacity to remove [error] is conditioned by having as its object a form distinct from that which accompanies the delusion.

But is it not observed that, even in the absence of a difference in their objects, one cognition is not opposed to error while another is opposed to error—as seen in the case of recognition (*abhijñā*) and re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*)? For instance, although the recognition "This is that same Devadatta" has the same object [as the previous perception], the error of perceiving two persons—such as "He is different from the one seen before"—is still observed.

In response to the objection that—even though the recognition "This is that same Devadatta" has as its object the identity of Devadatta, it is observed to be incompatible with duality; therefore, despite the lack of difference in their objects, it is logical for a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) to sublate an error—the author says: "This has been stated. The word "nature" (*svabhāva*) is used to show that while there exists a nature such as truthfulness and cognitivity, this [nature] is not distinct from the essential form (*svarūpa*) itself. By this, the difference in the objects of immediate perception (*abhijñā*) and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is also indicated.

In a single act of direct perception (*abhijñā*), it is understood that a single subject (*dharmin*) is related to one place and one time, but not that it is related to two times and two places. That [latter], however, is understood through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). The cognition of being related to one place and one time is not incompatible with duality. Indeed, the fact that a single subject is related to two times and two places constitutes unity; since this [unity] is incompatible with duality, its apprehension dispels the error of duality.
Therefore, it follows that even in that case, there exists a disparity between the objects [of the two cognitions].

Now, he states "moreover" (*kiñca*) to show that the meaning of the third verse culminates in a refutation [of the opponent's position]. Being a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñānatva*) is pervaded by being a remover [of error] (*nivartakatva*). Therefore, because the nature of Brahman, which serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), lacks the status of being a valid cognition, it does not have the capacity to remove error. In response to the doubt that—since it is the substratum like mother-of-pearl and the like—the nature of Brahman is not opposed to error and thus requires another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), he says: "But mother-of-pearl and the like... (*śuktayādayastu*).

Being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) is pervaded by being the object of another cognition. Therefore, by the cessation of the pervader, there is the cessation of being the substratum; thus, even when the nature of Brahman flashes forth as the substratum itself, it would require another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But this is not so. For it is precisely because of its insentience (*jaḍatva*) that objects such as mother-of-pearl require another means of knowledge even when their own nature flashes forth, not because they are substrata. Consequently, being the substratum is a conditioned attribute (*sopādhika*).

If it is argued that here, because [the Self] is non-inert (*ajaḍa*), there is no dependence on another means of knowledge for the manifestation of its own nature, then [we reply]: in that case, it is precisely because of inertness that the shell and so forth require another cognition for the cessation of error, not because they are the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, that [error regarding the shell] is *sopādhika* (conditioned). Thus, the intention is that in the case of the non-inert [Self], there would be no dependence on another means of knowledge, nor would there be [dependence] for the cessation of error. In the phrase "but the shell and so forth," the word "but" (*tu*) is intended to distinguish the Brahman from the shell and other such objects.

For those who maintain non-duality (*advaitin*), there are indeed two possible positions: either that valid knowledge regarding Brahman removes delusion, or that knowledge regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) removes delusion. Of these, the first position has been refuted. Now, in order to refute the second position, he raises an objection with the words "Now it might be argued" (*athocyeta*). He refutes it with the words beginning with "No" (*na*). Regarding the phrase "this": [the opponent asks] how can the reality of the phenomenal world be called ignorance (*ajñāna*)? For ignorance is that which obstructs knowledge.

Indeed, the reality of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) does not obstruct anyone’s knowledge. True; it is the concealing ignorance (*āvaraṇa-ajñāna*) that is of such a nature. However, this was stated according to the opponent's own admission, namely that the reality of phenomenal manifestation and its appearance constitute the projecting ignorance (*vikṣepa-rūpa-ajñāna*). He refutes the first position with the words "not that" (*atad*). To the question, "How is it that because it does not have that as its object, it is not in contradiction with the ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman? he replies: "Of knowledge and ignorance... The meaning is that cessation occurs only when there is a contradiction.

He refutes the second head with the words "prapañca" (the world). He raises the objection that the knowledge of the falsity of the world results in the cessation of ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman, using the phrase "brahmasvarūpa" (the nature of Brahman). "Sadvitīyatvam" means the cognition of having a second. For mere existence does not constitute the ignorance regarding the nature of Brahman as being accompanied by a second, because such existence is not ultimately real (*apāramārthya*).

When ignorance, which has as its object Brahman qualified by non-duality (*advitīyatva*), ceases, the knowledge that has as its object the substantive portion (*viśeṣya*) also ceases; thus, how can there be the establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpasiddhi*)? To this he says: "But the essential nature... He refutes it with "No. With the intention of the following dilemma—whether non-duality is the essential nature or a property (*dharma*)—he first refutes the position that it is the essential nature with "No. Regarding the position that it is a property, he states the contradiction with his own established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*) with "Non-duality... He concludes the impossibility of a substratum (*āśrayānupapatti*) with "Therefore..."; the meaning is "precisely because of the aforementioned contradiction. In this way, the impossibility of a substratum has been stated.

Now, he states the impossibility of concealment (*tirodhāna*) with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). [Objection: But even in your view, there is the eternal manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*); nevertheless, for them too, the delusion of identifying the body as the self would not occur without the concealment of their true nature (*svarūpa*), so the logical inconsistency is equal. [Reply: True. There is indeed the manifestation of the true nature, and its concealment is not admitted. Furthermore, the manifestation of the true nature is not what contradicts delusion; rather, it is qualities such as eternality, atomicity, and partlessness that contradict delusion.

These [attributes] are to be known through scripture; their concealment (*tirodhi*) consists of a contraction characterized by the absence of the expansion of knowledge regarding them. Therefore, because it is admitted that there is a concealment of other forms distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no consequence of the destruction of the Self (*ātman*). If it is argued that error is untenable because the Self’s unique form—that is, knowledge—manifests, we say no; for its uniqueness does not manifest. Indeed, it is observed that a property which manifests as unique is opposed to error, as in the case of "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) and so forth.

For the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*), having been previously known as the unique characteristic of mother-of-pearl, subsequently sublates the error. However, consciousness has never before been observed as a unique attribute of a self distinct from the body; therefore, error is possible. Since superimposition (*adhyāsa*) occurs because the unique attributes of the self are not perceived, and the non-perception of unique attributes occurs because of superimposition, this circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) is resolved by [the doctrine of] beginninglessness (*anāditā*).

If it is argued that since you accept both the eternality and the concealment (*tirodhāna*) of knowledge that has become the nature of reality (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), it would follow that knowledge itself is subject to destruction, we say no. For knowledge is a substance (*dravya*). It is accepted that, apart from its essential nature (*svarūpa*), it possesses two states consisting of contraction and expansion. Therefore, its concealment is the contraction of that [knowledge] caused by karma; its cessation, however, is its expansion, which is precisely its manifestation (*prakāśa*). And that [manifestation] is non-eternal.

Even though that [state] is non-eternal, the doctrine of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the eternal substance of consciousness (*jñānadravya*) is based on its fitness for the outward expansion of its own luminous form. Therefore, because the two states are subject to appearance and disappearance, the substance itself is indeed eternal. For you, illumination is equivalent to our state [of cognition]; that alone is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). Consequently, concealment is simply the cessation of that [expansion]. With this meaning in mind, it is said that Brahman has the sole nature of light (*prakāśaikasvarūpa*).

Therefore, since one does not admit two states called "manifestation" and "concealment" that are distinct from the essential nature (svarūpa), the meaning is that concealment would necessarily be the destruction of the essential nature itself.

Now, he states the impossibility of its own nature with the words "moreover" (*api ca*). For, since [qualities] such as being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) are not ultimately real, they require other defects; it is in this sense that the sequence beginning with "without an object" (*nirviṣaya*) is presented here as an illustration, serving to establish the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that will be discussed later. Alternatively, the statement regarding the non-existence of the distinctions between objects, substrata, and appearances is made because they serve as the cause for imagining defects. The phrase "because it is not admitted" (*anabhyupagamāt*) implies that if these were ultimately real, it would entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita*).

He states "tathā sati" (if that were so) to show that only three alternatives are possible for refuting the position that [the world] is not ultimately real. The refutation—that there would be an infinite regress due to the dependence on further underlying defects because of its non-ultimate reality—is common to all three alternatives. He then demonstrates that there is an additional refutation specifically regarding the position that it is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*). He begins with "na tāvat" (not first...).

Is perception (*dṛśi*) undifferentiated (*anavacchinna*), or is it differentiated (*avacchinna*)? With the intention of raising the dilemma as to whether, in the case of its being undifferentiated, it is something other than its own nature (*svarūpa*) or simply its own nature itself, he refutes the position that it is something other than its own nature under the heading of the "undifferentiated" alternative, stating: "because no difference from the nature of perception is admitted. This means that two undifferentiated perceptions are not admitted. He then refutes the position that it is its own nature under the heading of the "undifferentiated" alternative, stating: "in [the case of] error," and so forth.

The infinite regress that will be stated as a refutation of the view that consciousness is limited (*avacchinna-dṛśi*) applies equally to the position that it is unlimited (*anavacchinna*); however, because two additional refutations exist in this case, it was not mentioned there. He refutes the acceptance [of consciousness] as both the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) and the seen (*dṛśya*) by means of its being limited and its being the seer and the seen with the words "of the seer and the seen. The meaning is "by way of being conceptual" (*kālpanikatvena*), which is to say, "by way of being non-ultimate" (*aparamārthatvena*). This conceptuality is the cause for the requirement of further defects.

Even in the view that [the self] is the delimited consciousness (*avacchinnadṛśi*), the fault of non-acceptance (*anabhyupagama*) applies equally to the alternative between its being the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or something distinct from it; for the essential nature of Brahman is not accepted as being delimited or as being unreal. Therefore, no such alternative is proposed in the case of the delimited view. As for the "infinite regress" (*anavasthā*) mentioned regarding the view that it is distinct from the essential nature: the meaning is that one wishes to avoid the fault that an infinite regress would result if it were unreal, whereas if it were real, it would entail the loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*).

The intention is that since experience itself is the defect, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*), and because it is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He refutes this with the words "Brahman alone," etc. By intending the similarity of its dependence on another defect due to its lack of ultimate reality, the term "equal to the phenomenal world" (*prapañca-tulya*) is used. Thus, the meaning is that [the opponent's view] is subject to the same refutations stated against the opposing position. To avoid the consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa-prasaṅga*), [the opponent claims] it is distinct from Brahman; to avoid the infinite regress, they claim it is ultimately real.

The opponents have avoided the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in three ways. Those who maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness avoid it by means of the logic of the seed and the sprout, [arguing] that the stream is beginningless; for their view is that the soul arises from ignorance (*avidyā*) and ignorance arises from the soul. Those who maintain that Brahman is consciousness avoid it by means of the beginninglessness of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). And both [groups] avoid it by means of its "inexplicability" (*durghaṭatva*); for inexplicability is an ornament of ignorance, not a defect. For the ultimate reality indeed requires logical justification.

In cases such as the swallowing of a palace, the logical argument—that it is impossible for a vast palace to be swallowed by a small mouth—does not apply. Therefore, the independence from logical justification (*upapatti*) establishes the non-ultimate nature [of the object]. Furthermore, because a defect (*doṣa*) is self-sustaining and does not require another defect, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

To this it is replied: the argument regarding the beginninglessness of the stream has already been answered by the proponent of Brahman-ignorance (*brahmājñānavādin*). Furthermore, since the eternity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established by scriptural texts and by the presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*) of other scriptural passages—such as those concerning the "attainment of what was not done" and the "loss of what was done"—the desired persistence of the soul until liberation would be forfeited [if its nature were otherwise]. Moreover, if [the soul] were not ultimately real, even its beginninglessness in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) would not avoid the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*); for if that were the case, it would result in the victory of the Madhyamaka position.

In this regard, [it was argued]: "If the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were established through error, that error would require another substratum; if that too were established through error, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, by means of the argument from infinite regress, the ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) of the substratum was established. However, if the Mādhyamika accepts that the substratum—which is not ultimately real—is beginningless by nature (*svarūpānāditva*), the infinite regress is avoided, and consequently, the non-ultimacy of the substratum itself would follow.

Furthermore, even if it is beginningless by nature, there is still a dependence upon a root defect (*mūladoṣa*), because you yourselves have admitted that the individual soul (*jīva*), though beginningless, is a conceptual construction of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, "inexplicability" (durghaṭatva) is untenable. Inexplicability means independence from logical justification (*upapatti*). If that were to establish the non-ultimate reality [of the world], then because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), being non-ultimate, would be independent of justification by virtue of its inexplicability, it would not depend upon a fundamental defect (*mūladoṣa*). Consequently, it would persist even when the subverting knowledge (*nivartakajñāna*) has arisen. If you argue that it does not persist due to contradiction, then ignorance (*avidyā*) would have to conform to logical justification.

There are two kinds of logical justification (*upapatti*): that based on ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and that based on non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*). In this context, "difficulty of comprehension" means independence from justification based on ultimate reality. For justification based on non-ultimate reality consists in the observation of defects (*doṣa*). If it is argued that it is therefore reasonable to postulate a fundamental defect for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then there would likewise have to be dependence on a defect consisting in justification based on non-ultimate reality even for that defect which is itself non-ultimate.

Consequently, the infinite regress remains exactly as it was. If you claim that the difficulty is resolved by the infinite regress itself, then even if the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were unreal, the infinite regress would be avoided. In that case, since the logical justification based on unreality would be unavoidable, one must say that there would still be an infinite regress due to the necessity of depending upon a substratum. This fault applies equally here as well, and thus the infinite regress is difficult to avoid. Even in the view that the series is beginningless (*anādi*), the infinite regress is easily avoided; for, like the succession of father and son, one accepts an endless succession of substrata.

The objection regarding the "impossibility" (*durghaṭatva*) raised by the proponent of Brahman-ignorance against the proponent of individual-soul ignorance applies equally to the doctrine of Brahman-ignorance as well. For instance, if the impossibility of ignorance were to apply, then ignorance would have to take refuge in either the liberated souls or the Supreme Brahman. If it is argued that pure-natured Brahman cannot be the locus of impure-natured ignorance due to their contradiction, then ignorance must indeed possess logical consistency. Consequently, the aforementioned objections—such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth—would necessarily follow; and this is equally true for you as well.

If it is argued that even in liberation (*mokṣa*), ignorance (*avidyā*) would have Brahman as its locus—on the grounds that once the subverting knowledge (*bādhakajñāna*) has arisen, ignorance, being unreal, cannot remain—it can indeed be said that our stated objections, such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), would follow; for ignorance is precisely defined by the logical principle that "the object to be subverted (*bādhyasiddhi*) cannot be established when the subverting factor is present."

If it is argued that just as a defect (doṣa) establishes itself and others, so too must the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) be so; and that its status as a self-establishing factor is established only once its status as a substratum for another is established—then we reply: the status of being a self-establishing factor is established only once its status as a defect for another is established, and since that very status [of being a defect] does not exist, the two cases would be equal. Furthermore, a distinction between the substratum and the superimposed object (āropya) is observed.

If it is argued that if the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were to establish itself and the superimposed (*adhyasta*) object simultaneously, it would follow that the locus and the superimposed are identical—then [we reply]: even in the case of a defect and its effect, such as the visual disorder (*timira*) and the double moon, a distinction is observed. It is the same [in your case]: if the defect were to establish itself and the superimposed object simultaneously, it would follow that the defect and the superimposed are identical. With this intention, it was stated that as long as one does not admit a metaphysically real defect distinct from Brahman, an illusion cannot be established. As the venerable Teacher (Sureśvara) has said:
"The difficulty of establishing [nescience] through its own nature or by means of itself and others, and furthermore the beginninglessness of the stream—

these four ways are indeed considered equal in their application to the path of a non-existent substratum, for they equally avoid the charge of infinite regress when nescience is declared to be unreal."

Now, he states the impossibility of indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*) with the words "And indefinability... Indefinability means that it is difficult to establish in the presence of the learned. To the question, "How is it devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," he replies, "This has been stated... [namely: "Everything would be the object of every cognition. The meaning is: even in the case of the cognition that something is "distinct from both the real and the unreal," its objects would still be only the real and the unreal. For it is in accordance with cognition that things such as blue or yellow are established.

Therefore, since cognition possesses the forms of both the existent and the non-existent, its object must likewise possess the forms of the existent and the non-existent, and not something distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. As stated in the *Khyātiviveka*: "For that which appears is not one thing and the object another; for an object is established by way of its appearing. If it is argued that it is untenable for a single object to possess the forms of both the existent and the non-existent because it contradicts the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti*), then the claim that it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is equally untenable due to the contradiction with the rule of pervasion.

For it is observed that existence is distinct from non-existence and non-existence is distinct from existence; however, it is never observed that a single entity possesses both distinctions simultaneously—thus there is a contradiction with the universal rule (*vyāpti*). This is the distinction: while being distinct from both existence and non-existence is nowhere observed, being of the nature of both existence and non-existence is indeed observed. As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*:

"It is not [unreal] because it is perceived, nor is it real because it is sublated; for that which is neither is not so because of perception alone. Why is the world not real simply because it is perceived? And why is it not unreal because it is sublated? In the determination of the nature of an object, there must be either existence (*sattva*) or non-existence (*asattva*); there can be no state distinct from these two. If it is argued that an existing thing such as a jar is seen to be distinct from both existence and non-existence, we say no; for if that were the case, it would follow that even Brahman is distinct from both existence and non-existence. If you claim that being distinct from existence and non-existence is precisely what is intended—meaning it cannot be identified with either one—that is equally applicable [to the world].

By asserting such a distinction from both existence and non-existence, you effectively accept existence itself under another name. Therefore, the "distinction from both existence and non-existence" favored by you is refuted due to its inherent contradiction.

If it is argued that "existence" consists in being apprehended as "it exists," while "sublatedness" consists in being the object of the cognition "it does not exist"—and thus there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence for a single entity, and that the intended meaning is a state distinct from both existence and non-existence—then, since every prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and established conclusion (*siddhānta*) has as its object a form mutually contradictory [to the other], the object to be proven would necessarily be distinct from both forms; consequently, the effort to establish the *siddhānta* would be rendered futile.

Furthermore, having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "difference is easily defined," and then having established the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by you that it is "difficult to define," [the object] would have to be distinct from both the easily defined and the difficult to define due to the contradiction between these two cognitions. Likewise, in debates concerning whether consciousness is real or false, insentient or sentient, eternal or non-eternal, and so forth, consciousness would possess a nature distinct from the forms of both the prima facie and the final conclusions. And that is not desired.

Therefore, the notion that two mutually contradictory cognitions can produce a distinction from the forms perceived is contrary to the rule of pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, the establishment of a distinction from both the existent and the non-existent is not achieved.

If it is asked, "In that case, what solution has been stated for the fact that neither manifestation (*khyāti*) nor sublation (*bādha*) would otherwise be possible?"—the answer is that the possibility has been explained quite differently: since manifestation and sublation are possible through "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) and other such theories favored by various respective disputants, provided that the object exists. [Objection: How can there be sublation of something that exists? [Reply: Because it is manifested elsewhere. [Objection: If it exists elsewhere, there is no sublation; if it does not exist [there], it follows that there is manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). [Reply: No, because it exists elsewhere.

"Anyathākhyāti" (the theory of misapprehension) is indeed the appearance elsewhere of that which exists elsewhere. It is the appearance elsewhere of what exists elsewhere due to the influence of a defect (*doṣa*). If it is argued that the capacity of a defect to cause an appearance elsewhere has never been observed, we reply that it is equally the case that the capacity of a defect to cause the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) has never been observed anywhere other than in our own position. Furthermore, your claim that the non-contradiction of a single object with two mutually contradictory perceived forms is something additional [to our view] is merely superfluous.

In the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātipakṣa*), since there is existence [of the object], the sublation of the cognition is established through the non-apprehension of difference. It is the appearance of that which exists precisely as something whose difference has not been apprehended; and the apprehension of difference is the sublation. Furthermore, the state of being sublated pertains to the activity [of the subject]. In the theory of the appearance of reality (*yathārthakhyātipakṣa*), however, because of the existence of things such as magical illusions and dream-objects, and because of the absence of their predominance, as well as the non-apprehension of their stability and their being experienced by a single subject, the sublation of the cognition is established. It is the appearance of silver, which indeed exists in the object present before one; and the apprehension of the predominance of the mother-of-pearl is the sublation.

Therefore, activity must be sublated; and that sublation consists in the impossibility of such activity. In the case of the fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and similar phenomena, however, its possibility is established just as it is in the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*). Consequently, since the possibility [of activity] is established in another way, the postulation of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) is untenable.

Thus, the impossibility of [the opponent's position] regarding the concealment of the substratum (*āśrayatirodhāna*) and the indeterminability of its nature (*svarūpānirvacanīyatva*) has been stated. Now, with the intention that—according to the maxim "for there is nothing impossible when what is perceived is present"—it is not proper to subvert an object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through mere reasoning (*tarka*), the opponent raises an objection concerning the claim of such a means of knowledge, saying: "Now, it might be so. To establish the aspects previously refuted, he says: "The nature of the thing... By this, concealment is expressed; by "internal and external," its nature is expressed.

For it is by virtue of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that its falsity (*mithyātva*) is established. Its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*), as being neither existent nor non-existent, has been stated. In the scriptures, for the sake of recognizing the words that convey this [meaning], it is said to be denoted by terms such as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and "nescience" (*ajñāna*). Although another form is about to be refuted by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*), he states it as the probandum (*sādhya*) in the phrase "knowledge of the true nature of things. The phrase "conditioned by that" (*tadupahita*) also refers to the locus (*āśraya*).

What is internal superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and what is external? Furthermore, how can Brahman be the material cause (*upādāna*) if ignorance (*avidyā*) is the material cause? To this, he says: "qualified by that" (*tadupahita*). He indicates the impossibility of the pure, abstract Brahman being the material cause by stating: "in the inner self (*pratyagātman*), whose nature is changeless, self-luminous consciousness alone. The meaning is that because it is changeless, self-luminous, and inward-turned (*pratyaktva*), a transformation into the form of an object that is external, insentient, and subject to modification is not possible.

To the question, "How can superimposition (*adhyāsa*) be possible for that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*)," he says: "whose true nature is concealed" (*tirohitasvarūpa*). To the question, "What is the concealer? he says: "by that very [cause]" (*tenaiva*). This means: by that very cause of superimposition itself. The ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*) constitute internal superimposition; the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) constitutes external superimposition. Regarding the action whose form is superimposition—that is, the state of being superimposed—it is said: "by a particular state of that very defect alone" (*doṣasyaiva avasthāviśeṣeṇa*), meaning by a certain occasional particular state, there occurs the superimposition of a snake on a rope and so forth. (This is the syntactical connection.)

Thus, the impossibility of pure Brahman being the material cause (*upādāna*) has been stated. He states the logical justification for a defect (*doṣa*) being the material cause with the words "of the whole" (*kṛtsnasya*). For it is observed that gold alone is the material cause of an ornament belonging to the class of gold; such is the sense. This is based on the force of the reason characterized by the observation that cause and effect belong to the same genus. Now he states the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with the words "the cause," etc. The explanation of "I am ignorant" (*aham ajñaḥ*) is "I do not know myself and another. "I am ignorant" is the mention of the very nature of ignorance.

The statement "I do not know myself or anything else" is an expression of the effect, which is concealment (*ācchādana*). By using the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*), there is an exclusion of ignorance that takes the form of an effect. Therefore, the ignorance pertaining to deep sleep (*sauṣuptika*) is what is intended. It has been stated by the author of the *Tattvaśuddhi* and others that in states such as waking, ignorance delimited by objects like jars is perceived through determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*); however, in deep sleep, there is the perception of the undelimited causal ignorance. The traditional doctrine (*saṃpradāya*), however, holds that this experience of ignorance occurs only in the waking state.

And because of the statement, "I do not know anything else," there is indeed no reflection upon another during deep sleep. Since ignorance—which is perceived as an obscuring factor in the form "I do not know"—is the cause [of that experience], it is said that [the experience] has ignorance as its object. The term "immediate manifestation" (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) is stated for the purpose of excluding indirect means of knowledge such as inference. Anticipating the objection that it might have the prior absence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) as its object, he refutes this with the words "But this... Anticipating the further objection that this too might be the object of the sixth means of knowledge (non-apprehension), he says: "But this..."

The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the remote (*parokṣa*) are distinct from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the meaning is that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is an object of a remote means of valid cognition, cannot be the same as ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is an object of a non-remote (direct) means of valid cognition. He states the refutation even if non-existence were cognizable by a means of valid cognition that grasps positive entities (*bhāva*): "of non-existence" (*abhāvasya*). He provides the reason: "on account of experience" (*anubhava*). At the time of the experience of non-existence, does knowledge exist or not? If it exists, there can be no cognition of non-existence because of the absence of an object to be grasped (*grāhya*).

If this were not the case, the meaning would be that because there is no cognizer (*grāhaka*), there can be no cognition of that absence; for contradiction exists only when existence and non-existence share a single object. Here, however, there is no contradiction, because the cognition whose object is absence is itself present as the cognizer, whereas the cognition of the other object is non-existent insofar as it is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that absence. In dispelling this doubt, [the author] establishes: (1) the presence of cognition at the time of experience; (2) the impossibility of cognizing the absence of cognition if it were non-existent; and (3) the lack of contradiction if cognition is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).

He explains this by saying, "This is what is meant. With the intention that if the prior non-existence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) were the object of apprehension, then even against one's will, existence and non-existence would result in having the same objective referent, he says, "I... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*): the word *jñāna* here is common to both knowledge whose object is the self and knowledge whose objects are jars and the like. In cases such as "there is no jar on this ground," it is observed that the apprehension of non-existence depends upon the cognition of both the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the locus (*dharmin*). Therefore, in this case as well, [the cognition of the absence of knowledge] must depend upon the cognition of the locus of that non-existence.

It must be stated that knowledge of the self exists; for the self is indeed distinct from non-existence. Therefore, even when there is knowledge having that [self] as its object, the claim that "knowledge whose object is distinct from non-existence is the counter-positive of non-existence" would be contradictory. If it is argued that "knowledge whose object is distinct from the triad consisting of the non-existence, the locus (dharmin), and the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is the counter-positive of non-existence," then one must admit that there is also a cognition of the knowledge itself by virtue of its being the counter-positive of non-existence.

Since the cognition being apprehended is apprehended as delimited by its own object, there is also the apprehension of the objects themselves. Thus, the point is that when objects are cognized as the delimiters of the cognition of a counter-positive (pratiyogin) of an absence, the absence of a cognition of those objects becomes untenable. He extends the aforementioned refutation to the case where absence is the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), stating "of the absence of cognition."

The sense is that even though there is no rule that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must have only existing things as their objects, [ignorance] cannot be shown to exist [in that way]. For ignorance is indeed perceived as being present in the form "I am ignorant. In this view, another additional refutation has been stated previously: it is established by the facts that it is impossible for that which is immediate (*aparokṣa*) to be the object of a mediate (*parokṣa*) means of valid cognition. He states "of this" (*asya*) to show that the aforementioned refutation does not apply if [ignorance] is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

The cognition of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is "the cognition of the locus and the counter-correlate. There is no contradiction between that [cognition] and ignorance (*ajñāna*) in its positive form; for it is the ignorance veiling a jar that is contradicted by the cognition of the jar, and not by the cognition of the object of the cognition of the jar, nor by the cognition of the locus—this is the meaning.

He raises an objection, saying "But surely," [arguing] that ignorance—which is to be removed by the knowledge of the true nature of reality—is opposed by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) which consists in the manifestation of the true nature of reality. He refutes this, saying "Not so. By the word "true nature" (*yāthātmya*), the intended meaning is the essential nature characterized as non-duality, stripped of all adjuncts. He states the reason, taking for granted the established falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), with the words "otherwise"; the meaning is: otherwise, if the mere manifestation of one's own witness-nature were itself the object of the true nature of reality.

(Or: "In the absence of being the object of ignorance") let there be the state of being the object of ignorance; to the question "What follows from that?", he says "Not indeed" (*na hi*). The meaning is: for silver is not removed by a cognition whose object is silver. Since visibility is observed even in color and so forth, which are qualifiers of the visible, [the opponent] objects again with the words "But this... (*nanu cedam*), intending to argue that because the "I-factor" (*asmadartha*), which delimits the ignorance of the visible, is not admitted to be visible, the ignorance delimited by the "I-factor" is not made an object [of knowledge].

The "particularity of the object" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*) refers to a particular delimiting factor (*avacchedaka-viśe�ṣa*). The word "that" (*saḥ*) refers back to that very same thing. He resolves [the objection] by saying, "This is not a fault. The referent of the first-person pronoun (*asmadartha*) is also included within what is denoted by the word "all" (*sarva*). Whether it be known or unknown, it is either dependent on another cognition or independent of it. The meaning is that it becomes an object of the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) and thus manifests through that witnessing consciousness. However, the status of the first-person referent as an object of the witnessing consciousness is merely figurative (*aupacārika*), because it is impossible for that which is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśa*) to be its own object.

Since an insentient entity cannot be self-luminous, its establishment depends upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it becomes a qualification of the object of perception (*dṭśya*). However, the "I" (*asmadartha*), being established by itself through its own self-luminosity, is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of ignorance—this is the meaning. As for the objection that it is "perceptible" (*dṛśya*) because it is a delimiting factor of the perceptible, the rebuttal is that this is based on its insentiency (*jaḍatva*) and is thus a fallacious argument (*sopādhika*). Therefore, the meaning is that there is a contradiction in the view that [ignorance] is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), whereas in the view that it is of the nature of an entity (*bhāva*), such a contradiction does not exist.

"Supported by reasoning" (nyāyopabṛṃhitena) means supported by reasoning in the form of either contradiction or its absence in both alternative positions. Thus, it is established by perception supported by reasoning that nescience (ajñāna) is of a positive nature, and that it is self-referential through the cognition "I do not know. Its exclusion from the "action" (karman) postulated by opponents—which is denoted by the word "nescience" in the scriptures—is established by its being perceptible. Furthermore, its status as being denotable by words such as "nescience" in the scriptures is established because it is the opposite of knowledge and because it is apprehended in the form "I am ignorant."

Now, ignorance—characterized by the features already established as being both an obscuration of its own object and something to be removed by itself—is also proven by inference through the passage beginning with "that which is the subject of dispute," and so forth. When it is said "knowledge," since it is impossible for the nature of Brahman itself to be preceded by another entity, the term "valid knowledge" (*pramāṇajñāna*) is used in order to exclude that [Brahman].

Nevertheless, because in a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*), each subsequent cognition lacks the quality of being preceded by another object intended to be established, the phrase "subject of dispute" (*vivādādhyāsita*) was stated in order to exclude that case. When the question arises as to what kind of cognition that is, the term "cognition through a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇajñāna*) was stated for the sake of clarification. In this way, the subject (*dharmin*) has been shown. Now, he states the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) with the words beginning "its own prior non-existence" (*svaprāgabhāva*).

If it were stated simply that "it is preceded by another entity," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since [darkness] is already established as being preceded by its own object, such as a jar; therefore, to exclude that, he says "located in its own place" (*svadeśagata*). If it were stated "located in its own substratum" (*svāśrayagata*), there would be a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example; for darkness does not reside in a lamp. Hence, the expression "located in its own place. To exclude *dharma* and *adharma*, he says "that which is to be removed by itself" (*svanivartya*).

Now, one might ask: how does the term "sublated by itself" (*svanivartya*) exclude merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)? For *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) which serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge is indeed destroyed by the arising of that knowledge. Not so; because not all *dharma* and *adharma* have knowledge as their fruit, and because those *dharma*s and others distinct from the producer of knowledge exist in their own location at the preceding moment. Alternatively, by the term "sublated by itself," there is the exclusion of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); for a mental impression is not sublated by knowledge.

To exclude [the definition from applying to] fear and so forth, he says "obscuring its own object" (*svaviṣayāvaraṇa*). Since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is of such a nature, he says "distinct from its own prior non-existence" (*svaprāgabhāvavyatirikta*) in order to exclude that. This is the exclusion by way of reverse order (*pratiloma-vyāvṛtti*). When it is said "preceded by another entity" (*vastvantara-pūrvaka*), since even non-existence is denotable by the word "entity" (*vastu*) as a category of existence (*padārtha*), he says "distinct from its own prior non-existence" in order to exclude that. To exclude [the application of the definition to] the pot and other such things which are their own objects, he says "obscuring its own object."

He says "svanivartya" (capable of being removed by itself) in order to exclude walls and the like. He says "svadeśagata" (situated in its own locus) in order to exclude the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the manifestation of consciousness residing in the object. For that is their established procedure: when ignorance is dispelled by valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*), the consciousness residing in the object becomes manifested. The state of being an obscuration of the object for the prior non-existence of manifestation consists in its opposition to light (*prakāśa*); it does not consist in its being an impediment to it. This is the exclusion in the direct order (*anuloma*).

He states the reason: "not being manifested" (*aprakāśitā*). Here, "manifesting-ness" (*prakāśakatva*) is intended to mean the state of being the cause that is conducive to non-sublated practical activity, whether directly or indirectly. By specifying "whether directly or indirectly," the application of the definition to both the light of a lamp and to cognition is established. The phrase "the state of being the cause conducive to non-sublated practical activity" is stated in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the cognition "this is silver."

When it is stated "because of being an illuminator" (*prakāśakatvāt*), since in a continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) each subsequent cognition possesses the quality of being an illuminator, yet lacks the property sought to be proven (*siṣādhayiṣita-dharma*), the reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*). To exclude that case, he says: "because of being an illuminator of an unilluminated object" (*aprakāśitārthaprakāśakatvāt*). It should be understood that the reason is qualified by the phrase "while being manifest" (*bhāsamānatve sati*) in order to exclude the inconclusiveness regarding the sense organs (*indriya*). He states the example: "in darkness" (*andhakāre*).

If it were stated simply as "like the light of a lamp," there would be a deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavikalatā*) because subsequent instances of light do not possess the quality of illuminating an object not previously illuminated; furthermore, there would be a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) because such light lacks the quality of being preceded by another entity that it itself dispels. To exclude these [faults], it is stated: "like the light of a lamp produced for the first time. Even so, since the light of a lamp during the day is not observed to have such characteristics, the word "darkness" (*andhakāre*) is used to exclude that case.

Anticipating the objection that the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), he refutes it with the words beginning "In the presence of light" (*āloke sati*). He states the nature of the accompanying phenomenon as either "the mere absence of the perception of form" (*rūpadarśanābhāvamātraṃ vā*)—since darkness is possible for owls and others even when light is present—or alternatively, he says "the perception of form" (*rūpadarśana*) in order to account for the experience of darkness by one who has closed their eyes. Here, he considers the refutation stated by the Naiyāyikas and others: that [darkness] is a distinct substance (*dravyāntaratva*) is refuted because neither its production (*utpādaka*) nor its cognition (*jñāpaka*) is logically tenable.

Even though atoms possess form (*rūpavattva*), they alone are unproduced (*anutpādya*). However, since darkness possesses form, it would follow that it is produced as something large (*bṛhat*). In this regard, because they lack form, substances such as air and space cannot be its producers; nor can other substances, due to their lack of touch, taste, and smell. For the production of specific qualities in an effect occurs through the sequence of the qualities of the cause. This is the impossibility of its production. Furthermore, because it is not assisted by light, the eye is not its perceiver.

Because it does not persist in the presence of light, it cannot be an object of perception. The cognition of it as possessing color is merely an illusion, like the appearance of blue when the eyes are closed; thus, its status as a known entity is untenable. To this, the Vārttikakāra offers a rebuttal: "Darkness is indeed mobile, blue, and possesses distinctions of priority and posteriority; because it differs from the properties of the well-known [nine] substances, it deserves to be distinguished from those nine. That very point is stated here.

In this context, the meaning of the terms "superior" (*parā*) and "inferior" (*apara*) is expressed by the words "abundance" (*bahulatva*) and "scarcity" (*viralatva*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), "mobility" (*calatva*) is indicated. By the phrase "possessing color" (*rūpavattayā*), the meaning of the term "blue" (*nīla*) is expressed; by the term "another substance" (*dravyāntara*), the status of being a tenth substance is stated. For the acceptance of nine substances is maintained by them on account of the mutual difference (*anyonya-vaidharmya*) among those substances, such as earth and the rest. Otherwise, one could say that earth alone is a substance and nothing else, because of the absence of the quality of smell (*gandhavattva*). In the same way, there are two substances, and so forth.

And that is not accepted; the meaning of the *Vārttika* is that because substances possess mutual dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and because it possesses a dissimilarity from the nine substances, a tenth substance must be admitted. The perception of blue during [the eyes'] closing has its object sublated; however, this [perception under discussion] cannot be like that, because it is unsublated. If it is argued that, nevertheless, since there is no perception at the time of perceiving color, it might still be a case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—just as with the closing of the eyes—the answer is: no.

For at the time when one perceives the form of an owl and so forth, there would arise the suspicion that even the perception of our own form is absent, since [the owl's] form is not perceived; and at the time when one perceives the form of an owl and so forth, there would follow the consequence that even the perception of our own form is suspected to be absent, because our own form is not perceived.

Furthermore, since any doubt has been dispelled by the natural consistency of the scriptures (*āgamasvārasya*), it is determined that darkness (*tamas*) is the tenth substance. For its being created, its being withdrawn, and its being a body are heard in such scriptural passages as: "The Blessed Lord created darkness," "There was neither day nor night, neither sky nor earth; there was no darkness, nor was there light, nor anything else," "He whose body is light," and "He whose body is darkness. Thus, these qualities—being created, being withdrawn, and being a body—are indeed attested in the Śruti.

Just as independence from light is observed to be occasioned by a particular cognizer, so too it is logically consistent that it may be occasioned by a particular object of cognition (*jñeya*). For in the world, the nature of an effect is the very basis for the postulation of its cause; indeed, an effect that is clearly ascertained does not deserve to be denied when investigating its cause. Thus, according to the principle that one must postulate the producer of darkness—which is established by uncontradicted perception—there is neither an impossibility of a producer nor an impossibility of a means of knowledge (*jñāpaka*). As our Teacher has said: [insert citation].
"We perceive darkness as a substance that is extremely subtle, black, and moving; yet no sublation of it has been observed by anyone anywhere.
Therefore, a cause must be postulated [for its perception], and verbal cognition (śābdī pramitiḥ) prevails; for the eye reveals it as being devoid of light, by virtue of that very observation."

That darkness (*tamas*) is a substance (*dravya*) is the opinion of the author of the *Bhāṣya*; for it is not refuted in the final system (*siddhānta*), and because [darkness] is heard in scripture to be something that is created, dissolved, and a body. Because it is a transparent substance, darkness is an effect of space (*ākāśa*). Its possession of color (*rūpa*) is established through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). Alternatively, darkness is an effect of light (*tejas*); because it possesses color, while its non-perception of touch (*sparśa*) is due to its being a transparent substance. Thus it is "without fault" (*niravadya*); the meaning is that it is without flaw because, being established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it cannot be sublated by reasoning (*tarka*).

Now he begins to state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words, "To this it is replied. The phrase "by mere perception" is stated as an illustration; the meaning is that once the refutation of the logical argument (*upapatti*) has been made, mere perception is not a means of proof. For there is a contradiction if the [non-existence] is taken as the object of the antecedent absence of knowledge (*jñāna-prāgabhāva*); he states that this contradiction is equal even if it is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*) with the words, "But as for that which... He establishes this equality with the words, "by way of being an object. By the word "perceived" (*pratipanna*), manifestation is meant. [The phrase] "to be removed by the knowledge of its own nature" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that "knowledge of its own nature" (*svarūpajñāna*) is the manifestation of its own nature; that is to say, it is that which is to be removed by the manifestation of its own nature, whether by itself or by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since it is observed that even when hundreds of cognitions produced by a means of valid cognition—such as "this is white and shining"—arise with respect to the [erroneous perception] "this is silver," the delusion is not removed, it is established as a matter of fact that being a cognition produced by a means of valid cognition is not the determining factor; therefore, it is stated that it is to be removed by the knowledge of its own nature.

The inner self (*pratyagartha*) is that which distinguishes [ignorance] by being its locus and its object, yet it is devoid of the cognition of itself as the locus or the object. The commentary, beginning with the words "by way of being an object" (*viṣayatvena*), demonstrates the equality of the contradiction involved in the apprehension of ignorance regarding one's own self. Even in the case of the perception of ignorance regarding objects such as a jar, has the jar been apprehended as the object that distinguishes the ignorance, or not?

If the jar is apprehended, how could the ignorance regarding that jar—which is to be removed by the knowledge of the jar's own nature—possibly persist once that jar has been apprehended? If the jar is not apprehended, how could ignorance, which is devoid of knowledge regarding its distinguishing object, be experienced? Thus, one should see the contradiction established by these facts.

Thus, having shown the contradiction between existence and non-existence by another [author], the contradiction between the sublated and the sublator was stated as a counter-argument (*prati-bandī*) to that. Now, he raises the objection that there is no contradiction due to the distinction between the clear and the unclear, beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The manifestation of the inner self (*pratyagartha*) through valid cognition is a "clear manifestation"; he states, "Alas, then," to show that this is equally present in his own position as well. That which has a clear nature as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) is "that whose object has a clear nature."

The clear nature (*viśadasvarūpa*) serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) by means of the cognition whose object is itself. The meaning is that even the antecedent non-existence of cognition is delimited by the cognition of the clear nature. Furthermore, cognition functions as the delimiting factor of non-existence by way of being its counter-correlate (*pratiyogitā*). This amounts to saying that the cognition of the clear nature is the counter-correlate of the antecedent non-existence. To establish the absence of contradiction, he states that the existing cognition is something other than that [antecedent non-existence] by means of the word "substratum" (*āśraya*). The cognition of this counter-correlate is the "cognition of the substratum-counter-correlate."

Regarding the phrase "having as its object an indistinct nature": the state of having an indistinct nature as its object for that which is being based upon means having as its object an indistinct sense of the self (*pratyag-artha*). The state of having an indistinct nature as its object for the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) means having as its object an indistinct cognition that constitutes the counter-positive of the absence. The subverting cognition (*nivartaka-jñāna*), which has itself as its object, now takes hold of the cognition as being the counter-positive of the absence.

In this context, because the inner reality (*pratyagartha*), which is the object of the subverting knowledge (*nivartakajñāna*), is currently indistinct, and because the subverting knowledge itself is not yet present, the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*)—the knowledge—is indistinct. For knowledge that is actually present, together with its locus, takes the form of immediate manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*); therefore, its lack of distinctness arises from its non-existence [at that time].

The meaning is as follows: the nature [of the object] appearing as the substratum (*āśraya*) is indistinct; the cognition being remembered as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is likewise indistinct because its object is currently indistinct and because it is non-existent. Thus, the cognition whose objects are both of these has an indistinct nature as its object. And that [indistinct cognition] exists. However, the distinct cognition is non-existent and serves as the counter-correlate of the absence [of that distinct cognition]; therefore, there is no contradiction. This is the point: you must admit, at the very least, the absence of the valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) intended to remove ignorance.

Otherwise, it would be impossible to experience ignorance as something that is sublated by valid knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*). Consequently, the very absence of valid knowledge—which you yourself accept—must be the object of the cognition "I am ignorant. Therefore, one should not postulate its positive nature on the grounds that the apprehension of an absence is otherwise inexplicable. If it is asked how the contradiction stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is thereby resolved, it is as follows:

For in that case, there is indeed a contradiction: when a cognition delimited by a certain object is said to be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence, then once that object which delimits the cognition of the counter-positive of the absence is apprehended, the absence of that cognition becomes untenable.

The resolution to this is as follows: it is the cognition of the counter-positive of the absence that is negated when it has ascended to the level of memory. Just as in the negation "there is no direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a jar," the direct perception of the jar is recalled. Since there is no rule that what is being remembered must exist at the same time as the memory, there is no contradiction in the fact that what is being remembered serves as the counter-positive of the absence at the time of the negation.

Furthermore, according to your view, since the subverting cognition (*nivartakajñāna*) that has ascended into memory cannot exist at the same time as the memory itself, even if it is apprehended as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of ignorance, you must admit that the subverting cognition residing in memory is not an opponent to ignorance. Therefore, it is more logically consistent to maintain that valid cognitions (*pramāṇajñāna*)—whether having the Self as their object or objects such as jars—become the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of non-existence when they are apprehended in an indistinct manner as having ascended into memory along with their own objects, namely the Self and jars.

For recollection arises only from that which has been experienced. If you ask, "By what was the knowledge of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) experienced? then by what was your own subverting cognition experienced? If you say, "From scripture," then for us as well, the direct realization of the Self is understood through the words that enjoin it. As for the direct realization of a jar and so forth, it is experienced by anyone through perception and the other means of knowledge. But how can the direct realization of Mount Meru be denied? For that was never previously experienced by any means of knowledge. It is said in reply:

In this world, how can it be said by a man who has never before seen an elephant at a crossroads that "there is no elephant at this crossroads"? If you argue that even when the relation (*saṃsarga*) is not experienced, the negation of one of the two related things (*saṃsargin*) in another place is possible through the mere experience of the two related things themselves—then, likewise, even when the relation between Mount Meru and direct perception is not experienced, the negation of that relation would be possible because both Meru and direct perception are known by someone.

As for the argument that because non-existence is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of valid cognitions, there can be no apprehender of it at that time—that has been refuted by the fact that it is impossible to experience the absence of all valid cognitions simultaneously, and because the absence of some specific cognitions can be apprehended through another means of knowledge (*māna*). Thus, the parity of the resolution of contradictions has been shown in the case where [non-existence] is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*).

Surely, it cannot be said that the contradiction is the same [in both cases]. For while ignorance must be understood precisely as being delimited by the counter-positive of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), that knowledge which is the counter-positive of the *nañ* appears as delimited by the inner self (*pratyagātman*), who is its own object and locus. Thus, when there is knowledge of the inner self—which serves as the object and locus—there is a contradiction with the persistence of the ignorance that is to be removed by it. Indeed, positive ignorance does not depend upon the apprehension of knowledge for its own manifestation.

Since it is possible to apprehend [ignorance] by its very own nature (svarūpa), one might object that a positive entity such as a jar is never seen to depend upon the knowledge of its counter-positive (pratiyogin) for its cognition; to this, he says: "of a positive entity" (bhāvarūpasya). To the question, "In what way does it depend? he says: "even though... [He continues: even if ignorance were a positive entity, it would still be established by its own nature; to this, he says: "as intended by you" (bhavadabhimata). If it is argued that its establishment by its own nature is seen in such expressions as "I am bewildered" or "I am deluded," [the reply is: no, for delusion belongs to a certain person with respect to a certain object.

In passages such as, “He of pure intellect does not fall into self-delusion,” and “How, moreover, could there be delusions such as the confusion of directions or the [illusory] circle of a whirling firebrand? delusion is indeed perceived as delimited by both an object and a substratum. By the expression “I am deluded,” its delimitation by a substratum is cognized; the object is also established by the force of the context. This refutation is the result of the direction stated in the passage: “Does consciousness succeed or not?”

Consequently, ignorance regarding one's own self is destroyed by the existence of the realization of the inner self (pratyag-artham), which serves as its substrate and object; however, ignorance regarding a jar or the like is contradicted by the cognition of that jar or object which serves as its substrate and object. If it is argued that when ignorance is understood through words such as "māyā," there is no requirement for a substrate or an object, we say no. This is because even words like "māyā" can convey meaning independently of etymological derivation, and since they are established as synonyms for "ignorance" (ajñāna) and so forth, their establishment in their own right is difficult to maintain. With this intention, it was stated that [ignorance] is never established in its own right.

[Objection: Even if ignorance delimited by its own nature (*svarūpa*) is established as being delimited by the knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—which is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—there is no contradiction between the sublated and the sublator; for that [ignorance] is established as being other than the knowledge that constitutes its own nature. Indeed, it is not the knowledge consisting of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) that removes ignorance, but rather only knowledge derived from a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*); therefore, there is no contradiction. [Reply: This is not so; for in the cognition "I do not know myself and the other," [ignorance] is perceived as being delimited by a knowledge that relates to the object, the locus, and their connection.
