For in your view, knowledge that constitutes the very nature [of the self] is not admitted to have a substratum (*āśraya*) or an object (*viṣaya*). Does the nature [of the self] delimit ignorance solely by way of being its substratum, or also by way of being its object? In the first case, your intended position is not established; for at that time, it would be established that the inner self (*pratyagartha*) is indeed qualified by something other than itself. If it were the delimiter by way of being the object, then ignorance would be an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) of the inner self. And obscuration consists in being an obstacle to the knowledge that has that [self] as its object.

Therefore, because the cognition of the means of knowledge regarding that [object] necessarily occurs, the contradiction with your own statement remains unresolved. Consequently, the acceptance of a cognition delimited by a knower who is identical with one's own nature is untenable.

Anticipating the objection that "since both the proof and the refutation are equal in both cases, let ignorance be accepted as having a positive (bhāva) nature," he refutes it by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), stating: "But [it is] the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge. This is indeed accepted. For while there is disagreement regarding the negative nature of what is apprehended in the cognition "I am ignorant," there is no denial of non-existence itself. Otherwise, since the prior non-existence of valid knowledge would be absent and thus beginningless, the impossibility of its arising would entail the non-arising of the positive ignorance that is to be negated by it.

The meaning is that you have thereby admitted the non-existence of knowledge. Furthermore, it is indeed perceived; for in the world, we observe the conventional usage "knowledge does not exist" when one intends to express the absence of such specific knowledge. Since an intention to speak is impossible regarding what is not apprehended, the meaning is that there is certainly a perception of the absence of knowledge.

Therefore, since the cognition "I am ignorant" is established by the very absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*) as commonly accepted, there is no reason to postulate anything further. By the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), that [absence] alone must be accepted as the object of the cognition "I am ignorant. [Objection: But there is no such thing as "absence" (*abhāva*) that is admitted by both parties. In our own system (*svamata*), absence is a positive entity (*bhāvāntara*); however, in the opponent's system (*paramata*), it is something distinct from a positive entity. So how can the cognition "I am ignorant" be established by means of something admitted by both? [Reply: It is said:

For it was not said that [the object] is accepted by both parties; rather, it was said that it is accepted by you. Some object denoted by the word "non-existence" (abhāva) is accepted by both of us. The point of contention is merely this: whether that [object] is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva-rūpa) or something distinct from it.

In this context, since the cognition "I am ignorant" can be accounted for by either that which is intended by you as a positive entity (*bhāvatva*) or that which is intended by the opponent as denoted by the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) by virtue of being distinct from it, it has been stated that the postulation of an object distinct from both is untenable; thus, there is no contradiction. Now, one might object: "By you, who maintain that non-existence is merely another form of existence (*bhāvāntarabhāva*), the term 'prior non-existence of knowledge' (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) would have to be accepted as a positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*). This is not so; for this objection arises from a lack of familiarity with the two established systems (*siddhānta*).

The state of self-luminous knowledge itself, which takes the form of contraction and is designated by the term "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva), is what we accept; whereas the existence of ignorance as a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) distinct from self-luminous knowledge is what others accept. Therefore, how could there be identity between these two?

If it is argued, "In that case, let us abandon the state consisting of the contraction of knowledge and accept the positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna) described by others as denoted by the word 'ignorance' (ajñāna), since there is no difference in their being positive entities," this is untenable; for it would mean abandoning what is supported by scripture and accepting what is not. [This is so because of such scriptural passages as: "There is no loss of the knower’s power of knowing" (*na vijñāturvijñāterviparilopo vidyate*); "The seer sees everything" (*sarvaṃ ha paśyaḥ paśyati*); and "And because it is concealed by that [ignorance], O King, the power known as the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) exists in all beings."

Since it is established by Śruti and Smṛti—beginning with "It exists in a graduated manner" and "Among insentient beings, that [power] is very slight," up to "Hiraṇyagarbha is characterized by a power far exceeding that of other men"—how can the gradation of knowledge and its contraction, which are thus authoritative, be rejected? On the other hand, positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna) is merely a postulate; and since the postulator is otherwise accounted for, how can that unauthoritative [postulate] be accepted?

For the principle of parsimony (*lāghavanyāya*) operates in the realm of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), but not with respect to an object established by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, in the cognition "I am ignorant," it is precisely the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge that is perceived.

Thus, it has been stated that if the perception "I am ignorant" has positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) as its object, there is a lack of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*)—namely, the impossibility of the position of positive ignorance and the impossibility of the position of negative ignorance (*abhāvarūpa*); now, sublation by contrary reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) is stated in the words beginning with "eternal" (*nitya*). The phrase "whose sole nature is eternal, liberated, self-luminous consciousness" contains a reason within itself (*hetugarbha*). "Eternal liberation" (*nityamuktatva*) means being, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), untouched by defects. Therefore, an ultimately real defect is not possible.

The meaning is that because its nature is one's own self-experience (*svānubhava*), the experience of another—which is not the ultimate reality—is impossible. Furthermore, the intention of the word "one" (*eka*) is due to the absence of any spatial differentiation (*pradeśabheda*) consisting of the experience of another. By the word "one," the absence of being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatvābhāva*) is also intended. He explains the intended inclusion of the reason by the phrase "because its nature is one's own self-experience. What is intended as the reason is the state of having the sole nature of one's own self-experience, which persists during the stage of the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) and is the opposite of the appearance of ignorance.

However, it is not merely the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) that exists even at the time of delusion; therefore, the meaning is that the nature of being solely one's own experience (*svānubhavaikasvabhāvatva*) exists even prior [to the delusion]. He raises the objection that "the experience of ignorance is possible because even the essential nature of one's own experience can be concealed" by the words *svānubhava*.

In order to explain his intended meaning and to demonstrate that there is no other possible meaning for the word *tirodhāna*, he states the meaning of the term by way of a question: "What is this state of having one's nature concealed (*tirohitasvarūpatvam*)? He then introduces the objection: "If it means 'having one's nature unmanifested (*apramāśitasvarūpatvam*),'... He refutes this with the words "svānubhava... (one's own experience), considering that it is contradictory for that which is of the nature of one's own experience to be unmanifested. He extends the previously mentioned refutation to the case where the nature is unmanifested due to something else, with the words "evam tarhi... (if that were so...).

He states another objection with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). [The opponent argues: Because it is not ultimately real (*aparamārthatvāt*), ignorance does not obscure through its own existence (*sattayā*), but rather it obscures by being perceived (*pratīyamānatayā*); thus, the obscuration is preceded by experience. Conversely, experience is preceded by obscuration, because it is impossible to experience the nature of Brahman—which is one's own experience—without first having obscured it. This is the meaning of the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*). Desiring to avoid this, the opponent suggests that the obscuration is indeed preceded by experience, stating: "It has been experienced. To that, he states the refutation: "If... (*yadi*).

The meaning is that since the experience of ignorance is possible even regarding that which is not concealed, the postulation of its concealment and the postulation of a veiling ignorance (*avidyā*) for that purpose are fruitless. He demonstrates this with the words "of Brahman."

The meaning is as follows: just as the experience of ignorance—which is not ultimately real—is possible even for that whose nature is unobscured, so too the experience of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is not ultimately real, is possible for that which is unobscured; therefore, the postulation of obscuration and the postulation of ignorance as its concealer are fruitless. He states the refutation by way of an alternative regarding the position that [the concealment] precedes the experience, beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca). In the view that [concealment occurs] inherently, there are two defects: the impossibility of liberation and the cessation of the very nature of Brahman.

By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "of the experience of silver also," the cessation of the silver itself is indicated. In the alternative view [where the silver is real], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). He raises an objection regarding the view that [the silver] is experienced after being set aside (*tiraskāra*): "Brahman... When it is said that [the silver] is the object of experience after being set aside, it would mean that Brahman sets it aside by its very existence (*sattā*), and not by way of being perceived (*pratīyamānatayā*). In that case, the fact that [the silver] is removable by knowledge as something ultimately real—like a cataract (*kāca*) or similar defects—would not be established. This is the meaning.

Now, he raises the doubt that the experience of concealment and [the experience of] the object might be simultaneous with the words "atha idam" (now this). He refutes this with the passage beginning "na etat" (not so), etc. The phrase "of the nature of its own experience" (*svānubhava-svarūpasya*) is a qualification containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). The meaning is that since being of the nature of one's own experience is intrinsic, the experience of another cannot be accounted for without a cause. Having raised the possibility of concealment by means of some other cause, he refutes it with the word "hetu" (cause), etc.

With the intention of showing that even the refutations of the two previously mentioned positions apply to the position of simultaneity (*yaugapadyapakṣa*), he says: "And the previously mentioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*) [follows]. This infinite regress also serves as an indication for the refutation regarding the impossibility of being sublated by knowledge (*jñānānivartyatva*); this is because it was mentioned immediately prior. He states the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) in the case of establishing witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) without the concealment of one's own nature (*svarūpatiraskṛti*): "If unconcealed... (*atiraskṛta*). Previously, a refutation was stated while accepting the appearance as either clear or unclear; now, however, he begins to refute that very point with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).

"One conceptualizes through ignorance"—this refers back to the previously stated refutation. Regarding "in the former" and "in the latter": the word *kim* is used in the sense of censure; the meaning is that it is untenable. The point is that since even words such as "Being," "Consciousness," and "Bliss" are admitted to refer merely to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the distinction between being obscured and not being obscured is untenable. [One must ask: what part of this is obscured, and what part is manifested?

This [statement] is also intended as an illustration of the question: "What specific feature is concealed, or what is revealed? This follows immediately from the preceding statement that [Reality] is partless (*niraṃśa*) and devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*). What is this "part"? The intention is that a division into parts cannot be asserted. He establishes this by saying "partless. In the phrase "in mere luminosity" (*prakāśamātre*), the suffix *-mātra* is intended to signify the absence of being an object (*aviṣayatva*). The meaning is "that which has not become an object. As for the phrase "they do not coexist simultaneously": you certainly do not maintain that manifestation and concealment occur at different times.

Rather, they occur simultaneously. The point is that at that time, because there is no distinction of parts and no distinction of forms, those two [manifestation and concealment] do not coexist. Thus, since the simultaneity of manifestation and concealment is untenable, he objects with the word "indistinct" (*aviśada*), beginning with "Now" (*atha*). The word "now" (*atha*) is used here to grant a concession. He refutes this with the words "manifestation," etc. What is its nature? The meaning is that it is untenable.

In response to the doubt as to how [the manifestation] is untenable, he says, "This has been stated," in order to teach the nature of clarity (*vaiśadya*) and lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*), and to demonstrate their untenability in this context. He teaches the nature of clarity with the words beginning "that which is partless" (*yassāṃśa*). He states the untenability of that [manifestation] in cognition with the word "therein" (*tatra*); the meaning is that because of the very absence of illumination (*prakāśa*), there is no lack of clarity of illumination, since the absence of a property follows from the absence of its substratum (*dharmin*).

He says, "Even with regard to the object" (*viṣaye 'pi*), because even in the case of the knowable, since the known portion is clear and the unknown portion remains unknown, a lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*) is not possible anywhere. The meaning is this: in a single entity, the non-manifestation of some parts or some aspects constitutes a lack of clarity regarding the totality (*samuditarūpa*); however, there is no lack of clarity regarding that portion which is actually shining forth therein. Therefore, the phrase "while its own nature is shining forth" (*svarūpe prakāśamāne*) does not connect with the preceding clause "in Brahman," but rather with the subsequent one.

The meaning is that when the true nature of an object (*vastu-svarūpa*) is manifesting, a lack of clarity (*avaiśadya*)—consisting in the non-apprehension of certain particularities—is not possible in the case of Brahman. The phrase "non-apprehension of certain particularities" is intended to include the non-apprehension of certain parts as well. He states another refutation with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*): [otherwise] its effect and its cessation would not exist; the point is that a clear essential nature (*viśada-svarūpa*) is by its very nature opposed to ignorance (*avidyā*). [Regarding the phrase] "because liberation would be an effect": this refers to liberation as the state of being released (*mukta-svarūpa*).

The meaning is as follows: since that which is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) is necessarily impermanent when it is an effect, and since clarity (*vaiśadya*) is of the nature of a positive entity, the refutation you stated against the opponent's view applies to you yourself. If you argue that the consequence of the impermanence of clarity—which was previously non-existent and subsequently produced—is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because its permanence is established by scripture, then the intention is that Brahman would thereby possess distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*).

He states "of this" (*asya*) to present the previously mentioned untenability of the substratum as a counter-argument (*pratikūlatarka*) against the opponent's definition of perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*). Keeping in mind that the refutations based on the beginninglessness of the nature [of consciousness] and so forth are merely parallel arguments (*pratibandī*), he states another objection with the words "moreover" (*api ca*). Just as the occurrence of error is possible even if the locus of defects and non-defects is not ultimately real, so too error is possible even if the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not ultimately real.

If it is argued that since the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is non-ultimate (*apāramārthya*), it too—like the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—is non-ultimate, and thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of another substratum, then by the same logic, since the defect (*doṣa*) is also non-ultimate like the phenomenal world, there would likewise be an infinite regress due to the requirement of another defect. If it is argued that even though the defect is non-ultimate, there is no infinite regress because its own nature (*svarūpa*) is beginningless (*anādi*), then [we reply] that even though the substratum is non-ultimate, there is no infinite regress because its own nature is also beginningless. Furthermore, the resolution based on being beginningless as a continuous flow (*pravāha-anāditva*) and being difficult to grasp (*durdharṭatva*) is equal in both cases.

If it is argued that the defect (*doṣa*) which brings about the perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and one's own philosophical system (*svadarśana*) is itself its own sustainer, and thus there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the requirement of further defects, we say: no. This is because it is impossible for something that is not ultimately real (*aparamārtha*) to be the sustainer of both itself and another. For instance, in a dream, the pressing of a finger—which is the cause of the cognition of two moons—is not independent of a defect in its own conceptualization. Even if it were possible for something unreal to sustain both itself and another, then even if the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) were not ultimately real, there would be no infinite regress, as it would sustain both itself and another.

If it is argued that the self-establishing nature [of the substratum] is established only once the ultimate reality's status as a substratum for another is established, then it is equally true that its self-maintaining nature is established only once the ultimate reality's status as a defect for another is established. If it is argued that its status as a defect is established because of the appearance of the world as something false, then its status as a substratum is likewise established from that very same fact; thus, the substratum's self-and-other-establishing nature is proven.

If it is argued that no error is observed when the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), the intention [of the author] is that this inquiry applies equally: even when the defect (*doṣa*) and its locus (*doṣāśraya*) are not ultimately real, no error is observed. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And therefore... Thus, it has been stated that the perception "I am ignorant; I do not know myself and others" is sublated by counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*). On this point, some say: the inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*) of the subsequent reflection (*parāmarśa*) of one who has risen from sleep—"I was not aware of anything"—is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for ignorance as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*).

How is it that [the experience] cannot be explained otherwise? It is as follows: the reflective awareness "I knew nothing" does not have the absence of cognition as its object; for during deep sleep, the absence of cognition has not been experienced. Indeed, if there were an experience of the absence of cognition, one would have to admit the manifestation of the counter-positive—the cognition—qualified by its objects. To admit that would contradict the state of deep sleep. Nor should it be argued that this is a cognition in the form of an inference, produced by the mark of non-remembrance, which has the absence of cognition as its object.

Because non-recollection is not necessarily pervaded by a lack of experience—for instance, grass or similar objects touched by one walking on a path are not remembered—therefore, the positive entity that is ignorance experienced during deep sleep is remembered as "I was not aware of anything. Consequently, the existence of positive ignorance is established through the otherwise inexplicability of this recollection.

This is not tenable, because even if ignorance were of a positive nature, its dependence on a counter-correlate (pratiyogin) has been established; and since no counter-correlate is manifest during deep sleep, there can be no experience of ignorance, and thus no recollection of it is possible. Furthermore, you yourself have stated that the manifestation of a counter-correlate would contradict the state of deep sleep.

Nor can it be argued that at that time there appeared as manifest a cognition whose nature consists of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of the object residing elsewhere; for we understand from the experience "I was not aware of anything" and "I do not know myself or another" that the cognition delimited by an object functions as the counter-correlative. Therefore, if that [cognition] were not manifest, the experience of ignorance would be impossible, and thus the recollection of it would be untenable.

Furthermore, is there an experience of positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) during deep sleep through either an indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) or a determinate (*savikalpaka*) mental operation (*manovyāpāra*)? In the first case, since it is not admitted that the indeterminate cognition—which you yourself maintain to be of the nature of the manifestation of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*)—can produce a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the subsequent recollection would be untenable. Nor is the second case possible; because of the contradiction with the state of deep sleep, a mental operation cannot occur at that time. Therefore, the cognition "I was aware of nothing" is not a memory.

However, non-apprehension characterized by non-recollection has as its object the absence of knowledge, taking the form of an inference. Nor is there a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the non-recollection of grass and such things touched while walking on a path; for there is no deviation when non-recollection is qualified by the absence of factors that obstruct the mental impression (saṃskāra), such as distraction toward other objects.
[The obstructing factors are: "Lack of intent toward that [object], lack of sharpness of cognition, intense pain and the like, insanity, lack of repetition, and long duration [of time]."

"In these cases [of non-recollection], an imperfection in the unseen (adṛṣṭa) must be postulated as obstructing the latent impression (saṃskāra). From the fact that recollection does not occur when these [obstructive factors] are absent, the absence of knowledge is inferred.

When one walking on a path touches grass and such things, they are not remembered because of the presence of something that opposes the arising of a vivid latent impression. For one walking on a path is distracted by thoughts of the destination and duties to be performed. Furthermore, there is no attention directed toward the grass and so forth, due to the absence of a purpose. Even in the absence of such [attention], the cognition of grass and such is not vivid—just like the sight of an elephant and other objects—because of the lack of the object's vastness, variety, and so on.

However, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from experience in a previous birth remains unawakened due to being overwhelmed by the intense suffering produced at death, in hell, and at rebirth. Furthermore, insanity is an obstacle to the awakening of latent impressions, as is lack of practice, since it is observed to be a cause of forgetfulness. Even the long duration of time is seen to cause its loss, as things experienced in childhood are not remembered in old age. Yet none of these causes exist during deep sleep (*suṣupti*); nor can any unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) be postulated that opposes the awakening of latent impressions.

Because there is no warranting factor (*kalpaka*), it is impossible to postulate either the ignorance of deep sleep or an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that obstructs the recollection of objects belonging to its domain. Even if something were imagined as a warranting factor, such a postulation would not be tenable when the matter can be resolved through non-postulation (*akalpanā*). Thus, this cognition—"I was not aware of anything"—consists in an inference of the absence of knowledge, characterized by the mark of non-recollection (*asmarana*) as qualified by the absence of causes that would otherwise obstruct the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of other [objects], such as being directed toward something else.

You yourself have also admitted the absence of knowledge during deep sleep; and it must be admitted that this is inferable solely from the aforementioned marks. That [absence] is equally [established] for us as well. Therefore, since the status of [the experience] as memory is untenable and its nature as an inference is established, the cognition "I did not know anything" is explained otherwise; thus, the existence of positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) is not proven by that. The untenability of such fallacious arguments is established by the refutation of the perception whose object is positive ignorance.

Now, he refutes inference with the words beginning "that which has been stated," etc. The phrase "due to the impossibility of inference" means that the inference you have stated is merely a fallacy (ābhāsa). To the question "In what way is it poorly stated? he replies: "Even in the case of ignorance," and so forth. In response to the doubt—"How is the proof of another instance of ignorance necessarily entailed? And why is that undesirable?"—he establishes its necessity by saying "therein. He establishes the undesirability of ignorance by saying "and in the case of a proof," etc. To the question "What follows from that? he says: "And therefore," etc.

Since this valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) illuminates an object not previously illuminated, it establishes another ignorance that serves as a veil over its own object; thus, that ignorance veils the very ignorance intended to be proven as that which obscures the nature of Brahman. Because it is veiled by that [other] ignorance, that ignorance is not directly perceived by Brahman. Since that which is unreal and unperceived cannot function as an effect, the postulation of such ignorance would be fruitless; for its postulation is indeed for the sake of an effect in the form of concealment (*tirodhāna*).

If that which is not itself directly perceived were to produce an effect, then, by producing an effect through its mere existence, it would—like glass or other such materials—be real and thus could not be sublated by knowledge. Thus, regarding the point that ignorance is not sublatable by knowledge and is therefore fruitless, it has been stated that it would establish another, unintended ignorance as its cause; and if it does not so establish it, the reason is shown to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Now, it may be argued: if the cognition produced by the stated reason is of the nature of a correct ascertainment, then due to that very contradiction, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the reason. If, on the other hand, it is not correct, even so there is no inconclusiveness of the reason, because the reason—"the illumination of an unillumined object"—does not apply to that case. It is replied: the avoidance of the inconclusiveness of the reason precludes the cognition of the object of the probandum from being of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramiti*); whereas the correctness of the cognition, however, precludes the avoidance of the inconclusiveness of the reason.

Therefore, if knowledge were correct, its being produced by the aforementioned cause would be contradicted, because that cause is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For correct knowledge is never produced by a defective cause. If it is argued that the aforementioned cause is not inconclusive, then its capacity to produce knowledge in the form of an incorrect ascertainment (*asamyag-niścaya*) is contradicted; for it is impossible for a non-defective cause to produce incorrect knowledge.

The intention [of the opponent] is this: since the excellence of the knowledge that avoids the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the reason and [the existence of] ignorance are mutually contradictory, they cannot be combined here; thus, even if one of the two is absent, there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*), and therefore inference is untenable. Now, it may be argued that there is no inconclusiveness of the reason, because the reason does not operate within the cognition whose object is the probandum. For it is not the case that this [reason] illuminates an unmanifested ignorance; what then? It merely performs a discrimination (*vivecana*) of the ignorance already established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), because [ignorance] is not something non-existent.

It is not so; for if ignorance were established by the self-luminous consciousness (*svarūpacaitanya*) which transcends the light that constitutes the attribute of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), then there would be the fallacy of a vicious circle (*cakraka*): the validity of inference would depend on the establishment of ignorance; the establishment of positive ignorance would depend on the validity of that inference; and the establishment of the experience of ignorance would depend on the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) which transcends that [inference], since even the knower is itself imagined by that [ignorance]. Thus, this circularity is insurmountable.

He states another objection with the words "And the example," and so forth. In this regard, there are four possible alternatives: (1) is it the state of being an illuminator directly; (2) or by way of a succession; (3) or merely the state of being an illuminator, whether directly or by succession; (4) or is it the state of being an illuminator consisting in the removal of the obscuration of its own object? Among these, in the first alternative, the example is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*). In the second, however, there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*) regarding the subject (*pakṣa*). In the third, however, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntyam*) with respect to the sense organs.

This is because they lack the quality of being preceded by another entity that is not itself reversible; for these [lights], whether directly or indirectly, possess the nature of being one or the other of two illuminators. Even if the sense organs (*indriya*) are taken as the subject of the proposition, it is improper to postulate that they too are preceded by such an entity, because the sense organs—being derived from *ahaṅkāra*—arise without being preceded by any other entity that either obscures their respective objects or occupies their own location; for only light possesses such a character.

Regarding the fourth alternative, however, with the intention that [the probans] would be non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*), he states the refutation of the first position: "and the example is devoid of the probans. In response to the doubt as to how cognition alone possesses the quality of being a direct illuminator, he establishes that point with the words "even though" (*satyapi*). By the phrase "cognition alone has the quality of being an illuminator," it is implied that in the second position, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). By the phrase "of the sense organs" (*indriyāṇām*), he intends to show that in the third position, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the sense organs.

The capacity of the light of a lamp to illuminate even through a succession [of objects] is far removed [from the case at hand]; thus he says, "In the case of a lamp," etc. He asks how there can be the conventional usage of "illuminating" [in the case of cognition], and so he says, "That which illuminates," etc. He raises the fourth alternative with the words, "Not by us," etc. [He explains] "by way of refutation" as meaning "through the medium of refutation. He states that [the reason] is non-different from the probandum (sādhyāviśiṣṭatva) with the words, "For indeed," etc. For cognition does not possess an illuminating nature consisting in the removal of a veil over the object; rather, that [removal] is the very probandum (sādhya), and it is not something already established (saṃpratipanna)—this is the meaning.

The suffix *-mātra* serves to exclude the delimitation of the object (*artha-pariccheda*). By the word *hi*, it is implied that the capacity to remove the veil over the object (*viṣayāvaraṇa-nirāsakatva*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). In this regard, he states "but rather" (*api tu*) to express the well-established nature of luminosity (*prakāśakatva*). To prevent the suspicion that the word *pariccheda* implies limitation (*parimiti*), he says "in terms of linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra*). "Fitness for linguistic usage" (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*) means being related to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-pratisambandhitva*). [Objection: But is this not a case where the reason (*hetu*) is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*)?

By the phrase "removing the obscuration of its own object," what is intended is the removal of its own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāva*). Therefore, the probandum (*sādhya*) is that [the cognition] is preceded by a removable entity in the form of a positive state (*bhāvarūpa*). This is not so; for the reason (*hetu*) "being the remover of its own prior non-existence" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when applied to the simultaneous operation with the sense organs. Even if the reason is qualified as "being the illuminator of an unilluminated object while itself being manifest," the same alternative options (*vikalpa*) would arise as before. In that case, regarding the direct position (*pakṣa*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

In the first case (*praṇāḍyā*), the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). In the third, there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to [inferential] marks (*liṅga*) and so forth. In the fourth, there is non-difference from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭatā*); for it is not admitted that the quality of removing the veil over the object is qualified by "being manifest" (*bhāsamānatva*).

Now, he states that this inference is refuted by counter-reasoning (*pratikūlatarka*) with the words "and the counter-arguments" (*pratiprayogāśca*). Because reasoning (*tarka*) is also rooted in pervasion (*vyāpti*), the term "arguments" (*prayogāḥ*) is used. Three counter-inferences are stated, taking ignorance as the subject (*pakṣa*), which are respectively opposed to [the properties of] being located in its own locus, being an obscuration of its own object, and being removable by itself. The phrase "residing in Brahman, not residing in that [object]" means "that which is the subject of dispute"; thus, there is an exclusion of the ignorance regarding nacre and the like.

For that [ignorance] has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus; and even though this positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) called ignorance is not established by valid means of knowledge, opposing arguments (*pratikūlatarka*) are stated on the basis of the admission that Brahman is pure consciousness alone. To the question of how the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and the like can have something other than consciousness as its locus, he says: "It has the knower as its locus. In this way, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is shown. What is meant is that if something is ignorance, it follows that it cannot have consciousness as its locus. He states another opposing argument with the words "in the dispute," etc. He demonstrates the pervasion with the words "obscuration of the object," etc.

The meaning is that if [Brahman] were ignorance (*ajñāna*), it would follow as a logical consequence that it is not an obscuration of knowledge (*jñānānāvaraṇatva*). Regarding the third syllogism as well, the meaning is that if Brahman were not an obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyānāvaraṇatva*), it would follow as a logical consequence that it is not removable by knowledge (*jñānānivartyatva*). Now, taking Brahman as the subject (*pakṣa*), three counter-arguments (*pratikūlatarka*) are stated beginning with the words "Brahman" and so forth. The meaning is that if Brahman were the locus of ignorance, it would follow as a logical consequence that Brahman is a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Regarding the second syllogism as well, the meaning is that if Brahman were an obscuration of ignorance, it would follow as a logical consequence that it is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).
Regarding the third as well, the meaning is that if Brahman were ignorance removable by knowledge, it would follow as a logical consequence that it is an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*).

Now, taking valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), he states the counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*) for its being distinct from antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) with the words "that which is the subject of dispute" (*vivādādhyāsita*). The meaning is that if [valid cognition] were valid cognition, it would follow that it is not preceded by an ignorance distinct from antecedent non-existence. Alternatively, this is indeed an inference (*anumāna*). For in the case of continuous streams of cognition (*dhārāvāhikajñāna*), it is appropriate for the first [cognition] to be the subject and the subsequent cognitions to be the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). By the statement beginning with "Cognition does not destroy the object," a negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*) has been stated.

He demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) in two ways with the words "yadvastunaḥ" (of whatever object). The reason (*hetu*) is indeed qualified as "because it is cognition (*jñānatva*) in the absence of being augmented by a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*). In that context, since there is no difference in being distinct from cognition augmented by a specific power—whether it be cognition augmented by a specific power or non-cognition (*ajñāna*) not augmented by a specific power—both are the ground for the negative concomitance; thus, the concomitance is shown in both cases.

Having taken positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*) as the subject of the argument, he says, "it is of the nature of a positive entity. The meaning is that if it were of the nature of a positive entity, it could not be removable by knowledge alone. He raises the objection regarding the failure of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that there is no necessary concomitance between being a positive entity and being removable by knowledge—on the grounds that fear and the like, though positive entities, are seen to be removable by knowledge, saying, "Now, it might be argued... [The phrase] "of those produced by prior knowledge" means "of those produced by prior erroneous cognition."

The sense is that fear persists prior to the arising of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), and fear and so forth cease after its production. He refutes this, saying "not so. For effects that perish [immediately] are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) in the sense that their destruction is dependent on the destruction of their own substratum (or, as the variant suggests, they possess a destruction dependent on the destruction of their own substratum). The aforementioned qualification excludes the flame [from being considered momentary in this specific sense]. Thus, the meaning is that fear and so forth also perish of their own accord after producing an effect such as trembling. If it is argued that fear and so forth do not possess momentariness because they are perceived over a long duration, we say no.

For the continuous arising of fear and so forth occurs through the persistence of the deluded cognition that serves as its cause; thus, there is a perception [of it] over a long duration. If it is argued that, in that case, the continuity of fear should be perceived at all times, he says in response: "And because of the non-arising later due to the cessation of the cause. The meaning is that because the continuity of the effect—fear and so forth—does not arise once the cause—the deluded cognition and so on—has ceased, there is no perception [of it] at all times. The phrase "non-arising later" (paścādanutpattiḥ) connects with the preceding [term] "due to momentariness" (kṣaṇikatvena), which is expressed in the ablative case.

The meaning is that because it does not arise later once its cause has ceased, its momentariness is established by its own destruction. Alternatively, in response to the doubt that "there is no momentariness," the connection is made with the sentence drawn forth by the force of the context: "momentariness is established. Thus, the objection concerning the necessary concomitance of momentariness has been resolved.

Alternatively, in order to establish the thesis of refutation—that it is not so [that fear ceases immediately upon the knowledge of its cause]—he states that the persistence of the nature of fear until its sublation is unproven by the phrase "due to momentariness. He further states that its cessation after the subverting cognition is otherwise accounted for by the phrase "and by the cessation of its cause. In response to the doubt as to how that momentariness is established, he demonstrates it with the words "and momentariness... For objects such as jars, being enduring, are observed to perish when their causes, such as the staff and the wheel, cease; however, this is not the case for cognitions, lamp-flames, and the like.

The meaning is that, likewise, even in the case of fear and so forth, momentariness is ascertained because their presence and absence follow the proximity and cessation of their causes. He states the refutation for the contrary position (*vipakṣe bādha*) with the words "if it were non-momentary" (*akṣaṇikatve ceti*). For stable objects such as jars are perceived as many arising at every moment simultaneously; the point is that the same would result here [in the case of fear] as well. Therefore, fear and so forth are not to be removed by knowledge; they perish of their own accord due to their momentariness.

The cessation of the continuity of fear occurs through the removal of the causal basis, which is the succession of erroneous cognitions. And that removal [of the cause] occurs through the removal of defects. The cognition "this is not a snake, it is a rope" is the cause for the practical engagement (*vyavahāra*) regarding its own object; however, it is not the direct cause for the cessation of fear and so forth. For the nature of being a rope is simply the exclusion of being a snake.

Therefore, the refutation has been stated according to the method accepted by all: because of the absence of the knowledge of "rope-ness" (which consists in the exclusion of the snake), the cognition of the snake persists, and consequently the subsequent fear persists; whereas through the knowledge of "rope-ness" (which consists in the exclusion of the snake), the conceit of the snake's reality ceases, and thus the fear ceases. In our own position, however, fear and the like are merely specific cognitions that perish of their own accord due to their momentariness. The persistence of the cognition in the form of fear and so on is rooted in the persistence of the delusion of the snake and such, caused by a defect; and with the cessation of that [delusion], there is the cessation of its continuum—this is the resolution.

Thus, the refutation of the meaning has been stated; now he states the refutation of the formal argument (*prayoga*) with the words "svaprāgabhāva" (its own prior non-existence). The words *sva* (own), *prāk* (prior), *abhāvavyatirikta* (distinct from non-existence), and *antara* (other) are redundant. For the word *vastu* (entity) indeed denotes existence (*bhāva*). He concludes the failure to establish ignorance as a positive entity through inference with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). Anticipating the objection that it is established through scripture (*śruti*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he says "śruti" (scripture).

He refutes in detail the reason stated by the opponent regarding indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) with the words "pratīti" (cognition), etc. "Cognition" (*pratīti*) is a form common to both error (*bhrānti*) and non-error (*abhrānti*). "Error" (*bhrānti*) is that which is produced by the apprehension of a common form preceded by the non-apprehension of an existing difference; it is characterized by its object being otherwise than it appears, and it serves as the cause for activity and so forth. "Sublation" (*bādha*) is a cognition that penetrates the nature of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is opposed to what has been superimposed. "It should not be accepted in that way" means that it should not be accepted as being indeterminable.

Intending the alternative that the establishment of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) occurs either through the mere mention of its own object by cognition, error, and sublation, or else through *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability), he first refutes the former with the words "that which is being cognized" (*pratīyamānam*). "Being cognized" means that which is being delineated by cognition. For the delineation of blue cannot be accepted as the delineation of yellow; for if that were the case, it would follow that everything is in chaos—this is the sense. He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "by these" (*ābhiḥ*).

By these perceptions—those conveyed by the terms "cognition," "error," and "sublation"—which are direct perceptions (*pratyakṣapratīti*); or by these worldly cognitions (*laukikapratīti*) as opposed to another cognition produced by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as that produced by scripture (*āgama*); or alternatively, the plural number is used with reference to the multiplicity of [erroneous appearances] such as the snake, the ground, and the stream of water, all having a single substratum (*ekādhiṣṭhāna*). By "another cognition" is meant a sublatting cognition (*bādhajñāna*).

To expand upon the concise refutation, he restates the opponent's view [beginning with] "in the case of mother-of-pearl, etc.," and [concludes with] "because it is impossible for one thing to appear as something else."

Now, one might ask: how is it that there is no possibility of appearing otherwise? It is said in reply: First of all, "appearing otherwise" (anyathākhyāti) does not consist in the identity between the property (*dharma*) and the substrate (*dharmin*). The white, shining fragment situated in front is not perceived as having the universal of silver-ness (*rajatatva*), nor is silver-ness perceived as having the nature of the white, shining fragment. Furthermore, the fragment is perceived as a fragment, and the universal is perceived as a universal. Therefore, there is no perception of either one as being the other.

Nor can there be the identity or transformation (*anyathātva*) of one substratum (*dharmin*) into another substratum. Is that [transformation] located in the object, or is it located in the cognition? If it exists in the object, then the cognition is indeed "according to the object" (*yathārtha*). If it does not exist [in the object], then the consequence follows that it is a manifestation of what is non-existent (*asatkhyāti*). If it is located in the cognition, then it is untenable for the object to be one thing and the cognition to be quite another; for it is impossible for the cognition of a jar to be the cognition of a cloth. Furthermore, this would entail the consequence of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), because silver and the like would possess the form of the cognition itself.

If it is argued that "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) is the appearance of a form that does not exist in the object itself, we say no; for this would entail the consequence of "the apprehension of the non-existent" (*asatkhyāti*). If it is argued that misapprehension is the appearance elsewhere of what exists elsewhere, we say no; for this would result in the erroneousness of perceiving "cowness"—seen in a spotted cow—when it is seen in a hornless one. If it is argued that misapprehension is the appearance elsewhere of what exists only elsewhere, how is its existence "only elsewhere" determined? If you say "because of sublation (*bādha*) here," we say no.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even real silver, which is sublated by erroneous cognition, would be determined as non-existent here. If it is argued that the determination of existence occurs elsewhere because of the sublation of the [subsequent] activity, we say no; for then there would be the undesirable consequence that even fire, when its capacity is obstructed by mantras or medicinal herbs, would be determined as false due to the sublation of the activity of producing a burn or similar effects. If it is argued that it is sublated here because it is the object of a cognition produced by a defective cause, then how is the fact of being produced by a defective cause itself determined?

If it is argued that [the falsity of the first cognition] arises from the emergence of a sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), then the preceding cognition itself would be the sublater. For it has already been shown that posteriority is irrelevant. Furthermore, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): once it is ascertained that the preceding cognition was produced by a defective cause, the sublativeness of the subsequent cognition is ascertained; and once the sublativeness of the latter is ascertained, the fact that the former was produced by a defective cause is ascertained.

Furthermore, as for that silver which appeared as being present before one, what is the proof for its existence elsewhere? It cannot be the prior cognition, for that makes it known as existing *here*. Nor can it be the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*), for that makes known its non-existence in another place. Nor can it be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the silver, for that indeed makes known the existence of silver in the marketplace, but not its identity with that which is manifested here before one.

If it is argued that because the appearance of what is non-existent anywhere is impossible, it is determined that only what exists elsewhere appears [here], we say no; for the impossibility of the appearance of the non-existent has already been abandoned in the case of the relation [of superimposition]. Indeed, neither the relation with the substrate (dharmī) of silver nor the relation with the universal (jāti) of silverness exists elsewhere in the object present before one. If it is argued that while there is merely a relation elsewhere, that very thing appears here—thus the appearance of what exists elsewhere occurs here—we say no, because two relations are not perceived.

In the case of a relation existing elsewhere appearing elsewhere, another relation would have to be required as if for the related entity itself. And if there were the appearance of yet another relation, there would be no appearance elsewhere of that which exists elsewhere, because a second relation does not exist anywhere at all.

If it is argued that because a relation does not depend on another relation, its manifestation in the object present before one is logical even in the absence of another relation—then, in that case, since there is a relation with another related entity and that which is present before one manifests without interval, this would simply be called "yathārthakhyāti" (the theory that cognition corresponds to reality); for the manifested portion exists, and nothing non-existent can ever be manifested.

Furthermore, it is also improper to attempt to prove that "the fragment of mother-of-pearl alone is the object of the cognition of silver, because—while being distinct from the means for obtaining silver—it is the object of the activity of one seeking silver. For instance, what is to be proven here is that the object "this" (idamartha) is the object of a cognition qualified by the universal of silverness; however, since this is necessitated by its being the object of uncontradicted activity, the reason is *sopādhika* (vitiated by a limiting condition). Moreover, there is sublation (*bādha*) by the inference: "The mother-of-pearl does not appear as silver, because it possesses the nature of mother-of-pearl, like any other well-established case. It is with the intention of pointing out such refutations, and on the grounds that "one thing appearing as another is impossible," that it was stated [in the previous verse].

"It does not corrupt [the object]," he says. "Apprehending as qualified by a form that exists elsewhere while it appears as being in front is *anyathākhyāti* (apprehension otherwise). Furthermore, the ascertainment of the absence of the perceived form in the thing standing before one arises from the cognition 'it is not,' which is accompanied by the sublation of the initial inclination to act. For it is well known that there is no cognition that 'the firehood of a fire connected [with smoke] does not exist' when one has a cognition of fire. In response to the inquiry, 'How is it that even in the case of *kalpanā* (conceptual construction) the occurrence of *anyathākhyāti* is unavoidable?', he says: 'For that which is being conceptualized...'"

If one accepts the cognition that [the object] is "indefinable," then that cognition would be of the nature of an error, and there would be neither sublation nor purposeful activity. The meaning is that if the indefinable were cognized as being definable, the appearance of reality (*tattva*) as something other than what it is would be unavoidable. And because that [appearance] cannot be avoided. "That" refers to the appearance as something else. This is the intended sense: "There is no appearance of one thing as another, because only that which exists is cognized. Reality is twofold: the transcendental reality (*alaukika-sat*) and the empirical reality (*laukika-sat*)."

If it is argued that "in the indeterminable (anirvacanīya), there exists a non-worldly existence (alaukika-sattva), and it is this non-worldly existent silver that is perceived here," then does that non-worldly existent appear as having non-worldly existence, or as having worldly existence? In the first case, there would be the impossibility of error, sublation, and purposeful activity. If the non-worldly is perceived as being a worldly existent, then there would be the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti).

If it is argued that the occurrence of activity and so forth is possible due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between the transcendental real (*alaukikasat*) and the empirical real (*laukikasat*), then—rather than postulating an indeterminable object (*anirvacanīya vastu*) there and establishing the falsity of the sublated error through the non-apprehension of its distinction from that [empirical] object—it is simpler by way of parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*) to establish the falsity of the sublated error through the non-apprehension of the distinction between the accepted silver and the nature of the mother-of-pearl (*śuktikātva*). With this sequence of arguments in mind, [the author states: "the indeterminable object is untenable," and so forth.

And it has been stated that this [error] is unavoidable. With the intention that among the views other than *yathārthakhyāti* (the theory that cognition is always of the object as it is), the view of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory that there is a misapprehension of the object) is the most powerful, he says, "by another theory of manifestation" (*khyātyantareti*). This means even after going very far and having abandoned a succession of arguments. He explains that with the words, "the non-existent" (*asaditi*). How is the Madhyamaka position? Is it perceived as merely "non-existent," or as "existent"? If you say it is perceived as "non-existent," then error, sublation, and purposeful activity would be impossible.

If it is argued that [the object] is "existent" (*sat*), the meaning is that there would be the appearance of one thing as another. Regarding the term "self" (*ātman*): this is the position of the Yogācāra school. Here, the word "self" refers to cognition (*jñāna*). Is it cognized as "what is cognition? or as "what is the object? In the first case, there is no possibility of activity, sublation, or error. In the second case, the meaning is that there is the appearance of one thing as another. Regarding the position of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*): is "this is silver" a single cognition?

Alternatively, intending the alternative that there are two cognitions, he raises the consequence of "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) regarding the object of knowledge under the view that there is a single cognition, stating: "the qualifier of one thing is [cognized] as the qualifier of another. It was established that "this is silver" is cognized as the qualifier of one thing being the qualifier of another, because it is perceived through a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consistent with the application of the mark (*liṅga*) of the superimposed [silver], just like a real piece of silver recognized as a unity; however, that specific position [of misapprehension] was not what was actually put forward [in the previous argument].

In the view that there are two cognitions, he points out the consequence of "misapprehension" (*anyathākhyāti*) regarding cognition by the word "jñāna. As for the dilemma: is the "two cognitions" perceived as exactly two cognitions, or as one? The refutation is as before. Regarding the phrase "the non-existence of the object": is it perceived as being non-existent, or is it perceived as being existent? In the first case, there is the impossibility of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth. In the second case, the meaning is that there is an appearance otherwise (*anyathābhāna*).

Now, he establishes the lack of a cause with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). Of that perception (*pratyakṣapratīti*): by its having that [non-existence] as its object, meaning by its having an existent thing as its causal object. For the sense is that a cause must necessarily precede [its effect]. This is an argument provided by the great [teachers].

The meaning is that it is utterly untenable [to claim] that the causal status of that cognitive function (*vṛtti-jñāna*) is accepted by admitting a state devoid of an object; for this would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Furthermore, if the occurrence of activity and so forth were established through its influence—as is the case for those who maintain the theory of cognition without an object (*nirviṣaya-khyāti*)—then the postulation of the "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*) would be useless. This is because it would imply production without the cause consisting of an object, and because it would imply a cessation of operation followed by a renewed activity. Now, regarding the phrase "the sense organs, etc. (*athendriyādi*): by the word "etc.," defects residing in the object or the inattention of the person are included.

Regarding the phrase "because it has the person as its locus": although defects such as distance reside in the object (*viṣaya*), since it is also possible for them to reside in the person (*puruṣa*), the effect must be produced in both; it cannot be produced in the object alone, as there would be no determining factor [to restrict it]. Therefore, the intention is that [the defect] cannot exist in the object in the same way it exists in the person. Now, one might object: even though the eye has the person as its locus, we observe that the visual ray, having issued forth and come into contact with the object, produces an effect therein. [The answer is: No.

Because the effect thereof—namely, cognition—is dependent upon the person (*puruṣa*), and because the portion consisting of defects does not produce an effect [in the object]. Now, one might argue that defects such as similarity reside solely in the object, and it is logical that their causal efficacy should belong to that very object alone. This is not so; for it would follow that similarity and the like, which persist as long as the substance exists, would produce [cognition] at all times. Furthermore, no other adventitious factor is observed there [in the object]. Moreover, the conjunction of the sense organ with the object is not established as a cause distinct from the cognition residing in the person. Finally, the analogy of the "poisonous gaze" (*dṛṣṭiviṣa*) is inapplicable here.

Furthermore, even if it were possible, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the effect] would be perceived by everyone. Now, one might object: "Just as the sense organs produce specific effects only in relation to a particular person due to their connection with him, so too, due to their connection with a particular object, let them produce something [specific] only in that very object. To this, he says: "Nor do the sense organs... The fact that the sense organs have the nature of being mirrors for the effect called "knowledge" residing in the person is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, no other effect produced by the sense organs is observed in the object itself. The intention is that the postulation of such an effect is refuted because it can be explained in another way.

Nevertheless, he says "nor are they defective" regarding the objection that, just as defects arise in places and so forth due to the proximity of wicked persons, so too might a specific effect regarding the object arise due to the proximity of defective sense organs. The point is that nothing can be established by a mere example while bypassing the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and the like.

What is the need for seeking another cause here? [The opponent might argue: "Ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is of the nature of an eternal entity (*anādibhāvarūpa*) and serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, can itself produce diverse effects such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. To this, he replies with the word *anādi* (beginningless). This is because its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is beginningless; consequently, the effect would have to exist even prior to its production. Furthermore, the sense organs and so forth, which might be suspected of acting as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), have already been refuted. Moreover, it is illogical for that which is illusory (*mithyābhūta*) to possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). And the impossibility of a substratum (*āśrayānupapatti*) and other such arguments have already been stated. This is the intended meaning.

Having thus stated the impossibility of the production of silver and the like—which are indeterminable—he states [the following] with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*) regarding the impossibility of the necessary concomitance of the cognition and the verbal designation of silver even if such production were to occur. He raises a doubt as to what might establish that [concomitance] with the words "Silver and the like" (*rajatādi*); the meaning is that this is due to the similarity between the illusory silver and the empirical silver which performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*). Intending to show that what has been stated does not constitute a valid establishing factor, he states another point to be proven regarding similarity according to observation with the word "Then" (*tarhi*).

If the cognition of that [cow] occurs with respect to something similar to it, then—just like the cognition of a cow in a gavaya—it would be a case of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension); this is the intended meaning of the word "eva" (only). One might object, using the example of silver and so forth: "Even if similarity does not account for it, the connection with that genus (*jāti*) is seen to account for the cognition. [The response is: "That is the genus of silver and so forth. [The objection continues: "Because a connection with an unreal [genus] is impossible, [it must be] a connection with a real individual; such is the meaning. The sense is that even when the individual is sublated, there would follow the consequence that the genus is not sublated. For even the genus is indeed sublated.

Indeed, there is no cognition such that "the individual is not present, but the universal is present. Rather, the understanding is precisely that "even the universal is not present. Nor should it be said that although the universal was previously apprehended, its subsequent non-cognition is due to the absence of the manifesting individual and not due to the absence of the universal itself; for even though the universal was apprehended at an earlier time when the manifestor was present, the subverting cognition (bādhaka-pratyaya) has as its object its non-existence precisely by virtue of its connection with that [later] time. For a subversion is a cognition that [an entity] does not exist within a locus that was previously apprehended.

He refutes the position that [the universal] is not ultimately real with the words "nor even" (*nāpi*). The meaning is: because it is impossible for there to be a connection (*anvaya*) with an ultimate reality, just as it is impossible for there to be a connection with an instance of silver existing in a marketplace. The underlying point is that even if the individual instance remains, there would follow the contingency of the universal being occasionally sublated. For the nature of silver (*rajatatva*) is never sublated in the case of silver found in a marketplace. He states the sublation (*bādhaka*) regarding the connection with an ultimately real individual: "not ultimately real" (*aparamārtha*), referring to the cognition and the word for what is ultimately real.

The meaning is as follows: if the universal (*jāti*) were not connected to the manifestation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then since it would never be observed to be the cause of either cognition or verbal expression regarding ultimate reality, it could not even account for the production of such cognitions and expressions in cases of error. Alternatively, he states another objection against the non-ultimacy of the universal—namely, the impossibility of its connection with cognition and verbal expression—by saying "if it were not ultimate" (*aparamārtha*). In that case, the phrase "of ultimate cognitions and words" (*paramārthabuddhiśabdayoḥ*) means "of cognitions and words that are themselves ultimately real."

This refutation is stated following the rejection of the arising of the real from the unreal. The statement that [the universal] is "not ultimately real" (aparamārtha) is intended to demonstrate the impossibility of the individual (vyakti) being its sustainer. The meaning is that it is illogical for a universal that is not ultimately real to be the sustainer of cognition and verbal designation, which are ultimately real; furthermore, the ultimate reality of cognition and verbal designation is established precisely because no sublation of them is observed.

Now, he shows that the theory of "manifestation of reality as it is" (*yathārthakhyāti*), which is about to be explained, is his own established tenet by saying, "Alternatively" (*athavā*). Demonstrating its traditional authority, he proposes it with the words, "as it is" (*yathārtham*). This means [the view] of Bhagavad-Bodhāyana, Nāthamuni, Yāmunamiśra, and others. To the question "Why?", he says, "From Śruti and Smṛti. He shows the Śruti passage: "May I become many," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) is intended.

Alternatively, "maintenance, dissolution, and so forth" refers to what is stated in the passage beginning with "having Being as their root. Regarding the section whose opening is creation and so forth—that is, in the context of creation and so forth—[the author asks: for what purpose is this half-verse? It is said in reply: By the order of the text, one understands that the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) occurs after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). However, the tripartition exists even prior to the creation of the egg, because the tripartition is for the sake of the creation of the egg. Tripartition is the means; the creation of the egg is the result. In the case of actual production, that result occurs later; but in the case of volitional intention (*saṅkalpa*), it occurs earlier.

It is established in common worldly experience that with respect to the production of things—such as in the inquiry "by what, what, and how"—the means (*upāya*) precedes the intention (*saṃkalpa*), while the intention follows. Therefore, in this sentence regarding the intention for the creation of individual beings—"I shall unfold name and form; I shall make each of these threefold"—the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), which serves as the means for the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), is mentioned subsequently.

In the passage concerning origination, "He evolved name-and-form; he made each of them threefold, threefold," although the evolution of name-and-form was mentioned previously, it is determined that the tripartition occurs prior to the creation that constitutes its fruit, because it is logical that the order of meaning (arthakrama) overrides the order of the text (pāṭhakrama), as in the case of "He offers the Agnihotra; he cooks the gruel. An illustration of this point is the statement at the beginning: "May I be many, may I procreate."

In this context, "May I be many" is the resolve regarding the fruit [of the action], while "May I procreate" is the resolve regarding the means thereto. By this, it is made known that—contrary to common worldly notions such as "by what, for what purpose, and how"—the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is determined to precede the creation which constitutes its fruit, both because of its logical priority and because of its conformity with the initial statement of resolve.

Thus, the half-verse beginning with "May I be many" has been cited to demonstrate that the tripartition exists prior to the creation of the cosmic egg, and to show that the initial statement of resolve is consistent with that fact.

In response to the doubt that—since the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is demonstrated in relation to fire and other elements existing within the cosmic egg—it must therefore occur after the creation of the egg, the author states the meaning of the scripture: "For it is thus perceived by direct perception. The point is this: the demonstration of the threefold nature in a few specific instances such as fire is not intended merely for that purpose; rather, because only what is contained within the egg is capable of being perceived, it is meant to demonstrate the possibility of the previously mentioned tripartition.

And [the author] clearly indicates in the Purāṇa that the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) exists even prior to the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍasṛṣṭi*). Since the creation of the three elements is mentioned in this Upaniṣad, the mixing of those [elements] described as having been created is stated here. This citation from the Purāṇa is intended to demonstrate that their mixing is also shown in the sections explaining the creation of other principles (*tattva*). By the term "Vaiṣṇava," its authority is indicated due to its being characterized by *sattva*.

This is because of the statement: "In all things characterized by *sattva*, the majesty of Viṣṇu is intended. There are two states: being conjoined (*saṃhatatva*) and having come together (*samāgatatva*). "Being conjoined" means merely a conjunction of those capable of existing separately; "having come together" refers to a specific kind of intimate union of those capable of existing separately. He says "possessing diverse powers" (*nānāvīryāḥ*) to indicate that they were unable to create due to the absence of these two states. He says "having come together," etc., to indicate that they created upon attaining both of these.

If all elements were present within each individual element, then all sounds would be employed everywhere; to this, he replies: "Because they are mutually dependent. One element is the support for the other elements that depend upon it. And the relationship between the supported and the support is based on the principle of relative deficiency and excess. The meaning is that the regulation of sounds is determined by that [relationship]. Immediately after the mention of "appropriated," the phrase "having attained unity entirely" expresses the state of being fully integrated.

Although the reading "mahadādayaḥ" (beginning with the Great Principle) exists, the Commentators stated "mahadādyāḥ" in their own composition in order to avoid breaking the meter. The phrase "sūtrety" indicates that the author of the Sūtras spoke thus in order to establish that this alone is the intention of the Śruti. The syntactical connection is: "tataḥ sūtrakāro 'pyavadat" (therefore, the author of the Sūtras also said). The meaning of "tataḥ" is: because this matter is established by both Śruti and Smṛti.

Thus, first, the existence of one element within another element has been stated, because this is useful for establishing the existence of one similar thing within a similar thing, which will be discussed hereafter. By this, the meaning is that the systematic arrangement of designations occurs through the multiplicity of designations. He states the existence of one similar thing within a similar thing with the words "In the absence of *soma*... [and so on]. The "experts in logic" are the investigators. The injunction, "In the absence of *soma*, one should press *pūtīka* plants," is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*), because in the absence of *soma*, there would otherwise be a spontaneous inclination toward other substances similar to it.

He says "vrīhī" (rice) to establish a point by means of an analogous reasoning. "From the state of being rice" means from the existence of the constituent parts of rice. To the question, "How can there be the existence of one similar thing in another similar thing?", he says "tadeva" (that very same). By this, it is concluded that the existence of the constituent parts of silver and so forth in mother-of-pearl and the like is established; thus he says "in mother-of-pearl and the like. It is "made known by the scripture itself" means it is established as being declared by the very scripture concerning substitutes (*pratinidhi*). Alternatively, its being made known is established by the very scripture concerning the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that, because of the process of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (triplication), a portion of silver (*rūpyāṃśa*) in abundance is established in the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*). To the question, "How is the linguistic determination (*śabdavyavasthā*) established?", he says "rūpya" [silver]. For it is when there is a similarity between the mother-of-pearl and silver that the existence of silver in the mother-of-pearl is established, as well as the establishment of the linguistic determination as being caused by abundance; to this he says "rūpyādi" [silver, etc.]. Alternatively, he states another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) for the existence of a portion of silver in the mother-of-pearl with the words "rūpyādi. To the question, "What follows from that?", he says "ataḥ" [therefore].

"Because of its being perceived as similar to silver" means because it is perceived as resembling silver. If there were a real presence of silver particles in the mother-of-pearl and such, they would always be perceived; there would always be an inclination toward action [to pick it up]; and sublation would not be possible. To this, he says "sometimes. Defect (*doṣa*) is the cause for the non-perception of the portion that is mother-of-pearl. Due to the absence of being overwhelmed by the perception of the more abundant [silver], and by the power of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), there is the perception of silver. For it will be stated later that "due to the power of *adṛṣṭa*, water is perceived [as fire]. This statement is made there [in the *Bhāṣya*] so that it may serve as a supporting precedent for other examples as well.

The absence of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is due to preponderance. Because of the preponderance of the mother-of-pearl, the cognition of it possesses the quality of being the sublater. From that very fact, the scarcity of the silver is established; by this, the meaning is that the cognition of silver is the sublated. When it is said "by preponderance," there might arise the suspicion that because the erroneous cognition [of silver] has a preponderance of silver, it would therefore sublate the cognition of the mother-of-pearl; to exclude such a doubt, he establishes the relationship of the sublated and the sublater through preponderance by stating "the mother-of-pearl," etc.

[Objection: But surely, even when there is completeness (*sākalya*), if a deficiency (*vaikalya*) is apprehended, that is "apprehension otherwise" (*anyathākhyāti*). [Reply: It is not so. For "the apprehension of a deficiency" does not mean the apprehension of a mere lack; rather, it is an apprehension due to the non-deficiency consisting in the abundance of the mother-of-pearl, an apprehension accompanied by that. The meaning is: because of the nature (*rūpa*) or essential character (*svabhāva*) of those two apprehensions—that is, because they consist in such a mode of grasping. Alternatively, it may be analyzed as a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The designation emphasizes the state (*bhāva*).
