The meaning is that the relationship of the sublated and the sublator exists between the preceding and succeeding cognitions because they possess such a form.

The sublation (*bādhyatva*) of a cognition does not occur by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), nor by way of its object (*viṣayataḥ*); rather, it consists in the sublation of the activity (*pravṛtti*) produced by it. Furthermore, the sublation of a subsequent cognition consists in its being the remover of the activity generated by the preceding cognition. Even in the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti-vāda*), the sublation of a cognition by way of its own nature is not accepted; rather, only the sublation of its object is accepted. Our distinction, however, is that sublation pertains to the activity which is the fruit of the cognition.

The sublation of activity consists in its being obstructed from arising or its being fruitless. "Not from this" [means]: by the terms *mithyārtha* (false object) and *satyārtha* (true object), the falsity and truth intended by the opponent are meant. "In this way" [means]: even though everything is everything, there is a fixed order of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-vyavasthiti*), a rule regarding rejection, acquisition, and so forth; the meaning is that this occurs through such abundance, totality, or deficiency.

The apprehension of common features (*sādhāraṇākāragrahaṇa*) and the non-apprehension of differences (*bhedāgraha*)—these defects must be accepted by all theorists. Even though activity and so forth are possible through that much alone, the postulation of further [factors] would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) for others. In this regard, activity arises from the uninterrupted manifestation of an object possessing a desirable form; cessation arises from the uninterrupted manifestation of an object possessing an undesirable form. "Uninterrupted manifestation" refers to the manifestation of the form and the possessor of form (*rūpa-rūpin*) without the appearance of their residing in a different substratum (*dharmyantaraniṣṭhatva*) or their dependence on other contradictory properties.

For this very reason, objections such as, "If activity arises from the apprehension of difference, then there would be no cessation of activity when the difference between a rope and a snake is not apprehended," find no footing. That which is accepted by the opponent as the cause for other types of erroneous cognition (*khyāti*) is precisely what we regard as the cause for activity and so forth. Since the Prābhākaras do not accept that mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) possess a definitive meaning, they maintain their position through the mere non-apprehension of difference alone.

In this context, however, there is a difference [between the two systems], because the authority of the Mantras and Arthavādas is accepted regarding their literal meaning; thus, the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) understood from the Upaniṣadic portions, as well as the fivefold partition (*pañcīkaraṇa*) demonstrated therein, are taken as a specific creation performed by the Lord (*īśvara*), and the explanation is carried out by relying on the principle of non-perception of difference (*bhedāgraha*) as a means of negation.

In that regard, some teachers maintain that while the delusion of one element within another element is clearly resolved through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), the delusion of one similar object within another similar object is resolved solely by the principle of substitution (*pratinidhi*), and triplication has no utility therein. However, the established tradition (*sampradāya*) holds that even triplication serves as a means for resolving the delusion of one similar object composed of heterogeneous elements within another similar object composed of heterogeneous elements.

This is understood from the natural sense of passages such as "of everything [the cause is] from the Śruti and Smṛti. Therefore, through the scriptural account of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (triplication), the traditional teaching of *pañcīkaraṇa* (quintuplication), and the logic of substitution (*pratinidhi-nyāya*), the correctness of the cognition of one similar thing in another similar thing is established. Now, one might ask: how is the *trivṛtkaraṇa* process of any utility regarding the error of one similar thing for another similar thing? For indeed, prior to *trivṛtkaraṇa*, there were no constituent parts of silver or the like.

If that were the case, there would be a mixing of silver and so forth with nacre based on the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*); but such is not the case, because the triplication occurs prior to the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). It is replied: even among objects composed of the five elements, a certain effect is produced by one particular element which predominates and possesses a specific mode of transformation.

In that regard, since a particular effect—which is composed of a certain kind of transformation and abounds in certain elements—exists within other effects as well because those elements possessing such a transformation are present there, it is logical that a cognition directed toward those other effects arises with respect to their being abundant in those same elements and producing similar effects.

Even though there is no specific intermediate form at the stage of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), nevertheless, because that element which has entered into the effect through tripartition can possess a dimension equal to the constituent parts of another effect, the correspondence of the cognition of one material object toward another material object becomes logically possible. Likewise, since a portion of fire (*tejoṃśa*) enters into mother-of-pearl through tripartition and transforms into its bright luster, it is established that it possesses the nature of a part of silver due to its extreme similarity to silver.

For it is precisely those specific elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*) endowed with such forms that are perceived as real silver and so forth. Therefore, the existence of parts of silver and so on within mother-of-pearl and the like is logically established. [Objection: But how can the parts perceived in mother-of-pearl and the like be considered parts of silver? For they were certainly not brought from silver and inserted there. [Reply: It is said: Their status as parts of silver consists simply in their having a form highly similar to the well-established parts of silver.

But it is not the case that [the substance] was brought from silver and other such things and inserted, as is the case with the parts of well-known silver and so forth. For the parts of silver found in a marketplace were not brought from some other source of silver and inserted there. In the very same way, the status of being "parts of the Soma plant" for the parts of the Soma plant perceived in *pūtīka* plants and the like consists precisely in their extreme similarity to the parts of the well-known Soma plant; and this is established by the most clear perception and remains uncontradicted.

For it is not the case that a subverting cognition arises [with the thought] that there is no similarity between fragments of mother-of-pearl, *pūtīka* plants, and the like, and silver, *soma* creepers, and so forth. Rather, due to the predominance of heterogeneous constituent parts (*avayava*), those [fragments] lack the capacity to produce [the expected effect], just as a small amount of water mixed with abundant milk, or a small amount of silver mixed with abundant gold, is possible [but ineffective].

But in that case, the "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) of the aggregate intended to be shell would be incomplete due to the contact with heterogeneous parts, just like "man-deer-ness" (*puruṣamṛgatva*) in a man-deer. If it is argued that "man-deer-ness" is a distinct genus (*jātyantara*) different from both "man-ness" and "deer-ness," and not merely an incomplete man-ness or deer-ness, then by the same logic, the aggregate intended to be shell would also possess a distinct genus different from both "shell-ness" and "silver-ness."

Consequently, just as the human convention applies to a "human-deer," the convention of "mother-of-pearl" would not be primary [in the case of the illusory object]. This is because the mother-of-pearl, which serves as the substratum for the error and is mixed with a heterogeneous element, lacks sufficient similarity to another piece of mother-of-pearl—just as a human-deer lacks similarity to a human. For the usage of "thatness" (tattā) is primary only when there is sufficient similarity; its absence renders the statement "Devadatta is a lion" secondary. Furthermore, the status of being mother-of-pearl is fully established due to the abundance of the constituent parts of mother-of-pearl.

If it is argued that for that very reason the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it is primary, then, because the silver-portion is not abundant, silverhood (*rajatatva*) would not exist; consequently, the silver-cognition would lack correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).

It is said in reply: Just as "humanity" (puruṣatva) [does not exist in its full form in a single atom], "mother-of-pearl-ness" (śuktitva) does not reside in a specific aggregate of parts; therefore, even in a single atom, mother-of-pearl-ness is complete. However, because "humanity" resides in a specific aggregate, it is incomplete in the absence of that aggregate, or else there would be a different universal (jāti) present there. But it has been stated that mother-of-pearl-ness is not like that. Therefore, both mother-of-pearl-ness and the linguistic usage based upon it are logically established in the constituent parts of the mother-of-pearl, since there is no presence of a contradictory universal therein.

However, in the aggregate intended as "mother-of-pearl," the determination of causal efficiency and the determination of verbal designation are both possible due to the predominance of the constituent parts of mother-of-pearl. Since the silver portion is not apprehended because it is overwhelmed by the abundant mother-of-pearl, it is logical that the word employed with reference to that [aggregate]—intending the apprehended mother-of-pearl—is primary (mukhya).

Nor does the mother-of-pearl that serves as the substrate of the error lose its similarity to other pieces of mother-of-pearl by virtue of being composed of heterogeneous parts; for even another piece of mother-of-pearl contains a small portion of silver. Thus, the perception of similarity to another piece of mother-of-pearl is possible due to the suppression of the silver portion. Furthermore, the mutual similarity between the constituent parts of the mother-of-pearl itself is more readily established. And according to the reasoning stated, the "silver-ness" of the silver portion is primary.

In that respect, because there is no inherence of a contradictory genus (*viruddhajāti*), there is a similarity with the parts of other pieces of silver. Since, at the time of error, that which is being perceived is not overwhelmed by the perception of abundant mother-of-pearl, the cognition of its similarity with the parts of other pieces of silver is logically established. For this very reason, the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding silver is primary. Therefore, the correspondence (*yāthārthya*) of the cognition of silver and so forth with respect to mother-of-pearl and so forth is established.

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) when a small amount of silver is apprehended as abundant, we say no; for there is no apprehension of abundance at all, but rather only the non-apprehension of its smallness. Since abundance is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), and since the mother-of-pearl—the counter-correlate—is not apprehended, it is impossible to act toward it [as silver] upon such an apprehension. Thus, because the abundance of the silver-element relative to the mother-of-pearl is not apprehended, there is no *anyathākhyāti*. Now, one might object: "Is not the non-apprehension of smallness simply the apprehension of abundance?"

If it is argued that, according to your view, non-existence (*abhāva*) is indeed another entity (*bhāvāntara*), and therefore there is the apprehension of something else (*anyathākhyāti*), we say no; for what is called the non-apprehension of smallness is not the apprehension of largeness, but rather the contraction of the cognition whose object is smallness. Thus, there is no apprehension of anything "otherwise. If it is asked what the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is in the statement "this is not silver," we reply: it is precisely the nature of the mother-of-pearl (*śuktikatva*). That specific form (*ākāra*) by the apprehension of which the activity or the cessation of activity produced by the previous cognition is prevented—that very form is the meaning of the negative particle.
And that form is expressed by words such as "this is not silver," which depend upon a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), as well as by words such as "mother-of-pearl," which do not depend upon one.

Thus, because one element exists within another that has already come into being, and because one similar thing exists within another similar thing, the validity (*yāthārthya*) of cognitions such as "silver in mother-of-pearl" has been established. [The opponent objects: "It cannot be said that dream objects possess either the existence of one similar thing within another similar thing, or the existence of one element within another element that has already come into being. To this, he says: "And in a dream... As for why some [dreams] are of the nature of pleasure and others are of the nature of pain, he says: "...in accordance with merit and demerit (*puṇyapāpānuguṇam*). [The term] "by the Lord" means by the Creator of the world himself.

To the objection that "in that case, it would be perceived by others as well, and it would be perceived at all times," he says: "tattat" (those respective things). To the question "How are they of a different class from what is seen? he says: "tathābhūtāḥ" (being such as they are). He shows the scriptural authority with the words "tathāhi" (for thus). In response to the doubt as to how this statement concerns the subject matter of a dream, he recalls the preceding sentence, "svapnaṃ paśyati" (he sees a dream), with the words "svapnaviṣaya" (having the dream as its object). "Rathayogāḥ" refers to horses and so forth. The meaning is: "they do not exist" means they are not of the same class as those things seen [in the waking state]. [The text continues: "ānandāḥ, mudaḥ, pramudaḥ" (joys, delights, and pleasures).

Joy (*prīti*) born from seeing objects of common enjoyment is *mud*; joy born from the knowledge that an object is not commonly enjoyed is *pramud*; joy born from its specific application (*viniyoga*) is *ānanda*. Alternatively, joy born from seeing an object of a distinct nature is *mud*; joy produced by the knowledge that such an object is fit for one's own application is *pramud*; and joy born from its application is *ānanda*. By these words, the objects are indicated indirectly (*lakṣyante*), because if they were used in their primary sense, it would be impossible for them to be of a different kind from what is seen. *Veśantāḥ* means houses.

Alternatively, "veśāntāḥ" means small ponds. To the question "How is this possible?", he says: "For He is the agent. The sense is: since the agent possesses all powers, what is impossible? The word "tat" (He) does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) under discussion, but rather to the well-known Supreme Self (*paramātman*). To avoid the suspicion of contradiction or tautology, he states the meaning of this scripture as follows: "Even though [the Lord] is all-pervading," and so forth.

In order to avoid contradicting the word "creates," the restriction of the negation "they do not exist" is indeed made according to the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*). Therefore, the negation refers to [objects] that persist through other times, are perceivable by other persons, or possess a specific form; it does not, however, negate their essential nature as being perceivable only by that specific person at that specific time. Thus, the meaning is: [the objects created in a dream] do not exist as things of the same class as those experienced in the waking state, nor are they perceivable by multiple persons, nor do they persist through other times.

He explains the section beginning with "for he is the agent" (*sa hi kartā*) as a justification for the meaning already stated, using the words "of that" (*tasya*). To clarify that the creation of dream-objects has God as its agent, he cites another scriptural passage: "He who [creates] these while they are asleep. To dispel the doubt that the meaning of this scripture might not be what it is—given the difference in the opinions of commentators regarding whether the objector (*pūrvapakṣin*) had proposed the reality of dream-objects and the author of the Sūtras (*sūtrakāra*) established their unreality—he states that the aforementioned meaning is indeed the intention of the author of the Sūtras, using the words "by the Sūtra-author" (*sūtreṇa*).

He states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words, "In dreams... [The opponent argues] that even for the individual soul (jīva), the manifestation of qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) is to be postulated during the state of dreaming; to this he replies, "In that world... For only that which cannot be established otherwise serves as a basis for postulation. Since the perception of dream-objects is accounted for by the Supreme Self alone through the hearing of marks (*liṅga*) belonging to the Supreme Self, the manifestation of the individual soul's own nature is not to be postulated—this is the meaning.

To the question, "How can traveling to another country and so forth be ultimately real for one lying in a room? he replies with the words, "In rooms and so forth. Furthermore, since it is impossible for [the Self] to create objects that bring about its own suffering, it follows as a matter of course that the manifestation of the individual soul's (jīva) true nature is not imagined at that time; this is because it has already been stated that [such experiences] consist of things like the cutting off of one's head. When one lies in another body of similar form, the worldly usage regarding the previous body is caused by the non-apprehension of difference, and not by the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti).

In this way, with respect to dream objects, activity and so forth occur due to the non-apprehension of distinctions—specifically, the fact that each is experienced by a particular person and that each is delimited by its own particular time.

To show that the scriptural statement regarding the yellow conch and so forth being created by Īśvara cannot be demonstrated [in this way], he says "pīta" (yellow). To address the objection that whiteness might also be perceived as yellow, he says "tatra" (therein). Then, to the objection that people standing nearby should also perceive the bile-substance, he says "pitta" (bile). Finally, to the objection that even they would not perceive the bile because of its subtlety, he says "pittopahatena tu" (but by one afflicted by bile).

To the objection—“Since the conch shell is at a distance, there is no extreme proximity [to the eye]; how then is the *pitta* substance located therein perceived?”—the author replies with the words “tadgrahaṇa” (perception of that). Just as a bird that has flown very far away cannot be seen, yet even so, if it is watched continuously from the moment of its flight while in close proximity, it is perceived by the eyes—even at a distance—due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [continuous observation]; such is the meaning. The Prābhākaras have stated that the yellowness of the *pitta* and the substance of the conch shell are both perceived without interruption.

However, the distinction here is that it has been stated that, because the eye has the capacity to perceive substances possessing color, the substance *pitta* (bile) is apprehended. This is the intended meaning of the example "like a conch shell smeared with gold. Now, if the linguistic usage of "yellow conch" arises from the non-apprehension of the difference between the *pitta* substance and the conch, then why would there not be the linguistic usage of "yellow" in the case of a cloth? Or, if you maintain the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), why is there no such usage of "yellow" in the case of the cloth? If you argue that when an error occurs, one must investigate its specific cause, and that an error need not occur everywhere, this is equally applicable [to both cases].

Regarding the claim that it is difficult to explain the contact of visual defects with the *japā* flower, crystal, and so forth, he says "japā" [and so on]. In cases such as the *japā* flower, crystal, mirage-water, fire-brand circle (*alātacakra*), and the confusion of directions, the explanation is that the cognition is not according to reality because of its connection with another substance. If it is argued that the perception of red arises from the connection with the light of the *japā* flower, then by that same connection, the same would occur for stones and other objects; to this he replies "svaccha" (transparent). [He then mentions] "marīcikā" (mirage).

The fact that the unseen (adṛṣṭa) acts as a regulator must be accepted by all proponents of other theories [of error], otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everyone would always and everywhere experience errors regarding all objects, or conversely, that no error would ever occur at any time. Regarding the phrase "alāteti" (as in the case of the fire-brand): it means that because the interval is not perceived—that is, because the interval between the successive conjunctions of the fire-brand with various specific locations occurring in prior and subsequent moments is not perceived—there is a non-perception of sequence. To the question, "If the interval is not perceived, how can there be correspondence with reality (yāthārthya)? he replies with the word "cakra" (wheel).

The perception of a circle is the correct perception of a circle. To the question "What is the distinction [between this and other perceptions]? he says: "In some cases," namely, "in mirrors and the like. If it is asked how there is a reversal of left and right, it is explained as follows: the status of being left or right is indeed relative. In that case, because the mirror has its left and right reversed in relation to one's own face, there is simply a failure to perceive the space between them. The reversal resides in the location of the mirror.

Therefore, in the case of the statement "the face has no intervening space," because the space between the mirror and the face facing it is not perceived, the cognition of that facing-ness is indeed true to reality; the same applies to [the cognition of] its blackness, smallness, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even in the confusion of directions": although all directions exist, the conventional usage of "east" and so on depends upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*). In that case, there is the immediate appearance of one direction as the counter-correlate to another direction. Thus, the object is real. Furthermore, the plurality of directions is understood from the passage: "The earth from the two feet, the directions from the ears."

Regarding the phrase "two moons": to the question "What follows from that?", he says, "In that case, one... Even though visual light naturally spreads straight, its curvature is possible, as is seen in the case of mirrors and the like. Here too, its occurrence is explained by the pressing of a finger, a disorder of the eyes, and so forth. To the question "What follows from that?", he says, "Therefore... The reason for the absence of the cognition "there are two moon-locations" is the non-apprehension of the oneness of the moon. To the question "How can that which has moved to another location possess that [moon] as its qualifier?", he says, "The location..."

To the question, "What follows from that regarding the validity of the cognition?", he says: "In that case, [it is] the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). By this, the two apprehensions of the moon as qualified by two locations are ultimately real. The sense is that the two apprehensions, due to extreme rapidity, have their sequence unperceived; for this very reason, their mutual difference is also unperceived. To the question, "Even when there are two apprehensions of an object qualified by two qualifiers, why is the identity of the qualificand not perceived?", he says: "In that case..."

For it is not observed that the eye alone is capable of apprehending identity in the case of Devadatta and others; rather, it is observed to be capable only when refined by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). The meaning is that because the impression arises with a delay, there is no apprehension of identity at that time. "Visual cognition remains just so" means that it remains with the moon alone as its object, without having grasped its unity. According to the reading *tasyaiva*, the meaning is that it persists as the grasper of the moon alone.

To the question, "How can there be two causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) for two eyes that constitute a single complex? he says, "of the two eyes. For the defectiveness of a sense organ that is inherently faultless must be inferred from its effect; the same applies to the duality of the causal complex—this is the intended meaning. To the objection, "In that case, the duality of the moon would always be perceived," he says, "but when [the defect] has departed. When it is asked how the cognition of unity arises once the defect has vanished, he states that the perception of duality is adventitious (*aupādhika*), saying, "caused by a defect," meaning the duality of the form of the object to be grasped.

The first form [of the object] is its being qualified by its own location; the second form is another location whose intervening space has not been grasped. Its "form-ness" consists in its being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*). Nor is there a misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) of that which is not a form as being a form; for only that which appears as subordinate while having its intervening space ungrasped functions as a qualifier. The Prābhākaras maintain that the visual function (*netravṛtti*) and the cognition (*vitti*) grasp the duality residing therein and the moon without apprehending the difference between them.

As stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi* during the presentation of the Prābhākara view: "The function of the eye becomes twofold, producing two cognitions; therein, for us, it simultaneously manifests both duality and the moon. Thus, there is a discrepancy here [in your argument], because [the Prābhākaras hold that] one grasps the moon along with a spatial duality whose distinction has not been apprehended.

The meaning is that two cognitions—produced by two sets of causal conditions consisting of the eye, light, movement, and distinct forms, which, due to extreme rapidity, do not perceive a sequence and do not perceive a difference between them—grasp the moon as having an unperceived unity and grasp another location as being without an unperceived interval. Therefore, there is the conventional usage of "two moons. Thus, the demonstration of *yathārthakhyāti* (the theory that all cognition is of an object as it truly is) is faultless. Regarding the phrase "khyāti... [at the end], he states that there is no effort required toward those various refutations of other theories of error (*khyāti*) because they have already been addressed against one another and are accepted [as untenable] by his own position.

Alternatively, the reading "athavā kimanena" and so forth is seen in many manuscripts and has been explained by the commentators. In that regard, a single subsequent answer serves as a refutation for all errors concerning objects other than the Supreme (parāgartha) and those involving non-apprehension (aparokṣabhrama). By the phrase "What will not be established?", the existence of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is stated. By the phrase "What is not possible?", the logical justification (upapatti) is stated. To the questions "What is the means of knowledge? and "How is the justification?", he says: "For it has been said by the Blessed One... and so on.

By the phrase "creating the entire world," it is indicated that this matter is rooted in the Śruti, because Brahman is the cause of the whole aggregate of effects. For the Śruti says, "It created all this. Since there is no difference in their being perceived, the meaning is that even this [the dream-world] was created by It. To the question, "In that case, how is the distinction between the sublated and the sublator established? he replies with the word "tatra" (in that regard). The point is that it is not the case that pleasure and so forth—which are experienced by a particular individual and which terminate at a particular time—are unreal.

Now, in order to refute the proof of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) through both scripture (*śruti*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he first applies the scriptural passages, beginning with "But that which... He explains the scriptural passage starting with "by the untrue" (*anṛtena*) as follows: "by the untrue. The sense is that since the indeterminable has already been rejected by the aforementioned method, there can be no linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) for it. He explains the word "untrue": "For the word 'untrue' refers to that which is other than the real (*ṛta*). By the word "for" (*hi*), the consensus regarding its referring to that which is other than the real is indicated.

The point is that since it is impossible for that which is non-existent (*ṛtābhāva*) or that which contradicts *ṛta* (*ṛtaviruddha*) to have Brahman—which is the very essence of *ṛta*—as its substratum, you too must state that the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is something other than those two. To extract the meaning of the word *anṛta*, he states the meaning of the word *ṛta*: "‘Ṛtam’ means... The sense is that it refers to merit (*puṇyakarma*), denoting action, but not the sense of truth (*satya*). Why? To this he says: "‘The two who drink the *ṛta*’ (*ṛtaṃ pibantau*). The sense is that in this passage it is stated, "In the world of good deeds" (*sukṛtasya loke*).

In such other passages, established usage is intended; for after stating, "Just as the fragrance of a tree in full bloom wafts from afar, so the fragrance of meritorious action wafts from afar," the word *anṛta* (untruth) is employed in contrast to merit (*puṇya*) in the phrase, "Thus one should recoil from untruth. Therefore, the word *ṛta* denotes merit. For even merit is an obstacle to liberation.

In response to the doubt as to how there can be the removal of "merely the evil denoted by the word *anṛta*," [the author] distinguishes the merit mentioned in the section on liberation by stating, "Righteous action (*ṛtam*) is karma. For both the well-done and the ill-done of one desiring liberation are indeed obstacles; thus, both of these constitute "evil" (*pāpa*). Therefore, the meaning is that the word *ṛta*, occurring within the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*), denotes action whose fruit has not been intentionally sought.

By the phrase "having the form of worshipping the Supreme Person, with the fruit of attaining Him," this is indicated: "By worshipping Him with one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. Since the word *anṛta* (untruth) refers to that which is opposed to the attainment of Brahman, it follows that the word *ṛta* (truth) denotes action other than that which causes bondage; he establishes this point by means of the preceding verse with the words "etam" (this).

Regarding the words *ṛta* and *anṛta*: since in such scriptural passages as "In this way, one should guard oneself from the untruth (*anṛta*)" they are well-known to refer to merit and demerit; and since in passages such as "Neither good action nor evil action [remains], all evils (*pāpmānaḥ*) turn back from there," and "His actions (*karmāṇi*) are exhausted," it is heard that even good and evil deeds are obstacles to liberation; and since in the contexts concerning liberation, both are denoted by the word "evil" (*pāpa*) because they yield the undesirable fruit called saṃsāra for the seeker of liberation—therefore, in this very sentence, this word *anṛta* [refers to both].

The meaning is that because it is heard [in scripture] that [ignorance] is opposed to the attainment of Brahman; because in passages such as "Within Him, O Maitreya," merit and demerit are heard to have fruits that are opposed to liberation; and because there is no etymological derivation for the word *anṛta* (untruth) as denoting the "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*), the word *anṛta* refers here—through an alternative etymology—to actions that are opposed to liberation.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Non-being was not," here the application of the terms "being" (*sat*) and "non-being" (*asat*)—referring to the nature of the pure Self denoted by the word *brahman* in the statement, "The beginningless Brahman, which is higher than Me, is called neither being nor non-being"—should be understood as a counter-argument (*prativandi*). He establishes that the terms "being" and "non-being" have as their scope the conditioned states of the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) in the verse beginning with "origination" (*utpatti*). For the dissolution (*pralaya*) and the origination of that which has been produced belong, according to scripture, to the conditioned states of both the conscious and the unconscious; therefore, the meaning is that their dissolution is what is being described here.

By the two words *sat* and *tyat*, the statement “It became *sat* and *tyat*” is recalled. Since the conscious entity in its state as an effect is denoted by the word *sat*, the negation here is made of the conscious entity in its state as an effect by the word *sat*, and of the unconscious entity by the word *asat*, which denotes that which is other than it; this is because [the present passage] must have the same meaning as other scriptural passages. With reference to the immediately following passage, “Darkness existed, hidden by darkness,” it is stated that [the negation applies] to the object denoted by the word *tamas*, which constitutes the collective totality of the unconscious.

And he states another reason with the words, "of the existent and the non-existent. For the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) is not accepted as existing at any particular time. He establishes that the term "darkness" (*tamas*) refers to the aggregate of non-consciousness (*acit-samaṣṭi*) with the word "here. Regarding the two statements, "Darkness existed" and "But Māyā is Prakṛti," he first shows the intention of their respective origins in the form of an objection with the word "true" (*satyam*). The intended meaning is that Māyā is what is denoted by the word "Prakṛti. He refutes this with "this is not so. To the question "Why?", he says "Māyā. The particle *iti* here indicates a reason.

The intention is that *prakṛti* is what is denoted by the word *māyā*. This is because we observe the use of the term "possessor of *māyā*" (*māyāvin*) in reference to magicians and the like; because the words *māyā* and *mithyā* (false) are synonyms; and because that which is indefinable (*anirvācya*) is false (*mithyā*). With this intention, he raises the objection: "Is it *māyā*? He refutes it: "That too does not exist. For the word *māyā* is not even a synonym for "false."

The point is that even if one were to accept [the existence of such a term], it is not logical for it to have that [indescribable object] as its referent, because the phenomenon is accounted for by either *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) or *bhedāgraha* (non-apprehension of difference). Thus, there is no such thing as a word denoting the "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*). He demonstrates this with the words "For indeed... (*na hīti*). The meaning is that falsity (*mithyātva*) does not persist across all instances where the word "māyā" is employed. He shows the use of the word "māyā" even regarding real things (*satya*) with the phrase "as it has been said" (*yathoktam iti*). For it is not the case that each individual thing sublated by knowledge is severable by a weapon.

Therefore, since it is stated that each individual illusion (*māyā*) is capable of being cut asunder, the word *māyā* refers to reality (*satya*). Because it is precisely the followers [of the illusions] that constitute the ground for the application of the term, he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*), meaning that among all the objects to which the word *māyā* is applied, the common factor (*anugata*)—wonderfulness (*āścaryatva*) alone—is the ground for the application of the word *māyā*. Wonderfulness means the state of being marvelous. And that [wonderfulness] arises from the capacity to produce a manifold creation of objects. The word "manifold" (*vicitra*) signifies "various kinds. Because it produces various kinds of effects, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is marvelous.

For it will be stated that the word *māyā* denotes that which is wonderful (*āścarya*). Therefore, being wonderful is indeed the basis for its application. Wonderfulness exists even among things that are unreal, as well as among those that are real, within the scope of the usage of the word *māyā*. He states "of *prakṛti*" to show that wonderfulness alone is the cause for *prakṛti* being denoted by the word *māyā*. He establishes this with the words "from this" (*asmāt*). Because it produces diverse effects, *prakṛti* has the nature of a wonder; thus, there is no contradiction with the commentary on the sūtra "Māyāmātram" (Māyā only).

Thus, the meaning of the word *māyā* has been stated. Now, in order to dispel the doubt that the Blessed Lord is subject to *māyā* upon hearing of His connection with it, he explains the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) in the term *māyī*: "And of the Supreme Person. The connection with *māyā* expressed by the term *māyī* does not mean being concealed by it; rather, it means being its master (*taccheṣitva*). On the other hand, it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that is to be concealed by it, because it is heard in scripture that concealment applies to him alone—this is the meaning.

Regarding the point that the subjugation by *māyā* belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, he cites the very words spoken by the opponent, beginning with "anādi": "In the passage 'Indra through *māyās*,' the fact that [the word] denotes multiple and diverse powers is understood from the use of the plural number. 'Mama' is clear. He concludes with 'iti. If the use of the word *māyā* is observed in reference to objects that are false, it would be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*); for since the object lacks reality, there is no basis for that [usage]."

The appearance (pratibhāsa), however, is of a wondrous nature because its object is duality and so forth, and mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like are also of a wondrous nature; thus, through that connection, it possesses a figurative character.

Now, he refutes the establishment of the indeterminable (anirvacanīya) through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) by saying "nor" (*na api*). He substantiates his initial proposition by saying "for not" (*na hi*). The intention is that there is no inconsistency in not postulating ignorance; rather, the inconsistency lies precisely in its postulation, because of the hearing of contradictory attributes. With this in mind, the qualifiers understood from the word *tat* (That) are stated. For, since identity is established by the hearing of the words in the same case-ending, that identity must not be abandoned; and since it is improper to discard what is directly heard in scripture, the specific qualities understood from the word *tat* must be accepted—this is the sense.

If it be argued that "the teaching of identity is untenable," he replies with the word *aikya* (identity). For the contradiction of identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) arises from their respective connections with what is to be abandoned (*heya*) and their lack thereof. If it be argued that when the identity of the Supreme Self, who has the individual soul as His body, is expressed, the use of a word denoting the individual soul to denote the Supreme Brahman who has that soul as His body is non-primary (*amukhya*), he replies with the word *anena* (by this). He concludes with the word *ataḥ* (therefore), establishing the point through scriptural implication (*śrutyarthāpatti*). He asserts that the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* do not have ignorance regarding Brahman as their primary subject matter by stating *itihāsa*.

Regarding the passage beginning with *nanu* and so forth: the intention is that it is proposed that Brahman alone is the single reality (*tattva*). This is because, since the identity of nature between the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*) is impossible, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) must be understood as having a sublationary sense (*bādhārthatva*); furthermore, in the subsequent verses, everything other than that [Brahman] will be declared to be false. The term *vijñāna* refers to that by which various things are known, or that by which things are known erroneously; thus, it is derived in the instrumental sense. *Vijñāna* here is ignorance (*avidyā*). However, its distinction [from Brahman] will be stated later in the passage beginning with "when it is pure" (*yadā tu śuddham*).

The construction "they have manifested through consciousness" (*vijñāne vijñānena vijṛmbhitāni*) is improper due to a lack of natural elegance. This is because it is impossible for the neuter term *vijṛmbhitāni* to function as a qualifier for the masculine word *bheda*; furthermore, since the word *vijṛmbhita* properly ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvārthapratyaya*), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is more appropriate. He says, "But when... (*yadā tu...*) to establish, by way of contrast, that everything other than Brahman is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). "Pure" (*śuddham*) means devoid of ignorance.

"Having its own form" means being devoid of the perception of distinctions created by that [mind]. "Free from defects" means being devoid of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like. Regarding the phrase "of the tree of conceptualization" (*saṅkalpataroḥ*): that by which something is conceived on all sides is "conceptualization" (*saṅkalpa*), which is a defect. In the expression "distinctions among things" (*vastubhedāḥ*), there is no intended meaning in the plural number of the word "things" (*vastuṣu*). The meaning is that distinctions residing in insentient matter do not exist within an object characterized by insentience. Alternatively, one instance of the word "thing" (*vastu*) refers to "form" (*ākāra*); the meaning is that distinctions of form (or nature) residing in insentient matter do not exist.

In the two verses beginning with "vastvasti kim" and "mahīghaṭatvam," the first states the nature of the object (*arthasvabhāva*), while the second provides an illustration; this is the distinction. In that context, the meaning is: "If this is so, from where could there be reality (*tattva*), and from where the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)? To address the doubt—"If everything is perceived as being non-ultimate, how can there be validity (*prāmāṇya*) therein?"—it is said: "by those whose certainty regarding the self is stilled by their own karma. This means: "due to the influence of karma which opposes the ascertainment of the true nature of reality."

Alternatively, the sense is that its unreality is perceived not only by those who know the Self, but even by the ignorant (*aja*). This implies that its falsity is established not only through the authority of the scriptures, but also through the empirical means of perception employed by worldly, insentient beings. Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), indicating that the half-verse beginning with "na vijñānam ṛte" concludes the negation of difference consisting of heterogeneous, non-self entities. The half-verse beginning with "vijñānam ekam" is intended to negate difference within the Self consisting of homogeneous forms.

"One's own karma alone is the root of the ignorance that causes the perception of difference. Here, "perception of difference" refers to the perception of difference among those of the same class. That [perception] is the cause of the ignorance regarding subsequent effects that arise later; the meaning is that even for that, one's prior karma alone is the cause. The intention of the particle *eva* ("alone") is to indicate that it is precisely that which is the cause of the various bodies, such as those of gods and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning is that the ignorance which is the cause of the cognition of the distinctions between the bodies of gods and others consists in the superimposition of forms such as "god-hood" upon the Self, and the cause of that is indeed karma alone.

It is also appropriate to designate the notion of a self (*ātma-buddhi*) with respect to what is not-self as being expressed by the term "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), because that too is an effect of fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). This is because it is said, "Listen also to the nature of ignorance, O delighter of your lineage: it is the notion of a self in what is not-self," and thus it is designated by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), which is a synonym for *ajñāna*. The phrase "pure knowledge" (*jñānaṃ viśuddham*) negates any internal differentiation within it. "Pure" (*viśuddha*) means "stainless" (*vimala*), in the sense that it is devoid of the perception of difference caused by ignorance and its products. He says "free from sorrow" (*viśokam*) to indicate that it is devoid of sorrow and other such states produced by that [ignorance].

"One and always one" (*ekaṃ sadaikam*) is a restatement of the absence of distinctions based on similarity and dissimilarity (*sajātīya-vijātīya-bheda*). Alternatively, "one" (*ekam*) is a restatement of the negation of distinctions based on similarity and dissimilarity, while "always one" (*sadaikam*) expresses, in the manner described, the absence of internal distinctions (*svagata-bheda*). He says "Supreme" (*parama*) to indicate that this is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone, which is denoted by terms such as "Supreme" (*parama*) and "Other Lord" (*apareśa*). He says "Being" (*sadbhāva*) to show that this is not a mere philosophical tenet (*paramatam*), but rather the Reality itself (*tattvam*) as it has been described. "Empirical" (*saṃvyavahāra*) refers to that which is fit for all-around worldly transaction (*samantād vyavahārārha*).

The meaning is that even in the case of that which "resides in the world" (*bhuvanāśritam*)—meaning it exists as having the world as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatayā*)—ignorance alone is stated to be the cause. Alternatively, the meaning is that even regarding this "truth established in the world"—which is "residing in the world" (*bhuvanāśritam*), i.e., dependent on the world, being of the nature of worldly transaction (*saṃvyavahārabhūtam*), or empirical (*vyāvahārikam*)—ignorance is stated to be the cause. It is indeed with this intention that it has been said that the truth of that world and so forth is "empirical" (*vyāvahārikam*). For such is the instruction observed [in the scriptures].
Therefore, the meaning is that it cannot be said that the doctrine of Brahman’s ignorance is not seen in the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*.

He refutes this with the words "this is not so," and so forth. The meaning is that what was stated—that pure consciousness, which is Brahman, is connected with ignorance, and that the world is false because it is imagined by ignorance—is not supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

If that were the case, [the non-existence of the world would follow] due to contradiction with the meaning, contradiction with the context, contradiction with the purport of the scripture, because terms such as "the Lord whose form is the entirety" would become figurative, contradiction with the means of valid cognition that apprehend the world as a substantive entity, because establishing that the Śruti refers to a qualified reality would result in the Smṛti having a meaning contrary to it, and due to contradiction with the previously stated reasoning.

Here, the contradiction in meaning consists in the contradiction between the qualities such as omniscience and the possibility of ignorance and so forth, as well as the impossibility of ignorance serving as the locus for concealment and the like. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with the context, namely the futility of the detailed exposition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). The rest is clear. In the *Daśaślokī*, words such as "existent" and "non-existent," "real" and "unreal," and "knowledge" and "ignorance" refer to the Self and the non-Self; thus, there is no disagreement on this point.

In this regard, concerning the inquiry as to whether the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the words *asatya* (unreal) and *śabda* (word) is their being sublated by knowledge or their being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), there is a natural consistency (*svārasya*) in favor of the position of transformation, because [the text] explains that "the earth becomes a jar. Furthermore, the word *ajñāna* does not refer to the "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*); rather, it refers exclusively to action (*karman*), because of the natural consistency of such statements as "sacrifice is an animal," and because of other declarations such as: "O King, these various bodily forms have their origin in action," "another [form] is called ignorance-action (*avidyā-karma*)," and "one whose intellect functions through external actions."

Intending to state that the discrimination between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is being performed here, he speaks of the appropriate connection with the words "here" (*atra*). "Here" means in this second part (*dvitīyāṃśa*). "Extensive" (*vistīrṇam*) is an adjective qualifying the essential nature (*svarūpa*). By the word "extensive," grossness (*sthaulya*) is intended. The sense is that after describing the mixed gross form, the unmixed subtle form is now described. Alternatively, "extensively" (*vistīrṇam*) may be an adverbial modifier of the action. If falsity (*mithyātva*) were intended to be expressed later on, how could it previously have been stated as "extensively" (i.e., in detail) without contradiction?

Indeed, it is not the case that one who is already deluded should be subjected to further delusion. Therefore, the sense is that since the structure of the universe (*bhuvana-kośa*) has already been described in detail, its falsity will not be stated here. The account of Ādibharata’s life, which is about to be told, exists in the mind in an extensive form; this [present passage] is its summary. Since both a summary of what is yet to be told and a summary of what has already been told are seen, he says "unspoken" (*anuktam*) in order to dispel the doubt that this might be a repetition of what was already stated.

To dispel the doubt that "another form" (*rūpāntara*) refers to something other than what has been stated, he says "another form. This means "separated" (*viyukta*). Since every [form] other than falsity (*mithyātva*) has already been mentioned, there arises the doubt: "Therefore, the 'other form' yet to be stated must be falsity itself, and nothing else. In response to this doubt, he states that the "other form" not mentioned apart from falsity is "the mixture of consciousness and the unconscious" (*cidacinmiśra*).

By the phrase "in the world consisting of the conscious and the unconscious," the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the expression "let the summary be heard again" is explained. In that very same world composed of consciousness and unconsciousness, its gross form was previously described; the meaning of the word "again" here is that this other form is now being stated once more. He states the qualification mentioned in such passages as "mere existence, beyond the reach of words, to be known by the self alone" with the words "the conscious aspect [is] beyond speech and mind."

Keeping in mind the meaning of such statements as "those who hold to duality are seers of the unreal," which are intent on negating difference, he says: "unaffected," etc. If it is intended that the conscious aspect (cid-aṃśa) has the sole form of knowledge and the unconscious aspect (acid-aṃśa) is the locus of transformation, then why are terms such as "existent" and "non-existent," or "real" and "unreal," stated as the grounds for their application? To this, it is replied:

In specific Vedic branches, regarding words such as *asti* (existent), *nāsti* (non-existent), *satya* (real), and *asatya* (unreal) heard in passages like "It became both *sat* and *tyat*," "Both consciousness and unconsciousness," and "Both truth and falsehood became truth," are these terms applied on the basis of being sublated by knowledge (*jñāna-bādhyatva*) or not being so sublated? Furthermore, what is the case for those [words] occurring in branches not studied [by oneself]?

Furthermore, in order to dispel the doubt as to whether [the meaning of terms like "unreal"] consists in being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) or not being subject to transformation (*apariṇāmitva*), [the text] states: "The meaning of words such as 'unreal' (*asatya*) refers precisely to being subject to transformation or not being subject to transformation, and not to being sublated by knowledge (*jñānabādhyatva*) or not being so sublated. This is for the purpose of making known the meaning of the recited and non-recited branches of scripture. It is observed that the earth and other elements possess the status of a body (*śarīratva*) with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*) only when they exist in a particular state of aggregation (*saṅghātaviśeṣāvasthā*); not in their individual form. Likewise, even human bodies and the like are observed to have the status of a body only when they exist in such a state of a composite whole (*piṇḍāvasthā*).

He says "both" in order to dispel the doubt that the state of being the body of the Lord might be absent in the specific states of either consciousness (*cit*) or matter (*acit*), such as the state of ashes and so forth. The meaning is that both the forms of consciousness and matter—whether conjoined with one another or isolated—are the body of the Lord.

Since it is established that the individual soul (jīva) is the body of the Blessed Lord when extracted [from its limiting adjuncts], it follows that its status as the Lord's body is based on its essential nature (*svarūpa*), being free from adventitious conditions (*nirupādhika*). Thus, the status of the jīva as the body of the Blessed Lord is proven even in the state of liberation (*mukta-avasthā*). This form is the meaning of "this aspect" (*etad-rūpa*). He establishes this with the passage beginning "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, in the *Daśaślokī*; for the specific identity with the Blessed Lord is not what is to be established there, as that is common to all the treatises.

However, the unique subject to be established is precisely the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Since this scripture is intent upon expanding upon the meaning of the Upaniṣads, the state of having the Blessed Lord as its essence is declared in the various sections on the *sāvarnya* (homogeneity) for the purpose of distinguishing it from the doctrines of the Sāṅkhya and other schools. It was stated previously that "another form [of the Lord] was not mentioned" with the intention that the unique subject to be established here is indeed the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

Indeed, it has been stated repeatedly previously that the state of having the Blessed Lord as one's self (bhagavadātmakatva) is common to all sections [of this work], and this will be further explained later. In order to indicate that the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) found in the *Daśaślokī* is based on the relationship between body and self, he cites the preceding verse beginning with "yadambu. He states the intended, resultant meaning as expressed by the Seer (Ṛṣi): "Of the water, Viṣṇu... and so forth.

For there is no identity of nature between the conscious [self] and the entity that constitutes the body during childhood and other stages; rather, the point is that in every stage, that entity is simply the body. And regarding the phrase "Viṣṇu is its Self," the meaning is "having intended" this. Or, the meaning is "the relationship of body and self of such a form. [This refers to] that which serves as a reinforcement for the teaching of identity found throughout all the Śrutis.

There is also an instruction regarding identity (*tādātmyopadeśa*) even in those recensional branches (*śākhā*) not studied [by oneself]; the "corroboration" (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of that instruction of identity consists in making known that "this is its very meaning. Alternatively, the so-called "corroboration" of the instruction of identity found in all directly perceived *Śruti* texts means making known that there is no teaching of a meaning contrary to that in the unstudied branches. Here, the manner of syntactical connection for the three occurrences of the word "iti" is as follows: "Having intended this meaning by means of this verse, the Blessed One said, 'This is the meaning.'"

It is not only here that, through the use of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the verses concerning individual creation—as opposed to the use of grammatical subordination (*vyadhikaraṇa*) in the verse concerning collective creation—it is understood that this coordination is based on the relationship between body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*); rather, in other passages, the fact that the states of individual existence are bodies with respect to the Lord, and that grammatical coordination is based on the relationship between body and embodied being, has been stated repeatedly and explicitly. Thus he says: "In this... [referring to the cited passage].

The fact that the identity of the body and the self is the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is stated explicitly in the verse: "Since Viśvarūpa is imperishable. Likewise, elsewhere it should be understood from such passages as: "Because the Infinite One is omnipresent, He alone am I," and "You pervade all, therefore You are everything. By the words "That this... and so forth, the meaning of the three quarters of the verse beginning with "the light" is expressed; the meaning is that the nature of the Lord constitutes the essence of the [universe] as a composite whole.

Since it has been stated that [the universe] consists of both sentient and insentient entities, beginning with *pradhāna* and ending with the *viśeṣas*, words such as "light" (*jyotis*) and so forth denote the individual soul (*jīva*) in its state of association [with matter]. Now, for the sake of connecting with the following verse, he demonstrates the meaning of the fourth quarter by restating the meaning of the qualified sentence: "In this, there exists the Self-nature. By the verse beginning with "That which was water," the fact that the aggregate states of the conscious and the unconscious have the Blessed Lord as their essential nature (*bhagavad-ātmakatva*) was declared through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

The identity with the Lord (*bhagavadātmakatva*) of those two—the individual state (*vyaṣṭyavasthā*) and the collective state (*samaṣṭyavasthā*)—whether they are unmixed or even when mixed, is stated by means of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the verse beginning with "the luminaries" (*jyotīṃṣi*). In that [verse], by the first three quarters, their non-identity with Him is stated when they are in a mixed state; however, by the fourth quarter, it is stated that even when they are extracted [from that mixture], they possess His nature. This is the meaning. He introduces the subsequent verse with the word "this" (*idam*).

For the insentient portion (*acid-aṃśa*), the intended meaning is not based on its being of the nature of the Self (*ātmakatva*); for it is precisely the doubt regarding the falsity of the insentient portion that must be dispelled. Therefore, because that portion is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), the intended meaning is simply that it is not of the nature of the Self. However, since the sentient portion (*cid-aṃśa*) is non-transforming, it follows that it is of the nature of the Self. With this intention, it was said: "And he states this as the reason for its not being of the nature of the Self. He takes up the *pratīka* (exemplar) from the text to be explained: "jñānasvarūpa" (of the nature of knowledge).

Regarding this, the fact that the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "the Lord whose nature is knowledge" is based on the relationship between body and embodied is understood not only from what was stated in the preceding verse—namely, "that which is the body of Viṣṇu, consisting of water"—but is also known from the expression "whose form is the entirety" in this verse as well; with this intention, he explains [the term] as "aśeṣa. If the word "entirety" (*aśeṣa*) were intended to include even the insentient (*acit*), then its status as a "form" (*mūrti*) would have to be predicated of the Lord, since such a status has not been previously established.

Consequently, the negation of the existence of things such as gods, humans, mountains, oceans, and the earth—expressed by the phrase "but not as real entities"—would otherwise be untenable. Therefore, with the intention that the word "entirety" (aśeṣa) refers to the individual souls (kṣetrajña), it is said: "as the self of all individual souls. Here, although words such as "consisting of the nature of knowledge" denote the ultimate substantive (paramaviśeṣya) as well, the function of the sentence lies in its qualification of the qualifier. Thus, the state of consisting of the nature of knowledge is predicated specifically of the individual soul, which serves as the qualifier.

Just as in the statement, "The priests proceed wearing red turbans," it is the redness residing in the qualification that is the object of the injunction, serving as a qualification for the priests' ritual activity through a traditional connection, so it is here. Examples such as "He who possesses hardness" and "The Blessed Lord in the form of Nṛsiṃha is white" should be observed. Furthermore, one should not suspect that in the phrase "whose nature is knowledge" (jñānasvarūpa), what is being stated is that the divine self-nature has knowledge as its essence.

Because the commentary [of Śaṅkara], "When all karma is exhausted, knowledge is free from defects," would otherwise be untenable; for there is no possibility of the divine nature of the Self being connected with such rejectable things as karma and the passion and hatred produced by it. He states the meaning of the phrase "but not as a real entity" with the words "not as a god, a human, etc. The mention of "mountains and so forth" (immobile beings) is intended to indicate all bodies, which is why the word "gods, humans, etc. is used. He explains the second half of the verse with the words "since it is thus."

By the statement "Know that the distinctions such as mountains, oceans, and the earth are the manifestations of consciousness," he elucidates the relationship of cause and effect [between consciousness and these objects] through the passage beginning with "tadvijñāna" (of that consciousness). He explains the word "vijñāna" with the word "tasya" (of that). *Vijñāna* means manifold knowledge (*vividha-jñāna*). How is it that the distinction between mountains, oceans, the earth, and so forth, is rooted in the synthesis of manifoldness?

Regarding the phrases "by those whose walls are divided by the distinctions of their own actions" and "upon the destruction of all actions," since it will be stated that action is the root, he says "devādī" (gods, etc. to show that action alone is indeed the root. The fact that the contemplation of various [Vedic] injunctions is the cause for the distinction between gods and others is mediated [by action]; this is because it accords with the meaning of the subsequent text, and because of other scriptural statements such as "action accumulated through ignorance," "born from the activity of external action," and "these, O King, have action as their source. This is the meaning.

Regarding how the meaning of the verse stated previously—beginning with "This [world] exists as having the nature of 'is'"—is consistent, he says "yataśca" (and because). The sense is that this is established by the phrase "the manifestations of consciousness" (*vijñānavijṛmbhitāni*). "Tadeva" (that very same thing): the formulation of the final position (*siddhānta*) is carried out by relying on those portions required among the points stated in the formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning is that he explains the state of being a manifestation of consciousness precisely by way of its opposite (*vyatireka*).

In the preceding verse, it was explained that the differentiation into gods and so forth is rooted in the contemplation of the manifoldness of one's own Self through an intermediary; in the subsequent verse, this is clarified by way of its opposite (vyatireka), based on the scriptural teaching that karma is the cause. To make this clear, he says: "in the form of gods and so forth. The detailed analysis of the meaning of the words "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*) and so on will be elucidated in the commentary on the verse beginning with "Pure knowledge" (*jñānaṃ viśuddham*); therefore, for the sake of brevity, it is not elaborated upon here.

"Faultless" means devoid of connection with the body. "Pure" means free from the passion, hatred, pleasure, pain, and so forth produced by that [body]. "Of its own nature" means having its true form manifested. He explains the word *saṅkalpa* by equating it with the term "imagining as one's self" (*ātmakalpanā*). For grammarians state: "the prefix *sam-* signifies unification. As before, he explains this as being mediated; that is, they are "resulting from karma rooted in imagining as one's self. The result of identifying the body and the self is the contemplation of one's own self as manifold through forms such as those of gods and so forth.

Of these two, each is established by implication within the term *vijñāna* and the term *saṅkalpa*. For pleasure and pain are the fruits of karma. To the doubt as to how the distinction between entities can be the fruit of karma, it is stated that they exist "for the sake of experiencing that. The meaning is that because they serve as the gateway for the experience of pleasure and so forth, the distinctions such as gods and others are the fruit of karma. By the phrase "for the sake of experiencing that," the meaning of the word *bhogya* (the object of enjoyment) in passages such as "having understood the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 1.12) is clarified.

The meaning is that "the state of being an object of enjoyment" (*bhogyatva*) consists precisely in the capacity to serve as the basis for enjoyment, the instruments of enjoyment, and the means for the accomplishment of enjoyment. The word *vastu* ending in the locative case refers to the body extending up to the individual soul (*jīva*); the second word *vastu* refers exclusively to the bodies of gods and so forth. "Distinctions among objects" (*vastubhedāḥ*) means the distinctions among the bodies of gods and so forth. Here, by the term "distinction among objects," since the distinction itself has the nature of an object, its ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) is also implied. Regarding the words connected here, he says, "those [bodies] among the gods and so forth," in order to explain the term to be explained.

The meaning is that among the objects beginning with the gods, which are conceived as the self, the first word "object" (*vastu*) refers exclusively to the body extending up to the individual soul (*jīva*). For the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) occurs only toward a composite form. He cites the phrase "those which have become objects of enjoyment" (*bhogyabhūtāḥ*) as an illustration to explain the previously mentioned term "for the sake of its enjoyment. By the term "those which have become objects of enjoyment," it is stated that the phrase "diverse objects" (*vastubhedāḥ*) refers solely to the insentient portion; however, this is not because [the text] says "diversity of objects" (*vastubheda*).

He states "devamanuṣya" etc., to show that the very distinctions mentioned in the preceding verse are intended here. For negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consists in the absence of the effect due to the absence of the cause; he clarifies this with the words "tanmūlabhūta. He declares the conclusion regarding the subject matter at hand with the words "ityacidvastunaḥ. In the explanation of the concluded meaning of the previous verse, the reason for the Self being denoted by the word "is" (*asti*) was not stated; here, however, he states the conclusion for that as well with the words "itarasya."

The mutability (*pariṇāmitva*) of distinct entities is established through two verses even by means of the manner in which the world is perceived. Regarding this, he states the meaning of the first sentence with the words "at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇam*). It was understood from the opening of the verse—*that which exists and that which does not exist*—that the purpose of the verse concerns the denotation of the word "non-existent. In this verse, there is instruction for the practitioner. He states the established meaning based on the opening "that which exists and that which does not exist," which serves as a means for connecting the sense of the question "What is the entity that exists? with the subject matter, using the words "the word 'exists'... (*astishabdeti*).

For only when [an entity] is denotable by the word "exists" (asti) due to its being of a constant, single nature, is it established that the absence of that [nature], as stated in the first half-verse, is the cause for being denotable by the word "does not exist" (nāsti). He explains the first half-verse with the words "insentient substance" (acidvastu). To the doubt, "What follows from this regarding the state of being denotable by the word 'does not exist'?", he introduces the second half-verse with the words "To the question 'what then? he says. He states the intention behind the present-tense reference in the word "goes" (yāti) with the words "at every moment" (pratikṣaṇam). He states the meaning of the phrase "it is no longer thus" with the word "that" (tat).

The meaning of the word *bhūyaḥ* (again/further) is "by attaining successive subsequent states. He explains the meaning of the phrase "it is not so" as "it abandons each preceding state. He explains the meaning of the word "therein" (*tatra*) as "of that which was in a preceding state, in a subsequent state. He explains the meaning of the phrase "whence its reality? as "there is no recognition" (*na pratisandhānam*). The meaning is that the state of being such-and-such (*tattvam*) results in the incapacity for recognition (*pratisandhānānarhatva*). Now, one might ask: "Whence is its reality? Whence is its state of being in a preceding condition? It has been stated [as follows].

How is the negation of reconnection [pratisandhāna] established? It is said: Why is the word *kutaḥ* intended to negate the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? When it is stated, "The mountain possesses fire," the expectation for a means of valid cognition is indeed indicated by the question "Why? (*kutaḥ*). Therefore, even the word *kutaḥ*, being intended as a negation, is intended to negate the means of valid cognition; its meaning is "from what means of valid cognition? Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the means of valid cognition for the continued existence of a thing in its previous state. Thus, the sense is that when the means of valid cognition is negated, reconnection is thereby negated.
Otherwise, there would be tautology with the phrase "it is not so in that way. By the word "hi" (for/since), he states the meaning as it has been established by the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

With the intention that the subsequent verse demonstrates through an illustration the training provided regarding the applicability of the term "non-existent," he says, "For instance" (*tathā hi*). He explains the verse beginning with "The earth [attains] the state of a jar" (*mahī ghaṭatvam*) by means of the passage starting with "by its own action" (*svakarmaṇā*). In the phrase "the earth [attains] the state of a jar," the verb "goes" (*yāti*) is supplied from the preceding verse. He states that the contradiction between action and the certainty of the Self is mediated by saying, "in the form of gods, humans, and so forth"; the meaning is: "through association with the bodies of gods and others."

"Stimittam" means obstructed. The sense is that the notion of objects being fit for enjoyment arises because there is a lack of firm conviction regarding the Self, which consists of a more stable happiness; this is due to "staimitya" (inertia or dullness). Alternatively, he says "tathā hi" (for instance) to show that even by those devoid of self-knowledge, the instability of non-sentient objects is perceived. He uses the word "ālakṣyate" (is perceived) because that term is frequently used in the context of visual cognition; to exclude that meaning, he specifies "anubhūyate" (is experienced). He indicates the conclusion of the commentary on the verse with the words "ityarthaḥ" (this is the meaning). He explains the meaning of "brūhi" (tell me) and so forth with the words "evaṃ sati" (this being so).

By this, the following word is explained: by the term *acidvastu*, the word *vastu* found in the verse is explained; the qualification beginning with "deserving the word 'is'" (*astiśabdārham*) is stated as being established by implication. Alternatively, he states the intended meaning of the verse [with the words] "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*).

However, because the word *vastu* is used in reference to the non-sentient (*acid*) in the Purāṇa text—where it says "but not a real entity (*na tu vastubhūtaḥ")"—and in the Bhāṣya—where it says "is there some non-sentient thing (*acidvastu kiñcit")", one should not suspect that the word *vastu* in the verse "What is that entity (*tadvastu*), O King? is equivalent to those instances. By the phrase "it exists" (*asti kim*), it is stated that the word *asti* found in the verse has the sense of "to be" (*bhavati*). Therefore, just like the word *asti* in the expression "that which exists" (*yadasti*), one should not suspect that it refers to the essential nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*).

The author states the conclusion with the words "na hi" (for not). Thus, by the natural force (*svārasya*) of the commentary (*bhāṣya*), it is understood that the phrase "asti kim" (is there anything?), which occurs at the beginning of the two verses, is explained as having the sense of the verb "to be" (*bhavati*). Alternatively, by the phrase "in what is denoted by the word 'asti'," the word "asti" in the expression "vastvasti kim" (does the thing exist? is explained; this is because of its uniformity with such passages as "yadasti" (that which exists) and "tasmānna vijñānamṛte'sti" (therefore nothing exists apart from consciousness).

The meaning of each of the two verses beginning with "Does the existent exist? (*vastvasti kim*) has already been stated; this serves as the basis for the application of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). He explains the first half of the subsequent verse with the words "because" (*yasmāt*): because it is thus, therefore [it is so] precisely because of its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), and not because of its being sublated by knowledge (*jñānabādhyatva*). By the term "non-sentient entity" (*acidvastu*), the meaning of the word "the collection of entities" (*vastujāta*) is expressed. The point is that the word *vastu*, when preceded by the word *jāta*, does not denote that which is eternal. [He concludes with: "that which is denoted by the word 'exists' alone."

The meaning of the word "asti" (is) in this verse is not the sense of mere existence; for that which is distinct from knowledge and has been described as eternal by such phrases as "this is imperishable and eternal" cannot be the object of negation, and because it is more appropriate to conclude [the discussion] with what was introduced at the beginning by "that which exists. The word "kevala" (exclusive/absolute) is used to exclude insentient objects—which possess prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—since they are denoted by the word "non-existent" (*nāsti*) and are expressed by the term "asti" only when qualified [by other factors].

Thus, the fact that an entity distinct from the Self is denoted by the word "non-existent" has been concluded. He explains the passage beginning with "consciousness" (*vijñānam*) with the words "the Self, however" (*ātmā tu*). The word "however" (*tu*) is intended to indicate its difference from non-conscious matter. [The term] "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) means in all bodies. He explains the word "one" (*eka*) as "by virtue of having the single form of knowledge" (*jñānaikākāratayā*). Just as in the phrase, "A single grain of rice, when fully ripened, brings prosperity to the people," this word "one" refers to the identity of form. And that form is the state of being knowledge (*jñānatva*), which is expressed by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); it is with this intention that he says "by virtue of having the single form of knowledge."

This is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is predominant; the meaning is "by way of having the single form of knowledge. Since there is no distinction in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) or attributes (*dharma*), the state of being knowledge (*jñānatva*)—whether mediated or immediate—is indeed the "form" (*ākāra*). In the phrase "by way of the single form of knowledge," the word "single" (*eka*) excludes contraction, expansion, the nature of suffering, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even though its essential nature is opposed to distinctions such as those of gods and others," its opposition to distinction follows from its having a single (undifferentiated) nature.
