He explains the word "intrinsic" (*nija*) and so on with the words "gods and others. He states the meaning of the word "distinction" (*bheda*) with the words "various" (*vividha*).

The meaning of the word *citta* is expressed by the word *buddhi*. The differentiation of the intellect (*buddhi*) arises from the distinction among objects in the form of deities and so forth that are superimposed upon the Self. The phrase "accepted as manifold" means being characterized by many modes such as divinity and so on. It is clear that the word "manifold" (*bahudhā*) refers to the diversity of forms. He states the resulting meaning: "not prompted by the nature of the Self. This means it is adventitious (*aupādhika*). To the question of what the true nature is when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are removed, he explains the following verse beginning with "the Self" (*ātma*).

He explains the term *viśuddha* (pure) as "devoid of karma. He explains the term *vimala* (stainless) by the words "from that very [state]. The word *mala-rūpa* (having the nature of impurity) is used to clarify the explanation of the term *vimala*. By the phrase "devoid of contact with the nature of impurity (*mala-rūpa-prakṛti*)," the meaning of the verse "when all karma is destroyed, knowledge is free from defects" is understood; for the term immediately following the one expressing the destruction of karma has been explained as referring to being devoid of connection with a body.

And thus says the Śruti: "Shaking off evil as a horse shakes its hair, and freeing myself like the moon from the mouth of Rāhu, having shaken off the body, I, with a perfected self, attain the world of Brahman. For here, after stating "having shaken off evil," it is said, "having shaken off the body. He explains the subsequent words with the phrase "tataśca" (and therefore). The meaning is "for that very reason. The word "ca" (and) indicates the independence of the cause. The meaning is: "one whose attachment to greed and all other [defilements] has been cast out."

He explains the term *ekam* (one) as "one because it is incapable of increase or decrease. Increase and decrease mean growth and decay; the state of being subject to those consists in having parts (*sāvayavatva*). It is precisely because of the absence of having parts that it is denoted by the word "one. The meaning is that partlessness is oneness. For that very reason, it is "always of one form"; the meaning is that because it lacks parts, it is devoid of the growth and decay caused by having parts. He explains the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "and that" (*tac ca*).

Because it has been stated that "the body of Viṣṇu is indeed water" and that he is "the form of all things," this is precisely the meaning. He explains that there is nothing other than this by the word *atad* (not-that). The meaning is that from *yataḥ*—that is, from Vāsudeva—there exists no other entity that terminates in itself. Alternatively, one may supply the word "from Vāsudeva" (*vāsudevāt*) and construe it thus: since there is nothing other than Vāsudeva, therefore [he is everything]. In this construction, the pronoun *tat* refers to what is well-known. For this reason as well, the previous construction is more excellent.

This is because it is natural for that [verse] to take the form of a reference back to the preceding verse, and because there is no need to supply a word ending in the fifth case (ablative). As for the division: the two verses beginning with *jñānasvarūpaḥ* and *yadvā tu* apply to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*); the two and a half verses beginning with *vastvasti* apply exclusively to the unconscious; and the one and a half verses beginning with *vijñānam* apply exclusively to the conscious. The half-verse beginning with *sadbhāva* was stated with the intention that what was expressed was not the view of another school, but rather the reality itself (*tattvam eva*).

In this context, he explains the meaning of the word "yathā" (as) by saying "cidaṃśaḥ" (the conscious aspect). "Yathā" means in whatever manner—that is, in the form of being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva) or not being subject to transformation (apariṇāmitva); it does not mean in the form of being sublated by knowledge (jñānabādhyatva) or not being so sublated. "Evamrūpā" (of such a nature) means in the manner of the relationship between the body and the embodied (śarīra-śarīribhāva), by which mode there is identity with the Blessed Lord; it does not mean identity of essential nature (svarūpaikya). In the verse, the word "evam" (thus) is the counterpart to the word "yathā."

The intended connection (*anvaya*) is that truth and knowledge are real, while anything else is unreal as it stands; thus, the true nature (*sadbhāva*) has been described. Therefore, the intended meaning of the word "as" (*yathā*) is the non-transformative nature (*apariṇāmitva*) and the transformative nature (*pariṇāmitva*) which sustain the applicability of the terms "real" and "unreal," as well as the state of having the Blessed One as one's self (*bhagavadātmakatva*). [An objection is raised: "Something different was introduced, yet something different is concluded; for one begins with the words 'is' and 'is not,' yet concludes with the words 'real' and 'unreal'. To this, he says: "In this regard... (*atrety āha*).

The intention behind the mention of different terms at the beginning and the conclusion is this: even when other words are heard in certain instances, their ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is precisely this same [one]. Intending the meaning of the second half-verse, he says "this" (*etad*). Intending the meaning of the two phrases "with all distinctions subsided" (*pratyastamitabheda*) and "beyond the range of words" (*agocaraṃ vacasām*), he says "equal by virtue of having the single form of consciousness" (*jñānaikākāratayā sama*) and "having a difference in nature that is not within the range of words" (*aśabdagocarasvarūpabheda*). By the particle *eva* (only/precisely), the contradiction is indicated.

He states the term that constitutes "residing in the worlds" as "mixed with the insentient. This means residing within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), located in the places of experience. He explains the word "conventional usage" (*saṃvyavahāra*) as "distinction fit for correct usage. The word "correctly" (*samyak*) refers to clarity. When there is an expectation as to what that action is, he says that the following verse is intended to explain it: "He explains that very [point]. And "desire consisting of heaven" means a longing directed toward heaven.

Because the fruit will be explained [later]. The deity and the fruit are included within "action" (*karman*) by virtue of being that which is to be sacrificed to and that which is to be accomplished, respectively. By the word "etcetera," giving, oblation, and so forth, as well as sin, are also indicated. By the word "earth" (*bhūḥ*) and so on, the fruit of sin is also indicated. Sacrifice itself—accompanied by its adjuncts such as cattle—is "action. Such action, consisting of sacrifice and characterized by giving, oblation, and the like, is the cause therein. It is "seen in the paths resorted to. This means it is seen in those various paths resorted to, namely the *varṇas* and *āśramas*.

He states the meaning of the subsequent verse with the words "the world," etc. For one who is subject to karma wanders everywhere; or rather, because one who is subject to karma indeed wanders everywhere, the meaning is that one should act in this manner. The sense is that one who is bound indeed moves about everywhere in a prison, and therefore one should strive for liberation from it. "Firm" (dhruvam) means immovable, always of a single nature—meaning uniform in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) as well as in its qualities (*guṇa*). Alternatively, it means uniform in its essential nature, qualities, and form (*rūpa*). Therefore, the connection with the preceding [verse] is: "it is not the case that this [world] is thus."

Having thus established that the verses are consistent with his own interpretation, he demonstrates their inconsistency with the interpretations of others by means of the passage beginning with "atra" (here). It should not be said that "not even a single word is seen [to support the opponent's view]"; rather, the intention is that in your position, words such as *parama*, *apareśa*, and so forth, do not achieve their primary meaning. He states another reason as well: "asti-nāsti-satya-asatya" (existent-non-existent-true-untrue). Here, the first *ca* (and) has the sense of "but. The intention is that there exists a disparity—namely, the fact that a word which is consistent with his own interpretation is inconsistent with the opponent's position.

The words *asti* (existent) and *satya* (true) have objects that are perceived. Just as the words *asti* and *satya* do not refer to something other than the existent (*sad-vilakṣaṇa*), so too the words *na-asti* (non-existent) and *asatya* (untrue) do not refer to something other than the non-existent (*asad-vilakṣaṇa*); this is the meaning. To the question, "How is there an inability to denote an indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) entity?", he says: "It does not exist" (*nāsti*). This is a contradiction by way of the object. To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataśca*). Alternatively, the absence of a [conventional] linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti-abhāva*) has been stated by the phrase "due to the inability to denote an indeterminable entity."

The state of having mutually contradictory meanings is stated here as another reason (*hetvantara*). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). If it is argued that, nevertheless, because of the absence of existence (*sattva*), either worthlessness (*tucchatva*) or falsity (*mithyātva*) is thereby implied, he says "here" (*atra*) in response. To the question "How [is this so] regarding perishability and the opposite?", he says "the entity" (*vastu*). When there is the suspicion that falsity is simply perishability, he clarifies the nature of perishability with the words "by one [form]" (*ekena*). Let there be the perception of something experienced at one time in a different form at another time; [this does not constitute falsity].

Then, in response to the doubt as to how destructibility (*vināśitva*) is excluded from being non-existent (*tucchatva*) or false (*mithyātva*), he clarifies the nature of non-existence and so forth with the words, "For non-existence... [and] "by means of transformation, etc. (*pariṇāmādinā*). Here, the word *pariṇāma* refers both to transformation in general and to its specific instances. This is just as the word *vāda* (discourse) is common to all types of discourse yet specifically refers here only to the discourse of those free from passion (*vītarāga*). In this context, the word *pariṇāma* denotes a state of increase, based on the usage: "by means of transformation, growth, and birth" (*pariṇāmarddhi-janmabhiḥ*).

This was stated with a view toward the forthcoming statement: "That which does not indeed acquire another name—even after a lapse of time—such as that produced by transformation (*pariṇāma*) and so forth. If the word *pariṇāma* were intended to mean mere modification (*vikāra*), then the word *ādi* would refer to movement to another location. To the objection—"How is it not a sublation (*bādha*) that what was experienced at one time is no longer perceived at another time?"—he replies: "By the difference of time. For sublation occurs only where there is contradiction; and the state of being sublated is, in his intention, nothing other than falsity (*mithyātva*). Thus he says: "Therefore..."

Regarding the two meanings of "transformed" (*pariṇāmitva*) and "untransformed" (*apariṇāmitva*), it is not the case that words such as "non-existent" (*nāsti*) and so forth are merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*); so how is their mode of expression [to be understood]? To the objection that it is untenable for even an object that is the locus of transformation to be denoted by the word "non-existent" because it is eternal, he says: "This is what is meant. The meaning is that having a single, constant form is the ground for the application of the word "existent," while containing the potential for destruction is the ground for the application of the word "non-existent."

In the state of a jar, the lump does not exist; in the state of potsherds, the jar does not exist; and in the state of powder, the potsherds do not exist. Thus, there is always the presence of destruction within. For the attainment of a subsequent state is indeed the destruction of the previous state, and that very [attainment] is the origination of that [subsequent] state. Therefore, non-sentient matter is denoted by the word "non-existent. However, because sentient matter—due to the absence of abandoning one state while undergoing another—is of a single uniform nature, it does not contain destruction within it. Consequently, it is denotable solely by the word "existent."

That which exists eternally is what is denoted by the word "exists. This term contains an element of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), just like the word "established" (*siddha*) in the phrase "when the relationship between word and meaning is established. For in that context, it is explained as "only established," taking examples such as "one who subsists on water" or "one who subsists on air. The meaning here is that it is the same in this case as well. He states the proof for the point that this alone is the ground for the application of words such as "exists" and "does not exist," saying "as it has been stated."

In response to the doubt that words such as "non-existent," "unreal," "existent-non-existent," and so forth possess a natural aptitude for establishing both falsity and non-falsity, [the author] shows that they are also pregnant with falsity by stating "deśa" (place), etc. Regarding the phrase "in relation to specific actions": existence and non-existence in the form of being a king, a father, and so on, depend upon the presence or absence of actions such as protecting and pleasing. The meaning is that when an object possesses existence only through limiting conditions (*upādhi*), its being an object of the cognition of possessing intrinsic existence is not ultimately real.

It has been stated that because the insentient (acit) lacks the nature of ultimate reality and is endowed with the sense of existence, it cannot be denoted by words such as "non-existent" (asat). Since the Self possesses an inherent existence, its being the object of that [conceptual] cognition is the ultimate reality; thus he says, "of the Self alone. He confirms for the listener the meaning already explained word-by-word in the *Daśaślokī* by way of restatement, saying, "and for the listener. [The term] "prādhānyataḥ" is an expression where the state (*bhāva*) is the primary focus, similar to the rule "dvayekayoḥ"; it means "predominantly. Predominance (*prādhānya*) means excellence (*utkarṣa*).

He states the meaning realized by the first half of the recapitulatory verse (*anubhāṣaṇaśloka*) with the words "The luminaries... (*jyotīṃṣi*). For the definition of a body is that it is a substance to be supported by a single [entity]. Therefore, by the phrase "having Viṣṇu as its support" (*viṣṇvādhāram*), the relationship of self and body (*ātmaśarīrabhāva*) is established. He states the meaning realized by the second half of the verse with the words "Conscious and unconscious... (*cidacid-iti*). The predominance of knowledge (*jñāna*) is explicitly stated; since the non-predominance of the unconscious object (*acidvastu*) is thereby established by implication, he says "and of the unconscious object. Predominance and non-predominance constitute excellence (*utkarṣa*) and deficiency (*apakarṣa*).

These two are characterized by being non-transformed and transformed, not by being non-erroneous and erroneous. For predominance and non-predominance exist only when there is a substratum (dharmin). Indeed, error is established only through cognition; therefore, the term "non-predominance" does not apply to that [substratum] by its own inherent force—this is the intended meaning.

Now, in order to state that the scriptural passages cited by the opponent do not have that meaning—since they are intended to show that the knowledge of the identity of the self with the attributeless Brahman (*nirviśeṣabrahmātmaikya*) is what effects cessation—he restates the opponent's position with the words "As for what was said. He refutes it with "That is incorrect. Therein, intending to refute both that knowledge has the attributeless reality as its object and that it has identity with the Self as its object, he first takes up the verse "I know [Him]" (*vedāham*) in order to eliminate the notion that it has the attributeless reality as its object.

By this, it is stated that the means (*upāya*) is precisely the knowledge of the object characterized by its form and so forth, and nothing else. Because it has the same meaning as this, he says, "All moments of time" (*sarve nimeṣāḥ*). For in that [context], there is an adoption of a representative passage (*pratīka*), namely: "Eight [verses] beginning with 'Hiraṇyagarbha was born from the waters'. By this [mention of the specific attribute], the word "lightning" (*vidyut*) is also explained; the meaning is "from that which has the color of lightning," because of its functional identity (*ekārthya*) with the phrase "having the color of the sun" (*ādityavarṇam*).

By the statement, "No one has mastery over him," it is established that there is no other means consisting of further knowledge, because there is no other object of knowledge remaining. The text shows that the means consists in the cognition of the Person as characterized by the aforementioned attributes through the words, "Those who know Him. The inclusion of these and other passages gathered under the word "etcetera" is for the purpose of demonstrating the contradiction of many [contrary] statements.

Now, one might object: since the cause-sentences such as "Being alone, one without a second" establish that Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*), the knowledge of that [Brahman] alone is the direct means to liberation; therefore, the status of the knowledge of the qualified (*saguṇa*) as a means would be mediated by that [knowledge of the attributeless]. Or else, even in those passages where the knowledge of the qualified is presented as the means, there is no intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding its qualified nature; rather, the underlying reality (*vastumātra*) alone is indicated. To this, he replies with the words "of Brahman."

Since it has been established that even the *Sadvidyā* and other such texts have as their object [Brahman] with attributes (*saguṇa*), and since knowledge whose object is the true nature of reality as it exists is alone the means to liberation, the meaning is that those [texts] also are intent upon being means for the knowledge of [Brahman] with distinctions (*saviśeṣa*). To the objection that this contradicts the purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*), he says "purificatory... and so on. Thus, the claim that knowledge has the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*) as its object has been refuted by citing passages that contradict it.

Now, in response to the doubt that "the knowledge of the attributeless [Brahman] alone is the means, because otherwise the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in statements such as 'That thou art' would be inexplicable," the text refutes the view that this [coreferentiality] has as its object the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). In purificatory statements (*śodhakavākya*), coreferentiality aims at the oneness of the reality by way of the exclusion of two [superimposed] aspects; whereas in statements such as 'That thou art,' the coreferentiality of the individual soul and Brahman aims at the oneness of the reality characterized by way of inclusion.

Regarding the identity of acid and Brahman, however, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) occurs in passages such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman" through the superimposition of a non-ultimate form; in cases such as "The luminaries are Viṣṇu," it is for the purpose of sublation (*bādhārtha*). For opponents accept fourfold types of coreferentiality in various contexts. Among these, in sentences such as "That thou art," having raised the possibility that they aim solely at the bare reality (*vastumātra*) by way of positive concomitance (*anvayamukhena*), or that they serve for the purpose of sublation due to a lack of other recourse, those possibilities are refuted.

In this regard, he first states "not [a text] having as its purport the identity of a featureless reality" (*na nirviśeṣavastvaikyaparam*) in order to refute the view that it has such a purport. To the question "Why?", he says "The *tat-tvam* [formula]. To the question "And how is that so?", he says "For the word *tat*... (*tatpadaṃ hi*). The particle *hi* indicates a reason. To the question "How is there the teaching of [Brahman] possessing attributes such as omniscience?", he says "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*). It is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti-siddha*) that the word *tat* refers back to the reality qualified by all its aforementioned aspects, just as in the case of: "My white, beautiful-eyed, full-horned, pot-bellied cow."

In expressions such as "Bring that cow" or "The cow stands, bring her," it is observed that the reference (*parāmarśa*) is directed toward an object devoid of qualifiers such as the action of bringing or the state of standing; and this [reference] is primary (*mukhya*). This is not so, because even though the qualifier of standing is capable of being construed simultaneously with the act of bringing, the intention (*vivakṣā*) is to specify the object as characterized by a prior time. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of bringing even a cow that is currently running.

A qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which conforms to the qualified object (*viśeṣya-vastu*) in such a way as to be compatible with it; indeed, the non-abandonment of that [object] thus conjoined is what constitutes its intendedness (*vivakṣitatva*). If even one among all the qualifications under discussion were abandoned, the very status of being "under discussion" would be lost. For example, when it is said, "Bring my white, beautiful-eyed, full-horned, pot-milking cow," even if the individual cow conjoined with all the qualifications other than whiteness is brought, the intended individual cow has not been brought, because the qualification of whiteness was not abandoned.

Therefore, while that which possesses attributes is the subject under discussion, the status of being the subject for that which lacks attributes is cast far away. Nor can the status of being the subject be established through the identity of the substratum (*dharmī*) alone even if all its qualifying attributes are abandoned; for when all forms are discarded, it is incapable of being the object of recognition. Indeed, when it is said, "There is a jar in the room, bring it," if the intention were not to refer to "jar-ness," there would be no establishment of the mere clay as the subject under discussion.

How is it that while it is impossible for [the substance] to be the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) when even a single aspect is abandoned, it becomes possible when all aspects are abandoned? If you argue that gold is indeed reconnected even when the state of being a ring is discarded—this is true, as established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—nevertheless, the word "that" (*tacchabda*) is incapable of producing a reconnection precisely when the specific aspect under discussion is abandoned. For this very reason, when one says, "Bring that ring," it is not merely the gold that is brought.

Therefore, since the subject under discussion is a reality that is incapable of reconnection once all its modes have been abandoned, it cannot even possess the status of being the "subject under discussion"; thus, the word *tat* would have to be used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to refer merely to a "reality" in general. If it is argued that because of the contradiction between omniscience and other qualities denoted by the word *tat* and ignorance and other qualities denoted by the word *tvam*, the two words must refer to a "reality devoid of distinctions," the author replies to that with the phrase: "co-referential with that" (*tatsamānādhikaraṇam*).

In oblique constructions such as "the whiteness of the jar," the word expressing the attribute does not extend to include the substratum; therefore, the phrase "co-referential with that" (*tatsamānādhikaraṇam*) was stated in order to exclude such cases. Regarding the expression "having the individual soul as its body, qualified by the non-sentient": the meaning is that the contradiction between attributes such as ignorance (in the soul) and attributes such as omniscience (in the Supreme Self) is resolved by means of an intermediary.

The term "the individual soul as qualified by the non-sentient" (acid-viśiṣṭa-jīva) is stated with the intention of indicating a specific orientation (*abhimukhya*) characterized by being the object to be addressed through the grounds for the application of the word *tvam*. To the question, "If there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), how can the word *tvam* refer to Brahman as qualified by the individual soul?", he replies: "existing in two modes" (*prakāra-dvaya-avasthitam*). This means "qualified by two modes. The word "two modes," referring to the grounds for the application of the word *tat* under discussion, serves to preclude any deficiency [in the meaning].

But it does not aim at the exclusion of three modes and so forth. He establishes this by saying, "the abandonment of two modes. He states another objection with the words, "of the two. The meaning is that when a primary reconciliation is possible without contradiction, it is not proper for even a single word to have a secondary figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*); for even if there were a contradiction, the absence of contradiction would be established through the figurative sense of only one word, and thus the figurative sense of both words is untenable. [Objection: But surely the figurative sense of both words is not a fault;

This is because [the identity] is observed in cases such as "This is that Devadatta. For in those instances, since there is a contradiction between a form qualified by one place and time being connected with another place and time, the two words must be taken in a figurative sense (*lākṣaṇika*). To this, he says: "This is that" (*so'yam*). Does the contradiction lie in one thing's connection with two places, or in its connection with two times? Having thus raised the dilemma, he says: "Past" (*bhūta*), etc. Indeed, there is no connection with another qualifier within a qualified form; rather, it is only with the substantive (*viśeṣya*) itself. Therefore, the connection with two times is not contradictory.

If it were contradictory, then the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) asserted by the Buddhists would necessarily follow; the implication is that the prescription of qualities to be accomplished over multiple times and the attainment of results would both become untenable. Regarding "difference of location" (*deśabheda*): if there were a contradiction in a single entity being connected to two different locations, then injunctions such as the "stepping of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇukramaṇa*) and bathing at sacred fords (*tīrthasnāna*) would be impossible; the implication is also that this would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). If it is asked how simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) is possible, it is explained as follows:

There is no simultaneous existence of the connection with two places or the connection with two times; rather, simultaneity belongs only to their cognition. Furthermore, cognition itself demonstrates that the connection with two places and two times occurs only in succession. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Otherwise, in cognitions whose objects are past or future, it would follow absurdly that the past and future objects are present, or that the cognition itself is past or future. He states another objection as well: "It [the Self] thought (tadaikṣata)."

The point is that in the section concerning the opening statement (*upakrama-adhikaraṇa*), the superiority of the opening statement has been established. Since identity is understood in the very beginning of the opening statement, there is no contradiction with the opening statement. Regarding the phrase "by the knowledge of one," he says this because the sentence asserting that through the knowledge of one everything is known occurs prior to the sentence, "It thought: 'May I be many. The meaning is that therein [in the opening statement] are established the attributes of being the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), as well as omniscience, omnipotence, and other qualities consistent therewith. Thus, the cause is indeed the qualified [Brahman].

That very [cause] in its gross state is the effect; thus, because there is no difference in substance (*dravyāntaratva*), the knowledge of the effect is logically established through the knowledge of the cause. For the proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*), however, if it is intended that the effect is included within the scope (*viṣayatā*) of the knowledge of the cause, there is a contradiction, because a false object cannot be the scope of a cognition whose object is real. Furthermore, one would have to supply the word "as being false" (*mithyātvena*) [to the text]. If, on the other hand, it is not included, then the linguistic usage of "known" regarding what is actually unknown would not be primary. Therefore, our position alone accords with the natural sense of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*).

He states the contradiction with another scriptural passage [the *Śrutyaṃtara*] with the words "of that whose nature is knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpasya*). By the phrase "of the omniscient one" (*sarvajñasya*), both the substrate (*dharmin*) and its attribute (*dharma*)—namely, knowledge—are intended. The contradiction consists in the fact that for one who is omniscient, there would be ignorance; for one who has discarded all defects and whose essence consists of all auspicious qualities, there would be the locus of infinite non-human goals (suffering). Furthermore, by the phrase "of that whose nature is knowledge," the impossibility of concealment (*tirodhāna*) is also indicated.

Thus, the view that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has as its purport the identity of a single, undifferentiated reality has been refuted. Now, he refutes the view that it has the meaning of sublation (*bādha*), stating: "And if [it has] the meaning of sublation. There is no such thing as grammatical coreferentiality in the form of "the rope is a snake" intended to mean sublation; for since grammatical coreferentiality presents two qualifiers (*prakāra*) with respect to a single qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it is contradictory for it to have the meaning of sublation. Therefore, if the primary meanings of both words are intended, grammatical coreferentiality cannot be established as having the meaning of sublation.

Having raised the objection that the illustrative sentence "the rope is not a snake" could be sustained by using the word "touch" (sparśa) to indicate the meaning of the negative particle (nañ), he states a refutation of the corresponding subject-sentence that is even more severe than that, on the grounds that it would have the sense of sublation (bādhārthatva).

And so on. In the phrase "of the two words *tvam* and *tat*," there is no intention to imply a specific order. The word *tat* indicates the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) alone, while the word *tvam* indicates the cessation of the state of being an individual soul (*jīvabhāva*). Alternatively, the word *tvam* indicates the substrate, and the word *tat* indicates the cessation [of that state]. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the following objections are intended: the loss of the defining characteristic of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), contradiction with the opening statement (*upakrama*), the impossibility of the promise that through the knowledge of one thing everything is known, and contradiction with other scriptural passages.

He states, "But this much is the distinction," because of the aforementioned example and because of the observed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is an additional refutation here. The meaning is that if [the statement] has the sense of sublation (*bādhārthatva*), the "distinction" does not consist in the removal of the previously mentioned refutations; rather, the distinction is simply the occurrence of two further refutations that will be stated along with those. He states the additional refutation: "Like 'this is not silver,' one would have to resort to the postulation of a sublation that is not even perceived."

In the case of "the mother-of-pearl is indeed silver," the postulation of sublation (*bādhakalpana*) occurs because sublation by another means of knowledge—namely, "this is not silver"—is already apprehended. Here, even though sublation is not apprehended, the meaning is that one must resort to the postulation of sublation due to the lack of any other alternative (*agatyā*). Furthermore, there would be no possibility of sublation if the word did not present a property distinct from the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In the case of "the mother-of-pearl is indeed silver," the word itself presents the contradictory property consisting of the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*); therefore, the postulation of sublation takes place therein.

The meaning here is that since the term *tat* (That) indicates only the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and does not bring to mind a contradictory property—just as the word "mother-of-pearl" [does not bring to mind its own specific qualities]—it is untenable to assume a sublation (*bādhaka*). If one resorts to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the sake of resolving the contradiction, then the figurative indication of either one of the two words alone would suffice to resolve the contradiction. Furthermore, it follows by implication that [the Brahman] would then possess attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). The assumption of a sublation occurs because the sublation is established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and because the contradictory properties are brought to mind by the verbal expression.

In this case, however, because both [the object and its contrary] are absent, it has been stated that [sublation] is untenable. To this, the objection is raised regarding the presentation of a contradictory form: "But the substratum... The phrase "as it occurs" (*yathā bhavati*) is an adverbial modifier meaning that the substratum is presented in such a way that its own nature remains unobscured. For the postulation of sublation consists in the manifestation of a contradictory aspect that was previously unmanifested; there is no rule, however, that the postulation of sublation consists merely in the presentation of a property (*dharma*).

Therefore, the meaning is that sublation is conceived because the nature of the substratum—the opposite of what was previously manifested—is revealed by that term [tat]. Here he says "no. Having raised the dilemma as to whether the substratum in its form as the opposite is manifested or not, he states the refutation for the position that it is not manifested with the words "the substratum... In the phrase "tadāśraya," the word *āśraya* refers to the object (*viṣaya*). Alternatively, the meaning is "of the delusion and the sublation which have that as their substratum. He raises the objection regarding the position that it is manifested with the words "delusion..."

In this context, the reading *bhramāśrayamadhiṣṭhānam* (the substratum is the locus of error) should be examined. The word *āśraya* here refers to the object (*viṣaya*). In the compound *bhramāśrayam*, it can somehow be resolved as a *bahuvrīhi* either through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—meaning "that by which error is its locus, that which is resorted to, or with which it is connected"—or through grammatical non-coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*)—meaning "that wherein there is the resorting to, or the taking as an object, of error. Alternatively, the intended meaning may be: "the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which serves as the locus for the form being superimposed."

The meaning is: "If it is argued that [the substrate] is not concealed because it is the locus of error. He refutes this with the words "that very same thing" (*tadeva*). With the intention of posing the dilemma—whether this substrate is of a contradictory nature or a non-contradictory one—the refutation is stated for the position that it is contradictory. For the position that it is non-contradictory, the refutation—that the postulation of sublation would be untenable and that error would never be eradicated—is clear, and thus it was not explicitly stated. Therefore... [ata iti].

The intended meaning of the term *pāramārthika* (ultimately real) is this: if the form that contradicts error were not ultimately real, then only the superimposed form would be real; just as, for example, if the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*) were not ultimately real, the nature of silver (*rajatatva*) would become real.

As for this objection—that even if the contradictory form is not ultimately real, the cessation of error is still possible; just as in the case of a bee that, due to the error regarding a cluster [of bees], clings to a *palāśa* flower while under the delusion that it is a cluster of bees, both the delusion regarding the *palāśa* flower being a forest fire and the delusion regarding the stalk being a cluster of bees cease—this is incorrect, as they say: "The female bee, through her delusion of a male bee, clung to the stalk of the *palāśa* flower, which she mistook for a forest fire. This is untenable.

Even in that case, the cessation of the object of error occurs only through a mode that contradicts the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The mode of being a *palāśa* flower, which contradicts the nature of a forest fire (*dāva*), is the ultimate reality; and the mode of being a stalk, which contradicts the nature of a bee (*bhramara*), is the ultimate reality. If these were not the ultimate reality, then the state of being a forest fire and the state of being a bee would have to be real, just as the state of being silver is [real] when the state of being mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is not the ultimate reality.

If it is argued that the cessation of the delusion regarding the nature of a firebrand (*dāvatva*) occurs through the delusion that it is a bee, then what of it? The cessation of the cognition of "firebrand-ness" is caused by the realization of the reality of "bee-ness"; consequently, an other delusion regarding the reality of an unreal object remains. The cessation of even that [second delusion] would require another delusion regarding the reality of an unreal object, such that, due to this succession of delusions, the complete cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) becomes impossible. Furthermore, even when the cognition whose object is "firebrand-ness" ceases, the cessation of "firebrand-ness" itself does not occur through the delusion that it is a bee.

Rather, it occurs precisely through the form of the ultimate reality as the flower. Otherwise, if there were a cognition of non-ultimate mother-of-pearl regarding an ultimately real silver, the cessation of the cognition of silver would entail that the silver itself becomes mother-of-pearl. Furthermore, if one delusion were to be removed by another delusion, there would be an infinite regress, since each subsequent delusion acting as a remover would require yet another remover, just as in the case of the series of delusions regarding a rope: [the delusions of] a snake, a strip of ground, and a stream of water.

Furthermore, after the cessation of the delusion regarding the bees, the subsequent delusion concerning the forest-fire—which arises from the knowledge that the means of cessation was not ultimately real—is itself dispelled precisely by the apprehension of the ultimate reality of the *palāśa* flowers.

Therefore, for one who maintains that liberation consists in the total cessation of ignorance, one must ultimately admit the existence of an ultimate form (*paramārthākāra*) in order to bring the succession of delusions to an end, just as there is the nature of the rope. If it is argued that the final delusion cannot exist of its own accord, we say no; for if it were to act upon itself as its own sublater, there would follow the contradiction between the object of an action and the agent of that action.

Furthermore, since the sublater (*bādhaka*) would be real and the sublated (*bādhyam*) would be false, if one were to accept that the very same thing is both the object to be removed and the remover, there would be a contradiction, as that single entity would simultaneously possess both falsity and reality. Moreover, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) itself, independent of a sublater, would have to remove its own self; and since destruction in its own right is merely a change of state, ignorance (*avidyā*) would remain in a subtle form. Furthermore, there would have to be another ignorance to account for that destruction.

He establishes, by means of an illustration, that error and its sublation are impossible when there is no concealment of the true nature of reality (dharmatattva) which contradicts the ultimate truth (paramārtha), stating: "For, in the substratum... Herein lies the analogy of the prince employed by the venerable commentator.

Thus, the sense of [the word *brahman*] having the meaning of "obstruction" has been refuted. Now, he states the words beginning with *jīvaśarīraka* to show that these objections do not apply to his own position. By the phrase "in its primary sense," the abandonment of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is stated; by the phrase "in two ways," the establishment of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is shown. By the phrase "of him who is devoid of all defects" and so forth, the contradiction with the qualities denoted by the word *tat* (That), as well as conformity with the opening statement, is addressed; thus, non-contradiction with the opening statements such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and "It thought" is stated.

Regarding how the proposition that "all cognitions [are known] by a single cognition" is established, he says: "subtle," and so forth. The meaning is that the proposition is established because the specific cause is itself the effect. He states the lack of contradiction with other scriptural passages in the words: "Of the lords... and so forth.

If it is a sentence, it must possess the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). For the subject is that which is already known, while the predicate is that which is to be enjoined and is not yet known. In this case, the word *tat* does not aim at presenting the subject, because the possession of attributes such as omniscience is not within the scope of perception or other means of valid cognition. Furthermore, if the word *tvam* refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*), its function as the presenter of the subject is untenable, since the Inner Controller is not an object of perception or other such means of knowledge.

Therefore, one must accept that the word *tvaṃ* (thou) points to the individual soul (*jīva*) alone, and its identity with Brahman is enjoined by the word *tat* (that). In this regard, he raises an objection with the intention of showing that grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible only when it refers to the unity of a featureless reality due to the absence of contradiction: "If it be asked how there can be a distinction between the subject and the predicate in the statement 'That thou art'? He answers: "Not so here."

In response to the inquiry, "How can there be a restatement (anuvāda) of an object that is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition?"—with the intention that a sentence is not merely restorative with respect to an object already apprehended by perception and so forth, but is also restorative with respect to an object understood through another sentence—the author demonstrates the attainment [of the meaning] from another sentence by stating, "This is its self-nature" (aitadātmyam).

The point is that within this very context, by the scriptural passage concerning the initial determination of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is understood that words denoting the sentient and insentient which constitute the body of the Supreme Self denote the Supreme Self as their ultimate referent. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "For [the scripture] applies where [the meaning] has not been reached. This means that scripture, having as its object a matter not yet established, possesses a purpose consisting in making known what was previously unknown. Therefore, only that [scripture] possesses the distinction between the subject to be indicated (*uddeśya*) and the predicate to be predicated (*upādeya*); it does not apply to a sentence that serves as a conclusion to the present topic.

Therefore, the meaning is that because this concluding statement (*nigamana*) has as its object a matter already established, it does not possess the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). Now, one might object: even the concluding statement is perceived to possess the distinction between subject and predicate; for example, in "therefore sound is impermanent" (*tasmācchabdo'nityaḥ*) or "therefore this [mountain] possesses fire" (*tasmādayamagnimān*), impermanence, possession of fire, and so forth are understood as the things to be enjoined (*vidheya*) with respect to the subjects, such as sound or the mountain. This is not correct;

For there is a contradiction in the conclusion (*nigamana*) having as its object a meaning already established, while [simultaneously] having as its object a meaning not yet understood. As for the [notion of] comprehension, it is merely an illusion of the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), arising from the recognition of the words denoting the subject and the predicate within the prescriptive sentence, and from the similarity in their respective positions as first and last in the statement. For those learned in logic maintain: "That which is connected with *yat*, that which is first, and so forth, is the definition of the subject."

Is it not the case that the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*) conforms to the intended referent (*uddeśya*)? For this very reason, in usages where *yuṣmad* and *asmad* are in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another word, or in mutual coreferentiality with each other, we observe the systematic application of the second and first persons according to the intended referent, as in: "You are the lord of beings," "I am the first-born of Cosmic Order (*ṛta*)," and likewise, "O Agni, if I were you, or if you were I, then your blessings would be realized here. And so forth.

"O Agni, if I were you, I would be a deity like you; if you were I, you would be a seeker like me; then your blessings would become true"—this is the meaning. Therefore, even in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), because the middle case is employed, one must accept that the word *tvam* (thou) serves to present the subject (*uddeśya*) and the word *tat* (that) serves to present the predicate (*upādeya*). This is not so; for the meaning understood from both words was already established by the preceding sentence.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the second-person (madhyama) designation [in the Mahāvākya] to be understood?", it is said in reply: Since both the *tat* and *tvam* words are employed, and because there is no distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), both the first and second persons would apply without distinction. However, since it is logical for the concluding statement (*nigamana-vākya*) to conform to the enjoining statement (*prāpaka-vākya*), and because the word *tvam*—which denotes the Supreme Self as qualified by the specific consciousness included within the world designated as "all this"—has as its object only a portion of what is denoted by the subject-word in the enjoining statement, the second-person designation is used in accordance with that.

To address the objection that, while the statement "all this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) describes the entry of Brahman into the insentient, the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) declares the identity of essence between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—the author replies: "By the phrase 'all this,' he points to the world together with the individual soul. The word "all" (*sarva*) does not refer merely to the insentient; for even though there is no restrictive factor [to limit its scope], it would be improper to violate the natural sense [of the term]. This is because in the preceding passage, "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support," the word "all" is specifically qualified by the term "creatures" (*prajā*).

The meaning is that the word *prajā* (progeny) refers specifically to sentient beings conjoined with insentient matter; furthermore, in other passages such as "He created all this," the world consisting of both sentient and insentient entities—denoted by the terms *vijñāna* (consciousness) and *avijñāna* (non-consciousness)—is indicated by the word *sarva* (all). He explains the term *aitadātmyam* (this-ness) with the phrase "this is its Self. The two words "this" (*idam*) and "all" (*sarvam*) provide the subject (*uddeśya*), while "this-ness" (*aitadātmyam*)—meaning "having this as its essence"—is the predicate (*vidheya*).

Although the distinguished Brahman is the subject under discussion as the cause, the word *etad* (this) refers to the substantive aspect (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) which is distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious, due to the force of the context. To the objection that "being of that nature" (*tadātmakatvam*) might imply identity of essence—as in the case of "a pot is of the nature of clay"—he replies: "And the reason for this has been stated. By the phrase "having Being as their support" (*sadāyatanāḥ*), the relationship of locus and located is expressed. Through this, the relationship of body and embodied (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) is established; for a body is a substance supported by a conscious being for as long as that being exists.

In this sentence, the nature of being the cause is not explicitly revealed; therefore, he says "All this, indeed... in order to clarify that. Here too, the fact of having "Being" (sat) as its abode is established by the act of breathing, since it has the same meaning as the passage beginning with "having Being as their root. In that context, "having Being as their root" expresses its origination from That; "having Being as their support" expresses its subsistence in That; and "having Being as their abode" expresses its dissolution into That. And that [status of being the cause] consists in being the cause of persistence through remaining within and supporting [the world] by means of governance.

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "The Teacher has entered within the people," and, "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable, all this remains held apart. Thus, since the nature of Brahman as thus abstracted cannot logically be the material cause or the locus of dissolution, and because everything is declared to be non-different from It, it is established that [Brahman] has the sentient and insentient as Its body (śarīra).

Therefore, the word *sat* refers to the Supreme Self whose body consists of both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) in their state as effects; whereas the word *brahman*, because it denotes unlimited greatness through its essential nature and attributes without restriction, and by the force of the meaning—that the isolated Brahman cannot logically be the cause—refers to that which is qualified by consciousness and unconsciousness in their causal state.

Thus, the meaning of this sentence is the identity of Brahman—which possesses both conscious and unconscious modes (*prakāra*) in its two states—as established by grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This constitutes the identity of the substrate (*prakārin*) in its causal and effected states. The possession of conscious and unconscious modes is understood from the nominal stems [of the words], while the identity of the single reality qualified by the two states is understood through grammatical coordination; therefore, there is no split in the sentence. Consequently, the meaning is exactly as stated.

Now, in order to clarify that the identity established by the statement "all this indeed" is based on the relationship between the body and the embodied one—through such factors as being the controller and the controlled—and to do so by means of the word "body," he cites scriptural passages with the words "tathā" (thus). The passage "He has entered within as the ruler" serves as an explanation of the term "the Self of all. By this, the relationship of body and self is established (expressed); for indeed, the state of being a body consists in being that which is entered within and governed.

To clarify this, he provides an illustration with the verse beginning, "He who [dwells] on earth. Through the two successive passages, "He who [dwells] on earth" and "He who [dwells] in the self," it is stated that both the sentient and the insentient constitute the body of the Lord. Since the expression "dwelling in the self" could be understood in a general sense—as in "fire dwells in the hearth" or "oil dwells in the sesame seed"—meaning merely an external or internal presence, he says "within the self" (*ātmano'ntara*) to make this clear. By the phrase "who controls from within" (*antaro yamayati*), the defining characteristic of a body is stated.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is His body because it is governed by Him. Nor is this designation like [the expression] "the body of a stone statue," for in the absence of a sublation, it is impossible to abandon the natural force of a designation of distinction. This is because the absence of any abandonment of the natural force of the designation of distinction—as seen in the passage "whose body is the earth"—is established by the context; and thus, in the absence of a sublation, it is improper to resort to a figurative sense even there.

Furthermore, because any natural contradiction [between the two] has been utterly refuted by such opposing attributes as the relationship between the locus and the occupant, the pervaded and the pervader, the ignorant and the wise, and the governed and the governor. The meaning of the illustration "whom the earth does not know" is this: just as an insentient being does not know, so too does a sentient being [not know]. In the subsequent section beginning with "He who is in the self," it is stated by way of a synonym that the pure self has the Lord as its body.

This is because the fact that specific conscious entities conjoined with the insentient—such as the stars, the moon, and the sun—are bodies of the Supreme Self has been stated separately; and furthermore, because the fact that even those individual souls not explicitly mentioned in the passage "He who dwells in all beings," yet are conjoined [with matter], are bodies of the Supreme Self has been stated separately. Moreover, the word *bhūta* does not refer solely to the insentient elements such as earth and so forth, because earth and other elements have been mentioned separately in passages such as "He whose body is the earth" and "He whose body is the waters."

The phrase "the Self which one does not know" is a negation of knowing it in terms of limited magnitude; or rather, it establishes that such knowledge is impossible without the grace of the Blessed Lord. To make known that even in its causal state the body of the Blessed Lord exists, and that the embodied being is a specific deity named Nārāyaṇa, he says: "He who moves within the earth. Here, *mṛtyu* (death) refers to *prakṛti* (primordial nature), as indicated by the fact that the word *mṛtyu* is used in place of the word *tamas* (darkness).

He states, "Having created that," to show that the relationship between body and embodied being is what establishes their respective designations. He says, "In this case as well," to show that the meaning of the term *aitadātmyam* is determined not only by conformity with other scriptural passages, but also from the statement within its own context. By this, it is established that Śvetaketu understood even the word denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) to extend in its ultimate sense to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), [the latter being] "by me, the living self, having the individual soul as my body"; just as in the expression, "Having become a tiger, many were devoured by me."

He explains the term *nāmarūpe* as "the state of being an entity" and "the state of being denotable by words. The meaning is: the state of being entities such as various gods and so forth, and the state of being denotable by words such as "god" and so forth. [An objection is raised: "Let the identity between non-sentient matter (*acid*) and Brahman be due to His entering into it; however, the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman must be due to their essential oneness (*svarūpaikya*) alone, because of the scriptural statement 'by me, the individual soul' (*mayā jīvena*). To this, he replies: "Having entered into that... (*tadanupraviśya*).

But surely, even for Brahman that has entered into the individual soul (*jīva*), its status as being denotable by a name is not established by the act of differentiation (*vyākaraṇa*); for the scriptural passage concerning the differentiation of names and forms does not have the purpose of establishing that [Brahman] is denotable by a name. Just as the differentiation of form is merely the production of form, and not the bringing about of the fact that the form itself is cognizable by it, so too the differentiation of names is merely the creation of words, and not the bringing about of the fact that [Brahman] is cognizable by them.

It is not so; for in the same passage—"In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form"—we hear that the Brahman, which is the Self of the world denoted by the word "this," having its name and form withdrawn during the state of dissolution, becomes differentiated by name and form at the time of creation. In the expression "by name and form" (*nāmarūpābhyām*), the instrumental case denotes a specific mode of being (*itthambhāve tṛtīyā*). The meaning is that it was made distinct (*viśiṣṭam akriyata*) by means of name and form.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that being qualified by a name consists solely in being the agent of naming, rather than being denoted by the name; for it is not established that a person who utters a name—such as "pot"—while teaching the relationship between a designation and its designated object is qualified by that name. Indeed, it is only that which is denoted by a name that is commonly recognized as being qualified by that name. Since the utterer lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the sound, they are not recognized as being qualified by the name.

If it is argued that since Brahman is the material cause of everything, it is logical for it to be qualified by names—just as it is qualified by forms—because it is the material cause of sound, we say no; for the qualification of the ether (*nabhas*) by names such as "pot" is not established. Indeed, when it is stated that the ether is qualified by names like "pot," its status as a name is not naturally understood. For the natural understanding of something being a "name" occurs only when it is related to a word as its denotation (*vācyatvena*).

Nor should it be argued that Brahman can be understood through those various names even by means of secondary (lakṣaṇā) or metaphorical (gauṇa) functions; for it is not well-known that the bank [of a river] and a young boy—being the objects of the secondary and metaphorical functions respectively—are "names" (nāmin) in relation to the words *gaṅgā* and *agni*. [Objection: But surely the word *śyena* has been determined to be a metaphorical name (*gauṇanāmadheya*) with respect to a particular sacrifice. [Reply: True; however, because its usage is otherwise accounted for through the similarity of the quality of "taking away life" (*prāṇahāritva*), the primary sense remains intact. For the scripture says: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes [its prey]."

For the understanding of a word as a name is naturally obtained for the primary [meaning] alone. In this case, however, since there is no sublation (*apavāda*) of the primacy that is naturally established, its abandonment is not appropriate. Therefore, by this sentence, the fact that [the world] is denoted by names is understood from the inherent force (*svārasya*) of the word itself. Due to this same consistency of meaning, in the passage "Let me evolve names and forms," the evolution of names and forms is intended to extend up to Brahman itself.

Furthermore, even the suspicion that this [passage] might be teaching the creation of phonemes (*varṇa*) cannot arise; for the word *nāman* is not synonymous with "mere phoneme. Since the production of the essential forms of all individual objects distinct from Brahman is already established by the statement regarding the "differentiation of form" (*rūpavyākaraṇa*), the production of the specific form of the sky—which is characterized by the word "space"—would also be established by that very same statement on the differentiation of form; thus, its separate exposition would be redundant.

Nor can there be a restriction of the term *rūpa* by the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*), because the restrictive factor—the instruction on the derivation of names (*nāmavyākaraṇanirdeśa*)—is established otherwise. Therefore, the derivation of names (*nāmavyākaraṇa*) must consist precisely in the etymological derivation of the words that denote those various forms as they are being produced.

In this context, since the phrase "May I be many" (tatra bahu syām) reveals that the multiplicity about to be created is a qualification of Brahman, and since even in this sentence the fact that manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*) is preceded by entry [into the world] is established, it is understood that the form being manifested is a qualification of Brahman. Therefore, due to its co-occurrence with a form that qualifies Brahman, it is understood that the name (*nāman*) is also a qualification of Brahman. It has been demonstrated that the name functions as a qualification precisely by virtue of being its designator.

Since it is understood that all forms are qualifiers of Brahman, and since names have as their basis for application those respective forms, it is understood that names qualify Brahman precisely by being its designators.

Since the word *bahu* (many), which refers to the multiplicity of things about to be created, is seen at the beginning [of the passage] to be used as extending up to Brahman, it is understood that the names denoting those various forms—which are subordinate divisions of the multiplicity mentioned in the opening—are designations of Brahman and thus function as its qualifiers. Furthermore, because in the context of the passages "That heat [tejas] thought" and "Those waters thought," words such as *tejas* and so forth are seen to be used with reference to the Supreme Self, these names are established as qualifiers of Brahman.

It is understood that [Brahman] is denoted by those names. This is known from such Smṛti passages as: "The supreme object of all speech," "Hari alone is expressed by all words," and "We bow to Him in whom the eternal foundation of all words resides. Furthermore, it is established that the Śruti text, "I shall manifest name and form," teaches that Brahman, as qualified by the sentient and the non-sentient, is indeed denotable by those names.

He concludes the explanation of the meaning of the term *aitadātmyam* with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). He concludes that words denoting the body extend to the embodied self with the words "consequently" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because the relationship between the body and the embodied self has been established by the cited passages, and because that [relationship] is the means of accounting for the body's participation in those respective names. Now, an objection: such an extension of denotation to the embodied self is not tenable, because it would entail a violation of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), since in common usage words are understood as referring only to the specific object itself.

Regarding the point that "because unity [in Brahman] precludes duality and plurality," he says: "Therefore, of all words... The meaning of the term *lokavyutpatti* (worldly linguistic convention) here is this: there is no contradiction with linguistic convention, because the established meanings [of words] are not abandoned. Since Brahman is not within the scope of worldly means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is an absence of linguistic convention extending up to it; however, this is not due to [words] being non-denotative. Thus, that [objection] is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*).

Just as those who maintain that the meaning of a sentence is an action (*kārya*) assert—on the basis of Vedic usage—that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and other such markers denote something not previously known (*apūrva*), thereby avoiding the charge that there is no linguistic derivation for them from worldly usage; in the same way, it is stated that even for Brahman, duality, plurality, and so forth, are established through their mediation by words qualified by their respective referents.

He states that the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) serves as a concluding statement by saying, "Thus, this is its self-nature" (*aitadātmyam*). This means that there is a conclusion regarding a specific detail through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). The sense is that what was proposed through non-coreferentiality is concluded through coreferentiality, and what was proposed in general terms is concluded in a specific detail. By the passage beginning with "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), the referent of the word "That" (*tat*) is understood; by the passage beginning with "This is its self-nature," the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) has Brahman as its self is understood.

Since it has been established by the passage beginning with “by this living soul” (*anena jīvena*) that words denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) ultimately refer to Brahman, there is no distinction here between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*). For such a distinction applies to sentences that convey an unestablished meaning, but not to concluding statements (*nigamana*), because those concern what has already been established. Furthermore, a conclusion is seen to be necessary for the purpose of confirming the stated meaning. Therefore, the objection regarding the distinction between subject and predicate in this concluding statement finds no footing; thus the resolution has been stated.

However, where there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and Brahman in a sentence whose primary purport concerns an object not yet established, it should be understood that what is to be enjoined is Brahman’s participation in those forms and names.

Thus, in order to reconcile the scriptural texts that teach difference with those that teach identity, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the statement "That thou art" has been explained by way of the relationship between body and embodied. Desiring to establish—by means of the principle of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*—that words denoting a body can denote the embodied being (just as words for a genus or a quality denote the individual or the possessor of the quality), [the author] proceeds to the section beginning with "A part [of Me], because of the various designations" (*aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*), which consists of a determination of whether words denoting a body fall within the scope of the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* principle.

He states the refutation regarding the matters constituting the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). The meaning is: because the scriptures establish the relationship between the world and Brahman as that of body and embodied soul, and because that [relationship] serves to justify their sharing various names; and by the term "proponents of difference-and-non-difference" (bhedābheda-vādin), there is a simultaneous mention of both those who maintain difference based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika) and those who maintain intrinsic difference (svābhāvika); by the term "mere difference" (kevalabheda), difference restricted to itself is intended, and its proponents are the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

And there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because the instruction takes the form "this is his Self. To the question, "How can the abandonment of the instruction regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self [be justified]? he says, "In one [entity]," in order to state the impossibility of that [instruction] under the view of those who maintain that [the world] is false. He raises an objection with "Of that very [Self]" and replies with "That. [The question is: Is there or is there not the comprehension of a further meaning beyond what is already comprehended by its own statement—the statement concerning the essential nature such as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth? In the first case, there would be the possession of attributes (*saviśeṣatva*).

The sense is that in the second case, the instruction regarding identity (*tādātmya*) would be purposeless. He raises a further objection with the words "imagined" (*kalpita*), and refutes it with "that" (*tat*). The sense is that [the word] presents two modes [of cognition]. "Co-referentiality as identity" means that identity is to be understood through co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). He states that it is not only ineffective, but even contradictory, with the words "co-referentiality, however. He points out its inconsistency within the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference based on limiting conditions (*aupādhika-bhedābheda-vāda*) with the words "difference-and-non-difference."

The Lord is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and so forth, and possesses qualities such as omniscience. Therefore, since the Lord is faultless, any teaching of identity with Him—which would entail the contradiction of His being non-Lordly, a state unworthy of Him—is logically inconsistent; this is the meaning. [The qualities] would be abandoned; that is to say, their abandonment is the logical consequence. Regarding the position of natural difference-and-non-difference (*svābhāvikabhedābheda*), he states its untenability with the words "natural" (*svābhāvika*): "Just as there are qualities, the defects would also be natural."

Just as qualities such as omniscience might be inherent to Brahmā by virtue of his being a portion of the Lord (*īśvara*), so too defects might be inherent to the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of its being a portion [of the Lord]. The meaning is that, because the flow of transmigratory existence is endless—as stated in the verse: "O twice-born one, the blessed Time is beginningless and no end of it is known; therefore, these processes of creation, maintenance, and dissolution are uninterrupted"—defects would be eternal. Alternatively, the meaning is that the fitness for connection with those respective defects would be inherent. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "thus, faultless... and so forth.

Having established that the Lord alone possesses the nature of Brahman—by demonstrating through the negation of any entity other than the Lord that words such as "Sat," "Brahman," and "Atman" ultimately terminate in the word "Nārāyaṇa"—and having in mind the faultlessness of Brahman as declared by scriptures such as "Niravadyam nirañjanam" (faultless and stainless), the contradiction with the teaching of identity with the faultless Brahman was stated; thus, the contradiction with the faultless scripture is the resulting conclusion.

If it is to be said that there is then a contradiction with the faultless *Śruti*, why is it stated that "the teaching of identity with the faultless Brahman is contradictory"? It is replied: Identity with that which is incapable of being abandoned (*heya*) is indeed the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). If there were identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), then because Brahman would be subject to what is to be abandoned, the cognition of identity with a Brahman that is subject to abandonment would not remove what is to be abandoned. Furthermore, the experience of such identity would itself not be a human goal. Consequently, due to the contradiction between being a means and being the goal attained, the sentence whose purpose is the teaching of identity would fail to result in its intended purpose.

For the meditation on a person being cut by a sword or being burned by the fire of cosmic destruction does not remove the suffering of the meditator. Nor is the cognition of identity with that [object] a human goal for anyone; thus, it has been stated that the teaching of identity is contradictory, in order to make this known. He refutes the position that difference resides in the thing itself (*svaniṣṭhabheda*) with the word "merely" (*kevala*). The meaning is: of two things that are absolutely distinct and devoid of the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*prakāra-prakāribhāva*). "In any way whatsoever" means that even from the perspective of the aspect of the substantive (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), identity is not established.

Having thus stated the untenability of the four preceding positions (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the distinction in his own position (*svapakṣa*) with the words "in its entirety" (*nikhila*). By the word "properly" (*samyak*), he intends to express primacy (*mukhyatva*). To the question "In what way is there primacy?", he says: "of genus and quality. To exclude [the case of] a staff and so forth, he says: "by being a body, that is, by being a qualifier. How can it be said that [this usage] is seen only in the primary sense? For even a non-primary usage is possible; and the non-primacy of the body follows from its being a substance (*dravyatva*).

For it is not observed that words such as *daṇḍa* (staff) or *kuṇḍala* (earring) denote their referents up to the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) while not being a substance, or being a qualifier while being either a genus (*jāti*) or a quality (*guṇa*), is the cause for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*). Thus, he states "even in the case of genus and quality" regarding the claim that the denotation of a word signifying a body up to the substantive is non-primary; by the particle *eva*, he excludes [the necessity of] being either a genus or a quality as the cause.

To the question "What follows from that?", [the author] says: "Because of being human" (*amanuṣyatvāt*). Here, the word *prakāra* (mode/type) refers merely to a qualifier. By the particle *eva* (only), the exclusion of [other qualifiers] such as a staff or earrings is intended. Regarding the statement "co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is pervasive": the meaning is that because co-referentiality is pervasive, that which pervades it must be stated as the cause [of the cognition]. Why should universality (*jātitva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and so forth, not be the cause? To this he says: "Not mutually... (*na paraspara...*). "Mutually excluded" means not following one another.

"Jātyādayaḥ" means "universality and so forth. This is the intended meaning: in expressions such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," since no recurring form—which serves as the basis for the application of the word "Gaṅgā"—is perceived in either the current or the bank, it is appropriate that the word there functions figuratively (lākṣaṇika).

In this context, however, it is improper to claim that a term is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) in certain instances simply because one resorts to a non-uniform basis for its application, when a uniform form is observed across all those instances where usage is seen to extend up to the substantive (viśeṣya). Otherwise, one could not even maintain that "being a qualifier while not being a substance" is the determinant for extending the denotation up to the substantive; rather, one might as well say that "being a universal" (jātitva) or "being a quality" (guṇatva) is the determinant, and everything else would have to be considered figurative.

And it is not as you maintain; for we observe that in usage both types of words—those denoting genus (*jāti*) and those denoting quality (*guṇa*)—are seen to terminate in the substantive (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, since we also observe in usage that words denoting the body likewise terminate in the substantive, and because a single recurring form is perceived across all such usages, it is improper to assume that one of the two is secondary by postulating another non-recurring form as the determinant. Thus, this co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also [established].

[The opponent says: "Just as in the case of words denoting genus (*jāti*) or quality (*guṇa*), [the word denotes] only the primary [object]. Now, one might raise the objection that it is untenable for words denoting a substance that serves as a mode (*prakāra*) to denote up to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) without depending on a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), since such a thing is not observed in the case of words like *daṇḍa* (staff). In response to this doubt, he explains what was previously intended by the phrase "only as a mode" with the words: "For even those [words] which are established in themselves... and so forth.

The meaning is that denoting a mode (*prakāra*) that is not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha*) is precisely what necessitates grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya*). Wherever there is the status of being a fixed mode, there the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is observed.
