However, in the case of the body, because the rule of simultaneous perception is absent, its status as a non-separately established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is untenable. Therefore, with the intention that such coreferentiality would be merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), he raises the objection: "If [the word] 'cow' [is used for] a horse... and so forth.

He shows the contrapositive of the pervader (*vyāpakaviparyaya*) in the case [of the opponent's position] with the words "but it is not so. He explains that with "for not... He asks "What follows from that? and answers with "Therefore... He refutes this with "This is not so. Intending to state the flaw in the necessity of simultaneous perception being the cause for the restriction of the mode [of existence], he first demonstrates that the body is apprehended as a non-distinct qualifier, using the words "human beings, etc."

The meaning is that "being a qualifier" (*prakāratva*) consists in being endowed with either "having the self as its sole substratum" or "having the same referent as that [self]. Alternatively, by the term "being a qualifier," what is intended is cognition precisely as a qualifier; for it will be stated later, in the explanation of "being a qualifier," that there is "cognition precisely as a qualifier of the self. By this, it follows that when the qualificand is apprehended, there is an absence of cognition as something existing separately, like a staff or an earring.

The meaning is that having the same substratum (*ekāśrayatva*), having the same purpose (*ekaprayojanatva*), and not being perceived as existing separately when the perception of the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is possible—these are the criteria for being an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Among these three, he demonstrates "having the Self as the sole substratum" with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*) by saying "ātmaikāśrayatvam"; he demonstrates "having the Self as the sole purpose" by saying "ātmaika-". Nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of hellish bodies whose sole fruit is suffering.

Even though suffering itself serves no purpose, it is because those [bodies] serve as causes for the purpose of the destruction of sins. Nor should one suspect an over-extension [of the definition] to the bodies of servants and the like, which are the causes of pleasure for a master and others, on the grounds that they have that [pleasure] as their sole purpose; for what is intended is the impossibility of their remaining in existence without being a means to achieve that purpose. Indeed, it is not established that a body fit for buying, selling, and so forth has that [pleasure] as its sole purpose; for it has been stated that its very existence is solely for the sake of experiencing the fruits of that [master's] karma.

Therefore, this is precisely the meaning of the term "having that as its sole purpose" (*tadekaprayojana*). Now, he demonstrates "being a mode of that" (*tatprakāratva*): the phrase "being a mode of that" intends to mean the absence of being perceived as established separately from the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), once the cognition of the qualificand has been established. The use of the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is figurative (*aupacārika*). Alternatively, the meaning is that it is described as being a mode of that for that very reason. Or else, when there is an absence of the perception of separate existence, a specific type of cognition is cited as the cause.

He shows that this triad—beginning with having a single substratum—is present even in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) by saying "for this very [is it]. He shows its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) by saying "having this nature. He states that such a mode of being is the cause for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) independent of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), by saying "gods, humans, etc. He states the alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*) for the reason of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*) by saying "of the genus and the individual."

The meaning is that the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is caused by being cognizable through the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*), and not caused by being an inseparably established qualifier (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). The mention of "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) is for the sake of illustration. He shows that the probans does not reside in the subject (*apakṣasthatva*) with the words "But of the self... (*ātmanastu*). Anticipating the objection that being cognizable through the same causal complex is the determinant for being an inseparably established qualifier, and therefore that [the self] lacks such a qualifier-status due to the absence of that [determinant], he says: "Because of the possibility of separate apprehension... (*pṛthaggrahaṇa...*). "Its own form" (*svaṃ rūpam*) means its essential nature (*svarūpa*); [it refers to] the property (*dharma*).

That whose very nature (*svarūpa*) consists solely of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) is "that which has the unique form of being a qualifier. By the word "solely" (*eka*), the possibility of its ever not being a qualifier is excluded; consequently, it differs from things such as a staff or an earring. Anticipating the following dilemma—whether the cause for being a non-separately established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is said to be "being cognizable by the same causal complex" (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*) due to the absence of any other cause, or whether "this [being a qualifier]" is also said to be a cause because of its persistence (*anuyāyitva*)—he first refutes the first horn of the argument with the words "jātyādi" (beginning with genus, etc.).

Regarding the phrase "because of the apprehension of having the single nature of being a mode (*prakāra*)," although the restriction to being a mode is already established by the word *svabhāva* alone, the use of the word *eka* (single) is for the purpose of excluding the nature of being cognizable by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatā*). If [it is argued that] only having the same substratum (*ekāśrayatva*) and so forth is the cause for the absence of separate qualification (*apṛthagviśeṣaṇatva*), then how is there a rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) in the case of universals (*jāti*) and the like? To this he says: "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*). By this, it is made clear that the previous mention of "being visual" (*cākṣuṣatva*) was intended to demonstrate cognizability by the same causal complex.

Now, regarding the second alternative among the previously mentioned options, the intended dilemma is as follows: Is this [reasoning], which is stated as being the cause for the lack of non-distinct qualification, applicable to all instances of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that do not depend on possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), or is it applicable only to those universals (*jāti*) and qualities (*guṇa*) that you yourself accept? In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable; for there is no single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*) that perceives both the body and the self.

Consequently, since the presence of a recurring *prayojaka* (efficient cause) entails that "not being a non-distinct qualifier" (*apṛthagviśeṣaṇatva*) is also recurring, it follows as a matter of course that it is untenable to resort to a non-primary status for all instances of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by accepting a non-recurring form as the *prayojaka*, thereby narrowing the scope of "not being a non-distinct qualifier" and relying on that [narrowed definition] as the basis for their non-primacy.

In the phrase "because it is understood to have a single nature as its mode (*prakāra*)," the word "single" (*eka*) excludes the nature of being cognizable by the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*). Now, stating a refutation based on the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of odor and so forth—which would otherwise follow the second horn of the argument as intended by the opponent—the author asserts that being cognizable by the same causal complex is neither a non-distinct qualifier nor a pervader, saying "just as" (*yathā*). For even though odor is not visible to the eye, there is no loss of its status as a mode necessarily restricted to earth. The word "thus" (*evam*) serves as a restatement corresponding to the word "just as" (*yathā*).

To the question "Why is it not apprehended?", he replies: "Because of the apprehension of the self. He states the consequence of the absence of pervasion: "Not by this much alone. That is to say, merely because there is no apprehension by the eye, there is no loss of its inherent nature as having that [object] as its mode (*tatprakāratva*). The sense is that [the nature of being a mode] is not pervaded by the state of being known through the same causal complex (*ekasāmagrīvedyatva*) or by non-distinctness as a qualifier (*apṛthagviśeṣaṇatā*), because other determining factors such as having the same substratum (*tadekāśrayatva*) exist. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The state of having that as its mode... Here, the word "one" (*eka*) is intended to exclude the nature of being known through the same causal complex.

The particle *eva* is for the purpose of excluding the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*). Regarding the body's state of being a non-distinct attribute, he says "the self" (*ātman*) to show that it would be perceived as such by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

He raises an objection that even the word [denoting a class] does not denote up to the individual possessing that body, saying "But surely... He refutes this, saying "Not so. With the intention that these two objections and refutations are the same as those in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*, he says, "Just as 'cowness'... If words such as "niṣka" and "arka," which do not denote up to the substantive, were the case, then words denoting sentient and insentient beings would not denote Brahman as their ultimate referent.

If it is argued that this is because words such as “self” (*ātman*) and “earth” (*pṛthivī*) are understood to be abstracting terms (*niṣkarṣaka-śabda*) in passages such as “whose body is the self” and “whose body is the earth,” we reply: an abstracting term is of two kinds—the optional abstractor (*vaivakṣika-niṣkarṣaka*) and the fixed abstractor (*niyata-niṣkarṣaka*). Among these, words such as “body” are fixed abstractors, whereas words such as “self” are optional abstractors—just like the word “cowness” (*gotva*) or the word “white” (*śukla*); for it is the usage [of the speaker] that determines [the status of a term].

For even the distinction between that which extracts [the quality] and that which does not extract it depends upon usage; likewise, this distinction [between substance and quality] is rooted in that. Now, one might object: words such as "white" (*śukla*) are exclusively extractors [of qualities]. Their extension to the substratum of the quality, however, results from the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*): "The elision of the suffix *matup* should be stated after words expressing qualities. This is not so; for like words denoting a genus (*jāti*), words such as "white" are no different in their denotation of a particular that is inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*).

The suffix *pratyaya*, however, like the dual ending found in the word *dvi*, does not have a meaning distinct from the base (*prakṛti*); it serves for the grammatical correctness of the word through its three genders and for specific accents. For this very reason, the lexicographers state: "Words such as *śukla* [white] are masculine when denoting a quality (*guṇa*), but they take the gender of the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) when referring to that which possesses it. This is because the rule regarding the elision of the possessive suffix *matup* applies only to words denoting qualities that inherently extend up to the possessor of the quality, for the sake of gender and accent.

However, for those [words] that lack the capacity to denote the substratum of qualities (*guṇin*), they cannot serve to denote that substratum; for this very reason, the word *rāga* (color) is not used as a synonym for the word *rakta* (colored). Therefore, words such as *śukla* (white) are abstractors (*niṣkarṣaka*) according to the speaker’s intention. Even for those abstractors that are restricted [to specific contexts], their status as such depends upon a particular counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); it is not universal. As it is said: "O son of Kuntī, I am the taste in water; I am the light in the moon and the sun."

Because words such as "taste" (*rasa*) and "smell" (*gandha*), as in the passage "there is a fragrant scent in the earth," are also employed in a sense extending up to the Supreme Self; therefore, words like "smell" possess a restricted denotative power only with respect to [their specific substrates] such as the earth. He concludes that words denoting the body extend to the embodied self by saying, "Therefore, [words] such as 'cow'... They have the capacity to extend up to the Self (*ātmaparyanta-śaktayaḥ*). The meaning is that the cognition of the Self through words denoting the body is primary (*mukhyatva*) because it is based on that [extended] capacity.

Now, it might be argued that although words denoting the body fall within the scope of the principle of *ākṛti* (form), nevertheless, the cognition of the embodied [individual] by means of them is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), because even in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*), the cognition of the individual is figurative. For figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) arises from either the impossibility of a relation or the impossibility of the primary meaning. Since the mere universal (*jāti*) is incapable of being brought and so forth, and because of its relation to the individual, the individual is understood through figurative indication by words such as "cow"; for when a usage can be established otherwise, it is improper to postulate a primary denotative power (*śakti*). This is not so.

Because the status of being a word denoting a qualifier that is not established as a separate entity (ayutasiddha) does not preclude the indication (lakṣaṇā) of the qualified object; otherwise, since there would be no difference in the impossibility of a relation for words such as "genus" (jāti) and so forth, it would follow that they too would sometimes be used to denote the individual (vyakti).

It is also not tenable to argue that "the form (*ākṛti*) alone is the object of the word’s power, whereas the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) arises through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*); just as in the case of recognition, the sense organ is aided by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too the word’s power is aided by the force of the meaning to constitute the causal complex for the cognition of the qualified [individual]. This is because the undesirable consequence follows that there would be a cognition of the qualified even upon hearing words denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like. For indeed, when the causal complex is present, its non-arising cannot be justified.

Objection: But words such as "cow" and the like denote the universal (*jāti*) as being dependent upon the individual (*vyakti*); therefore, from them there arises a cognition extending up to the individual. Words such as "universal" and the like, however, denote only the essential nature of the universal; therefore, from them there is no cognition extending up to the individual. Reply: This is not so; for if words such as "universal" do not convey dependence upon a substance (*dravya*), it would be impossible for the universal to be cognized as distinct from the substance.

[Objection: Is it not the case that what is intended to be expressed is not the cognition of dependence in the sense of having a single nature consisting in being a qualifier (*prakāra*) of a substance, but rather the cognition of dependence in the sense of being incapable of connection with other qualifiers or of functioning as a *kāraka* (grammatical participant)? [Response: It is said in reply: By words such as "cow" (*gavādi*), such a cognition of dependence is brought about by the denotation of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) within a single word. For when "one who has earrings" (*kuṇḍalī*) is said, there is no connection of the earring with qualifiers such as "beautiful," nor does it possess the status of a *kāraka*, as is the case in the expression "adorned with an earring" (*kuṇḍalena bhuṣitaḥ*).

This being the case, if it is admitted that the dependent nature is not understood because the individual is not understood, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*): the dependent nature is not understood because the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is not understood, and the qualified object is not understood because the dependent nature is not understood. Furthermore, if words such as "cow" lacked the capacity to convey the qualified object, they would necessarily lack the capacity to convey dependence, just like words denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like.

Since the incapacity to convey a substratum (*dharmin*) pervades the incapacity to convey dependence upon another—as observed in the case of words denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like—how could this incapacity to convey dependence, when it is excluded from words such as "cow" (*go*), not also exclude its own pervaded counterpart, the incapacity to convey a substratum? One should not say: "Let there be no power (*śakti*) regarding the substance-component; yet words such as 'cow' may still convey the universal's dependence upon an individual. For if that were so, it would follow that even words denoting universals—which lack power regarding the substance-component—would nonetheless convey the dependence [of the universal] upon a substance.
Therefore, the cognition of a substance by means of words such as "cow" is necessarily based solely on the power of the word itself.

Furthermore, if the genus alone were the primary meaning, then there would be the undesirable consequence of words such as "cow" being used predominantly for the genus alone even when applied to substances that are merely secondary (metaphorical) correlates of that genus; for we observe that words are frequently used in their primary sense even when applied to objects related to qualities inherent in that primary sense. For instance, words such as "Ganges," "fire," and "lion" are seen to be used predominantly in their primary senses even when applied to objects such as a riverbank, a boy, and so forth.

However, there is no such usage as "the cow is established in the individual" (*vyaktiniṣṭhā gauḥ*) or "the buffalo is established in the individual" (*vyaktiniṣṭho mahiṣaḥ*). If the universal (*jāti*) alone were the primary meaning of words such as "cow," then in usages where the word refers solely to the universal, there would be independence from suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*. For words like *gaṅgā* are not employed with abstract suffixes when they refer to the current and so forth. If it is argued that the absence of frequent usage and the dependence on abstract suffixes for words like "cow" are due to the impossibility of a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) regarding the individual, we say: no.

For "established usage" (*nirūḍhi*) consists in following frequent application (*pracuraprayoga*). Consequently, the rebuttal that "the absence of frequent application [of the secondary sense] follows from the absence of frequent application [of the primary sense]" is untenable; for an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) cannot be avoided by the mere absence of the thing to which it would apply. Indeed, the consequence of being possessed of fire is not avoided by the absence of fire. Furthermore, the consequence of not depending on an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is difficult to avoid.

Even if one accepts that words such as *śukla* (white) possess a conventional secondary signification (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) when denoting the possessor of the quality, we observe that in expressions such as *paṭasya śuklaḥ* ("the whiteness of the cloth"), which denote the quality alone, there is no requirement for an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*). For others accept that words like *śukla* have a secondary signification whose matup-affix (*-matup*) has been elided—just as in compounds, it is accepted that the nominal stem signifies the meaning of an unexpressed case-ending. If it is argued that "conventional usage" (*nirūḍhi*) means being followed in all applications [of the word], this is not so; for otherwise, it would follow that the word *go* (cow) lacks such conventional usage.

The linguistic usage "cow" is applied even to the mere nature of being a cow (gotva) because it is followed [by that usage]. Furthermore, a function (vṛtti) that conforms to all usages would not be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) at all, just like a function whose object is the generic form (ākṛti). [Objection: But surely, a function that cannot be established otherwise is primary (mukhya). [Reply: True; and such non-alternative establishment has already been shown, since it was demonstrated that words denoting qualifiers that are inseparably connected (ayutasiddha) lack the capacity for figurative indication of the qualified (viśeṣya).

Now, an objection may be raised: "In your view, it is accepted that words denoting a substratum (dharmin) possess a secondary figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding a primary part when there is a reference primarily to the state (bhāva); whereas in our view, words such as 'cow' (go) have lakṣaṇā with respect to the individual (vyakti). In that case, for you, there would be the burden (gaurava) of postulating that the word's expressive power (śakti) has both the qualifier and the qualified as its objects. It is indeed so. However, this is not a fault here, because a burden is not considered a defect in a situation where it cannot be avoided by a simpler solution (lāghava). Indeed, the impossibility of resorting to lakṣaṇā has already been demonstrated.

Furthermore, if the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) in cases such as "village-leader" (*gāmanaya*) arises through the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*), then the substance (*dravya*), which is the counter-correlate (*pratisambandhin*) of the intended universal (*jāti*), would be perceived only as a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Consequently, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—such as in "this is a brindled cow"—just as there is none in the expression "the son is the father."

In the command "Bring the son," even though the word "by me" is not uttered, Devadatta—who is understood as the father related to the intended son—is perceived as subordinate (*guṇatayā*) to the son; he is not perceived as the substantive (*viśeṣyatvena*) or the primary element, because his function is merely to delimit that [son]. In words such as "cow," however, the substance itself is perceived as the primary element. In the expression "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā," since the current is not intended to be expressed, there is no perception of the bank as being subordinate to it.

In the case of "Those with umbrellas are going" (*chatriṇo gacchanti*), however, because those without umbrellas are not perceived as being related to the umbrella-bearers, there is no perception [of them] as subordinate to the umbrella-bearer. Therefore, even though it is perceived as being connected to the intended meaning, a substance that is perceived as primary is understood through the very power of the word itself; this is like the son perceived by the word "having-a-son" (*putrin*) in the phrase "This man has a son" (*ayaṃ putrī*).

Furthermore, since the cognition of color is observed through the word *rūpin*, which possesses the power [to denote] the substantive portion (*viśeṣya*), whereas the cognition of the substantive is not observed through the word *rūpa* when it is devoid of that [power], it is determined by the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the cognition of the substantive as conjoined with a specific word is based upon the power of that word. Therefore, the capacity of words such as "cow" (*go*) to convey the substantive is based upon their inherent power.

[Objection: But surely, because individual instances (*vyakti*) are infinite, it is impossible to grasp their relationship [with a word]. If the derivation of a word’s denotative capacity (*vācyatā-vyutpatti*) occurs with respect to only one individual instance, then other instances would not be denoted by that word "cow. [Reply: This is not so; for the derivation takes the form: "the word applies wherever the universal (*jāti*) is present. Therefore, since the basis for denotability (*vācyatā-nimitta*) is one and the same, there is no need for a separate derivation for each individual. The denotative capacity is derived simultaneously for all individuals, and yet the establishment of the denotability of each individual instance is also possible, because the basis for denotability is fully present in each individual instance.

If it is asked, "How is it possible to project infinite individuals into the mind?"—you who deny that individuals are denotable by words, do you admit those individuals or not? If you do not, then the denial of their being denotable by words is untenable; for as it is said: "Only something that has been apprehended somewhere can be denied as being such. If they are admitted, are only a few individuals admitted, or all of them? In the first case, it is impossible to deny the denotability by words of all individuals.

In the second case, however, everyone would arrive at and become proficient in all individual instances just as you do. Therefore, words such as "cow" and the like denote individuals through their own inherent power (*sva-śakti*). Similarly, it is established that words denoting the body also denote the embodied being (*śarīrin*) through their own inherent power alone.

In this way, words denoting the body would extend to include the embodied being. To the question, "What follows from this regarding the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting the Supreme Self and the sentient and insentient [world]? he says: "Thus. Stating the underlying motive, he concludes with: "Therefore. Thus, by the sentence "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), the oneness of Brahman—possessing a sentient and insentient body—in its causal state and its effected state is established. Nor should it be suspected that there is a split in the meaning or a split in the sentence due to a difference between the identity of the modes (*prakāra*) and the identity of the effect and cause; [for they are not distinct].

Because the state of being the subject (prakāritva) is understood from the word [“that”]. For that word denotes the subject under discussion; and the subject under discussion is the cause characterized by attributes such as omniscience, having the world as its body. This is because of the scriptural hearing of the acts of reflection, oneness, entering, and the subsequent differentiation of names and forms, as well as the sustaining [of the world], in passages such as: “It reflected,” “One only,” “May I become many,” “It emitted heat,” and “Having entered, let me differentiate names and forms,” and “They have Being as their support, Being as their foundation.”

Therefore, the term *tat* (That) refers to Brahman, whose body is the universe and who possesses attributes such as omniscience; and the term *tvam* (Thou) refers to Brahman as qualified by a specific individual soul (*jīva*) which is a product and conjoined with non-conscious matter (*acit*). Consequently, from the two words, it is understood that Brahman, in both its states [of cause and effect], has consciousness and non-consciousness as its modes (*prakāra*). Furthermore, through the identical case-ending applied to both words, the oneness of Brahman in its causal state and its effected state is apprehended; thus, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*).
Therefore, the identity of the substratum (*prakārin*) in its causal and effected states is established by the sentence "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*).

How can the world be the body of the Supreme Self? If this were established, there would be defects resulting from being embodied. What is the supporting evidence for the reasoning already stated? How is the contradiction with etymological derivation to be avoided? In response to such doubts, he says: "The meaning is this."

He explains the aphorism and the statement of the author of the *Vākyakāra*, which were cited by the opponent as being intent on the identity of essential nature, with the words "This very... and so forth. Here, this meaning should be reflected upon in summary: the proponents of falsity (the Mṛṣāvādins) have offered various ways to resolve the problem of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Among those, the view that coordination aims at the bare reality (*vastumātra*) by means of the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyāvṛtti*), as illustrated by the analysis of sentences such as "Truth, etc. (*satyādi-vākya*), has been refuted; for if the exclusions are taken as mere secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), other words [in the sentence] would be redundant.

Furthermore, since the primary meaning is possible, it is improper to accept a figurative sense when the status of being a qualifier has been admitted. Moreover, in the sentence *tat tvam asi*, if it were intended to convey the pure identity of essence through a process of positive correlation (*anvaya*), there would be a violation of the word *tat*’s function as a reference to what has been previously mentioned; there would be a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of both words; there would be a loss of the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the absence of a distinction between their respective grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*); if one resorts to an adventitious ground for application as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), other words in the sentence would become redundant; and there would be a contradiction with the opening statement, "That [Self] thought" (*tadaikṣata*).

The following objections have been stated: contradiction with the method of approach (*upakrama*) and the method of conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), contradiction with other scriptural passages (*śruti*), and contradiction with reasoning (*tarka*) regarding the possibility of concealment (*tirodhāna*) and so forth. Furthermore, if [the word "Brahman"] were intended to convey sublation (*bādha*), there would be the defects of two-word indication (*padadvayalakṣaṇā*), such as indication of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ-artha-lakṣaṇā*) and indication of the essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇā*). Two further objections have also been stated: that since no sublation is observed through perception, it is untenable for the text to be intent upon sublation; and that since there is no contradiction because no contrary attribute is presented by another word, the postulation of sublation is untenable.

Likewise, in the passage "All this, indeed, is Brahman," it is improper to maintain that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is based on the superimposition of a form that does not belong [to the object], because the defining characteristic of coreferentiality—the sharing of a single substratum by "allness" and "Brahman-ness"—is absent; furthermore, since true identity is possible through ultimate coreferentiality, it is illogical to resort to a basis in non-ultimate unity. For if unity were ultimately real, the authority of the scriptural statement of coreferentiality would be lost.

Because the identity intended to be established is false. Thus, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the insentient and Brahman is untenable due to the absence of identity between the real and the unreal.

Furthermore, because there is no identity between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the coreferential expression "I am Brahman" (*brahmāhamasmi*) is not logically possible. If it is argued that this is justified because the word "I" denotes consciousness as qualified by the internal organ, we say no.

Since the word "I" (ahaṃ) does not denote consciousness as qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), it is untenable for the word "I" to denote consciousness as qualified by that [organ]. For instance, just as in the usage "I desire," "I hate," and so forth, desire and the like are treated as qualifiers of the referent of "I," the word "I" does not denote desire and so forth as being qualified by the internal organ; likewise, because of the usage "I know," it is also illogical for the word "I" to denote consciousness as qualified by it [the internal organ]. Indeed, consciousness itself is not qualified by consciousness.

Since there is no cognition whatsoever—distinct from the knower, the known, and the cognition delimited by them—that exists like the horn of a hare and thus falls outside the scope of worldly experience, it is not possible to justify the use of the word "I" with the intention of referring to such a thing. Consequently, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) is untenable. Furthermore, because there is no identity between two internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and because, according to the reasoning previously stated, words such as "I" do not denote the consciousness (*jñapti*) conditioned by that organ, the coreferentiality found in passages such as "I was Manu" (*ahaṃ manur abhavam*) is likewise unestablished.

Because there is no identity between the insentient vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the living being (*jīva*), such statements as "I am the vital breath, the conscious self," "I alone am all this," and "From me comes all, I am all" would be incorrect. Furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as words denoting the insentient and the Lord—as in "I am Hari, all this is Janārdana"—is untenable; for the individual soul, the Lord, and the earth and other elements are all superimposed upon pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Indeed, there is no mutual coreferentiality among words denoting a rope, a snake imagined upon it, a patch of ground, and a stream of water [all superimposed on the same locus].

If it is argued that words such as "I," "this," and "all"—which denote superimposed objects—have a single referent because they ultimately refer to Brahman, which serves as their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), we say no. This is because, unlike words denoting a generic form (*ākṛti*) which extend to the individual (*vyakti*), there is no linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) for words denoting a superimposed object to denote its substratum. For instance, the word "silver" here does not have a conventional meaning as denoting the substance that is the locus of the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*). Furthermore, such a convention is absent because the "silverness" and other properties that serve as the grounds for applying words like "silver" do not exist in fragments of mother-of-pearl and the like.

If it is argued that words denoting a superimposed object have their primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) in the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because there exists an etymological derivation rooted in the linguistic usage of elders such as "this is silver," we reply: the determination that a word denotes a particular object is based on the fact that its employment with the intention to convey that specific meaning cannot be established otherwise. In this regard, it must be asked: if a word denoting a superimposed object extends as far as the substrate, is its root cause the usage of a person under delusion, or the usage of one who is fully awakened?

The first [alternative] is not tenable; for since the silver and the object present before one are neither superimposed nor the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) [of each other], the employment of the word "silver" there occurs simply through the cognition [of the object] as not being superimposed. Thus, that [usage] does not prove that a word denoting a superimposed thing extends to its substratum. Indeed, the employment of the word "Devadatta" due to ignorance of someone's not being Devadatta does not constitute a basis for the word "Devadatta" denoting Yajñadatta.

Furthermore, in the second case, the usage "the rope is a snake" cannot have its root in the assumption of a power directed toward a superimposed object, because it is merely a restatement of a usage based on a cognition that was previously not superimposed. If it is argued: "It is accepted that words denoting inseparable qualifiers (apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa) extend to the substratum (viśeṣya); and the superimposed is an inseparable qualifier of the substratum, since it appears only when that [substratum] exists and does not appear without it"—we say no.

Otherwise, there can be no non-separate qualification (*apṛthaksiddhi*) of an existing qualifier with respect to that which stands before one; for in the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), both the status of being superimposed and the status of being the substrate are absent. Furthermore, in the theory of illusory manifestation (*mṛṣāvāda*), just as a jar or the like—which is a transformation of clay—cannot be a non-separate qualifier of gold, so too silver, which is a transformation of the defect called ignorance (*avidyā*), cannot be a non-separate qualifier of that which stands before one.
Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is untenable.

Furthermore, regarding sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), does the word denoting the individual soul (*jīva*), such as "thou" (*tvam*), stand in grammatical apposition with the word denoting Brahman by abandoning its primary meaning, or without abandoning it? In the first case, the reality would possess attributes (*saviśeṣa*), and the identity between that which is subject to defects and that which is not subject to them would be untenable. In the second case, the identity of the individual soul and Brahman would not be established; nor could it be established that the state of being an individual soul is illusory and that only the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is ultimately real.

This is because a case-ending (*samānavibhakti*) intended to express the unity of the primary referent (*prakṛti*) lacks the capacity to establish the unity of that which is not so intended as its referent; and furthermore, it lacks the capacity to establish the falsity of those qualifiers that are not intended as its referent. Indeed, in the cases "the country is delighted" (*prahṛṣṭo janapadaḥ*) and "the boy is fire" (*agnirmāṇavakaḥ*), neither the unity of the country and the delight, nor the unity of the boy and the fire, is established by the falsity of "country-ness" and "fire-ness," nor is the ultimate reality of the substratum alone thereby proven.

If it is argued that by the word *janapada* (country) that which is external to the denoted object is indicated (*lakṣyate*), whereas by the word *tvam* (you) a portion of the denoted object is indicated, and thus—since their identity as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is impossible due to contradiction—the falsity of the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) is established; [we reply] no, because words such as *tvam*, when in grammatical apposition with the term for the knower (*jñātṛpada*), cannot be established as signifying pure consciousness (*jñapti*) through a lack of co-referentiality with consciousness, and therefore it is difficult to maintain that they indicate a portion of the denoted object.

Even if that [identity] were established, neither the oneness of the substratum nor the falsity of the other form would be proven. For instance, when one sees a fire blazing at the peak of a distant mountain and says, "The mountain is burning," it does not follow that there is identity between the mountain and the fire, nor that the rest of the mountain—including its ridges and other parts—is false, such that only the substratum would be ultimately real. Therefore, the intended oneness and the falsity of the state of being a living soul (jīva) are not established. Consequently, all cases of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are contradictory for those who maintain the doctrine of universal illusion (*mṛṣāvāda*).

Even in the view that difference and non-difference are adventitious (*aupādhika*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable in its primary sense. For, according to that system, Brahman is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*). Since the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord, as well as the insentient (*acit*) and the Lord, possess mutually contradictory natures—characterized by being subject to afflictions, karma, and so forth, versus being free from them, and by being subject to transformation versus being unchanging—the words denoting them cannot be coreferential, just like the words "pot" and "cloth. If it is argued that coreferentiality is possible because non-difference exists alongside difference, we say no.

Even though there is identity in some respect, when a difference in the qualified portion—characterized by the presence or absence of the ground for application—is perceived, a single case-ending lacks the power to convey oneness.

For, since the non-difference— which cannot tolerate even partial difference between the qualificand understood from one word and the qualificand understood from another word— is precisely what is conveyed by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it follows that if non-difference were admitted [only] as in the case of "the broken" and "the shaven" (as individuals and universals), or "the jar" and "the bowl" (as cause and effect), or "the cow" and "the tail" (as whole and part), there would still be an absence of coreferentiality in such expressions as "the broken is the shaven," "the jar is the bowl," and "the cow is the tail."

[Objection: Since consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit) are both parts of Brahman, their grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—such as in the statement, "The manifest is Viṣṇu, as well as the unmanifest, the Person, and Time"—is justifiable, just like [the expression], "This cloth is white, black, and red. [Reply: It is not so; for even when the relation of part and whole exists, we do not observe grammatical coordination such as "The finger is the person. [Objection: Why should it not be similar to words like "white" and so on? [Reply: It is said: *Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence. The following is a continuation of the argument based on standard Advaita Vedānta exegesis.* It is stated: [The case is different because]... [The text continues with the explanation that the relationship between the part and the whole is not one of identity, whereas the relationship between the qualities of whiteness, etc., and the cloth is one of identity-in-difference (bhedābheda), which allows for grammatical coordination.]

Even though words such as "white" and so forth lack mutual coreferentiality prior to hearing the word "cloth" when there is a distinction of parts in the cloth, because whiteness and the rest are inseparably established qualifiers (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), the referent denoted by the word "cloth" does not differ even in part from the referent denoted by the words "white" and so forth—which denote the qualifier up to the ultimate substrate—when they are combined; thus, coreferentiality exists, just as it does with the word "variegated" (*citra*) which denotes the same substrate.

Parts such as the hands and so forth, which are subject to cutting and other forms of injury, do not possess the quality of being inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*) with respect to the whole [body], because even when they are cut, the sense organs are not destroyed and the respective physical bases (*golaka*) do not lose their essential nature. If it is argued that, this being the case, since the dead body is perceived without its essential nature having been lost—just like a severed hand or foot—it would follow that the body is not inseparably established with respect to the Self, we say: no; for the Self departs immediately after the disintegration of the aggregate known as the body.

This is because, subsequently, the cognition of the body is of the nature of an error, according to the analogy of the cognition of a cloth [arising] when a cloth has been burnt. However, the distinction regarding fingers and so forth is that, at the stage of being cut, their own parts—which were not loose—subsequently become loose. Therefore, since words denoting those [parts] denote only the hand and so forth, and since the whole (ekadeśin)—which consists of a collection of parts such as the hand—is distinct from the mere hand and so forth, the identity characterized by non-distinction cannot be conveyed by a word with a common case-ending, as it would contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[Objection: Surely properties such as "hand-ness" (*hastatva*) and so forth are non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*), like whiteness and the like, and they reside in a single part of the body, just as [color resides] in a jar. Therefore, just as one says "the cloth is white" or "the cloth is black," it would be logical to say "the hand is a man" or "the foot is a man. [Response: It is because of ignorance of this logic that common people do not employ such expressions. To this we reply: although ignorant of the logic—or even though they are knowledgeable—common people employ words such as "white" as extending up to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), but they do not employ words such as "hand" as extending up to the possessor of the part (*ekadeśin*).

Therefore, that which establishes the application of the designations "the known" (*abhijñāta*) and "the knower" (*abhijñātṛ*) must be stated. We shall explain this: certain properties that are inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*) with something else exist necessarily in only one part [of that thing]; others exist either in that one part or elsewhere without such necessity. Among these, words denoting properties that exist necessarily in a specific part refer only to the substance that constitutes that very part, because they are restricted to producing the cognition of being a "part. For it is precisely as parts that hands and the like are perceived.

Words denoting a property (*dharma*) that exists in only one part [of a substance] and which lack a restriction [to that part alone] function with respect to the substratum (*viśeṣya*), having abandoned the restriction to the cognition of being a mere part. Therefore, since words such as "white" abandon the state of being a mere part and present only the locus of that [quality], and because the locus presented by them is not distinct from the locus of the cloth-ness (*paṭatva*), it is logical for the word "cloth" to stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with them.

Since words such as "hand" denote only a single part, they do not denote the possessor of that part; therefore, because the referent exceeds the substantive (viśeṣya) presented by the nominal stem *hasta* and so forth, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable. If, however, coreferentiality is observed in some instances, it must occur either through the word "hand" indicating the possessor by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), or through the word "man" indicating a part thereof, or by means of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) based on an intention regarding predominance and so forth.

In the case of the expression "the aperture is space" (*chidram ākāśaḥ*), since the property of being space (*ākāśatva*) does not reside in the aggregate [of parts], there is no indication of a single part (*ekadeśalakṣaṇā*) in the aperture because it exists there in its fullness. Furthermore, according to your own view, properties such as being a living soul (*jīvatva*) or being consciousness (*cittva*) reside necessarily only in a single part of Brahman; therefore, words denoting these [properties] cannot stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting the Lord (*īśvara*) in a primary sense.

But is it not observed that the usage "the head, the hand, the belly, and the foot are the body" occurs? True; when many constituent parts are taken as a whole, there is the possibility of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) because the whole does not exceed those parts. However, coreferentiality with each part individually would be merely figurative, as it would entail the fallacy of indicating only a single portion [of the whole]. Likewise, it would be improper for words denoting specific aspects of consciousness to be coreferential with a word denoting the Lord in reference to each individual aspect.

Because words denoting parts lack the power (*śakti*) to denote the whole, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) for each individual term in such passages as: "The manifest is Viṣṇu, likewise the unmanifest," "The luminaries are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu," and "Beings are Viṣṇu, the worlds are Viṣṇu. Similarly, in the statement "I am everything," it is improper to maintain coreferentiality between the words denoting the non-conscious (*acit*) and the individual soul (*jīva*), as they would function merely as designations. If coreferentiality were established everywhere by bringing Brahman to mind through a secondary sense (*amukhyā vṛttiḥ*), that same defect would apply; for when primary coreferentiality is possible, it is unjustifiable to resort to a secondary sense.

Even on the view that [Brahman] possesses both difference and non-difference by its very nature (*svābhāvikabheda-abheda*), since the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller are all admitted to be portions of Brahman, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the insentient and the individual soul, of the insentient and the Lord, and of the individual soul and the Lord—such as in the expression "the pot is a bowl"—is untenable; this remains established. For grammatical coreferentiality makes known only a non-difference that cannot tolerate any difference in the substantive, even in part; therefore, their coreferentiality with Brahman must also be reconsidered.

If the common form that expresses the existence and substantiality of words denoting Brahman were the ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), then when it is said "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it would be as if saying "Thou art an existent substance" (*sadasidravyamasi*). In that case, the instruction would be purposeless, for no one thinks, "I am non-existent" or "I am not a substance. If it is argued that what must be taught is identity with another existent, we say no; for such identity cannot be understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) indeed conveys the connection of a previously mentioned substantive (*viśeṣya*) with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) presented by another word; it does not, however, convey the identity of that [substantive] with another object qualified by that same qualifier. For when it is said, "You are a Brāhmaṇa," the identity of the person indicated by the word "you" with another Brāhmaṇa is not established; rather, only the possession of the qualification of being a Brāhmaṇa is conveyed for him. Therefore, since the intended unity is not established, the instruction would be entirely futile.

If the specific aspect that is not common [to others] were the basis for the application of the term (*pravṛttinimitta*), then there would be a contradiction when words such as "Brahman" are used in grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words expressing other aspects. If, on the other hand, unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśayabṛhattva*) were the basis for the application of the term, then when it is said, "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it would be equivalent to saying, "Thou art the unsurpassably great. Consequently, there would be a contradiction regarding the atom-like individual soul (*jīva*) possessing unsurpassed greatness. If the meaning is "Thou art a part (*aṃśa*) of the unsurpassably great reality," then this involves a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on being a single portion.

For indeed, a single part of the word *brahman* (such as the root *bṛh*) is not its primary meaning. In this same way, one should observe that the same untenability applies even if another unique characteristic were taken as the ground for the application of the term.
Therefore, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) which counters the three false views belongs primarily to the position of the Commentator alone.

What difference is there between the interpretation you have provided and that offered by other commentators? Furthermore, the relationship of body and embodied being (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) is established only if a distinction between the self (*ātman*) [and the Supreme Self] is proven; yet that very distinction does not exist, because their identity is taught at certain times. This is because the origin and dissolution of both the conscious and the unconscious are established through such passages as, "Both these [the individual soul and the subtle body] dissolve into the Supreme Self," and "In the same way, the selves indeed emerge from the Self"; and because cause and effect are of one and the same substance.

For a single entity cannot simultaneously be both the body and the embodied; therefore, in order to dispel the doubt that it would be better to maintain consistency by adopting the view of transformation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*), in order to make known the primary sense of all the scriptures, and in order to facilitate easy comprehension by synthesizing and demonstrating the meanings stated scattered across various passages, he begins [this work] with the words: "In this matter, the truth is as follows."

The word *ca* (and) [is used] because both [the objects and the subject] are included within a single category as that which is to be ruled (*īśitavyatvena*), namely, as the object of enjoyment (*bhogyatvena*) and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtvena*). He cites the verse "But the Māyā-possessor... (*māyī... asmāt*) in order to extract the meaning of the word *māyā*; and he says "The perishable is the *pradhāna*" (*kṣaraṃ pradhānam*) to clarify that the Self is denoted by the word "other. He explains the word *hara* as "the *pradhāna*" because it is the cause of confusion regarding other meanings.

In this context, because the preceding statement, “The Lord sustains the manifest and the unmanifest universe,” is heard, the distinction characterized by the relationship of the supported and the supporter is established. He shows the distinction consisting of the nature of the ruler and the ruled with the words, “He is the cause. For the purpose of explaining the term “Lord of the lords of the instruments,” he says, “of Pradhāna,” etc.; [he is] the Lord of the Guṇas, the controller of the Guṇas—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. He demonstrates the state of having no other lord with the word “the Master” (pati); by this, the distinction characterized as the relationship between the subordinate and the sovereign is also established.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *pati* is derived from the verbal root *pā* (to protect), it denotes a protector and not one who is the object of service (*śeṣin*); for the word is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the one who is served. Otherwise, since the word *go* is formed from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍoḥ*, it would follow that the word *go* could denote humans and other such beings.

If it is argued that because the term is not applied to all moving beings (*gatimat*), yet is applied even to a standing cow, its application there is based on conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*), [we reply: by the maxim, "An aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even by performing a hundred improper acts," the word *pati* is not applied to a son who protects his parents in preference to the parents themselves; furthermore, since the word *pati* is applied to a master even when he does not protect the house and so forth, the word *pati* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of the one who is the principal (*śeṣin*).

Likewise, the use of the terms "servant," "subordinate," and "master" is seen in the scriptures of the Lord, such as: "Indeed, all individual selves are by nature servants of the Supreme Self," and: "The Supreme One is the master to be adored, and the others are declared to be the adorers; this relationship between the adorer and the one to be adored is not based on any external purpose."

Even in the absence of words such as "husband" (*pati*), just as in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*) and so forth, where the accusative *śruti* establishes that the act of sprinkling and the like have the rice-grains and so forth as their subordinate purpose (*śeṣatva*), so too—because the world is understood through passages such as "whose body is the Self" (*yasyātmā śarīram*) to be the body of the Supreme Self, and because the fact that a body exists for the sake of another is well-established by such [Sūtras] as "because an aggregate exists for the sake of another" (*saṅghātaparārthatvāt*)—the relationship of subordinate and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*) between the world and Brahman is established.

Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. He demonstrates the establishment of difference through another approach with the words "the Knower and the ignorant" (*jñājñau*). He demonstrates the teaching on the absence of origination and dissolution with the words "the eternal among the eternals" (*nityo nityānām*). He states the difference by means of another aspect with the word "the enjoyer" (*bhoktā*). He shows that the Blessed One is untouched by defects with the words "of those two" (*tayor*). He states that the knowledge of difference is the cause of liberation with the word "separate" (*pṛthak*). He states the difference in the state of liberation with the word "unborn" (*ajām*).

In order to clarify the inherent difference and the distinctness between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he says, "On the same tree" (*samāne*). Between two scriptural passages which teach that the knowledge of their separation is the means to liberation, the verse beginning with "The one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*) is cited because it shares the commonality of being connected to the discussion of *pradhāna* (primordial matter), as seen in both "on the same tree" and "the one unborn female. "Juṣṭam" means being delighted by. As for the phrase "also in the Smṛti": by the statement "My nature is divided eightfold," the existence of difference is established even in the causal state.

The same applies here [in the verse] "they go to my own nature at the end of the kalpa. In the passage "taking hold of my own nature, I send them forth," that [distinction] is likewise established. However, in the phrase "by me as the supervisor," both the non-confusion of natures and the distinction in the causal state are established. In the word "nature" (*prakṛti*), there is a mention of its beginninglessness; and in the word "my" (*mama*), the distinction in the causal state is also established. He explains the portion requiring interpretation in the cited Smṛti passages with the words "the source of the world" (*jagadyoni*).

By the term *jagadyoni* (the source of the world), the statement "That which consists of the three qualities is the source of the world" is recalled. The expression "subtle element" (*bhūtasūkṣma*) is used for the purpose of excluding the state of being an effect. Thus, in response to the doubt—"Since there is a distinction between the conscious [individual] and the Lord, how can the determination of oneness be justified?"—he introduces the corroborating scriptural passages with the word "evam. It is heard in the Subālopaniṣad: "He who moves within the earth... Here, he explains the word *mṛtyu* (death) in order to exclude its primary meaning of death.

This is because of the statement "it dissolves" (*līyate*); the meaning is that it is due to the recognition of a sequential order. For the sequence—namely, "of whom the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the body, of whom the imperishable (*akṣara*) is the body, of whom death is the body"—is consistent with the sequence: "the unmanifest dissolves into the imperishable, the imperishable dissolves into darkness (*tamas*). Only the unification (*ekībhāva*) of darkness is heard in the scripture, not its dissolution (*laya*), because there is no abandonment of its nature as darkness. Its unification occurs within the Lord, whose body is the darkness that is not employed for any effect, while [the imperishable] is that which is employed for effects.

Since darkness characterized by death is heard of as having the nature of a body (*śarīratva*), its unification with the "unmanifest darkness" (*tamasā tamasaḥ*) is appropriate. To explain its being the self of all, he says, "having entered within. By this also, the relationship of being a body is established; for being a body consists in being that which is governed after [the Self] has entered within. Through the two—entering within and the teaching [of it as such]—kings and the sky are excluded. This definition of a body is also intended by the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*).

He states the meaning of the passages concerning unity in a way that does not contradict the scriptural texts that establish difference, beginning with the word "evam" (thus). The phrase "sanmūlāḥ" (having Being as their root) is cited as an example of such an establishing text. The phrase "atrāpi" (here also) means in both the Chāndogya section and the Taittirīya section. "Hantāham" and so forth occurs in the Chāndogya; "tatsṛṣṭvā" and so forth occurs in the Taittirīya. He says "anena" (by this) for the purpose of explaining the term "jīvenātmanā" (by the living self).

He says, "of such a nature," because even though the entry (*anupraveśa*) is not explicitly heard [in some texts], the general statement regarding the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) results in a differentiation of name and form preceded by entry, according to the maxim of the general and the particular. Alternatively, according to the maxim of the uniformity of all recensions (*sarvaśākhāpratyaya*), that which is not stated in one place may be taken from another; since entry is required for its utility in the task at hand when known in one instance, it must be accepted elsewhere as well. Thus he says, "thus. The word "evambhūta" (of such a nature) refers to being preceded by entry.

By this mention of the "manifestation of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) and "hearing" (*śruti*), it is stated that the birth and dissolution of living beings consist in the manifestation of name-and-form and its absence, respectively, and not in the production or destruction of their essential nature (*svarūpa*). By this, the previously raised objection is also resolved; for it is understood that the unity mentioned at a particular time refers merely to the absence of the manifestation of name-and-form, and not to identity of essential nature.

Now, demonstrating that all the Śrutis have primary authority on this point, [the author] states "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that what was previously mentioned—that the knowledge of one thing resulting in the knowledge of all things is untenable in the opponent's view but tenable in his own—is indeed established. For the realization of non-duality (*advaita*) occurs in three ways: through the teaching of the identity of cause and effect, through the promise of the knowledge of all by means of the knowledge of one, and through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Here, the first two of these are shown to be tenable according to the method we have explained; this is what is expressed by the commentary beginning with "Therefore."

The cause is the qualified [entity], and that very thing is the effect; thus, there is non-difference of the effect from the cause. Therefore, for those scriptural passages dedicated to the identity of cause and effect, what is intended to be established is merely their being a single substance (*ekadravyatva*), and not the negation of their qualified nature, since that qualified nature has been enjoined. Likewise, the "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is exactly the same. Just as when, by means of a lump of clay, there is knowledge of its effects, there is no negation of the color and other qualities residing in that lump, so it is here.

By the use of the suffix *tarap* in the word *upapannataram*, the intention is to express that [this] is the primary meaning in all cases. Thus, he states the primacy of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "I these. To the question of how the non-confusion of the natures of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) and being the self (*svabhāva*) is established, he says: "Therefore, gross... Being the material cause is indeed the relinquishing of a prior state by one who possesses a particular subsequent state. Therefore, those two particular states are indicated by the terms "gross" and "subtle."

It follows that this determination of oneness delimited by a specific time is intended to signify the absence of differentiation between name and form (*nāmarūpa*). He states that even though [the cause] is the material substrate (*upādāna*), there is no confusion of their respective natures, using the word "subtle" (*sūkṣma*). He establishes this point through an illustration with the words "just as" (*yathā*). Now, one might object: white, black, and other threads are indeed distinct even in the state of the cause; nor is any one of them the cause of any other. Therefore, in that case, there is no confusion of natures.

But here, although the universe is the material cause of the aggregate, in the causal state only the Supreme Self is heard by its own name, and not the sentient and the non-sentient. Furthermore, the oneness of the Supreme Self prior [to creation] and the origination and so forth of the other two from Him are heard in scripture. Therefore, there is no confusion of natures; to this he says: "Of the threads," etc. For there is no relation of mutual subordinate and principal among the threads, and thus the aggregate is not denoted by a word signifying any one of them.

The meaning is as follows: here, however, it is established that the Blessed One is denotable by every kind of word; thus, even by any one of those words, only the qualified [Brahman] is expressed. Since the cause is precisely the qualified [Brahman], difference exists even prior [to manifestation], and therefore the non-confusion of essential natures (*svabhāva*) is logically consistent. To the question "In what form is there similarity?", he says: "By its own nature" (*svabhāva*). Anticipating the objection that Brahman might undergo a change of state—like other substances coming into contact with *rumā* salt turning into salt—he says: "And thus" (*evañca*).

To the objection that "in that case, the very nature of being the material cause (upādānatva) is untenable," he replies with the words "of the gross state" (sthūlāvasthasya). To the question "Since it exists as the Self (ātmatayā), how can there be causality (kāryatva)?", he replies with the word "state" (avasthā). The meaning is that while the scriptural texts concerning immutability (*avikāratva*) refer to the absence of any modification consisting of a change in the essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*) residing in the primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the meaning of those scriptures asserting causality is that Brahman's causality consists in its attainment of a different state (*avasthāntara*) characterized by the governance of the sentient and insentient beings in their causal condition.

For the determination of the causal state does not constitute the determination of the effected state. The specific forms of the controller of the various states of the sentient and insentient are the direct (advāraka) states of Brahman; whereas modifications such as change of essential nature, contraction of knowledge, and so forth, are the indirect (sadvāraka) states—this is the meaning.

Just as, when objects mentioned in proximity are understood to be subordinate to the supreme *apūrva* by virtue of being grasped by the "grasper" (the primary ritual), the subordination of the sacrifice, the rice-grains, and so forth is understood to be direct (*advāraka*), while the subordination of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth is understood to be mediated (*sad-vāraka*), so too, when all states are understood to belong to the Supreme Self by virtue of being grasped by the "grasper" through the [Vedic resolve] "May I become many," the belonging-to-the-Supreme-Self of both the mediated state—consisting of the contraction of knowledge and the alteration of one's own nature—and the direct state—consisting of the respective governance [of those states]—is likewise established.

The sense is that it is indeed primary. Regarding the term "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*), such passages as "free from evil" (*apahatapāpman*) have been explained here to some extent. As for the phrase "scripture itself": in the interpretations offered by other schools, there is both the abandonment of what is stated in scripture and the assumption of what is not stated; however, in this case, the interpretation is based solely on scripture and is consistent with scripture—this is the intended distinction.

Now, in order to refute the [opponent's] denial of the qualities of the object (*arthaguṇa*), he states the meaning of the scriptural passages favored by others, beginning with the words "jñānasvarūpam. The phrases such as "of the omniscient one" (*sarvajñasya*) are intended to call to mind those statements that enjoin specific auspicious qualities. Here, the two ways of explaining [the nature of Brahman] have been stated exactly as established by the sūtras beginning with "tadguṇasāratvāt. Because the Lord is a knower (*jñātṛ*), it is said that He is defined solely by knowledge; for knowledge is the defining characteristic of a knower. The suffix *-tarap* signifies preeminence (*mukhyatva*).

He cites the scriptures—beginning with "He who is all-knowing"—which refer to [Brahman] as having the nature of knowledge and possessing the quality of knowledge. The meaning is that both [views] are tenable, because both the state of having the nature of knowledge and the state of possessing the quality of knowledge have been established; that is, [the texts] show the suitability for the designation "knowledge" in both ways. As for the objection regarding the impossibility of knowledge being the substratum of itself, that has already been resolved previously.

He states the meaning of the scriptural passages that negate difference with the words, "He desired... This means the manifoldness of diverse entities by way of their having the nature of the various stable and moving things; or alternatively, it means [the world] consists of the nature of the stable and the moving. The phrase "not having Brahman as its self" (abrahmātmaka) means "not being Brahman. Such being the case, the negation of the difference between cause and effect would be established.

The meaning is this: since the scriptures concerning unity (aikya-śrutis) are intent upon the identity of the modes (*prakāra*), even the negation of difference—which is a specific instance within those scriptures of unity—must, in accordance with them, be understood as a negation of the difference between the possessors of the modes (*prakārī*). For a general negation is seen to apply to matters other than those for which a specific injunction is observed, as in the case of "one should not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*) and so forth. He says "but not... with the intention that if a specific injunction were to override a general negation, it would follow that ritual killing (*vaidhahiṃsā*) would result in demerit (*adharma*).

He establishes the stated point by means of the very opening [of the Upaniṣad] with the words, "But when for him... and "whoever [sees] other than the Self. The indeclinable *anyatra* is a synonym for the word *vināśa* (destruction). The meaning is that there exists nothing separate from Brahman, nor anything devoid of its inseparable connection [with it]. The intention is that because a specific negation of difference is seen there, the general negation of difference also culminates in that very same place, according to the maxim: "The goat [is the animal to be sacrificed], on account of the wording of the mantra."

Other commentators, including yourselves, have also proposed ways of reconciling [the texts]; to the question "What is the distinction here?", he says "In this way. Our proposed reconciliation is stated by the Śrutis themselves and is in accordance with the Śrutis; whereas the reconciliation proposed by them is contrary to the Śrutis, is not found in the Śrutis, and is rooted in fallacious reasoning (tarkābhāsa). The phrase "rooted in an improper method" and "contrary to all the Śrutis" applies to every instance. By the word "of another," he refers to both the doctrine of natural difference-and-non-difference and the doctrine of difference residing in the Self.

He establishes this point by means of a Vedic illustration, beginning with the words "of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord. There are six sacrifices: the Āgneya, the Agniṣomīya, the Upāṃśuyāja, two Aindras, and the Aindrāgna. These are established by their originative injunctions (*utpattivākya*), such as: "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is never omitted at the new moon and the full moon [festivals]," and so forth. An "originative injunction" is defined as a statement that produces the initial cognition of a rite. [These sacrifices] are produced separately and established separately.

By the two sentences that restate the aggregate—namely, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon"—[the text] says "by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa. The meaning is that, having unified them under the form of being the means for attaining heaven, it enjoins their performance. Likewise, [the author] shows the presentation of the meaning here with the word "tathā" (thus). [The phrase] "become the body" means...

The meaning is that, by way of a specific verbal formulation stating that the Supreme Self alone exists in both the causal state and the effected state, [the text] establishes three distinct entities which were previously understood as separate. Regarding the question of how the designation of a whole can occur here through a word denoting the Supreme Self—whereas it is not observed in the case of a collection such as the Āgneya sacrifice and others, where words denoting any single member are used—the author says: "the conscious and unconscious entities. He provides an illustration with the words "just as... [yathā].

In that [other case], because there is no relationship of "part" and "whole" (prakāra-prakāribhāva) between the members, the word denoting any one member does not denote the whole collection; however, here it is appropriate because such a relationship exists. How so? It is said: by virtue of the power of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*) and the power of the word (*śabdasāmarthya*). Since consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) are inseparably established as modes (*prakāra*) of Brahman, and since it is impossible for a Brahman abstracted from its modes to be the cause, it is established that a word denoting the possessor of the modes (*prakārī*) brings about the cognition of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*).

The two words *sat* and *brahman* are capable of presenting the qualified [entity] because they are connected with existence (*sattva*) and greatness (*bṛhattva*). And the word *ātman* presents the qualified [entity] because its ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), which is the nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*), is dependent upon that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). Alternatively, [it is supported by such passages as]: "From the Imperishable, the universe comes into being," and "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

Therefore, in passages such as "From that, this Brahman is born—name, form, and food," and "From the Self, space was produced," the cause is denoted by words that refer exclusively to the Supreme Self. These words lack the power to denote the sentient and insentient entities which serve as its attributes. Even if one resorts to *lakṣaṇā* (indication), the same defect remains. Consequently, in all cases, a modification of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) would naturally follow; to this, he replies with the words "sentient and insentient."

The sense is that, because a modification of the essential nature [of Brahman] is impossible on the strength of other scriptural passages (*śrutyantara*), a qualifying attribute—even if not explicitly stated—that is required for its function as an effect, must be understood as being brought to mind by implication (*arthasvabhāvena*) according to the principle of the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter). He confirms this very point through common usage with the words "just as" (*yathā*). In the statement "this self is happy," when happiness is predicated of a specific self, since such sensory happiness is impossible for a self devoid of a body, it follows by implication (*arthataḥ*) that the self is qualified by a physical aggregate such as that of a human being, which is suitable for such happiness;
the meaning is that it is exactly like that.

He restates [the opponent's position] in order to show the impossibility of its cessation, beginning with "yat punar" (as for what again...). He refutes it with "tadayuktam" (that is incorrect), and so forth. Both the fact that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by knowledge and the fact that knowledge has unity as its object are accepted by the opponent. Regarding these, he first states the impossibility of sublation by knowledge, beginning with "bandhasya" (of bondage). He establishes the ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) of [the world] as being consistent with all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), beginning with "puṇyāpuṇya" (merit and demerit). The restriction of the relation between cause and effect is untenable for that which is established merely through appearance (*pratīti*).
