Because [the object] is the domain of one's own will, independent of its being a means to achieve some other internal purpose that serves as a cause for one's own pleasure; therefore, since one perceives an inability to endure the suffering of others—whether out of compassion (*kṛpā*) or affection (*sneha*)—it is established that the welfare of another constitutes the supreme purpose (*paramaprayojana*). Thus, there is no impossibility regarding the definition of the "subordinate" (*śeṣa*). Nor should one suspect that this definition is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), since the quality of conferring a supreme excellence upon another—which constitutes the nature of the supreme purpose—is also possible in the case of friends and the like.

This is because there is no rule that their sole purpose is to serve another. For that [purpose] is not necessarily fixed for them either by a specific form, or for as long as they live, or with respect to a particular person; it is also not fixed across different persons. In the case of servants, however, that is fixed: even in the absence of a restriction to a specific master, the fact that a servant exists for the sake of another persists as long as his own existence, regardless of who that person may be. If such a nature is not observed, they do not possess the status of being servants.

Alternatively, although those such as slaves born in the house (garbhadāsa) and others—unaware that their sole purpose is for the sake of another—might consider even the conferring of excellence upon the beneficiary to be for their own sake, nevertheless, that [notion] is an error, just like the cognition of the self as non-different from the body in the thought "I am fat. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion in the definition, because the cognition of something being for one's own sake is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition of the self as being fat. Nor is the quality of being for the sake of another lost merely through the error of thinking it is for one's own sake.

For the delusion "I am stout" does not cause the Self to lose its distinction from the body; likewise, since the notion of independence regarding consciousness and the intellect is sublated by scripture, there is no lack of pervasion of the definition. Indeed, even if rice and other grains are not known to be intended for sacrifice, they do not lose their status as being subsidiary to the sacrifice.

If it is asked: "How can one who possesses the conceit of independence, and who does not necessarily bestow upon another an excellence that constitutes a supreme purpose, possess the defining characteristics [of a devotee]?"—the answer is no. For even if such a state is not perceived due to a lack of understanding, in reality, because he is an instrument for the divine play (*līlā*) of the Supreme Self, an excellence in the form of the essence of the rasa of that play is necessarily established within the Supreme Self. Furthermore, his being invariably known by those who know the truth as an attendant of the Lord (*īśvara*) is his specific function.

Therefore, by virtue of being accompanied by such a retinue, the excellence consisting in the state of being known as such would be established for the Supreme Being. As it has been said by those learned in political science (*nītivid*): "Let there be some degree of assistance to everyone; this is because [the Lord] is known to have them as His retinue. The fact that the Supreme Self possesses an excellence such as the rasa of divine play (*līlā*) imparted by things that have become His subordinates (*śeṣa*) does not contradict His having attained all desires. For the attainment of all desires consists precisely in the possession of a retinue suitable for the intended application whenever there is a desire.

As the venerable author of the Bhāṣya states in the Vedāntasāra: "For this one who is satisfied in the Self, the state of having attained all desires is indeed the constant presence of all desired objects of enjoyment and their means. Therefore, the previously stated definition of the *śeṣa* (the subordinate) is established.

Thus, having accepted our definition of "subsidiarity" (*śeṣatva*), opponents are unable to define it as "being subsidiary to an action" (*kṛti*) or "being the intended object of an action" (*kṛtyuddeśyatva*), because such definitions cannot withstand logical scrutiny. Do you intend by "being subsidiary to an action" that it is being subsidiary to the means (*dvāra-śeṣitva*), or that it is being subsidiary to the final result (*phala-śeṣitva*)? In the first case, even the verbal root-meaning (*bhāvārtha*) would be subsidiary to the action, since it is produced by the action. In the second case, heaven (*svarga*) would be subsidiary to the action, since the unseen potency (*apūrva*), which is produced by the action, is itself a means to heaven.

Therefore, the status of being the intended object of an action (kṛtyuddeśyatva), which consists in being that which remains after the action is performed, is not established for the fruit or the meaning of the verbal root (bhāvārtha) by way of a distinct form.

Now, he refutes the position that "being the purpose of an effort" means "being the objective of an effort" with the words "nor also" (*nāpi*). For what is called "effort" (*kṛti*) is not itself some conscious entity that possesses a purpose. Therefore, the meaning of "the purpose of an effort" is the purpose of the person who possesses that effort. When the question arises as to what follows from this, he says "and that" (*sa ca*), concluding that it amounts to being "desired. Thus, the "task" (*kārya*)—defined by its being achievable through effort and its having effort as its primary element—is indeed difficult to define. By the term "having effort as its primary element," sweating and other involuntary bodily functions are excluded.

By the term "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatā*), the self (*ātman*) is excluded; for the self possesses the status of being the object of effort (*kṛtiśeṣitva*). Since the definition consists of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), when the substratum (*viśeṣya*) therein is difficult to establish, the qualified entity itself remains unestablished—this is the meaning. Thus, the nature of purpose (*prayojanatva*) as the third form has been refuted.

Now, [the author] refutes the notion that being a purpose (*prayojanatva*) consists in being desired for its own sake (*svataiṣṭatva*), as well as the state of being achievable through an effort prompted by that [desire], starting with the words "niyogasyāpi" (even of the injunction). *Īṣiḥ* means desire. Here, "being desired for its own sake" (*svataiṣṭatva*) is intended to mean being desired as such, in the absence of being a means to any other object that is the content of that desire. This [quality of being desired for its own sake] is common to both pleasure and the cessation of pain. Furthermore, being desired for its own sake and being achievable through an effort prompted by that very desire belong to those two alone.

Therefore, the meaning is that by virtue of being desired for its own sake, both the status of being achievable through an effort prompted by that [desire] and the status of being the means for that which is desired are established for the *niyoga*. He explains how it is established as being desired as a means with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva hi*). He states that otherwise, if the form of being a means were not admitted, the verbal root-meaning itself would have to be the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished), with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). He elaborates on this with the words "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). [He concludes with] "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is that, prior to the syntactical connection with the term *svargakāma* (“one desiring heaven”), there is the comprehension of the mere meaning of the verbal root as the object to be accomplished (*kāryatā*); and upon its connection [with the desire for heaven], it is comprehended precisely as the means (*sādhana*) to that [heaven]. Thus, because the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) is first understood as an end-in-itself, the *apūrva* itself subsequently becomes the means to the attainment of heaven, in order to fulfill the status of that end-in-itself which was initially apprehended as having no other purpose.

The meaning is as follows: just as a master grants what is desired by his dependents in order to accomplish his own preeminence, so too does [the Vedic injunction] grant heaven to the person who accomplishes his own [heaven] while regarding even the unprecedented [apūrva] as primary for the sake of establishing his own preeminence. As it says in the *Pañcikā*: "In order to establish the qualified agent (*niyojya*) who is favorable to the accomplishment of his own self, even heaven and the like are, for us, merely the primary task (*kārya*)."

"Upahāsya" means being laughed at even by those standing nearby. He explains the meaning of the word "ataḥ" (therefore) with the words "svargakāma" (one desiring heaven). With the intention of raising the dilemma—whether the comprehension of the task (*kārya*) occurs at the moment of hearing the single word [“svarga”], or at the moment of its connection with the word “svargakāma”—the first alternative is refuted by the statement, "otherwise, the action alone would be the task. Furthermore, within that same position, another refutation is stated by way of concession: "Let the task be comprehended from the single word as having no other purpose;"

Nevertheless, at the stage of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of the related), the very meaning that is apprehended is the correct meaning; therefore, it is not the case that [the word] lacks another purpose. The refutation of the second alternative is stated as "connected with the word *svargakāma*. The meaning is that since it is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth as connected with the word *svargakāma* precisely as a means to that [heaven], it is not proper to say that it was first apprehended as having no other purpose. At the stage of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*), there is an acquisition of the *apūrva* as being the means.

To address the doubt that at the time of denotation one might understand the body (*kārya*) as being non-contingent on any other purpose and as something stable, [the author] says "pleasure" (*sukha*), stating that even for a person who has never before learned the meaning of the word, it is impossible to perceive its non-contingency upon hearing a single word. According to the maxim, "A universal is not without particulars," even when denoted in general terms as "something to be accomplished" (*sādhya*), it is understood as residing in a particular instance. Only three things are achievable through volitional effort (*kṛti*): pleasure, the cessation of pain, and the means to those two.

Therefore, among these three, one must be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Among them, since it is impossible for [the action] to be pleasure itself or the cessation of suffering, it is understood that it is the means to those two that constitutes the object to be accomplished. For volition (*kṛti*) has as its object only one of these three; this is because such is observed. And one must accept [this] in accordance with what is observed. Indeed, because volition is not observed to have anything other than an action as its object, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*) is introduced as the constituent element of both the volition and the *apūrva*.

Therefore, the meaning is that in the absence of being any one of these three, there would be no cognition at all of [the object] as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Furthermore, the proponent of *anvitābhidhāna* (the theory that words denote meanings as already connected) must maintain that the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth denote the task (*kārya*) only when conjoined with the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). At that time, by the force of that proximity, it would be understood only as a means to that [heaven], and thus it could not be apprehended as having no other purpose. Alternatively, the meaning of the passage beginning with "pleasure" (*sukha*) is as follows: because it is distinct from pleasure and the cessation of pain, its being achievable through volitional effort (*kṛtisādhya*) is untenable on the grounds of being desired for its own sake (*svata iṣṭatayā*).
Since it is distinct from the means to that [end], and since it is desired by each [person] individually, its being "to be accomplished through volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*) is also untenable.

Previously, the nature of being a purpose (*prayojanatva*) consisting of the third form [of cognition] was refuted; now, the nature of being a purpose consisting of being inherently desired (*svataiṣṭatva*) has been refuted because it is distinct from pleasure and the cessation of pain. Now, he begins to refute the possibility of the nature of being a purpose consisting of pleasure—which might be imagined for the sake of establishing inherent desirability and for the sake of strengthening the argument that [the injunction] has no other purpose—by saying, "Moreover" (*api ca*). He asks: "What is this 'being a purpose' of the *niyoga*? The particle "what" (*kim*) is used here in the sense of an objection. He raises a doubt: "Like pleasure" (*sukhavat*)."

Considering that being "conducive" (*anukūlatva*) is untenable for anything other than pleasure (*sukha*), he asks: "What [is it]? He explains his intention: "For it is indeed pleasure... He raises a further objection: "Like a particular kind of pleasure... The word *apara* (other) is used because there is the possibility of numerous synonymous terms for what is otherwise called *niyoga*. "Another pleasure" means: just as a pleasure such as that of heaven is conceived as distinct from earthly pleasure, so too this [pleasure] is another pleasure distinct even from that.

He says "What then? in order to state the absence of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For pleasure derived from sandalwood and the like is established by one's own experience (*svānubhava*). Therefore, it is stated by the passage beginning with "If [it were] one's own experience," that one's own experience, worldly speech, Vedic injunctive passages concerning desired ends (*kāmyavidhi*), passages concerning obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika*), and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not, respectively, serve as valid means of knowledge for the fact that the mandate (*niyoga*) is of the nature of pleasure.

Because that [action] has suffering as its essential nature and is the object of an activity, it is taught by him [the author] merely as something to be accomplished through volition (*kṛtisādhyatāmātra*) precisely by way of being a means to pleasure and so forth. The meaning is: because only the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), which consists of suffering and serves as a means to pleasure and so forth, is taught as being "to be done" (*kartavyatā*). By the phrase "of an action with a fixed worldly result," etc., non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is expressed. This means: of an action with a fixed worldly result, an action for which no obstruction has arisen. By this, there is the exclusion of the supreme *apūrva* (unseen potency) which depends upon the final funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*).

Now, he refutes [the view that] being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*) [is the meaning of the optative suffix], stating: "Therefore, even in injunctive sentences... Having kept in mind the following alternatives—whether [this property] is accepted as a meaning distinct from the root-meaning because it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), or for the sake of establishing its status as a human goal (*puruṣārthatā*), or for the sake of establishing its status as an indirect human goal characterized as a means to happiness—he states the answer to the first and second positions with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is this: because there is no etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) for anything beyond the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) in the manner described, and because such a thing lacks intrinsic status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The activity of the agent is effort (*prayatna*). He states that the natural consistency of the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*) also exists in our position by saying, "it is established precisely by the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*). Regarding the claim that one must accept an object distinct from the action in order to establish its status as a means (*sādhana*), he says, "and of the meaning of the verbal root. The intention is that the verbal root is indeed "yaj, in the sense of worshiping the gods," and so forth.

He states "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that the reason for commencing the present inquiry into Brahman is established. The meaning is that the initial acquisition of knowledge regarding an already established entity occurs either through deliberate reflection or by chance; furthermore, such establishment is possible even otherwise, as an entity may be known as a subordinate element (*vidhiśeṣatayā*) within an injunction. Now, he dispels the objection regarding the non-establishment of the qualifying attributes with the words "the four-monthly sacrifices," etc. It should be understood that the fact that ritual actions yield perishable fruits is established because their repetition is enjoined.

Intending the passage beginning with, "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes," he says, "because of the teaching that its fruit is perishable. He states the resolution of the scriptural hearing of imperishable fruits with the words, "and air" (*vāyuśca*). For the hearing of imperishable fruits in the passages concerning the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and others is not rejected on the grounds of being merely an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*); rather, [it is understood] because of the injunction for the repetition of rituals and because of the teaching that their fruits are perishable. Therefore, the determination that the fruits of actions are perishable is established. Consequently, the qualifying portion of the reason is proven.

He concludes the subject matter [of this section] with the word *ataḥ*. The subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this section is the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmamīmāṃsā*); the doubt (*saṃśaya*) is whether it should be commenced or not; the deliberation (*vicāra*) is whether there is no derivation of the meaning of words regarding an already established entity; the conclusion (*nirṇaya*) is that such a derivation does exist; and the purpose (*prayojana*) is its commencement—these are the five constituent parts of a section (*adhikaraṇāṅga*). As they say: "The subject matter, the doubt, the deliberation, and likewise the conclusion, together with the purpose—this shall be the fivefold set of constituents."

The passage beginning with "Having examined the worlds" (*parīkṣya lokān*) is intended as an injunction regarding the rule of approaching a teacher (*gurūpasadana*), following an restatement of the principle established in the first Sūtra; for it has been stated that "one should approach a teacher alone. It cannot be argued that this Sūtra lacks the status of a sentence because there is no object to be enjoined once activity has proceeded from natural inclination (*rāga*); for a sentence is characterized by the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), and the predicate is indeed what is to be enjoined. This must not be said, because [the Sūtra] makes known what was previously unknown. For that which is to be enjoined is precisely what is made known by the sentence when it was previously unknown.

Even for one who has engaged in the inquiry into Brahman out of passion (*rāga*), it is understood from the statement that there is no comprehension (*vyutpatti*) regarding an established entity (*siddhavastu*) that [the inquiry] need not be commenced. For such a person, the communication that the inquiry must be commenced because comprehension of an established entity is possible is indeed the communication of what was previously unknown; thus, the Sūtra possesses the distinction between the subject to be indicated (*uddeśya*) and the predicate to be expressed (*upādeya*). For here, when a person proceeding out of passion is on the verge of desisting due to the reasons for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the respective refutations of those reasons—which were not yet understood—are enjoined.
Thus concludes the section on the desire to know (Jijñāsā-adhikaraṇa).

Now, among the seven types of *saṅgati*—distinguished by the categories of scripture (*śāstra*), section (*kāṇḍa*), pair (*dvika*), chapter (*adhyāya*), quarter (*pāda*), basket (*peṭikā*), and topic (*adhikaraṇa*)—since the other forms of *saṅgati* are clear, he states the *saṅgati* of the topic (*adhikaraṇa-saṅgati*) with the words "What, moreover... (*kiṃ punar iti*).

The connection with the *śāstra* (the treatise) is indeed most evident because it consists of an inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas; the connection with the *kāṇḍa* (section) is because it consists of an inquiry into the meaning of the Vedānta; the connection with the pair (*dvika*) is because its subject matter is the Cause; the connection with the *adhyāya* (chapter) is because it takes the form of reasoning upon the scriptural statements concerning the Cause; the connection with the *pāda* (quarter) is because it culminates in the exclusion of non-connection; and the connection with the *peṭikā* (sub-section) is because it serves as the introduction to the commencement of the *śāstra*. Therefore, the "intermediate connection" (*avāntara-saṅgati*) is stated by the commentary beginning with the words "niṃpunaḥ" and so forth.

"Jijñāsya" means that which is to be investigated; the meaning is that which has been described as the object of inquiry by way of being both the goal to be attained and the means [thereto], preceded by the renunciation of all other human goals and their means. For Brahman is indeed understood in a preliminary manner as both the goal to be attained and the attainer; by this term "jijñāsya," there is an exclusion of the figurative and modern meanings of the word "Brahman"—such as the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) or the Vedas—since it is established that such exclusions must be stated through a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).

That which is denoted by the word *brahman* is, by its very nature and its attributes, endowed with unsurpassed greatness (*bṛhattva*). This is because of the etymological definitions found in Śruti and Smṛti: "It grows (*bṛhati*) and it causes to grow (*bṛhayati*); because of its greatness (*bṛhatvāt*) and its nourishing nature (*bṛṃhaṇatvāt*), it is traditionally recited as *brahman*. In this regard: "The Brāhmaṇa is indeed all the deities"; "None is superior to you, O Indra"; "Agni is all the deities"; "Rudra is indeed one alone"; and "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth."

Because the reality of the meaning is confused by such [scriptural passages] as "He is the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu," and "The waters indeed are all this," through which even Brāhmaṇas, Agni, Indra, and others are perceived as being devoid of any equal or superior, therefore—among those [entities]—that Brahman, which is the object of inquiry for one afflicted by the three-fold suffering, possesses what kind of characteristics? This is the meaning.

Even though it is understood that all [entities] are devoid of equals or superiors, that [understanding] is contradicted by what is known from other passages [of scripture] and is therefore to be disregarded. With the intention that in the contexts of creation and dissolution—which primarily concern reality—it is precisely that which is described as the unsurpassedly great (*niratiśaya-bṛhat*) that must be investigated, the author of the Sūtras composed the first aphorism, *janmādy asya yataḥ*, keeping this meaning in mind. Thus, with that intention, he said: "What, then, is that Brahman which is said to be the object of inquiry?
For he did not say, "What, then, is Brahman? [as a mere definition].

He takes up the Sūtra: "That from which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed" (janmādy asya yataḥ). He explains the first term, "origin and so forth," as creation, maintenance, and dissolution. The other two terms will be explained during the construction of the sentence-meaning; however, because the explanation of the first term—being intended to determine the meaning of the compound—is incapable of being included within the construction of the sentence-meaning due to its dependence on the determination of the compound's sense, it is explained separately.

In the expression *sṛṣṭisthitipralayam*, the word *sṛṣṭi* refers to origination (*utpatti*), as seen in such usages as "at the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution" (*sṛṣṭisthityantakāleṣu*) and "that which effects creation, maintenance, and end" (*sṛṣṭisthinyantakaraṇī*). The use of words denoting the activities of the prompted (*prayojya*) and the prompter (*prayojaka*) in a transposed manner is based on the intention that Brahman alone is both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). The compound *sṛṣṭisthitipralayam* is a collective (*samāhāra*) *dvandva*. It is a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*) because there is a connection between the three in a single effect, where they function as equal producers through mutual dependence.

Just as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices with respect to heaven, there is no intention to express them as a collective aggregate (*samuditāvivakṣā*); rather, this very [instance] is a *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective copulative compound) when there is an intention to express a collective aggregate. Consequently, the singular number and the neuter gender are employed. Therefore, in the phrase "creation, maintenance, and dissolution" (*sṛṣṭisthitipralaya*), a *samāhāra-dvandva* has been formed; however, for the purpose of connecting the meaning of the sentence, an *itaretarayoga-dvandva* (distributive copulative compound) is formed as "creation, maintenance, and dissolution" (*sṛṣṭisthitipralayāḥ*), since the result is the same in both cases.

In the phrase "janmādi" (birth, etc.), by means of the particle *iti*, the intention behind the singular number (*ekavacana*) is understood. In the construction of the meaning of the words there, the singular number of the sūtra-word is followed by the word ending in the singular number, namely "sṛṣṭisthitipralayam" (creation, maintenance, and dissolution). There too, the singular number is used for the purpose of making it known that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the aggregate of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and not each one individually.

That the definition [of Brahman] consists of the aggregate [of the three clauses] is determined from the natural force (*svārasya*) of the scriptural text: "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart. For in this passage, it is not stated that "that is Brahman" with respect to each individual sentence; otherwise, one or another of the definitions would be redundant. Nor is the definition the sum of all parts, because there would be nothing to be excluded [if only one were used].

If it is argued that there is no entity whatsoever that serves as the efficient or material cause for the origin of the world—which would then be excluded by the term "cause of being" (*sthitikāraṇa*) and so forth—this is true; indeed, nothing to be excluded is intended here. Nevertheless, the author of the Sūtras spoke thus in accordance with the Śruti. For the Śruti, in the injunction "Desire to know That," employs the collective expression [of the three causes] in order to exclude the suspicion of a lack of greatness in that unsurpassed greatness which is conducive to the meditation one wishes to perform. Even by means of excluding what was suspected, the passage possesses a purpose.

For it is impossible to determine the nature of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) without first dispelling doubts that contradict its defining characteristics (*lakṣyākāra*). Furthermore, the status of being the cause of only one of the [six] states such as birth (*janma*) is not capable of dispelling doubts contrary to the nature of the object to be defined. To explain: even if "being the cause of origination" is stated, if it is not also the cause of subsistence and so forth, then—due to the absence of the corresponding power of knowledge and because other entities exist that serve as the causes of subsistence and dissolution—the unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśaya-bṛhattva*) of that which is the cause of mere birth would not be established.

Since liberation is included within absorption (*laya*), and because that which is worshipped as the bestower of liberation is itself what is to be attained, "greatness" (*bṛhattva*) is not established by qualities merely conducive to bestowing liberation or being the object of attainment. Therefore, although the status of being the cause of birth alone is capable of distinguishing [Brahman] from all other things, it is the status of being the cause of the entire collection—birth and so forth—that is necessary for unsurpassed greatness; thus, it is made known that the definition is the causality of the entire collection of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

In this context, the status of being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) for the aggregate is not intended. Since the term *janmādi* (birth and so forth) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound whose primary referent is an external object (*anyapadārtha*), birth is already included therein; thus, he says "tadguṇa... [referring to the rule *tadguṇasaṃvijñāno bahuvrīhiḥ*]. There are two types of *bahuvrīhi*: those where the qualities of the members are understood (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) and those where they are not (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*). An example of the former is "all pronouns beginning with *sarva*" or "bring the long-eared one. An example of the latter is "bring the man with the brindled cows."

By the word *tat* (that), the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is intended, and by the word expressing a quality (*guṇa*), the qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*). The prefix *sam-* signifies unification. The meaning is that it makes known both the qualifier and the substantive as being conjoined through their participation in a single effect. Even so, there is no violation of the rule that the Bahuvrīhi compound has a meaning external to its constituent members (*anyapadārtha-pradhānatva*), because it is logically consistent to intend the aggregate qualified by the meanings of its own members—or the possessor of that aggregate—as the external referent.

For even that which is denoted by a word standing within a compound is appropriately treated as the "referent of another word" (*anyapadārtha*) by virtue of its being included within the specific aggregate [of the compound], since the word itself alone does not denote it in that particular form. The word *asya* ("of this") is the citation of the term to be explained; he explains it with the words beginning with *acintya* ("inconceivable"). If it is asked: "Since the meaning of the word *asya* could have been stated simply as 'of the world' (*jagataḥ*), for what purpose is this elaboration?"—it is for the sake of stating the meaning intended by the author of the Sūtras. And that intention follows the intention of the Śruti (the Veda). If it is asked how the intention of the Śruti is known, it is said: [as follows].

Although the category of effects is denoted by the word *bhūta* (beings) in the phrase "from which indeed these beings are born," the term *imāni* (these) refers to the specific forms of that category of effects as established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend their substratum. In this context, the fact that the world is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*) is not relevant to the inquiry into Brahman; rather, the term *imāni* is intended to convey its manifold variety (*vaicitrya*), in order to make known that Brahman possesses a pre-eminence of attributes suitable for producing such effects.

The intention of the author of the Sūtras, who points to [the world] with the word "this" (*idam*) in the scriptural passage, is also precisely this: although the plural number is used in the Śruti as "these worlds" (*imāni*), the singular number in the Sūtra is intended to indicate that the entire universe possesses a single agent by virtue of its being a single effect; and it is also intended to show that the term "beings" (*bhūta*) refers to the entire collection of effects connected with the act of becoming—the "world"—rather than being restricted merely to the four classes of beings beginning with the gods.

For this very reason, it was stated as "of the world" (*jagataḥ*) in the Bhāṣya. In that context, because the category of effects consists of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), he expresses the inconceivable variety of those respective conscious and unconscious elements through the two terms beginning with "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Now, an objection may be raised: In the *Gṛhādhikaraṇa*, regarding the statement "he cleanses the house" (*gṛhaṃ sammārṣṭi*), it was stated that there is no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the singular number because there is no desire to emphasize the qualifiers inherent in the subject (*uddeśya*). By that same logic, since the word "this" (*idam*) is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*) in the form of a reference to what is already well-known, and thus lacks intentionality regarding the qualifiers of the subject, the text should not be explained in this manner. This is not so.

For in the context of the *gṛha-adhikaraṇa*, it is not denied that one may intend to express a specific qualification of the subject (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*); rather, what was stated there is that there is no intentionality regarding a qualification that contradicts the meaning expressed in the original injunction (*prāpaka-vākya*) which serves as the basis for the restatement (*anuvāda*). Indeed, singularity is contrary to the plurality of houses established by the originative injunction (*utpatti-vākya*). Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that even in the case of the rule "one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa boy at eight years of age," there would be no intentionality regarding qualifications such as being eight years old.

In these injunctive passages, however, the very diversity of the world is clearly evident. Alternatively, wherever there is a lack of syntactic coherence due to the non-intentionality of the meaning of a word employed, the intentionality of the qualifiers of the subject (*uddeśya*) has been accepted in those respective instances. Therefore, it is proper to explain it in this manner.

In this regard, he describes the variety of the non-conscious portion with the word beginning with "inconceivable" (*acintya*). "Inconceivability" (*acintyatva*) means the impossibility of being conceived as having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its creator. "Diversity" (*vividhatva*) refers to the distinction between ether, air, and so forth. "Variety" (*vicitratva*) refers to the multiplicity of each respective individual aggregate (*vyaṣṭi*). The meaning is "of such a construction" (*racanasya*); here, "construction" (*racanā*) signifies structural arrangement (*saṃsthāna*). Next, he describes the variety of the conscious portion with the word "determined" (*niyata*).

In this place and at this time, this fruit must be experienced by this [being]—such is the fixed law that applies without distinction to all beings from Brahmā down to a tiny ant. For even for Brahmā, it is impossible to live longer than his own allotted span of a hundred years, to enter another cosmic egg, or to enjoy a fruit greater than the sovereignty over that egg. Thus, by describing the diversity of the conscious and the unconscious, it is indicated that agency is untenable for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) alone. He takes up the third word, "yataḥ" (from which).

The explanation was provided in accordance with the intention expressed by the hearing of the preceding word; however, here, even though such a word is not heard, how is there the statement of multiple qualifiers? It is said in reply:

The reference "from which, by which, and that which" is made as if it were already well-known, for such a reference depends upon the source-texts (*prāpakavākya*). Since the Sūtrakāra’s intention is that the very same specific subject (*dharmiviśeṣa*)—endowed with those particular qualifications suitable for being the cause of the world and the object of inquiry—which was described in those source-texts, is intended here in the Śruti by the word *yat*, it is stated that the word *yataḥ* in the Sūtra has as its purport that specific subject characterized by those respective qualifications.

Regarding the word *yataḥ*: since the suffix *-tas* here functions as a general case-ending (*sārvavibhaktika*), there might be a suspicion that it refers to some other case. Consequently, one could suspect that the definition of Brahman is merely its being a locus—just like space or time—in the sense that "the origin and so forth of the world occur therein. Furthermore, because the suffix *-tasi* is common to the singular, dual, and plural, and because the causal texts designate the cause by various terms such as *sat*, *brahman*, and others, there might be a suspicion that the causes are manifold. To exclude both of these [suspicions], the word *yasmāt* (from which) is used.

By means of the words beginning with "sarva" (all), he demonstrates the qualifiers intended by this Śruti passage, which are established by various scriptural statements that bring about [the realization of] those [entities], and which are applicable both as the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*), as well as in their capacity as causes. According to the view of Yādavaprakāśa, "Brahma" refers to the three forms or parts (*mūrti/aṃśa*). It is the opinion of some that the Pradhāna and Puruṣa constitute the causality.

In order to exclude such [other entities] that are either deficient or excessive in their essential nature (*tattva*), the term "Lord of all" (*sarveśvara*) is used, in accordance with such scriptural passages as, "Him, the supreme Great Lord of lords," and "He is the cause, the Lord of the lords of the organs. He then states the specific form that distinguishes Him from both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), which is established by the purificatory passages (*śodhaka-vākya*) that serve as supplements to the causal texts (*kāraṇa-vākya*) and is useful for the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*): "from whose nature all defects are entirely alienated."

By the word "entire" (*nikhila*), the six modifications of being (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*) pertaining to the non-conscious (*acid*) and the afflictions, karma, its fruition, and latent impressions (*kleśakarmavipākāśaya*) pertaining to the conscious (*cit*) are intended as the things to be abandoned. By the word "antithetical" (*pratyanīka*), the state of being devoid of those [afflictions] while yet possessing the fitness to be abandoned is excluded. To the objection that if it were antithetical [to evil], its status as the material cause of the world would not be tenable, he says: "from its own nature" (*svarūpāt*). The meaning is that a direct connection with what is to be abandoned is excluded, but not one mediated by an intermediate factor (*sadvāraka*).

Regarding the point that even in the qualifying aspect of being "contrary to what is to be abandoned" (*heyapratyanīkatva*), there is no possibility of anything being abandoned—because it is opposed to such a connection and because it is impossible for it to produce its own opposite—the author says: "Because of His true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpāt*). He is capable of effecting a connection with what is to be abandoned and its subsequent removal among those who take refuge in Him, in accordance with His own resolve. Furthermore, the sense is that nothing is "to be abandoned" in relation to the Lord; since it can be warded off by His resolve, it actually serves as a source of delight for His divine play (*līlā*).

The quality of having true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) establishes the state of being opposed to all that is to be discarded (*heyapratyanīkatva*) and is useful for [establishing] the Lord as the object of inquiry as the Cause. By the two terms "from Him who is opposed to all that is to be discarded" and "who has true resolves," the passage beginning with "He is free from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*) is recalled. He states the auspicious nature of the subject's essence, which is useful for its being an object of inquiry, by saying "knowledge," etc. Blissfulness is the state of being favorable to oneself. By the word "etc.," reality (*satyatva*) and infinity (*ānantya*) are intended. The state of being opposed to all that is to be discarded was stated previously.

The phrase "bliss of knowledge" (*jñānānanda*) is an indication of the abstract state (*bhāvapradāna*), as in the rule "the dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively]. The meaning of the word "infinite" (*ananta*) is that the qualities of being knowledge, bliss, and truth are not limited or partial. Although infinity is already included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is no contradiction in stating the eternity of all-pervasiveness—which is the statement of temporal infinity—and the omnipresence of eternity—which is the statement of its existence in all places and its fitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with every object.

"Kalyāṇatva" (auspiciousness) means being favorable even to other experiencers. The meaning is: "from Him who possesses auspicious qualities such as knowledge and so forth. Just as in the case of a lamp, which is the substratum of light, the qualities of being four-finger-breadths in size, being luminous, and so on belong to the substratum itself apart from the light, so too for Brahman, the qualities of being knowledge, bliss, and eternally uniform are qualities of its very nature (*svarūpa*). There is no contradiction in both the substrate (*dharmin*) and the attribute (*dharma*) being knowledge, because they are distinct individual manifestations.

The common form shared by *dharma* (attribute) and *dharmin* (the possessor of attributes) is blissfulness and so forth. Just as when it is said that "of one who is indeed a man, the king has men as his attendants," there is no contradiction because of the difference in individuals, and "manhood" is the common form shared by both; it is the same in this case. He states that [Brahman] possesses knowledge as its attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) by the word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*). Omniscience is useful for being the efficient cause (*nimitta*), while omnipotence is useful for being the material cause (*upādāna*). By this, it is also intended that [Brahman] has the sentient and insentient as its body (*cidaciccharīraka*), otherwise being the material cause would be impossible.

Furthermore, omniscience is useful for knowing the obstacles to that [omniscience] expected by the seeker and the manner of their removal; omnipotence is useful for removing what is opposed to it; and supreme compassion is useful as the cause for being an object of inquiry. For creation proceeds out of pity upon beholding the multitude of sentient beings as if they were non-existent during the state of cosmic dissolution. And accessibility to those who have taken refuge arises precisely through compassion, as in: "Nārāyaṇa is mother, father, brother, abode, shelter, friend, and goal."

Regarding the statement that "such a Lord is the means (upāya) and the goal (upeya) is something else," he says "from the Supreme" (parasmāt). In this context, it should be understood as "the mother and the father. To determine the specific deity, he says "of the Person" (puṃsaḥ).

Regarding the causal statements, according to the logic of the sūtra, "Or the goat [is the victim], because of the wording of the mantra," general terms such as *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman* culminate in specific designations like *puruṣa* and *nārāyaṇa*. Thus, the intention of the author of the sūtras—that the heart-meaning of passages such as "from which indeed these beings [are born]" culminates in Nārāyaṇa alone—is the opinion of the commentator (the Bhāṣyakāra). By the word *puṃsaḥ* ("of the Person"), it is also indicated that the reality which serves as the cause possesses both form (*mūrti*) and manifestation (*vibhūti*).
This is because it is heard in the *Puruṣasūkta*: "Three-quarters of him are the immortal in heaven. [The phrase] "the meaning of the Sūtra" means the literal meaning and the intended meaning.

Now, if the Lord is what is intended to be defined, then why was "being the cause of birth and so forth" formulated in the Sūtra, while disregarding statements such as "truth, knowledge," etc., which establish His unique attributes like omniscience? It is said in reply: If the essential nature (*svarūpa*) were defined solely by its attributes (*guṇa*), then it would follow that the manifestation (*vibhūti*), which exists externally in relation to that nature, would not be included within the object of meditation.

However, when the true nature [of Brahman] is indicated by its manifestations (vibhūti) which have creation and so forth as their objects, it cannot even be suspected that these manifestations are not included among the qualities (guṇa), precisely because they require the governing and sustaining [of those qualities]. Therefore, the definition beginning with "birth" (janmādi) was formulated in the Sūtra in order to make known that both the qualities and the manifestations are included within the object of inquiry (jijñāsya). Furthermore, the inclusion of the manifestations within the object of inquiry will be established through the threefold nature of meditation and the principle of parity (tattulyanyāya).

[Objection: Even so, it is not established that the entire manifestation (*kṛtsnavibhūti*) is included within the object of inquiry, because the three-quarter manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*) is untouched by the "origin and so forth" (*janmādi*). [Reply: Not so; for even though that [three-quarter manifestation] is untouched by the origin and so forth, its inclusion is established within Brahman—the goal to be attained by the liberated—which is indicated by the word "that" (*yat*) in the dissolution-verse, "to which they go" (*yat prayanti*).

For instance, the term "they proceed" (*prayanti*) refers without qualification even to liberation (*mokṣa*), which consists of absolute dissolution; thus, by the word *yat*, Brahman is indicated as that which is to be attained by the liberated. And Brahman, characterized by the form of that which is to be attained, is here restated as being established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, other means of knowledge declare that Brahman, distinguished by its two-fold manifestation (*vibhūti*), is the object to be attained. Moreover, the fact that the object to be attained is also the object of meditation is established by the principle of "according to the nature of one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*).

Thus, by the inclusion of the aspect of dissolution (*layāṃśa*) within these very characteristics, the inclusion of the three-pada manifestation (*tripādvibhūti*)—as characterized by that [dissolution]—within the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) is established as indicated by the aphorism. Now, an objection may be raised: since the ablative case in the word *yataḥ* in the aphorism signifies the sense of material cause (*upādāna*), Brahman would be the material cause. Consequently, because there exists another [separate] efficient cause, there would follow the possibility of the position of the *Vyomātīta* school, which states: "The Blessed Lord is the material cause, while Maheśvara is the efficient cause. This is not so; for the ablative case in *yataḥ* has as its scope the mere sense of cause (*hetu*). And that it has the sense of cause is understood from its common applicability to birth (*janman*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*laya*).

However, unlike the rule for the designation of the *apādāna* (ablative) as seen in "the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth," no such rule for the designation of the *apādāna* is observed for the agent of persistence or for the locus of birth, persistence, and dissolution. Therefore, this fifth case (*pañcamī*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Consequently, since there is no distinction in the causality of both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), the word "whence" (*yataḥ*) encompasses both types of causality.

Because the word *yataḥ* in the passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*) has a dual scope, it is logical that the word in the Sūtra likewise possesses a dual scope. Now, one might object: since the relative pronoun *yat* occurs three times in the sentence "from which indeed these [beings arise]"—as in "from which" (*yataḥ*), "by which" (*yena*), and "which" (*yat*)—the word *yataḥ* does not have a common application to origination, maintenance, and dissolution. Therefore, in that context, the ablative case in *yataḥ* refers exclusively to the material cause (*upādāna*), because it connects specifically with the verb "they are born" (*jāyante*). For the meaning of the ablative is understood precisely as "the material cause of that which acts as the agent of birth" (*janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ*).

Furthermore, even though the ablative case in the Sūtra has "mere cause" as its general scope, it must ultimately resolve upon a specific type of cause—namely, the material cause—as expressed by the ablative case in the scriptural passage, since it is appropriate for the Sūtra to have the same meaning as the Śruti. Therefore, because the ablative case in both the Śruti and the Sūtra refers exclusively to the material cause, Brahman is the material cause and not the efficient cause. This is not so.

In the Śruti, although the word *yataḥ* (from which) lacks the commonality of referring to birth, maintenance, and dissolution, because the pronoun *yat* functions as a reference (*anudā*), and because a reference depends upon a source-statement (*prāpakavākya*), it is impossible for it to convey a meaning contrary to that source. Furthermore, in those source-statements—such as "One only, without a second," "It thought: May I be many," and "It emitted heat"—the Brahman, who is the material cause itself, is shown to have no other efficient cause; having declared the resolve, "May I myself become many in the form of the world," [He acted] according to that resolve.

Since it is established that the creation has Him as its agent, the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) in the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) that restates this refers to both [origination and dissolution]. Because it conforms to the Śruti and because it is common to origination, maintenance, and dissolution, the word "from which" in the Sūtra likewise refers exclusively to both. Therefore, the doctrine of another cause (as the material cause), being not opposed to the Veda, is simply to be disregarded. If it is argued that, in that case, there would be a redundancy with the *Prakṛti-adhikaraṇa* (the section on Primordial Matter), we say no.

For in that [previous] case, the fact that the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause is established by scripture is being supported; whereas here, however, the objection regarding the impossibility of that twofold causality being a defining characteristic is resolved by taking the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause as already established—thus there is a difference between the two.

Now, if the Lord (Īśvara) alone were Brahman, then it should be defined by such characteristics as "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth, rather than by "birth and so forth" (janmādi), because it is impossible for the Lord to be the cause of all things in every respect. For in the Vedāntas, it is held that the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) and the material cause (upādāna) are one and the same. Therefore, this statement of the definition beginning with "birth and so forth" would be favorable only to the proponent of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda-vādin) who accepts a Brahman distinct from the Lord. This is not so.

Because the Lord alone—being qualified by consciousness and matter (cid-acit) and possessing the power of true resolve (satya-saṅkalpa)—is capable of the contemplation "May I become many," it is logical that He alone is the cause in every respect. This is because pure existence (san-mātra) or pure consciousness (cit-mātra) cannot possess true resolve; and because the Lord, who is intended [by some] as a part of Brahman or as superimposed upon Him, cannot be denoted by words in grammatical apposition with another part or another superimposed entity. Thus, in the doctrine of identity-in-difference (bhedābheda) and in the doctrine of illusoriness (mṛṣāvāda), causality preceded by the resolve "May I become many" is not tenable.

Thus, this definition [of the world] is untenable for the opponents alone. Furthermore, the definition of that which is desired to be known must be stated; and that which is desired to be known is the object of meditation (*upāsya*). The Lord alone is both the object of meditation and the goal to be attained. Meditation has a specific object as its domain, because a threefold nature of meditation will be explained later. Attainment also has a specific object as its domain, since it is produced by the state of meditation. Moreover, "the origin and so forth" is the definition of the object of meditation, because of the teaching: "Seek to know That. However, "truth, knowledge," and so forth, are the definitions of the substantive portion [of the object].

But not [the Brahman] as qualified [by attributes]. Therefore, since only the qualified [Brahman] is the object of worship, the definition of the Brahman to be known (*jijñāsya*) is precisely "having its origin and so forth" (*janmādi*). Because the word "from which" (*yataḥ*) is of the nature of a restatement (*anuvāda*), and because of the statement that it is to be known in the phrase "you should desire to know" (*vijijñāsasva*), the meaning of the purifying statements (*śodhaka-vākya*) useful for establishing what is to be known is contained within the relative pronoun *yat*. Consequently, the qualifying attributes beginning with "from which" (*yasmāt*) have been stated.

Now, regarding the question—"What is the proof for birth and the others being the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and for birth being included therein, and furthermore, for that which is comprised therein being the defining characteristic?"—the author of the Sūtras shows the Śruti intended as the subject matter by citing the passage beginning with "Bhṛgu... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1]. The scripture (*śāstra*) is the subject matter of the inquiry. Although a mere statement such as "From whence indeed these... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1] should have been cited, the passage beginning with "Bhṛgu... was cited instead in order to indicate its status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), to make known the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of its purpose, and to demonstrate that the context (*prakaraṇa*) is not directed toward anything else, since it deals with Brahman.

Since entities such as Agni and Indra appear at first glance to be the most excellent, yet it is impossible for all of them to be the most excellent—rendering their true nature difficult to ascertain—the question, "Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman," arises from a desire to know that specific individual who is the locus of unsurpassed greatness. In that context, the definition of that specific individual is stated: "From which indeed these [beings arise]," and so forth. By the connection with the relative pronouns *yataḥ*, *yena*, and *yat*, the state of being the cause (*kāraṇatva*) is restated.

The statement "That [is] Brahman" prescribes that the cause is Brahman; by this, it is established that causality is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman. The injunction "Seek to know That" is not an injunction for inquiry or for meditative worship (upāsanā). Knowledge consisting of inquiry cannot be enjoined, as it is already attained through natural inclination (rāga).

However, since knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*) is already established by another sentence within the context, namely, "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," and because the initial question, "Teach me, O Blessed One, Brahman," refers to the true nature of reality (*tattva*) and does not concern a means [to that end], knowledge consisting of meditation is not what is to be enjoined here. Therefore, the injunction "Desire to know" (*vijijñāsasva*) is stated for the purpose of directing attention toward the subject being taught, or for the purpose of removing doubt, just as in the statement, "Know that which possesses fragrance to be earth."

Therefore, the very fact that being the cause is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman is what must be enjoined by this sentence. This is just as when it is said, "Wherever there is a crane, that is Devadatta’s field," the connection with the crane is stated to be the defining characteristic of Devadatta’s field. In that case, Devadatta’s field is the object of inquiry and resides in the mind, and the connection with the crane is perceived; however, its status as the defining characteristic of Devadatta’s field remains unknown. Thus, that alone is what must be enjoined by the sentence.

Thus, while unsurpassed greatness (*niratiśaya-vṛhattva*) is perceived at first glance in many things, and causality (*kāraṇatva*) is understood from the scriptural passages that establish [it], its character as the definition of the unsurpassably great reality remains unestablished; therefore, that is what must be enjoined here. Since a definition has the inherent nature of differentiating [its subject] from both homogeneous and heterogeneous entities, the exclusion of the suspicion that other things might possess unsurpassed greatness follows as a result. Consequently, it is established that unsurpassed greatness belongs only to that specific entity denoted by particular terms such as Nārāyaṇa.
For this very reason, it was stated: "from the Supreme Person" (*parasmāt puṃsaḥ*).

If it is argued that the unsurpassed greatness of the specific entity which serves as the cause is already known through the originative (prāpaka) statements alone, so what is the purpose of this defining (lakṣaṇa) statement? This is not the case; for even in the case of fire and other elements, their status as the most excellent is understood from the ritualistic (karmabhāga) statements. Therefore, in order to dispel the suspicion of such "greatness" regarding them, this statement is intended to demonstrate that the causal statements—unlike those [ritualistic ones]—do not have another purpose, but rather have the reality itself as their purport.

Now, if it is argued that the Śruti itself establishes the definition, then what is the purpose of the Sūtra? To this objection, wishing to state the intended meaning of the Sūtra, [the author] first demonstrates the arising of doubt by means of the very reasons found in the Śruti, in order to show the doubt. The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "in such a case. The term "therein" was used with the intention of indicating that the specific qualifications—which are numerous and favorable to the *pūrvapakṣa*—and the unity of the word "Brahman" within a single recitation, which is favorable to the *siddhānta*, serve as the causes for the doubt.

He demonstrates the nature of the doubt with the words "kimasmāt" (what from this?). The first inquiry is whether the Brahmamīmāṃsā should be commenced or not. For that purpose, there is a second inquiry common to all four sūtras: whether the Vedāntas are a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman or not. Anticipating the objection that a scripture cannot propound a Brahman whose nature is already established, he says at the beginning of the *Samanvaya* section: "That Brahman can indeed have the status of being known through the authority of that scripture."

For the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself will state that this section has the purpose of establishing the validity (*prāmāṇya*) which serves as the cause for undertaking the treatise. Thus they say: "The absence of linguistic derivation, the difficulty of comprehension, establishment by another means, and lack of fruit—these very reasons for not undertaking [the work] are refuted by the mere husk of the Sūtra."

Thus, intending that the pair of investigations [into the cause and the nature of the world] is established here by implication, the specific form of the doubt unique to this section is shown by the words "whether from this... and so on. The doubt is as follows: is the passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]" capable of defining Brahman through its characteristics, or not? To that end, it is further doubted: is it possible for creation and the other [stages of cosmic process] to serve as the definition of Brahman, either as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), or is it not?

For that purpose, regarding the position that [the adjuncts] are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), is there a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*) due to the difference in the qualifiers, or not? For that purpose, does the status of being a qualifier consist in the exclusion of all attributes belonging to its own substratum, or rather in the exclusion of contradictory attributes? Regarding the position that they are mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), is there the cognition of another form, or not? The prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that the status of being a qualifier consists in the exclusion of all attributes, and that there is no cognition of another form.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) functions precisely by excluding contradictory attributes, and that there is indeed the apprehension of another form [of the object]. If being a qualifier consisted in the exclusion of all attributes, it would follow that the qualified entity itself would be divided, which makes it impossible for "birth" and so forth to function as qualifiers. Furthermore, because there is no apprehension of another form, they cannot function as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). Since the status of being a definition (*lakṣaṇatva*) is thus untenable in either way, this sentence is incapable of establishing Brahman through its definition; thus, due to the defect of the definition, regarding Brahman—

In the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position, the conclusion was that since the scripture lacks authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*), an inquiry into it need not be commenced. In the final position (siddhānta), the conclusion is that an inquiry must indeed be commenced because the excellence of the definition establishes the authoritative validity of the scripture regarding Brahman. This is so because, although a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) functions precisely by excluding contradictory attributes, there is no difference in the nature of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*); thus, birth and the other characteristics can appropriately function as qualifiers. Furthermore, since they convey a different aspect of the object, they can also appropriately function as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). Since the status of being a "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is possible in both ways, this sentence is capable of presenting Brahman through its definition. Thus, by virtue of the excellence of the definition, the authoritative validity of the scripture with respect to Brahman is established, and consequently, the necessity of commencing an inquiry into it is proven.

In this regard, he introduces the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "it is not possible. Having in mind the dilemma as to whether the birth and other characteristics constitute the definition of Brahman by way of being qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) or by way of being indicators (upalakṣaṇa), he first refutes the former with the words "not, for instance" (na tāvat). To the question of how they do not define it by way of being qualifiers, he says: "because of multiplicity" (aneka). To the question of how there is the consequence of multiplicity or how there is the exclusion [of others], he says: "for qualification... (viśeṣaṇatvaṃ hi).

The meaning is as follows: according to the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) "that by which something is distinguished is a *viśeṣaṇa*," it is well known that the distinguisher is the *viśeṣaṇa* and the thing to be distinguished is the *viśeṣya*. This is observed in such cases as "the humped one, the shaven-headed one, the full-horned one," "blue, white, yellow," and "goat, elephant, buffalo. He raises an objection in the manner of the Siddhāntin with the word "nanu" (but surely). He refutes it with "naivam" (it is not so). "Upasaṃhāra" means the final conclusion. "Otherwise" means in the absence of the cognition of identity through another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

"In that case as well"—that is, even in the case of Devadatta and others—he states the disparity in this instance with the words "But here... The intention of one who asserts that unity is not apprehended by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: even by such [scriptural passages] as "One only, without a second," there is no certain determination of oneness, because even there, due to the difference between qualifiers such as "one" and so forth, there would result a plurality. Furthermore, there is the possibility of explaining the words "one" and so on [in a non-literal sense], just as in the expression "one grain of rice" (*eko vrīhiḥ*). [Objection: But surely the cognition of unity is not derived from other means of knowledge alone; there is also a verbal [cognition of it].

If that were the case, there would be no plurality of substrata (*dharmin*). Here, one might object—by the phrase "the word *brahman*," etc.—that the identity of the singular-ended term denoting the substratum serves as an indicator of the identity of the qualified (*viśeṣya*). The sense of this objection is that there is neither the repeated utterance "That Brahman, That Brahman" nor the plural form "those Brahmans. He refutes this with "No. To the question "How so? he says: "Because it is unknown. The identity of the singular-ended term denoting the substratum depends upon the plurality of qualifiers; it does not sublate the plurality of the qualified.

In the case of "the broken-horned, the hornless, the full-horned cow," there is the cognition of plurality. [Objection: The identity of the subject-expressing word ending in the singular number inherently conveys the identity of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), whereas the cognition of plurality in the case of "broken-horned" and so on is due to perceptual sublation (*pratyakṣabādha*). [Reply: This is not so; for even when a sentence such as "the broken-horned [cow]" is uttered with respect to cows that are not before one's eyes, there is still a cognition of plurality. Therefore, the intention behind stating "of the unperceived individual" is that the plurality of qualifiers brings about a difference in the qualified (*viśeṣya*).

The meaning is: "of a cow-individual not previously known through perception," that is, of a cow-individual currently being seen by the senses. The phrase "of one who desires to know" (*jijñāsoḥ*) is stated in order to exclude the impossibility of employing sentences such as "He is a *khaṇḍa* (a broken-horned cow)" or "He is a *muṇḍa* (a hornless cow)" [in reference to a cow already seen]. Since, when there is knowledge of the universal "cow," a desire to know arises because the specific cow-individual has not been seen, the employment of such sentences is possible.

Having in mind the alternative as to whether creation, maintenance, and dissolution possess individual characteristics or occur collectively, the refutation regarding the individual case has been stated; now he states the refutation regarding the collective position with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). This means: for this very reason, because the distinction among qualifiers inherently brings about a distinction among the qualified objects.

He refutes the position that [the adjuncts] are mere indicators (upalakṣaṇa) with the words "Nor also... (*nāpi*). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of another form" (*ākārāntara*). The sense is that when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is excluded, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is necessarily excluded. He establishes the status of being a pervader with the words "of the indicators" (*upalakṣaṇānām*). When there is a cognition of the indicated object (*upalakṣya*) by means of an indicator, three forms are unavoidable: the indicator itself, the form of the indicated object, and the previously cognized form; for this is seen in cases where there is common consensus. For example, the connection with the *sārasa* bird is the indicator.

The meaning is as follows: the state of being related to Devadatta is the character to be indicated (*upalakṣya*); the state of being a field (*kedāratva*) is the previously apprehended form. Therefore, since there is no apprehension of a third form here, it is untenable for [the field] to function as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). If it is asked how there can be three forms in the case of "The moon is at the tip of the branch," it is said in reply: the connection with a specific place at a specific time is the character to be indicated; the tip of the branch is the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*); and the relationship between the branch and the moon is their being situated in a straight line.

And that relation is understood from the sentence. The third form is the lunar configuration (*candrasaṃsthāna*), which is denoted by the word "moon" and serves to distinguish it from the sun and other objects. The form of being a field (*kedāratva*) and so forth is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, "moon-ness" (*candratva*) resides in the intellect because it was previously experienced. Thus it is when there is a desire to know "Where is the moon? When there is a desire to know "What is the moon?", its status as the denotation of the word is to be apprehended as a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣya*).

The curvature and so forth perceived through perception—whether by its own inherent nature or by means of a perception rooted in a desire to know (bubhutsā) aroused by words—is a previously apprehended form; by this, it is implied that in the doctrine of a featureless reality (nirviśeṣavastuvāda), even the status of being a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇatva) is untenable. He raises an objection, saying "But surely... [nanu ca], and refutes it, saying "No" [na]. Are truth and the other qualities [satyatvādayaḥ] defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) as qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa), or as secondary indicators (upalakṣaṇa)? Regarding the first alternative, the refutation has already been stated.

Furthermore, if there is a requirement to apprehend another form [of Brahman], and this is done by means of another sentence, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it were done by itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, the apprehension of another form must be stated by means of the sentence beginning with "from which indeed these... (*yato vā imāni*); and consequently, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*)—this is the sense. "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) means: because it is impossible for it to be either a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).

He introduces the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words: "This being the case, it is replied. This means that when the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) intended by the author of the Sūtras has been reached, the refutation of that position as intended by you is now stated. An *upalakṣaṇa* is a means of cognizing [an object] that is external to what is to be cognized (*jñāpya*). A *viśeṣaṇa* is a means of cognizing [an object] that is internal to what is to be cognized. Furthermore, there is no contradiction in one and the same thing being both the cognized and the cognizer.

Since the status of being an object (*viṣayatva*)—consisting in being a cause for the arising of cognition by virtue of being the counter-correlate of sense-organ contact in the case of a jar and so forth—is observed [in the world], and since he will later state that a qualifier is that which, by being present in the mind through verbal expression, serves as a cause for the cognition of its own qualified [substratum], the definition is established in both ways. Thus, just as in the verse, "Salutation to the one whose nature is both one and many, whose self is both gross and subtle," he first sets forth the latter-mentioned view of the *upalakṣaṇa* (secondary indicator) by way of its presence in the mind, and makes his formal declaration with the word "the universe."

To the objection that an inconsistency has been stated regarding the view that [the term] is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an incidental indicator), he says: "And not... An "other form" (*ākārāntara*) is a specific form (*ākāraviśeṣa*); and since that is distinct from the form of the object indicated (*upalakṣya*), there is no tautology. Desiring to show two forms in order to demonstrate a separate third form, he first states the form of the object indicated with the words: "For the object indicated... In the *Atharvaśiras*, it is said: "It expands and causes to expand; therefore it is called the Supreme Brahman."

In the *Śrīmad Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa*, the statement beginning with “Because of its vastness (*bṛhattva*) and because of its causing growth (*bṛhaṇatva*), it is traditionally recited as ‘Brahman’” is indeed a word intended to indicate the well-known etymological derivation (*nirvacana*). The *ca* (and) particles occurring here and there are to be understood as serving to indicate the distinctness of the three forms. To the question, “How is the realization of unsurpassed vastness and the quality of causing growth attained? he replies with the word “of the root *bṛh*. The meaning is that this is because the root *bṛh*, ending in the suffix *manin* and supported by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), has that very [meaning] as its sense.

Alternatively, regarding how the understanding of "greatness" (*bṛhattva*) and "expansiveness" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*) arises from the word *brahman*, he says: "of the root *bṛh*. The sense is that since greatness is intended both in its essential nature and in its qualities, expansiveness—which is the form of greatness—is also included within the meaning of the verbal root. He states the manner of this indication: "that indication... [and so forth].

Now, one might object: "The relationship between birth and so forth with Brahman must be stated as being like that of a crane with a field; furthermore, if Brahman were the material cause (*upādāna*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its being presided over by another instrumental cause—as in the systems of outsiders—and thus the 'bigness' (*bṛhaṇatva*) characterized by the possession of qualities such as 'truthful resolve' (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) would not be established. Dispelling these two doubts, he introduces the sentence that presents the third form [of Brahman] with the words "from which," "by which," and so on. To the question "Where and how is this well-known? he replies: "And the well-known [usage is as follows]."

In response to the inquiry "And how is that so?", he demonstrates its exposition by way of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the words, beginning with "That also... (*tadapi*). "That" refers to the causality consisting in being the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*). The demonstration of the exclusion of any other material cause or supervisor has already been established by the passages "It thought, 'May I be many'" and "It created. To exclude the notion of becoming manifold in the form of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth, it is shown that the becoming manifold occurs in the form of the universe (*jagat*), as indicated by the passage "It created fire. Here, he states the resulting relationship: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

Just as a field has a relationship with its delimiters by way of being their locus, and just as there is a relationship between the moon’s position and the reed in terms of straightness, so too it is stated that Brahman has a relationship with its defining characteristics (upalakṣaṇa), such as birth and so forth, by way of being the possessor of those causes; this is because the sentence functions as a restatement (anuvāda) according to what is already well-known. Furthermore, by implication, any suspicion of other [possible] causes is thereby set aside.

Thus, the causality consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*), which takes the form of an indicative connection (*upalakṣaṇa-sambandha*) and impels the third aspect, has been stated. Now, he states that third aspect implied by it, beginning with the word "the world" (*jagat*). For, in the causal sentences recalled by the word "since" (*yataḥ*), there is the comprehension of omniscience and other attributes; therefore, it is said that [this aspect] is implied by the world's being both the efficient and material cause. The phrase "by way of the greatness of its aspects" (*ākāra-bṛhattvena*) is stated in order to make known the fitness of Brahman—qualified by those [attributes]—to be denoted by the word "Brahman," due to the unlimited nature of those qualities.

Because the omniscience and other attributes understood from statements such as "He who is all-knowing" (*yaḥ sarvajña*) do not function as mere secondary indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is no circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, it will be explained that a plurality of qualifiers does not necessitate a difference in the qualified entity (*viśeṣya*); thus, there is no contradiction. The phrase "iti ca" concludes the refutation of the impossibility of the *upalakṣaṇa* position; "iti ca" means "for this reason," and "ataśca" means "and for that reason."

The interpretation of the commentary beginning with "upalakṣyaṃ hi" (*for that which is to be characterized*) is as follows: the intended meaning lies in the term "limitless and unsurpassed" (*anavadhikātiśaya*). That which is to be characterized (*upalakṣyam*) is limitless and unsurpassed greatness (*bṛhattva*) and expansiveness (*bṛṃhaṇatva*).
