Furthermore, "limitless greatness" means greatness that is limitless in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*), qualities (*guṇa*), and manifestations (*vibhūti*). Thus, it is stated that the specific distinction between greatness and expansiveness is what is to be characterized.

Consequently, it follows that the previously apprehended form consists merely of "bigness" (*bṛhatva*) and "nourishingness" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*), which are constituent parts of the defining characteristic (*upalakṣya*). This is because such is observed in the world. For instance, in the case of "Devadatta’s field," it is the field itself that is the object defined; yet it is not merely the relationship with Devadatta, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding jars, cloths, and so forth. Furthermore, the prior cognition occurs by means of its being a field, which is a part of that [whole] entity. Therefore, with the intention that it is the object to be defined, it was stated: "the exceedingly great and the nourisher of the great."

Because it is characterized by the specific qualities of vastness (*bṛhattva*) and nourishingness (*bṛṃhaṇatva*), the mere state of vastness and nourishingness is the form previously apprehended; this is established as the meaning [of the word "Brahman"], as indicated by the word "hi" (for). To the question, "How is that apprehension [attained]? he says: "Of the root *bṛh*. The connection with the ablative case in the phrase "because it has that as its meaning" (*tadarthatvāt*) is with the sentence supplied [in the commentary]: "The mere state of vastness is the form previously apprehended. Alternatively, it connects with the preceding sentence beginning with "na ca" (nor...). He states the form of the characterization: "That characterization... (*tadupalakṣaṇa*).

Desiring to state another third aspect, he introduces the sentence that establishes it; by stating the relationship between the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and the indicated (*upalakṣya*), and by means of the words "since" (*yataḥ*) and so forth, he also dispels the suspicion of any other cause. The meaning is as before. He states the intended third aspect with the word "the world" (*jagat*). Now, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate another third aspect.

Just as the state of being a field (kedāratva) is conducive to its being the locus of water and its being related to Devadatta, so too omniscience and other such qualities are conducive to [the Lord's] being the cause of birth and so forth, characterized by infinite, unsurpassed, and great expansion.

Now, he establishes that [the attributes] function as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by virtue of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), stating: "of the world's birth and so forth. How is there no fault? For it has been stated that, in the absence of a subverting means of knowledge (*apavādaka-pramāṇa*), the distinction between qualifiers brings about a distinction in the qualified, which constitutes a fault. To this, he replies: "even though they are defining characteristics. This means: even though they are differentiators (*vyāvarttaka*). Alternatively, it means: even though the qualifiers that constitute the definition have the inherent nature of excluding [the subject] from its own class (*sajātīya*) and from other classes (*vijātīya*).

The meaning is: "excluded from that which possesses a qualifier residing in a necessarily distinct locus" means it is excluded from what is opposed to itself, but not excluded from what possesses a non-opposed qualifier. This section concerns the subject (pakṣa). Regarding the point that "opposition" consists simply in being a qualifier when there is no evidence to sublate the plurality [of instances], he says: "unperceived," etc. This, however, concerns the similar instance (sapakṣa). The intended example here is: "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," and so forth.

The meaning is that even when the object is not perceptible, the identity of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is understood due to the unity of the word expressing the subject (*dharmin*) in the singular number. Here, in response to the inquiry as to what establishes this identity of the qualificand, he demonstrates the identity of the qualificand in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) with the words "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). The meaning is that, by the natural force of the words, there is the cognition of the qualifiers as being connected to a single substratum; thus, it is established that non-contradictory qualifiers reside in a single substratum. Therefore, it is stated that the state of having non-contradictory qualifiers is the determinant of the identity of the qualificand.

Alternatively, the phrase "whose nature is unknown" (*ajñātasvarūpa*) is also a subject of the proposition (*pakṣaviṣaya*). In the previous text, it was stated that the various qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) serve as differentiators (*bhedaka*) because they reside in contradictory qualities, thereby effecting a distinction within their own substratum. [The argument is: being a differentiator consists precisely in having distinct qualifiers while remaining non-perceptible (*apratyakṣatva*).

He says, "Save [us] from the charge of being 'unknown' (*ajñāta*). The meaning is that even in that case, a difference among non-contradictory qualifiers does not entail a difference in the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). Why is this so? To this he says, "Of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). The meaning is that since we observe non-contradictory qualifiers residing in a single substratum in instances such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned, young, and red-eyed," their application is likewise possible in the subject under consideration (*pakṣīkṛta*), which is also a single entity. Thus, it has been stated that non-contradictory qualifiers do not bring about a difference in the qualified object.

Regarding the fragments and so forth that constitute the opposing view, he states the rule for their multiplicity: "But the states of being fragments, etc. From this, he points out the disparity with the [proponent's] position: "But here, however... The intended meaning of the phrase "by means of a difference in time" is as follows: even if there were a multiplicity of Brahman as the substrate (*viśeṣya*), since the simultaneous occurrence of the origination of the world and so forth would be contradicted, one must resort to the absence of contradiction by means of a difference in time; likewise, even when the substrate is one, there is no contradiction in the same way.

In this regard, the following point should be considered: the plurality of qualifiers inherently brings about a difference in the qualified object, as is seen in cases such as "the one with a cleft lip" and "the shaven-headed. In instances such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," the cognition of identity arises because it is sublated by perception.

If it be argued that, therefore, regarding Brahman—which is not an object of perception—the multiplicity of the substratum (the qualified) necessarily follows from the multiplicity of its qualifiers, [we reply: the unity of the substratum expressed by a single word ending in the singular number is seen in cases such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," where the word itself intends the unity of the qualified. In cases such as "Khaṇḍa" and "Muṇḍa," the cognition of multiplicity arises because of the contradiction with perception. Therefore, in the case of Brahman, which is not an object of perception, unity is indeed established by the unity of the word expressing the substratum in the singular number. [Objection: It is not so.

The multiplicity of the qualified (viśeṣya) dependent upon the difference of the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa) does not contradict the singularity of the word denoting the substratum (dharmin) ending in the singular number; rather, it is perception itself that contradicts it. For the position of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is this: even when a person who has not seen a specific cow utters sentences such as "the spotted one" or "the bald one," there is a cognition of multiplicity despite the singularity of the word denoting the substratum. To this, the reply is stated with the words beginning "ajñāta-": the singularity of the word denoting the substratum indeed contradicts multiplicity.

Even when Devadatta is not visible, when one employs a sentence such as "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young," although there is a multiplicity of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), there is still the cognition of the oneness of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Likewise, in this case [of the Self], despite being devoid of the distinction between the perceptible and the imperceptible, there occurs both the cognition of multiplicity and the cognition of oneness. If it is asked, "In this matter, what is the decisive factor regarding multiplicity and oneness?"—the answer is: the multiplicity of qualifiers observed to have fixed, distinct substrates is opposed to the oneness of the qualificand; however, the multiplicity of qualifiers observed to have unfixed, non-distinct substrates is not opposed to oneness.

Now, he states the justification for *satya-jñāna* and so forth being definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the resolution of the previously mentioned circularity (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*), with the words "from which [verily]... (*yato vā*). By this sentence defining the definition, it is stated that causality itself is the definition; thus, this constitutes a statement regarding causality. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those scriptural passages such as "Being alone... (*sadeva*) which establish causality are included. [Objection: But surely, by means of the very causality of birth and so forth—which serves as its definition—the exclusion of Brahman from things of the same class (*sajātīya*) and different classes (*vijātīya*) is established; otherwise, it would be impossible for that [causality] to function as a definition.

How, then, can it be said that by the statement of the Truths (*satya*) and so forth, there is an expression of the denotation of exclusion from everything else? It is replied: exclusion is of two kinds: (1) consisting in the non-connection with specific properties unique to each genus, which are impossible in other individuals; and (2) consisting in the non-connection with those very same properties. Among these, when there is a connection with distinct properties, difference from other individuals is established; however, non-belonging-to-that-genus (*atajjātīyatva*) is not [established]. This is because the suspicion of belonging-to-that-genus—which depends on the connection with properties that manifest belonging-to-that-genus—is not apprehended [in the case of mere exclusion].

However, when there is no such connection [with that property], the exclusion from belonging to that class is established. For example, although a jar is established as distinct from everything else by its specific configuration, it does not lose its membership in the class "earth" because of its possession of odor, which is the determinant of earth-ness; and because water and other elements lack that [odor], their exclusion from that class is accepted. In the same way, even though Brahman possesses the unique attribute of being the cause of the universe, the suspicion that it might belong to the class of non-sentient matter (acit) or the class of individual souls (jīva) persists.

Since the exclusion of other classes (tajjātīyatāvyāvṛtti) is conveyed by the sentence "Truth, Knowledge, etc.," it is logical to state that this [sentence] makes known a nature that is excluded from everything else.

Regarding the question of how there can be a designation of a nature that is excluded [from all else], he says "therein" (*tatra*). By some particular modification, the existence of that which is in such-and-such a state is "existence with conditions" (*sopādhika-sattā*); therefore, "existence without conditions" (*nirupādhika-sattā*) is the state of being changeless. He states what is excluded by the word "real" (*satya*) with the words "by that" (*tena*). To the question "how?", he says "by another name" (*nāmāntara*). Since the word "real" (*satya*) without an adjunct does not restrict its scope, it makes known the single uniform nature both in terms of essence and attributes; thus, there is an exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) who is associated with the mind (*citta*).

He states the meaning of the word "jñāna" (knowledge) with the phrase "the term jñāna. Now, by means of the term *jñāna* devoid of qualifiers such as "in this object," he demonstrates the non-restricted nature (*asaṅkucitatva*) and eternality (*nityatva*) of knowledge. That which has the form of being eternal and unrestricted knowledge is therefore "that whose sole form is eternal and unrestricted knowledge. By this, there is an exclusion of insentience (*jaḍatva*) in Brahman at any time or in any location. This state of being eternal and unrestricted knowledge constitutes the form of the Supreme Self, both directly (*advāraka*) and through its attributes (*dharmadvāraka*).

From such passages as, “The self-luminous one, the resplendent,” and “By what, O friend, would one know the knower?,” we understand that both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its attribute (*dharma*) are of the nature of knowledge; thus, by the unrestricted application of the term ‘knowledge,’ it is established that [the Self] has the form of knowledge both mediately and immediately.

Now, what is the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of this term "knowledge" (*jñāna*)? If it is the state of being a substance called knowledge that penetrates an object, then because [the series of attributes] would never end, it would be stated that [the Self] has knowledge as its attribute (*jñānadharmakatva*), but not that it is of the nature of knowledge (*jñānasvarūpatā*). If, on the other hand, the ground for the application is "knowability" (*jñānatva*) in the form of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*), then it would be stated that it is of the nature of knowledge, but not that it has knowledge as its attribute. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra: "Because that [Brahman] has the quality of intelligence as its essence" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*).

Furthermore, if words such as "cow" were intended to refer to the Supreme Self, it would not be possible for both the substance called knowledge (jñāna) and its attribute, knowability (jñānatva), to serve as the grounds for the word's application (pravṛttinimitta), as is the case with the class-property "cowness," the individual body, and the individual soul, which stand in the relationship of the door and the one who enters through the door. For the attribute of knowability residing in the essential nature of the Self does not inhere in the attribute of knowability belonging to the transmigrating knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna), such that there could be a relationship of door and door-keeper between them.

If "cognitiveness" (*jñānatva*) alone—pervading both the cognition that has become a property (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) and the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—were the sole ground for the application of the term, then, like the two individual forms of a humpbacked and a hornless cow, two distinct instances of cognition would be denoted by the word "cognition. Consequently, because they are not expressed through the relationship of the door and the doorkeeper (*dvāradvāribhāva*), there would be no perception of a property-and-possessor relationship (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between those two cognitions. Furthermore, if the essential nature were denoted as qualified by the substance of cognition (*jñānadravya*) which is itself specified by the quality of cognitiveness, and [simultaneously] as specified by the quality of cognitiveness, it would entail a simultaneous bifurcation of the word's function.
Therefore, by the term "knowledge," the nature of the self as having the form of knowledge, both in its own essence and in its true nature, would not be established.

It is said: the basis for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the state of being knowledge (*jñānatva*) consisting in self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*). Nor does this contradict the Sūtra, "Because that [Self] has the quality of knowledge as its essence" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*); for even when the term refers to the substance of attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), the state of being knowledge remains the basis for its application. Furthermore, the self-nature’s (*svarūpa*) state of being knowledge is established by the Sūtra, "And like light, because it is not purposeless" (*prakāśavaccāvaiyarthyāt*). Nor is there a simultaneous division of the word's operation when denoting the self-nature, whether through a medium or without a medium.

Whether directly or indirectly, since the mere nature of being knowledge (*jñānatva*)—without regard for such distinctions—is the cause of engagement (*pravṛttinimitta*), and because the power of the word is not restricted, there is an understanding of the state of being qualified by the nature of knowledge through both direct and indirect means; thus, its status as having the nature of knowledge as its property and its essential nature as knowledge itself are established.

Nor is the relationship of attribute and substratum (dharmadharmitva) unestablished on the grounds that they are not designated as the door and the one who enters the door, as in the case of the individuals Khaṇḍa and Muṇḍa; for the fact that both the Supreme Self and the individual soul possess knowledge as their attribute and have knowledge as their very nature is established by such scriptural passages as: "The Self is light, O Emperor," "By the wise Brahman," "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous," and "For he is the seer, the hearer, the taster, the smeller, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the person whose essence is consciousness."

Furthermore, because the word *jñāna* (knowledge) functions without restriction, it possesses the capacity to convey the qualification of "being knowledge" (*jñānatva-vaiśiṣṭya*) with respect to both the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇa-aṃśa*) and the qualified portion (*viśeṣya-aṃśa*) of the self of knowledge. This is just as, for example, in such expressions as "the king was seen with his retinue," "the house was bought with its furnishings," or "the cow was bought with her calf," the connection of the qualifying portion and the qualified portion with the properties of being "seen" or "bought" is conveyed by the single operation of the word.

Furthermore, the connection with "being seen" (*dṛṣṭatva*) or "being purchased" (*krītatva*) does not apply to either the qualifying element (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*) or the qualified element (*viśeṣyāṃśa*), because there is no impossibility of perceiving the connection between "being seen" or "being purchased" for one part in the absence of the other part of the qualifier or the qualified. For it is not the case that, as in the example of the sound of a river being the dwelling place of a village (*ghoṣaprativāsatva*), the "being seen-ness," "being purchased-ness," and so forth, of the qualified element is untenable without the qualifying element.

Nor is there a cognition of the connection of the qualifying portion with that [action] by virtue of the object's capacity, characterized by its fitness for being seen, bought, and so forth; for even in the case of a pavilion, a field, or a cow-pen—which are fit for being seen, bought, etc.—such a connection is not cognized. And the non-cognition of that [connection] is established because doubt arises when there is a desire to know. Nor is the establishment of the connection of the qualifying portion with that [action] achieved through the force of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*); for in the expression "the virtuous king was seen," the virtue (*dharma*) is not cognized as having been seen.

If it is argued that *dharma* is not an object of the eye, and that its connection [with the verb] is established by the force of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) given its fitness (*yogyatva*), then it would follow that the verbal nature (*śābdatva*) of its connection must also be asserted for the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*). For being understood through a connection based on expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and fitness does not exclude the verbal nature of that understanding.

[Objection: Is it not the case that in such instances as "the king was seen with his retinue," since both the qualifying element (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified element (*viśeṣya*) are presented by the word, the connection with the intended form is appropriate even in the case of the qualifying element; whereas here, because that [presentation] is absent, the connection with the intended form is impossible in both cases? [Reply: This is not so, because the qualified entity itself is presented by the word *brahman* alone.

For instance, the Brahman that is stated as the object of inquiry for one desiring liberation in the passage "Let him desire to know That," and which is described in such passages as "That [Brahman] thought" as the cause characterized by true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*) and other attributes, is precisely what the word *brahman*—occurring in the "Satya" and other passages engaged in defining that [Brahman]—refers to as a specific cause characterized by true resolve and so forth. Indeed, the meaning of the word *brahman* is also "expansion" (*bṛṃhaṇatva*).

And that [knowledge] is the cause of the gross transformation of the insentient through its own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*), and the cause of the expansion of knowledge for sentient beings, as stated in the passage: "And that leads to infinity. Furthermore, because it qualifies the specific entity apprehended by the word "Brahman"—which presents an object characterized by such qualities as having true volitions—the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*), with its power uncontracted, conveys the connection of "knowability" (*jñānatva*)—which serves as its own ground for application—to both the qualified part (the subject) and the qualifying part (the attribute).

In cases such as "the king was seen with his retinue," a qualified entity is presented by means of a word co-occurring with other words; however, here the distinction is that [the qualified entity] is presented by the word *brahman*, which depends upon a definition located in another sentence that serves as its own basis. Once the qualified object has been presented, the fact that both the qualifying portion and the qualified portion are connected to the form intended to be enjoined is the same in both cases.

When a qualified entity is presented by a word that depends on other words as its own basis of meaning, it is observed that the form intended to be enjoined is connected to both [the qualifier and the qualificand], as in the examples: "The king has arrived with his retinue," and "I have honored the king"; or, "A cow with her calf stands there," and "She [the cow] has been given. Therefore, it is logical that the term *jñāna* (knowledge) denotes for the Supreme Self both the possession of the attribute of knowledge and its nature as consciousness. This same principle applies automatically to terms such as *ānanda* (bliss) and the like.

However, when there is a contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the presumption] ceases. Therefore, the meaning as stated is established. Thus, by demonstrating that [the Self] has the single form of eternal, uncontracted knowledge—both directly and through implication—he states the establishment of the exclusion of the liberated state by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) with the words "by that" (*tena*). He explains the meaning of the word "infinite" (*ananta*) with the words "infinite" (*ananta*). Here, "spatial non-limitation" (*deśāpariccheda*) is the impossibility of delimiting it as "this is here, not elsewhere. "Temporal non-limitation" (*kālapariccheda*) is the unsuitability for delimiting it as "this is now, not at another time."

But this does not mean the absence of space and time. Likewise, the non-limitation of an entity (*vastvapariccheda*) is not the absence of other entities; rather, it is simply the incapacity for limitation such that "this is not that. In other words, the non-limitation of an entity consists in its capacity for co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all entities. If one accepts a collection of positive ignorance and its effects distinct from Brahman, then the opponent's claim that the non-limitation of an entity consists in the absence of other entities becomes untenable.

If it is argued that this [non-existence] is the absence of another real entity (*satyavastvantarābhāvaḥ*), then it would be better to accept that it is the absence of another entity residing within itself (*svaniṣṭhavastvantarābhāvaḥ*), because this does not contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the absence of another real entity is contradicted by those very means of valid cognition that apprehend the respective substrata (*dharmin*). Furthermore, he states that there is infinity even in terms of qualities (*guṇa*) by the phrase "because it possesses qualities" (*saguṇatvāt*). While qualities possess limitations of space and time, they do not possess the absence of limitation by an entity characterized as previously described; rather, that [absence of limitation] belongs to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) alone.

Alternatively, he states the absence of the delimitation of an object by another means, beginning with the words "because it possesses qualities" (*saguṇatvāt*). The absence of delimitation of an object is the non-delimitation of an entity as "this is such-and-such" by its own nature; for example, even when there is equality of form and equality of time, gold of six colors is inferior in comparison to gold of ten colors, and silver and the like are inferior in comparison to that [gold]. That inferiority is the delimitation of an object.

In comparison with various other things, gold and the like are superior by virtue of qualities such as weight, brilliance, and purity, which exist in ten degrees. The state of that superiority being beyond all further gradation is "non-limitation of the object" (*vastvapariccheda*). Such non-limitation of the object is appropriate for both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and the attributes (*guṇa*), because even their excellence—consisting in the nature of being opposed to everything that is to be abandoned—is itself limitless. Thus, what is meant by "non-limitation of the object" is the unsurpassed excellence of the attributes, which serves as the cause for the absence of anything equal or superior.

Inclusion within this [Brahman] also entails the capacity for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things that have been produced. For that [capacity] consists in being the body of all; and that, in turn, is the ultimate limit of being the controller, the sustainer, and the sovereign. By the word "thereby" (*tena*), he states what is excluded by the term "infinite" (*ananta*): namely, that its essential nature and qualities are subject to degrees of excellence (*sātiśaya*). Its essential nature is subject to degrees of excellence because of its atomic dimension (*aṇutva*). Furthermore, qualities such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and the rest, which are distinct from knowledge, are also subject to degrees of excellence because they lack the capacity for the activity of the universe.

And although knowledge is eternal and all-pervading, it is nevertheless characterized by degrees of excellence because its nature as such is dependent upon the eternal will of the Supreme Self. Since the excellence consisting in independence from another exists in the Supreme, the word "own" (*sva*) is used to indicate that even though the qualities are innate, they possess gradation. He states the reason for this description of differentiation with the words "of the qualifiers" (*viśeṣaṇānām*). He shows that the charge of mutual dependence has been avoided with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*); "therefore" means because differentiation is thus established.

"Whose essential nature has been understood" means whose unique form has been understood. For the state of being the cause of birth and so forth is indeed the unique form; the meaning is that this has been understood as a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). "The specific nature of the substantive entity" refers to the reading *vastu-viśeṣya-svarūpam*. Alternatively, there is the reading *brahma*. The meaning is that since the purificatory statements (*śodhaka-vākya*) serve to exclude defects marked by the causality of Brahman—which has already been characterized by its causality—the purificatory statements must precede the defining statement (*lakṣaṇa-vākya*), and not the other way around; thus, there is no circular dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*).

The reason why the author of the Sūtras did not state "truth," "knowledge," and so forth as defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) is also demonstrated by this very point: truth, knowledge, and the rest are the definition of the qualified object (viśeṣyāṃśa), but not of the qualified whole (viśiṣṭa). Since it is the qualified whole alone that is the object of worship and the goal to be attained, the intention of the author of the Sūtras is that the definition of Brahman—the object of inquiry—is precisely "the origin and so forth" (janmādi).

It has been stated that Brahman, the cause of the world, is the object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*). In this Sūtra, the meaning of the purificatory statements (*śodhaka-vākya*), which serve as a supplement to that [definition] by excluding the defects suspected in the status of being the cause, is also intended by the author of the Sūtras. This is because causality alone—being consistent with the status of being the object of inquiry—is intended as the definition (*lakṣaṇa*); for since it is impossible for that which is inherently a locus of what is to be abandoned (*heya*) to be the object of inquiry, the status of being the object of inquiry depends upon the meaning of the purificatory statements.

Since there is no other sūtra whose subject matter is the passage beginning with "Truth, Knowledge, etc. (*satyajñānādi*), and since the sūtras "Like the Intelligent One" (*prājñavat*), "And like light" (*prakāśavacca*), and "And like light and so forth" (*prakāśādivacca*) are intent upon establishing a different point by taking the passage on Truth and so forth as an illustrative example, the Commentator has stated the qualification "whose nature is opposed to everything that is to be discarded" (*niḥśeṣaheyapratyanīkasvarūpa*), with the intention that the meaning of the passage on Truth, Knowledge, and so forth is what is intended here.

He concludes the section on the subject matter with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). "Therefore" means: because birth and the rest function as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) both as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*). With the intention that the causal reality—qualified by the very form understood from the purificatory passages (*śodhakavākya*) which are conducive to its being the object of inquiry—is what is effectively established in the passage beginning with "from which indeed these [beings arise]," he says "faultless" (*niravadyam*). His statement of that [reality] is made with the intention that the collection of attributes such as omniscience, though implied by its causality, is here restated in the word "from which" (*yataḥ*).

He states the inconsistency of these two sutras with the position of those who maintain that Brahman is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣavādin*) with the words "But those who... (*ye tu*). He establishes the inconsistency of the first sutra with the words "In the unsurpassed... (*niratiśaye*). The intended etymological definition is that which is stated in the *Atharvaśiras* and the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa*. The sense is: "No, for [Brahman] is defined as 'Brahman devoid of distinctions' (*nirviśeṣaṃ brahma*). He explains the inconsistency of the second sutra with the words "And that... (*tacceti*). The sense is: "For it is not intended to be characterized by the statement that 'the world is superimposed upon [Brahman]' (*jagato 'dhyāso yataḥ*)."

Thus, by stating that the discussion is inconsistent with the Sūtras, it is also implied that the passages concerning those subjects are likewise inconsistent. With the word "evam" (thus), he states that the subsequent Sūtras and their respective subject-passages are also not in accordance with the position of the Nirviśeṣa (the doctrine of the attributeless). Regarding the phrase "sūtragaṇeṣu" (in the groups of Sūtras), the meaning is that it is not each individual Sūtra or passage that is contradictory, but rather the entire framework of each topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) and the collection of passages concerning its subject matter that are contradictory. He states the lack of conformity with reasoning with the words "tarkaśca" (and reasoning); here, the word *tarka* refers to inference (*anumāna*).

Or [the definition of Brahman] is one that relies on reasoning (*tarka*) which supports the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even regarding the interpretation favored by the opponent, he states that a featureless entity (*nirviśeṣavastu*) is not established, citing the phrase "the origin, etc., of the world. He adds, "even in the case of the theory of creative imagination (*sotprekṣāpakṣe*). The intention here is as follows: in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras—such as "Just as, my dear, by one clod of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known," "He made himself by himself," "By means of distinctions such as bracelets, crowns, and earrings," "Because of being self-made," and "Because of transformation"—one observes statements concerning transformation (*pariṇāma*), along with corresponding examples and their justifications. However, nothing is observed that is consistent with the theory of illusory appearance (*vivarta*).

For neither is there a scriptural statement such as, "O dear one, by means of a single piece of mother-of-pearl, the entire collection of silver would be known," nor is there a sūtra stating, "[The world is] an illusory manifestation (vivarta). Therefore, the meaning that Brahman is that from which the delusion of the world's birth and so forth arises is merely self-invented; it is not established by scripture. Regarding the position imagined by others, [the author] demonstrates the failure to establish its featureless nature by saying, "the root of delusion. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "For witnesshood..."

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "But luminosity... Luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is the state of being denotable by the word "luminosity. Regarding the phrase "by having as its nature the production of fitness for linguistic usage" (*vyavahārayogyatāpādana-svabhāvena*): the very production of fitness for linguistic usage is its nature; therefore, the meaning is that luminosity is precisely that nature which consists in producing fitness for linguistic usage regarding both self and other. He states that such an admission implies a focus on qualified [entities] with the word "tathā" (thus). He states the refutation of not admitting this with the words "tadabhāve" (in the absence of that).

Then he states the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) with the words "the birth of the world, etc. To the question "How is it improper? he replies with "For that... The sense is that once it is established that [Brahman] is cognizable by the word in general, its status as being known through the Vedāntas—which are specific types of words—is established. And why is that? For it is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); to this he replies with "by inference" (*anumānataḥ*).

Objection: This section need not be commenced for the purpose of refuting the doctrine of the Lord’s (Īśvara) being the material cause, because such a refutation is impossible through scripture when the subject matter falls within the scope of other means of valid cognition—both supportive and subversive—and furthermore, such a refutation is not required. For even if a mere agent is established by inference, it is possible to establish the identity of the efficient and material causes as well as the creation of the ether and so forth, which are not apprehended [by that inference].

If it is argued that a scripture does not intend to establish a portion that is contradicted by inference, and therefore the refutation of inference is for the sake of establishing that [scriptural portion], we say: no; because contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) itself constitutes a defect in inference, it is impossible for inference to obstruct scripture. It is replied: A scripture indeed does not establish what is already established by another means of proof, nor does it establish what is sublated by another means of sublation. As they have said: "By the word 'not proximate' (*asannikṛṣṭa*), two things are here intended to be abandoned... [Ślokavārttika 1.1.4].

"Determination occurs either by way of that very form [of the object] or by its opposite. In this context, both the status of being the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) are understood through the scripture. Since the status of being merely the efficient cause is already established by inference, its mention in the scripture would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). Because a restatement depends upon what has been established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the restatement of the efficient cause necessarily depends upon inference.

Furthermore, since inference is based on the pervasion (vyāpti) that [an effect] has an agent distinct from the material cause (upādāna), which resides in everything other than incorporeal substances, the scripture is unable to establish the identity of the efficient and material causes or the production of ether and so forth, due to contradiction with the inference that apprehends the subject (dharmin).

Thus, because the causal statements have their scope already established in one part and are sublated in another part, the identity of the efficient and material causes and so forth would not be proven; therefore, this section must be commenced for the purpose of refuting the inference of a mere efficient cause in order to establish that [identity].

If it is argued that even by those who maintain the validity of inference (anumānavādins), the fact that God is accessible through scripture (āgama) is admitted, and that inference is stated merely as a corroborator of scripture—therefore its refutation is not appropriate—it is not right for those who hold that the validity [of knowledge] is extrinsic (parataḥ prāmāṇyavādins) to say this; for if inference were a corroborator of scripture, then scripture alone would be the primary means of valid cognition regarding God.

For the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is that which is to be favored [by the Lord], and they accept the authority of the Vedas on the grounds that they were spoken by Īśvara. Therefore, if Īśvara is established, the authority of the Vedas is established because they were composed by Him; and if that [authority] is established, Īśvara is established—thus, it is argued, there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*). If this is said, we reply: No. To exclude the possibility that their acceptance [of the Vedas] is rooted in delusion, one must state that it is rooted in the knowledge of His faultlessness. Furthermore, the knowledge of His faultlessness arises from the knowledge that He is a speaker endowed with excellence (*guṇavat*). Thus, the circular dependency would indeed remain.

If it is argued that the status of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is established through inference and thus there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*), then since God would be established as the speaker of the Veda from that very same inference, what is the use of the Veda? Therefore, in order to avoid the charge of the treatise (*śāstra*) being useless, its refutation must be carried out; thus, the commencement of this section is justified.

"Because [Brahman] has the scripture as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt). To exclude the interpretation as a genitive *tatpuruṣa* favored by other commentators, he says: "the scripture of which. To exclude the sense of the word *yoni* as meaning "material cause," he states that it means "cause" in the general sense. In response to the doubt, "How can the scripture be the cause of Brahman, who is the cause of all? he says "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) in order to exclude the sense of being a cause of origination.

Regarding the question of how the word *yoni*, which denotes a cause (*kāraṇa*), can denote a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "By the knowledge of Brahman. The sense is that the word *hetu* (cause) is employed for a communicator (*jñāpaka*) just as it is for a producer (*utpādaka*); likewise, the use of the word *yoni* is possible with the intention of signifying a cause.

In response to the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that Brahman is not known through scripture because it is knowable by other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), [the author] addresses the objection that the probans (hetu) of the final position—“because it is knowable through scripture” (śāstravedyatvāt)—would be indistinguishable from the probandum (sādhya). He demonstrates the grammatical connection between the word expressing the probans ending in the fifth case and the word expressing the probandum, stating "atyantā-": "Because Brahman, in its essential nature, has no connection with the sense organs, nor does its indicative mark (liṅga) have such a connection, nor even its indicative mark's indicative mark. With this intention, he says: "by being entirely beyond the senses" (atyantātīndriyatvena).

For this very reason, it was stated that [Brahman] is not an object of means of valid cognition such as perception (*pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, the sense is that there is neither "being seen" in the form of a particular (*vyakti*), nor "belonging to the same class as what has been seen," which is necessary for universal concomitance (*vyāpti*). The difference in meaning between the words *indriya-pratyakṣa* (sensory perception) and *śabda* (verbal testimony) arises from the intention to refer to the instrument (*karaṇa*) and its resulting knowledge (*jñāna*), respectively. The phrase "because it has scripture alone as its means of valid cognition" (*śāstra-eka-pramāṇaka-tvāt*) implies an exclusive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), just as in the expression "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣa*); such is the intended meaning of the term *śāstra-yoni*.

Consequently, since its being beyond the scope of other means of knowledge is established, Brahman—being fit to be presented by the Word as something not within the range of other means of knowledge—is what specific passages such as "From which indeed these [beings arise]" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1) make known; this is what is meant. The very same thing that was to be proven in the previous Sūtra is proven here through a different approach; this is the intended meaning of the particle *eva*. Here too, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the Śāstra by way of passages such as "From which indeed these [beings arise]"; the doubt (*saṃśaya*) is also established by implication.

Two common lines of inquiry are to be considered. First, there is the doubt: "Is the statement beginning with 'From which indeed these [beings arise]' a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, or not? For that purpose, one must determine: "Is Brahman within the scope of other means of knowledge, or not? For that purpose, one must determine: "Does inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa-anumāna*) lead to the understanding of something distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), or not? When it does lead to such an understanding, then, because it falls within the scope of other means of knowledge, the statement "From which indeed these [beings arise]" and so forth does not establish Brahman. Consequently, since the Vedāntas would lack authority regarding Brahman, the non-commencement of their inquiry is the result in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, since inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭānumāna*) lacks the status of a means of valid knowledge regarding that which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), Brahman is not within the scope of other means of knowledge. Consequently, such scriptural passages as "From which indeed these [beings arise]" constitute the authority for Brahman; thus, because all Vedānta texts possess authority therein, it follows that the inquiry [into Brahman] must be commenced.

In the application of the words of the Sūtra, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin), unable to accept the meaning stated in brief, raises an objection with the word "nanu. "Śāstrayonitvam" means having the scripture as its source of authority (*pramāṇa*). To the question, "If [Brahman] were knowable through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how would it be impossible for the scripture to be its source? he replies: "But when [the object] is not already attained, the scripture is purposeful. The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). For lexicographers state: "'Syuḥ', 'eva', 'tu', 'punar', 'vai', and 'ca' are words expressing emphasis. Or, it may signify a distinction (*vaiṣamya*).

Since perception is accomplished without effort because it apprehends what is not sought to be known (*abubhutsita-grāhitva*), the fact that it does not communicate its purpose to the knower is not a defect; however, since scripture is accomplished through effort because it apprehends what is sought to be known (*bubhutsita-grāhitva*), the fact that it does not communicate its purpose to the knower is a defect. This being so, there would be no possibility of engaging in hearing and other such practices [with regard to scripture], just as there is none with respect to statements concerning the heat of fire, the existence of wind, or the number of teeth in a dog.

Regarding this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), a certain proponent of the established view (*siddhānty-ekadeśin*)—a Mīmāṃsaka—raises an objection with the words "What then? He is a proponent of the established view because he refutes the inference of a Lord (*īśvara*); he is a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*) because he does not accept a Lord at all. "What then? means "nothing at all. To the question "How so?", he says "Not, first of all... He states that perception is of two kinds in order to demonstrate that even all perception lacks the capacity [to prove the object]: "For that [perception]... He further states that the first kind is also of two types: "That which arises from the sense organs..."

And [the phrase] "and internal occurrence": by the word *āntara* (internal), the mind (*manas*) is intended. Regarding the first [point], he states the impossibility [of perception] with the words "the external sense organs. By the word *vidyamāna* (existing), which specifies spatial proximity (*deśa-sannikarṣa*), temporal proximity (*kāla-sannikarṣa*) is also established. By the word *yogya* (suitable), natural proximity (*svabhāva-sannikarṣa*) is expressed. By this, there is the exclusion of merit, demerit, and so forth; by the word *sva* (own), there is the exclusion of sound and so forth with respect to the eye and other [senses].

Alternatively, by the term "its own object" (*svaviṣaya*), there is an exclusion of that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and that which is the object of another sense-organ. By the term "suitable" (*yogya*), however, there is an exclusion of that which is unsuitable due to factors such as non-manifestation (*anudbhava*), even in the case of things belonging to the same class as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are restricted to their respective sense-organs. He answers the second [objection] with "nor... (*nāpi*). The meaning is that the mind (*manas*) does not produce cognition of that [external] object. In the phrase "internal pleasure, pain, etc. (*āntarasukhaduḥkhādi*), the word "internal" (*āntara*) refers to the self (*ātman*) and its attributes (*dharma*). For it is precisely because it grasps those [internal things] that the mind itself is considered internal.

"Suffering, pleasure, and so forth" is an explanation of the internal [objects of perception]. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), desire, aversion, and the like, as well as the self, are included. By the term "distinct" (vyatirikta), it is established that form and the other [sensory objects] are external. To show that [perception] produced by yoga is untenable, he says, "Nor by yoga. Having in mind the dilemma—whether yogic perception is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose object is not greater than what was previously experienced, or whether its object is greater than what was experienced—he states the refutation regarding the case where the object is not greater, saying, "by cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

The meaning is that because it has no object beyond [that of its source], it is merely memory and thus lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); consequently, its being a specific sub-type of a valid means of knowledge is utterly discarded. He establishes the lack of an additional object by stating, "because there is no cause for an object exceeding that. The cause is the connection with the sense organ. The meaning is that there is no validity because of the absence of the causes of valid cognition. He states the refutation regarding the case of having an additional object with the words, "if that were so."

The meaning is that even in the absence of a connection with the sense organs, if it has an object exceeding what was previously experienced, it is nothing but an error (bhrānti), because it is rooted in a defect (doṣa). He states that it is not within the scope of the two kinds of inference by means of the words "nor" (na api) and so forth. "Niyata" means pervaded (vyāpta).

The proponent of a partial prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣaikadeśin*) challenges the disputant who objects by casting the shadow of the established conclusion (*siddhānticchāyayā*), saying: "But surely... His status as a partial proponent of the prima facie view arises from his propounding an inference stated by certain Naiyāyikas. "Recipient" (*sampradāna*) means the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). "Purpose" (*prayojana*) means application (*viniyoga*). To establish that there is a single agent, he states another inference: "That which is insentient... He provides an example for [the world] having an agent who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth, saying: "For everything... And he provides an example for its being dependent on a single conscious being, saying: "That which is insentient..."

The terms *aroga* (healthy) and *sva* (own) are used for the purpose of excluding a body that is afflicted by disease. For once the fact of being an effect is established, the establishment of its having an intelligent agent who knows the material cause and so forth follows; regarding this, [the author] says, "by virtue of having parts" (*sāvayavatvena*). By this, the removal of the suspicion of the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason—that it is not originated by the insentient—is also achieved as a consequence. Thus, the proponent of a particular position within the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣaikadeśin*) refutes the point stated by another proponent of the prima facie view with the words beginning "it is said" (*ucyate*). Because it resides in the intellect, he refutes the subsequent inference with the question, "What is this? (*kim idam*).

Regarding the phrase "dependence on a single volition" (*ekacetanādhīnatva*), one must consider the following alternatives: does it mean that its arising and subsistence are dependent upon that [volition], or that its activity is dependent upon that? Even regarding the first alternative, what is meant by "arising and subsistence being dependent upon that"? Is it that its arising and subsistence are dependent upon its [the volition's] desire, or that its arising and subsistence are dependent upon its unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)? The word "what" (*kiṃ*) is intended for the purpose of setting aside these various alternatives.

In this regard, since the state of having its production and subsistence dependent upon His will is not observed [in the example], the refutation known as "deficiency of the probandum" (*sādhyavaikalya*) is well-established; thus, with this in mind, he refutes the second alternative with the words "For the example... He explains the deficiency of the probandum with the words "For not... To the question "Why?", he says here: "Of that body... Alternatively, the passage beginning with "First of all, not... concerns the two states: having its production and subsistence dependent upon His will, and having its production and subsistence dependent upon His unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*).

It is common [to both positions]. In that regard, since the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) is obvious in the case where [the persistence] is dependent on desire, he explains the deficiency of the probandum in the case where it is dependent on the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) with the words "For not... (*na hi*). For origination and persistence were refuted together. Now, having considered persistence separately, he says "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) in order to refute it. The statement regarding persistence as consisting in inherence in its own parts is made in accordance with the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others. [The phrase] "it does not depend on a conscious being" (*na cetanam apekṣate*) [is used].

For dependence on consciousness (cetanā) must occur either by way of its own nature, or through the medium of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), or through the medium of desire (icchā). Among these, its mere nature is ineffective, because destruction is observed even when that nature is present. Since the answer has already been given regarding dependence on the unseen, this [argument] refutes the position of dependence on desire. The meaning is that it does not depend on the desire of a conscious being. With the intention that the argument regarding stability—characterized by non-laxity until the time of destruction—has also already received its answer, that point is not mentioned here.

Now, although the previous alternative has been refuted by the critique of the aforementioned options, he takes up another alternative for refutation because other critiques still exist, beginning with the words "prāṇaneti" (by means of breathing). "Prāṇanā" is characterized by being accompanied by the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose characteristic is the act of breathing. "We do not perceive [it]"—the intention here is that this constitutes a *kālātyayāpadeśa* (an argument where the evidence is presented after the time for its application has passed). He raises the objection regarding the position that "dependence on that" means dependence on a single conscious agent, with the words "tadāyatteti. He states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the reason "being composed of the non-conscious" with the word "aneketi" (many).

"In those things accomplished by multiple conscious agents" means "those things set in motion by multiple conscious agents. He states "merely by a conscious agent" to show that [the argument] would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*) if the singularity of the conscious agent were not intended. Thus, dependence on a single conscious agent has been refuted. With the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*), he points out that the reason (*hetu*) of being an effect (*kāryatva*) results in proving what is already established by way of the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*). By the phrase "of those established for both disputants," the reason for parsimony is stated; for they say, "When there is a conflict between what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what is to be postulated (*kalpya*), it is proper to accept what is already established."

For when another course is possible, the principle of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*) applies; however, when no other course is possible, the postulation of something additional is not a fault—to this he says, "And not... Why so? To this he says, "Of all... He establishes that sentient beings possessed the capacity for direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) in a previous time by means of the method observed [in the present], saying, "Just as... "At present" implies that it was likewise in a previous time. Anticipating the objection that agency is impossible due to the absence of direct perception of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), he says, "By means of instruments... [meaning] in the form of the power [to perform] sacrifices and the like.

The meaning is that [the result] consists of a specific excellence (atiśaya) produced within one's own self by sacrifices and other such acts. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the direct perception of that" (*tatsākṣātkāra*). If so, how is there a rule regarding the necessity of directly perceiving clay and so forth in the creation of a jar and the like? To this he says: "Possessing power" (*śaktimat*). By the word *śaktimat*, that which is connected to power (*śakti*) is expressed. Since the relationship between the produced and the producer is a specific kind of connection, the term *śaktimat* is applied to sacrifices and the like, which produce unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) in the form of power. Because power also shares the quality of being required [for the effect], its direct perception is likewise required.

Otherwise, one might argue that even persons who have not understood the power (*śakti*) of an object could perform its effect by means of it; to this he says, "But of the power" (*śaktes tu*). The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to highlight the distinction that, although the power must be known just as the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) must be, there is a specific difference [in the manner of knowing]. He establishes the lack of utility for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the power with the words "for not" (*na hi*). Even if direct perception of the power is unnecessary, a mere knowledge of the power is required; and that is accomplished in the case of the staff, the wheel, and so forth, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). But how is it so in the case of sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like? To this he says, "But here" (*iha tu*).

Thus, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) has been stated. Now, with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*), he states that the probans (*hetu*), namely "being an effect," is subject to contradiction due to two types of adventitious conditions (*upādhi*). He states that the condition does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*) by saying "the earth, mountains, etc. He states that the condition is co-extensive with the probandum (*sādhyasamavyāptatva*) by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Since the probans would lack the necessary pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) when an adventitious condition exists, this constitutes the defectiveness of the condition (*upādhi*). It is stated that the goal is to prove "having an intelligent agent as its precursor" (*buddhimatkartṛpūrvakatva*) in order to exclude the possibility of having a sentient being as its agent who possesses unseen merit (*adṛṣṭavat*).

Now, he states that the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is contradicted by its own specific property (*viśeṣaviruddhatva*) with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). [The opponent argues: "By one who is non-omniscient (*anīśvara*), subject to karma (*karmavaśya*), and possessed of acquisitions (*parigrahavat*), that is to say, possessed of instruments (*upakaraṇavat*). Anticipating the objection that this would lead to the annihilation of all inference (*sarvānumānoccheda*), he says "and not" (*na ca*). To the question "How so?", he replies "the possessor of the mark" (*liṅginī*). To the objection that the same would apply to the subject (*pakṣa*) as well, he says "but here" (*iha tu*). He explains the distinction intended by the word "but" (*tu*) with the words "the subverting" (*nivarttaka*). He concludes the view of a certain proponent of a partial position (*siddhāntyekadeśimatam*) with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). [The meaning is: "If it were established, there would be no means of knowledge other than scripture (*āgama*)."

Therefore, the meaning is that [the argument] is refuted by the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), being vitiated by a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*), and being contradictory (*viruddhatva*).

Now, he introduces the proponent directly with the words "here they say. Anticipating the objection that the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), he dispels it by stating "because of having parts" (*sāvayavatvāt*). The phrase "precisely because of having parts" means "from that very [reason] previously introduced. By this, the existence of other reasons is also indicated. Thus, both explicitly and through implication, he elucidates the established reasons through their formal application (*prayoga*) with the words "they exist" (*bhavanti*).

The phrase "the term under dispute" (*vivādādhyāsitapada*) is a gloss on the term "earth, mountains, and so forth" (*bhūbhūdharādipada*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the specific individual instances (*vyakti*), while the phrase "under dispute" serves as a collective designation for them. Alternatively, the word "under dispute" is used to exclude those portions of the subject that are already commonly accepted among the very things being made the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*). For there are indeed portions of the earth produced by the filling of the hollows with earth; portions of the ocean produced by the sons of Sagara and others; and mountains and the like produced by [the power of] weapons and so forth.

The terms "ocean" (*jaladhi*) and "body" (*tanu*) are employed by repeating the proposition (*pratijñā*) in order to indicate the possibility that these two might not be effects—given that the ocean persists even during the dissolution (*pralaya*) and the Creator’s body persists even when all else is non-existent. Between the second and third applications [of the reason], the term "large" (*mahattva*) excludes atoms (*paramāṇu*). The terms "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*) and "corporeal" (*mūrta*) exclude space (*gagana*) and other such entities.

The insertion of the word "ocean" (*jaladhi*) between the words "earth" (*avani*) and "mountain" (*mahīdhara*) is likewise intended to indicate that both of those [the earth and the mountain] also possess trembling. For the trembling of the earth and mountains is well-known to occur during portents and similar events. [Objection: But is it not improper to take the body as the subject (*pakṣa*), because there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the case of bodies such as ours, while in the case of God’s body, there is the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*)? [Reply: Not so; for there is no insistence on taking the body specifically as the subject.

The inclusion of that [term "having parts"] is for the purpose of making it known that even the body of the Lord (Īśvara), which is accepted as belonging to his own side [of the argument], is an effect (*kārya*). Alternatively, this is the underlying intention: one does not establish that [the world] possesses an origin by means of having parts, and then subsequently prove that it has an agent (*sakartṛkatva*); rather, by the very fact of having parts, its status as an effect—in the form of being producible by volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*)—is established. And since volitional effort does not exist without a substratum, its substratum, namely the agent, is established in a general sense.

[Objection: If that is so, then when "having an agent" is to be proven on the grounds of "being an effect," the reason would be non-different from the probandum. [Reply: No; for there is a distinction, as "being producible by volitional effort" is the reason, whereas "having an agent who is cognizant of the material cause and so forth" is the probandum. For this very reason, it will be stated later that "it is produced" (kriyate), and not "it arises" (utpadyate). And it is said: "Having ascertained the state of being an effect, one immediately infers the diversity of the agent's knowledge and power," and so on.

And thus, when the probandum is defined as "being achievable through volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*), the body also qualifies as the subject (*pakṣa*) because it is the point of dispute. Now, he refutes [the objection] regarding the presence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*) in general with the words "in those things possessing parts" (*sāvayaveṣu*). "Possessing parts" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); for both "possessing action while being large" and "possessing form while being large" share the same locus as "possessing parts" and are co-extensive with it. Thus, the exclusion of these two as limiting conditions is established. "Another form" means another configuration. He raises the doubt regarding a limiting condition with the words "being an effect" (*kāryatva*).

He refutes this, saying "no. [The opponent argues: "In the case of the *sapakṣa* (similar instance) which is admitted to be an effect, and elsewhere in the *pakṣa* (the subject), even in the *sapakṣa* such as a jar where the capacity for knowledge is to be inferred from its being an effect—since the state of being an effect is likewise recognized in the *pakṣa*, the capacities for knowledge [and action] are inferred; thus, it is not the case that [these capacities] are incapable of being produced, but rather that they are capable of being known. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*).

Is the probans (*upādhi*) "the state of having the capacity to produce" and "the knowledge of the capacity for the material cause and so forth" applicable even to one who is not the maker, or is it applicable only to that maker? In the first alternative, it cannot be a valid *upādhi* because it does not follow the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). In the second alternative, it cannot be an *upādhi* because it exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) as well. For the intended meaning of an *upādhi* is that which follows all similar instances but is absent from the subject. This alternative is intended by the phrase "the variety of the maker's knowledge and power."

To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: because of the reason [of] having parts (*sāvayavatva*) and so forth, being free from limiting conditions (*nirupādhikatva*). Thus, when "being an effect" (*kāryatva*), defined as being produced by volitional effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*), is to be proven on the grounds of having parts, the limiting condition (*upādhi*) such as "being capable of being produced" (*śakyakriyatva*) has been set aside. By this, when "having an agent" (*sakartṛkatva*) is to be proven on the grounds of "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*), the reason of "having an origin" also becomes free from limiting conditions. Furthermore, when "having an origin" is to be proven on the grounds of "having parts," the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the limiting condition in the case of *dūrvā* grass and the like is established;
for *dūrvā* grass and such, though they originate, are not capable of being produced by beings such as ourselves.

He says "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) in order to refute the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and to present another inference. The phrase "even if [the world] were caused by merit and demerit" (*dharmādharmanimitte 'pi*) indicates the suspicion that the argument might be proving the already established. The statement of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—"because [creation] would be impossible for two [causes] that are not presided over"—is stated for the sake of strengthening the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*). He provides an example with the words "by a carpenter" (*varddhakinā*).

The phrase "even when there is the presence of numerous auxiliary factors such as place and time" is stated in order to dispel the suspicion that the failure of tools like an axe to produce effects such as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is caused by the absence of some other non-conscious auxiliary factor. The formal structure of the inference is as follows: merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are capable of producing effects only when presided over by a conscious being who directly perceives them, because they are insentient, just like an axe and similar tools. Since it is impossible for individual souls (*jīva*) to possess direct perception of merit and demerit, or to preside over them based on such perception, the existence of a being distinct from the individual soul is established.

Since that which is not presided over cannot perform an action, and since direct perception by individual souls (jīvas) and the resulting presiding over it are impossible, the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) is avoided. Furthermore, the "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) argument—which claims that the production of effects can be accounted for by unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from the application of human effort toward pleasure and so forth, thereby rendering the opponent's subverting inference (the *bādhakatarka*)—which asserts that no effect could arise in the absence of an agent—likewise becomes refuted by this very [point].

He dispels the doubt that there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—since even insentient things like seeds, when not presided over by an intelligent agent, are seen to produce sprouts—by means of the phrase "seed-sprout. By the inclusion of the word "sprout," the removal of the suspicion of deviation in the case of the sprout and similar effects from the reason of "being an effect" is achieved. He anticipates and then refutes the objection that the reason of "insentience" is deviant with respect to pleasure and the like, which are themselves insentient yet produce goosebumps and so forth without being intended by an intelligent agent or presided over by one; he does so by the very same [phrase].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), suffering and so forth—which are not presided over by volition—as well as the mind and other factors that produce pleasure and so on, are intended. By this, the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason "being an effect" (*kāryatva*)—which might otherwise arise from specific instances of pleasure and pain produced without one's own will, and from their effects such as horripilation and trembling of the limbs—is avoided. This is according to the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*).

Fearing that the argument might be subject to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) because the reason is otherwise established, he refutes this with the words "And not... (*na ca*). When the question "Why? arises, he explains the reason intended by such words with the phrase "Of those... (*teṣām iti*). Although the postulation of a single sense-organ (*ekendriya*) is simpler, since a single sense-organ lacks the capacity to grasp all objects such as sound and so forth, one must postulate multiple sense-organs. Therefore, the point is that it is improper to postulate the performance of a function for something that lacks the power [to perform it], even for the sake of simplicity. He demonstrates this very point with the words "Perception... (*darśana iti*).

For that which is logically possible alone should be postulated; the meaning is that the power of living beings to perceive the subtle, the concealed, and so forth, has not been observed. By the phrase "the subtle, the concealed," etc., this [objection] is also refuted—that it is only the direct perception of the possessor of the power that is required, and not the direct perception of the power itself—since even atoms and other such possessors of power are not established as being directly perceived by the individual soul (kṣetrajña). He states "nor is there... to show that there is no such impossibility in the case of the Lord (Īśvara).

He concludes the proof of the Lord through intermediate inference with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). One might object: "Granted that by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), a creator endowed with knowledge and power appropriate to the effect is established; however, how is his distinction from the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) proven? For knowledge is dependent upon the body, senses, and so forth. To address this doubt, he states the point established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) with the word "samartha" (capable). The term "natural direct perception of all objects" (*svābhāvika-sarvārtha-sākṣātkāra*) is intended to exclude the possibility that [the Lord's] knowledge and power might be limited according to karma, which would be the case if they were not natural.

Now, with the words "But as for... (*yattu*), etc., he dispels the charge that the reason (*hetu*) "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is contradictory (*viruddha*). To the question "How so?", he replies: "In the case of the similar instance" (*sapakṣe*). Does the acquisition of a body and so forth result from mere observation of coexistence, or from [the body's] being the cause? It cannot be the first, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor can it be the second, because its status as a cause is unestablished—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, by the phrase "of effects which do not have [them] as their causes," the absence of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) is also intended.

[Objection: "But surely, since [the cause] is observed together with all similar instances (*sapakṣa*), its causality for the body must be postulated; that being so, how can it be said that there is non-attainment in some cases and attainment in others? To this, he says: "This has been stated. In order to avoid the contradiction regarding specific particulars, he states the necessary distinction: "by something... [and so on]. To the objection that "since it is observed together with similar instances, ignorance and the like should also be postulated as causes," he says: "by its own creation... [and so on]. [The phrase] "of that which is ineffective... [is used].

For the determination of causality is indeed based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be established otherwise. In this regard, if some distinct causal efficiency (*kiñcitkāra*), which is not produced by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), were observed to remove ignorance (*ajñāna*) where other [causes] lack such capacity, then there would be "establishment otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddhi*). However, no additional causal efficiency is observed; nor can it be postulated, because in the absence of a cause characterized by the incapacity of ignorance, there is no cessation of the effect.

Just as an effect does not arise without the cognition of its own object, its capacity, and its material cause (*upādāna*), so too it is never observed that an effect fails to arise without the cognition of others’ incapacity; therefore, its status as a cause should not be postulated. For being present when [the effect] exists is not what constitutes causality; rather, the point is that [the cause must exist] only when [the effect] exists. He demonstrates this very lack of efficacy through the method of alternatives, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). [He says] "In all cases," etc.

The meaning is this: the absence of the capacity for knowledge conducive to the production of walls and such things is not the cause for the production of a jar, because we observe that even one who possesses the capacity for knowledge conducive to those [walls] can still produce jars and the like. As for the claim that—because it is observed in the sapakṣa (similar instances)—there is an exclusion of those specific properties in the subject (liṅgin) which have been contradicted by the means of valid cognition apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), but not of others; this too has been refuted by the statement that [the property of] being an effect is not a prover of [those specific properties].

Because there is no concomitance (vyāpti) with those properties observed together [with the effect] that are otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*) as being useless for the probandum (*sādhya*), they cannot be attained due to the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Even among things observed together, there would be no attainment of those that are useless for the effect; for the body alone is useful for the effect—thus [the opponent] objects regarding the potter and others. [The author] refutes this, saying "no. To the question "How so?", he says "by volition" (*saṅkalpa*). [The opponent] objects again, "How? [The author] refutes this, saying "no. To the question "What is the reason?", he says "the mind itself" (*mana eva*). To the question "Does that exist?", he says "that... [and so on].

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because it is an effect. The mention of the Lord's connection with the mind is according to the view of a certain school of Nyāya. He raises an objection again: "Is it mental? He refutes this: "No," because of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*), that is, due to the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*). There is inconclusiveness because the connection with the mind exists even in one who is bodiless. Furthermore, although the mind is eternal, the capacity of a conscious being to produce effects depends upon its connection with a body; for even though the mind is eternal, the liberated soul lacks the capacity to produce effects.

Indeed, there is no objection that the mind of a liberated soul produces cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth. Here, keeping in mind the rebuttal by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*) directed at the Mīmāṃsaka, he concludes the proof of God (*īśvarasiddhi*) by demonstrating the force of the "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*). Thus: "Therefore, [He is] one whose diverse parts... By these two phrases—"one who is bodiless" and "the manifold expansion of diverse structures produced solely by the instrument of volition"—the intention of the rebuttal by way of a counter-objection is understood.

Although it is a rule that objects such as a jar—which possess conjunction with all-pervading substances and are characterized by motion—must possess tangibility, the Prābhākara does not admit that the mind possesses tangibility, even though it possesses conjunction with all-pervading substances and is characterized by motion. This is the rebuttal directed against the Prābhākara.
