Furthermore, although it is observed that there is a rule regarding the perception of color in luminous matter endowed with the quality of magnitude (mahiman), the perception of color is not admitted in the case of the eye; thus, the pervasion of having parts (sāvayavatva) by being the originator of an effect is refuted in the case of atoms.

Therefore, to avoid numerous contradictions, it is logical to abandon the [universal] pervasion of a single [attribute]. Consequently, the point is that when the mind performs an action, its dependence upon a connection with the body must be accepted as being necessitated by its nature as the mind (manastva) which is an instrument of experience. Thus, because this is established by other proofs, he concludes that the scripture lacks authority regarding the entity that is the cause of the world, stating: "Therefore, [it is not a source of knowledge] regarding the means of valid cognition... etc.

Having raised the objection that the scripture possesses authority regarding Brahman because its subject matter exceeds that of inference—since the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause, as well as the creation of space and so forth, are not objects of inference—it is stated [in the commentary] with "Moreover" (*kiñca*) that the scripture lacks authority there, because it is sublated by another sublation. Since the scripture, which merely restates the efficient cause, is dependent upon inference, it cannot establish through the scripture the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause, which is contrary to that [inferential conclusion].

Since it has already been established that among substances such as earth and the rest—which have been made the subject of inquiry—it is precisely the state of having parts (*sāvayavatva*) that is the determinant of being an effect (*kāryatva*), and thus that a partless substance (*niravayavadravya*) is not an effect, the scripture does not subsequently teach the production of a partless substance. The point is that even among the means of proof such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), priority and posteriority are the causes of relative strength and weakness. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

He begins to state the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words, "Thus it being the case" (*evaṃ prāpte*). He declares the ultimate thesis (*paramasādhya*) with the words, "As has been stated" (*yathokta*). He states the reason (*hetu*), preceded by an inquiry, with the word, "Why? (*kutaḥ*). The meaning is: because the scripture alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is, because it does not fall within the scope of any means of valid cognition other than the scripture. To ward off the charge of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*), he restates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words, "As has been said" (*yadukta*). He refutes it with the words, "That is incorrect" (*tadayuktam*).

With the intention of considering the following alternatives—namely, whether the proponent of the difference between the Field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) [and the Creator] based on the strength of the property of being a subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) asserts this by including the rule that the creator of vast effects must be a single entity, or by the mere fact of their vastness, or by virtue of perceiving supersensuous material causes and so forth, or by virtue of a creation independent of a body—he first refutes the first alternative with the verse beginning "The earth... (*mahī*). He establishes the absence of being constructed by a single deity acting alone with the passage beginning "Nor by one... (*na caikasya*).

The word "one" (*eka*) indicates the doubt that the single nature of being an effect (*kāryyatva*), like that of a jar and so forth, is capable of having a single agent simultaneously. The "oneness" of being an effect means its being preceded by a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*); for the sake of establishing that, the word "of one" (*ekasya*) was stated. For indeed, a single individual entity is not produced by multiple causal complexes, because all causes delimited by a single effect constitute a single causal complex.

Even though [the pot] is a single entity, the word "pot" (ghaṭa) intends to exclude those things like city gates that have multiple makers; rather, it intends the fitness for connection with a single maker at one and the same time. The kind of "being an effect" (kāryatva) observed in a single pot—which resides in a limited, single composite whole—is precisely what gives rise to the possibility of its being produced by a single maker at one and the same time. And that [kind of being an effect] is not observed in the case of the earth, mountains, and so forth—this is the meaning. The word "syāt" (might be) expresses mere possibility.

For there is no rule that even a single jar must have a single maker, since it is possible for many people to produce a single jar together. When the question arises as to what follows from this, he states the opposite case regarding many and vast effects with the words "in separate [beings]. In the phrase "in separate [beings]," vastness is also implied, because of the previous statement, "just like a single jar."

Since no rule regarding the identity of agent and time is observed in the case of many vast effects, there is a lack of evidence for the claim that the earth and so forth were created at one and the same time by a single agent. The connection of the text is to be understood by supplying the phrase "because of the lack of evidence, that [claim] is untenable. Nor is "being an effect" itself proof for the identity of agent and time, because it cannot withstand critical analysis. Does this mean merely being an effect, or being a vast effect, or being an effect whose agency by a living being is impossible—an effect unique to the subject under consideration? In the first case, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).

In the second [case], there is contradiction (*viruddhatva*), because it is observed that for vast effects, there is a multiplicity of agents over a long duration of time. Or rather, there is simply inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*). In the third case, the intention is that there is an inconclusiveness due to being too restricted (*asādhāraṇānaikāntya*). Regarding the claim that when an agent is to be postulated by the force of the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), the distinctness from the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*) is established by the force of the attributes of being more vast and more subtle, and the oneness of the agent is established by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), he says "And not... (*na ca*).

By the word "various" (*vicitra*), what is intended is its extreme vastness and extreme subtlety, in the sense that it is impossible for people such as ourselves to comprehend. To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) alone. For if something were to be postulated in addition to the knowers of the field, then since multiple postulations would be required, it is more logical to postulate only one. The meaning is that since agency is possible for the knowers of the field themselves, nothing additional to them should be postulated. The phrase "of those who have accumulated specific merits" is stated in order to demonstrate the diversity of capacity even among those who belong to the same class (*sapakṣa*).

The phrase "by means of the possibility of an extraordinary unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)" refers to the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*). Through such statements as "the Jyotiṣṭoma [is for] all desires," the possibility of an extraordinary *adṛṣṭa* conducive to the creation of the earth and so forth is established. Furthermore, the perception of subtle, concealed, and other such objects by means of yoga is accepted by opponents as belonging to *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) alone. A diversity of cognitive power is observed among ourselves and among the gods. Moreover, the strength of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not capable of setting aside those properties that are established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Because [merit and demerit] are the sole causes for the increase or decrease of qualities established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even knowledge and the desire to act could be lost. Regarding the phrase "beyond that": the sense is that, according to the maxim "it is better to postulate a property than to postulate a substratum," it is better to postulate a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*) rather than the postulation of God (*īśvara*). Furthermore, the argument that merit and demerit produce their effects only when presided over by a conscious being because they are insentient—like an axe or similar tools—is untenable.

Because of the deviation [of the reason] in the case of the knowledge and activity of Īśvara, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding either one [of the two alternatives]. Now, if it is argued that since the *kṣetrajña* (the individual soul) requires a body for creation, and since he lacks a body at the time of universal dissolution, the agent at that time must be distinct from the living being (*jīva*) as he is independent of a body—the author replies with "And not" (*na ca*). Regarding the objection that sequential production and destruction are observed now, whereas the simultaneous occurrence of production and destruction would have to be postulated [if the world were created all at once], he replies with "By being an effect" (*kāryatvena*). Here, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) means "being producible by volitional effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*).

And here, the third [case-ending] has the sense of "being in such a state" (*itthambhāva*); that is to say, because there is no contradiction, meaning there is no contradiction with the pervasion (*vyāpti*). Thus, the instruction on the matter useful for refuting the opponent's view has been given. Now, he shows the resulting refutation with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The word "therefore" refers to the fact that the points stated starting from "that is incorrect" (*tadayuktam*) serve as the reasons (*hetu*). The word "intelligent" (*buddhimat*) is used to exclude the kind of agency characterized merely by being the substratum of action, as in the case of grass and so forth in movements like swaying.

Is what is to be proven (sādhya) the state of having a single intelligent creator, or merely the state of having a creator in general? Regarding the first [alternative], is it merely the state of having a single intelligent creator in a general sense that is to be proven, or is it the state of having a single creator who is omniscient and omnipotent? Having in mind this dilemma, [the author] states that in the first case there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntya), because the property of being an effect is present in things such as chariots and city gates, which have multiple creators; this is the intended meaning. He states the refutation regarding the position that the creator is omniscient and omnipotent with the words "of the subject" (pakṣasya).

For the state of being created by an omniscient and omnipotent agent is not observed elsewhere in the same way that being preceded [by another] is. Thus, the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikalatā), because such a creator is not seen in the case of effects such as jars and the like. He establishes both "the unestablished nature of the qualifier" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) and "the deficiency of the probandum" (sādhyavaikalya) with the word "sarva-". Since it was stated [in the original thesis] "by one skilled in the creation of all," it is understood that these two defects apply to the position that there is an omniscient and omnipotent creator. If, however, this were intended for the previous position alone, then the charge of "unestablished nature of the qualifier" would not be applicable.

For it is not unestablished that there is a single agent. Regarding the objection against the mere position that [the world] has an agent, he says "by an intelligent [being]. It should not be said by the Vedāntins that this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), because they do not admit that individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) are agents. If it is argued that even for individual souls agency is admitted only as instrumental (*dvārakartṛtva*), we say no; for even in the case of the collective principles (*samaṣṭitattva*), there is no instrumental agent, nor is that [collective] being made the subject of the inference, since it is not an object of worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*).

If it is argued that those who are established by scripture are also included within the subject class (*pakṣīkāra*), then by that same logic, the agent is also established; thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*).

He analyzes the reason (*hetu*) by way of another perspective, [stating] "by omniscience" (*sārvajñyena*). This is the intended meaning: it has already been stated that a specific creator cannot be established merely by the fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which is pervaded by the mere status of having a creator in general. Therefore, a specific creator must be proven by a specific nature of being an effect that depends upon the particularity of the subject (*pakṣa*). For, from a specific effect such as a jar, one infers a specific creator such as a potter, but not from the mere fact of being an effect. Consequently, the specific nature of being an effect that depends upon the subject is what is being refuted here.

"What does 'simultaneously' mean? [The questioner asks: "In what two ways could the excellence of the cause, which depends on the intensity of the subject (*pakṣaprakarṣa*), possibly be observed? Either through the simultaneous production of vast effects such as mountains and the like, or through the infinity of effects that occur sequentially over the three periods of time? In this regard, by what kind of intensity of the subject is the specific quality of the cause intended to be expressed? He refutes the first [alternative] with the word "simultaneously."

The meaning is that because a universal dissolution is not established—and because there is no proof for the simultaneous production of mountains and other such things—the distinction in the causes (hetu-vailakṣaṇya) which is based on that [simultaneity] and intended to prove a distinction in the agent (kartṛ-vailakṣaṇya) remains unestablished. He refutes the second [position] with the words "by succession" (krameṇa).

Even if it were possible for each individual agent, such as a potter, to produce infinite effects even over the course of a thousand births, nevertheless, because the effects produced by weavers and others during the same time as those [specific] births would not have that [potter] as their creator, all effects do not have a single creator. Therefore, the property of being an effect (*kāryatva*), as qualified by its subsistence in all things existing in the three periods of time, is pervaded by a plurality of creators; thus, it is contradictory to the proof of a single creator. This is the meaning of the phrase "in the proof of a single creator" used here as well.

The meaning is that there is a rejection of the observed fact—found in the case of jars, cloths, chariots, and so forth—that they possess distinct makers, since this [distinctness of maker] is intended to be pervaded by the state of having a specific effect. Regarding those things established by perception as having distinct makers, there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*). As for others: "A jar existing on another continent has a potter as its maker other than this [present one], because, while being caused by factors outside the scope of this [potter's] activity, it possesses the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*), like a jar produced by a different potter in a well-known location."

The fact that the staff and other causes of a pot existing on another continent fall outside the scope of this [agent's] activity is determined by the certainty that he does not go there. Therefore, there is a contradiction with such inferences. He explains the contradiction with scripture [as follows]: "the potter is born" and "the chariot-maker is born"—this is the intended meaning, not the literal order of the text. For if the pot and the chariot were made by the same agent, the separate birth of the potter and the chariot-maker would not need to be stated;
the point is that it would result in a redundancy due to them having the same designation.

He states another form of contradiction with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*). Considering that the fact that pleasure and so forth are effects of the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* is seen in the scriptures, and thus must be accepted by one who maintains the authority of those scriptures, he adduces an undesirable consequence; however, this is not based on what the opponent himself accepts. By the terms "pleasure" and so forth, pleasure, pain, and delusion (*sukha-duḥkha-moha*) are intended.

The "concomitance with pleasure and so forth" (sukhādyanvaya) of the body and other things means their concomitance with the states that cause pleasure and so forth; it means having as their material cause substances characterized by the qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva*. To the question, "What are these [qualities] like *sattva* and so forth, and how do they cause pleasure and so forth?", he says: "By the diversity of bodies. This refers to the specific differences residing in the causes. The word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) here refers generally to both efficient and material causes. To the question, "What follows from this regarding the agent's subjection to the qualities?", he says: "Of those effects... [and so on].

The meaning is that the Puruṣa brings about the dependence of effects upon itself by means of the modifications of its own internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is endowed with *sattva* and the other qualities (*guṇas*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And of the Puruṣa... The opponent had argued that properties which do not contribute to an effect do not attach [to the Puruṣa]. However, since *sattva* and the others are instrumental to the effect, the connection with action dependent upon them is unavoidable; thus the proponent says: "Like the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)."

It is established by the scriptures that pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth, have *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as their causes. Furthermore, it is established by the scriptures that the agent who effects the appropriation of the body and other instruments—which serve as the causes of pleasure and the rest—is endowed with the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the others; this is seen in passages such as: "How can the agency of creation and so forth be attributed to Brahman, who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), immeasurable, and pure, even though he is stainless? (ŚV, Sambandhākṣepaparihāra 102).

Therefore, the Puruṣa presides over the substance—the body and so forth—which has the qualities (guṇas) such as *sattva* as its material cause (*upādāna*), while his own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is modified by the influence of those very qualities like *sattva*. And since this connection with the qualities is rooted in karma, the consequence is that he would be subject to karma. He states another reason for this connection with karma by saying "knowledge," etc. If it is argued that the manifold creation does not arise from the diversity of the power of knowledge, but rather from mere will (*icchā-mātra*), he replies to that: "of will," etc., meaning [will] as qualified by specific objects.

The meaning is that desire has as its object the creation, maintenance, and so forth [of the world], and even therein, it has as its object the diverse creation and so forth; this is rooted in *sattva* and the other *guṇas*, and thus has karma as its root. Thus, because one observes the concomitance (*vyāpti*) between agency and being a knower-of-the-field (*kṣetrajña*), he says "therefore" [in the verse] to show that there is no establishment of anything distinct from those two.

He states the counter-reasonings (*pratitarka*) with the words "and there are... and "the body, the world, etc. This is either a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) or a counter-reasoning (*pratitarka*). Others are indeed counter-reasonings alone. The meaning is: if [the world] were an effect, it would follow that it has an individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) as its agent; if it had an agent, it would follow that he is dependent on something else; and if he were an agent, it would follow that he possesses a body. Anticipating and refuting the objection that the reason "being bodiless" is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*), he says "not so. "Beginningless" means beginningless in its continuous flow (*pravāha*), like the seed and the sprout.

If "presiding" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) means the first connection with a body, it is refuted by the beginninglessness of the stream of subtle and gross bodies; just as the assumption of a youthful body is [effected] by one characterized by a childhood body, so too is this case. If "presiding" means impelling (*preraṇa*), it is refuted by the principle of self-sustaining systems (*svaparanirvāhakanyāya*). For while an impeller distinct from the body requires a body, the body itself does not; indeed, being a body entails the capacity for impelling independently of another body.

Likewise, even if the world is the body of the Lord, there is no consequence of His being subject to karma due to possessing a body. Just as the body is both the instrument for the arising of its own cognition and the object of that karma, and just as a jar, by its mere existence, is the cause for the arising of cognition regarding itself and subsequently becomes the object of that cognition, so too is the body [the cause] for the impelling of its own objects; thus, there is no contradiction between [the Lord] being the object of action and the agent. Nor is there a non-apprehension of the body in sprouts and the like, given its suitability [for such apprehension].

This is because invisibility is possible, as in the case of the bodies of *piśācas*, *siddhas*, and others; and because impelling [an effect] by means of intention through a body situated in another location is also possible, just as in the case of poison and the like. He states another counter-argument with the words "vimati" (disagreement). Here, since time—distinguished by specific counts of the sun’s revolutions—is made the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of its prior and posterior aspects, there is no lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). He refutes the inference from another perspective with the words "api ca" and so forth. He sets up a dilemma (*vikalpa*) in order to state the refutation with the word "kim" (what).

"It does not first corrupt that which resides in the intellect" refers to the refutation of the previously stated position that a bodiless [self] could possess agency through the mind; this is addressed by the words "mental [cognitions]. To the question "Why?", he says "of the mind. By the word "api" (also/even), it is indicated that in his own view, permanence is not admitted. He refutes the position of having a body with the words "nor even... To explain the inability to withstand the alternatives, he presents the options with the words "that [body]... He refutes the first alternative with the words "not first... [The term] "jagataḥ" refers to the world, such as the earth, mountains, and so forth.

He refutes the second [position] with the words "nor even... He states the reason: "because of that which is distinct from it. This means because there is no other body for the cause of that [first] body. To avoid this refutation, he himself raises an objection stated by another: "by himself," where the word "himself" refers to the Lord (*īśvara*). He refutes this with "no," because that [Lord] is not joined with [the body], and thus cannot be the cause. Again he objects: "by another. He refutes this with "no," on account of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

If it is argued that there is no fault because this is the tradition of authoritative teachers, the implication is that [the Lord] would be subject to karma due to possessing a body. Since the consequence of being subject to karma was already mentioned previously, it is understood here as well that the refutation of infinite regress (anavasthā) is intended to culminate in the consequence of being subject to karma. He refutes this by raising an alternative possibility with the words "What is that? [The opponent asks: If he were bodiless and devoid of activity, and if there were no causal agency for one devoid of activity, the analogy would be the liberated soul (muktātman).

And the "activity" (vyāpāra) intended here is effort (*prayatna*). For if a specific desire were the cause [of the world], the consequence of being subject to the *guṇas* would follow, as was stated previously. Regarding the claim that "desire alone is the activity," he says: "The effect is the world. By the word "alone" (*mātra*), there is an exclusion of the connection with the *guṇas* such as *sattva*, their underlying connection with karma, and so forth. Now, one might object: subjection to karma and the like should not be attributed to the Creator, because it is not universal (*avyāpaka*).

Indeed, there is no pervasion (vyāpti) either by your position or by our position, because neither you nor I admit [the existence of] God. This is not so; for it is stated by people like us—having set aside scripture (*āgama*)—in response to one who claims that God is established even without scripture. If the inference of God is established by setting aside the pervasion I have stated on the strength of scripture that establishes God, then the validity of inference as independent of scripture would fail to be proven, and thus scripture would be established as apprehending what has not yet been reached [by other means].

Alternatively, since agency is pervaded by subjection to karma and other such qualities, it cannot be known solely through non-worldly means of valid cognition (*alaukikapramāṇa*). Thus, the direct perceptions of those proficient in the scriptures, yogis, and liberated souls are what are designated here as "non-worldly."

He concludes the refutation of inference with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). The term "Lord of All" (*sarveśvara*) is intended to indicate that the Supreme Brahman is not distinct from Īśvara; by this, the Śruti passage, "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among the lords," is brought to mind. The term "Supreme Person" (*puruṣottama*) is for the purpose of determining the specific deity and for the purpose of recalling the Śruti passage, "The Great Lord, the Puruṣa, is indeed the impeller of sattva. To the objection that the aforementioned defects would still apply even then, he replies with the words "the scripture, however" (*śāstraṃ tu*).

The term "sārvajñya" (omniscience) indicates that [Brahman] is entirely distinct from all other classes of entities. The compound word "sārvajñasatyasaṅkalpatvādi" (omniscience, truthfulness of resolve, etc. is either a qualifier of Brahman or a qualifier of its attributes; for all other attributes consist of the nature of those [primary ones]. The meaning is that the attributes are "unlimited"—that is, they are immeasurable and beyond numbering, being singular and possessing no higher degree of excellence.
Thus concludes the section entitled "The Scripture Being the Source."

Just as, although clay possesses the capacity to produce a jar and the potter possesses the power of creation, there is still a dependence upon the apparatus of the staff, the wheel, and so forth; likewise, although the Word (śabda) possesses the capacity to convey the perfectly established Brahman, and although Brahman can indeed be apprehended through the Word, there exists a dependence upon the apparatus known as the desire to know (bubhutsā) for the production of valid cognition (pramiti). Because it is to be accomplished through effort, this desire to know is required. And that [desire] is prompted by [the object being] unknown and by its being a human goal (puruṣārtha).

Therein, by means of the first sub-section consisting of two sūtras, the possession of power (*śaktimattva*)—both through the medium of words and through the medium of meanings—is established. Now, following these two sūtras, there begins another sub-section dedicated to defining the cause of the desire to know (*bubhutsāhetu*). Among those, by the first [of this second sub-section], the third sūtra, the cause of the desire to know in the form of "being unknown" (*ajñātatva*) is stated. Next, the cause of the desire to know in the form of "being a purpose" (*prayojanatva*) is stated by the fourth [sūtra]. For it is only when an object has been cognized that there arises an inquiry into whether it is purposeful or not.

And because [the nature of] practice must be defined by its characteristics, the second aphorism, *janmādi*, was formulated. Since the doubt that "if birth and so forth are the defining characteristics, their establishment would have to depend on another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*) is well-founded, the third aphorism, *śāstrayonitvāt*, was formulated. Even if something is unknown, there is no desire to know it if it serves no purpose; therefore, its nature as a purpose is established here. This is precisely the sequence. Regarding the aphorism *sū tattu samanvayāt*, he states the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) with the words "even though... (*yadyapi*).

The meaning is that although "unknownness" exists as a cause for the desire to know (*bubhutsā*), the purpose (*prayojana*) consists of pleasure and the cessation of pain. The scripture culminates in that [purpose] by means of teaching the engagement in the means thereto. And that [culmination] does not exist if the scripture is directed toward an already established entity (*siddha*), because such an entity lacks the nature of engaging in or desisting from action. Therefore, the meaning is that since it lacks the culmination in a purpose, the requisite condition known as the desire to know is absent; thus, the scripture does not produce valid cognition regarding an established entity.

In response to this doubt, he cites the Sūtra: "But that [is so] because of the connection" (samanvayāt). Here too, two common preliminary investigations are established by implication: first, whether it is possible for Brahman to have the scripture as its means of valid cognition; and secondly, whether the Vedānta passages—which appear to lack a purpose consisting of engagement or withdrawal—can be connected with Brahman as their primary purport.

To that end, is the authority of the word (*śabda*) based on its being directed toward activity and cessation (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*), or rather on its being directed toward the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? If the authority of the word were based solely on its being directed toward activity and cessation, then because Brahman—which is of an established nature—would lack the status of having scripture as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaka*), an inquiry into it would not be commenced. However, if the authority of the word is based solely on its being directed toward the human goal, then since Brahman, which constitutes the human goal, possesses the status of having scripture as its means of valid cognition, it follows that an inquiry into it must indeed be commenced.

Thus, intending to explain the Sūtra with the aim of resolving doubts regarding the subject matter once the purpose has been established, and wishing to include the word-analysis within the very analysis of the sentence-meaning, he explains the word *tu*, which requires separate explanation, by saying "prasakta... [and so on]. Although all Sūtras are introduced in response to their respective specific doubts, in this particular Sūtra, the word *tu* serves the purpose of indication (*pradarśanārtha*). The word to be explained is *tat*; he explains it as "the fact that Brahman has the scripture as its means of valid cognition" (*śāstrapramāṇakatvaṃ brahmaṇaḥ*).

The phrase "it is indeed possible" is the result of the word "tu" (but). He shows the expectancy for the word "cause" by asking "from what? Since the term "samanvaya" (concordance) will be explained in detail later, he now explains it briefly as "by way of being the supreme human goal. In response to the expectation—"Of what, with what, and of what kind is the concordance?"—he says "parama" (supreme). The meaning is: because Brahman, who constitutes the supreme human goal, is in concordance [with the scripture] as its subject matter (*abhidheya*).

Because the treatise (*śāstra*) resides within the intellect, there is no explicit mention of "by the treatise. Once it has been asserted that Brahman has the treatise as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is appropriate to state the reason (*hetu*) as residing in the subject (*pakṣa*); therefore, the "concordance" (*samanvaya*) is explained as having Brahman as its agent, and not as having the treatise as its agent. In response to the inquiry, "How is such a connection [possible]?", he establishes this with the words "In this way" (*evam*). The word *iva* has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*).

The meaning is "just so. The sense is that the collection of words belonging to the Upaniṣads is indeed coherent (*samanvita*) as a means of establishing Brahman, which constitutes the supreme human goal. "Collection of words" means a sentence. Although there is a multiplicity of Upaniṣadic sentences, they are expressed in the singular number to indicate their unity as a single mass, since they share a single purpose through the relationship of being syntactically connected as parts of one whole (*vākyaikavākyabhāva*). The statement that they are "coherent" is made with reference to the authorship of the sentences [by the sages], intending the resultant meaning; it is not intended as a formal application of the Sūtra.

The phrase "of those who are united with Brahman" applies in the same way to what follows as well. In accordance with the sequence of comprehension, he first takes up the definition statement: "From which [verily]... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1). Then, he states the causal statement that establishes [the nature of Brahman]: "Being alone, my dear... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and so forth. Since the word *sat* (Being) is common to both the vast (*bṛhat*) and the non-vast (*abṛhat*), he takes up the qualifying statement: "Brahman indeed... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).

If it is argued that when the defining statement "That from which [this world arises] is Brahman" is uttered, and the causality of Being (*sat*) has been stated, the fact that this Being is Brahman is established, and thus the determination of its greatness does not depend on the sentence "or Brahman"; we say no. For the defining statement merely restates the cause and is dependent upon the originative statements. Indeed, the sentence "or Brahman" is employed precisely to provide knowledge that determines the specific nature among those very originative statements upon which it depends.

Although the two words "sat" and "brahman" refer to a reality excluded from the non-conscious (acid-vyāvṛtta) due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their connection with "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), there is no certainty regarding that exclusion from the non-conscious based solely on the semantic power (*śabda-sāmarthya*) of those two words because they are common [to other entities]. Therefore, the sentence "Ātmā vā" is introduced for the purpose of making known the specific [nature] by means of the word's own capacity. The "commonality" (*sādhāraṇatva*) of the word "brahman" consists in its being employed in many different senses; it does not, however, consist in the commonality of the ground for its application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*).

Alternatively, it may refer to the capacity of unsurpassed greatness—which serves as the basis for the application of the term—to admit doubt regarding its application to anything other than the two Blessed Ones (Brahmā and Viṣṇu). For once it is understood that the word *ātman* has its natural primary meaning [referring to Brahman], there can be no doubt that unsurpassed greatness applies to non-sentient matter (*acid*). In the *Śāṇḍilyavidyā*, the word *ātman* occurs in the concluding section as "That is the Self" (*sa ātmā*); therefore, the sentence "Verily, the Self" (*ātmā vā*) is cited from the introductory section in order to determine the specific [referent] by means of that very word *ātman*.

Even though the cause is indicated by the word *ānanda* in the passage beginning with "From bliss indeed, verily, these beings are born," within the very context starting with "From which indeed these [beings arise]," the certainty of the exclusion of the non-sentient (*acid-vyāvṛtti*) is obstructed because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *ākāśa* in the phrase "If this space were not bliss. With the intention that the exclusion of the non-sentient might be easily understood, the sentence "Or rather, the Self" (*ātmā vā*) is introduced.

He cites the passage, "From that very Self," in order to demonstrate—by means of the principle of the "corroboration by all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*)—that even without the immediate context, the word "Brahman" refers to the Self; and furthermore, he cites it to show that this meaning is established because the passage is situated within a context that teaches the nature of bliss as required for this specific section. For it is there that "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite" is the subject under discussion, and it will also be stated there: "Another inner self consists of bliss" and "Knowing the bliss of Brahman."

In this context, according to the principle that "the goat [is the victim] because of the wording of the mantra," he shows that general terms culminate in a specific deity with the words, "For there is indeed one... and "That very deity reflected... and "He who ordains Brahman in the beginning, who indeed sends forth the Vedas to him."

Regarding that very God—of whom it is said, "He is the Lord of this universe, for there exists no other cause for His lordship," "The Ruler of what has been and what is to be," and "The Supreme Great Lord of lords"—the words such as "deity" (*devatā*) and so forth found in these passages, although they are specific terms relative to each preceding [context], do not directly reside within the causal statements. Furthermore, even though those words like "deity" possess conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), they lack conventional usage with respect to a specific individual; and as for words like "Lord" (*īśa*), [it is said]: "He is the Lord of the universe, for there exists no other cause."

Because the intention to convey the meaning of the individual components is made even more explicit by the mention of the word ending in the genitive case—such as in the phrase "īśanāya"—and because the conventional (rūḍhi) sense [of the term] has been submerged, and since that [conventional sense] is common [to other deities], the author, with the intention that the convergence of those [meanings] upon that [single deity] would be established by implication through the presentation of the final qualifying word, has cited the passage beginning with "eko ha vai nārāyaṇaḥ," while disregarding sentences such as "seyaṃ devatā."

The intention is that words such as *Hiraṇyagarbha* are unsuitable for [denoting] the intended object—just like words such as *ākāśa* or *prāṇa*—and that words such as *Śiva*, because they are used in many senses, are common [to many referents] and thus, unlike words such as *sat* (Being), are incapable of bringing about the apprehension of a specific [referent].

By the principle that "the words [are authoritative] because they express something not previously known," and "but there is an injunction in the case of holding, because it is something not previously known," this Mahopaniṣad passage—like the sentences "The cake for Agni is on eight potsherds" and "For he holds [the vessel] above for the gods"—establishes its own meaning independently of anything else, because it presents a matter not otherwise established and, unlike passages concerning ether or the vital breath, does not present an impossible object.

If it is argued that this statement has an inappropriate meaning because it contradicts the statement, “It is neither being nor non-being, but is solely the auspicious (śiva) alone,” we say no; for by contradicting the statement, “In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone” (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), the statement “neither being nor non-being” and so forth would itself result in having an inappropriate meaning.

If it is argued that because the common word *sat* is not incompatible with its ultimate resolution in Śiva, it does not have an unsuitable meaning here, then likewise, since the word *Śiva* is used in many senses, the common word [referring to him] is not incompatible with its ultimate resolution in Nārāyaṇa; therefore, it does not have an unsuitable meaning here.

For the fact that Brahmā, Śiva, and others are effects—just like Indra and the other gods—is established by many scriptural passages in the Yajurveda: "In the navel of the Unborn, one [lotus] was placed, upon which this entire world is supported; from it the divine Viśvakarman was born"; "He, Prajāpati alone, came into being upon the lotus-leaf"; "From him Virāj was born, and from Virāj the Puruṣa"; and in the Mahopaniṣad: "Therein Brahmā, four-faced, was born"; and in the Subālopaniṣad: "From the waters, the earth."

"Then that [universe] became an egg. Having remained thus for the duration of a year, it split into two parts: the earth below and the sky above, with a divine person in the middle; 'The Puruṣa has a thousand heads'... starting from there, up to: "In the beginning, he created death among beings. Brahmā was afraid of him. He entered into Brahmā himself. Here, it is heard in scripture that Brahmā was produced from the Puruṣa, who is the Supreme Self, because two distinct words for "Puruṣa" are heard and because the state of being subject to fear of death is mentioned.

In the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, from the passages, "I know this great Puruṣa," "The Puruṣa is indeed the great Lord, the impeller of this being (sattva)," and "He who first created Brahmā," the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha is understood.

Likewise, in the Mahopaniṣad: "The three-eyed, trident-bearing Person was born"; in the Subālopaniṣad: "From his forehead, Rudra, born of wrath, was born"; and in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka: "In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman alone. Being alone, it did not flourish. It brought forth that form which is superior—the Kṣatra; these other divine Kṣatras: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna."

Likewise, in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, beginning with "This [world] indeed became established," and continuing through "Prajāpati consecrated himself for the sake of the year among the beings; Bhūtānām-pati was the householder (gṛhapati), and Uṣas was the wife," and so forth; it says: "Bhūtānām-pati poured his seed into Uṣas during the year. In the year, a boy was born. He wept. Prajāpati said to him: 'Boy! Why do you weep, since you have been born from toil and austerity? He replied:"

"I am indeed one whose evil has not been struck down, and my name has not yet been assigned. Give me a name for the striking away of evil. He said to him, "You are Rudra. Thus he gave him that name. Fire became his form. Thus begins the account of the conferring of names such as Śarva, Paśupati, and others, as well as the granting of forms consisting of earth, water, and so forth; and from the very words of Rudra, his state of having evil struck down is heard in the Śruti.

And in that very *Śatarudrīya Brāhmaṇa*: "The deities who had issued forth from Prajāpati departed; only one god did not leave him—Mahāmanyu (Great Wrath) indeed remained hidden within him. He wept. Those tears of his which fell, they settled upon this Manyu. He became this hundred-headed Rudra. Here, it is stated that Rudra, in the form of Manyu, originated from the tears born of the anger of the enraged Prajāpati.
Furthermore, it is well known that anger is a cause of tears, as in: "From the eyes of him who was enraged, drops of tears fell, like flaming drops of oil from two blazing lamps."

Likewise, in the *Śailālī Brāhmaṇa*, beginning with "Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerities," the text describes the origin of fire, wind, the sun, and the moon, as well as their emission of seed. It continues: "That Prajāpati fashioned a golden vessel, one fathom in length, extending both upwards and across. Into it he poured the seed. Thereupon there arose [a being] with a thousand eyes and a thousand feet. With a thousand attendants, he assailed his father, Prajāpati."

He said to him, "How do you approach me? He replied, "Give me a name. [Prajāpati said,] "I shall not eat food under an unordained name. He said, "You are indeed Śarva," and "Bhava indeed. Having thus described the conferring of names such as Bhava, Śarva, and so forth, and the granting of the forms (mūrti) such as Salila and others, it is stated even more clearly that Prajāpati ordained the possession of eight names and eight forms, saying: "This very Mahādeva has eight names and is established in eight ways."

At the commencement of a ritual action, those who study the *Talavakāra* recite: "I shall perform this rite; may it prosper for me, may it succeed for me. Homage to Virūpākṣa, the tooth-anointer, the son of Brahmā, the eldest, the most excellent, the unfailing lord of rites."

Likewise, at the commencement of the ritual for the Chāndogas, it is stated: "Obeisance to that Virūpākṣa, the one with joined palms, the impeller, the all-knowing, the thousand-eyed, the son of Brahmā"—thus, by means of these two mantras, Rudra’s status as the son of Brahmā is declared. Furthermore, in the *Ghṛtasūkta*, it is said: "He who brought forth Brahmā from Brahmā, the Lord of Prāṇa, clad in animal skins, the wielder of the Pināka bow"—here, Rudra’s emergence from Brahmā is stated. The word *ujjahāra* means "he brought forth" (*udabhavat*).
Therefore, since it is understood that Hiraṇyagarbha and others are effects, words such as "Being" (sat) are unsuitable for them; thus, these words ultimately refer to Nārāyaṇa alone.

But is it not said: "In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose," "Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone exists," "Verily, Nārāyaṇa was alone," and "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra—they are all produced from Him"?

Since the status of being the cause and the agency of the body are heard of without distinction in respect to all three deities, and since the doubt regarding their unfitness is equal in all three cases, and since the removal of the objection of unfitness—on the grounds that birth is a matter of will—is easily stated for all three, and because the determination of the oneness of the cause must be respected and the non-abandonment of conventional usage follows naturally, the supreme causality should be accepted by resorting to the identity of all three. [Objection: It is not so.

Because there is no scriptural statement regarding the three [entities] being equally objects of action (*kāryatva*) without distinction, the suspicion that all three are unfit [for meditation] does not apply equally to them all. For at the beginning of that section, it is understood that the intent is to enjoin the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) through the words "And who is to be meditated upon?"; thus, their status as objects of action is restated (*anūdyate*). And this restatement must conform to what has already been established elsewhere. In the *Uttaranārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, which concerns the Lord of Lakṣmī, the birth and incarnations of the Blessed One are heard; therefore, it is in that very passage that there is a restatement of the Blessed One's incarnations.

Since there is no scriptural statement regarding the descent (*avatāra*) of Brahmā and Śiva, their birth is merely restated as being equal to that of Indra, Varuṇa, and others; thus, there is no hearing of their being created without distinction [from other beings]. Furthermore, it is established by general rule that if there is birth, there is a connection with a body dependent on karma. And this has not been set aside for Brahmā and Śiva, whereas for Nārāyaṇa it has been set aside by the scriptural statements concerning his descents. In the passage, "Prajāpati created the gods; they were born fettered by evil (*pāpman*)," the connection of the gods created by Prajāpati with evil is heard as a general rule.

Specifically, the fact that Rudra is untouched by evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) is demonstrated in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* from its own words: "This is the inner self of all beings, untouched by evil, the divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"; "His eyes are like a lotus with petals as yellow as a monkey's bottom"; "His name is 'Ud' (Risen), for he has risen above all evils"; "He is untouched by evil, free from old age, and free from death"; and "He is the Supreme Person. Thus, it is stated that the Lotus-Eyed One possesses a form not produced by karma.

Thus, since the discrepancy is so evident that any suspicion of an equality of origin has been utterly destroyed, it is untenable to claim that words such as "Brahmā" and "Śiva"—which have inappropriate referents—do not abandon their conventional meanings, just as words like "Nārāyaṇa," which have appropriate referents, do not.

If you, who are most devoted to the existence of the divine, assert that Rudra is the supreme cause and that his manifestation [as Indra] is an incarnation, then what is this hatred toward Indra on your part? For it is heard in scripture that Indra, like Brahmā and Śiva, possesses both the status of effect and cause: "Indra moves in manifold forms through his powers of illusion," and "Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—all these are brought forth.
Therefore, why is the suitability of the word "Indra" not accepted by relying upon Indra’s status as the supreme cause and the fact that his manifestation is an incarnation of that supreme cause?

If it is argued that Indra’s birth, conduct, and inferiority are established because he is heard in scripture to have been created by Prajāpati ("Prajāpati created Indra"), because he is heard to have been overwhelmed by the Brahman-slaughter consisting of the killing of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, and because penances for that act and so forth are heard of—then why should Kṛṣṇa’s birth in the house of Vasudeva and his flight due to Kālayavana not likewise be considered a divine play (līlā)?

If it is argued that this is not so—because there would result the fallacy of circular reasoning (cakraka-āśraya), wherein Indra’s identity with the Supreme Cause exists only if he is the subject of the *Uttara-nārāyaṇa* hymn; his birth, activities, and association with defects are merely sport (*līlā*) only if that identity exists; the word "Indra" possesses its appropriate meaning only if those [qualities] exist; and Indra’s identity with the Supreme Cause exists only if he is the subject of the *Uttara-nārāyaṇa* hymn—and furthermore, because within a single sentence he is perceived as a created being, like Soma, Varuṇa, Yama, and others; then, [the same logic applies] to Rudra’s identity with the Supreme Cause.

Because there would be the fallacy of a circular argument—namely, that the Lord is the subject matter of the *Uttaranārāyaṇa* section; by that, His acts of birth and work are established as mere sport (*līlā*); by that, words such as "Śiva" and so on are shown to have appropriate meanings; and by that, the identity of the Supreme Cause with the individual Self is established—and because in that very same passage He is heard to be both created and withdrawn, like Soma and Varuṇa, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that words such as "Śiva" do not have Him as their appropriate referent.

However, there is no fallacy of circular reasoning (*cakraka*) if [the Lord] is understood as having the nature of an incarnation at birth; for the incarnation of the Lord of Lakṣmī—the Supreme Person who is designated as the cause in the passage "From Him Virāṭ was born," and who is recognized by the term *mahāpuruṣa* in the Uttara-Nārāyaṇa hymn—is established by such statements as "He who is not being born."

If it is argued that there is no lack of fitness [of the term *nārāyaṇa*] because words such as *śiva* have different meanings when applied to the effect and the cause, we must ask: do the words *śiva* and so forth, when applied to the effect, refer to the well-known Rudra, or do they refer to the Cause? In the first case, since the well-known Rudra is a created being like ether and other elements, it is unavoidable that the words *śiva* and so forth—when applied to something distinct from him—must refer to that specific entity presented by the word *nārāyaṇa*.

If it is argued that words such as "Śiva" and others, when referring to the cause, refer to the well-known Rudra, whereas when referring to the effect, they refer to something distinct from him—then why could it not be the case that the word "Indra," when referring to the cause, refers to the well-known Indra, while the word "Indra," when referring to the effect, refers to something distinct from him?

If it is argued that the word *indra* is derived [as a name] for one who performs the slaying of Vṛtra and other such acts, [we reply: the word *śiva* and others are likewise derived as synonyms for "the three-eyed one," "the trident-bearer," and so forth, as in: "The three-eyed, trident-bearing Person was born"; and "Umāpati, Paśupati, Śitikaṇṭha, the son of Brahmā—Śiva spoke this Pāśupata knowledge at the very beginning. Furthermore, since words such as "trident-bearer" are used with reference to the effect (the manifested deity), it is improper to restrict words like *śiva*, which refer to the cause (the primordial source), to the well-known Rudra alone.

It is indeed appropriate that words such as "Nārāyaṇa" and others, which refer to both the cause and its effects, have as their well-established meaning Viṣṇu; for it has been demonstrated that there is a scriptural basis for the identity of nature between the cause and its incarnations, and thus no difference in substance exists. Indeed, only when there were a difference in substance would the question arise as to which among those terms referring to Nārāyaṇa and others—whether they pertain to the effect or the cause—possesses the established meaning and which possesses a meaning distinct from that.

It has been stated that if there were identity between the attributes of Rudra as cause and effect—just as there is identity between the attributes of Indra—it would unavoidably lead to the fallacy of a logical circle (*cakraka*). Therefore, by accepting a difference in meaning for words such as "Śiva" when applied to the effect and the cause, those words like "Śiva" referring to the cause denote an object other than the one commonly known [as the individual soul], and thus they do not express identity with Nārāyaṇa.

Since there is no difference in meaning between words such as *Nārāyaṇa* and others due to the fitness of their well-known referents, and since the identity of the substratum (*dharmy-aikya*) is established by valid means of knowledge, the sense is that the terms *Sat*, *Brahman*, and so forth, ultimately converge upon Nārāyaṇa alone as propounded in the *Mahopaniṣad*.

Now, he states the purificatory statement (*śodhakavākya*)—"It is Truth"—which removes the suspected defects from Brahman as designated by way of being the cause. He says, "Brahman is Bliss," in order to establish that Brahman, characterized by the aforementioned qualities, manifestations, and so forth, constitutes the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). For blissfulness is the state of being favorable (*anukūlatva*). Favorableness, moreover, is the state of being desired for its own sake; and that too is the state of being desired even without [the presence of] being a means to something desired or the removal of what is unfavorable. And that [desirability] resides in the object itself.

Because the knowledge of that [Bhagavān] is also favorable [to the self], it possesses the nature of bliss (*ānandatva*). Because the Bhagavān is the unsurpassed object of enjoyment for the liberated souls, he possesses the nature of bliss by virtue of being favorable through both his essential nature (*svarūpa*) and his attributes (*dharma*). Furthermore, because the knowledge of one’s own object and one’s own essential nature are favorable toward oneself, they possess the nature of bliss. Such is the sense. This connects with the preceding phrase as "the collection of words belonging to the Upaniṣads."

When sentences are thus construed, what meaning is understood as being useful for the human goals under discussion? Is that meaning apprehended merely on the surface, or is it the ground of the intended purport (*tātparya*)? It cannot be the first, because it is impossible to determine its ultimate reality. Nor can it be the second, because that would be untenable due to the absence of engagement in action or desisting from action. To this doubt, [the response is: the connection with engagement and desisting is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of validity; therefore, since validity is pervaded by that, it cannot be established in its absence. Why then do you say [otherwise]?

Alternatively, one might intend the following dilemma: Is the connection with activity and cessation (*pravṛtti-nivṛtty-anvaya*) pervasive of the purpose (*prayojana*), and since the purpose is pervasive of validity (*prāmāṇya*), it is argued that in the absence of the connection with activity and cessation, the purpose—which is pervaded by it—is absent, and consequently its pervader, validity, is not established? Anticipating this alternative, [the author] states "and not" (*na ca*) to show that the connection with activity and cessation is not pervasive of validity. The phrase "established through linguistic usage" (*vyutpatti-siddha*) is a restatement of the meaning of the first sūtra.

It should not be argued that because an established entity (*siddhavastu*) is not a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), the scripture is unable to teach it; nor that even if it were taught, there is no primary intent (*tātparya*) toward it, since there is no linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*) regarding an established thing. The point is that proficiency can indeed be established with respect to an established entity. To dispel the suspicion that [the scripture] is secondary (i.e., non-authoritative) because its subject matter falls within the domain of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*), he states the meaning as understood from the cited causal statement (*kāraṇavākya*) beginning with "all" (*akhila*).

He states the meaning established by the purificatory passages (*śodhaka-vākya*) and the causal passages (*kāraṇa-vākya*) with the words "without remainder" (*aśeṣa*). The sense is that it is difficult to maintain that the [Vedas] have as their ultimate goal the *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* favored by the followers of Śaṅkara. He says "whose nature is bliss" (*ānanda-svarūpa*) to exclude the possibility of having another goal, since there is no purpose beyond the fulfillment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). "Having another goal" means a lack of *tātparya* (purport); the meaning is a lack of authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*) regarding Brahman. To the question, "How can there be authoritative validity if there is an absence of connection with engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)? he replies with "with respect to its own object" (*sva-viṣaya*).

The meaning is that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) culminate in the comprehension of their own respective objects, but not in activity or cessation. Now, having accepted that the connection with activity and cessation pervades [the existence of] a purpose (prayojana), he states that the purpose does not pervade the status of being a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya) with the words "na ca prayojana... (And not the purpose...). He explains this with the words "prayojanaṃ hi... (For the purpose...). The word "hi" indicates a reason. Alternatively, the word "hi" is intended to signify the well-known fact that the purpose does not pervade the status of being a means of valid cognition.

As it is said in the *Tantraṭīkā*: "Indeed, for one who perceives a clod of earth, the perception of that [clod] is not purposeless, such that it could be imagined as a perception of gold. In that case, its status as a cause is established by the fact of the matter (*arthasiddha*). Let it be that the pervasion of the purpose (*prayojana*) belongs to the connection with engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtty-anvaya*); therefore, upon the cessation of that [connection], the purpose itself ceases, but not the validity (*prāmāṇya*), because the purpose lacks the pervasion of validity—this is the meaning. And in the phrase "na ca," the word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the negation of the two types of pervaders.

The meaning is that just as it is incorrect for the concomitance of engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtty-anvaya*) to be a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of validity, so too it is incorrect for a purpose (*prayojana*) to be a pervader of validity. In response to the doubt that although a purpose may not be a pervader of validity in the case of perception and so forth, it might nonetheless be a pervader of validity in the case of a treatise (*śāstra*), [the author] says, "And not engagement..."—implying that even if the validity of a treatise were pervaded by its purpose, nevertheless, a purpose does not possess the property of being pervaded by the concomitance of engagement and withdrawal.

The word "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the perception of a connection with human purpose" (*puruṣārthānvayapratīteḥ*). This refers to the subject under discussion (the thesis). The meaning is that even though [the sentence] lacks the form of engagement or withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*), there is a perception of a connection because Brahman—which is itself the human purpose—is the object denoted (*abhidheya*). And in the phrase "na ca," the word "ca" serves to conjoin two negations of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*).

The meaning is that just as validity (*prāmāṇya*) lacks the property of being pervaded by concomitance with activity and cessation (*pravṛtti-nivṛtty-anvaya-vyāpyatva*), so too the purpose (*prayojana*) lacks the property of being pervaded by concomitance with activity and cessation. The absence of validity’s concomitance with activity and cessation is established by the passage beginning with "the cognition of its own object" (*svaviṣayāvabodha*). With the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he demonstrates the concomitance with human goals (*puruṣārtha*) even in worldly sentences that refer to established facts (*siddhapara-vākya*), which are intended as similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Just as having an orientation toward activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*) does not constitute the fulfillment of a purpose, but rather the orientation toward the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), so too, having an orientation toward activity or cessation, or an orientation toward an established entity (*siddhavastu*), does not constitute the fulfillment of a purpose; rather, it is stated that the fulfillment of a purpose for a sentence consists precisely in its connection with a human goal, whether that goal is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or already established (*siddha*). This is because it has been stated [above] that this is due to the cognition of the connection with a human goal. Thus, the meaning has been stated briefly for the sake of construing the words of the Sūtra.

Now, in order to state the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), he introduces the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in detail with the words "here [the opponent] says" (*atrāha*). The meaning is that once this much of the subject matter of the section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been stated, the opponent—who finds an occasion for refutation—speaks. He asserts the non-establishment of Brahman as the subject matter of the scripture with the words "not by the Vedāntas. Since the status of being the source of the scripture (*śāstrayonitva*) was referred to by the word "that" (*tat*) in the Sūtra, it is understood that the opponent is also asserting its absence.

He establishes what was promised [in the opening verse] with the words, "devoid of connection with engagement or withdrawal. The sense is that in the absence of such a connection, the very act of exposition would not be fulfilled. And thus says the Vārttika:

"As long as words do not effect the engagement or withdrawal of cognizers, so long there is no cognition free from expectancy. Regarding the word *śāstrasya* (of the treatise): it is called a *śāstra* because it instructs (*śāsana*). And instruction consists of engagement and withdrawal. On this point, the Vārttika states:

"Whether it be engagement or withdrawal, that by which men are instructed—whether by means of what is eternal or what is produced—that scripture is indeed untenable. Having raised the doubt regarding the aforementioned capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to cognize their own respective objects, [the author], while establishing that [capacity] within a specific type of *pramāṇa*, states that the scripture must necessarily culminate in its purpose with the words "Even though... He demonstrates this with the words "For not..."; he states that there is not only non-perception, but also logical inconsistency, with the words "Not anything..."

The meaning is that [the utterance] may concern something related to oneself or something related to another, and it may be slight or abundant; for the employment of a sentence is to be accomplished through effort, and effort is not possible without a purpose. Indeed, it is precisely because sentences must culminate in a purpose that tautology constitutes a fault due to the absence of a purpose; for the employment of a purposeless sentence, or the hearing of it, would be irrational.

Then, what follows? [The author] states "And that" (*tacceti*) because the sentences under discussion—which culminate in a purpose—must have as their purport either engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*); for even if they culminate in something already established (*siddha*), it is still possible for them to culminate in a purpose. He demonstrates the usage of these two [words, *sat* and *asat*], according to worldly practice, by means of the passage beginning with "one who desires an object" (*arthārthī*).

In response to the doubt that a sentence may be seen to have a purpose even in the absence of being intent upon activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation (*nivṛtti*), the author restates the opponent’s position—described as being "intent upon an established fact" (*siddha*)—in order to refute it, beginning with the words "But as for [the claim]... (*yat punar*). He analyzes this by means of an alternative (*vikalpayati*). Anticipating the acceptance of the second alternative because the first alternative is untenable, he raises the objection with the words "Even though [it exists]... (*sato ’pi*). He refutes this with the word "then" (*tarhi*). The conclusion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated with the words "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

There exist two positions among the proponents of the doctrine of illusion (*māyāvādin*): one is the theory of the injunction for the removal of phenomenal plurality (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa-niyogavāda*), and the other is the theory of the injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-niyogavāda*). Intending now to state the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) against the opponent of the present section—who has refuted these two views as well as the system of Śaṅkara and others by means of the proponent of the injunction for meditation—the author introduces the theory of the injunction for the removal of phenomenal plurality with the words, "Here someone says. He announces that [position] with the words, "The Vedānta... and so forth.

Anticipating the question of how a statement directed toward a task (*kāryapara*) can possess the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an established entity (*siddhavastu*), he asks: "How? He provides the answer: "As that which is free from phenomenal proliferation" (*niṣprapañca*). Here, the word *iti* following *kuryāt* indicates the manner [of the action]. When there arises the expectation as to what the connection of Brahman is with the injunction to make it free from phenomenal proliferation, he states the connection: "Of Brahman. The meaning is that the connection is by way of being its object (*viṣayatvena*).

The phrase "by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcapravilayadvāreṇa*) was stated in order to dispel the doubt that Brahman, whose nature is already established (*siddhasvarūpa*), cannot be the object of an injunction (*vidhi*). Herein is implied that the status of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) for that which is already established is not contradictory, due to a difference in form (*ākārabheda*). In this context, the word *iti* marks the conclusion. Alternatively, it serves as the answer to the question "How? by meaning "In this way. To show the injunction, he raises an expectation with the question: "What is that [injunction]? (*ko'sau*)?

The intention is that for one who is incapable of destroying even a few things, the procedure for destroying the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is impossible. "Procedure" (*vidhi*) here refers to an injunctive statement. Alternatively, with the intention that the dissolution of the phenomenal world—which is rooted in ignorance—is possible in the form of a mere cessation of the intellect (*buddhinivṛtti*), he cites the passage beginning with "not from sight" (*na dṛṣṭeḥ*). Since there is no distinction in their being distinct from sight, the negation of the knowable (*jñeya*) is also implied. This is also explicitly stated by other scriptural passages indicated by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

The sense is that because absolute cessation has not yet been established, it is appropriate for it to be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). By the word "void" (*śūnya*), absolute cessation is intended; by the word "only" (*mātra*), the cessation of ignorance—which is the conceptualizer of the seer and the seen—is intended. For it is precisely from that [cessation] that the establishment of absoluteness follows. To the doubt as to how the already established Brahman can be something to be enjoined, he explains at length the previously intended meaning—that it is by means of the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—with the words: "even though it is self-established," and so forth.

Alternatively, previously the impossibility of anything other than an action (*bhāvārtha*) being the object of an injunction was refuted; here, however, by the passage beginning with "of that which is self-established," the impossibility of even an established entity (*siddharūpa*)—by way of the dissolution of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*)—being the object of an injunction is refuted; this is the distinction. Even heaven and the like are distinct from actions; yet they do not possess the quality of being established (*siddhatva*), for they are indeed things to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

The Mīmāṃsaka, who is the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) regarding this topic, refutes that [position], saying: "That is incorrect. To the question "How so?", he says: "By the injunction... (*niyoga*). By the etymological derivation "that which qualifies the object" (*viśiṃṣan viṣaya*), the "object" (*viṣaya*) is the sacrifice and so forth. At the time of the comprehension of the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) as something to be accomplished by human effort (*kṛti*), that [sacrifice] is the "object" insofar as it delimits that effort; that very same thing becomes the "instrument" (*karaṇa*) upon the accomplishment of the task. [These points] must be stated. The sense is: "But you are not able to state them. First, he speaks [the following] in order to refute the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya-viśeṣaṇa*). "In that case... (*tatra*).

Regarding those things that must be stated therein: a qualification of the person enjoined (*niyojya*) is not something to be accepted (*anupādeya*). That which is to be accepted is the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*); the meaning is that it is distinct from that [qualification]. He states the twofold nature of the qualification in order to refute it through an alternative analysis, beginning with "And that... (*tacceti*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says "In this case" (*atre*). "In this case" refers to the injunction for the removal of the manifold world (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa-niyoga*). He raises an objection regarding the nature of the qualification of the person enjoined, beginning with "The nature of Brahman... (*brahmasvarūpeti*). He refutes its status as a causal motive (*nimitta*), beginning with "Then... (*tarhīti*). To the question "Where?", he says "Like living, etc. (*jīvanādivaditi*).

The meaning is that it is not the same as in the case of the injunction, "One performs the Agnihotra for as long as one lives," where living is already established and thus serves as a condition (*nimitta*). He says, "And even if it were a condition," regarding the objection that [the rite] would become a condition whenever it is established—such as at the birth of a son—and would therefore continue to be performed even after liberation (*apavarga*). There is no possibility of such performance even after liberation, because there is no rule for performance as long as the condition exists; indeed, the absence of such a rule is observed in the case of those devoid of the necessary equipment (*parikara*).

If it is argued that there can be no performance [of duties] at that time due to the absence of the instruments (the senses) and the body, then, alas, you yourself are merely exposing your own refutation. For instance: since experience characterized by the manifold world lacks the nature of a true experience (*yathārthānubhava*), the experience of reality occurs only after liberation. At that time, even in the absence of the instruments and the body, is the engagement with objects possible or not? If it were impossible, then it could not be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Therefore, one must say that it is possible.

The sense is that, because the cause (*nimitta*) is eternal and the effect (*naimittika*) is therefore always possible, it would follow that its performance must be eternal. He states the refutation regarding the case where [the result] is a qualification by way of being the fruit (*phala*), saying "nor also" (*nāpi*).

In order to state that the subject matter of *niyoga* (an injunction) is untenable, [the author] asks: "What? He raises an objection: "Brahman itself. He refutes it: "No. He states the reason: "Because of its... [The meaning is: because it is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhavya*), because it is not something to be accomplished (*asādhya*), and because it is not a positive entity (*abhāvārthatva*). The phrase "words denoting action are those whose meaning is existence" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*) implies that [Brahman] lacks the nature of an action (*kriyārūpa*). Since the fruit (*phala*) also possesses the quality of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the term "positive entity" (*bhāvārthatva*) serves to exclude that; the sense is that both [these conditions] are absent [in Brahman]. He raises an objection regarding its being something to be accomplished in the form of the cessation of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*): "The state of being free from phenomenal proliferation."

He replies: "Even in the case of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). [The opponent says: "It is precisely the state of being a fruit (*phala*). [The author replies: If it were the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*), it would have to be distinct from the fruit. The intended meaning is that since there is no distinction from the fruit, its status as an object is untenable. Showing another reason explicitly, he refutes its status as an object by stating: "Because it has a negative referent (*abhāvārtha*), it cannot be the object of an injunction (*vidhi*). Thus, the impossibility of the qualified [negation] being the object has been stated.

Now, intending to demonstrate the impossibility of the qualified part (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifying part (*viśeṣaṇa*) being objects [of cognition], he raises a dilemma with the words "And as for its being the probandum" (*sādhyatvam ca*). Alternatively, since the status of the qualified [whole] as an object was refuted by accepting that the qualified [whole] is the probandum, he now raises a dilemma with the words "And as for its being the probandum" in order to refute the status of the qualified [whole] as the probandum itself.

Indeed, the impossibility of a qualified entity being the probandum (*sādhya*) would follow from the impossibility of the qualifier, the qualified, or both being the probandum. Among these, the option "of both" is not explicitly stated because it shares the same refutation as the other two horns [of the dilemma]. He refutes the first [option] with the words "not, for... (*na tāvad iti*). To the question "Why?", he replies: "Because [the qualification] is already established and because it would entail impermanence. (*siddhatvād anityatvaprasakteś ceti*).

The meaning is that because [Brahman] is already established (*siddha*), it cannot be an object of proof (*sādhya*); however, if one were to accept its status as an object of proof, then since it would possess the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), it would follow that it is non-eternal (*anitya*). He raises the second objection with "Now" (*atha*), and refutes it with "In that case, not" (*na tarhi*). The meaning is that if the cessation of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca-nivṛtti*) is the object of proof, then Brahman itself lacks the status of being an object of proof, and thus it cannot be the subject of an injunction (*vidhi-viṣayatva*). Having raised the possibility that the cessation of phenomenal manifestation is the subject of an injunction, he refutes it with the words beginning with "of the phenomenal manifestation" (*prapañca...*).

He establishes its status as a fruit with the words, "For the cessation of phenomenal manifestation (prapañca-nivṛtti) itself... [is the fruit].
