To the objection, "Let the cessation of phenomenal manifestation be liberation; what of it? It cannot be an object," he replies, "And that... Since the cessation of phenomenal manifestation is the nature of liberation, and liberation is a fruit, that which constitutes the fruit cannot be an object—this is the meaning. He states another refutation with the words, "And of this... Although one should have said "of this" (asyāḥ), the word "of this" (asya) is used with the intention of emphasizing its status as a fruit.

The meaning is that if one accepts two aspects—namely, being the result (*phalatva*) and being the object (*viṣayatva*)—there arises a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañcanivṛtti*) would be accomplished by the mandate (*niyoga*) because it is its result, and the mandate would be established through the cessation of the phenomenal world because it is its object. Alternatively, he states "Moreover" (*api ca*) to offer another refutation of the view that [the world] is rendered devoid of phenomena (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa*). Or rather, since the mandate has already been refuted by the refutation of its object and by the demonstration of circularity, he now refutes the mandate by yet another method with the words "Moreover."

He raises a doubt by asking "What [is it]? and first refutes it by saying "It is false. He then anticipates an objection regarding its efficacy by saying "But the injunction... and refutes that with "That... The meaning is: from one's own statement [of the falsity of the world], and from other statements [regarding the falsity of the phenomenal world and the non-differentiation of Brahman]. By stating the refutation of the injunction’s fruitlessness, the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) is also refuted; for the qualification of the person to be enjoined consists in the very result to be accomplished by the injunction, and such a result is impossible here.

He states another refutation with the words "vākyārthajñānādeva" and so forth. To refute the second alternative among the two previously considered options, he says "prapañcasya. This means that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were real, it could not be something to be removed by an injunction (*niyoga*). Having raised the alternatives with the word "kim," he refutes the first with "yadi" and so forth; then, in order to refute the second, he raises the opponent’s position with "atha," and refutes it with "tasya."

By the passage beginning with "of that" (*tasya*) and ending with "destroyed" (*naṣṭa*), the refutation of the agent (*prayoktṛ*) is accomplished. By the passage beginning with "the cessation of phenomenal proliferation" (*prapañcanivṛtti*), the mandate (*niyoga*) is refuted by way of stating the absence of a result even if phenomenal proliferation were real. With the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*), he refutes the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). He asks "how? (*katham*) in order to explain the absence of the procedure. He replies "thus" (*ittham*). Regarding the position that [the mandate] is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), he states its twofold division with the words "if it is of a positive nature" (*bhāvarūpā cet*).

The production of the body as an instrument (karaṇa-śarīra) is intended to be twofold—both seen and unseen purposes—just like threshing and sprinkling. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "It is of both kinds. This means it is both productive (niṣpādikā) and supportive (anugrāhikā). Regarding the position that it is productive, he first states the refutation concerning its having a seen purpose: "For not... The meaning is that a seen purpose consisting in the absence of the producer of the body as an instrument—which takes the form of the cessation of the entire phenomenal world—is not possible.

If it were for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the reality of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-satyatva*), as well as a lack of epistemic authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*); this is so obvious that it was not explicitly stated. Now, he refutes [the view that it serves] as a favor (*anugraha*) with the words "nor even" (*nāpi*). He establishes the impossibility of that [favor] with the words "anugrāhaka... (the favorer). For the favorer occurs subsequent to the instrument (*karaṇa*); if the favorer were to remain after the instrument—which consists in the cessation of the entire phenomenal world—then the instrument itself would not have been established.

When the instrument (*karaṇa*) is established, there is no longer an auxiliary (*anugrāhaka*); thus, the meaning is that an auxiliary is impossible. He raises an objection regarding the establishment of the instrument by way of the existence of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), saying "of Brahman. He refutes this with "by that very [instrument]. The meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is as follows: the mandate (*niyoga*) is to be produced by the instrument and so forth, and the fruit (*phala*) is to be produced by the mandate. If the instrument were to perform its own function, then, because of its non-existence [prior to that], its status as an instrument would be untenable. This is the meaning.

Now, he refutes the view that the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) consists of non-existence (*abhāva*) with the words "in the case of its being of the nature of non-existence. The meaning is: precisely because it is non-existent, the *itikartavyatā* consisting of non-existence lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇikatva*). The point is that cessation (*nivṛtti*), tranquility (*śama*), and so forth cannot constitute an *itikartavyatā* of the nature of non-existence, because they serve to bring about knowledge and thus cannot logically bring about the instrument (*karaṇa*) which is the cessation of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*).

Here, by the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "precisely because of non-existence," it is understood that the intention is to show the lack of authoritative basis for a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) consisting of an entity that was previously unperceived. He concludes the refutation with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). "Injunction" (*vidhi*) means "command" (*niyoga*); the meaning is that the command has as its object the removal of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa*). Thus, the final result is that it cannot be asserted that the nature of Brahman is established by an injunction that prompts action alone.

Now, he introduces the position of those who maintain that meditation (*dhyāna*) is the primary injunction by saying, "Another also says. Having accepted that the Vedānta texts lack independent authority regarding Brahman, he says, "Even though... To the question, "In that case, how is [Brahman] established? he replies, "Nevertheless... With the intention of pointing out a contradiction, he asks, "Why? He states the reason: "By means of the injunctions for meditation. What is the injunction for meditation, and how does its efficacy work? To this he replies, "For it is exactly thus..."

The meaning is: "in exactly the same way as sentences, even though they are devoted to meditation (*dhyāna*), establish the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*). He states the scriptural passages prescribing meditation with the words "The Self, verily... (*ātmā vā*). By the phrase "it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), meditation is expressed; by "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavyaḥ*), its nature as a form of vision is indicated; and by "it is to be sought to be known" (*vijijñāsitavyaḥ*), a general term is used. By the word "Self" (*ātman*), the meditation on identity is expressed.

"Ātmānam" (the self) refers to the meditation on one's own identity with the universe. He shows the capacity for this in the word "atra" (here). [Objection: Let the object of meditation be implied; however, how is it known that "that" is Brahman? To this he says: "And that which is to be meditated upon... The underlying thought is: when there is an expectancy, if what is in close proximity is suitable, it is not proper to abandon it; for this is seen to be the case in expressions such as "Bring the cow."

He states [in the verse] "What is its form? that even those causal purificatory statements (*kāraṇa-śodhaka-vākya*) which teach the mere essential nature [of Brahman] possess authority only by way of providing the necessary complement for the injunctions. Since the purified essential nature is the object of meditation, the statement "Being, etc. (*satyādi-vākya*) is presented first. Because its meaning is concordant with that, the causal statement "Being alone... (*sadeva...*) is cited afterwards. The phrase "entered into the body of meditation" implies the principle: "For the distinction between cognitions occurs through the object itself, since they are devoid of form. [The word] "it certainly exists" (*astyeva*).

The sense is that, like the statement "in which there is no heat" and so forth, which concerns results such as heaven understood from one's own words [of scripture], its authority exists as a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatayā*). For the nature of Brahman, which is the object of meditation, has entered into the very body of the meditation; since the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does not enter into the body of the meditation, how can there be an intention (*tātparya*) to negate difference? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). Therefore, because there is an intention toward an established fact (*siddhārtha*) in that which is a supplement to an injunction, non-dual Brahman is the object of meditation.

The scriptural texts negating difference have as their purport the non-duality of Brahman; the meaning is that since the non-duality of Brahman itself constitutes the falsity of difference, the intention [of these texts] lies in the negation of difference once one has entered into the body of meditation. To dispel the doubt that the scripture does not establish Brahman as non-dual because it contradicts the means of knowledge that apprehend difference—just as in the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun"—the author accepts that there is a cognition contradictory to perception and other means of knowledge, stating: "by perception and so forth."

He removes the doubt with the words "of difference and non-difference. The meaning is that since the perception of difference is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhatvāt*), the unity understood from the scripture—which is not established otherwise—is the ultimate reality. [Objection: In that case, one must state the object, the instrument, the agent, and the fruit; furthermore, if it were something to be accomplished by an injunction (*niyoganirvatyatve*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the world being real, and because the state of Brahman is eternally attained, it cannot be the fruit. To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*). By the phrase "by the injunction of meditation" (*dhyānaniyogena*), the status of meditation as the object is stated.

If liberation were [attained] through *niyoga* (an injunction), then the doubt that "liberation is not from knowledge" is dispelled by the phrase "by means of the fruit of its direct realization. The meaning is that the status of *niyoga* as a means is mediated by knowledge. By the words "dispelled," etc., it is stated that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the fruit. That very [cessation] is the qualification of the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*) by virtue of being the fruit; the sense is that for us, it is established that the worshiper is the agent (*prayoktā*), while tranquility (*śama*) and so forth constitute the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). He refutes the proponent of liberation through mere knowledge of the sentence-meaning with the words "not," etc.

He states the contradiction with direct perception [in the words]: "because non-perception persists despite the observation of various distinctions. He states the contradiction with scripture [in the words]: "and such being the case..."

Now, the proponent of Māyā, desiring to state his own position later on, first anticipates the objection from the school that maintains liberation results from the application of ritual injunctions (*dhyāna-niyoga-vāda*), saying: "Now it might be argued... He states, with supporting arguments, that bondage is to be removed by knowledge alone: "This is a rope... For the falsity of that which is to be removed is accepted by both parties; therefore, he asserts the independence [of liberation] from injunction: "No... Otherwise, he points out the undesirable consequence: "By an injunction... He further states the undesirability of liberation being non-eternal: "Of liberation..."

He says "moreover" (*kiñca*) to show that [liberation] would yield a contrary result. By the words ending with "by means of the door" (*dvāreṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the consequence (*prasañjanīya*) and the proponent of the consequence (*prasañjaka*) is demonstrated. By the words ending with "inevitable" (*avarjanīya*), the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is stated. To the question "What follows from that? he replies with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This means: because of the consequence that it would have *saṃsāra* as its fruit; by the removal of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which is having *saṃsāra* as its fruit, the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—namely, being achievable through religious duty (*dharma*)—is also removed. Furthermore, he states that liberation cannot be achieved through ritual injunction (*niyoga*) based on the scriptural testimony that liberation is of the nature of being bodiless (*aśarīra*); this is expressed by the words "And likewise" (*tathā ca*).

Since liberation, which consists in bodilessness (*aśarīratva*), is heard in scripture to be devoid of connection with the pleasant and unpleasant—which are the fruits of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—it follows that liberation cannot be accomplished by means of *dharma*. This is what is stated in the phrase "thus, [liberation] consisting in bodilessness. In this way, the scriptural presumption (*śrutyarthāpatti*) has been stated: namely, that if liberation were accomplished through a ritual injunction (*niyoga*), it would be impossible for scripture to declare its freedom from the results of *dharma* and *adharma*.

Just as the cessation of evil is stated to be the fruit of a specific injunction (*niyoga*), so too the cessation of bondage can be the fruit of a specific injunction; to this he says, "And not... By the terms "specific injunction" and "specific fruit," the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and the destruction of sin are intended. To the question "Why?", he says, "Because of the state of being bodiless" (*aśarīratva*). Since the state of being bodiless is the very nature [of liberation], he cites scripture, saying, "As they say... [The verse begins] "Without breath" (*aprāṇa*). Because of the absence of connection with breath and mind, the state of being bodiless is established.

The sense is that the connection between the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) belongs to one who possesses a body; therefore, the meaning is that because bodilessness is understood to be the very nature of the Self, it cannot be something to be accomplished through ritual injunction (*niyoga*). He states, "And so says the Śruti," to show that not only is its non-attainability through injunction established by the absence of any connection with the fruits of action and by its being natural, but it is also explicitly stated [in scripture]. By the words "other than dharma and adharma" (*anyatra dharmād adharmāt*), the absence of any connection with dharma is expressed.

The meaning is that the relationship [between them] is that of the probandum and the probans. Here, by the words "done" (kṛta) and "not done" (akṛta), the "being done" (kriyamāṇa) is expressed; and by the words "past" (bhūta) and "future" (bhavya), the past and the future are expressed.

With the words "Moreover" (*api ca*), he refutes the position that liberation (*mokṣa*) is something to be accomplished through injunction by means of another approach. Stating the various ways in which being an effect (*sādhyatva*) can occur, he declares their impossibility with the words "In its production" (*utpatti*) and so forth. Regarding the dilemma as to whether the word "liberation" intends the essential nature (*svarūpa*) from which ignorance has ceased, or rather the cessation of ignorance itself: if the essential nature is intended, he states the impossibility of it being any of the four kinds of effects with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvat*) and so forth. It will be explained later that even if cessation were something produced, it would nonetheless be imperishable because its nature is that of a non-existent destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "For [it is] a refinement" (*saṃskāro hi*), etc.: here, by the term "eternally pure" (*nityaśuddha*), what is intended is the absence of connection with defects from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). It has been stated that an eternally pure, undifferentiated reality cannot be the object of a refinement—which consists of the removal of defects or the addition of qualities—because it is eternally pure and because no excellence can be added to it. Now, the absence of being an object of refinement is stated through the phrase beginning with "eternal," etc., on the grounds of its not being an object of action (*kriyā*).

How is it that, by virtue of being changeless (*nirvikāra*), there is an absence of being an object of action? It is as follows: whatever has become an object of action is observed to possess change (*savikāra*). When a mirror is rubbed on the palm of the hand, the action has the mirror as its locus (*āśraya*); when the hand is rubbed against the mirror, the action has the hand as its locus. Thus, the example of the mirror illustrates both actions that have their own locus and those that have another locus. To the objection that something may be an object of refinement (*saṃskārya*) even in the absence of being an object of action, he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

To the question "In that case, what is it that is refined?", he says "But rather" (*kintu*). "Seized by ignorance" (*avidyāgṛhīta*) means "constructed by ignorance" (*vidyākalpita*). By this, it is indicated that [the self] possesses the capacity for modification conducive to the production of excellence (*atiśaya*). Alternatively, by the phrase "seized by ignorance," it is shown that because of the delusion regarding purity and impurity, it is dependent upon purification. Since the agent of egoity (*ahaṅkartṛ*) is distinct from the body, how can there be an excellence in it through bathing and so forth belonging to the body? To this he says "associated with that" (*tatsaṅgata*). "Associated with that" means associated with the body.

Regarding the claim that "the self alone is to be refined because it is the enjoyer of the fruit," he says: "tatphala... (Because of that fruit...). If the enjoyer of the fruit is the referent of the "I" (ahamartha), then that itself would be the self; to this he says: "na cāham... (And not the "I" [is the self]). He states the reason: "tad... (That...); the sense is that whatever is the witness of something cannot be that very thing. He provides the proof for its being the witness: "tathā ca... (And thus...). The meaning of the passage beginning with "tayor anyaḥ" (One of the two... is as follows: between the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and the conscious self (jñapti-ātman), one is the enjoyer of the fruit, while the other does not eat.

The verse beginning with "ātmendriya... clearly demonstrates that the *ahaṅkāra* (ego) alone is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Here, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the body. Since the state of being an enjoyer arises from the connection with the body and other factors, and because scripture declares that the Self is "without body, without breath, without mind," and further declares it to be a non-enjoyer through the phrase "not eating," the intention is that the Self is distinct in nature from the enjoyer. Alternatively, the word "Self" may refer to consciousness (*saṃvid-ātman*). In that case, since the state of being an enjoyer belongs to that which is joined with [consciousness], the [pure] Self lacks the quality of being an enjoyer; thus, the intention is that the *ahaṅkāra* alone is the enjoyer.

In the phrase "the one God," the word *kevala* (alone) is intended to signify the absence of connection with any fruit; this is its relevance here. "Without qualities" (*nirguṇaḥ*) means not being subject to the qualities (*guṇas*), and thus not an enjoyer (*abhoktṛ*). The sense is that while the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is active, he remains as a mere witness (*sākṣin*) and is therefore not an enjoyer. Regarding the phrase "he has pervaded": *śukla* means free from ignorance (*avidyā*) or free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). *Śuddha* means untainted by evil, which implies being devoid of the fruits of action and devoid of action itself. "He has pervaded" (*paryagāt*): roots meaning "to go" also mean "to understand."

The meaning is "he thought. He states the nature of the Self as endowed with the form established by the cited scripture in the words "ignorance" (avidyā). The grammatical connection is that [the Self] is distinguished from the agent of egoism (ahaṅkartṛ). He concludes the non-attainability of liberation [through effort] with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).

He raises the objection that knowledge would be useless with the words "If it were so"; he refutes this with "Liberation... He states that the fact that the cessation of obstacles alone is what is to be accomplished is established by scripture with the words "And thus..."; he concludes that the cessation of obstacles is what is to be accomplished with the words "Therefore...". To the objection that the cessation of obstacles would be non-eternal because it is something to be accomplished, he replies with "The cessation... If it is argued that this same refutation applies equally to the position that [liberation] is to be accomplished through a ritual injunction (*niyoga*), we say no.

It has been stated that the intention is that if [Brahman] were to be accomplished through an injunction (*niyoga*), the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would follow. Regarding the position that it is accomplished through an injunction, he says "Brahman" to show the loss of the natural sense of the scripture (*śruti*). The meaning is that the natural sense of the scripture itself does not tolerate any delay. How is the intervention of an injunction obstructed? For the establishment of Brahman occurs as a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) to an injunction.

In response to the doubt that an injunction (*niyoga*) must be accepted for the sake of accomplishing that [knowledge], he says "And not by knowing" (*na ca vidīti*), stating that being subordinate to an injunction is impossible in either way—whether as the object of the act of knowing (*vidi*) or as the object of the act of meditation (*dhyāna*). "Knowing" (*vedana*) means cognition; "meditation" (*upāsana*) is a specific kind of cognition. Here, the word "knowing" (*vedana*) ultimately rests upon a specific kind of cognition that effects the removal of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa*), depending on the intended meaning. Consequently, this also results in the refutation of the theory that there is an injunction to effect the removal of the phenomenal world.

Regarding the absence of being an object of knowledge (*vidi*) or meditation (*upāsi*), he cites the scripture: "Other than this" (*anyat*). "From the known" (*viditāt*) means from that which is to be known; "from the unknown" (*aviditāt*) means from the knower. "Other indeed" (*anyad eva*) is the negation of its being an object of knowledge; "that very same" (*tad eva*) is the negation of its being an object of meditation. [This concludes the section on] the object of knowledge.

Fearing that, in the absence of [Brahman], the scripture would be rendered objectless because its status as something to be known would be unestablished, he raises this objection and refutes it with the words "And not... [na ca]. He states that Brahman's status as an object of knowledge is perceived through such scriptural passages as "He knows Brahman" and "The knower of Brahman"; to this he replies, "Not indeed as 'this' (idantayā). "As 'this'" means as an object of cognition characterized by spatial or temporal limitation. "But rather" (api tu) means that the scripture establishes the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) as being devoid of distinctions and beyond the scope of objective categories. He demonstrates that the purpose of the scripture is the cessation of duality with the words "And thus" (tathā ca).

Anticipating the objection that "if the cessation of bondage results from knowledge alone, there would be a contradiction with scripture and perception," he first dispels the contradiction with scripture by stating, "And not from knowledge [alone]. Regarding the point that "the injunctions for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth would be rendered purposeless": since the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) has also stated that hearing and reflection are themselves to be enjoined, there is no contradiction. To the question "Why?", he says: "By its own nature" (*svabhāva*). By the term "spontaneous activity" (*svabhāva-pravṛtta*), what is intended is the state of being primordially active.

Now, he dispels the contradiction with perception by saying, "And not merely from knowledge. To the question "How so?", he says, "Of bondage... How is its continued existence untenable? This is the doubt that "bondage indeed persists," which will be resolved by the passage beginning with "But for whom there is bondage... For the very reason already stated, he declares the independence from the fall of the body by saying, "For this very reason... He establishes this through an illustration by saying, "For not... He explains the point shown in the illustration in the case of the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) by way of its contrapositive (*vyatireka*) by saying, "If..."

He states the opposite of its being ultimate reality with the words "But that... The meaning is: that which is subject to misconception is not ultimately real, because it is distinct from Brahman, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. If it is argued that its persistence after the time of knowledge is untenable, he says "But for whom... regarding how bondage continues: for one who has the cognition that it has not ceased—that it is "not ceased"—knowledge itself has not arisen, because no effect of such knowledge is observed.

The meaning is as follows: although the absence of the effect is not pervaded by the mere absence of the cause, it is nevertheless pervaded by the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Since true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) constitutes the causal complex for the cessation of error, the absence of such knowledge is postulated due to the absence of that complex; thus, there is no contradiction with perception. He concludes the cessation of bondage immediately after the arising of knowledge with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). As for the phrase "let the body persist or not": [it means this is irrelevant].

The meaning is that, just as the appearance of a cloth persists or ceases upon a burnt cloth, so too the appearance of the body may persist or cease. "He is indeed liberated" means that because the root of bondage has been severed, he is like a burnt cloth, incapable of producing effects; this is the sense. He states "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that Brahman is not established as a subordinate element of an injunction by means of those reasons which prove that the cessation of bondage is independent of such an injunction. "Therefore" means because [liberation] is accomplished merely through the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence.

To the question, "In that case, how is Brahman established? he says, "But rather... (*api tu*). "By those [statements] intent upon that" means that it is established as being devoid of distinctions by means of sentences whose purpose is the negation of difference. Alternatively, it means "by those intent upon the meaning of an already established form. The word "is established" (*sidhyati*) implies "Brahman" as the understood object.

The proponent of the doctrine of the application of meditation refutes this with the words "that is improper," and so forth. To the question "Why?", he says "because of the meaning of the sentence. To the question "How can it be said by the proponent of the falsity of the phenomenal world that the cessation of bondage through knowledge is untenable?", he says "Even though... He states the disparity even when the cessation by knowledge is admitted with the words "Nevertheless... Regarding the fact that indirect knowledge does not sublate an immediate error, he provides an illustration with the words "in the case of a rope, etc. By the word "etc.," items such as a piece of ground are included.

The cognition of a rope is the sublation of the cognition of a snake. If fear were not removed by that [cognition], the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*) would be rendered useless; therefore, he says, "of the instruction of a reliable person. By this, the meaning of the commentary on the first sūtra is understood: "However, the effect such as fear ceases because it is sublated by a more powerful means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For the meaning of that commentary is that the instruction of a reliable person serves as the cause for the cessation of effects such as fear by means of the activity initiated through the immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of the true nature of reality (*vastuyāthātmya*).

He demonstrates this point through an illustration with the words "tathā hi" (for instance). One might object: "Let it be that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) alone is the opponent of such an error; yet, the word itself generates immediate knowledge. Anticipating this doubt, he says "na ca" (and not). He states the reason with the words "tasya" (of that). He shows the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "jñāna" (knowledge). Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the reason on the grounds that light and the like, though not sense organs, are seen to generate immediate knowledge; for what is intended [as the reason] is the state of not entering into the causal complex of knowledge in which the sense organ is predominant.

And this has been indicated by the phrase "in the causal complexes of knowledge" (*jñānasāmagrīṣu*). This means: in the causal complexes of knowledge together with their accessories—namely, the sense organs, inferential marks, words, similarity, presumption, and non-apprehension. Regarding the statement "the sense organs alone," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "together with [auxiliaries] such as light. Having raised the objection that "the sense organ itself makes known even what is obstructed and so forth to the yogi, and likewise the speech of a specific intended person generates immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*)," he refutes it with the words "and not... [referring to the sense organ]. "[Of] this person" refers to the yogi. He states the reason: "because [the capacity] has ceased," and so on.

Having kept in mind the two phrases beginning with "unintended" (*anabhisaṃhita*), he states the two qualifiers: "even when the obstacle has ceased and [the mind] is intent upon that. In the phrase "by showing the non-transgression of its own object" (*svaviṣayaniyamātikramādarśanena*), the word "object" (*viṣaya*) refers to the probandum (*sādhya*). The meaning is: "by showing the non-transgression of the knowledge of its own probandum. The knowledge produced by a word is necessarily indirect (*parokṣa*); the point is that a word does not transcend the indirect knowledge that it itself produces. Since the mind is a cause common to both indirect and direct knowledge, whereas a word—like a logical mark (*liṅga*)—is a cause of indirect knowledge alone.
The sense is that there is no equality with the mind of a yogi [through mere verbal testimony].

Now, an objection is raised: "But isn't it the case that immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge is produced even by a word? For we observe the arising of the immediate knowledge 'I am the tenth' from the sentence 'You are the tenth. That is not so; because immediately following the instruction, through a cognition produced by the causal complex for perception—which arises swiftly—the prior cognition is superimposed as being perceptual due to the non-apprehension of its difference [from the new one]. For at that time, by the force of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the previous counting of the nine [persons] occurring before the instruction, an unimpeded enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) indeed arises.

Just as when it is said, "This is a jar," the immediate perception (*aparokṣapratīti*) of one who sees the jar is produced by the sense organ, and not produced by the sentence "This is a jar"; for the sentence is merely the cause of the operation of the eye, which is the instrument of that immediate perception—so too, the sentence "You are the tenth" is the cause of the recollection of the object required by prior impressions, which serves as the basis for the cognition "I am the tenth. It is not, however, the cause of the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*), because a sentence, being separated from the respective causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for such a perception, cannot constitute that specific causal complex itself.

The point under dispute is that perceptual knowledge is not produced by a sentence, because it is perceptual knowledge, like the cognition "I am the tenth" in one who has not been instructed by a sentence. Furthermore, the point under dispute is that a sentence is not a generator of perceptual knowledge, because it is a sentence, like any other accepted sentence. Thus, the intended meaning of the *Bhāṣya*—namely, that the objection is refuted by the fact that [the sentence] is otherwise established through the swiftness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) and by being the cause of activity based on the immediate intuition of the true nature of reality—is as follows.

Nor should it be argued that even in a cognition produced by a sentence, the qualifier-part—which enters into the qualified object—is also perceptual merely because the "I" (the self), which serves as the qualificand, is perceptual. Furthermore, there is no rule that a cognition expressed by a word co-referential with "I" must necessarily be immediate; for instance, in the case of a person who has inferred merit or demerit from pleasure or pain, one observes no immediacy regarding that merit or demerit in cognitions such as "I am a doer of merit" or "I am a doer of demerit."

If the dharma were perceived merely by the perception of the substratum (*dharmin*), then in the inferential cognition "the mountain possesses fire," it would follow that the fire itself is also perceived. All of this is intended [to be refuted] by the point that such [a claim] is untenable because no transgression of the restriction regarding one's own object is observed.

Thus, the capacity of the word to produce immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*) has been refuted. Now, he refutes the idea that meditation (*dhyāna*) is a means to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence by pointing out the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*), beginning with the words "And not... (*na ca*). To avoid this mutual dependence, one might suggest that the knowledge preceding meditation has one object and the subsequent knowledge has a different object; however, resorting to such a distinction of objects is improper. To this, he says: "And not through meditation... (*na ca dhyāna...*). Why? To this he replies: "If that were so... (*tathā sati*).

To the question, "How is there a loss of its being a means? he says: "For there is no other meditation. Even though they have the same object, the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence—which brings about cessation—would require meditation; as to how meditation requires the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, he says: "The object already known," and so forth.

One might raise the objection that the knowledge which serves as the cause for meditation (*dhyāna*) is produced by other causes, whereas meditation is not rooted in the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence that arises subsequently; thus, due to the difference in their causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), one might avoid the charge of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Anticipating this, [the author] states "the object of meditation" (*dhyeya*), etc., to show that such a difference in causal complexes is impossible. The implication is that because Brahman is beyond the reach of perception and other means of knowledge, no other cause for its knowledge is possible. Then, having raised the objection that there is a difference in the sentences themselves to resolve that issue, he says "nor," to show that it is improper to speak in such a manner.

He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating, "meditation has knowledge as its root. If they have the same object, that very same fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśrayatva) arises. The meaning is this: if knowledge were produced by another statement, then because it would have the same object as the knowledge produced by the sentence "That thou art," that knowledge too would require meditation, and meditation would require knowledge of the meaning of the sentence; thus there is mutual dependence. He states the refutation regarding the two sentences having different objects with the word "bhinna" (different).

He states "moreover" (*kiñca*) to show that meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed opposed to the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "the meditator and so forth," tranquility (*śama*) and other such qualities are included. Regarding the phrase "by way of the seen" (*dṛṣṭadvāreṇa*): the opponents, who are excessively fearful of [logical] consequences, have abandoned the utility [of meditation] by way of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), for fear of the undesirable consequence of the reality of the latent impressions of duality (*dvaitavāsanā*), which they seek to refute. This is the intention of those who maintain the doctrine of the injunction of meditation (*dhyānaniyogavādin*).

He states "yataḥ" (since) to establish that the refutation of *jīvanmukti* follows from the rejection of the cessation of ignorance through the mere knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. "Dūrotsāritā" (completely cast aside): even if direct (*aparokṣa*) knowledge were possible from a sentence, *jīvanmukti* is cast aside due to contradictions and so forth; the sense is that it is "completely cast aside" because direct knowledge cannot arise from a sentence. "And what is this?"—the word "what" (*kā*) is used in a derogatory sense, or it is intended as a question regarding the various alternatives. He raises a doubt concerning its nature with the words "saśarīrasya" (of one possessing a body). He states the contradiction with the words "mātā" (mother).

He points out the contradiction with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). He raises that view as an objection in order to avoid the contradiction, beginning with "now" (*atha*). By the statement "the cessation of embodiedness," the proponent of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) intends to show that the root of embodiedness has been severed. He refutes this with "no" (*na*).

Since the reality of the body is not admitted, its cessation in the form of total destruction is not intended; therefore, what is meant must be either the cessation of appearance or the cessation of the conceit regarding the reality of that appearance. With this intention, [the author] first restates the first alternative and refutes it by showing that what is desired is not established, saying "it is false," etc. "Possession of a body" refers to the appearance of possessing a body, because in the subsequent text there is a reference to "appearance. [The question is: "How can there be liberation for one who possesses a body?"

The meaning is that liberation cannot be said to belong to one who possesses a body. He establishes this very point with the words, "even for one not living. By the term "false appearance" (*mithyā-pratibhāsa*), erroneous cognition (*bhrānti-jñāna*) is intended. The meaning is that since there would be no distinction between the liberation of one living and one not living, liberation could not be said to belong to the body. He raises the second alternative with the word "now" (*atha*). Here, the intended meaning of the preceding passage beginning with "while the appearance of possessing a body is present" is elucidated. He refutes it with "no" (*na*).

To the question "How so?", he says: "Brahman," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "ignorance, karma, etc.," latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are included. "Sublated by that very [knowledge]" means sublated by the sublating knowledge (*bādhaka-jñāna*). Regarding the point that the persistence of what has been sublated is observed in cases such as the cognition of two moons, he says: "In the case of the [cognition of] two moons, etc. The sense is that the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not removed merely by the knowledge of the true nature of the rope.

In the first sūtra, regarding the refutation of the persistence of what has been sublated, the persistence of error was mentioned because the defect is ultimately real and thus not sublatable by knowledge; here, however, the persistence of the cognition of two moons is mentioned because the defect remains unsublated since it is not an object of the cognition of the oneness of the moon—this is the distinction. Furthermore, this disparity is stated because even the ancient Māyāvādins accept the falsity of everything in its entirety. He states the contradiction with Śruti regarding liberation while living (jīvanmukti) with the words "Moreover" (kiñca); he states the contradiction with Smṛti with the words "This very... (saiṣā).

By the word "Veda," the actions that are the means for attaining the three aims of life (trivarga) are expressed; their fruit is expressed as "this world and the next. When the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences has arisen in the intellect, the attainment of security is liberation (mokṣa).

The meaning of the plural number in the phrase "contradicted by the scriptures" (*śāstrair*) is as follows: there is contradiction with numerous scriptures—those intended for injunctions regarding meditative worship (*upāsana*) that follow the knowledge of the meaning of the sentences; those intended to enjoin the persistence [of the practice] until death, such as "conducting oneself thus for the duration of one's life"; those intended to show that liberation depends solely upon the falling away of the body; those intended to describe the departure through a specific channel, such as "going upwards by those two, he attains immortality"; and those intended to describe the attainment of a specific location via the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*). Thus, there is conflict with many such scriptural passages.

"Contradicted" (*vipratiṣiddham*) means specifically prohibited. It is not merely obstructed by [authorities] of equal strength, but rather struck down by those that are stronger. The reason for this superiority is the principle: "The majority shall be more powerful" (*bhūyasāṃ syāt balīyastvam*). Smṛti itself states the contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the verse beginning with *buddhe cet*. By this, the other [contradiction] is explained. By this contradiction between scripture and direct perception, whatever else was stated according to the view of Auhulomi is also explained.

The meaning is that everything has been rejected. Alternatively, the meaning is that just as there is the perception of suffering now, so too will there be after death. Or else, the meaning is that just as the cessation of suffering is not perceived, so too is the cessation of happiness not [perceived]. By means of the statement cited for the purpose of refuting *jīvanmukti*, he says "by this," indicating that liberation through the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentences is also effectively refuted. He concludes the refutation of *jīvanmukti* with the word "therefore."

He states "tasmāt" (therefore) to establish the stability of his own position by refuting *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). He says "na ca niyogena" (nor by injunction) to show that the rebuttal of the objection stated by the proponent of liberation through mere knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic texts is equally applicable to him as well. Anticipating the objection that if [the world] were to be removed by an injunction (*niyoga*), the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would follow, he says "kiñca" (furthermore). The word "kiñca" is employed because he intends to address the untenability of the view that liberation results from the injunction to meditate (*dhyāna-niyoga*).

The meaning is that the power of the *niyoga* (injunction) to bring about cessation is mediated by knowledge (*jñāna*), and therefore there is no requirement for the reality of that which is to be ceased. He asks, "How? with the desire to know the specific mode of operation (*kiñcitkāra*) of the *niyoga* in the production of knowledge. The sense is: "Indeed, no visible mode of operation is possible for the *niyoga* regarding knowledge; therefore, that must be stated. He answers by way of a counter-objection: "Or how [is it]? [He replies: "It is the cause for the arising of cognition. By this, what is intended is its being the cause for the arising of cognition through the mediation of desire (*icchā*).

For it will be quoted later: "desiring to know. He anticipates an objection regarding the mind (*manas*). He states its similarity with the words, "It is the same for me too. He raises the objection again with the words, "But for me," meaning: since the mind is a common cause, even when that exists, a specific (uncommon) cause is still required; I possess such a cause, whereas you must state what yours is. This is the sense.

He refutes [the objection] by stating "meditation" (dhyāna), on the grounds that the mind alone is the uncommon cause—just as in the case of mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa) accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, or like the yogic perception established in such passages as "By the power of dharma, you see all that exactly as it is," which has the mind alone as its cause when assisted by preeminent unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). The intended meaning is that although the mind in general is a common cause, it is logical that a specific, exceptionally pure mind serves as the uncommon cause.

He raises an objection regarding the indicator [of the truth] with the word "by what? He asks "or by you? in order to show the disparity in his own position characterized by the natural fitness of the indicator. He cites the scriptural passages favored by the opponent as authoritative for the arising of the knowledge that turns one away [from the world] through the *nididhyāsana* of one whose mind has been turned away from objects, beginning with "those who desire to know... The opponent's intention is that by the word "knowing" (*vedana*) in the passage "he who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence is intended.

He shows the proof for the mind being the instrument of knowledge with the words "so too for me. The sentence beginning with "not by the eye" is naturally inclined toward the mind alone as the instrument. However, in the phrase "he knows Brahman," it is not naturally understood that the word "knowledge" (vedana) refers to the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence; nor is its reference to that [sentence-meaning] understood through consistency with another scripture, because there is no other scriptural passage that explicitly states that the knowledge of the sentence-meaning serves as the means [to liberation]. All objections and resolutions based on the premise of falsity are the same [in both cases].

The phrase "how so" (*katham*) and so forth serves as a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) to resolve various objections, demonstrating the disparity [between our view and yours] by showing that in your position there are further defects: namely, that even indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) would have to remove direct error (*aparokṣabhrama*), which contradicts both scripture and perception, and which results in the abandonment of the natural sense of the *śruti*. The word "iti" is not the remainder of the immediately preceding sentence, but rather the remainder of the entire section (*prakaraṇa*).

He raises the objection regarding the prohibition of being an object of meditation with the words, "Not this. He refutes it with, "Not so," meaning that such an interpretation of that passage is not tenable. To the claim that a negation of being an object of meditation is perceived there, he replies, "Not here. To the question, "What then is the meaning? he says, "But rather... To the question, "How is the presentation of dissimilarity [between the two] established? he says, "That which is this... The sense is that in the phrase "that which they meditate upon as this," the purport of the negation lies in the referent "this."

For the objects of worship in the meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) enjoined by such passages as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" are indeed limited; this [Brahman under discussion] is not that. Rather, the meaning is that it is the unlimited, supreme Brahman itself. By this, it is explained that the passage beginning with "That is indeed other than the known" is also intended to show the world's dissimilarity [to Brahman]. The phrase "otherwise" expresses a contradiction with one's own statement [that Brahman is beyond speech].
The phrase "futility of the injunction to meditate" expresses a contradiction with another scriptural passage. He concludes his own position with the word "therefore."

Now, this proponent of the necessity of meditation (*dhyānaniyogavādī*), in order to refute the view of Bhāskara, restates the latter’s position regarding the non-contradiction of difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedāvirodha*) with the words beginning "As for that which... He first refutes it briefly, saying "That is incorrect. Contradiction (*virodha*) is twofold: characterized by necessarily having different substrata, and characterized by non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the relationship of destroyer and destroyed—as in the case of grass and fire—is intended. He states "For not... to show that contradiction exists between difference and non-difference as well.

Now, he introduces the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) in detail with the words "Then it might be said" (*athocyeta*). He instructs on the matter relevant to what is about to be said with the words "For everything" (*sarvaṃ hi*). The point is that even in cases such as cold and heat, contradiction is dependent upon cognition. To the question "What follows from this?", he says "And everything" (*sarvaṃ ca*). To the question "In what way is there both difference and non-difference?", he says "By way of the nature of the cause" (*kāraṇātmanā*). He says "Like a shadow" (*chāyā*) in order to state the dissimilarity between this case and the two previously mentioned instances where contradiction is perceived. To the question "What follows from this?", he says "The effect... (*kārya...*).

He states the perception [of coexistence] without contradiction by saying "on the contrary" (*pratyuta*). He demonstrates this perception through a gesture of illustration by saying "just as" (*yathā*). He states the non-perception of a non-dual entity by saying "and not" (*na ca*). He asserts that there is no third type of contradiction characterized by the relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer by saying "nor of grass and so forth" (*na ca tṛṇādeḥ*). By the term "contradiction of entities," the contradiction characterized by the relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer is intended. He establishes the absence of such a contradiction by saying "clay, gold, etc. (*mṛtsuvarṇa-*) .

In response to the doubt—namely, how a single entity can possess both difference and non-difference, given that non-difference resides in the universal (*jāti*) while difference resides in the individual (*vyakti*)—the author establishes the mutual difference and non-difference between the universal and the individual with the words "And not of the non-different... and so forth. The meaning is: "of the non-different" refers to the universal, and "of the different" refers to the individual. Is it by some decree of God that one must accept that the form of the universal is exclusively non-difference and the form of the individual is exclusively difference? The point is that no matter should be accepted by force, in disregard of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*).

He anticipates the acceptance [of the opponent's position] on the strength of common cognition (pratīti), saying "because it is cognized. Likewise, he states that his own view must also be accepted, saying "precisely because it is cognized"; the purpose of the word "precisely" (eva) is to indicate that this follows from what you yourself have said. Regarding the phrase "even the two-fold nature," the intention of the word "even" (api) is to include "even that which is undesirable. He establishes that it is indeed cognized by saying "for not... The meaning is that only when one distinguishes, "this is the universal (jāti)" and "this is the individual (vyakti)," would it be appropriate to say, "here there is non-difference" and "here there is difference"; however, they are not distinguished in that manner.

To the question, "How then is there cognition [of this]? he says, "But rather... (api tu). The meaning is that a single entity alone is perceived as both distinct and non-distinct by way of its universal nature (*jāti*) and its individual nature (*vyakti*). By the expression "this is a clay pot" (*mṛdayaṃ ghaṭaḥ*), he states the argument establishing both difference and non-difference: namely, the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that does not depend on a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*). He raises an objection regarding their distinction based on persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) with the words, "By persistence... (*anuvṛttīti*). He refutes this with, "Not so" (*naivamiti*).

He explains the non-perception of distinct forms with the words "not even the most subtle. For if there were perception of distinct forms, it would be possible to determine that "in this part there is the state of being cognized by a cognition of persistence," and "in this part there is the state of being cognized by a cognition of exclusion. The meaning is that "distinct form" (*ākārabheda*) refers to "distinction of parts" (*aṃśabheda*). To the question "In that case, how is there perception?", he replies: "as is commonly agreed upon. "Particular" (*viśeṣa*) means the individual instance (*vyakti*).

The meaning is that just as the oneness of the effect and the oneness of the individual (vyakti) are admitted, so too the cognition of oneness arises between cause and effect, as well as between the genus (jāti) and the individual. By the phrase "cognition of oneness," a cognition permeated by the word "one" is expressed. By this, the rule of simultaneous perception and the apprehension [of the two] as non-different at the first grasping of the individual object are implied by the sense of the argument; for it is stated that one is unable to distinguish [them].

Thus, the mutual difference and non-difference between the genus (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) has been stated. Now, the mutual difference and non-difference among individuals (*piṇḍa*) is stated with the words "in the very same way. The distinction of place and time is evident. The distinction of form consists in [qualities] such as blueness or being a fragment. "Absolute difference" means a difference that cannot tolerate non-difference. Here, he anticipates an objection with the words "Now, it might be said."

The sense is this: even if the identity of the body and the self as existing substances is accepted, their oneness—whether in the form of the body or in the form of the self—is unauthenticated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, their being both different and non-different (*bhedābheda*) is undesirable. He refutes this with the words "this [is] that. The meaning is: this was stated by one who does not understand that uncontradicted grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) establishes difference-and-non-difference, and that such difference-and-non-difference is the true nature of reality (*tattva*). He explains this further with the words "for instance" (*tathā hi*). He teaches the point necessary for the refutation with the word "uncontradicted" (*abādhita*).

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "devādī" (gods, etc.). To the objection that the same might apply to both genus and individual, he says: "khaṇḍa" (a fragment). Thus, the difference-in-identity (*bhedābheda*) of worldly objects has been stated. Relying upon that, he states the difference-in-identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman even with respect to Vedic matters, saying: "ata eva" (for this very reason). The meaning is: because difference and non-difference are not contradictory. In the phrase "by being a part of Brahman," the Sūtra "aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt" (He is a part [of Brahman], because of the various designations) is recalled.

It is the view of both Bhāskara and Yādava that the difference and non-difference between consciousness (*cit*) and Brahman are innate; however, the author says "therein" (*tatra*) in order to exclude the position of Yādava, who holds that "the difference and non-difference of consciousness and Brahman are innate. The question "how? means: what is the proof for the existence of both difference and non-difference, and specifically for the fact that it is non-difference alone that is innate therein?

Because non-difference is primary due to its being inherent, he first states the scriptural passage concerning the portion of the sūtra "and otherwise," namely: *tat tvam asi*. He states the passage concerning the portion beginning with "the Daśas and Kitavas," namely: *brahmaivedam*. He states the passage concerning the portion [of the sūtra] "on account of the designation of multiplicity," namely: *nityo nityānām*. Regarding "by means of actions, qualities, and self-qualities": actions and qualities are the causes of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*); self-qualities are the causes of liberation (*mokṣa*).

The meaning is that it is the cause of their conjunction. To the question, "How is it understood here that difference (*bheda*) is adventitious (*aupādhika*)?", he replies with the word "therein" (*tatra*). The meaning is that the designation of attaining that very nature and the negation of difference are the indicators that non-difference (*abheda*) is not adventitious. Since difference is negated precisely at liberation (*mukti*), the fact that difference is adventitious is established by implication. He raises an objection while showing that difference exists at liberation, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*). The objector’s intention is that the word "together" (*saha*) refers to the coexistence of the enjoyer.

He avoids [the objection] by means of the cognition that [the enjoyer and the enjoyed] are co-existent, saying "not this. Intending to avoid the perception of difference, he shows that difference in liberation is contrary to scripture, saying "not another. He avoids the perception of difference by saying "he enjoys. The meaning of the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that it is expressed by the sentence "he enjoys" (*so 'śnute*).

"He attains the qualities along with Brahman and experiences both the qualities and Brahman. In response to the inquiry as to whether he attains them as something separate from Brahman or as non-separate, that must be understood from other scriptural passages; thus, for the time being, there is no perception of duality here. He establishes this by saying "otherwise" (*anyathā*). The sense is that non-predominance would be a defect if it were in relation to another enjoyer, but it is not a defect in relation to one's own qualities which constitute the objects of enjoyment. He states his own intended meaning regarding the sūtra cited by others: "the world," etc.

The meaning of the *sūtra* is that there is no difference [between Brahman and the liberated soul], because if a difference between Brahman and the liberated one were to exist, it would follow that [the liberated soul] is devoid of the activity of governing the world. He establishes this with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). He concludes the inherent nature of non-difference with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). By the use of the particle *eva*, he intends to show that the conditioned nature (*aupādhikatva*) of difference is established by implication from the negation of difference in the state of liberation. In response to the question "What is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)?", he says: "But the difference... The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate a distinction consisting in its being conditioned, or else it serves to express a doubt.

Regarding the claim that because Brahman possesses omnipresence and partlessness, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) must reside in Brahman itself—and thus, due to the absence of any region unconnected with it, a distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*) is impossible—the author says, "Even though... He addresses the suspicion of mutual dependence by saying, "Nor is it..."; for since there is no connection with limiting adjuncts such as the intellect (*buddhi*) produced by karma in the portion that is the Lord, the conjunction with an adjunct is necessarily preceded by [an already existing] distinction.

He avoids [the objection] by means of the "beginninglessness of the stream" (*pravāhānāditā*), [stating] "of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*). To the doubt—"How can there be a beginninglessness of the stream for the limiting adjuncts and their conjunction with those who are themselves devoid of karma? And how, by that, is the avoidance of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) achieved?"—he explains this with the words "this has been said. [The phrase] "karma from that which is joined with it" means as follows: being subject to karma is indeed what constitutes the state of being a *jīva*. The state of being a *jīva* arises through the limiting adjunct; because the nature of a *jīva* [precedes] the further limiting adjunct, it is beginningless. He states the resulting meaning with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). He points out the disparity regarding the non-conscious portion (*acidaṃśa*) with the words "furthermore, of the limiting adjuncts."

Furthermore, the meaning is as follows. He states two reasons for the inequality with the words "of the limiting adjuncts" (*upādhīnām*). He concludes the position that [the self] is both different and non-different with the words "therefore, by the karma of the individual soul" (*ato jīvakarma*).

Now, the proponent of the doctrine of meditative application (*dhyānaniyoga*) refutes the position of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) with the words "To this it is said," and so forth. To show the point of connection that introduces the position previously commenced with the words "As for what someone has said," he says "It is non-dual. He indicates that point of connection by saying "In that regard, as for what was said. Intending to refute the cognition concerning difference and non-difference, he first states their essential nature in order to establish their mutual contradiction, beginning with "From something... Here, "distinctness" (*vilakṣaṇatva*) means "otherness" (*anyatva*).

The cognition regarding difference and non-difference is expressed as "this is not that" and "this is that. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Of those two. "Difference and non-difference" is not the name of any single property. The meaning is that if the meaning of the words "difference and non-difference" is accepted in accordance with worldly convention, then the contradiction between existence and non-existence becomes unavoidable. Furthermore, it cannot be asserted by this [position] that there is no contradiction anywhere, because three kinds of contradiction are observed.

If there were no contradiction between existence and non-existence, then there would likewise be no contradiction even between one’s own words and the words of others regarding whether difference-and-non-difference exists or does not exist. [The opponent] restates the claim made by another—that the difference-and-non-difference of two lumps is not contradictory due to a difference in form—by saying "in the nature of the cause. [The author] refutes this by means of an alternative analysis, beginning with the word "no" (*na*). Regarding the phrase "in one form": the word "form" (*ākāra*) here refers to an entity (*padārtha*). Regarding the phrase "in the former alternative":

In this regard, with the three alternatives in mind—whether there is mutual difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), or non-difference, or both difference and non-difference—he first refutes the first position with the words "located in the individual" (*vyaktigata*). He restates the second with "the universal" (*jāti*). He refutes it with "then indeed" (*tarhi*); the meaning is that the contradiction remains precisely as it is. He refutes the third with "and in one" (*ekasmin ca*); the meaning is that the contradiction between existence and non-existence—namely, that the universal both is and is not the individual—remains precisely as it is.

The second alternative, which was stated explicitly as the first option, refutes the second head [of the argument] with the words "but in the second case. Here, there is an additional fault, namely that no entity distinct from both genus (*jāti*) and individual (*vyakti*) is apprehended; this is what is intended by the phrase "that very thing is unapprehended" (*apratipannam*). Even if one were to grant that it is apprehended, he states the refutation with the words "even if a third is granted. The meaning of "not otherwise" is that [the number three] would not exist [otherwise].

Regarding this third point, the author raises the objection that there is no contradiction because difference and non-difference are established through two distinct aspects (*ākāra*). He introduces this with the words "by means of two aspects. Having in mind the following alternatives—whether these two aspects are different from their own substratum, or non-different, or both different and non-different—he first refutes the first position with the words "from itself" (*svasmāt*). The three occurrences of the word *sva* (self/own) all refer to the substratum. For indeed, contradiction exists only when difference and non-difference reside in a single substratum.

For the two forms that effect non-contradiction do not serve as the substratum for both difference and non-difference; therefore, they cannot be what effects non-contradiction. The meaning is that the two forms—tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) and brilliance (*aujjvalya*)—residing in fire do not effect the coexistence of the two contradictory properties in the form of coldness and heat within that same fire. He refutes the second alternative with the word "non-distinct" (*avilakṣaṇa*). It was previously stated that when two distinct forms are possible, it is impossible for a single [undifferentiated] thing to effect the coexistence of two contradictory properties.

In this context, however, since even the two forms themselves do not exist, the impossibility of the coexistence of contradictory properties is absolute; it is with this intention that the phrase "how much more so" (*kathaṃtarām*) is stated. He refutes the third alternative with the words "of the two forms and their substratum. The meaning is as follows: another pair of forms would be required to establish the difference-and-non-difference between the two forms and their substrate; if that [second] pair also possesses difference-and-non-difference with its own substrate, then yet another pair of forms would be required to establish the non-contradiction of that, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, in response to the doubt as to what could possibly be "inexplicable" regarding that which is perceived, he refutes the cognition concerning difference and non-difference with the words "na ca" (and not). He states the reason with the words "yataḥ" (since). He then demonstrates the qualifier and the qualified by distinguishing them within that cognition with the word "tatra" (therein).

By this, the following fourfold set of reasons is also refuted: (1) grammatical coreferentiality independent of possessive suffixes (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), (2) the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*), (3) cognition permeated by a single word, and (4) the apprehension of non-difference between the genus and the individual at the first grasping of the object. The reason for [the identity of] grammatical coreferentiality independent of possessive suffixes is the state of being a qualifier that is not established separately (*apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*).

Furthermore, the non-separability (*apṛthaksiddhi*) of the qualifier (*prakāra*) and the qualified (*prakārī*) is established solely through the necessity of their relationship. Therefore, there is no room for postulating identity—which contradicts the difference apprehended in the relation of qualifier and qualified. Moreover, the very necessity of their relationship is the cause for the necessity of their simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*). Even the cognition "this is one cow" has as its object the unity of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), just like [the cognition] "one who has a staff" (*eko daṇḍī*); it does not have the unity of the qualifier and the qualified as its object. Even at the time of the first apprehension of an individual (*piṇḍa*), the cognition occurs precisely as a distinction due to the relation of qualifier and qualified.

Furthermore, even coexistence (*sahatva*) is a proof of difference, for coexistence belongs only to two things. Moreover, the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is not a proof for either [difference or non-difference], because it is inconclusive due to being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇānaikāntika*); it is not observed in cases where things are currently perceived as either distinct or non-distinct. If one were to accept that something unobserved in both distinct and non-distinct things could prove both difference and non-difference, then the property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*), which is excluded from both eternal and non-eternal things, would prove both the eternity and non-eternity of earth.

Furthermore, since the restriction of the means of proof (*sādhananiyama*) is the cause for the restriction of the object to be proven (*sādhyaniyama*), the restriction of co-occurrence (*sahatvaniyama*) is itself the cause for the restriction of difference (*bhedaniyama*). In this context, the non-apprehension of a distinction in location—such as "here is the universal" and "here is the individual"—is due to the fact that the universal exists pervasively within the particular instance (*piṇḍa*). And that [non-apprehension] is included within the restriction of co-perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*). For the restriction of perception with respect to both space and time is indeed what constitutes the restriction of co-perception. Therefore, the restriction of co-perception is brought about by the restriction of the relation [between the two] in terms of both space and time. Moreover, the restriction of co-perception is unestablished (*asiddha*).
In the cognition "this is silver," there is the perception of the substrate individual apart from the universal of "silver-ness" (śuktitva); therefore, this does not establish identity.

Relying on the contradiction between difference and non-difference regarding worldly objects, he states that this same [contradiction] exists even in the case of the Vedic [reality] with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is that because difference and non-difference are contradictory, they cannot both logically subsist in a single entity. Relying on the refutation of difference and non-difference, he asserts that non-difference alone is the ultimate reality with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He raises an objection by way of the connection with defects with the word "now" (*nanu*). He refutes it as being unreal with the words "not so" (*naivam*). He states that the defect alleged by the opponent belongs to the opponent alone with the words "but for you" (*bhavatas tu*).

He establishes this with the words "for not" (*na hi*). Just as cutting is impossible for a finger and the like, Brahman possesses the quality of being indivisible (*acchedyatva*); the reason for this is its partlessness (*niravayavatva*). Even if it were divided, the meaning is that there would still be no distinction of specific locations as there is in the case of hands, feet, and so forth. Because of its partlessness and indivisibility, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot bring about a connection with Brahman through either spatial division or physical cutting. This is the meaning.

Even though [the Self] is partless and indivisible like space, one might raise the objection that the existence of both "faultiness" and "faultlessness" is possible through the distinction between its conditioned (upahita) and unconditioned (anupahita) aspects. Anticipating this, he says, "If one should think... To avoid the fallacy of mutual dependence—where the state of being a *jīva* arises from the limitation by adjuncts (*upādhi*), and the limitation by adjuncts arises from the state of being a *jīva*, and where the state of being a *jīva* arises from karma, and karma from that state of being a *jīva*—it is stated that [this relationship] is beginningless (*anādi*). To refute this, he says, "This person must be questioned," and then offers the following alternatives: "What is it? etc.

Since the word *aṇu* in the Śruti can possibly intend the sense of "subtle," the third alternative arises. The fourth and fifth alternatives were formulated with the intention that there is no other way [to resolve the difficulty] than through these two options, and not by adopting the views of others. The fourth alternative is based on the fact that the word *brahman* can be used figuratively (*upacāra*) for the individual soul (*jīva*). The fifth is based on the acceptance of the identity-in-difference between the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and Brahman. He refutes the first position first, stating: "Because it is indivisible" (*acchedyatvāt*).

He states another objection: "having a beginning" (*ādimattvam*). He explains that [objection] with the words: "of that which is one" (*ekasya sataḥ*). He refutes the second [position] with: "but in the case of the second" (*dvitīye tu*). He states another objection: "in the case of a limiting adjunct" (*upādhau*). Since that [objection] cannot be avoided without [the assumption of] attraction, he addresses that suspicion with: "and if there were attraction" (*ākarṣaṇe ca*). Anticipating the objection that this is untenable and thus not accepted, he dispels it by means of the previously mentioned refutation: "since it is partless" (*niraṃśasya*). He states another objection: "if it were uncut" (*acchinna-*) and, anticipating its refutation, he says: "due to the difference in location" (*pradeśabhedāt*).

He refutes the third [alternative] with the words "In the third case... [meaning]: there would be the establishment of an unconditioned Brahman (*anupahita-brahma*). For it is the opponent’s own admission that the scriptural texts concerning the faultless and auspicious qualities have as their object the unconditioned Brahman. The meaning is that there would follow the consequence of the non-existence of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the consequence of the non-existence of mutual distinction among individual souls. He refutes the fourth and fifth [alternatives] with the words beginning "But in the fourth case... and so on. [The word] "last" [refers to the final alternative].

The intention is that because it is stated that only non-conscious substance (*acit-dravya*) possesses consciousness, its identity with the conscious Brahman is untenable. Concluding the refutation of the theory of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*), he states "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to establish his own position. He concludes the establishment of Brahman as being subordinate to the injunction for meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*) with the word "hence" (*ataḥ*).

The Mīmāṃsaka refutes the position of those who advocate for the injunction of meditation (*dhyāna-niyoga-vādin*), stating that even that is untenable. The sense of the word "also" (*api*) is that not only is the theory of an injunction for the removal of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañcīkaraṇa-vidhi-vāda*) illogical, but this view as well is untenable. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of meditation... [and so forth]. If [the Upanishads] were subordinate to an injunction regarding meditation, how could they have the capacity to convey the reality of the object? Alternatively, would they possess authority regarding Brahman independently, setting aside their status as subordinate to an injunction? To this, he says: "This has been stated... [and so forth].

He analyzes [the opponent's position] in order to refute it, stating "as the nature of Brahman. He refutes the first alternative with the word "one" (*eka*). "Oneness of statement" (*ekavākyatvam*) means the unity of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). He refutes the second alternative with the word "different" (*bhinna*). "Incapacity to produce understanding" arises because there would be no engagement in hearing and so forth, which are difficult to accomplish. Anticipating the objection that Brahman might be established as a subordinate element of an injunction under the view of oneness of statement, he says, "And it should not be said... Why? To this he replies, "Because of the injunction for meditation" (*dhyānavidheḥ*).
