In injunctions for contemplative identification (*dṛṣṭividhi*) such as "One should meditate [on the name] as Brahman," even though the substantive (*viśeṣya*) is real, the unreality of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) makes the unreality of the qualified whole unavoidable; and here, the meaning is that it is exactly the same. He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its essential points by saying "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). [Objection: But how is it consistent that the first sūtra establishes the authority regarding Brahman as being supplementary to an injunction, while in the prima facie argument of this present section, the establishment of that [authority] as being supplementary to an injunction is rejected? [Reply: It is thus:

In that context, however, its establishment was stated as being by way of a result (*phala*), because if that which is established as a result were not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), it would follow that even heaven and the like would be unreal. Therefore, the demonstration of its establishment as a result is more effective for proving its ultimate reality. Here, however, its establishment is set aside by virtue of being the object (*karman*) of the injunction to meditate (*dhyāna-vidhi*); it is not established as a result. Thus, there is no contradiction.

With reference to the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) thus set forth, the author of the Sūtras composed this aphorism; he states this with the word "therein" (*tatra*). [The opponent] accepts [the objection], and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) follows; or rather, the meaning is that it becomes known. He explains the term *samanvaya* in detail with the words beginning "coherence" (*samanvaya*), fulfilling the expectation of what is coherent with what by stating the meaning of the sentence.

"He joins with the Supreme" (*yojayati parama*): the word "unlimited" (*anavadhika*) establishes that this is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). For being a human goal consists in being sought after by a person. It is a human goal by virtue of its nature as bliss; and because that bliss is unlimited and unsurpassed, it is the supreme human goal—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, since even a means to happiness that is not itself agreeable can still be a human goal, the phrase "unlimited" and so forth excludes that possibility. He explains the word "that" (*tat*) as "having the scripture as its means of valid knowledge" (*śāstrapramāṇakatva*).

He states the meaning obtained from the word "tu" (but), which serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), as follows: "It is indeed established. For one who asserts that the cessation of ignorance occurs through the mere knowledge of the meaning of the sentence whose purport is the instruction on the nature of reality—such as "That thou art"—and that the sentence's purpose is fulfilled thereby, would be a speaker of falsehood; for the futility of the injunction to meditate (*dhyānavidhi*) would follow, since the utility of such meditation for the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence has already been refuted.

In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, Brahman remains unestablished; thus, being questioned regarding these two-fold defects, [the author], desiring to demonstrate the authority of the Vedānta texts with respect to Brahman by means of a particular mode of presentation, first intends to show that Brahman possesses a superior status as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) because it is the object of enjoyment for all people in every way through its own nature, whereas activity and cessation lack the status of a human goal due to their consisting of suffering. Consequently, he addresses the objection based on the absence of a culminating human goal in those [texts] which lack the purpose of inciting activity or cessation.

He dispels the suspicion of invalidity with the word *nirasta* (“dispelled”). One who dwells in the royal palace, is born in the royal family, or is an intimate of the royal court. *Kauleyakas* are dogs; they are understood here as either dogs or Mlecchas who subsist on dogs. Although, in the context of a collection of sentences, one would expect a person dwelling in the royal palace to be understood [as the subject], nevertheless, by the force of the sense, this designation results in referring to the person who comprehends the meaning of the sentence.

The statement that a sentence concerning the supreme goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) which is intrinsically unlimited is devoid of purpose is untenable; its meaning is false. How is it that Brahman possesses a preeminence as a *puruṣārtha* by virtue of being of the nature of unlimited bliss? And how is there a deficiency in the status of *puruṣārtha* regarding engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*)? Where is the culmination in *puruṣārtha* observed for a sentence concerning the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman]? In response to the inquiry, "If that were so, how could the injunction to meditate (*dhyānavidhi*) be efficacious?", he says: "This has been stated."

He states the superiority of Brahman as the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) with the words beginning "beginningless" (*anādi*). His intention is that the individual knowers (*kṣetrajña*) lack knowledge of its status as a human goal because their experience is obstructed by karma, not because of any deficiency in that [Brahman] itself; thus he says "beginningless karma. The enumeration of gods, asuras, and so forth is for the purpose of demonstrating that they possess fixed objects of enjoyment. The phrase "possibility of experience" (*anubhavasambhava*) is stated to eliminate the doubt regarding the non-perception of a suitable object.

For being conducive to the knowledge of that [object] is not possible without being conducive to it. Therefore, by the statement that Brahman generates an unsurpassed and unsurpassable bliss, its state of being unsurpassed and unsurpassably conducive is established, and thus its nature as bliss (*ānandatva*) is demonstrated. By the words "in its own nature" (*svarūpa*) and so forth, its being an object of enjoyment in every way is stated; thereby, its superiority as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is established. By the words "activity" (*pravṛtti*) and so forth, the deficiency of activity and cessation from activity as human goals is stated.

Because it is to be accepted as a means for attaining even a small portion of desired pleasure, and because, being of the nature of suffering, it lacks inherent enjoyability [as a goal], [the author] avoids the charge of the futility of injunctions regarding meditation and so forth by stating "of such a nature. Since even indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) is of the nature of bliss, sentences whose primary purport is the essential nature [of Brahman] indeed culminate in the human goal; for they inform one who desires its direct realization of the means thereto, and thus even sentences enjoining meditation are not fruitless—this is the meaning. He illustrates this point with an example, beginning with "just as."

Thus, even though a statement that produces knowledge of something beyond the senses culminates in the human goal (puruṣārtha), the engagement in meditation is nevertheless appropriate with a view toward a specific result. This is just as, in such injunctions as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," and "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," although each individual rite—such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa—is a means to heaven, one undertakes another ritual action in view of a specific result [of that particular rite]. It is the same for a single ritual action.

And recurrence is also possible; the intention is that just as for one who has experienced joy upon hearing of the birth of a son, an inclination toward activity subsequently arises out of a desire for the direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of the pleasure of seeing his face, so it is here as well. In this regard, two examples—the king’s treasure and the prince—are stated to distinguish between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), in order to make known that the quality of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) residing in both belongs to Brahman. As the Śruti says: "Just as those ignorant of the field (*akṣetrajña*), though walking over and over it, might not find a treasure of gold buried there."

He shows that the statement "there is a treasure" has as its ultimate purpose the human goal by saying, "being satisfied. In accordance with such Śruti and Smṛti passages as "the boys were unknown," "I am the Lord's son, servant, and disciple," "mother, father, and brother," "he who is the imperishable father of beings," "Indra alone became the king of the world," and "the supreme king of all," the term "prince" is used for the Blessed One to demonstrate his sovereignty over sentient beings, thereby showing that he is the source of every kind of enjoyment.

And his status as a son has been described. Here, one should observe the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Kuśa and Lava. By the phrase "intent on childish play," the outward-directed inclination of conscious beings toward external objects is indicated. By the phrase "departed from the royal palace," his state of being outside the presence of the Blessed One is shown; and by the phrase "fallen from the path," his lack of connection to the means such as ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) is made known, as well as his failure to attain the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*).

By the phrase "nurtured by the best of the twice-born," the connection with a preceptor who brings about the completion of study and other disciplines—which serve as the cause for establishing the fitness for the realization of the Lord’s knowledge—is intended. The meaning of "sixteen years old" is that he is in the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and yet also in the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). By the description "a mine of all auspicious qualities," fullness through the qualities favored by the Lord—such as those stated in passages like "This Self consists of liberation, consists of knowledge, and is stainless"—is indicated. Through the words "His father... and so forth, the multitude of the Lord's qualities is suggested.

Depth (*gāmbhīrya*) and the other qualities are those employed for accessibility (*saulabhya*) toward the devotee (*upāsaka*); heroism (*śaurya*) and the others are included within transcendence (*paratva*). Depth is the disregard for the gravity of what is being given due to the ease of bestowing it. Magnanimity (*audārya*) is the state of perceiving that [the gift] has been received as if it were already accomplished, through the absence of any conceptual distinction between giver and recipient; or alternatively, it is the disposition of thinking, "My debt has increased," even after giving away one's very self and possessions. Affection (*vātsalya*) is the perception of virtues even in faults, as a mother feels toward her calf.

Good character (*suśīlatva*) indeed consists in having a nature of close intimacy with the great even when they are dull-witted; possessing that quality is *sauśīlya*. Heroism (*śaurya*) is the capacity to enter into the midst of enemies as if it were one’s own home. As in the expression “the brave, the coward, the poet, the fool,” heroism is the opposite of cowardice. Prowess (*vīrya*) is tirelessness. Valor (*parākrama*) is valorous action. Although not explicitly mentioned here, fortitude (*dhairya*) should also be understood; and that consists in regarding the provocation of enemies as if it were mere grass.

By the words "desiring to see," the intention of the Blessed One—that "that Great-Souled One is very difficult to attain"—is indicated. By the term "excellent city," residence within the body known as the City of Brahman (brahmapura) is intended, or else a connection with the manifestation consisting of three quarters (tripādvibhūti). By the word "most proficient," the Guru who bestows the knowledge of the Blessed One is meant. It is intended that his distinction from others is expressed by the phrase "by someone."

When the preceptor who causes one to study and so forth is himself capable of being the instructor of Brahman (*brahmopadeṣṭā*), then this term "most proficient" (*abhiyuktatama*) refers specifically to the aforementioned best of the twice-born. In the absence of such a person, it intends any person whatsoever who can instruct in Brahman. Here, the intended meaning of the phrase "by someone" should be understood as either by that same [preceptor] or by another. By the phrase "if he hears," the difficulty of attaining knowledge of the Blessed One is intended.

By the statement "he becomes endowed with unsurpassed joy," it is shown that the purpose of this passage is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, by the word "and the king," the practitioner who occupies the position of a king is intended. By this, it is made known that since all kinds of objects of enjoyment are fully present in the Blessed One, the enjoyment found in a virtuous son is also present therein; for the knowledge of the Blessed One is not of a remote (indirect) nature.

By the statement "one becomes one who has attained all human goals," it is shown that the purpose of the sentence culminates in this result. Furthermore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "And the king... is not contradictory even as it is understood at first sight. It is stated that "he subsequently exerts himself in its acquisition" and "subsequently those two come together" in order to make known that the futility of the injunction for meditation is established by both examples.

In this regard, as previously stated, because of the citation of sentences such as "one desiring wealth should go to the king's court" and "one with weak digestion should not drink water," and because of the presentation of the analogy of the treasure here, this point is also established by implication: does the sentence conclude its purpose only by having as its purport an action-transcending effect (*kārya*), or is the view that it concludes its purpose only by denoting a meaning that is either an action-effect or something transcending it, which serves as the motivator (*pravartaka*)?

Not the first [alternative], because such statements as "one who desires wealth should serve the king" possess a purpose. Not the second, because treatises devoted to the examination of gems—characterized by identifying ground containing treasure and so forth—possess a purpose. Nor can it be assumed that even in those cases the sentences are intent upon injunctions for digging, holding, and so on; for those two [actions] are prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), and the manner of digging and so forth is already established in the world. For a scripture is meaningful only with respect to what is not [otherwise] established.

The avoidance of defective gems is also achieved through the desire to abandon what is harmful. However, the sentences [in question] terminate merely in making known the qualities and defects of possessing a treasure. Therefore, the rule that the purpose must terminate solely in an impelling object is broken.

Now, he restates what was said by the opponent: "As for [the statement] 'yat punar... The proposition (*pratijñā*) is that the Vedānta texts do not possess authority regarding the actual existence of an object; for that purpose, the intended reason (*hetu*) is "because they culminate in human goals even in the absence of the actual existence of an object. He refutes this, saying "that is incorrect" (*tadasat*). To the question "Why?", he replies: "Because of the actual existence or non-existence of the object. This statement refers to the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), or it applies commonly to both the proposition and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Its status as a reason (*hetutva*) is implied.

The meaning is that when there is certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of an object, there is no finality in the human goal (puruṣārtha). In response to the doubt that a human goal is seen even when the object does not exist, he states "of children, the sick, and so forth" as a limiting condition (upādhi) for the lack of certainty regarding the object's existence in those cases. He demonstrates this very point with "of those very [people]. Then, in anticipation of the question "What of it?", he clarifies the point shown in the similar instance (sapakṣa) by applying it to the subject (pakṣa): "even among the followers of the Upaniṣads."

If it is argued that, as in the case of persuasive statements addressed to children, the sick, and others, there may be a finality regarding human goals here too due to the delusion that the literal meaning exists, [we reply]: "Drink milk; drink decoction; your crest-lock will grow."

Just as in the case of sentences intended for engagement or withdrawal—such as "If you roll in the dust, your teeth will not erupt"—one might wonder why sentences like "One who desires heaven should sacrifice" and "One should not eat *kalañja*" would not likewise terminate in human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), due to the delusion that their meaning exists [as something other than such a purpose]. However, because the Vedic sentence is authorless (*apauruṣeya*), it is improper for it to terminate in human purpose in the same way as a sentence rooted in a desire to deceive, which is inherently misleading.

If it is argued that, such being the case, since the scripture must be understood by one who investigates it, the engagement in teaching and so forth toward one's own sons, disciples, and others would be untenable—[we reply that] the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) and the futility of engagement in teaching and so forth are equally applicable to the Vedānta texts as well. If it is argued that because the injunctions for ritual action (*karmavidhi*) depend upon the knowledge of a self distinct from the body, the engagement in teaching and so forth is justified as the Vedānta texts are supplementary to those injunctions for action—we say no.

Even if there were no actual difference between the body and the self, as long as the suspicion remains that the body could be the cause of the delusion regarding its existence, it would be impossible to provide encouragement by means of that [delusion]; consequently, teaching and other such acts would be untenable as being subordinate to an injunction (*vidhi*). If it is argued that the real distinction between the body and the self is established by flawless scripture supported by reasoning (*tarka*), then the same applies even when the Supreme Self, which constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is the subject to be expounded.

If it is argued that there is no certainty regarding [the body] being a cause of error because of the corroboration by other means of proof establishing the difference between the body and the self, then the difference between the body and the self would be established by those very other means of proof alone; consequently, since there would be no need for Vedāntic statements to inform one of that [difference], it would be illogical to teach them as supplementary to injunctions (*vidhiśeṣatayā*).

Thus, with the intention of using the arguments of the *pravṛttaka* (those engaged in worldly activity) as a counter-example—since a scripture whose subject matter is thus defined would fail to culminate in human purpose due to the delusion that its subject matter actually exists—the commentary begins with the words "In the case of the Upaniṣadic [texts] as well... and so forth.

Showing that the stated reason culminates in its opposite, he concludes the subject matter with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). He states the meaning of the causal statements with the word "nikhila" (entirety); the word "nikhila" is intended to indicate that even space and other elements, which are considered eternal by opponents, are in fact effects. The word "eka" (one) indicates the identity of the efficient and material causes.

With the intention that the meaning of the purificatory statement (*śodhakavākya*)—beginning with the words "from which these [beings arise]" (*yato vā imāni*)—is profound, he says: "devoid of all... (*nirasta-*, etc.). Here, by the word "all" (*nikhila*), what is intended are the afflictions (*kleśa*), karmas, and so forth, as well as birth (*janman*) and the like, pertaining to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). By the word "fragrance" (*gandha*), which excludes the possibility of any connection with defects at any time, its perpetual opposition to such defects is expressed. He states the qualities necessary for being the cause [of the universe] with the words "omniscience," etc. He states the matter established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words "limitless," etc.

The meaning is as follows: [the scripture] "makes known" (bodhayati) Brahman characterized as described above through such passages as "from which indeed these... and so forth. This is because, for the purpose of teaching and the like, it is necessary that the scripture culminates in human goals (*puruṣārtha*). For a rational person who is a qualified seeker, once there is certainty regarding the existence or non-existence of the subject matter of a treatise, it would be impossible for it to culminate in a human goal if that subject matter did not exist. Therefore, in order to make that possible, one must accept the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the sentences that convey it with respect to the actual existence of the subject matter, just as one does for sentences that incite action. Thus, the scripture makes known Brahman as defined.

This set of four aphorisms (*catuḥsūtrī*), intended for the successful commencement of the treatise, is not consistent with the position of those who maintain that [all things] are false; for according to their view, the treatise ought not to be commenced due to the impossibility of establishing both its subject matter (*viṣaya*) and its purpose (*prayojana*). To explain: what is the subject matter—is it Brahman, or the falsity of difference, or the identity of the individual soul and Brahman?

The first [alternative] is not tenable; for Brahman is not admitted to be an object of cognition (*vedyatva*), and it has already been stated by you yourself that if it were an object of cognition, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that it is not an experience (*ananubhūtitva*), just like a jar. If it is argued that "objectivity exists only on the conventional level (*vyāvahārika*)," then since the objectivity of a jar is likewise merely conventional, the consequence that it is not an experience is as unavoidable as before. Furthermore, if the absence of real objectivity is what is to be proven regarding Brahman, then a jar cannot serve as a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*); for there is no absence of the absence of real objectivity in the case of a jar.

Experience (*anubhūti*) is not an object of cognition in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), because it is experience. Whatever is an object of cognition in the ultimate sense is not experience, just as a pot (*ghaṭa*); this is stated as a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*), for [otherwise] it would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavyāvṛtta*). Indeed, a pot is not an object of cognition in the ultimate sense. Even if one were to disregard the consequence that being an object of cognition entails not being experience and were to accept that Brahman is an object of cognition, it would still be improper for Brahman to be the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of the scriptures.

In your view, which accepts that perception grasps only pure existence (*sanmātra*), there follows the consequence that the scripture (*śāstra*) is purposeless; for "scripture is meaningful only with respect to what has not [already] been attained."

Not the second; for one who considers the falsity of difference through such marks as "visibility" (dṛśyatva) and so forth, there would follow the consequence that the scripture is purposeless. Since the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva)—which contradicts the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception, that apprehend those respective substrates—cannot be established by the scripture (just as the identity of the sacrificial post and the sun cannot be), the scripture would be rendered devoid of an object. For a scripture is meaningful only with respect to what is not already established. Indeed, "non-establishment" (aprāptatva) consists in being outside the scope of both sublation (bādhaka) and proof (sādhaka).

Furthermore, the threefold disparity regarding the inference from the difference in flames has already been explained in detail. It was also stated previously that contradiction by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is an indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparya*), and thus the impossibility of the intended meaning applying to a sense contrary to that [contradiction] has already been established. Therefore, it is untenable for the falsity of difference to be the object [of the Upanishads].

And the third alternative is untenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that Brahman itself is an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*). For the scripture does not state the identity of a jar and a cloth; rather, it states the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman. At that time, if Brahman were not made known by the word "Brahman," how could the oneness of that [Brahman] with the individual soul be asserted? Indeed, [the scripture does not state] the individual soul...

When "one" is said, the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established, just as when one says "the pot is one," the identity of the pot and the cloth [is not intended]. If, in the scriptural statements teaching identity—such as "This Self is Brahman"—the fact that Brahman is the object denoted by the word must be accepted, then why is it not admitted that Brahman alone is the primary subject matter of the scripture? To deny this results in contradicting the natural meaning of such scriptural passages as, beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim," and ending with "That is the supreme state of Viṣṇu."

Furthermore, regarding the identity being taught, is it non-different from the nature of Brahman, or is it different? If it were different, it would necessarily fall under the position that [Brahman] is known through its own nature alone; and in that case, defects such as the futility of the teaching would follow, since the mere nature [of Brahman] has already been realized. If it were different, is that [identity] ultimately real or not ultimately real? In the first case, the doctrine of the absence of attributes (*saviśeṣatva-bhaṅga*) would be undermined.

In the second case, just as the non-ultimate reality of the identity of the flame [with the wick] or the identity of the body with the self entails the ultimate reality of the difference between the flames and the body, or the difference between the self and the body, so too would the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman be ultimately real.

Furthermore, what is this so-called identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman? Is it the identity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and consciousness (*saṃvit*), or that of the internal organ as delimited by consciousness and consciousness itself, or that of consciousness as delimited by the internal organ and absolute consciousness? It cannot be the first, because the identity of the insentient and the sentient is logically untenable. Nor can it be the second or the third, because if the identity of the qualified entities is admitted, it would follow that the internal organ—which is included therein either as a qualifier or as the qualified—must also be identical with consciousness.

And it has been stated that identity between those two is untenable, given their respective qualities of being non-insentient and insentient, and being real and unreal. If it is argued that the object of the teaching is the identity of consciousness as qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), then with what is that consciousness qualified [by the internal organ] said to be identical? Is it with itself, or with another consciousness? Not the first, because the teaching would be purposeless; for it is not necessary to teach that any entity is non-different from itself, since there is no possibility of its being different from itself.

If [the difference] is due to another cognition, is it ultimately different or non-different [from the object]? Not the first, because it is neither accepted nor logically tenable. If it is non-different, does the perception of difference exist or not? If it does not, then the teaching of unity would be purposeless. If it does exist, then the teaching of unity would be nothing other than a teaching regarding the falsity of difference. Since the falsity of difference is presumed to be established by inference, the scripture would then be rendered devoid of subject matter.

If it is argued that the scripture—supported by such reasonings as "if difference were ultimately real, its being an object of perception would be untenable"—is the authority for the falsity of difference, and therefore the scripture does not lack a subject matter, we say: no.

If it were argued that [the distinction between cognitions] would not exist because it is sublated by reason—just as the scriptural injunction "one should not kill" establishes that the ritual slaughter of animals is unrighteous (adharma), making it impossible for that [slaughter] to be considered dharma—it is incorrect. For it is impossible for a scripture to establish the falsity of a distinction that is itself established by scripture; because, just as in the case of conjunction, desire, and so forth, which are differentiated by their respective correlates, the mutual distinction between cognitions is established by perception and other means of knowledge. Therefore, since it contradicts such evidence, the falsity of the distinction between cognitions—which is unfit [to be established by scripture]—cannot be established by scripture.

Furthermore, because the demonstration [of such unity] is untenable: "I do not indeed at this time know myself as 'I am this'"; "when one has fallen asleep and does not see any dream"; "from the vital breaths (prāṇas) come the deities (devas), and from the deities come the worlds (lokas)"—where "deities" refers to the sense organs and "worlds" refers to perceptions. Thus, the mutual difference among cognitions (jñaptis) with respect to time, object, and locus is established by scripture and by perception and other means of knowledge. If it is argued that the scriptural statement concerns a difference in the modifications (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), we say no.

For there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): if dream-hearing has as its object a mental modification (*vṛtti*), then there is the unity of consciousness; and if there is the unity of consciousness, then the hearing of the difference in cognition has as its object a mental modification. Furthermore, if knowledge—which is perceived as delimited by the knower and the known—is merely an activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-kriyā*), then a knowledge that transcends this triad would be like the horn of a hare. Consequently, the demonstration of the falsity of the difference between them would be equivalent to demonstrating the falsity of the difference between the horns of a hare; thus, the subject-matter of the scripture cannot be established.

The mutual difference among those very cognitions that have been apprehended is false because it contradicts both scripture and perception—just as [the view that] the immolation of animals is not dharma, or as [the view that] the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the sun are one. Scripture is not capable of establishing such a thing.
Therefore, since there is no subject matter for the scripture, it should not be commenced.

Likewise, the purpose [of the treatise] is not tenable; for the purpose of a treatise is twofold: the intermediate purpose, which serves as the means, and liberation, which is the ultimate purpose. In this regard, it is undisputed that the knowledge arising from the sentence produced at present does not remove [ignorance]; furthermore, it is utterly improbable that knowledge unarisen even in Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, and others should arise in others. If such knowledge had arisen in them, the appearance of duality would not exist.

If it is argued that he (the individual self) will be turned back [from transmigratory existence], then for that very reason, others who are non-different from him would also be turned back; thus, the scripture need not be commenced. Furthermore, because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is real, it cannot be sublated by knowledge; therefore, knowledge that does not effect such sublation cannot be an intermediate fruit, and the scripture need not be commenced for that purpose. Moreover, the supreme goal is not accomplished, because the cessation of the real distinction between the knower and the known is impossible.

Furthermore, does the qualification for hearing the scripture belong to mere consciousness (*jñaptimātra*) or to the knower (*jñātṛ*)? Not the first, because mere consciousness lacks the capacity to be a hearer. Not the second, because since the destruction of the knower is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), it would be illogical for such a knower to engage in hearing and so forth. That to which pleasure and the cessation of suffering belong is indeed the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). For the cognition (or inclination) is: "May I be free from suffering and happy."

How can there be the destruction of that which possesses a human purpose (puruṣārtha)? Or how could another human purpose belong to that seeker in the absence of such a [seeker]? How indeed could there be a human purpose if he were non-existent?

Now, it might be argued: "In your position, does the authority for the scripture belong to one who is bound or to one who is liberated? In the first case, there would be no engagement [with the scripture] because one's own destruction is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). For the destruction of the nature of the bound self as qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is indeed its own destruction. In the second case, however, the liberated one has no authority because he is independent of scripture. If you argue that the destruction of the form caused by adjuncts is not a non-goal because it results in the abiding in one's natural state free from suffering, then [we reply]: since the state of being a knower is caused by adjuncts, when that ceases, the essential nature remains; thus, it is not a non-goal."

It is not so; for we do not admit that consciousness possesses actual subjectivity (*jñātṛtva*). If one were to superimpose it upon it, then its existence would necessarily have to be established elsewhere [in a real subject]. Furthermore, no other subject lacks the property of being a knower (*jñapti-dharman*). If cognition (*jñapti*) were the very nature [of consciousness] and the knower were its attribute, then this [objection] would constitute a valid counter-argument (*pratibandī*).

Since it is universally accepted that "I am happy" or "I am suffering" indicates that happiness and suffering are attributes (*dharma*) of the referent of "I" (*aham-artha*), and that this referent is perceived as the substratum (*dharmin*), the destruction of that very substratum—which serves as the locus for the cessation of happiness and suffering—is certainly not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). If the substratum has perished, for whom would the cessation of suffering constitute a human goal?

The state of being bound by the insentient primordial nature (prakṛti) brings about suffering through limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Just as for a person who possesses the cognition "I am stained," the removal of that stain is not a non-purpose of man (apuruṣārtha), so too is the removal of that [bondage] not a non-purpose of man; for the essential nature of the subject (dharmin), which is extremely cherished, remains intact, and because the cessation of the undesired bondage is itself desired.

Is it not the case that the "I-sense" (ahamartha) constitutes the very nature [of the self] either according to worldly cognition or according to the cognition of the investigator? In the first case, since it is apprehended through worldly perception as "I am fat," "I am thin," and so on, the cessation of the body characterized by fatness and the like would also constitute a non-human goal (apurushārtha). In the second case, just like fatness and so on, the "I-sense"—though it is the knower—is superimposed and thus not the true nature [of the self]; therefore, its destruction would not be a non-human goal. Even from the perspective of worldly experience, the "I-sense" (the *ahamartha*) is perceived as distinct from the body, as evidenced by such cognitions as "my hand" or "my foot. Furthermore, since it has already been demonstrated that the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras establish the "I-sense" itself as the Self (*ātman*), and since the very nature of the "I-sense" is what is perceived even in the cognition of the one who investigates [the truth], the cessation of the "I-sense" cannot be equated with the cessation of the body; consequently, its status as a non-human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*) is unavoidable. Therefore, due to the absence of both subject matter (*viṣaya*) and purpose (*prayojana*), the position of the proponents of illusion (*mṛṣāvādins*) remains that the scripture need not be commenced.

It has already been stated that the meaning of the word *atha* as explained by others is untenable, because it is impossible for the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal (*nityānityaviveka*)—which occurs later—to have existed previously. Furthermore, the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal produced by other scriptures is not a cause for the inquiry into Brahman, because it contradicts the Vedānta and because one’s desire is satisfied by those very scriptures through their instruction on the means to liberation. Moreover, a superficial perception (*āpātapratīti*) of the eternal and the non-eternal is common to both parts [of the Veda], and thus it lacks the exclusivity required to be a cause for the inquiry into Brahman. This is also the case with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

Because cognitions such as "eternal" or "non-eternal" produced by that [discrimination] are seized by doubt and error, they lack the capacity to generate the desire to abandon the three aims of life (*trivarga*); consequently, they cannot serve as a cause for the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmavicāra*). Therefore, the meaning of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) is untenable. Furthermore, the conjecture that the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal things consists in the discernment that "that which is eternal is to be accepted, and that which is non-eternal is to be abandoned" is also incorrect.

Because it would follow that there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*): the understanding that the Vedāntas teach the eternal human goal (*nityapuruṣārtha*) depends upon their being commenced [for that purpose], and their being commenced for that purpose depends upon the understanding that they teach the eternal human goal. Furthermore, because other scriptures might also be thought to contain the eternal human goal, they lack absolute necessity as a cause for the inquiry into Brahman. Moreover, since the absence of such a goal in other scriptures and the certainty of its presence in the Vedāntas depend upon the *Tarkapāda* (the section on logic), there is once again the risk of a circular argument, just as before.

Furthermore, since the existence or non-existence of the eternal human goal (*nityapuruṣārtha*) in the Vedānta and other scriptures is understood through the words of a teacher, and since the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*) is likewise understood through the words of a teacher, it would follow that the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* (the Investigation into the Body [of Brahman]) need not be commenced, as it would be unnecessary. Moreover, if one accepts that the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is the subject matter of the scripture, then the section concerning the "Inquiry into Brahman" (*brahmajijñāsā-pāda*) would not be coherent; for it is from the Word (*śabda*) that the status of Brahman as the object of inquiry is understood, not the identity of the individual soul and Brahman.

Just as the term *dharmajijñāsā* (enquiry into dharma) expresses that dharma alone is the object of enquiry, and not the unity of dharma and adharma, so it is with the term *brahmajijñāsā*. Furthermore, the statement of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) for a featureless reality is untenable: if it were a definition by way of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it would entail that the reality possesses qualities (*saviśeṣatva*); if it were a definition by way of an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would be useless because there is no other form to be made known by the indicator that exceeds the form already previously apprehended; and if such a form were admitted, it would again entail that the reality possesses qualities.

If it is argued that the very nature of the thing itself is what is made known by the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), then has that nature already been apprehended or not? If it has been apprehended, the secondary characteristic is redundant. If it has not been apprehended, then the thing would lack self-luminosity (*svaprakāśakatā*), and it would be impossible for it to be characterized. For being "characterized" means that something already cognized in its aspect as, say, a field (*kedāratva*), is subsequently made known as belonging to Devadatta by means of a crane (*sārasa*).

If it is argued that the exclusion of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-vyāvṛtti*), previously unapprehended, constitutes the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣyākāra*), [we reply: if this exclusion of phenomenal proliferation were distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman], it would follow that Brahman possesses attributes (*saviśeṣatva*). If it is not distinct, then its essential nature would have already been manifest even prior [to the realization of Brahman], and thus the secondary characteristic would be useless. Furthermore, how can there be an exclusion of phenomenal proliferation when "causality" is the defining characteristic? For so-called causality consists in being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the effect, which is the world.

If it is argued that there is a distinction of the substrate, Brahman, from the superimposed unreal phenomenal world (prapañca) by virtue of its reality, we say no; for then, just as clay—the substrate of a jar and so forth—is itself unreal, it would follow that Brahman too must be unreal. This is because even clay and other such causes are themselves superimposed upon further causes and are therefore unreal.

If it is argued that Brahman cannot be unreal because nothing else exists as superimposed upon Him—who is the substratum of all effects throughout the three periods of time—we say no; for since the scripture states, "In the beginning this [world] was," we hear that the mere aggregate of effects denoted by the word "this" has Brahman as its substratum, which does not contradict the fact that Brahman Himself may be superimposed upon another cause. Furthermore, this is logically consistent with the beginninglessness of the causal series, according to the analogy of the seed and the sprout.

If it is argued that Brahman, being the cause of all effects, possesses reality because it is not itself an effect due to the negation of any other cause for it—and thus there is an exclusion of the phenomenal world (prapañca)—then, since the exclusion of the world is established merely by its being non-an-effect, the mention of its being the "cause" would be redundant. Consequently, only the scriptural text concerning its being non-an-effect should have been cited as the defining statement (lakṣaṇavākya), and not the scripture beginning with "From which indeed these [beings arise]," and so forth.

If it is argued that the scriptural statement regarding non-producedness (*akāryatva*) alone is intended [to define Brahman], then, because the scriptural statement on non-producedness—namely, "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him"—has as its object the Lord denoted by the term "lord of the lords of the senses," the featureless nature (*nirviśeṣatva*) of the indicated reality would not be established. Furthermore, the specific characteristic of being the cause of the world, which belongs to the indicated reality, is contradictory to its featureless nature, since that characteristic necessarily implies attributes such as omniscience.

If it is argued that even though omniscience and so forth are implied, they merely serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the bare reality (*vastumātra*), we say no. For once the reality is indicated by means of omniscience, other indicators such as omnipotence would be redundant. Indeed, when the moon is indicated by its branch, there is no need for the top of a palace. Furthermore, indicating the undifferentiated reality through omniscience is contradictory; for it is impossible to convey the undifferentiated nature of a substrate that is itself qualified by its own [attribute], and because omniscience lacks the capacity to convey the absence of other specific attributes such as omnipotence. Therefore, the *lakṣaṇa-sūtra* contradicts the position of the undifferentiated [Brahman].

The third sutra is also untenable; for if the subject matter intended is a reality devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-vastu*), what purpose is served by establishing omniscience and other attributes implied by its being the cause? Nor is it logical to establish such attributes even as a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), because that would contradict its quality of being without distinctions. Furthermore, the inference—that the scripture consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth has as its material cause one who possesses knowledge of a subject matter greater than its own, because it is a collection of sentences—is also incoherent.

To explain: is it being proved that [the Veda] has as its material cause (*upādāna*) one who possesses knowledge of a subject matter greater than that [of the Veda], or that it was spoken by such a person, or that it was uttered by such a person? In the first case, the example is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because sound, which is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), does not have Kālidāsa or others as its material cause. It is not the second, because it would entail the consequence that the Veda is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*). It is not the third, because of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*); for children and others who merely utter Vedic or other sentences do not possess knowledge of a subject matter greater than that [of the sentence they are uttering].

Furthermore, the interpretation that the meaning of the Sūtras consists in having the Śāstra as the means of valid cognition is untenable for those who do not admit that Brahman is an object of experience.

Furthermore, in the fourth sutra, because Brahman is not primarily indicated as the source of the scripture (*śāstrayoni*), it is not natural for the word "that" (*tat*) to refer to Brahman. Moreover, the claim that the Upanishadic statements find their purpose in generating the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence—which removes error—is untenable; for the cessation of bondage through the mere knowledge of the sentence-meaning contradicts both scripture and perception, and the refutation of any other possible justification for this has already been established.

Furthermore, whose delusion is it that ceases? Is it that of *jñapti* (pure consciousness), or of the conscious being (*cetana*)? It cannot be that of *jñapti*; for, being insentient (*acetana*), it lacks the status of being the locus of delusion. Indeed, the conscious being is the locus of delusion, not the insentient (*jaḍa*).

If you argue that [the absence of error] is the determinant for not being a locus of error, then because the absence of being a locus of error is non-existent in the knower whom you consider to be insentient (jaḍa), the positive concomitance with the probandum is unestablished. Furthermore, on your view, even the cessation of error would not be a human goal for a sentient being, since the knower himself would be included within the category of things to be removed. Moreover, self-destruction cannot be a human goal for him. If you argue that the cessation of the knower is a human goal—just as a king's removal of enemies is so for the king—because the Self is of the nature of knowledge, we say no.

Because the knower alone is the self (*ātman*). Knowledge, being understood as an attribute of the knower—like desire, aversion, and so forth—cannot be the self. Even if its status as the self were admitted, since it would lack the state of being one who seeks the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), it would be impossible for it to have a relationship with those goals; consequently, the cessation of the knower with respect to knowledge could not constitute a goal of human life. For that alone is considered a "goal of human life" which is sought after by the person.

Even if it is accepted that knowledge possesses the nature of the self and is related to human goals (*puruṣārtha*), it is improper to claim that the cessation of the knower—who is dependent upon that knowledge—is itself a human goal; for the knower is not any one of the following: suffering, the cause of suffering, or pleasure, which is the object of knowledge. Indeed, for the enjoyer of pleasure and pain, the causes of pleasure and the cessation of suffering and its causes constitute human goals. For the knower is not of the nature of suffering due to cognition, nor is he the producer of suffering, since it is impossible for knowledge itself to be the experiencer of suffering.

Furthermore, you yourself have rejected the conclusion that a treatise culminates in a purpose by being directed toward engagement or desistance, in your refutation of the doctrine of meditation as a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, the claim that your [view of] the treatise culminates in a purpose is untenable.

The followers of Yādavaprakāśa, however, explain the meaning of the first sūtra as follows: because a person does not engage in the means for the cessation of the threefold suffering immediately after being struck by that suffering, it is Brahman alone that is to be investigated, and not primordial matter (pradhāna) and the like. [The opponent objects: Let it be that Brahman is the object of inquiry; yet this does not imply that primordial matter and the like are not objects of inquiry, since one of those very things is the referent of the word "Brahman," for the scripture restates Brahman and enjoins knowledge of it.

Since it is impossible for a single statement to simultaneously enjoin and restate a single object, a restatement (*anuvāda*) necessarily depends upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Furthermore, since all the specific modes of reality imagined by various disputants have already been conceived through other means of valid cognition, it is impossible to conceive of any further reality. Therefore, the *Janmādi-sūtra* is intended to dispel the doubt that the scripture merely restates one among those [already known] objects in order to enjoin that it is to be known.

The subject to be established here is the origin and subsistence of the entire expanse of the sentient and insentient (*cid-acit-prapañca*) from the one, non-dual Brahman, who consists of pure existence (*san-mātra-vapus*) and possesses manifold powers. Therefore, they state that since such a reality has not been conceived by other disputants, none of the objects imagined by them can be the meaning of the word "Brahman"—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. If this is so, then since it is not established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there would be the possibility of the scripture merely restating what is already known; in response to this doubt, it is said: "Because [Brahman] is the source of the scripture" (*śāstrayonitvāt*).

They state that the purport of the Sūtra is this: it is logical for a statement already established by some sentence within the Vedāntas to be restated by another sentence, for the greatness of the Word (śabda) lies in its capacity to convey matters never before perceived by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, they explain the *Samanvaya* Sūtra as being intended to resolve the doubt that Brahman cannot be the subject matter of the scripture, on the grounds that there is no linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding an established entity and that a sentence lacks purpose in the absence of engagement or withdrawal from action.

In that regard, first of all, the claim that the knowledge of the affliction by the threefold suffering (duḥkhatraya) must have occurred previously has already been refuted in the first sūtra. This is because, if that knowledge is intended to be established through perception and other means, its removal is already accomplished by the Ayurveda and other sciences; and since even the knowledge that heaven and so forth are included within the threefold suffering depends on other systems such as Sāṅkhya, the means to liberation would likewise be easily available therein, rendering the Vedānta unnecessary.

Furthermore, because the knowledge of that [Pradhāna] depends upon an inquiry into ritual action (*karma*), it would follow that such inquiry must have preceded it. Moreover, the claim that the Sāṅkhya and other systems are intended merely to show that Pradhāna and the like are not to be inquired into has already been refuted; for you yourselves accept the authority of Sāṅkhya and other scriptures in those parts that do not contradict the Vedas, while their lack of authority in contradictory parts is established by the logic of the *Virodha-adhikaraṇa* (the section on contradiction), and the defects of their objects of knowledge will be demonstrated in the *Tarka-pāda*. Finally, since it will be stated in the *Īkṣati-adhikaraṇa* and elsewhere that the Vedānta passages do not have that as their primary purport, the Sūtra would otherwise be rendered superfluous.

Furthermore, it is improper to claim that the *Janmādi-sūtra* (1.1.2) differs from the reality of the Upaniṣads according to the constructions of other disputants, and that the word "Brahman" is intended to exclude as its object any one of the categories such as *pradhāna* imagined by them; for if the multiplicity of the qualified entity—which depends upon the distinction between qualifiers—is not avoided, it would be impossible to establish that the non-dual reality is the cause of the entire universe.

Indeed, you have stated that the reality taught in the Upaniṣads differs from the principles postulated by other schools because it is the non-dual cause of the expansion of the sentient and the insentient (*cid-acit-prapañca*). However, the distinction of the reality known through the Vedānta from *pradhāna* and other such principles cannot be established by the method you have described without recourse to the logic of the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* and others; for no other distinct line of reasoning has been stated here apart from those yet to be mentioned, and because the objections to be raised later cannot be resolved without those very arguments that are yet to come.

Furthermore, since the distinction of the principles from [the Brahman] and the fact that *pradhāna* and so forth are not objects of inquiry would be established precisely from what is to be stated hereafter, [the present section] would be redundant.

Moreover, it is improper to claim that the *Śāstrayoni* section merely aims to show the possibility of restating what has been established by one sentence through another sentence, precisely because of such redundancy. In the *Pūrvakāṇḍa*, it is well known that there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by the sentence "He offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) of the oblation already enjoined by the sentence "He performs the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

It is well known from various sources that the group of six sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya—which were not enjoined by their own originative injunctions—are merely restated (anūdyante) in the two sentences, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day" and "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day. Therefore, the possibility of both injunction and restatement through syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) need not be further investigated here.

Furthermore, although the *Samanvaya-sūtra* does not have as its primary aim the [establishment of] engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*), it is accepted that its purpose is to demonstrate that the scripture possesses a meaningful goal. However, the claim that its aim is to establish linguistic usage regarding established entities (*siddha*) is incorrect, because the establishment of linguistic usage regarding established entities has already been justified by the first sūtra alone.

Furthermore, since it has been demonstrated that those three sūtras would be purposeless if they were intended to convey the meaning you have stated—due to the absence of any support for such a claim regarding established entities (*siddhavastu*) alone, and because, in the absence of a justification for the word’s power to denote an established entity, there would be no need to investigate the distinction from established entities, the nature of injunctions or restatements (*anuvāda*), or their respective purposes—it follows that the emergence of the three sūtras beginning with "janmādi" must necessarily be preceded by [the establishment of] that [word’s power]. Moreover, if they were to emerge merely by depending on what is yet to be explained, there would be a lack of consistency in the sequence of comprehension (*pratipatti-krama*).

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the first sūtra to be intent on enjoining what is not required when there is already a required injunction [already established], it is therefore logical that the four sūtras have as their purport the *Atharva* Veda, exactly as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Thus concludes the Section on Concordance (Samanvayādhikaraṇa).

In the first Sūtra, the subject matter was stated; in the second, the definition was given. In the third and fourth [Sūtras], the doubts regarding [the definition] being already known and being purposeless—which arise from the nature of the definition and the nature of the defined object, Brahman, respectively—were removed for the sake of establishing that Brahman is fit to be investigated. Now, it is investigated whether the object to be defined is distinct from both sentient and insentient things, or not distinct. Alternatively, having previously restated causality, its status as a defining characteristic was declared.

The two-fold doubt concerning the relationship between the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the thing defined (*lakṣya*) has been resolved. Now, the statements that establish [Brahman] as the cause—which serves as its defining characteristic—are examined. Alternatively, the four sūtras have established the preliminary framework for investigating whether the Vedānta texts possess authority regarding Brahman; now, the investigation into the specific object of knowledge (*prameya-viśeṣa*) is undertaken—such is the structural connection (*peṭikā-saṅgati*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* need not be commenced? For, since the *Samanvaya-adhikaraṇa* has already established that Brahman—which is the very goal of human life—is the subject to be propounded, there is no possibility of the Pradhāna (primordial matter), which is a locus of things to be abandoned, being introduced here. [Reply: This is not so; for the objection arises by taking into account the point stated in the *Samanvaya-adhikaraṇa*, namely, that it is impossible for Brahman to be the subject to be propounded if one propounds the Pradhāna and other such things that are not the goal of human life.

This is the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*); with this intention, he states the divisions of the sections (*peṭikābheda*), their connections, and the intermediate connections, beginning with the words "from which indeed these... Thus, the definition of Brahman, which was previously mentioned, has been stated.

The definition-statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) has been introduced with the intention that the examination of what has been characterized will now proceed; for, by restating [the Lord's] causality, its status as a defining characteristic is prescribed. Furthermore, the inclusion of the definition-statement is intended to indicate that, since the determination of the cause's distinction from the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) depends upon the investigation of the scriptural passages concerning causality, the causal statements are being examined in this section (*adhikaraṇa*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those scriptural passages that establish [Brahman] as the cause are included; for this very reason, it was stated that [the Sūtra] "teaches that the world has Brahman as its cause" in a manner common to both restatement (*anuvāda*) and prior assertion (*purovāda*). The qualifying attributes such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) are useful for the intermediate connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) which serves as the basis for raising an objection regarding the meaning of the section on "Concordance" (*samanvaya-adhikaraṇa*). By stating "it is to be desired to know," the meaning is that it is to be examined as being authoritative (*prāmāṇika*). With the intention that examination follows immediately after that, he says: "Now" (*idānīm*).

By this group of four sūtras, the immediate succession of the section on *samanvaya* (the concordance of the Vedas), which is devoted to establishing that Brahman is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is also stated. By the phrase "from the Pradhāna and so forth inferred through reasoning," it is indicated that there is an intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) because [this section] arises by way of challenging the immediately preceding *samanvaya*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "Pradhāna and so forth," the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*) alone, as well as specific instances of consciousness (*cid-viśeṣa*) and specific instances of insentience (*acid-viśeṣa*), are included; or alternatively, the meaning is that [these are excluded] by the remainder of the chapter, beginning with the sūtra "Because of seeing [Brahman is not the Pradhāna], for that which is not based on scripture [is not the cause]" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*).

He illustrates the subject matter (*viṣaya*) with the word "this" (*idam*). The subject matter is a causal statement that possesses a proposition (*pratijñā*) and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), which expresses a conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) and contains a general term. Among these, the *sadvidyā* passage alone is the direct subject matter of this section; other such causal statements become subject matter only by way of the *sadvidyā*, and not directly, because at the time of selecting the specific scriptural passage for the subject matter, those other passages were not selected.

Furthermore, because the lamp and the essence among those [examples] are non-appropriated (anupātta), and because the contradiction with the initial proposition and the merging (*pratyaya*)—which occur in this very context—are themselves formulated in the Sūtras; because the "similarity of transition" found in other Upaniṣads is taught here as a supporting factor for that [merging]; because, according to the sequence of intellectual comprehension, the doubt regarding insentience—which is appropriate given its status as the material cause—is to be refuted first; and because, among sentences marked by terms such as *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*, the sentence marked by general terms must be examined first.

For a particular (viśeṣa) ascends to the intellect by means of a universal (sāmānya). When there is an apprehension or a rejection of the universal, there is scope for doubt regarding the particular. However, when the particular itself is the counter-position, the expectation for a universal does not flow spontaneously; it is only when something is doubted that the application of logic (nyāya) proceeds. Therefore, he states the existence of doubt with the word "therein" (tatra). Doubt arises from the perception of both the similarity of this effect—denoted by the word "this" (idam)—to its cause, and the necessity [of such a cause]. He demonstrates the body of the doubt with the word "whether" (kim).

By the phrase "denoted by the word *sat*," it is shown that the subject-term (*dharmin*) is common [to both possibilities] and thus susceptible to doubt. By the phrase "the cause of the world," the grounds for doubt are confirmed: because it is the material cause (*upādāna*), its similarity to the effect is difficult to avoid; yet because it is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), its primary status as a perceiver (*īkṣitṛ*) remains. The sense is that the phrase "stated by others" indicates that disagreement (*vipratipatti*) also serves to reinforce these two causes of doubt. The term "inferred" (*ānumānika*) is used to highlight the sūtra-word intended to recall the seed of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The aforementioned characteristics refer to the characteristics such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). Through the two terms "inferred" (*ānumānika*) and "aforementioned characteristics" (*uktalakṣaṇa*), the two causes of doubt are indicated. Furthermore, there is an inquiry common to the remainder of this chapter: Are the Vedānta passages concerning the cause of the world intended to propound the *pradhāna* and so forth, or are they intended to propound the Brahman that is distinct from them? Here, however, for that purpose, the inquiry is: Do the passages on the "Knowledge of Being" (*sadvidyā*) intend to propound the *pradhāna*, or do they intend to propound the Brahman possessing the aforementioned characteristics? For that purpose, [the question is: What is the "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) here?

Is it secondary (*gauṇa*) or primary (*mukhya*)? To that end, do the form of inference and the association with "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) exist [in a secondary sense]? Or not? To that end, do the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) imply the reason (*hetu*)? And are words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth denotative of fire and so forth alone, or are they directed toward the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? To that end, is the word "Self" (*ātman*) non-contradictory to the fact that words such as "fire" and so forth do not refer to Brahman, or is it contradictory?

The inquiry is as follows: should those factors that cause the abandonment of the natural sense of the word *ātman* be followed, or rather those factors that support it? The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the factors causing the abandonment of its natural sense should be followed. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that only those factors which support it should be followed.

When, for the sake of avoiding a violation of the natural sense [of the text], the word *ātman* must be made subordinate, and since there is no contradiction in the words *tejas* and so forth not referring to Brahman, those words like *tejas* denote only fire and the rest; and when both the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) imply a logical reason (*hetu*), then—given that such an implied reason exists along with the association with secondary (metaphorical) seeing—the seeing mentioned first is taken in its secondary sense. Consequently, because the passages of the *Sadvidyā* refer to the Pradhāna, all causal texts, by virtue of having the same meaning as that, [refer to the Pradhāna].

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the relationship between the means and the end (*phala-phalibhāva*) is that the [passages] are primarily concerned with *pradhāna*. However, when—because the reason that reinforces the natural force of the word "Self" (*ātman*) must be followed, and because the word "Self" is incompatible with the non-Brahman nature of the words "light" (*tejas*) and so forth—the words "light" and the rest refer to the Supreme Self; and when the initial proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) do not imply a [separate] reason, then, due to the non-establishment of the forms of inference and the association with secondary seeing (*gauṇekṣaṇa*), the primary seeing is non-secondary. Thus, the sentences of the *Sadvidyā* [are concerned with Brahman].

Since [the words] refer to the Supreme Brahman, it follows by virtue of their having the same purport that all causal statements refer to the Supreme Brahman; such is the conclusion regarding the relationship between the subject and the result. In this regard, the author shows the expectation for a determination based on the logical validity of one or the other position in order to state the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), asking: "What is obtained? By "obtained," the meaning is "that which is logical. The proponent of the prima facie view asserts his own position as being logical, stating: "The Pradhāna."

The meaning is that between the two positions embraced by doubt, the former position is "possessed of reason" (*yuktimat*). He shows the expectation for a specific reason with the word "Why? (*kutaḥ*). He establishes that [reason] with the words "Being alone... (*sadeva...*). With the phrase beginning with "of that which is denoted by the word 'this'," he states the qualifiers that serve to establish the primacy of the cause and which oppose its being a distinct Puruṣa of a different nature. The point is that the word "this" (*idam*) naturally applies to an external object (*parāg*), and not to the internal conscious self (*pratyag-rūpa-cetana*).

Since the world consists of both the sentient and the insentient, he says "of that which has become the object of enjoyment for the sentient" in order to exclude the possibility that even the sentient is included within the denotation of the word "this" (idam). Because the conscious portion cannot logically be an effect or a cause, it is not included among effects; rather, its status is solely that of an enjoyer (bhoktṛ), whereas only the object of enjoyment (bhogya) possesses the nature of being an effect—this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the intention is that it is improper for the sentient to have the nature of the world, whose sole essence is being an object of knowledge (jñeya).

He states the qualification "consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*," which serves to establish the enjoyability of the effect and the primacy of the cause. The intention is that because the world is observed to be connected with pleasure, pain, and delusion—which are the effects of *sattva* and the other qualities—it consists of *sattva* and the rest; furthermore, there is the underlying concern as to how that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) could be the cause of that which consists of qualities. He says "beginning with ether" (*viyadādi*) in order to demonstrate its status as an object of enjoyment.

Alternatively, regarding the question of what the distinction is between being an effect and being a cause when the substance denoted by the word "this" (idaṃ) is the cause, he says: "the ether and so forth. The meaning is that the cause is in a state of unity, while the effect is in a state of multiplicity; this is the distinction. The underlying thought is that it is untenable for a single-natured Puruṣa to exist in the form of various-natured effects.

If it were necessarily the case that the cause must possess the same characteristics as its effect, then it would be impossible for the conscious [Brahman] to be the cause of that which is denoted by the word "this" (the world); for the state of being a cause resides in a different substance that serves as the material substrate of the effect. To address this doubt—namely, how there can be a necessary identity of characteristics—the author states that the cause and the effect are one and the same substance, using the words "of the substance which is the cause. Then, in response to the question "What follows from that?", he states the resulting rule regarding the necessity of the identity of characteristics between cause and effect with the words "Therefore... (ataḥ).

To the question "What follows from that?", he states that the effect possesses the same characteristics as the primary cause (pradhāna) with the words "and consisting of sattva, etc. He describes the similarity between the primary cause and its effect by saying "existing in a state of equilibrium of the guṇas. The phrase "existing in a state of equilibrium of the guṇas" is stated to dispel the doubt that because inequality among the guṇas is observed in the effect, the cause must also be of such a nature; it does not mean that [the cause] is "consisting of the guṇas."

The point is this: since everything that exists in a state of imbalance is observed to be an effect, it follows that its cause must likewise be so; furthermore, if that cause were also to depend on another cause, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress. Thus, the equilibrium of the gunas in the *pradhāna* is established. Moreover, if the *pradhāna*, which is a state of equilibrium of multiple gunas, were the cause, the determination of it as a single entity would be untenable.

Regarding the point that it is only when Brahman alone is the cause that [the scriptural statements] are logically consistent, he says: "That very [Brahman] is withdrawn... With the intention that the phrase "one only" excludes the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*), while "without a second" excludes inequality of attributes (*guṇavaiṣamya*), it is stated that "[all] particularities have been withdrawn. The sense of "pure existence" (*sanmātra*) is that the phrase "Being alone" excludes occasional non-existence; this is the meaning of the word "iti" used here as a reason (*hetu*). He states "from that very [source]" in order to establish that Brahman alone is the cause by means of another argument.

The point is this: it is precisely because the *pradhāna*—which consists of the three *guṇas* and is the cause of that which is denoted by the word "this"—is itself denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*), that the non-difference between cause and effect is established; for there can be no non-difference between two things of different natures. To the objection that such non-difference might not exist, he says: "If that were so. For if non-difference exists, then the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one is established; however, that is not possible on the view that the cause is something distinct from both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).

Thus, the reasoning consisting of the establishment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been stated. Alternatively, the non-difference (*ananyatva*) [of cause and effect] was intended in the preceding text because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "this was then being," and because of the rejection of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) in the passage "Now, some say. He states another reason: "If that were so. This means: "if there were primacy of the cause as the material source. The sense is that since the purport of the statement of the proposition is the non-difference of effect and cause, the use of the singular word "one" (*eka*) there is also appropriate due to the unity of the aggregate of qualities (*guṇasamudāya*).

He states another argument with the words "otherwise. The intention is that the examples of insentient things such as a lump of clay, iron, or a magnet do not fit when they are used as illustrations for a sentient cause. Alternatively, the meaning is that the example of a homogeneous cause and effect, such as a lump of clay and a jar, is not applicable when the cause and effect are heterogeneous. Intending to show that this is consistent with the *Kapila-smṛti* as a supporting reason, he says: "the cause of the world... and so forth.

The sense is that, according to the reasoning already stated, it is not proper to reject the Smṛti on the grounds of its non-contradiction with Śruti. By the phrase "by the great seer," the Śruti passage, "The great seer Kapila, who was born... is recalled. He states another reason: "the proposition" (pratijñā). This is said with the intention that the proposition and the illustrative example imply a logical reason, and thus it takes the very form of an inference. [Objection: But the proposition does not have the cause as its object; rather, it has the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one as its object.

Therefore, it should not be argued that even if [the argument] takes the form of an inference, the status of the Pradhāna as the cause is not established; for the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" is to be resolved through the non-difference (*ananyatva*) of everything from the One, and since this non-difference is based upon the relationship of cause and effect, the proposition that the Pradhāna is the cause is thereby proven. Here, the intended formal argument (*prayoga*) should be understood as follows: The world has a material cause non-different from itself, because it is an effect, like a jar.

Alternatively, this world must be known through the knowledge of its single cause, because it is an effect, like a jar and other objects produced from a single lump of clay; thus he concludes the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa).

The word *iti* here indicates a reason (*hetu*). The first reason for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the principle denoted by the word "this" (*idaṃśabda*), which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—and is to be inferred through pleasure, pain, and delusion—is the cause [of the world]. The second reason is the declaration that through the knowledge of one thing, there is the knowledge of all, which results from the non-difference of cause and effect; this serves to support the former, and the cognition in the form of an inference is the other reason. Showing that the Sūtra has been introduced to establish the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) against this prima facie position, he says: "Thus, when this [view] has been reached."
