The prior citation of the Sūtra is for the purpose of indicating that the objects, doubts, and prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa) being discussed belong to this specific section (adhikaraṇa). The present citation, however, serves to indicate that this is a Sūtra containing the final conclusion (rāddhānta) and to provide a word-by-word commentary; thus, there is a difference between the two cases. In response to the doubt—"How can that which is intended to be known through the Word (śabda) be 'non-scriptural' (aśabda)?"—he says "in which" (yasmin). The intention is that this [Sūtra] contains an exclusive emphasis (avadhāraṇa), just as in the expressions "one who drinks only water" or "one who subsists on air."

If it be argued that there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that [Brahman] besides verbal testimony (*śabda*), he says: "It is inferential" (*ānumānikam*). If it is then objected that scripture would not be teaching what has already been established by another means of knowledge, the answer is no; for although the cause is apprehended in its general form through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), its specific characteristics remain unapprehended, and thus it is taught by scripture in its qualified form.

The intention of the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) is that the Mīmāṃsakas hold the view that "instruction is purposeful only when [the object] has not been previously attained," whereas this is not the view of the Sāṅkhyas. Furthermore, the term *aśabda* ("not based on scripture") is employed to indicate the untenability of that [Sāṅkhya position]. With the intention of stating that the status of being inferable (*ānumānikatva*) applies equally to the sense organs as it does to atoms, and thus to exclude [the latter], he says "pradhāna" (primordial matter), following the singular number used in the Sūtra.

For *pradhāna* is a single cause of many [effects], whereas atoms, being multiple, are the causes of each individual effect; moreover, the sense organs are many causes of cognition, but not causes of the object. Thus, the exclusion of that [pradhāna] is established. Dispelling the suspicion that the word "not" (*na*) serves to negate the very nature of *pradhāna*, he connects the meaning of the sentence with the words "not that" (*na tat*).

The meaning is that, although the scripture is intent upon negation, because it is intent upon defining the sentence and because the nature of the verbal root is presented by the word "cause" (hetu), what is intended is the status of being negated in the capacity of being the subject matter to be established.

The absence of being conveyed by the sentence would have to arise either from its being established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or from its being sublated, because the sentence would then be intent upon something else. However, since there is no non-perception of what is perceptible and so forth, and since there exists a specific qualification of a form not previously apprehended, sublation and establishment by other means are impossible. Furthermore, the claim that the sentence is intent upon something else has already been refuted by the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, with the intention that the reason (*hetu*) is not possible, he shows the expectation for a reason by asking, "Why? (*kutaḥ*).

He explains [the reason] as "that which is denoted by the word 'sat'" (*sacchabdavācya*) in order to exclude both the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhi*) and its establishment otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*). By stating "related to that which is denoted by the word 'sat'," he excludes the fallacy of being unestablished due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*). The point is this: it is precisely the "Being" (*sat*) under discussion that is referred to by the pronoun "it" (*tat*) in the passage "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*). By using the term "specific activity" (*vyāpāraviśeṣa*) and the term "denoting word" (*abhidhāyiśabda*), he excludes establishment otherwise.

For that which is denoted by the verbal root *īkṣ* is not merely a tendency toward an effect common to both sentient and insentient things; rather, it is a specific activity unique to a sentient agent as its performer. The point is that when the primary meaning is possible, a figurative usage is not appropriate.

By the grammatical rule, "The suffixes *ik* and *tip* should be stated for the mention of a verbal root," the word *īkṣati* is used here to denote the verbal root itself, not its meaning; for if it were the meaning, one would have to say *īkṣiteḥ*. With the intention of indicating the natural aptness of the word for its intended sense, he says "of the verbal root."

The refutation of the objection regarding the non-establishment of knowledge from hearing is what is intended by the sūtra, "Because [the root] *īkṣati* is heard" (*śrūyamāṇād īkṣateḥ*). However, that result has been explained here by extracting it through the genitive case; whereas in the *Vedāntadīpa* it was explained for the sake of the natural sense of the meaning—that the word *īkṣati* indicates (or denotes) the act of seeing—here it is explained according to the natural sense of the words themselves.

Now, one might object: the two statements, "That heat [tejas] thought" and "Those waters [āpas] thought," suggest that the act of seeing (īkṣaṇa) is connected with non-conscious matter; likewise, in the passage "This deity thought," it would be appropriate for the seeing to belong to non-conscious matter, since it is impossible for the word "deity" (devatā) here to have a meaning different from the word "deities" (devatāḥ) found in the immediately preceding sentence, "Come now, let me enter these three deities. Furthermore, because the first instance of seeing is connected with the "Being" (sat) referred to by the pronoun "this" (sā) in the phrase "this [Being]," it too must belong to non-conscious matter. To this doubt, the author replies: "That [Being] thought" (tadaikṣata).

The sense is that it is not proper to violate the natural force of the opening statement (*upakrama*) for the sake of conforming to the final sentence (*caramavākya*); thus, "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) is primary. To the objection that there is no inconsistency here because the meanings of verbal roots are actions and an insentient thing can possibly be connected with action, he says: "seeing is an action. The meaning is that this particular kind of action is impossible [for an insentient thing]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This means: therefore, because seeing is impossible for an insentient thing, it contradicts your own position.

By the phrase "capable of such seeing," the exclusion of non-conscious matter (*acetana*) is stated. By the word "such" (*īdṛśa*), which is a term for a specific conscious entity, and by the fact that the nature of seeing has been realized as its fruit, the exclusion even from mere consciousness (*cetanamātra*) is stated; the sense being: how could that which is not possible even in mere consciousness be possible in the non-conscious? He states the established attribute [of the Self] with the words "all-knowing" (*sarvajña*), referring to "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*). He states the meaning realized as the fruit with the words "all-powerful" (*sarvaśakti*), referring to "May I be many" (*bahu syām*).

The term "Puruṣottama" indicates the point of culmination for the general notion of "Being" (sat), which is established by the force of the distinguishing marks that differentiate between consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit). The intention is that even the word "deity" (devatā) in the passage "This is that deity" (seyaṃ devatā), being supported by the capacity of the specific act of seeing and by the logic of the "goat-sacrifice" (where the general term is restricted to a specific animal), refers to a specific deity mentioned in another context. He establishes that the statement regarding the Knowledge of Being (sadvidyā) has the aforementioned meaning as its primary purport by means of the natural consistency of many other scriptural passages, stating "And thus" (tathā ca).

In this context, there is no citation of another scriptural passage as the subject sentence (*viṣayavākya*). [The word] "in all" (*sarveṣu*) is used in the sense of "in every single one"; by this, abundance (*prācurya*) is intended. The point is that if one were to resort to a figurative sense for the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), it would result in the violation of the natural sense of numerous scriptural passages. The meaning of "it is perceived" (*pratīyate*) is that perception (*pratīti*) is, at the very least, undisputed. Having stated the proof for his own position, he introduces an objection in order to refute the arguments of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*).

The similarity of characteristics between cause and effect must indeed be admitted, as it is observed in the case of clay and its products. Now, is this similarity to be accounted for by Brahman’s connection with the nature of the three *guṇas* (sattva, rajas, and tamas), or by the world being devoid of those qualities? In the first case, it is the acceptance of *pradhāna* under a different name. In the second case, there is a contradiction with the perceived association of pleasure, pain, and delusion [with the world]. This is the sense. He refutes this with the word "satyam" (true). The word "satya" implies partial admission. The conformity of the effect has been admitted, but not [Brahman’s] status as *pradhāna*.

The word "all" (sarva) implies that the Pradhāna alone is unsuitable for all effects, because it lacks the form conducive to being a cause in relation to the consciousness that has entered into the effect; this is the intended meaning. The two terms "omniscient" (sarvajña) and "omnipotent" (sarvaśakti) are used to establish its status as both a material cause (upādāna) and an instrumental cause (nimitta) suitable for the effect. He states the result of these two [attributes] with the phrase "of true resolve" (satyasaṅkalpa); the meaning is that because his omnipotence is unrestricted, there is no possibility of any obstruction to his volition.

The words "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and so forth are used in order to establish that modifications (*vikāra*) and the rest possess a medium [of manifestation], because causality is impossible in the absence of the aforementioned form. To show the scriptural statements regarding its possession of that [form], he cites the passage beginning with "Of this, the other... (*parāsya*). As to how the sentient and the non-sentient constitute the body, and how the possessor of that body might incur defects such as being subject to karma if it were indeed a body—he says "That very [Self]... (*tadetad*). Anticipating the objection that these sūtras are redundant with those beginning with "Because of the difference in nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*), he says "In this regard, concerning creation... (*atra sṛṣṭau*).

"Contradiction with reality" (*vastuvirodha*) means contradiction with the capacity of the object (*arthasāmarthyavirodha*). The distinction is this: here, the determination of the meaning is achieved through the reasoning of the Vedic statement (*vākyatarkeṇa*), whereas there, it is achieved by way of investigating and refuting external reasoning based on fallacious pervasions (*vyāptyābhāsa*) rooted in mere conceit (*ābhimānika*). In this manner, the causality of that which is denoted by the word "this" (*idaṃśabdavācya*)—which consists of the qualities such as *sattva*—and the promise of knowing all through the knowledge of one (*ekavijñānena sarvavijñānapratijñāna*), which serves to support that [causality], are both resolved.

Now, he restates the other reason mentioned by the opponent with the words, "As for what was said. He states its invalidity with the words, "That is incorrect. To the question "How so? he replies, "Because of the non-employment of a reason. The meaning is that if the speaker intends to state an inference, the reason—the principal member of the syllogism—must necessarily be employed; since it is absent here, there is no such intention to speak. He further states that it is also improper to imply a reason through the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) alone, with the words, "By which [the unheard is heard]."

For that which is not established otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*) is what implies [the probandum], since this applies universally to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Having taken for granted that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is established otherwise, it is stated that it is improper for the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to imply the reason (*hetu*). The point is this: the presentation of an example is not solely for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*), but also for the purpose of demonstrating the exclusion of impossibility; therefore, because it is established otherwise, it does not imply [the probandum].

The sense is this: the impossibility of that [knowledge] in every respect means that the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is possible only if there is identity of nature (*dharmmaikya*), or a uniform positive concomitance (*ekākārānvaya*), or a negative concomitance with other things (*vastvantaravyatireka*). However, in the case of jars, cloths, and so forth, none of these three is possible; for in jars, cloths, and the like, there is an absence of identity of nature, of positive concomitance, or of the connection of a common form, whether by way of difference from others or otherwise.

Granted that the example possesses commonality (sādhāraṇya) both in its being a constituent of inference and in its serving to demonstrate possibility; nevertheless, one might argue that even in our own view, such possibility would be merely occasional (pākṣika). To this, he says: "Because of 'seeing' (īkṣati) and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the reasons to be stated later are intended. The objection was raised that there is inferential status due to the commonality between the proposition (pratijñā) and the example; however, with the intention of showing that this doubt is also refuted by the existence of unique reasons such as "seeing," it is stated: "there is not even a scent of inference."

In order to introduce the subsequent sūtra, he raises the objection that the term "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) is used figuratively by saying, "Now, it might be argued... The sense is that one must consider the context here; [the opponent suggests] that "sentience" (caitanya) refers to what belongs to sentient beings, whereas "insentience" (acetanatva) conforms to what belongs to the primary cause (pradhāna). Since the first "seeing" cannot belong to insentient effects such as fire and so forth, the word *pradhāna* is used [figuratively]. He states the reason for this with the words, "That fire... (tatteja...).

The two statements are cited for the purpose of showing what is generally observed; the sense is that even the principle of "the majority" (*agrayaprāyanyāya*) does not constitute a sublation [of the primary meaning] as long as there is no contradicting evidence. The thought is that the word *devatā* in the phrase "this is that deity" (*seyam devatā*), by this very same logic, is appropriate as referring to non-conscious entities—just as in the case of "these three deities"—and thus it does not sublate its primary sense through figurative usage. He shows an instance of figurative usage with the words "and it occurs. The term "attributes of a conscious being" (*cetanadharma*) is used to include other attributes such as joy, which share the same status as "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*).

Two types of usage are observed both in common worldly parlance and in the scriptures. Concluding the discussion on figurative usage (*gauṇatva*) and in order to dispel the aforementioned doubt, he states "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that the present Sūtra has been introduced. He says "having restated" (*anubhāṣya*) because the doubt did not arise outside the scope of the Sūtra itself.

"If it be argued that [the term 'Self'] is secondary, no, because of the word 'Self'. Anticipating the objection as to by what connection with a quality it could be secondary, he applies the Sūtra while refuting that doubt, stating: "As for what was said... With the intention that the subject under discussion is the act of seeing (*īkṣati*), which is qualified by the masculine secondary term, he says "the designation of seeing" (*īkṣaṇavyapadeśa*). When it is stated that "seeing is not secondary," the use of the pronouns *yat* and *tat* is explained as being intended to negate the qualification, in order to dispel the doubt that the subject itself might be rejected; the meaning is: "that [quality] by virtue of which secondary status was alleged does not exist."

The word *sarga* has a secondary meaning: the state prior to creation (*sargaprāgavasthā*). In that context, the "conjunction of qualities" (*guṇayoga*) means conformity to the effect, characterized by necessary antecedence. With the intention that the word *ātman* occurring in both sentences—specifically the two words *ātman* found in the phrases "this world has that as its essence" (*aitadātmyam*) and "that is the Self" (*sa ātmā*)—is intended without distinction by the sūtra-word "by the word *ātman*," both sentences have been cited.

The meaning is that the word *sat* (Being) is established as the referent because, in the passage "this world has that as its essence" (*aitadātmyam*), the word *etad* (that) and the word *sa* (he/that) in the phrase "that is the Self" (*sa ātmā*) both refer back to the subject under discussion. Furthermore, regarding the concern that the word *ātman* (Self) might mean nothing more than the thing's own nature—as in "the pot has clay as its essence" (*mṛdātmakaḥ*) or "clay is the essence of the pot"—the author says: "This has been stated."

The phrase "by way of indicating the manifold of sentient and insentient things" means that the term "all" (*sarva*) is inherently unrestricted by its very nature—as seen in the statement "all this," and in harmony with the preceding passage "all creatures have Being as their root"—and furthermore, in agreement with other scriptural passages such as "He created all this; it became both the manifest and the unmanifest, both the conscious and the unconscious. Thus, the sense is that the word "all" refers to the world consisting of both the sentient and the insentient. The phrase "not in the insentient" means that it is impossible for the sentient to have identity of essence with the insentient.

Thus, having accepted the association with figurative seeing (*gauṇekṣaṇa*), the refutation was stated. Now, he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to show that such [figurative seeing] does not even exist. "Therefore" means because the world (*prapañca*), consisting of consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), has the Self as its essence. For what purpose is food (*anna*)—which lacks the instruction of seeing—taken up as a material cause? It is said:

This is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that food might not have Brahman as its self—a doubt based on the absence of an explicit teaching regarding "seeing" [Brahman]. Otherwise, since it would not be understood that the entire body has Brahman as its self, the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "this is Being" would be untenable, and thus the promise that "by knowing one, all is known" would not be fulfilled. Therefore, by taking up that [teaching], the fact that food has Brahman as its self—which was established through the praise of "entering"—is shown here as a secondary point (anuṣaṅgika) for the sake of fulfilling the initial promise.

The intention of the word "even" (*api*) is that there is not even the slightest thing that does not have that as its essence; or, it means "even those things you consider to be of a different nature. The intention of the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) is that that alone is the primary object of the first perception, by virtue of being its substratum. The sense of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "light and so forth also" is that they are like the word "existent" (*sat*); or, it means that even though these terms are conventionally understood in the world to refer exclusively to light and so forth.

The sense is that the Supreme Self alone is what is to be established as the primary subject by way of being the qualificand; light and the other elements, however, are merely the means [to that realization]. He establishes that [the word "Being"] denotes the Supreme Self with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*). "The state of being a thing" (*vastutvam*) means the state of being a thing whose nature is that [Supreme Reality]. The state of being a thing for light is "lightness" (*tejastvam*); the state of being a thing for water is "waterness" (*aptvam*); the state of being a thing for earth is "earthness" (*pṛthivītvam*); and the state of being a thing for gods, humans, and so forth, is "godhood," "humanity," and so on—the meaning is that it consists in assuming those respective states.

Being the possessor of a name means being denotable by a name. Now, one might ask: how is it established that the Supreme is denotable by a name, merely from the scriptural hearing that He is the expounder of names? It is said in reply: because in the same sentence—"It is differentiated by name and form"—the state of being differentiated is heard, and indeed, the differentiation of a name consists in its being differentiated [by the Supreme]; furthermore, it is well known that the differentiation of a name takes the form of being denotable by that name, and not merely the state of being its producer.

For indeed, there is no well-known designation of space, or of parents and so forth, as being "Devadatta" or by any other specific name; therefore, "being unmanifested by name" means being expressible by a name. Consequently, because they share the same meaning, what is intended here also is being expressible by a name.

The meaning of the phrase “the supreme object of all words” is also stated here; thus, he states the result of establishing that words such as *tejas* (fire/heat) and others denote the Supreme Self in the passage, “That fire thought. The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). He states the result of its primary [meaning] with the word *ataḥ* (therefore). The word *api* (also/even) is intended to include the grounds for suspecting a secondary sense; the suspicion of a secondary sense based on [the Lord’s] being the cause of the world denoted by the word *idam* (this) has been refuted, and the suspicion of a secondary sense is also dispelled by the association with the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), which is primary.

Alternatively, the sense is that even by means of what establishes your own position, your position is refuted. Regarding the phrase "completely cast aside": although there is an association with the secondary (gauṇa) sense, the suspicion of a secondary meaning in the passage "That [Self] thought" (*tad aikṣata*) has been cast aside by the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word *ātman*—which denotes the primary correlate of the word *sava*; the meaning is that it has been completely cast aside because the association with the secondary sense is not established.

"Even though there is an association with the secondary seeing (*gauṇekṣaṇa*), the first seeing is non-secondary because of the word 'Self' (*ātman*); moreover, the association with the secondary seeing is unestablished precisely because of the word 'Self. How can these two points be stated by a single sūtra? To this he says: "This is the intention of the sūtra. It is clear from the two sūtras that what is to be demonstrated in this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is: (1) that the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) do not imply a reason (*hetu*), and (2) that among those factors that support both the primary and the secondary meanings, the supporter of the primary meaning must be followed.

Introducing the subsequent Sūtra while dispelling the doubt that [the preceding discussion] might concern a subordinate object of proof, he says, "For this reason also" (*itaśca*). By defining the attribute of *īkṣaṇa* (seeing/contemplation) as being conducive to causality, the status of the Existent (*sat*) as the Supreme Self was established. Now, the connection is as follows: through the attribute of being the unique bestower of liberation—which belongs to the causal reality—by means of the scriptural statement, "But the Cause is to be meditated upon," its status as the Supreme Self is further proven.

Because liberation is taught for one who is intent upon that. Demonstrating that the word *tanniṣṭhasya* (of one intent upon that) in the Sūtra is the explanation of the word *tasya* (of him) in the Śruti passage "For him, so long as... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2], and elucidating the meaning of the words *tat* and *niṣṭhā*, he states the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "for the seeker of liberation."

The doubt that this might be an injunction for the contemplation of the exalted *pradhāna* as the material cause of the entire world—since such an injunction for the contemplation of a result within the realm of the finite (*arvācīna*) is possible regarding a conscious being—is dispelled by the word "seeker of liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*). With the intention of making known that the word "that" (*tat*) in the sentence which teaches the nature of Being (*sad-ātmatva*)—instructing the seeker to contemplate their identity with Being through the formula "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*)—refers to the "Being" under discussion, the word "that" is used in the Sūtra.

It has been stated that [the Self] consists of Being (*sad-ātmaka*). By the word *anusandhāna* (synthesis/contemplation), the meaning of the word *niṣṭhā* (finality) has been expressed. Here, how is it understood that the purpose of the instruction is synthesis? It is said: at the beginning, in the passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known," the word *vijñāna* (knowledge), which occurs immediately after hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), refers to meditative worship (*upāsana*), because it has the same sense as the statement, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be synthesized (*nididhyāsitavya*"). And in the conclusion, it says, "He indeed understood it."

The phrase *vijajñau* ("he understood") is repeated for the sake of that same meaning. Furthermore, even in the middle [of the passage], the statement "A man who has a teacher knows" (*ācāryavān puruṣo veda*)—which describes the specific knowledge of the object as the fruit of having a teacher—is a sign (*liṅga*) that the object taught by the teacher is to be reflected upon (*anusandheya*). Thus, by these reasons, it is understood that the instruction regarding the nature of Being (*sad-ātmaka*) is intended for meditative worship (*upāsanā*). By the word *antarāya* ("obstacle"), delay (*vilamba*) is indicated; the meaning is that the delay lasts until the fall of the body.

When it is said, "until I am liberated," how is liberation from the body established? It is explained as follows: when "liberation" (mokṣa) is mentioned, one expects some cause of bondage from which there is liberation. When the question arises as to what that cause is, it is understood from the hearing of the departure from the body in this very knowledge-text, beginning with, "Now, when his speech merges into the mind," and elsewhere in, "Having risen up from this body, having attained the highest light... shaking off the body," and "Neither pleasure nor pain touches one who is bodiless."

From the scriptural hearing that "[the two] touch [it]" and from the traditional smṛti texts such as "having abandoned the body, he does not undergo rebirth," it is understood that [the object] is the body. The sense is that [the state] characterized by union with Brahman is "liberation" (mokṣa), because Brahman itself—established by another scriptural passage, "Then I shall be united," and "At that time, my dear, one becomes united with Being"—is the very "action" (karman) denoted by the term "union" (sampatti).

The intention is that for the word "liberation" (*mokṣa*) used in the Sūtra, the meaning is precisely the attainment of Brahman preceded by the falling away of the body, and not merely the destruction of the body. Then, in response to the expectation of what follows from this distinction regarding the primary subject, he explains what is intended by the phrase "for one desiring liberation" (*mumukṣoḥ*) with the words "if, moreover" (*yadi ca*). How is there an inconsistency? To the doubt—namely, why should the non-intelligent object of meditation (*acid-upāsana*) not be conducive to liberation on the strength of the scriptures, just like the service of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and holy fields (*kṣetra*)—he says: "according to one's resolve" (*yathā kratuḥ*).

The meaning of the Śruti is that one partakes of a fruit corresponding to the nature of the meditation; consequently, it is illogical that the abandonment of what is to be discarded should result from meditating upon that which is to be discarded. "Attainment of the insentient" (*acetana-sampatti*) means reaching the state of being insentient (*acit-prāpti*); for transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) is indeed the connection with the insentient caused by karma. That the word *sampatti* has the sense of "attainment" is made clear by the immediately following commentary: "the attainment of the insentient, which is the cause of being struck by the threefold affliction. To the question, "Let there be attainment of the insentient; what follows from that?", he says: "And not... (*na ca*).

In this context, the Purāṇic statement, "For the scripture is more affectionate than a thousand mothers and fathers," has been recalled. The meaning is that while parents are intent merely upon nourishing one in a single lifetime, the scripture is intent upon providing every form of protection across many lifetimes, both in this world and the next. By the phrase "the threefold affliction," the intention is that the purpose of the scripture would otherwise not reach its ultimate fulfillment.

Thus, the utility [of Sāṅkhya] for liberation has been refuted on the grounds of its contradiction with principles established by scripture (*śruti*) and its lack of a culminating purpose. To show agreement with the views of others (*paramata*) regarding this point, he says: "By one who is established in Pradhāna. The sense is that even by the Sāṅkhya, who speaks thus—"From the discernment of the Manifest, the Unmanifest, and the Knower"—only the mere thorough knowledge of Pradhāna is intended, as in the case of a disease, and not its meditative worship (*upāsana*).

One might object: "The statement 'That thou art' (tattvamasi) is not an instruction for the contemplation of the self as being of the nature of Reality (sat), but rather a restatement of the delusion that the body is the self, such as 'I am stout. Therefore, the insentient thing denoted by the word 'sat' is to be known by the seeker of liberation for the sake of its abandonment. Anticipating this doubt and intending to show the connection with the following sūtra, he says: "For this reason also" (itaśca).

"And because there is no mention of it being something to be discarded. He says "on the contrary" to show that it is not merely a lack of favor toward the Supreme, but rather that there is even hostility toward it. Just as the identification "I am fat" and so forth is established as something to be discarded, the identification with the True Self is not taught as something to be discarded, but rather its very nature as something to be accepted is stated.

Furthermore, that [word] is inappropriate if it refers to *pradhāna*, because in passages concerning *pradhāna*—such as "asleep through beginningless *māyā*, constrained by *māyā*," "he grieves and is deluded by his lack of lordship," and "the other, the unborn, leaves her behind once she has been enjoyed"—it is presented solely as something to be abandoned; this is the meaning. Thus, the reasons found in the subsequent passages starting from "That thought" (*tadaikṣata*) have been stated, and the word "and" (*ca*) is employed at their conclusion.

Alternatively, the word "ca" (and) is used here for the purpose of unifying the two points—namely, the stated acceptability and the unstated non-acceptability—which are presented by the two preceding sūtras as being mutually connected through the nature of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). For this very reason, the conclusion of the meaning of the previous sūtra has been made with the words "on the contrary" (pratyuta), and so forth.

Now, he dispels the doubt that—since there is a contradiction with the opening statement—the primary subject matter must be what is established, because the reasons found in the subsequent sentences are weak; [he does so] by stating "because of the contradiction with the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodhāt*). Filling out the expectation as to in what sense there is a contradiction, he explains: "in the case of the causality of Pradhāna. The sense is that the intention of the author of the Sūtras is this: that very thing which was stated in accordance with your own view is, in fact, contrary to your own view. To the question "How so?", he says: "For, at the beginning of the passage... and so forth.

Although the word "all" (*sarva*) is absent from the initial statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*), it is stated that the knowledge of everything is indeed proposed, because of the unity of meaning with statements in the same context—such as "O Blessed One, when what is known does all this become known? and "Verily, my dear, when the Self is seen, heard, thought, and known, all this becomes known"—and because of the natural force of the term "all creatures" (*sarvāḥ prajāḥ*) which is about to be mentioned. Nor should it be said that the "knowledge of all" refers only to the knowledge of the insentient world as an effect, as in the expression "all that is made of clay"; for [the text intends] the knowledge of everything.

The meaning is that since even sentient beings—understood through the natural force of the word *prajā* (progeny) which stands in grammatical apposition with the word *sarva* (all) in the passage, “O dear one, all these progenies have Being as their root”—are included among all effects that must be known as having Being as their root; [the opponent asks] what follows from this, and [the author] replies: “And that [Being]... The sense is that there is no non-difference between consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*) by way of the non-difference between cause and effect.

[Objection: "But even if [the world] is different [from Brahman], the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is still possible, because while earth and the other elements are effects, the conscious element (cidaṃśa) is not an effect, and thus its knowledge can arise. To this, he says: "of the manifold of sentient and insentient things that have become its effects. The sense is that, by the force of the examples of the lump of clay and its products, and from the natural force of the word *prajā* ("progeny") in the statement "All beings have Being as their root," it must be stated that even the sentient is known precisely as an effect.

The point is this: it must be established as being known precisely through its own nature; thus, like the knowledge of a village through the knowledge of Devadatta, the "knowledge of all" here is not figurative. For if the knowledge of all were merely figurative, the question "How indeed, O Venerable One? would be inappropriate, as such knowledge is already evident in the world. Furthermore, one observes that the knowledge of all is established in its primary sense by means of examples such as clay and its effects, which are non-different from it. He shows the contradiction with the initial proposition by stating "that [is]... in the opposite manner of what was previously stated.

The proposition that all cognitions are [contained] within a single cognition is based on the relationship of cause and effect; likewise, the dissolution of consciousness into the Supreme Self during deep sleep is also based on that same relationship. Intending to state that the dissolution in deep sleep is logically consistent because of this commonality of being based on the relationship of cause and effect, he says: "For this reason also: because of its merging in itself" (*svāpyayāt*).

The intention is that he dispels the suspicion of a different meaning based on the fact that the word *sat* has the same referent as the word *ātman*, which designates the individual soul (*jīva*), by stating "that very thing is what is denoted by the word *sat*"; thus, even here, the word *sat* refers exclusively to the reality that is the cause of the world. The phrase "wherever... whenever" conveys this sense.

[Objection: "But surely, attainment (*sampatti*) with 'Being' (*sat*) must be contact with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whereas the deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is its abiding in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); thus, the two words 'own' (*sva*) and 'Being' (*sat*) would have different meanings, and this statement would not contradict the doctrine that primordial nature is the cause. Refuting this, [the author] explains: "The one who is asleep" (*suṣuptam*). He clarifies the phrase "he has merged into his own" (*svam apītaḥ*) by saying "merged in himself" (*svasmin pralīnaḥ*).

The intention is as follows: the word *svam* (one's own) is used with the accusative case (*dvitīyā*), while *satā* (by being existent) is used with the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) in the sense corresponding to the locative case (*saptamī*) in the phrase *sampadya* (having become), because the result is the same; however, the difference in designation arises from the difference in the nature of the verbal roots. The accusative indication is used because merging (*apīti*) is of the nature of attainment (*prāpti*), for there are other scriptural passages such as, "Being Brahman, he attains Brahman," and, "That toward which they go, into which they enter."

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used because of the co-occurrence (*sāhitya*) with the word *sat* (Being), or alternatively, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) in *sampannaḥ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). At that time, since the attainment of perfection (*sampatti*) takes the form of reaching [the goal], the third case is employed to express the agency (*kartṛtva*) of that which already exists, as in the phrase "embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvaktaḥ*). As for the use of the seventh case (*saptamī*), it is due to the fact that dissolution (*apyaya*) requires a locus. Because words denoting dissolution inherently require a locus, and this requirement is more prominent [than the requirement for an agent], the explanation has been given in accordance with the seventh case.

Thus, it has been stated that the two words *sampatti* and *apyaya* have a single meaning insofar as they refer to dissolution (*pralaya*), and it has also been stated that the two words *sva* and *sat* have a single meaning insofar as they refer to the locus of dissolution. This is the intended sense: "O dear one, at that time he becomes united with the Existent; he is united in the Existent"—in this statement, which constitutes the conclusion of the proposition, it is evident that there would be a syntactical inconsistency if the phrase situated between the proposition and the conclusion were to refer to some other matter not required by the statement regarding the soul's merging into itself (*svāpyaya*).

Furthermore, because of the abundance of scriptural usages such as, "Then, finally, they go even to this; being Brahman, he attains Brahman," and "Then he becomes united with Brahman," it is appropriate that the dissolution (pralaya) established by the natural force of the words *apīti* and *sampatti* serves to indicate the locus [of the soul]. Moreover, it is fitting that the two words *sva* and *sat* should result in having a single identical meaning.

In the phrase "By the living self, thou art That" (*jīvenātmanā tattvamasi*), it is appropriate—by virtue of the context—that both the words *tvaṃ* (thou) and *tat* (That), as well as the words *sva* (own) and *sat* (Being), have a single referent, since they both concern the causal reality existing in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, this unity of meaning is logical because, if the [individual soul] were distinct from that reality, there would arise the doubt that its dissolution [into Brahman] is impossible; therefore, it is necessary to demonstrate that what is denoted by the word *sva* culminates in *sat*, and thus their identity of meaning is established.

Granted that the two words *svasañjña* (one’s own name) and *sva* (self) may have the same referent; however, this is possible even if both words—by taking *sva* to mean "belonging to oneself"—refer to the Pradhāna. To this, he says: "And dissolution... Dissolution (*laya*) indeed consists in the merging into a cause by abandoning a dissimilar state characterized by being an effect. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Nor... [The meaning is: "because it is insentient" (*acetana*), i.e., because it lacks consciousness (*acittvāt*).

To dispel the doubt that the word "Being" (*sat*) might refer to the individual soul (*jīva*)—since the gross state of the soul can logically dissolve into its own subtle causal state which is endowed with existence—the author says: "Likewise, [the text speaks of] deep sleep. The intention is that, because this passage refers to the Supreme Cause characterized by qualities such as seeing and so forth, independent of the body and senses to be created, and because it accords with other concordant scriptural texts, the word "Being" here does not refer merely to the individual soul in its subtle state of extremely contracted knowledge.

Objection: Is it not the case that the dissolution (*laya*) of the eternal individual soul (*jīva*) is untenable? Because of the non-difference between cause and effect, and because it is impossible for the Supreme—who is distinct from the individual soul—to be its cause, the dissolution of the individual soul within that [Supreme] is likewise untenable. Reply: This is not so, because the causal relationship, in the form of a particular state, is possible for the Supreme Self which is always qualified by the individual soul. To explain:

In the passage "he has merged into his own self" (*svam apīta*), the word "own" (*sva*) does not refer merely to the individual soul (*jīva*), because the word "own" has the same referent as the word "Being" (*sat*) in the statement, "then, my dear, he becomes united with Being; he has merged into his own self," and because in this context the word "Being" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Nor does it refer to the abstract Brahman, because that which is eternally changeless cannot logically be a material cause (*upādāna*) and thus cannot be the locus of merging.

For the dissolution of an effect occurs only in its material cause; therefore, it must be stated that the reference here is to the Supreme Self abiding in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*). Even in that case, there is no dissolution of the soul as there is of silver in mother-of-pearl, because that would entail the cessation of the soul's own essential nature. Nor is there a dissolution like that of the space within a jar into the great space (*mahākāśa*), because the limiting adjuncts such as the body and so forth continue to exist.

Nor is there a dissolution [of the individual soul] upon the surface of the earth like that of a jar; for if the state of being a living being (*jīvatva*) were abandoned just as the nature of a jar is, it would contradict the scriptural texts regarding the eternity of the soul. Furthermore, since the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) remains, the abandonment of the state of being a living being is impossible. Moreover, if this state of being a living being—which persists until liberation—were to cease through mere sleep, it would follow that the means to liberation are useless, and it would entail the fallacies of experiencing the results of actions not performed (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so forth, as well as contradicting recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). This is evident from the text: "Embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña*), one knows nothing external, nor anything internal."

Furthermore, because at that time there is a designation of difference based on ignorance and omniscience, and because the state of deep sleep (*svāpyaya*) must be accepted by all as existing within the very condition of being a living soul (*jīvatva*); therefore, due to this very difference, the word "self" (*sva*) refers to the Supreme Self as qualified by the living soul. For this very reason it is stated in the *Sāra*: "The meaning is that the living soul has gone back into the Self itself; for the Supreme alone is the true nature of the living soul, according to the scriptural text concerning the differentiation of names and forms."

Its "attainment" (*sampatti*) means abiding in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) devoid of the outward-flowing expansion of consciousness; its "exit" (*nirgama*) means the outward-flowing expansion of consciousness. Now, one might ask: how can there be a dissolution of the substratum-part (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) while the soul, characterized by the body, remains within that very body? It is not so; for just as there is the persistence of attachment, aversion, and so forth in the substratum-part, it is likewise logical that there is the persistence of a state consisting of dissolution in that very same part.

But then, since there is no maintenance of the body by consciousness during deep sleep, and since maintenance by its own nature is equally present even in the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), it would follow that the body's non-separate establishment from the individual soul (jīva) and the definition of the body as such are untenable.

No; for since the living self does not abandon the body, and since the body is capable of being sustained by its [the self's] volition, the definition of the body as being non-separately established (*apṛthaksiddha*) is appropriate. Therefore, the meaning of the Śruti is this: the Supreme Self, while characterized by the living self in the waking state—which possesses an outward-turned expansion of cognition corresponding to attachment, greed, and so forth, along with the conceit of names and forms such as "human" and the like—is, when embodied by the living self that is free from the turbidity of conceiving internal and external forms based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the names and forms of gods and humans, as well as passion, hatred, greed, and delusion, contained within Himself.

Because dissolution (*apyaya*) is of the nature of an attainment, the accusative case is used in the *Sāra* as "the Self" (*ātmānam*). Because dissolution requires a locus, it is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) that [the individual self] is "merged in itself. The designation of the relationship between locus and located for the single Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is intended to refer to a distinction of parts (*aṃśabheda*); for even though a part of the earth—the material cause of a jar—is not itself the jar, it is still regarded as the cause because it belongs to the same class as the cause. However, in the case of Brahman...

The relationship between the locus (*sthāna*) and the occupant (*sthānin*)—distinguished by the difference between the specific individual soul (*jīva-viśe� causality*—is due to the identity of the substrate (*dharmyaikyāt*). The inclusion within the substrate that persists through the causal state is uniform everywhere. The effect-state is characterized by the individual soul as distinguished by an identification with its limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-ākāra-abhimāna*), while the causal state is characterized by the individual soul lacking such identification. In this regard, there is indeed a dissimilar state for the portion that is being dissolved, compared to the causal state of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which serves as the locus of dissolution.

The state of being qualified by the individual soul (jīva) is like the expansion of knowledge that conforms to the conceit of forms conditioned by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth; therefore, "deep sleep" (svāpyaya) is logically established as abiding in one's own self, which is the causal state characterized by the absence of conceit regarding those conditioned forms. For this very reason, there is no contradiction with the eternity of the individual soul, because there is no abandonment of its status as a soul apart from the specific contraction and expansion of its knowledge.

Indeed, even by opponents, the stability of the state of being a living soul (jīva) until liberation must be admitted; therefore, its dissolution (svāpyaya) should be described in a manner that does not contradict this. In this way, there is no contradiction with the teaching of distinction found in the passage, "embraced by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā sampariṣvakta*). Furthermore, it must be accepted that such a dissolution is indeed the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), because the objections regarding partiality and cruelty can be avoided by accepting the plurality of souls, their beginninglessness, and the persistence of specific karmic impressions.

Nor is there any contradiction with the scriptural teaching on the eternity of knowledge, namely, "There is no loss of the knower's knowledge," for that [scripture] does not imply unreality, as it merely refers to the absence of contraction. Furthermore, one should not suspect the substance of knowledge to be unreal simply because its expansion and perception are absent; for the non-existence of the unobstructed luster of a gem is not established by the absence of its expansion and perception. As it is said: "The light of a gem is not created by the washing away of its impurities."

"For knowledge of the Self is not produced by the mere removal of defects," so says the Smṛti. This aforementioned manner is also consistent even with absolute dissolution (*atyantikapralaya*), because at that time [the soul] abides in the Supreme Self in its causal state, through the non-abandonment of the semblance of identification with forms conditioned by name and form (*nāmarūpa*). For the "causal state" of the Supreme consists in being qualified by a soul that is devoid of the state of being an effect—characterized by the fitness for identification with conditioned forms; that is to say, it is being qualified by a soul that is free from modification (*vikṛti*).

That [state] is the same both at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and in liberation (*mukti*). Now, it might be argued: "Since in deep sleep one is embraced by the conscious Self (*prājña-ātman*) and knows nothing external nor internal—thus a difference consisting of consciousness and unconsciousness is understood—and since in liberation a difference such as being the Lord (*īśvara*) and being the object of His rule (*īśitavya*) is admitted to persist, the mode of dissolution favored by you is untenable. This is not so.

This is because, with reference to the causal state (*kāraṇāvasthā*), a dissimilar state is intended; the causal state is the state of being qualified by a *jīva* who is devoid of the conceit of forms conditioned by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth, whereas the dissimilar state in relation to that is the state of being qualified by a *jīva* possessing such conceit. Since the abandonment of that [conceit] exists here, dissolution (*laya*) in deep sleep is logically established.

Furthermore, the inequality in liberation by way of the state of being subject to His rule does not contradict the final dissolution, because being subject to His rule is not of the nature of a temporary state (*avasthā*); for a state is indeed a contingent property (*kādācitkadharma*), whereas being subject to His rule and so forth is eternal, according to such scriptural passages as: "He is the Lord of this world eternally; no other cause exists for His lordship," "Whose body is the Self," and "Who rules the Self from within."

Therefore, there is no fault in not abandoning even that which has the form of a counter-example—such as the state of being ruled over (*īśitavyatva*) and so forth—as non-existent; hence, the dissolution (*svāpyaya*) is exactly as previously described. He connects the scriptural reason with the ultimate probandum by saying "therefore" (*tasmāt*). He says "the Supreme Brahman" (*paraṃ brahma*) to establish that the place of dissolution is the ultimate cause. The word "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) is used for the purpose of excluding the individual soul (*jīva*), for the Śruti says, "by the conscious Self" (*prājñenātmanā*); this is in agreement with [the passage] "That thought" (*tad aikṣata*).

The term "Supreme Lord" (parameśvara) is used to indicate that He is the controller of the individual soul even at the time of dissolution, and to exclude any reality superior to God. The term "Supreme Person" (puruṣottama) is intended to show His distinction from a person in deep sleep and to designate a specific deity. To preclude other interpretations, he says: "He said that."

The phrase "by means of attainment and non-attainment" (sampattyasampattibhyām) means by means of the attainment and departure previously mentioned—namely, "Being, having attained [this world], they do not know; Being, we shall attain," and "Having come from Being, they do not know; Being, we are coming. Alternatively, it means by means of attainment in the Supreme Self and non-attainment elsewhere. This is the intention of the Commentator (*vṛttikāra*), that even non-attainment is intended by the term "dissolution into one's own nature" (*svāpyaya*). The meaning is that this constitutes the causality of the Supreme Brahman.

In the preceding sūtra, because another scriptural passage concerning deep sleep—beginning with "by the intelligent Self"—was present in the mind as supporting the subject at hand, the fact that the cause is the Supreme Self is also established by other scriptural passages concerning the cause, due to the uniformity of their purport (gatisāmānya).

Since it was previously stated [in the Sūtra] that "if it is argued that [the Self] is secondary, no, because of the word 'Self'," he cites scriptural passages containing the word "Self," beginning with "The Self, verily... In the passage "Of this very one, indeed... the word "Self" is also heard; likewise in "The Self, my dear, should be seen," "When the Self, my dear, is seen," and "By whom else than the Self all this is known. And in the passage "Of this very one, indeed...", there is the phrase "he knows all from the Self. He explains the term "going" as "activity."

The word *pravṛtti* is intent upon the operation of making known, just like the word *pravṛtti* in the expression “of those having different grounds for application” (*bhinnapravṛttinimittānām*). He states that the identity [of the words] is mediated by their referents in the phrase “identical with that” (*tatsamāna*). To the question “What follows from that?”, he says “And in them...”. To the question “What follows from that too?”, he says “Therefore...”. Furthermore, he states that the fact that the Lord of All is the cause is clear not only in other Upaniṣads but in this very one as well, in the passage beginning with “Because it is heard [there]” (*śrutatvācca*). He demonstrates the agency of fashioning names and forms through His nature as the Self in the passage beginning with “by means of this living soul” (*anena jīvenātmanā*).

Omniscience and omnipotence have already been demonstrated by such passages as "It thought: May I be many," and it has also been indicated that [all things] have Being as their root. The text shows that [Being] is the substratum in the phrases "having Being as their abode" and "that which belongs to this. Furthermore, it shows that it is the sustainer by virtue of being the Self in the phrase "this is its essence. The point here is that what is intended is not merely the status of being the substratum of effects by way of being their cause. Moreover, the passage beginning with "that which... is also useful for establishing the quality of having true desires.

He shows the qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*) by saying, "This is the Self. Then, for the purpose of clarifying the qualities already mentioned, for the purpose of showing qualities not yet mentioned, and for the purpose of making explicit His lordship (*īśvaratva*) and His status as a specific deity (*devatāviśeṣatva*), he cites other scriptural passages (*śruti*) intended in the previous sūtra but not previously quoted, beginning with "And thus... (*tathā ca*). However, these are not cited as the specific textual passages (*vākya*) for the subject matter of this particular sūtra; for it has been stated even in the *Dīpa* and *Sāra* that this sūtra has the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* alone as its scope: "For it is indeed heard in this very Upaniṣad."

There is no intention here to express a sequential order. "Liṅga-śarīra" refers to the subtle body. By the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*), he concludes that the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is not what is being propounded, in accordance with the introductory sūtra "Not that which is based on sound" (*na śabdaṃ*). By the phrase "hence" (*ataḥ*), he concludes that it follows as a result that Brahman is indeed what is being propounded. "Omniscience and so forth" (*sarvajñatvādayaḥ*) are the qualities useful for [Brahman's] being the cause of creation and so on. The qualities mentioned in the purificatory passages are those stated in the words beginning with "having all defects removed" (*nirasta-nikhila-doṣa*).

By the words beginning with "anavadhika" (limitless), the fact that [the Lord] is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) is shown. If the word "ogha" (flood) is present, it shows that the qualities do not terminate elsewhere; the word "mahārṇava" (great ocean) shows the greatness of that which is the substratum even beyond those qualities. The two words "Puruṣottama" and "Nārāyaṇa" demonstrate that the purificatory statements regarding the Cause culminate in the specific attributes established by the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, while showing His distinctness from both the conscious and the unconscious, as well as the fact that they constitute His body.

By the word "entire" (*nikhila*) in the phrase "the single cause of the entire world," even the ether and other elements are subsumed. By the word "single" (*eka*), it is intended that [Brahman] is both the efficient and the material cause.

It was previously stated that these sūtras are inconsistent with the doctrine of Brahman-as-ignorance (*brahmājñānavāda*); this is now explained in detail with the words "for this very reason. The phrase "by the author of the sūtras" implies "by the author of the Nyāya treatise" (Bādarāyaṇa). The term "by these" (*ābhiḥ*) is intended to convey the sense of being expressive of meaning; the underlying idea is: "by the Śrutis which are clear in meaning and supported by reasoning (*nyāya*)."

Furthermore, since it is observed in the world that even one who is authoritative may have the conceit of being non-authoritative—resulting in a fallacy of position (apasiddhānta)—and that even an established tenet (siddhānta) may be non-authoritative due to being rooted in error, the mention of both the Sūtra and the Śruti is for the purpose of excluding both of these possibilities. "Is to be understood as refuted" means that the refutation has been accomplished. He explains what was stated by the words "pāramārthika" (ultimately real), etc.

The intention of the word "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*) is as follows: if the act of seeing were not ultimate, then the *pradhāna* favored by the Sāṅkhyas would itself be Brahman; for if the nature of mother-of-pearl were not ultimate, then silver alone would be the ultimate reality. Thus, the refutation of the Sāṅkhya position would be untenable. Furthermore, since the essential nature denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) is susceptible to doubt, there must be something distinct from it that serves as its differentiator; this is the sense of the word "attribute" (*guṇa*).

The meaning is that the refutation of the *nirviśeṣa* (devoid of attributes) position is effectively established by those sūtras which intend to convey the reality of qualities such as *īkṣaṇa* (seeing), for the purpose of excluding the possibility that words like *ātman* and *sadā* refer to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) favored by the Sāṅkhyas. [An objection is raised: "Sentences such as 'It saw' (*tadaikṣata*) refer only to the state of being a witness (*sākṣitva*), and not to specific qualities; even by mere witnesshood, the exclusion of the *pradhāna* intended by the sūtra is established. To this, he replies: "nirviśeṣa... [and so on].

The meaning is that, according to your own view, even the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*), since it does not exceed the nature of the object of dispute presented by the word "real" (*sat*). The intention of the word "also" (*api*) is that it has already been stated previously that the status of being a witness cannot be established in the absence of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). To the question, "What would follow from its being non-ultimate? he says: "The Vedānta... The sense is that a superimposed form is not the object of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka*), nor is Brahman the subject proposed here as something to be investigated (*jijñāsya*) in a merely recent or superficial sense. He then asks, "What of it? and replies: "And that... (*tac ca*).

What follows from this? For we do not say that [the cause] is insentient; to this he replies: "Sentience (caitanyatva) consists in the possession of the quality of consciousness. The intention is that being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*) is not merely the nature of consciousness itself. He concludes by summarizing the result of the refutation of the featureless [Brahman]: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). For here, the distinction of the Pradhāna is not indicated by the mere nature of consciousness alone; rather, it is by the possession of the quality of seeing. The meaning is that for one who does not accept that [quality], there would be no exclusion at all in the absence of a differentiator.

By the words "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*) and so forth, the contradiction with this current section (*adhikaraṇa*) is stated. By the words "Vedānta" and so forth, the contradiction with the preceding sections is stated. Alternatively, [the opponent might argue that] being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of Brahman] and not an attribute (*dharma*); therefore, it is not ultimately unreal. To this, [the author] says "Vedānta. If it were merely the nature [of Brahman], then since that would already be established by the previous sūtras, there would be no additional matter to be propounded; thus, the intention is that sūtras such as "because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*) would be rendered redundant.

If it is argued that the specific nature (*svarūpaviśeṣa*) is not established, is the nature itself the specific feature, or is it a specific feature of the nature? In the first case, the previously mentioned defect applies. In the second case, Brahman would possess specific features (*saviśeṣatva*). In response to the doubt that since Brahman was established in the preceding sūtras as being the cause, but not in its conscious form, the sūtras beginning with "Because of seeing" (*īkṣateḥ*) ought to be commenced, [the author], accepting that Brahman is to be presented in its conscious form, says: "And that... (*tac ca*).

He clarifies the nature of consciousness (*caitanyatva*) in order to state that the exclusion of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) cannot be established unless there is an absence of the quality of consciousness: "What is called consciousness... Here, the word "quality" (*guṇa*) refers to a property (*dharma*). To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Therefore... The meaning is that because there would be no differentiator, the exclusion [of the *pradhāna*] would not be established. If the word "consciousness" were intended to refer merely to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the futility of beginning this section of the treatise would be self-evident. Furthermore, it does not imply equality with the *pradhāna*, since luminosity (*prakāśatva*) is admitted [for consciousness].

"Just as, in your view, there is the exclusion of non-sentience (*acidvyāvṛtti*) for knowledge that has become the self or its attributes—even though it cannot be related to another knowledge—so it is here"; to this he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). To the question, "How is it difficult to establish? he says, "For illumination... (*prakāśo hi*). "Fitness for linguistic usage" (*vyavahārayogyatā*) means being the counter-correlative (*pratisambandhitā*) of linguistic usage. The meaning is: because of the absence of both forms—that is, because of the absence of being the cause of its own linguistic usage and the cause of the linguistic usage of another. Now, he raises the doubt regarding the capacity for both: "If it possesses both... (*tadubhaya...*).

Having conceded that this [position] is tenable, he states the refutation with "That is not so. He says "Now" (*atha*) in order to show the lack of an alternative for the opponent. He responds with "Alas, then! (*hanta tarhi*). He states that such tenability does not exist at all with "And if there were capacity," etc. The meaning is: if a specific effect lacks proof, then there is an absence of the fitness to establish the distinction between self and other; and in the absence of a defining agent (*nirūpaka*), there is an absence of the thing to be defined (*nirūpya*). Even though its status as a real entity (*vastutva*) is possible, its similarity to *pradhāna* has been stated.

Now, [the author] says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) to show that reality itself (*vastutva*) is not established. Reality consists in being excluded from the void (*tuccha*). Why? To this he says: "by perception" (*pratyakṣa*). Although self-experience (*svānubhava*) is included within perception, its status as a separate means of knowledge is stated here by way of accepting the view of others. "Having particulars as their object" (*saviśeṣagocarāḥ*) means, in fact, having real objects possessing particulars as their domain. Reality is common to both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). And that [reality] consists in being excluded from the void; the meaning is that this is not established.

After refuting the opposing position, he concludes his own position with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). However, the following interpretation of the Sūtra offered by others is not appropriate: "Pradhāna is not what is to be propounded, for it is 'non-scriptural' (*aśabda*); that is, it cannot be propounded by the Word (the Veda), and because [the Sūtra] mentions 'seeing' (*īkṣati*) and so forth, it is incapable [of propounding it]. This is incorrect because one must supply a word in the thesis-statement (*pratijñāvākya*) that establishes the subject (*dharmin*), and because even when it is said "for it is non-scriptural," there remains an expectancy for a further reason.

In the sūtras such as "Not [the Self] through inference, because of the word 'that'" (*nānumānamatacchabdāt*) and "Some [say there is] also that which is inferential" (*ānumānikamapy ekeṣām*), just like the words "inferential" (*ānumānika*) and so forth, the word "not-scriptural" (*aśabda*) is also capable of presenting the subject (*dharmin*) by way of its etymological meaning; thus, since it does not require supplementation (*adhyāhāra*), it is established that the very seed of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—consisting of the apprehension of the form of inference—is manifested by the sūtra itself through its own component power (*avayava-śakti*). Therefore, the interpretation favored by the author of the Bhāṣya is more excellent, having relied on the fact that in the sūtra "If [it be argued it is] figurative, no, because of the word 'Self'" (*gauṇaścen nātmaśabdāt*), the word "Self" (*ātmaśabda*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, it is also untenable to claim that the act of seeing is non-figurative because, having mentioned the *jīva*, [the Self] is designated as the very nature of that which is denoted by the word "Real" (*sat*); for that [Self] cannot possibly possess figurative seeing, and because this contradicts the intended meaning of the Sūtra. Indeed, it was not stated [in the Sūtra], "If it were figurative, [it would not be so] because of the word *jīva*," that the word *ātman*—when referring to the essential nature—is dependent [on something else]; for without its co-occurrence with a term denoting the *jīva*, the word *ātman* lacks the capacity to exclude non-sentient matter (*acid-dravya*).

However, the word *ātman* refers primarily to consciousness (*cetanā*). By demonstrating that this entire phenomenal world, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, has the Self as its essence in the statement, "All this has that as its Self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*), it is utterly free from any further expectation regarding the exclusion of the unconscious. Therefore, since the indication of a reason for being free from expectation is superior even to the indication of a reason for having an expectation, the meaning of that Sūtra also is exactly as stated.

Since the word *ātman*, which denotes the inner self of the entire world consisting of both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), cannot be suspected of being figurative—because, unlike the expression "Bhadrasena is my *ātman*," there is no impossibility of its primary meaning—it is not figurative; and because it does not depend on any other sentence as a statement of a proposition (*pratijñā*), it is appropriate that the third *sūtra* also expresses the reason for the ultimate probandum.

Since the Śvetāśvatara passage is already included by the very sūtra on the uniformity of approach (*gatisāmānya*), which demonstrates the unanimity of all Vedānta texts, it is improper to rely on the Śvetāśvatara passage as the subject matter of the sūtra [“*śrutatvāt*"].

As for what was stated by the followers of Yādavaprakāśa—that the phrase "endowed with the Existent" (satā saṃpannaḥ) expresses merely the attainment of the Existent and not identity—even if the word *sat* refers to the Pradhāna, the state of being "endowed with" it is possible; and as for the "dissolution in itself" (*svāpyaya*), this is taught in the *Gatisāmānya-sūtra* to refute the doubt that the dissolution of all individual souls might occur separately within themselves, by showing that in deep sleep there is a single object to be reached by all souls, and therein their attainment of oneness.

And as for the scriptural passage regarding the object [of the analogy], namely: "Just as, my dear, honey-makers collect the juices from various trees and reduce those juices to a single unity, and just as those juices do not distinguish themselves there, thinking 'I am the juice of this tree' or 'I am the juice of that tree,' even so, my dear, all these creatures, having merged into Being, do not know [this]"—that too is incorrect. For instance:

Does the passage beginning with "having attained [the Being]" (*sati sampadya*), which conveys unity supported by an illustrative example, exclude the primacy of the *pradhāna* by relying on its being the cause, or without relying on its being the cause? In the first case, the Sūtra on the uniformity of interpretation (*gatisāmānya*) would be redundant, because the exclusion of the *pradhāna*'s primacy would already be established by the Sūtra on deep sleep (*svāpyaya*), since deep sleep consists in the attainment of the state of being the cause. Furthermore, there would be an inconsistency regarding the illustrative example, as it has not been shown that many tastes dissolve into a single cause.

For in that case, what is observed is simply the attainment of a common flavor among the flavorful parts by way of their sweetness. And as for the second [alternative], what kind of unity of the individual souls (jīvas) could exclude the primacy of the Existent (sat)? It cannot be an unity of the Existent through the abandonment of their status as individual souls, because you do not admit the abandonment of the state of being a soul, and because it would contradict the scriptural texts on the eternity of the soul, such as: "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman), he knows nothing without nor within"—referring to the ignorant soul at that time.

Furthermore, this is because it contradicts the scriptural teaching that [the soul] is presided over by the Intelligent One (prājña), and because the experience of the fruits of established karma and so forth would again be untenable. Nor is there oneness in the form of existence (sadrūpa), for since that exists even during the waking state, as in that case, there would be no contradiction between the individual souls' abiding in their own nature and their primary contact [with the Supreme] during sleep; thus, your desired conclusion is not established.

Nor can there be oneness through the absence of the conceit of internal and external conceptual distinctions such as godhood, humanity, passion, and hatred; for even that [oneness] does not establish the exclusion of its own essential nature from the primary [state], since the coexistence of abiding in one's own essential nature and the state of being the substratum of manifestation and dissolution is not contradictory. Therefore, because either the suspicion of the futility of the Sūtra or the failure to resolve it must necessarily occur, it is improper to maintain that the Sūtra has the meaning asserted by the opponent.

Furthermore, the collection of passages beginning with the statement of the proposition in the sūtra *śrutatvāt* (because it is so stated in scripture), such as "This is that subtle essence" (*sa eṣo 'ṇimā*) and "This is its nature" (*aitadātmyam*), which were taken as the subject matter [of the objection], is also untenable; for it would contradict the initial proposition and result in redundancy with the words of the sūtras such as "Not so, because of the word 'Self'" (*nātmaśabdāt*). Therefore, the meaning of the sūtras is exactly as previously stated.

Now, he states the connection between the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) and the preceding one with the words, "Thus, of that which has been sought to be known. Once it has been established by the four aphorisms (*catussūtrī*) that the cause of the world is to be defined, [the opponent] first resorts to the non-conscious [nature], because of its superior renown as being established through perception and other means. Then, having turned away from that non-conscious [nature] by means of [the attributes of] "seeing" and so forth, the intellect is directed toward a conscious entity. Now, although the internal self (*pratyagātman*)—established by the notion of "I"—is less renowned than the non-conscious [nature], it is more renowned than the Supreme Self; therefore, the meaning is that the intellect is now turned away from that [internal self].

"Consisting of bliss, because of repetition. Since the passage concerning the cause, "From this very Self," will be cited later by way of raising an objection and its resolution, the text beginning with "That indeed is this person" is first introduced as the starting point for the explanation of the word "Self. For this very reason, the passage beginning with "From this very [Self]" is cited in another section of the treatise. The intention here is that a doubt arises regarding that [bliss] on account of its being corporeal and its abundance of bliss.

In the *Sadvidyā*, the term “denoted by the word ‘jīva’” is used to indicate that the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase “by the self which is the living soul” (*jīvenātmanā*) is the seed for the arising of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The first inquiry is: Are all the Vedāntas, which teach the Cause, devoted to the nature of the perfectly pure inner Self (*pratyagātman*), or are they devoted to something different from that? For the sake of that inquiry, it is asked: Is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) the inner Self in its state of perfect purity, or is it the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)?

For that purpose, it must be investigated here whether the bodily connection established here is unique to the individual soul (jīvātman) or not. For that purpose, one must investigate whether the suffix *-maya* denotes either its own primary meaning or the sense of a modification (*vikāra*); or whether it denotes abundance (*prācurya*). For that purpose, one must investigate whether the reasons consistent with meanings such as "modification" are to be followed, or whether the reasons consistent with meanings such as "abundance" are to be followed. Finally, one must investigate whether the term *vijñānamaya* refers merely to consciousness (*vijñāna*), or whether it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*).

For that purpose, is the suffix *mayaṭ* there used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*), or not? For that purpose, does the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the passage "Consciousness performs the sacrifice" refer to mere cognition, or to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) which possesses the quality of cognition? The former alternatives are prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the others are the established conclusions (*siddhānta*).

When, because it must conform to reasons such as its having the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is either pleonastic (*svārthika*) or has the sense of a modification, then—since no unsurpassed abundance (*prācurya*) is understood and since mere bliss is possible in the individual soul (*jīva*)—there is no contradiction in the connection with a body being a characteristic unique to the individual soul as it is understood to be naturally suited to the soul; thus, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the individual soul. And when the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the verse refers to consciousness alone, then the same applies to the word "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*).
