Since the word "vijñāna" can refer to the intellect (*buddhi*) because it ends in the suffix *-maya* used in a derivative sense (*svārthika*), it is possible for it to denote the intellect; thus, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the blissful one (*ānandamaya*) that follows it must be the inner self (*pratyagātman*). This is the relationship between the conclusion and its consequence.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, when—on account of the necessity of following the reason consistent with the sense of abundance—the suffix *mayaṭ* in the term "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is taken to mean abundance, then, because that abundance of bliss is understood to be limitless, it is impossible to assume unmentioned limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that would contradict the scripture; furthermore, since such [limitless bliss] is inherently unsurpassed, it cannot exist in the individual self (*jīvātman*). Moreover, because of this contradiction, bodily connection—which is rooted in the specific karma of the individual—is not possible for the individual self. Thus, the one "consisting of bliss" is not the inner self (*pratyagātman*). And when the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in the verse...

When [the term] refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) whose quality is consciousness (*vijñāna*), then because the word *vijñānamaya* also denotes the inner self by virtue of ending in the suffix *-maya* in the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), it follows that the one within that is the *ānandamaya*, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This constitutes the relationship between cause and effect (*phala-phalibhāva*). He raises an objection against the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Now, if... (*nanu ceti*). By stating that he enumerates the *annamaya* and the others for the sake of easy comprehension, he indicates that the context concerning the cause of the world (*jagatkāraṇa-prakaraṇa*) remains uninterrupted.

The meaning is that being the cause of the entire universe establishes [the Self] as the substratum of an excellence of bliss dependent upon the preeminence of its manifestations (vibhūti), as will be explained by the subsequent analysis. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "And it is the cause of the universe. The term "cause of the universe" is mentioned again in order to make known the utility of its power of knowledge. He refutes [the objection]: "True," [we grant] the admission [of its existence] regarding its sentience and so forth; however, there is dispute concerning its distinction from the individual soul (jīva).

Let there be the designation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); what follows from that regarding the lack of distinction from the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this he says: "Grammatical coreferentiality. Regarding the claim that its distinction from the individual soul is stated because of the hearing of the term "seeing" (*īkṣati*), he says: "Seeing. The particle *eva* (indeed) indicates a lack of natural appropriateness [in that interpretation]. The sense is that being a witness (*sākṣitva*) alone constitutes being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*).

By stating "and because of the designation of difference" (*bhedavyapadeśācca*)—thereby citing the designation of difference as the reason for the final conclusion (*siddhānta*)—it is understood that the author of the Sūtras intended the designation of identity (*aikyavyapadeśa*) to serve as the reason for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Thus, due to the logical necessity of its arising and by virtue of the reason stated in the Sūtra, the designation of identity is presented as the reason for the prima facie position. The sense is that, since the distinction from the individual soul (*jīva*) was not established by the preceding section, a new section must be commenced.

An objection may be raised: in the passage "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," Brahman is heard as that which is to be attained (*prāpya*); subsequently, its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is stated, wherein truthfulness (*satyatva*) and infinity (*ānantya*) are included. Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is eternally attained, it is illogical for it to be the object of attainment; and since it is already known, its definition need not be stated. Furthermore, specific characteristics such as truthfulness and infinity are not possible for a limited knowledge that is uniform in nature. Therefore, the Supreme Self alone is what is being propounded. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Therefore, [the text says] 'the knower of Brahman'."

Therefore, the meaning is that because the state of being embodied is heard [in scripture] and because oneness is established through the force of grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya), it must be inferred that the text aims at the attainment of the essential nature (svarūpa) as dissociated from the non-sentient (acit). He says "dissociated from the non-sentient" to show that both the statement of the definition and the description of its specific qualities are possible only in that essential nature dissociated from the non-sentient. He says "of that form" to indicate that the state of being the object of attainment for the essential nature dissociated from the non-sentient follows not only from the force of the grammatical coordination with the state of being embodied, but is also explicitly stated.

The word *hi* indicates what is well-known from the Śruti; alternatively, it suggests the natural force of the term *mokṣa* (liberation) as being merely the cessation of adventitious forms while the essential nature remains. He shows the very Śruti passage with the words "na ha vā..."—the phrase "because of such hearing" is to be supplied. Finally, he concludes by demonstrating that [liberation] possesses the status of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) consistent with its being something to be attained, using the words "ataḥ" (therefore).

[Objection: Is it not the case that here the nature of the individual soul (jīva) as dissociated from the non-intelligent (acid) is not being taught, because of the mention of its connection with a body in the passage, "That indeed is this person consisting of the essence of food," and because of the mention of its being unlimited bliss? To this, he says, "For thus... The meaning is: the body is merely an indicative mark (upalakṣaṇa), not a qualifying attribute (viśeṣaṇa); therefore, by means of its dissociation [from the body], its state of being unlimited bliss and so forth is being taught.

And regarding the phrase "the intellect which is situated within that": since the suffix *mayaṭ* in the terms *prāṇamaya* and *manomaya* has its own primary meaning (*svārthika*), the *mayaṭ* in *vijñānamaya* is likewise *svārthika*. This is because [the text] will later state, "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) performs the sacrifice," without employing the suffix *mayaṭ*; furthermore, because the words *buddhi* and *vijñāna* are used interchangeably as having the same meaning in such passages as "But know the charioteer to be the intellect (*buddhi*)" and "But know the intellect (*vijñāna*) to be the charioteer. The sense is that *vijñāna* is the intellect (*buddhi*), based on the etymological derivation: "that by which one cognizes (*vijñāyate*) is *vijñāna*."

Regarding the question of why there is an instruction beginning with "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and so forth, he says: "for the purpose of facilitating the entry of the intellect into each respective stage. It is established by implication that even the state of being unlimited bliss is possible for the nature of the completely pure Self.

The summary of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because of the scriptural mention of being embodied; because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*); because the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); because attributes such as being an object to be attained are possible even for the pure essential nature; because it is possible for the soul to be attained in its nature as dissociated from the body by taking that body as a mere secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*); and because the suffix *-maya* is used in its primary sense (*svārthika*) and thus does not imply a modification (*vikāra*), this sentence has as its subject the pure nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). In this regard, two reasons are conclusive (*sādhaka*), while the others are merely intended to refute potential objections or establish alternative interpretations.

Thus, standing on the side of the proponents of falsehood (the Mṛṣāvādins), he challenges the Sāṅkhya opponent who maintains that the word *ānandamaya* refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*), saying: "But surely... The meaning is this: from the phrase "its tail" (*tasya puccham*), the genitive case indicates a relationship between the whole and its part; since such a relationship resides in two relata, there is an understanding of distinction (*vyatireka*) by way of the relation between the support (*pratiṣṭhā*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*), and thus there is otherness. He refutes this, saying: "Not so."

It was stated that [Brahman] is "characterized by being in the form of a person" for the purpose of recalling the scriptural statement, "Following him, he becomes of human form. It is characterized by being in the form of a person. He establishes its non-difference [from the preceding] with the word "just as": since in this context it is seen that [the Self] is characterized by having the tail as its support through its own parts which are not different from itself, here too the meaning is that Brahman, characterized as the tail and support, is not different from the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).

The meaning is that the use of the genitive case is justified because it is based on the relationship between a whole and its parts. Now, one might object: "In the passage 'Bliss is the Self,' bliss is described as the whole (the possessor of parts), not as a part; so how can it be said that 'joy, delight, and supreme bliss' are described as its parts? This is not a fault, because the word "Self" (ātman) does not denote itself [as a mere part].

Indeed, the middle portion of the body is what is denoted by the word "Self" (ātman), as seen in such usage as: "The ten fingers, the ten toes, the two thighs, the two arms—the twenty-five-fold Self. For this very reason, the natural force of the genitive case in the expression "bliss is the Self of that" (*tasyānanda ātmā*) is established; therefore, bliss is described as being the middle portion. But even so, would it not follow that Brahman is accepted as being designated as the "tail"?

What follows from that? What, then, is to be refuted? It is the non-Brahmanhood of the *ānandamaya*; therefore, by means of its refutation, the inclusion of the "tail" within it is stated. He states another reason with the words "if, moreover. An objection is raised: "But surely, because of the statement 'from this *ānandamaya* there is another inner self, which is Brahman,' the difference must be expressed precisely as an inner self; is there not a fixed rule [to that effect]? Anticipating this doubt—that difference can be established through other distinguishing characteristics, just as in the cases of "the Self distinct from the impeller" or "the Lord of the universe"—he says: "This has been stated."

The meaning is that since the context is intent upon establishing distinctness precisely through their mutual internal relationship, a statement situated within that context must be of such a nature. In response to the doubt—namely, how it is understood that the word *ātman* has been explained by the scripture itself—it is stated, "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]," and so forth; this is done both to show that the explanation of one's own statement is established by the context itself, and because it is useful for proving that what is designated by the word *ātman* is indeed Brahman.

In this context, the explanation of the word *brahman* is completed in the passage beginning with "truth, knowledge," and the explanation of the word *ātman* is completed in the section concerning the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Consequently, when the doubt arises as to whether the status of being *brahman* belongs to the one consisting of bliss alone, [the author] shows that the very subject under discussion denoted by the word *brahman* is what is pointed out by the word *ātman*, stating: "That very same [is this]. The intention is that the words *tat* and *etat* refer back to the subject previously introduced. Again, he raises an objection: "But surely..."

In the preceding verses, it was observed that those subjects beginning with the *annamaya*, which were primarily discussed, were referred to by their respective specific terms; likewise, if the *ānandamaya* were the primary subject here, it too should have been referred to by its own specific term in the verse concerning it. Alternatively, if the explanation of the word "Self" (*ātman*) had reached its conclusion regarding the *ānandamaya*, then it should have been referred to by the word "Self"; however, this was not done, but rather it was referred to by the word "Brahman."

Therefore, the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not the primary subject; hence, the meaning is that Brahman alone, as the "tail," is the principal thing to be established. Anticipating the objection that there is no fault in designating it with the word "Brahman" once it has been established that the word "Brahman" refers to the one consisting of bliss, he offers another argument while implicitly resolving that doubt: "Nor [is there a fault] regarding the one consisting of bliss... By the word "objection" (*āśaṅkā*), the meaning contained within the two scriptural passages cited has been explained.

The meaning is that since something well-known to the whole world cannot be denied, it is improper to raise a doubt regarding its existence as if it were non-existent; even when its existence is certain. He refutes this with "not so. Having understood clearly that once the identity of the words *brahman*, *ātman*, and *ānandamaya* is established, the mention of the word *brahman* is equivalent to the mention of the word *ānandamaya*, he states the reasoning for the primacy of the *ānandamaya* with the words "this is the tail."

The meaning is that, since the preceding verses in this context do not have the purpose of establishing the tail alone, this verse as well does not have the purpose of establishing the tail alone. He removes the objection regarding the impossibility of doubting the existence or non-existence of the well-known bliss by saying, "of the one consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*). Then, intending to employ a counter-argument (*pratibandī*), he says, "of the Brahman-tail as well."

When it is objected that—since Brahman’s nature as bliss has been stated in such passages as “Brahman is consciousness and bliss” (*vijñānamānandaṃ brahma*) and “Bliss is Brahman” (*ānando brahma*), and since bliss is well-known—the doubt regarding its existence or non-existence is not appropriate; [the reply is: you must establish that Brahman, whose nature is bliss, is unknown precisely because its bliss is unlimited (*aparicchinna*). This point is the same here as well. [The opponent] objects: “One suspects the head and so forth. [The author] refutes this: “Of Brahman... Being a “tail” means being a specific limb.

"Being the foundation" (*pratiṣṭhātva*) means being the substratum (*ādhāratva*). If it is argued that it is untenable for Brahman to have parts (*avayavin*), the meaning is that having parts (*avayavatva*) is likewise untenable. He raises the objection that "having parts" is merely a figurative representation (*rūpaṇamātra*) with the word "Now" (*atha*). He refutes this with "Alas, then" (*hanta tarhi*). "Because of not being pleasure" (*asukhāt*) means that specific exclusions from what is not-pleasure are represented as the head and so forth. To the question, "Since the state of being excluded from everything else is already established by the statement 'Truth, Knowledge,' etc., what is accomplished here?", he replies with "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

Since Brahman, which is designated by the word "Truth" (satya), cannot be a modification of anything else, it is also incorrect to claim that it is denoted by the term "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya); to this, he says, "And therefore" (tataśca). This means: because the aforementioned logical inconsistencies have been resolved, and because there exist other supporting arguments.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because the causal reality is designated by the masculine pronoun *saḥ* (He) in the sentence "He desired," the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) must be the Supreme Brahman—and that this masculine designation refers to the Self indicated by the word "Self" in the passage "From this very Self"—we say no; for since that which is proximate is to be grasped rather than that which is remote, it is the one consisting of bliss who is to be understood here. This is because the phrase "His very Self is this, the embodied one" (*tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā*) is recited immediately after the statement "Brahman is the tail, the support."

If it is argued that the word *ātman* occurring in the phrase *itivākya* refers to the [Self] because there is no intervening element, and thus the masculine designation *saḥ* (he) is used with that intention, whereas the *ānandamaya* is not referred to by it because it is separated from this sentence—this is not so;

for since the *ātman* occurring in the sentence *tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā* is common to all the sections (*paryāya*), this particular section is not its primary subject of exposition, and because it is the natural function of a pronoun to refer to the primary subject, the word *saḥ* refers precisely to the *ānandamaya*.

In the passages, "He understood Brahman to be consciousness" and "He understood Brahman to be bliss," as well as in the passages, "having reached the self consisting of consciousness" and "having reached the self consisting of bliss," one understands through the authority of their context that the words *ānanda* (bliss) and *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) have the same meaning; furthermore, since it is well known that the word *ānanda* refers to the Supreme Brahman, the *ānandamaya* is the Supreme Brahman.

Nor should it be said that in the passage "Bliss is Brahman," the word *ānanda* (bliss) likewise refers to an external sheath, as does the word *ānandamaya*; for, unlike after the cognitions "Food is Brahman" and "Breath is Brahman," there is no further approach of Bhṛgu to Varuṇa after the cognition "Bliss is Brahman. Indeed, it is not heard again that "Having understood that, he once more approached his father Varuṇa."

This is what is meant: In the passage, "He understood that food is Brahman," is it stated that there is a realization of Brahman indicated by food and so forth; or is it the introduction of the notion of Brahman into that which consists of food and the rest? In the first case, there would be no approach to Varuṇa after the knowledge that "food is Brahman," because Brahman would have already been apprehended through that which serves as its indicator. In the second case, however, the notion of Brahman directed toward bliss would be in accordance with reality, since there would be no further approach to Varuṇa.

Furthermore, you yourselves have explained that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) in the passage "Bliss is Brahman" refers to Brahman; for Śaṃkara has stated: "In the case of the Bhārgava-Vāruṇī knowledge—'He understood that bliss is Brahman'—since the suffix *mayaṭ* is not heard there, and since [qualities] such as 'having joy as its head' are not heard, it is appropriate that bliss is Brahman."

And therefore, since the sentence "Brahman is bliss" refers to the Supreme Self, by the authority of its context (*sthānapramāṇa*), the word "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) in the passage "the self consisting of bliss" must also refer to the Supreme Self. Furthermore, it should be understood that the "consisting of bliss" is to be purified in the sense of removing the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and other such [defects] consistent with that [nature]. Anticipating the objection—"If the very nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is indeed the form of unlimited bliss, how is it that the gradations of suffering and happiness among individual souls (*jīva*) are perceived?"—he concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Therefore... (tasmāt).

Because the genitive case in the word *tasya* ("of him"), which expresses a relationship, conveys a sense of distinction; because the subsequent verse concerning Brahman does not have the *ānandamaya* as its subject, it is understood that the Brahman described as the "tail" is indeed the primary subject; because it is illogical to entertain doubts regarding the existence or non-existence of the *ānandamaya*—which is known in the world through forms such as pleasure (*priya*) and joy (*moda*)—since it would then lack a basis for such inquiry; because it is impossible for the partless Supreme Self to possess limbs; and because it is impossible for the changeless to undergo modification; [the text states]: "Of that, this very one is the embodied self."

Thus, because the other self understood from the passage concerning the *ānandamaya* must be the Supreme Self, it is illogical for the *ānandamaya* itself to be the Supreme Self; and because the state of being purified—as heard in the scripture, "May my *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya* be purified"—is incompatible with the eternally pure Supreme Self, the *ānandamaya* is not the Supreme Self. Rather, Brahman alone, which is indicated as the "tail," is the Supreme Self. This is the summary of the reasons for the doctrine that Brahman is the tail (*pucchabrahmavāda*).

Since this section is devoted to the metaphorical representation of the head, wings, and so forth by means of its own constituent parts which are not distinct from itself, the explanation of the word *ātman* as being internal to that [section] culminates in the *ānandamaya*. Furthermore, because the verses situated within this section concerning the *annamaya* and others have the tail as their subject matter, the immediately following sentence, "He desired" (*so 'kāmayata*), which establishes [Brahman's] causality, must refer to the *ānandamaya* alone—which is proximate to it—by the pronoun *saḥ*, ending in the masculine gender, which refers back to the primary subject under discussion.

Because it is logical; for the word *ānanda* is accepted as referring to Brahman in the passage "Brahman is bliss" (*ānando brahma*), and since the words *ānanda* and *ānandamaya* have the same meaning—as seen in "He understood that Brahman is bliss" (*ānando brahmeti vyajānāt*) and "having approached the Self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamayam ātmānam upasaṅkramya*)—the word *ānandamaya* also refers to the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, because no mention is heard of Varuṇa’s approach after the knowledge of Brahman denoted by the word *ānanda* (which has the same meaning as *ānandamaya*), and in accordance with the natural sense of the Sūtra, [the Self] consists of its own parts which are not distinct from itself.

Since it is appropriate to understand the use of the genitive case as being based on the relationship between a whole and its parts—given that it conforms to the context of the subsequent section which describes [Brahman] in the form of a head, wings, tail, and so forth—it is logical that any one of the terms *ānandamaya*, *ātman*, or *brahman* should be used in the verse concerning them, as they all share the same referent. Furthermore, because unlimited bliss (*aparicchinna-ānanda*) is not well-known, there arises a doubt regarding its existence or non-existence, similar to the doubt concerning the existence of the "tail-Brahman" accepted in the statement "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānando brahma*). Therefore, just as it is described as a part, it is likewise described as a whole.

Regarding the statement that [Brahman] is "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) because of the possibility of transformation (*rūpaṇa*), there is no contradiction with the changelessness of Brahman, since the suffix *mayaṭ* here does not denote a modification (*vikāra*), whether it is taken in its own primary sense (*svārthika*) or in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). Furthermore, the sentence "This is indeed His embodied self" (*tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā*) is intended to establish that [the blissful self] is non-different from the Self. In the mantra "May my self consisting of food, the self consisting of vital breath, the self consisting of mind, the self consisting of consciousness, and the self consisting of bliss be purified," purification refers to the performance of duties appropriate to each respective entity; thus, this applies to the position that [the *ānandamaya*] is the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

This is a summary of the arguments for refuting the doctrine that the "tail-Brahman" (puccha-brahman) is distinct from the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). Because it is to be purified by the removal of saṃsāra, and because, on the view of its being distinct, the state of being purified—which consists in the pacification of impurity and is accomplished through surrender (prapadana)—is logically possible only for the Blessed One, the tail-Brahman is not distinct from the one consisting of bliss; thus, the one consisting of bliss alone is the Supreme Self. Among these, the first group of six reasons establishes the final conclusion (siddhānta), while the other group of reasons is intended to refute the arguments raised by the opposing side.

When this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been established, he introduces the sūtra of the final conclusion (siddhānta) with the words, "Thus [the view] having been reached. Therein, completing the portion of the proposition (pratijñā) with the word that conveys the thing to be proven, he explains it as "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya). In the subsequent section, the word "other" (anya) is employed in the phrase "And because of the designation of difference, [He is] other"; here, the meaning obtained by drawing that [word] back is stated as "the Supreme Self" (paramātman).

Alternatively, he states the meaning obtained by supplying the two words *na* and *aśabdam* from the two preceding sūtras (*pūrvādhikaraṇa-sūtra*) to the word *paramātma*: "That which has no verbal testimony as its means of knowledge is indeed *aśabda* (non-verbal). Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is established through self-luminous perception, inference, and so forth, its being *aśabda* is also logically consistent. As it is said in the *Ātmasiddhi*: "Thus the Self, being established by itself, shines forth clearly through scripture, through inference, and through the perception born of the practice of yoga."

Alternatively, with the intention that the probandum portion (*sādhyāṃśa*)—namely "not the other" (*netaraḥ*)—found in the very sūtra of this section is intended here as well, he says "the Supreme Self" (*paramātmeti*). The designation of the subject (*dharmin*) by the term "Supreme Self" is intended to indicate the culmination of the series of "inner selves. Since the state of consisting of bliss (*ānandamayatva*) is perceived in the scripture through repetition (*abhyāsa*), he asks "Why? (*kutaḥ*) to demonstrate the requirement for a reason regarding the probandum, thereby dispelling the doubt that the reason might be stated in reference to the state of consisting of bliss itself.

[Objection: Surely, since the designation of difference, being more manifest as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), serves as an independent reason and is situated within the very same passage, that alone should be stated first; it should not be the repetition found in another passage, which depends upon corroborative reasoning. [Reply: Not so.

Because of the designation of difference found within its own statement, and because the suffix *mayaṭ*—which denotes abundance—is dependent on a corroboration that is nonetheless more proximate [to the subject], it is proper to state first that repetition (*abhyāsa*) alone, which culminates in the unsurpassed state and serves as the explanation thereof, is the cause. Filling the expectation of "from the repetition of what?", he explains the word "cause" with the passage: "This very [repetition] of bliss... Repetition means counting or recurrence.

With the meaning of the passage "from which words turn back" in mind, it was stated that [the bliss] culminates in a state beyond all comparison (*niratiśaya-daśāśiraska*). With the meaning of the sentence "That is one measure of the bliss of Brahman" in mind, it was stated that it is "being repeated" (*abhyasyamāna*), because it is multiplied in a sequence of hundredfold increments.

If one were to accept that the sentence "That is one measure of the bliss of Brahman" refers to the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā (*caturmukha*), while the sentence beginning with "from which words turn back" refers specifically to the bliss of Brahman, then the reason "because of repetition" (*abhyāsāt*) would be irrelevant (*vyadhikaraṇatā*).

Furthermore, this word *brahman* denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because the word *brahman* has its primary application (*mukhyatva*) only in reference to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*). This is because in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]" (*brahmavidāpnoti*) and "Brahman exists" (*asti brahmeti*), the word *brahman* is employed specifically with reference to the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*). Moreover, in the preceding and following sentences—"From which words turn back"—the word *brahman*, ending in the superlative suffix (*iṣṭhan*) and denoting that which is related to bliss (*ānanda*), is seen to refer to the Supreme Brahman, as in the statement: "This is the inquiry into that bliss. (*saiṣānandasya mīmāṃsā*)

Because a conclusion regarding the bliss of Brahman under discussion is required, the word *tat* (That) in the immediately following sentence—"And that which is this in the person"—which refers back to what was under discussion, determines that the word *brahman* in the preceding sentence refers to the Supreme Brahman; otherwise, it would follow that the four-faced Brahmā is the inner self of all and the ultimate cause, [a conclusion contradicted] by the introduction of the verse concerning the bliss of the Blessed Lord with the words, "On this there is also this verse."

This is because [the passage] does not depend on the context of the bliss of the Blessed Lord; because the word *prajāpati* without an epithet has its natural application (*svarasa*) in reference to the Four-faced One (Brahmā); because there is no natural fitness for the singular number if it were intended to refer to Dakṣa and others; and because in this context, the plural number is employed for many individuals—as in "of the gods," "of the divine Gandharvas"—while the singular number is used for each individual entity, as in "of Indra" and "of Bṛhaspati."

Likewise, because it shares the same meaning as the passage from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "That which is the bliss of Prajāpati in the world—[the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and undisturbed by desire—is a hundredfold greater than that; and that which is the bliss of Brahmā in the world—[the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and undisturbed by desire—is a hundredfold greater than that; this indeed is the supreme bliss, this is the world of Brahmā, O Emperor," it is established that the statement "That is the one bliss of Brahman" refers to the bliss of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Nor [is this conclusion undermined] by the designation "that one."

The statement regarding the limited nature of Brahmā’s bliss refers merely to its relative superiority, as that is the intended purport of the sentence. This is just as the sentence, “He moves like a discharged arrow,” aims at negating the slowness of the sun’s motion rather than asserting equality with an arrow, since it is established by authoritative means of knowledge that the sun traverses many *yojanas* in the mere twinkling of an eye; likewise, here too, because the state of having unlimited bliss is established through the preceding and following sentences, it is understood that the sentence “That is one” intends to express the superiority [of that bliss] over the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā.

Or rather: "Infinite universes revolve within your pores. "Thousands upon thousands of universes, tens of thousands, and likewise hundreds of millions upon millions of such [universes] are there; like the stream of sand from the Ganges when it rains during the day."

"The grandfathers (pitāmahas) who have passed away cannot be counted in this world," and so forth—since from such passages we understand that the cosmic eggs (*aṇḍas*) and their respective four-faced lords (*caturmukhas*) are innumerable, and since it is stated that the Controller possesses a hundredfold the bliss of those who are controlled, it follows as a matter of course that the Blessed Lord, whose bliss is understood to be a hundredfold greater than that of the innumerable four-faced ones, possesses unlimited bliss. Therefore, the meaning is exactly as stated. Regarding the word "being practiced" (*abhyasyamāna*), the intention is that the term *abhyāsa* ends in the suffix *ghañ*, which denotes the action itself.

Alternatively, even though *ānanda* has the sense of a state of being (*bhāva*), the fact that it is multiplied (*abhyasta*) is what is intended by the term; this is stated in order to dispel the suspicion that the reason [for its increase] might belong to a different category. Now, "multiplication" means increasing; for the bliss of Prajāpati increases by a factor of a hundred, whereas the bliss of Brahman does not. True; nevertheless, the statement is made figuratively, meaning that the bliss of Prajāpati itself, when multiplied, is the bliss of Brahman—just as one says, "four handfuls of rice have been multiplied."

The meaning is that *brahmānanda* (the bliss of Brahman) is being presented as a single part, similar to those various multiplied joys. Alternatively, "repetition" (*abhyāsa*) refers to the repeated mention [of the joys], by which the presence of the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*) is suggested. [An objection is raised: "Let it be that bliss is unlimited; what follows from that? To this he replies: "by endless suffering" (*anantaduḥkha*). By this, the connection with a quality contrary to unsurpassed bliss is stated. By "limited" (*parimita*), the absence of unsurpassed bliss is stated.

The meaning is that [the opponent's position] is impossible because of the perception of contradictory attributes and the perception of non-existence. How is it impossible? Regarding the scriptural statement that the liberated one possesses unlimited bliss (*aparicchinna-ānandatva*), the author says: "Of all that is to be discarded... Here, "antagonism" (*pratyanīkatva*) is intended to mean "that which causes cessation. For even for the liberated one, the attainment of unsurpassed bliss preceded by the cessation of everything to be discarded occurs only through the grace of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). However, in this context, unlimited bliss is understood as belonging to [Brahman] inherently, because no cause is heard [in scripture], and because it is impossible to postulate a cause that would contradict the scriptural hearing of its unsurpassed nature.

Furthermore, the liberated soul does not possess unlimited bliss by its own nature, because of scriptural texts stating that it is dependent on the Supreme Self: "Then he becomes fearless," "For He alone causes bliss," and "Having obtained the essence (rasa), he indeed becomes blissful. Indeed, the bliss of the Supreme Self is not heard in scripture to be dependent on another; for in the passage, "And [the bliss] of one learned in the Vedas and unaffected by desire," the liberated soul is mentioned separately. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied the Vedānta.

One who is "unstruck by desire" (*akāmahata*) is one from whom all afflictions have ceased through meditation; as another scriptural passage states: "And he who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and unstruck by desire. Furthermore, because the liberated soul lacks involvement in the governance of the world, the possession of unsurpassed bliss belongs to the Supreme Self alone by its very nature. Thus, it is established that the term *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) refers to the Supreme Self, supported by the reasoning that such unsurpassed bliss is incompatible with the individual soul (*jīvātman*).

It is not only because it is favored by the inherent power of the reality whose nature is unsurpassed bliss that its distinction is understood; he says, "as he said," to show that this distinction is also explicitly stated. Now, one might object: "This is indeed the subject passage for the sutra 'Because of the mention of difference' (B.S. 1.1.17). How then can this [passage], which is to be explained later, be cited here and how is its meaning established? It is replied:

The reasoning (tarka) that the unsurpassed bliss is unsuitable for the individual soul (*jīvātman*) has indeed been stated as the basis for establishing that the term *ānandamaya* refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); since this reasoning is implied by this sentence, the sentence is presented here as an indicator of it. For in this context, by the phrase "from this" (*etasmāt*), [it is understood]: "Consciousness performs the sacrifice."

Furthermore, by the preceding statement, "and he performs actions," it is intended that the individual soul (jīva) possesses specific qualities such as being subject to karma; yet, by the word *vijñānamaya*—which ends in the suffix *maya* and denotes the substratum itself—the natural form of the soul, entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and characterized by uncontracted knowledge, is shown through the primary power (*avayava-śakti*) of the term.

By this statement, it is established that even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is pure by nature, because it is a vessel for infinite suffering produced by karma, unsurpassed bliss is impossible for it; thus its distinctness from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is demonstrated. This [passage] is cited here to refute the view that the word *vijñānamaya* in this sentence refers merely to the intellect (*buddhi*), as indicated by the phrase "for he consists of consciousness" (*vijñānamayo hi*). The word *hi* (for) serves to highlight the well-known scriptural authority: "This person who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart."

Or [the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*)] may indicate the well-known fact established by perception which supports the natural sense of the word; for the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is indeed perceived of the self in the cognition "I know. Intending to show that it is unnatural for the word *vijñānamaya*—which denotes the act of knowing—to refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) based on the etymology "that by which one knows," he says, "not mere intellect" (*na buddhimātram*). He clarifies the intended meaninglessness of the suffix (*pratyaya*) by means of the suffix *mayaṭ*. Anticipating the objection that it might have its own primary sense due to the context, he says, "but in the case of 'consisting of breath' (*prāṇamaye*)," etc.

Because there is no other possible meaning due to the lack of an alternative and the abundance of modification (*vikāra*), he states the disparity in the alternative view with the words "But here... (*iha tu*). The meaning is that the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*) is possible [in this case] by the rule *tadvat*. Here, the meaning of the suffix *-mayaṭ* is not possible; for the Self has the nature of pure consciousness (*jñapti-mātra-svarūpa*), and the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*); moreover, even that does not exist in the state of liberation (*mukty-avasthā*), as he says with the word "bound" (*baddha*). A resolution was previously stated by accepting the suffix *-mayaṭ* in its own primary sense (*svārthika*) in the case of "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) and so forth.

Then, he says that very thing does not exist in the case of the "consisting of breath" (prāṇamaya) and so forth. Since the word *vijñānamaya* has the same meaning as the word *vijñāna* found in the verse concerning that subject, he asks, "How then? with the intention that the suffix *mayaṭ* here is used in its own primary sense (*svārthika*). The point is that it is not possible for consciousness to be the substratum of another consciousness. He shows the ground for the application of the word *vijñānamaya* to the knower by saying, "of the knower alone."

The particle *eva* indicates the absence of any suspected contradiction, while the word *api* refers to the commonality of the cause for both the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its attributes (*dharma*). He demonstrates that the term can also be maintained by having the same meaning as the word "knower" (*jñātṛ*) in the phrase "having knowledge as its sole [nature]" (*jñānaika-*) and so forth. To the question "What follows from this?", he says "essential nature," etc. Words that denote the defining attributes of the essential nature are words that express inseparable properties (*ayutasiddha-dharma*). He provides an example of a word accepted as falling under the principle of "form" (*ākṛti-naya*) in the phrase "cow, etc. (*gavādi*). Thus, two ways of maintaining the position have been stated through both the aphorism (*sūtra*) and reasoning (*nyāya*).

Now, he explains the two-fold resolution according to the requirements of grammar with the words "kṛtya" and so on. In the first case, the status of being the agent (*kartṛ*) must be assumed; in the second case, inclusion within a different grammatical class (*gaṇa*) must be assumed. The use of the word "resort" (*āśrayaṇa*) applies to both instances. The sense is that the term *vijñāna* should be resolved in accordance with the word *vijñānamaya*, which is more powerful because it is consistent with direct perception, because of the recognition of another scriptural passage (*śruti*), because it is heard first, because of the natural fitness of the base (*prakṛti*), and because the meaninglessness of the suffix (*pratyaya*) would otherwise be untenable.

He states another argument found within his own statement, beginning with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: "precisely because the word *vijñāna* refers to a conscious being. To the question, "Since agency in performing sacrifices and so forth is heard [in scripture], how can that which is denoted by the word *vijñāna* be conscious?", he replies: "of mere intellect" (*buddhimātrasya*). The intention is that agency belongs only to the cognizer, as established by direct scriptural texts and the Sūtras. Now, it might be argued that all things possess agency with respect to their own respective functions.

True; however, it is not merely that much which is intended here, but rather a specific agency unique to consciousness, characterized by being the substratum of effort—that is, the status of being the agent of sacrifice and so forth, as has been stated. In this regard, the natural force (*svārasya*) of the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is equal for both [the individual soul and the Supreme Self], whereas the lack of natural fit regarding the status of being the agent of sacrifice and so forth is greater in the case of the other (the individual soul).

Now, one might object: "In the case of the *annamaya* [self], where it is said 'it is eaten and it eats beings,' agency is metaphorical; likewise, since there is no difference in its being an instrument, agency could also belong metaphorically to the *buddhi*. To this he replies: "For among insentient things... The intention is as follows: when there is no subverting evidence, metaphorical usage is indeed a defect; and that defect would have to be tolerated only if it were consistent with the context (*prakaraṇa*). But there is no such consistency here, because that [metaphorical agency] is interrupted in the *prāṇamaya* and *manomaya* [sheaths].

He shows another usage [of the term] where the word *vijñāna* refers to consciousness (*cetana*) with the words "for this very reason, it is conscious. The meaning is: for this very reason, because the word *vijñāna* refers to consciousness. The point is that here no division is being made between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the non-internal organ; rather, the division is precisely between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). To the question "Why?", he says: "because of being the place of dissolution," and so forth.

The sense is that it is impossible for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is a specific modification of *acid* (intellect), to be the locus of the universe, as it is maintained by consciousness in the manner described in the passage, "O mighty-armed one, that which has become the individual soul (*jīva*) by which this world is supported"; furthermore, the Supreme [Lord] does not admit its reality. Moreover, it is improper to take the word *vijñāna* to mean pure consciousness (*saṃvit*), because of the mention of "entering" (*anupraviśya*); for the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is not accepted by the Supreme [Lord] as being something that can pervade another self.

He shows another usage [of the term] when the word *vijñāna* refers to consciousness (*cetana*) with the words "likewise" (*tathā*). Since *vijñāna* is heard in place of the word *ātman*, it is untenable for it to refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nor can the word *ātman* itself refer to the internal organ; for, just like the word *vijñāna*, it is also inherently unsuitable for that sense. Just as the etymological derivation of *vijñāna* as "that by which one knows" (*jñāyate 'nena*) is strained when applied to the substratum [the internal organ], so too the word *ātman* is inherently unsuitable for things other than consciousness.

If both terms *vijñāna* and *ātman* were taken to refer to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there would be an inconsistency for both; however, if they are taken to refer to the conscious self (*cetana*), there is an inconsistency only for the word *vijñāna*, but not for both—this is the distinction.

In this context, it is difficult for the opponent to maintain that the word *ātman* refers to the consciousness (*saṃvit*) intended by [the author], as the supreme self (*paramātman*), because in the passage "He who dwells in the self," there is mention of dwelling within another self; and since it is not established that that which pervades other selves is the supreme self. Furthermore, regarding the word *vijñāna*, which is used everywhere: if it ends in the suffix *-lyuṭ*, it must take the gender appropriate to its substantive; therefore, how could it be neuter when its object is the self? To this, he says: "Vijñānam."

The phrase "tadevam" connects the established meaning with the ultimate point to be proven. That is, by means of the arguments stated therein; the meaning is that thus the word *vijñāna* is established as referring to the conscious [self]. By demonstrating that the word *vijñāna* in the verse refers to the knower (*jñātṛ*), it has been shown that the word *vijñānamaya* also refers to the knower. Now, even though the verse itself lacks the sense of a knower, he states that the word *vijñānamaya* does refer to the knower with the words "yadyapi" (even though).

The meaning is that since the referent of the suffix *mayaṭ* is abandoned in a sentence devoid of that suffix, it should not be abandoned even in a sentence where it is present. To the question, "In that case, how can there be identity of meaning (*aikārthya*) between the Brāhmaṇa passage and the verse (*śloka*)," he says, "Just as... The verse shares identity of meaning with the former because its subject matter is a portion of the meaning stated in the preceding Brāhmaṇa passage; the meaning is that it is like the verse concerning the *annamaya*. The phrase "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*) is a restatement of the meaning of the suffix *mayaṭ* found in the Vedic sentence; "its modification" (*tadvikāra*) is its explanation.

Warding off the suspicion that the group of meanings already stated might contradict the Sūtras, and demonstrating their utility for the Sūtras that are about to be explained, he says: "All this. The meaning is that by stating the sentence, "From this very one, which consists of consciousness," the author of the Sūtras—asserting it to be a proof of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para)—speaks while keeping in mind that the word *vijñāna* refers to the knower (*jñātṛ*) and its justification.

In the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), two reasons were stated: the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*) and the scriptural mention of being embodied (*śārīratva*). Therein, in order to demonstrate that this coreferentiality actually implies difference, [the author] refutes the prima facie reason—which was restated in the passage beginning with "that which was said" and ending with "is taught"—by stating, "That is incorrect."

Since non-difference is established through the cognition of the superimposition of contradictory attributes—both by means of the sentences relevant to the context and by the nominal stems of the words in grammatical apposition—the opponent’s reason is like a "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) reason; it does not prove the probandum. To state this refutation, [the author] shows the establishment of difference—which contradicts the unity favored by the opponent—by means of the contextual sentences that provide the specific particulars denoted by those terms, beginning with the words "of the individual soul" (jīvasya).

The meaning is that the agency of creation is untenable for one who is bound, because during the state of dissolution—when the instruments (the senses) and the body have been withdrawn—it is impossible for one subject to karma to bring about the manifold creation of the world by mere volition. To the objection that this is possible for one in a pure state, he says "pure" (śuddha). He raises a doubt to refute what has been stated: "by the cause" (kāraṇa), etc. The question is: how can there be the logical establishment of identity as understood from the identical case-endings? And how [is it so]? This means: how can there be the syntactical connection of the qualifiers as understood from the nominal stems?

By the words beginning with *nirasta* (cast off), the connection of the qualifiers understood from the nominal stem *tat-pada* is demonstrated. Since it is heard in scripture that the world was created according to His will—as in "That [Being] willed" and "It created"—the qualities such as having true volition (*satya-saṅkalpa*) are understood to be unobscured; thus, with the intention that His fitness for association with anything base or obscuring is established by implication, He is described as being "devoid of even a trace of all defects."

Intending that other qualities conducive to the governance of the world—which are explicitly mentioned elsewhere—are established here by the principle of the uniformity of application (*gatisāmānyanaya*) within the *Sadvidyā*, it is stated that [the Lord's qualities] are "unlimited" (*anavadhika*). The connection with the qualifiers understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) of the word "thou" (*tvam*) has been shown by the term "of various kinds" (*nānāvidha*). Regarding the phrase "the very nature of the individual soul" (*jīvasvarūpatvam*): this refers to identity of essence (*svarūpaikyam*) with the individual soul. Since the expression "the state of being the individual soul" (*jīvatvam*) could also imply that [Brahman] has the individual soul as its body (*jīvaśarīrakatva*), the term "the very nature of the individual soul" is used to exclude that possibility.

Intending to refute the position—directly favored by the opponent—that the two words abandon the qualifiers understood from them, [the author] raises the two possible alternatives with the words "of either one" (*anyatarasya*). This means: of either of the two qualifiers apprehended by the words *tat* and *tvam*. He poses the question "of which? (*kasya*) to provide the options. The underlying thought is that the collection of qualifiers understood from the word *tat*, being established by both perception and scripture, is difficult to abandon. With reasons and without contradiction, he anticipates the opponent’s acceptance of the first alternative with the words "contrary to what is to be abandoned" (*heyapratyanīka*).

That which is to be abandoned is suffering; false appearance is erroneous cognition. Just as a cloth inherently pure possesses a stain that is merely adventitious, or as a crystal essentially stainless appears red due to superimposition, so too the Brahman’s exclusive devotion to faultless, auspicious qualities and its connection with that which is to be abandoned are not contradictory—whether distinguished as inherent versus adventitious, or as ultimate versus non-ultimate. For the contradiction arises only if one were to admit that both [the defects and the auspicious qualities] are equally inherent and real; this is the intended objection.

"It vitiates [the argument] because it is contradictory" means that he demonstrates the contradiction by stating "being the locus of ignorance. The meaning is that not only is suffering alone to be abandoned (*heya*), but its cause, its appearance, and its manifestation are also to be abandoned. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "being related to that. The meaning is that being the locus of those things to be abandoned—namely ignorance, its effects (suffering), and their manifestations—and being the opposite of them are contradictory. He raises the objection that there is no contradiction because the relationship is false, saying: "Even so..."

"Even so" (*tathāpi*) means even though ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest are to be abandoned (*heyatve*). "Of that" refers to the relationship consisting in being the substratum (*āśrayatva-rūpa-sambandha*). He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "even though it be false" (*mithyābhūtamapi*). The meaning is that even if the state of being a substratum is false, it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). He establishes this lack of being a human goal with the words "for the purpose of whose removal" (*yannirasanāya*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "it must be removed" (*nirasaniyeti*).

This is what is meant: Is falsity (*mithyātva*) absolute non-existence, or is it the state of being sublated by knowledge? In the first case, since there would be no object to be negated, the commencement of the scripture for the purpose of such negation would be unnecessary. In the second case, does that which is false lack the status of being a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*), or not? If it does not, then because there would be no object to be discarded, the commencement of the scripture would be futile. If, on the other hand, it does lack the status of being a human goal, then the contradiction with the principle that [the scripture] must be opposed to what is to be abandoned (*heya*) is difficult to avoid.

He raises an objection, saying "What can we do?", suggesting that even if there is such a contradiction, the connection with what is to be abandoned (*heyasaṃbandha*) must still be accepted on the strength of scripture (*śruti*). He refutes this, saying "Scripture and reasoning. That which is "unreasonable" is contradicted by logic (*tarka*); that which is "contradictory" is opposed by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Examples from scripture include: "Free from evil," "Free from sorrow, free from hunger," "For he has risen above all evils," "The other, not eating," and "Being deluded, he grieves through lack of mastery."

There would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "When he perceives the other, the Lord, who is beloved," and "I take refuge in the deity who is free from suffering. There would be a contradiction with reasoning (*tarka*) because it is impossible for contradictory attributes—such as being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned and being the locus of all that is to be abandoned—to coexist in a single entity. [The opponent] raises another head [of argument] with the word "Now" (*atha*). [The author] refutes this with "Alas, if that were so" (*hantaivam iti*). The sense is that the scripture would result in a lack of purpose, which would lead to the consequence of its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). [The opponent] then raises the abandonment of both positions, which is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the other, with the words "Now, this... (*athaitad iti*).

He dismisses [the objection] with "Aho bhavatām" (Oh, of you!). This is an investigation consisting of the determination of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through two words and a sentence suitable for extracting the meaning, as well as this treatise, other treatises, the secret doctrines (*upaniṣad*), other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and reasoning (*tarka*). First, he shows the contradiction with the introduction of this treatise by saying "eka" (one). To the question, "Even if everything were real, how would it be established?", he replies with "yathaika" (just as one).

The sense is that there would be a discrepancy between the two cognitions if one had the ultimate reality as its object and the other had a false object. Regarding the phrase "and included within that": the meaning is that by means of the cognition of the assembly, the persons situated therein are indeed known, but those outside of it are not. The inclusion of the cognition within that consists in its being included within its object. Alternatively, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "everything is included within that. He establishes the point—that what has the ultimate reality as its object is included within that—by means of a negative argument (*vyatireka*), stating: "For [it is] not the case that the ultimate reality... and so forth.

For it is not the case that mother-of-pearl and silver are the objects of a single cognition; this is the point. Even though there is a difference in their states—such as oneness and totality—the knowledge of all is established through the knowledge of one because of the identity of the underlying attribute (*dharma*). For "knownness" and "totality" reside in a single substratum; indeed, totality is not defined by the form qualified by knownness, nor is knownness defined by the form qualified by totality. Even in the thought "this was already known by me," the knownness belongs to the substrate alone, and not to that which is qualified by a particular state.

[This is] due to the difference of place, time, and so forth. For it is not the case that once Brahman alone is known as the sole reality—qualified by this particular time and so on—everything else would thereby be known as false; thus [the opponent] raises the objection with the words, "Now, if it be said... [The author] refutes this with, "In that case, it would not be so... The meaning is: either it would be heard in scripture that "everything is known as false," or that "everything has ceased to exist."

And this being the case, there is the fault of having to supply (*adhyāhāra*) the word "falsity" (*mithyātvena*); there is a discordance (*vairūpya*) between the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "word" (*śabda*) because they would then refer to two different subjects (*dharmyantara*); for their natural state is to possess a single uniform form as knowledge, and that is violated; and there is the fault that [cessation] characterized by disappearance would result from the absence of the knower, the known, and the knowledge delimited by them—these three faults are intended. With the words "by which," he states that the manner of connection (*anvaya*) found in what is actually heard is contradictory to the opponent's position. Thus, the lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*) in the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been explained.

Then, he states that [the example] is inconsistent with the illustrative statement by saying "by being the cause. He explains the lack of logical connection (*aghaṭitatva*) by saying "the lump of clay," etc. The point is that the cessation of silver through the knowledge of mother-of-pearl is not shown to be analogous to the cessation of a jar or the like through the knowledge of a lump of clay. He raises an objection regarding the lack of contradiction with the example by saying "even there," etc. He refutes it by stating that the presentation [of the example] is untenable as if it were well-known, saying "of the modification of clay," etc. To the claim that the unreality of the modification of clay is understood through inference and so forth, he replies, "And not," etc.

"Unassisted" (ananugṛhītam) is intended to mean that which produces only a superficial cognition, like the perception of the unity of a flame. He shows the failure to consider the subsequent statement with the word "tathā" (so). Being the abode of all (sadāyatanatva) results in its being the cause of its own activity and its own sustaining of life. For its support is by means of its command (praśāsana), and its life is sustained by that support. To dispel the doubt that this might be a restatement of qualities for the sake of negation, he says "śāstraika-". The sense is that a positive injunction cannot be a mere restatement.

He shows that there is no consideration of other scriptural passages [by stating]: "even in other contexts, by virtue of being connected to that. The meaning is that its nature consists of being free from sin and so forth, which is the state of having all defects removed. To demonstrate that the mark of the purport (*tātparya*) regarding the qualities is their being "unprecedented" (*apūrvatā*), he says: "they are the objects of all other means of knowledge. Then, fulfilling the expectation of what follows from this, he shows the absence of consideration for the two words [of the compound] by saying: "thus..."

By the phrase "thus distinguished by infinite particularities that are not within the range of others," the contradiction with the contextual statement is intended. By the phrase "of the word *tat* which refers back to the Brahman under discussion," the contradiction with the etymological derivation of the word *tat*—which refers back to whatever qualified form is under discussion—is stated. Regarding the term *tvam*, he states that if it were to refer merely to the bare reality (*vastumātra*), its primary meaning would be abandoned; thus he says, "And the word *tvam*... The meaning of the word *tvam* is a conscious being directed toward oneself.

The sense is that "being directed toward" (ābhimukhya) means being capable of being understood through one's own words, and such capability is naturally possessed by the ignorant transmigrating soul. Therefore, the referent of "thou" (tvam-artha) is characterized by those qualities suitable for being made an object of instruction; consequently, it is [the limited ego] that is abandoned. He states "nirviśeṣa" (without attributes) to show that the aforementioned [idea of the soul] was not preceded by an investigation into valid means of knowledge and reasoning. Since the state of being without attributes resides in the intellect once the two limiting adjuncts (the words "that" and "thou") have been discarded, the failure to investigate the inconsistency of that [prior notion] has been demonstrated.

In response to the doubt that the acceptance of a featureless reality follows from the force of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), he states the refutation regarding the metaphorical and non-metaphorical nature of the two words with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). The meaning is: and this being the case, if it is accepted that the purpose is to present a featureless essential nature, then by admitting the cognition of the mere thing through its connection with the primary sense, one must resort to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Now he introduces the view of another by saying, "It is further said. The passage beginning with "of those functioning in grammatical coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇavṛttānām*) is intended as a summary of the subject under consideration. The phrase "because it is impossible for there to be an intentionality regarding the qualifying portion" implies that otherwise, due to the multiplicity of qualifiers, the status of having a single referent (*ekārthatva*) would not be established. The force of the particle *eva* ("only") is to indicate that this has already been stated previously; indeed, it was stated many times in the first sūtra. Alternatively, the particle *eva* is intended to signify independence from anything else. Thus, there is no risk of [the definition] becoming over-extensive (*lakṣaṇaprasaṅga*).

The meaning is that [the word] expresses something not external to its primary denotation (*vācya*). Thus, having briefly stated the point regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), he establishes it with the words "as follows" (*yathā*) and so on. In that regard, even in the example cited from the *Mahābhāṣya*, he has provided the illustration by taking for granted that there is no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇāṃśa*). To the question, "How is there a lack of intention regarding the qualifying portion in that case? he replies: "If there were an intention toward that... He shows the undesirability of such a consequence with the words "for then" (*tat tu*).

Considering that if both were denoted simultaneously, there would be the undesirable consequence of losing the distinction between the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*), and furthermore, that if the identity of a single qualified entity—presented by the basic meanings (*prakṛti*) of two words—is conveyed by a common case-ending (*samānavibhakti*), it would follow that not only the substratum (*viśeṣya*) but also the qualifying portions, namely the universal (*jāti*) and the quality (*guṇa*), would become identical, one must accept the position of sequential denotation; keeping this in mind, he says: "For indeed... (*na hi*).

Even in the view that [the sentence] is understood sequentially, one must consider the following dilemma: Is the identity between the object qualified by the form apprehended from the preceding word and the object qualified by the form apprehended from the subsequent word conveyed by the co-occurrence of identical case-endings (*samānavibhakti*)? Or is it the connection of another qualifier with the object already apprehended as qualified by the preceding word? With this dilemma in mind, having established that in the first alternative there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the identity even between the genus and quality which serve as qualifiers, he states "of the genus and the quality" (*jātiguṇayoḥ*) regarding the second head of the dilemma, pointing out the consequence of their inherence in a different substratum (*anyasamavāya*).

Demonstrating the utility of a qualifier even when it lies outside the primary purport (*tātparya*), he states the resulting conclusion with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). In the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpalam*), although the connection with the qualifier is clear, it was stated that there is no primary purport [for that connection]; since in that instance the connection with the qualifier was not manifest, he shows another example where there is no manifest purport regarding the connection with the qualifier with the word "Likewise" (*tathā*).

He says "even though" (*yadyapi*) because, if a word denoting a qualified entity were to function with respect to the mere nature of the qualificand—which is related to it by being a single part of that qualified entity—while abandoning the qualified entity itself, that would indeed be *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication). He refutes this with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The sense is that the qualificand is external to the qualified entity, which is the primary meaning (*vācya*) and the object of the word's direct denotative power (*śakti*).

The meaning is that because the primary portion (*pradhānāṃśa*)—as the object of intention and as the grammatical subject (*dharmin*)—is not excluded from being the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there is no *lakṣaṇā* (indication), even when the non-primary qualifier is abandoned; this is like the word "man" (*puruṣaśabda*) when applied to someone who lacks fingers and so forth. Although the status of being the primary meaning is equal [in both cases], he shows the distinction based on the stage of conveying a qualified entity by saying "but rather" (*api tu*). By "mere lack of intention to express" (*avivakṣāmātra*), he means that while there may be an absence of function regarding what is impossible, there is no incapacity regarding the aspect that constitutes the object of the function.

Previously, the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) was stated regarding the *pūrvapakṣa*; now, it is made clear regarding the *sapakṣa*. To the objection that there would be a lack of natural consistency (*asvārasya*) if the qualification were not intended, he says "in all cases. Because origination (*utpatti*) is of such a nature, there is no lack of natural consistency in its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For there is a lack of naturalness (*asvārasya*) when one does not follow the conventional etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*); therefore, the sense is that the lack of naturalness occurs precisely when one intends to express a qualification that contradicts the established etymological derivation of the term's unity of meaning. He rejects this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words, "This is without substance" (*tadidamasāram*). First, he refutes the recourse to an alternative etymology—which had been present in the mind because it was mentioned last—with the words, "In all [cases]" (*sarveṣveva*). This means: in all sentences, whether they are grammatically coordinate (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or non-coordinate (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

In sentences with different grammatical subjects (vyadhikaraṇa), such as "Bring the cow" or "Bind the horse," it is not necessary to assume a distinct linguistic convention (vyutpatti) for each sentence regarding the meaning of the words. This is because, according to the maxim "When there is a conflict between what is already established and what must be assumed, the acceptance of the established is proper," since the communication of their own meanings is possible through the already established convention alone, it is illogical to assume another convention. The point is that even in sentences with the same grammatical subject (samānādhikaraṇa), one need not assume a separate convention for the words directed toward an object qualified by the same basis of application (pravṛttinimitta).

The phrase "merely a specific relation between meanings established through linguistic usage" (*vyutpatti-siddhārtha-saṃsarga-viśeṣa-mātra*) is intended to demonstrate that even in the absence of a separate process of learning word-meanings (*vyutpatti*), it is possible for sentences to differ from one another. The intention is that the difference between sentences arises from a specific relation between meanings already established through usage, and not from the postulation of some other meaning for the nominal stem (*prakṛti*) that was not previously understood through usage. Having thus stated the form common to all sentences, he states the resulting meaning in the case of co-referential (*samānādhikaraṇa*) sentences with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

Regarding those sentences, he demonstrates by means of an example how words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) serve as the cause for the cognition of a single qualified object, using the word "for instance" (*yathā*). There are two examples: one concerning a perceptible object and one concerning an imperceptible object; for this very reason, it is said that [the object] is "brought" (*ānīyate*) or "cognized. With the intention that the presence of case endings denoting a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) does not contradict grammatical apposition, the phrase "bring the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam ānaya*) is stated. It is precisely that which is qualified by blueness and so forth that is brought.

The intention is this: if a collection of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) were to convey only the bare object (*vastumātra*), then because there would be no distinction in being merely the object, even something that is not blue would be brought forth. Furthermore, what is the reason for the abandonment of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) by words in apposition? If it is argued that it is the unity understood through the identical case-endings (*samānavibhakti*), we say no; the identical case-ending cannot establish unity against the force of the connection with the qualifiers understood from the nominal stems (*prātipadika*). Therefore, the latter [position] alone is logical.

Even when a case-ending (vibhakti) is present, the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is predominant; for in instances such as "aditiḥ pāśān" ("Aditi [cuts] the bonds") and "grahaṃ saṃmāṣṭi" ("he cleanses the cup"), the meaning of the case-ending is disregarded. If it is argued that [the word] refers to identity because usage is seen regarding identity, we reply that since usage is also seen in connection with qualifiers, it conveys connection with qualifiers as well. Verbal cognition pertains only to the thing-in-itself; however, the connection with qualifiers is accepted on the strength of perception.

If it is argued that when [the object] is not within the range of perception (*pratyakṣāgocara*), there is no cognition of the qualifier according to the word, we say no. For while the connection with the qualifier is the object of verbal cognition (*śābdapratīti*), why could it not be that identity (*aikya*) is accepted through the force of perception? If it is argued that even in cases beyond the range of perception—such as the usage "Devadatta is dark-complexioned and young"—identity is seen to be the object of cognition, and thus identity is the object of verbal cognition, [we reply: in that very case, since the connection with the qualifier is also cognized in usages concerning an imperceptible object, the connection with the qualifier is indeed verbal (*śābda*).

"It is not established by perception. Thus, with reference to the final stage, two examples have been shown to demonstrate that words in grammatical apposition (samānādhikaraṇa), devoid of the distinction between direct and indirect [perception], are observed to convey a single object qualified by multiple qualifiers.

Therefore, according to the principle of the *lokavad-ādhikaraṇa*—namely, "whatever is worldly is the same as what is Vedic"—it is stated that "thus, in the Vedānta texts," the meaning must be understood even in the Vedānta sentences without abandoning the specific qualifiers apprehended from the two words. He avoids the contingency of mutual inherence (*anyonyasamavāya*) by saying "not so. A detailed refutation will be provided in the *Aruṇādhikaraṇa*, but here it is given in brief. The sense is that one should not speak in such a way that an inconsistency would arise.

Keeping in mind the simultaneous denotation [of all attributes], it has been stated that the very nature [of the subject] is the qualificand (viśeṣya) by means of all the qualifiers (viśeṣaṇa). He states "tathā hi" (for it is thus) to show that the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is consistent with the nature being the qualificand through all the qualifiers. The meaning is that grammatical coreferentiality is not defined as the presentation of the connection of another qualifier to a form already qualified by another qualifier. He explains the section on the definition of grammatical coreferentiality with the words "by way of positive concomitance (anvaya) or by way of exclusion (nivṛtti)."

The meaning in the form of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) need not be conceived as having the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). The sense is that, according to linguistic usage, whether by way of positive concomitance or by way of exclusion, the function of a collection of words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) is to convey that a thing possesses a different aspect from the aspect conveyed by other words. He provides an example of this with "as follows" (*yathā*): "dark-complexioned and young" (*śyāmo yuvā*) is an illustration of the qualification by multiple grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) by way of positive concomitance.

The example of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through the method of negative exclusion (*vyatireka*) begins with the words "not wretched" (*adīna*) and so forth. Here, "wretchedness" (*dīnatva*) means lack of luster and lack of mental clarity; "miserliness" (*kṛpaṇatva*) means poverty. The point here is this: if these were stated in sequence, even in sentences with different grammatical loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), there would arise the problem that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) would be construed as qualified by the instrumental factor (*karaṇa-kāraka*), or conversely, the other factors would be construed as qualified by that [locus]. Thus, the objection regarding the mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) applies equally even to sentences with different loci.

In this regard, even though the same defense applies here as well, there is no contingency of the qualifiers being mutually inherent at the stage of recollection, because—as stated in the verse: "The entire collection of words heard recalls their respective meanings without yet showing their connection; subsequently, its manifestation is brought about by logical reasoning (nyāya), and it then conveys the sentence-meaning"—all words individually recall their own meanings during the state of recollection. Furthermore, at the stage of reflective synthesis (parāmarśa), this contingency does not arise, as the synthesis occurs in whatever manner is appropriate.
