Since the meaning of the sentence is understood simultaneously by all the words at once, there is no consequence of mutual inherence (*samavāya*); therefore, because there is no sequence in the simultaneous presentation of a single qualified substantive as characterized by its respective grounds of application (*pravṛttinimitta*) through words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), there is no mutual inherence.

In the text stating that "the very nature [of the substance] is the qualificandum by means of all the qualifiers," this is the intended meaning. By introducing here the section on the definition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), another objection is also resolved: namely, the objection that if there is simultaneous denotation, the identical case-ending would establish the identity of the two qualified entities, and consequently, just as there is identity between the qualified entities, there would also have to be identity between the qualifiers.

The resolution here is as follows: "Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence [of words] in reference to a single object. Since this demonstrates the identity of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) alone through the use of identical case-endings, it does not imply the identity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). If it is asked: "When both the qualifier and the non-qualifier (the qualificand) are understood from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), what is the restrictive factor that determines that the identical case-ending is intended solely for the identity of the qualificand, and not for the identity of the qualifiers?"

What is the determining factor that a case-ending with identical inflection (samānavibhakti) conveys identity rather than difference? If you say it is linguistic usage (vyutpatti), that applies equally here as well. Furthermore, when the word "ghaṭa" (pot) is used without being co-referential with another word, what is the determining factor for the fact that the case-ending attached to it does not convey the identity of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation—conveyed by the nominal stem (prātipadika)—but instead conveys the identity of the qualified object alone? For linguistic usage is rooted in perception (pratyakṣa), and perception is [as follows]:

If it is argued that [the word] shows the identity of the substantive alone, but not the identity of the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation—and therefore that linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) based on perception is the regulator [of meaning], then it is the same here as well: that very [usage] is the regulator. If, in this way, one must accept only that meaning established by linguistic usage everywhere, then there would never be the postulation of another function (*vṛtti*) or the postulation of another linguistic usage; to this, he says: "But where... (*yatra tu*).

The phrase "the two qualifiers" is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for three or more as well. In every case, the acceptance of the meaning established by etymology (*vyutpatti*) is what is naturally obtained; however, when that [meaning] is unfit for syntactic connection (*anvaya*) due to contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the assumption of another mode of operation (*vṛttyantara*) follows. When even that is impossible, the assumption of a different etymology follows. For instance, if the word *go* were to signify "rays," one would have to assume a primary denotative power (*śakti*) because no other mode of operation would exist [for it]. Even when there is an assumption of another mode of operation, at that time one must assume that one of the two words is non-primary (*amukhya*); by that much alone [the problem is resolved].

This is due to the reconciliation of contradiction, but not because of all the words [being non-literal], for that would entail the impossibility of determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*). For in the expression "The Vāhīka is an ox" (*gaur vāhīkaḥ*), it is only the word "ox" (*go*) that is non-primary, and not the word "Vāhīka" either; yet even when one of the two words is understood through a different mode of signification (*vṛttyantara*), there is no intent to convey a featureless reality (*nirviśeṣavastu*), because even if the qualifiers brought forward by the primary mode of signification do not connect, they do connect with the qualifiers brought forward by the other mode of signification—this is the intended meaning.

He states "nīla" etc., because there is no reason at all to postulate another mode of operation (*vṛtti*) in sentences such as "blue lotus. He raises the objection that the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) must differ due to the difference in qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) with the words "atha manyase" etc. "Being related to a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇapratisambandhitva*) means being characterized by a qualifier. The expression "being determined as being related to a single qualifier" is a statement emphasizing the state (*bhāva-pradhāna-nirdeśa*). What is intended here is the state of being so determined.

The meaning is that being related to one qualifier is distinct from being related to another qualifier. Alternatively, the meaning is that an object, when defined by its relation to one qualifier, is distinct from the entity that serves as the qualificandum for that other qualifier, because of its relation to that other qualifier. He demonstrates that the difference in the nature of the qualificandum follows from the difference in its relations to qualifiers, using the example "like a jar and a cloth."

Just as there is a difference between a jar and a cloth—the two subjects qualified by those attributes—due to the difference between the qualification by "jar-ness" and the qualification by "cloth-ness," so too, even when expressed with the same case-ending, a difference between the two subjects is unavoidable due to the difference between the connection with one qualifier and the connection with another qualifier; thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not capable of establishing the identity of the qualified entities. This is the meaning.

The sense is this: although the cognition of the connection with the qualifier is unavoidable because the text is not intended solely to establish a distinction, there is no *tātparya* (intentional focus) upon that [distinction]. He says "but rather" (*api tu*) to address the point that since it is impossible to bring to mind the substantive (*viśeṣya*) which is the counter-correlate of the qualifier if the qualifier is abandoned, the identity of the two would also be difficult to establish. The meaning is that the establishment of the cognition of the identity of the two is possible, because the cognition of the substantive is accomplished by the mere fact of its being perceived at the stage of reflecting upon the qualifier, even though that qualifier is not the object of the primary intention (*tātparya*).

He addresses this with the words "it might be so. For even in a case where unfitness (*ayogyatva*) is admitted, it is indeed the status of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) that is the cause of that unfitness; therefore, even a qualifier such as "blueness" would be contradictory. To this he replies: "And unfitness... The sense is that [unfitness] is established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), and not that unfitness is caused by the status of being a qualifier.

Another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) also makes known the contradiction characterized by the fact that "pot-ness" and "cloth-ness" have different substrata; however, that same contradiction applies equally to "blueness" and "lotus-ness," since they are observed separately in the six-spoked flower (*ṣaṭpada*) and the water-lily (*kumuda*). To this he replies with the words "In cases such as 'the blue lotus,'" and so on. The point is that contradiction does not consist merely in having different substrata, but rather in the necessity thereof; and there is no such contradiction between blueness and lotus-ness, because they are sometimes perceived together.

Regarding the phrase "having punished," [the author] explains that the staff and so forth are *yutasiddha* (separately established), while form and so forth are *ayutasiddha* (inseparably established). Thus, having resolved the contradiction between the two sections of the text by means of the principle of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*), he now resolves the contradiction with statements such as the *Kalpasūtras* raised by the opponent by means of that very same principle, saying: "In this case..."

This is the demonstration of the apparent contradiction here: having begun with the statement, "The Brāhmaṇas are injunctions regarding ritual action," the venerable Āpastamba states that all four types of arthavādas—namely, explanatory praise (arthavāda), censure (nindā), praise (praśaṃsā), traditional accounts (parakṛti), and ancient legends (purākalpa)—are supplementary to the Brāhmaṇas. Other instances should be understood in the same way. Thus, how can it be said that the arthavādas possess authority regarding Brahman without being supplementary to an injunction? To this, he gives the reply: "The answer has already been given."

The meaning is as follows: the statement that explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi*) is a general rule. Here, however, the assertion of the independent authority of explanatory passages concerning Brahman is an exception (*apavāda*) to that very rule. Therefore, since the contradiction is resolved by this very principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), the charge of contradicting the *Smṛtis* is indeed untenable. He specifically clarifies this same principle of the general rule and its exception for the sake of the disciple who does not understand it, by saying "the general rule," and so forth.

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration found within that same statement, beginning with the word "tataḥ. For in that very statement of Āpastamba, the mutual distinctness between a mantra and an injunction is stated later on: "Other than those are the mantras. That is to say, "other than those"—namely, the injunctions and explanatory passages (arthavādas)—are the mantras. This, however, is merely a general rule, since it is accepted that mantras also possess injunctive power; for the Tantric authorities indeed say, "A mantra enjoins."

Just as you accept that the statement regarding the difference in the injunctions of mantras is the general rule (*utsarga*), while the statement regarding their injunctive nature is the exception (*apavāda*), so too here, may you be satisfied by accepting that the statement regarding [the mantras] being supplementary to the Brāhmaṇa is the general rule, whereas the statement regarding their independent expressive power is the exception.

While many grounds for validity exist, the Mīmāṃsakas who deny the existence of Īśvara argue that their refutation of the Upaniṣadic statements is nothing but a rash act, and in demonstrating this, he sets up a counter-argument against the repudiation of all Vedic paths with the words "by those [statements] recorded in scripture" (*āmnātaiḥ*). In the Veda, following the authority of statements regarding perceptible results—such as "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī"—the validity of statements regarding imperceptible results, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," is postulated.

The phrase "by means of those that are flawless and effective" means that in certain cases, such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others, the non-attainment of the result occurs precisely due to defects in the ritual action (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the instrumental factors (*sādhana*). Regarding the phrase "by means of augury, astrology, and so forth": just as the attainment of results is described through the flawless and effective Vedic rites such as the *Kārīrī*, in exactly the same way, the attainment of results is likewise described through the flawless and effective [practices] such as augury and astrology, even though they are not Vedic. Thus, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is perceived in some instances regarding those things whose results are directly observable.

Likewise, he states "pāratrikyā" (pertaining to the next world) to show that the authority of the Veda is ascertained everywhere even by the activity of the learned toward ends that are not perceptible. The meaning of "atinipuṇā" (extremely subtle) is that the authority of the Veda is ascertained even by the activity of those of great spiritual power (*mahānubhāva*) which has the other world as its cause. By this, the acceptance [of the Veda] by the great multitude (*mahājana-parigraha*) is expressed.

When the authority of the Veda has been established through many such reasons for the sake of providing confidence in the scriptures, the author states "the word" (*śabda*) to indicate the absence of any cause for non-authority. By the phrase "when there is the word and the resulting cognition," the rejection of non-authority characterized by non-origination is expressed. Regarding the "object of another," namely the subject of God (*īśvara*), the phrases "free from defects and sublation" (*doṣabādhavyapeta*) serve to exclude both the defect in the cause and any sublating cognition.

Since it possesses an unbroken tradition from time immemorial, lacks defects in its cause, concerns suprasensory objects, and is free from subverting cognitions, the Veda is authoritative; and since no cause for non-authoritativeness exists—whether [alleged] authority does or does not—it remains a valid means of knowledge regarding the Supreme Brahman. Thus, if one were to assert the non-authoritativeness of the Vedānta passages without such a basis, then by that same logic, one would have to assert the non-authoritativeness of the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) as well; the meaning is that this would result in the total repudiation of the path of the Veda.

Having thus explained the meanings of the four *adhikaraṇas* by way of their distinctions, and having first restated their general meaning, he addresses the objection that there might be redundancy (*paunaruktya*) with the subsequent *kāraṇatva-adhikaraṇa* and *ubhayaliṅga-adhikaraṇa* which are to be discussed later—since those two will establish the same points as these two, namely the *janmādi-adhikaraṇa* and the *samanvaya-adhikaraṇa*. He states that there is no such redundancy because, while the latter sections will establish the specific arguments for those respective topics, the present section expresses those very meanings by relying upon the points that are to be stated later.

By the words "In the Śāstra," etc., two specific points are thus established: first, that the words *brahman* and so forth culminate in Śrīnivāsa, as stated in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*); and second, that Brahman, who is to be known through the Vedāntas, is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, as stated in the fourth section. In this regard, it is most excellent that the former [point] depends upon the subsequent section on causality (*kāraṇatvādhikaraṇa*), which is yet to be discussed, while the latter depends upon the subsequent section on the dual characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa*).

Having here shown, both generally and specifically, the meaning of the first section consisting of the four aphorisms which constitute the cause for the commencement of the Śārīraka-śāstra, he next states the connection between those two by expressing the meaning of the second section, which consists of the commencement of the Śāstra itself, with the words "In the Self thus... (ātmany evam). For in these four sections, the unity of purpose is that "the Self is to be known," while the division of the meaning of the sections consists of the fourfold set of actions beginning with "not being made" (akṛta) and "being the locus of thought" (mata).

Because all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) establish specific aspects of Brahman, [the author] now, by way of restating the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the second section (*peṭikā*), demonstrates the connection (*saṃgati*) as well as clarifying the manner in which that section proceeds, stating: "Suchness" (*īdṛktvam*).

The meaning is that the collection of points stated in the preceding section—that they belong respectively to *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—is refuted in sequence by the two subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇas*), which demonstrate that [the opponent's view] is untenable because [the soul] is not subject to inference and so forth, and is untouched by suffering. Alternatively, the passage beginning with "suchness" (*īdṛktvam*) and ending with the word "iti" constitutes the very statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since the status of Prakṛti and Puruṣa as the cause of the world and so forth is not established by valid means of knowledge, and since they lack the capacity for inference and the like, as well as the quality of being untouched by suffering—this objection raised against the preceding section is resolved by the following arguments through appropriate explanations. This is done either by the immediately subsequent peṭikā (section) or by the remainder of the pāda.

For it was previously stated, in the *Śāstrayoni* and *Samanvaya* sections, that the object known through the Vedāntas is incapable of being known by inference and the like, and is untouched by suffering; neither of these two [qualities] would be possible if either *prakṛti* or *puruṣa* were accepted as the object known through the Vedāntas. Thus, the connection with the preceding intermediate section (*avāntarapeṭikā*) is also stated here.

In the first section, by the words "It is uncreated," he shows that the state of being uncreated—stated in the subject-sentence "The uncreated is not [attained] by the created"—is the primary meaning. In this same manner, it should be understood in sequence that in the second section and those following, the status of being the cause of the universe and so forth is the primary meaning.

For in that context, since the first pāda—concerned with the Vedānta texts as excluding other [entities] from Brahman—provides the resolution that the statement of the exclusion of connection with *prakṛti* and so forth is for the sake of supplementing the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and not as a primary purpose, the lack of consistency regarding the *Īkṣati-adhikaraṇa* and subsequent sections is not to be suspected. Indeed, this is the division of the "boxes" (*peṭikā-vibhāga*): in the first pāda, the four *adhikaraṇas* intended for the commencement of the Śāstra constitute one [box], while two of those constitute intermediate boxes.

It is stated that the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* and the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa* constitute a single section (*peṭikā*). Beyond this, it is established that all five *adhikaraṇas* form a single section because they share the common characteristic of referring to specific aspects of either Prakṛti or Puruṣa. Alternatively, the three beginning with the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* may be considered one section, since the refutation by means of specific marks such as "seeing" (*īkṣati*) is identical for the opponent who has raised an objection based on general scriptural texts regarding the nature of the Sat, the Self, and Puruṣa.

For the experts in the Tantras maintain that, between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the specific indicative mark is more powerful than a general scriptural statement. Consequently, the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—which has arisen from specific scriptural statements concerning the ether, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), light (*jyotis*), and so forth—is refuted by the two sections on Ether and Vital Breath (*ākāśaprāṇādhikaraṇa*) through the acceptance of the etymological meaning of the scriptural terms in accordance with reason. In the case of the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), however, only their etymological meanings are accepted; for conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not override etymology (*yoga*).

By the maxim that "a well-established connection subverts a figurative application," [the figurative sense] is set aside. Consequently, the status of the *ākāśa* and *prāṇa* sections as intermediate sub-sections (*avāntara-peṭikā*) is established. However, in the *jyotis* and *indra-prāṇa* sections, since the abandonment of figurative application is set aside in favor of the view that they refer to the Supreme Self qualified by those respective conventional meanings, their status as distinct sub-sections is likewise established. Regarding these four sūtras, those who desire a correct understanding of the meaning must exert themselves in summarizing the subject matter (*prameya-saṃgraha*).
Furthermore, the *Śatadūṣaṇī* composed by the Teacher (Vedānta Deśika) should certainly be consulted.

Previously, it was stated that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is that which is known through the Vedāntas. Now, it is being explained that the same status of being known through the Vedāntas cannot possibly belong to primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest. In this regard, since primordial nature—which has transformed into the form of the universe—is well-known to all people according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems, and since the Spirit (puruṣa) is subtler than that, it is primordial nature alone that is refuted first; such is the connection [of the argument].

Alternatively, it may be argued that in the preceding section it was stated that the reality known through the Vedānta constitutes the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), but that is untenable because Prakṛti alone—being of the nature of what is not a human goal—is the cause. Or else, it may be argued that in the preceding section it was claimed that all Vedānta passages have as their purport Brahman who transcends both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, yet the *Sadvidyā*, which is the essence of all Vedānta, actually describes Prakṛti itself; so what is the use of other spurious passages? Such other possible connections (*saṅgati*) should also be mentioned as they arise.

The subject matter, however, is the Supreme Brahman itself; the distinction from the previous [section] on the commencement of the scripture lies therein. Furthermore, the doubt is: is Brahman, as known through the *Sadvidyā*, distinct from *prakṛti* (primordial nature), or is it *prakṛti*? The cause for the arising of this doubt is the scriptural mention of the general term "Being" (*sat*). This is because the word "Being," which denotes all existing things, is common to *prakṛti*, *puruṣa* (the individual soul), and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The investigation into that meaning is as follows: does the word *sat* refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), or does it refer to primordial nature (*prakṛti*)? If it refers to primordial nature, does the "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) mentioned in the phrase "It saw" (*tadaikṣata*) not occur, or does it occur? For that purpose, it is further investigated whether this seeing is primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, it is investigated whether there is an association with secondary seeing here, or whether such association certainly exists. In that regard also, it is investigated whether the seeing of fire and the other elements in passages such as "That fire saw" (*tatteja aikṣata*) is primary or non-primary.

For this reason as well, it is investigated whether the reasons corresponding to the primary [meaning] must be followed, or whether even the reasons corresponding to the secondary [meaning] are to be accepted, and so forth. However, because there exist here many arguments corresponding to the secondary meaning regarding the relationship between cause and effect—since the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) in the passage "That heat [or fire] saw" is figurative, and since the presence of association with that figurative seeing exists here, making the seeing mentioned in this context also figurative—it is argued by the Sāṃkhyas and others that the seeing described here is consistent even if it refers to primordial matter (*prakṛti*).

In the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), it is held that the word "Being" (sat) here denotes primordial matter (pradhāna) alone; however, in the established conclusion (siddhānta), the relationship between cause and effect is the reverse. He explains the aforementioned point in sequence with the words: "because of its association with [the term] 'seeing' used in a secondary sense."

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the observation of becoming manifold is certainly not primary; for the proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādinaḥ*) refute the causality of *prakṛti* on the grounds of its association with the quality of observing. Yet, that observation is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), just as in the cases of "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*) or "the rice plants are pleased by the rain. This is because the attributes of a conscious being can be attributed even to an insentient thing. In this context, the very fact that the text mentions figurative observation in passages such as "That heat observed" (*tatteja aikṣata*) serves as the basis for its figurative nature.

Furthermore, he states "by means of examples and so forth" because it appears that this is merely the inference of *pradhāna* as stated by the Sāṃkhyas—beginning with "the transformation of the elements"—based on the examples of clay and its effects. Nor is this a mere appearance based on scripture; he says "from such [a source]" because this is also consistent with reason: it is logical that an insentient effect arises only from an insentient cause. Anticipating the objection, "How can the word 'Being' (*sat*) apply to *pradhāna*, which is subject to modification? he says "Being."

In response to the prima facie argument—that while the modifications such as the *mahat* (intellect) and so forth might not be denoted by the word "Being" (*sat*) because they are localized, the unmodified *prakṛti* (primordial nature) must be denoted by that word because it is eternally established—the author states the final conclusion: "That is incorrect. This is because of the scriptural testimony, specifically the use of words such as "Self" (*ātman*), which are unique to the conscious [Brahman]. Furthermore, there is the cessation of *prakṛti* and the other categories.

He further states, "by your own accepted [scriptures]," indicating that this very meaning is determined not only by scripture, but also by indicative marks (*liṅga*), sentences (*vākya*), and context (*prakaraṇa*) that refute the doctrine of *prakṛti* as the cause, such as the mention of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*).

Here, having raised the objection that this is a recognition of the Sāṃkhya method of inference, [the author] refutes it with the words "jñāta" (known). Here, indeed, the opponent thinks as follows: first of all, the proposition that through the knowledge of one thing there is the knowledge of everything is seen in such passages as, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and so forth. It is not merely a proposition; there is also an illustrative example, as he says, "mṛttaditi" (clay, that...). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the examples mentioned in the Śruti, such as the nail-cutter, are included. Thus, [he addresses] those who hold the Śruti to be primarily based on inference.

He says, "By this [word]," meaning that by establishing the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this statement would merely be a restatement of the inference propounded by the Sāṃkhyas. He refutes it with the word "in vain. He states the reason for that: "Because of the non-statement of the probans (*hetu*). This means because the probans, which is the most essential among the members of an inference, has not been stated. If it is argued that the Sāṃkhyas do have probans such as "similarity" (*sārūpya*) and so forth, he says "of similarity and the rest," meaning that this is not so, because they will be refuted later in the section on the Sāṃkhya (*sāṃkhyādhikaraṇa*).

Anticipating the objection that there is tautology between the refutation here and that [in the previous section], he says: "In this case. In the subsequent section, the reasons that establish the Pradhāna as the cause will be uprooted without exception; here, however, only the mere possibility of inferring the Pradhāna as the cause is refuted. Thus, there is no room for the charge of tautology.

Having thus set aside the method of the opposing view, he summarizes the reasons that favor his own position through the word "ādeśa. In the opening passage, "But did you ask for that instruction (ādeśa)? the term *ādeśa* first points to Brahman, which is denoted by the word *Sat*. Furthermore, the word *ādeśa* denotes the instructor (*ādeṣṭṛ*) himself. Moreover, being an instructor is nothing other than being a controller (*niyantṛ*). And that is not possible in the case of the Pradhāna, because it is insentient.

The word "Self" (ātman) is also heard here in the phrase "That is the Self. This term is unique to the conscious being alone. In that context, regarding the state of deep sleep, the Supreme Self—the locus of deep sleep—is indicated by the word "own" (sva) in the passage, "He becomes merged in his own (self). Because He is the inner ruler (antaryāmin), the Supreme Self alone is worthy of being designated by the word "own," and not the Pradhāna; for the Pradhāna lacks the status of being the inner ruler with respect to deep sleep.

"By those that have no other refuge" means by those that are not established otherwise. For these words are primary when referring to the Supreme Self, whereas they function only in a secondary sense when referring to the Pradhāna. He states another reason as well: "Thou. Here, the identity of the word "thou," which denotes the individual soul (jīva), with that which is denoted by the word "that" is declared. If the word "that" were intended to refer to the Pradhāna, then this would be an instruction of non-identity.

This is because the teaching of identity between the conscious and the unconscious is a cause of delusion, similar to the teaching that the body is the self. Here, he provides further proof with the words "by the *jīva*. The meaning is "by his own self-nature. This is because, in the passage, "Having entered by means of this *jīva*-self, let me evolve names and forms," there is an entry of the non-conscious aggregate—which is distinct from the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*)—preceded by the first-person singular pronoun (*uttamapuruṣa*) established as the sense of "I. Thus, the meaning here is that the Supreme Self, having the *jīva* as its body, enters the collection of unconscious things distinct from the *jīva* through the medium of the *jīva*.

It is stated that it is not logical for an insentient object (*acidvastu*) which is to be entered to possess an entry characterized by the ego (*sāhaṅkaraṇa*), that is, an entry accompanied by the ego. Furthermore, the proposition of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is seen [in the scripture]: "By which the unheard becomes heard. That, moreover, is consistent only with God being the cause, and not with Pradhāna being the cause, because Pradhāna is not a conscious cause; thus he says "eka" (one). He states another reason as well: "sarva" (all), in the passage: "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*).

For it is heard [in scripture]: "If the Pradhāna were the cause, how could the identity with that [Brahman] be predicated of the individual soul (jīva), who is included within the term 'all'? This is the meaning. Not only is the causality of Brahman understood from the *Chāndogya-śruti*, but also from another *śruti*. In the *Chāndogya* as well, it is not understood solely from the passage concerning the Knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*), but also from the passages concerning the *dahara-vidyā*, the *avyākṛta-vidyā*, and so forth. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the corroborating *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, and other texts are included. In this context, the term "knower of all" (*viśvavit*) is intended to establish its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*).

The distinction is as follows: "omnipresence" (*sārvajñyam*) is understood [in the first part], while "the universal form" (*viśvamūrtiḥ*) is understood as the state of having all things as its body, which is applicable to its being the material cause (*upādānatva*). In this regard, the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), as well as the analysis of the objections, should be seen in the *Śrībhāṣya*, the *Nyāyasudarśana*, and other such works. Furthermore, the consistency of the opening and concluding statements of the great aphorism (*mahāvākya*), as well as the sequence of the sūtras intended to illuminate other scriptural passages and other meditations (*vidyā*), should also be investigated therein.

Having stated the two types of connection between the preceding and following sections, he briefly presents the subject matter of the subsequent section with the words "mukhya" (primary), etc. One connection arises from the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): if the primary act of seeing is intended for the Existent (*sat*), then since the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses consciousness and is thus capable of primary seeing, the soul itself must be the cause of the world. Another connection is that in the *Sadvijñāna* passage, the identity of the soul and Brahman is demonstrated nine times by the three words of the formula "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); and so, the soul alone would be the cause of the world.

"Brahmā, indeed"—thus arises the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). To refute the opponent who is rising up with such an objection, the Creator of the Universe, who was introduced previously as the innermost Self (*antarātman*) even of the individual soul (*jīva*) and who possesses unsurpassed great bliss (*mahānanda*), is established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*). The investigation into its meaning concerns the statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme": is that which is called the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) here the individual soul or the Supreme Self? Furthermore, it is deliberated whether the suffix *-maya* here signifies a modification (*vikāra*) or an abundance (*prācurya*).

For that purpose, it is investigated whether, following the fact that the suffix *mayaṭ* in the word *annamaya* occurring at the beginning has the sense of "modification," it is likewise appropriate here for *mayaṭ* to have the sense of "modification" alone, or rather the sense of "abundance. Furthermore, it is investigated whether there is an interruption in the middle—by means of *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, and so forth—of what was understood from the beginning, or not, and so on.

Regarding the relationship between cause and effect in this context: since the sense of "modification" (vikāra), understood from the introductory passage, is equally applicable here due to the lack of interruption, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that the suffix *-maya* in the word *ānandamaya* signifies modification, and thus the *ānandamaya* is the individual soul (*jīva*). In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, the relationship between cause and effect is established by reversing this position.

Regarding this, someone says: "Since the creation itself is described by such passages as 'From the Self, space was produced,' and since in the earlier passage, 'This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food (annarasamaya),' the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen to denote a modification (*vikāra*), let it be the same in the final passage as well, 'Another inner Self, consisting of bliss (ānandamaya). Let the suffix *mayaṭ* here also have the sense of a modification, because of the recognition of the previously mentioned *mayaṭ* as having that meaning. To this he replies: "It is seen. He refutes that with: "That is incorrect."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "in the middle. This means because one observes the refutation of the sense of being a modification (*vikāra*) in the case of the sheaths consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) and the others. He states the conclusion: "abundant" (*pracura*). Anticipating the objection, "What is the fault in [interpreting it as] having the sense of a modification?", he says: "of another. This means that since any entity other than the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is sublated, the sense of being a modification is thereby sublated.

[Objection: "But surely, Ānanda, if 'abundance' (prācurya) is being predicated here, there must be a corresponding scarcity of suffering, just as when one says 'a country abundant in Brāhmaṇas,' the scarcity of Śūdras is implied. [The author] refutes this with the word "ānanda" (bliss). Here, the abundance of bliss—extending from human bliss up to the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā—is established by having the limited bliss of the supreme subject under discussion as its upper limit; therefore, it does not depend upon a scarcity of suffering, but rather upon the cessation of the abundance of bliss residing in [lower beings] such as the four-faced Brahmā.

As in the passage, "The sacrifice consists of food," and so forth. Now, one might object that an abundance of bliss (*ānandaprācurī*) can also be described by the paucity of suffering; anticipating this doubt, he says "pareti" (in the other). He destroys the misfortunes of those who have taken refuge in Him and shatters the sins of His devotees; for thus it is heard in the scripture: "Consisting of bliss. Indeed, we have studied hundreds of such scriptural collections, such as: "Then he becomes free from fear," "This [bliss] indeed does not afflict him," and "He is not smeared by evil action."

Therefore, the suspicion that there might be a small amount of suffering here does not arise. Furthermore, he says "of the ruler," because there is a contradiction between the state of being a ruler and having little sin, for the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is established as the ruler through such passages as "From fear of Him the wind blows," "By His command indeed, O Gārgī," and "The ruler of all."

But surely it was said by you that the mark consisting of being "made of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is contradictory in our position. This contradiction is singular for us, whereas for you there are many contradictions. Even regarding the one made of bliss, the statement of another self—namely, "This very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the former"—is contradictory. Furthermore, the mention of being "embodied" is not tenable because the body is the fruit of karma. Nor is the doctrine of its being something to be purified (*śodhya*) applicable to the supreme Brahman, as there is no possibility of impurity in it.

For it is heard even regarding the *ānandamaya* that there is a statement concerning its being something to be purified: "May my [selves] consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss be purified. Furthermore, in that very same *ānandamaya*, when the state of the fruit is indicated, it is said to be something to be reached; that too is contradictory. How can there be a new reaching (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) for a living self (*jīva*) that is already eternally present in the Supreme Self? Having thus pointed out these four contradictions, [the author] proceeds with the four quarters in their respective order.

"He composes himself as the Self"—this process of composure is indeed intended to exclude any other self, just as the statement "the Self of that very [one]" regarding the *ānandamaya* is like saying "the ascetics themselves are servants. What contradiction is there in this? Furthermore, the description of the Lord's having a body is especially appropriate for the *ānandamaya*, since He is the indweller of all bodies. Even the need for purification refers simply to the *ānandamaya* being one who is to be propitiated, as in the expression "the king’s heart is indeed pure."

Furthermore, there is no specific purity whatsoever in the previously mentioned auspiciousness. Even in common worldly usage, such as in the phrase "the king’s heart is pure," it is simply the cessation of harmful intent that is expressed; for only a favorable meaning is to be accepted in each respective context. Moreover, compatibility (*yogyatā*), like expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*), is a necessary factor in determining the meaning of a sentence. Here, indeed, only "approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) remains [as the intended sense], and that too is consistent; for "approaching" is said to be "attainment" (*prāpti*). And this attainment refers to Brahman, which was not previously experienced.

Subsequently, there arises the experience [of enjoyment]. This very point is expressed in the words: "He enjoys all desires together. Alternatively, it is indeed the attainment of a specific location that we are able to describe; this is precisely what is stated in the passage: "In Vaikuṇṭha, in the supreme world. Therefore, in our view, there is no room for contradiction. Here, the status of these terms as constituent parts of the meaning must be understood by oneself.

Here, the proponent of the view that the tail is Brahman (pucchabrahmavādī) objects, saying "it is bodiless. For if the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were indeed Brahman, then—given its partlessness—the postulation of fivefold limbs through distinctions such as head and wings, as expressed in the passage "joy is its head," would be untenable.

Therefore, it is said that "the tail is the support"; because it serves as the substratum for all beings, the tail itself—which is the form of the support of the universe—is the Supreme Brahman, since the designations of head, wings, and so forth are inappropriate for the Bliss-filled (Ānandamaya) being in its capacity as Brahman. He begins to refute this position with the words "soḍhā" (having endured): How can it be logical to speak of the tail of Brahman—whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss and which you yourselves accept as being devoid of limitations in space and time?

If you say, "We must accept the conceptualization of a tail for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda," then, alas! You, long-lived one, should likewise be satisfied with the fact that we too must accept the conceptualization of a head, wings, and so forth in the case of the partless *ānandamaya*, intended to express the various divisions such as joy (*priya*), delight (*moda*), and so on. Thus he asks, "How [is this]?"—meaning, how is the other [part], such as the head and wings? In that case, this would be utterly contradictory, namely, that the *ānandamaya* is Brahman itself whose nature is self-established; yet that is not the case.

The statement that [Brahman] is its own support is for the purpose of declaring that it has no other substratum; for, according to the manner of another Śruti—"In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own glory"—it is precisely the exclusion of any further support for Brahman, who is the support of all, that is stated here. What contradiction is there? As for the many refutations of those who maintain that the "tail" is Brahman, they have been clearly set forth in the Commentary itself; therefore, having merely demonstrated the meaning of the verse, we shall desist.

In the subject-sentence of the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, it is stated in the passage "for him, there is delay only so long" (*tasya tāvadeva ciram*) that the connection with suffering lasts until the fall of the body. On this basis, one might suspect that the "embodied self" (*śārīra ātmā*) referred to in the phrase "of him, this very one is the embodied self" (*tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā*) must be the individual soul (*jīva*). This suspicion is refuted in the *Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa* by the point that it is only the assumption of instruments and a physical body under the influence of karma that constitutes the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and not the universal embodiment (*viśva-śarīra*) which is natural to [the Self].

From this point forward, the section concerning the Inner Sun (Antarāditya-adhikaraṇa) proceeds. In this section, the relationship between the body and the Self is not stated merely by way of the state of being the inner controller; rather, there is a person connected to a body that possesses the distinctions of hands, feet, eyes, hair, and so forth. Since such a connection with a body is possible only for the individual soul (jīva), the connection [of this section] arises through the raising of a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa). Furthermore, the connection is that whereas previously the individual soul in general was refuted, now a specific type of individual soul is refuted. This is what he expresses by the word "bhūyiṣṭha" (in abundance).

Indeed, it has been stated previously that among humans up to the level of Prajāpati, there are certain individuals who possess sovereignty awakened by the power of the accumulation of abundant and infinite merit. It is further argued, as another point of connection with the preceding section, that one among these very individuals must be postulated as the Lord (Īśvara) existing in the form of a continuous stream. The meaning of this is: let there not be those for whom sin predominates, nor those for whom merit and sin are equal; rather, let certain individuals for whom merit predominates be postulated as possessing lordship. To this, the answer is: "That is not so."

In that regard, he summarizes the reasons according to the authoritative means of knowledge as "akarma" (non-action). He possesses a divine body that is not dependent on karma. "Jani" means birth. "Mahimā" means greatness. He is the natural controller of all persons. "Nityaśrīḥ" means he is eternally possessed of the connection with Lakṣmī.

Such a person is the Supreme Person, heard of in the orb of the sun (the solar disc) as the one taught in the section beginning, "That which is this space within the heart"; He alone is heard of in the *Antarāditya-vidyā* in the passage, "This [Person] who is within the sun. Thus, there is no room for the suspicion that he is a particular individual soul (*jīva*). For it is heard in that very same context: "He has risen above all evils; indeed, he rises above all evils who knows thus."

One should reflect here on such passages as: "O King, that in which all these powers are established," for therein it is stated: "She is not born from the cause of karma. Furthermore, the historical account—"Clearly, this is a great yogi"—is also well known. As for the quality of being the Ruler mentioned here, since it is established by many authorities such as "He who has entered within is the Ruler of people, the Self of all" and "The Ruler of all," it must be understood as pertaining to everything.

This is the summary here: because the form of the Blessed One residing within the solar orb is not dependent on karma, is non-material (aprākṛta), and exists for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who have taken refuge [in Him], any statement suggesting that it is merely a particular individual soul (jīva) simply by virtue of its connection with a body is the mere prattle of the most wicked haters of the Supreme Person. Here, even a brief investigation into that matter is set forth: Is the Person residing within the solar orb a particular individual soul, or is He the Supreme Self?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether the connection with a body and so forth—characterized by the differentiation of hands, feet, and the like—establishes the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) or not. For that purpose, it is further investigated whether this connection with a body is dependent on karma or independent of karma. Furthermore, it is investigated whether the scriptural statements regarding its arising from all sins and so forth preclude dependence on karma or not.

For that purpose, it is further investigated whether the word *pāpman* (evil) there refers merely to sin, or whether it refers to action (*karman*) consisting of both merit and sin. As for the relationship between cause and effect: if the word *pāpman* were restricted to sin alone, then statements such as "having risen above all evils" would not preclude dependence on action; rather, since the connection with a body is invariably dependent on action, the person within the egg is the individual soul (*jīva*). In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the relationship between cause and effect should be inferred by the students themselves.

Regarding this, an objector says: In the *Antarāditya-vidyā*, it is stated that the Blessed One is "risen above all evils" (*sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ uditaḥ*), which expresses His freedom from all sins. According to the method of the logicians (*tāntrikāṇām*), when there is a specific negation, there is an implied permission for the remainder; thus, since sin is denied in the case of the Person dwelling within the solar orb, there must be an implied permission for merit. This is what [the objector] states with the words beginning "from all," etc. [The author] refutes that with "not so," and here he states the reasons with the words beginning "it is declared," etc.

Through numerous proofs such as "no one has mastery over him," the fact that the Blessed One is not subject to the commands of another is understood. For a king’s servant, being subject to another's command, would incur sin from the transgression of that command, whereas by its observance he would obtain a favorable result. Since the Lord is not subject to the commands of another, even "good deeds" (sukṛta) consisting of compliance with the commands of another are impossible for him, like evil deeds; this is one reason. He states another reason in the words "svavaśa" (self-dependent).

According to the principle that "the fruit [arises] from this [Brahman] because it is logically consistent," it is stated that the Blessed One alone bestows the desired or undesired fruit for others; how, then, can His connection with good deeds (sukṛta) be possible? Furthermore, since the connection with good deeds is effectively rejected by the meaning of the text, "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action," that [position of yours] is contradictory. To the question, "In that case, how is the word 'pāpman' (evil) applied to merit (puṇya)? he says: "It may be so."

Even in the case of merit (*puṇya*), the word "evil" (*pāpman*) is employed here because it possesses the characteristics of evil. For indeed, even merit possesses the characteristics of evil, owing to its connection with undesirable results. In the world, what is a desirable result for one person may be undesirable for another. Thus, even a desirable result such as heaven is undesirable for those who know the supreme self; therefore, with respect to specific qualified persons, even optional ritual action (*kāmya-karma*) is indeed evil. Regarding this, he states a powerful regulatory principle in the form of a Vedic usage, beginning with the words "not well-done" (*na sukṛtam*).

For here, having indeed pointed out both good and evil deeds, the designation of both by the word "evil" (pāpman) is made quite clearly. Therefore, since even good deeds—just like misfortunes—are denotable by the word "evil," it is established that the statement regarding the rising above all evils also implies the cessation of good deeds.

Here, however, an objection is raised: "It has been stated by you that the Supreme Brahman possesses a form (*vigraha*). Is that form composed of *prakṛti* (material nature), or is it non-material (*aprākṛta*)? Even if it is non-material, is it the very essence of the Lord Himself, or is it a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*)?

In the first case, the flaw of being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), as previously mentioned by us, would follow—this is the 'logic of the ruined cart' (*ghaṭṭakuṭīnyāya*). In the second position, there is the undesirable consequence of the transformation of His essential nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*). The third position also does not hold, because there exists no distinct principle apart from *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, *Īśvara*, and *kāla*. Therefore, how can that be? He refutes this with the words: "It is well-known" (*prakhyātam*).

It is well-known from such passages as: "A foot of Him are all beings; three feet of His are the immortal in heaven"; "In the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha"; "The Creator beyond darkness"; and "Sattva which illumines its own existence. Pure *sattva* is that which serves as the substratum for *sattva* devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*. It is a certain divine substance. Its sinlessness is stated because it lacks any role in promoting the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Its distinctness from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is explicitly declared by the statement, "Three feet of His are the immortal in heaven."

By this [statement], he declares that the form of the Blessed One is neither ordinary nor its own natural state, but rather a non-ordinary, distinct substance; thus he says, "that form. Lord Parāśara has stated: "That form of Hari is another, great form, which is the opposite of the universal form (*viśvarūpa*). Here, *vairūpya* means "dissimilarity" (*virūpa*). By this, the arguments of opponents—such as "the form under discussion is ordinary because it possesses the nature of form," or "it is impermanent because it has parts"—are refuted.

Regarding the establishment of such a form, there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*), because it is established by valid cognition precisely through its association with specific attributes such as being non-material and eternal. Furthermore, if it were not so established, there would be a lack of a locus for the argument (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, let the logician himself recall his own system. If it is asked, "Granted that the Blessed One has such a form, what is the status of Ananta, Garuḍa, and the others?"—the answer is that the Blessed One alone is their refuge.

Because hundreds of authoritative proofs—such as "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" and "Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, dwells together with his devotees, the Bhāgavatas"—have refuted this, the demoness of doubt is dispelled. One might object: "Granted that the resident of Vaikuṇṭha has such a form, yet what is the means of certain knowledge regarding its eternality and other attributes? Anticipating this, he says "eternal," with the intention of referring to the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and so forth.

"One always beholds [Him]" (Sadā Paśyanti), "Eternal, possessing an eternal form" (Nityaṃ Nityākṛtidharam), "O Pauṣkara, when His form and His intent are eternally established," and "The Śrīvatsa-marked chest, eternal glory"—thousands of such authorities are to be considered.

One might raise the objection: "Granted that the entire collection of qualities belongs to the Lord who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha; however, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others are merely *prākṛta* (subject to material nature), experiencing pleasure, pain, and so forth under the influence of karma. How then can our attainment of liberation (*āpavargikī siddhi*) result from their worship? Anticipating this doubt, the author describes the collection of qualities—such as being non-material (*aprākṛtatva*) and the like—in the remainder of the text beginning with the words "ajahat" and so on, in accordance with the views of Parāśara, Pārāśarya, and others. The statement "possessing all powers" (*samastaśakti*) and so forth is the word of Parāśara.

The statement of Pārāśarya (Vyāsa), "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of an aggregate of elements," should also be kept in mind. Furthermore, the one born from a termite hill (Vālmīki) also said, "This great yogin is the manifest, eternal Supreme Self. Therefore, it should be understood that the imitation of grief, delusion, and so forth during incarnations is merely for the sake of diversion, like actors in dramas. The division into the categories of Para, Vyūha, and so on, is clearly to be found in the Pañcarātra and other scriptures.

Stabilizing the very point already stated by means of a *pratibandī* (reductio ad absurdum) following a restatement of the opponent's position (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] also demonstrates that being subject to suffering and so forth is the result of acting like an actor, using the phrase "because of being a body" (*dehatvāt*). Here, the *pratibandī* is as follows: if sublation (*bādha*) is admitted in some cases regarding matters known solely through scripture, then there would likewise be sublation in the case of the killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) and other such acts. To this, if one attempts to release the *pratibandī* by arguing that there is no sublation here because it is established by Śruti, then the release of the prisoner (*bandīmocana*)—that is, the resolution of the original dilemma—would occur in exactly the same manner.

It has been stated that because the form of the Blessed One and so forth are established by the Vedas (*śruti*), the mention of their being mixed with suffering and the like is for the purpose of deluding the *āsuras*. The *āsuras* are Kaṃsa and others. Thinking that the childhood and other performances of Kṛṣṇa and the rest are merely a dramatic play (*naṭana*) and not ultimate reality, they would repeatedly act in opposition; through that very activity, they would be destroyed. Thus, the meaning is that the performance of childhood and so forth has as its fruit the destruction of the evil-doers, as stated in the verse: "And for the destruction of the wicked."

Regarding the sections (adhikaraṇas) mentioned here, since they share a single purpose, they constitute a single "box" (peṭikā). Fearing that the subsequent sections up to the end of the chapter might be redundant due to a lack of specific difference in their subject matter, the author—demonstrating how they possess utility through a variety of methods—explicitly declares the primary purpose common to all these sections: namely, the contemplation of the specific qualities of the Blessed Lord, stating "In this manner."

Although, by means of the threefold knowledge taught in the three sections beginning with "Sadvidyā," there may be a superiority of the Blessed One—the cause of all things consisting of the sentient and insentient, both stationary and moving—over primordial matter (*pradhāna*), the class of individual souls (*jīva-varga*), and even the sun and other luminaries; yet...

Nevertheless, the meaning of the word *iti* is this: by restraining in this chapter the opponents who have arisen in succession according to the stated order—"more indistinct, indistinct, distinct, and following the shadow"—through the distinction of the doors of their arising, and who are characterized by a gentle beginning and a cruel conclusion, [the author] especially illuminates the qualities of the Blessed One through the remaining topics (*adhikaraṇa*).

The point here is this: just as in battles involving infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots—where each subsequent unit is weaker than the preceding one—the stronger forces are employed upon the defeat of the weaker; so too, when the signs of life become increasingly obscure, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) proceeds by the successive abandonment of each preceding stage and the adoption of each succeeding one. Without the curbing of such activity, even the knowledge of reality that has arisen does not become firmly established. Therefore, the remainder of this chapter must indeed be commenced.

Furthermore, our position is that in all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), the specific qualities (*guṇas*) of the Lord are manifested individually according to each section; therefore, the purpose of the remainder of the chapter is the comprehensive contemplation of those qualities. However, for those who maintain the doctrine of the attributeless (*nirviśeṣavādin*), since the attributeless reality is established by a single topical section alone, there is an absence of any further qualities to be expounded; thus, the heart of the matter is that the subsequent topical sections would be entirely fruitless.

Having thus stated the connection of the remainder of the chapter with the preceding section (peṭikā), he now specifically elucidates the nature of both the preceding and succeeding sections in order to state the connection of the remainder of the quarter (pāda): "By means of words... In the first section of the Śārīraka-śāstra, which begins with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā), it was stated that Brahman is the object of inquiry.

Regarding that Brahman, which is understood through words common to the assembly hall of Brahmā (*brahmasadana*), the Self (*ātman*), the Puruṣa, and the Person (*puruṣa*): is it *prakṛti*, or the individual soul (*jīva*), or some particular soul distinguished by accumulated merit? Since the word "sin" (*pāpman*) is common [to both], even if it arises from sin in the form of both merit and demerit, one might suspect whether it is the lotus-eyed one (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*), or someone else such as the four-faced one (*caturmukha*) or the three-eyed one (*virūpākṣa*). Having raised this doubt, it was determined in the preceding section that it is indeed the lotus-eyed one. In that regard, he states the distinguishing marks that exclude others, beginning with "will" (*saṃkalpa*).

From the mention of "volition" (saṃkalpa), there is an exclusion of Pradhāna. From the repetition of "bliss" (ānanda), the commonality with the individual soul (jīva) is excluded. Even though the individual soul possesses a specific accumulation of merit due to its non-material form, it is also excluded because of the scriptural hearing of the "lotus-eyed" nature (puṇḍarīkākṣatva); the underlying intention is that even the four-faced Brahmā and others are excluded.

The meaning is "by those [marks] that are not inconsistent with it and are not otherwise established. Here, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) objects: "In the three preceding sections, you have asserted the exclusion of Pradhāna and other such entities by means of marks (liṅga) through the sublation of general scriptural statements (sāmānya-śruti). However, specific scriptural statement (viśeṣa-śruti) is stronger than a mark, for it functions through its conventional power (rūḍhi-śakti). Therefore, by means of specific scriptural statements regarding ether (ākāśa), breath (prāṇa), light (jyotis), the sense organs (indriya), and so forth, one should set aside the marks and accept the well-known ether and the rest themselves as the Brahman to be known."

By this, the consistency of the section consisting of the remaining quarters has been stated. This very point he expresses with the words "the element" (*bhūta*). Space (*ākāśa*) is of two kinds: one is that accepted by the knowers of the inner self (*adhyātmavit*), namely, "If there were no bliss in space..."; the other is the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), which is well-known to all the world without distinction between the common folk and the investigators. Therefore, in accordance with the preponderance of common usage, it is the elemental space alone that should be understood here. The same should be observed regarding breath (*prāṇa*) and the others as well.

Thus, having set aside the inferential mark (liṅga) stated in the three preceding sections by means of specific scriptural mentions (viśeṣa-śruti) regarding ether and so forth—and having refuted it according to the opponent's view—the proponent (siddhāntin) again protects—that is, preserves—that very same inferential mark which establishes Brahman and distinguishes it from Pradhāna and the like, by demonstrating the impossibility of a collection of specific attributes such as ether and so forth. This is because, according to the rule "bhujo 'navane," the middle voice (ātmanepada) is prescribed when a meaning other than protection (rakṣaṇa) is intended.

The intention here is as follows: it is already established that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymological derivation (*yoga*); nevertheless, the conclusion of those learned in logic is that an etymological derivation determined by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) indeed subverts conventional usage. And in this context, the expression "sarvāṇi ha vā imāni" is seen as a reference to what is well-known, because we observe the indeclinable *ha vai*, which indicates what is well-known. And this well-known status resides in the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*).

And in those [passages], the fact that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme referent is already established by the principle of the goat-sacrifice and others. Therefore, it is entirely logical that the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is set aside by its etymological derivation (*yoga*), which is determined by the mark of being the cause of all things found in a sentence that cannot be explained otherwise and which contains a designation similar to well-known indicators of Nārāyaṇa. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.

Beyond this, he states that the division of the four subsequent sections consists of two pairs, which are also mutually connected, beginning with the words "ākāśa" (space). The terms *ākāśa* and *prāṇa* have no other possible resort; they are not fit for being understood as referring to the well-known [elemental] space and breath. Therefore, setting aside their conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) in favor of the Supreme Brahman, they must be explained solely through their etymological power (*yoga*). By this, the status of these two sections as a single group (*ekapeṭikatva*) is established.

Likewise, since the two subsequent sections (adhikaraṇas) have as their purport Brahman qualified by the conventional meaning [of the terms] without abandoning that conventionality, their status as a single section (ekapeṭikatva) is established. In that regard, he demonstrates that the word *jyotis* (light) has as its purport that which is qualified by its conventional meaning, stating: "Light. For a collection of scriptural authorities is found, such as: "The sun does not shine there," "It neither rises nor sets," and "The splendor residing in the sun."

In this same manner, the word "senses" (*indriya*) and others must also be interpreted by relying on their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) without breaking it, while concluding that they refer only to the qualifying attributes, insofar as they denote the Supreme Self characterized by Indra and the rest. Thus, he concludes with the words "in this way," showing that the establishment of two sections (*peṭikā*) results from the difference in meaning. The sequence of the application of words is such that in one case there is etymological power (*yaugika-śakti*), while in the other there is conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) that terminates in the qualifying attribute alone.

Previously, in the passage beginning with "This golden person who is within the sun," it was stated that a certain person residing within the sun is to be known through the Vedāntas on account of specific indicative marks. Now, the connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that space (ākāśa) might also be known through the Vedāntas due to the absence of such marks and the presence of specific scriptural texts regarding it, that doubt is now being refuted.

One should reflect for oneself that the common application of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) to both the well-known physical ether and Brahman is the seed of doubt, and so forth. The investigation into its meaning, however, concerns whether the word "ether" in the Chāndogya passage beginning with "All these beings, indeed... refers to the well-known physical ether or to the Supreme Self.

For that purpose, it is investigated whether this word "ākāśa" functions by means of conventional power (rūḍhi-śakti) or not; for that purpose as well, it is investigated whether there exists another principle that sets aside the general rule that "conventionality overrides etymological derivation" (yoga), or whether such a principle does exist. Furthermore, it is investigated whether the mention [of Brahman] as being established—as if it were the well-known element—and its stated causality and so forth refer exclusively to the conscious (cetana), or whether they refer to both the conscious and the unconscious (acetana), and so on.

Regarding the statement "The state of being the fruit and the fruition is austerity—these beings," since there is no other logical principle (nyāya) to establish a figurative power (yoga-śakti) for the restatement of causality concerning an object already established as such, the word *ākāśa* functions solely by its conventional meaning (rūḍhi); thus, this word refers to the well-known ether. This must be stated by the proponent himself even in his own final position (siddhānta).

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that in the *Chāndogya*, the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is seen to denote the cause of the origin and dissolution of all things; yet that same ether is stated in the *Taittirīya* to be unproduced from anything else, in the passage: "From the Self, ether was produced. Its state of being unproduced from anything else is logical precisely because it is eternal as the cause of all. This is what he expresses with the words beginning "here," etc. He refutes that [view] with "not so."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "because it is established. Since this sentence, which contains the expression "it is so" (*havai*) as a reference to what is already well-known, has the nature of a restatement of an established fact, a prior establishment must necessarily be presupposed. And that establishment exists in the causal texts (*kāraṇavākya*), and it has already been stated that those refer to Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, the meaning is that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) does not refer to the commonly known ether. Furthermore, in the passage "the ether is the supreme resort," the ether's status as the ultimate goal to be attained is heard right here [in this very text].

Those who know the Self declare that nothing insentient can be the supreme goal. This is what [the author] states with the word "atha" (now). The meaning is that the status of being the supreme goal is not possible for that ether (*ākāśa*). He states another objection with the word "tat" (that): in passages such as "That [Self] thought," "That fire thought," and "Those waters thought," the agent of those actions is indeed heard to be the All-seeing (*vipaścit*). Consequently, manifold seeing is not possible for ether. Alternatively, the phrase "its agent" means "the agent of ether."

In the Brahmavallī, the entity that is the cause of the world is heard of as being "Vipaścit" (the All-seeing) by means of the term "Brahman. They have explained that "vipaścittva" (the state of being Vipaścit) is indeed the quality of seeing variously. Therefore, the word "ātman" denotes the Supreme Self (Paramātman). As for what was said—that in the passage "From the Self, space [arose]," the production of space from one's own self is being stated—there is a contradiction if the primary meaning is accepted; if the non-primary meaning is accepted, that same fault remains.
Therefore, with the intention that the meaning is simply this—"Space was produced from the Self, i.e., the Supreme Self"—he says: "Obstructed... (vihata).

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks as follows: "Since the origination of the world in the well-known ether (*ākāśa*) is not perceived, it is logical to abandon the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word 'ether' there; however, here in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because we observe that the activity of all persons indeed depends upon the vital breath, that very thing which is a favorable indicative mark (*anukūlaliṅga*) for us is an unfavorable indicative mark for you. Therefore, the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word 'prāṇa', being accompanied by such a favorable indicative mark, should not be abandoned. He states this with the words, "dependent on the vital breath" (*prāṇāyattam*). [The author] refutes that with "not so" (*tan na*).

Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*). By the phrase "all indeed," it is stated that the entire phenomenal world—without distinction between sentient and insentient—is subject to activity dependent upon the vital breath. The meaning is that even among certain insentient things, such as stones and wood, they should be accepted as denotable by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) by relying on the etymological derivation "that in which the vital breath resides. He applies the reason stated in the preceding section here as well with the words "as before"; the meaning is that the word "indeed" (*havai*) is present in both instances.

Regarding this, he states with an illustration the Vedic usage of the word *prāṇa* for the Blessed Lord: "As [in the case of] *ākāśa*," etc. Just as the word *ākāśa* refers to the Supreme Self because that word is found in various places in the Śruti concerning the Supreme Self, so too the word *prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Self because the act of breathing (vivifying) all living beings is seen to be predicated of Him. The relationship between the inquiry into its meaning and its resulting fruit should be understood by oneself, as in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the connection (*saṅgati*) is one of extension (*atideśikī*).

The author reveals the difference between the preceding and subsequent sections by stating that here, for the benefit of the students, the refutation of the rising prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—which was based on the absence of the subject-matter sentences (*viṣayavākya*) for the two aforementioned sections—is carried out by another method. This refers to the procedure of contradiction and non-contradiction: that which is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) favorable to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is opposed to the prima facie position, whereas that which is an indicative mark favorable to the prima facie position is itself not opposed to the final conclusion.

In this context, by means of specific terms such as "space" (*ākāśa*) and so forth, a definitive conclusion regarding the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) has been reached through the strengthening of the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) that correspond to the tenets establishing the respective subjects in the two preceding sections. Herein, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that while in the two preceding sections they cite specific indicative marks (*liṅga*)—such as being the cause of all things—that distinguish [the subject], no such specific indicative mark is cited in the two subsequent sections.

Furthermore, he shows that there is also an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—such as the identity with the gastric fire—that is favorable to the well-known light and the sense organ mentioned in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), by stating "it exists. That very same [mark] is contrary to the status of the supreme Brahman, which constitutes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). He shows that we do not speak merely on the basis of an indicative mark, but also on the basis of the primary scripture (*śruti*), by stating "the word" (*śabda*). The meaning is: a specific word whose referent is nothing else.

Thus, the summary of the opponent’s specific intention is that, for four reasons, the Supreme Self is not known through the Vedic texts concerning light and so forth. Now, one might object: "If there is no mention of being the direct cause in the passages concerning light and so forth, how can there be any room for the suspicion that light and the rest are the cause? Anticipating this, [the author] says "viśva... (the universe), meaning: even in the absence of a statement of being the direct cause, it is somehow possible to even suspect that light and the rest are the cause by means of certain indicative marks—such as the appearance of some semblance and unsurpassed splendor—which imply causality.

He refutes him who objects in this manner by means of the two immediately preceding sections with the word "obstructs" (*rundha*). The meaning of the word is that he "obstructs" by demonstrating the specific distinction between sentient and insentient beings as corresponding to the Lord's own power of manifestation (*māyā-śakti*).

In these three sections concerning ether and the subsequent elements, the connection consists of the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and its resolution, following the sequence stated in such scriptural passages as "From ether, air [is produced]. The cause of doubt is the common usage of the word "light" (*jyotis*) for both the well-known physical light and the Supreme Self in various places. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: in the passage beginning with "Now, that which is beyond heaven," does the word "light" denote the well-known physical light, or does it denote the Supreme Self?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether, even in the absence of a mark (liṅga) unique to the Supreme Self within its own sentence, the mark unique to the Supreme Self situated in the introductory section establishes that the word "light" (jyotis) denotes the Supreme Self, or whether it does not. For that purpose as well, it is investigated whether there is or is not a mark unique to the Supreme Self even in the introduction. And from that, [the main point] is investigated.

Does the word *gāyatrī* in the introductory passage, "The *gāyatrī* indeed is all this," set aside the interpretation that [the *gāyatrī*] refers to the Supreme Self, or not? Furthermore, it is investigated whether the designation of the quarters beginning with "beings" (*bhūta*) found in this same passage excludes the view that [the *gāyatrī*] refers merely to the *gāyatrī* meter, or does not exclude it.

The relationship between the cause and the effect is to be inferred by oneself. Here, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that, unlike in the sections concerning Ākāśa and Prāṇa, in the subject-sentence of the section on Jyotis (Light), no characteristic mark (liṅga) contrary to the well-known light—such as being the cause of all—is found to establish that the word "light" denotes the Supreme Person. On the contrary, a favorable characteristic mark is found: the identity with the gastric fire. This he states in the words "kaukṣeya" (of the stomach). And thus, that [gastric fire] alone is the cause of the universe.

It is not only through this *vidyā* that [the Lord] is recognized; rather, He is also recognized as the cause of the universe in the *Vaiśvānara-vidyā*. Thus, he says, "of that" (*tasya*). He states the conclusion with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). He refutes [this view] with "not so" (*maivam*). He provides the reason with "by the *Puṃsūkta*" (*puṃsūktena*).
