For at the beginning, by the statement "all beings are one foot of Him," the passage from the *Puruṣasūkta*, "all beings are one foot of Him," and so forth, is made to be recognized. Indeed, the fact that the *Puruṣasūkta* has Nārāyaṇa as its primary subject is well-established.

And that causality belongs to Nārāyaṇa because of the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the Lord of Lakṣmī in the passage, "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," and because of the statement of Parāśara: "The word 'Bhagavān' [refers to Him]. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the identity with the gastric light mentioned in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*)?"—the answer is that its status is simply sublation (*bādha*), due to its conflict with the logical principle (*nyāya*). For those who know the logic maintain that between the opening and the conclusion, the opening is stronger. In this regard, the very logic of the "sacrifice for receiving a horse" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi-nyāya*) serves as the illustration.

One might object: since the opening statement of the entire section, “The Gāyatrī indeed is all this,” demonstrates that the focus is on the Gāyatrī, does not the introductory passage establish the Gāyatrī alone and not the Supreme Person? Anticipating this doubt, the author states the word “Gāyatrī” to show that this [identification] is established otherwise. The mention of the Gāyatrī is due solely to the similarity of having four feet, and not because of its being the very nature of the Gāyatrī. Anticipating the question as to what the reason for understanding it thus is, he states the restrictive reason with the words “Moreover” (api ca).

In this passage, indeed, the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart are indicated by way of similarity with the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*. The fact that the Supreme Self is the soul of the universe (*viśvātmakatva*) is the restrictive factor establishing that the word *gāyatrī* refers to the Supreme Self—not merely to the *gāyatrī* as a collection of syllables; for it is possible to explain the concluding portion in accordance with the introductory statement itself. Thus, the conclusion is reached that that which is denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*) is none other than the Supreme Brahman.
And the word "light" (jyotis) is applied even to the supreme Brahman in other passages, such as "That which the gods know as the light of lights," and so forth.

In the *Śrīmadbhāṣya*, for the sake of those with dull understanding, he raises the doubt regarding a mutual contradiction between the preceding and following statements and resolves it with the passage beginning with "utthānam" and ending with "ittham."

At the beginning of this section, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* themselves stated that in the pair of sections starting with "Jyoti" (Light), there is an emergence [of the topic] from a mark (*liṅga*) pervaded by the cause; yet, at the time of presenting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) once again, they remarked—even though it was indicated as if it were well-known—that because no specific marks of the Supreme Self contained within its own sentence are observed, it is like the case of "Ākāśa," "Prāṇa," and so forth. Therefore, how is there no contradiction? To this, he states the reason for the refutation: "viśva... (the whole).

This, indeed, is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers that there exists an indicative mark (liṅga) consisting of the manifestation [of the Lord], such as "on all sides, behind everything, in the unsurpassed, supreme [worlds]," which implies His status as the cause.

Furthermore, [the opponent] might argue that there is no contradiction because there is no mark (*liṅga*) within its own statement—such as being the cause of the world—that establishes the Supreme Person as characterized by having both genders and so forth. To this, he says: "contradiction" (*vyāhati*). The meaning is this: although the author of the Commentary intends that there is indeed a mark unique to the Supreme Person in this sentence, "Now, that light which is beyond the sky," as presented in the commentary on the statement of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The employment of the two qualifiers—"shining in the unsurpassed and supreme worlds"—is appropriate only for that light which dwells in the extraordinary divine realm, and not for mere light existing within the cosmic egg; such is the intended meaning.

The connection here has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself with the words beginning "niratiśaya" (incomparable). Having rejected the term "supreme light" as applied to the sun and other luminaries, Indra—who is postulated by others as the supreme lord over all lights—is now suspected of being the cause of the world and is likewise rejected.

Alternatively, the refutation of the meaning stated in the concluding portion on the basis of the predominance of the opening statement was already explained in the previous section; therefore, by that same principle, in the Pratardana-vidyā as well, the conception of the Supreme Person—though established by the words of the concluding passage—is sublated due to the predominance of the opening statement. This constitutes the connection [of the present discussion] by way of raising such a prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view. The inquiry into its purpose is as follows: in the Pratardana-vidyā, is it the well-known Indra who is taught, or is it the Supreme Self having Indra as its body? The same should be said regarding Prāṇa as well.

For that purpose, it is deliberated whether, according to the principle of the section on "commencement" (*upakrama*) stated in the preceding section, it is proper here also to describe the meaning [of the passage], or not. Furthermore, it is deliberated whether there exists a principle subsequent to the principle of the section on "commencement"—namely, that when there is a contradiction between the introductory statement and the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the great sentence alone must be followed—or whether such a principle does not exist. Again, it is deliberated whether, in this sentence, a collection of reasons establishing the nature of the Supreme Brahman is found everywhere, or whether it is not found.

Here the opponent thinks: You have stated that it is logical to explain the concluding portion in accordance with the opening statement; however, in the Pratardana-vidyā, the word *Indra* is employed first in the opening, and since that is a specific scriptural mention (*viśeṣa-śruti*), there is indeed conformity with the scripture situated in the opening. Furthermore, it is likewise stated that he is the object of meditation as the most beneficial thing: "Choose for yourself a boon from me, whatever you consider most beneficial for a human being. And that...

The mark of being the Supreme Brahman [is present]; therefore, by both the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) found at the beginning, Indra alone is the Supreme Person. Furthermore, characteristics such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, which are well-known to Indra and are contrary to your intended Nārāyaṇa, are observed; and that is indeed inconsistent with the Supreme Person. He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*tad*); for that reason, this one denoted by the titles Śakra and so forth is Indra alone, the creator of the world. He refutes this, saying: "No."

The intention is as follows: it is not possible for the well-known Indra to be the object of meditation as the "most beneficial" (*hitatama*), nor can he be the object of meditation for the sake of liberation (*apavarga*). For the well-known Indra is merely a member of the host of gods, an inhabitant of limited realms such as heaven, and is like a mere insect; how could he be the object of meditation as the most beneficial? Therefore, because of this contradiction in meaning and in order to establish that the denotation of the word is not restricted, the Supreme Person alone is designated by the word "Indra," for [the root] *idi* signifies supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*).

They explain [this]: "Upon careful examination, even the Grandfather (Brahmā) is but a *udumbara* worm; how much more so the well-known Indra, who was defeated by Meghanāda and others? Reflect on this yourself! Then Indra instructs him to worship himself, saying, "Therefore, worship me. Furthermore, in this very context, deeds such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son are proclaimed—marks that are contrary to the Supreme Person and favorable to the well-known Indra. If one asks, "How can that be?", the author provides the resolution here with the passage beginning with "brahma" and ending with "svātmanā ca."

The intended meaning is as follows: Brahman, the object of meditation, is indeed threefold—namely, meditation on Brahman as qualified by the non-sentient (acid-viśiṣṭa), meditation on Brahman as qualified by the sentient (cid-viśiṣṭa), and meditation on the Supreme Self alone (kevala-paramātma). By this [threefold classification], even well-known figures such as Indra are designated as objects of meditation by virtue of being attributes of Brahman. Consequently, for the purpose of realizing those well-known figures like Indra who serve as qualifiers, even indicative marks (liṅga) such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son are meaningful and are not contradictory.

This is the conclusion here: because he is the object of the most beneficial meditation and for other such reasons, it is already established that in the Pratardana-vidyā, the Supreme Person alone is the primary denotation of the word "Indra. Nevertheless, by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son and so forth, the well-known Indra is also accepted as a qualifying attribute. In this same way, let the well-known vital breath (prāṇa) also be accepted through the specific indicative marks belonging to the context, but not in its own right. For meditation upon the Supreme Self in its own essential nature is already well-established.

Therefore, since the specific attributes of Indra and others—which are well-known and not shared by [other deities]—are mentioned in the Pratardana-vidyā for the purpose of establishing the threefold nature of the worshipper, there is no contradiction. Consequently, it is established that in the Pratardana-vidyā, the Supreme Self alone, qualified as Indra and so forth, is the object of worship; thus, by means of the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word "Indra," there is an expression that refers to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) while setting aside the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Anticipating the objection, "How then can the meaning of a sentence be determined when it contradicts the opening statement (*upakrama*)," he says: "Prāṇa, Indra... and so on.

Both [the introductory statement and the concluding summary] are elucidated here; however, between the introductory statement (*upakrama*) and the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*), the introductory statement is more powerful. Furthermore, when there is a contradiction between an introductory statement and a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the great sentence alone is more powerful. But this applies only when there is indeed a contradiction. Here, however, the intention of the Commentator is that there is no contradiction at all, because those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*) interpret even the introductory statement within the great sentence as referring to the Supreme Self characterized by Indra.

Having raised the objection that the commencement of this section (adhikaraṇa) is untenable here, he resolves it with the words "yat... (that which...). This is the meaning: regarding the mark (liṅga) stated by you as residing solely in the cause—that which was spoken concerning the Jyotis (the Light), namely, its possession of unsurpassed radiance in the highest worlds as expressed in the passage beginning "Now, that which is beyond this..."; and that which was intended concerning Indra, namely, his being the object of meditation for those seeking liberation for the sake of direct liberation, as in "Meditate upon me"—both of these are well-known to reside exclusively in the Cause (Brahman) as its defining characteristic.

The two marks (liṅga) have been previously established as being co-extensive with the state of having space as their substratum, which is exclusively devoted to Nārāyaṇa as is well known. How so? Just as the causality of the entire universe was previously established as having the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) as its object, so too these two marks are established in that very same way as being co-extensive with Him; this is the meaning. He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).

Since the marks (*liṅga*) consisting of being endowed with unsurpassed radiance and being an object of meditation for those seeking liberation have already been established as residing in the Supreme Person, it is not tenable for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) to arise on the basis of the mark of being the cause, which is pervaded [by that same nature]. Thus, the refutation has been stated regarding the consideration of these two marks as residing in the Supreme Person; he now states the refutation even in their absence, beginning with the words "aprāpte" (when [the conclusion] is not yet reached).

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a reflection on the two marks as residing in all causes, let there be some light endowed with those two marks, or let there be some Indra; yet by this much, the previously stated causality based on a single locus, which is supreme causality, does not fall away—what is the purpose of these further deliberations?"—he refutes it by accepting half of the point, saying "True."

Even if there were no specific purpose for this section (*adhikaraṇa*), there is nonetheless some purpose; and even if the two marks (*liṅga*) belong exclusively to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), that very Supreme Person exists by assuming the state of Upendra (Viṣṇu). Therefore, he too is indeed an object of worship. Some of childish intellect, however, might be confused, thinking that the Śruti—just like the Purāṇas and other texts—merely speaks of the birth of Upendra. The meaning is that this section is commenced in order to dispel such a doubt.

The meaning is that Upendra’s status as the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa) is well-known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas; likewise, it is well-known in those very same sources that Indra is a servant of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).

Having thus resolved the apparent contradiction between the two subject matters mentioned, [the author] demonstrates the distinction between what is accepted and what is not accepted regarding the position held by the opponent. Furthermore, he shows that the purpose of the identity with the gastric light—which was stated as a contradictory mark—as well as the marks such as the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), lies in their being for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*), stating: "The light... Words such as "light" are accepted as denoting the supreme reality qualified by its attributes; they are not accepted as denoting the mere attribute alone.

The identity with the light within the belly is for the purpose of meditation; likewise, the characteristic mark of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is for the purpose of illuminating the specific nature of the object of meditation—such is the summary of the meaning of the verse. The remainder is quite clear.

Here, for the sake of favoring the disciples and for the purpose of clarifying the meaning stated in the section beginning with "ākāśajyotiḥ," he demonstrates the rule regarding the application of words denoting other things to Brahman according to their different referents, starting with the word "kāryam" (the effect).

When Brahman is indicated by well-established (nirūḍha) or conventional terms—such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth, which are firmly determined to be effects, or "belonging to Prajāpati" (*prājāpatya*) and so forth, which are firmly determined to be subject to karma—the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) must be set aside in some cases where words like "ether," used for states of the Self, have no other possible application. Here, "no other application" (*agati*) means the impossibility of maintaining the conventional sense; by that lack of alternative, the convention is barred, and thus only the etymological meaning (*yoga*) is resorted to. This is the sense.

In another place, he explains the resolution by means of a different method, saying "that" (*tad*). The meaning is that in the case of the light (*jyotis*), the mark (*liṅga*)—namely, the identity with the gastric fire—and in the case of Indra, [the marks] such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, are both non-otherwise-established (*ananyathāsiddha*) and pervading (*vyāpta*). Through the power of knowledge, because those respective marks are non-otherwise-established, there would be a state of having as its object that which is qualified by those specific attributes. Regarding this, he states four examples, beginning with "light": the word "light" refers to Brahman qualified by light; furthermore, the word "Indra" refers to [Brahman] qualified by Indra.

In the statement "Thus, I am Brahman," the word "I" (ahaṃ) denotes the Supreme Self as qualified by one's own self. Here, the phrase "with the Aindrī [verse]" remains to be explained; we shall discuss that as well. In the case of "With the Aindrī [verse], [one worships] the Gārhapatya [fire]," since the word "Indra" lacks a conventional meaning (rūḍhi-śakti) applied to the Gārhapatya fire, one must resort either to a figurative application (gauṇī-vṛtti) or an etymological derivation (vyutpatti). Regarding both of these, they say: "The status of Indra in Agni would be figurative, caused by its connection with sacrifice; or, following the sense of the root 'ind' (to rule), he too is indeed a lord over his own domain."

Therefore, it is perfectly consistent that we accept the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the words "space" (*ākāśa*) and "breath" (*prāṇa*) as referring to the Supreme Brahman. This is the meaning: "Through etymological derivation, the various designations may reveal the Supreme Self; provided that its characteristic marks (*liṅga*) cannot be established otherwise, they take hold of Him as qualified by those marks."

Previously, it was established that the subsequent sections (adhikaraṇas) have as their purport the manifestation of each individual attribute of the Lord, based on the principle of "it praises Him because of His qualities. Now, however, he explains that the purport of the seven past sections lies respectively in the seven attributes of the Lord, beginning with "conquest" (*jaitra*) in the section on Jitavītahavya, and "endowed with excellence of strength, manliness, and so forth" in the section on Anuśāsana, using the words "by His own will," and so on. The term "Auspiciousness" (*śubha*) means infinite and boundless joy consisting of the splendor of auspicious qualities.

"Without substrate" (anupadhika) means being devoid of limitations by space, time, or substance. "Possessing breath" (saprāṇa) means being the cause of life for both those with breath and those without breath. In that context, the mention of "the Lord" (prabhu) is for the purpose of manifesting the majesty described in the Sarvādhikāra section.

The third quarter (pāda) of the first chapter: By means of the two preceding quarters, those scriptural passages containing signs of the individual soul (*jīva*) and others that are less clear or unclear have been examined. Now, by means of the two subsequent quarters, those passages containing signs of the individual soul and others that are clear or clearer will be examined in succession. For this very reason, the mutual connection between the second and third quarters is established. As for the connection between the sections (*adhikaraṇa*), at the end of the previous quarter it was stated that the one connected with heaven, earth, and so forth is the Supreme Self; that very point is now raised as an objection and subsequently resolved.

Furthermore, in the very section concerning the "Invisible One" (Adṛśyatvādy-adhikaraṇa), it was established that [the subject] is the Supreme Self by virtue of having the three worlds as its body; in connection with that, even in the section concerning Vaiśvānara, the possibility of it being the individual soul (jīva) was raised and refuted. Here, however, at the conclusion of that incidental discussion, the same passage concerning heaven, earth, and so forth (dyubhv-ādi-vākya) is resolved once more by stating the remaining points of the matter already discussed in the preceding section. Its placement here in the third pāda is due to the fact that the marks (liṅga) of the individual soul and others to be refuted are clearly evident here.

In this fourth quarter (pāda), exactly seven topical sections (adhikaraṇas) are directly connected. One might raise the objection that the three sections beginning with the "Deity Section" (Devatādhikaraṇa) in the middle are not connected because they deal with different subjects; anticipating this, the author refutes it by saying, "by clear [marks]. In this third quarter, speech resting on Brahman is established through clear marks such as those pertaining to the individual soul (jīva). As for the mention of the qualification for knowledge (vidyādhikāra) in the three intermediate sections—what is its purpose? It is stated there because it arises from the context; since the topic of qualification occurs in the passage, "But with reference to the heart, because humans are the qualified," it is appropriate that it be mentioned here as well.

Furthermore, the refutation of the "half-Lokāyata" Mīmāṃsakas—who deny the existence of a Lord—as set forth in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* and other sections, is indeed useful for establishing the present subject matter: namely, that the Supreme Person is the cause of the entire universe, from the four-faced Brahmā down to a tiny ant. For if deities did not exist, it would be impossible to establish His causality in relation to them. Moreover, by virtue of being the object of worship even for those deities, the preeminence of the Blessed One as Brahman is established; thus, even the delusion regarding the identity of those deities with the ultimate cause is completely dispelled.

Therefore, there is a direct connection between the seven topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), while for the others it is by way of incidental context (*prasaṅga*). Having restated this, he says "the principles" (*nyāyāḥ*) regarding the mutual connection between the sixth and tenth [sections] among the seven that are directly connected. Thus, exactly seven principles are joined here in this chapter (*pāda*) by virtue of their being directly related to the subject matter of the subsequent [section].

Furthermore, the intended purport of this quarter is to establish that the Lord’s own glory (*svamahiman*) is His abode and His lack of dependence on any other support, by means of the sequence stated [in the scripture]: "He is the support of all; He is that very Self; on what is He established? On His own glory. For it has already been stated previously that "the Creator, the embodied one, is self-abiding," just as in the expression, "The ascetics are themselves their own servants. To confirm this purport, the various groups of topics concerning the Lord’s status as the ruler of all and so forth—which have been discussed in their respective sections—should be considered as woven together and interconnected with one another.

If one then raises the objection as to how there can be a connection when the sixth and tenth sections are separated by three intervening sections, the answer is that the mutual relationship is indeed established: the Lord’s status as the Sovereign of All, which was determined in the sixth section, must be protected by the tenth section through the establishment of His very nature as the bestower of liberation. Thus, the connection is proven.

It should be understood that the inclusion of the two words "dyu" (heaven) and "bhū" (earth) in the Sūtra is for the purpose of indicating the upper worlds. Here, having raised an objection regarding the commencement of this section, he provides a resolution with the words "siddham" (established), etc. This was already established in the previous *Adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa* (Section on Invisibility). In the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*, the Supreme Brahman is indeed established as possessing distinctness through its various specific attributes which define it; and because of the mention of distinction—that is, because of the direct statement of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*).

And that being the case, for what purpose does he grind this Upaniṣad like grinding flour—meaning, why does he grind it specifically again and again? He provides a reply by partially accepting the point, beginning with "True" (satyam) and so forth. Let it be granted that the passage from the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad has already been examined; nevertheless, as to why it is examined once more, he says: "The Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña).

The doubt, which had arisen due to the uncommon attributes of the individual soul (jīva) such as being the support of the channels (nāḍīs), is uprooted by the means of knowledge beginning with direct scriptural testimony (śruti), preceded by the word [of the Veda], so that it does not arise again. The meaning is this: since the qualities of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) are recognized in both passages of the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad, there is no doubt at all regarding a difference in context. Furthermore, the connection with the channels and other such factors are merely fallacious reasons (ābhāsa). Therefore, they should be resolved by the appropriate reasons for reconciliation intended by the Commentator (the Bhāṣyakāra) himself.

The investigation into that meaning is as follows: Is the abode consisting of heaven, earth, and so forth the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (paramātman)? To determine this, it is further investigated whether the collection of passages beginning with "In whom heaven... is distinct from the context characterized by attributes such as invisibility, or not distinct. To determine that, it is further investigated whether the connection with the vital breaths (prāṇas) and so forth is based on the relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, or is characterized by the relationship of container and contained.

Furthermore, for that purpose, is the connection with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth based on the relationship of the benefactor and the beneficiary, or is it characterized by the relationship of the container and the contained? For that purpose, do attributes such as being the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth, and being the bridge of immortality, belong to the individual soul (*jīva*), which experiences the fruits of karma, or not?

Here, he summarizes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words beginning "In whom [the earth] is woven," and so forth. If it be argued that—in passages such as "In whom heaven and earth..."—the mind is woven in, meaning it is continuously connected, to another agent; and that which is described as being born in various ways, as the support of the channels (*nāḍī*), and as moving within the body—that is none other than the enjoyer of the fruits of action who possesses the instruments (the senses) such as the eyes; [the author] rejects this stated position with the word "no. He states the reasons for this with the word "because of all" (*viśva*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: because the Supreme Person is described in this section as the self who is the support of the universe; because it is established that He is the bestower of liberation through the statement, "He is the bridge to immortality"; because it is established that He is the goal to be attained by the liberated; because there is no break in the previously mentioned context of Brahman; because of His possession of unsurpassed radiance due to the absence of being an enjoyer of the fruits of action—as expressed in "the other, not eating, looks on"; and because of His association with other qualities exclusive to Brahman (indicated by the word "and"), what you have stated is untenable.

Now he begins to state the alternative establishment (*anyathāsiddhi*) of the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), starting with the words "pervaded" (*vyāpta*). The meaning is: if all the senses and so forth are woven into the Lord who is all-pervading, then what is there that would not be possible here? If it is argued that the birth of the Lord is not possible, he says "birth" (*janma*) to show that this too is possible because birth occurs by His will; for it is heard in scripture: "Being unborn, He is born in many ways."

"Abiding in the form of the heart within the network of channels" means existing by virtue of being situated inside the heart; for all the channels are connected to the Supreme Person residing within the heart, as it is heard in scripture: "There are one hundred and one channels of the heart. If it is asked how that which is all-pervading can be contained within [the heart], he restates that point and provides the answer with the word "unwavering. Indeed, the Lord’s nature as the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) is twofold: one through the assumption of a formal body (vigraha), and another through His all-pervading essential nature (svarūpa).

In the case of the *vigraha* (embodied form), "moving within" (*antaścaraṇa*) refers primarily to moving within the body; however, "moving within by way of one's own nature" (*svarūpeṇāntaścaraṇa*) is indeed applicable here as well, just like the "moving within" that consists of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all things, as taught in the Subālopaniṣad in such passages as "He who moves within the earth. The meaning is that, by virtue of being the inner controller, the mere act of presiding over [all things] is what is denoted by the word "moving within."

Since the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad establishes that the subject matter pertains exclusively to the Supreme Self (paramātman) from beginning to end due to the absence of any interruption in the context of the Supreme Self, the prima facie argument arises that in the Chāndogya’s Bhūmavidyā, because there is no interruption in the context of the individual self (jīva), it is the individual self alone that is being propounded. Thus, the connection [of this section] is established by way of this logical proof.

The connection is also stated by way of the subject matter (*artha*). In the preceding passage, "The mind is woven together with the vital breaths," the person associated with the vital breaths was mentioned; here too, it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that is denoted by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) due to its association with the vital breaths. The inquiry into the meaning of this, however, is whether the one indicated by the word "plurality" (*bhūman*) is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) or the supreme self (*paramātman*). Is the inner self indicated by the extensiveness that is the basis for the word "plurality," or is it the supreme self?

Is the *bhūman* (the Infinite) concluded with the question and answer concerning the inner Self designated by the word "prāṇa"? Furthermore, having stated that "he who sees thus, thinks thus, and knows thus becomes an 'exceeding speaker' (*ativādī*)"—referring to the one who exceeds the *prāṇa*—the text then prescribes for that "exceeding speaker of *prāṇa*" the practice of speaking the truth as a subordinate part, saying, "But he indeed is an exceeding speaker who exceeds by means of the Truth (*satya*). Or, does it designate the Supreme Self by the word "Truth" and [prescribe] for the one who exceeds that?

"He speaks as one who speaks beyond [the vital breath]"—does this statement, "But he indeed speaks beyond," involve the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the speaker regarding the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or not? And does the word "but" (*tu*) contradict that recognition? Here, the author summarizes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "The Self" (*ātman*). Indeed, in this knowledge of the Infinite (*bhūmavidyā*), Sanatkumāra is the teacher and Nārada is the disciple.

Although he had mastered every branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), Nārada was nonetheless not free from sorrow due to his longing for self-knowledge, thinking, "I am devoid of the Blessed One’s wisdom," and saying, "In this way, O Blessed One, I am indeed a knower of mantras, but I am not a knower of the Self. To this Nārada, the discourse initiated by Sanatkumāra culminates in the vital breath (*prāṇa*). He establishes that very point with the word "the vital breath. And that which is called the vital breath is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), because in that very context it is described as being incapable of being harmed.

Furthermore, fearing that the object denoted by the word "ground" (*bhūman*), which is being described here as having few adversaries, might be the individual soul (*jīva*)—the locus of unlimited happiness—the author refutes this with the word "not. He explains this very point with the words "from that called *prāṇa*. For there, after first using the term *prāṇa* to denote the individual soul and stating that one who knows *prāṇa* is a superior speaker (*ativādin*) because his happiness surpasses the happiness of others, it is finally established that even for that individual soul, only one who knows the happiness of the Supreme Self is truly a superior speaker, since the individual soul itself is limited.

Therefore, it is stated that in this context, the Supreme Brahman alone—which is denoted by the word "Truth" (satya) and is superior to that which is called "vital breath" (prāṇa)—is the primary subject to be expounded.

Having stated the opponent's position in detail, he likewise states his own view, beginning with the word "nāma" (name). Since the sequence of questions and answers continues as far as the knowable object extending to the ends of the quarters, and since it is observed that each subsequent stage is spoken of as having a superior result and being further specified, and because such a designation is seen to find its rest in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the instruction concerning the Self under discussion must terminate at the vital breath. Consequently, there is no instruction regarding the Self beyond the vital breath by means of the term "Truth" (*satya*).

He rejects the stated point, saying "it is not so. Here, in this context, it has been stated that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), like name and the rest, is born from the Supreme Self. How can that which is born possess the nature of the Supreme Self? Anticipating the objection that the word "Self" (*ātman*) here refers to one's own self, and that there would thus be no contradiction with the context because [the breath] is born from itself, he rejects it, saying "no. He provides the reason for this: "because of the dissolution" (*vighaṭanāt*). This is because of the dissolution of the natural case-ending that expresses the relationship of cause and effect.
The relationship of cause and effect is also inherently based on difference; the notion that something could arise from its own self is indeed a strained one—this is the intended meaning.

In order to awaken the disciple, having analyzed the intention of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the appropriate reply as well, beginning with "the seer of prāṇa. For here, the seer of prāṇa is mentioned as one who speaks beyond [ordinary speech]; reiterating that, speaking the truth (*satyavāda*) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*). Therefore, if it be argued that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of "I" in its entirety, is indeed prāṇa—the producer of all principles by way of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—he rejects this with the word "no. He explains the reason for this rejection with the word "this" (*eṣa*).

Anticipating the objection that—"In the passage 'But indeed he is an Agnihotrin who speaks the truth,' the word *eṣa* (this) is also preceded by the word *tu* (but), yet no other qualified person (*adhikārin*) is postulated there; likewise, it might be so here"—he says "tadvat" (like that). For in that case, two Agnihotras were not established as authoritative, whereas here they are indeed established as authoritative.

Having first spoken of one who speaks excessively regarding the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), it is stated once more, "But he indeed speaks excessively who speaks excessively by means of truth"; thus, the state of being an "excessive speaker" is mentioned twice. This is not the case with the statement concerning the *agnihotra*, where the status of being an *agnihotrin* is not mentioned twice. Therefore, it is logical that speaking the truth is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) for the previously mentioned *agnihotrin*. Here, however, the distinction is that by means of the word "this" (*etad*) accompanied by the particle "but" (*tu*), another "excessive speaker" is understood.

Otherwise, even in this context, another qualified subject would not be heard [in the text]: "But he indeed speaks transcendentally who speaks transcendentally by means of Truth. Furthermore, if the sentence were to find its rest in the individual soul (jīva), then there would be an inconsistency regarding the attributes unique to the Supreme Self mentioned in this section. Therefore, the fact that all attributes are logically possible only in the Supreme Self, who abides in His own glory, also serves as a reason for establishing the Supreme Self.

In this context, regarding the knowledge of the levels (bhūmavidyā), he states a summary verse beginning with "Name" (*nāma*) for the purpose of understanding the essential nature of the entities starting from Name and ending with Hope (*āśā*). First is Name; above that is Speech (*vāk*); after that is Mind (*manas*); then the one called Volition (*saṃkalpa*); after that is Consciousness (*citta*); immediately following that is Meditation (*dhyāna*); after that is Knowledge (*vijñāna*); after that is Strength (*bala*); from that comes Food (*anna*); from that, Water (*toya*); from that, Fire (*tejas*); then again Space (*ākāśa*); after that, Desire (*manmatha*); then Hope (*āśā*); and finally, above all these, the Living Being (*jīva*) denoted by the word "Breath" (*prāṇa*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*), the controller of all—all of which is understood to be this very [Self].

In the preceding section, it was stated that [the Lord] is established in His own glory; however, since that same quality is heard of even in reference to one distinct from the Supreme Person, there is a connection by way of raising an objection (*pūrvapakṣa*). Alternatively, the connection is that while in the previous section the status of being denoted by the word "Truth" (*satya*) was established for the Supreme Brahman—having pointeded Him out with the two words "Truth" and "Imperishable" (*akṣara*) in the passage, "By whom the true Imperishable Person is known"—here the status of being denoted by the word "Imperishable" is established.

Or rather, in the previous [section] there was a refutation of the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas here there is a refutation of both the individual soul and primordial matter (*pradhāna*). The inquiry into that meaning concerns whether that which is designated by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*) in the passage, "This indeed, O Gārgī, is that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare," is primordial matter, the individual soul, or the Supreme Person.

To that end, it is considered: "In what, indeed, is space woven like warp and woof? Here, the question arises whether the state of being the substratum of space perceived in this passage belongs to the *pradhāna*, or to the individual soul (*jīva*), or indeed to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone. Furthermore, does the word "space" (*ākāśa*) here refer to elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) or to unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*)?

Regarding this, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in succession, beginning with the phrase "Because it is well-known. One position is that, because in passages such as "In what, indeed, is space woven like warp and woof," the *pradhāna*—which is denoted by the word "the Imperishable" (*akṣara*)—is intended, since it carries its own effects starting with the well-known space.

Even that *pradhāna*, which is determined as "space" (*ākāśa*) through the etymological derivation "it spaces itself" (*ākāśate*) by virtue of being the causal space, is designated as the substratum [of the syllable]; yet the *akṣara* (the Imperishable), which is described as supporting the entire aggregate of the worlds, must be the *jīvatattva* (the principle of the individual soul) alone, because *prakṛti* is presided over by the *jīva*. He rejects both these positions with the words, "Not so."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because [He] is the Seer. This is because the attributes such as being the Seer of all—which are impossible for both the conscious and the unconscious, and which are unique to the Blessed Lord—as well as the fact that [the world] is maintained by His own teaching in the manner stated in the Sūtra, "And she [is Brahman], because of His presiding over it," depend upon His instruction. Furthermore, in this context, the exclusion of any other seer is observed; and that is possible only in the case of the Supreme Self, not in the case of the individual soul (jīva), because there exists a Supreme Self who is the Seer of all, distinct from the individual soul.

Therefore, the refutation of another seer is precisely the refutation of another Lord. This is what [the author] states with the words "of another seer. The meaning is that the exclusion of a seer other than the Supreme Person—who is the seer of the universe by virtue of being its sustainer and controller—is the rejection of another similar Lord who exists as a controller of the Supreme Person by virtue of being superior to Him.

In the Sūtra, the masculine designation "he" (saḥ) is intended to refer to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). Indeed, in the preceding [Sūtra], it was stated that the Supreme Self is "the unseen seer" (adṛṣṭo draṣṭā), meaning He is not seen by others; therefore, the connection [of this Sūtra] arises from the objection that if He were designated as the object of seeing (īkṣatikarmatva), He could not be the Supreme Person.

Alternatively, they say that the connection [of the discussion] arises from the following doubt: "Just as it was previously established that the word 'ether' (ākāśa) refers to something else due to a contradiction with its primary meaning, so too might the word 'intermediate space' (antarikṣa) be explained by another etymological derivation. Or rather, since the word 'ether' refers to everything up to the celestial vault (ambarānta), there is a connection because the term 'world of Brahman' (brahmaloka) can likewise be explained otherwise.

The inquiry into its meaning, however, concerns whether the one specified in the passage, "But he who meditates upon that Supreme Person by means of this very syllable 'Om' consisting of three morae," is the four-faced Brahmā or the Supreme Self; whether, in the phrase "he sees the Person," the object of the act of seeing is the four-faced one or the Supreme Self; whether the term "the aggregate of individual souls" (jīvaghana) includes the four-faced one as well or not; and whether the word "Brahma-world" (brahmaloka) here refers to the abode of the four-faced one or to the supreme ether (paramavyoman).

Regarding the phrase "that which the seers know" (*yattatkavayo vedayante*) in the verse [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.14], it is not recognized as referring to the state of Viṣṇu because of its connection with being the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*). Having stated the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) here, he refutes it step by step, beginning with the words "the one who has become the object" (*lakṣībhūta*). According to the principle that in this context the fruit corresponds to the mode of meditation, both disputants agree that the person who is the object of both the acts of meditating (*dhyāti*) and seeing (*īkṣate*) is the one to be attained; and that is primarily the single individual soul (*jīva*), the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

He alone is the Lord of the Egg (the cosmic egg). The statement, "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city [of the body], who is higher than the high," is the designation of Him precisely as the object of that vision. His state of being "higher than the high" is due to his being higher than the individual soul (jīva), which itself is higher than primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest. He states the fault in not accepting this [view] with the words, "If it were not so. He refutes [that objection] with the words, "That is incorrect. For it would be improper to describe the qualities of the Supreme Self—such as peace and immortality—and to repeat them in reference to that Supreme Reality which is the object of meditation on the Praṇava. Therefore, because of the connection with attributes unique to the Supreme Self, the meaning is that the one to be established in this context is indeed the Supreme Person.

Here, an objection is raised with the words "nanu" (but surely). Since the world of Brahmā, which was previously mentioned as being counted among the earth and the intermediate space as the fruit of meditating on the *praṇava* consisting of one or two measures (*mātrā*), is now being presented as the fruit of meditating on the *praṇava* consisting of three measures, it might—on account of the aforementioned proximity—be considered to be the world of Caturmukha (Brahmā) alone. He says "maivam" (not so) to show that this is not the case. He states the reason for this with the words "pāponmuktena" (by one freed from sin).

In this context, the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), which is heard of as being attained by one who is completely liberated from all sins, cannot be the perishable abode of the four-faced Brahmā. Furthermore, since the world of Brahman is heard of as being attained preceded by union with the sun—according to the text, "He is united with the heat in the sun"—and because of the recognition of the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga) in the passage, "From the year [he goes] to the sun," it must be Vaikuṇṭha alone that is to be attained by the liberated soul.

In this context as well, the state of being the Sun is expressed by the words, "that which the poets declare. This is what he means by saying, "preceded by the attainment of the status of the Sun. If it is objected that, due to its proximity to the atmospheric world (antarikṣaloka), it must be the world of the Four-faced One (Caturmukha) itself, we say no; for there is an absence of such proximity because of the intervention of many worlds, such as heaven (svarga) and others, in between. If it is argued that such an extensive interval must be tolerated, the solution is the same. He states here, beginning with the words "it must be tolerated," that even the intervention of the world of the Four-faced One must likewise be tolerated.

Furthermore, since at the beginning [of the passage] it says, "One should meditate upon the Supreme Person," it must be stated that the object of meditation alone is the object of the act of seeing (*īkṣati*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the principle of "according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*); such refutations are to be inferred. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Self alone is designated as the object of the act of seeing.

In the preceding section, it was established that the "Person dwelling in the city" (*puriśaya-puruṣa*) mentioned in the passage "higher than the high, the Person dwelling in the city" is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Here, the connection [of the present discussion] is that the status of the Supreme Self for the one who dwells in the city and is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) is being refuted. Furthermore, previously it was stated that the term "world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) refers to the abode of the Supreme Self; similarly, here the connection arises from the doubt that the terms "world of Brahman" and "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*) might likewise refer to a location.

Alternatively, just as in the previous [section] the well-known sense of the word *antarikṣa* was set aside, so too here it is established that the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) does not refer to the well-known subject of ether; this is the connection. Since it is untenable for the Supreme [Self] to be perceived as something else to be sought after, and since the relationship between the standard of comparison and the object compared is untenable in either of the two [other] positions, there arises a doubt. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is the small ether the elemental ether, or the individual soul (*jīva*), or the Supreme Self?

Is the mention of something else to be sought for that purpose contradictory to the small ether being the Supreme Self, or not? Does the mention "that which is within it" refer to a collection of qualities or to another object? Are the attributes such as freedom from sin mentioned in the statement "this is the Self" the same as the qualities of the individual soul (jīva) mentioned in the Prajāpati discourse, or not? If they are qualities of the individual soul, does the natural force of the scriptural texts regarding freedom from sin and so forth remain intact, or not?

The relationship between the result and the consequence is as follows: when the statement "that which is within it" (Chāndogya Up. 8.1.1) is intended to refer to something other [than the self], then, since the word "to be sought" (*anveṣṭavya*) would not have the qualities as its object, the small ether (*daharākāśa*) would be the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*). However, when there is a natural consistency in the eight qualities mentioned in the sentence "this is the Self" being attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) as described in the Prajāpati section, then, because the sentence "this is the Self" refers to the individual soul, the small ether would be the individual soul; such is the relationship between the result and the consequence in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

When the statement "that which is within it" refers to the collection of qualities (*guṇajāta*), then, because the word "to be sought" (*anveṣṭavya*) would likewise refer to the collection of qualities, the small ether (*daharākāśa*) would be distinct from the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*). However, when the natural sense of the sentence "this is the Self" does not lie in referring to the attributes mentioned in Prajāpati’s discourse, then—by virtue of its naturally signifying the Supreme Self as qualified by the eightfold qualities—that small ether would be the Supreme Self; such is the relationship between the conclusion (*siddhānta*) and its result.

Having first refined the subject sentence, he summarizes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words: "The small [space] within the lotus of the heart. This is the meaning: in the *Taittirīya* [Upaniṣad], in the passage "Therein is a small inner space," the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is used as a synonym for the "ether of the sky" (*gaganākāśa*), and thus it refers to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) alone; for while the word "space" is well-known to apply to Brahman, its primary renown is as the elemental ether. Thus he says: "Because of the pre-eminence of its well-known usage."

He rejects this [interpretation] with the words "no. He states the reason for this with the words "by opposing qualities" (*pratyanīkaiḥ*). This is because that which is indicated here by the word "ether" is qualified by attributes such as being the self without adjuncts (*nirupādhika-ātmatva*), freedom from evil (*apahatapāpmatā*), and the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), which are found in Vedic passages such as "This Self is free from evil" and are unique to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, there are two kinds of well-known usage: the Vedic and the worldly.

In this matter, the Vedic usage among those learned in the Vedas is more authoritative; therefore, that which is designated by the word "ether" (ākāśa) here is indeed the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the well-known usage of the word "ether" with respect to the Blessed Lord is stronger, as it is supported by such marks (liṅga) as being "without attributes" and "free from sin," and is established by other scriptural passages such as, "If this ether were not bliss. This is what he means by saying, "and it is based on scripture. He says, "by groups of marks," to show that there are not only scriptural usages, but also supporting marks.

Furthermore, he summarizes the scriptural passages and reasons that refute [the view] that the space within the heart is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) in the first half-verse beginning with "The external ether," and so forth. This is its meaning: the relationship of comparison and object of comparison expressed in the passage, "As large as this external ether is, so large is this ether within the heart," is not possible if the small ether (*daharākāśa*) were the elemental ether, because the relationship of comparison and object of comparison necessarily involves a distinction between the two.

If it is argued that the relationship of analogy (upamānopameyabhāva) is based on the limitation [of the Self] to the heart, then in that case, it would be impossible for that which is limited to the heart to be the locus of all things, as taught in such passages as, "In Him are both heaven and earth. Furthermore, the status of being denotable by the words "Truth," "Brahman," "City," "Self," and so forth—as specified in the passage beginning, "This is the true Brahman-city; this is the Self"—is not possible in the case of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa). He states this very point with the word "satya" (truth).

If it be objected that the "small ether" (daharākāśa) is not the Supreme Self because of the mention of another object to be sought within it—"What is within that, that is to be sought"—the author replies with the words "and the support of desires. Here, that which was reckoned—that is, calculated—as the support of desires is the very same eternal reality that is expressed by the term "small ether"; therefore, the statement "this is its Self" is a restatement of that very [reality], and the phrase "desires to be meditated upon" refers to its qualities. This is the construction.

The meaning is as follows: preceded by the question, "What is there in this that is to be sought? [the text] first enjoins the meditation upon the Supreme Self—designated by the term "small ether" (daharākāśa)—and the eightfold qualities residing within it, stating, "In Him all desires are contained. For this very reason, in the statement regarding the fruit—"Now, those who depart from here having discovered the Self and these true desires"—both are indicated as objects of meditation; thus, the small ether is the Supreme Self.

Therefore, that collection of qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth, which must be sought within [the Self], is denoted by the word "desires" (kāma). Desires are so called because they are desired; they are auspicious qualities.

In the *Chāndogya*, the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); however, in the branch of the Vājasaneyins, it is stated: "That which is this ether within the heart—within it he lies, the ruler of all, the lord of all. Thus, it is the one lying within the ether who is designated as the Supreme Self. If it were argued that the well-known (physical) ether alone is being expressed by that word, how could there be consistency between the two? To this, the author provides the resolution: "The Lord of All," etc.

In the Vājasaneyi-śākhā, however, the space within the heart (hṛdayavyoman) is designated as the substratum of the Lord of All; therefore, we accept that what is denoted by the word "space" there is indeed the well-known ether (ākāśa), due to the specific characteristic mark (liṅga). In the Chāndogya, the word "ākāśa" refers exclusively to the Supreme Person, because of the characteristic mark consisting in the statement that it is the substratum of all desires.

If it is objected that in the *Chāndogya* the word *brahmaloka* is employed, yet the compound is not *brahma eva lokaḥ* (Brahman itself is the world), because it is more logical to adopt a genitive determinative compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*) as in *brahmaṇo lokaḥ* (the world of Brahman), we reply: no. Since in the case of the injunction "one should request the *niṣādasthapati* with this [formula]," a descriptive determinative compound (*karmadhāraya*) is indeed adopted, we have explained—following that same principle—that *brahmaloka* means "Brahman itself is the world"; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

Regarding this, he says "the Chāndogya. For when there is an absence of a decisive reasoning (*nirṇāyaka-nyāya*), another meaning is suspected. And it is appropriate that this Brahman, by virtue of being the support of all, should be denoted by the word "world" (*loka*). He shows that Āpastamba also expresses this very same point by saying "Āpastamba."

The verse, "He indeed is Vaibhājana, both what has been and what is to be," establishes that Brahman alone, having become the self of all, exists as the city (*pura*) of all things. "Vaibhājana" is a place fit for standing by means of the individual distribution (*vibhajana*) of all objects. It also says, "All living beings (*prāṇinaḥ*) are indeed the cities of Him who dwells in the cave. This means that all living beings are the cities of the Supreme Self who dwells in the cave. Thus, living beings are the cities—that is, the dwelling places—of the Supreme Self.

That too, even so; that too, even Brahman; their city, because it is the substratum of all, since everyone dwells within it. By this, the meaning of the word *Vāsudeva* is recollected, according to the [scriptural] statement: "Because he dwells everywhere and everything dwells in him."

Thus, having raised and refuted the objection that the small ether (daharākāśa) is the well-known physical ether, the possibility that it is the individual soul (jīva) is now raised and refuted. The word "jīva" [is used] to express this doubt: "If that were so, even though its being the well-known ether is set aside because it is untenable for it to be the substratum of qualities, yet since qualities such as 'freedom from sin' (apahatapāpmatva) are possible [in the soul], and since the phrase 'this is the Self' refers specifically to the individual soul, and furthermore, because its limited size is mentioned in the words 'therein is the small ether, free from sorrow,' the small ether must be the individual soul itself. Anticipating this objection, the author rejects it with the word "no" (asat). Here:

He states the reason with the words "from that which is without substrate" (*anupadhikāt*); the meaning is "from that which is natural. For the Supreme Self possesses by nature such qualities as the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpatva*), whereas for the individual soul (*jīva*), these are obtainable through His grace, according to the scriptural statement: "Having reached the highest light, he emerges in his own form. Furthermore, the fact that the Supreme Person is the substratum of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is mentioned here; therefore, it is the Supreme alone who is being established. Now, an objection might be raised: "Its smallness (*daharatva*) has been stated; how can that be so? Anticipating this, he resolves it with the word "conditioned" (*aupādhikī*).

The meaning is that the smallness of the Supreme Self is not stated here as being inherent, but rather it is stated as being based on its limitation by the heart. Now, one might object: "In the Prajāpati discourse, even the individual soul (jīva) is described as possessing the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin; therefore, how can the exclusivity of these qualities to the Lord be established? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the Prajāpati [discourse]..."

This is the meaning: the Prajāpati discourse, which is recorded in the context of the Discourse on the Subtle (Dahara-vākya), is indeed a supplement to that very Discourse on the Subtle; furthermore, the individual soul (jīva) taught therein would be one who has been refined by the mass of qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) through attaining a state of equality with Him, obtained by the grace of the Supreme Person. And thus, there is no fault whatsoever.

In that case, the Prajāpati statement would indeed be distinct from the Dahara statement, and the individual soul (jīva) taught therein would be entirely independent; why then do you establish a mutual connection between these two statements, both of which are self-sufficient? Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "the space within the heart" (daharākāśa). We do not here postulate a mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), but rather [the connection] arises from the very nature of the statements themselves.

For here, in the preceding passage, the mention of the individual soul (*jīva*) is intended to establish that the Blessed Lord is the bestower of liberation; the *saṃprasāda* is the individual soul, because its nature is serene due to its delight in the essence of knowledge regarding its relationship with the Blessed Lord. Furthermore, in the subsequent passage concerning Prajāpati, the Supreme Self is mentioned within that same discourse in order to determine the specific goal to be attained by the individual soul who is the subject of exposition.

Since both sentences are connected through their mutual proximity, expectancy, and semantic competency, one should not postulate a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Thus, one should not suspect a contradiction between the preceding and following sentences, nor should one assume independence (*nairapekṣya*). According to the maxim that "when a single unified sentence is possible, a split in the sentence is not desired," since a single unified sentence is possible, it is improper to accept a split in the sentence.
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras shows by the word "that" (*tat*) that he intends the very harmony of both sentences.

In the previous section, regarding the Dahara-vidyā, it was established by the sūtra, "If it be argued that on account of the scriptural mention of smallness [the Supreme is not meant], that has already been answered," that the term "the Supreme Person" (parama-puruṣa) refers to the one heard as being small. The connection of this present discussion is stated in the Bhāṣya itself: the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arises from the fact that this possession of a small dimension is heard elsewhere in scripture in reference to the individual soul (jīva) alone. The inquiry into its meaning, however, concerns whether the "Person the size of a thumb" mentioned in the text is the inner self (pratyagātman) measured by a thumb, or the Supreme Self (paramātman).

The inquiry into that matter is as follows: Is this lordship dependent upon the body, the senses, and so forth, or is it independent of everything? To determine that, the inquiry is: Does the status of being established by the opening statement contradict the natural force (*svārasya*) of the mark (*liṅga*) of lordship, or not? For that purpose, it is investigated whether that status of being established is consistent with the individual soul (*jīva*), or whether it is inconsistent in both cases. The subject passages for this should be clearly seen in the *Bhāṣya* and *Dīpikā*. Having stated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) therein, he refutes it with the words "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*).

"The lord of the vital breaths (prāṇa) moves about by means of its own actions, thumb-sized and having a form like the sun"—this Vedic scripture is intended here. Moving about by its own actions through the vital breath itself, it is described in one part of the scripture as being "thumb-sized. Furthermore, in another passage it is seen stated: "Yama forcibly drew out the person the size of a thumb. Therefore, the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) is that the Upaniṣad declares this individual soul (jīva) to be of the measure of a thumb, as established by such authoritative evidence.

That is incorrect, because it has already been refuted by the mark (liṅga) of lordship and so forth stated in his own words, namely, "the Lord of what has been and what is to be. If one asks, "How then can the Lord be measured by the thumb? [the author] says, "Not [in that sense]. His being measured by the thumb is stated with reference to the limitation of the worshipper's heart, and not as something inherent.

In this context, within the discussion of the *adhikaraṇas*, three *adhikaraṇas* are mentioned because of the incidental topic (*prasaṅga*) of the qualification of human beings. Thus, since there is an investigation here into the qualification established in the third chapter, one might object that there is a confusion of chapters. To this, he replies with the words "Not so" (*na hi*), and so forth. Indeed, someone thinks as follows: previously, the measurement of the Supreme Person by the size of a thumb was stated, and it was said that this is in reference to the heart; for it is not the case that the hearts of all living beings are measured by the size of a thumb.

"Because of the absence of a thumb, it cannot be said that the heart—the abode of all living beings—is measured by a thumb. This is true; however, it is not stated that the heart which is the support of all is measured by a thumb, but rather the heart of the worshiper. Therefore, the statement regarding the Supreme Brahman—which is all-pervading—being measured by a thumb should be understood as being made in some instances with reference to the human capacity [for meditation].

In connection with that discussion on *adhikāra*, within this section consisting of four sūtras, a specific *adhikāra* is considered through three sections (*adhikaraṇas*) placed between each pair of sūtras. However, it is not intended here that the *adhikriyā* (the subject matter to be established) should be understood by means of the sections belonging to the third chapter; therefore, there is no contingency of violating the structural arrangement of the chapters. This is what he expresses by the words "by those belonging to the third [chapter]. The term *itikartavyatā* refers to the collection of subsidiary elements (*aṅgakalāpa*).

In the preceding section, it was stated that the qualification for the meditation on Brahman belongs to humans, based on the sūtra: "But with respect to the heart, [the meditation is] for humans and others, because they possess a body. Now, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt: "In that case, would there not be no qualification for gods and others in the knowledge of Brahman? The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is there or is there not a qualification for gods and others in the knowledge of Brahman? And is it possible or not possible for the mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) that establish their corporeal forms to have that [knowledge] as their primary purport?

Is it possible for them [the deities] to possess a physical body, or not? Is it possible that the mantras and *arthavādas* which set forth such bodies have that [possession of a body] as their primary purport, or not? Can it be asserted that there is no intentionality regarding the possession of a body as it appears in the mantras and *arthavādas*, given that those mantras and *arthavādas* primarily aim at either revealing the meaning of what is to be performed (*anuṣṭheya*) or providing praise (*stuti*), or not? And is the possession of a physical body useful for the revelation of the meaning of what is to be performed or for the purpose of praise, or not?

Having stated the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the section on deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), he refutes it with the words "the word itself is the self" (*śabdātmā*). [The opponent argues: Is the deity merely the word ending in the dative case, or is it the object such as the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*) and so forth, or is it the word conjoined with its object that constitutes the deity? In any case, meditation upon Brahman with respect to such a deity is not possible. [The term] "non-ṛṣic" (*anārṣa*) means non-Vedic. If there were no deity, the deity's capacity to bestow fruits would simply not exist.

And thus, there would be the abandonment or rejection of the satisfaction of the deity mentioned in the scripture in the passage, "Being thus pleased, he pleases [the deity]"; or else, there would be the postulation of something not heard in the text, such as the *apūrva* (unseen potency) or the literal meaning, depending on the difference of opinion. And that is indeed improper, because the abandonment of what is heard and the postulation of what is not heard are extremely base.

[Objection: "If this is so, then since the inference regarding God (īśvarānumāna) was refuted in the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa*, how can there be an acceptance of a deity here? [Response: Anticipating this objection—that even God is included among the deities—the author provides the answer: "the creator of the universe. In that [section], we refute the inferential nature of God, but not His scriptural nature (*āgamikatva*). Therefore, the Supreme Person established by the scriptures—which were previously shown in the *Śāstrayonitvādhikaraṇa* to be uncontradicted and full of intended meaning—cannot be denied even by one who possesses all powers. Thus, for us, who maintain that God is known through scripture (*āgamika*), there is no fault whatsoever.

Because of the existence of both desire (*arthitva*) and capability (*sāmarthya*), he specifically establishes the qualification (*adhikāra*) of the deities as already stated, saying "capability" (*sāmarthyam*). Qualification is said to be fourfold: one who is desirous, capable, learned, and not excluded by the scripture. Alternatively, qualification is twofold: desire and capability. Capability, moreover, is threefold: capability of birth, capability of action, and capability of intellect. It is said that all of this belongs to the deities, expressed by the phrase "for those who have assumed suitable bodies."

Since the connection with a body is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there certainly exists both the capacity of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the capacity for action (*karman*). Indeed, the capacity of the intellect is observed in some cases through the non-forgetting of previous births, and in others through instruction; for it is heard in scripture that Indra and others were instructed in the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). The capacity of birth consists simply in the assumption of a body produced from the constituent elements (*sattva*).

Since the state of being a seeker arises precisely from being afflicted by the threefold suffering, even those deities possess the qualification for the category of worshiping the Blessed Lord. Here, the atheistic Mīmāṃsakas raise an objection: "The Veda proclaims only that which is not perceived through the body and so forth; such is the established rule of the system."

And thus, since it is cognized by the *arthavāda* portions of mantras which convey objects not apprehended by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the entire [corpus] including the corporeal form of the deities and so forth must be accepted as true, provided there is an absence of defects in the cause or of subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). As for those Mīmāṃsakas who proclaim such things to be false because they deny the existence of God (*nirīśvara-mīmāṃsaka*), they forget their own stated principle that the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*). For the established rule of the Mīmāṃsakas is that validity is intrinsic, whereas invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*);
the meaning is simply that in this case, there is no defect in the cause or the like.

Regarding this, someone says: "The experts in the Tantras state that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like have praise as their primary purpose; however, if the object [of the praise] is not ultimately real, its status as praise is contradicted. He dispels this doubt with the words, "The function is twofold. For praise is the expression of the relationship between a quality and the possessor of that quality. That is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and figurative (*aupacārika*). The primary is according to the actual fact, such as "free from evil, stainless," and so forth. The figurative, however, concerns objects such as kings, as in "You are Indra, you are the Moon," and so forth.

Even there, the description of the connection with the various qualities of Indra, Candra, and so forth, pertains exclusively to the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); all of this has been stated here in the preceding verse. To explain: in praise (*stuti*), there are two modes of operation—one by way of one's own qualities and another by way of the qualities of another. Among these, the former is "literal" (*ārthī*), as it does not deviate from the primary meaning. Even in the latter type of praise, a portion of the primary attribute must be inferred by those of subtle intellect.

One might object: "Is it not the case that even falsehood is spoken for the purpose of enticing children, and since that takes the form of praising medicine and the like, the falsity of praise is indeed observed? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says: *rucyarthāyām* ("when the sense is 'to please'"). This is the meaning: even where a falsehood is uttered for the sake of pleasing someone, if the listener is not deluded, the act of persuasion (*prarocanā*) is not accomplished through the telling of a lie. If, on the other hand, the listener is deluded, that statement pleases him precisely because he perceives it as having a reference to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Therefore, the ultimate reality of the meaning [of the Veda] is indeed useful for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). Now, it might be argued that the sages have stated, "What praise could there be regarding a thing as it actually is (*bhūtārtha*)?", and poets have also said, "For the utterance of a fact as it is is not praise of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*). From this, it might be claimed that praise lacks ultimate reality; but that is not so, because those statements are intended to exclude figurative (*aupacārika*) praise. It is not, however, that the ultimate reality of praises is denied in every respect. The meaning is that the praise of the Supreme Lord is not figurative praise, but rather is real (*tāttvikī*).

Here, with the words "not so," he refutes the idle chatter that the deities have no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) because of the rejection of the fivefold [attributes] such as the body, by means of the passage beginning with "the body, the taking of oblations," and so forth. It is well known from the *Śruti*, *Purāṇas*, and other sources that the gods and others are capable of assuming various bodies; therefore, how could the simultaneous presence of such deities, endowed with such powers, at a ritual performance not be possible?

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is maintained that deities possess forms and perform specific activities, then because those [deities and activities] are non-eternal while the Vedas are eternal, the fault of 'conjunction of the eternal and the non-eternal' (nityānitya-saṃyoga-doṣa) would follow. Anticipating this, the author refutes it with the words "tattad" (those respective...). He provides the reason for this with the word "pravāhāt" (due to the continuous flow).

Even regarding the impermanent bodies of deities and their respective narratives of that kind, the Śrutis do not suffer from the defect of association with impermanence, because they have as their subject matter the continuous succession of Indras and others. If it is argued: "In that case, you claim the Śrutis are eternal, yet this is untenable; for in passages such as 'The Kāṭhaka [is the work] of Kaṭha' and 'The hymn (sūkta) of Viśvāmitra,' their status as having an author is perceived. To this, he replies: "No, [it is said] at the beginning of the sections (kāṇḍa)," etc. In the Śrutis, the assertion of authorship for certain individuals arises only from the act of promulgation (pravacana), and not from being the direct creator.

If it is asked how that is so, he states the reason therein: "because the eternity of the Veda is established by means of valid cognition. This means that even if Vyāsa, Viśvāmitra, and others were merely the initiators of the Veda in the interim, [the Veda remains eternal].

Anticipating the objection that "in the first kalpa, the Blessed Lord himself creates this various Veda," as established by such scriptural passages as, "Verily, this is the breath of that great Being," the author refutes it with the word "Īśa" (the Lord). By the statement, "The Creator fashioned [it] as before," the Blessed Lord's role as the initiator according to the sequence of previous kalpas is declared. Although the Veda is the teaching of the Blessed Lord, nevertheless, because the Blessed Lord is the ruler through an eternal and uniform utterance, its eternity is established.

The doctrine that the teaching of the Blessed One does not fall into corruption [is stated as follows]: "Even here, in the production of phonemes (*varṇasarga*)," whereby impermanence is admitted regarding phonemes. By this, the distinction [of our position] from the non-theistic Mīmāṃsakas, who maintain the eternity of phonemes, is established.

Here, having restated the position of the proponents of logic (Nyāyavādins), he refutes it with the words "the non-authoritativeness of the Vedas. Since it has been stated that "in every Manvantara, a different Veda is ordained," if it were accepted that the sequence of the Vedas—due to the intellect of the Lord—is subject to destruction and becomes otherwise in those Kalpas, then the same alteration would apply to the mantras employed in sacrifices and other rites. Anticipating the objection that "let there be such alteration," he rejects it with the word "no. He states the reason for this with the word "vrīhi" (rice).

The meaning is this: in the world, the relationship between cause and effect is observed to be strictly fixed; for example, a jar [is produced] from potsherds and cloth from threads.
