Indeed, according to the proponents of logic (*nyāyavādin*), even in alternative scenarios (*kalpa*), a jar is never produced from threads, nor is cloth produced from potsherds. Likewise, in Vedic examples such as "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" and "one should sacrifice with Soma," in all possible scenarios, it is simply not possible to alter the mantras that serve as the causes for those respective effects.

And thus, the eternity of the Veda is established. [Objection: "Let there be a fixed order for the mantras because it is necessary, but let there be no such requirement for the injunctions (*vidhi*) and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). To this, he provides the answer: "In this way" (*ittham*). The meaning is as follows: Just as with the mantras, the injunctions and explanatory passages also possess causality toward their respective cognitions; in that regard, they do not have the status of a cause without a fixed order.

Thus, you yourself must reflect and be satisfied that there can be no cause in the absence of a fixed order; and so, there is no room for the suspicion that the relationship between cause and effect could be otherwise. Here, if out of audacity you say, "It is an order taught by God," even then, a fixed order has indeed been admitted by you at some point. Therefore, with the intention that this position is superior because this fixed order must be accepted as eternal, he says: "partial" (*pākṣika*).

"In that case, why do you, who maintain the doctrine of difference, abandon the path of logic? "It is indeed abandoned," he says with the words "the position. The meaning is: "Let this position of Akṣapāda reach the extreme limit of the systems of our Vedāntins' opponents; what loss is there for us?"

If one raises the objection, "If deities possess embodied forms, why are they not perceived by us?", he explains the multiplicity of causes for non-perception with the word "due to subtlety" (*saukṣmyāt*). For in the Sāṅkhya treatises, the causes for the non-perception of even existing things are enumerated as: "due to extreme distance, due to proximity," and so forth.

Non-perception occurs due to subtlety, as in the case of atoms and the like; due to being overwhelmed by something similar, as in the case of a drop of oil poured onto oil-soaked ground; due to the departure of the auxiliary conditions, as in the case of a jar and so forth existing in darkness due to the absence of auxiliary factors; due to an obscuring agent, as in the case of objects covered by a cloth; due to preoccupation with something else, as in the case of objects standing before one whose mind is distracted; due to extreme proximity, as in the case of what is on one's own eyes; and due to excessive distance, as in the case of what is located in another land.

The connection [of the reason] with all cases is as follows: due to being overwhelmed by something more powerful, the light of a meteor at midday does not manifest; due to the nature of the collection of ocular rays and so forth, there is non-perception of an object situated in front of one whose eyes are impaired by disease. For all these reasons, even things existing in front are not perceived. In the same way, the host of deities such as Agni and Indra is also not perceived due to their power of invisibility (*antardhāna-śakti*).

Furthermore, in the scriptures, specific supernatural powers (siddhis) arising from greatness are well-known to result from birth, austerity, yoga, mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth. Through birth, there is the power of invisibility for Piśācas and others; through austerity, for the great seers (maharṣis); and through yoga, for yogins—this is indeed an established fact. It is therefore rightly said that the power of invisibility of gods and others is not perceived [by ordinary means].

In the preceding section, it was considered whether those belonging to the various classes of deities have the qualification for the meditation on the Lord; now, however, the qualification for specific meditations upon specific deities is being determined—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, while the possibility of such qualification was stated previously, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises here because that possibility is denied in the case of the *Madhu-vidyā* and other such meditations—this is the connection. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: in the *Madhu-vidyā* and other meditations, does a deity who is the object of worship possess the qualification for them, or not?

Does she possess the capacity to withdraw that knowledge or not? Is only the deity such as Vasu to be meditated upon in the Madhu-vidyā, or is it Brahman in that state? Is the fruit of the knowledge merely the status of being a Vasu, or is it the status of being a Vasu culminating in the attainment of Brahman? Having thus restated the mode of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) contained within the statement of the connection, he refutes the two objections raised against that prima facie view by saying, "It might indeed be so."

Just as among humans there is a commonality in the worship of the Supreme Person within the general category of deities, so it is indeed here; nevertheless, in certain meditations such as those on the *madhu* (honey) and others, there would be no possibility for certain deities to be the objects of worship. Furthermore, for those deities who are established as the goal to be attained (*prāpya*), their status as the attainer (*prāptṛ*) is a direct contradiction. Thus, due to the contradiction between the object of action and the agent (*karmakartṛ-virodha*) regarding the worshipped and the worshipper, there would be no qualification (*adhikāra*) for the deities in the *madhu-vidyā* and similar meditations.

As for the meaning of the words: since the Vasus and others, who are being enjoyed by the Sun as objects of worship, are established as qualifiers [of the Sun], their status as worshippers is indeed contradictory. Furthermore, because the attainment of the Supreme Self preceded by the attainment of the Vasus constitutes the fruit [of the meditation], there would be a contradiction even in that regard; for the Vasus already existing beforehand cannot be attained by the word "Vasu. Consequently, there could be no qualification for that [meditation] at all. He refutes this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "Not so" (naivam).

Therein, he first dispels the contradiction regarding worship by stating, "the inner self of all. It is not only one's own self that is to be worshipped, but rather the Supreme Self as qualified by that [individual self]; therefore, there is no lack of qualification for the worship of the Self, which has the Supreme Self as its primary object. Nor is there a contradiction even regarding the attainment of the fruit; thus he says, "from desire. If the fruit were merely the attainment of the status of a Vasu while existing as a Vasu in the present, then indeed there would be a contradiction. However, here the attainment of the status of a Vasu in another Kalpa or Manvantara is obtained as the fruit. And so, what contradiction is there?

It has been stated that deities other than humans—specifically particular deities such as the Vasus and others—possess eligibility because they possess both the desire [to know] and the capacity [to practice]. If that is so, one might raise the objection that certain specific types of humans, such as Śūdras and others, would also possess eligibility due to their having both desire and capacity; this is the connection [of the present discussion]. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: Does a Śūdra have eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman, or not? Does he possess the capacity to undertake it, or not?

Is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), which consists of a mental modification directed toward Brahman, possible even for one who has not studied the Vedas, or not? Is the realization of Brahman derived from the Veda alone, or is it also possible through the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth? [If it is possible through them: Is the status of the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas* as causes for the realization of Brahman due solely to their acting as supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the Veda, or is it by their own independent authority?

Does the fact that Jānaśruti Pautrāyaṇa was addressed as "Śūdra" before the instruction of knowledge strengthen the view that the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* do not provide an independent realization of Brahman? Or is it not so? Is the word "Śūdra" here intended for the caste of the *vṛṣala*, or is it derived by analyzing it as "śug-asya" (he who has grief) and applying the suffix *rak* according to the rule "śucer daś ca," thus referring to one characterized by sorrow? Even though in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*), the venerable Jaimini stated that Śūdras have no qualification for ritual action because they lack the sacred fires and Vedic knowledge; [nevertheless...]

Furthermore, anticipating an objection regarding eligibility based on the Lord’s own words—“For even those of sinful birth, O Pārtha, and likewise women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, they too attain the supreme goal” (Gītā 9.32)—the author presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) as stated by Jaimini: “Because [eligibility] is enjoined by Jaimini. [The opponent argues: “Since the Lord himself has declared in the passage ‘For me’ that Śūdras possess eligibility, therefore eligibility does exist. Nevertheless, one might object: “In the absence of knowledge (*jñāna*), how can meditative worship (*upāsana*) be properly joined? Anticipating this doubt, he says: “Because of their capacity to hear (*śrotṛtva*), etc. The meaning is this: let there be no knowledge of the Lord for Śūdras and others preceded by the study of the Vedas.

Moreover, there certainly exists [the capacity for knowledge] preceded by the hearing of the *Bhārata* and other such works, because one is a listener of the *Bhārata* and so forth; that is to say, one is fit to hear them. Granting that knowledge arises from hearing the *Bhārata* and so on, one might again raise the objection: "How can the meditation upon the Lord arise through His truthful word for one whose impurities (*kaṣāya*) have not been ripened by ritual actions (*karman*)? Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "svajanī" (relatives).

The meaning is this: just as Brāhmaṇas and others effect the destruction of sins that obstruct knowledge through rites such as sacrifices performed according to their respective qualifications, so too may a Śūdra effect the destruction of sins that obstruct the meditation on Brahman through service and other duties appropriate to his own qualification. Having thus restated the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the author refutes it by saying "that is improper. He shows the reason for this by stating "because [the qualification] has been attained."

When the instruction in Brahman is attained, the necessity of the existence of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has been demonstrated by the author of the Sūtras themselves through such aphorisms as "Because of the reference to the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), and because of the mention of their absence [in the case of others]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.30–38). Therefore, the meaning is that only those of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) have the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, and not Śūdras and the like.

Anticipating the objection as to why the hearing of the *Mahābhārata* and similar texts is permitted for Śūdras and others, he says "of the Śūdras," etc. The meaning is that this is for the sake of pacifying sins, and not for the sake of Vedic knowledge, nor for the purpose of clarifying the meaning understood from the scriptures. He explains that very point with the words "the meaning of the Vedas. The sense is: if a Śūdra were to have even a superficial understanding (*āpātabuddhi*) of the meaning of the Vedas, then at that time the Śūdra would be supplemented by the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and would be rendered possessed of clear knowledge. However, a Śūdra does not possess even such a superficial understanding.

Because he lacks the status of a Brahmin, there is no initiation for him; because of that absence, there is no study of the Vedas. Therefore, even a superficial understanding does not exist [for him]. Furthermore, that superficial understanding which has no locus other than a Śūdra—that is, which is not supported by a Śūdra—is not supplemented by the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*; the meaning is that he is not nourished by them through the possession of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore, the hearing of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* for a Śūdra is solely for the purpose of destroying sin, and not for the purpose of increasing knowledge of reality.

Alternatively, the meaning of the passage beginning with "the initial cognition of the Vedic meaning" (*vedārthāpātabuddhi*) is as follows: The Veda is indeed twofold—studied (*adhīta*) and unstudied (*anadhīta*). The studied belongs to the Brāhmaṇas and others; the unstudied, however, belongs to the Śūdra. The studied Veda generates an initial cognition (*āpātapratīti*), whereas the unstudied does not. Thus, that which is the locus of the initial cognition of the Vedic meaning—which does not arise from the unstudied Veda—that unstudied Veda is not supplemented by those [texts] such as the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

For *upabṛṃhaṇa* (supplementation) consists in clarifying a meaning that has been only superficially understood. However, since the Veda does not produce even a superficial comprehension in the case of a *śūdra*, it is not logical for the Veda to be supplemented for him. Furthermore, the Blessed Lord himself explicitly taught in the *Mahābhārata* to Yudhiṣṭhira that the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), which were declared by me as purifiers for the wise, must not be touched by a *śūdra*: "At the very outset, I declared these purifiers for the wise;
therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, these must not be touched by *śūdras* and others."

How then are the hymns of praise to the Blessed One from the Itihāsas and Purāṇas recited by Śūdras? It is as follows: the distinction is that their recitation is by way of mere chanting (saṃkīrtana), and not for the purpose of supplementing the Veda. Therefore, etc.—the meaning is that because there is thus no means for knowing the meaning of the Veda, Śūdras, who possess deficient intellects and limited knowledge, would have no entitlement to meditative worship (upāsā).

Raising the objection: "How is it possible that even Śūdras and others are told to worship another [deity], given such statements as 'by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas' and 'For by taking refuge in Me alone, O Pārtha'?"—he says "It has been sung," etc. There is no contradiction, because their practice consists merely of performing duties appropriate to their own caste, such as making garlands, lighting lamps, circumambulating, prostrating, and anointing.

Now, one might object: "In that case, you claim that Śūdras lack the qualification for meditative worship (*upāsanā*); if that is so, then the scriptural accounts of the practice of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) by Dharmavyādha and others would be inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Dharma... [and so on]. Dharmavyādha, Tulādhara, Vidura, and others were indeed beings of great majesty who attained perfection through practice in previous births; they did not possess the knowledge produced by the study of the Vedas and other means in this very life. Thus, there is no contradiction even in that regard.

Let this be the resolution; however, it is observed that there is an objection: "The address 'Śūdra' used for the purpose of instructing Jānaśruti in the knowledge of Brahman is inexplicable. Anticipating this, [the author] states, "It is established otherwise" (*tadapyanyathāsiddham*). Addressing Jānaśruti, the teacher Raikva uses the word "Śūdra" merely to indicate the Śākala [sacrificial fee] belonging to Jānaśruti, and not to denote his status as a member of the Śūdra caste.

Anticipating the objection—"Why is the etymological (yoga) meaning accepted by abandoning the conventional (rūḍhi) sense of the word *śūdra*, since this would contradict the principle of the chariot-maker (*rathakāra*), and it is improper to abandon a conventional meaning?"—the author says: "Because of the commands to the *kṣattṛ*," and so forth.

The *kṣattṛ* is the executor of the king’s command; his *praiṣa* is the sending forth. This is the meaning: through the dispatching of the *kṣattṛ* for the purpose of identifying Raikva, as well as by other indicative marks (*liṅga*) found in the sūtras such as "and because of the subsequent mention of Caitraratha," Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya is indeed very clearly known. Consequently, the word *śūdra* is applied to Jānaśruti based on the etymological derivation from the root *śuc* according to the rule "of *śuc*, *da*" (Pāṇini 3.2.140)—that is, "he is a *śūdra* because he grieves"—in accordance with the *Nirukta*; it is not used there because of his belonging to the *śūdra* caste. This is the conclusion.

Previously, in the Daharādhikaraṇa, the smallness of the "small ether" (daharākāśa) was stated on account of its being limited by the size of the heart. In connection with that, in the Antarādhikaraṇa, it was stated that the Supreme Self alone is measured by the size of a thumb. In that very context, three intermediate sections were inserted because of the incidental discussion regarding the eligibility of human beings. Immediately thereafter, the remainder of the preceding section was also concluded.

Now, the connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that the section beginning with "Ākāśa, indeed, by name..."—which is studied immediately after the previously mentioned Dahara-vidyā—is intended to refer to the individual soul (jīva) because it serves as the locus for its knowledge, that doubt is now refuted. The inquiry into its meaning concerns whether the entity designated by the word "ākāśa" in the Chāndogya passage, "Ākāśa, indeed, is the revealer of name and form," is the liberated soul or the Supreme Self.

Does the phrase, "having shaken off the body, being self-made, [he attains] the uncreated," indicate that the word "ether" (ākāśa) refers to the liberated one because it is mentioned immediately after the liberated one? Or does it not? Is the capacity to sustain names and forms possible even for the liberated one, or is it not? Does the capacity to sustain names and forms here consist in the enjoyment of names and forms, or in the agency of creating names and forms? Does the designation, "that which is between them," establish the capacity to sustain as being due to agency, or not?

The "ether" (ākāśa) heard in the passage, "Ether, indeed, is the revealer of name and form," is none other than the individual soul (jīva) already established in the preceding text, "Having shaken off the body, he, having made himself immortal... This is because it is logical to accept the subject under discussion throughout. That soul assumes name and form at the time of bondage; subsequently, upon attaining the state of Brahman, it abandons name and form. Therefore, the very soul mentioned in the prior sentence is presented in the subsequent sentence as if distinct [from the ether].

Having restated the prima facie view—that "he who is liberated is indeed space"—the author refutes it with the passage beginning with "having shaken off" (*dhūtvā*) and ending with "is improper" (*anyāyyam*). He explains that very point with the words "as previously stated. This is the meaning: two things were indeed previously mentioned in the phrase "having shaken off the body" (*dhūtvā śarīram*); namely, one is the individual soul (*jīva*) who is to attain [the state], and the other is the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who is to be attained.

Because of the mention of that very same entity by the word "Brahmaloka" in the phrase, "May I attain the world of Brahman," and because the word "Brahmaloka"—through grammatical coordination according to the *niṣādasthapati* maxim—refers to the Supreme Person, it is that very Supreme Person previously mentioned as the one to be attained who is again referred to in the subsequent sentence by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*). Therefore, it is well-established that the word "ether" here refers back to the subject under discussion; for it is the Supreme Person, who is the primary subject at hand, that is being taken up.

Now, one might object: in the passage "May I attain the world of Brahman," it is the individual soul (jīva) itself in its state of liberation that is denoted by the term "world of Brahman," and not some occasional form of liberation produced by specific ritual actions. Therefore, it is inconsistent to claim that the soul's status as Brahman consists merely in its assuming a subsequent state after abandoning a prior state.

Furthermore, you assert that the individual soul (*jīva*) was previously unliberated, non-sovereign, and not Brahman, yet in its state of liberation it becomes omniscient, sovereign, and Brahman; this is indeed contradictory to scripture. For in the *Śrutis*, the individual soul and Brahman are designated as distinct entities simultaneously in the passage: "The two unborn ones, the knower and the ignorant, the Lord and the non-Lord. Therefore, it is established that the Supreme Person alone—endowed with the eternally perfected qualities of vastness (*bṛhatva*) and expansion (*bṛṃhaṇatva*)—is denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*).

He describes the qualities of the Blessed One, which constitute the primary meaning of the ten topics already mentioned, beginning with the words "the Soul of the Universe" (*viśvātmā*). He is the inner controller of all, distinguished by infinite sovereignty; through His governance, He is the substratum of all effects; His nature is that which is to be enjoyed by the liberated; He is the support of all worlds within His own limited form; as the Lord of all, He is the object of worship for gods and others in His state of being measured by the heart; He is to be served by the Vasus and other deities as their inner controller; He is worthy of worship even by Śūdras and others; and He is the sole creator of names and forms.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa was awakened here in the third quarter; the meaning is that he was made conscious.
May it be auspicious.

Thus, in the first three quarters (*pādas*), those scriptural passages (*vākyas*) which contain signs (*liṅgas*) such as the individual soul (*jīva*)—whose nature is either very obscure or somewhat clear—were raised as potential references to the individual soul and then determined to refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Now, in the fourth quarter, those passages containing even clearer signs of the individual soul and so forth are likewise determined to refer to the Supreme Self; this is the connection between the quarters (*pādasaṃgati*). These very passages are designated as "following the shadow" (*tattacchāyānusāriṇī*) of their respective [preceding] contexts.

In the preceding [section], having raised the doubt that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) mentioned in the immediately preceding sentence, it was indicated that it actually refers to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) as understood from that very passage. Similarly, here too, having raised the doubt that the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*) refers to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) as propounded by the Sāṃkhyas, the proponent establishes that it refers to the body as described in another passage that sets forth the metaphorical arrangement. This constitutes the connection between the sections (*adhikaraṇasaṃgati*).

Alternatively, the connection [between this and the previous section] is as follows: in the preceding section, having refuted that the individual soul (jīva) is the subject to be expounded and having stated that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the subject to be expounded, here again, having refuted that the primordial matter (pradhāna) is the subject to be expounded, it is stated that the Supreme Self is the subject to be expounded. The investigation of its meaning concerns the *Kaṭhavallī*: whether, in the passage "Higher than the senses are the objects," the term "unmanifest" (avyakta) denotes the primordial matter which is non-Brahman in nature, or not.

Is there an identification of the procedure established in the Tantras within this mantra or not? Is "supremacy" here to be understood as being subject to control (*vaśīkāryatā*), or rather through a specific Tantric causal principle? Here, after first stating the connection between the third and fourth quarters, [the author] explains that the eight topics situated in the fourth quarter also constitute two groups (*peṭikā*). Thus it is said: "It has been determined. In the third quarter, the collection of scriptural passages containing clear indicatory marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, which relate to the Supreme, has been determined.

In the fourth quarter (pāda), however, the collection of statements that follow the shadow of various Sāṅkhya doctrines establishes the Supreme Person alone; such is the connection between the quarters. Regarding this, he states the internal division of sections with the words "by six," and so forth. The division is as follows: he rejects the objections raised by the Sāṅkhya doctrine through six topical discussions (adhikaraṇas), and he rejects the doctrine established by Yoga through two topical discussions. Thus, there are two *ghaṭṭas* (sections) and [one] *peṭikā* (sub-section). The meaning of *jāghaṭṭaḥ* is that they fit together with one another.
Furthermore, some teachers say that the eighth section is a conclusion (nigamana) of the meaning already stated, because this section consists in the completion of the chapter.

Regarding that, he states with two [verses] that there is a distinction even among the eight topics (*adhikaraṇa*) based on their internal differences, as they occupy the position of the fourth quarter [of the book]. By means of two topics, the *pradhāna* favored by Kapila is to be refuted. Immediately thereafter, by one topic, the enumeration of principles (*tattva-saṃkhyā*) favored by Kapila is refuted. And by the fourth topic, it is established that even for the term "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*), when functioning through the door of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the limit is the all-pervading Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) alone.

And thus it is established; this is the meaning. Immediately thereafter, in the pair of topics (adhikaraṇa), it is to be demonstrated that the pure and impure souls—whether bound or liberated—are not the Supreme Reality; this is the meaning. The remaining two topics serve to refute the "Lord who is merely the instrumental cause" as taught in the Yoga-tantras; such is the division of the meaning of the topics in the fourth quarter.

In this regard, the first half of the verse—beginning with "akṣādī"—refutes the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) which states that the passage in the Kaṭhavallī beginning with "Higher than the senses are the objects" enumerates insentient categories starting from the senses up to the Unmanifest (avyakta), and then subsequently distinguishes the Puruṣa as the ultimate limit of reality, thereby merely repeating the system propounded by other schools.

He explains the very lack of propriety [in the opponent's view] with the words "tattra" (therein). This is the meaning: here, indeed, a succession of causes in ascending order is not being stated; rather, having described a succession of objects to be mastered (*vaśīkārya*), it is said that the "subsequentness" (*paratva*)—meaning primacy—of one object to be mastered over another belongs to the latter in relation to the former object to be mastered. This is the syntactical connection (*padānvaya*) here: because it is an expression of the primary sequence of objects to be mastered as established by the statements situated within that context.

Furthermore, in this section, Viṣṇu alone is identified as the Lord of the place to be reached by the liberated, through the statement: "He reaches the end of the path, that supreme abode of Viṣṇu"; and He is recognized as such by the subsequent declaration: "There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. Since He is not the individual soul (jīva), he states that this entire section refers exclusively to the Supreme Person by the words "śāntātmā" (the one whose self is peaceful).

Having here demonstrated the absence of the recognition (pratyabhijñā) asserted by the Sāṅkhya through the presentation of many contradictions in their meaning, he concludes that the statement indeed refers to the Supreme Person with the words, "for the objects [are not... (na hyarthāḥ). Regarding this, it was said: "The objects are indeed higher than the senses. Now, in the system of the Sāṅkhya tenets, the objects are certainly not said to be the material cause (prakṛti) of the senses. Furthermore, "the mind is not desired as their cause"—that is, it is not the position of the Sāṅkhyas that the mind is the cause of these objects of the senses, because all the senses are derived from the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra).

In that regard, it is said: "But the intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind. According to the Sāṅkhya system, the intellect itself is the Great One (mahat); therefore, it might be argued that what is meant is that the Great One is produced from it. However, even that is not tenable. If one objects that in this context it is not logical for the Great One to be "superior," we reply: the individual soul (jīva) alone is the enjoyer, and the qualification "Great One" is appropriate for it; thus [the author] says, "It is great."

Now, one might object: since the expression "the Unmanifest is beyond the Great" (mahataḥ paramavyaktam) designates the Unmanifest as the cause of the Great, and since the expression "the Person is beyond the Unmanifest" (avyaktātpuruṣaḥ paraḥ) designates the Person mentioned by the Sāṅkhyas, this [text] merely causes one to recognize what was already stated by the Sāṅkhyas; to this, he replies: "By way of elimination" (pāriśeṣyāt).

The meaning is as follows: in the preceding passage, by the mantra beginning with "Know the Self as the rider, and the body as the chariot," the self, the body, and so forth were metaphorically described as the rider, the chariot, and so on. Regarding those metaphorical entities, when the doubt arises as to why one is more fit to be controlled than another, the superiority of the controllability of one over another is stated in the passage beginning with "For objects are superior to the senses. Here, all the matters mentioned in the previous mantra are indicated in the subsequent mantra; however, the body alone is not [the sole object of control].

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is shown that that very *śarīra* (body) is what is expressed here by the word "unmanifest" (*avyakta*). Therefore, he says "that," meaning there is no recognition of Kapila’s system in this context.

Now, an objection may be raised: "In the previous section, it was established by means of the principles of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) and position (*sthāna*) that the word 'Unmanifest' (*avyakta*) denotes only the body, which is an unmanifest effect; therefore, in the same manner, the passage beginning with 'The one unborn female' (*ajāmekām*) must denote that very Unmanifest accepted by both [sides]. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) by way of such an objection. The inquiry into its meaning, however, concerns whether or not the mantra from the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "The one unborn female," denotes primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is non-Brahman in essence.

Is the word *ajā* in the mantra used in its etymological sense (*yaugika*) as referring to primordial nature (*prakṛti*) that is not of the nature of Brahman, or does it refer to primordial nature that is of the nature of Brahman? Does the status of the word *ajā* as a constituent part of the sentence "creating many offspring" indicate that it refers independently to creation, or not? And does the status of the word *ajā* in the Taittirīya passage "the one *ajā*" as a constituent part of the sentence beginning with "Light" (*jyotis*) contradict its indication of independent reference to creation, or not?

Furthermore, [the opponent argues that] the state of being unborn (*ajātva*) and the state of having light as its starting point (*jyotirupakramatva*) are contradictory; this is not so. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states his intention with the words "by way of independence" (*svātantryeṇa*). In the passage "one unborn female" (*ajāmekām*), the phrase "bringing forth" (*janayantīm*) expresses the agency of the Pradhāna through its independence in generating many offspring. Moreover, in the Śvetāśvatara statement "creating" (*sṛjamānām*), that same agency is indeed expressed. And in the passage "for one unborn, alone, enjoying, lies along with her," the lying along with that very same unborn female is described for the bound soul who is "enjoying," meaning filled with pleasure.

By the passage beginning with “he abandons this,” even the abandonment of that [Prakṛti] by the liberated one is stated. Anticipating the objection that this statement, though found in the Śruti, might nevertheless be based on the Tantras—specifically established in the *Kapila-tantra*—the author refutes it, saying “no. He states the reason for this: “because only the state of being unborn (*ajatva*) is mentioned. This is the meaning: here, indeed, only the state of being unborn is expressed; it is not said that the Unborn is non-Brahman in nature. Therefore, the claim that there is a mention of the Unborn as being non-Brahman in nature—as asserted by the Sāṅkhya—is unproven. He states another reason: “because its lack of independence is well-established.”

Indeed, the lack of independence of the insentient primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is well-known throughout all the worlds. Then, how can there be a statement regarding her being the agent of creation in the words "generating" (*janayantīṣu*) and "creating" (*sṛjamānām*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The root *sṛj* [is used here]. For in the world, agency is of two kinds: that of the instigating agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*) and that of the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛtva*).

The meaning is that the agency of the primordial material cause (mūlaprakṛti), as heard [in scripture], should not obstruct the fact that it is impelled by the Supreme Self, which is established by valid means of knowledge. In the previous section, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) raised by the Sāṅkhya—based on such scriptural passages as "the one unborn female" (ajāmekām), which point to an unmanifest principle (avyakta) that is not of the nature of Brahman—was refuted. Now, the refutation is being made of that same argument as it arises again, this time relying on a scriptural passage that sets forth the number of principles (tattvas) as taught by the Sāṅkhya. This constitutes the connection (saṃgati).

The investigation into its meaning concerns whether the mantra, "In whom the five groups of five reside," is intended to propound the principles established in the Sāṃkhya system, or not; whether the term "five groups of five" (pañcapañcajana) conveys the twenty-five principles, or not; and whether by the term "five groups of five" the five pentads are meant, or rather five categories of objects.

Is the compound *pañcajanaḥ* intended as a collective aggregate (*samāhāra*), or is it intended as a technical name (*saṃjñā*) according to the rule "Directional words and numerals [form a compound] when they denote a name"? Is there, in the case of the collective aggregate compound, a basis for the application of an intermediate number, or not? And does the separate mention of space (*ākāśa*) contradict the application of an intermediate number? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains: "In the sentence 'In whom the five groups of five persons [dwell],' that which is indicated by the locative case in the word 'in whom' (*yasmin*) is the multitude of Puruṣas beyond the *Prakṛti* mentioned in the Sāṅkhya system."

The twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are indeed what are referred to by the expression "five fivefold groups" (*pañca pañcajanāḥ*). Thus, it is well known that these five categories, when calculated by the number five, amount to twenty-five. He restates this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words beginning with "In which... and ending with "...let it be so. The phrase "not resting on anything else" (*ananyaniṣṭhaḥ*) means being devoid of resting upon the Supreme Self. He rejects the aforementioned prima facie argument with the words "Not so" (*maivam*). Therein, he states two reasons, beginning with "Of the ether... (*ākāśasya*).

For in the Sāṅkhya system, there exist exactly twenty-five principles (*tattva*s), and not twenty-seven. Here, moreover, there is a separate mention of space (*ākāśa*), and by the word "in which" (*yasmin*), ending in the locative case, the Person (*puruṣa*) is also separately indicated. Therefore, the meaning is that through these two [separate mentions], there is no recognition of the twenty-five principles spoken of in the Sāṅkhya. Raising the objection, "In that case, who is said to be 'in which' according to your own position?", he says: "the twenty-sixth."

The twenty-sixth is the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), as established by the Vedic scripture: "They call him the twenty-sixth. He, however, being the support of all, is referred to by the word "in whom" (yasmin). The reason for this is stated as "by [attributes such as] Brahman-hood and so forth"; the meaning is that he is determined to be the Supreme Self by the marks of Brahman-hood, immortality, and so on, which are understood from the context.

On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that this is a collective compound (samāhāra-samāsa). Thus, as in the case of "pañcapūlī" and similar forms, by the Vedic grammatical process (chāndasa-prakriyā), the term *pañcajanāḥ* is used in the masculine plural to denote a collective aggregate; and when that aggregate is qualified by the number five, the establishment of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) follows.

Refuting this position, he states that "pañca pañcajanāḥ" is a technical designation (*saṃjñopādhi*), according to the grammatical process prescribed by the rule "dik-saṃkhye saṃjñāyām," just as in the case of the expression "saptasaptarṣayaḥ. He says "it is a technical designation" to indicate this. Then, raising the doubt as to what the group of five (*pañcaka*) to be explained is by virtue of being a technical designation, he replies: "the group beginning with breath" (*prāṇādyam*). This group of five, consisting of the cognitive organs (*jñānendriya*), extending from breath up to the mind, is clearly stated in the Śruti itself in passages such as "the breath of breath" (*prāṇasya prāṇam*).

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that in some places, in the Kāṇva recension, 'food of food' is not seen? How then is the state of being fivefold established? Anticipating this, he says, "light. The meaning is that the state of being fivefold has been established by the author of the Sūtras himself in the words, "For some, [the fifth element is] light, since food is absent. To the question, "How can there be a deficiency in that regard? he replies, "deficiency. The sense is that even where there is a deficiency in one place, it should be supplemented by what is observed elsewhere.

Anticipating the objection that since there are six organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), how can their number be established as five here, he says "the nose" (*ghrāṇam*). In this context, the word "food" (*anna*) denotes both the nose and the tongue together; thus, the number five is established. Then, anticipating the question of where the organ of touch (*tvagindriya*) is mentioned, he provides the answer with the words "the vital breath" (*prāṇa*). For here, because the organ of touch is nourished by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the word "vital breath" indicates the organ of touch itself through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); this is indeed accepted by all. This is very clearly explained in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) itself.

Thus, having established through three *adhikaraṇas* that the statements following the shadow of what was spoken by the Sāṃkhya refer exclusively to the Supreme Self, [the author] now declares that even the force of terms such as "the Undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*), which those same Sāṃkhyas have accepted as referring to the Pradhāna—which is not of the nature of Brahman—is perfectly consistent only when it refers to the Supreme Person. In doing so, he reflects upon the reality of the meaning stated in the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* and other sections according to the logic of the "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*), thereby establishing what has been set forth by the collection of sound reasonings (*nyāyakalāpa*). This is the connection (*saṃgati*).

The investigation into that matter is as follows: Is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) taught in the Vedānta texts as the cause of the world the *pradhāna* mentioned by the Sāṃkhyas, or is it Brahman? Does the word "non-existent" (*asat*) in the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," refer to Brahman in its state where name and form are undifferentiated (*avyākṛta-nāmarūpa*), or does it refer to something other than the undifferentiated? And does the reference to [Brahman] as a witness in the statement, "Regarding that, there is this verse," lead one to understand that the word "non-existent" in "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" refers to the previously mentioned Brahman, or not?

Does the term "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) in the passage, "Was that undifferentiated [state] then? denote Brahman with an undifferentiated body, or rather the unmanifest (*avyakta*)? And does the passage, "This very one, having entered here unto the tips of the fingernails, sees though eyeless," convey that the conscious ruler possesses the nature of Brahman with an undifferentiated body, or not? Here, he restates the argument of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The universe," etc. The scriptural mention of "Being," "Non-being," and "the Undifferentiated" as the material cause of the universe conforms only to the "Undifferentiated" as asserted by the opponent.

The meaning is this: since it is firmly established by both worldly usage and Vedic authority that words such as "ātman" denote primordial matter (prakṛti), other words like "ātman" must somehow be interpreted in accordance with that [matter]. He rejects this doubt with the word "no" (na). He explains that very rejection in the passage beginning with "wherein" (yatra): in whatever sentence "non-existent" (asat) or "undifferentiated" (avyākṛta) and so forth are seen, in that very same sentence there is the mark of the Supreme Person—such as omniscience and the rest—as gathered from the context of the statement "May I be many."

Rather, because it is endowed with the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the agreement between the opening and the conclusion, it is indeed firmly established. Therefore, the meaning is that words such as "Self" (*ātman*) and "Nārāyaṇa" found in causal statements—such as "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" and "Verily, Nārāyaṇa alone existed"—are not sublated, as they rely upon the causality of *prakṛti*.

Now, raising the objection: "If words such as 'the unmanifest' (avyākṛta) do not denote primordial nature (prakṛti), how can they possibly denote the Supreme Self?"—he explains the manner in which they denote it in detail with the verse beginning "It existed" (āsīt). Here, indeed, by the statement beginning with "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (asadvā idamagra āsīt), only the state of dissolution of the manifest universe (prapañca) as it is presented in that passage is described.

Nor does it mean being a mere lump of consciousness, having the nature of non-existence, having the nature of absolute non-existence, or having the nature of absolute unreality. If one asks how the statement, "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here," is then to be understood, the author addresses this by saying, "Not at all. For in the Vedāntic doctrine, dissolution (*vilaya*) means simply the attainment of another state, not the destruction of the essential nature of a substance. To the question "How so?", he replies: "Because of the negation of emptiness and the like. For the claim that dissolution is the destruction of the essential nature of a substance is merely the prattle of the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

But that [position] has indeed been refuted by those who accept perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To the question, "In that case, how can there be the state of being unmanifest (*avyākṛtatva*)?", he says: "Of everything.

The state of being unmanifest for every object whatsoever is said to exist in its causal state because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa-vibhāga*). Having thus considered the general meaning of the word "unmanifest," he applies it to Brahman as well: "Of such a kind. For that reason, the Supreme Person alone—the inner self of the collection of various substances characterized by states such as being unmanifest—is determined by those proficient in the Vedānta to be denoted by the words "existent" (*sat*), "non-existent" (*asat*), and "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*).
Therefore, one should not fall into the error of thinking that there is no meaning for the term "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) when it refers to the Blessed One.

In the preceding section, having raised the doubt that the term "Unmanifest" (avyākṛta) and others might refer to primordial matter (prakṛti) based merely on their conventional designations as "indeterminate" (anaikāntika) and so forth, it was established that they refer to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa) due to the superior force of context and other factors that cannot be otherwise explained. Now, the connection [of this section] arises from the following doubt: "In that case, let the twenty-fifth principle (pañcaviṃśaka), being drawn forward by the force of unambiguous indicative marks (liṅga) such as its being an object of action (karmatva) and so forth, be the Supreme Reality itself. This is the doubt with which the present section begins.

Another connection is also stated according to the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*): previously, having set aside the view that the word "unmanifest" (*avyākṛta*) refers to primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it was determined that it refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*); now, however, having set aside the view that the word "action" (*karman*) refers to actions in the form of merit and demerit, it is stated that it denotes the world in its state as an effect. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: is the one taught in the Vedānta texts as the cause of the world the *puruṣa* who presides over primordial matter, or rather the Supreme Self?

Is the person being designated as the agent in the phrase "the maker of these persons" the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (paramātman)? Furthermore, regarding the phrase "he whose work this is," does the word *karman* denote meritorious and demeritorious actions, or does it denote the world? Is it appropriate that the word *karman* denotes the world, given its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the pronoun "this" (*etad*), which—by virtue of its connection with the context and other factors—refers to the world perceived through direct perception in its unrestricted sense?

Does the mention of the marks of the individual soul (jīva) and the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa)—beginning with "The two came to a sleeping man"—strengthen the view that [the passage] refers to merit and demerit? Or is it not so? Are these marks intended for the individual soul, or are they intended for the Supreme Self? Furthermore, do the question and answer—"O Bālāki, where did this person lie? Now he becomes one with the prāṇa alone"—aim at establishing the Brahman who is distinct from the individual soul, or not? In this section, the author sets forth the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) starting with the words "Of whom... (yasya).

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is as follows: since it has been stated, "O Bālāki, he who is indeed the maker of these persons being seen here, and whose [work] consists of all human efforts—merit and demerit—which are not seen but have their results in visible sons and so forth; he indeed is to be known, he is to be sought after," it follows that the one to be known is the individual soul (jīva) alone, who is the agent of the actions that result in those fruits, and not the Supreme Person.

As for the meaning of the words: that very Puruṣa who, as the result of his own karma, acts as the agent of sons and other men, and who exists as their father—that Puruṣa alone is to be known. [The opponent] refutes this with the words "begun" (*upakrānta*). He explains [the refutation] with the words "Bālāki. Indeed, here Ajātaśatru is teaching a reality that Bālāki does not know; he is not teaching what is already known, because there would be no purpose in making known what is already known. This is what [the author] states with the words "the statement of one who knows that is useless."

This is what is meant: "O Bālāki, he who is indeed the maker of these persons"—all these persons indicated by this word are already known to Bālāki. Therefore, there is no purpose in making them known [again]. Consequently, it is stated that the Supreme Person alone, who is distinct from the individual soul (jīva), is the creator of the entire universe which constitutes his own work of creation; "he indeed is to be known. This is what is expressed by the word "jagati" (the world). By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "that which is made is *karman*," the description of the world as the *karman* (object) in relation to the Lord is indeed primary.

Anticipating the objection as to why there is a description of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the chief vital breath (*prāṇa*) in this section, he states—from the words "In this way" (*evam*) up to "one should meditate upon" (*upāsīta*)—that because the individual soul and the vital breath are the body of the Supreme Self, the Lord is to be meditated upon as qualified by them. Thus, since the Supreme Self as distinct from the individual soul is the subject established in this section, the mention of the individual soul and the chief vital breath does not here result in any deficiency or contradiction. To the question "Why so?", he replies with the word "Thus" (*tathā*).

The meaning of the words is this: that being so, when there is a description by way of being qualified by that [the Supreme], meditation upon that which is thus qualified is also possible. He states that this [rule] is universal with the words "of the vital breath" (prāṇasya). For in the Vājasaneyaka, in the Antaryāmin Brāhmaṇa, the Supreme Person is described as the substratum even of the living soul (jīva) who possesses the vital breath, by virtue of being its body.

And this being the case, by that very same logic, the description of things other than that [Brahman] is for the sake of making Brahman known; thus, in various places, there is a description of substances in the form of attributes for the purpose of meditating upon the Supreme Self as qualified by those attributes. This is the meaning: our established position holds true on every ground.

"In the preceding section, it was stated that the quality of being denotable by the word 'karma'—which was intended as a probans (*liṅga*)—is not a valid probans because it is inconclusive. Here, the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) states a probans intended to be unique for determining the Person (*puruṣa*). How so? Starting from "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen," up to "Having arisen from these elements, which are a mass of consciousness, one perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death"; and "Everything else would discard him who knows everything as other than the Self"; and "Where [the Self... [and so forth].

For [the Upanishads] negate anything other than the twenty-fifth principle (the individual soul), stating, "When there is duality, as it were," and "By what, my dear, should one know the Knower? and because [the Supreme Self] is designated merely by its marks (*liṅga*). To this, he says, "On account of the syntactical connection of the sentences" (*vākyānvayāt*). Thus, the connection was clearly established by the venerable Viṣṇucittārya in his *Saṃgatimālā*. Therefore, in this context, a single section consisting of three sub-sections proceeded by way of raising doubts regarding the Sāṃkhya methodology. Now, however, [the next section proceeds] by means of three [arguments] such as being the cause, and by two marks such as having the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) as its object.

The teachers also maintain that this constitutes a separate section (*peṭikā*), because, following the instruction on the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, the possibility that the presiding cause (*prakṛti-adhiṣṭhātṛ*) might be the individual soul due to their absolute non-difference is raised and then refuted.

The inquiry into that subject concerns whether the cause of the world taught in the Vedānta is the *pradhāna* presided over by the *puruṣa*, or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). In the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, beginning with "Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear," and continuing with "The Self, verily, is to be seen," the question arises whether the "Self" refers to the twenty-fifth *puruṣa* or the Supreme Self. Does the connection with the dearness of husband, wife, sons, and so forth at the beginning of the passage indicate that the word "Self" refers to the *puruṣa*, or does it not?

Do all the constituent parts of the sentence have the capacity for syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the Supreme Self alone, or with the individual person (*puruṣa*)? Here, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented: "Of the husband and so forth. In the opening passage, "Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear," and so on, the Śruti reiterates the dearness of the husband and others; the meaning is that they are dear for the sake of fulfilling the desires of the Self—that is, for the accomplishment of what is desired by oneself.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing his own desired conclusion, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this self is indeed the individual soul (*jīva*), which experiences the fruits arising from merit and demerit, by demonstrating that sons and other such things are dear to it. He refutes that [view] with the words "from the introductory context" (*prakramādīti*). This means that [the opponent's position] is contrary to the introductory context and so forth. Anticipating the objection, "If what I have said is not present in this passage, then what is being stated here?", he replies with the words "that and that" (*tattaditi*).

The meaning is that the dearness of those sons and others depends upon the will of the Supreme Person alone, who bestows the enjoyments occasioned by them; that is to say, when the Lord has willed, "Let this son be dear to this father," their dearness comes to be exactly so. Here, by the word *ātman*, the Blessed Lord alone is meant, and not the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of a father or other relative.

Furthermore, in all the Vedāntas, the Lord Puruṣottama alone is heard of as that which is to be seen for the sake of liberation; therefore, He alone is the Self, as is recognized by the word "Self" in the passage, "The Self, verily, is to be seen. This is because the uniformity of the teaching (gatisāmānya) has already been stated.

Regarding this, one position is that the words denoting the self (*ātman*) employed here refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by virtue of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). The third [position] is that a word denoting the individual soul (*jīva*) refers to the Supreme Self alone by means of the individual soul. This division of the three positions is stated in the first half of the verse beginning with "by etymological derivation" (*vyutpattayaḥ*). Here, for the sake of favoring his disciples, he clarifies in the second half of the verse beginning with "due to the identity of the individual" (*vyaktyaikyāt*) the previously mentioned positions favored by the three sages concerning the fact that words denoting the individual soul refer to the Supreme Self.

Āśmarathya maintains that because of the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, the term "individual soul" denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Auḍulomi, however, says that due to the non-duality in the state free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupadhika-daśā*), the term "individual soul" denotes the Supreme Self in the state of liberation. Kāśakṛtsna, on the other hand, says it is because the individual soul abides in That; since the individual soul is the body of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self is established in it. Among these views, that of Kāśakṛtsna alone is accepted as the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
Having refuted the position of Auḍulomi, [the author] establishes the position of Kāśakṛtsna as his own view with the words, "Because of difference," and so forth.

The view of Auḍulomi—that this individual soul (jīva) would attain the state of Brahman upon the removal of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance (avidyā)—is incorrect. Why? To this he says: "Because that difference is eternally perceived. This is because the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme (para) is directly seen to be eternal through such scriptural texts as, "The Eternal among the eternals... Furthermore, he provides another reason with the words, "Because it transcends... and so forth.

The meaning is this: since the scriptures speak of "equality" (*sāmya*) and "attaining similarity" (*sādharmya*)—in the passages "When all fetters have fallen away, the soul, stainless, attains the supreme equality" and "Having attained similarity with Me"—and since these two terms imply a distinction [between the two states], [the opponent objects]. If that is so, how can the analogy of clay and its effects mentioned in the scripture be consistent with your assertion of an absolute difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*)? Anticipating this doubt, I say: "clay and its... [and so forth].

For one should not state that there is an absolute identity between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*); rather, they must be consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with hundreds of scriptural texts (*śruti*). Thus he says, "contradicted by hundreds of scriptural texts. The meaning is that the very nature of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord is determined by directly distinguishing them through scripture itself, as in: "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the Self" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10). He concludes this stated point according to the opinion of Kāśakṛtsna by saying, "therefore."

Because words denoting the individual soul (jīva) possess the capacity to denote the substantive [the Lord] through their function as inseparably established attributes (apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa), Kāśakṛtsna held that "He alone is the one who breathes through all" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22); this indeed is the established doctrine (siddhānta) of the venerable Vedavyāsa. The other two positions are simply to be rejected.

In the preceding [sūtra], it was stated that the Lord's grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the individual soul (*jīva*) arises because He abides as its controller, according to the view of Kāśakṛtsna, who held that "it is because of His abiding [in the souls]. Against this, someone raises an objection: "Just as in the expression 'the king is the kingdom,' where the king abides as the ruler of the kingdom, the coreferentiality here is merely figurative (*aupacārika*) and does not imply that he is the material cause (*upādāna*); likewise, in this case too, the Lord may be only the efficient cause (*nimitta*), not the material cause. It is on account of the arising of such a doubt that the present section is connected [to the previous one].

The investigation into that matter is as follows: Is Brahman the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of the world, or is it also the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*)? Do the Vedāntic texts, which teach the cause of the world, establish that Brahman is also the material cause, or do they establish only its status as the efficient cause? Furthermore, does the rule observed elsewhere—that the efficient cause and the material cause are distinct—determine that Brahman is merely the efficient cause, or not?

Is there a contradiction between the two—the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" and the illustrative examples—given that [the cause] merely establishes itself as the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)? Here, having restated the method proposed by the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins to refute it with the words "of the lump of clay, etc. For in the world, the potter and others, who are the instrumental causes of the lump of clay and so forth, are perceived as distinct from the material cause; likewise, why should the primal creator of the worlds not be the material cause? Having raised this doubt, he states the reason: "because of being devoid of modifications" (*vikārair virahataḥ*), which means because of being free from modification. He negates the stated point with the word "no" (*na*).

He explains that very point: "As a door. Just as when one says "the child has become a youth," there is no modification in the living self (*jīva*) because the modification occurs in the body which serves as a door, so too here, although there is modification in the Lord who is the specific attribute of the material cause of the world, there is no modification in the Lord Himself—this is the meaning. Now, an objection might be raised: "The example of clay and its effects is shown; however, in the case of the illustrative examples such as clay, the modification occurs in the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the substance. Likewise, here too, the modification should occur in the very nature [of the Lord]. Anticipating this, he says "clay" to show that it is not so.

Indeed, it is not required that there be a complete similarity between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*); rather, only such similarity as is appropriate is accepted. In this case, however, since a modification of its own nature is impossible for the Blessed One, the attainment of a different state is observed solely through association with non-conscious matter. This is what he expresses by the word "body" (*deha*). By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), examples such as "as hair and body-hair [grow] from an existing person" are included. Because his activity has been shown—that is, because the activity of the Blessed One has been demonstrated.

For it is observed in the world that the spider’s attainment of a different state occurs neither in its body alone nor in the self alone, but rather in the self as qualified by the body; likewise, it is entirely consistent that the attainment of another state occurs in the Supreme Self as qualified by primordial matter (prakṛti).

Others prattle that for a single entity, being the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) and being the material cause (*upādānatva*) are mutually contradictory. To demonstrate the point they have stated by means of an example from their own accepted system, [the author] begins with the words "svajñānādyavat" (like one's own knowledge, etc.). Those proponents of Nyāya who reject the Lord’s status as the material cause fall away precisely due to the contradiction within their own system. Indeed, they postulate three types of causes: the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Furthermore, some assert that whatever is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) is also the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). For example, with respect to its own cognition and so forth, the individual soul (jīva) produces its own cognition, desire-to-act, effort, and the like, which are produced by itself, through the practice of the scriptures and other means. Therefore, because it is the agent therein, it constitutes the efficient cause.

Nevertheless, it is itself the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), because the definition of an inherent cause is clearly perceived as that wherein the effect—such as its own cognition—inheres. Furthermore, God himself also brings about the conjunction of Himself, who is all-pervading, with all atoms and so forth, since He is the cause of all effects; thus, in that regard, He is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) by virtue of being the agent.

Inherence-causality (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) is also observed in Him with respect to that [effect], because the conjunction of atoms and so forth resides in God. Therefore, just as in your own system both agency and inherent causality reside in God alone, so too in our system both instrumental causality (*nimittatva*) and material causality (*upādānatva*) reside in a single reality; what contradiction is there?

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: since inherence (*samavāya*) lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) and because the theory of the arising of a new cognition (*pratyayotpatti*) is extremely inferior, we accept only the occurrence of a transition to another state. Regarding the phrase "he creates" and so forth, the syntactical connection of the words is that God (*īśvara*) creates his own conjunction with another. In that context, he explains God’s status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) by the words "through conjunction. "Tat" means for that reason.

The meaning is that even primordial matter (*pradhāna*), being an efficient cause (*nimitta*) through its own activity, becomes an instrumental cause (*nimitta*) in the Lord’s conjunction with material forms; it is also the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) in the conjunction of the Lord with those material forms. The meaning is that, by means of the action residing in itself, it itself becomes an instrumental cause. Here, an objection is raised: "How can there be the becoming many for the one Lord, as in 'May I become many'? He resolves that objection with the words "of the one."

Just as it is established by authoritative means that Saubhari alone, having resolved upon assuming fifty bodies, was born in those forms, so too there is no contradiction in the fact that the Blessed Lord is born through His own volition alone in various forms distinguished by diverse attributes. Anticipating the objection that one scripture speaks of non-duality while another speaks of duality—and that duality and non-duality are mutually contradictory—the author states "bhedābheda" (duality-non-duality) to show that in our established doctrine, not even a scent of contradiction exists.

If one maintains that the scriptural texts concerning difference are justified by the difference in essential natures (*svarūpa*), while the texts concerning non-difference are justified by the unity of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-ekya*), then we alone emerge victorious.

He briefly demonstrates the collection of arguments that establish the stated causehood and the non-contradictory nature of being the material cause (upādāna) in the words "kāryaikye" (in the identity with the effect). In this regard, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)—which teaches that through the knowledge of one, all is known—is not possible without the Blessed One’s status as the material cause. The meaning is that the proposition holds only when there is an identity between the cause and the effect. Accordingly, the group of examples such as clay and its products was cited precisely to conform to the proposition of the identity between cause and effect.

Thus, its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been stated. Now he states its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) with the words "of the Creator. The meaning is that the scripture expresses the creative meditation (*abhidhyāna*) of the Lord, the Creator—namely, "May I be"—and thereby declares His status as the efficient cause. However, another scripture, taking the status of the efficient cause for granted, directly declares [Brahman] itself to be the material cause, the auxiliary cause, and so forth, through the passage beginning with "What was the wood? The repetition of the verb "states" (*vakti*) in the phrase "states the state of being wood and the state of being trees, etc. is for the sake of including both. "What was the wood? is a question regarding the material cause.

"What was that tree? is a question regarding the material cause (*upakaraṇa*). From which material cause (*upādāna*) did the Blessed One fashion (*niṣṭatakṣuḥ*) heaven and earth? The change in verbal form (*vacanavyatyaya*) is Vedic. Alternatively, the meaning is that the wise ones fashioned [it] with their mind—that is, they determined it through their intellect (*buddhi*). The sense is that they resolved in their minds that the origin of everything is from the Blessed One alone, who serves as the material cause. Or else, since the word *manīṣiṇaḥ* connects with what follows as well, it is to be taken as a vocative.

The syntactical connection of the Śruti passage beginning with “yad adhyatiṣṭhat” is as follows: the Lord, who sustains [the world] by being its inner ruler (antaryāmin), presided over that which served as His instrument. In the phrase “brahma vanam,” Brahman is the material cause (upādāna). In the phrase “brahma sa vṛkṣaḥ,” the meaning is that Brahman alone is the instrument (upakaraṇa). What is being stated here is this: while the subtle [state of] the sentient and insentient [world] qualified [by Brahman] is the material cause of the universe, that same [Brahman], when qualified by time and other factors that serve as instruments, is the instrument itself.

"O wise ones, ask this with your minds"—the meaning is: "O wise ones, listen to this together with mental attentiveness. In the phrase "I declare it to you with my mind, O wise ones," he says: "I speak to you who are listening, preceded by grace and with a special degree of attentiveness. Regarding the phrase "that upon which [He] presided," it was already stated previously that the Blessed Lord presided over that instrument; thus, because He is the presiding controller of all, the Blessed Lord's status as the efficient cause is established.

Furthermore, from the statement, "He himself made Himself his own self," it is seen that the Blessed Lord alone, by Himself, assumes different states of His own self; thus, His status as both the material cause (*upādānatva*) and the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is revealed. Regarding the statement that He is the source of beings (*bhūtayonitva*), in the passage, "The wise perceive Him as the source of beings," His very nature as the source of beings is stated directly. Therefore, both His agency (*kartṛtva*) and His material causality (*prakṛtitva*) are established by valid means of knowledge; thus he concludes with the words, "Therefore."
The phrase "the inner self of all principles" contains a reason within itself; the meaning is that everything is integrated because [He] is the inner controller of all.

Regarding this, someone says: "The definition of a causal factor has been stated by the Naiyāyikas and others as follows: that which is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) and that which is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)—any cause distinct from these two is the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa). Consequently, since the rule is established that what is the material cause (upādāna) cannot be the instrumental cause, and what is the instrumental cause cannot be the material cause, the doctrine of the identity of the instrumental and material causes is untenable. Anticipating this objection regarding a contradiction with the definition, he refutes it with the words: "It is not the material cause."

No material cause (*upādāna*) can be the instrumental cause (*nimitta*). For those who know the nature of instrumental causes maintain that an instrumental cause is a factor distinct from the material cause. Thus, the syntactical connection of the words is as follows: that which is established as being the instrumental cause does not partake in the state of being the material cause. He rejects the stated position by saying, "This is incorrect" (*ayuktam*). He demonstrates this very incorrectness through its contradiction with what is well-known in common experience and the Veda, beginning with the words "from the desired [sacrifice]," and so forth.

For in the world, according to the logic of the conventional usage of the means of measurement (*pramāṇa*) and the object of measurement (*prameya*), when a single entity possesses all characteristics, its capacity for being treated as manifold is established through the difference of its forms; this being the settled rule, the claim that the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*) and the material cause is distinct from the efficient cause—this artifice of propounding mutual contradiction is a fallacious argument, the ripening of childish thought. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, even in the absence of being denotable by a word whose meaning is established through convention (*saṃketa*), the agency of the material cause itself is well-established. Thus, the Lord’s status as both material cause and agent is not contradictory; there is no difficulty whatsoever.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the dissolution—that is, the destruction—of an effect into its own cause has been stated in such passages as "earth dissolves into water," and since the dissolution of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa has also been established by the venerable Parāśara in the statement, "And these two, Puruṣa and Prakṛti, dissolve into the Supreme Self," it follows that they are destroyed at the time of Pralaya; how then can you maintain that the universe is created from the Puruṣa as qualified by subtle Cit and Acit? Anticipating this doubt, [the author states: "At the time of creation, etc."

The manifestation as many by the one Lord alone—meaning the becoming many according to the expression "May I be many"—is established by the logic of Saubhari. Just as it is proven by authoritative evidence that Saubhari, though being only one, took on fifty bodies through his own resolve and was born in those forms, so too is it established by the logic of illustration that the Blessed Lord likewise arises from His own resolve alone in various forms distinguished by diverse attributes. This is the meaning within this established doctrine.

Furthermore, there would be no contradiction between the scriptural texts concerning difference and non-difference, because of the possibility of a unity of the qualified [nature]. The texts stating difference, such as "Two birds, united, friends," "The perishable is the primary matter (pradhāna), the imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over the perishable self," and "The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious," and so forth; and the texts stating non-difference, such as "There is not even the slightest diversity here," and so forth—there is no mutual contradiction between these two types of scriptural texts, because the texts on difference have as their purport the difference of essential nature, while the texts on non-difference [have as their purport the identity] of the underlying reality.
The meaning is that [the existence of the Self] is established through its connection with volition, non-volition, specific types of effects, activity, and purposefulness.

He briefly demonstrates the collection of arguments that establish the stated causehood and the non-contradictory nature of being the material cause (upādāna) in the words "kāryaikye" (in the identity with the effect). In this regard, the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*)—which teaches that through the knowledge of one, all is known—is not possible without the Blessed One’s status as the material cause. The meaning is that the proposition holds only when there is an identity between the cause and the effect. Accordingly, the group of examples such as clay and its products was cited precisely because they are consistent with the proposition of the identity of cause and effect.

Thus, its nature as the material cause (*upādānatva*) has been stated. He also states its nature as the instrumental cause (*nimittatva*) by the word "of the Creator" (*sraṣṭuḥ*). The meaning is that the scripture expresses the meditative reflection (*abhidhyāna*) of the Lord, the Creator, in this [Prakṛti], thereby expressing His status as the instrumental cause. However, another scripture, taking for granted His established status as the instrumental cause, directly states His own nature as the material cause and as the auxiliary cause (*sahakāritva*) through the passage beginning with "What was the forest? (*kiṃ svid vanam*).

The word "vakti" (he speaks) is connected through repetition to both "vanatām" (the state of being a forest) and "vṛkṣatādim" (the state of being a tree, etc.). "What was the material cause (*upādāna*) of that forest? is the question regarding the material cause. "What was that tree? is the question regarding the instrumental cause (*upakaraṇa*). "From which [cause] the Blessed One fashioned (*niṣṭatakṣuḥ*) heaven and earth"—here, the verbal substitution *niṣṭatakṣuḥ* for *sasṛje* (he created) is a Vedic usage.

Alternatively, the meaning is that the wise ones (manīṣiṇaḥ) mentally and intellectually carved out (niṣṭatakṣuḥ) the forest—that is, they determined it. The meaning is that they resolved in their minds that the origin of all things is from the Blessed Lord alone, who serves as the material cause. Alternatively, since the word *manīṣiṇā* is connected with what follows, it is in the vocative case; thus the syntactical connection of the scripture is: "That which He presided over," meaning the Lord, sustaining [the world] as its inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) through the universe, presided over whatever instrument [He employed]. In the passage beginning with "The Brahman is the forest," the Brahman is the forest, serving as the material cause (*upādāna*).

"Brahman is that tree"—the meaning is that Brahman alone is the instrument (*upakaraṇa*).
