What is intended is this: the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe, which is characterized by the subtle sentient and non-sentient [principles], is that very same [Brahman] when characterized by time and other factors that serve as its instruments.

"O wise ones, ask this with your mind. The meaning is: "O wise ones, listen to this with your minds," that is, with attentive concentration. In the passage, "O wise ones, I declare it to you with my mind," the word "to you" (*vaḥ*) means that I speak for the sake of favoring you who are listening, by means of a particular kind of attentive concentration. As for the phrase "that upon which He stood," it has already been stated that the Blessed Lord presided over that instrument. Thus, because He is the presiding controller of all, the Blessed Lord's status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*) is established.

Furthermore, in the passage, "He made Himself His own self," it is seen that this very Blessed Lord, by Himself, through the assumption of a different state of His own self, possesses both the nature of the material cause (*upādānatva*) and the efficient cause (*nimittatva*). Thus, His being the source of all beings (*bhūtayonitva*) has been stated; for in the verse, "The wise perceive Him as the source of all beings," His very status as the source of all beings is declared with scriptural authority. Therefore, He concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), establishing that both His status as the agent (*kartṛtva*) and His status as the material cause (*prakṛtitva*) are proven by valid means of knowledge. The qualifying phrase "the inner Self of all" contains a reason: the meaning is that because He is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all, everything is logically consistent.

Regarding this, someone objects: "The logicians have stated the definition that the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is a cause distinct from both the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Consequently, since the rule is established that whatever is the material cause (*upādāna*) cannot be the efficient cause, and whatever is the efficient cause cannot be the material cause, the doctrine of the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause is untenable. Anticipating this objection regarding a contradiction with the definition, he refutes it by stating, "It is not the material cause. That is to say: no material cause whatsoever is [exclusively] the efficient cause.

It occurs thus: those who know the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) maintain that the efficient cause is a cause distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*). Thus, the syntactical connection of the words is that whatever is established as being the efficient cause does not partake of the nature of the material cause. He refutes the stated position with the word "untenable" (*ayuktam*). He demonstrates its untenability by means of what is well-known in the world and the Veda, beginning with the words "from the desired," and so forth. For in the world, according to the logic of the transaction between the instrument of measurement and the object measured on a scale, when a single entity possesses all the characteristics [of both], [it is untenable].

The meaning is as follows: since the rule that the application of the conventional usage of "diversity" is established through a difference in form (*ākārabheda*) has been proven, the attempt to introduce mutual contradiction—by means of a logic fabricated from one's own imagination—that the efficient cause (*nimitta*) is distinct from the material cause (*upādāna*) and the material cause is distinct from the efficient cause, is a fallacious argument and the ripening of a child’s fancy. Furthermore, even in the absence of being denotable by the term "efficient cause" as established by your own convention, it is well-known that the material cause itself possesses agency (*kartṛtva*). Thus, the Lord’s status as both material cause and agent is not contradictory; there is no difficulty whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "Has it not been stated that the dissolution (*laya*)—that is, the destruction—of an effect into its own cause occurs in such passages as 'Earth dissolves into water' (*pṛthivyapsu pralīyate*)? Furthermore, the dissolution of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* has been established by the venerable Parāśara in the statement, 'And these two, [the individual] soul and [nature], dissolve into the Supreme Self. Since they are thus destroyed at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), how can you assert that the universe is created from a *puruṣa* qualified by subtle consciousness and matter? Anticipating this objection, [the author] points out the distinction established by scripture based on the fact that the dissolution of earth and other elements—which are effects—is different [from the dissolution of the causes].

He demonstrates this with the words "having said," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: here, two kinds of dissolution (*laya*) are intended. One is the attainment of one's own state; the other, however, is the attainment of a specific kind of conjunction that is incapable of being divided from another entity, without abandoning one's own state. For example, [the dissolution] of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*: without abandoning the nature of *prakṛti*, which is eternally established because it is uncontradicted, there is the attainment of a specific conjunction incapable of division with the Blessed Lord, who is the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

That very darkness becomes one with the Supreme; thus, it is designated by way of a specific unity. Previously, however, in such passages as "the earth dissolves into water," the word *laya* (dissolution) itself is employed directly. Therefore, the distinction is that the Puranic expression "both of these dissolve" (*līyete*) speaks only of a state of unification. Furthermore, the word *laya* is also used for a particular kind of contact, as in "birds settle (*līyante*) upon the trees," where the word *laya* itself is used in its direct sense.

All of this is to be understood according to the reading in this verse. As for the grammatical connection (*anvaya*): having stated the dissolution of the other principles (*tattva*) in such passages as "the earth dissolves into water," it is further stated that darkness attains oneness with the Blessed Lord alone, in the words "darkness becomes one. By this, there is no destruction of those two, namely *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Moreover: "Know both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* to be indeed beginningless; [know] *prakṛti* to be insentient, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly changing."

In such passages and in the statements of Parāśara and others who know the supreme Veda, the beginninglessness of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa is declared; therefore, their dissolution cannot be direct. The statement regarding dissolution found in the Purāṇas, along with its illustrative example, is interpreted otherwise by the phrase "it may be like the case of iron and water. Just as water held within iron that has been transformed into the form of a weapon remains in the very form of water—otherwise, because of the impossibility of the persistence of its fluidity and so forth.

In the same way, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), though capable of existing in a state of non-distinction within the Blessed Lord, become objects of the conventional usage of "oneness" through a mere specific conjunction; thus, they specifically assist in the creation of the world and other such processes. He concludes the stated point with its supporting reason by saying, "Therefore."

The creation of the universe from the Blessed Lord—who is accompanied by the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and so forth—is well-established, as this is proven by the Śruti texts skillfully determined along with their supporting expositions (upabṛṃhaṇa). Here, by the word "and so forth" (prabhṛti), the connection with time is intended. By that, the meaning is that the status of being the material cause (upādānatva) is established for Him as qualified by the subtle sentient and non-sentient, while His status as the instrumental cause (upakaraṇatva) is established through His qualification by time.

At the commencement of this treatise, the Lord’s status as both the efficient and material cause of the universe—as declared in the Sūtra on "Birth and so forth" (Janmādy-asya yataḥ)—was introduced and concluded in the section concerning Primordial Matter (Prakṛty-adhikaraṇa). Hereafter, since it is impossible to exhaustively state all remaining Vedic passages due to their infinite number, the reconciliation of them in that very same manner must be inferred by oneself; such is the connection [of the present section].

Regarding this, Viṣṇucittārya states the connection between the four quarters (pādas) mentioned in the first chapter through an analysis of their meaning: "In this way, by means of the first quarter of the first chapter, together with the definitions of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the Supreme Person—who is accepted by all Vedāntins as the ultimate cause—is established. By the second and third [quarters], the nature of His manifestations and the manner of His relationship [to them] are shown. By the fourth quarter, the refutation of opposing views is accomplished."

Thus, he says "by this" (*eteneti*) to indicate that the reconciliation of all the Śruti texts has been stated. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: Do those specific passages concerning the cause (*kāraṇavākya*) not cited here refer to Brahman, which is characterized by the aforementioned duality of consciousness (*cit*) and non-consciousness (*acit*), or not? To determine that, one must ask whether those passages fall outside the scope of the aforementioned principles (*nyāya*) or within it. To determine that, one must ask whether it is possible for them to be within the scope of those principles or not. In this section on extension (*atideśādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that the reconciliation of even those causal passages not previously determined can be achieved through the method applied to the causal passages already established.

In response to the doubt as to which those sentences are, he begins to state that by citing certain sentences and following their lead, all such sentences are to be interpreted; thus he says, "In the beginning. First, there appears one sentence establishing the supremacy of Hiraṇyagarbha: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists."

Likewise, another statement, "Neither being nor non-being, Śiva alone is absolute," is also seen as if it were establishing the supremacy of Rudra; for there, by the words "When there was darkness, neither day nor night," it is prima facie understood that the persistence of Rudra alone at the time of dissolution is being described. This is what [the author] expresses by the word "devoured" (grasta).

These two statements have been cited; indeed, there exist many such statements. In order to suppress a specific doubt—that there might be something superior to Nārāyaṇa arising from those [other] statements—the author of the Sūtras extends (atidiśati) the very same previously mentioned logical principles to other cases. Why is this for? He says "for the sake of instructing the disciple" (*śiṣyaśikṣārtham*), meaning "such as these. This is the sense: although the principle learned in one instance is to be applied elsewhere, and thus the intended meaning is established by itself, nevertheless, out of favor toward his disciples, the venerable author of the Sūtras has explicitly declared it in words. ||149||

In this scripture, you assert that Śrīpati alone is the Lord of all; yet it is Śrī herself who is declared by the Veda to be Brahman, as she is designated as the culmination of the triad of forms—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—and the worldly convention regarding these three forms is well-established. Furthermore, since Brahmā and Śiva are subject to karma, Viṣṇu, who is mentioned alongside them, must likewise be subject to karma. Thus, in the *Ghaṭukūṭā*, the distinction of the Blessed Nārāyaṇa from others is clearly shown.

"Since you have set out to establish [the Lord's uniqueness], you have once again fallen into the very state of similarity (sālakṣaṇya) that you sought to avoid. Anticipating this objection with the first half-verse, he says, "O Lord of the Universe" (*viśveśa*). [The opponent argues: He is subject to suffering because of His subjection to karma, and thus shares the common characteristics (*sādharmya*) of Brahmā and Rudra, who are likewise subject to suffering. He rejects the stated point, saying, "Not so" (*maivam*). He explains that very point: "In the forms of the Fish and others" (*matsyāditi*). Even in the states of the Fish incarnation and so forth, what is observed is merely the Lord’s dramatic imitation (*anukaraṇa-nāṭyam*) of His own manifestations (*vibhūtis*), such as the Fish and others, by virtue of their belonging to the same genus.
Thus, this is merely a dramatic performance (nāṭya) by Brahmā and Rudra, who have become His own manifestations. To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "By Brahmā and Īśa, the creators."

Beginning with the words, "In the beginning, indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed," and continuing, "Therein Brahmā, the four-faced, was born; then, from the forehead of him who remained absorbed in meditation, sweat fell; from the sweat a bubble arose; from the bubble a three-eyed, trident-handed person was born"—the meaning is that this is a dramatic performance (*nāṭya*) imitating the majesty of the Supreme Brahman, whose essential nature is infinite greatness, and who is acknowledged as the creator of both Brahmā and Rudra.

In this context, for the sake of easy comprehension by the students, he summarizes the process of raising the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the eight topics situated in the fourth quarter and their subsequent refutation, beginning with the words "sāṃkhyoktā" (as stated by the Sāṃkhya).

In the *Ānumānika-adhikaraṇa*, [the Sūtra refutes] the process described by the Sāṃkhya; in the *Camasa-adhikaraṇa*, the process of creation from the *pradhāna*—which they claim is not Brahman—as stated by them; in the *Saṃkhyopasaṃgraha-adhikaraṇa*, their formulated enumeration of principles (*tattva*); in the *Kāraṇatva-adhikaraṇa*, the identity of the cause with the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) as asserted by the Sāṃkhya; in the *Jagadvācitva-adhikaraṇa*, that the word "karman" refers to one's own actions in the form of merit and demerit; and in the *Vākyānvaya-adhikaraṇa*, the connection with the defects of the fruits of action consisting of wife, son, and so forth.

In the Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa, the author of the Sūtras refuted the distinction between the efficient cause (nimitta) and the material cause (upādāna), as well as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that Brahmā, Rudra, and others possess causality, which was addressed in the Sarvavyākhyānādhikaraṇa.

In this treatise, the use of the ablative case is for the purpose of demonstrating, by way of analysis, the specific reasons for the emergence of the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) views. Regarding the word "refuted" (*kṣiptam*) and so forth: from these reasons imagined by the proponents of the prima facie view, the Sūtrakāra has protected the meaning stated in the first three quarters [of the work] by revealing the heart of the Śruti in the fourth quarter, thereby clearly illuminating the meanings of the sacred texts.

Thus, when the subject matter of the first chapter has been established with certainty, the author, desiring to commence the second chapter, restates the connection between the preceding and succeeding chapters by the words "as the object of inquiry" (*jijñāsyatvena*). The phrase "once [the Self] is established" (*siddhe*) simultaneously conveys the meaning of the four aphorisms that serve as the introduction to the treatise (*śāstropodghāta*) as well as the meaning of the first quarter (*pāda*). The phrase "the embodied beings, both moving and stationary, consisting of conscious and unconscious matter" conveys the meaning of the second quarter. The phrase "the reality of Brahman" (*brahmatattva*) conveys the meaning of the third quarter, since the word "Brahman" reveals the Lord’s nature as the support of all things.

By the phrase "by direct assertion and so forth" (*śrutyādyaiḥ*), the meaning of the fourth quarter [of the first chapter] is also summarized along with those [other means]. The syntactical connection is as follows: it is well-stated that this natural function of the words of the Vedic tradition—which teach causality—[is established] by the means of proof consisting of direct assertion, indicative mark, syntactical connection, and so on. Now, he states the subject matter of the second chapter, which is about to be discussed, with the word "sublation" (*bādham*).

In this regard, the first two quarters (pādas) are devoted to resolving external contradictions by way of the cause; there too, the distinction is that one [quarter] resolves sublation (*bādha*), while the other is devoted to resolving counter-argument (*pratirodha*). The latter two quarters are devoted to resolving internal contradictions by way of the effect. Internal contradiction, moreover, refers to the mutual contradiction between scriptural statements. And here, since it is precisely the contradiction based on the effect that is resolved, it follows that the distinction from the first two quarters—which resolve contradictions based on the cause—is established. This is what is being stated.

As for the meaning of the words: those who describe sublation (*bādha*) and obstruction (*pratirodha*), as well as external and internal roots, in manifold ways are "Musalyas"—that is, strikers with clubs—or alternatively, they are called "Musalyas" because they are to be slain with a club; the sense is that they should be expelled or cast out. Anticipating the question "For what purpose?", he says: "for the sake of establishing the immovability of the *Niṣads* and the *Upaniṣads*."

In this regard, there exists a certain Upanishad, renowned by the name *Mūla-śruti*, which illuminates the meaning expressed in the *Pañcapātra* and is cited by the Bhāgavatas; furthermore, since it is well known that we designate this as the essence within all the Vedas, there is nothing further that needs to be said here.

Beginning with this refutation, [the author] sets forth at the end of the chapter a rebuttal of the opposing view, stating that the entire collection of topics expounded in the first chapter is untenable for those who maintain the doctrine of a Brahman devoid of distinctions, using the verse beginning with "In the beginning. The meaning is: "Let the status of being an object of inquiry (jijñāsyatā) be set aside from the start, as it has been struck down by many refutations. Here too, the very first aphorism, "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), was propounded; in this aphorism, the fact that Brahman is an object of inquiry is stated.

Furthermore, even the proponents of non-dualism (advaitavādins) must concede that Brahman is an object of inquiry; for if Brahman were not an object of inquiry, then the entire scripture would have to be abandoned, which they cannot accept even against their will. Consequently, since the consequence of falsity arises through the logic that "if Brahman is an object of inquiry, then because it is an object of perception, it must be false," the proponents of non-dualism are left with nothing but ridicule—caught on both ends like a rope. This is what is meant by the phrase "struck down by many refutations. The term [from the previous verse] is also to be applied here according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*).

The defining statement, "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]," is accepted even by the proponents of non-duality (Advaitavādins). A "definition" (lakṣaṇa) is, by its very nature, a unique property (asādhāraṇo dharmaḥ). Therefore, for the Advaitavādins, the description of a definition for a Brahman devoid of all attributes (nirdharmaka) is untenable.

Now, is it not the case that there are two kinds of definitions—a defining characteristic by way of distinction (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) and a defining characteristic by way of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*)? The defining characteristic by way of essential nature is that which is set forth by such statements as "Truth, Knowledge," namely, reality, consciousness, infinity, and so forth; this, moreover, is presented through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And the defining characteristic by way of distinction is the causality of the universe and the like; this, moreover, is expressed through non-coreferentiality, as it is presented by such statements as "From whence indeed these [beings arise]. And thus, let there be no defining characteristic by way of essential nature for Brahman.

Let there be an extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), since there is no relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*); just as when it is said, "The moon is at the tip of the branch," the tip of the branch is not actually connected with the moon, so too the causality of the world and other such attributes, though they define Brahman, are not conjoined with the real Brahman. Therefore, Brahman remains strictly without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*); thus, we have no fault whatsoever.

To this, the reply is as follows: if the definition of essential nature (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) does not exist in Brahman, then the statement "Being, Consciousness, etc. (*satya-jñānādi-vākya*) would fail to be a means of establishing Brahman at all; this would be a great blow [to your position]. If you argue that it establishes Brahman by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-mukhena*), then since exclusion itself is inexpressible, the very same defect remains in the definition.

If it is argued that even figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) must be accepted in accordance with the intended purport of the sentence, then let it be so; however, you yourself must specifically demonstrate what the indicated object is. If you say it is "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), then we shall analyze this: is exclusion the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of the entity], or is it something additional? If it is the nature itself, then since the nature would be indicated by a single word alone, there follows the consequence of the other words being redundant. If it is something additional, then there follows the consequence of falling into the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*).

Furthermore, the designation of various characteristics is meaningless, because even by means of those respective characteristics, there is no specific form of the object to be characterized; or, if such a form did exist, it would entail the consequence of actual difference. This is the general direction of the argument. Regarding the third aphorism as well, let us examine the statement that the scripture is its source (*śāstrayonitva*). By the word *mṛṣyāmaḥ* ("we tolerate"), it is indicated precisely that [the opponent's view] is not to be tolerated. By this, the phrase "it is struck down by many refutations" is also to be supplied here. Consequently, even the conventional usage of "harmony" (*samanvaya*) in the aphorism "But that [Brahman is known] from harmony" (*tattu samanvayāt*) would be utterly untenable.

"Coherence" (samanvaya) means the convergence of all causal statements upon Brahman as their primary purport. And that coherence cannot be asserted by you regarding Brahman; for you yourselves have asserted it while resorting to a refutation [of our position] based on the weakness of establishing your own view, through the refutation of the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakabhāva) and so forth. If it is argued: "Let there be a refutation of the primary mode of operation (mukhyavṛtti); we shall resort to a figurative mode of operation (aupacārikī vṛtti) regarding Brahman," even that is merely laughable.

If the primary sense is absent, how can a figurative usage (*aupacārikī vṛtti*) be asserted? For it contradicts the definitions established by all the world that "indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is the application of a word to another object connected with its primary meaning, while "secondary usage" (*gauṇī*) is the application to another object possessing qualities similar to the primary meaning. Furthermore, secondary usage is indeed a type of usage; for "usage" means the communication of a meaning by a word. Thus, even through secondary usage, Brahman is certainly capable of being understood.

Thus, please uphold your own statement that "because it is an object of cognition, it is false. If you argue that there must therefore be the function of *tātparya* (intentional import), we reply: that too is indeed a [linguistic] function; and so, whether it be a snake or a scorpion, the capacity to cause harm is common to both—enough of this elaboration. We shall endure everything said by the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), but we will not endure this one thing.

Beginning with the sūtra “Because of seeing [Brahman], not that which is non-scriptural” and ending with “By this, all [sūtras] have been explained, have been explained,” is there or is there not a single meaning for each individual sūtra to be established through its distinctions?

If there is, then the consequence follows that there is a doctrine of duality (bheda-vāda). If there is not, then the sūtras would be utterly meaningless. If it is argued that there are meanings, but they are merely conventional (vyāvahārika), then if the meanings of the Vedānta-sūtras are conventional, tell me: what is the ultimate reality (pāramārthika)? If you say there is nothing at all, then for what purpose is this Śārīraka-śāstra commenced?

Furthermore, if the subject matter of the Śārīraka-śāstra were non-ultimate, then because the meanings asserted by others would also be non-ultimate, the futility of commencing the scripture would once again be very well stated by you. Here, the syntactical connection of these sūtras—which possess clear meanings and referents—is as follows: how could your doctrine of the difference between Brahman and Prakṛti-Puruṣa be consistent with the view of non-dual identity without attributes, given that the qualities such as "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) and so forth, which are the primary subjects to be established as the meaning of the sūtras and constitute the attributes of Brahman, [are taught] through these words?

If the difference between the Brahman propounded in the Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa and primordial matter (prakṛti) and the individual soul (puruṣa) were false, the section would be rendered purposeless; if it were real, it would entail the doctrine of dualism (bhedavāda). Since the fallacious resort to "empirical reality" (vyāvahārikatva) has already been refuted, we shall not labor over it here.

In the first chapter, across its four sections (pādas), the opponent has presented four types of passages containing very obscure indications (liṅga) regarding the individual soul (jīva) and so forth; the proponent has countered these with their respective opposing statements. This concludes the first section of the second chapter.

In the first chapter, across its four quarters (*pādas*), the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) has presented four types of scriptural passages containing indistinct marks (*liṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, while the proponent (*siddhāntin*) has presented passages that counter them. Therein, the arguments of the opponent undergo a gradual depletion quarter by quarter, according to the maxim of "the destruction of the descendant of Pulastya and others. Because those [arguments] once destroyed do not arise again, and because the logical reasons and scriptural passages introduced in each subsequent quarter are rendered weak due to their lack of support, their total extinction occurs in succession.

Furthermore, because the arguments of the established doctrine (siddhānta)—like those of Sugrīva’s soldiers—remain unimpaired with every step having repelled opposing views, and because each successive subject to be established, such as scripture, tradition, and reasoning, possesses its own support and thus gains increasing strength, the method of the established doctrine proceeds entirely free from thorns; thus, there is the attainment of victory on all fronts. When the positions of the Sāṅkhya and others have been refuted by the preceding chapter and the opponent is defeated—like one who, when his gambling fortune is lost, seizes upon worthless grass (balbaja)—[the following is stated].

According to the maxim "one should act [in such a way]," since the arguments here begin by asserting contradictions based solely on the initial course of the discussion, this constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) with the second chapter. Furthermore, because at the conclusion of the first chapter the positions of Sāṅkhya and Yoga were refuted in succession, the Sāṅkhya proponent first states the contradiction with the Vedānta, and then the Yoga proponent does so; thus there is a connection between the sections (*adhikaraṇa-saṅgati*) and they belong to a single group (*ekapeṭikatva*).

Regarding this, the author states the connection between the preceding and subsequent chapters along with an illustration: "Although the attainment of satisfaction for those of great intellect who are skilled in the methods of various systems of logic (*tattādṛgvidhatarkatantra*) may be achieved through the manner explained in the first chapter, nevertheless, the author of the Sūtras—anticipating an attack (*āskanda*) by rationalists (*haituka*) upon those of dull intellect and childlike understanding—stabilizes the very nature of Brahman as the cause, according to the maxim of 'digging in a pillar' (*sthūṇānikhananyāya*)."

Furthermore, whatever kind of "being an effect" (kāryatva) belongs to space and so forth, that very same [nature] he establishes; thus there is a further connection. This is the meaning: the author of the Sūtras stabilizes, by way of the "burying the pillar" (sthirīkaroti) analogy, the causality of Brahman and the effect-nature of space and so forth, along with their specific modes, so that they cannot be assailed by opponents who possess the intellect of children. Thus it is said that the function of the second chapter is precisely the stabilization of the matters already stated in the first chapter; consequently, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy.

The connection between the first and second chapters was previously stated; now, however, the mutual connection between the two preceding quarters (pādas) and the two subsequent quarters within the second chapter is being explained. Furthermore, other points concerning the true nature of reality that are supplementary to that [connection] are also elucidated therein by the words "the pair of quarters," and so forth.

As for the meaning of the words: the first pair of quarters in the second chapter sequentially removes the affliction—consisting of contradiction and obstruction—regarding Brahman, the supreme cause, as expressed by those outside the Veda. Furthermore, the subsequent pair of quarters—the quarter on ether (*viyat*) and the quarter on breath (*prāṇa*)—removes the contradiction arising through the effects [of Brahman] in order to pacify internal agitation.

By means of these two—sublation (*bādha*) and contradiction (*pratirodha*)—the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) characterized by the non-arising of the knowledge of the Supreme Self is also refuted. "Internal agitation" (*āntarakṣobha*) refers to the mutual contradiction among the Vedānta statements. Thus, the connection between the first pair of quarters [of the *Brahmasūtra*] with the subsequent pair of quarters has been explained. Furthermore, he states the difference in meaning and the connection in another way, beginning with the word "causality" (*hetutva*). By the preceding pair of quarters, the refutation of the impossibility of God being the cause was accomplished.

However, by the second pair of quarters, the refutation of the impossibility of that very causality being universal is performed. This is the meaning: the proponents of Nyāya think thus: "Granted that God may be a cause; nevertheless, because space and so forth are eternal, He cannot be their cause. Therefore, God's causality is not universal. That too is dispelled by the quarter concerning space and the rest. The phrase "it results" does not mean the direct sense, but rather the sense resulting from the overall context.

When the fact that space and so forth are effects is established, the dependence upon God results in His own status as an effect being automatically proven. Now, one might object: "The eternality of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is heard in scripture; how then can there be a challenge to the universal applicability of God’s causality? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that [objection]. That challenge to the universal applicability would apply only by setting aside the eternality established by scripture. The meaning is that while God is the cause everywhere except where there is a scriptural statement of eternality, He is the cause in all other cases.

The meaning is that the sovereignty of God—which is common to both the eternal and the non-eternal—is the definition of causality characterized by being invariably antecedent, and this [causality] is restricted to what is merely non-eternal.

The connection with the previous chapter has already been stated; now, however, the connection between the first quarter of the second section (lakṣaṇa) and the fourth quarter of the first section is being declared in this [section]. In the previous quarter, which serves as the basis for the "shadow of the treatises" (tantra-chāyā) regarding the Upaniṣads, it was established that they do not themselves have another purpose [than liberation]; yet, since those Upaniṣads are weaker than the treatises, the opponent raises the objection that it is more reasonable to follow them [the treatises], which constitutes "following the treatises" (tantrānusaraṇa).

This is the meaning: in the section on the "Exposition of All Explanations" (*sarvavyākhyānādhikaraṇa*), it was stated that "the Upaniṣads have been explained. And this explanation is indeed an amplification (*upabṛṃhaṇa*). That amplification of the Śruti must be carried out by means of Smṛti. However, the Smṛti of Manu and others, because it is intent upon propounding ritual action (*karman*), serves as an amplification of the ritual portion (*karmabhāga*) of the Veda.

Thus, because it lacks specific instruction, the poor Upaniṣad relies upon the Sāṃkhya Smṛti for the reinforcement of its reasoning. Therefore, since it is weaker than the Sāṃkhya Smṛti which is to be accepted as authoritative, the conclusion that this Upaniṣad must be interpreted in accordance with that [Smṛti] emerges; thus, the connection by way of the introduction of the present section (*adhikaraṇa*) also becomes manifest here. He states "thus" (*ittham*) to show that the author of the Sūtras resolves the confusion brought about by the opponent in the subsequent section.

The passage beginning with "tattad" and so forth refutes the excessive violence conceived through the logic and traditional doctrines (smṛti) of various schools such as Sāṃkhya; having warded it off with counter-weapons capable of rejecting those respective views, it confirms the meaning stated in the preceding section.

He dispels the charge of pointlessness regarding the commencement of the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter with the words "It has been determined," and so forth. For in the Karma-kāṇḍa, in the section concerning contradictions and elsewhere, it was determined that the Vedic scriptures remain unshakable even when there is a conflict with Smṛti or reasoning. Since the Vedānta is also indeed Śruti, this present discussion for its sake—that is, for the sake of establishing what was already established in the previous [section]—would render the first quarter of the second chapter entirely useless. He says "Not so" to refute this, and explains that very point with the word "profound."

For one of dull intellect who might perceive that—given the profundity of the Upaniṣads and the resulting suspicion that their subject matter is difficult to comprehend—the pursuit of knowledge regarding the true meaning has already been achieved through the words of the most authoritative sages such as Kapila and through the logic that serves as an embellishment thereof, this [present work] is composed to refute such a misconception; thus, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy.

Anticipating the doubt as to where the removal of contradictions with Smṛti occurs and where the removal of contradictions with logic (nyāya) occurs, [the author] demonstrates by dividing them, saying "by two," etc., that the removal of contradictions with Smṛti takes place through two sections (adhikaraṇas), while the removal of contradictions with logic takes place through eight sections. He states the resulting meaning of both these removals with the words "by that" (tena): the sense is that the Lord's status as both material cause (upādānatva) and efficient cause (nimittatva) is established with great firmness.

The meaning is as follows: "and we are likewise" indicates that in some cases there is the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), while in other cases it manifests both the status of being the material cause and the efficient cause (*nimittatva*). When the various mutually contradictory ontological principles imagined by different disputants are refuted one by one, and when the range of doubts regarding the existence or non-existence of the remaining principles proceeds according to the maxim of the scale's beam rising and falling, the author of the Sūtra—having placed his intellect with equanimity during this investigation—blocks partiality and establishes equanimity itself;
such is the application of the second half of the verse.

The connection (*saṃgati*) here has already been stated. The investigation into its meaning, however, concerns whether the previously stated fact that Brahman is the cause of the world can be subverted or not; whether the Vedānta texts establish Brahman as the cause or not; whether the contradiction with the Vedānta texts—due to following the *Sāṅkhya* Smṛti which lacks scope—establishes that they refer to *Pradhāna* or not; whether the *Sāṅkhya* Smṛti provides an expansion (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) of the Veda or whether it is the Smṛtis of Manu and others that do so; and whether the *Sāṅkhya* Smṛti is rooted in error or not.

In this regard, he states the reason why the Vedāntas must necessarily follow the Smṛti of Kapila in due order, saying: "The Smṛti-kāra... This sage Kapila is heard of in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad itself in the passage, "The seer Kapila, who was born first," as one who has realized the true nature of reality. For "sage-ness" (ṛṣitva) consists in being advanced in knowledge; this is an unassailable reason. Furthermore, it is well known from the Rāmāyaṇa that Kapila is a portion (aṃśa) of Vāsudeva. And since error is not possible for Vāsudeva, [his teaching is authoritative].

Moreover, it is heard everywhere in the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other texts that he possessed a mind skilled in making vows and a mind highly proficient in the practice of Yoga. The underlying intention is this: Manu, Yājñavalkya, and others were performers of ritual action (karmīs) alone, whereas he was solely devoted to knowledge (jñāna). Therefore, by his very words, the Vedānta is further elucidated. Thus, because he possessed such excellence, even regarding matters not perceptible to us, the definitive conclusion concerning the "Crown of the Śrutis" (Upaniṣads) would be reached through his statement alone; hence he says, "Therefore."

"Do not say so," he says, [concluding] with "it would not be [the case]. In that regard, he states four reasons beginning with "having a single purpose. Because the statements of Manu and others have a single purpose, they lack mutual contradiction; because it is heard in scripture that "whatever Manu said is medicine," [his words] serve as the medicine for all worldly diseases; because they were composed by one who is supremely peaceful and untainted by defects such as misplaced anger like Kapila; and because of his great erudition—it is only right to follow those [Manu's] statements.
Therefore, since the knowledge of reality is established through those very statements, following the statements of Kapila is improper—this is the meaning.

In this context, the connection with the *Bhāṣya* itself is made very clear by the statement expressing a further doubt: "Since the Yoga-smṛti also accepts Īśvara and describes yoga as enjoined in the Vedānta as a means to liberation, and since its author, Hiraṇyagarbha, is authorized to expound all the Vedāntas, it is logical that the Vedānta is supplemented (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) by that Smṛti. The inquiry into its meaning, however, concerns whether the doctrine of Brahman as the cause remains as it is or not; that is, whether the Vedāntic passages have Brahman as their cause as their primary purport (*paratva*), or whether they have something else as their purport.

Is that cause the *pradhāna* presided over by Īśvara, or is it Brahman? Does the *Yoga-smṛti*, which leaves no room for doubt, serve as a supplement to the Veda, or is it superseded by the *smṛtis* of Parāśara and others? Is the *Yoga-smṛti* rooted in error or not? And is it possible for its author, Hiraṇyagarbha, to have been subject to error or not?

In all these cases, the relationship between cause and effect (*phala-phalibhāva*) is to be inferred by oneself. This is because, in both positions, the relationship of cause and effect exists in the form of demonstrating that if the subsequent points—reached through a succession of investigations into those meanings—are reversed, then each preceding point is likewise reversed. Therefore, since the relationship of cause and effect in both the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is to be inferred by oneself, we do not demonstrate it in detail.

Since the subject matter, the cause for the arising of doubt, the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusions (*siddhānta*), the methods of reasoning (*nyāya*), the definitive resolutions (*nirṇaya*), and their respective fruits—all of which have been introduced—are already clearly elucidated in the *Bhāṣya* and the *Dīpa*, they need not be discussed here in detail. Therefore, we shall elaborate extensively upon the connection (*saṅgati*) and the investigation of its meaning alone. In this regard, he demonstrates the methods of the prima facie and established conclusions by distinguishing them, beginning with the words "the Vedas" (*vedān*).

It is heard in scripture that in former times the Blessed One was appointed by the Creator to distribute the Vedas, as stated: "He who ordains the Brahmās in the beginning, and who indeed sends forth the Vedas to him. This is the first reason why he was appointed as the initiator of all branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). Furthermore, his renown as the Lord of Speech (*vāgīśatva*) throughout all the worlds is the second reason. And thirdly, because of these three reasons, the Vedānta itself undergoes movement [of authority] due to the contradiction with the statement of Hiraṇyagarbha.

He rejects this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) stated above, saying, "Not so. He states the reason for this: "tasyāpi" ("of him too"). Since even Hiraṇyagarbha is seen to have encountered calamities—foremost among them the theft of the Vedas caused by Madhu and Kaiṭabha—it follows that, due to his being a "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña), that is, having a body composed of the three guṇas of primordial nature (prakṛti), error and the like are possible for him. Consequently, because it is impossible to resolve in any way the contradiction with the Vedas found in his words regarding matters for which there is no other recourse, we conclude that his word is indeed non-authoritative, just like the words of Kapila. This is because of the contradiction with the Vedas.
If it is impossible to carry out [the injunction], we understand that very statement to be non-authoritative.

Regarding this, the connection [of the topic] has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself: "Once again, those who maintain the position of contradiction with Smṛti stand forth, relying upon reasoning."

The venerable Viṣṇucittāryas have stated this very point: "Having abandoned the teachings of Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others, one opposes [the Vedānta] by attempting to interpret the meaning of the Veda otherwise through the arguments propounded by them. The inquiry into that meaning is as follows: Is it possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world, or not? Furthermore, is the emergence of an insentient world from a sentient Brahman possible, or not? And does an effect arise from a cause of the same genus, or from one of a different genus?

Is the inference based on the similarity between cause and effect inconclusive or not? In this regard, he introduces the subject matter of the Sāṅkhya statement—which was cited as the regulating principle for the similarity between cause and effect—by saying "the universe. Indeed, the Sāṅkhyas say this: because the universe consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, it is composed of the three *guṇas*; therefore, it must arise from that which possesses the three *guṇas*. It cannot arise from what is "non-similar" (*asama*), meaning from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is devoid of the three *guṇas*. Thus, it cannot come into being from such a source.

Having set forth the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it, saying "this is untenable. Here he analyzes the alternatives: is the identity of cause and effect asserted by you in every respect, or in some respect? Within that [latter case], there is a further division of alternatives: is it in the specific form that determines the existence of cause and effect, or in just any form whatsoever? Therein, he refutes the first alternative with the word "sarva" (all).

The identity of cause and effect cannot exist in every respect, because they are observed to have distinct forms as effect and cause respectively. He has already refuted the third position—that there is identity in some respect—by stating "it is accepted. Furthermore, they say: "The status of being an entity (padārthatva) is established in both the mountain and the atom. Thus, it is not at all necessary to establish an identity in some respect whatsoever.

Therefore, the second position—that there is similarity by way of the form that determines the causal relation—remains; yet he says "no" to that as well, stating "shattered" (bhagna). The meaning is: there is no equality of qualities suitable for establishing the causal relation—that is, no equality of qualities such as being cow-dung—which would determine the status of cause and effect between the scorpion and the cow-dung. This is because the quality of being cow-dung exists in the cow-dung but is absent in the scorpion. Thus, the construction is: "the equality of qualities is shattered."

Therefore, it is easily understood that the Blessed Lord, whose body consists of subtle consciousness and non-consciousness (cid-acit), abides in a form characterized by gross consciousness and non-consciousness. Consequently, every objection is refuted; for we have stated that the causal relationship consists merely in the subsistence of that very same substance in its subtle state in the form of its gross state. Indeed, we do not assert that the Lord Himself, in His own essential nature, undergoes transformation into the forms of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

In this regard, a certain person of dull intellect standing nearby thinks: "Since consciousness is perceived in the effects—given that 'that heat [tejas] thought' and 'those waters thought'—consciousness is seen in the effect; furthermore, its presence in the causal substance is established by the perception of consciousness in the statement 'It thought: May I become many. Thus, there is a similarity of characteristics between cause and effect. This is what he says with the word "īkṣā" (thinking). The meaning is this: when the cause exists, such thinking as "May I become many" is observed in the case of heat and water, as seen in the passages "that heat thought" and "those waters thought."

When an objection was raised by one of duller intellect—that the Self, as the cause, must possess similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) with the world, its effect, through the connection with consciousness (*caitanya*)—the following correct answer was given: the opponent, having denied this very point that the Supreme Person, whose form consists of fire and so forth, possesses this act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), attempted to evade it by means of another interpretation, claiming that such statements as "That fire saw" and "Those waters saw" are designations based on the presiding deities (*abhimānivyapadeśa*).

Furthermore, he states generally that this designation refers to the specific deities presiding over those respective principles (tattvas), such as fire and so forth; however, he does not state it by distinguishing whether it is a designation for the Supreme Self or refers merely to those individual deities. Therefore, since this is a conventional usage of the opponent, we incur no fault.

Thus, having refuted the Sāṅkhya position—which possesses unavoidable defects because it is rooted in fallacious reasoning that lacks logical validity, because it is unstable, and because it contradicts the Vedānta—the author extends this [refutation] by indicating that the positions of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and others are likewise to be abandoned due to the same logic and the aforementioned defects. This is the connection (*saṅgati*). Previously, too, in the passages "For this very reason, Prāṇa," "By this, all [other systems] are explained, they are explained," and "By this, Yoga is answered," a connection based on extension (*ātideśika-saṅgati*) was stated; here, that same [connection] is being expressed.

The investigation into that meaning, however, concerns whether it is possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world or not. That is to say: do the Vedānta passages have as their purport that Brahman is the cause of the world, or do they have another purport? Do the contradictions with the logic (tarka) of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and others lead to the conclusion that the Vedānta passages have another purport, or not? And even when the doctrine of atoms—the cause of the world accepted by many—is refuted, does the reason of the "unfoundedness of logic" (tarkāpratiṣṭhāna) remain effective or not?

Having restated the manner in which the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) arises here, [the author] also explains the method of its refutation with the words "because of correspondence" (saṃvādāt). The opponent's intention is as follows: the doctrine of primordial matter as the cause (prakṛti-kāraṇavāda) is propounded only in Sāṅkhya and Yoga; however, the doctrine of atoms as the cause (paramāṇu-kāraṇavāda), being accepted by many schools such as those of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda), Akṣapāda (Gautama), and the Kṣapaṇaka mendicants, is therefore to be respected in every respect.

"The universe must have that [atom] as its cause"—thus, by the sequence beginning with dyads and so forth, the universe would have atoms alone as its cause. This is merely a restatement of the "dog-and-boar" logic by those of dull intellect and small understanding. For dogs, though mutually hostile toward boars, at that moment cast aside their mutual enmity and pounce upon them. Likewise, even opponents of the Vedānta, casting aside their mutual hostility, proceed to subvert the Vedānta; such is the dog-and-boar maxim.

He states the manner of refuting that [opponent] with the words "anyonya" (mutually). The syntactical connection is as follows: "The sun of Vedānta shines for us, which, through its multitude of counter-arguments, dispels the faults of sophistry and the many deceptions involving mutually contradictory meanings. For in the world, even universal darkness is instantly uprooted by the mere rising of the sun; likewise, by the mere introduction of the Vedānta doctrine, the systems of others perish of their own accord.

The untenability [of the opponent's position] has been demonstrated due to the abundance of mutual contradictions and other flaws among the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣas*). If that is so, then even in your own position—that the Supreme Self, whose subtle body consists of consciousness and matter, creates the universe in the form of the Supreme Self whose gross body consists of consciousness and matter—there is an untenability of the reality (*vastu*) due to many contradictions. Thus, the introduction of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) occurs by raising the doubts of those very disputants who were previously refuted; this is the connection (*saṅgati*).

The investigation into that matter concerns whether the distinction stated—that Brahman, whose body is the individual soul (*jīva*), possesses a nature of unsurpassed bliss from the individual soul who constitutes His own body—is possible or not; whether, if Brahman has a body, it follows that He partakes in the pleasure and pain of the individual soul who is His body, or not; and whether such participation in suffering and so forth is caused by the body or caused by something else.

Does the scriptural text, "For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant," indicate that the experience of suffering is caused by the body or not? In this regard, is the word "body" (śarīra) meant to denote the body alone, or does it refer to a body produced by merit and demerit (puṇyāpuṇya)?

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) thinks as follows: "He who has even a single body becomes a partaker of manifold and infinite sufferings; if, for you, the universe is the body of the Supreme Self, how could that Supreme Person fall into suffering caused by the universe which has become His own body? This is what he expresses with the words, "ekaḥ" (one).

Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī), wishing to deny the boundary between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) based merely on their connection with the body, should find peace—that is, attain composure—upon seeing the similarity and difference between the Vedas, which are the source of the lineage of Brahmā, Rudra, and others who are subject to censure, and the analogy of the king’s servants, according to the maxim of the sovereign and his servants. For kings themselves enjoy sovereignty independently, whereas the king’s servants enjoy such a state of enjoyment only through service to him.

In the same way, the Lord’s possession of all bodies and so forth is indeed natural; however, it is only through the grace of the Lord that the four-faced Brahmā and others, having attained their respective offices, experience enjoyment according to their own past actions. This much does not establish equality with the Lord, for a clear disparity is indeed observed. Therefore, it is action alone that is the cause of worldly enjoyment, and not the state of possessing a body.

In this regard, the Lord Commentator himself has directly stated the connection [of the present topic] in such passages as, "If it be argued that it is non-existent, no, because it is a mere negation," and so forth, wherein the non-difference of the world, which is the effect, from Brahman, which is the cause, was established. Now, that very non-difference is raised as an objection and subsequently resolved.

Thus [ends the previous section]. Alternatively, in the preceding section (*navilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa*), the Sāṅkhya—who asserts the similarity between cause and effect—was refuted by demonstrating their dissimilarity. Now, however, the Vaiśeṣika and others—who assert that just as there is a difference between the two, so too must there be a difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*)—are being rejected by demonstrating the non-difference (*ananyatva*) of cause and effect; such is the connection (*saṅgati*).

Thus, the distinction is this: previously, the Sāṅkhya, who maintains that both substance and state are eternal, was refuted; now, however, the Vaiśeṣika, who maintains that both of those are non-eternal, is being refuted. As for the investigation into its meaning: it concerns whether the stated possibility of Brahman being the cause of the world is tenable or not; whether the world, which is the effect of Brahman, is non-different from Brahman or different; and whether the effect is merely the cause itself having attained another state, or whether the effect is something other than the cause.

Are differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth based on a difference in state (*avasthā*), or are they based on a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*)? Do scriptural passages such as, "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," lead us to understand that these differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth are based on a difference in state, or not?

Here, he first presents the position of the proponents of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) with the words "the effect. The effect must be distinct from the cause, because it is characterized by contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyastatvāt*). Whatever is characterized by contradictory properties in relation to something else is indeed distinct from that thing, just as a jar is distinct from its shards; this is the inference used by the proponents of *asatkāryavāda* to establish the difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its product (*upādeya*). Regarding this, he states the supporting argument (*anugrāhakatarka*) with the words "activity" (*vyāpāra*). Otherwise—that is, if there were no difference between the material cause and its product—[activity would be impossible].

The activity of the causal factors (*kārakas*) would be purposeless; for it is not tenable to say that the activity of the causal factors is for its own sake alone, because that would involve a contradiction. Having thus restated this position, he begins to refute it with the words: "In the statement of the Ardhavaināśikas. The *vaināśikas* are the Buddhists, because they maintain the doctrine of the destruction of substance (*dravya*). The *ardhavaināśikas*, however, are the Vaiśeṣikas, who assert the destruction of the whole (*avayavin*) in composite substances, but not [the destruction] of atoms (*paramāṇu*) or the infinitely large (*paramamahat*).

Therefore, they are called "half-nihilists" (*ardhavaināśika*). He demonstrates the manner of refuting that [position] with the words "in the unity of substance" (*dravyaikye*). Even though there is unity of substance between the two substances consisting of cause and effect, everything—including the superimposition of contradictory attributes—is consistent through the distinction of states (*avasthābheda*), according to the maxim of the *tālī* leaf and the earring (*tāṭaṅka*). Anticipating the objection, "I have spoken of a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*), whereas you speak of a difference in state; what is the distinction here?", he provides the answer: "due to the difference in the states intended by him" (*tadabhimatadaśābhedataḥ*).

The meaning is this: for one who maintains that there is a difference between substances as causes, a difference in the states of the cause must also be admitted, as well as a difference in the substance itself; thus, admitting both types of difference involves complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, it is better to follow the path of parsimony (*lāghava*) by admitting only a difference in states. For by that very difference in states, all the faults you have raised—such as the distinction based on contradictory properties—are satisfactorily explained.

The underlying point is that if one does not admit a difference in states (*avasthābheda*), even a difference in substance (*dravyabheda*) would not be established for you. And as for the phrase "the power of non-existence": by the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," the non-existence of the universe in its causal state is asserted, because the effect-state does not exist within the causal state. Now, having raised the doubt—"What is the determining factor for your adopting [our position] while abandoning your own?"—he states three reasons for that determination, beginning with the words "from perception" (*adhyakṣāt*).

First, perception [establishes this]: for indeed, apart from the threads, nothing called a "cloth" is perceived; rather, it is the very threads that, having reached the state of being a cloth, are designated by the different name "cloth. He states another reason: "because of parsimony" (*lāghavāt*). There is complexity (*gaurava*) in accepting both a cloth-substance and a difference in the state of the threads; there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting the mere state. It is logical to abandon the position of complexity and follow the position of parsimony. [He says] "stated in scripture" (*śrutikathita*).

The third reason is stated: the identity between the world and Brahman, which stand in the relation of effect and cause, is expressed in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. Indeed, those who know the principles of logic do not approve of abandoning what is explicitly stated in scripture or imagining what is not so stated.

Here, someone objects: "By means of the distinction between subtle consciousness and unconsciousness, [Brahman] would undergo different states; thus you establish the non-difference of cause and effect. But this being the case, the scriptural teaching of 'non-duality' (*advaita*) regarding the causal state would be contradicted, because the two qualifiers of Brahman—consciousness and unconsciousness—would continue to exist even in the causal state. Having restated this objection, he begins to resolve it through a counter-argument with the words "Māyā" (Illusion).

The point here is this: for those who maintain that Brahman as conditioned by *māyā* is the material cause of the world—whether they hold it to be differentiated by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), or differentiated by its own power (*svaśakti*)—in their view as well, since entities such as *māyā* exist as specific states of Brahman in its causal condition, the contradiction with the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*advaita*) remains exactly the same.

If others resolve the contradiction with the scriptural teaching of non-duality (*advaita-śruti*) by claiming that *māyā* and the like are not primary, then we too shall resolve the contradiction with the non-duality scripture by claiming that both the sentient and the insentient are not primary. This being the case, there is no fault whatsoever in this position, wherein the cause is characterized by subtle consciousness and matter, and the effect is characterized by gross consciousness and matter.

For those for whom the verbal connection [of the world] has as its root the Supreme Brahman—whose own power is manifested through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Māyā—and who thus regard the phenomenal world (prapañca) as non-different from it, even they validate the scriptural teaching of non-duality here by means of the subordinate status of the qualifiers within their respective qualified entities. Likewise, for us too, there is a connection of Prakṛti and Puruṣa as qualifiers in the form of gross and subtle aspects within a sentence where the Inner Self is primary; thus, the non-difference of the effect, which is the world, from the cause, which is Brahman, is established.

Having thus explained the manner of the world's origin in accordance with all the Vedas according to his own established doctrine, he states—in the verse beginning with "viśvārambhe"—that the positions imagined by various disputants are false positions because they contradict the sacred tradition (āmnāya).

*Vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is like the false imagination of a snake, a patch of ground, a leaf, or a stream of water upon a rope and so forth; *śakala-pariṇati* (partial transformation) is the partial transformation of the non-conscious portion within the three-fold Brahman—consisting of consciousness, unconsciousness, and the Lord—into the form of the non-conscious, while that portion remains ultimately real; *śakti-śeṣa-sūti* (production from the remaining power) is the creation of the various distinctions of power within the supreme Brahman, which consists of the triad of powers of consciousness, unconsciousness, and the Lord; and *abhivyakti* (manifestation) is the manifestation of an effect already existing in its cause, like the appearance of the limbs of a tortoise that were previously present.

They vainly imagine that the meaning of various scriptural passages is this: that the blossoming of the universe is like the blossoming of a flower that was not yet manifest during its bud-stage; that emission is like the pouring out of material from within a bellows; that modification is the transformation of Brahman, which is pure Being alone, into the form of the phenomenal world; and that creation is indeterminate within the series of principles, such that sometimes water comes from fire and sometimes fire from water, without any fixed rule for the creation of the world.

The meaning is that those who are mostly like children have been cast aside and refuted by those who cherish the uniformity of all the Vedas. The truth is this very one: that from Brahman as qualified by subtle consciousness and matter (cid-acit), Brahman itself as qualified by gross consciousness and matter arises. All doctrines contrary to this are to be rejected; such is the meaning.

Regarding this, the connection [of the topics] has been clearly stated by Śrī Viṣṇucittārya: "In the section beginning with 'If it be said that [the effect] is non-existent,' non-difference (*ananyatva*) was indeed introduced; however, because it constitutes a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was not established therein, since the present section on 'Originating Material' (*ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*) is dependent upon it and because there is a difference in the mode of exposition. Having thus established non-difference, he says 'The others... to address an undesirable consequence that has arisen. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: whether or not the stated fact of Brahman being the cause of the world is possible.

Does the charge of defects such as failing to act for the benefit [of others] attach to Brahman’s being the creator of the world, or not? Is the identity understood through the grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in "That thou art," characterized by oneness of essential nature, or is it characterized by the relation of self and body? Is the consistency of scriptural passages concerning difference—such as "The Illusionist [from whom this world proceeds]" and "He makes himself distinct from himself"—maintained if identity is characterized by the relation of self and body, or even if it is characterized by oneness? Having stated the prima facie position here, he states its refutation with the words "It has been said."

In the preceding section, the non-difference between cause and effect was stated. On this view, since even the conscious being (cetana) is an effect, its non-difference from the Lord must also be asserted. However, that consciousness, along with its connection to the suffering of saṃsāra, is manifested here. As for the syntactical connection of the words, once you have stated it thus regarding the position of non-difference, the conscious being would also be a transformation (pariṇati) of Brahman; therefore, for that reason, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) understood from such texts as "That thou art" would necessarily be upheld. Let there be such identity indeed.

Nevertheless, a contradiction is observed: the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed an ocean of suffering. To the objection, "Let the soul be an ocean of suffering; what does that matter to us?", he says: "Unerring" (*abhrānta*). Is the Lord (*īśvara*) erring or unerring? If He were erring, He would not be the Lord at all. If He is unerring, does He know the identity of Himself and the soul, or not? If He does not know it, He would not be omniscient. If He does know it, how could He produce suffering in the soul, which is one with His own self?

If it is argued that play produces suffering, that is not so. Anticipating the prima facie objection that no sane person would cut off their own head for the sake of play, he refutes it with the words "it is not so. He explains this very point with the phrase "by way of being for the sake of that" (*tātthyena*). The meaning is this: we do not assert the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman on the basis of their identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*); rather, as stated in the Sūtra, "Because of the abiding [of the Lord within], [the non-difference is] according to Kāśakṛtsna," it is precisely because the Blessed Lord abides as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of the individual soul.

And that state of abiding as the inner controller (antaryāmin) arises precisely from the relationship of the body and the self, which is established by the scriptural texts that produce the cognition of such a relationship within the adhyātma-śāstras; this is the meaning.

"The fact that it is not contradictory for the supreme Brahman—who is omniscient and whose will is true—to be the Self of all in every way by having all sentient and non-sentient things, in their gross and subtle states, as His body, and to be distinct from everything else, has been established. Now, it is established that it is not contradictory for the supreme Brahman, whose will is true, to possess the capacity for the creation of the manifold world through His mere will. Thus the connection [of the topics] was stated by the author of the Commentary himself.

The investigation into that meaning, however, concerns whether it is possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world or not; and whether the causality of a cause capable of producing an effect necessarily depends upon other auxiliary factors, or is indeed independent of them. For while in the previous [sūtra] the contingency of defects such as non-action (akartṛtva) was refuted, here he refutes yet another such defect asserted by the opponent, stating "the capable" (śaktām).

This is the meaning: let that [Supreme Being] be either the agent or the material cause; for even though both possess their own inherent power (*svarūpa-śakti*), it is observed that they produce an effect only when the necessary instruments and auxiliaries are present. Therefore, regarding the statement, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad evedam agre āsīt*), one might ask: at the time of universal dissolution, what instrument would the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*)—who consists of both the instrumental and material causes—require, or what auxiliary would He employ? He refutes the aforementioned prima facie view with the word "non-existent" (*asat*). He states the reason for this here: "Because of the distinction of powers" (*śaktibhedāt*).

For in the world, causes are indeed determinate, and their powers (*śakti*) are also determinate. Power is of two kinds: the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) and the auxiliary power (*sahakāri-śakti*). Thus, it is observed that there are certain powers for the production of a jar and other powers for the production of a cloth; this fact cannot be denied. Likewise, the powers consisting of Nature (*prakṛti*), Spirit (*puruṣa*), and Time (*kāla*) belong to God (*Īśvara*) even in His causal state. Therefore, there is no fault; such is the meaning.

Regarding the employment of various appropriate auxiliary powers (*sahakāri-śakti*) in this context, he provides many examples beginning with the word "milk" (*kṣīra*). Milk produces curd through the process of churning (*ātañjana*); however, churning serves both to bring about the state of curd quickly and to produce a specific flavor. A magnet attracts iron merely by its proximity. A spider weaves a thread together with its saliva. Gods and sages perform their respective diverse effects endowed with their innate power (*svābhāvikaprabhāva*). In this manner, other examples should also be understood.

Having observed these examples, you should be satisfied; the meaning is that you should abandon improper speech and abide in happiness. He states the example—which is well-known to all the world and cannot be disregarded even by opponents—beginning with the words "from volition" (*saṅkalpāt*). For the individual soul (*jīva*), like a potter and others, impels the body through mere volition, [using] a stick and so forth situated within its own body to move the wheel and such; the meaning is that it performs whatever action is required in whatever place it is needed.

Thus, he says "Viśvarūpa" (the one whose form is the universe) to show that Īśvara is likewise; the meaning is that because He has the universe as His body, Īśvara also brings forth everything by mere volition.

Or, even if Brahman—the cause of the universe—is accompanied by external auxiliary causes in the form of time, there still arises the following objection: how can the Supreme Self, who is partless and inherently endowed with all powers of consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*), resolve "May I become many" and yet exist in the state of manifold effects? To address this, the inquiry concerns whether the previously mentioned status of being the cause of the universe is possible or not; specifically, whether the scriptural teaching of Brahman’s partlessness is contradicted if it is the cause of the universe, or not.

Having previously resolved the general objection regarding causality based on the absence of auxiliary causes, the author now states the following point: "The whole [is transformed]," which provides the rebuttal for one who raises a specific objection concerning the particular nature of causality as material transformation (*upādānatva*). Herein lies the dilemma: does Brahman, as the cause, transform entirely into the nature of a single effect, or only in part?

If [Brahman transforms] in its entirety, then because there would be no remainder once Brahman has transformed into the nature of a single effect, there could be no further transformation into other effects. If, on the other hand, the transformation were by way of a single part, there would be a constant contradiction of the scriptural texts concerning its being partless (*niṣkala*) and its being without parts (*niravayava*). This objection applies not only to the view that Brahman is the cause in its own essential nature, but is equally applicable to the view that it is the cause as qualified by sentient and insentient beings; thus he says "this" (*idam*).

"In that Brahman" is the meaning. Having thus stated the refutation, he states the consequence for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Brahman," etc.; the syntactical connection is: "In this way, the status of Brahman as the material cause (*upādānatva*) is not tenable. Anticipating this objection and wishing to refute the prima facie position, he says "No" (*na*). The proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādins*) hold that Brahman qualified by Māyā is the cause; the followers of Bhāskara hold it to be qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); and the followers of Yādavaprakāśa hold it to be qualified by power (*śakti*). Therefore, he says "in their own positions" (*svapakṣeṣu*), indicating that the refutation is the same even in those views.

Having thus stated the counter-argument (*pratibandī*), he says "tanmānāt" (on account of that authority) to show that their intended resolution of the counter-argument is likewise equal [to our own]. This, indeed, is their resolution of the counter-argument: "We accept such a Brahman on the strength of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes Brahman as qualified by power (*śakti*) with *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)."

Thus, if you accept your own position by the force of fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), then you should instead accept our own position—which is supported by hundreds of direct scriptural authorities (*śruti*) and consists of Brahman characterized by both the conscious and the unconscious, and which is favorable to all the worlds. The sense is that other positions are unfit to be accepted because they contradict the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), whereas our position is fit to be accepted because it is not contradicted by either worldly experience or the Vedas.

In this way, those who argue according to logic (nyāyavādins) and who reject the identity of the body and the self must also be refuted; for even in their position, regarding the relation of ether, composite wholes, atoms, and so forth, the dilemma of "in whole or in part" (kṛtsna-ekadeśa-vikalpa) applies equally to the subject of relation. Having briefly addressed the objection stated against his own position, the author, wishing to refute it at length, restates the Mādhyamika’s method of the "whole or part" dilemma, beginning with the words "saṃyoga" (conjunction): that the creation of dyads and so forth arises from the conjunction of two atoms and so on.

The system of the Vaiśeṣikas and others: therein they assert that the Lord, the creator of the world, being himself all-pervading, joins with the atoms and presides over them. To this, the Mādhyamika objects: do two atoms join with one another entirely (*kārtsnyena*), or by way of a single part (*ekadeśena*)? If entirely, then because the two atoms would be submerged into each other’s own nature, a composite effect such as a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) of greater dimension could not be initiated. If, however, by way of a single part...

There would be the consequence of [the atom] having parts. Thus, if the atom (*paramāṇu*) and the omnipresent Lord (*īśvara*) were to be conjoined in their entirety, it would follow that they possess equal dimensions; consequently, the atom would become as omnipresent as the Lord, and the omnipresent Lord would become as minute as the atom. If, on the other hand, there were conjunction by way of a single part, it would follow that both the Lord and the atom possess parts, whereby their very status as partless substances (*niravayava-dravya*) would be destroyed. And thus, because of their partless nature, any assertion that they have parts is indeed mere audacity.

It might be argued: "In the absence of partless material atoms (*paramāṇu*), one must also abandon dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and the rest, since they exist as dependent upon those [atoms] as their parts.
