Thus, if the meaning stated by the Mādhyamika for the purpose of refuting his own position were directed against the Vedāntin by one who adheres to the school of Kaṇabhakṣa (the Vaiśeṣika) and others, then the Mādhyamika himself would sink. This is the syntactical connection here: the effect known as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would have to occur either between two all-pervading substances, or between God and an atom, or among atoms themselves, or between one atom and another.

In that case as well, there would be alternatives such as whether [the whole] exists in its entirety or in part; by stating "that is indeed refuted" to us Vedāntins, the proponent of the opposing view would himself sink into the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), like a Mādhyamika. One might object: "Let this be a refutation of the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain that atoms are the cause; what is the refutation of the Sāṅkhya? Anticipating this, he says: "The Sāṅkhya also... The method of the Sāṅkhyas is indeed as follows: Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) creates the universe, and it is all-pervading (*vibhvī*).

Furthermore, that [Prakṛti] consists of a composite of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Thus, while performing its effects, does it do so by joining with the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* that constitute its own self individually, or by joining them together? If by joining them together, then is this conjunction of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* total or partial? If it were total, then since all the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* would be entirely employed toward a single effect, there would be nothing remaining for the commencement of any other effect.

If the connection were by way of a single part, then it would follow that those [guṇas]—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are composed of parts; and thus, the postulation of their all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) would be contradicted. If, on the other hand, each one individually were the cause, then the effect would not possess the nature of the three guṇas, since one thing would be created by sattva alone, another by rajas, and yet another by tamas. Thus, the system propounded by the Sāṅkhya is struck down by a multitude of such refutations. As for the question, "How could there be a creation deficient from that?", this is its meaning: [the answer follows].

For the Sāṅkhya, who accepts a pervasive primordial nature (*prakṛti*), how could there be a creation of anything inferior? This is because [the Sāṅkhya position] is flawed in the manner already stated. In this way, by means of the process of refuting the positions of the Sāṅkhyas and others, the same objections should be inferred for the positions that hold Brahman to be conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā* and its power (*śakti*). One might object: "Granted that our positions and yours are equal, yet what is the distinction in favoring your position? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As declared in the conclusion" (*nigamanigadita*).

This is the distinction here: since our own position is established by hundreds of scriptural passages such as, "The perishable is Pradhāna; the immortal and imperishable is Hara; the one God rules over both the perishable and the self," any attempt to refute that [position] is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehend its subject (the scripture itself). Our position, however, remains firm because it is in harmony with the scriptures. Thus he says: "The path remains unimpaired."

In this regard, the Bhāṣya provides a specific indication of the connection [between the two sūtras]: "Even if the Lord, being one alone prior to creation, is capable of creating the diverse world by Himself—being distinct from everything else and endowed with the power for all purposes—nevertheless, the Lord’s status as the cause is not possible, because the diverse creation must have a purpose, and the Lord lacks any such purpose. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: does the aforementioned causality of the world belong to Brahman or not?

Is it possible for one who has attained all desires to create the world as a mere sport (*līlā*), or not? Is there no purpose for such sport even for one who has attained all desires? Having raised these alternatives, he refutes them with the words beginning "for his own sake" (*ātmārtham*). Does the Lord’s role as the creator of the universe exist for his own sake or for the sake of others? First of all, it cannot be for his own sake, because he has attained all desires. This is what he expresses by the phrase "of one who has eternally attained all desires."

If the position is that [the Lord acts] for the sake of others, it must be said that the creation of the universe proceeds out of compassion; yet even that cannot be maintained, as he says with the words "out of compassion" (*kāruṇyāt*). If He creates the universe out of compassion, then He would create the universe as consisting solely of happiness, and not as consisting of suffering.

One might object: "But [the Lord] creates even that which is of the nature of suffering, and that too is surely out of compassion; just as a physician who administers a treatment consisting of pain is called a protector, so too the Lord, by creating the universe—which is of the nature of suffering—must be considered a physician and a protector. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). The intended meaning here is this: a physician, because his power is limited, creates suffering for the sake of healing; [the Lord], however, is not like that.

Therefore, for that reason, the objection that the omniscient Lord, satisfied in His own Self, cannot be the cause of the world's creation, is merely the argument of the blind. He establishes this very point with the verse beginning with "līlā. The author of the Sūtras himself has clearly stated the refutation of this objection: "But as in the case of the world, [His] mere play [is the motive]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.33). Just as a sovereign emperor, though already fully accomplished, engages in a game of dice; in this regard, the verse of the Teacher beginning with "While the Śrutis are watching," etc., should indeed be recited.

An objection is raised: "Is it not the case that gambling consists in obtaining an object that was previously non-existent through a particular stroke of luck? How, then, can the Lord be said to have all His desires already fulfilled? Anticipating this, he says: "Abhimata" (desired). Whatever is desired, at that very time its accomplishment constitutes the state of having all desires fulfilled; it does not mean that future human goals must have been accomplished beforehand. Likewise, for the Lord as well, by virtue of His resolve such as "May I become many," at whatever time He desires the creation of the world and so forth, or the bestowing of liberation and so forth—at that very time [His purpose is realized].

The non-attainment of that [liberation] is itself the state of having attained all desires; therefore, this claim that "the attainment of all desires" and "engagement in divine play" are contradictory is merely the prattle of delusion.

Here, someone raises an objection: "If the Lord creates a universe that is entirely composed of suffering and is uneven, his conduct would be inconsistent. This is what is expressed by the word "viśvam" (the universe). In this context, "unevenness" refers to one being happy while another is miserable, and so forth.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: "If the *līlā* (sport) of the Lord, who constantly creates even the entire universe—which consists solely of suffering—were to arise from an improper sequence (*asamañjasakramataḥ*), it would arise according to the narrative account of someone named *Asamañja*, who is well-known in the Purāṇas as one who acts contrary to his own karma. From that, defects such as the Lord's cruelty would follow. He rejects this point with the words "not so" (*maivam*). He explains that very method of rejection with the verse beginning "bījīṅkura... (the seed and the sprout).

This is the meaning: this beginningless stream of the wheel of karma, ignorance, and so forth, proceeds for each individual, and it is manifold. At various times, the ripening (*vipāka*) of that stream occurs; ripening is the state of being oriented toward the yielding of a fruit, and that occurs in many ways. All established philosophical systems (*siddhāntika*) accept this point, for otherwise, according to the methodological process of any given school, there would follow the impossibility of establishing the necessary restriction regarding the performance of specific actions by individuals.

Therefore, the general principle is that the Lord creates everything in accordance with past karma; nevertheless, even so, the inequality corresponding to those respective karmas is not lost. This means that because both compassion and impartiality are not abandoned—namely, because the Supreme Lord does not relinquish either the performance of the universal task or the inequality therein that conforms to past karma—the Lord, indeed, does not alter the rules of merit and demerit established by His own beginningless volition, nor does He alter their ripening at their respective times.

If it is asked what the authority for this point is, it is simply the Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth; otherwise, the killer of a father would attain heaven, while one of virtuous character would go to hell. How then is it that those of sinful character, such as Caidya and others, attained liberation? This has already been answered: it is due to the sequence of their past karma. In this regard, according to the logic established in the world:
"If He were to create the universe for sport, His state of having fulfilled all purposes (kṛtārthatā) would be impaired;
yet, if He were to create the world out of compassion, He would lead the world toward a state of singular happiness."
Thus, this objection raised by the followers of Kumārila—that God does not create because of the force of inference—has also been answered.

For the Vaiśeṣikas, who postulate objects not previously perceived, it is logical that their postulation follows what is observed; therefore, they would be subject to the refutation of the "whole-or-part" dilemma (*kṛtsnaikadeśavikalpa*) and other faults characterized by the absence of conformity to observed facts as asserted by the Mādhyamikas and others. For us, however, who establish the reality of the object by relying on the scriptures (*āgama*) that reveal unprecedented meanings, there is no necessity of conforming to what is observed; thus, we are able to establish the entire reality of the object in a perfectly coherent manner.

"By the observation of common principles"—this is the meaning of the word here: by the method of observation (*dṛṣṭanyāya*), that is, by the mode of what is observed, the conscious Lord (*cit īśvara*) is the progenitor of the universe; furthermore, that Lord is postulated through inference (*anumāna*). The unconscious atom (*acetana-paramāṇu*) is the progenitor of the universe; furthermore, it is postulated through the inference of the triad (*tryaṇuka*) from the atom. Thus, in both cases, the conceptualization arises solely from inference.

In that case, since the effect would be produced by one who possesses limited knowledge, there would likewise be confusion (*vaiyākulī*) regarding that [creation]. If the state of having a limited-knowledge agent were established in the subject (*pakṣa*) by the force of the property of being an effect, then God (*īśvara*) would not be proven; however, if it were the state of having an omniscient agent, then there would be a contradiction with the specific [property of being an effect], and thus confusion would arise. In this way, one should also consider the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would consequently possess parts. Having thus stated the fault in the position of those who maintain a creator based on inference, and having stated the fault in the opponent's position, [he now states it] in his own position.

He states the absence of defects with the words "atyanta... (absolutely unperceived). Since the scripture, which is engaged in proclaiming the meaning that the Lord, whose body consists of both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*), is the cause, establishes the existence of the Lord who is the agent of all, there is indeed the compatibility of all attributes—being dependent on the knowledge of reality that is incapable of being sublated or obstructed. Thus, for all attributes such as being the efficient cause (*nimitta*), the material cause (*upādāna*), omniscience, and partlessness, their compatibility certainly exists. Therefore, the sublation of the Lord established by scripture is simply not to be respected, like the inference that a human head is pure; hence, there is no sublation.

Demonstrating specifically the manner in which the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) for the ten topics already mentioned arise, [the author] also shows their general refutation by means of the phrase "due to contradiction with the Sāṅkhya-smṛti" and so forth: 1. Due to contradiction with the *Sāṅkhya-smṛti*, in the section concerning Smṛti (*Smṛty-adhikaraṇa*); 2. Due to contradiction with the *Caturmukha-smṛti*, in the section concerning Yoga (*Yoga-adhikaraṇa*); 3. Due to the dissimilarity between cause and effect, in the section concerning Non-difference from the Dissimilar (*Vailakṣaṇya-adhikaraṇa*); 4. And again, in this very section concerning those not accepted by the learned (*Śiṣṭāparigraha-adhikaraṇa*), because [the opponent's view] is subverted by the maxim of multiple systems having a single purpose (*ekārthāneka-tantra-nyāya*) regarding Brahman as the sole cause.

The meaning is that [the Sūtra] pierced—that is, refuted—the opponent who was disputing on the basis of the following: in the *Bhoktrāpatya* (The Enjoyer and the Offspring) section, because the body is inseparable from experience; in the *Ārambhaṇa* (Commencement) section, because of the statement regarding the difference between the material cause and its effect; in the *Itaravyapadeśa* (Designation as Another) section, because of the contradiction with the performance of what is beneficial to one's own self; in the *Upasaṃhāradarśana* (Observation of Effort) section, because of the absence of auxiliary causes; in the *Kṛtsnaprasakti* (Total Involvement) section, because of the sublation by the dilemma of whether the whole or a part [of Brahman] would be involved; and in the *Naprayojanavattva* (Absence of Purpose) section, because of the further point that the Lord’s activity would be purposeless. Thus he struck down the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).

Having thus resolved the contradiction between the statements of the two sections by means of the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), he now resolves the contradiction with statements such as those of the *Kalpasūtras* raised by the opponent, using that very same principle, [saying] "In this case... (*tredha*).

This is the demonstration of the apparent contradiction here: having begun with the statement, "The Brāhmaṇas are injunctions regarding ritual action," the venerable Āpastamba declares that all four types of *arthavāda*—namely, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), eulogies (*praśaṃsā*), censures (*nindā*), traditional narratives (*parakṛti*), and ancient legends (*purākalpa*)—are supplementary to the Brāhmaṇas. Other instances should be understood in the same way. Thus, how can it be asserted that *arthavādas* possess authority regarding Brahman without being supplementary to an injunction? To this, he provides the answer: "The answer has already been given."

The meaning is as follows: the statement that explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) are supplementary to injunctions (*vidhi*) is a general rule. Here, however, the assertion of the independent authority of explanatory passages concerning Brahman is an exception (*apavāda*) to that very rule. Therefore, since the contradiction is resolved by that same principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), the charge of contradicting the Smṛtis is entirely untenable. He specifically clarifies this very principle of general rule and exception for the sake of the disciple who does not understand it, stating: "the general," and so forth.

He establishes this very point by means of an illustration found within that same statement, beginning with the word "tataḥ. For in that very statement of Āpastamba, the mutual distinctness of the mantra and the injunction (*vidhi*) is stated later on: "The mantras are other than those. That is to say, "other than those"—namely, the injunctions and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)—"are the mantras. This, however, is merely a general rule, since it is accepted that mantras also possess injunctive power; for the experts in the Tantras say, "A mantra indeed enjoins."

Therefore, you accept that the statement regarding the difference in the injunctions of mantras is the general rule (utsarga), while the statement regarding their injunctive nature is the exception (apavāda). In the same way here as well, may you be satisfied by accepting that the statement regarding [the mantras] being supplementary to the Brāhmaṇas is the general rule, whereas the statement regarding their independent expressive power is the exception.

While many grounds for validity exist, the Mīmāṃsakas who deny the existence of Īśvara argue that the refutation of the Upaniṣadic statements is merely a rash act based on their own arbitrary conventions; thus, demonstrating this, he sets forth a counter-argument that subverts all Vedic paths with the words "By those [Vedic texts] which are recited. In the Veda, following the authority of statements regarding perceptible results—such as "One desiring rain should sacrifice with the Kārīrī"—the validity of statements regarding imperceptible results, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," is established.

The phrase "by means of those that are flawless and successful" means that in certain cases, such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice, the non-attainment of the fruit results precisely from a deficiency in the ritual action (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the instrumental factors (*sādhana*). Regarding the phrase "by means of augury, astrology, and so forth": just as the attainment of results is described through the flawless and successful Vedic rites like the *Kārīrī*, in exactly the same way, the attainment of results is likewise described through the flawless and successful [practices] taught in the Vedas, such as augury (*śākuna*) and astrology (*jyotiṣa*). Thus, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is perceived in some instances regarding those things whose fruits are perceptible.

Likewise, he states "pāratrikyā" [in the verse] to show that the authority of the Veda is ascertained everywhere even by the activity of the learned (śiṣṭas) toward ends that are not perceptible. The meaning of "atinipuṇā" is that the authority of the Veda is ascertained even by the activity of those of great spiritual power (mahānubhāvas), which has the other world as its cause. By this, the acceptance by the great multitude (mahājanaparigraha) is expressed.

When the authority of the Veda has been established through many such reasons for the sake of providing confidence in the scriptures, [the author] states "in the word" (*śabde*) to indicate the absence of any cause for non-authority. By saying "and when there is cognition from that," the rejection of non-authority characterized by non-origination is expressed. Regarding the "object of another," namely the object of God (*īśvara*), the phrase "free from defects and sublation" (*doṣabādhavyapeta*) rejects both the defect in the cause and the sublating cognition.

Since it possesses an uninterrupted tradition from beginningless time, lacks defects in its cause, concerns suprasensory objects, and is free from subverting cognitions, the Veda is indeed authoritative regarding the Supreme Brahman—provided that no cause for non-authoritativeness exists. Thus, if one were to assert the non-authoritativeness of Vedāntic statements without such a cause, then by that same logic, one would have to assert the non-authoritativeness of the ritual (karma) section as well; the meaning is that this would result in the total repudiation of the Vedic path.

Having thus explained the meanings of the four sections (*adhikaraṇa*) through their respective divisions, [the author] anticipates the objection that there might be redundancy between the two current sections—the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* and the *Samanvayādhikaraṇa*—and the subsequent sections on "Being the Cause" (*Kāraṇatva*) and "Possessing Both Marks" (*Ubhayaliṅga*) which are to be discussed later. He states that there is no such redundancy because the establishment of the meaning of those respective sections will occur later, whereas here the explanation of those meanings proceeds by presupposing the points that are yet to be stated.

By the words "In the Śāstra," etc., two specific points are thus established: first, that the words *brahman* and so forth culminate in Śrīnivāsa, as stated in the second section (*adhikaraṇa*); and second, that Brahman, who is to be known through the Vedāntas, is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, as stated in the fourth section. In this regard, the former [point] relies upon the subsequent section concerning causality (*kāraṇatva*), while the latter relies upon the section concerning the possession of both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*); thus, this is most excellent.

Having here shown, both generally and specifically, the meaning of the first section consisting of the four aphorisms that constitute the cause for the commencement of the Śārīraka-śāstra, he then states the connection between those two by expressing the meaning of the second section, which consists of the commencement of the Śāstra itself, with the words: "In this way, in the Self... Here, indeed, in these four sections (adhikaraṇas), the unity of purpose is that "the Self is to be known"; the division of the meaning of the sections consists of the fourfold set of actions beginning with "not being made" and "being thought."

Because all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*) establish specific attributes of Brahman, [the author], while demonstrating the connection by way of restating the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) of the second section (*peṭikā*), also clearly shows the manner in which that section proceeds with the words "suchness" (*īdṛktvam*).

The meaning is that the collection of points stated in the preceding section—that [the qualities] would belong respectively to *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—is refuted in sequence by the two subsequent sections, which demonstrate that [the qualities] are neither suitable for inference and so forth nor untouched by suffering. Alternatively, the passage beginning with "suchness" (*īdṛktvam*) and ending with the word "iti" constitutes the very statement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Since the status of Prakṛti and Puruṣa as the cause of the world and so forth is not established by valid means of knowledge, and since they lack the capacity for inference and the like, as well as the quality of being untouched by suffering—this objection raised against the preceding section is resolved here through appropriate statements. This is done either by the immediately following section (peṭikā) or by the remainder of this chapter (pāda).

For it was previously stated in the *Śāstrayoni* and *Samanvaya* sections that the object known through the Vedāntas is unfit for inference and the like, and is untouched by suffering; neither of these two [qualities] would be possible if either *prakṛti* or *puruṣa* were accepted as the object known through the Vedāntas. Thus, the connection with the preceding intermediate section (*avāntarapeṭikā*) is also stated here.

In the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), by the phrase "It is uncreated," he shows that the state of being uncreated—stated in the subject sentence "The uncreated is not [attained] by the created"—is the primary meaning. In this same manner, it should be understood in sequence that in the second section and those following, such things as being the cause of the universe are the primary meanings.

For in that context, since it is established in the first pāda—which is devoted to the exclusion of other [meanings] regarding the Vedānta passages concerning Brahman—that the statement of the exclusion of connection with other things such as *prakṛti* is for the sake of supplementing the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and not as a primary purpose, one need not suspect a lack of coherence regarding the *Īkṣati-adhikaraṇa* and the subsequent sections. Indeed, this is the division of the "boxes" (*peṭikā-vibhāga*): first, there is one group consisting of the four *adhikaraṇas* intended for the commencement of the Śāstra; therein, two constitute intermediate boxes.

It is stated that the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* and the *Ānandamayādhikaraṇa* constitute a single section (*peṭikā*). Beyond this, it is established that all five *adhikaraṇas* form a single section because they concern specific aspects of both Prakṛti and Puruṣa. Alternatively, the three *adhikaraṇas* beginning with the *Īkṣatyadhikaraṇa* constitute one section, since the refutation by means of specific marks such as "seeing" (*īkṣati*) is uniform for the opponent who has arisen based on general scriptural texts concerning the nature of the eternal Self and Puruṣa.

For the experts in the Tantras maintain that, between direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*), the specific indicative mark is stronger than a general scriptural statement. Consequently, the prima facie opponent—who has arisen on the basis of specific scriptural statements regarding space, breath, light, and so forth—is refuted by the two sections concerning Space and Breath through the acceptance of the etymological meaning of the scriptural terms in accordance with logic. In the case of the words "space" (*ākāśa*) and "breath" (*prāṇa*), however, only their etymological meanings are accepted; for a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) does not override an etymological one (*yoga*).

By the maxim that "an established application of a term sets aside its conventional meaning," [the conventional sense] is sublated. Consequently, it is established that the *ākāśa-prāṇa* section (*adhikaraṇa*) constitutes a subordinate sub-section (*avāntara-peṭikā*). However, in the *jyotis* and *indra-prāṇa* sections, rather than abandoning the conventional meaning, it is stated that they refer to the Supreme Self as qualified by those respective conventional meanings; thus, it is established that these two also constitute separate sub-sections. Regarding this group of four sūtras, those who desire a correct understanding of the meaning must exert themselves in summarizing the subject matter (*prameya-saṃgraha*), and the *Śatadūṣaṇī* composed by the Teacher (*Ācārya*) should certainly be consulted.

Previously, it was stated that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is that which is known through the Vedāntas. Now, it is asserted that the same status of being known through the Vedāntas cannot possibly apply to primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest. In this regard, since primordial nature—which has transformed into the form of the universe—is well-known to all people according to the Sāṃkhya and other systems, and since the Spirit (puruṣa) is subtler than that, it is primordial nature itself that is refuted first; such is the logical connection.

Alternatively, it may be argued that in the preceding section it was stated that the reality known through the Vedānta constitutes the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), but that is untenable because Prakṛti alone—which is not of the nature of a human goal—is the cause. Or else, it may be argued that in the preceding section it was claimed that all Vedānta passages have as their purport the Brahman that transcends both Prakṛti and Puruṣa; however, the *Sadvidyā*, which is the essence of all Vedānta, actually describes Prakṛti alone. What, then, is the use of these other spurious passages? In this way, another possible connection (*saṅgati*) should also be stated.

The subject matter, however, is the Supreme Brahman itself; the distinction from the previous [section] on the commencement of the scripture is therefore based on this. Furthermore, the doubt is whether the Brahman to be known through the *sad-vidyā* is distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), or whether it is primordial nature itself. The cause for the arising of this doubt is the scriptural mention of the general term "Being" (*sat*). This is because the word "Being," which denotes all existing things, is common to primordial nature, the individual soul (*puruṣa*), and the Lord (*īśvara*).

The investigation into its meaning is as follows: does the word *sat* refer to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) or to primordial nature (*prakṛti*)? If it refers to primordial nature, then does the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) expressed in the phrase "It saw" (*tadaikṣata*) not apply, or does it apply? For that purpose, it is further investigated whether this seeing is primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, it is investigated whether there is an association with secondary seeing here, or if indeed there is none. In that regard also, it is investigated whether the seeing of fire and the other elements in passages such as "That fire saw" (*tatteja aikṣata*) is primary or non-primary.

For this reason as well, it is investigated: should the reasons be followed according to their primary nature, or should the reasons also be followed according to their secondary nature, and so forth? Regarding the relationship between cause and effect, although there exist here many arguments consistent with a secondary sense, the Sāṃkhya and others have argued that the "seeing" mentioned here is compatible even if [the cause] refers to primordial matter (prakṛti), because the "seeing" in the passage "That heat [thought]" is figurative, and because the association with such figurative seeing exists here, making the seeing spoken of in this context also figurative.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is held that the word "Being" (*sat*) here denotes primordial matter (*pradhāna*) alone; however, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the relationship between cause and effect is the reverse. He explains the stated meaning in sequence with the words: "because of its association with [the term] 'seeing' used in a secondary sense."

The opponent indeed maintains that the observation of becoming many is not primary; for the proponents of Brahman (brahmavādins) reject the status of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) as the cause on the grounds of its association with the quality of observing, yet they consider that observation to be figurative (*gauṇa*). This is because a property of a conscious being can be attributed to an insentient thing, as in such expressions as "the bank wishes to fall" (*kūlaṃ pipatiṣati*) or "the rice plants are pleased by the rain. In this context, the very fact that the text mentions figurative observation in passages such as "That heat observed" (*tatteja aikṣata*) serves as the basis for its figurative nature.

Furthermore, [the author] states "by means of examples and so forth" because it appears that this is nothing other than the inference of *pradhāna* as stated by the Sāṃkhyas—beginning with "the transformation of the elements"—based on the examples of clay and its effects. Nor is this merely a matter of the appearance of the Śruti; he says "from such [a source]" because this is also consistent with reason: it is logical that an insentient effect arises only from an insentient cause. Anticipating the objection, "How can the word 'Being' (*sat*) apply to *pradhāna*, which possesses modifications? he says "Being."

In response to the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa)—that while the modifications beginning with the Mahat might not be denoted by the word "Being" (sat) because they are localized, the unmodified Prakṛti, being eternally established, must be denoted by the word "Being"—the author states the final conclusion (rāddhānta): "That is incorrect. This is because of the Śruti, specifically through the use of terms such as "Self" (ātman), which are unique to the conscious [Brahman]. Furthermore, there is the cessation of [the existence of] Prakṛti and the rest.

He states that this very meaning is determined not only by Śruti, but also by the indicative marks (liṅga), sentences (vākya), and contexts (prakaraṇa) such as "seeing" (īkṣaṇa), which refute the causality of Prakṛti as you maintain: "by the indicative marks and sentences such as 'seeing' which set aside the causality of Prakṛti as you intend."

Here, having raised the objection that this is a recognition of the inferential method taught by the Sāṃkhya, he refutes it with the words "jñāte" (when [the one] is known). Here, the opponent indeed thinks as follows: first of all, the proposition that through the knowledge of one thing there is the knowledge of all is seen in such passages as, "By which the unheard becomes heard," and so forth. It is not merely a proposition; there is also an illustrative example, as he says, "mṛttat" (from clay, that [is made]). By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the examples mentioned in the Śruti, such as the nail-cutter, are included. Thus, regarding these two—the Śruti and the inference—wherein inference is predominant:

He says, "By this [word]," meaning that by establishing the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this statement would merely be a restatement of the inference propounded by the Sāṃkhyas. He refutes this with the word "in vain" (*vṛthā*). He states the reason for this: "Because of the non-statement of the reason" (*hetvanukteḥ*). This means because the reason, which is the most essential among the members of an inference, has not been stated. If it is argued that the Sāṃkhyas do have reasons such as similarity (*sārūpya*) and so forth, he says "of similarity, etc. (*sārūpyādeḥ*), meaning that this is not so, because those [reasons] will be refuted later in the section on the Sāṃkhya (*sāṃkhyādhikaraṇa*).

Anticipating the objection that there is tautology between the refutation here and that one there, he says: "In this [context]. In the subsequent section, the arguments establishing the Pradhāna as the cause will be uprooted without remainder; here, however, only the mere possibility of an inference for the Pradhāna’s causality is being refuted. Thus, there is no room for the charge of tautology.

Having thus set aside the method of the opposing view, he summarizes the reasons that are favorable to his own position with the words, "The instruction. First of all, in the opening passage, "But did you ask for that instruction? the term "instruction" (ādeśa) refers to Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Sat. The word "instruction" also denotes the instructor itself; furthermore, being an instructor is precisely the state of being a controller. And that is not possible in the case of the Pradhāna, because it is insentient.

The word "Self" (ātman) is also heard here in the phrase, "That is the Self. This term is unique to that which possesses consciousness. In that context, regarding the occasion of deep sleep, the Supreme Self—the locus of deep sleep—is indicated by the word "own" (sva) in the statement, "He becomes merged in his own (self). Because He is the inner ruler (antaryāmin), the Supreme Self alone is worthy of being designated by the word "own," and not the Pradhāna; for the Pradhāna is not the inner ruler with respect to deep sleep.

"By those that have no other refuge" means by those that are established as having no other possible referent. For these words are primary when referring to the Supreme Self, whereas they are secondary (jaghanya-vṛtti) when referring to the Pradhāna. He states another reason as well: "Thou. Here, the identity of the word "thou," which denotes the individual soul (jīva), with that which is denoted by the word "that" is predicated. If the word "that" were intended to refer to the Pradhāna, then this would be a teaching of non-identity (atatva-upadeśa).

Because the teaching of identity between the conscious and the unconscious is a cause of delusion—just like the teaching that the body is the self—the author provides another proof here with the words "by the *jīva*. The meaning is "by its own nature. This is because, in the passage, "Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva*), let me evolve names and forms," the entry of the collection of insentient things—which are distinct from the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) established by the first-person pronoun—is preceded by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). Thus, the meaning here is that the Supreme Self, having the *jīva* as its body, enters the mass of insentient objects distinct from the *jīva* through the medium of the *jīva*.

By this, it is stated that it is not appropriate for the non-intelligent entity (*acidvastu*) which is to be entered to possess the state of being an enterer accompanied by the ego (*sāhaṅkaraṇa*). Furthermore, the declaration of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is seen in the passage, "By which the unheard becomes heard. That [declaration], moreover, is consistent only with God (*īśvara*) as the cause, and not with *pradhāna* as the cause, because *pradhāna* is not a conscious cause; thus he says, "one" (*eka*). He states another reason as well: "all," in the passage, "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*).

For it is heard [in scripture]: "If the Pradhāna were the cause, how could identity with that [Brahman] be predicated of the individual soul (jīva), who is included within the meaning of all words? This is the sense. Not only is the causality of Brahman understood through the *Chāndogya-śruti*, but also through another *śruti*. In the *Chāndogya* as well, it is not understood solely from the passage concerning the Knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*), but also from the passages concerning the "small ether" (*dahara-vidyā*), the "Golden Embryo" (*hiraṇyagarbha-vidyā*), and so forth. Here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the corroborative *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, and other texts are included. In this context, the term "knower of the universe" (*viśvavit*) is employed for the purpose of [establishing] its status as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*).

The distinction is as follows: "omnipresence" (sārvajñyam) is understood as omniscience, while "having a universal form" (viśvamūrtiḥ) is understood as having all things as one's body, which is applicable to being the material cause. In this regard, the presentation of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the final conclusion (siddhānta), as well as the analysis of the objections, should be consulted in the *Śrībhāṣya*, the *Nyāyasudarśana*, and other such works. Furthermore, the consistency between the opening and the conclusion of the great statement (mahāvākya), as well as the sequence of the sūtras intended to illuminate other scriptural passages and other meditations, should also be investigated therein.

Having stated the two types of connection between the preceding and following sections, he briefly presents the subject matter of the subsequent section with the words "mukhya" (primary), etc. One connection arises from the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): if the primary act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*) is attributed to *Sat*, then since it possesses consciousness and is thus fit for primary seeing, let the individual soul (*jīva*) alone be the cause of the world. Another connection is that in the *Sadvijñāna* passage, the identity of the individual soul and Brahman is demonstrated nine times through the three words of the formula "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*); and thus, the individual soul alone would be the cause of the world.

"Brahmā, indeed"—thus arises the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To refute the opponent who is rising up with such a conjecture, the Creator of the Universe, who was introduced previously as the innermost Self (*antarātman*) even of the individual soul (*jīva*) and who possesses unsurpassed, supreme bliss, is established in this section (*adhikaraṇa*). The inquiry into its meaning concerns the statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme": is that which is called "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) here the individual soul or the Supreme Self? Furthermore, it is deliberated whether the suffix *-maya* here signifies a modification (*vikāra*) or an abundance (*prācurya*).

For that purpose, it is investigated whether, following the fact that the suffix *mayaṭ* in the word *annamaya* occurring at the beginning has the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), it is appropriate here as well for the suffix *mayaṭ* to have the sense of modification, or rather the sense of abundance (*prācurya*). Furthermore, it is investigated whether there is an interruption in the middle—by means of *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, and so forth—of what was understood from the beginning, and so on.

Regarding the relationship between cause and effect (*phala-phalibhāva*) therein: since the meaning of "modification" (*vikāra*), understood from the initial context, is equally applicable here due to the lack of interruption, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that the suffix *-maya* in the word *ānandamaya* signifies a modification, and thus the *ānandamaya* is the individual soul (*jīva*). In the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, this relationship of cause and effect is established by reversing [the positions].

On this point, someone says: "Since the creation itself is described by such passages as 'From the Self, space was produced,' and since the suffix *mayaṭ* is seen in the earlier statement, 'This person, indeed, consists of the essence of food (*annarasamayaḥ*),' as denoting a modification (*vikāra*), let it be the same in the final passage as well—'Another inner self, consisting of bliss (*ānandamayaḥ*)'; let the suffix *mayaṭ* here also have the sense of a modification, because of the recognition of the previously mentioned *mayaṭ* as having that meaning. To this he replies with the words "It is seen," and then refutes that view with "That is incorrect."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "in the middle. This means that in the case of the *prāṇamaya* and others, one observes the sublation of the sense of being a modification (*vikāra*). He states the conclusion: "abundant" (*pracura*). Anticipating the objection, "What is the fault in [interpreting it as] having the sense of a modification?", he says: "of another. This means that because there is a sublation of any entity other than the *ānandamaya*, the sense of being a modification is itself sublated.

[Objection: "But surely, Ānanda, if there is a statement regarding abundance (*prācurya*), it must imply a smallness of suffering (*duḥkhālpatva*); for instance, when it is said that 'the region is abundant in Brāhmaṇas,' a smallness of Śūdras is understood. [The author] refutes this with the word *ānanda*. Here, the abundance of bliss (*ānanda-prācurī*)—extending from human bliss up to the bliss of the four-faced Brahmā—is limited by the smallness of the supreme bliss under discussion; therefore, it does not depend upon a smallness of suffering inherent in the Blissful One (*ānandamaya*), but rather upon the cessation of the abundance of bliss residing in the four-faced one and others.

As in the passage, "The sacrifice consists of food," and so forth. Now, one might object that an abundance of bliss can also be described by the relative paucity of suffering; anticipating this doubt, he says "para-" (the other). He who shatters the misfortunes of others destroys the misfortune of those who take refuge in him, for it is heard in scripture: "He consists of bliss. Indeed, we have studied hundreds of such scriptural passages, such as: "Then he becomes free from fear," "This indeed does not afflict him," and "He is not smeared by evil action."

Therefore, the suspicion that there might be a small amount of suffering here does not arise. Furthermore, he states "of the ruler" (*śāsituḥ*), meaning that for the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), who is established as the ruler through such passages as "From fear of him the wind blows," "By his command, O Gārgī," and "The ruler of all," there is a contradiction with having even a small amount of evil.

But surely, you have stated that in our position the characteristic mark of being "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamayatva*) is contradictory. This contradiction is only one for us, whereas for you there are many contradictions. Even regarding the "consisting of bliss," the mention of another self in the passage, "This very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the former," is contradictory. Furthermore, the mention of being "embodied" is not tenable because the body is the fruit of karma. Nor is the doctrine of its being something to be purified applicable to the supreme Brahman, as there is no possibility of impurity in it.

For it is heard even regarding the *ānandamaya* that there is a statement concerning its being something to be purified: "May my [selves] consisting of food, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss be purified. Furthermore, in that very same *ānandamaya*, when the state of the description of the fruit is reached, it is said that it is to be "approached" (*upasaṃkramitavya*); that too is contradictory. How can there be a new "approaching" for a soul (*jīva*) who is already eternally abiding in the Supreme Self? Having thus raised these four contradictions, [the author] proceeds with the four quarters (*pādas*) in their respective order.

"He composes himself as the Self"—this process of composure is indeed intended to exclude any other self, just as the statement "the Self of that very [Self]" regarding the *ānandamaya* is like saying "the ascetics are themselves servants. What contradiction is there? Furthermore, the mention of being "embodied" (*śārīratva*) is especially appropriate for the *ānandamaya*, because the Lord is the indweller of all bodies. Even its being "to be purified" refers simply to the *ānandamaya*'s state of being gracious, as in the expression "the king's heart is indeed pure."

Furthermore, there is no specific purity whatsoever in the previously mentioned auspiciousness. Even in common worldly usage, such as in the expression "the king’s heart is pure," it is simply the cessation of punishment that is being expressed; for in each such instance, only a favorable meaning is to be accepted. Moreover, compatibility (*yogyatā*), like expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and proximity (*sannidhi*), is a necessary factor in determining the meaning of a sentence. In this context, only "approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) remains [as the intended sense], and that too is consistent; for "approaching" is said to be "attainment" (*prāpti*), and attainment refers to the Brahman not previously experienced.

Thereafter, the occurrence of experience follows. This very point is expressed by the words, "He enjoys all desires together. Alternatively, it is precisely the attainment of a specific location that we are able to describe; this is what is stated in the passage, "In Vaikuṇṭha, in the supreme world. Therefore, in our view, there is no room for contradiction. Here, the status of these terms as constituent parts of the meaning must be understood by oneself.

Here, the proponent of the tail-Brahman (pucchabrahmavādī) objects, saying "without body. If the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) were indeed Brahman, then because it is partless, the arrangement of fivefold limbs through distinctions such as head and wings—as stated in "His joy alone is the head," and so forth—would not be tenable.

Therefore, it is said that "the tail is the support"; because it serves as the substratum for all beings, the tail itself—which is the form of the support of the universe—is the Supreme Brahman, since the designations of head, wings, and so forth are inappropriate for the Bliss-filled (Ānandamaya) being in its capacity as Brahman. He begins to refute this position with the word "soḍhā" (how can it be endured): How can it be logical to describe as a "tail" that Brahman which you yourselves accept as being of the nature of Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda) and devoid of limitations by space and time?

If you say, "We must accept the imagination of a tail for the sake of establishing the authority of the scripture," then, alas! You, long-lived one, should likewise be satisfied with the fact that we too must accept the imagination of a head, wings, and so forth in the case of the partless *ānandamaya*, intended to express the various distinctions such as joy (*priya*), delight (*moda*), and so on. Thus he asks, "How [is this]?"—meaning, how is the other [part], the head, wings, and so forth? In that case, this is utterly contradictory: that the *ānandamaya* is Brahman itself, whose nature is self-established; and yet that [self-established nature] does not exist [in the imagined limbs].

The statement that it is its own support is for the purpose of declaring that it has no other substratum; for, according to the manner of another Śruti—"In what, O Venerable One, is He established? In His own glory"—it is precisely the exclusion of any further support for Brahman, who is the support of all, that is stated here. What contradiction is there? Since many refutations of those who maintain that the "tail" is Brahman have already been clearly set forth in the Commentary itself, we shall desist after merely demonstrating the meaning of the verse.

In the subject-sentence of the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*, the phrase "for him there is delay only so long" (*tasya tāvadeva ciram*) declares that the connection with suffering lasts until the fall of the body. On this basis, one might suspect that the "embodied self" (*śārīra ātmā*) referred to in the passage "this is his very embodied self" (*tasyaiṣa eva śārīra ātmā*) must be the individual soul (*jīva*). This suspicion is refuted in the *Ānandamaya-adhikaraṇa*, where it is established that the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) consists precisely in the assumption of a body and its instruments under the governance of karma, and not in the natural state of having the universe as one's body.

From this point onward, the section concerning the Inner Sun (*antarādityādhikaraṇa*) proceeds. In this section, the relationship between body and self is not stated merely by way of the state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); rather, there is a connection with a person who possesses a body characterized by the distinctions of hands, feet, eyes, hair, and so forth. Since such a connection with a body is possible only for the individual soul (*jīva*), there is a thematic connection through the raising of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). Furthermore, there is a connection in that previously the individual soul in general was refuted, whereas now a specific type of individual soul is refuted. This very point is expressed by the word "mostly" (*bhūyiṣṭha*).

Indeed, it has been stated previously that among humans up to Prajāpati, there are certain individuals who have attained sovereignty through the power of having accumulated a vast and infinite store of merit; it is further argued that among these very beings, some one must be postulated as the Lord (Īśvara) existing in the form of a continuous stream. This is the meaning: let there not be those for whom sin predominates, nor those whose merits and sins are equal, but rather let certain ones for whom merit predominates be postulated as the Lord. To this, the reply is: "That is not so."

In this regard, he summarizes the reasons in accordance with the authoritative means of knowledge as "akarma" (non-action): one who possesses a divine body not dependent on karma; "janiḥ" (birth) refers to birth; "mahimā" (greatness) refers to majesty; "sarvapuṃsām svābhāvikaniyantā" (the natural controller of all persons); and "nityaśrīḥ" (eternally possessed of fortune) means one who is eternally connected with Lakṣmī.

Such a person is the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), heard of in the solar orb—the maṇḍala of the sun—as stated in the section beginning, "That which is this space within the heart" (*sa ya eṣo'ntarhṛdaya ākāśaḥ*). He is one and the same who is heard of in the *Antarāditya-vidyā* as "this [Person] within the sun" (*eṣo'ntarāditye*). Thus, there is no room for the suspicion that he is a particular individual soul (*jīva*). For it is heard in that very same context: "He has risen above all evils; indeed, he rises above all evils who knows thus. (*eṣa sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ uditaḥ...*)

"One should reflect here on such passages as: 'O King, that in which all these powers are established'—for it is stated therein: 'She is not born from the cause of karma. Furthermore, the historical account, beginning with 'Clearly, this is a great yogi,' is well known. As for the quality of being the ruler mentioned here, because it is established by many authorities such as 'He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all' and 'The ruler of all,' it must be understood as pertaining to the entire domain."

This is the summary here: because the form of the Blessed One residing within the solar orb is not dependent on karma, is non-material (*aprākṛta*), and exists for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who take refuge in Him, any statement suggesting that it is merely a particular individual soul (*jīva*) simply by virtue of its connection with a body is the mere prattle of the most wicked haters of the Supreme Person. Here, even a brief investigation into that matter is set forth: Is the Person residing within the solar orb a particular individual soul, or is He the Supreme Self?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether the connection with a body and so forth—characterized by divisions such as hands and feet—establishes the state of being a *jīva* or not. For that purpose, it is further investigated whether this connection with a body is dependent on karma or independent of karma. Furthermore, it is investigated whether the scriptural statement regarding the rising above all sins and so forth precludes dependence on karma or not.

For that purpose, it is further investigated whether the word *pāpman* (evil) there refers merely to sin, or whether it refers to action (*karman*) consisting of both merit and sin. As for the relationship between cause and effect: if the word *pāpman* were restricted to mere sin, the statement "having risen from all evils" and so forth would not preclude dependence on action; since the connection with a body is invariably dependent on action, the person within the sun is the individual soul (*jīva*). In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), the relationship between cause and effect should be inferred by the students themselves.

Regarding this, an opponent says: In the *Antarāditya-vidyā*, it is stated that the Blessed One is "risen above all evils" (*sarvebhyaḥ pāpmabhyaḥ uditaḥ*), which expresses His freedom from all sins. According to the method of the logicians (*tāntrikāṇām*), when there is a specific negation, there is an implied permission for the remainder; thus, since sin is denied in the case of the Person dwelling within the solar orb, there must be an implied permission for merit. This is what [the opponent] states with the words "from all," and so forth. [The author] refutes that with "not so. He states the reasons for this with the words "it is declared," and so forth.

Through many proofs such as "no one has authority over him," the fact that the Blessed Lord is not subject to the command of another is understood. For one who is subject to the command of another—such as a king's servant—would incur sin from violating that command, and would obtain a favorable result from its observance. Since the Lord is not subject to the command of another, even "good deeds" (*sukṛta*) in the form of following the commands of another are impossible for him, like "evil deeds" (*durita*); this is one reason. He states another reason in the words "svavaśa" (self-dependent).

According to the principle that "the fruit [arises] from Him because of its logical possibility," it is stated that the Blessed One alone bestows the desired or undesired fruit for others; how then can His connection with meritorious deeds (sukṛta) be possible? Furthermore, since the connection with meritorious deeds is effectively rejected by the meaning of the text, "He does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action," this contradicts your position. To the question, "In that case, how is the word 'pāpman' (evil) applied to merit? he says: "It may be so."

Even in the case of merit (*puṇya*), the word "evil" (*pāpman*) is employed here because it possesses the characteristics of evil. For even in merit, there is indeed a connection with the characteristics of evil, owing to its association with undesirable results. In the world, what is a desired result for one person may be undesirable for another. Thus, even a desired result such as heaven is undesirable for those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*); therefore, with respect to a particular qualified seeker, even a desirable action is indeed evil. To this, he states a powerful regulating factor in the form of a Vedic usage, beginning with the words "not good deed" (*na sukṛtam*).

For here, having pointed out both good and evil deeds, the designation of both by the word "evil" (pāpman) is made quite explicitly. Therefore, since even good deeds—just like misfortunes—are denotable by the word "evil," it is established that the statement regarding the rising above all evils also implies the cessation of good deeds.

Here, however, an objection is raised: you have stated that the Supreme Brahman possesses a body; is that body composed of material elements (*prakṛta*), or is it non-material (*aprākṛta*)? And even if it is non-material, is it the very nature of the Lord Himself, or is it a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*)?

In the first case, the very state of being a transmigrator (*saṃsāritva*) that we have previously described would result; this is the "logic of the ruined shed" (*ghaṭṭakuṭīnyāya*). In the second position, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of a modification of its own essential nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*). The third position also does not hold, because there exists no other principle distinct from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the person (*puruṣa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and time (*kāla*); therefore, how could that [state] be? He refutes this with the word "well-known" (*prakhyātam*). It is well-known: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven."

By such statements as "In Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme world," "The Creator beyond darkness," and "Sattva which illuminates its own existence," it is shown that *śuddhasattva* is the substratum of *sattva* devoid of *rajas* and *tamas*. It is a certain divine substance. Its state of being "sinless" (*anaghātva*) is said because it lacks any role in promoting the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). Its distinctness from the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is explicitly stated in the passage: "Three-quarters of Him are the immortal in heaven."

By this [statement], he says that the form of the Blessed One is not an ordinary (*prākṛta*) nature, but rather an extraordinary (*aprākṛta*) distinct substance; thus he says, "that form. Lord Parāśara has declared: "That form of Hari is another, great form, different from the universal form (*viśvarūpa*). The word *vairūpya* means "dissimilar" (*virūpa*). By this, the arguments of opponents—such as "the form under dispute is material because it is a form," or "it is impermanent because it possesses parts"—are refuted.

Regarding the establishment of such a form [of the Lord], there is a contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), because it is established by a means of knowledge precisely through its association with qualifiers such as being non-material and eternal. Furthermore, if it were not so established, there would be a lack of a substratum (*āśrayāsiddhi*). Thus, let the logician himself recall his own system. If it is asked: "Granted that the Blessed One has such a form, what is the status of Ananta, Garuḍa, and the others?"—the answer is: the Blessed One alone is their refuge.

Because hundreds of authoritative proofs—such as "That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu" and "Viṣṇu, whose nature is inconceivable, dwells together with his devoted Bhāgavatas"—have refuted this, the demoness of doubt is dispelled. One might object: "Granted that the resident of Vaikuṇṭha has such a form, what is the definitive proof for its eternity and other attributes? Anticipating this, he says "eternal," intending to refer to the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and so forth.

"One always beholds," "the eternal one who possesses an eternal form," "O Pauṣkara, when His form and His devotion are eternally established," "He whose chest bears the Śrīvatsa, the eternally glorious"—these and thousands of other such authorities are to be considered.

One might raise the objection: "Granted that the entire collection of qualities belongs to the Blessed Lord who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha, yet Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others are material beings who, under the sway of karma, experience pleasure, pain, and so forth; how then can our attainment of liberation result from their worship? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] describes the collection of qualities—such as being non-material—in the remainder of the text beginning with "ajahat," in accordance with the views of Parāśara, Pārāśarya, and others. The statement "samastaśakti" and so forth is the word of Parāśara.

The statement of Vyāsa (Pārāśarya) should also be kept in mind: "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of a collection of elements. Vālmīki also said: "This great yogi is manifest as the eternal Supreme Self. Therefore, it should be understood that the imitation of grief, delusion, and so forth during incarnations is merely for the sake of diversion, like actors in plays. The distinction between the Para, Vyūha, and other forms is clearly to be found in the Pañcarātra and other scriptures.

Stabilizing the very point already stated by means of a *pratibandī* (reductio ad absurdum) following a restatement of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] demonstrates that even the fruit of acting as an actor—such as suffering—is [unreal], using the phrase "because of being a body" (*dehatvāt*). Here, the *pratibandī* is as follows: if sublation (*bādha*) is admitted in some cases regarding matters known solely through scripture, then sublation would also apply to the killing of the sacrificial animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya-hiṃsā*) and other such acts. To this, if one attempts to release the *pratibandī* by arguing that there is no sublation because it is established by Śruti, then the release of the prisoner (*bandīmocana*) would likewise occur in the original case.

It has been stated that because the form of the Blessed One and so forth are established by the Śruti, the mention of their being mixed with suffering and the like is intended for the purpose of deluding the *āsuras*. The *āsuras* are Kaṃsa and others. Thinking that the acting out of childhood and other stages by Kṛṣṇa and the others is merely a supreme reality, they would repeatedly act in opposition; through that very activity, they would be destroyed. Thus, the meaning is that the acting out of childhood and so forth has as its fruit the destruction of the wicked, as stated in the verse: "And for the destruction of the doers of evil."

Regarding the sections (adhikaraṇas) mentioned here, since they share a single purpose, they constitute a single "box" (peṭikā). Anticipating the objection of the opponent—that the subsequent sections up to the end of the chapter might be redundant due to a lack of distinct subject matter—the author demonstrates their utility through a variety of methods. He then explicitly declares the primary purpose common to all these sections: the contemplation of the specific attributes of the Lord, stating "In this way... [ittham].

Although, by means of the threefold knowledge taught in the three sections beginning with "Sadvidyā," there may be a superiority of the Blessed One—the cause of all things consisting of the sentient and insentient, both stationary and moving—over primordial matter (pradhāna), the class of individual souls (jīva), and even the sun and other luminaries; yet...

Nevertheless, the meaning of the word "iti" (thus) is that, by restraining the opponents—who arise in succession according to the stated order of "very indistinct," "indistinct," "distinct," and "following the shadow" due to differences in their means of emergence—and who are characterized by a gentle commencement and a cruel conclusion, the Blessed One specifically illuminates His own qualities through the refined topics (*adhikaraṇa*) presented in this chapter.

The point here is this: just as in battles between infantry, cavalry, elephants, and chariots—where each subsequent unit is weaker than the preceding one—the stronger force prevails upon the defeat of the weaker, so too does the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) proceed by the repeated rejection of those whose signs of life are increasingly obscure and the subsequent adoption of others. Without the neutralization of that [prima facie] activity, even the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) that has arisen would not become firmly established. Therefore, the remainder of this chapter must indeed be commenced.

Furthermore, our position is that in all the topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), the specific qualities of the Lord (*bhagavad-guṇas*) shine forth individually according to each particular section, and the purpose of the remainder of the chapter is the comprehensive contemplation of those qualities. For those who maintain the doctrine of a qualityless [Brahman] (*nirviśeṣavādins*), however, since the qualityless reality is established by a single topical section alone, there is an absence of any further qualities to be expounded; thus, the heart of their argument is that the subsequent topical sections would be entirely fruitless.

Having thus explained the connection of the remainder of the chapter with the preceding section (*peṭikā*), he further elucidates specifically the nature of the preceding and succeeding sections in order to state the connection of the remainder of the quarter (*pāda*): "By means of words," etc. In the first section of the *Śārīraka-śāstra*, beginning with the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*), it was stated that Brahman is the object of inquiry.

Regarding that Brahman, which is understood through words common to the abode of Brahmā, the Self, the Puruṣa, and others—whether it be *prakṛti*, or the individual soul (*jīva*), or some particular soul distinguished by accumulated merit; and since the word "sin" (*pāpman*) is common [to both], even if it arises from sin in the form of both merit and demerit—is it the lotus-eyed one (Viṣṇu), or some other such as the four-faced (Brahmā) or the three-eyed (Śiva)? Having raised these doubts, it was determined in the preceding section that it is indeed the lotus-eyed one. In this regard, he states the distinguishing marks that exclude the others, beginning with "volition" (*saṃkalpa*).

From the mention of "volition" (saṃkalpa), there is an exclusion of Pradhāna. From the repetition of "bliss" (ānanda), the generic class of individual souls (jīvasāmānya) is excluded. Even among individual souls, one who has accumulated specific merit is distinguished by his non-material form; furthermore, because the state of having lotus-eyes (puṇḍarīkākṣatva) is heard of in that context, the intention is that even the four-faced Brahmā and others are excluded. Thus is the internal meaning.

"Not inconsistent with that" means "not otherwise established. Here, the opponent objects: "In the three preceding sections, you have asserted the exclusion of *pradhāna* and other such entities by subverting general scriptural texts (*sāmānya-śruti*) on the basis of inferential marks (*liṅga*). However, specific scriptural texts (*viśeṣa-śruti*) are stronger than inferential marks, for they function through their primary (conventional) power. Therefore, by means of specific scriptural texts concerning ether, breath, light, the senses, and so forth, one should subvert the inferential marks and accept the well-known ether and the rest themselves as the Brahman to be sought after."

By this, the consistency with the section consisting of the remainder of the [previous] quarter has been stated. This very point he expresses with the words "bhūta" (the element). Space is of two kinds: one is that which is accepted by those who know the inner self (adhyātmavit), according to the text, "If there were no bliss in space"; the other is the elemental space (bhūtākāśa), well-known to all the world without distinction between the common folk and the investigators. Therefore, following the preponderance of common usage, the elemental space alone is to be understood here. The same should be observed regarding the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth.

Thus, having set aside the inferential mark (liṅga) stated in the three preceding sections by means of specific scriptural mentions (viśeṣa-śruti) regarding ether and so forth—thereby refuting it according to the opponent's view—the proponent (siddhāntin) again protects (bhunakti)—meaning he preserves—that very same inferential mark which establishes Brahman and distinguishes it from primordial matter (pradhāna) and the like, by demonstrating the impossibility of a collection of specific entities such as ether and so forth. This is because, according to the rule "bhujo 'navane," the middle voice (ātmanepada) is prescribed when one intends a meaning other than protection (rakṣaṇa).

The intention here is as follows: it is indeed established that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) sets aside etymological derivation (*yoga*); nevertheless, the conclusion of those learned in logic is that an etymological derivation determined by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) overrides conventional usage itself. And in this context, the expression "sarvāṇi ha vā imāni" is seen as a reference to what is well-known; for we observe the indeclinable particle *ha* used to indicate what is well-known. And this well-known status resides in the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*).

And in those cases, the fact that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme referent is already established by the logic of the "goat-sacrifice" (chāgapaśunyāya) and others. Therefore, it is entirely reasonable that the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word "ākāśa" is set aside by its etymological application (*yoga*), which is determined by the mark of being the cause of all things found in a statement that cannot be explained otherwise and which is accompanied by a reference to Nārāyaṇa as a well-known identifier. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.

Beyond this, he states that the division of the four subsequent sections consists of two pairs, which are mutually connected, in the verse beginning with "ākāśa. The words *ākāśa* (space) and *prāṇa* (breath), having no other possible resort and being incapable of being understood as referring to the well-known space and breath, must—setting aside their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) in favor of the Supreme Brahman—be interpreted solely through the power of etymological derivation (*yoga*). By this, the unity of the two sections within a single group (*peṭikā*) is established.

Likewise, since the two subsequent sections (adhikaraṇas) have as their purport Brahman qualified by the conventional meaning [of the terms] without abandoning that conventionality, their status as a single section (ekapeṭikatva) is established. Therein, he first demonstrates that the word *jyotis* has as its purport that which is qualified by its conventional meaning: "Jyotis," etc. For such a collection of scriptural authorities is found, such as: "The sun does not shine there," "It neither rises nor sets," and "That light which resides in the sun."

In this same manner, the word "senses" (*indriya*) and others must also be interpreted by relying on their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) without breaking it, while concluding that they refer solely to the qualifying attributes, as being directed toward the Supreme Self characterized by Indra and the rest. Thus, he concludes with the words "in this way," showing that the establishment of two sections is due to the difference in meaning: in one case there is etymological power (*yaugika-śakti*), and in the other case there is conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) which terminates in the qualifying attribute alone; such is the sequence of the application of words.

Previously, in the passage beginning with "This golden person who is within the sun," the fact that a certain person residing within the sun is to be known through the Vedāntas was stated on the basis of specific indicative marks (liṅgas). Now, the connection [of this section] is as follows: having raised the doubt that space (ākāśa) might also be known through the Vedāntas due to the absence of such marks and the presence of specific scriptural statements regarding it, that doubt is now being refuted.

One should reflect for oneself that the common application of the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) to both the well-known physical ether and Brahman is the seed of doubt, and so forth. The inquiry into its meaning, however, concerns whether the word "ether" in the Chāndogya passage beginning with "All these beings, indeed," refers to the well-known physical ether or to the Supreme Self.

For that purpose, it is investigated whether this word "ākāśa" functions by means of conventional power (rūḍhi-śakti) or not; for that purpose as well, it is investigated whether there exists another principle that sets aside the principle that "conventionality overrides etymological derivation" (rūḍhir yogam apaharati), or whether such a principle does exist. Furthermore, it is investigated whether the mention [of the Lord] as if He were well-known, along with His being the cause of this world and so forth, refers exclusively to a conscious being, or whether it refers to both conscious and unconscious entities, and so on.

Regarding the statement "This austerity [is] the state of being the fruit of fruits," since there is no other logical principle to postulate a derivative power (*yoga-śakti*) for the restatement of causality concerning an object whose meaning is already well-known—namely, that it refers only to insentient things—the word *ākāśa* functions by its conventional sense (*rūḍhi*) alone; thus, this word refers to the well-known ether (*ākāśa*). This must also be stated by oneself even in the final established view (*siddhānta*).

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that in the Chāndogya, the word ‘ether’ (ākāśa) is seen to denote the cause of the origin and dissolution of all things; yet that same ether is described in the Taittirīya as not being produced from anything else, in the passage: “From the Self, ether was produced. Its state of not being produced from anything else is logical precisely because it is eternal by virtue of being the cause of all. This is what he states with the words beginning “here,” etc. He refutes that with the words “not so” (maivam).

Regarding this, he states the reason with the word "siddha" (established): because this sentence, which contains the expression "it is so" (*havai*) as a reference to what is already well-known, concerns the restatement of an established fact, a prior establishment must necessarily be presupposed. And that establishment exists in the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*), and it has already been stated previously that those refer to Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, the meaning is that the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) does not refer to the ether as commonly understood. Furthermore, in the passage "The ether is the supreme goal," the ether's status as the ultimate object of attainment is heard right here.

The knowers of the Self declare that nothing insentient can be the supreme goal; this is what [the author] expresses with the word "atha" (now). The meaning is that the status of being the supreme goal is not possible for that ether (*ākāśa*). He states another objection with the word "tat" (that): in passages such as "That [Being] thought," "That fire thought," and "Those waters thought," the agent of those acts is indeed heard to be the Omniscient One (*vipaścit*). Consequently, manifold seeing is not possible for ether. Alternatively, the phrase "its agent" means "the agent of ether."

In the *Brahmavallī*, the entity that is the cause of the world is heard of as being "Vipaścit" (the All-seeing) by Brahmā; for they have explained that "Vipaścit-ness" is the state of seeing variously (*vividhaṃ paśyac-cittvam*). Therefore, the word "Ātman" denotes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). As for what was said—that in the passage "From Ātman, space [arose]," the origination of space from one's own self is being stated—there is a contradiction if the primary meaning is accepted, and that same fault remains if a non-primary meaning is accepted. Therefore, with the intention that the meaning is simply "Space was produced from the Ātman, i.e., the Supreme Self," he says: "It is refuted... (*vihata*) and so forth.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks as follows: "Since the origin of the world in the well-known ether (*ākāśa*) is not perceived, it is proper to abandon the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) of the word 'ether' there; however, in the case of 'breath' (*prāṇa*), because we observe that the activity of all persons whatsoever is dependent upon breath, that very thing which is a favorable indicative mark (*liṅga*) for us is an unfavorable indicative mark for you. Therefore, the conventional power of the word 'breath,' supported by such favorable indicatives, should not be abandoned. He states this with the words, "dependent on breath. [The author] refutes that with the words, "that is not so" (*tan na*).

Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*). By the phrase "all indeed," it is stated that the entire phenomenal world—without distinction between sentient and insentient—is subject to activity dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). The meaning is that even among certain insentient things, such as stones and wood, they should be accepted as being denoted by the word *prāṇa*, based on the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "the vital breath resides in them. He applies the reason stated in the previous section here as well with the words "as before"; the meaning is that the word "indeed" (*havai*) occurs in both instances.
