Regarding this Blessed One, he states with an illustration the Vedic usage of the word *prāṇa*: "Ākāśa," etc. Just as the word *ākāśa* refers to the Supreme Self because that word is found in various places in the Śruti concerning the Supreme Self, so too the word *prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Self because the act of breathing (*prāṇana*) of all living beings is seen [to be attributed to Him]. The relationship between the inquiry into its meaning and its result should be understood by oneself, as in the previous section (*adhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, the connection (*saṅgati*) is one of extension (*atideśikī*).

The author states this for the benefit of the students to clarify the difference between the preceding and succeeding sections (*peṭikā*): whereas in the two previous sections the arguments supporting the conclusions were refuted by the rising opponent due to the absence of the subject matter of those two sections in the scriptural passages under discussion, here the refutation of that same rising opponent is performed by another method. This is the procedure regarding contradiction and non-contradiction: a mark (*liṅga*) that is favorable to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is opposed to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), while a mark that is favorable to the prima facie view is itself not opposed to the final conclusion.

In this context, by means of specific terms such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth, the determination of the final conclusion (*siddhānta-nirṇaya*) has been established through the reinforcement of the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) which are consistent with the established tenets (*siddhānta*) that present their own respective probanda in the two preceding sections. Herein, the proponent of the prima facie view maintains that, whereas in the two preceding sections they cite specific indicative marks (*liṅga*) such as being the cause of all things, no such specific indicative mark is cited in the two subsequent sections.

Furthermore, he shows that there are also indicative marks (*liṅga*) favorable to the well-known light of the eyes mentioned in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), such as the identity with the gastric light, by saying "it exists. That very [mark] is, however, contrary to the status of the supreme Brahman which constitutes the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). He shows that we do not speak merely on the basis of indicative marks alone, but also on the basis of the primary scripture (*śruti*), by saying "the word" (*śabda*). The meaning is: a specific word whose referent is nothing else.

Thus, the summary of the opponent's specific intention is that, for four reasons, the Supreme Self is not known through the Vedic texts concerning light and so forth. Now, one might object: "If there is no mention of being the direct cause in the passages concerning light and so forth, how can there be any room for the doubt that light and so forth are the cause? Anticipating this, [the author] says "viśva... (the universe), meaning: even in the absence of a statement regarding direct causality, it is somehow possible to raise the doubt that light and so forth are the cause, by means of certain indicative marks—such as the appearance of some semblance and unsurpassed splendor—which imply causality.

He refutes one who objects in this manner by means of the two immediately preceding sections with the word "obstructs" (rundha). The meaning of the word is that he "obstructs" by demonstrating the specific distinction between sentient and insentient beings that is appropriate for the Lord and conforms to His splendor.

In these three sections concerning ether (*ākāśa*) and the others, the connection (*saṅgati*) consists of the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and its resolution (*samādhāna*) according to the sequence stated in the scripture beginning with "From ether, air" (*ākāśādvāyuḥ*). The cause of doubt is the common usage of the word "light" (*jyotis*) for both the well-known physical light and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in various places. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: in such passages as "Now, that which is beyond heaven," does the word "light" denote the well-known light, or does it denote the Supreme Self?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether, even in the absence of a mark unique to the Supreme Self within its own sentence, the mark unique to the Supreme Self situated in the opening passage establishes that the word *jyotis* denotes the Supreme Self, or whether it does not. For that purpose as well, it is investigated whether there is a mark unique to the Supreme Self in the opening passage or whether there is not. And from that, [the main point] is investigated.

Does the word *gāyatrī* occurring in the introductory passage, "The *gāyatrī* indeed is all this," set aside the interpretation that [the *gāyatrī*] refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), or not? Furthermore, it is investigated whether the designation of the quarters beginning with "beings" (*bhūta*) found in this same passage excludes the view that [the *gāyatrī*] refers merely to the *gāyatrī* meter, or whether it does not so exclude it.

The relationship between the cause and the effect is to be inferred by oneself. Here, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) considers that in the subject-sentence of the section on Light (*jyotir-adhikaraṇa*), unlike the sections on Space (*ākāśa*) and Breath (*prāṇa*), no characteristic mark (*liṅga*) contradictory to the well-known light—such as being the cause of all—is found to establish that the word "light" denotes the Supreme Person. On the contrary, a favorable characteristic mark is found: the identity with the light within the body (*kaukṣeya-jyotis*). This he states with the words "the light within the body" (*kaukṣeya*). And thus, that very [light] is the cause of the world.

It is not only through this *vidyā* that [the Lord] is recognized; rather, He is likewise recognized as the cause of the universe even in the *Vaiśvānara-vidyā*. Thus he says, "In that [text]. He states the conclusion with the words, "Therefore. He refutes [the opponent's view] with the words, "Not so. He provides the reason with the words, "By the *Puruṣasūkta*. For at the beginning, by the statement, "All beings are one foot of Him," the passage from the *Puruṣasūkta*, "All beings are one foot of Him," and so forth, is made to be recognized. Indeed, the fact that the *Puruṣasūkta* has Nārāyaṇa as its subject matter is well-established.

And that causality resides in Nārāyaṇa because of the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being the husband of Lakṣmī in the passage, "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives," and also because of the statement of Parāśara: "The word 'Bhagavān' [refers to Him]. If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the identity with the gastric light mentioned in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*)?"—the answer is that its status is simply sublation (*bādha*), as it contradicts the logical principle (*nyāya*). For those who know the logic of interpretation maintain that between the opening and the conclusion, the opening is more powerful. In this regard, the very principle of the "sacrifice for receiving a horse" (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi-nyāya*) serves as the illustration.

One might object: since the opening statement of the entire section, “The Gāyatrī indeed is all this,” demonstrates that the subject matter is the Gāyatrī, does not the introductory sentence establish the Gāyatrī itself and not the Supreme Person? Anticipating this doubt, he states the word “Gāyatrī” to show that even this [identification] is established otherwise. The mention of the Gāyatrī is due solely to the similarity of having four feet, and not because of its being the actual nature of the Gāyatrī. Anticipating the question of what the reason for understanding it thus is, he states the restrictive reason with the words “Moreover” (api ca).

In this very statement, the elements, the earth, the body, and the heart are indicated by way of similarity with the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the word *gāyatrī*. The fact that the Supreme Self is the soul of the universe (*viśvātmakatva*) is the restrictive factor establishing that the word *gāyatrī* refers to the Supreme Self, and not merely to the *gāyatrī* as a collection of syllables; for it is possible to explain the concluding portion in accordance with the introductory statement. Thus, the conclusion is reached that that which is denoted by the word "light" (*jyotis*) is indeed the Supreme Brahman.
Furthermore, the word "light" (jyotis) is applied to the Supreme Brahman alone in such passages as "That which the gods worship as the light of lights," and in other places as well.

In the *Śrīmadbhāṣya*, for the sake of those with dull intellects, he raises the objection that there is a mutual contradiction between the preceding and following statements and resolves it with the section beginning with "utthānam" and ending with "ittham."

At the beginning of this section, in the pair of sections concerning *jyotis* and so forth, the Commentator himself stated that there is an emergence from a mark (*liṅga*) pervaded by the cause; yet, at the time of presenting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) once again, he remarked—even though there is a reference as if it were well-known—that because no specific marks of the Supreme Self are seen within its own sentence, as is the case with *ākāśa*, *prāṇa*, and so on, [the conclusion does not follow]. Therefore, how is there no contradiction? To this, he states the reason for the refutation: "viśva... (beginning with the word *viśva*).

This, indeed, is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) considers that there exists an indicative mark (liṅga) consisting of the manifestation [of the Lord], such as "on all sides, behind everything, in the unsurpassed, highest [worlds]," which implies [the Lord's] status as the cause.

Furthermore, [the opponent] says "there is no contradiction" because there is no mark (*liṅga*) within its own statement—such as being the cause of the world—that establishes the Supreme Person as characterized by having both genders (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) and so forth. The meaning is this: although the author of the Commentary intends that there is a mark unique to the Supreme Person in the sentence, "Now, that light which is beyond the sky," as presented in the commentary on the statement of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

The employment of the two qualifiers, "shining in the unsurpassed and supreme worlds," applies only to the light residing in the extraordinary divine realm; it does not, however, apply to mere light existing within the cosmic egg—this is the intended meaning.

The connection here has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya himself with the words beginning "niratiśaya" (unexcelled). Having rejected the term "supreme light" as applied to the sun and other luminaries, Indra—who is postulated by others as the supreme lord of lights—is now suspected of being the cause of the world and is likewise rejected.

Alternatively, the refutation of the meaning stated in the concluding portion on the grounds of the superior authority of the opening statement was already explained in the previous section; therefore, by that same principle, in the Pratardana-vidyā as well, the conception of the Supreme Person—though understood from the concluding sentence—must be set aside due to the superior authority of the opening statement. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*) by way of raising the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: in the Pratardana-vidyā, is it the well-known Indra who is taught, or is it the Supreme Self having Indra as its body? The same should be said regarding the Prāṇa [in the subsequent section].

For that purpose, it is deliberated whether, according to the principle of the section on "commencement" (*upakrama*) stated in the preceding section, it is appropriate here also to describe the meaning [of the passage], or not. Furthermore, it is deliberated whether there exists a principle subsequent to the principle of the section on "commencement"—namely, that when there is a contradiction between a "commencement" and a "great sentence" (*mahāvākya*), one must follow the great sentence—or whether such a principle does not exist. Again, it is deliberated whether, in this sentence, a collection of reasons establishing the status of the Supreme Brahman is observed everywhere, or whether it is not so observed.

On this point, the opponent considers that it has been stated by you that it is logical to describe the conclusion in accordance with the opening; however, in the Pratardana-vidyā, the word *Indra* is employed first in the opening, and since that is a specific scriptural mention (*viśeṣa-śruti*), there is indeed conformity with the scripture situated in the opening. Furthermore, it is likewise stated that he is the object of meditation as the most beneficial thing: "Choose for yourself a boon from me, whatever you consider most beneficial for a human being. And that...

The mark of being the Supreme Brahman [is present]; therefore, by both the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and the indicative mark (*liṅga*) located at the beginning, Indra alone is the Supreme Person. Furthermore, characteristics such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, which are well-known to be common to the celebrated Indra and are contrary to your intended Nārāyaṇa, are observed; and that is indeed inconsistent with the Supreme Person. He states the conclusion: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Thus, this very Indra, denoted by terms such as Śakra, is the creator of the world. He refutes this, saying: "No."

The intention is as follows: it is not possible for the well-known Indra to be the object of meditation on that which is most beneficial (*hitatama*); likewise, meditation for the sake of liberation is the meditation on that which is most beneficial. However, the well-known Indra is merely some insignificant being included among the hosts of gods, a resident of limited realms such as heaven; how could he be the object of meditation on that which is most beneficial? Therefore, because of this contradiction in meaning and in order to establish the non-restriction of the word’s referent, the Supreme Person alone is denoted by the word "Indra," for [the root] *idi* signifies supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*).

They explain that upon careful investigation, even the Grandfather (Brahmā) is but a "fig-worm" (*udumbarakīṭa*); how much more so, then, the well-known Indra who was conquered by Meghanāda and others? You yourself must reflect on this! Thus, Indra enjoins his own worship, saying, "Worship me," and the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ's son and other such deeds are proclaimed in this very context as marks (*liṅga*) favorable to the well-known Indra and contrary to the Supreme Person. If it is asked how this can be so, the author provides the resolution here with the words beginning with "brahma" and ending with "svātmanā ca."

The intention is as follows: for the Brahman to be meditated upon is threefold—namely, meditation characterized by the non-sentient (acid-viśiṣṭa), meditation characterized by the sentient (cid-viśiṣṭa), and meditation on the Supreme Self alone (kevala-paramātma). By this, even well-known figures such as Indra are designated as objects of meditation by virtue of being attributes of Brahman. Therefore, even signs such as the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son are indeed meaningful for the purpose of recognizing the well-known Indra who serves as an attribute; they are not, however, contradictory.

This is the conclusion here: because he is the object of worship as the most beneficial means and so forth, it is already established that in the Pratardana-vidyā, the Supreme Person alone is the primary denotation of the word "Indra. Nevertheless, by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son and other such deeds, the well-known Indra is also accepted as a qualifying attribute of Him. Likewise, let the well-known vital breath (prāṇa) also be accepted through its specific indicative marks pertaining to the context, but not in its own right. For meditation upon the Supreme Self in its own essential nature is already well-established.

Therefore, because the specific attributes of well-known beings such as Indra—which are not shared by others—are mentioned in the Pratardana-vidyā for the purpose of establishing the threefold nature of the worshipper, there is no contradiction. Consequently, it is established that in the Pratardana-vidyā, the Supreme Self alone, qualified by [the form of] Indra and so forth, is the object of worship; thus, by means of the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) of the word "Indra" and the like, there is an expression that refers to the substantive (*viśeṣya*) while setting aside the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*). Anticipating the objection—"How then can the meaning of a sentence be determined when it contradicts the opening statement?"—he says: "Prāṇa, Indra, etc. (*prāṇendrāti*).

Both [the introductory and concluding statements] are elucidated here; however, between the introductory statement (*upakrama*) and the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), the introductory statement is stronger. Furthermore, when there is a contradiction between the introductory statement and the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), the great sentence alone is stronger. But this is only true when a contradiction exists. The intention of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) here, however, is that no contradiction exists at all, because those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*) understand even the introductory statement within the great sentence as referring to the Supreme Self qualified by Indra.

Anticipating the objection that the commencement of this section (adhikaraṇa) is untenable, he provides the resolution with the words "yat" (that which). This is the meaning: as for the mark (*liṅga*) stated by you to reside solely in the Cause—namely, in the case of *jyotis* (light), what was said in the passage beginning "Now, that which from this... regarding its possession of unsurpassed radiance in the highest worlds; and in the case of *indra*, what was intended by "You are I," namely, being the object of worship for those seeking liberation for the sake of direct liberation—both of these marks are well-known to belong exclusively to the One Cause by virtue of its causality.

The two marks (liṅgas) are first established as being co-extensive with the state of having space as their substratum, which is well-known to be exclusively devoted to Nārāyaṇa. How so? Just as the causality of the entire universe is first established as having the Supreme Person as its object, likewise, the two marks, being equally co-extensive with that [causality], are also established in that very same way; this is the meaning. He states the conclusion with the word "ataḥ" (therefore).

Since the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of being endowed with unsurpassed radiance and the state of being an object of meditation for those seeking liberation have already been established as residing in the Supreme Person, it is not tenable that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from a mark pervaded by causality. Thus, the refutation has been stated regarding the consideration of these two marks as residing in the Supreme Person; he now states the refutation even in their absence, beginning with the words "aprāpte" (when [the object] is not [otherwise] obtained).

Anticipating the objection—"In the absence of a reflection upon the two marks (liṅga) as being situated in all causes, let there be some light endowed with those two marks, or let there be some Indra; yet, by this much, the previously stated causality residing in a single [source], namely the status of being the supreme cause, does not fall away—why then is this section undertaken?"—he refutes it by accepting half of the point, saying "True."

Even if there is no specific purpose for this section (*adhikaraṇa*), there is nevertheless some purpose; and even if the two marks (*liṅga*) pertain exclusively to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), that very Supreme Person exists by assuming the state of Upendra. Therefore, he too is indeed an object of worship. Some of childish intellect might be confused, thinking that the scripture—just like the Purāṇas and other texts—merely describes the birth of Upendra. This section begins in order to dispel such a doubt; this is the meaning.

The meaning is that Upendra’s status as the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣatva) is well-known in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas; likewise, Indra’s status as a servant of the Supreme Person (puruṣottamakiṅkaratva) is well-known in those very same sources.

Having thus resolved the apparent contradiction between the two subject matters mentioned, [the author] demonstrates the distinction between what is accepted and what is not accepted regarding the position maintained by the opponent; furthermore, he shows that the purpose of the identity with the gastric light—which was cited as a contradictory mark—as well as the marks such as the chief vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), lies in their being for the sake of meditation (*upāsanā*). He states: "The light," etc. It is accepted that words such as "light" denote the supreme reality qualified by its attributes; it is also accepted that they denote the attributes alone.

The identity with the gastric light is for the purpose of meditation; likewise, the characteristic mark of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) is for the purpose of illuminating the specific nature of the object of meditation. This is the summary of the meaning of the verse. The remainder is quite clear.

Here, for the sake of favoring the disciples and for the purpose of clarifying the meaning stated in the section beginning with "the light of the ether" (ākāśajyotiḥ), he demonstrates the rule regarding the application of words denoting other things to Brahman according to the distinction of their respective objects, starting with the word "effect" (kārya).

When "that which is to be accomplished" (kārya) is firmly established as referring to ether and so forth, and when "that which is subject to action" (karmavaśya) is firmly established as referring to the world of Prajāpati and so forth, and these two are designated by their well-known conventional (rūḍha) terms within the context of Brahman—then, in certain instances where words such as "ether" refer to states of the Self, the conventional meaning must be set aside because there is no other possible recourse. Here, "no other recourse" (agati) means that it is impossible to maintain the conventional sense due to a lack of any alternative; by that lack of recourse, the conventional meaning is precluded. Therefore, the meaning is that only the etymological (yoga) sense is to be resorted to.

In another place, he explains the resolution through a different method with the word "tat" (that). The meaning is that in the case of the light (*jyotis*), the mark (*liṅga*) is the identity with the gastric fire; whereas in the case of Indra, it is the slaying of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son and so forth—both of which are unestablished otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*) and thus pervading [the respective subjects]. Through the power of knowledge, because those respective marks are not established otherwise, there would be a state of having as its object that which is qualified by those specific attributes. Regarding this, he states four examples beginning with "light": the word "light" refers to Brahman qualified by light, while the word "Indra" refers to [Brahman] qualified by Indra.

Thus, in the phrase "I am Brahman," the word "I" (ahaṃ) denotes the Supreme Self as qualified by one's own self. Here, the expression "with the Aindrī [verse]" remains to be explained; we shall discuss that as well. In the case of "with the Aindrī [verse] [one worships] the Gārhapatya fire," since the word "Indra" lacks a conventional (rūḍhi) power of denotation with respect to the Gārhapatya fire, one must resort either to a figurative application (gauṇīvṛtti) or an etymological derivation (vyutpatti). Regarding both, they say: "The state of being Indra (indratva) in Agni would be figurative, caused by his connection with the sacrifice; or, according to the sense of the root 'to rule' (ind), he too is indeed a lord (īśvara) over his own functions."

Therefore, it is perfectly consistent that we accept the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "breath" (*prāṇa*) as referring to the Supreme Brahman. This is the meaning: "By means of etymological derivation, the various designations may reveal the Supreme Self, provided that His characteristic marks (*liṅga*) are not established otherwise [than by Him], and provided that those designations depend upon Him as their specific qualifier."

It was previously established that, according to the subsequent sections, each one has as its purport the manifestation of a single quality of the Lord. Now, however, [the author] explains that the purport of the seven past sections lies respectively in seven qualities of the Lord—beginning with "conqueror" (*jaitra*), "Vītahavya," "conqueror," and "one who has overcome"—and that He is endowed with excellence in strength, prowess, and so forth, as seen in the *Ānuśāsana-parvan* and elsewhere, stating "by His own will" and so on. The term "auspicious" (*śubha*) means infinite and boundless joy consisting of the glory of auspicious qualities.

"Without substrate" (anupadhika) means being devoid of limitation by space, time, or substance. "Possessing breath" (saprāṇa) means being the cause of life for both those with breath and those without breath. In that context, the mention of "the Lord" (prabhu) is for the purpose of manifesting the majesty described in the section on the "Supreme Authority" (sarvādhikaraṇa).
The third quarter (pāda) of the second chapter:

Here, the connection between the preceding and subsequent quarters is stated very clearly in the Bhāṣya itself: "It has been stated that systems outside the Veda, such as Sāṅkhya and others, lack consistency because they are rooted in fallacious reasoning and involve contradictions. Now, in order to demonstrate that our own position is free from even the slightest scent of defects such as contradiction, the manner in which the world—consisting of the conscious and the unconscious—is produced as an effect of Brahman is being clarified."

In this regard, we have already stated previously that there is a connection between the first two quarters and the latter two quarters: the first two quarters are intended to resolve external contradictions by way of the cause (*kāraṇa*), while the other two are intended to resolve internal contradictions by way of the effect (*kārya*). Following this, the author summarizes his own position—which consists of the refutation of the opponent’s method—by concluding with the word "all" (*sarvam*) at the end of the two quarters intended to resolve contradictions concerning the effect.

In this regard, four positions are to be refuted. The Sāṅkhyas assert that everything, both substance (*dravya*) and non-substance (*adravya*), is eternal. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that everything is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Those who recite the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) as taught by the Jina declare that everything is both eternal and non-eternal. Even those who claim that [reality] is eternal in its substantial nature (*dravyātmanā*) but non-eternal in its modal aspect (*paryāyātmanā*) speak erroneously; for they assert that what is indeed eternal is non-eternal, and conversely, that what is non-eternal is eternal in certain respects.

The Vaiśeṣikas indeed assert that consciousness is eternal, yet they claim it is non-eternal; likewise, they do not accept that the form and other attributes of the Lord are established by valid means of knowledge as being eternally so, and thus they treat even the non-eternal as eternal. For example, although the relationship between two non-eternal things—a jar and its properties—is of the nature of inherence (samavāya), they declare it to be eternal. Having thus restated the opposing views, the connection [of the sūtras] is that he joins the sections on the ether and the vital breath (viyatprāṇapāda) with the very scriptures (śruti) to restrain those who have arisen [in opposition] by relying upon the scriptures.

Regarding the connection with the *adhikaraṇa*: in the *Śrīpāñcarātra-adhikaraṇa*, it was stated that [the mention of] the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth refers to Saṅkarṣaṇa and others who preside over the individual soul, and is therefore figurative (*aupacārika*). Now, the doubt arises: "In that case, by that very same logic, the doctrine of the origination of ether (*viyat*) must also be merely figurative. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Does ether originate or not? Specifically, does the statement, "From the Self, ether was produced," establish the origination of ether or not?

Is the word *sambhūti* here intended in its primary sense of "origination," or is it used figuratively? Does the observation elsewhere of the non-origination of that which is partless indicate that this [Brahman], which is known solely through scripture, is capable of origination, or not? Here, having first shown the connection between the preceding and following sections and having restated the position favored by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), the author refutes it with the words "In the previous [section]... (*pūrvatra*).

This is the meaning of the words here: in the preceding section, it was established that the scriptural statement regarding the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) is sublated by the statement establishing the eternity of the Person (*puruṣa*). Similarly, some maintain that even regarding the scriptural passages concerning the origination of space (*ākāśa*), since there is a conflict between the two declarations—one establishing eternity and the other non-eternity—the same principle applies, and thus the statement of non-eternity is sublated by the statement of eternity. Having thus set forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*) states his own view.

The meaning is this: the origination of space is established by numerous scriptural passages; there is no way to establish it otherwise. While many scriptural passages that cannot be explained otherwise remain authoritative, a single fallacious argument devised by an opponent—which is not primary—is not even fit to survive. Therefore, we abandon what you have asserted.

Anticipating the objection that the eternity of space (*ākāśa*) has been stated by the scripture itself in the passage, "The wind and the intermediate space—this is the immortal," and that if this were rejected, there would follow the rejection of the statement regarding the immortality of the individual soul (*jīva*), the author demonstrates the disparity pointed out by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) with the words beginning "vāyu... (the wind). This is indeed the disparity here: for many scriptural passages declare the birth or origin of space, whereas one scriptural passage merely restates its eternity. For this reason, [the latter] is set aside; and it is utterly weakened by its being mentioned in conjunction with the wind.

For the impermanence of air is indeed acknowledged by the entire world; here, however, the very permanence of the living self is acknowledged by all the Vedas. The doctrine of its production is found only in some isolated instances, and that is established otherwise [by other means]. Therefore, it is logical that the self is permanent in accordance with the many scriptural passages established otherwise; the opposite is illogical. Thus, the distinction is established: space is permanent.

In this context, regarding the demonstration of the eternity of space (*ākāśa*), [the author] clearly refutes the many unstated reasons imagined by the opponent for the sake of instructing the student, beginning with the words "because fire comes first" (*tejaḥprāthamya*) and so on. Here, the collection of reasons intended by the opponent is as follows: in the *Sadvidyā* [of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad], it is stated that "it created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*), and thus the creation of fire alone is mentioned without first mentioning the creation of space. Therefore, the non-mention of the creation of space implies the eternity of space; this is the first reason.

Because of the statement of immortality immediately following [the mention of wind], namely, "And the air and the intermediate space—this is immortal," [the author] says "Amaraḥ. The third [reason] is "because of the state of being a substance that is without parts. Therefore, the statement regarding the origin of the ether must have as its object only that which is conditioned (upahita), such as the ether within a jar; thus, the doctrine of the origin of the Self is reinterpreted as having the assumption of a body as its object, and this same counter-argument (pratibandī) applies here as well. He rejects what was restated by saying "No. As for what was said previously—"because of the observation of the mention of the creation of fire first"—that is not so, because priority is not heard [in the text]. For here, "first" is not [stated].

"The word 'originating from fire' (tejassṛtaḥ) is heard first"—this is what is heard. Anticipating the objection that even if there is no hearing of its being first, it might still be inferred merely on the basis of its being read first, [the author] refutes this with the words "on account of being read first. The meaning is: because it is sublated by another statement—namely, "From the Self, space was produced," and so forth—which is supported by many Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and principles of logic (nyāya). For an assumption is merely inferential (laiṅgika).

The meaning is that because of the ablative case-nirdeśa in the phrase "from this very Self," the fact that space is an effect is perceived directly by the Śruti itself. Furthermore, the word *saṃbhūta* also denotes birth. The word *amṛta* remains; however, like words such as *amartya*, which denote merely lasting for a long time, it does not establish eternity. Regarding this point, he states the reason for the determination: "because of the uniformity of many sentences. For those learned in logic determine that "in a conflict between two, the word of the majority prevails."

The Vaiśeṣikas indeed employ the inference: "Space is not produced, because it is a partless substance. That is incorrect, because the qualification is redundant; for all substances are established as eternal by valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, the mere property of being a substance (*dravyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) according to your own position. [Objection: But then how is the production of jars and so forth explained? [Reply: We say: precisely because of the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*).

Furthermore, there is no production of a substance such as a jar; for it is simply the lump of clay and so forth that, having acquired a form characterized by a broad base, a belly, and other features, is called a "jar" and the like. And this is indeed consistent with reason, because apart from a specific substance existing in the state of an non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), no other distinct substance is perceived even in the state of the effect. Moreover, this position is supported by the scriptures (*śruti*). Therefore, the qualification "because of being a partless substance" is entirely redundant.

Therefore, because those various substances are produced through states that deserve different names, this theory of creation is very well-founded. This is what he expresses with the words beginning with "yuktaḥ" (it is logical). "Yuktaḥ" means "consistent with reason. It is "endorsed by the Śrutis," for it is said [in the Upaniṣads]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

The illustration, "Just as, my dear, by one [clay]," applies to this very position: the possession of its qualities by the individual soul (*jīva*), as well as conjunction and so forth in the Lord (*īśvara*) and others even when devoid of those effects such as clay; likewise, the mutual conjunction of eternal atoms, the production of qualities born of baking (*pākaja*) in earth-atoms, and so on, should be understood by oneself. This is the distinction here: they maintain that "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) consists in the attainment of another state within the nature of the material cause (*upādāna*), which is worthy of receiving a different name.

"Otherwise, it would be of the nature of attaining another state. He concludes the point thus established for the sake of clarity with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that the origination of ether and the other elements mentioned in the scriptures is not contradicted, because it is analogous to the origination of air, fire, water, and earth. This is the sense: if one refutes origination on the grounds of [the self] being partless (*niravayava*), one is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); however, if one refutes the origination of a state that is fit to assume a different name, there is a contradiction with worldly experience, the Veda, and reasoning.

On this point, it has been stated very clearly in the Saṅgama-bhāṣya itself: "It has been declared that everything other than Brahman is an effect of Brahman. Now, it is considered whether the remote effects arise solely from their respective immediate causes, or rather from Brahman in those specific forms. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: do all the principles (tattvas), such as Mahat, Ahaṅkāra, and the rest, arise solely from their preceding principle alone, or from Brahman in the form of each of those [subsequent principles]?

Do the words "ether" and so forth in such scriptural passages as "From ether, air [was produced]" refer merely to ether and the rest, or do they refer to Brahman in those respective states? Does the indicative mark of reflection found in passages such as "Fire thought" lead one to understand that the words for fire and the rest refer to Brahman in those respective states, or not? If the words for fire and the rest were to refer to Brahman in those respective states, would there be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or not?

Is there a defect such as contradiction with linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) when words like "splendor" (*tejas*) and so forth denote Brahman through an unlimited application (*aparyavasāna-vṛtti*), or not? Having restated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) on this point, he refutes it [with the words] "from the immutable" (*kūṭasthāt*). For, based on scriptural passages such as "From Him is born the vital breath" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*), two possible interpretations (*gati*) are conceivable.

From this Brahman, there is one view that the creation of the universe proceeds through the sequence beginning with *prakṛti* and ending with earth; another view, however, holds that the entire universe, from earth upwards, is created directly from Brahman itself, whose body consists of each preceding principle (*tattva*) such as *prakṛti*. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that the creation of the universe proceeds through a lineage from the immutable Brahman alone—according to the analogy of sons, grandsons, and so forth—by interpreting the statement "from this [Brahman] comes *prāṇa*" in that manner.

In this passage, it is understood that the sequence is established according to the order of recitation (pāṭhakrama) in the text: "Space, air, light, water, and the earth, the supporter of all. However, since the Vedic sequence found in the text "From space, air [arises]" is also observed here, and because of its agreement with other Śrutis and the force of its being read in conjunction with them, the order of recitation perceived even in the passage "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses" is intended; yet, it does not mean that the creation of the universe proceeds directly from Brahman.

An objection is raised: "But [passages] such as 'From this, the vital breath (prāṇa) is born,' 'From that, this Brahman, name, form, and food are born,' and 'It created fire' do not fit your position. Anticipating this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) refutes it with the words "From this," etc. The meaning is as follows: by words such as "from this," mere causality is expressed; and since that causality is common to both the positions of being immediate and mediate, it is easily established even in our own view. He refutes [the objection] with the words "In this case," etc., stating that "confusion" is the error here.

This is the meaning: it is the settled conclusion of those learned in logic that, between two things separated by an interval and one not so separated, the cognition refers to the one that is not separated. Therefore, since it is possible for Brahman alone to be the immediate cause, the postulation of an intermediate cause is not more parsimonious.

Furthermore, when the possibility of construing the meaning of the sentence by supplying the word "from this" (*etasmāt*) from the phrase "from this [it] is born" (*etasmāj jāyate*) has been considered, it is altogether improper to explain the meaning through such verbal formulations as "From this is born the vital breath (*prāṇa*); from the vital breath, the mind (*manas*); from the mind, the senses (*indriyāṇi*); from the senses, space (*kha*)" and so forth, involving the supply of preceding terms and the modification of their grammatical forms.

Furthermore, in the passage "from this Brahman," there is a disparity: the direct origination of the breath (*prāṇa*)—which is the self that has become the cause of Brahman—is stated, whereas the origination of the mind (*manas*) and the rest is said to occur through a succession. Since consistency is possible, an interpretation based on such disparity is indeed inferior. Moreover, in the *Subālopaniṣad* and elsewhere, as well as in many *smṛtis*, *itihāsas*, and *purāṇas*, there are accounts stating: "The earth dissolves into water," and so forth; that the creation of the mind proceeds from the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the creation of the senses from the mind, and the creation of space (*ākāśa*) from the senses.

Here too, having raised the objection of "unestablished sequence" (anyathāsiddhi), he refutes it with the passage beginning with "prāṇa" and ending with "atiprasaṅgāt. The meaning is this: indeed, your intention is that in the passage "Space [is] Air," the very sequence established by another scriptural text is perceived, on account of the indicative mark of its being recited together with that [other text].

Regarding the statement “the mind [is the source] of all the senses,” one must follow the very order of the text; thus, the alternative order well-known from the *Subāla Upaniṣad* and other sources is set aside. However, this is without substance, for it is logical to explain the meaning of a single, unestablished sentence in accordance with many established statements, rather than imagining the opposite. This is because imagining a meaning contrary to logic would result in the abandonment of the entire scripture. Therefore, the sequence is not intended here.

Moreover, the universe originates from Brahman itself, which is distinguished by each preceding reality (*tattva*). To show that the scripture itself supports this point, he states another reason: "Because of [the act of] seeing" (*īkṣā*). In passages such as "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), "That heat thought" (*tatteja aikṣata*), and "Those waters thought" (*tā āpa aikṣanta*), the act of seeing is seen to be continuously present in Brahman, which serves as the cause. And that [act of seeing] is logical only if the universe originates from Brahman as qualified by those respective realities; this has been established everywhere in the scripture, beginning with the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa*.

He concludes the stated point with the word "firstly": just as Brahman, having the *prakṛti* as its body, creates the principle of *mahat*, so too Brahman, having the *mahat* as its body, creates the *ahaṅkāra*; in this manner, the sequence should be applied down to the earth.

The connection here is stated in the Commentary with the words "of ether and so forth," and so on. This is the intended meaning: in the section concerning ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*), the production of ether and the other elements—which had been accepted as eternal by the opponents—was established. In the immediately following section, however, [the same is treated] in the fourth quarter of the second chapter.

Here, [the author] raises an objection regarding the commencement of another section on the grounds that there is no increase in purpose, and then provides a resolution, beginning with the words "akṣādi" (senses, etc.). The meaning of the words here is as follows: the demonstration of the non-origination of the Self and the demonstration of its nature as a knower must indeed be undertaken because they possess specific results. However, the discussion of the origination of the senses and so forth, which are of the nature of insentient particulars, serves only the purpose of removing extreme misconceptions. If it is argued that a new section is commenced merely to dispel some minor doubt, even that is not clearly seen here.

This is what he means by saying "insignificant. Anticipating the objection that there is indeed a superior fruit in the thorough knowledge of the number of the sense organs and so forth, he says, "of their number, etc. For there is no purpose whatsoever in knowing the number of crows' teeth; likewise, we perceive no fruit at all in the detailed knowledge of whether the sense organs are eleven or six, and so on. He rejects the suggested point with the word "no" (na). He clarifies the reason for this rejection with the words "in these," etc.

In the present context as well, it has indeed been proposed that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is an effect of Brahman. If the status of certain things as effects of Brahman were not established, some dull-witted person might experience doubt or lack of comprehension due to apparent contradictions in the scriptures. For the author of the Sūtras undertakes his work solely for the sake of favoring his disciples. Therefore, the commencement of this section (pāda) for the purpose of purifying [the understanding of] the effects such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is indeed meaningful.

In this regard, there is a distinction: the first section, which establishes that [the creation] is the work of the Prāṇa, and the final section, "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the scriptural teaching," have a direct connection with the present context, whereas the intermediate sections have a contextual (incidental) connection.

In this quarter (pāda), he again demonstrates the number of topics, the distinction between their subject matters, and the purpose of each respective topic by stating "eight. Eight topics are declared here in this quarter. Among them, in the first topic, the principle regarding space (viyat) and the sense organs is stated.

Just as the origin of ether was stated in the section on ether (*viyatpāda*), so too is the origin of the sense organs stated here in the section on breath (*prāṇapāda*). Although the origin of the eyes and other organs is asserted by both the followers of Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣikas) and those of Akṣapāda (Nyāya), their origin is not asserted for the mind (*manas*); therefore, because it provides a specific point of refutation, the commencement of this section is indeed purposeful.

He states the purpose of the final section [of the book] with the words "tejo'banna" (fire, water, and food). The sense is that, just as it was established that the Supreme Self, having fire, water, and food as its body, performs successive effects during the creation of the aggregate (samashți), so too, by establishing that the Supreme Self, having the four-faced Brahmā and others as its body, performs their respective functions during the creation of the individual (vyashți), the final section is indeed purposeful.

Anticipating the objection that the consideration of number, transformation, and so forth in the middle [of the section] is for what purpose, since it is not useful for establishing the relationship between cause and effect, he says: "Number. Even in the consideration of the number, magnitude, and other attributes of the senses, there is a purpose because, within those specific branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), one meditates upon the Supreme Self as qualified by those respective numbers, magnitudes, and so on; and according to the maxim that "a cognition does not grasp its qualifiers unless they are themselves apprehended," all such consideration in this section is indeed fruitful.

He states its fruitfulness by another method as well, beginning with the words "from the vital breath and so forth. By such statements as, "The individual soul is other than the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and intellect, and is the means for their mutual functioning," the individual soul (jīvātman) is indicated by Yāmunācārya and others as being superior to the body and the rest. In that regard, the investigation into specific details such as size and number is indeed purposeful; thus, this entire section (pāda) is fruitful.

Regarding this, the connection between the sections is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "When it has been declared that everything other than Brahman, such as the ether and so forth, arises as an effect, [the author] has refuted the idea that for the individual soul (*jīva*), even though it is an effect, there is an arising characterized by a change in its essential nature (*svarūpa-anyathābhāva*). In connection with that, the essential nature of the soul was purified."

"Now, the manner of the origin and so forth of the senses—the instruments of the individual soul (jīva)—and of the vital breath (prāṇa) is being clarified. The investigation into that matter is as follows: do the senses not originate, like the individual soul, or do they originate, like ether (viyat) and the other elements? Does the scriptural statement, "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses," establish their origination or not?

Does the word *prāṇa* refer to the sense organs (*indriya*) or to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? Does the word *ṛṣi* in the passage, "The *ṛṣis* are indeed the *prāṇas*," lead one to conclude that the word *prāṇa* refers to the Supreme Self, or not? Here, the author refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) by beginning with the words "In the beginning... and so forth. "In the beginning, this world was non-existent (*asat*). Regarding this, they ask: 'What existed then? The *ṛṣis* indeed existed then as that non-existence. Regarding this, they ask: 'Who were those *ṛṣis? The *prāṇas* indeed were those *ṛṣis*. It cannot be said that this [passage] is intended to state what occurred at the time of the world's creation. [The term used is] "*ṛṣayaḥ*" (the *ṛṣis*).

The statement that "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*) refers to the senses because of the contradiction with the plural number, and that this establishes the eternity of the senses, is a restatement of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). The author refutes it, saying: "Not so. Because there are hundreds of passages in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas that speak of the creation of the senses, a statement asserting their existence at the time of dissolution is simply not tenable. If it is then argued that there remains the contradiction with the plural number, that too is not a fault; for, as in the case of the mantra "the bonds of Aditi" (*aditiḥ pāśān*), plurality is used figuratively (*aupacārika*). Indeed, in the section concerning the "bonds" (*pāśādhikaraṇa*), the plurality of the bonds [is explained as being figurative].

Since the oneness of the *pāśa* (the bond) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the elders of the Nyāya school have determined that [the plural number] refers to the multiplicity of the parts of the *pāśa*. Therefore, because there is a multiplicity of attributes constituting Brahman as qualified by sentient and insentient beings, the use of the plural number is indeed appropriate. He states this very point with the words, "the plural number. Now, one might object: "The status of being a 'means of knowledge' (*pramāṇatva*) is well-known in the case of the sense organs; and since the status of being a 'seer' (*ṛṣitva*) is also somehow possible for them due to their nature as indicators, why should it not apply to the Supreme Self? Anticipating this, he says, "regarding the state of being the vital breath and the seer. Since He is the cause of the vitalizing function (*prāṇana*) of all living beings, His state of being the "vital breath" (*prāṇatva*) is certainly appropriate. Furthermore, His state of being the "seer" (*ṛṣitva*) is likewise [appropriate] in the Supreme Self.

This is all the more appropriate because of his seniority in wisdom (*jñānavṛddhatva*). He states this with the word "that" (*tat*). If the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is the same, and if the conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is also the same—since it can be asserted by us as well that the conventional usage applies to Brahman alone—or else, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the abundance of usage (*prayogaprācurya*) is intended.

Thus, the nature of the sense organs as effects has been stated. Now, their number is also being considered; this is the connection [of the topic]. The inquiry into that matter is: are there seven sense organs, or are there eleven? Does the scriptural mention of the movement of seven—"These seven persons move within them"—imply that the sense organs are seven in number, or not? [The opponent asks: Is it not so because the hands and other limbs do not move along with the individual soul (*jīva*), and because they are beneficial to the person and exist in the body only by depending on the vital breath (*prāṇa*)? [The proponent asks: What of the statement, "These ten, and the one who..."?

The statement, “The vital breaths (prāṇāḥ) are a part of the Self,” indicates that those designated by the word *prāṇa*—numbering eleven—are indeed the sense organs (*indriya*), and not otherwise. Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: “There are seven vital breaths. The number seven of the vital breaths is declared in the scripture: “Seven vital breaths move about. Furthermore, they are specifically mentioned in the context of yoga, in the passage establishing yoga: “When the five [perceptual] knowledges, together with the mind, come to rest, and the intellect does not stir—that, they say, is the supreme goal. Thus, the number of the vital breaths is seven.

This is the meaning. Because it consists of going toward the supreme goal—that is, liberation—it is called *yoga*. Since it is established in this manner, there are exactly seven sense organs (*indriya*). He refutes this by saying, "It is not so. He states the reason for this as "because of the mention of more" (*adhika*). Since other passages speak of a greater number of sense organs, the statement that there are seven is intended for another purpose. This has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The designations of fewer [organs] in various places are prompted by specific functions, such as movement, which are intended to be discussed therein. However, the number seven does not apply to the sense organs in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, the number seven is stated by way of their movement through the seven worlds; and that movement is indicative of all eleven [faculties] on the strength of authoritative evidence. When the word "five" does not refer to a numerical count in the context of establishing the supreme goal, then—given that the status of being a faculty belongs to all eleven faculties by virtue of possessing the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa)—one might ask: "What then is that characteristic? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The characteristic... (lakṣma).

The meaning is this: the definition of a sense organ (*indriya*) is being a modification of the substance of *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). This is indeed common to all eleven. If so, why is the mind mentioned separately in the statement "the five internal organs together with the mind," when the other five organs have already been mentioned in general? To this, he states the specific purpose by saying "by way of distinction. The point is that this separate mention of the mind—both from the [external] organs and from the cognitive organs—is fruitful insofar as it demonstrates its preeminence.

In this quarter, having described the specific modes of acceptance for the various positions regarding the diversity [of sense organs], he says "deha" (the body), implying that their refutation is also established by the very force of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). Some say: there is only one sense organ pervading the body; it is designated as manifold due to its residence in specific locations such as the hands and feet which constitute the limbs of the body, and it performs various functions. Others, however—those who have turned their faces away from the words of the Vedas, such as the followers of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda—have abandoned the organs of action through their petty logic, asserting that only the organs of knowledge exist.

"Not the ear, etc., as organs. Others, however, on the mere basis of hearing the Purāṇas and other texts, assert that the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the person (puruṣa), possesses fourteen organs along with the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and mind (citta). Yet others have declared that there are thirteen instruments (karaṇa), excluding the mind. The author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) has refuted them by implication through his demonstration that there are eleven [organs]; the meaning is that the rejection of numbers both less than and greater than this is established here as a matter of course.

The enumeration of the sense organs has been stated; now their essential nature and dimension are being considered—this is the connection [of the topic]. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: are the sense organs all-pervading (*sarvagata*), or are they of the size of atoms (*paramāṇu*)? Does the statement regarding their infinity in the passage, "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite," lead one to understand their all-pervasiveness or not? Is the hearing of their infinity intended to signify a multiplicity of results for the practice of meditation—as in, "Now, he who meditates upon these as infinite"—or is it intended to signify their all-pervasiveness? Thus [the doubt].

Regarding the scriptural statement on departure, "When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs, all the vital breaths depart," the question arises whether this indicates that the senses are minute because they are limited yet not perceptible, or not. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is presented: "In all [the senses]" and so forth.

Since there is a scriptural reading of the infinity of all the senses—stating that "all these are equal and infinite"—and since no specific limitation of measure is mentioned for each sense such as "this is the measure of this particular sense," it follows that the pervasiveness of the senses is established. This [view] is rejected with the word "no."

Regarding the phrase "because of their departure from the body": the meaning is that when all [the senses] depart from the body, they go to another place and then return again. Now, raising the objection as to how there could be the perception of distant objects if the sense organs were atomic in size, he says: "by means of their function (*vṛtti*). It is stated elsewhere that "function consists of the material elements used for nourishment. Function is an extension; for that [extension] arises through the nourishing elements. This is the meaning.

Even though the sense organs are atomic (*aṇu*), although they lack pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) by virtue of their own essential nature, a state of pervasiveness is nonetheless established through the elements that nourish them, consisting in the apprehension of all objects existing within the interior of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). This is just as the followers of Kaṇāda maintain: although the eye resides within the cavity of the socket, it perceives objects located within the cosmic egg due to its light radiating in all directions. Thus, the statement regarding the infinity of the sense organs in passages intended for the injunctions of their worship is [figurative].

Anticipating the objection, "How so?", he says, "by their own effects. This means by the effects of the sense organs. For even though the sense organs are limited in number, it is indeed observed—just like the light of a lamp—that they grasp innumerable objects when there is an absence of obstacles. Now, one might object: "If the sense organs reside within the heart itself—the root of all the senses—within those various bodies, how can there be extensiveness? Anticipating this, he says, "the root" (kanda). The meaning is that extensiveness is logical because, being composed of transformable fluid matter, they spread out in all directions.

On the basis of the fact that the production of the *śreṣṭha-prāṇa* (the chief vital breath) is established by the same reasoning as before, an investigation is now conducted regarding its specific nature. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is the *śreṣṭha-prāṇa* merely the element of air or its activity, or is it air having attained a particular state?

Here, according to the reasoning previously stated, the fact that even the preeminent *prāṇa* is produced by another has already been established. Its true nature is now being investigated: is it merely the air (*vāyu*) within the body, or is it merely its activity? He restates this [dilemma] with the words "the breath. He denies both possibilities with the word "no. He provides the reason for this with the word "separately," because of the statement regarding the separate origin of *prāṇa* from the [Supreme Self]—namely, "From Him is born *prāṇa*, mind, and all the senses"—and because of the declaration that it is distinct from the air mentioned in the passage "ether, air, light," etc., within the category of substances.

And because of its being mentioned [in the list], it is indeed a substance; thus, the status of being air (*vāyutva*) and the status of being the movement of air (*vāyukriyātva*) have been refuted. Anticipating the objection that it might therefore be a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*), he refutes it. He states the reason for the absence of its being a distinct principle with the words "In the state of fire" (*tejastve*) and so forth. If, by abandoning the state of air and abandoning the state of fire, there were the attainment of the state of vital breath (*prāṇatva*), then it would be a distinct principle; but this is not the case. Therefore, the vital breath is merely a particular state of air.

In the passage beginning with "And [He is] the best," it is established by the same reasoning that the preeminent vital breath (*prāṇa*) is also an effect of Brahman; its specific nature was described in the sūtra, "Or rather [it is] not [Brahman], because of the separate instruction regarding Vāyu. Now, however, its atomicity (*aṇutva*) is further elaborated.

The investigation into its meaning, however, concerns whether the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is all-pervading or atomic. Does the designation of infinity in the passage, "He is equal to these three worlds," lead one to understand its omnipresence (*vibhutva*), or not? Does the scriptural mention of the movement of the breath in the passage, "When the breath departs, all the vital breaths depart," indicate that the hearing of its infinity is figurative—intended as praise because its stability depends upon [the Self]—or not? In this regard, because of the statement of equality with the three worlds, "He is equal to these three worlds," he...

With the words beginning with "it has been said," the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "May [the prāṇa] be all-pervading. He refutes that position with the word "improper" (*ayuktam*). He provides the reason for this with the word "jīva": the departure (*utkrānti*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), the sense organs, and likewise of the *prāṇa* from the body is heard in scripture; therefore, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is not tenable, because [otherwise] there would be a contradiction regarding its departure, going, and returning. Anticipating the objection—"How can the scriptural texts concerning universal equality, such as 'He is equal to these three worlds,' be explained here?"—he resolves it by stating that they are "for the purpose of praise" (*stutyartha*). He further provides the reason even for their being for the purpose of praise with the word "instruments" (*karaṇa*).

The meaning is this: in the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the cause of the instruments, the field, and sustenance, there exists the quality of being highly beneficial toward the body. And that breath is divided tenfold by its various functions (vṛtti). For wind is seen to be fivefold in the form of prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna. Likewise, there are five winds distinguished as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya, well-known in the Ayurveda and other sciences and detailed in the Yoga-tantras; they are differentiated according to their specific ways of assisting [the body]. Therefore, it is appropriate that [the breath] is the object of praise.

The connection here is stated in the Commentary: "The origin of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from Brahman, along with their excellence and their specific measure, has been declared. Furthermore, the fact that these vital breaths are presided over by deities such as Agni was already established in the context of the previous discussion by the sūtra: 'But there is designation of the presiding deities because of the distinction and the following [of the breaths]' (*abhimānivyapadeśastu viśeṣānugatibhyām*). Moreover, it is well known in the world that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the presiding controller of these means for its own experience."

This is also established by such scriptural passages as: "In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths (prāṇas), he moves about at will within his own body. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether this presiding over the vital breaths by the individual soul (jīva) and the deities such as Fire is dependent upon itself or dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātman): [The opponent argues: It is dependent upon itself. Why? Because of the independence [implied] by the mention of "at will" (yathākāmam). Furthermore, the scripture states: "He, becoming Yama, goes along with death; he, becoming Agni, leads forward the oblation; he, becoming Vāyu, moves through both the worlds; becoming the moon, he presides over the nakṣatras; becoming Brāhmaṇa, he rules over the people; becoming Rudra, he watches over the creatures; becoming Indra, he protects the hosts; becoming Viṣṇu, he traverses the three strides. Since these various activities—such as going along with death, leading the oblation, moving through the worlds, presiding over the nakṣatras, ruling the people, watching over creatures, protecting the hosts, and traversing the three strides—are impossible for the Supreme Self, they must belong to the individual soul. Moreover, the scripture says: "He who dwells in the breath and controls the breath from within," and so on, which shows that the individual soul presides over the breaths. Therefore, the presiding over the vital breaths is independent. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. Why? Because of the statement of dependence. For the scripture declares the dependence of the individual soul and the deities upon the Supreme Self: "Entered within, the ruler of all beings, the self of all, who makes his one form manifold"—and so forth. Furthermore, the scripture says: "He who dwells in the breath and controls the breath from within—he is your self (ātman), the inner ruler, the immortal. The term "self" (ātman) here refers to the Supreme Self, as is known from its usage in other contexts. Moreover, the scripture says: "He who dwells in the earth and controls the earth from within," and so on, showing that the Supreme Self presides over the earth and other elements. Since the individual soul and the deities are subject to His control, their presiding over the vital breaths is necessarily dependent upon Him. As for the mention of "at will," that is intended to show the absence of external instruments of action, not the absence of dependence on the Supreme Self. Therefore, the presiding over the vital breaths is dependent upon the Supreme Self. Furthermore, the scripture says: "When the breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it," which indicates that the departure and remaining of the vital breaths are governed by the Supreme Self. Thus, the conclusion is that the presiding over the vital breaths by the individual soul and the deities is dependent upon the Supreme Self.

The investigation into that matter concerns whether the luminaries and so forth—namely fire and the other elements—as well as the individual soul who presides over the sense organs, are dependent upon the Supreme Self or independent. Is the perception of their independence found here and there correct, or is it rooted in error? Is there any subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the perception of such independence? Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "Of the experiencers" and so on. This refers to the individual souls who are the experiencers within their respective bodies, as well as the deities such as Fire who are the presiding agents of the eyes and other senses.

"The presiding over the body, senses, and so forth, is not dependent upon God, because [the soul] is granted independence. This is the meaning: God indeed bestows independence upon all sentient beings in general by granting them knowledge, volition, effort, and so on. It would therefore be logical that the individual soul (jīva), having been granted independence by that Lord, should itself engage in the presiding over the instruments, the body, and the rest. He refutes this with "no" (na). He explains that very point with the words "tanubhṛtaḥ" (of those who bear bodies).

This is the meaning: all embodied living beings are indeed the body of the Lord. And they have determined that a body is necessarily presided over, necessarily governed, and necessarily subservient [to another]. Therefore, living beings are invariably dependent on another. This is because it is established by hundreds of authoritative proofs such as, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," and "Without Him, not even the tip of a blade of grass exists. Consequently, the general rule of sovereignty does not apply at all to one who is dependent upon the Lord.

Indeed, even vassals, though possessing independence in matters such as breathing, thinking, and blinking, do not act contrary to the king's command. But in those who are dependent upon God, there is not even a scent of independence. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "as the vital breaths. For one does not breathe only in the waking state, but also in the state of deep sleep. It is your own established doctrine that one in deep sleep does not engage in breathing and so forth with an independent consciousness, but rather is impelled solely by God.

If one objects: "In that case, how can the individual soul (jīva) possess sovereignty over the range of effects, given its lack of independence in impelling the instruments [of action]?"—the author provides the following rebuttal: "Sovereignty" means that even the sovereignty of living beings over their own sphere of capability is entirely dependent upon the Supreme Self, because the soul acts as an *prayojya-kartṛ* (an instigated agent), whereas God alone is the *prayojaka-kartṛ* (the instigating agent). Furthermore, the term "over what is possible for itself" (*sva-śakyataḥ*) is stated in order to assert that there is no possibility of agency regarding impossible tasks, such as leaping across the ocean.

Previously, it was stated that upon the departure of the individual soul (*jīva*), "the principal breath (*prāṇa*) departs after him, and as the principal breath departs, all the breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) depart after it. In that context, the present section is commenced again for the purpose of establishing a specific rule of usage: whether the term "sense-organ" (*indriya*) applies to all the breaths, or only to those distinct from the principal breath. This constitutes the connection (*saṅgati*).

The investigation into that meaning, however, is as follows: Are all "prāṇas" sense organs (*indriyas*), or are they distinct from the principal *prāṇa*? Does the word "prāṇa" apply to the ear and other senses, as well as to the principal *prāṇa*, on the basis of a single etymological ground, or on the basis of different grounds? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the *prāṇa* is also a sense organ (*hṛṣīka*).

"May it be so. "Exceedingly so. For it is indeed the very nature of the sense organs (*indriya*) to be beneficial to the living being (*jīva*); however, that [benefit] is accomplished through the departure (*utkrānti*) and other functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is observed in the world. Therefore, the vital breath alone is the primary sense organ. He negates what was stated with "No. He states the reason for this with the word "separately" (*pṛthak*).

Regarding the statements, "From this [Self] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind (manas), and all the sense organs," and "When the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart following it," since the vital breath is mentioned separately, it is distinct from the sense organs. To the objection that, by the same logic, the mind must also not be a sense organ because it is mentioned separately in the phrase "the mind and all the sense organs," the author provides the resolution: "Because it is explicitly stated [as such]."

Regarding the phrase "the senses with the mind as the sixth," since the mind is explicitly stated to be a sense organ, its status as a sense organ is indeed established so that there may be no abandonment of what has been heard in scripture. One might then raise the objection that since "the senses" were mentioned in general terms, stating specifically that the mind is a sense organ is redundant; anticipating this, he resolves it by saying, "it is like the maxim of the cow and the bull. He further states another point of distinction: "but not the vital breath (prāṇa)."

The definition of a sense organ (*indriya*) is indeed being a modification of the *sāttvika* ego; since that [definition] exists in the mind (*manas*), but because the vital breath (*prāṇa*) lacks that defining characteristic, it does not possess the status of a sense organ. Having raised the weak objection that it might nonetheless be a sense organ merely by virtue of being denotable by the word "prāṇa," he refutes it with the words "sound" (*śabda*). For the meaning is that the Vibhītaka tree and others do not possess the status of a sense organ merely by being denotable by the word "akṣa" (axle/tree), nor do the senses and so forth possess the status of a specific type of tree.

Regarding this, the *peṭikā-saṅgati* (the thematic connection of the section) in the Commentary states: "It was previously stated [in the third quarter] that the collective creation of the elements, the sense organs, and so forth, as well as the agency of individual souls, proceeds from the Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, it was reiterated for the sake of stabilization that the individual souls' presiding over their own sense organs is dependent upon the Supreme Self."

(The meaning is: immediately following this [in this section]. Now it is considered whether this creation of the individual world (*vyāṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), consisting of the manifestation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*), is the work of Hiraṇyagarbha alone—who is the collective soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*)—or rather, whether it belongs to the Supreme Brahman who has Hiraṇyagarbha as His body, just as He created fire and the other elements while having them as His bodies. Thus [it is said].

This is the meaning: here, beginning from the third quarter (*pāda*), there is one section (*peṭikā*) prior to this point. Within that, the description of the creation of the aggregate of the elements and the senses, followed by the description of the individual creation (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*), constitutes the coherence of the section. Furthermore, because the individual creation serves as an instrument (*upakaraṇa*), the description of its creation constitutes the coherence of the quarter (*pāda*).

In the preceding section, the agency of the Supreme Self was stated in passages such as "Space, wind, fire... Now, however, there arises an intermediate connection by way of raising a doubt: that the creation of individual manifestations (vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi) appears to have the individual self (jīvātman) as its agent. Furthermore, this is intended: the origin and so forth of the vital breaths (prāṇas), which are the instruments of the individual self, have been examined.

For it was stated that the creation of the individual (vyaṣṭi) is the act of the Supreme Self (paramātman) consisting in the bringing about of the soul's conjunction with those [organs]; now, however, there arises a doubt that the creation of the individual appears to have the individual soul (jīvātman) as its agent. This constitutes the intermediate connection (avāntarasaṅgati). Furthermore, this is intended: the origin and so forth of the vital breaths (prāṇas), which are the instruments of the soul, have been described; and the connection is that the creation of the individual consists in the bringing about of the soul's conjunction with them.

The investigation into that matter is as follows: Is it logically tenable that the scripture teaches Brahman’s direct causality of all things, or is it not? For that purpose, one must determine whether the manifestation of individual names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) has Hiraṇyagarbha alone as its agent, or whether it has Brahman in that state as its agent. For that purpose, one must determine whether the scriptural statement regarding the agency of the generic soul—“by this living self” (*anena jīvena*)—implies that it is the agency of Hiraṇyagarbha alone, who is the substratum of the collective totality of souls (*jīvasamaṣṭi*), or whether it implies that it is the agency of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as qualified by the individual souls (*jīva*).
