For that purpose, is it possible for there to be a single agent for both the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) as they are heard in scripture, given that [the latter] has Hiraṇyagarbha alone as its agent? For that purpose, is the agency of Hiraṇyagarbha possible regarding the tripartition, or not? For that purpose, does the tripartition occur after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), which is the place of origin for Hiraṇyagarbha, or before it? For that purpose, [does the text say]: "He differentiated names and forms"?

Regarding the statement, "He made each of them threefold, threefold," does the order of the text—which demonstrates the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) occurring within the cosmic egg—and the scriptural account of the tripartition of food and the other elements, lead us to understand that this tripartition takes place after the creation of the egg, or not? Are these three reasons strong or weak?

If those [arguments] were stronger, then since the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) would be understood as occurring after the creation of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), it could possibly have Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent; thus, the scriptural statement regarding the identity of the agents of tripartition and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) would be justified. Consequently, the reference "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) would indicate that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the agent, and the differentiation of individual names and forms would belong to Hiraṇyagarbha alone. In that case, the Supreme Brahman’s status as the direct cause of all things would not be established.

Since the order of recitation and other criteria are weak, it is not established that the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) occurs after the creation of the cosmic egg; consequently, because Hiraṇyagarbha cannot be the agent therein, it is impossible for there to be identity of agent between the tripartition and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*). To justify this, the phrase "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) indicates that the tripartition is performed by the Supreme Self whose body is the aggregate of individual selves (*jīvasamaṣṭiśarīraka*); thus, the differentiation of individual names and forms (*vyaṣṭināmarūpavyākaraṇa*) is performed by the Supreme Self whose body is Hiraṇyagarbha.

Thus it is established that the status of the Supreme Brahman as the direct cause of all is logically consistent. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) maintains: Manu and other great sages state and record in their Smṛtis that the dweller in the lotus (Brahmā) alone is the agent of the differentiation of names and forms, as in the verse, "And [He is the creator] of the names and forms of beings. Nor is this merely a Smṛti; there is also Śruti: "By means of this living self (jīva). Therefore, he suspects that the sequence of action here is like that of a servant, such that one must enter by way of a messenger and then marshal the enemy forces; thus he says, "by Manu and others."

It was stated that [the objection] does not fall into being without a counter-argument; he explains that very point with the words "one. For it is taught that there is indeed one creator: "Having entered by means of this living self," "He made each of those threefold," and "He unfolded name and form. By this, the fact that the three [acts] have a single agent is established. Then, raising the doubt as to how the Supreme Self can be the agent when the four-faced Brahmā is the agent, he says "that and that."

Just as in passages such as "That fire thought" and "It created the waters," the agency belongs to the Supreme Self as qualified by fire and so forth; likewise, the meaning is that the Supreme Self alone, as qualified by the four-faced Brahmā and others, is the cause even in the creation of the collective totality (samaṣṭi).

Having here refuted by means of his own position the method propounded by the opposing school, he concludes with the words "yā jīvena" (that which [is done] by the individual soul), clarifying the meaning of the scriptural passage "anena jīvena" for the instruction of his disciples. The Śruti statement "anena jīvenātmanā" does not declare the identity of the individual soul and Brahman; for the eternal distinction between them has already been established previously through the Śruti, Smṛti, Sūtras, and their supporting commentaries, such as: "The one alone is the inner Self; all things are His body."

Having thus refuted the view of others, [the author] concludes with the word "tena" (by that) that the agency in the differentiation of names and forms, as well as in the subsequent entry, belongs to the Supreme Self alone, albeit in a mode qualified by the individual soul (*jīva*). Because it has been established in this way, the agent in the differentiation of names and forms and in the entry is indeed the one qualified by that [soul], specifically qualified by the individual soul. This is because the soul is His instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being His body; for the word *karaṇa* can denote the limbs of the body, according to the rule: "The word *karaṇa* refers to the most effective means (*sādhakatama*), as well as to the field, the limbs, and the senses. Alternatively, it means by virtue of the soul being the most effective means of the Self itself. For it is the Lord who is intended here, according to the principle: "The factors of action (*kāraka*s) become [the agent]."

According to logic, it can be designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*) by virtue of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*). Its status as the independent agent (*kartṛ*) is indeed well-established through common usage. Regarding the position that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the agent of entry, he states the primary defect: "The individual soul. The scriptural statement regarding the individual soul's agency in entry is not tenable, because the individual soul is the agent of entry while the Lord is the one who differentiates names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākartṛ*).

Now, an objector might say: "In the case of fire and other elements existing within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), a threefold nature has been stated through various forms, such as in the passage beginning, 'That which is the red form of fire. And in passages such as, 'Food, when eaten, becomes divided into three parts,' this very process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) is clearly explained; therefore, the agency of triplication belongs to Caturmukha (Brahmā) alone. Such is what some dull-witted person asserts with the words "in fire and so forth. He refutes that with "not so," and explains that very point with the words "the cosmic egg... and so on.

In the verse beginning with “nānāvīryāḥ,” it is stated that only the elements already made tripartite (trivṛtkṛta) possess the capacity for creation. [One might ask: if there was no prior tripartition before the creation of the cosmic egg, how could the creation of the Brahmāṇḍa occur? As for the statement, “Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts,” that merely refers to a threefold transformation, not to tripartition itself. For tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) means the unification of three things, not their division. This is the threefold transformation mentioned here;
the other [statement] means that one observes the proximity of one element within the others among the elements.

In this quarter (pāda), he explains the meanings of the eight topics by dividing them, beginning with the words "of the senses" (akṣāṇām) and so forth: the birth of the senses; their number as eleven; their dimension, namely atomicity (aṇutva); the nature of the principal vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa); the atomicity of that very principal vital breath; the dependence of the deities and the individual souls upon the principal and secondary vital breaths as their substrate; therein, the non-sensory nature of the principal vital breath; and the differentiation of names and forms of the various individual manifestations of the sentient and insentient.

These matters have been clearly explained in the Prāṇapāda [of the Pañcapādikā]: that [the individual soul] arises from the Supreme Person, who is the Supreme Brahman Himself—the primordial source from whose own navel the four-faced body (Brahmā) emerged, who is the cause of the creation of the aggregate through His bodies of fire, water, earth, and so forth, and who is the cause of the quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) for the purpose of creating those respective effects.

The refutation of the opponent's position has already been accomplished by the first two quarters [of the verse]. To someone who might inquire as an utter child, "What remains to be refuted in these latter two quarters?", he proceeds here to state the positions to be refuted in succession, beginning with "permanence" (*nityatvam*) and so forth.

In the section concerning the ether (*viyad-adhikaraṇa*), [the following misconceptions are addressed]: the eternity of space; the eternity of atoms such as air and so forth; the insentience of the *puruṣa* due to the absence of the nature of knowledge, like a stone; the nature of being ether (*ākāśatva*) in the sense organs such as the ear; the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) in the mind; the status of being a distinct eternal principle separate from material objects; the state of being a primary or secondary vital breath (*prāṇa*) apart from the category of eternal principles; the attribution of the status of the Self (*ātman*) to the host of celestial beings and the assembly of deities; and likewise, the agency of living beings (*jīvas*) through independence in governing those subject to their own control.

The meaning is that the defeat of those disputants—who claim independent agency in their own instruments and who assert that even the Grandfather (Brahmā), the lord of the immortals, possesses the power of independently fashioning names and forms through the sequence of a mechanical process—occurs at these two feet.

He states, beginning with "by means of reasonings" (*tarka*), that the chapter on non-contradiction (*avirodhādhyāya*) is indeed not opposed to the position of the proponent of falsehood. Herein lies the dilemma: is the lack of contradiction asserted by means of reasonings that are conventionally true (*vyāvahārikasatya*), or by those that are ultimately true (*pāramārthikasatya*)? It cannot be the first, because if the reasonings establishing non-contradiction are only conventionally true, then contradiction would have been established in the ultimate sense. Nor can it be the second; for if you claim non-contradiction by means of reasonings that are, in reality, incorrect, then your own self-conceit is undermined.

If one were to establish the ultimate reality of an object distinct from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it would constitute a deviation from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*). This is what he means by saying “by those who know correctly. Having thus stated the refutation, he states the conclusion with the words “therefore. For this so-called “non-contradiction” is indeed contradictory for the proponent of the doctrine of illusion (*mṛṣāvādin*), who is bound by the intellect. Anticipating the objection—“How then do you refute the opposing position using reasonings that have been rejected by the author of the Sūtras on the grounds that ‘reasoning is not firmly established’?”—he says: “That [refutation] is scriptural... (*sautrī*).

Indeed, reasoning (tarka) is of two kinds: that which is contrary to the Vedas and that which is not contrary to them. Therefore, the statement regarding the instability of reasoning should be applied—according to the manner stated in the verse "the teaching of the Dharma by the Ṛṣis"—to refer specifically to reasoning that contradicts the Vedas. It does not, however, concern reasoning that constitutes the procedural methodology (itikartavyatā) of the Veda; so enough of this miserable effort at refuting such people.

Thus, the reflection on the first two sections (dvika), which concern the determination of the accomplished object (*siddhaviṣaya*), has been completed. Now, regarding the reflection on the latter two sections, which concern the determination of the object to be accomplished (*sādhyaviṣaya*): within the reflection on the means (*sādhana*) in the third section—prior to the portion of the object to be accomplished that is to be determined in the fourth chapter according to the order of origination—the connection between the sections (*dvikasaṅgati*) and the connection between the chapters (*adhyāyasaṅgati*) are all explained in detail in the Commentary itself starting with the words "Having transcended" (*atikrānta*). Therefore, they should be consulted there.

The connection between the two quarters (pādas) of the third chapter is also clearly stated in that very same commentary (*bhāṣya*): "And [the topics to be treated are] the means most conducive to the commencement of meditation, and the absence of thirst for anything other than the object to be attained. For the sake of establishing these, the defects of the individual soul (*jīva*) as it wanders through other worlds—whether waking, dreaming, deep asleep, or in a swoon—and the fact that the supreme Brahman is free from those defects and is a mine of auspicious qualities, are demonstrated in the first and second quarters."

The connection with the subsequent section will follow later. Here, someone raises an objection: "Is liberation something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) or not? If it is not, then the formulation of the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) would be rendered fruitless. If it is something to be accomplished, then that liberation would be transitory.

Consequently, how could there be final liberation (*apavarga*) characterized by the absence of rebirth? He refutes this, saying, "Not so. He demonstrates the manner of this refutation by stating, "Brahman... and so forth.

For a person who possesses external objects, [the self] must first be established as unestablished and then proven; anticipating the objection that, "in that case, because experience would be something to be proven, it would follow that it is impermanent," [the author] proceeds by means of the very method of the opponent's own system.

He dispels [the charge of] impermanence with the words, “by the contraction of the intellect” (*dhī-saṅkoca*). The very destruction of the contraction of knowledge is the experience of Brahman. Even opponents admit that although a cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*) is produced, it has no further destruction. Therefore, the meaning is that the experience of Brahman, being of the nature of a destruction, lacks a subsequent limit. This is the point: even in our own position, since we accept non-existence as a positive entity (*bhāvāntara-abhāva*), non-existence itself would be a positive entity. Furthermore, its permanence is established by the authority of the scriptural testimony: “And he does not return again.”

In the Vedānta system, the expansion of the intellect (dhi) is indeed innate; its contraction occurs due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). When that contraction ceases, the innate expansion alone remains; for this is explicitly stated by the Śruti itself in the passage: "And he becomes fit for infinity."

In this third chapter, he demonstrates the division of the subject matter between the two pairs of preceding and succeeding quarters, as well as the distinct meaning of all four quarters, by means of the phrase "by the two quarters. The meaning is that through the quarter on detachment (*vairāgya-pāda*) and the quarter on the two-fold marks (*ubhaya-liṅga-pāda*), he generates the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahma-vidyā-adhikāra*) in living beings (*bhavin*); subsequently, by means of both those quarters, he demonstrates that very same knowledge of Brahman together with its constituent limbs (*aṅga-sahitām*).

He demonstrates the distinctions in meaning among the four quarters (pādas) in sequence, beginning with "In sovereignty and so forth" (*aiśvaryādau*). The distinction is as follows: in the *Vairāgyapāda*, there is detachment from sovereignty and the like; in the *Ubhayaliṅgapāda*, there is the arising of unsurpassed longing for the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) who possesses boundless majesty; in the *Guṇopasaṃhārapāda*, there is the non-apprehension of differences between various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*); and in the *Vidyāṅgapāda*, there is the perfection of the requisites for knowledge. This is the division.

Regarding this, someone has raised an objection: "At the time of hearing the Vedānta, one who is already dispassionate from the very beginning engages [in the inquiry]; therefore, since dispassion is already established beforehand, it need not be cultivated again in the third and subsequent pādas. To this, he says: "saṃsāra... (In this Śārīraka-śāstra, the individual soul whose mind is distressed by the cycle of transmigration alone is the qualified seeker). Thus, dispassion is established at the very commencement of the treatise. Why, then, is a pāda on dispassion commenced here once again?

He offers a response by accepting half [of the objection], saying "True. For detachment (*vairāgya*) is indeed twofold: one is conducive to the hearing of the scriptures, and another is conducive to the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*). Since that [latter kind] is being defined here, there is no fruitlessness in the commencement of this chapter. He clarifies this very point with the words "having attained," etc.

"These indeed, O dear one, are hells compared to the abode of the Supreme Self"—this contemplation on heaven and the like as being equivalent to hell, in relation to the station of the Supreme Self, is useful for the commencement of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*); since this is established in this very chapter (*pāda*), the beginning of this chapter on detachment (*vairāgya*) is fruitful. He states this very point, saying that it would be appropriate at the commencement of the means to liberation (*mukti-upāya*), and he clarifies that same point by saying, "Hasten."

The Supreme Person, the Lord of all, has clearly realized His own nature; I, however, like an ordinary man, am merely fit for the experience of Him. Nevertheless, due to the power of karma, I wander in saṃsāra. Thus, one who possesses clearly perceived self-knowledge—like the prince who previously lived as a hunter—should hasten toward the uncontracted experience of Brahman by means of the perfect contemplation of his own true nature. This is the meaning.

In the preceding section, under the sūtra "But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the tripartition, because of the teaching," the matter of *mūrti* (form) was introduced. Now, however, setting aside one form, we investigate whether, upon reaching another form in another location, the soul goes enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) associated with the previous form, or not. The inquiry into that purpose is as follows: Does the individual soul (*jīva*), when going to another body, proceed enveloped by the subtle elements which are the seeds of the body, or does it proceed unenveloped?

Regarding the question and answer, "Do you know how, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'?", does this imply that the soul, enveloped [by subtle elements], moves upward, or not? Do the words "faith" (*śraddhā*) and so forth refer to substances such as water that have entered into particular states, or do they refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) enveloped by them?

Does the use of the word "Soma" in the passage, "This King Soma,"—which occurs in the context of the return of those who perform only sacrifices and works of public utility (iṣṭāpūrta) by way of the path of the fathers—indicate that the word "Soma" refers to the individual soul (jīva) possessing a somal body? Or does it not? [The opponent asks: Does the statement, "From that oblation, King Soma comes into being," make one understand that the word "Soma" refers to the individual soul possessing a somal body? Or not?

Here he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The soul is enveloped by the subtle elements" (*dehādhyam*). For a person who has departed from a previous body and reached another location, there is indeed the accomplishment of new bodies, sense organs, and so forth, corresponding to his karma and arising from *apūrva*, just as the objects of enjoyment are found there. Therefore, the hypothesis that he goes away already completely enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and the life-breaths (*prāṇādhyaiḥ*) taken from the previous body would involve unnecessary complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*).
Now, raising the objection—"How can the movement of the living being (*jīva*) be possible without a connection to the [gross] elements?"—he says: "Of the living being" (*jīvasya*).

For having a limited size is indeed the cause for movement; therefore, the movement of the atomic soul (jīva) is logically established precisely because of its atomicity. To assume that it is conjoined with another substance would be the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava). It is the Lord alone who, through the process of vitalization—expressed in the words, "He leads the prāṇa upward and the apāna downward"—produces the movement of the soul as well.

He rejects the aforementioned position with the words "not so. He explains that very point with the verse beginning "acting according to his own will" (*svacchanda*). Whatever is established by scripture as being done by the Lord must be accepted as such by those who follow authoritative means of knowledge. Furthermore, one should not cite defects such as "complexity" (*gaurava*) regarding the Lord's actions which are established by scripture; for proponents of logic (*nyāyavādinaḥ*) cite the defect of complexity only in the case of inferential postulation (*ānumānikī kalpanā*). Therefore, this statement of a reason—that it is improper to allege complexity regarding the Lord’s independent activity when His nature is determined by scripture—is beyond dispute.

Now, it is said by you that in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the individual soul (jīva) departs enveloped by the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma). In that regard, what is this word denoting the five elements? If it is argued that the word *śraddhā* itself, which denotes water, signifies the five elements by way of synecdoche (*upalakṣaṇanyāya*), then one might ask: how is the word *śraddhā* a denoter of water? Anticipating both these doubts, the author refutes them in succession with the words beginning "nānājātīya... and so forth.

The meaning is this: even in the world, people commonly refer to objects that consist of an aggregate of various substances by the name of the substance that predominates; this is clearly observed when a medicine containing a great deal of ghee is called simply "ghee. Furthermore, the word *śraddhā*, while denoting water, also refers to other elements conjoined with water. Anticipating the objection—"How can a word denoting one element denote another element?"—the author states "on account of predominance" (*prācuryāt*), explaining that because water is most abundant in the body, the word denoting water appropriately denotes the other elements as well.

The principle expressed by the word *śraddhā* (faith) is the same even for the word *āpaḥ* (waters), as in the passage: "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (*pañcamyām āhutāv āpaḥ puruṣavacaso bhavanti*). Thus he says, "In this way" (*evam*). If one then objects: "Why should creation not occur from a single element alone?"—anticipating this doubt, he says, "The individual manifestation" (*vyaṣṭim*). For it is observed that in all cases, such as the body and so forth, creation occurs only from elements that have been "pentadified" (*pañcīkṛta*). Furthermore, a relative gradation is also observed therein; indeed, the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*) in bodies arises precisely from the predominance of the respective imbalances among those elements.

He states that gradation [is established] by the word *tadita*. A second objection remains: how can the word *śraddhā* denote water? To this, the answer is given: "The word *śraddhā*... He provides the reason for this: "In the Vedic scripture (*nigama*). For in the Vedic scripture, it is said: "Water, indeed, is faith (*śraddhā*)," thus water is described by the designation *śraddhā*.

Anticipating the question, "What here are conceived as the five fires, what are the things to be offered, and who are the offerers? the text demonstrates all of this by stating, "The sky," and so forth. The five fires are: the sky, Parjanya (the rain-god), the earth, the man, and the woman. By the phrase "along with their adjuncts" (*saparikarān*), the inclusion of the necessary implements for the conceptualization of the fires is expressed. *Śraddhā* (faith), *soma*, rain, food, and semen are the things to be offered. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) called *śraddhā* becomes, through a gradual transformation, the forms of *soma*, rain, food, and semen.

"With the living" (sajīvam) means accompanied by the *jīva*, that is, the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*). The intended meaning is that the *jīva* as qualified by the subtle elements is to be offered, because the *jīva* alone is primary. The meaning is that they offer the extremely subtle vital breaths (*marut*) which sustain the body of the ancestors.

Regarding this, the connection [of the present section] with the commentary is as follows: It is recorded in scripture that those who perform only sacrifices, works of merit, and acts of charity travel by the path of the fathers via smoke and so forth, and return again at the conclusion of the fruits of their karma, according to the text: "Having gone as far as the end of their work, they return again by this very same path. In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether the soul descending returns possessed of a remainder of its works (*anuśaya*), or not.

The inquiry into that matter is as follows: Do those who return—having dwelt [in the world of the fathers] for as long as their allotted time lasts—return with residual karma (*sānuśaya*), or do they return without residual karma (*niranuśaya*)? Does the statement, "for as long as their allotted time lasts" (*yāvatsampātam*), lead us to understand that they return without residual karma—since the word *sampāta* refers to all karma rather than specifically to the karma set in motion for the yielding of results—or does it not?

In this context, does the word *sampāta* refer to action (*karman*) in general, or does it refer specifically to that action which is engaged in the process of yielding its fruit? Does the statement, "Those whose conduct here has been pleasant, they will quickly attain a pleasant womb," lead us to understand that the word *sampāta* refers to action engaged in the process of yielding its fruit, or not? And does the word *caraṇa* in the phrase "those of pleasant conduct" refer to mere behavior (*ācāra*), or does it refer to ritual action (*karman*)? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that it refers to sacrifices such as the *iṣṭāpūrta*.

Whatever *śrauta* and *smārta* ritual action one performs here, having experienced the fruit of all that even in another place such as heaven, one returns here again at its conclusion. Therefore, one returns without any residual karma (*niranuśaya*). "Residual karma" (*anuśaya*) refers to that collection of actions which lies latent within the self until the exhaustion of their results; thus, the opponent’s intention is that one returns only after having exhausted all karma by experiencing its fruits. He rejects that view, saying, "That is not so. He provides the reason for this: "Because it contradicts what is observed" (*dṛṣṭabādhāt*).

If all actions were experienced only in the next world, then upon returning immediately thereafter, the observed disparity—where some enter the womb of a *caṇḍāla* while others enter the womb of a *brāhmaṇa* according to their respective karma—would be contradicted. Furthermore, in the passage "having reached the end of that action," it is not heard [in the scripture] that one reaches the absolute end of the entire action; rather, having reached the end of the specific action being experienced, one returns along with another action. This is clearly consistent with the nature of the effect. He states another argument as well, beginning with "sukṛta-": [The text continues: "By the force of the momentum of good and evil deeds, they return again to this world. This indicates that there is a remainder of karma. Otherwise, if all karma were exhausted by experiencing its fruit in the other world, there would be no reason for them to return here again. Therefore, it is established that there is a remainder of karma. Moreover, the scripture says: "Those who perform good deeds go to a bright world, and those who perform evil deeds go to a dark world. If all karma were exhausted by experiencing its fruit in the other world, there would be no basis for the distinction between "bright" and "dark" worlds. Therefore, it is established that there is a remainder of karma. Furthermore, the scripture says: "Having enjoyed the fruits of their good deeds in heaven, they return to this mortal world. If all karma were exhausted by experiencing its fruit in the other world, there would be no basis for the mention of "having enjoyed the fruits of their good deeds. Therefore, it is established that there is a remainder of karma. And so on. Thus, it is proven that there is a remainder of karma. This is the meaning. "Those of pleasant conduct will attain a pleasant womb; those of foul conduct will attain a foul womb"—thus it is understood from the study of the different classes [of beings] as being the fruits of good and evil deeds. He concludes the stated point with the words "Therefore. By the phrase "by the remnants of what has begun, together with the other," the meaning is this: in the treatises on the distribution of karma, it is declared that for a single action, there is first the fruit such as heaven, and at its conclusion, further fruit pertaining to this world must also be experienced.

Therefore, it must be understood—without contradicting any means of valid knowledge—that even one who has begun to experience the fruits of their actions returns again, joined with the remainder of that unexhausted fruit as well as other intervening karmas; this is shown by the scriptural authority: "Those who desire objects of desire obtain the state of going and returning," which describes him as a traveler on the path to heaven.

In this regard, since the section of the Sūtra beginning with "yathetamanevañca" (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15) states the difference between going and returning, it demonstrates that very difference [with the words] "dhūmam" and so forth: "The deceased performer of ritual action reaches smoke, night, the dark fortnight, the six months when the sun moves southward, the world of the ancestors, and even the moon."

Upon returning, however, the journey proceeds from the moon to the sky, from the sky to the wind, from that to smoke, from that to mist (*abbhra*), and from mist to the cloud (*megha*). Here, the words *abbhra* and *megha* are not redundant because they differ in meaning; by the word *abbhra*, which is derived from the root *ap* (water) with the suffix *bhṛ* (to bear), it is simply called "that which bears water. Yet, by means of the specific form characterized by the state of pouring (*miha* = to sprinkle), that very same thing is called a "cloud" (*megha*).

"Vrīhyādīn" means rice and other grains that are to be consumed by the ancestors (*pitṛ*). "Retassig" refers to the progenitor. The grammatical construction is: "then he goes to the mother. "Yātanācakravartī" means one who exists within the wheel of torments (*yātanācakra*); or alternatively, one who is a sovereign (*cakravartī*) everywhere upon the path of saṃsāra.

In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) considers that what you have stated—that one descends by means of the remainder of previously performed karma and attains birth and so forth—is untenable; for by the scriptural passage beginning with "those of foul conduct [attain] a foul womb," it is specifically *caraṇa* (conduct) that is mentioned, and that consists merely of behavior. This he expresses with the words "conduct" (*ācāra*). For one who has arrived [in a new state], birth, experience, and so forth would be achievable through mere conduct alone, because of the mention of *caraṇa*.

Now, one might object: "Is conduct not itself action, and is action not itself conduct? Anticipating this doubt, he states the distinction with the word "action. For it is heard in scripture: "Those actions which are not censurable should be practiced; those which are our own good deeds [should be followed]. He rejects this view with the words "not so. He provides the reason for this: "because there is no other way" (*gatyabhāvāt*). Even though the term "conduct" (*ācāra*) denotes action, both "action" and "conduct" are observed in that same scriptural passage; therefore, such a statement is made for the sake of the meaningfulness of the terms, as there is no other alternative.

He establishes this very point with the words "the primary [meaning]. Even regarding action (*karman*), the term "conduct" (*caraṇa*) is used in its primary sense through both engagement and non-engagement; it is not to be restricted to a single part, namely mere behavior (*ācāra*). For the common usage is well-known in such expressions as "he performs a meritorious action" (*puṇyaṃ karma ācarati*) and "he performs a sinful action" (*pāpaṃ karma ācarati*). Thus, since caste and so forth arise from the distinctions of action, they constitute the ripening of action (*karmavipāka*).

The meaning is that since it is established by various scriptural passages—such as "the fallen one is born as a Caṇḍāla after death" and "one who has fallen from yoga is born into the house of the pure and the prosperous"—that which is accomplished through conduct is indeed inconceivable and should not be deliberated upon, because it is established by very firm evidence. For it is observed that, by virtue of being accomplished through conduct, there is the loss of eligibility for subsequent rites and so forth, as in such texts as: "One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts."

In this context, he states the necessity of right conduct (*ācāra*) as a matter of incidental discussion with the words "having obtained" (*prāpta*). Indeed, some might think: "The attainment of heaven and other goals results solely from the performance of ritual acts (*karma*); what is the use of this conduct? To that, the answer begins with "having obtained," and so forth. Regarding the obligatory rites such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) that have been obtained, the sages have declared for every single step in the *Ṛtivṛtti* the occurrence of transgressions (*pratyavāya*). The meaning is that they declare defects such as the loss of eligibility for subsequent rites. Furthermore, they state that by following that—that is, by conforming to right conduct—there is the destruction of previously committed sins.

It is heard in such [Vedic] passages as, "Whatever evil I have done this day," and so forth. Furthermore, based on the rule "A rite must be performed by one who is pure" and other such statements, they declare that one is worthy of performing meritorious acts only by following established conduct (ācāra). Thus, for these reasons, he says "not from this" (nātaḥ), meaning that the abandonment of conduct is not appropriate, based on the notion that heaven results from virtuous action alone.

He shows the authority for this in the passage beginning with, "They do not purify one devoid of conduct. The meaning is that in a person who has fallen away from conduct, even the entire collection of Vedas will not be a purifier, being like water in a dog's skin-bag.

Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "It has been stated that those who perform only sacrifices (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and acts of charity (*datta*), having gone to the moon, return with their residual karma (*sānuśaya*). Now, a doubt arises as to whether even those who perform wicked deeds (*aniṣṭādikārin*) go to the moon or not. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: do even those who perform wicked deeds, after experiencing the torments of Yama, go to the moon and then return, or not?

Does the sentence "Whoever they may be" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1) indicate that even those who perform sacrifices for specific desires (*iṣṭādikārin*) reach the moon, or not? In this regard, does the word "all" refer to deceased persons in general, or only to those deceased persons who perform sacrifices for specific desires? Is the journey along the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*) intended only for those who perform sacrifices for specific desires? And does the introductory passage, "Those here in the village who perform sacrifices and works of public utility" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.3), indicate that the path of the fathers applies exclusively to those who perform sacrifices for specific desires, or not?

Regarding the response to the question, "Do you know how that world is not filled?", which begins with "Now, of these two paths... and concludes with "Being born and dying—this is the third place; by that, that world is not filled," [the opponent argues that] this does not indicate the absence of ascent to the heavenly world (*svarloka*), nor does it make known that the third place lacks the production of human status without the fifth oblation. Here, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words, "Of all... and so on.

It has been stated that upon the fall of the body, the attainment of the moon is a rule for all; therefore, even for those characterized by sin—those afflicted by excessive evil—the attainment of the moon is preceded by a journey to hell. [The author] refutes this [view] with the word "no. He explains the refutation itself with the word "loka" (the world). This is the meaning: by the phrase "all of them go to the moon," you assert that the attainment of the moon occurs even for those who perform undesirable acts, based on the force of the term "all" which implies no restriction of meaning.

"By the force of the statement, 'Therefore that world is not filled,' it follows that contraction [of the path] is not a defect. He concludes the stated point with the words "ta" (they): those performers of undesirable acts and the like, by the command of Yama, after reaching the moon at the end of their torments, enter into a contemptible womb.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that birth is described for those who possess birth only with reference to the fifth libation? How then can there be birth for those dominated by sin in the absence of the fifth libation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Birth. First of all, the birth of beings such as the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) is indeed established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, it is simply impossible to maintain a dependence on the fifth libation, because we do not observe the entry of the [soul] from the father's body into the mother's body.

Raising the objection, "In that case, how is it that there is a statement regarding the requirement of the fifth libation? he says, "By the majority" (*bhūyiṣṭhaiḥ*). This is the meaning: the statement regarding the requirement of the fifth libation is a general rule (*sāmānya*); however, it finds scope only where there is no exception (*apavāda*), and not elsewhere. Draupadī, Dhṛṣṭadyumna, and others, who for the most part have not been born in this life [as a result of their past actions], do not require the fifth libation. Likewise, even those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) and so forth do not require it, because they are produced by a preponderance of sin.

The meaning is that, just like the requirement for the fifth libation, the path beginning with smoke (dhūmādimārga) is likewise devoid of speech. Regarding this point, how many are heard of in scripture who, due to their specific excellence of merit, having departed while assuming a naturally attained divine body and so forth until reaching the world of Brahmā, are taken as examples for the assumption of a body without requiring the fifth libation? This is the intended sense.

In this regard, the connection is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Those who perform sacrifices and other rites, enveloped by the subtle elements of the body and accompanied by their residual karma (anuśaya), descend from the moon. And the manner of that descent is as follows:

From the scriptural statement: "Then they return again by this very path as they came—to space; from space, to air; having become air, he becomes smoke; having become smoke, he becomes mist; having become mist, he becomes a cloud; having become a cloud, he rains down," it has been stated that [the soul's journey] is both "as they came" and "not so. In that regard, when [the soul] attains the state of space and so forth, does it attain the state of space etc. in the same way as it attains the state of gods, humans, and so on, or is it merely an attainment of similarity to them?

The investigation of that meaning concerns whether the state of being ether and so forth—expressed in the passage, "Just as this [soul] reaches the ether"—consists in actually assuming a body made of ether and the like, similar to the assumption of bodies as gods or humans, or whether it is merely the attainment of similarity to them. On this point, some hold the view that among the five oblations, the fact that the first and the last oblations possess a bodily nature is beyond dispute, because the possession of a body is explicitly stated in the passages: "From that oblation King Soma arises" and "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'."

Likewise, birth itself would have to occur for the person even in space, air, and so forth, because of the connection with the verbal root *bhū* (to become) as heard first in the phrase "he becomes King Soma. He states this very point in the words "of the two oblations. He refutes that [objection] with the word "āsāram" (the flow). He clarifies that same point with the words "retassig" (the one who discharges semen).

The meaning is as follows: just as upon entering the father’s body there is merely a state of conjunction, so too in the case of becoming ether and the other elements, the word used by the proponent of ether and the rest denotes only the unfitness for separate designation due to a particular kind of conjunction. He states the reason for this point with the words "between heaven and earth" (dyubhvoh). This means that since the assumption of a body in the interval is for the purpose of experiencing the fruits of merit, the fruit of merit would also be heard of [in scripture]; yet no such experience is observed.

The connection here is stated in the Commentary: "Regarding the interval from the attainment of space up to the attainment of rice and so forth, there is a doubt as to whether it stays for a long time at each stage or if there is no fixed rule. The inquiry into its meaning, however, is: does it stay for a long time in space and the other stages prior to the attainment of rice and so forth, or does it depart from them quickly?

Regarding the attainment of rice and other grains, the statement, "From this [state], indeed, it is more difficult to emerge" (*ato vai khalu durniṣprapataram*), indicates that there is an exit from elsewhere after a long time; is this not so? Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "In the ether, etc. (*vyomādīti*). In this case, since there is no explicit mention of a distinction between a long and a short duration for the soul's state of abiding in the ether and so forth, there would be no fixed rule, just as in the case of the state of the semen in the mother's body.

Indeed, it is observed that the state of being white (the white path) lasts for a long time during its stay until the completion of the womb, whereas in the case of falling [from the dark path], it lasts for a long time again. He refutes this with "No. Therein he states the reason: "by way of their natural tendency" (*svārasikyā*). The meaning is: because there exists a scriptural passage proceeding by way of its own natural tendency, namely, "From here, indeed, it is more difficult to emerge. He expresses that very quality of being natural with the words "from rice and so forth."

For the specific statement, "from rice and so forth it is more difficult to escape," declares that from others it is easier to escape. By this, it is understood through the power of the sentence itself that there is a rapid abandonment of those respective states previously mentioned. The meaning is that the mention of being "more difficult to escape" in a particular context precludes such difficulty in other cases.

The connection [of this section] with the commentary itself is clear: "It is heard in scripture that descending souls are born in the form of rice and so forth: 'Having become a cloud, he rains down'; 'These are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. In this doubt—whether they cling to rice and other plants already inhabited by other experiencers, or whether those very experiencers are born with rice and other plants as their bodies—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because of the word "are born," they possess the bodies of rice and so forth, just as one says "a god is born" or "a human is born. To this, the following is stated: "Thus it is said."

The investigation into that matter concerns whether the scriptural statement—"Those [souls] are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans"—refers to those descending souls being born with bodies consisting of rice and so forth, which serve as the bodies for other experiencers, or not.

Regarding the statement "they are born" (*jāyante*), does it refer to actual origination—as in "a god is born" or "a human is born"—or does it refer merely to a connection? The hearing of the word "are born" does not imply a mere conjunction, like the phrase "those of foul conduct" (*kapūyacaraṇāḥ*) which indicates an absence of connection with ritual action; rather, it signifies actual birth. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that it is birth: for here, in the phrase "they are born in the form of rice and so forth," only birth is heard. Therefore, this must be a case of birth, just as [the same term] denotes divinity or mortality.

"Now, surely there is no self (nairātmya) in stationary objects; therefore, how can there be the birth of a living being in the form of a stationary object?"—so says someone. He states that this is the speech of one who stands outside the Vedānta: "No-self. He refutes this prima facie argument with "No," and explains that very point with "Of merit... and so forth.

In the *Pañcāgnividyā*, the fruit of merit for those who perform rites such as *iṣṭāpūrta* is indeed declared. Thus, while in the context of declaring the fruits of merit primarily, it is stated that "a man goes to the state of a stationary being through the defects of actions born of the body," it is not correct to say that this declares the fruit of sin in the form of attaining birth as a stationary being.

If this is so, one might ask: how can the direct act of being born be expressed by the word "are born"? Anticipating this objection, [the author replies that] just as the term for "being born" is used when a soul presides over the body of a father, so too the term for "being born" applied to the soul descending into the bodies of rice and other plants is merely figurative; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

On this point, someone objects: "For that which is based on tradition (ānuśravika) is like that which is seen (dṛṣṭa), insofar as it is associated with impurity, decay, and excess. Thus, the followers of Sāṅkhya maintain that sacrifices and the like are partially impure due to their connection with non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Consequently, the fruit of the meritorious portion is heaven and so forth, while the fruit of the sinful portion is rebirth as rice and other such things; therefore, even when discussing the results of merit, it is entirely appropriate to mention the results of sin. He restates this [objection] with the words "violence" (*hiṃsā*).

It is logical that sacrifices such as the *iṣṭi*, even though enjoined by the Śruti, are impure because they involve acts of violence such as the immolation of animals. Therefore, the one who has performed meritorious deeds experiences his portion of sin starting from the state of being rice and so forth. He rejects this restated argument with the words "it is improper. He states the reason for this: "because it has been said [otherwise]. Indeed, through mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*), this violence is declared to be for the benefit of the animal. For example, the mantra begins: "Verily, you do not die here" (*na vā u etan mriyase*). There is also an *Atharva* explanatory passage: "With a golden body, he goes upward to the heavenly world. [The opponent objects: But surely the Śruti would only express a meaning that is appropriate?

Anticipating the objection as to how "saṃjñapana"—which consists of the production of suffering—can be for the benefit of the animal, he establishes the point by means of an analogy: "that is like medical treatment. For in the world, even acts such as cutting with a blade, applying caustic, or using fire, which consist of slight pain but serve as the cause for attaining greater pleasure, are indeed designated as "beneficial" (hita); the meaning is that it is just like that. Now, one might object that in that case, even the killing of a prisoner would be beneficial; anticipating this, he says "speak," with the intention that the distinction between what is beneficial and what is harmful is to be understood solely through the scriptures.

The venerable Manu, possessing the authority of the statement, “Whatever Manu has said is indeed medicine,” declares that in a sacrifice there is no such thing as killing; the meaning is that there is no nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*). For the nature of violence attaches itself only to the separation of life through a non-scriptural method. Just as the slaying with weapons by kings in battle is not violence, so too is the slaying of thieves. It is precisely because of the difference in context that the distinction between merit and demerit is established in all cases.

"Even self-sacrifice sometimes accumulates millions of merits, as it is said: 'One should completely renounce one's life for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow. Therefore, there is no violence in sacrifices and the like, nor is there the experience of their [sinful] results; nor is there any fault touched by the injunction, nor is there any state of being a perpetrator of violence for the followers of the Veda—this is a pleasing conclusion. Now, raising the objection: "In the context of knowledge, in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, censure of ritual action is seen here and there; how is that to be understood? he says: "It praises... and so forth.

According to the maxim that "criticism does not function to criticize the object of criticism, but rather to praise something other than the criticized," the condemnation of action in various places is intended solely for the purpose of praising the desired knowledge and so forth. Furthermore, this is not an absolute condemnation of actions that must necessarily be performed, because the intent (*tātparya*) in the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) lies precisely in the condemnation of attachment to results, agency, and the like. For the experts in logic maintain that "the word is authoritative only with respect to the intended meaning" (*tātparye hi śabdaḥ pramāṇam*).
Otherwise, the entire *Gītā* scripture, including such passages as "He who sees inaction in action," would be rendered inconsistent.

Regarding this, someone says: "What is the use of this somewhat forced justification? Indeed, the Sāṅkhyas, who are the foremost among the knowers of reality, declare that the act of immolation (*saṃjñapana*) is a fault. Otherwise, how could the Purāṇas and other texts speak of the contingency of using flour-made animals and the like? Such indeed is the intention of the Sāṅkhyas: the prohibition "one shall not kill" refers to killing prompted by passion (*rāga*), whereas the scriptural injunction "one should immolate" refers to ritual killing (*vaidha-hiṃsā*) which is prompted by a Vedic command.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that when there is a conflict between an injunction (*vidhi*) and a prohibition (*niṣedha*), the prohibition must be restricted to a domain distinct from that of the injunction; thus, they establish the distinction between injunction and prohibition by means of a difference in scope (*viṣaya-bheda*). This, however, is not tenable, for a distinction based on a difference in scope should only be made when a conflict actually exists. Such a conflict is simply not present here. For the injunction regarding the ritual slaughter (*saṃjñāpana-vidhi*) declares that the immolation of the animal brings excellence to the sacrifice, whereas the prohibition, "One shall not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*), declares that killing is a cause of sin.

Since a single action, through both injunction and prohibition, produces two effects consisting of both pleasure and pain, what contradiction is there? Therefore, according to the maxim of eating food mixed with poison, sacrifices and the like take the form of both the beneficial and the harmful. He restates this with the words "of the agent. The phrase "devotees of Sāṃkhya" is a term of derision.

The meaning is that even though the logical path has been stated, the opponent merely continues to urge his point again and again, prattling about the method of the Sāṅkhya doctrine out of mere devotion. This is the conclusion here: since the prohibition against causing harm remains valid, and since the authority of the injunction regarding animal sacrifice is established by both reasoned mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas) as well as by the acceptance of great men, how could a follower of Sāṅkhya advocate such a mixture of sin? He expresses this with the words, "completely shaken off."

Raising the objection, "How then is the practice of using flour-made animals and so forth described in the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and other texts?", he replies with the word "piṣṭa" (flour), stating that even this is not contradictory because it is a specific dharma restricted to a particular time. Just as the regulations of dharma concerning the arrangement of time-measures such as the *ghaṭikā* are accepted only by those who are righteous (*dhārmika*), so it is here as well; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Furthermore, he adduces another defect in the Sāṃkhya position with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). He establishes this with the words "In the case of general injunctions" (*utsarge*). This is the meaning: although in optional injunctions such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," a person engages in violence that assists the sacrifice—the means to heaven—due to a passion for heaven, it is said there that because the element of violence is of the nature of sin, its fruit is experienced in the form of stationary beings such as rice plants.

Nevertheless, for you who abandon the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*) in this context, how could obligatory violence (*nityahiṃsā*)—such as that enjoined by the injunction "In autumn one should sacrifice an animal"—be established? For in those cases, violence is obligatory and not produced by passion (*rāga*). If it is argued that even there passion exists, because it is stated that all social classes (*varṇa*) attain immeasurable happiness through the performance of their own duties (*svadharma*), we say no; for that would entail the undesirable consequence of abandoning both obligatory and optional rites.

This is what he says: "What kind of constant injury (nityahiṃsā) [is there]? The meaning is that constant injury itself would not be established. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because constancy can be established even through flour and the like, he says in response: "For you" (tava hi). This means for you who abandon the principle of general rule and exception (utsargāpavādanyāya) everywhere. In the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other texts, in the context of the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), it is said: "Five slaughter-houses (pañcasūnā) exist for the householder day after day."

Since grinding with a mortar and pestle and so forth is also described as violence by such statements, there is nothing whatsoever among your prescribed acts that falls outside the scope of prohibition. If you say, "Let it be so," we reply: no, because the contradiction with the Mantras and Arthavādas has already been stated.

Now, one might object: since [the texts] prescribe the telling of falsehoods in passages such as "at the time of marriage" and "during sexual union," and then prescribe an expiation for it—stating that "having reviled one who should not be reviled, or having spoken a falsehood, one shall eat no food containing pungent or saline substances for three nights"—how can this be? To this he replies: "It is true; there, that recourse is taken out of necessity. He explains this by saying, "where there is a scriptural injunction regarding untruth and so forth. The meaning is that, just as there is an injunction for the telling of falsehoods, there would likewise be an injunction for the expiation.

Alternatively, since a fault exists when that [falsehood] is committed, no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed; rather, as in the case of the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, some occasional rite (*naimittika*) is prescribed for it. Thus, he says, "Or rather, it is merely caused by that," meaning that the telling of a lie is merely an occasion, just like the birth of a son.

He demonstrates that this quarter [of the verse] is particularly helpful for refuting the positions of the Sāṃkhya and the Māyāvādins by stating, "embraced" (*āśliṣṭam*). Indeed, some Sāṃkhyas and certain Māyāvādins say as follows: "The sky, though struck by pestles, is not affected; likewise, they say, the Self (the 'owner of the field') is not affected by the afflictions of the body and so forth. For just as the sky is not struck by blows from pestles, so too the reality of the Self—though spoken of as being subject to affliction by the Sāṃkhya and the proponents of Illusion—is not actually afflicted, because it is devoid of attachment (*asaṅgatatvāt*).

Having thus stated that there is no enjoyer of the fruits [of action], he says "the non-doer of action" (karmākartaṃ) to show that there is also no agent. Here too, the phrase "they say" (āhuḥ) is to be supplied from the previous context. Then, raising the doubt as to where the fruit resides if the individual soul (jīva) lacks agency, he says "the fruit," etc. The meaning is that it resides in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the soul. Then, raising the further doubt as to whether the worldly fruit belongs to the ego-sense and so forth, while liberation (mokṣa) belongs to whom, he says "of the unmanifest" (avyaktasya) to show that liberation also belongs to Nature (prakṛti).

"Prakṛti, having various substrates, transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated"—such is the Sāṅkhya system. "Therefore, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate"; thus they declare the beginningless liberation of the *jīva*. "The *puruṣa*, however, is always untainted, like a lotus leaf"—this is the teaching of the Sāṅkhyas. In all these cases, the offering is that which is the age.

The author of the Sūtras refuted this view held by both the Sāṅkhyas and the proponents of illusion (Mṛṣāvādins), because it establishes that the connection with transmigratory existence belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone; thus he says, "Of them," meaning that in this section on dispassion (vairāgyapāda), he set aside and refuted the doctrine of the Sāṅkhyas and the Mṛṣāvādins. Herein lies the distinction: for the Sāṅkhyas, primordial nature (prakṛti) is real, while the defects such as pleasure and pain caused by the connection with that nature are false.

Furthermore, for those who speak falsely, even illusion is false, and consequently, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) associated with it is also false; this is one position. The meaning is that both positions are refuted by demonstrating the ultimate reality of the connection to saṃsāra.

In this [section], the author demonstrates by dividing the distinct meanings of the six topics mentioned here; thus he says "pāda. In this pāda, six topics are to be established. He states those very topics in their proper order, beginning with "vapuḥ": (1) The first point is that the living soul, when abandoning the body, departs together with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*). (2) Another is that one who has experienced heaven descends again by the same path and in the same manner, but with a remainder of karma (*sānuśaya*). (3) Furthermore, the third is that for those who resort to the path of hell—those traveling by way of the infernal regions—there can be no attainment of the moon.

The fourth [view] holds that there is merely a similarity to space and so forth, but not birth in the form of those [entities]. The fifth holds that the descent from space and so forth occurs very quickly. The sixth also holds that there is merely a long-term conjunction with another body, such as rice and so forth; "conjunction" (yoga), however, means mere contact.
Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter.

Here, having raised an objection regarding the commencement of the quarter on "The Two Indications" (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*) immediately after the quarter on "Dispassion" (*vairāgya-pāda*), he connects [the topics] with the words "Brahman alone" (*brahmaiva*). Previously, through both chapters, Brahman was established as being endowed with all its own inherent natures. And this is the chapter on the means (*sādhana-adhyāya*). The intention of the objector is: "What is the purpose of bringing back and reflecting upon Brahman—which was already established in the chapters on 'Harmony' (*samanvaya*) and 'Non-contradiction' (*avirodha*)—once again in this chapter? He refutes this objection with the words "Not so" (*maivam*).

This is the intended meaning here: it is true that this is the chapter on the means (*sādhana-adhyāya*); nevertheless, reflection upon Brahman must indeed be performed specifically. For the means (*sādhana*) is twofold: the means to what is to be accomplished (*sādhyopāya*) and the means that is already established (*siddhopāya*). The established means is the Lord (*īśvara*). The means to what is to be accomplished is devotion (*bhakti*) itself, which possesses distinctions such as *vidhi* (the path of injunction) and so forth. And the distinction between these paths arises from the difference in their forms (*rūpa*). Furthermore, the form of the path primarily consists of Brahman, who is to be known. And the distinction therein arises from the difference in its qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, by virtue of being the object of devotion—which is the very form of the means taught in the chapter on the means—and by being itself the established means (*siddhopāya*), [Brahman is the subject of this inquiry].

Since reflection on Brahman is a means [to liberation], it is appropriately included specifically in the *Sādhanādhyāya* (the chapter on the means). Regarding that, he first states that reflection on Brahman is an auxiliary to the injunctions with the words "vidhyā" and so forth. As for the phrase "taddhi tadrūpabhedāt," the meaning is that this clarification of Brahman—due to the distinction of its forms (*tadrūpabheda*) and the distinction of its qualities (*tadguṇabheda*)—implies that Brahman, endowed with such specific attributes as having both genders, is what must be reflected upon here. To demonstrate that this reflection on Brahman is fruitful by establishing it as a perfected means (*siddhopāya*), he says "siddha" and so forth.

Two points must be specifically established regarding Brahman: its being the means (*siddha-upāyatva*) and its being the goal attained (*siddha-prāpyatva*). The demonstration of both these points is for the sake of establishing a particular longing (*tṛṣṇā-viśeṣa*) for Brahman as the object to be attained. Indeed, in the absence of such a particular longing, a person would have no qualification (*adhikāra*) for the means at all. For just as one who desires heaven is qualified for sacrifices and the like, so too one who desires the attainment of the Supreme Brahman is qualified for the meditations upon Brahman.

And thus, since this section on the "Two Characteristics" (ubhayaliṅga-pāda) specifically assists in the practice of meditation, it constitutes the very essence of the Śārīraka-śāstra; therefore, there is no risk of it being purposeless. Regarding the phrase "for the expansion of thirst" (tṛṣṇā-prathimne), it is said for the sake of increasing thirst. For thirst increases here in the manner stated: "He himself bestows the fruit," meaning that when Brahman is fully realized by itself as its own means of attainment, [thirst increases]. This is the intended sense.

Furthermore, this "Chapter on the Two Attributes" (Ubhayaliṅga-pāda), which is devoted to establishing that Brahman is solely composed of auspicious qualities that are the opposites of all things to be avoided, is indeed fruitful, as it specifically assists in the refutation of opponents such as the Mṛṣāvādins (proponents of illusionism). Thus he says: "The absence of qualities" (nairguṇyam). If Brahman were devoid of qualities, then the distinction between the injunctions regarding Brahman and its various auspicious attributes—as established by the differences in qualities set forth in the "Chapter on the Two Attributes" within the sections of the "Chapter on the Compendium of Qualities" (Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda)—would be rendered false.

Now, he restates the opponent’s position—that the distinction between Brahman and ignorance might exist through qualities that are themselves merely imagined—by saying, "He says, 'That [is not so]... He refutes that with the words, "...because it would contradict the scriptural tradition. For if the meaning of the Śruti, which is accepted as having an unbroken tradition without beginning or end, were itself imagined, what then would be non-imagined? Thus, the meaning is that one who asserts the imagined nature of these qualities falls outside the scope of the Vedānta.

One might object: "In the Vedānta as well, in passages such as 'One should meditate on the mind as Brahman,' an injunction for a figurative meditation (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is observed—just like [the injunction] 'One should know oneself as Garuḍa. Therefore, it might be the same in this case as well. Anticipating this objection, the author refutes it with the words "not here. The meaning is that one cannot claim that because an injunction for figurative meditation must be accepted in one instance out of necessity, it must therefore apply everywhere in that same way; for an injunction for figurative meditation consists precisely in the contemplation of one thing by superimposing the qualities of another upon it.

The meaning is that Brahman’s possession of truthfulness, knowledge, and so forth is sublated by the doctrine that these are merely attributes of its own nature (*svarūpa-guṇatva*). Thus, having stated the defect of the proponent of falsehood due to its contradiction with the evidence establishing the exclusive devotion to auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇa-guṇa-ekatānatva*), he now states the flaw of the proponent of falsehood on the grounds of its contradiction with the evidence establishing faultlessness (*nirdoṣatva*): "Faultlessness," etc. If you assert, in accordance with the evidence, that the faultlessness of Brahman is indeed eternal, then—since there would be no transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) distinct from Brahman—the [faultlessness] of Brahman...

Furthermore, because [Brahman] is eternally faultless, the effort involved in hearing the Vedānta and so forth for the sake of pacifying the defects in the form of saṃsāra would be merely vain and useless; thus, the commencement of the scripture would be purposeless. Anticipating the opponent's intention—namely, "In that case, we shall assert that the faultlessness of Brahman is something to be inferred"—the author refutes it with the words "is to be inferred. If faultlessness were to be inferred, then defectiveness itself would become the very nature of Brahman, and thus the commencement of the scripture would again be futile. It is precisely for the sake of refuting such opponents that the *Ubhayaliṅga* section (1.2.2) is indeed fruitful.

Having thus seen the defect in the falsity of the attribute-less nature, [the author] says "Furthermore" (kiñca) regarding the many defects of the deluded false-speaker who, seeing that, again asserts its reality.

If the absolute non-differentiation (*nirviśeṣatva*) of Brahman were its ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*), then the initial injunction that "the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken" would be untenable; likewise, its being within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇagocaratva*) would be impossible. Furthermore, how could all such a collection of attributes—which constitute the very essence of one's own established doctrine—exist in a non-differentiated Brahman? These include its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), its nature as bliss (*ānandarūpatva*), its status as the substratum for the superimposition of the universe (*viśvādhyāsādhiṣṭhānatva*), and its volition to become manifold, expressed as "May I be many" (*bahu syām*). The meaning is that none of this could possibly exist.

If these qualities are ultimately real, then it follows that [Brahman] possesses qualities (saguṇavāda). If they are not ultimately real, then since self-luminosity and bliss would also be non-ultimately real, there would be a destruction of the very root of one's own established doctrine; furthermore, what distinction would there be from the Buddhists and others? This contradiction with reason has been stated. Now, he states the contradiction with scripture as well:

The word "all" [refers to all means of knowledge]. Having stated the contradiction with the authority of scripture (*śruti*), he also states the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana*). It is well known that for a speaker of falsehood, the assertion of things contradicted by all means of knowledge, such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, is established; for it is said: "The difficulty of being established is an ornament of ignorance, not a defect."

If that "ornament" were indeed Brahman itself, then it would be an ornament of the very highest order—even such utterly impossible claims as "error is without a substratum" and "Brahman is without luminosity"—which would merely sound the victory-trumpet for the Mādhyamikas. Furthermore, for those speakers of falsehood who have fallen into a miserable state through the audacity of their *māyā* (as expressed in the phrase "the audacity of *māyā*," etc.), their conception of the eight feet [of the Lord] deserves to be uprooted from its very roots; consequently, all worship of the Lord with attributes (*saguṇopāsana*), which is the subject matter of the chapter on the "Combination of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*), must likewise be eradicated, resulting in a total contradiction of all the scriptures.

Regarding this section on the "Two-fold Characteristics" (Ubhayaliṅga-pāda), one might raise the objection: "If Brahman is said to be the object of contemplation here, then how can the description of the individual soul's (jīva) state of dreaming be consistent? Anticipating this, [the author] resolves it by stating that even the perception of sleeping and so forth is accomplished solely through the will of the Lord; thus, since demonstrating this also serves to reveal the majesty of the Lord, its inclusion in this section is logically appropriate. This is what is meant by the phrase "it has been stated."

This is the meaning of the word here: if Brahman—which is free from defects and rich in qualities—were to be meditated upon again here [in this context], then there would arise the doubt as to how such a meditation on Brahman as being in the state of dream could be consistent with the section on detachment (*vairāgya-pāda*) that precedes this present section. He refutes this very doubt with the word "no" (*na*). He explains that very point by saying "in a dream," and so forth.

The Lord alone is the creator even of the objects of a dream; this reflection on the state of dreaming is undertaken here for the purpose of establishing the manifold greatness of Brahman—beginning with His status as that creator—and to demonstrate that this living being is in a state of absolute dependence, as if liberated from itself. The meaning is this: the individual soul (jīva) is not spoken of here as being primary; rather, it is for the sake of demonstrating that the Supreme Self is the agent of all states, such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, that the Supreme Self alone is spoken of throughout this section (pāda) as the primary subject.

Regarding this, some say: "In this section on the two-fold marks (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*), the first half refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and serves as a supplement to the section on dispassion (*vairāgya-pāda*); the second half refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*. He restates this [view] with the words "of the section" (*pādasya*). He refutes this partial view (the view of the *ekadeśin*) with the word "this," stating that it is not at all pleasing to the heart. He provides the reason for this: "because of the variegated nature" (*śabalitā*). This is because there would be a reversal of skill regarding the description of mixed topics.

Then, raising the objection as to why the defects of the individual soul (jīva) are mentioned in the first half of the verse, he answers that it is for the purpose of manifesting the qualities of Brahman; the meaning is that by describing the transmigrating jīva, the majesty of the Supreme Self (paramātman), who liberates from saṃsāra, is established. As for the literal sense of the words: "the mention of the jīva's defects here is, however, a means [to that end]."

Here he raises an objection: "You claim that the creation in a dream is ultimately real; how can this be consistent? For one sees even things past and future in a dream. Indeed, the perception of impossible objects is false in the waking state, so how much more so in a dream? Therefore, the creation in a dream is not ultimately real. To this he says: "In a dream... The grammatical connection here is as follows: let objects be created in a dream.

Moreover, various delusions are difficult to abandon here in a dream, because there is the experience of fathers and others as if they were present now, and because there is the delusion of stability and so forth regarding gold and other things obtained in a dream, even though they are unstable; therefore, you must state that the dream is not ultimately real. He refutes this by partially conceding the point, saying "True. Therein, he shows by distinguishing between what is conceded and what is not conceded, beginning with "By scripture," etc.

Since it is impossible to abandon what is established by scripture and other means of valid knowledge, we do not discard the meaning established by the Śruti; rather, accepting that the Lord, the creator of all, creates at those respective times objects to be experienced only by specific individuals, and acknowledging—due to the very fact of contradiction—that there is delusion regarding utterly inconsistent matters just as in a dream, we maintain that everything is consistent.

Then, raising the objection as to how the movement to another place in a dream could be ultimately real for one who is himself situated in a single location, [the author] says "someone" (*kaścit*), explaining that everything is possible through the power of the will of the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, just as it is for a yogin who assumes various bodies. Here is the grammatical connection of the words: "A certain yogin, by the power of yoga, like the manner of moving at will between his own house and another's, having emerged from his former body, enters and attains another body, the body of another."

By that very [subtle body], one performs activities such as wandering there; furthermore, having previously abandoned the body, one returns and regains it. Likewise, some have maintained that in a dream, the dreamer abandons the previous body and attains another body created by the Lord, and at the end of the dream, regains the previous body once again.

This is what he says with the word "thus" (ittham). He also states another alternative view with the words "by the activity of breathing" (śvāsavṛttyā). This is indeed the intention of others: if a person lying in a dream were to abandon his former body and take up another body, then there would be no activity of breathing in the former body. Therefore, the living self (jīva) remains in that very same body.

However, regarding the other bodies created by the Blessed One within his own dream, they have determined that the assumption of those other bodies occurs through the pervasion of knowledge as a quality (dharmabhūtajñāna) alone; for, according to the principle to be stated—namely, "the entry [of the self] is like a lamp"—the logic of Saubhari is established through the pervasion of knowledge as a quality.

The connection here is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Thus, by means of the conjunction with going, coming, birth, and so forth corresponding to his karma, the suffering of the individual soul (jīva) while awake has been made known; now, its state of dreaming is examined. Regarding the investigation of that meaning, beginning with the text, "There are no chariots there, no yoke-poles, no roads," the creation of dreams is recorded in the scripture; the inquiry is whether that [creation] is ultimately real or merely illusion (māyāmātra).

Does the designation, "For he is the creator who creates," indicate ultimate reality or not? Does this designation refer to the agency of the creator of the creation, or does it refer to an agency similar to that in dream-cognition? Is it possible for a creation to arise from mere volition in a dream for a living being (jīva) whose will is true, as understood from the Prajāpati discourse, or is it not?
