"Who, while these [senses] sleep, remains awake, creating each desired object at will"—this [passage] makes known that the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses the power of creation through mere volition during dreams, or does it not? Is this statement concerning the *jīva* or concerning the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? Indeed, in this section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is deliberated whether the creation of dreams is the work of the *jīva* or the work of the Supreme Self.

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that it has been stated. For it has indeed been stated in the Prajāpati-vākya, which forms the supplement to the Dahara-vidyā passage, that the quality of having true resolves (satyasaṅkalpatva) belongs to the Lord of Creatures (prajāpati), and like the small ether (daharākāśa), it also belongs to the individual soul (jīva). The word "bhavinī" is used in the locative case; the meaning is "in the soul. Therefore, by its own resolve, creation in a dream is appropriate for the soul alone.

Furthermore, although it is stated here that sons and so forth are created, the relationship with sons and the like belongs only to the individual soul (jīva), because chariots and such things serve as indicators of objects favorable to the soul. Therefore, the meaning is that the individual soul, under discussion as the agent of sons and so forth, creates its own desired dream-objects. He rejects this point with the words "not so" (maivam). Therein he states the reason: "in liberation" (muktau).

Because of the mention of those qualities; that is to say, because it is stated that the individual soul (jīva) undergoes the manifestation of the eightfold qualities such as being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva), how could the soul, which is like one who is blind during the state of dream, attain those eight qualities such as being free from sin? He states another reason as well: "anabhimata" [and so forth].

If the individual soul (jīva) were to create its own objects for its own sake within a dream, then it would necessarily create only what is favorable. Yet, one who is asleep sometimes sees even unfavorable things in a dream. That is not logical; for if the soul possessed the power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva), how could it create for itself that which is contrary to its own interests? He states a third reason as well: "because dreams are indicative [of future events]."

The meaning is that one should understand that all white [dreams] bring about auspicious results; thus, even in a dream, those indicating good or evil have come of their own accord through the volition of the Lord (Īśvara). Therefore, the Lord's status as the creator belongs solely to the manifold world of dreams. This is what he expresses by the words "the entire universe."

Regarding this, one might raise the doubt: in the scriptural passage (*viṣayavākya*) "creating whatever he desires" (*kāmaṃkāmaṃ puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ*), does the term denote the suffix *ṇamul*, or does it denote the specific objects of desire as the accusative case (*karman*)? Anticipating this, [the author] states "kāmaṃkāmaṃ," asserting that the suffix *ṇamul* alone is appropriate for expressing the creative agency of the Blessed Lord whose resolve is ever-true (*satyasaṅkalpa*). This is because a living being (*jīva*), whose resolve is not true, lacks the capacity for such creative agency; thus, it is the Lord alone who is being meditated upon.

And this Supreme Self remains awake while persons are asleep; therefore, its agency in performing wondrous deeds is logical—this is the meaning. He states that its waking is established by scripture, saying "clearly": for it is heard in the Śruti, "Embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman)."

One might object: "If even a dream, like waking life, consists of a creation that is ultimately real (*paramārtha*), how is it that it is restricted to specific times, or how is it experienced by only one particular individual? Anticipating this doubt, the author resolves it with the intention that it is due to the specific volition (*saṅkalpa*) of the unrestrained and independent Lord (*īśvara*), stating: "that [and] that. It is not only in dreams that there is a creation of effects delimited by specific times; rather, even in the waking state, the emergence of clouds and so forth is observed to be characterized by such [temporal and subjective] limitations.

If it is objected that even so, the state of being experienced by only a single person is not observed, we reply that this too must be understood as resulting from the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). Indeed, through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, perfected eye-salves (*añjana*), and so forth, specific objects are seen to be experienced by particular individuals alone. Furthermore, he states another reason for the fact that things are created by the Lord: namely, the bestowing of fruits in accordance with respective actions (*karman*). Since the vision of dreams consists of pleasure and pain, it is the fruit of action; and since action is a specific form of the Lord’s will, the entire collection of dream-objects is dependent upon the Lord alone.

For the sinner indeed sees a dream corresponding to his sin, while one whose dharma predominates sees one corresponding to that; thus, this great path is certainly not to be transgressed by anyone. This has also been stated by the authoritative teachers (āpta), the intention being as follows: when some person attains auspiciousness at a certain time, and subsequently attains inauspiciousness, this is explained by the learned through the science of omens (nimitta), physiognomy (sāmudrika), the movements of various planets, and so forth. If, due to an obstruction or other cause, that [result] does not occur, then it will not be obtained even in a dream.
It is designated by those very same terms; therefore, it is established that dream happiness, suffering, and so forth, are indeed the fruits of karma.

In this context, relying merely on the employment of the word *māyā* in the sūtra, "But [the world] is mere illusion in its entirety," those who follow the teachings of Sugata—the Buddhists who masquerade under the guise of Vedic discourse—declare that the universe is false. He refutes their view with the words "māyā" (etc.). Since that falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) was already stated by them at the commencement of their own scripture, to state it again here would result in both redundancy and incoherence.

Therefore, what is stated here is simply that the Lord’s manifold creation is like the world-appearance in a dream; it is not, however, the falsity of the universe. For this assertion of those who maintain the doctrine of falsehood (mṛṣāvādins) rests solely upon the word "māyā" alone; yet even that is not their actual basis, as he says: "the word *māyā*. Indeed, lexicographers do not record the word *māyā* in common usage as a synonym for "falsehood."

For the lexicographers state that "māyā is indeed knowledge" (māyā tu vayanaṃ jñānam), and thus they employ the word *māyā* specifically for a particular kind of knowledge. In passages such as "Indra moves in many forms through *māyās*" (*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate*), it is said that the Lord is perceived in various forms by means of His specific volitions (*saṅkalpa*). And Parāśara says: "O Lord of men, He creates by His own sport many forms possessing diverse powers, designated as gods, animals, and humans, and endowed with activity."

"For the benefit of the worlds, it is not born from the cause of karma. Thus, *līlā* (sport) is said to be one's own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*). And that volition, as well as knowledge (*jñāna*), is *māyā*. Therefore, the word *māyā* does not denote "falsehood," but rather denotes "wondrous creation," or else it denotes a specific power (*śakti*) that serves as the cause for such creation, or else it denotes a specific volition that serves as the instrumental cause and basis for each respective creation. Indeed, usages are seen such as: "created like the *māyā* of a god. For if it were false, it would be designated as "imagined" (*kalpita*). Furthermore: "By that [missile] of Śambara, which moves swiftly, he [destroyed] that thousandfold *māyā*..."

"By protecting the body of the fool, [the body] was destroyed one by one. Here, the word *sūditaṃ* (destroyed) expresses precisely the state of being subject to destruction (*nāśyatva*). For destruction (*nāśa*) is the annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*) of that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*). Otherwise, it would be expressed as "sublated" (*bādhyatva*). For those who propound false doctrines (*bhṛṣāvādinaḥ*) say that sublation (*bādha*) is the state of being negated within the locus in which it was perceived. Indeed, in the statement "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti," the phrase "one should know Prakṛti" is stated precisely to exclude the meaning of "false" (*mithyā*) from the word *māyā*. Therefore, in the passage "The illusory deer (*māyāmṛga*) was killed," the actual annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*) of Mārīca is described.

Even in cases such as Meghanāda’s illusions, the term "māyā" is applied specifically to those ultimate serpents (*paramārtha-sarpa*) that are accomplished through particular mantras. Otherwise, how could it be logical for them to be neutralized by the specific powers of Garuḍa? Furthermore, this usage is well-established throughout the world. In the treatises on political ethics (*nīti-śāstra*), seven expedients are specified: conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, punishment, illusion (*māyā*), sorcery (*indrajāla*), and indifference. Among these, the distinction between *māyā* and *indrajāla* is stated as follows:

Māyā is the creation of an ultimately unreal snake and so forth due to a specific power of mantras and the like; likewise, the fruit of *indrajāla* (sorcery) is the breaking of an enemy's army by displaying unreal elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry through that very same specific power of mantras and the like. Other examples should be understood in this way as well. Now, raising the objection that the word *māyā* is used even in reference to falsehoods within the Purāṇas and in the common parlance of the ignorant, he provides the answer: "Let it be used figuratively."

The meaning is that figurative usage does not restrict the specific power (*śakti*) of a word. To this he says, "What of it? [meaning: it has no such effect]. He states, "In truth," indicating that even in the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, where usage is frequent, it is observed to be truly applicable only to things such as Asuras, Rākṣasas, and weapons. Even in the *Purāṇas* it is recited, beginning with "The rising of clouds, the ebbing of the ocean," and concluding with "The diverse illusory powers (*māyās*) of Viṣṇu come forth."

If it is then asked what determines that the entirety of an effect is denoted by the word *māyā*, he says: "because of its appropriate restriction. This is the meaning: a specific kind of effect characterized by wonder is called *māyā*; the application of the word *māyā* to a magician’s trick (*indrajāla*) is merely figurative because there is no difference in its nature as a wonder. Thus is the distinction between *māyā* and *indrajāla*. The statement, "For this is My divine *māyā*, consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is difficult to overcome," clearly establishes that the word *māyā* denotes the very cause of the creation of the manifold world, which consists of the three *guṇas*.

The connection here is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Now the locus of deep sleep is examined. The meaning is that while the dream state was previously defined, the locus of deep sleep is now being considered. The investigation into its purpose concerns whether the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman are the loci of deep sleep for the individual soul (jīva) as alternatives, or as a collective whole. Furthermore, is there a difference in their function—like a couch, a bed, and a sofa—or not?

Regarding the hearing of Brahmā’s awakening with the words, “We have come to the presence of the Existent,” which makes known that Brahmā occupies the position of a couch, does this make known a difference in function or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that it does, based on such statements as, “This is the station of the living being,” and so forth.

The scripture states that during deep sleep, the soul’s location is not fixed, mentioning the channels (nāḍīs), the pericardium (purītat), and Brahman as its possible sites. Therefore, since these three locations are mutually independent, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that there is an option (vikalpa) among them—namely, either the channels, or the pericardium, or Brahman. He refutes this stated position with "That is not so," and explains the refutation through reasoning with the words "Like a palace" (prāsāda). The meaning is this: an option is logically appropriate only when there is no difference in the resulting effect despite the combination [of alternatives].

Furthermore, in this case, since the options are joined together through a distinction of purpose—according to the maxim of the palace, the couch, and the bed—a choice (vikalpa) between the *nāḍī*, the *purītat*, and Brahman is simply not logical. Moreover, that choice is indeed tainted by eight defects. He states this very point: "In every alternative. Regarding the two options, "One should sacrifice with rice" and "One should sacrifice with barley," when rice and barley are to be performed as alternatives, if rice is performed first, there are two defects concerning the scriptural injunction regarding barley: the abandonment of the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the barley-scripture and the acceptance of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).

Immediately thereafter, when the barley ritual is being performed, there are two defects: the abandonment of the authority of the rice-scripture and the acceptance of its lack of authority. At that very same time of performing the barley ritual, there are likewise two defects: the acceptance of the authority of the barley-scripture (which had been abandoned) and the rejection of its lack of authority (which had been accepted).

Furthermore, in the third performance, which consists of turning back to the performance of the *vrīhi* scripture, there are two defects: the acceptance of the validity that was previously abandoned for the *vrīhi* scripture, and the abandonment of the invalidity that was previously accepted. Thus, both scriptures are tainted by eight defects across the three performances—four defects for each. This should be reflected upon by the wise, having analyzed it with the understanding that there are two defects at the time of the first performance, four at the time of the second performance, and again two defects at the time of the third performance.

The Teacher states that there is also corruption by eight defects from another perspective regarding the scope of the alternative: if one performs the ritual with rice (*vrīhi*) while the injunction for barley (*yava*) is present, there is the sublation of the performance, the apūrva, and the fruit according to the [barley] injunction—thus there are four defects. Likewise, if one performs the ritual with barley while the injunction for rice is present, there is the sublation of the performance, the apūrva, and the fruit according to the [rice] injunction—thus there are four defects. This constitutes corruption by eight defects.

Therefore, this is the meaning: when no other course is possible, an alternative (vikalpa) must be accepted; however, when a course is possible, there should be a combination (samuccaya). In this case, since a combination is possible according to the maxim of the palace, the bed, and the couch, an alternative should not be accepted. By stating that [the alternative] is "endowed with four faults arranged in sequence," he reiterates that the three applications are corrupted by eight faults. Thus, the impression of children that "therefore, from the second application... is a false impression.

In the *Saṅgati* (Introduction), it is stated: "When the doubt arises as to whether it is the very same one who was in deep sleep who rises at the time of awakening, or whether it is another. The investigation into that matter is as follows: Does another than the one in deep sleep rise at the time of awakening, or is it that very same one? Is there a complete liberation from all adjuncts (*upādhi*) during deep sleep, or not? Do the arguments based on action, recollection, and scriptural testimony lead to the conclusion that there is no complete liberation from all adjuncts, or not?

Now, an objection is raised: "Is not deep sleep (suṣupti) essentially like liberation? For liberation is indeed described by the Śruti as being devoid of the multitude of miseries and free from the aggregate of suffering; it is merely an absorption into Brahman, which is itself the dissolution (pralaya). Therefore, the embodied soul who awakens after that deep sleep must be someone else. This restatement of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is made under the heading "Liberation. The author refutes this position, saying: "It is not so."

The author demonstrates the distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and deep sleep (*svāpa*) by means of the passage beginning with "due to the persistence of karma" (*karmānuvṛtteḥ*). This refers to what is stated in the commentary: because one observes the results of past karma, such as pleasure and pain, there is a persistence of karma. Furthermore, if liberation were merely the state of deep sleep, how could injunctions for the sake of liberation be consistent? For what purpose would effort be required for that which is obtained without effort?

This is because of the restatement of his own state [in deep sleep] through such passages as, "Indeed, I was not thus," and because of the restatement of the state of one who has fallen asleep in, "I did not see even this much of an object of enjoyment; I have gone to my destruction. It should be understood that the person who was already ancient and nearly destroyed becomes awakened.

Here, one might object: "Why is it established that there is a re-arising at the time of awakening for one who was merely in deep sleep, given the absence of any specific purpose? Anticipating this doubt, he states a very pertinent specific purpose in the verse beginning with "the beginninglessness of the individual soul" (*jīvānāditva*). If this Sūtra is intended to establish the beginninglessness of the individual souls, then it has already been stated therein: "If it be said [that the soul does not exist] because of the non-differentiation [of the world] due to karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness," and so forth.

If it is argued that by this sūtra the rejection of the imitation of defects in liberation and the rejection of delusion are being performed, that too will be dealt with later on. If it is argued that by establishing permanence the activity of living beings for the sake of attaining heaven is being established, even that has already been understood through scripture and the reasoning supporting it, since such activity for the sake of heaven is impossible without the permanence of the entire Mīmāṃsā system as known from the method of the scriptures.

If it is argued that the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established by proving the stability of the self (*ātman*), that too has already been proven in the *Saugatādhikaraṇa* and other sections. If this section is intended for the purpose of refuting the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Lord (*īśvara*) during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), then it has been stated in various places that even at the end of a kalpa, the soul's oneness consists merely in the relinquishing of name and form (*nāmarūpa*), and not in an identity of essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, that statement is also restricted in its scope.

Thus, he refutes the objection of a certain person who is like a child, who suggests that no further reflection need be made regarding deep sleep (suṣupti), by demonstrating the establishment of the desire to abandon [the world] and so forth through the state of dissolution (pralaya). Some stubborn Naiyāyikas claim that liberation (mokṣa) is merely like a stone. If that were so, then even deep sleep—which is censured in such passages as "I see nothing enjoyable here" and "he has gone to utter destruction"—would be liberation; yet this is not what is sought by the wise as liberation.

Thus, by censuring that liberation which is like a stone in the *Vairāgyapāda*, even the specific desire to abandon it is established; therefore, this incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*) is not purposeless—this is the meaning.

The connection [of the topic] is as follows: after having thoroughly examined the specific states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the state in the form of a swoon, which is equivalent to deep sleep, is now investigated.

Because waking and dreaming are characterized by the presence of consciousness (*prajñā*), while deep sleep and fainting (*mūrchā*) consist in the loss of consciousness, there is a mutual connection between them. An inquiry into their meaning is as follows: Is fainting one of the states such as waking, dreaming, or deep sleep, or is it a distinct state? Can a difference be established through its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) or not? And is the connection with the subtle vital breath (*sūkṣma-prāṇa*) the defining characteristic of fainting, or not?

On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: "Indeed, four distinct states are well-known in the world through the division of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death. Among these, waking and dreaming are not devoid of external cognition; deep sleep is [distinct] because it is filled with breath; and fainting is not death, because the group of senses and vital breaths has been stilled. He restates this with the words "waking," etc., and rejects it with "no," etc. First, he establishes the difference between fainting and death by means of the difference in their causes, starting with "from death," etc.

One reason is that there is a distinction between the causes of fainting and death: fainting results from a mere blow and so forth, whereas death results from such things as the severing of the head. He states another reason: "sthitau" (in the case of duration). People are uncertain whether one who has fainted will remain in that state until the end or whether he is dead; this doubt makes known the difference between fainting and death. He states a third reason as well: "utthiteḥ" (because of rising). Among those who have fainted, someone may rise again due to the influence of mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like.

The meaning is that one who has died goes only to the next world because the time of rising [from death] is uncertain. Then, suspecting what this specific state called "fainting" (mūrchā) might be, he says: "to die. Having begun to die according to the natural course, one faints midway; thus, the specific state of the fulfillment of the purpose of dying should be understood as "fainting. The meaning is that fainting is half-death.

Here, by establishing the mutual distinction in meaning among all eight topics (*adhikaraṇas*), [the author] describes the division of the section (*peṭikā*) and the internal subdivisions (*avāntarapeṭikā*) in the subsequent section with the words "of living beings" (*jantūnām*). Thus, by means of four topics, the calamity that afflicts living beings during the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, has been demonstrated. Beyond this, however, even while in conjunction with all these states, Brahman—which is itself inherently faultless and possessed of auspicious qualities—is being purified; such is the division of the section.

In the *Uttara-peṭikā* as well, he states the disparity between the first and second sections by way of their different meanings, beginning with the words "saṃsarga" (contact) and so forth. Through both of these sections, he removes the defects rooted in mere contact and those rooted in the expression of identity (*tādātmya*). Then, regarding the meaning of the latter two sections, he says "hīnatva" (inferiority) and so forth.

Since worship is impossible in the absence of being superior to all else and in the absence of unsurpassed magnificence, he refutes the loss of being superior to all and the lack of unsurpassed magnificence through the latter two sections; such is the mutual distinction.

The connection [between this section and the previous one] is as follows: having described in the preceding section the individual soul (*jīva*) transmigrating and subject to the state of death for the sake of establishing an excellence of detachment (*vairāgya*), the dual-natured character (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) of the Blessed Lord is now stated for the sake of establishing a specific longing for that which is to be attained. This very point is clearly demonstrated by the words "freedom from qualities" (*nairguṇyam*). Here, this section proceeds specifically to refute the position of those who speak falsely (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*) after first stating their view.

They indeed say: "without qualities (nirguṇa) and stainless (nirañjana). Thus, the qualitylessness of Brahman alone is authoritative. Then, raising the objection as to what the status of the descriptions of qualities—such as "whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"—might be, he says: "the description of qualities."

The meaning is that the description of qualities is merely a discourse on dharmas and objects imagined through ignorance, intended for the purpose of enticement. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, if qualities are absent, are you saying that Brahman possesses defects by its very nature?"—he says, "freedom from defects" (*nairdoṣyam*). The point is this: both the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and the absence of defects (*nirdoṣatva*) are inherent in Brahman. This is what he expresses by the phrase "as a reality" (*vastuvattvena*).

Raising the objection, "In that case, would the qualities, form, and so forth of Brahman established by the Śruti and Purāṇas, as well as its connection with the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra) well-known to all the world, not be [negated]? he says: "That other" (taditarat). We have stated only a portion of this. Thus, in order to refute those who are deluded by the deceptive doctrines (kuhanāvāda) intent on robbing the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) of their sovereignty, the section beginning with "Not even from a change of place" (na sthānato'pi) is commenced. "Many-horned" means having many forms.

The connection [of this section] with the preceding one is made clear by the commentary beginning with the words "doṣadarśanāt" (due to the observation of defects), and has already been demonstrated by us previously. The purpose of that inquiry is as follows: whether those undesirable states that befall the individual soul (*jīva*) while situated in states such as deep sleep and departure from the body also necessarily apply to its inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) and to that which constitutes its body, or not. That is to say: is the soul's connection with undesirable states caused by its connection with the body, or is it caused by its connection with *karman*?

Does the fact that Brahman possesses both characteristics, as established by scripture even when it has a body, lead one to understand that the connection with karma is the very cause of its being a non-human goal (apuruṣārtha), or not? Is the possession of both characteristics established by scripture real (tāttvika) or unreal (atāttvika)? And does the statement, "Now therefore the instruction: 'not this, not this'," constitute a negation of all previously mentioned specific attributes, or a negation of the limited nature previously described?

Is the consistency between the opening and the conclusion of the passage maintained by the negation of all specific attributes (*sarvaviśeṣaniṣedha*), or by the negation of the limited nature of what has been previously described (*prakṛtaitāvattvaniṣedha*)? Here, having specifically presented the position of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the author also demonstrates its refutation according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "this is to be rejected" (*heyam*). Indeed, the proponent of the prima facie view thinks as follows: just as immersion in pus and blood is to be avoided by a king’s servant, so too must it be avoided by the king himself; otherwise, that [immersion] would not even be something to be avoided by him.

In that case, even for Īśvara, abiding in a body like a *jīva* would necessarily be a cause of suffering. Anticipating the objection that "the *jīva* dwells in the body under the control of karma, whereas Īśvara does so by his own will, and therefore there is no fault," he refutes it with the words "even by his own will. Even by his own will, immersion in pus, blood, and the like is seen to be a cause of suffering, because the nature of things cannot be questioned. He rejects the stated position with the word "no" (*na*), and states the reason for this with the phrase "because he is without adjuncts" (*nirupādheḥ*).

This is the meaning: in the world, indeed, the relationship between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted is altered according to the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*). For example, warmth that is favorable in the morning is unfavorable at midday, and coolness that is favorable at midday is unfavorable in the morning. Likewise, it is observed even through the difference of persons: grass and such things that are favorable for animals are unfavorable for humans. Similarly, even through the difference of states, food that is favorable to one who is hungry—even if it is delicious—is unfavorable to one who has already eaten.
This very point was stated by the venerable Parāśara:
That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, arises again as a source of suffering;
for it likewise arises as a cause of anger and as a cause of serenity.

"Therefore, nothing has suffering as its nature, nor does anything have happiness as its nature. Thus, the distinction between pleasure and pain is observed even according to the difference in the perceiver. In the case of one and the same child, there is pleasure when it is said, "This is your son," but there is pain when it is said, "This is the son of an enemy. In this way, the transformation of pleasure and pain due to various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is well-known and witnessed by all the world. Likewise, the distinction between the pleasure and pain of living beings (*jīva*), which arises under the influence of the limiting adjuncts of actions consisting of merit and demerit, cannot be denied.

Just as in the world, the imbalance of objects characterized by being favorable or unfavorable for those possessing wind, bile, and phlegm is taught in the *Āyurveda* and other sciences, and is likewise observed; therefore, it is not appropriate to speak of the Lord’s connection with karma or his connection with pleasure and pain resulting from that [karma] on account of his abiding in bodies. Anticipating the objection that the Lord too might have a connection with karma precisely because of his connection with a body, he provides the rebuttal: "eternal" (*nitya*).

In this regard, there is this dilemma: does the word "Lord" (īśvara) refer to the sovereign master and controller of the entire universe, or merely to a king and the like? If it refers to the latter, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because even kings and others are clearly observed to experience pleasure and pain. If it refers to the former, the very nature of being a Lord is not established, because there is a contradiction in saying that one who experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth is a Lord; for the experience of pleasure and pain is indeed the fruit of karma.

Karma is indeed a specific excellence (*guṇaviśeṣa*) produced by the non-transgression of the preservation of the Lord’s command; or, according to the principles of the *adhyātma* scriptures, it is the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the Lord, the Ruler, to restrain or favor. How, then, could there be the consequence of the Lord experiencing pleasure or pain? If you say that, out of delusion, there is some ruler even of the Lord, let the scripture itself—"No one equal to Him or superior to Him is seen"—deal you a blow upon the cheek.

"Even if you are struck, if you still prattle on, let the exponents of Brahman (brahmavādins) cast you out! Therefore, because there is no other Lord who issues commands to this Lord, He is not subject to the scriptures. Due to the absence of subjection to the scriptures, there is no connection with karma. And due to the absence of connection with karma, there is no consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain occasioned by connection with a body; such is the path of the great-souled ones who are experts in the discrimination between the authoritative and the non-authoritative. He states "by the scripture itself" to show that this very meaning has been clearly demonstrated by the scripture itself through its own analysis.

For the Śruti text, "Two birds," speaks of the experience of the fruits of karma by one among the two—the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—who reside in a single body, while the other is characterized by the absence of such experience and possesses unsurpassed radiance. It has already been established that in the verse "Two birds," it is precisely the individual soul and the Supreme Self that are distinguished and described.
Furthermore, the absence of contradiction with the Paiṅgi-Śruti has been clearly demonstrated in that very place; therefore, we shall desist here.

Here, someone, not understanding the true nature of the matter due to blindness and excessive pride, raises an objection again: "For instance, according to the position of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and others, since God acts as the impeller of merit and demerit, even though He exists within another body, He lacks corporeality; therefore, He is not denotable by words such as 'Brāhmaṇa'. Consequently, [the injunction] 'A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice'..."

"In such sentences as 'A Kṣatriya should sacrifice,' there is no possibility at all of [the subject] falling within the scope of an injunction. Furthermore, according to your own established doctrine, since words such as 'Brahmin' and 'Kṣatriya' primarily denote the Lord (Īśvara), it is the Lord alone who becomes the object of an injunction. [But] because He would be subject to commands such as 'He should do' or 'He should not do,' His very nature as the Lord is undermined."

This is restated in the verse beginning with "brahmakṣatrādi. The meaning of the words here is as follows: within the bodies of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and others, the Lord, though all-pervasive like the atomic individual soul (jīva), abides as the Self by way of being the impeller of the body; thus, while being denotable by those respective terms, He becomes expressible by the words "Brahmin" and so forth through Your permission.

Therefore, how could that Lord, being qualified by limiting adjuncts such as Brahminhood and so forth, not be subject to those respective injunctions? If you argue that he is not subject to them because he is the Lord himself, we reply: no, for one must not embrace atheism regarding a matter directly established by the Śruti. Consequently, it follows that the Lord—who is the very object of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions—is a mine of all defects. This [is merely] blind prattle.

He refutes this, saying "it is not so," and explains that very point with the words beginning "it is not made known. Herein lies the dilemma: do you assert that an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in making known what was unknown, or in impelling one to act who had not previously acted? First of all, making known what was unknown is not possible in the case of God; thus he says, "He is not made known. He states the reason for this as follows:

"Because he has not experienced separation" means "because he is omniscient. Indeed, no benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the sun by a lamp. Nor is it possible for him to be impelled toward what he has not already undertaken. To strengthen the stated point, he provides an example of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) from the perspective of worldly experience, saying "one who knows only a little," and so on. For in the world, it is observed by everyone—and cannot be denied—that servants and others are informed regarding their duties because they know only a little, and are urged to act because they are dependent on others.

Therefore, the claim that the omniscient Lord must be both the object of knowledge and the one who is impelled is not the discourse of the wise, but rather that of the unintelligent; thus do the virtuous mock it. As for the argument that even the Lord—who is denoted by terms such as "Brahmā" and so forth—is subject to being commanded because this is established by scripture (*śruti*), that too is laughable. For scripture speaks only of what is appropriate, and never of what is utterly inappropriate or contradicted by other scriptures; may you consider this yourself as well.

In this section concerning the two-fold characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga-adhikaraṇa*), indeed, the state of being the adversary of all that is to be rejected and the state of being solely composed of auspicious qualities are described by way of these two characteristics. And this is to be established by means of three logical principles (*nyāya*). Regarding the injunctions "One should not harm any living beings" and "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma," the principle of general rule and exception (*utsarga-apavāda-nyāya*) applies, because the prohibitive scripture has as its scope matters other than those specifically ordained.

In passages such as "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," the principle of the section on the opening statement (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*) applies; for the opening statement is stronger than the concluding statement, because the opening statement is free from contradiction while the concluding statement is subject to contradiction. In cases where there is a conflict between two [rules] whose sequence is not fixed, such as "If the Udgātṛ should be cut off," the principle of the section on the subsequent cutting-off (*apacchedādhikaraṇanyāya*) applies. This is because, according to the rule "The arising of the latter is not established without subverting the former," the latter can only arise after the former has been subverted.

On this point, the proponents of falsity (mṛṣāvādins) say: First, there arise statements concerning the qualified (saguṇa), and these are indeed prior because they convey meanings in the form of injunctions (vidhi). The statements concerning the unqualified (nirguṇa), however, are subsequent because they convey meanings in the form of prohibitions (niṣedha). For it is well known in the world that prohibition is preceded by an injunction. Therefore, because the enjoining [texts] and direct perception (pratyakṣa-pramāṇa) occur first, they are sublated; whereas the subsequent status of the prohibitive statements—such as "without qualities, stainless" (nirguṇaṃ nirañjanam) and "there is no diversity whatsoever here" (neha nānāsti kiñcana)—constitutes their sublativeness. The same applies to inference (anumāna) as well.

The same applies to the ritual scriptures (*karma-śāstra*). Furthermore, those statements even within the Vedānta that are devoted to the meditation on Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-upāsana*) must likewise be sublated, as they are equivalent to the ritual scriptures. Moreover, certain statements asserted by proponents of the qualified view (*saguṇa-vādin*) which concern the nature of Brahman with attributes must also be sublated, because they fall within the scope of injunctions and are antecedent [to the realization of the absolute]. However, the statements concerning the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) persist as authoritative, because they fall within the scope of negation and, being posterior, possess the power of sublation.

Just as in the *Apacchedādhikaraṇa*, when two mutually contradictory expiations arise due to the occurrence of two causes—the disconnections of the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartṛ*—the expiation caused by the later disconnection is performed, overriding the expiation caused by the earlier disconnection; so too here, authoritative persons must accept the qualitylessness (*nairguṇya*) that is the subject of the statement regarding the absence of qualities, overriding the quality that is the subject of the injunctive statement.

This [objection] he refutes by means of the two other principles (*nyāya*), stating "by way of a general rule" (*utsargeṇa*). "One should not harm any living beings" is the general rule (*utsarga*); "One should sacrifice a beast to Agni and Soma" is the exception (*apavāda*). In this regard, it is the method of the systematizers (*tāntrika*) that the general rule is indeed set aside by the exception, but the exception is not set aside by the general rule. By that logic, "devoid of qualities, stainless" is the general rule.

The statement "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true" is an exception (apavāda), because one [statement] has a general scope while the other has a specific scope. Therefore, the conclusion of those learned in the principles of interpretation is that the statement regarding the absence of qualities (nirguṇa-vākya) must be restricted by the statement regarding qualities (saguṇa-vākya) to the sense of qualities that are to be abandoned. This is what he expresses with the words "Therefore... (tasmāt).

The prohibition of qualities and so forth in the passage from the *Brāhma* [section], "without qualities, stainless," would remain as something that transcends the scope of injunctions such as "whose desires are true, whose resolves are true. Having thus explained the removal of contradiction between the passages concerning the qualified and the unqualified through the principle of general rule and exception (*utsargāpavāda*) by means of a difference in their respective objects, he states—once the contradiction has been resolved—that there is no need for the application of the principle of the section on the "simultaneous disconnection" (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*): "For not when they have the same object. Indeed, the principle of the section on the simultaneous disconnection applies only when there is equality of object.

Because the two cases of disconnection (*apaccheda*) are equal by virtue of being disconnections, here the contradiction is pacified by a difference in subject matter established through another principle of reasoning (*nyāya*). Therefore, the principle of the section on disconnection (*apacchedādhikaraṇanyāya*), which is the cause for that pacification, is indeed to be disregarded due to its pointlessness. Just as when one bitten by poison has the defect of the poison removed by any one of various gems or mantras, what is the use of another pseudo-remedy? In this context, [the author] demonstrates that the application of the principle of the section on disconnection is merely a fallacy by stating, "it is seen."

The meaning is this: the principle of the section on "truncation" (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*) applies where there is no fixed order of sequence; for instance, sometimes the *udgātṛ* is truncated first and sometimes the *pratihartṛ*, and therefore in that case the latter prevails. Here, however, the order is indeed fixed: the injunction comes first and the prohibition follows. For in the section on the "introductory statement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), when considering whether the horse-sacrifice offering belongs to the giver or the receiver, it was determined—following the introductory statement—that it belongs to the giver alone.

Therefore, even in this case, it must be determined that because the former is stronger, the passages concerning the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇa*) alone possess greater authority, and not the passages concerning the unqualified [Brahman] (*nirguṇa*). All that remains to be said on this matter should be consulted in the *Tattvaṭīkā* and other commentaries on the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya* itself, at the very first sūtra, it is stated: "The claim regarding the superior authority of the latter [passages] is ridiculed as being a mere deviation from the victory of the Mādhyamikas. This very point should be investigated in detail by attentive students.

Furthermore, experts in logic speak of a contradiction with that upon which one depends for subsistence. As they have said: "In those cases where cognitions arise independently of one another, it is indeed observed that the subsequent is stronger than the preceding."

Therefore, for those who have not studied Mīmāṃsā or have forgotten what they studied, this statement—that the scriptures negating difference possess greater authority because they depend upon the perception of difference regarding both the essential nature [of Brahman] and its own validity—is merely a claim. For even in the *Apacchedādhikaraṇa*, there can be no determination of relative strength or weakness without the perception of difference such that "this is prior" and "that is subsequent. Nor can there be a determination of validity without that perception; thus, we shall desist from further elaboration.

"In that case, let us rely upon the Śruti itself; for it declares everywhere that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is indeed false. That alone is the truth; surely a mother does not give her child poison."

Therefore, some people boast that the very nature of reality is the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca), because this is established by such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent. This [view] he refutes by means of a careful consideration of the scriptures itself with the words, "The effect is existent" (sattvaṃ kāryasya). The meaning is this: for the statement, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent? accepts the existence of the effect while rejecting only the non-existence of the cause. By this, it is stated that the effect is existent and the cause is also existent.

Therefore, because of the use of the word "some" (*eka*) in the phrase "Now some say" (*taddhaika āhuḥ*), it is understood that non-existence (*asattva*) is indeed the position of the opponent. As for the connection of the words, the inquiry—"How can there be existence from non-existence?"—makes known the existence of both cause and effect. Anticipating the objection, "Let this sentence not be our support; rather, let the sentence 'Just as, my dear' (*yathā somya*) be our basis," he provides the rebuttal: "Because it is different from the substance" (*dravyānyatvam*).

The meaning is that even that statement merely rejects the numerical difference between cause and effect as distinct substances; it does not, however, establish the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*). To the objection that, in that case, you must not say that the scriptural declaration, "There is no diversity whatsoever here," is our support, he replies with the words "because of inclusion" (*antarbhāvāt*). Since the qualifiers are included within the qualified Lord, the statement "There is no diversity here" also rejects only that diversity which is not of the nature of Brahman.

If it is argued that the sentence "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), which directly negates the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is our family treasure, [the author] replies that even that is like gold found in a dream, stating: "Having specified... (verse 17). Having previously stated certain attributes of Brahman, the doctrine of "not this, not this" removes the doubt of a dull-witted person who might think that the very extent thus specified constitutes the entirety of Brahman. By saying "not this, not this," only the specific modes previously mentioned are negated, but not the collection of qualities yet to be described.

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras stated: "For [the scripture] denies that the nature of Brahman is limited to what has been previously described, and then declares further beyond that. Thus, since the authority of all the Śrutis is established through their distinct subject matters, it is only those who maintain that Brahman possesses qualities (saguṇa) who achieve excellence in determining the meaning of the Vedānta; the doctrine of the absence of qualities (nirguṇa), on the other hand, is merely the arbitrary chatter of those who claim there are no qualities.

"Granted that these may be the solutions, yet this one point remains unestablished: the illustration provided—that the Lord, who resides everywhere, is like the sun reflected in reservoirs of water—actually demonstrates their falsity (mithyātva)," so thinks someone; to him he gives the reply: "tattaddṛṣṭi... (according to each respective perception). For in the case of intended meaning (*tātparya*), the word itself is the authority (*pramāṇa*). Here, the falsity of individual souls (*jīva*) is not what is intended to be expressed, because that would contradict authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-viruddha*).

Moreover, although Brahman is omnipresent, it is merely denied that it participates in the specific increase and decrease belonging to this or that particular object. Just as the reflection of the moon's orb appearing in waves does not truly possess the increase, decrease, and so forth belonging to the waves, so too the supreme Brahman, abiding as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) of all, has no connection with the distinctions arising from those respective objects.

This is merely an illustration showing that, due to the specific power of Brahman existing here [in the individual soul], there is no occurrence of defects caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: the Supreme Self, who is perceived as complete with all attributes in every object and location, is devoid of distinctions such as increase or decrease; for thus it is said: "Like the sun in various receptacles of water."

Since the meaning must be described in accordance with the intended purport (*tātparya*), why is this strained interpretation (*kliṣṭakalpanā*) adopted? One might suspect that the illustration is given here precisely for the sake of showing non-connection (*asaṃsarga*); that is, the meaning here is that Brahman is untouched by anything at all. To this, he gives the reply: "No" (*na hi*). For the great sages do not provide only a single illustrative example.

In one place, as in the verse, "Like the sun in various reservoirs of water," and in another, "Just as the single ether appears distinct within jars and other vessels," a reflection that does not actually exist is cited; whereas elsewhere, the ether itself, which truly exists, is cited. Therefore, for the sake of consistency between both examples, the appropriate object must be cited, rather than merely its state of being untouched by the defects inherent in those [reflections]. Otherwise, if only one were employed, the other would be excluded, and thus neither would be established.

Having thus established the reality of the meaning in detail, he concludes that [Brahman] possesses both characteristics with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). It is "possessing two characteristics" (*dviliṅgam*), meaning endowed with both sets of qualities because it is the opposite of everything to be abandoned and is solely composed of auspiciousness. It is "possessing a twofold majesty" (*dvividhavibhavam*), meaning distinguished by both types of manifestation. The sense is that it is distinguished by the two kinds of manifestations well-known from such scriptural authorities as "The Person alone is all this. For this has been explained by the venerable Parāśara in passages such as "He consists of all auspicious qualities," and so forth.
The mention of the "Vedānta position" is for the purpose of relegating the position of the proponents of falsehood (the Mādhyamikas) to the category of the Buddhists.

The connection [of this section] with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is stated as follows: "Now, the manner in which that insentient entity (*acidvastu*) has the nature of Brahman is considered for the purpose of establishing the faultlessness of Brahman.

This is the meaning: in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the faultlessness of Brahman was asserted. For the sake of establishing that faultlessness, it is now considered whether the insentient entity has the nature of Brahman according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils (*ahikuṇḍalanyāya*), or according to the analogy of light and its radiance (*prabhāprabhāvannyāya*), or else by way of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Thus is the connection with the preceding section.

The investigation into that meaning is as follows: Is the nature of Brahman in non-conscious (acid) entities according to the analogy of the snake and its coils (*ahikuṇḍala-nyāya*)? Or is it in the manner of light and that which possesses light (*prabhā-prabhāvad-rūpeṇa*)? Or is it through the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāvena*), as part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitvena*)? Does the negation of non-conscious attributes in passages such as, "He indeed is this great unborn Self, undecaying and immortal," lead one to understand the world's nature as Brahman through the relation of qualifier and qualified, or not? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "Of the creator of the universe... and so forth.

For the Supreme Person, the creator of the universe, there is no possibility of suffering for Himself when generating the insentient category (*acid-varga*) from His own portion (*svāṃśa*), because the insentient lacks suffering. Furthermore, if the status of being a "portion" is attributed to the insentient, then the numerous examples cited—such as clay and its effects—are perfectly consistent with the proposition and occur quite naturally. Therefore, Brahman alone, by virtue of His playful inclination (*vihāra-vaśāt*), undergoes modification even while creating the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*) and other things; thus, it follows that the creation of the insentient in the form of a modification is indeed logical. [The author] rejects this view with the words "no" (*na*).

He explains that very point with the words "His own part" (*svāṃśa*). This is the meaning: for misfortune (*anartha*) is indeed twofold. One is the production of suffering; the other is the induction of delusion regarding an object capable of yielding unsurpassed bliss. Although there is no production of suffering because insentient matter (*acid-vastu*) is distinct from consciousness (*cit*), the induction of delusion—by way of its being of the nature of insentient matter—regarding the Reality which is essentially unsurpassed knowledge and bliss, is indeed the induction of misfortune for oneself. Therefore, the creation of His own part consisting of insentient matter is simply not possible.

Having restated other positions along with the position already mentioned, he refutes them with the words "some say" (kaścit). Previously, the view that Brahman itself brings about the state of non-consciousness within itself was raised as an objection and refuted. Now, in order to avoid the aforementioned defects, some say that there exists a certain eternal, non-conscious portion (acid-aṃśa) which is established from time immemorial and undergoes various transformations.

Even in that case, the contradiction remains as it was, because it is utterly untenable to conceive of the omniscient Brahman as having a nature eternally conjoined with such ignorance. He restates another position: "Like foam, etc. Others say that within the ocean of Brahman, which is pure Being (*sanmātra*), the triad of principles consisting of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord arises through the process of transformation, according to the analogy of foam, waves, and bubbles. That too is exactly the same [as the previous case].

Furthermore, because one imputes modification to that which is changeless, the fault of causing one's own ruin remains as it was. Moreover, some maintain that the world and Brahman possess the same genus (*sājātya*) according to the analogy of the moon and its light; however, this is utterly unworthy of consideration, as it is inconsistent with those Vedāntic statements that establish the identity of the world and Brahman.

If "sameness of genus" were intended merely in the sense of being real entities, then it would not be something to be known through the Vedānta, since it is already well-known to everyone. If, on the other hand, it refers to sameness of genus by virtue of being the Self (*ātmatayā*), then it simply does not exist in the case of insentient matter.

If [it is argued that] there is a commonality of genus (*sājātya*) by virtue of being the Lord (*īśvara*), this is refuted by the established doctrine of the three principles (*tattvatraya*). Furthermore, it contradicts the Śruti: "The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller. Therefore, the conclusion of those who know the reality of Vedānta is that oneness exists through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Consequently, all disputants are to be terrified here because they contradict the internal consistency of all Vedānta statements; such is the syntactical connection of the words.

In the commentary itself, the connection (*saṅgati*) is stated by means of the introductory sentence of the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*), which is linked to the concluding sentence of the preceding section: "Since Brahman is established as possessing both characteristics—being free from defects and being a mine of auspicious qualities—it is now refuted, after having been raised by certain fallacious arguments, that there exists some supreme reality even beyond this Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause of the world in the form of both its efficient and material cause."

The investigation into that meaning, however, concerns whether this Brahman, which possesses both characteristics, is there anything further beyond it, or not; and whether, if it is indeed the supreme, the designations of "bridge," "measurement," "relation," and "difference" can be logically justified, or not. In this regard, the author of the Sūtras, having sequentially restated the reasons for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), demonstrates the refutation in accordance with the order of the Sūtras, beginning with the word "setum."

Because of the statement that it is something to be crossed, namely, "having crossed this bridge"; because of the statement that Brahman is limited, namely, "Brahman has four quarters and sixteen fruits"; because of the mention of a relationship with something to be attained, namely, "this is the bridge to immortality," where it is designated as being related to another, distinct immortality by virtue of being its means of attainment; and because of the scriptural testimony of another's superiority, namely, "he goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high."

And because of the Śruti passage, "That which is higher than the high, greater than the great," there is another [entity] beyond everything. According to the proponents of the doctrine of that which transcends space (*vyomātītavādinaḥ*), this Supreme Person—who is the cause of the universe—must be merely the *attainer* by way of being the "conductor" (*ativāhika*) who leads one across, and not the object attained; for the object attained must be something else entirely. He refutes this, saying "it is not so. That which is the cause of the world is itself the object of meditation, according to the rule: "But the Cause is to be meditated upon."

And that which is to be meditated upon is precisely that which is to be attained, because of the determination of the identity between the attainer and the attained in such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Therefore, the conclusion of those who maintain the final Vedantic truth is that the bridge to immortality is itself immortality. If it is asked how there can be a statement regarding the nature of a "bridge" in relation to this Brahman, the answer here is: "As a bridge. One should accept a function [for Brahman] that is not contradicted by many means of valid knowledge.

The fact that the Lord alone is both the goal to be attained (*prāpyatva*) and the means of attainment (*prāpakatva*) must certainly be accepted, as this is established by all the Vedānta scriptures. Therefore, the meaning of the arguments concerning His being a "bridge" (*setu*) and so forth must be explained by postulating a suitable sense. Otherwise, there would be no distinction in the world between primary and secondary usage;

secondary usages would have to be abandoned, and even the explanation of the meaning of sentences in various contexts by the learned—achieved through purifying the marks of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*) such as the introduction and conclusion—would not be possible, resulting in a total collapse of all the scriptures.

It has been stated here that the previous mention of "being a bridge" (*setu*) and so forth is to be interpreted by postulating suitable meanings. He demonstrates those very suitable meanings in their proper order, beginning with "the state of being a bridge" (*setutvam*). "The state of being a bridge" means the state of being a support and regulator, like a bridge; that is to say, the capacity for sustaining and restraining. For the Lord alone is indeed the sustainer of all. He provides another meaning as well: "from binding" (*bandhanāt*), for that same Lord binds the entire collection of principles (*tattva-jāta*) without confusion. He also states the interpretation for the expression "limitation" (*parimiti*): "even though [He is] all-pervading" (*vyāpte 'pi*).

Even though this supreme Brahman is all-pervading, the description of it as having limited dimensions is purposeful; this has indeed been stated in various contexts concerning the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) and so forth. As for the statement "Brahman has four quarters," it should be understood as a figurative construction consistent with the respective scriptural passages—such as "All beings are one quarter of Him"—even though Brahman is infinitely vast. Furthermore, the phrase "This is the bridge to the Immortal" should be construed either as "of Brahman, who is of the nature of the Immortal," or as "of the Immortal, which is liberation consisting in the attainment of Brahman."

In this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) describes how, having accepted the supremacy of Nārāyaṇa, the supremacy of one even higher than him is asserted; and he provides an illustrative example for that: just as in the passage "higher than the Imperishable (*akṣara*)," the term "the higher" (*para*) refers to one who is other than the Imperishable, so too is another "higher" spoken of. To point out the disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) when this has been stated, he says: "of another."

The meaning is as follows: In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), when the superiority of that which is designated by the word "the other" (*para*) in the nominative case is asserted, that which is designated by the word "the other" in the ablative case is seen to function as the limit (*avadhi*). And its status as being denoted by the word "the other" is determined from the statement that it is so in relation to the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, which are its effects. In that context, it could be said that either the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is "other than the Imperishable" (*akṣarāt paraḥ*) in relation to its own effects. But here, however—

For by the words, "Indeed, there is nothing else higher than this 'Not this, Not this'," any entity superior to the Supreme Self is rejected; therefore, another superior reality must certainly not be postulated. Now, some have said that in the passage, "That which is higher than that," the pronoun *tat* refers back to the previously mentioned Supreme Person, and thus a different principle higher even than Him is indicated, implying that there exists a reality superior to the Supreme Person. He refutes this with the phrase, "Because of the word *evam*. In that context, the reason is restated as "because of the word *tataḥ* (from that)" and "because of the word *evam* (thus)."

The meaning is that it has already been established through many proofs that the Supreme Person alone is the supreme reality (*paratattva*). Therefore, the passage beginning with "that which is higher than the high" (*yaduttarataram*) refers to the Supreme Person alone, and not to some other principle. He also provides an alternative interpretation for the word *tataḥ*: "or else. In this case, the construction is: "that which is higher than the aforementioned phenomenal world (*prapañca*) because it is pervaded by the Supreme Person—[that which is] formless and free from affliction. Here too, the Supreme Person alone is spoken of as the supreme.

If it were asserted that there exists a reality superior to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), then, at the commencement of this section, by means of the recognition of the Puruṣasūkta, [there would be a contradiction] regarding anything superior to the Supreme Person.

The sense is this: because of the rejection [of the alternative], and because it is logical that the beginning (upakrama) is stronger than the conclusion (upasaṃhāra), the concluding statement must be interpreted in accordance with the beginning precisely according to the method we have stated. This is the application of the words here: in a discourse on the superiority of another Lord—such as in the passage "higher than the high Imperishable"—wherein Prakṛti and the rest are seen as the limit (avadhi), in that very same example, the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and so forth would be the limit in relation to Him.

Furthermore, He is designated as being "higher than the high" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*) by virtue of His transcendence over the entire class of His own effects. However, in this context, where it is taught that there is nothing else higher than what is taught as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), because of the absence of any further limit, it is illogical to speak of anything else higher than that which has been declared as the highest. Therefore, the conceptualization of "the higher" culminates in the Supreme Person alone.

Regarding the phrase "that which is higher than that" (*tato yaduttarataram*), one interpretation is that the word *tat* (that), ending in the ablative case, has the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Another interpretation is that even if it has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*), it refers by means of the word *tat*—as being the subject under discussion—to that which was previously mentioned as being pervaded by the Supreme Person.

Regarding this, he states the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections with the words "ārādhya" (as one to be propitiated). For it is well known in the world that he alone who possesses both supremacy (*paratva*) and magnanimity (*audārya*) is to be served; because even if one possesses supremacy, a miserly person is not to be served, and likewise, even if one possesses magnanimity, a pauper is not to be served. Therefore, in the preceding section, the supremacy of the Lord was stated for the purpose of establishing His status as the object of worship to be expounded in the subsequent quarter-verse.

Furthermore, magnanimity (*audārya*) is stated here by way of describing the bestowal of fruits; this constitutes the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Having thus reiterated that supremacy of the Blessed One which is declared everywhere in the *Trikāṇḍī*, his magnanimity, as conjoined with that [supremacy], is now proclaimed. As for the meaning of the connection: "In whom all the Vedas become one," and "In whom all the Hotṛ-priests become one."

By such authorities as "by one who conforms to the conduct of the castes and stages of life," it was determined in the first section (*kāṇḍa*) that Viṣṇu alone is the object of worship for all ritual acts. In the middle section (*kāṇḍa*) as well, by the statement "Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest," he alone was established as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all deities and their presiding authority.

Furthermore, in this section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*), it has already been demonstrated most clearly in this very chapter that, as expressed throughout these ten chapters, the sole goal is the meditation upon Him who is the means for those terrified by the fear of worldly existence to attain [liberation].

Now, at the conclusion of the chapter on the two-fold marks (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*), at the commencement of the exposition of knowledge (*vidyā*), it is clearly established for the sake of accomplishing the undertaking of knowledge that [the scripture] bestows fruits corresponding to the duties of engagement (*pravṛtti-niṣṭha*)—which consist of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites—and the duties of renunciation (*nivṛtti-niṣṭha*)—which consist of the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of devotion, and so forth. For the activity of living beings is not possible without a purpose, nor is a purpose possible without one who bestows it.

Furthermore, the state of being a donor cannot exist without both supremacy and magnanimity; nor can these two qualities possibly exist anywhere other than in the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, who is the great benefactor who bestows His own self, distinguished by both types of opulence. This is the intended meaning.

The connection has been stated. Now, an inquiry into its meaning is as follows: does the production of the fruits of heaven and liberation arise from ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsana*) preceded by that [connection], or rather from the Lord (Brahman) alone, who exists in the state of Vāyu and others, and who is pleased by ritual action and meditation? For it is said: "He alone leads him to prosperity," and "He is to be attained by whomsoever He chooses."

Does this remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*)—beginning with "thus," etc.—indicate that [Brahman] in its state as air and so forth, as well as in its isolated state, is the bestower of results, or not? Is this remainder of the sentence to be understood according to its literal meaning, or is it intended for something else? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks: "From agriculture and so forth. It is undisputed in the world that there is a result from agriculture and even from activities such as massaging.

Otherwise, activity would be impossible. Furthermore, that result arises solely through a visible means and not through an invisible one, as that would entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*). When a result is produced without mediation, even a visible means is not required. Moreover, the status of ritual factors (*dharma*) as means must certainly not be abandoned, because it is understood through direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Nor is the Vedic revelation here sublated, as in the case of "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*). Therefore, since they are understood through Vedic revelations free from the defect of sublation, the status of ritual factors as means truly exists.

Thus, even though it is heard that the factors (dharmas) are the direct means of accomplishment, it is proper to conclude that the statement "the fruit [arises] from the grace of God" is intended solely for the purpose of praising God. He refutes the suspected view with the word "no. He states the reason for this as "scriptural" (śrauta). Herein is the distinction: one position is that karma alone bestows the fruit occurring at a later time; another is that there is something distinct from karma called the "unseen force" (apūrva); and the third is that a particular deity, pleased by the propitiation in the form of karma, [bestows the fruit].

In the first case, because the action has been accumulated and then destroyed, its very status as the cause of the fruit is impossible. In the second case, however, there are two faults: the abandonment of what is stated in scripture (*śrutahāni*) and the assumption of what is not stated (*aśrutakalpanā*). For it is heard in such passages as, "He, being pleased, pleases him," that the deity alone is the bestower of the fruit. Therefore, the third position must be accepted because it is scriptural and free from contradiction with the facts; thus, it is established that the deity alone is the bestower of the fruit.

This, however, is common [to all]: "For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices"—thus it is stated that He is to be propitiated by all ritual actions and is the bestower of the fruits of all ritual actions. For the lordship of one who does not have the habit of giving would be like any one of the following: a sky-flower, a tortoise's hair, or a rabbit's horn. Therefore, the Commentator determined that "lordship" refers precisely to the state of being the bestower of fruits, because that alone is appropriate to be spoken of in that particular statement and is what is required by the context.

Here, fearing that there might be tautology due to the repetition of the previously stated specific meaning in various places where the status of being the bestower of fruit is mentioned, he refutes this with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). For, in the previous *Devatādhikaraṇa*, by rejecting those who assert that "pleasure and the bestowing of fruit do not exist for deities," the status of being the bestower of fruit has already been established.

However, immediately following this, even in the sūtra, "But [the Lord] takes account of the effort made, because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless," etc., it is stated that the Lord impels merit and demerit in accordance with prior karma, and thus the fruit of action is dependent upon the Lord. Why, then, is the status of being the bestower of fruits stated here as well? Anticipating this very objection, he refutes it with the words, "Even so... (tathāpi).

In various Vedāntic passages such as “He is the witness, the perceiver” and “He is beyond speech and disregard,” because of the mention of His being a witness and His disregard [for worldly affairs], the very engagement in meditation might collapse for a devotee who fears upon merely hearing those statements. Therefore, in this section, the primary quality of the Supreme Lord—the Consort of Śrī, who is supremely magnanimous and whose mind is solely intent on protecting those who have sought refuge—is His very magnanimity, intended to remove the fear of that devotee whose intellect has been muddied by the apprehension that the Lord is indifferent.

The author of the Sūtra establishes this so that it may bear fruit; thus, there is no room for even a scent of tautology. He establishes the manner in which the Lord bestows fruits through the analogy of a king and his sons, following a method observed in the world, stating: "Like a sovereign. For in the world, some fathers among certain sons become sovereigns themselves; they are compassionate, know what is appropriate regarding what ought and ought not to be done, treat all their sons with impartiality, and are generous.

The meaning is that even magnanimity is common to all sons. From such a father, sons—constrained by their respective differences in inclination—attain and obtain that particular object desired by each according to their own wish. Similarly, from the Supreme Person who is endowed with this collection of qualities, all those persons who are His servants and are like sons obtain their own desired objects; this is the implied sense.

In this regard, He clearly demonstrates through the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) that everything—including the goal to be attained, the means of attainment, the obstacles thereto, and the pacification thereof—is present in the Lord as well, according to the analogy of the father and son.

That which is to be obtained by oneself, such as houses, fields, and so forth, in the form of an inheritance, whose loss occurs due to causes such as disobeying the father’s command; and its restoration, which comes through returning once more and prostrating at his feet; and that which is to be given, such as wealth, ornaments, turbans, garments, umbrellas, and fly-whisks; and furthermore, in the absence of a specific pardon for the offense, even punishment and discipline according to worldly custom—all this would likewise apply here.

For a king’s servant, however, the punishment for violating the king’s command is the amputation of a foot or similar corporal penalties; for his son, it is the restriction of livelihood and so forth. Likewise, for those who are not devotees (*abhāgavatas*), the fruit of sin as declared in the scriptures consists of falling into hell and the like. But for devotees (*bhāgavatas*), even when an offense occurs intentionally, [the Lord says]: "Indeed, devotees do not go to the domain of Yama; rather, some disturbances occur to them right here. Thus, their punishment consists merely of such things as blindness or lameness.

Therefore, since—according to the principle stated as, "A light punishment is for one who has surrendered, like the offense of a prince"—the infliction of a penalty disproportionate to the offense upon those who have surrendered would be far too meager, this section encourages the very commencement of meditative worship (*upāsanā*), asserting that the practice of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) should be undertaken immediately through faith in the Lord, who is supremely compassionate and the bestower of all fruits.

By manifesting the specific distinctions among the primary meanings of the words, he illuminates the understanding of the Lord’s supremacy with the phrase "Śuddhānanda" (Pure Bliss). This is the meaning of the words here: because it has been established in this way, [the Lord] is the Supreme Brahman whose essential nature is Pure Bliss, an ocean of auspicious qualities, possessing His own body which is true and eternal, and who is endowed with a supreme reality-form; He is preeminent through the Goddess, ornaments, weapons, attendants, retinues, and so forth, and is characterized by the two-fold manifestation of His radiant play of enjoyment. Thus, he states that [the Lord] is distinguished by these two manifestations (*vibhūti*).

The term *kanat* denotes the state of being intensely radiant; for the Śruti says: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven.
