Regarding the phrase "being the one to whom everything else is subordinate" (*śeṣitva*), the essence of the determination of the truth of Vedānta is as follows: the world constitutes the body of the Lord through its status as the supported, the commanded, and the subordinate; conversely, the Lord constitutes the body [of the world] through His status as the support and so forth. The permanence of the relationship means its eternally established nature. By the phrase "the progenitor of heaven and liberation," he specifically states the meaning of the adhikaraṇa (section) beginning with "The fruit [comes] from Him, because that is logical" (*phalamata upapatteḥ*).

The meaning is that while Hari is thus constituted, our gaze is unblinking and our scripture alone is an uncontradicted means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the sense is that no dispute should be raised by followers of the Veda regarding these matters established by scripture. Consequently, for all those opponents who seek to negate the attributes, form, and manifestations of the Lord by means of fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) equal in status to mere sophistry, scripture itself is their adversary. Thus, let them pay homage to the inference of the purity of the headless [corpse], and let them also hold in high regard such statements as, "Wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa."
Alternatively, it would result in mere mockery if they were to disparage even their own Brahminhood by means of their humanity and so forth.

In this section (pāda), for the purpose of explaining the distinctions among qualities within the various divisions of knowledge (*vidyā*) that follow, the author elucidates each of the distinct purposes stated in every individual topic (*adhikaraṇa*). [The Lord is] the creator of objects related to the dream state; the sustainer of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), meaning the support of deep sleep; the protector of the sleeping, meaning the guardian of the sleeper by virtue of the absence of destruction while asleep; the awakener of the fainting, meaning that He sometimes brings about the awakening of one who has fainted; and "sometimes death," etc., is the meaning of the words [of the text].

The phrase "anaghaśubhaguṇa" (one whose auspicious qualities are faultless) expresses His possession of both genders [male and female]. The phrase "acidbhir aṃśī svadehaiḥ" (the possessor of parts through His own bodies, which are non-conscious) expresses the meaning of the *ahikuṇḍala* (serpent-coil) and other such analogies. Next, the meaning of the *parādhikaraṇa* (section on the Supreme) is given as "pāramyasya ekasīmeti" (the sole limit of supremacy); the meaning is that He alone is supreme, and there is no one superior to Him. The phrase "sakalaphalada" (bestower of all fruits) expresses the meaning of the *phalādhikaraṇa* (section on the fruit). Having raised the doubt, "For what purpose is the Blessed Lord described in this way?", he says: "bhaktibhūmnaḥ" (for the sake of the abundance of devotion). The meaning is: for the sake of increasing the devotion consisting of the Brahma-vidyā to be described hereafter.

"Let it be that such a collection of qualities is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*); we too say this," so argue the proponents of falsehood. To this, he gives the reply: "For [it is] in truth" (*satye hi*). When it is stated thus—that the qualities and so forth are indeed real—only then can the distinctions of form and so on regarding supreme devotion and the like be explained in the subsequent chapter (*pāda*). This is the meaning: the Vedānta scripture establishes reality itself. If the collection of objects it propounds were unreal, what would reality be? If one says "nothing at all," then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of merging with the Mādhyamikas follows.

If it is argued that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is non-reality while the qualified alone (*viśeṣya-mātra*) is reality, who has said this? If you say "the Śruti," then by virtue of being expressible (*vācyatva*) and cognizable (*vedyatva*), Brahman would once again become illusory. If you say that it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), then what is this self-luminosity? If you say it is "being conducive to immediate empirical usage (*aparokṣa-vyavahāra*) while being free from defects," then by the very fact of being conducive to empirical usage, its illusoriness (*mithyātva*) would emerge once more.

If you argue that there is no fault because self-luminosity is false, then since self-luminosity is illusory, it follows that being illuminated by another is the reality; thus, you once again establish the falsity of Brahman through its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*). We feel ashamed even to engage in debate with such an incoherent speaker. In this way, by means of the ten quarters previously mentioned, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) conducive to the means of liberation has been established.

In what follows, the meditation that serves as the cause for the fruit consisting of the attainment of the Supreme Brahman will be clearly elucidated through six verses; thus, he states the connection between the preceding and the subsequent sections with the words "tattvajñāna" (knowledge of reality). For the person about to be liberated, the most beneficial meditation is permeated by the knowledge of reality. To explain this further, [the author] now—having shaken off the delirious arguments of opposing disputants, which are like the great delirium caused by a fever of logic regarding the subject of reality—proceeds since the awakening to reality has been achieved and the knowledge of reality has arisen.

"Because all his obligations have been burnt away by the fire of knowledge of Brahman, the sage who lives according to the root of the Śruti would no longer be a servant of the Veda. To those false-speakers who thus deny being servants of the Veda, [the scripture declares]: "He, indeed, living in this manner for as long as he lives, attains the world of Brahman."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: [the scripture] declares that the worship of Murāri (Viṣṇu), established by the Vedas (*śruti*), must be pursued throughout one's life for the sake of attaining liberation (*mukti*). Thus, indeed, the proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādī*) maintains this view: for only he who is possessed of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) and the like is a servant of the Veda; since agency (*kartṛtva*) and enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*) are not attributes of the Self (*anātman-dharma*). Now, agency in performing optional rites (*kāmya-kartṛtva*) has already been rejected for the knower (*jñānin*) because it is a cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Agency in the meditation upon Brahman (*brahmopāsana-kartṛtva*) is likewise rejected, because that too is included among the attributes of transmigratory existence.

But Brahman is neither to be known, nor to be meditated upon, nor even to be attained. Nor is this matter made known by the Vedas; for it is eternally self-luminous. Even its self-luminosity cannot be defined. If it is asked, "How can Brahman be established if it cannot be defined?"—let there be no establishment of Brahman. For this very reason, the knowers of the supreme self (adhyātmavidas) declare: "He taught by means of silence alone."

Thus, those who speak incoherently and hold false views abandon even the *Sadvidyā* (the Knowledge of the Six), which they have accepted as the very essence of their own system, let alone the various distinct branches of knowledge such as the *Daharavidyā*, which are endowed with diverse qualities and refinements. Therefore, the refutation of that [view] is now commenced. Here, by the words "bhīmābhya" and so forth, he demonstrates the difference in meaning among all four quarters (*pādas*) of the third chapter, the mutual distinction between each pair of chapters due to the difference in their subject matter, and the fixed order of succession.

In this regard, it is clearly elucidated that within the first two quarters [of the work], both the cause for the attainment of qualification (*adhikāra-sampatti-hetu*) and the qualification itself—which consists of a conjunction of detachment from worldly existence (*saṃsāra-virakti*) with a yearning for the Blessed One (*bhagavati tṛṣṇā-yoga*)—are expressed by the two quarters respectively. Therein, the meaning of the quarter on detachment (*vairāgya-pāda*) is stated by the verse beginning with *bhīmābhyo*, and the meaning of the quarter on the dual characteristics (*ubhaya-liṅga-pāda*) is stated by the verse beginning with *tṛṣṇām*.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: "As long as one directs one's thirst toward the ocean of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa, so much has been said"—thus he states the meaning of the latter two quarters with the word *ittham*. The syntactical connection here is as follows: that complete means (*sāṅga-sādhana*) in which one who has obtained authority through both quarters proceeds—that complete means he explains in the subsequent pair of quarters as being "barbarous with many divisions," meaning he explains it as being made uneven and diversified by many distinctions.

The author of the Sūtras [states]: "This is the meaning: indeed, specific forms of the knowledge of Brahman have been taught as distinct, supported by authoritative evidence, in the words 'on account of the difference of words and so forth. Then, in the words 'there is an option because the fruit is not different,' those very same means are presented as optional alternatives since they achieve a single result. Thus, the collection of means endowed with both aspects is indicated."

This is the sequence here: for first, upon the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*), a thirst for what is to be attained arises; once that has arisen, there follows the qualification for the means (*upāya*). When the means have been determined for the qualified person who has engaged in them, subsequently arises the desire to undertake all those ritual actions (*karman*) which serve as auxiliaries (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and function as its instruments (*karaṇa*); thus, the section on the auxiliaries of knowledge (*vidyāṅgapāda*) occurs later.

Now, regarding the statement by the venerable commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) concerning the subject matter of this section (*pādārtha*): "Now, for the sake of determining the combination or optionality of attributes in the meditations on Brahman, an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of these meditations (*vidyā*) is commenced. What, then, is this subject matter of the section? Is it an inquiry into difference, or an inquiry into non-difference, or perhaps an inquiry into difference in some cases and non-difference in others, or an inquiry into both difference and non-difference? It cannot be the first, because such is not the case everywhere. For that very reason, it cannot be the second either.

Nor is it the third [alternative], because a recurring (anuvṛtta) object is not established. Nor is it the fourth, because reflection upon an object consisting of both difference and non-difference is untenable due to its internal contradiction. Furthermore, if one were to define the word "reflection" (cintā) as deliberation in the form of doubt and then state two opposing positions, the very purpose of this section—namely, the reflection on whether there is a combination or non-combination of qualities—would be lost. For that alone is the primary subject of this section, as evidenced by its designation as the "Section on the Combination of Qualities" (Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda). Having all this in mind, he says: "In one... (ekasmin).

This is the meaning of the words here: in this section (*pāda*), a person who has mastered the subtle method of reasoning should accept only one single meaning. There should be no deliberation or investigation into two [contradictory] views. The single meaning known as "difference-and-non-difference" does not exist at all; for even if it were to exist merely through the use of words—like a hare's horn—it is only that [single, non-dual] reality which should be contemplated in this section, and not the contemplation of other matters such as the inclusion or non-inclusion of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra-anupasaṃhāra*). This is what he says: "because of the consequence of abandoning the other."

He concludes by summarizing the point already stated with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Thus, because this section (*pāda*) is flawed by its conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*), the expansion of logic (*nyāyavistara*)—the detailed application of reasonings scattered throughout—is considered lax. Consequently, when an objection is raised against the *prekṣita* (investigated) text, an inquiry is made into the difference or non-difference of the sciences (*vidyā*). When there is an objection from a certain person regarding the text of the *Dṛṣṭabhāṣya*, the intended meaning and purpose of this section is established as follows: this section is that which effects the restriction of the sciences as delimited by their objects of knowledge (*vedya*).

This is the meaning: here, neither difference nor non-difference is primarily intended; rather, difference and non-difference serve solely the purpose of determining the inclusion or non-inclusion of qualities. Consequently, the establishment of the section on the inclusion of qualities is also appropriate. If it is objected that the question of whether there is inclusion or non-inclusion arises once more as the subject matter of the section, the resolution is that the subject matter of the section is the determination of either inclusion or non-inclusion as appropriate; thus, a single unified purpose is established.

"This [vidyā] is the regulator of knowledge as delimited by its object. Thus, if the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is different, the vidyā is different; if it is non-different, that [vidyā] is also non-different. Therefore, since the regulation of vidyā conforms to the object of knowledge, the unity of the subject matter of the "feet" (pādas) is established. Here, the difference between objects of knowledge arises from the difference in qualities (*guṇa*), and not from a difference in Brahman. Consequently, the establishment of the section on the "compendium of qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*) is all the more appropriately integrated.

In the preceding verse, it was established that the single purpose of this section (pāda) is that this [section] determines the unity of knowledge as delimited by the objects of knowledge. Here, someone says: "Granted that there is a single purpose; nevertheless, since this section aims to demonstrate the unity of knowledge, its sole subject matter must be non-difference (*abheda*), and not the difference of knowledge (*vidyābheda*). If so, why do the commentators speak of 'an inquiry into the difference and non-difference of knowledge'? To this we reply: let it be an illustration of an exception (*apavāda*); the actual subject matter of the section remains the unity of knowledge itself.

It is shown that since identity is impossible in certain cases, there may even be difference; thus, this is merely an exception (apavāda) being demonstrated, and not that difference constitutes the primary subject matter of the section. He restates this doubt with the words "that which possesses a designation" (ākhyāvantam). The meaning of the word here is as follows: they have designated this section as the "Section on the Combination of Attributes" (Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda) because it consists of the combination of attributes.

Therefore, for that reason, because of the power of the introductory statement (*ākhyā*), in this section (*pāda*) which establishes the unity of knowledge, the consideration of difference is introduced merely as an exception (*apavāda*), and not as the primary subject matter of the section itself. It was precisely to ward off this doubt that the Commentator stated: "The consideration of the difference and non-difference of knowledge. He says "thus" (*ittham*) to this effect. If one asks, "What then is the subject matter (*pādārtha*) that runs through the entire section? he replies: "The object" (*viṣaya*).

Here, someone objects: "It has been stated by you that there is a distinction between the knowledges (*vidyā*) due to the distinction in their qualities (*guṇa*). In that case, there must also be a distinction in their fruits. For it is heard in scripture: 'As a person acts in this world, so does he become after departing from here,' and also, 'In whatever manner they meditate upon Him, so indeed do they become. Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is that one attains the Lord exactly as He is qualified by those qualities with which one worships Him."

Since it is a logical principle that when a specific injunction is made, there is an implied prohibition of everything else, the attainment of the Lord as qualified by attributes other than those to be meditated upon would be effectively prohibited; thus, the claim that liberation is the experience of the complete Brahman would be a mere assertion.

He restates this [objection] with the words "boundless" (*nissīma*). If one were to divide the Supreme Self—who is a mass of infinite, unconditional, and abundant qualities that serve as the cause for the excellence of boundless bliss—into various forms of meditation based on distinctions arising from the different forms of the object of knowledge, then even the attainment of Brahman would occur only partially, that is, in a single portion.

To the objection that the form of the object to be attained must be exactly as great as the form of the object of meditation, and that consequently the fruit would not be the experience of the complete Brahman, [the author] refutes this with the words "not so. He explains the refutation itself with the words "by these very [means]. This is the meaning: in the passage, "According to the nature of his resolve (kratu) in this world, such does a person become," it is stated that the attainment occurs without any deficiency in the form of the object of meditation; for by the phrase "it becomes exactly thus," the attainment of the entire form of the object of meditation is declared.

Furthermore, if there were a deficiency [in the attributes], the completeness of the form of the object of worship would be destroyed. However, neither the connection with additional forms nor their absence is enjoined here, nor is it prohibited. If it is argued that it is prohibited by the principle that when a specific attribute is enjoined, all others are excluded, this objection is based solely on a misconception. For an implied prohibition (*ārtha-niṣedha*) would only be accepted in the absence of another authoritative means of injunction; but here, such an injunction exists, because the very scripture stating, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," declares supreme equality.

Furthermore, that this supreme equality pertains only to experience will be established by the authors of the Sūtras themselves in the aphorism: "And because there is a mark [indicating] equality only in respect to experience" (BS 4.4.21). Therefore, since logic has no power when it contradicts a scriptural statement, the restriction [of equality] based on logic is a conclusion only for those who do not understand the true principles of reasoning. If it is argued that by accepting equality with the Lord, the status of being the Lord would follow for the individual soul (jīva) as well, we say no; for this objection has already been refuted by the authors of the Sūtras through their use of the word "only" (mātra).

Brahman alone—complete with those qualities of the Lord which are praised as the literal meaning of the words and thus fit for meditation, as well as accompanied by those qualities not so praised and unfit for meditation—is the goal to be attained by the liberated one whose desires are fulfilled; there is no other fruit here. However, it is well known that in the case of means such as [the pursuit of] heaven and the like, the object of meditation is one thing and the fruit is another. Therefore, in this context, by the principle of "as is one's resolve (tatkratu)," that very Brahman, characterized by both meditated and non-meditated qualities, is what is to be attained; thus the principle of "as is one's resolve" is established. Consequently, there is no possibility of a discrepancy in the fruits across the various forms of knowledge (vidyās).

Regarding this, the connection between the sections (*pādasaṅgati*) is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "It has been said that everything up to the fact that Brahman is the bestower of fruits must be explained in order to generate the desire to meditate upon Brahman. Now, the inquiry into the difference or non-difference of the meditations (*vidyā*) is commenced for the purpose of determining the combination or non-combination of their attributes. He also states the introduction to the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words beginning "First, however," and so forth.

In the aphorism "The fruit [results] from Him, because that is logical," the primacy of Brahman as the object of meditation in bestowing all fruits was stated; now, however, the Vaiśvānara-vidyā—which consists of the meditation on Brahman with form through the conceptualization of [the body] from the head down to the feet—is first investigated, as it is more principal than other forms of higher knowledge (paravidyā).

For this very reason, the Blessed Parāśara, in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), stated that Brahman with form (savigraha) alone is to be meditated upon first because it is the auspicious substratum; however, he declared that the true nature of Brahman (brahmasvarūpa) is not to be meditated upon by one engaged in yoga, but only by one who has already ascended to yoga (ārūḍhayoga).

And since this science contains the entire collection of logical principles (nyāya) stated in the various sections of the earlier portion of the Vedas, the intention is that this very science is investigated first, because it is appropriate to investigate other sciences only after this investigation. This is indicated by the two words "first of all" (*prathamam tāvat*). The inquiry into its meaning concerns whether the Vaiśvānara and other such sciences studied in various recensions (*śākhā*) are distinct for each recension, or whether they are one and the same.

Is there recognition [of identity] across different recensional branches (*śākhā*) or not? Does the restrictive rule for the teaching of knowledge—stated in the passage, "One should impart this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow (*śirovrata*) has been performed according to the rules"—which pertains to the *Atharvaṇikas* who observe the head-vow, serve as a subverter of recognition by establishing a difference [between the branches], or does it not? And is the head-vow a constituent part of the knowledge (*vidyā*), or rather a constituent part of the study (*adhyayana*)?

Having stated the non-difference [of rituals] here by means of the principles of non-difference taught in the section concerning other branches (*śākhāntara*) within the *Karmakāṇḍa*, the author of the Sūtras then raised an objection using the principles of difference and re-established non-difference itself by demonstrating that those factors of difference have another purpose. He states this with the words beginning "Difference," etc. This is the meaning: for in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, the unity of rituals is stated on the basis of the non-distinction of connection (*saṃyoga*), form (*rūpa*), injunction (*codanā*), and name (*ākhyā*). "Connection" refers to the connection with a result; "form" refers to the substance and the deity.

The ritualists maintain that the form (*rūpa*) of an action consists of the material substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*). An injunction (*codanā*) is a word denoting an activity (*kriyāvāci-śabda*) headed by verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), or the gerundive (*tavya*). A name (*ākhyā*) is a designation such as *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth. Because these [factors] are not distinct [in different passages], there is the unity of the action; this is the meaning of the sūtra: "Because there is no distinction in the connection, the form, the injunction, and the name. The means of proof for difference (*bheda-pramāṇa*), however, are "differentiation by another word" (*śabdāntara*) and the rest. Differentiation by another word (*śabdāntara*) is a non-synonymous term, such as *yajati*, *juhoti*, *dadāti*, and so forth.

Repetition (*abhyāsa*) consists of repeated recitation, such as "he sacrifices to the *samidhs*" and "he sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*. Number (*saṅkhyā*) is observed in cases such as "he offers three oblations," where there is a triad and so forth. Quality (*guṇa*) refers to things like *vājina* mentioned in passages such as "one pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the *vājina* for the Vājins. A different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is found in passages such as "having performed the *upasad* rites, he performs the *agnihotra* for a month."

Even a name is seen to be a differentiator, as in such passages as, "Now this is Jyotis, now this is Viśvajyotis, now this is Sarvajyotis. Therefore, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been explained by means of the various differentiators and non-differentiators consisting of the methodological principles stated in the earlier portion (*pūrvakāṇḍa*). Among those, the differentiation of injunctions (*vidhi*) through synonyms and other criteria was established and demonstrated in the second chapter of the Karma-kāṇḍa, regarding the syntactical connection of words.

From the fact that [the ritual] is determined by its origin, from its being a composite, from the unity of conjunction and so forth, and from the lack of distinction in the names of the injunctions regarding conjunction and form, another non-difference among rituals has been established. Because the sections on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*) and Brahman (*brahma-kāṇḍa*) belong to a single treatise (*eka-śāstrya*), and because the application of reasoning (*nyāya*) is likewise equal in both, the very method of ritual action is indeed the method for knowledge (*vidyā*) as well. Having thus stated the reality of the matter in general, [the author proceeds to] this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*).

The author of the Sūtras demonstrates that, because the commencement of a final conclusion (*siddhānta*) must be preceded by its introduction, he first states the final conclusion, then raises an objection from the perspective of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and finally re-establishes that very same final conclusion; this is shown by the word "at the beginning" (*ādau*). As for the connection of the words: since there is no difference in the injunctions (*codanā*) within that very section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), the method of other recensional branches (*śākhāntara*) was stated at the beginning.

Having set aside [the objection] by means of scripture itself—having set it aside by means of a differentiating authority contained within that very scripture—he established the previously stated point as a resolution. He states the reason for this: "by the statement that the differentiating [authority] has another purpose. The meaning is: because the differentiating authority has a different intended meaning (tātparya).

Having stated that the refutation previously mentioned against the Sāṅkhya, who asserts eternal liberation, applies equally to the proponent of falsehood as well, [the author] now clearly demonstrates liberation according to his own position by its very nature, beginning with the word "mokṣa. Herein lies the dilemma: does the proponent of eternal liberation, being a speaker of falsehood, say that future liberation simply does not exist, or does he say that liberation is established through delusion? In either case, it is untenable. To explain: if liberation were non-existent, then this means of attainment, along with its accessories, which is being contemplated, would be in vain, because there would be no future fruit in the form of liberation.

If it is argued, "In that case, let us adopt the position that liberation is established by delusion," there too a dilemma arises: is liberation established by a present-day delusion, or is it established by a delusion produced at the time of liberation? It cannot be the first, because since the delusion of saṃsāra currently exists, a delusion regarding liberation cannot arise. Nor can it be the second; for if that were so, because the delusion whose object is the superimposed liberation would persist during the state of liberation, there would be nothing but delusion as long as the nature of the self endures.

Furthermore, for you who assert that the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is eternally liberated, the chapter on the means (*sādhanādhyāya*) would be entirely fruitless, because there can be no chapter on the means for one who is eternally liberated. If it is argued that the chapter on the means is for the purpose of pacifying delusion (*bhrānti*), then, due to the existence of that which is to be removed (*nivartya*), the status of eternal liberation is not established. However, if there is no thing to be removed, then that same fruitlessness of the chapter persists. If it is then argued that the cessation of all worldly suffering (*saṃsārika-duḥkha*) is the effect of the knowledge of Brahman, we raise the objection that since an effect is non-eternal, upon its destruction, there would be the undesirable consequence of the resurgence of *saṃsāra*. Anticipating this, he says "pradhvaṃsa" (destruction). According to the position of those who know the Nyāya system:

Their position is that liberation consists of the form of absolute destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). For even though destruction is an effect, they maintain that it is eternal; therefore, there is no consequence of its being impermanent. If you then ask, "In your view, does it not have the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*)?", the answer is: indeed it does. For us, their very non-existence is our positive entity.

Just as the proponents of logic (nyāyavādins) maintain that liberation, being of the nature of non-existence, is eternal even though it is an effect, so too for us—who maintain that non-existence is merely another form of existence—the eternity of liberation is established despite its positive nature. This is because liberation consists in the manifestation of the eight qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), which is supported by the authority of scripture stating, "He does not return again. Enough with this elaboration.

Having previously established the position that non-existence is a distinct entity (*bhāvāntarābhāva*) according to worldly conventions and in accordance with the *Purāṇas*, [the author] now demonstrates the eternity of liberation through two positions. Regarding the phrase "the continuum as the self": indeed, based on the authority of statements by Parāśara and others—such as "the pot-ness [disappears] from the pot, [becoming] shards"—and because in the world destruction is observed to be merely the continuous succession of subsequent states, the expansion [of consciousness] occurs precisely when the contraction of the intellect, the senses, and the vital breaths ceases. That which is not of such a nature—the eternally established essential form—would, moreover, be attained here through scripture (*āgama*). The scripture, however, includes such passages as: "He does not return again."

"Non-return" (apunarāvṛtti) means the absence of further contraction of expanded knowledge. This accords with the statement of Śaunaka: "Just as the moonlight of a gem is not produced [anew] by the removal of its impurities. Regarding this, he states another view with the word "is considered" (manyate). One view holds that expansion is eternal by its very nature. Here, having raised an objection against the commencement of the section on the "marks of both" (ubhayaliṅga-pāda) immediately after the section on "detachment" (vairāgya-pāda), he connects them with the words "Brahman itself" (brahmaiva).

In the two preceding chapters, Brahman was established as being endowed with all its own inherent natures; this, moreover, is the chapter on the means (sādhanādhyāya). In this chapter [is treated] Brahman, which was the subject matter propounded in the chapters on reconciliation (samanvaya) and non-contradiction (avirodha).

Drawing it back again, the question "for what purpose? expresses the intention of the objector. He refutes that which is to be questioned with the words "it is not so. This is the intended meaning here: it is true that this is the chapter on the means (*sādhana-adhyāya*); nevertheless, the contemplation of Brahman must indeed be performed specifically. For the means are of two kinds: the means to that which is to be accomplished (*sādhyopāya*) and the means that are already established (*siddhopāya*). The established means is the Lord (*īśvara*). The means to be accomplished is His very devotion (*bhakti*), which is differentiated by the various forms of ritual practice (*vidhi*) and so forth. And the differentiation of these practices arises from the differentiation of their forms.

And since Brahman alone is primarily the object to be known (*vedya*) through the injunction to know (*vidhi*), its differentiation arises from the differentiation of its qualities. Thus, because it is the subject matter of the *bhakti* that serves as the means (*sādhana*) expounded in the Sādhanādhyāya, and because it is itself an established means (*siddhopāya*), reflection upon Brahman is particularly relevant in the Sādhanādhyāya as a means. In this regard, he first states that reflection on Brahman is auxiliary to the injunction with the words "vidhyā" [etc.].

"For that [is] due to a distinction in its nature" means that this clarification of Brahman is "due to a distinction in its nature," that is, due to a distinction in its qualities; therefore, the meaning is that Brahman, endowed with such attributes as possessing both genders (liṅga), is to be meditated upon here. To demonstrate that this meditation on Brahman is fruitful by showing it to be an established means (*siddhopāya*), he says "established" (*siddha*). Indeed, two things are to be specifically established: that Brahman is an established means and that it is an established goal (*siddhaprāpyatva*). The demonstration of these two [aims to produce] a particular longing for Brahman as the object to be attained.

For the sake of spiritual attainment (*siddhi*): indeed, in the absence of a specific desire, there would be no qualification for a person to employ the means [of practice]. For one who desires heaven is qualified for sacrifices and the like; likewise, one who desires the attainment of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) is qualified for the meditations on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*). Thus, this section [the *Upāsanā-pāda*], which specifically assists in the performance of meditations, constitutes the essence of the *Śārīraka-śāstra* (the Vedānta system); therefore, there is no risk of it being purposeless.

Regarding the phrase "for the expansion of craving," it is said for the purpose of the increase of craving; for here craving indeed increases. The sense is that, according to the manner stated in the verse "he himself bestows his own fruit," when Brahman is fully known by itself as the means of its own attainment, [craving ceases].

Furthermore, this "Chapter on the Two Attributes" (Ubhayaliṅga-pāda), which is intent upon establishing that Brahman is solely composed of auspicious qualities that are the opposites of all things to be abandoned, is indeed fruitful, as it specifically assists in the refutation of other schools such as the Mṛṣāvādins (the proponents of illusion). Thus he says, "Nairguṇyam" (The absence of qualities): if Brahman were devoid of qualities, then the distinction between the injunctions regarding Brahman and the various auspicious qualities established by the "Chapter on the Two Attributes" within the sections of the "Chapter on the Compendium of Attributes" (Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda) would be rendered false.

"Now, might there not be a distinction between Brahman and ignorance through qualities that are themselves imagined?"—thus he restates the opponent's position with the words "so 'stu" (let it be so). He refutes that with the words "śrutimatavihatiḥ" (contradiction of the scriptural view). If the meaning of the Śruti, which is accepted as having an unbroken tradition from time immemorial without beginning or end, were merely imagined, what would remain non-imagined? Thus, the meaning is that one who asserts the imagined nature of these qualities falls outside the scope of the Vedānta.

One might object: "In the Vedānta as well, in passages such as 'One should meditate on the mind as Brahman,' an injunction for a *dṛṣṭi* (contemplative identification) is seen—just like [the injunction] 'One should know oneself as Garuḍa. Should this not be the case here too? Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "not here. The meaning is that while one might have to resort to an injunction for *dṛṣṭi* in a single instance out of necessity, it cannot be asserted that it must be so in every case. For an injunction for *dṛṣṭi* consists precisely in the mental contemplation of one thing by superimposing the qualities of another upon it.

The meaning is that the truthfulness, omniscience, and other attributes of Brahman are not sublated because they constitute its essential nature (*svarūpa-guṇa*). Having thus stated the defect of the proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādin*) due to his contradiction with the evidence establishing that Brahman is solely intent upon auspicious qualities, he now states the flaw in the proponent of falsehood’s position due to its contradiction with the evidence establishing Brahman’s faultlessness: "Faultlessness," etc. If you maintain, in accordance with the evidence, that the faultlessness of Brahman is indeed eternal, then—since there would be no transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) distinct from Brahman—the [faultlessness] of Brahman...

Furthermore, because [Brahman] is eternally faultless, the exertion involved in hearing the Vedāntas and so forth for the sake of pacifying the defects in the form of saṃsāra would be merely vain and useless; thus, the commencement of the scripture would be purposeless. Anticipating the opponent’s intention—namely, that one might say "then we must postulate the faultlessness of Brahman"—the author refutes this with the word "kalpyam" (to be postulated). If faultlessness were to be postulated, then defectiveness itself would become the very nature (*prakṛti*) of Brahman, and thus the commencement of the scripture would again be futile. It is precisely for the sake of refuting such opponents that the *Ubhayaliṅga* section is indeed fruitful.

Having thus seen the fault in the falsity of the attributeless nature [of Brahman], the author speaks of many further faults against the deluded false-speaker who asserts its reality once more, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). If the attributeless nature of Brahman were ultimately real, the initial injunction that "the inquiry into Brahman must be undertaken" would not be possible; likewise, its being within the scope of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as well as its own-sufficient luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*)—which is the very essence of his own doctrine—and its nature as bliss (*ānandarūpatva*), its status as the substratum for the superimposition of the universe, and [its desire] "May I become many" (*bahu syām*) [would all be untenable].

Thus is the resolve for his own manifold becoming. How could such a collection of qualities exist in Brahman, which is devoid of distinctions? The meaning is: it could not exist in any way. If these qualities were ultimately real (*paramārtha*), then there would be the consequence of the doctrine of Brahman possessing qualities (*saguṇavāda*). If they are not ultimately real, then since self-luminosity and bliss would also be non-ultimate, the very root of one's own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*) would be destroyed. Furthermore, what distinction would there be from the Buddhists and others? This contradiction with reason has been stated. Now, he states the contradiction with scripture (*śruti*) as well:

"Everything. Having stated the contradiction with the authority of scripture (*śruti*), he also states the contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana*). It is well known that for a liar, the speaking of things contrary to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception and so forth, is indeed a "decoration" rather than a "defect," according to the maxim: "The difficulty of explaining ignorance (*avidyā*) is its ornament, not its flaw. If that [difficulty] were an ornament, then Brahman itself would be ignorance, error would be without a substratum, and Brahman would be devoid of luminosity; thus, even such extreme difficulties would become the most excellent ornaments, and this would be nothing but the victory-trumpet of the Mādhyamikas.

If it were claimed that this [practice] is merely deceit and audacity, then for those who have fallen into a miserable state due to such deceit and insolence, the very conception of the eight limbs would become a mere falsehood; consequently, all meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*), which are established here as the "feet" to be integrated as qualities, would deserve to be uprooted from their very foundation—thus resulting in a contradiction with all the scriptures.

Raising the objection: "If Brahman is said to be the object of meditation in this section (*pāda*) on that which possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*), then how can the description of the individual soul (*jīva*) in its state of dreaming be consistent?"—the author provides the following resolution: even the perception of sleeping and so forth is accomplished solely through the will (*saṅkalpa*) of the Lord; therefore, since demonstrating this also has the purpose of revealing the majesty (*māhātmya*) of the Lord, its inclusion in this section is logical. This is what is meant by the phrase "it is abandoned" (*tyaktam*). The meaning of the words here is: if Brahman—which is free from defects and rich in qualities—is further meditated upon here, then...

There is a doubt as to how the contemplation of the soul’s state in dream could be consistent with this present section (pāda), which follows the section on dispassion (vairāgya). He dispels this doubt with the word "no" (na). He explains that very point with the words "in dream" (svapna): "The Lord alone is the creator even of the objects of the dream; thus, this contemplation of the soul’s state in dream is performed here for the purpose of establishing the manifold greatness of Brahman—beginning with His being the creator of those [dream objects]—and to demonstrate that this living being is in a state of absolute dependence, even in its own liberation."

The meaning is this: the individual soul (jīva) is not spoken of here as being primary; rather, it is for the purpose of establishing that the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the agent of all states, such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, that the Supreme Self alone is spoken of throughout this section (pāda) as the primary subject.

Regarding this, some say: "In this section on the two-fold characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*), the first half pertains to the individual soul (*jīva*) and serves as a supplement to the section on dispassion (*vairāgya-pāda*); the second half pertains to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*. He restates this [view] with the words "of the section" (*pādasya*). [They argue that] the latter half is directly connected here in this section for the purpose of meditation (*upāsti*), because it describes various qualities of the Lord. He refutes this partial view (the view of the *ekadeśin*) with the word "this" (*etad*), stating that it is not at all pleasing to the heart. He states the reason for that [rejection] with the word "intermingled" (*śabalita*): [it is so] because it is a confused narration.

Regarding the phrase "due to the reversal of cleverness": one might then ask, for what purpose is the mention of the defects of the individual soul (jīva) in the first half-verse? Anticipating this, he answers with the word "Brahman," meaning that it is for the sake of manifesting the qualities of Brahman.

The sense is that by describing the transmigrating soul, the majesty of the Supreme Self, who liberates from saṃsāra, is established. As for the literal meaning of the words: the mention of the soul's defects here is the "means" (mukha), which means the instrument or method.

Regarding this, an objection is raised: "It is asserted by you that the creation in a dream is ultimately real; how then is this consistent? For one sees even things past and future in a dream. Indeed, the perception of impossible objects in the waking state is false, so how much more so in a dream? Therefore, the creation in a dream is not ultimately real. To this, he says: "In a dream... The grammatical connection here is as follows: let objects be created in a dream; nevertheless, there is manifold delusion in this dream.

Because there is no present experience of those fathers and others who have departed, and because there is the delusion of stability and so forth regarding things like gold obtained in dreams—even though they are unstable—therefore, you must state that the dream is not ultimately real. He refutes this by partially conceding the point, saying "True," and then proceeds as follows: In that regard:

He demonstrates the distinction between what is accepted and what is not accepted by stating "śrutyādi" (by scripture, etc.). Since it is impossible to abandon what is established by scripture and other means of knowledge, we do not reject the meaning established by the scriptures; rather, while accepting that the Lord, the creator of all, creates at each respective time objects to be experienced by specific individuals alone, we maintain that even in cases of utterly contradictory matters, there is only sublation (bādhā), and thus, like waking experience, we accept them as being illusory (bhrānti) and thereby reconcile everything.
Thus, we do not cast aside the meaning established by the scriptures.

Then, raising the objection as to how the movement to another place in a dream could be ultimately real for one who is himself situated in a single location, [the author] says "some say" (kaścit), explaining that everything is possible through the power of the volition of the Blessed Lord, the creator of the universe, just as it is for a yogi who assumes various bodies. This is the grammatical connection of the words here:

Some maintain that a certain yogin, by the power of yoga, having emerged from his own body, enters another body—the body of another—just as one moves freely between one's own house and another's; he even performs activities such as moving about therein, and subsequently returns to and regains his former body. Similarly, some have asserted that in a dream, the dreamer abandons his previous body and attains another body created by the Lord, and at the end of the dream, he again regains his former body.

This is what he expresses by the word "thus" (*ittham*). He also states another alternative view with the words "by the movement of breath" (*śvāsavṛttyā*). This is indeed the intention of others: if a person sleeping in a dream were to abandon his previous body and take up another body, then there would be no movement of breath in the former body; therefore, the *jīva* remains in that very same body. However, regarding the other dream-bodies created by the Lord, [the soul's presence occurs] according to the principle to be stated later: "an entry like that of a lamp" (*pradīpavad āveśaḥ*).

They have determined that the assumption of another body occurs solely through the pervasion of knowledge as a constituent element (dharmabhūtajñāna), because the principle of Saubhari is established by such pervasion.

The connection [of this section] with the commentary is stated as follows: "In this way, the state of suffering of the individual soul (jīva) while awake—due to its association with going and coming and birth in accordance with its karma—has been explained. Now, its state of dreaming is being examined. Regarding the investigation of that meaning: beginning with the passage, "There are no chariots there, no yoke-animals, no roads," the creation of the dream state is recorded in scripture. Is that [creation] ultimately real, or is it mere illusion (māyāmātra)? Does the scriptural indication, "He creates, for he is the agent," [support the former]?

It does not indicate ultimate reality. Is this description intended to convey that the creator possesses true agency, or rather that his agency is like that in a dream-cognition? Does the statement from the Prajāpati discourse—that the individual soul (jīva), whose will is known to be true, can create through mere volition alone in a dream—hold true or not? Does the passage, "He who wakes among these who sleep, creating each desired object," establish that the jīva is a creator by mere volition in a dream, or not? What is this?

Regarding whether this statement refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*): in this very section (*adhikaraṇa*), it is deliberated whether the creation in a dream is the work of the individual soul or the work of the Supreme Self.

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that it has already been stated. For it was indeed stated in the Prajāpati discourse, which forms a supplement to the Discourse on the Subtle (*daharavākya*), that just as the quality of having true resolves belongs to the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*), so too does it belong to the individual soul (*jīva*), like the subtle ether (*daharākāśa*). The locative case ending (*saptamī*) [in the word *bhavinī*] signifies "in the soul" (*jīve*). Therefore, by his own resolve, creation occurs in a dream.

[The agency] belongs to the individual soul (jīva) alone. Furthermore, it is stated here that the son and others are the objects created; for the relationship with sons and so forth pertains only to the individual soul, since chariots and the like are indicative of things favorable to the soul. Therefore, the meaning is that the individual soul, acting as the agent of the son and others, creates the desired object of its own dream. [The author] rejects this point, saying "Not so," and states the reason therein: "In liberation... (muktāv iti).

The meaning is as follows: because of the mention of those qualities—that is, because it is stated that the individual soul (jīva) manifests the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*)—how could the soul, which is like a blind person in the state of dreaming, attain the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin? He states another reason as well: "anabhimata" (unpleasant).

If the soul itself were creating its own objects for its own sake in a dream, then it would necessarily create only what is favorable; yet, one who is asleep sometimes [experiences] even unfavorable things.

He sees [these things] in a dream; that is not logical, for if the individual soul (jīva) possesses the power of true resolve (satyasaṅkalpatva), how could he himself create something contrary to his own interest? He states a third reason as well: "because dreams are indicative" (svāpnānāṃ sūcakatvāt). The meaning is that one must understand that even in dreams, white objects bring about auspicious results and so forth—all these, having arrived by the will of the Lord (īśvara), are indicators of good and evil. Therefore, the creation of the dream-phenomenon belongs solely to the Lord. This is what he expresses by saying "the entire world" (nikhilajagat).

Regarding this, one might raise the doubt: in the subject passage, "A person creating whatever he desires" (*kāmaṃkāmaṃ puruṣo nirmimāṇaḥ*), does the suffix *ṇamul* denote the act itself, or does "whatever he desires" (*kāmaṃkāmaṃ*) denote the specific objects that serve as the karma? Anticipating this, [the author] states "whatever he desires" (*kāmaṃkāmaṃ*) to show that the suffix *ṇamul* alone is appropriate for expressing the creatorhood of the Blessed One, whose resolve is true; for a living being (*jīva*), whose resolve is not true, agency is impossible. Thus, it is indeed the Lord who is being referred to.

And this Supreme Self remains awake while persons are asleep; therefore, its agency in performing wondrous deeds is logical—this is the meaning. He states that its waking is established by scripture, saying "clearly": for it is heard in the Śruti, "He is embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman)."

One might object: "If even a dream, like waking life, consists of an ultimately real creation, how is it that it is restricted to specific times, or how is it that it is experienced by only one particular individual? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides a solution with the word "tattat" (that respective), intending to show that this is due to the specific volition of the unrestrained and independent Lord. It is not only in dreams that there is a creation of effects limited to specific times; rather, even in the waking state, the appearance of clouds and other phenomena is observed to be of such a nature. One might further object: "Even so, being experienced by only one person is not observed."

If this is argued, then it should be understood that even that [diversity] arises from the volition of the Lord (Īśvara). For indeed, through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, perfected eye-salves, and so forth, specific objects are observed that are experienced by particular individuals alone. Furthermore, he states another reason for the fact that the world is created by the Lord: namely, the distribution of fruits in accordance with respective actions (*karma*). Since the vision in dreams consists of pleasure and pain, it is the fruit of action; and since action is a specific volition of the Lord, the entire collection of dream-objects is dependent upon the Lord alone.

For a sinner indeed sees a dream corresponding to his sin, while one preeminent in dharma sees one corresponding to that; thus, this great path is certainly not to be transgressed by anyone. This has also been stated by the authoritative ones (āptas), the intention being as follows: when some person attains auspiciousness at a certain time, and then again attains inauspiciousness, this is declared by the learned through the science of omens (nimitta), physiognomy (sāmudrika), the movements of specific planets, and so forth. If, due to an obstruction or other cause, that [result] were not to occur, then it would not be obtained even in a dream.
Thus it is stated by those very [authorities]; therefore, it is established that dream happiness, suffering, and so forth are indeed the fruits of karma.

In this context, relying merely on the employment of the word *māyā* in the sūtra, "But [the world] is mere illusion in its entirety," those who follow the teachings of Sugata under the pretext of Vedic discourse—those proponents of falsehood—assert the falsity of the entire universe. He refutes that view with the words "Māyā... Since that falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) was already stated by them at the commencement of their own scripture, to state it again here would result in redundancy and irrelevance.

Therefore, what is stated here is simply that the Lord’s diverse creation is like the manifold world of a dream; it is not, however, the falsity of the universe. For this assertion of those who maintain the doctrine of falsehood (mṛṣāvādins) rests solely upon the word *māyā*; yet even that word provides them no support, as he says: "The word *māyā*. Indeed, lexicographers do not record the word *māyā* in common usage as a synonym for "falsehood.

For the etymologists employ the word *māyā* specifically for a particular kind of knowledge, stating: "But *māyā* is weaving, [which is] knowledge. As it is said: "Indra moves in many forms through his *māyās*."
In such passages, it is indeed stated that the Lord is experienced in various forms through His specific volitions (*saṅkalpa*). And Parāśara says:
"O Lord of Men, He creates by His own play many forms possessing diverse powers, designated as gods, animals, and humans, and endowed with activity."

"For the benefit of the worlds, it is not born from the cause of karma. Thus, *līlā* (sport) is said to be nothing but one's own volition (*saṅkalpa*). And that volition, as well as knowledge (*jñāna*), is *māyā*. Therefore, the word *māyā* does not denote "falsehood," but rather denotes "wonderful creation," or else the specific power (*śakti*) that serves as the cause for such creation, or alternatively, the specific volition that serves as the instrumental cause and basis for each respective creation. Indeed, usages are seen such as: "created like divine *māyā*" (*devamāyeva nirmitā*). For if it were false, it would be designated as "imagined" (*kalpita*). Furthermore: "By that swift-moving [weapon], he [reduced] to ashes the thousand *māyās* of Śambara..."
"By protecting the body of a fool, it is destroyed one by one.

Here, the word "sūdita" (destroyed) expresses precisely the state of being subject to destruction (*nāśyatva*). For destruction (*nāśa*) is the annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*) of that which exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthasat*). Otherwise, it would be expressed as "sublated" (*bādhyatva*). For sublation (*bādha*) indeed...

Proponents of false doctrine (bhṛṣāvādinaḥ) maintain that the state of being negatable (niṣedhyatva) applies only under certain conditions (pratipannopādhau). Indeed, in the statement "one should know Māyā as Prakṛti," the phrase "one should know as Prakṛti" is used precisely to exclude the meaning of "Māyā" as something merely false (mithyā). For this very reason, in the passage "the illusory deer was killed," the actual destruction of Mārīca himself is described. Furthermore, even in cases such as Meghanāda’s illusions, the term "Māyā" refers to actual serpents produced by specific mantras.

Otherwise, how could it be logical for [the enemy] to be overcome by the specific powers of Garuḍa? Furthermore, this is a convention well-known to the whole world: in the treatises on political science (*nītiśāstra*), seven expedients are specified—conciliation, dissension, bribery, punishment, illusion (*māyā*), sorcery (*indrajāla*), and indifference. Among these, the distinction between illusion and sorcery is now stated.

Māyā is the creation of a real snake and so forth through the specific power of mantras and the like; likewise, the fruit of *indrajāla* (sorcery) is the breaking of an enemy's army by displaying unreal elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry through that very same specific power of mantras and the like. Other examples should be understood in this way elsewhere as well. Now, anticipating the objection that the word *māyā* is used even in reference to falsehoods within the Purāṇas and in the common usage of the vulgar, he provides the answer: "Let it be metaphorical. For a metaphorical application of a word does not [invalidate its primary meaning].

The meaning is that it restricts a specific power (*śakti*). This is what he says with the words "What follows from this? He says "It is real" (*satya*) to show that even in the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth, the abundance of usage is seen primarily in reference to things like the weapons of the Asuras and Rākṣasas, which are indeed real. In the *Purāṇas* as well, it is recited, beginning with "The rising of clouds, the ebbing of the ocean," and continuing, "The diverse *māyās* of Viṣṇu come forth. If, then, the entire range of effects is denoted by the word *māyā*, what [is the point]?

Anticipating the objection that [Māyā] must be a regulator, he says: "in the regulation of what is appropriate. This is the meaning: Māyā is said to be a specific type of effect characterized by wonder;

the application of the word "Māyā" to a magic trick (indrajāla) is figurative because there is no difference in its nature as something wonderful. Thus is the distinction between Māyā and indrajāla. The statement, "For this divine Māyā of mine, consisting of the Guṇas, is difficult to overcome," clearly establishes that the word "Māyā" denotes the three Guṇas themselves, which are the cause of the creation of the manifold phenomenal world.

The connection [of this section] with the commentary is stated as: "Now the locus of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is examined. The meaning is that while the dream state was previously defined, the locus of deep sleep is now being considered. The inquiry into its purpose is as follows: Are the channels (*nāḍī*), the pericardium (*purītat*), and Brahman the loci of deep sleep for the individual soul (*jīva*) as alternatives, or as a combination? Is there a difference in their function—like a cushion, a bed, and a couch—or not? [This is raised because] we hear of the awakening from Brahman in the passage: "We are coming back to Being."

Does that which makes known Brahman’s status as being like a couch-bed imply a difference in function, or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that the place of the living being [is indefinite], citing such passages as "the place of the living being. Scripture declares, without restriction, that during deep sleep the place of the living being is the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), the pericardium (*purītat*), and Brahman. Therefore, among these three places...

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is an option (*vikalpa*)—namely, whether it is the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*), or the pericardium (*purītat*), or Brahman—because they are mutually independent. [The author] rejects the stated point with the words "That is not so" (*tan na*). He explains this very rejection through reasoning with the words "Like a palace" (*prāsāda* etc.). The meaning is as follows: An option is indeed logical only when there is no difference in the effect (*kāryabheda*) in the case of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). Here, however, because there is a difference in the effect, the channels, the pericardium, and Brahman are joined in conjunction according to the maxim of the palace, the bed, and the couch; therefore, an option is simply not logical. And that...

Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed corrupted by eight defects. He explains this very point with the words "the alternative and the alternative": regarding rice and barley when they are performed as alternatives according to the injunctions "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley," first, when rice is performed, there are two defects concerning the scope of the barley-injunction: the abandonment of its authority (*prāmāṇya*) and the acceptance of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Immediately thereafter, if at some point the barley-injunction is performed, there are two defects concerning the rice-injunction: the abandonment of its authority and the acceptance of its lack of authority. In that very same [case]...

At the time of performing the first rite, there are two defects in the *yava* scripture: the acceptance of its validity which was previously abandoned, and the abandonment of its invalidity which was previously accepted. Then, upon returning to the third performance in the form of following the *vrīhi* scripture, there are again two defects in the *vrīhi* scripture: the acceptance of its validity which was previously abandoned, and the abandonment of its invalidity which was previously accepted. Thus, due to the three performances, both scriptures are tainted by eight defects—four defects for each; specifically, there are two defects at the time of the first performance.

The wise should contemplate this by dividing it according to their understanding: at the time of performing the second [alternative], there are four defects, and again at the time of performing the third, there are two defects.

Furthermore, the Teacher states that the eightfold defectiveness regarding the object of the alternative (*vikalpa*) can be explained in another way: when rice (*vrīhi*) is performed, there are four defects in the case of the barley (*yava*) injunction—namely, the non-performance of the preparatory rite (*pratipatti*), the non-origination of the unseen potency (*apūrva*), and the sublation of the fruit. Likewise, when barley is performed, there are four defects in the case of the rice injunction—namely, the non-performance of the preparatory rite, the non-origination of the unseen potency, and the sublation of the fruit. Thus, there is an eightfold defectiveness.

Therefore, the meaning is this: when no other course is possible, an alternative (vikalpa) must be accepted; however, when a course is possible, there should be a combination (samuccaya). In this case, since a combination is possible according to the maxim of the "palace, bed, and couch," an alternative should not be accepted. By stating that [the alternative] is "endowed with four faults occurring in succession," he reiterates that the three applications are corrupted by eight faults. Thus, the impression of the "children" that [the argument proceeds] "by way of the application" is a false impression.

In the *Saṅgati* (Introduction), it is stated: "There arises a doubt as to whether it is the very same one who was in deep sleep who rises at the time of awakening, or whether it is someone else. The investigation into that matter concerns whether it is someone other than the one in deep sleep who rises at the time of awakening, or whether it is that very same person. Does the state of deep sleep involve a complete liberation from all adjuncts (*upādhi*), or not? Do the criteria of action (*karman*), recollection (*anusmṛti*), and scriptural testimony (*śabda*) indicate the absence of a complete liberation from all adjuncts, or not? Now, is it not the case that what is called deep sleep is virtually liberation itself, for liberation indeed—?

The Śruti itself declares that the state where the multitude of joys and sorrows has ceased and one is free from the aggregate of suffering—namely, non-attachment to Brahman—is indeed dissolution (*pralaya*). Therefore, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is restated as follows: "Upon awakening after such deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the embodied soul is indeed another [person]; this is what liberation (*mukti*) is. This position is rejected with the words, "It is not so."

He demonstrates the distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and deep sleep (*svāpa*) by means of the passage beginning with "due to the persistence of karma. Because the persistence of prior karma is observed through the experience of its fruits—such as pleasure and pain—the persistence of karma is evident. Furthermore, how could memory be possible if [the two states] were different? There is also the scriptural statement cited in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "They become tigers here," and so forth. Moreover, if liberation were identical to deep sleep, how could injunctions for the sake of liberation be consistent? For what purpose would an effort be directed toward that which is obtained without effort? [This is supported by the phrase] "from the repetition of his own state": "I am not..."

This is because of the statement beginning with "Indeed, he [thinks] thus," and because of the description of the one who has fallen into deep sleep as saying, "I do not perceive even this much of enjoyment; indeed, I have gone to destruction. Therefore, it should be understood that the person who was already nearly destroyed in the previous state becomes awakened.

Here, one might raise the objection: "Why is it established that there is a re-emergence at the time of awakening for one who was in deep sleep, given the absence of any specific purpose? Anticipating this, he states the extremely relevant specific purpose in the verse beginning with "the beginninglessness of the individual soul" (*jīvānāditva*). If this Sūtra is intended to establish the beginninglessness of individual souls, then that has already been stated there [in the *Brahma-sūtras*] in such passages as: "If it be said that [the soul is not eternal] because of the non-distinction [of the soul from the body] due to karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness. If, however, by this Sūtra the casting away of the comparison to a snake's slough in liberation—that is, the rejection of the notion of being deluded—is intended; [then the following applies].

That too will be addressed later. If it is argued that the activity of living beings directed toward heaven and other goals is established by proving the permanence [of the soul], even that is untenable without the permanence of the entire Mīmāṃsā system as known through the method of the Śruti; for the activity directed toward heaven and other goals has already been [established] by the Śruti and the reasoning that supports it.

If it is argued that the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has already been established through the demonstration of the soul's stability (*ātma-sthairya*) in the *Saugatādhikaraṇa* and other sections, [we reply: if this section were intended merely to refute the identity of the individual soul with the Lord during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), then it has already been stated in various places that even at the end of a kalpa, the soul remains one only in the sense of having abandoned name and form (*nāmarūpa*), and not because of an identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*). Therefore, that statement is also restricted to a specific context. Consequently, for someone who is like a child, there is no need to further deliberate upon deep sleep.

He addresses the objection raised by the opponent with the words: "by the establishment of the desire to abandon [the state] through the attainment of the state of dissolution (pralaya-samadaśā) and so forth. Some stubborn Naiyāyikas assert that liberation (mokṣa) is indeed like a stone. If that were so, then even deep sleep (suṣupti)—which is censured in such passages as "I see no object of enjoyment here" and "he has gone to utter destruction"—would have to be liberation;

yet this is not what is sought by the wise as liberation. Thus, in the Vairāgyapāda, by censuring that [stone-like] liberation, there is also a specific desire to abandon it, as in the case of one who is like a stone.
The meaning is that this consequential argument (prasaṅga) serves that purpose; therefore, it is not devoid of utility.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: after having analyzed the specific states consisting of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the state in the form of fainting—which is similar to deep sleep—is now investigated.

Since waking and dreaming are characterized by the presence of consciousness (*prajñā*), whereas deep sleep and fainting consist in the loss of consciousness, there is a mutual relationship between these two pairs. The investigation into their meaning, however, is as follows: what...

Is fainting (mūrchā) one of the states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, or is it a different state altogether? Can its distinction be established through defining characteristics or not? Is the connection with the subtle vital breath (sūkṣma-prāṇa) the defining characteristic of fainting or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: Four distinct states are indeed well-known in the world—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and death. Among these, waking and dreaming are not devoid of external cognition, and deep sleep is not [devoid of it] because of the presence of breathing.

"Fainting is indeed death, because the group of senses and vital breaths has been pacified"—this is what [the opponent] restates with the words "waking" (*jāgrad*). He refutes that with "no. First, regarding the difference between fainting and death, he states the difference in their causes: "from the departure of life and so forth. Fainting arises from mere blows and the like, whereas death arises from such things as decapitation; thus, the first reason is that there is a difference between the causes of fainting and death. He also states another reason: "in the state of persistence" (*sthitau*). One who is in a state of extreme persistence is said to be "fainted," or one who persists [in life] is said to be "dead."

They lie down. And that doubt indicates a disparity between fainting and death. He states a third reason as well: "because of rising. Among those who have fainted, someone may rise again due to the influence of mantras, medicines, and so forth; however, one who is dead goes only to the next world. Thus, the meaning is that because rising is not certain [in the case of the dead], it must be fainting. If that is so, then [the term] "fainting" (mūrchā)— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the distinction between *mūrchā* (fainting) and *maraṇa* (death) based on the possibility of revival.]

Anticipating the question, "What is this particular state? he says, "to die. Having begun to die according to destiny, to be obstructed midway—that particular state of death characterized by the non-attainment of its purpose—should be understood as "fainting" (mūrchā). The meaning is that fainting is half-death.

Here, by establishing the mutual distinction in meaning among all eight topics (*adhikaraṇas*), [the author] describes the division of the section (*peṭikā*) and the internal sub-divisions of the section in the subsequent section with the words "of living beings" (*jantūnām*). Thus, by means of these four topics, the calamity that befalls living beings in states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep has been demonstrated. Hereafter, however—

Even though all [the topics] are connected, Brahman—which is itself free from fault and possesses auspicious qualities—is being purified; such is the division of the *peṭikā* (box-section). Furthermore, in the subsequent *peṭikā*, he states the disparity between the first part and the second part due to the difference in their subject matter, beginning with the words "saṃsarga" and so forth. By means of both these sections (*adhikaraṇas*), he removes the defects rooted in association (*saṃsarga*) and those rooted in the assertion of identity (*tādātmya*). Then, he states the meaning of the latter two sections, beginning with the word "hīnatva. [This refers to] the absence of supremacy over all things and the absence of unsurpassed magnanimity.

The distinction between the two is as follows: since it would be impossible for [Brahman] to be an object of worship, the subsequent two sections refute both the loss of its supremacy over all things and its lack of unsurpassed magnificence.

The connection [between this section and the previous one] is as follows: having described in the preceding section the individual soul (*jīva*) transmigrating and subject to the state of death for the sake of establishing an excellence of dispassion (*vairāgya*), this section now declares the dual-natured character (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) of the Lord for the sake of establishing a specific longing for that which is to be attained. This very point is clearly demonstrated by the words "nairguṇyam" (freedom from qualities). Here, this section proceeds specifically to refute the position of those who speak falsely, in order to reject it in particular. They indeed say: "It is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and stainless (*nirañjana*)," thus asserting the very qualitylessness of Brahman.

[Objection: If that is so, then what is the status of such descriptive statements of qualities as "one whose desires and resolves are true"? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The description of qualities.

The meaning is that the description of qualities is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding attributes imagined through ignorance, intended for the purpose of inducement. [Objection: If that is so, in the absence of qualities, are you asserting that defectiveness is indeed the inherent nature of Brahman? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Freedom from defects. The point is that both the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*) and the absence of defects (*nairdoṣya*) apply to Brahman.

Regarding the term *svābhāvikam* (intrinsic), he says this: "as the reality is. Then, one might ask: "In that case, what would become of the qualities, form, and so forth of Brahman established by the Śruti and Purāṇas, as well as the connection with saṃsāra which is well-known to all the world? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "that other [is not intrinsic]. We have stated only a portion of this. Thus, in order to refute those who are deluded by the deceptive doctrines (*kuhanāvāda*) intent on robbing the soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) of their sovereignty, the section beginning with "Not even from a change of place" (*na sthānato'pi*) is commenced. "Many-horned" means having many forms.

The connection [of this section] is made clear by the commentary beginning with the words "doṣadarśanāt" (because of the observation of defects), and has already been shown by us previously. The purpose of that inquiry is as follows: whether those undesirable states (apuruṣārtha) that befall the individual soul (jīva) while situated in states such as deep sleep and departure from the body also accrue to its inner ruler (antaryāmin) and to its body, or not. That is to say: is the soul's connection with undesirable states caused by its connection with a body, or is it caused by its connection with karma? [And is there any such undesirable state for] Brahman even when it possesses a body?

The fact that [the Self] possesses both sets of characteristics (ubhayaliṅgatva), as established by scripture, leads one to understand whether the connection with ritual action is indeed a cause for it not being the supreme human goal, or not. Is this possession of both characteristics, established by scripture, real (tāttvika) or unreal (atāttvika)? Is the negation of all specific attributes (sarvaviśeṣa-niṣedha) the subject under discussion in the passage, "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'Not this, not this'"? Or is it the negation of the limited extent of what has been previously described (prakṛtaitāvatva-niṣedha)? Is there consistency between the beginning and the conclusion of the sentence if all specific attributes are negated? Or is there consistency if the negation is only of the limited extent of what was previously described?

Thus [it is said]. Here, having specifically presented the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he also demonstrates its refutation according to the intention of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "it is to be abandoned" (*heyam*).
