Indeed, the proponent of the prima facie view thinks as follows: just as immersion in pus and blood is to be abandoned by a king’s servant, so too it must be abandoned by the king himself; otherwise, it would not be something to be abandoned for him at all. And likewise, even for the Lord (*īśvara*), abiding in a body like that of a living being (*jīva*) would necessarily be a cause of suffering. [Objection: But the living being is dependent on karma regarding the body...

Anticipating the objection that "the Lord acts solely by His own will, therefore there is no fault," he refutes it with the words "by His own will. Even by His own will, immersion in pus, blood, and so forth is seen to be a cause of suffering; this is because the intrinsic natures of things cannot be questioned. He rejects the stated position with the word "no" (na), and states the reason for that: [The text continues: ...He states the reason for that: "Because [the Lord] would be subject to censure. This means: if the Lord were to create such a world through His own will, He would be censured as being like a cruel executioner or a butcher. Furthermore, if He were to create such a world by His own will, He would be censured as being like a madman who acts without purpose. Moreover, if He were to create such a world by His own will, He would be censured as being like a wicked person who inflicts suffering on others without cause. Therefore, the view that the Lord creates the world by His own will is untenable. Thus, the conclusion is that the Lord does not create the world by His own will. This is the meaning.

"Without limiting adjuncts" (nirupādheḥ): this is the meaning. For in the world, the relationship between what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted is altered by the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi). For example, warmth that is favorable in the morning is unfavorable at midday; likewise, coolness that is favorable at midday is unfavorable in the morning. This is also observed through the difference in persons: grass and such, which are favorable for animals, are unfavorable for humans. Similarly, even through the difference in states, food that is favorable to one who is hungry becomes unfavorable to one who has already eaten, even if it is delicious. This very point was stated by the venerable Parāśara:
That very same thing, having become a source of pleasure, again gives rise to suffering;
for it is that which arises as both anger and serenity.

"Therefore, nothing has suffering as its essence, nor does anything have happiness as its essence. Thus, a distinction between pleasure and pain is observed even according to the difference in the perceiver. In the case of a single child, there is happiness when it is said, "This is your son," but there is pain when it is said, "This is the son of an enemy. In this way, the transformation of pleasure and pain due to various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is well-known and witnessed by all the world. Likewise, the distinction between the pleasure and pain of living beings, resulting from the influence of the limiting adjuncts of actions consisting of merit and demerit, cannot be denied.

Just as in the world, it is taught in the Āyurveda and other sciences that those possessing an imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*) encounter a disharmony of objects that are either favorable or unfavorable, and this is indeed observed accordingly; therefore, it is not appropriate to speak of the Lord’s connection with karma or his connection with pleasure and pain resulting from that [karma] on account of his abiding within bodies. Anticipating the objection that the Lord might also have a connection with karma precisely because of his connection with a body, he refutes it by stating "eternal" (*nitya*). Here, the following alternative arises: does the word "Lord" (*īśvara*) refer to the sovereign of all who governs the entire universe? Or...

Or [the subject] may be merely a king and so forth. If it is the latter case, there is indeed the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*), because the experience of pleasure and pain is clearly perceived even in kings and others. If it is the former case, it results in the proof of nothing other than [the existence of] God; for there is a contradiction in saying that one experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth, yet is God. Indeed, the experience of pleasure and pain is the fruit of karma. Karma...

This is simply a specific quality produced by the non-transgression of the preservation of the Lord’s command; or else, according to the principles of the Adhyātma-śāstra, it is the will of the Lord, the Ruler, regarding restraint and grace. How, then, could there be the possibility of the Lord experiencing pleasure or pain? If you say that, out of delusion, there is some other ruler even of the Lord, let the very scripture stating, "No one equal or superior to Him is seen," strike your cheeks. Even if struck, if...

"You prattle on; let the exponents of Brahman expel you! Therefore, because there is no other Lord who issues commands to the Lord, He is not subject to the scriptures. Because He is not subject to the scriptures, there is no connection with karma. And because there is no connection with karma, there is no consequence of experiencing pleasure and pain occasioned by a connection with a body—such is the path of those high-souled ones who are experts in the discrimination between the authoritative and the non-authoritative. He says "by the Śruti itself" to show that this meaning has been clearly demonstrated by the Śruti itself through its own analysis.

For the Śruti text, "Two birds," speaks of one among the two—the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (paramātman)—residing in a single body as the enjoyer of the fruits of karma, while the other is characterized by the absence of enjoyment of karmic fruits and is endowed with unsurpassed radiance. It has already been established that in the verse "Two birds," it is precisely the individual soul and the Supreme Self that are distinguished and described.
Furthermore, the absence of contradiction with the Paiṅgi-Śruti has been clearly demonstrated in that very place; therefore, we shall desist here.

In this regard, someone—failing to understand the true nature of the matter due to blindness and excessive pride—raises an objection once more: "For instance, according to the position of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and others, since God acts as the impeller of merit and demerit, even though He exists within another body, He lacks corporeality; therefore, He cannot be denoted by words such as 'Brāhmaṇa. Consequently, in injunctions such as 'A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice' and 'A Kṣatriya should sacrifice,' there is no possibility whatsoever of Him being the object of the injunction. In your own established doctrine, however, regarding the words 'Brāhmaṇa,' 'Kṣatriya,' and so forth..."

"Because He is primarily the designator of the Lord (Īśvara), it is the Lord alone who becomes the object of injunctions; [yet] because He would be subject to the command 'one should act' or 'one should not act,' His very nature as the Lord would be destroyed. This is what he restates with the words "brahmakṣatrādi" (the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, etc.). Here is the meaning of the words: within the bodies of the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, and so forth, the omnipresent Lord—just like the atomic individual soul (jīva)—abides as the Self by way of being the impeller of the body; thus, while being denotable by those respective terms, through Your permission, He indeed becomes expressible by such words as "Brahmin" and so on. Therefore, that Lord...

"How is it that [the Lord], being qualified by limiting adjuncts such as Brahminhood and so forth, does not become subject to those respective injunctions? If you say, "He does not become so because He is the Lord," then no; for one must not accept atheism regarding a matter directly established by the Śruti. Therefore, the claim that the Lord—who is the object of both injunctive and prohibitive scriptures—is a mine of all defects is refuted by the words "not so" (*maivam*), which dispels this blind prattle. He explains that very point with the words beginning "it is not made known" (*na jñāpyate*). Herein lies the dilemma: is it the making known of what was unknown, or the impelling of one who has not yet acted?

Or is it said by you that [the scripture] is an injunction (*vidhi*)? First of all, it is not possible for the Lord to cause something unknown to be known; therefore, he says: "He is not made known. He states the reason for this: "Because of the absence of anything unknown" (*aviditavirahāt*), which means because of His omniscience. Indeed, no benefit whatsoever is conferred upon the sun by a lamp. Nor is it possible for Him to instigate one who has not yet acted. To strengthen the stated point, he provides a negative example based on worldly observation: "A person of limited knowledge," etc. For in the world, servants and others [are instigated] by a king...

Because they possess limited knowledge, they are made aware of their duties; because they are dependent on others, they are impelled to act. This is observed by all the world and cannot be denied. Therefore, the claim that the omniscient Lord would be both one who must be made aware [of his duties] and one who must be impelled is not the argument of the wise, but rather that of the unintelligent—so the virtuous mock it. As for the argument that the Lord, who is denoted by terms such as "Brahmin" and so forth, must also be subject to governance because this is established by the *Śruti*, that too is laughable; for the *Śruti* speaks only of what is appropriate, not of what is utterly inappropriate.
And that it is also contradicted by other scriptural passages—let your honor reflect upon this yourself as well.

In this section concerning the two-fold characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa*), indeed, the state of being the opposite of everything to be rejected and the state of being solely composed of auspicious qualities are expressed by way of these two characteristics. And this is to be established through three principles that have been defined. Regarding the [injunction] "One should not harm any living beings" and the [injunction] "One should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma," there is the principle of the general rule and its exception (*utsargāpavādanyāya*), because the scripture of prohibition has a scope distinct from what is specifically enjoined. Regarding [the narrative] "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa," and so forth, there is the principle of the introductory context (*upakramādhikaraṇanyāya*).

The introductory statement (*upakrama*) is more powerful than the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), because the former has not yet encountered any contradiction, whereas the latter has already encountered one. In cases such as "If the Udgātṛ should be interrupted," where there is a conflict between two statements of indeterminate priority, the principle of the section on interruption (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*) applies: "For the arising of the subsequent [statement] is not established without subverting the prior. This is because the subsequent [statement] arises only after the prior has been subverted. Regarding this, the proponents of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*) say: first, the statements concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavākya*) proceed; however, those...

The former [scriptures] are indeed prior because they convey meanings in the form of injunctions; the latter, however, are the passages concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*), because they convey meanings in the form of prohibitions. For this is well known in the world: prohibition is preceded by an injunction. Therefore, because the enjoining [texts] and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are antecedent, they are subject to sublation. The subsequent nature of the prohibitive passages—such as "without qualities, stainless" and "there is no diversity whatsoever here"—constitutes their power of sublation. The same applies to inference (*anumāna*).

The same applies to the ritual scriptures (*karma-śāstra*) as well. Furthermore, those statements even within the Vedānta that are devoted to the meditation on Brahman with attributes (*saguṇopāsana*) must likewise be set aside, because they are equivalent to the ritual scriptures. Moreover, as for those few statements cited by the proponents of the qualified Brahman (*saguṇavādin*) which purport to describe the nature of Brahman with attributes, these too are subject to sublation because they fall within the scope of injunction (*vidhi*).

Because they arise earlier, they are sublated. However, the statements regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavākya*), by virtue of being the object of negation and because they arise later and are sublatives, remain as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Just as in the *Apacchedādhikaraṇa*, when two mutually contradictory expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are occasioned by two causes—the simultaneous impairments of the *udgātṛ* and the *pratihartr*—the expiation occasioned by the prior impairment sublates that occasioned by the subsequent impairment, and only the latter is performed; so too here, the quality which is the object of the injunctive statement...

Therefore, those who accept authoritative testimony must acknowledge that *nairguṇya* (the state of being devoid of qualities), which is the subject matter of the statements concerning the absence of qualities, is what prevails. He refutes this very point by means of two other logical principles, beginning with the words "by way of a general rule" (*utsargeṇa*).

"The injunction 'one should not harm any living beings' is a general rule (*utsarga*); 'one should sacrifice an animal to Agni and Soma' is an exception (*apavāda*). In this regard, the established method of the system (*tāntrika-prakriyā*) is that the general rule is set aside by the exception, but the exception is not set aside by the general rule. Accordingly, the statement "devoid of qualities, stainless" is the general rule.

"Having true desires and true resolves" is an exception (apavāda), because one [statement] has a general scope while the other has a specific scope. Therefore, the conclusion of those learned in the principles of interpretation is that the statement concerning the absence of qualities (nirguṇa-vākya) must be restricted by the very statement concerning qualities (saguṇa-vākya) to refer to qualities that are to be discarded. This is what he expresses with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). The prohibition of qualities and so forth in the passage from the *Brāhma* [Upaniṣad], "Without qualities, stainless," transcends the scope of injunctions such as "having true desires and true resolves."

It should remain so. Having thus explained the resolution of the contradiction between the passages concerning the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman through the distinction of their respective domains by means of the principle of general rule and exception (utsargāpavādanyāya), he states that once the contradiction is resolved, there is no need at all for the principle of the section on "simultaneous disconnections" (apacchedādhikaraṇanyāya): "For it does not apply when the subject matter is equal. Indeed, the principle of the section on simultaneous disconnections operates only when the subject matter is identical, because the two disconnections are equal insofar as they are both disconnections. In this case, however, the contradiction has been pacified by the distinction of subject matter established through another principle. Therefore...

The principle of the *apaccheda-adhikaraṇa* (the case of simultaneous or successive interruptions), which serves as the cause for pacifying that [conflict], is indeed not to be relied upon because it is purposeless. When the poison of one bitten by a snake is neutralized by any one of the various remedies such as gems or mantras, what is the use of another pseudo-remedy? Here, the author demonstrates that the application of the *apaccheda-adhikaraṇa* principle is merely a fallacy by stating "it is seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). This is the meaning: the application of the *apaccheda-adhikaraṇa* principle occurs only in cases where the sequence of priority is not fixed; for example, when sometimes the *udgātṛ* is interrupted first.

Sometimes the *pratihartṛ* [priest] is [the subject], and therefore in those cases the subsequent statement has greater force. Here, however, there is a fixed sequence: the injunction (*vidhi*) comes first and the prohibition (*niṣedha*) comes after. For in the *Upakramādhikaraṇa*, when it was considered whether the horse-sacrifice offering belongs to the giver or the receiver, it was determined—following the introductory statement—that it belongs to the giver alone. Therefore, here too, because of the greater force of what precedes, it must be concluded that the statements concerning the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-vākya*) have greater force, and not the statements concerning the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇa-vākya*).

The remainder of what is to be said here should be seen in the *Tattvaṭīkā* and other commentaries on the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*. Furthermore, in the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the very first sūtra, it is stated: "The assertion that a subsequent [authority] is stronger is ridiculed as being a mere pretext for the victory of the Mādhyamikas. This very point should be investigated in detail by attentive students. Moreover, logicians speak of a contradiction with that upon which another depends. As they say:
"In that case, indeed, the superiority of the later over the earlier is perceived."

"Where there may be the birth of cognitions that are mutually independent. Thus, for those who have not studied Mīmāṃsā, or for those who have forgotten the Mīmāṃsā of the Śruti, the statement that the scriptures negating difference possess greater authority—while [the things themselves] depend upon the cognition of difference regarding their own nature and their own validity—is merely a fabrication. For even in the *Apacchedādhikaraṇa*, the determination of relative strength and weakness does not occur without the cognition of difference such as "this is prior" and "this is posterior. Nor can the determination of validity occur without that cognition; thus, [our argument] concludes.

"In that case, let us rely upon the Śruti itself; for it declares everywhere that the world of plurality (prapañca) is indeed false. That alone is the reality. Indeed, a mother does not give her child poison."

On this basis, some boast that "the reality is precisely the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca), because it is established by such scriptural passages as 'In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent'. He refutes this very point by reflecting upon the scriptures themselves with the words: "The effect is existent" (sattvaṃ kāryasya). The meaning is this: for the statement, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?", accepts the existence of the effect while rejecting only the non-existence of the cause. By this, it is stated that both the effect is existent and the cause is existent.

Therefore, because of the use of the word "some" (*eka*) in the phrase "On this point, some say," it is understood that non-existence (*asattva*) is indeed the position of another school (*parapakṣa*). As for the connection of the words, however, the inquiry—namely, "How can there be the arising of the existent from the non-existent?"—makes one understand that both cause and effect possess existence (*sattva*). Now, one might object: let this sentence not be our support; rather, let us rely on the sentence beginning with "Just as, my dear."

Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "dravyānyatvam" (the difference in substance). The meaning is that even that statement merely rejects the difference in substance between cause and effect; it does not, however, establish the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*). Furthermore, you should not say that the scriptural statement, "There is no diversity whatsoever here," is our authority; to this he replies with "antarbhāvāt" (because of inclusion). This is because, in the case of the qualified Lord (*viśiṣṭe bhagavati*), the qualifiers are included [within Him]; thus [it is said], "There is no diversity here."

Even a sentence [of scripture] rejects only the manifoldness that is not of the nature of Brahman. If it is argued, "In that case, the sentence 'Not this, not this' (*neti neti*), which directly negates the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is our family treasure," [the author] replies, "That too is like gold obtained in a dream," by saying "having pointed out... After first stating certain qualifiers of Brahman, [he proceeds].

The teaching "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) removes the doubt of the dull-witted that the extent of Brahman has been fully specified. This means: "not this," "not this"—only the specific modes previously mentioned are negated, but not the multitude of qualities yet to be described. For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras stated: "For [the text] negates the limited nature as it was presented, and then declares more beyond that. Thus, since the authority of all the Śruti texts is established through their distinct subject matters, it belongs only to those who maintain that Brahman possesses qualities (*saguṇa*).
The claim that the determination of the meaning of Vedānta possesses excellence is merely the idle chatter of those devoid of qualities, spoken according to their own whims.

"Now, let these be the solutions; nevertheless, this one point remains unestablished: the illustration provided—that 'the Lord, though abiding everywhere, is like the sun in reservoirs of water'—is said by some to demonstrate the very unreality (mithyātva) [of the individual souls]. To that person as well, he gives the reply: 'tattaddṛṣṭi...'. For in the case of the intended meaning (tātparya), the word is the authority. Here, the unreality of the individual souls is not what is intended to be expressed, because it would contradict the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa)."

Moreover, although Brahman is present everywhere, it is only the participation in the increase and decrease pertaining to various particular objects—which do not constitute its true nature—that is denied. Just as the reflection of the moon seen in waves does not, in ultimate reality, participate in the increase, decrease, and so forth of the waves, so too it is with Brahman abiding as the inner controller of all.

The Supreme Brahman has no connection with the defects arising from the distinctions associated with this or that particular object. Here, the illustration is intended merely to show that, despite the presence of Brahman, there is no possibility of the imposition of adventitious defects due to its specific power (*prabhāvaviśeṣa*). The logical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: the Supreme Self, who is visible and complete in all attributes in every location and object, is devoid of distinctions such as increase or decrease; for it is said, "Like the sun in various receptacles of water."

Since the meaning must be described in accordance with the intended purport (*tātparya*), for what purpose is this strained interpretation (*kliṣṭakalpanā*)? One might suspect that the illustration here is stated precisely for the sake of non-connection (*asaṃsarga*), thinking: "If [the objection is] 'the example of the untouchable'. The meaning is that here Brahman is said to be untouched by anything at all. To that, he gives the reply: "Not indeed" (*na hi*). For the great sages do not state only a single illustrative example; in one place it says, "like the sun in reservoirs of water," and in another, "just as the one space [is present] in jars and so forth."

The phrase "it would be separate" is used in one instance to illustrate a reflection that does not exist [independently], while in another instance it refers to space, which does indeed exist. Therefore, for the sake of consistency between both examples, the appropriate meaning must be illustrated; it is not merely the state of being untouched by the defects inherent in those [examples]. Otherwise, if only one were employed, the other would be excluded, and thus neither would be established.

Having thus established the reality of the meaning in detail, he concludes that [Brahman] possesses both characteristics with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). It is "possessed of two characteristics" (*dviliṅgam*), meaning endowed with both sets of qualities because it is the opposite of everything to be abandoned and is solely composed of auspiciousness. It is "of twofold glory" (*dvividhavibhavam*), meaning distinguished by both types of manifestation (*vibhūti*); the sense is that it is distinguished by the two manifestations well-known from such scriptural authorities as "All this is indeed the Person" (*puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam*). For this has been explained by the venerable Parāśara in the passage beginning, "He consists of all auspicious qualities," and so forth. The mention of "the Vedānta position" is for the purpose of relegating the position of the proponents of falsehood (the Mādhyamikas) to the category of the Buddhists.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the connection [of this section] is stated as follows: "Now, the manner in which that insentient entity (*acidvastu*) has the nature of Brahman is considered for the purpose of establishing the faultlessness of Brahman.

This is the meaning: in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), the faultlessness of Brahman was asserted. For the sake of firmly establishing that faultlessness, it is now considered whether the insentient entity has the nature of Brahman according to the analogy of the serpent and its coils, or according to the analogy of light and its radiance, or else by way of the relationship between a qualifier and the qualified. Thus, it is connected with the preceding section.

Regarding the term "conjunction" (*saṅgati*): as for the investigation of its meaning, is it that some object possesses the nature of Brahman according to the analogy of the snake and its coils, or rather in the manner of light and its possessor, or else...?

"By way of the relationship of qualifier and qualified, or part and whole. Does the negation of non-conscious attributes—such as in the passage, "This great unborn Self is ageless and immortal"—through the relationship of qualifier and qualified, lead one to understand that the world has Brahman as its nature, or not? Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "Of the creator of the universe... For the Supreme Person, the creator of the universe, there is no possibility of being the cause of His own suffering when producing the aggregate of non-conscious matter from His own parts, because non-conscious matter lacks suffering. And if one were to postulate that [the world] is a part [of Him], it would possess the nature of non-consciousness.

The numerous examples cited, such as clay and its effects, are well-established and naturally persuasive. Therefore, Brahman alone, by virtue of its creative play (*vihāra*), undergoes modification even in the creation of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) and so forth; thus, it follows that the creation of insentient matter (*acit*) in the form of a modification is indeed possible—this is the meaning. He rejects this with the word "no" (*na*). He explains that very point with the words "its own part" (*svāṃśa*). The meaning is as follows: evil (*anartha*) is of two kinds. One is the production of suffering. [The other is] regarding an object capable of yielding unsurpassed bliss...

Another [teacher] maintains that it is the "inducing of delusion. Even though the non-sentient entity (acid-vastu), being distinct from consciousness (cit), does not itself produce suffering, the inducing of delusion—by way of its portion consisting of non-sentience within the Reality whose nature is unsurpassed knowledge and bliss—is indeed the bringing about of one's own ruin. Therefore, the creation of a portion consisting of non-sentience is simply not tenable.

Having restated other positions along with the position already mentioned, he refutes them with the words "some say" (*kaścit*). Previously, the objection was raised and refuted that Brahman itself brings about its own non-consciousness within itself; now, in order to avoid the aforementioned fault, some say that there exists a certain eternal, beginningless portion of non-consciousness (*acid-aṃśa*) which undergoes various transformations. Even in that case, the contradiction remains as it was, because [it would imply] that the omniscient Brahman is eternally...

Because such a conceptualization of a form conjoined with such ignorance is utterly untenable, he restates another position: "From foam, etc. Others say that within the Brahman, which is pure Being (sanmātra) like an ocean, the triad of principles consisting of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord arises through the process of modification, according to the analogy of foam, waves, and bubbles. That too is exactly the same [as the previous case]; for by imagining modification in that which is changeless, the fault of causing one's own ruin remains as it was. Furthermore, some [hold] by the analogy of the moon and its moonlight...

They assert that there is a single genus (*aikajātya*) between the world and Brahman; however, because this contradicts the Vedāntic texts that establish the identity (*aikya*) of the world and Brahman, it is indeed to be disregarded.

If their commonality were based merely on the quality of being a reality (*vastutva*), then, since this is well-known to all the world, it would not be something to be known through the Vedāntas. If their commonality were based on being the Self (*ātmatva*), such a thing does not exist at all in insentient matter (*acidvastu*).

If their commonality were based on being the Lord (*īśvaratva*), it is refuted by the delineation of the three distinct principles (*tattvatraya*). Furthermore, it would contradict the Śruti: "The enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller. Therefore...

The conclusion of those who know the truth of the Vedānta is that identity [of Brahman and the individual self] exists through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*). Therefore, the syntactical connection of the words is that all disputants are not to be terrified here, because they do not contradict the purport of all Vedānta statements.

In the commentary itself, the connection (*saṅgati*) is stated by means of the introductory sentence of the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*), which is linked to the concluding sentence of the preceding section: "Since Brahman is free from defects and is a mine of auspicious qualities, its possession of both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅgatva*) is established. Now, from this supreme cause, which is both the efficient and material cause of the universe—"

"Some, raising doubts through fallacious arguments, maintain that there exists a reality even beyond the Supreme Brahman; this [view] is now refuted. An investigation into the meaning of this [sūtra] is as follows: Is there some further reality beyond this Brahman which possesses both characteristics (ubhayaliṅga), or not? Is the designation of the "bridge" (setu), "measure" (unmāna), "relation" (sambandha), and "distinction" (bheda) possible only if this [Brahman] itself is the supreme? Or is it not? Here, the author of the sūtras, having restated in sequence the reasons for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that were introduced, [proceeds].

He also shows the refutation according to the sequence of the Sūtras with the words, "the bridge" (setum). Because of the statement that it is to be crossed—“having crossed this bridge”—because of the statement regarding the limited nature of Brahman—"Brahman has four quarters and sixteen parts"—because of the mention of its connection to something to be attained—“this is the bridge to immortality”—and because it is designated as being connected to another immortality to be attained by virtue of being its means; and also because of the scriptural text concerning the superiority of another—"he goes to the divine Person who is higher than the high."

"Higher than the high, greater than the great"—from this and other scriptural passages stating that there is something else beyond everything; and because of the principle of "carrying across" (*ativāhika*), this Supreme Person, who is the cause of the universe, must be the one who leads [the soul] to the goal, and not the goal itself. The proponents of the doctrine of the "Beyond-the-Sky" (*vyomātīta*) maintain that the goal must be something else entirely. He refutes this by saying "it is not so. That which is the cause of the world is precisely what is to be meditated upon, according to the rule: "But the Cause is to be meditated upon."

And that which is to be meditated upon is precisely that which is to be attained, because of the determination of the identity between the goal and the means in such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Therefore, the conclusion of those who propound the final end of the Vedas (*trayyantavādinaḥ*) is that that which is the bridge to immortality is itself immortality. If it is asked how the description of this Brahman as a "bridge" and so forth is possible, the answer here is: "As a bridge. Accept that its function is not contradicted by many authoritative means of knowledge. First of all, the Lord alone is the object to be attained.

Furthermore, its status as that which leads [to liberation] must indeed be accepted, as it is established by all the Vedānta scriptures. Therefore, the meaning of the arguments regarding its being a "bridge" (setu) and so forth must be explained by postulating a suitable sense for them. Otherwise, there would be no distinction in common usage between primary and secondary applications; secondary usages would have to be abandoned, and even the explanation of the meaning of sentences in various contexts by learned scholars—achieved through the refinement of the marks of purport (tātparya-liṅga) such as the introduction and conclusion—would not be possible, resulting in the total collapse of the entire scripture.

It was stated here previously that the mention of "being a bridge" (*setu*) and so forth is to be applied by means of imagining appropriate meanings. He demonstrates those very appropriate meanings in their proper sequence, beginning with "the state of being a bridge. "The state of being a bridge" means the state of being like a bridge, due to the supporting and regulating, that is, the restrictive sustaining; for the Blessed Lord alone is the sustainer of all. He states another meaning as well: "from binding," for that same Blessed Lord binds the entire collection of principles without confusion. He also provides the interpretation for the statement regarding "limitation": "even though [He] is all-pervading."

It has already been stated in various contexts concerning the "small ether" (*daharākāśa*) and so forth that even when this supreme Brahman is all-pervading, descriptions of its limited dimensions are purposeful. As for the statement "Brahman has four quarters," it should be understood as a figurative construction consistent with specific scriptural passages—such as "All beings are one quarter of Him"—even though Brahman is infinitely vast. Furthermore, the phrase "This is the bridge to the Immortal" should be construed either as referring to Brahman, which is of the nature of the Immortal, or to liberation, which consists in the attainment of Brahman and is itself immortal.

In this context, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) describes how, having accepted the supremacy of Nārāyaṇa, the supremacy of another even beyond him is asserted. An illustration for this is also stated: just as in the passage "higher than the Imperishable is the High" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*), the term "the High" (*paraḥ*) is used to denote one who is higher, distinct from the Imperishable. When this has been said, [the author] points out the disparity between the illustration and the thing illustrated by the words "of another" (*anyasya*). The meaning is this: in the illustration, since there is a statement of the superiority of that which is designated by the word "the High" (*para*) in the nominative case, [it is not the same as the present case].

That which is indicated by a word ending in the fifth case (the ablative) is perceived as the limit (*avadhi*). And its status as being denoted by the word "para" (beyond) is determined by the statement that it is so in relation to the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, which are its effects. In that context, it could be said that either the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is "beyond" the Imperishable (*akṣara*), in relation to its own effects. However, here, in the passage "For there is nothing else higher than this 'Not this'," anything beyond the Supreme Self is rejected. Therefore, no other entity beyond that should even be postulated.

Now, some have said that in the passage, "That which is higher than that" (*tato yaduttarataram*), the pronoun *tat* refers back to the Supreme Person under discussion, and thus another principle higher even than Him is being indicated; therefore, there exists a reality superior to the Supreme Person. He refutes this with the words, "But because of the word 'thus' (*evam-tu-āt*). In that context, the reason is restated as "because of the word 'thus' (*evam-tu-āt*) following the word 'from that' (*tataḥ*)."

The meaning is that it has already been established by many proofs that the Supreme Person alone is the ultimate reality (*paratattva*). Therefore, the passage beginning with "that which is higher than the high" (*yaduttarataram*) refers to the Supreme Person alone, and not to some other principle. He also provides an alternative interpretation for the word *tataḥ*: "Or else... Here, the construction is: "That which is higher than the aforementioned phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—by virtue of being pervaded by the Supreme Person—is formless and free from suffering. In this case as well, it is the Supreme Person himself who is spoken of as the ultimate.

If it were asserted that there exists a reality superior to the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), then, at the commencement of this section, by means of the recognition of the Puruṣasūkta, [there would be no room for] anything superior to the Supreme Person.

The intention is that, because the rejection [of a contrary view] is established, and because it is logical that the beginning (upakrama) is stronger than the conclusion (upasaṃhāra), the concluding statement must be interpreted in accordance with the beginning precisely according to the method we have stated. This is the application of the words here: in the statement of the superiority of another Lord, such as "higher than the Imperishable," where Nature (prakṛti) and so forth are seen as the limit (avadhi), in that very same example, the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and so on would be the limit in relation to that [other Lord]. Thus, in comparison to that limit, this [Lord] would be the limit.

Furthermore, He is designated as being "higher than the high" (*akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ*) by virtue of His transcendence over the entire class of His own effects. However, in this context—where it is taught that there is nothing higher than what is taught as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), and where the subject is taught as being devoid of any further beyond—it is improper to speak of anything else as being higher than Him. Therefore, any conceptualization of a "higher" state culminates in the Supreme Person alone.

Regarding the phrase "tato yaduttarataram" (that which is higher than that), one interpretation is that the word *tat* ending in the ablative case has the sense of a cause (*hetu*). Another interpretation is that even if it has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*), it refers by means of the word *tat*—as being the subject under discussion—to that which was previously mentioned as being pervaded by the Supreme Person.

Regarding this, he states the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections with the words "ārādhya" (to be propitiated). For it is well known in the world that he alone who possesses supremacy (*paratva*) and magnanimity (*audārya*) is worthy of service; because one who lacks supremacy, even if possessing magnanimity, is not to be served, and likewise, one who lacks magnanimity, even if possessing supremacy, is not to be served. Therefore, for the purpose of establishing the Lord as the object of worship to be propounded in the subsequent quarter-verse (*pāda*), [he says...]

Supremacy (*paratva*) was explained in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*). Here, however, magnanimity (*audārya*) is described by way of stating [the Lord's] capacity to bestow fruits; thus, there is a logical connection between the preceding and succeeding sections. Having restated this supremacy of the Blessed One as it is declared everywhere in the *Trikāṇḍī*, His magnanimity, which is conjoined with that supremacy, is now proclaimed. The meaning of the connection is as follows: "In whom all the Vedas become one," and "In whom all the Hotṛ-priests become one."

By such authorities as "by one who follows the conduct of the castes and stages of life," it was determined in the first section (*pūrva-kāṇḍa*) that Viṣṇu alone is the object of worship for all ritual acts. In the middle section (*madhyama-kāṇḍa*) as well, through the statement "Agni is the lowest of the deities, Viṣṇu is the highest," He alone was established as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all deities and their presiding authority. In this final section on Brahman (*brahma-kāṇḍa*) as well, it has already been stated in this very chapter (*pāda*) that, throughout these ten chapters, the sole objective is the meditation upon Him as the means for those terrified by the fear of worldly existence to attain [liberation].

This has been established most clearly. Now, at the conclusion of the chapter on the "Two-fold Characteristics" (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*), at the commencement of the exposition of Knowledge (*vidyā*), it is explained in detail for the sake of ensuring the successful commencement of that Knowledge:

[the Lord] bestows fruits corresponding to the various duties—both those of active engagement (*pravṛtti-niṣṭhā*) consisting of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, and those of renunciation (*nivṛtti-niṣṭhā*) consisting of the yoga of action, the yoga of knowledge, the yoga of devotion, and so forth—which are appropriate for the subject matter of the respective scriptures. For the activity of living beings is not possible without a purpose, nor is a purpose possible without one who bestows it, nor...

The state of being a donor cannot exist without supreme status and magnanimity; nor can these two qualities exist elsewhere than in the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, who is the great benefactor who bestows His own self, distinguished by both types of opulence—this is the intended meaning.

The connection has been stated. Now follows the investigation into its meaning: Does the production of the fruits of heaven and liberation arise from ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsana*) preceded by that [connection], or rather from the Lord (*para-brahman*) alone, who exists in the form of Vāyu and others and is pleased by ritual action and meditation? Does the supplementary scriptural passage (vākyaśeṣa)—"He alone leads him to prosperity," "He is to be attained by whomsoever He chooses"—indicate that the one abiding as Vāyu and others, as well as the absolute Lord, are the bestowers of the fruit, or not? Is this supplementary passage to be understood according to its literal appearance?

"And as for the claim that it has another purpose": here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) thinks [the following]: "Regarding agriculture and so forth"—it is beyond dispute that in the world there is a fruit for agriculture, as well as for activities such as massaging and the like.

Otherwise, activity would be impossible. Furthermore, that result arises solely through the medium of the visible (*dṛṣṭa*), and not through the medium of the invisible (*adṛṣṭa*), because that would entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). When a result is produced without mediation, even the visible medium is not required. Moreover, the status of ritual duties (*dharma*) as means to an end must certainly not be abandoned, since it is understood through direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*). Nor is the Vedic revelation here sublated, as in the case of [the figurative statement] "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*). Therefore, because they are understood through Vedic revelations free from the defect of sublation, the status of ritual duties as means to an end truly exists.

Thus, even though it is heard that the factors (dharmas) are the direct means of accomplishment, it is proper to conclude that the statement "the fruit [comes] from the grace of God" is intended solely for the purpose of praising God. He rejects the suspected view with the word "no. He states the reason for this as "because it is based on scripture" (*śrauta*). Herein is the distinction: one position holds that karma alone bestows the fruit occurring at a later time; another position holds that there is something distinct from karma called the "unseen force" (*apūrva*); and yet another holds that it is a specific deity who is pleased by the performance of the ritual form of worship.

The third [point]: In the first case, because the action has been accumulated and then destroyed, its status as a cause for the fruit is simply not possible. In the second case, however, there is the abandonment of what is stated in scripture and the assumption of what is not stated.

There are two faults [in the other views]. For it is heard in such passages as, "He, being pleased, pleases him," that the deity alone is the bestower of the fruit; therefore, the third position must be accepted because it is consistent with scripture and lacks contradiction in meaning. Thus, it is established that the deity alone is the bestower of the fruit. This, however, is the general principle: "For I am indeed the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices," whereby the state of being worshipped by all rites and the state of bestowing the fruits of all rites are declared.
Indeed, the status of a Lord belongs to one whose nature is not to withhold [the reward].

The commentators have determined that "sovereignty" (prabhutva) refers precisely to the capacity to bestow results, as this applies to things such as sky-flowers, the hair of a tortoise, or the horns of a rabbit; for it alone is both fit and required to be expressed in the sentence.

Regarding the statement here that [the Lord] bestows the fruit, the author anticipates the objection of redundancy—given the specific meanings already stated in various preceding passages—and refutes it with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*). For previously, in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, by refuting those who assert that "pleasure and the bestowing of fruits do not exist for the deities," the fact that [the Lord] bestows the fruit was indeed already established.

Immediately following this, even in the sūtra, "But [the Lord] depends on the effort made, because otherwise the injunctions and prohibitions would be rendered meaningless," etc., it is stated that the Lord impels merit and demerit in accordance with prior karma, and thus the fruit of action is dependent upon the Lord. Why, then, is the quality of being the bestower of fruits mentioned here as well? He rejects this very point by accepting it [as a premise]:

"Nevertheless": because of statements such as "He is the witness, the knower" and "He is beyond speech and indifferent" found here and there in the Vedāntic texts, the very engagement in meditation would perish for a worshiper who fears upon merely hearing those [passages]. Therefore, for one whose intellect is mired in the terror of doubt regarding the Lord's indifference and so forth, [meditation on] the Lord...

In this context, the author of the Sūtra establishes as the preeminent quality of the Supreme Lord, the Consort of Śrī—who is most magnanimous and whose mind is solely intent on protecting those who have sought refuge—the very quality of His magnanimity for the purpose of dispelling fear; thus, because it serves a specific purpose, there is no room for even a scent of redundancy.

He establishes the manner in which the Lord bestows fruits through the analogy of a king and his sons, according to a process observed in the world, beginning with the words "the sovereign. For in the world, some fathers among certain groups of sons become sovereigns themselves; such a one is compassionate, knows what is appropriate regarding what ought and ought not to be done, maintains equanimity toward all his sons, and is generous. The meaning is that even his liberality toward all his sons is common to each. From one who is thus constituted—

Just as sons, though constrained by differences in their fixed inclinations, obtain each their own desired object according to their respective wishes, so too from the Supreme Person—who is endowed with this collection of qualities—all His servants, who are like His sons, obtain their own desired objects; this is the implied meaning. In that regard, He clearly demonstrates through the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) that everything—namely, the goal to be attained, the means of attainment, that which opposes it, and its pacification—is present in the Lord according to the analogy of father and son.

That which is to be obtained by oneself, such as houses, fields, and so forth, in the form of an inheritance—since its loss occurs due to causes such as transgressing the father’s command; and since its restoration occurs through returning once more and prostrating at his feet; and that which is to be given, such as wealth, ornaments, turbans, garments, umbrellas, and chowries; and furthermore, in the absence of forgiveness for an offense, even punishment and instruction according to worldly custom—all of this would apply here as well.

For a king’s servant, however, the punishment for violating the king’s command is the cutting off of a foot or similar corporal penalties; for his son, it is the restriction of livelihood and so forth. Likewise, for those who are not devotees (*abhāgavatas*), the fruit of sin as declared in the scriptures consists of falling into hell and the like. But for devotees (*bhāgavatas*), in the event of an offense committed intentionally, [it is said]: "Indeed, devotees do not go to the realm of Yama; here in this world alone certain afflictions occur for them. Thus, their punishment consists merely of blindness, lameness, and the like. Therefore, "the punishment for one who has sought refuge is light, like that for a prince's offense."

In the manner thus described, punishment for the offenses of those who have sought refuge would be exceedingly meager; therefore, this section encourages the very commencement of spiritual practice by instilling the conviction that one should immediately undertake the practice of the knowledge of Brahman through faith in the Lord, who is supremely compassionate and the bestower of all fruits.

By manifesting the specific distinctions among the primary meanings of the words, he illuminates the understanding of the Lord’s supremacy with the phrase "Śuddhānanda" (Pure Bliss). This is the meaning of the words here:

because it has been established in this way, [the Lord] is the Supreme Brahman whose essential nature is Pure Bliss, an ocean of auspicious qualities, whose own body is eternally real, who possesses a supreme reality-eternal form, who is preeminent through the Goddess, ornaments, weapons, attendants, and retinue, and who is characterized by the two-fold manifestation (*vibhūti*)—namely, the radiant play of enjoyment (*kanadbhogalīlāvibhūti*). By the word "kanat" (radiant), he expresses His being distinguished by these two manifestations.

Its state of being intensely radiant is stated [in the scripture]: "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.13.7). Regarding the term *śeṣitva* (the state of being the principal): the essence of the determination of the truth of Vedānta is that the universe constitutes the body [of Brahman] by virtue of its being supported (*ādheya*), its being subordinate (*vidheya*), and its being subsidiary (*śeṣa*); whereas the Lord constitutes the body [of the universe] by virtue of being its support (*ādhāra*) and so forth. The permanence of the relationship means its eternally established nature. [The Lord is described as] "the progenitor of heaven and liberation," according to the principle: "The fruit [arises] from Him, because that is logical" (Brahma Sūtra 3.2.38).

Thus, for the purpose of establishing the point, he speaks specifically: when Hari is in such a state, our gaze is unblinking; this is the meaning, and our own scripture is the uncontradicted authority. By that—

The meaning is that no dispute should be raised by those versed in the Vedas (*vaidika*) regarding these matters established by the *Śruti*. Therefore, for all the opposing disputants (*pūrvavādin*) who seek to negate the attributes, form, and majesty of the Lord through fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*) that are equal in status to [legitimate] inference, the *Śruti* itself stands as their adversary. Consequently, they must bow down even to the inference regarding the purity of one who has severed his head; and they must also honor such statements as, "Wine may be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa.
Alternatively, since they would thereby deny even their own Brāhmaṇahood on the grounds of being human and so forth, nothing remains but laughter.

In order to explain the distinctions among qualities within the subsequent divisions of knowledge (*vidyābheda*), this *pāda* takes up each of the distinct objects mentioned in every section (*adhikaraṇa*) and elucidates them.

He is the creator of objects related to the dream state; he is the sustainer of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), meaning the support of deep sleep; he is the protector of the sleeping, meaning the guardian of the sleeper through the absence of destruction. He is the awakener of the fainting, meaning that he sometimes brings about the awakening of one who has fainted; "sometimes death" and so forth is the meaning of the words. He is sinless and possesses auspicious qualities.

Thus, His possession of both genders (masculine and feminine) is stated. By the words "the Lord of the insentient [souls] with his own bodies," the meaning of the *Ahi-kuṇḍala* (Snake-Coil) and subsequent sections is expressed. Now follows the meaning of the section concerning the Supreme (*parādhikaraṇa*):

"The limit of supremacy. This means that He alone is supreme; there is no one higher than Him. "The bestower of all fruits" is the meaning of the section concerning the fruit (*phalādhikaraṇa*). Thus it is said.

Anticipating the question, "For what purpose [did the Lord do this]?", he says, "on account of the abundance of devotion" (*bhaktibhūmnā*). The meaning is: for the sake of increasing the devotion consisting of the Brahma-vidyā which is about to be described. Now, those who speak falsely might argue, "We too say that such a collection of qualities may be merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*"); to that, he gives the reply: "for it is in truth" (*satye hi*). When the qualities and so forth are thus established as real (*satya*), only then can the distinctions of form and so forth be described in the subsequent section regarding supreme worship and the like. This is the essential point (*tattvam eva*).

[The opponent] establishes the Vedānta-śāstra. If the collection of objects propounded therein is not reality (*atattva*), what then is reality? If you say it is nothing at all, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of merging with the Mādhyamikas. If you say that the qualifier is unreal while the mere substantive (*viśeṣya*) alone is reality, who says so? If you say "the Śruti," then by virtue of being expressible (*vācyatva*) and cognizable (*vedyatva*), Brahman would once again be false. If you say that it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), then what is this self-luminosity?

If you argue that [the definition of falsity] is "being blameworthy while being conducive to immediate empirical usage," then falsity would emerge once again simply because of that conduciveness to empirical usage.

If you say there is no fault because self-luminosity is false, then since the truth of self-luminosity lies in its being revealed by another, you are once again establishing the falsity of Brahman due to its being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*). We are ashamed even to engage in debate with you, who speak such incoherent things.
Thus ends the second quarter of the third chapter.

In this manner, through the ten preceding quarters, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) conducive to the means of liberation has been established. Hereafter, through the six subsequent quarters, meditation (upāsana)—which is the cause of that [liberation] and is conjoined with the fruit consisting of the attainment of the supreme Brahman—is clearly elucidated. Thus, he states the connection between the preceding and succeeding sections with the words "tattvajñāna" (knowledge of reality).

In order to explain later on the most beneficial meditation for the person seeking liberation—which is permeated by the knowledge of reality—the author first shakes off the delirious ravings of rival doctrines, which are like the great collapse of feverish delusions caused by the heat of speculative reasoning regarding reality. This is because, once the awakening to reality is accomplished, the knowledge of reality has been attained; as it is said: "Since all his obligations have been burnt away by the fire of the knowledge of Brahman, the sage, though still living according to the Veda, is no longer a servant of the Veda."

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: to those false-speakers who deny their status as servants of the Veda, [the author] declares that for the sake of attaining liberation, one must practice the worship of Murāri (Viṣṇu) throughout one's entire life—a practice established by the Śruti text: "He, indeed, conducting himself thus for the duration of his life, reaches the world of Brahman. This is precisely what the false-speaker imagines. Whoever [it may be]:

Indeed, it is that very [self] joined with egoism and the like that is a servant of the Veda; for agency and enjoyership are not attributes of the Self. First of all, agency in performing actions motivated by desire is already discarded for the knower, because it is a cause of saṃsāra. Agency in the meditation upon Brahman is likewise discarded, since that too is included among the attributes of saṃsāra. But Brahman is neither an object of knowledge, nor an object of meditation, nor even something to be attained. Nor is this fact made known by the Vedas. Because it is eternally self-luminous, even its self-luminosity cannot be defined.

If it is asked, "How can Brahman be established if it cannot be defined?", we reply: let there be no establishment of Brahman. For this very reason, the knowers of the supreme self (adhyātmavidaḥ) declare: "He taught by means of silence alone. Thus, those who speak incoherently and are proponents of falsehood abandon even the Knowledge of Being (sadvidyā), which they have accepted as the very essence of their own system; how much more so would they abandon the various distinct meditations (vidyābheda), such as the Dahara-vidyā, which are adorned with diverse attributes? Therefore, the refutation of that [position] is now commenced.

In this third chapter, [the author] demonstrates the distinction between the meanings of all four quarters (pādas), the mutual distinction between each pair of quarters due to their distinct meanings, and the rule governing their sequential order, beginning with "bhīmābhyo" and so forth. Here, in the first two quarters, there is the cause for the attainment of qualification (adhikāra-sampatti) and the qualification itself, which consists of a thirst for the Blessed One conjoined with detachment from saṃsāra.

It is clearly demonstrated that both of these [sections] are designated by both feet. Therein, by the words "to those who are fearful" (*bhīmābhyaḥ*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the section on detachment (*vairāgya-pāda*); and by the words "thirst" (*tṛṣṇām*) and so forth, he states the meaning of the section on the dual characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga-pāda*). Here is the syntactical connection of the words: as long as one directs thirst toward the ocean of the nectar of Kṛṣṇa, so much has been said; thus he states the meaning of the two subsequent sections with the word "thus" (*ittham*). Here is the syntactical connection of the words: where, having obtained authority through both feet, there is the practice of the means together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-sādhana*).

That means of attainment proceeds with its constituent parts in the [first] two pairs of chapters; the author of the Sūtras explains it as being rendered variegated and differentiated by many divisions. This is the meaning: indeed, specific forms of the knowledge of Brahman have been taught as distinct, supported by evidence, in the [sūtra] "On account of the difference in words and so forth" (BrSū 3.3.56). Then, in the [sūtra] "There is an option because the fruit is not distinguished" (BrSū 3.3.57), those very same means are presented as options since they lead to a single fruit. Thus, the entire collection of means, characterized by both these aspects, is indicated here.

This is the sequence here: for first, upon detachment (*vairāgya*), there arises a thirst for what is to be attained—that is, a desire to seek the object to be attained. Once that has arisen, there follows the qualification for the means. For the qualified person who has engaged in the means, once the means have been determined, there subsequently arises the desire to undertake all the ritual actions (*karma*) which serve as limbs (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman and function as instruments (*karaṇa*). Thus, the section on the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅgapāda*) occurs later.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the venerable author of the Commentary stated, "Now, for the sake of determining the combination or optionality of attributes in the meditations on Brahman, an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of these meditations is commenced," what is the subject matter (*pādārtha*) of this section? Is it an inquiry into difference, or an inquiry into non-difference, or an inquiry into difference in some cases and non-difference in others, or an inquiry into both difference and non-difference? It cannot be the first, because that is not universal. For the same reason, it cannot be the second.

Nor is it the third [alternative], because a recurring object [of meditation] is not established. Nor is it the fourth; for since that which consists of both difference and non-difference is contradictory, reflection upon it is impossible. Although the word "reflection" (cintā) denotes an inquiry consisting of doubt, and although both sides of the argument have been stated, in this section (pāda), there is a reflection on whether there is a combination or non-combination of qualities.

[Otherwise] it would be deficient. For that very reflection (*cintā*) is the primary subject in this section (*pāda*), as evidenced by its designation as the "Section on the Synthesis of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*). Having all this in mind, he says: "In one [section]. This is the meaning of the words here: in a single section, only a single purpose is to be accepted by a person who employs subtle reasoning. [Any] deliberation upon two [purposes]...

There would be no deliberation (*vicāra*). The single entity called "identity-in-difference" does not exist at all; for even if it were to exist merely through the use of words—like a hare's horn—it would be this very thing that must be deliberated upon in this chapter (*pāda*), and not anything else, such as the inclusion or non-inclusion of qualities. He states this with the words, "lest there be the consequence of abandoning another [topic]. He concludes by summarizing the point already stated with the word, "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Thus, because this section (pāda) is marred by such conceptualization (*vikalpa*), the expansion of methods (*nayavitati*)—the elaboration of logic (*nyāyavistara*)—is considered lax; therefore, when an objection is raised against the *prekṣita* text, an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of the branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is undertaken. When there is an objection from some person regarding the text of the *Bhāṣya*, the capacity of the intended meaning (*aidamarthyatātparyasamarthya*) is established as follows: "This section is that which establishes the restriction of knowledge (*vidyāniyamakṛt*) as delimited by the objects of knowledge (*vedya*). The meaning is this: neither difference nor non-difference is investigated here as the primary subject; rather, difference and non-difference exist solely for the purpose of the inclusion or non-inclusion of secondary qualities (*guṇopasaṃhārānupasaṃhāra*). Therefore...

If it is argued that even the establishment of the "Chapter on the Compendium of Attributes" (Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda) is appropriate, yet the objection re-emerges that whether there is a compendium or no compendium constitutes the meaning of the chapter, [the response is:

the determination of either compendium or non-compendium as appropriate is the meaning of the chapter; thus, the unity of purpose is established. Since this [chapter] effects the restriction of knowledge according to the objects of knowledge, the objects of knowledge are distinct.

If knowledge (*vidyā*) is distinct [in one case] and non-distinct [in another], or if it is non-distinct and thus identical, then the restriction of knowledge conforms to the object of knowledge (*vedya*); thus, the unity of the subject matter (*pāda-artha*) is established. In this regard, the distinction between objects of knowledge arises from the distinction between qualities (*guṇa*), and not from a distinction in Brahman itself. Therefore, the establishment of the section concerning the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*) is all the more appropriately integrated.

In the preceding verse, it was established that the single purpose of this section (*pāda*) is to determine the identity of knowledge as delimited by its objects of cognition. Here, someone raises an objection: "Granted that there is a single purpose, nevertheless, since this section aims to demonstrate the unity of knowledge, its sole subject matter (*pādārtha*) must be non-difference (*abheda*) alone, and not the difference between knowledges. If so, why do the commentators speak of 'an inquiry into the difference and non-difference of knowledges'? To this we reply: let it be an illustration of an exception; the actual subject matter of the section remains the unity of knowledge itself.

Since identity is impossible in certain cases, difference must also exist; thus, only an exception (*apavāda*) is being demonstrated, and not that difference constitutes the primary subject matter of the section. He restates this doubt with the words "bearing its name" (*ākhyāvantam*). Here is the meaning of the words: they have designated this section as "the section on the combination of qualities" (*guṇopasaṃhārapāda*) because it deals with the combination of qualities.

Therefore, for that reason, by virtue of the power of its name, the consideration of difference in this section—which aims to establish the unity of knowledge—is introduced solely as an exception, and not as the primary subject.

In order to dispel this very doubt regarding the meaning of the *pāda*, the authors of the Commentary stated: "An inquiry into the difference and non-difference of the Vidyās. He says "in this way" (*ittham*) to that effect. If it is asked, "What then is the meaning of the *pāda* that recurs throughout all [sections]? he replies: "The subject matter" (*viṣaya*).

Here someone objects: "It has been stated by you that there is a distinction between the knowledges (*vidyā*) due to a distinction in their qualities (*guṇa*). In that case, there would also be a distinction in their fruits (*phala*). [The opponent continues: "As it is said: 'According to one's resolve in this world...'"

For it is heard in scripture: "As a person is in this world, so does he become after passing away," and also, "In whatever way one meditates upon Him, so indeed does he become. Therefore, the meaning of the scripture is that one attains the Blessed Lord endowed with exactly those qualities with which one worships Him. Since it is a logical principle that when there is a specific injunction, there is an implied prohibition of the remainder, the attainment of the Blessed Lord as qualified by attributes other than those of the object of worship is effectively prohibited; otherwise, the claim that liberation is the experience of the complete Brahman would be nothing more than a mere assertion.

This is restated as "nissīma" (boundless). If one were to divide, through various forms of knowledge characterized by distinctions based on the forms of objects of cognition, the Supreme Self—which is a mass of infinite, unconditional, and abundant qualities that serve as the cause for the excellence of boundless bliss—then the attainment of Brahman would also occur only partially, by way of a single portion.

Whatever form constitutes the object of meditation, that very same form would be the form attained; and thus, it would follow that the fruit is not the experience of the complete Brahman. To refute this objection, [the author] says, "Not so. He explains the refutation itself with the words, "by those very [means]. This is the meaning: in the passage, "As one's resolve (kratu) is in this world, so does a person become," the attainment of the form of the object of meditation is stated to be non-deficient; for by the statement "he becomes exactly so," the attainment of the entire form of the object of meditation is declared.

Furthermore, if there were deficiency, the completeness of the form of the object of worship would be destroyed. However, neither the connection with additional forms nor its absence is enjoined here, nor is it prohibited. If it is argued that it is prohibited by the principle that when a specific [form] is enjoined, the remainder is prohibited, this objection is also based solely on delusion; for [this principle applies] only in the absence of another authoritative means of injunction.

A prohibition based on mere reasoning would have to be accepted here; however, there is a positive injunction: "The stainless one attains supreme equality," for the scripture itself declares supreme equality. Furthermore, that this supreme equality consists solely in enjoyment will be established by the author of the Sūtras himself in the aphorism: "And because of the indicative mark of equality in respect of enjoyment alone. Therefore, when there is a contradiction with a scriptural statement, mere reasoning has no power; thus, a prohibition of additional attributes based on reasoning is a conclusion reached only by those who understand bad logic.

If it is argued that by accepting the equality of the individual soul (*jīva*) with God, the status of being God would follow for the soul as well, we say no; for this has already been refuted by the author of the Sūtras himself through the use of the word *mātra* (only). The meaning of the words is as follows: for the liberated one whose desires are fulfilled, the object of attainment is Brahman alone—complete with those very qualities of the Lord which are to be meditated upon, as well as accompanied by other qualities which are not to be meditated upon. There is no other fruit here. For in the means leading to heaven and the like, it is well known that the object of meditation is one thing and the fruit is another. Therefore, in this case...

According to the principle of "as is one's thought, so is one's attainment" (*tatkratu-nyāya*), that very Brahman, characterized by qualities whether they be attributes of the object of meditation or not, is what is to be attained; thus the *tatkratu-nyāya* is established. Consequently, there is no possibility of any discrepancy in the results across various meditative knowledges (*vidyās*).

Regarding this, the connection of the sections (*pādasaṅgati*) is stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "It has been said that everything up to the point where Brahman is established as the bestower of fruits must be explained in order to generate the desire to meditate upon Brahman. Now, the inquiry into the difference or non-difference of the various forms of knowledge (*vidyā*) is commenced for the purpose of determining the combination or non-combination of their attributes. He also states the introduction to the topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words "First, then," and so forth.

In the sūtra "phalamata upapatteḥ," the primacy of Brahman as the object of meditation in bestowing all fruits was stated; now, however, because the Vaiśvānara-vidyā—consisting of the meditation on Brahman with form through the conceptualization [of Him] from the head down to the feet—is superior to other forms of higher knowledge (paravidyā), that very [knowledge] is first [discussed].

This is now being considered. For this very reason, the venerable Parāśara, in the context of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), stated that Brahman with form (*savigraha*) alone is to be meditated upon first because it is the auspicious substratum (*śubhāśraya*); however, he further declared that the essential nature of Brahman (*brahmasvarūpa*) is not to be meditated upon by one who is merely practicing yoga (*yogayuk*), but only by one who has already ascended to yoga (*ārūḍhayoga*).

Since this entire collection of logical principles (*nyāya*) stated in the various sections (*adhikaraṇa*) of the previous portion [of the Mīmāṃsā] is present within this science (*vidyā*), and since it is appropriate to investigate other sciences only after first investigating this one, the intention is that this very science is investigated first. This is indicated by the two words "first" (*prathamam*) and "at the outset" (*tāvat*). The investigation of its meaning concerns whether the sciences such as the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, which are studied in various recensions (*śākhā*), differ with each recension or are identical. Which...?

Is there recognition [of identity] across different recensions or not? Does the restrictive rule for the teaching of this knowledge to the followers of the Atharva Veda—stated in the passage, "One should teach this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to the rules"—act as a contradiction to recognition by way of establishing a difference [between the recensions], or does it not? Is the head-vow a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the knowledge?

Or rather, [it is] a limb of study (*adhyayanāṅga*). Here, having first established non-difference by means of the arguments for non-difference stated in the section concerning other branches (*śākhāntara*) of the ritual portion (*karmakāṇḍa*), the author of the Sūtras then raised an objection by means of the arguments for difference, and finally re-established non-difference alone by demonstrating that those points of difference have other purposes. He states this with the words "Difference," etc. This is the meaning: in the ritual portion, indeed, the unity of rituals was asserted on the grounds of the non-distinction of connection (*saṃyoga*), form (*rūpa*), injunction (*codanā*), and name (*ākhyā*). "Connection" refers to the connection with a fruit; "form" refers to the substance and the deity.

The ritualists maintain that the form (*rūpa*) of an action consists of the substance (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*). An injunction (*codanā*) is a word expressive of an activity (*kriyā*) headed by verbal suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*), the imperative (*loṭ*), or the gerundive (*tavya*). A name (*ākhyā*) is a designation such as *Jyotiṣṭoma* and so forth. Because these [factors] are not distinct [in different cases], there is the unity of the action; this is the meaning of the sūtra: "Because of the non-distinction of connection, form, injunction, and name. The means of proof for difference, however, are "differentiation by another word" (*śabdāntara*) and so forth. Differentiation by another word (*śabdāntara*) refers to non-synonymous terms, such as *yajati*, *juhoti*, *dadāti*, and so on. Repetition (*abhyāsa*), however, [is seen in passages like] "the *samidhs*..."

Repetition (*punaḥ-pāṭha*) consists of repeated recitation in such forms as "he sacrifices" or "he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt. Number (*saṅkhyā*) is observed in instances such as "he offers three oblations," where the number three and so forth is seen. Quality (*guṇa*), however, refers to substances like *vājina* mentioned in passages such as, "He pours curds into heated milk; that is the *āmikṣā* for the Viśvedevas, and the *vājina* for the Vājins. A different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is found in passages such as, "Having performed the *upasad* rites, he performs the *agnihotra* for a month. Name (*nāmadheya*) is also a differentiator [of actions].

This is seen in passages such as, "Now this is the Jyotis, now this is the Viśvajyotis, now this is the Sarvajyotis. Thus, this section (*adhikaraṇa*) has been analyzed by means of the various factors of differentiation and non-differentiation set forth in the logical arguments of the earlier *Kāṇḍa*. In that regard, the application of words—specifically how differentiation among injunctions is established through "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and other criteria—was determined and demonstrated in the second chapter of the *Karma-Kāṇḍa*.

From the fact that [the acts] are determined by their origin, from their being combined, from their conjunction, and from their unity; and because there is no distinction in their conjunction, form, injunction, and name, another non-difference of ritual actions has been established. Since the two sections—the *karmakāṇḍa* and the *brahmakāṇḍa*—constitute a single scripture (*ekaśāstrya*), and since the application of reasoning (*nyāyapravṛtti*) is likewise equal, the very method of ritual action (*karmanīti*) is itself the method for knowledge (*vidyā*). Having thus stated the reality of the matter in general, and since this section begins with the presentation of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), the author of the Sūtras first states the conclusion, then raises an objection from the perspective of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), and finally re-establishes that same conclusion.

Thus he shows [this] with the word "in the beginning.
