As for the connection of the words: by that very section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*), because there was no distinction in the injunctions, the method of other recensions (*śākhāntara*)—which had been stated at the outset—was challenged by the scripture itself; having challenged it by means of a differentiating authority (*bhedaka-pramāṇa*) inherent within the scripture, he established that aforementioned point by resolving it. He states the reason for this:
"by stating that the differentiating [authority] has another purpose. The meaning is: because the differentiating authority has a different intended meaning (*tātparya*).

In this context, [the author] clarifies the very solution stated in the Bhāṣya by first restating the objection that the previously mentioned meaning constitutes a difference between the Vidyās, beginning with the words "In the Śākhās... The meaning is as follows: because of the repetition of the statement without qualification and because of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*), a difference between the Vidyās alone is appropriate here. This is just as in the case of "He offers the *samidh* oblation," "He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation," and so on, where there is a repetition of "he offers" (*yajati*) without qualification; and as in the case of "Having performed the *upasad* rites, he performs the *agnihotra* for a month."

Furthermore, a difference in ritual action (*karmabheda*) is observed due to a difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*). Likewise, here too, a difference in knowledge (*vidyābheda*) must certainly be accepted for those same two reasons. The logical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: in the various branches (*śākhā*) that teach the knowledge of Brahman, different methods (*prakriyā*) are seen in each respective place; and here, moreover, repetition without distinction is observed. Therefore, there would be a difference in knowledge. [The author] refutes this with "no" (*na*). Both of these—the repetition without distinction and the difference in context—are indeed appropriate because of the difference among the students (*adhyetṛbheda*). This is the meaning: such indeed is the established rule (*maryādā*) of the Mīmāṃsakas.

The repetition of a statement without distinction and a change of context bring about a difference in what is to be enjoined only if there is no difference among the students; when there is a difference among those who understand, the repetition without distinction and the change of context do not constitute a differentiator.

Therefore, since there is a difference in the practitioners (*pratipattr-bheda*) here, there is no contingency of a difference in the knowledge (*vidyā-bheda*). Now, one might object: "Since there is a rule for the instruction of the knowledge of Brahman only for those who have performed the 'head-vow' (*śirovrata*) according to the injunction—namely, 'One should teach this knowledge of Brahman only to those by whom the head-vow has been performed according to the rule'—let there be a difference in the knowledge. Anticipating this intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), he states the refutation even in that case with the words "it is improper" (*ayukta*). To the question "How is it improper?", he says "svādhyāya... [and so on].

Thus, in this context, the term *brahmavidyā* denotes the Veda itself (*svādhyāya*) and not knowledge (*vidyā*), because it is stated that the study of the Veda is connected with the Vedic observances (*vedavrata*) in the passage: "One who has not performed the vows should not study this. This is the meaning.

Here someone objects: "If the unity of the knowledge (*vidya*) is established by the identity of form (*rūpa*), what else remains to be combined? If you say that the identity of form itself is that [unity], we say no, because it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the unity of knowledge from the identity of form, and the identity of form from the unity of knowledge. Or rather, it would result in a circular argument (*cakraka*): the unity of knowledge from the identity of form; the combination of the forms, qualities, and attributes of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) from the unity of knowledge; and the identity of form from the combination of those qualities. If it is then argued that there is some quality other than the form of the object of knowledge that is to be combined, [we reply:]...

And is that other [entity] contradictory or non-contradictory? If it is contradictory, then, by accepting the coexistence of two contradictory properties in a single locus, there would be no distinction whatsoever anywhere in the world. If the coexistence of heat and cold in one place were possible, what else could serve as a differentiator? Therefore, [this applies] to actions or to knowledges.

If there were an inclusion of those respective unique differentiating attributes, there would be no distinction at all between sacrifices, gifts, oblations, and so forth, nor between the Sadvidyā, Daharavidyā, Bhūmavidyā, and others. Now, one might argue that the inclusion could occur through option (*vikalpa*), such that at one time there is a connection with its own attributes, and at another time a connection with other attributes opposed to them. That too is not tenable, because an option is marred by eight defects (*aṣṭadoṣa*).

Furthermore, no option (vikalpa) is even possible here, because its own inherent attribute has been taught by the scripture itself, while no other contradictory attribute has been taught by the scripture. An option occurs between two equal things, not between unequal ones. Therefore, one might ask: "What is this attribute that is to be combined? Consequently, the claim that the investigation into difference and non-difference is for the purpose of determining the combination or non-combination of attributes is a useless statement. He restates this [objection] with the words "because of the identity of form" (rūpaikyāt). If the identity [of the meditation] is established through the identity of form, what else remains to be combined? If it is another attribute—provided that the attribute is established as belonging to a different meditation or the like.

Otherwise, there would be no distinction established anywhere between actions or knowledges based on a difference in form. What is it that is to be deliberated upon here? Here, "what" is used in the sense of a negation. That form which is to be deliberated upon does not exist here at all, because it is unique to each specific knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, by this demonstration, the inquiry into difference and non-difference does not serve the purpose of the integration of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) and is thus fruitless. To this, the reply is: "No. [The author] clearly shows the distinction between what is to be integrated and what is not to be integrated with the words: "the form of the object of knowledge" (*vedyākāra*).

It indicates that the identity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) consists in the identity of the forms of the objects of knowledge (*vedyākāraikya*). However, that identity of the forms of the objects of knowledge is not to be combined [from different sources], because it is already established beforehand.

Therefore, there is neither a circular argument (*cakraka*) nor mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Thus, once the identity of the knowledge is established, that which is "additional" to it is something entirely distinct from the form that brings about the identity of the knowledge.

If a certain limb [of a ritual] is drawn out [from one branch], and it is heard in all those respective branches, then it is indeed not to be combined [into others], because it has already been heard there. But if it is heard only in some places, then, due to the identity of the knowledge (*vidya*), it must be combined even in other branches; such is the path of logic. One might suspect: "Is this very rule indeed devised by you yourself? To which [the author replies]:

He confirms his own stated position with the agreement of all learned people by saying, "Even in ritual action" (*karmaṇyapi*). The meaning is that if what we have said were not accepted, there would be a contradiction of all the scriptures. The grammatical connection here is as follows: even in *karman*—that is, even in the *Karmakāṇḍa*—in this very same manner, the quality that is the subject of the conclusion has been accepted as being distinct from the qualities that serve as differentiators. For here, among the various distinct rituals such as sacrifice, giving, and oblation, [the quality is established].

If a certain property distinct from the respective unique differentiating properties is established as being one and the same action due to the non-difference in form, injunction, and name, then because of that very unity, it is to be subsumed everywhere. This is the meaning: among ritual actions, a mutually contradictory property is not to be subsumed; even though unity is established through the identity of form and so forth, the very form that brings about that unity is also not to be subsumed. However, if a property other than that [unifying form] is recognized in one instance, it may be subsumed in the other.
And that [property] exists in both cases.
If it is established, then it is indeed not subject to further sublation; such is the conclusion of those who have reached the end of the tantric assemblies.

Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states the connection: "Thus, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth, the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikatva*) is established; and since there is unity, the combination of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) must be performed. Hereafter, with reference to certain knowledges, it will be determined by investigating whether or not there is a non-difference in the injunctions and so forth—which serves as the cause for recognition. The investigation into that purpose is as follows: There is the Udgītha-knowledge among both the Vājasaneyins and the Chandogas; is there unity of knowledge in both cases, or is there a difference between the knowledges? For that purpose, it is investigated: is there [non-difference] in both cases?

Is there a recognition of the same knowledge here or not? Is the object of worship in both cases the *udgītha* itself, or is it the *praṇava*, which is a part of the *udgītha*, for the followers of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad? Is the word *udgītha* used in both places to denote the *udgītha* itself, or is it used by the followers of the Chāndogya to denote the *praṇava* that constitutes a part of the *udgītha*?

Does the fact that the word *udgītha* occurs at the beginning of the passage, "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*," indicate that the word *udgītha* refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), or not? Previously, it was stated that the Vaiśvānara-vidyā is a single meditation because there is no difference in its connection, form, injunction, and name; if that is so, then in other meditations as well, a unity of meditation should be accepted on that same ground of non-difference. To illustrate this, the *udgītha*-vidyā is first cited as an example.

He says "as before" regarding this very point. One might suspect that, as in the case of the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, the Udgītha-vidyā would be one and the same despite the difference in Vedic branches (*śākhā*), with its distinctions pacified. Anticipating this, he refutes it by saying "that is not so. He states the reason for this: "in both ways. For among all factors that differentiate [vidyās], a difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*) is the primary one; and that difference in form is not perceived here in a single way, but rather in both ways. Therefore, due to the abundance of means of proof for differentiation, difference itself must be accepted.

He demonstrates the very two-fold nature of the means of differentiation already mentioned by the word "udgātā. In some cases, such as in the Udgītha-vidyā, the *udgātṛ* (chanter) is mentioned as the object of meditation; in another case, however, it is the *geya* (the song). This is one difference in form (*rūpabheda*). He states yet another difference in form with the word "geya": the distinction is that in some instances there is meditation upon the entire song (*sakalageya*), while in others there is meditation upon a partial song (*asakalageya*).

Thus, when a difference in form has been established—whether through the form itself, conjunction, injunction, or name—the non-difference of conjunction and the other factors, even if they are distinct from the form, does not at all lead to the conclusion that the knowledge (vidyā) is non-different. He explains this very point with the word "bheda" (difference). Indeed, this is the established rule of the Mīmāṃsakas: that even if there is oneness of conjunction, form, injunction, or name, a difference in ritual action (karma) is nonetheless established. Likewise here, once a difference in even a single principal form is established, a difference in the knowledge must necessarily be admitted.
Furthermore, here the difference in the nature of the principal [deity] is seen in both ways; the sense is that by this, the distinction between the Vidyās is all the more firmly established.

Previously, in order to establish the difference between the two Udgītha-vidyās, a distinction in the form of the objects of knowledge was asserted; now, he clearly demonstrates that very distinction in the form of the objects of knowledge with the words "In the Chāndogya... In the Chāndogya passage, the word *udgītha* in both instances refers specifically to the *praṇava*, which is a constituent part of it. He states the reason for this as: "Because of its established usage from the beginning of the context."

Since, at the beginning of the passage in the *Chāndogya*, the word "udgītha" is designated as referring to the *praṇava*, whereas in the *Vājasaneyaka*—due to the absence of any restrictive context or other such factors—the word "udgītha" denotes the entire *udgītha*, a difference in form is established: in one case it denotes the *udgītha*, while in the other it denotes the *praṇava* which is a constituent part of the *udgītha*. It is well known that there is a distinction between these two: the *udgītha* is a specific division (*bhakti*) of the *Sāman*, and the *praṇava* is a constituent part of that. If this is so, then...

If it is argued that the word *udgītha* occurring at the beginning [of the passage] as applied to the horses (*vājinaḥ*) must be figurative because the word *udgītha* is used for the *udgātṛ* priest, and thus the very use of the term is a defect of figurativeness—[the author] says "that" (*tat*) to show that there is no defect of figurativeness here. This is the meaning: the *udgātṛ* is the performer of the *udgītha*; and with respect to the task to be accomplished by that performer, the *udgītha* itself possesses the status of an instrument (*sādhana*), according to the maxim "that which is not grasped as a qualifier cannot be grasped as the qualified. Therefore, since the instruction is given that the *udgītha* itself is the instrument in the phrase "we shall cross over by means of the *udgītha*," there is no occasion for figurativeness.

Such is the meaning of the word. "In the pacification of enemies" means in the defeat of foes; this is because there is no contradiction in stating that [the pacification of enemies] is its fruit, for there is no contradiction in the statement that it is the fruit of the *udgītha*.

In the *Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*, it is the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) alone that should be contemplated, because this is a treatise on the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*), and thus it is that very knowledge which is contemplated everywhere. Nevertheless, raising the objection as to why the *Udgītha-vidyā*—which is itself not the knowledge of Brahman and has other minor fruits such as the defeat of enemies—should be contemplated here, he states the resolution in two ways with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*). First, the solution stated by the *ekadeśins* (partialists) is set forth: even though this [Udgītha-vidyā] is indeed not the knowledge of Brahman and has a minor fruit, it need not be adopted here.

In the *Mokṣaśāstra*, although this is so, according to the maxim "because there is no difference in the injunction regarding the form of the connection," and because there is no difference in the fact that [this knowledge] must be contemplated, the view of the *ekadeśins* (partial authorities) is that it is contemplated here. However, for others, this knowledge, though pertaining to desires (*kāmya*), is taught as a means for the removal of obstacles to the practice of *brahmavidyā*; since a specific utility exists, it is included within *brahmavidyā*, and thus it is to be contemplated specifically therein.

For enemies are indeed debates and the like, which are obstacles to the practice of knowledge, as well as the persons who instigate them; and their defeat brings about the very excellence of that knowledge. Thus, reflection on the Udgītha and other such meditations is especially appropriate in this very context.

Regarding the fact that the meditation on the *udgītha* knowledge should be considered right here, he states two further reasons by way of another method in the verse beginning with "ajñāta" (unknown). Indeed, these two reasons are as follows: meditations such as that on the *udgītha* take the form of viewing [the object] as Brahman; and those cannot even be performed in the absence of a thorough knowledge of the Brahman that is to be seen. Therefore, the meditation on the *udgītha* and other such meditations finds its proper connection right here. For this very reason, the *Vaiśvānara-vidyā* and others concerning the Brahman to be seen were considered first in this very section (*pāda*).

Now, the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, which consist of the vision of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*), are being considered. This is the syntactical connection here: how indeed could one who has not known the true nature of the essence of Brahman contemplate the vision of Brahman in relation to the *udgītha* and other such elements? Therefore, since it is impossible to even conceive of injunctions for the vision of the *udgītha* and so forth without knowledge of Brahman, these must be considered right here in this very section on Brahman (*brahmakāṇḍa*), and not again in the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*).

Because of the absence of such an association [with other meditations], this one reason has been stated for why the contemplations on the Udgītha and so forth must be performed right here [in this context]. He shows another reason, consisting in a specific utility, by saying "they would bestow" (*ādadhyuḥ*). According to the text, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," the Udgītha-vidyā is a qualification [of the ritual] because it brings about greater power (*vīryavattara*) in those actions that have knowledge as their constituent part (*vidyāṅga-karman*). This "greater power" means that the fruits of those actions having knowledge as their constituent part are unimpeded.
For when obstacles are absent, the ritual acts that are ancillary to knowledge (*vidyā*) are able to accomplish the knowledge of Brahman immediately;

therefore, because they serve to remove the obstacles to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman and because they themselves consist of the vision of Brahman, both types of knowledge—such as that of the *udgītha* and so forth—are to be considered here alone.

The meaning is that it is appropriate. This is the conclusion here: because the rites that are ancillary to knowledge possess an excellence of potency (*vīryavattva*) in bestowing their own fruits, the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth should indeed be applied to them. Therefore, the contemplation of the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth, by generating an excellence in the rites intended for the meditation on Brahman, is precisely what is required by the context at hand.

In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was stated that there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to a difference in form; prior to that, in the *Vaiśvānara* section, it was established that there is identity of knowledge due to the identity of form. Now, having raised the doubt—similar to the previous section—that there is a difference in knowledge due to a difference in form, and having refuted that, the identity of knowledge due to the identity of form is once again firmly established as in the *Vaiśvānara* section; such is the connection (*saṅgati*).

The investigation into that matter concerns the Praṇa-vidyā as taught by both the Chandogas and the Kauṣītakins: whether there is identity of the meditation in both places or a difference; whether the meditation in both cases possesses qualities such as being the "best" (*vasiṣṭhatva*) and so forth, or whether for the Kauṣītakins it is devoid of those qualities; and [the question] regarding the Kauṣītakins...

Whether or not the attainment of qualities such as being the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhatva*) is also part of the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇa-vidyā*). For, although there is no explicit restatement in the Kauṣītaki recension—such as "Insofar as I am the most excellent, you are that most excellent"—is the attainment of such excellence by speech and the other organs understood from the knowledge of the vital breath, on account of the initial statement regarding their subsistence and functioning depending upon the vital breath? Or is it not? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: In the Chāndogya, Vājasaneyaka, and Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇas, qualities such as seniority (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*) are studied in relation to the vital breath.

In the Kauṣītaki-vidyā, although this entire collection of qualities is identical [in both versions], the fact that speech and the other organs possess the quality of being "most excellent" (vasiṣṭha) and so forth—whereas my own excellence and yours depend upon him—is not restated by speech and the others with reference to Prāṇa. Thus, due to such differences in form, the Prāṇa-vidyā is established as manifold across many Śākhās.

"Let it be divided"—thus he restates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). He refutes that with "Not so. Since there is no difference in the description of speech and the other organs as being subject to the control of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) regarding their respective qualities of seniority (*jyaiṣṭhya*), excellence (*śraiṣṭhya*), and preeminence (*vāsiṣṭhya*), [the text] merely records the attribution of their own respective functions to the vital breath by speech and the others.

It was not done; however, that does not constitute a difference in form (*rūpabheda*). Since it has been established that the pre-eminence (*vasiṣṭhatva*) of speech and the other organs depends upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it follows by implication that the pre-eminence of speech and the rest is the pre-eminence of the vital breath; thus, nothing remains to be stated separately. Therefore, there is no room for a difference in meditative knowledge (*vidyābheda*) on account of a difference in form. All of this has been clearly and well-explained in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) itself, so there is nothing remaining for the Teachers (*Ācāryas*) to elaborate upon, and thus we conclude.

Previously, in three sections, an inquiry into the difference and non-difference of various meditations (*vidyās*) was conducted. Among those, in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, air (*vāyu*) was conceived as the object of meditation in the form of the breath of the Supreme Person, according to the text "Air is the breath" (*vāyuḥ prāṇaḥ*). Furthermore, in the Udgītha-vidyā, there arose a discussion regarding the breath in the form of viewing the Udgītha and other elements as the breath. In the section immediately preceding this one, the actual breath itself was defined. Thus, there is a mutual consistency among these preceding sections.

It has been stated that qualities such as being the eldest (*jyaiṣṭhya*) and so forth must also be considered, as they are included within the presentation of attributes; this follows from the fact that Brahman is the object of knowledge for all branches of learning (*sarvavidyāvedyatva*).

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is stated that attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*) and others, which define the essential nature of Brahman, must be meditated upon as being included within the definition of that very nature. This connection is clearly seen in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*): "Here, it is deliberated whether there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of the qualities of the nature of Brahman across all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), or not. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: are qualities such as bliss to be synthesized in all meditations, or only where they are explicitly heard?

Is it that qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth possess merely a non-difference from the substratum (*guṇin*), like sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) and other attributes; or rather, do they possess an inseparable connection with the cognition of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), just like the nature of Brahman itself? Demonstrating the connection [of this section] according to the view of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he first states the prima facie position: "Not by different words" (*nānāśabda*), etc.

The meaning is as follows: you yourself have previously stated that there is a difference in knowledge (*vidyā*) due to a difference in qualities (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is established that the other qualities heard in various places are restricted [to their respective meditations]. Similarly, the opponent's intention is that even such attributes as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and the like, which are distinct from the very nature of Brahman, are restricted according to the difference in knowledge. Later, the author of the Sūtras will state that the knowledge of Brahman is divided by the difference in qualities, saying: "It is manifold because of the difference in words and so forth" (*nānā śabdādibhedāt*).

Therefore, a quality belonging to one Vidyā, which is mentioned in its own specific context, should not be applied to another Vidyā. However, if a quality is mentioned in both contexts, let it indeed be applied to both; for this is precisely the rule established by those who know the principles of interpretation. Consequently, since this is determined by the boundaries of such logic, the opponent’s prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that qualities such as truthfulness, knowledge, infinity, bliss, and purity—just like other qualities—should also be restricted to their respective places. He refutes this with the words "Not so" (maivam). He explains the manner of this refutation with the word "Brahman."

This is the meaning: in the world, the qualities of things are of two kinds; among them, some define the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a thing, while others qualify the essential nature once it has been defined. That which defines the essential nature follows everywhere in connection with the essential nature of the thing.

Just as "jar-ness" is present in the context of a jar, whereas specific qualities such as redness or blackness—which define its particular nature—are restricted to this or that individual jar; so too, because they define the essential nature [of Brahman], bliss and the other [attributes] persist everywhere, while others, such as having joy as the head, are restricted to their respective locations. Thus, bliss and the rest are indeed common to all meditations (vidyās).

"Of the nature of Brahman" means that since it arises from the realization of the nature of Brahman, it must be regarded as possessing that very nature in all meditations (*vidyās*). This is the "ascent" (*anvāroha*). The essential point is that because these are attributes that define its true nature, they serve solely for the purpose of realizing that true nature.

He demonstrates the nature of truthfulness and so forth by distinguishing them according to their essential forms, beginning with the words "truthfulness. Truthfulness exists in the Supreme Brahman, the cause of the universe, due to the abandonment of the manifold web of transformations belonging to both the conscious and the unconscious. Knowledgehood exists [in the individual soul] because of its state as a knower. The word "knowledge" (jñāna) is also used in the sense of the agent, since the suffix *lyuṭ* can be applied even to denote the agent according to the rule "the kṛtya and lyuṭ suffixes are used diversely" (*Pāṇini 3.3.113*).

This is because it can be established by relying on the use of the suffix *lyu* in the sense of the agent alone, according to the rule: "The suffixes *lyu*, *ṇini*, and *ac* are applied after [roots ending in] *nandi*, *grahi*, *pacati*, and so forth"; and because the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) can also be employed in the sense of that whose essence consists of the quality of knowledge, according to the principle: "But its designation as such is due to its having that quality as its essence."

Furthermore, because the nature [of Brahman] is self-luminous, the word *jñāna* (knowledge), which denotes that very self-luminous nature, is appropriately applied to it alone. Now, one might object: "Since the meaning can be established in many ways here—whether as the agent (*kartṛ*), as an existent entity (*bhāva*), or even through non-difference from the Self—there must be a difference in accent (*svara*) due to the difference in meaning. Anticipating this, he provides the answer even to that point with the words, "due to the abundance of accents" (*svarabahulatayā*). The meaning is that since the accent is optional, wherever there is no inconsistency regarding the accent, it should be accepted exactly as it stands.

Furthermore, where a difference in accent must be accepted, there is no difficulty whatsoever because of the rule "bahulaṃ chandasi" (in Vedic usage, [rules apply] diversely), which allows for the diversity of accents and so forth. Otherwise, how could even the venerable Pāṇini have made such declarations as "uṇādayo bahulam" (the uṇādi suffixes are formed diversely)? To explain the infinity of Brahman—which consists in the absence of the three kinds of limitation—he states the modes of limitation with the words "tridvyekābhiḥ" (by three, two, or one). Pots and the like are limited by three, because they are delimited by space, time, and substance.

An atom is delimited by two [dimensions] because of its minuteness and its lack of continuity. Time, however, is delimited by only one [dimension], for while it possesses omnipresence and eternity, it is delimited as a real entity solely by its lack of continuity. He also states the infinity of Brahman with the words "of that": the Supreme Brahman is infinite because of its non-connection with the three types of delimitation.
The expression "the abode of eternally pure bliss" is intended to demonstrate that bliss is the preeminent quality among the attributes of Brahman.

[Objection: "But has not the definition of Brahman already been stated in the very Sūtra *janmādi*? And since that definition, by virtue of being a definition, excludes [Brahman] from both similar and dissimilar classes, that definition alone is sufficient; for what purpose is this 'definition of essential nature' consisting of truth (*satyatva*) and so forth being stated? Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by stating its specific purpose with the words "It has been said. Indeed, this doubt is indicated by the particle *nanu*. [The opponent argues: "By that [first definition] alone, there would be comprehension of the essential nature; therefore, truth and so forth are here entirely useless."

If that very Brahman is expressed by the word "Truth" (*satya*) and so forth, there is tautology; if it is something else, then it would not be Brahman, for there is no second Brahman. If it is another definition, then it is useless precisely because its purpose has already been fulfilled. "If there is a specific purpose, then explain clearly what that is"—this is the opponent's intention. He refutes this with "No. He explains that very point with the words "Because of the reason... (*hetor iti*).

The author of the Bhāṣya himself has already stated that once Īśvara is established as the cause of the world, the qualities such as truthfulness (satyatva) and so forth are predicated for the purpose of removing the defects suspected in that causality. This is because [these qualities] serve to exclude, respectively, non-sentient matter, the bound soul (jīva), the liberated soul, and the eternal [entities]. Therefore, since the sentence beginning with "truth" (satya) also serves to purify the nature of Brahman as it is understood through its distinction from everything else, there is no risk of it being rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, in our view, the attribution of various qualities to Brahman is either for the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*) or for the purpose of contemplation at the time of the attainment of the fruit; thus, the efficacy of everything is established.

Now, you have stated that for the purpose of meditating on Brahman, its truthfulness and other attributes must be reflected upon; however, one might then object that meditation on Brahman could also be accomplished by reflecting on its having "pleasure as its head" and so forth. Anticipating this, the author shows the difference [between the two cases] with the word "nanu. The meaning of the words here is as follows: the meditation on Brahman could indeed be accomplished even by means of such passages as "Pleasure is its head," and so on.

Anticipating the objection that qualities such as "having joy as its head" (*priyaśirastva*) and so forth should also be invariably meditated upon with respect to Brahman, he says "Certainly" (*bāḍham*), thereby granting partial assent. The meaning is this: some of what you have stated is accepted, while some is not. Joy and the other qualities are accepted because they are included within Brahman, which is of the nature of supreme bliss; however, the wings and other parts are not accepted because they are merely the products of another's imagination. Therefore, since even joy and the others serve as means for realizing the true nature of Brahman, those qualities beginning with joy are present throughout all [meditations].

The meaning is that the realization of that [Brahman] occurs through "dear things" (priya) and so forth; that is, the realization of the nature of Brahman occurs through "dear," "delightful," "joy," and so on. Then, one might object: "In that case, attributes such as being the 'tail' should also be considered, since they are studied in passages such as 'Brahman is the tail, the support'. Anticipating this, he says "the portion consisting of the tail and so forth" to indicate that it is not so, because of impossibility. He explains this very impossibility by stating: "In Brahman, which is partless, there can be no such thing as a portion consisting of a tail and so forth"—this is the syntactical connection.

One might object: "In that case, there would be the viewing of Brahman as having a tail; for in an injunction for viewing, the visualization of something not [actually] present is indeed an ornament. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "not so" (*na ca*). For an injunction for viewing consists in the enjoining of viewing a superior thing in what is inferior, as in "one should meditate on the mind as Brahman," and so forth. In the present case, however, if there were a viewing of Brahman as having a tail and so on, it would be quite the opposite; for it is impossible to enjoin the viewing of an inferior thing, such as a tail, in the superior Brahman.

To the objection, "In that case, how can there be such a conceptualization here as 'His very dear [Brahman] is the head'? he states the justification for that conceptualization with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). Since it has been thus established that the qualities of having the dear as the head and so forth are merely mental constructs, it is entirely appropriate to conceive of the Supreme Brahman here as having a head and other limbs, just as the fire-altar is figuratively described in the subsequent section.

Having stated the different meanings of words such as "Ānanda" according to various positions, he concludes his own intended meaning in the manner favored by the author of the Bhāṣya with the words: "Ānandatva... and so forth.

In this regard, some explain the word *ānanda* from the Sūtra as primarily signifying the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of being of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpatva*). Others, however, say it denotes the bliss that is an attribute (*dharmānanda*); according to the principle "because that is its essence" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*), the word *ānanda* expresses precisely the state of being blissful (*ānanditva*). Likewise, he states the third position: "the expression of both. This means that the word *ānanda* conveys both the state of being blissful and the state of being bliss itself. In this context, both positions are presented as alternative options (*vikalpa*) within a single category.

This is the meaning: some say that only "being bliss" (ānandatvam) is expressed; others say only "being blissful" (ānanditvam), or both; or, according to some, by repeating the words, all three positions should be stated as distinct alternatives for the three groups. Here, he extends the scope defined by the word "bliss" to the word "knowledge" as well, saying "in the mention of knowledge": whether it is "being knowledge" (jñānatvam), "being a knower" (jñānitvam), or both, is what is expressed by the word "knowledge. Having thus stated the different positions, he shows the position intended by the author of the Commentary (the Bhāṣyakāra) for the sake of clarity: "equality with the other."

The meaning is this: at the time of realizing the true nature of Brahman, as many attributes as are necessary to prevent any suspicion of similarity with objects other than Brahman must be maintained; thus it is established here that these attributes are to be meditated upon in the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of all Brahma-vidyās, within the context of the term "the abode of manifold enjoyment. Furthermore, those attributes—truth, consciousness, infinity, bliss, and purity—have been established in the Commentary itself according to their sequential utility, and may be seen there in detail.

The connection [of this section] with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is due to its being a remainder of what was previously introduced. The investigation of its meaning concerns whether the two passages from the *Chāndogya* and the *Vājasaneyaka* are intended to enjoin the viewing of the garment as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) while using water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), or not. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "One should sip water. Since the meaning of the sentence is explained in detail in the *bhāṣya*, only the syntactical connection of the words is demonstrated here.

Here, because of the hearing of the injunction "one should sip water" (*ācāmet*), and because an injunction is purposeful only when [the matter] is not already established—according to the maxim "scripture is meaningful where there is no prior attainment"—another sipping of water distinct from that already established by Smṛti and custom is enjoined for the sake of a new transcendental result (*apūrva*). He rejects this position with the words "not so. He states the manner of the rejection with the words "by Smṛti, etc. Since the sipping of water as an auxiliary to eating is already established by Smṛti and other sources, what is enjoined here is simply the contemplation of it as the "garment of the vital breath" (*prāṇavāsas*).

Therefore, because this [text] prescribes a specific act not previously established, there is no subversion of the injunction (*vidhibhaṅga*) in this view. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, since the previous rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) is already established, how can there be the hearing of an injunction in the form 'one should rinse' (*ācāmet*) when there is no prescription of a new rinsing?"—he says: "One should eat" (*bhujjīta*).

Just as in the case of the injunction "having bathed, one should eat," where the act of eating is already established, yet the injunction is heard specifically for the purpose of prescribing the previously unestablished act of bathing; even so, although the injunction "one should sip water" (ācāmet) may indeed be heard regarding the sipping of water which is already established by prior rules, the injunction here must nevertheless be understood as being directed toward the previously unestablished mental reflection on the clothing of the vital breaths (prāṇāvāsastva). Therefore, there is no contradiction in the syntactical connection of the words.

It is indeed accepted by the experts in the Tantras that even when an injunction for listening (*śravaṇa*) is situated elsewhere, its application may be resolved through connection with another [act] by means of an examination of the indicators of intent (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introduction (*upakrama*) and conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*); therefore, it should be the same in this case as well. By the phrase "resting on the meaning of the verbal root already established," the previously established act of sipping water (*ācamana*) is referred to. The meaning is: let there be the act of listening (*śravaṇa*) there, yet the intent (*tātparya*) lies elsewhere.

In this case as well, the fact that the purport of the passage is the injunction for the meditation on the waters used for sipping as the garment of Prāṇa has been explained in the Commentary itself through an examination of the introduction, conclusion, and other criteria; therefore, I shall desist here for fear of prolixity. Now, one might raise the objection of a fool: "Since the knowledge of Prāṇa was already mentioned previously, why is it being stated again now? To this, he provides the resolution with the word "previously" (prāk).

Previously, in the discussion of the knowledge of Prāṇa, considerations regarding difference and non-difference were undertaken; now, however, a subsidiary element (aṅga) consisting of the meditation on the waters used for sipping as the garment of Prāṇa is considered within the knowledge of Prāṇa. Thus, the distinction between the two sections (adhikaraṇa-bheda) is justified.

Even though the subject matter has been stated in this way, [the author] speaks beginning with the word "first" (*ādau*), summarizing both the stated and unstated specific reasons for the sake of clarity for the disciples. The wearing of the garment (*vāsaḥ-paridhāna*) at the beginning and the conclusion [of the section] is one reason. He states another reason as well with the word "they think" (*manyati*). By the use of the term *manyati* in the phrase "they think," it is intended solely for the purpose of enjoining the vision (*darśana-vidhi*). Now, one might object: "Let there be the state of being the breath's garment; what is the purpose of this? Anticipating this doubt, he states the purpose: "for the sake of pleasing the One to be worshipped" (*ārādhyapriyārtham*).

The meaning is this: for an enjoined action, only a purpose suitable to it should be postulated. Just as the purpose of the enjoined act of sipping water (ācamana) is the propitiation of the one to be worshipped, so too the purpose of the contemplation on being the garment of the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the propitiation of the one to be worshipped. And that [propitiation] is the meaning of the root *man* (to honor/propitiate), which refers to what is dear to the one to be worshipped; such is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*). Now, an objection:

Anticipating the objection that the statement regarding the investigation into the "breath-vestment" might itself be a mere hymn of praise (*stuti*), he refutes it with the words "It is a praise. For a hymn of praise is to be welcomed only when there is no other way [to understand the passage]; since here there is the possibility of a consistent interpretation (*gati*) through the injunction of a previously unknown matter (*apūrvārthavidhāna*), a mere praise cannot be assumed. And in this case—

Since the specific purpose of the act of "encircling" (*paridhāna*)—which is otherwise unprecedented (*apūrva*)—is specifically established by the statement, "He encircles it with waters," it is entirely appropriate that this is an injunction for the mental contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of Prāṇa as being clothed. Furthermore, Prāṇa is presented here as the object of worship; and since the mention of encircling with water is an auxiliary part of the worship of a particular deity who is to be propitiated, it is indeed fitting. One should understand that just as in the world the gift of clothing is an auxiliary to the propitiation of a deity, so it is here as well.

In this context, the preceding section was discussed by way of incidental connection as a supplement to the knowledge of the vital breath (*prāṇavidyā*); in that previous section, it was stated that those attributes which define the essential nature [of the Self] are to be combined because they are included within the cognition of that essential nature. Now, however, the combination of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth—which are included within the quality of "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—is being stated; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). The inquiry into its meaning concerns the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā as recorded in the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyaka and in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: is there a single vidyā here?

Is there a difference [between the two], or not? Is there a difference in form in both cases, or not? Is there the attainment of powers such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth in the *Agnirahasya*, or not? Does the mention of being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) and "having true resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpa*) alone lead to the attainment of mastery and so forth through the recognition of the possessor of those qualities, or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that, because of the repetition of the same description without distinction—as in the case of "He offers the *samidh* oblations"—the difference between the two meditations (*vidyābheda*) is unavoidable. Nor should it be argued that the repetition without distinction is due to a difference in reciters, and therefore no difference [in the meditation] arises from that.

Because when there is unity of the *śākhā* (branch of scripture), a difference among the students is impossible; for it is a general principle that a difference among students is not possible within a single *śākhā*. Therefore, in this case, there must be a difference between the two meditations (*vidyā*). Furthermore, no injunction regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*) is observed here by which one might rely on the unity of the meditation. If there were a mention of qualities here, then indeed one could say that the repetition is for the purpose of enjoining qualities within the very same previous meditation. Therefore, a distinction between the meditations must be accepted.

This is what he says with the words "in the case of the unity of the Śākhā. The meaning of the words here is as follows: once the unity of the Śākhā is established, it cannot be asserted that there is a difference among the students. No quality (*guṇa*) whatsoever is to be enjoined here; therefore, one must not say that there is a re-statement for the purpose of enjoining a quality. Consequently, how could the hearing of the aforementioned non-distinction not cause the knowledge (*vidyā*) to be non-different? He rejects the stated position with the words "it is not so" (*maivam*). He explains the manner of this rejection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).

Regarding this, what you have stated—that there is no injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)—is indeed so, because no other quality to be enjoined is observed here. Nevertheless, this is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, analyzed for the sake of clarity and for the purpose of manifesting the meaning already expressed; it is also for the sake of the students' ease of understanding. To illustrate this, he provides the example beginning with "addiction" (*vyasana*).

For in common worldly usage, people express a meaning that has been stated briefly by means of an expanded analytical sentence; likewise here, that which was already expressed by the term "having true resolve" (satyasaṅkalpatva) and is included within it—namely, "mastery" (vaśitva) and so forth—is further explained by the words "mastery" and so on. Therefore, since this is a restatement for the sake of clarification, there is no fault whatsoever.

Here someone raises an objection: "Surely the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, recited in two places in the Vājasaneyaka passage, was adopted by the Commentator; however, it was not investigated whether the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā recited in both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka are different or non-different. For what purpose [was this done]? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the reply with the words "by the Chandogas," meaning that since the principle determined in one place applies to the other as well, the Commentator’s intention is that the students may understand this for themselves.

This is the meaning of the words here: the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is clearly recited by both the Chāndogyas and the Vājasaneyins; why then has the commentator not demonstrated the consideration of difference and non-difference in this illustrative example? He removes this doubt with the words "To that we say. He explains that very point with the words "Wherever... and so on.

The meaning is that whether in the Vājasaneyaka or the Chāndogya, wherever an additional recitation of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth is observed, since it is appropriate to state that those additional qualities are included within other qualities such as "truthfulness of resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), the general statement—whether [the qualities] are more or fewer—is justified. This is because there is no need for a further declaration of a matter already established by a principle determined in one instance.

In order to provide extreme clarity regarding the meaning of what has been restated, [the author], while demonstrating the difference in form of the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā as taught in the Vājasaneyaka, states "the pair of locations" (*sthānadvandva*) to establish the identity of the vidyā by showing the absence of any difference in its essential nature (*rūpa*). For in the *Agnirahasya* of the Vājasaneyaka, the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā is recited as being endowed with qualities such as "consisting of true resolve" (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) but devoid of qualities such as "lordship" (*vaśitva*); whereas in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, that same vidyā is recited as not being devoid of lordship and the other such qualities.

If it be argued that, because there is a difference in form due to the difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*), one must therefore assume a difference in the Śāṇḍilya-vidyās, he rejects this with the word "no" (*na*). He explains that very point with the word "in the *Āraṇyaka*. If the qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) mentioned in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* were distinct from the "truthfulness of resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatā*) mentioned in the *Agnirahasya*, then one could say that the vidyās are different due to the difference in form; however, these are not distinct, since mastery and the other qualities are merely an elaboration of truthfulness of resolve. Therefore, since there is no difference in form, there is no difference in the vidyā.

He establishes that very point with the words "sā" (that). That [quality of] having true resolve was studied in the *Agnirahasya*. Since the [qualities of] mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth are of the nature of an elaboration of having true resolve, they too are effectively studied in that very same place. Therefore, because there is no difference in form, there is no difference in the knowledge (*vidyā*); thus he says: "due to the absence of anything additional."

Previously, it was stated that the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā constitutes a single meditation because there is no difference in its form; well then, the same must apply to the meditation concerning the Person residing within the solar orb and within the eye as described in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

Having raised the objection that there is identity of knowledge because there is no difference in form, it is stated here that there is a difference in form due to the difference in location; this is the connection [of the topic]. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: regarding the two names recorded as residing within the sun and within the eye, are these two names established according to their literal sense for each respective location, or are they to be combined in both places without such restriction? Is there identity of knowledge here, or not? Does the fact that the body consisting of the *vyāhṛtis* is the object of meditation lead to the conclusion that there is identity of knowledge in both cases, or not? Is the mere unity of the qualities of the object of meditation the cause of non-difference, or is the unity of location also a cause?

Is the place [of meditation] included within [the object], or not? Here, having raised the doubt that the two meditations on the Person residing within the eye and the one within the sun might be identical because of the identity of their forms, [the author] will demonstrate that they are distinct meditations due to the difference in form resulting from the difference in location; thus he says "akṣi" (eye). As for the meaning of the words: worship of the Lord, who is indicated by the eye and the sun, would be one and the same because of the identity of connection, form, injunction, and so forth. Consequently, there would be no restriction to either of the two names regarding the Supreme Brahman situated in both locations.

He rejects this position with the word "no. He states the reason for this as "due to location" (*sthānataḥ*), because a difference in form exists due to the difference in location. He establishes that very difference in form by stating "location" (*sthānam*). For the location of the Blessed One is taught indeed for the purpose of realizing His abiding in those respective locations. In this regard—

He states a counter-argument with the words "if not" (*na cet*). The meaning is that if the location (*sthāna*) is taught as being devoid of purpose, then its form (*rūpa*) would likewise be of that same nature. He concludes the stated point along with its supporting reason with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*); the meaning is that the conclusion is reached precisely through the systematic distinction between these two names.

In the preceding section, a systematic arrangement was established based on the difference in location of the names [of deities]. Here, however, the same principle of difference in location is used to establish the systematic arrangement even for those qualities such as *sambhṛti* (accumulation) and so forth, which are studied outside of specific contexts (*anārabhyādhīta*). This is the connection. The investigation of its meaning is as follows: in the *Khila* texts of the Rāṇāyanīyas, sentences such as "The heroic powers, with Brahman as the eldest, were accumulated" are heard; therein, qualities such as accumulation and pervasion (*dyubhyāpti*) are mentioned. Should these be combined in all meditations (*vidyās*), or only in certain ones?

For that purpose, it is deliberated whether those [qualities] taught as unconnected to any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*) are to be applied to all meditations (*vidyā*), or only to some; and whether their inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*) applies them to all meditations, or only to some. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "The collection [of qualities] and so forth. This means that the multitude of qualities such as "the collection" (*sambhṛti*), mentioned in passages like "Brahman is the eldest" (*brahma jyeṣṭhā*), should be connected to all meditations because they are not recited within a specific context (*prakaraṇa*). The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is stated: "No. The reason for this is stated: "In some cases... (*kvacid*...).

This meaning does not apply everywhere, but only in certain instances; for it has been established that [the inference] occurs only in some cases due to the lack of any other possible explanation (*agatikāt*). The "lack of any other possible explanation" regarding the inferential mark (*liṅga*) means its being not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddhatvam*). That alone is the cause of its strength, because reasons that are otherwise established are weak. He clarifies this very state of being not otherwise established with the word "alpa" (small). The meaning is as follows: in the mantra "Brahma is the eldest," it is said, "Brahmā first stretched out the vast sky," thus expressing Brahmā’s pervasion of the universe.

Furthermore, this quality of pervading the universe (*viśvavyāpitvam*) is not possible in the case of limited sciences (*vidyā*), but rather applies only to the meditations on Brahman through its all-pervasiveness. Therefore, since the qualities such as "pervading the universe" mentioned in this mantra must necessarily reside in their own appropriate locus, the other attributes such as "sustaining" (*saṃbhṛti*) and so forth—which are recited in the same mantra alongside the "pervading the heaven" (*dyuvyāpti*)—are "co-located" (*tatsamasthāninaḥ*); that is, they reside in the very same place where the "pervading the heaven" resides.

The connection [of the present topic] is as follows: it was stated that the *sambhṛti* (accumulation) and other rites, which are recited in proximity to the meditation on the *dyu* (heaven), belong to that single meditation because they enter into its same context; now, it is stated that the *puruṣavidyā* (meditation on the person), which is recited in proximity to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), is a subsidiary part of that knowledge of Brahman. The inquiry into this matter is as follows: in the Taittirīyaka, regarding "for him who thus... [the text continues].

The Puruṣavidyā is taught in the passage beginning with "Of the sacrifice of the wise man," and likewise the Puruṣavidyā is taught in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad as well, in the passage beginning with "Man indeed is the sacrifice. Now, is there identity of the two knowledges (vidyā) in both places, or is there a difference between the knowledges? For that purpose, it is investigated whether or not there is a difference in the form, the fruit, and the connection [to the ritual] in both cases.

Is the attainment of the lifespan mentioned in the *Chāndogya*—namely, "Does he not live for one hundred and sixteen years?"—the fruit in both cases, or is the fruit in the *Taittirīya* Puruṣavidyā the attainment of Brahman? Is the *Taittirīya* Puruṣavidyā a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the previously introduced Brahmavidyā, as indicated by the injunction, "One should yoke the self with 'Om' unto Brahman, the Great," or is it not? Does the reference, "Of him who knows thus," lead one to understand its status as a subordinate part of the Brahmavidyā, or does it not?

Having set forth the prima facie view here, he refutes it with the words "because of the identity of name and so forth. [The opponent argues: "Because of the identity of connection, form, injunction, and name, there is non-difference between the two meditations on the Person. He refutes this very point, saying "it is improper. It is improper to claim that the two meditations on the Person are identical because of the lack of distinction in their connection, form, injunction, and name. He demonstrates this very impropriety with the words "because of the different arrangement of the forms of sacrifice and so forth. Just as there is an arrangement of the forms of sacrifice and so forth in the Taittirīyaka, it is not so in the Chāndogya.

Because a disparity is observed in both cases, there is a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*) due to the difference in their form. Furthermore, in the *Taittirīyaka*, the "Puruṣavidyā" is subordinate to the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, the very fruit previously mentioned as belonging to the knowledge of Brahman is indicated here as its fruit. In the *Chāndogya*, however, the attainment of longevity is stated as the fruit. Thus, since there is a difference in the fruit in both instances, it is not the case that they are identical because of the non-difference in [the syllable] *om* and so forth. Therefore, the meditations are distinct.

Regarding this, someone raises the objection: "The discussion of the *puruṣavidyā* (the knowledge of the Person) should not even be undertaken here, because there is no clear reason for a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To refute that objection, he restates it with the words "clearly" (*sphuṭa*). Since the difference in form and other attributes between the two *puruṣavidyās* is evident, the prima facie argument asserting their identity based merely on the similarity of names arises through sheer force; thus, being extremely weak, it is unworthy of mention, and this section (*adhikaraṇa*) would be entirely useless. He refutes this doubt with the word "no" (*na*).

He states the reason for the rejection [of the previous view] with the word "another" (*anyā*). Indeed, there are two types of knowledge here: the "knowledge of ritual surrender" (*nyāsavidyā*), previously enjoined in the passage, "One should yoke the Self with 'Om' unto the Greatness of Brahman," is one; this, however, is another, namely the "knowledge of the Person" (*puruṣavidyā*) recorded in the passage, "Of him who knows thus," which is subordinate to that former one. Therefore, in order to emphasize the primacy of the knowledge of ritual surrender, the knowledge of the Person, being its subordinate part, is again clarified here.

Furthermore, the Puruṣavidyā found in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad is prescribed for the purpose of attaining longevity; therefore, it is not an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). Since this Puruṣavidyā does not share identity with [the Brahmavidyā], there is no contingency of their being one and the same. This has been clearly stated in its entirety in other treatises, such as the Nyāsa-viṃśati and others, and thus is not elaborated upon here.

Here, by the words "yadi haivam," [the author] demonstrates that the deliberation on the adhikaraṇa (section) conceived by the Commentator is consistent even under both views, having restated the two alternative positions regarding the subject of the Puruṣavidyā as propounded by various partial teachers. In this regard, the position of some is as follows: here, the visualization of the sacrifice (*yajñadṛṣṭi*) is not to be constructed; rather, for the purpose of demonstrating the majesty of one established in the previously mentioned vidyā of the cosmic person (*nyāsavidyā*), the entire collection of ritual acts exists within his very body by way of the sacrificial arrangement.

It is said that this is merely a commendatory statement (praśaṃsāmātra), because it is conceived as occurring in the midst of the Cāturmāsya and other sacrifices which are constituent parts of the ritual. Others, however, think thus: "The Veda is indeed of an unassailable nature; therefore, by virtue of its authority, there exists another such sacrifice, and thus a certain 'human science' (puruṣavidyā) also exists, consisting of the conceptualization thereof."

Since a difference between the two Puruṣavidyās is also established, their identity is not proven. Therefore, in one view, identity is not proven due to the absence of both [Puruṣavidyās], while in another view, identity is not proven due to the difference in their forms and so forth; thus, this section (adhikaraṇa) is appropriately structured for the purpose of refuting their identity. Having all this in mind, he says: "Let it be. In both views, the manner of the section as conceived by the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) remains perfectly consistent.

If one asks, "What then is this ultimate reality (paramārtha)?", let it be stated according to the traditional lineage (sampradāya); for a position not based on tradition is not to be accepted. Thus he says generally, "the tradition," meaning that the former [position] alone is to be adopted because it is consistent with reason.

It has been stated that the Puruṣavidyā is an auxiliary to the Brahmavidyā because it is recited in proximity to the Brahmavidyā; now, however, there arises a connection based on the doubt: might the mantras such as "śanno mitraḥ," which are likewise recited in proximity to the Brahmavidyā, also be auxiliaries to the Brahmavidyā? The inquiry into this matter is as follows: are the mantras studied at the beginning of the Upaniṣads—such as "śukraṃ pravidhya" and "śanno mitraḥ"—as well as rituals like the Pravargya, auxiliaries to the knowledge (vidyā), or not?

Is the application of these [mantras] restricted to ritual acts by means of direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and syntactical connection (*vākya*), or is their application to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) due to the context (*prakaraṇa*)? Is their inclusion in this context for the purpose of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the rite, or rather for the sake of being recited as part of the *divākīrtya* and *āraṇyaka* sections? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "They would be joined. Because mantras such as "May there be peace for us" (*śannaḥ*) are recited in the vicinity of the knowledge of Brahman, and because there is no distinction in their being subordinate to that knowledge, they would be joined as auxiliaries to all forms of knowledge. He refutes this with: "No."

Regarding this, he states the reason: "tadudita" (arising from that). The meaning is as follows: from the indicative mark (*liṅga*), it is understood that [the rites] are subsidiary to those respective actions; from proximity (*sannidhi*), they are subsidiary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). In this regard, it is universally accepted by all that between an indicative mark and proximity, the indicative mark is far more powerful.

In that regard, since the fact that the mantra beginning with "śanno mitraḥ" is a subordinate part of the study [of the Veda] is clearly seen through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "namo brahmaṇe," its status as a subordinate part of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) would have to be inferred by the extremely weak means of proximity (*sannidhi*). Consequently, even for the mantra beginning with "śukraṃ pravīdhya," which is recited in proximity to the knowledge of Brahman, there would likewise be the status of being a subordinate part of the knowledge of Brahman.

This is indeed contradictory; for since an action consisting of the infliction of pain upon others—such as "piercing the vital organ" (śukram) and "piercing the heart" (hṛdayam)—is opposed to the knowledge of Brahman, it is impossible to conceive of it as a subsidiary part of that knowledge. Furthermore, the mere proximity of the text is weaker than an indicative mark (liṅga). Therefore, since it cannot be a subsidiary to the knowledge of Brahman, how could it be appropriate to conceive of it as a subsidiary to all forms of knowledge?

In this context, it has been stated that the mantras such as "piercing the bright [seed]" (*śukraṃ pravidhya*), which are recited in proximity to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), are not auxiliary parts of that knowledge. Likewise, the reflection on the discarding and acquiring [of the senses], being recited in proximity, follows immediately; thus there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, while it was previously stated by means of *liṅga* (indicative power) that the mantras beginning with "piercing the bright" are subsidiary to their respective ritual acts, here, however, because of the *liṅga* of semantic capacity—namely, that the act of acquiring has the act of discarding as its object—it is stated that both [acts] must be kept in mind in both places, due to the rule of mutual connection between the two. Thus there is a logical connection.

Regarding the investigation of that meaning: in some places, the shaking off of good and evil deeds is taught, as in "Shaking off evil like a horse its hairs, and like the moon emerging from the mouth of Rāhu," and "so the knower, having shaken off merit and sin. In other places, the acquisition [of these deeds] is taught, as in "Friends take over his good deeds, and enemies his evil deeds. In yet other places, both are taught, as in "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his beloved kinsmen take over his good deeds, and those not beloved take over his evil deeds. In this regard, what is the case?

Should the contemplation of loss (*hāni*), the contemplation of attainment (*upāyana*), and the contemplation of both be combined or optionally chosen? Is the attainment a subordinate part of knowledge as a supplement to the loss, or is it independent? Is the statement regarding attainment—though studied in another recension (*śākhā*)—a supplement to the statement regarding loss, or is it independent? And does the mention of both by the Kauṣītakins contradict the status of the statement on attainment as a supplement to the statement on loss, or not?

Here, having clarified the subject matter and refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) without relying on the [specific] text, he correctly establishes the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) through both means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and logic, stating: "There are two branches. This is the syntactical connection of the words here: two branches describe the relinquishment of merit and demerit for a person destined for liberation at some point; another branch, moreover, speaks of the entry of merit and demerit into the beloved and its opposite at the time of the transfer of the wife. The meaning is that it declares the transfer of merit and demerit between the beloved and the unbeloved.

In some places, both the discarding (*hāna*) and the taking up (*upāyana*) are taught together; thus, it is established that in other cases where these two are recorded separately, their conjunction is proven by the scope of valid means of knowledge supported by logic. Anticipating the objection—“How can there be a mutual connection between sentences located in different recensions (*śākhā*) that are not present [together]?”—the author reminds us here of the previously mentioned principle of "cognition based on all recensions" (*sarvaśākhāpratyaya-nyāya*). This is what the sentence [means].

The opponent previously asserted that the abandonment [of karma] and its acquisition [through knowledge] were optional; this has been refuted by means of both authoritative testimony (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*). Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that those two are not optional, nevertheless, there may still be optionality regarding the contemplation (*cintana*) of them. Anticipating this, he says "ittham" (thus) to show that even this is not so. This is the meaning of the words here: "It may well be that the knowledge of Brahman, the abandonment of ritual action, and the relinquishing of action are thus inseparably connected with the cessation of the pleasant and the unpleasant. However, let there be only a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) or an option (*vikalpa*) regarding their contemplation. Why?

To this he replies: "Because they are not recited separately. He refutes that by saying "no," meaning that although a uniform conception might be possible everywhere, it is improper to conceive of things with a diversity of forms when they could be conceived uniformly. He expresses this by saying "because of the difficulty of such a conception. He clarifies the impropriety of conceiving a diversity by saying "of all": for all those who partake in liberation, both the abandonment and the attainment—both together—are equally to be accomplished according to their respective meditations.

Thus, it has been stated that there is indeed the relinquishing (*hāna*) and the taking over (*upāyana*) of merit and demerit. Similarly, just as the contemplation of relinquishing and taking over must be performed by the qualified worshipper who knows the majesty of the knower of Brahman, so too must the contemplation regarding both relinquishing and taking over be accepted. This is because, according to the rule that "the attainment of the fruit follows the mode of meditation," the attainment of the fruit in the form of relinquishing and taking over would be impossible in the absence of such contemplation. Indeed, in the world, everyone considers that the attainment of the desired or undesired fruit is itself the result of the contemplation of the desired or undesired.

Therefore, since the knowledge of Brahman is the fruit of both the means of removal (*hāna*) and the means of attainment (*upāya*), the conclusion is that one must indeed contemplate the fruit during the stage of meditation (*upāsanā*). For the contemplation of the fruit during the stage of meditation is heard in the scriptures: "May I attain the world of Brahman," "Having departed from here, I shall attain Him," and so forth. Furthermore, it is well known that for those who know Brahman, the removal of obstacles to devotion to Viṣṇu—such as the prayer, "May Viṣṇu be victorious, not the Asura"—is itself the very fruit to be prayed for.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that here the transference of merit and demerit (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) between the beloved and the unbeloved is taught? This is indeed contradictory, for an action performed by one does not transfer to another, nor does the fruit of one's action arise elsewhere, as that would entail the fallacies of 'attaining what was not done' (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and 'the loss of what was done' (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). Therefore, this which you have stated is contradictory. Thus the objector raises the doubt. The syntactical connection (*śabdānvaya*) here is as follows: it has been established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that the fruit of an action must be experienced by the very same agent who performs that action.

For it is observed that "the fruit of the action belongs to the performer. Therefore, it is not tenable that the karma of one who knows Brahman should transfer to a friend or an enemy. He rejects this [objection] with the words, "This is improper. Regarding the phrase "by the greatness of knowledge," the meaning is as follows: we do not say that there is a transference of merit and demerit residing in the knower of Brahman to a friend or an enemy, nor do we say that the pleasant and unpleasant fruits are produced in a friend or an enemy; rather, it is said that the very fruit of one's own actions accrues even to friends and enemies.

For both he who shows affection toward one who knows Brahman and he who bears malice toward him—since the good and evil deeds performed by each of them respectively become fruitless—the result of their own actions alone is what is spoken of here.

If that is so, how can there be a statement regarding the transfer of the fruit of karma when one experiences the fruit of one's own karma? Listen with an attentive mind: since it is impossible for the karma of one person to transfer to another, and impossible for the fruit of one person's karma to be produced in another, there is neither a transfer of karma nor a transfer of the production of its fruit; rather, what is being stated is merely the equality of the measure of the fruits of those respective karmas.

The Blessed One, who is supremely compassionate, has stated that as long as the fruit of merit is not given to those who know the inner self, so long is that fruit of merit given to those who are hostile toward the knowers of the inner self, by way of the fruit of their own contrary actions; and as long as the fruit of evil is not given to those who know the inner self, so long is that fruit of evil given to those who are hostile to the knowers of the inner self, by way of the fruit of their own contrary actions. Therefore, what is expressed here is merely a demonstration of the measure of the fruit being given to those who are favorable or unfavorable to the knowers of the inner self; it does not mean, however, that there is a transference of one's karma to another. Thus, everything is fully resolved.

In the *Bhāṣya*, regarding the section on "Conjunction" (*saṅgati*), it is stated: "The abandonment and the taking up of good and evil deeds (*sukṛta-duṣkṛta*) must be considered in all meditations (*vidyā*). Concerning the doubt as to whether that abandonment occurs at the time of separation from the body and during the journey after the soul has departed from the body, or only at the time of separation from the body—the investigation into its meaning is as follows: Does the abandonment of good and evil deeds occur both at the time of separation from the body and during the journey, or only at the time of separation from the body? Is there scriptural mention of abandonment in both cases, or only at the time of separation from the body?

Does the phrase "he shakes off his good and evil deeds," which is heard last in the sequence beginning with "Having entered this path of the gods, he goes to the world of fire," connect syntactically with what precedes it—"he comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it with his mind"—or does it connect according to its position in the text?

Is it more reasonable to describe the prior connection [of the soul] in accordance with the scriptural hearing that "pleasure and pain do not touch one who is indeed bodiless" (*aśarīram vāva santam na priyāpriye spṛśataḥ*), such that there is no experience of pleasure or pain for the bodiless state; or is it more reasonable to describe the connection according to the literal text in order to maintain the existence of a subtle body, in accordance with the scriptural hearing of the journey by the path of the gods (*devayāna*)? Here, the description [in accordance with the literal text] is more reasonable.

On this point, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) maintains that the Tāṇḍins indeed study the shaking off of good and evil deeds at the time of separation from the body, in passages such as, "Like a horse shaking its hair... The Kauṣītakins, however, state: "He comes to the river Virajā; he crosses it with his mind; there he shakes off his good and evil deeds. Thus, the shaking off of good and evil deeds occurs after crossing the Virajā. This reflection must also be performed by the knower of Brahman; let it be so in that respect as well. He states this [in the verse]: "The shaking off of karma."
