As for the connection with scriptural texts (*śabdānvaya*), in one Upaniṣad the shaking off of karma by the seeker of liberation at the time of separation from the body is heard, while in another Upaniṣad it is heard on the path; therefore, both are authoritative. [The opponent suggests: "Let it be thus in two separate parts—let there be the thought that for some karmas there is shaking off at the time of separation from the body, and for others on the path. This he refutes with "let it not be so. He explains that very point with "for not... (na hi).

If any fruit were declared for the path (*mārga*), then it could be said that there remains a residue of karma for the sake of that fruit; however, since there is no fruit to be experienced on the path, the meaning is that all karma, together with its fruit, perishes in the next world (*sāmparāya*). Now, one might object: if all karma were to perish at the conclusion of the body, then there would be no journey at all by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*); consequently, the effort of those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*) would be entirely purposeless.

Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the word "atha" (now). [The opponent asks: "If the knowledge of Brahman alone were to effect the persistence of the body for the sake of reaching [the goal], then, since the two means of knowledge would possess equal force, how can there be the restriction that [liberation] occurs only at the end of the body? Anticipating this, [the author] explains the meaning by setting aside the destruction of karma on the path—which is obtained through the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*)—in favor of the destruction of karma at the end of the body, which is obtained through the order of meaning (*arthakrama*), because the order of meaning is more powerful than the order of recitation. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

It might be argued as follows: if the entire karma of the knower were to perish right here, then the statement, "For him, the delay is only so long," would find its finality merely at the end of the gross body. And in that case, he would become liberated at that very moment. This being so, the purposefulness of the journey via the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) would not exist. Nor can it be said that the journey via the path of light does not exist.

"Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form. Since liberation is thus recorded as occurring immediately after reaching the Supreme Person by traveling via the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), a certain doubt arises: "How then can there be the total destruction of all karma at the conclusion of the gross body? This [doubt] is restated in the words "without remainder" (*niśśeṣam*). He refutes the aforementioned doubt with the word "inappropriate" (*ayuktam*). He establishes that very inappropriateness with the word "it would be" (*syāt*).

The meaning is this: although the entire collection of karma, which is the cause for attaining results such as pleasure and pain, comes to rest at the end of the body, nevertheless, until the attainment of one's own true nature upon reaching the supreme light, a residue of subtle karma persists; this residue is the cause solely for the contraction of knowledge. If it is asked how this is so, it is because of the authority of the scriptural text: "Having reached the supreme light, he appears in his own form."

Indeed, it cannot be asserted that for a person possessing innate knowledge, there is a contraction of knowledge for such a duration without any cause; nor is there any other cause for this except the Lord’s restraint (*nigraha*). Therefore, since it is directly stated in the Śruti that the perfection of *oṅkāra*—which consists of the experience of uncontracted Brahman—belongs only to one who has attained the Lord, it is established that the cessation of the Lord’s restraint occurs only through a gradual process.

In the preceding section, it was proposed that the destruction of all gross karma occurs precisely at the conclusion of the gross body upon entering the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), and that the manifestation in one's own true form belongs only to one who has reached the Supreme Light while retaining a residue of subtle impressions (*saṃskāra*). Now, the connection [of the present discussion] is as follows: it is considered whether this path under discussion—the path beginning with light—belongs only to one established in that specific knowledge in which it is studied, or rather to one established in all forms of knowledge.

The investigation into that matter is as follows: Does the path beginning with light pertain only to those established in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), or to all who are established in [Vedic] knowledge? For that purpose, it is examined whether the injunction regarding the path beginning with light is heard in the context of the *pañcāgnividyā*—in the passages, "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and truth, they pass into the light"—and "Those who know this thus, and those who in the forest worship faith and austerity, they pass into the light"—thereby referring to others as well, or not.

"Intending only those who have reached the culmination of the knowledge of the five fires"—does this mean that there is the practice of another form of meditation here by means of the presentation of the Brahman to be meditated upon through the words *śraddhā* (faith), *satya* (truth), and *tapas* (penance), or not? Does the reference to the path in the Upakośala-vidyā—namely, "But the teacher will tell you the way"—strengthen the understanding of another form of meditation, or not? Having set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) preceded by such a doubt, he reveals the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) as well with the words "The path."

First, he shows the nature of doubt as stated in the Bhāṣya. For this is the statement of the Bhāṣya: "In those meditations on Upakośala and others where the journey via the path beginning with light (arcirādi) is heard, is the attainment of Brahman by those devoted to them [achieved] through that [path] alone?"

"Or rather, for all those who are devoted to the meditation on Brahman. Here, by the words "beginning with" (*prārabhya*) and so forth, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The meaning is this: starting from specific meditations such as that of Upakośala, wherever the path of light (*arcir-ādi*) is prescribed, there alone should the journey via light and so forth occur; accordingly, the contemplation of that [path] should also be performed only there, and not elsewhere. He rejects this with the word "no" (*na*). He explains that very point with the words "of all" (*sarvāsām*).

The meaning is this: in the Pañcāgni-vidyā (the knowledge of the five fires), after referring to those established in the Pañcāgni-vidyā with the words "those who know thus," and then referring to those established in other forms of knowledge with the words "and those who [meditate] here in the forest," the path beginning with light (*arcis*) is prescribed. Therefore, the path beginning with light is indeed common to all forms of knowledge as their fruit. Consequently, since reflection on the fruit is necessarily required for those established in the knowledge of Brahman, reflection on the path beginning with light must likewise be common to all, just like the path itself.

For those who are intent upon the means, meditation is not possible without the pursuit of the fruit; therefore, it was previously stated by us as well that the thought, "May I attain the world of Brahman," must necessarily be cultivated.

He further establishes the necessity of contemplating the paths (*gaticintanādi*) by referring to the words of the Blessed One in the verse beginning with *heyopādeya*. This is the meaning: the path to be abandoned is the path of smoke (*dhūmādimārga*), while the path to be adopted is the path of light (*arcirādimārga*). By teaching both paths, the Blessed One—the giver of liberation—declared the necessity of contemplating the paths in the verse: "Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogi whatsoever is deluded."

Therefore, from this reflection upon the words of the Blessed One, which clarifies the meaning that was not yet clear in these ten chapters, there arises a *praṇihita*—that is, a *praṇidhāna* (earnest application) directed toward the entire subject matter conducive to the attainment of Brahman; *niṣṭhā* (the state of completion) is used here in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāve*). This is the conclusion reached here, and it is not merely [a conclusion] regarding this [section].

The method for contemplating the path is now stated: moreover, whatever is found here to be authoritative as being conducive to the attainment of Brahman, all of that must be contemplated. Since everything—from the exhaustion of all karma at the end of the body, to the transition through the pleasant and unpleasant, to the crossing of the Virajā river on the path beginning with the *arciḥ*—is a result, it must all be contemplated during the stage of the means (*upāya*).

Here, having raised the objection that the discussion of the abandonment [of defects] and the attainment [of qualities] by the authors of the Sūtras is not relevant to this section (pāda), he refutes it with the words "hānādeḥ" (of abandonment, etc.). The intention of the opponent here is as follows: the contemplation of abandonment, attainment, and so forth is indeed an auxiliary (aṅga) to knowledge; and as an auxiliary, it ought to be discussed later in the section on the auxiliaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga-pāda). Since this present section is devoted to the description of the essential nature of knowledge, how then can there be a connection here?

Why has the deliberation by the authors of the Sūtras regarding the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) and so forth, as well as the path of descent (*hāna*), been stated here? If it is for the sake of establishing their status as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), then let that discussion occur in the immediately following section on the auxiliaries of knowledge (*vidyāṅga-pāda*), not here. He rejects this doubt, saying "not so. For the Sūtra concerning the deliberation on the path (*gati-cintana*) and so forth certainly belongs to this very place. Why? To this he says: "In [the context of] being an auxiliary element of knowledge (*vidyāṅgatāyām*)."

Although the reflection on the path and so forth are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*), they are nevertheless like ritual service (*bhajana*) which serves as a means, or like meditation (*upāsana*) which is an auxiliary part of worship; and in order to state that this reflection on the path and so forth is also distinct from ritual action (*karman*) and the rest, it is formulated here [in the Sūtra]—this is the connection with the word "sthānapātin" (occurring in its proper place).

The meaning here is as follows: among the auxiliary parts of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*), some consist of cognition (*jñāna*) and some consist of action (*kriyā*). The contemplation of those consisting of cognition, such as the reflection on the goal (*gati*), is presented here for the purpose of demonstrating their equality with the primary knowledge itself; whereas the other parts, which consist of ritual action, are contemplated extensively in the section on the auxiliaries of knowledge (*vidyāṅgapāda*). Thus, there is no room for the suspicion that the contemplation of the goal and so forth is misplaced, as it is mentioned in its proper place.

In the previous [section], because it was heard that the meditation on the rays and so forth is common to all branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), it was established that such meditation is also logically applicable to all branches of knowledge by virtue of its being common to them. Now, however, the question is considered as to whether the meditations on the syllables (*akṣaradhiyaḥ*) are common to all branches of knowledge or not; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, the connection is that just as in the previous section the context (*prakaraṇa*) was the reason for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), so it is here as well.

Regarding the investigation of that meaning: in the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, it is stated, "O Gārgī, the Brāhmaṇas indeed declare this Imperishable (akṣara) to be neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," and so forth. Here, the question is whether these qualities such as non-grossness and the rest are to be subsumed only in that specific context, or in all meditations (vidyās). To that end, it is investigated: is it only the negative attributes such as non-grossness that define the nature of Brahman by virtue of being its unique characteristics, or is it rather [attributes] such as pure consciousness and bliss alone?

Is there a cognition of the exclusion of all suspected defects without [the qualities of] non-coarseness and so forth, or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) thinks: "Surely, in certain passages such as the Gārgī-brāhmaṇa, only qualities like 'imperishability' (akṣaratva) are recorded; however, in whatever meditation (vidyā) a specific collection of qualities is recorded, only that much should be combined there, because it is recited within that particular context."

Otherwise, since everything would have to be applied everywhere, there would be a confusion of attributes among the *sadvidyā* and other meditations; however, it has already been stated that the realization of the nature of Brahman occurs through [attributes] such as bliss (*ānanda*) alone. Therefore, what is the use of this attribute of imperishability (*akṣaratva*) and so forth—which is like a nipple on a goat’s neck—in the realization of the nature of Brahman? He restates this with the words "in which" (*yasyām*). He states that it is not to be applied elsewhere with the words "not in another" (*nānyasyām*). He provides the reason for this with the words "because of the loss of authority" (*mānahāneḥ*).

The meaning is that there should be a synthesis of every single attribute in every instance. Having thus restated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with "No. He clearly demonstrates the manner of rejecting the prima facie view with the words "as the cause," and so forth. The intention here is as follows: it is not merely the attributes of Brahman that are stated here; rather, it is a specific attribute which serves as the means for realizing His essential nature by removing the defects suspected in [His being] the Cause. That [attribute] is, moreover, stainlessness (*amalatva*), along with truthfulness (*satyatva*) and the others.

For instance, "truth" (satyatva) excludes insentient matter which is subject to modification; "knowledge" (jñānatva) excludes the individual soul (jīva), which is devoid of consciousness when in a state of bondage; "infinity" (anantatva) excludes the liberated soul, which possesses a prior limit; and "bliss" (ānandatva) excludes the Lord as conceived by opposing disputants, who is held to be devoid of bliss. Thus, by means of "purity" (amalatva), the eternal [nature] is distinguished from all else.

Although the term "infinite" (ananta) itself excludes the atomic nature and eternality [of the soul], nevertheless, because infinity exists in it in some sense by virtue of its attribute-knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna), space, and time, it can be described as infinite in that manner. However, purity (amalatva) is indeed the differentiator for all [souls]. Although eternal, because it is a dependent consciousness, it possesses the capacity for transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) in its essential nature; yet, solely due to the absence of the auxiliary capacity consisting of the Lord's displeasure, it remains eternally non-transmigrating.

The Lord (Īśvara), however, because he is an independent consciousness, is devoid of the natural fitness for transmigratory existence (saṃsāra). Therefore, this very purity (amalattva) is unique to the Lord alone. Furthermore, the power to bring about the cessation of the transmigration of others is unique to the Lord, and that is indeed purity itself. Thus, because He is Himself free from impurity and because He is the adversary of the impurities of others, the Lord alone is called "pure. If it is then objected: "Let there be only purity; what is the use of [the other attributes] such as reality (satyatva) and so forth?", the author says "hetutve" (in the state of being the cause) to show that such an objection does not apply here.

Indeed, the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is stated in two ways: one view holds that the exclusion of the entire class of non-definable objects (*alakṣya*) is accomplished by a single qualifier alone; the other, however, maintains that the nature of the definable object (*lakṣya*) is determined through the exclusion of non-definable objects by means of various qualifiers, following a sequence of mental comprehension, such that one arrives at the realization "this is it. This is the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. The meaning of the words here is as follows: defects residing in other things are suspected on account of their being causes [of error]; the removal of these is effected by the terms "Being" (*satya*), "Knowledge" (*jñāna*), "Infinite" (*ananta*), "Bliss" (*ānanda*), and "Pure" (*amala*).

By that means, there occurs a gradual realization of the removal of defects. To facilitate this realization, he provides an illustration regarding the comprehension of specific meanings through a sequential order, beginning with the word "Ānanda. In the section concerning the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss), the *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya* selves are realized as being progressively superior in successive order. In the same way, here too, the Blessed Lord is established as being supreme above all through this sequential progression.

Thus, the objection—"Since the Lord's preeminence over all is established by His being stainless from the very outset, what is the purpose of these qualifiers such as 'truthfulness' and so forth?"—is already answered; for this principle of sequential understanding is universal, meaning it is well-known throughout the entire world.

Here someone objects: "The comprehension of the essential nature [of Brahman] has already been stated through qualities such as truthfulness (*satyatva*) and so forth, as being accompanied by all forms of ignorance; therefore, this present section would be entirely redundant regarding other attributes such as imperishability (*akṣaratva*) that possess similar characteristics. He restates this objection with the words "by truthfulness and so forth. He refutes the unspoken point with the word "no" (*na*). He explains the very manner of the refutation with the words "by some" (*kaiścit*).

According to the principle that "when a certain form has been apprehended in some instance, something else similar to it is negated," once the nature of an entity is understood and established through various qualifiers, the comprehension of its exclusion (vyāvṛtti) occurs only subsequently. Thus, some maintain that [the concept of] exclusion does not assist in the comprehension of the entity's own nature; this is the "unperceived" (anadhyakṣita) principle. The meaning is that this section is indeed fruitful for the purpose of refuting that view.

The point here is this: in the world, in cases such as "a quality is that which, while being distinct from action, is the locus of mere genus," the apprehension of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is also useful for the apprehension of the specific nature of the quality and so forth. Similarly, in this case as well, the apprehension of exclusion is useful for the apprehension of the nature of Brahman.

In that case, what is the meaning of the statement: "When a certain form has been apprehended in some respect, something else is negated"? There is no fault whatsoever, for when an entity is established in any manner, another mode consisting of the exclusion of others (*itaravyāvṛtti*) is also cognized. This is the meaning: after an entity has first been understood in some way through a positive form (*vidhi*), the operation of negation (*niṣedha*) subsequently occurs; it does not, however, occur with regard to that which is absolutely unapprehended.

On this point, someone says: "Since the things to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) are infinite, their exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) must also be infinite. Furthermore, if that [exclusion] is infinite, its indicator (*vyāvartaka*) must likewise be said to be infinite. And in that case, it simply cannot be performed. For no one instructs others on the crossing of the ocean if it is impossible. Otherwise, if an impossible injunction were given, it would follow that the sentence lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*), characterized by its non-implementation. He restates this [objection] with the words "vyāvartya... and so forth.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: because the things to be excluded are infinite, the exclusion itself would also be infinite; therefore, the investigation of that—that is, the investigation of exclusion—would not be taught as something achievable by one of limited knowledge.

Regarding that which is impossible to teach, he provides an illustration: "like crossing the ocean. He refutes this with the words, "not so. He demonstrates the manner of this refutation with the words, "that and that. Just as in the world, by employing general properties such as substantiality (*dravyatva*), quality-ness (*guṇatva*), and action-ness (*karmatva*), there is an exclusion of even infinite individual instances, so too here, by employing general properties, there would be an exclusion of the properties to be refuted.

Alternatively, [the author] says "anavama" (not inferior), meaning that the exclusion of all other phenomena will be accomplished by a single qualification alone. The meaning is: let the inclusion—that is, the collective grasping and acceptance—of all those other inferior things which are to be rejected be understood through this single qualification, "Brahman is not inferior."

If being the opposite of that which is to be abandoned were the unique characteristic of Brahman, then Brahman would be characterized by the transcendence of hunger and so forth; however, if it were characterized by being the vitalizer and so forth, it would be the individual soul (jīva). This is the connection [of the doubt]. The inquiry into its meaning is based on the questions of Uṣasta and Kahola: "Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all," and "Explain to me that very Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all."

The counter-argument is as follows: In one place, the reply is, "He who breathes with the vital breath (prāṇa), that is your Self, the innermost of all"; and in another place, it is, "He who [transcends] hunger and thirst, grief and delusion," and so forth. Is there identity of the meditation (vidyaikya) in both cases, or is there a difference of meditations? Is the individual soul (jīva) the object of worship in the former case and the Supreme (para) in the latter, or is it the Supreme alone in both cases? Furthermore, in that context, is the one referred to in the passage, "He who breathes with the vital breath, that is your Self, the innermost of all," etc., conditioned by limiting adjuncts (aupādhika), or is it the unconditioned (nirupādhika)?

Upon reflecting on the sequence of questions and answers, such as "Do you not see the Seer of seeing? Do you not think the Thinker of thinking? and the subsequent realizations, "He who is within the Self" and "Who indeed could breathe?", it is understood whether or not Brahman’s being the innermost of all and its status as the agent of animation are established without limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Alternatively, does the meaning of the sentence "Do you not see the Seer of seeing" (*na hi draṣṭurdṛṣṭeḥ*) imply that one should not conceive of Brahman as the Seer by means of the instrument of seeing (*dṛṣṭi*), or rather, that one should not conceive of the Seer of experience (*dṛṣṭi* = *anubhūti*)?

In this commentary, two positions are set forth. In one position, having raised the doubt that [the passages] in certain instances refer to the individual soul (jīva), it is determined that they all refer to the Supreme Self (paramātman). In the other, although both [passages] refer to the Supreme Self, it is argued that in the former case, because different qualities are accepted, the subject is Brahman characterized by a different form; whereas in the latter case, because of the connection with qualities exclusive to the Supreme Self—such as being beyond hunger and so forth—the subject is the Supreme Self characterized by a different form. Having raised these doubts, [it is concluded that] in both cases...

It is determined that because there is no difference in form, the reference is to the Supreme Self which is of a single form. Here, [the author] shows the reason for both alternatives and the discrepancy between them by means of the Sūtra. In the former alternative, the reason is the attainment of the natural sense of the Sūtra, because the individual soul (jīva) is seen in the phrase "like the aggregate of beings. In the latter, however, the cause is the attainment of the natural sense of the Śruti, because in both questions the nature of Brahman is seen to be questioned in the words "Brahman, which is immediate and direct."

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: because it accords with the natural sense of the Sūtra, first the "possessor of breath" (asubhṛt), i.e., the individual soul (jīva), is introduced in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa); however, in the final conclusion (siddhānta), Brahman is introduced. This is for the purpose of removing the suspicion regarding the child (toka-śaṅkāpanuttyai), meaning for the sake of dispelling the doubts of the ignorant. Then, for the purpose of removing the suspicion regarding the child, he restates the subsequent alternative interpretation as well, beginning with the word "directly" (sākṣāt).

Considering that for those learned persons who reflect upon the two interrogative statements permeated by the word "Brahman"— namely, "That Brahman which is immediate and direct"— no further doubt could possibly arise, [the author], finding dissatisfaction with the previous [interpretation], has formulated a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) in the subsequent commentary (bhāṣya) regarding the Supreme Self.

Here, for the sake of the students' easy comprehension, he clearly elucidates his own intended formulation of the final position (uttarapakṣa) by means of the distinction between the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta), beginning with the words "That which directly... (yatsākṣāt).

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: in the sentence "that which is immediate" (*yatsākṣāt*) and in the sentence "that which is indeed immediate" (*yadeva sākṣāt*), let the Supreme Brahman alone be the object of knowledge. Nevertheless, the difference in the answers differentiates the form; and from this difference in form, a difference in the meditation (*vidyā*) is established. He says "difference of meditations" (*vidyābhid*) to show that a difference in meditations is established not only from the difference in form, but also from the difference in the questioners. The meaning is that the difference in the questioners also differentiates the meditation.

In one place Uṣasta is the questioner, and in another Kahola; the word "yadi" (if) indicates the restatement of the prima facie view. He rejects this with "no" (na). He states the reason for that: "having restated" (anūdya). The meaning is: because, having restated with emphasis the very Brahman previously heard in the words "That which is directly and immediately perceived as Brahman," Uṣasta again puts forth a question regarding that same Brahman. Then, raising the objection that the state of being beyond hunger and so forth mentioned later must differentiate the knowledge, he says "mentioned later" (paścādukta) to show that even that does not differentiate it.

The meaning is this: the state of being beyond hunger and so forth, which was mentioned later, is indeed included within the state of stainlessness (amalatva) discussed in the preceding section. And that stainlessness, because it is common to all meditations (vidyās), does not differentiate the meditation. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is common to both questioners, as they were together in their studentship (sabrahmacarya). Thus, since the unity of the meditation is established, the point is that the difference between the questioners does not differentiate the meditation, for the sake of clear understanding.

Now, it might be argued: "In the Bhāṣya, commonality was established by means of the example of the Sadvidyā; we accept that there is identity of the questioner in that case, and therefore let there indeed be commonality for all the answers as well. But here, since there is a difference of questioners, how can there be commonality of the answer? To clarify this very point for some objector who does not understand [the matter], [the author] states: "In the Sadvidyā... and so forth.

This is the point here: let it be granted that in the *sadvidyā* there is identity of the questioner, and let it be granted that in this [present case] there is a difference of questioners; nevertheless, the commonality of the answer must certainly be accepted. For in the world, when two disciples have approached a single teacher and asked about the same matter, the two points explained by him—each addressed individually—are both understood, adopted, and kept in mind by both. Likewise here, the answer given in both places is indeed common to both.

If it is asked what the reason for this is, it is simply their shared life as religious students (*sabrahmacarya*). Indeed, both arrived together and both received the answer; this is in accordance with worldly observation.

This is the syntactical connection of the words here: when it is established through an examination of the introduction, conclusion, and other criteria that these are indeed injunctions, then—just as in the *Sadvidyā* a difference in the answers reveals the Supreme Deity as the specific object to be meditated upon in accordance with the difference in the questions—by that same principle, one should meditate by synthesizing what was heard by Uṣasta and Kahola, and what was heard by Kahola and Uṣasta, [realizing] that the Brahman which is within all is the very same.

Now, it might be argued that in the *Sadvidyā* (the knowledge of the True), there is the specific qualification "one questioner," and therefore let there be identity of the knowledge (*vidyaikyam*) there. If so, then here too there is a specific qualification; for [the text] says, "Furthermore, together with his fellow-student" (*sabrahmacaryam*), which is like a fruit-bearing result. Just as in the world, when many fellow-students are listening to the study of a scripture, the instruction is common to all, intended to resolve the individual doubts of each listener, so too it is said here that Uṣasta and Kahola, having combined what they had heard, both should meditate upon Brahman as the innermost of all. Thus, it is stated that both of them together should contemplate the Brahman that is within everything.

The unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) was established on the grounds that the attributes of being the "breather" (*prāṇitṛtva*) and so forth, as well as the states of being beyond hunger and thirst (*aśanāyādyatītatva*), reside in a single substratum (*dharmin*). Here, however, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises from the suspicion that there is a difference in the substrata for the eight qualities beginning with freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and the qualities beginning with mastery (*vaśitva*); such is the connection (*saṅgati*).

The investigation into that matter concerns the following: In the *Chāndogya*’s Dahara-vidyā, "Now, that which is within this [city]," the object of meditation is Brahman characterized by freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth; whereas in the *Vājasaneyaka*, it is characterized by mastery (*vaśitva*) and so forth. Thus, the question arises whether, in both cases, it is characterized by freedom from sin and the rest, or not. To that end, it is investigated whether, in the *Vājasaneyaka*, there is an understanding of freedom from sin and the other qualities—occurring in association with truthfulness of resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*)—by way of specific subordinate attributes such as having the heart as its abode (*hṛdayāyatanatva*) and mastery (*vaśitva*), or not.

In this regard, the consideration of whether there is a difference or non-difference between the two vidyās in the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka passages has been clearly stated in the Bhāṣya; however, the passage of the Tāṇḍins was not cited. Nevertheless, having restated that even that passage of theirs has as its object Brahman as established by reasoning, [the author] now clarifies—by removing every doubt—the method set forth in the Bhāṣya for demonstrating that the Chāndogya and Vājasaneyaka passages constitute a single vidyā, beginning with the words "ākāśam."

The meaning of the sentence here is as follows: Some raise the objection that the *Tāṇḍins* teach that space (*ākāśa*) is the object of meditation, whereas the *Vājasaneyins* teach a person (*puruṣa*) reclining in space; therefore, the meditative knowledge (*vidyā*) must differ in the *Tāṇḍin* passage and the *Vājasaneyaka* passage. He refutes this with the word "no" (*na*). He states the reason for this: "because it is determined that both kinds of instruction are instructions regarding Brahman. Since both types of description are established as being instructions on Brahman, it is proven that there is no difference in the meditative knowledge between the *Tāṇḍin* and *Vājasaneyaka* passages.

Henceforth, however, following the sequence of the Bhāṣya, an investigation into the difference between the passages from the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka is continued. Based on the Lord’s unique attributes, beginning with being the substratum of all, it is established that the word *ākāśa* in the Sāma-veda chant—"The small *ākāśa* within this [heart]"—refers to the Supreme Self.

In the Vājasaneyaka, however, it is said: "He who lies within this space (ākāśa) in the heart—[he who is] the controller of all, the lord of all. Because of this statement that the Blessed One, endowed with qualities such as sovereignty, lies within the space, the word *ākāśa* here denotes the cavity that serves as the substratum for the Supreme Self. Having raised the objection regarding a difference in form between these two meditations, [the author] refutes it by stating: "But the form..."

"It is not different. In both the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, it is stated that the Supreme Person alone, characterized by qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), is to be meditated upon; thus, since there is no difference in form, there is no difference in the meditation (*vidyā*). This has been explained in detail in the Bhāṣya itself.

Having explained the method for establishing the absence of contradiction between the statements of the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka, and having thereby established the absence of contradiction between the statements of the Tāṇḍi and the Vājasaneyaka in that very same manner, he declares that the statement concerning the "small [ether]" (dahara) as spoken in the Taittirīyaka must likewise be explained by this same method.

Regarding the phrase "of the Chāndogyas": this is the meaning. For the Chāndogyas, the Brahman to be meditated upon is well known as being endowed with the eight qualities beginning with "freedom from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*). That same Brahman is described in the text of others, the Vājasaneyins, as possessing qualities such as "lordship" (*vaśitva*) and so forth; thus, let there be a difference in form. Therefore, let there be a difference in the meditations (*vidyā*); such is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*). He refutes this, saying, "Not so. He explains the manner of refutation by saying, "That which... That collection of qualities beginning with lordship is indeed non-different from the quality of "truthful resolve" (*satyasaṅkalpatā*). For lordship...

"Abiding in one's own control," or "causing others to abide in one's own control"—this is the etymological derivation. This is simply another way of expressing the state of having one's will fulfilled as reality (*satyakāmatva*). Thus he says: "That here is the distinction. This means that the identity of meaning is established; that is, the identity of meaning between the two passages from the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka is firmly established. In this way, the pair of passages from the Tāṇḍin and the Vājasaneyaka has been determined.

Likewise, the passage concerning the "small [space]" (*dahara*) found in the Taittirīyaka should also be investigated in the same manner as the passages from the Chāndogya and the Vājasaneyaka. This is the meaning.

One might object: "Has not the passage concerning the 'small' (dahara) already been examined previously in the Daharādhikaraṇa? Why, then, is it introduced here? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it by stating that there is no redundancy due to a specific purpose. Someone might argue: "It was already stated in the Daharādhikaraṇa that the small ether is the Supreme Self, the Highest Person, on the basis of its unique attributes and so forth; therefore, there is no possibility of suspecting it to be anything other than the Supreme Self, and thus this present section need not be undertaken. He rejects that view, saying "No."

He establishes the absence of redundancy with the words "transcending space" (*vyomātīta*). This is the meaning: the *Daharādhikaraṇa* was previously undertaken for the purpose of refuting those who maintain that [the Self] transcends space; those who claim that the subtle ether (*daharākāśa*) is the Supreme Person as the material cause, and that there exists some further instrumental reality beyond it, were already rejected therein. Therefore, while the *Daharādhikaraṇa* primarily focuses on that refutation, this present section primarily concerns the investigation into whether the meditations (*vidyā*) are distinct or identical. Thus, [there is no redundancy].

There is no tautology because the purposes differ; for although those who maintain that [reality] transcends space were previously refuted, they are here rendered rootless by way of a consequential argument (*prasaṅga*).

In the preceding section, it was stated that qualities such as having true desires (*satyakāmatva*) and having true resolves (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) are to be combined [in meditation]. The connection [of the present section] arises from the objection that, in the same way, meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth should also necessarily be combined. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: regarding meditations on the *udgītha* and other elements based on the subsidiaries of ritual action—such as "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the *udgītha*"—are they to be undertaken in rituals as a rule, or without a rule?

For that purpose, it is investigated: are these [meditations] auxiliary to the sacrifice by way of being parts of the *udgītha* and so forth, or are they for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), like the *godohana* vessel and other such things? Does the observation of non-restriction in the passage, "By this both perform [the rite], he who knows this thus and he who does not know," indicate their status as being for the sake of the person, like the *godohana*, or not?

Regarding the statement, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful," is this a *phalārthavāda* (an explanatory praise of the result) like the hearing of the *apāpaśloka*, or is it an injunction for a result (*phalavidhi*)? In this regard, according to the principle stated in the *Parṇamayī-adhikaraṇa*—"for whom the *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa*-wood"—the worship performed toward the *udgītha* and other such auxiliary parts of the ritual would become an integral part of the action (*karmāṅga*).

Even in the *Parṇamayī-Adhikaraṇa*, it was established that qualities such as being made of *parṇa*-wood are auxiliary to the sacrifice precisely by way of the *juhū* ladle and so forth, which have an inseparable connection with the sacrifice. In that context, just as the hearing of the "fame of sinlessness" and so forth is merely an arthavāda (laudatory statement) regarding the fruit, so too the statement of the fruit beginning with "Whatever one performs with knowledge" and ending with "that alone becomes more powerful" must be an arthavāda. This is because in both cases—the passage "He whose *juhū* is made of *parṇa*-wood... and "Whatever one performs with knowledge..."—the same principle applies.

This is because the present tense designation is not restricted [to the time of performance]. He states this very point with the words "in the case of the udgītha, etc. He rejects the aforementioned prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "as in the case of the godohana, etc. Now, one might object: "In the case of the godohana and so forth, since another fruit—the cattle—is seen apart from the primary fruit, it was accepted that these are for those already qualified [for the main rite], and it was said that they are 'enjoined' by relying on this very fact; but here, on the contrary, there is no such thing. Anticipating this doubt, the rebuttal is stated with the words "of heaven and so forth," meaning that even here, another fruit is observed.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: in the case of sacrifices, heaven and the like alone constitute the fruit; however, in the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth—which have the sacrifice as their locus—there is an "excess of vigor," meaning a fruit that is indeed superior to the previously mentioned fruit. In this context, "possessing greater vigor" means having a fruit that is unobstructed by other ritual acts. For in the world, the fruit of an action is often obstructed by the fruits of more powerful intervening actions.

The meaning is that the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth produces the capacity to ward off obstructions caused by previous karmas; thus, the result of the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth is its state of being "more powerful" (*vīryavattara*). For it is observed in the world that a cause naturally performs its own effect, but when an obstacle arrives, it suppresses that power; conversely, an enhancer—such as a gem or a mantra—intensifies that very power of performance.

Therefore, this is the meaning: if ritual action is accompanied by meditations such as that on the *udgītha*, it would produce its own result immediately; if not, it would not produce it immediately. Consequently, the *udgītha* and so forth are subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the ritual action, because they possess fruit only through the fruit of the primary action. Meditation, however, is not a subsidiary part of the ritual action, because it possesses a different fruit in the form of a greater potency exceeding the fruit of the primary action. But [subsidiaries] such as being made of *parṇa*-wood lack a separate fruit of their own.

[The *parṇa* wood] is indeed a subsidiary element (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice by way of the *juhū* ladle and so forth, which have an inseparable connection with the sacrifice. Now, since the two statements—"He whose [ladle] is made of *parṇa* wood"—and "Whatever [is done] through knowledge"—are similar in that both mention a fruit, how can a difference be asserted here? It is as follows: listen attentively to this. Because the hearing of the sentences is of a dissimilar nature, in one case the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) "through knowledge" (*vidyayā*) is heard; and that instrumental case directly teaches the status of being a means to the fruit.

In the sentence concerning the "leafiness" (of the ladle), however, there is no mention of the instrumental case; therefore, there is no connection with a fruit [in that context]. Consequently, it is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). This very point he demonstrates clearly with the words "in the case of leafiness and so forth. If it does not express instrumentality, what then does it say there? To this he replies: "And it speaks of the action, except in the case of meditation. The meaning is that, in the performance of ritual action other than meditation (*anupāsti*), the sentence speaks only of the action consisting in the taking up of the *juhū* ladle and other implements which have become subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the rite.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis, meaning "it speaks of the action alone."

Here someone objects: regarding the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) in the *udgītha*, a different result from the fruit of the sacrifice—such as being more vigorous (*vīryavattara*) and so forth—is indeed referred to; for this very reason, in the previous section titled "Otherwise, because of the word" (*anyathātvaṃ śabdāt*), an inquiry into the difference or non-difference of meditations was conducted. Therefore, the raising of a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) based on the aim of a further result is already refuted. He restates this with the words "In the *udgītha*," and he rejects it with "Not so. He explains that very point with "In this case... and so forth.

This is the meaning: regarding the *udgītha*, two points are established. Here, however, there is a determination that it is not an auxiliary (*anaṅga*) to ritual action because it serves a different purpose (the attainment of fruits). In that [previous] case, however, the inquiry into whether the meditations (*vidyā*) are identical or distinct proceeds by depending upon the matter determined in this present section, according to the principle of "anticipating what is yet to come" (*anāgatāvekṣaṇanyāya*). Therefore, there is no tautology. This is the syntactical connection here: for the qualified listener whose mind is firmly fixed on the fact that [the *udgītha*] is not an auxiliary, the doubt as to the identity of the meditations arises; and since that has been refuted, this is stated as the resolution.

He states another resolution with the words "having abandoned" (tyaktvā). Having set aside the status of these [elements] as either auxiliary or non-auxiliary, there was previously an inquiry as to whether the two knowledges are separate or not; since the separateness of the two knowledges has been determined therein, what is established here is merely that the knowledge possesses the character of an action based on a substrate by virtue of having separate fruits.

The previous section was introduced by way of a contextual transition; now, the determination of the subject matter of the *daharavidyā* (the doctrine of the small [space] within the heart) is undertaken here—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). The inquiry into its meaning concerns the passage: "Those who depart from here having understood the Self and these true desires," wherein the meditation on qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*) is also enjoined separately. In that regard, the question is whether, during the contemplation of the qualities, the meditation on the *dahara-ātman* as qualified by those qualities must be repeated or not.

For that purpose, it is considered whether the meditation on the qualities is also accomplished by the meditation on the small [space] alone, or not. On this point, someone says: "Because of the force of the statement which mentions them separately—'those who depart after having discovered here the Self and these true desires'—the meditation on the qualities is distinct from the meditation on the possessor of qualities. For that reason, let there be a separate enumeration of the possessor of qualities for the sake of meditating on the qualities; let the mention of the possessor of qualities be by way of a single rule (tantra), occurring only once."

The meaning is this: when the substratum (dharmin) has been apprehended for the sake of meditating upon the attribute (dharma), one need not apprehend the substratum again for the sake of meditating upon that same attribute, because the substratum is established by the very apprehension of it made previously, even for subsequent meditation. He restates all of this with the words "desires" (kāmān). He refutes this with the words "it is improper" (ayuktam). He establishes its impropriety with the words "that and that" (tattad).

In the meditation characterized by the multitude of qualities such as being free from evil (*apahatapāpmatva*), because there is a distinction based on the specific qualities [meditated upon], for each injunction prescribing the meditation on Brahman qualified by those respective qualities, the repeated contemplation of the substratum—Brahman—is required; that is, it is not excluded from the purpose. Therefore, regarding the contemplation of the substratum enjoined previously by the phrase "having understood" (*anuvidya*), and in the case of the phrase "having understood these true desires (*satyakāmān*) and departing," the meaning is that the contemplation of the substratum must be performed individually for each instance of the contemplation of Brahman qualified by those respective qualities.

In this context, the author of the Sūtras shows the principle stated in the Pūrvakāṇḍa as an illustrative example by the words "by means of [attributes] such as kingship," etc. This is the meaning: in passages such as "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra the King," the ritual act called "offering" is repeated with respect to Indra as qualified by each respective attribute. Likewise, since the Supreme Brahman abides as qualified by various attributes such as being free from sin (apahatapāpmatva), the repetition of that very same Supreme Brahman is meaningful.

Regarding this, someone says: "In this context, two kinds of worship have indeed been described: one is the worship of the nature [of Brahman] devoid of attributes (nirguṇa-svarūpa), and the other is the worship of Brahman as qualified by attributes (guṇa-viśiṣṭa). And here, according to the principle that 'the fruit corresponds to the manner of worship,' from the worship of the nature devoid of attributes comes the attainment of Brahman devoid of attributes; this is stated in the passage: 'Having reached the supreme light, he appears in his own form. Furthermore, from the worship of [Brahman] with attributes comes the attainment of Brahman with attributes; this too is stated here: 'Eating, playing, and rejoicing.'"

By such statements [as these], we postulate that there is liberation by stages (kramamukti) alone; thus, having attained the qualified [Brahman] through the meditation on the qualified, one subsequently attains the unqualified [Brahman] through meditation on the unqualified. He restates all of this with the words "that respective enjoyment" (*tattadbhoga*). He rejects that view with the word "untenable" (*asad*). The meaning is this: do you postulate both types of meditation here by following some authority, or not? Not the first, because all meditation whatsoever has the qualified [Brahman] as its object. Nor the second, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

If it is argued that the qualities (*guṇas*) are indeed unreal, we say no; for the reality of those very qualities is established with great emphasis in the passage, "These desires are real" (*ta ime satyāḥ kāmāḥ*). Furthermore, immediately after the statement, "Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own form," there is the teaching of the fruit consisting of qualities: "Eating, playing, and rejoicing. Moreover, it has already been established that the passages concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-vākya*) have as their scope the negation of qualities that are to be abandoned. Therefore, there is no such thing as a [scriptural] doctrine of absolute qualitylessness.

Whence could there be meditation upon that [Brahman], whence could there be the attainment of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahma*), and whence, moreover, could there be the postulation of a difference in the meaning of the scriptural statements based on the variety of fruits resulting from meditation? He restates the very point already mentioned for the sake of clarity with the words "in this scripture" (*asmin śāstre*). Indeed, in this scripture, starting from "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*) up to the final aphorism "No return, because of the scriptural statement; no return, because of the scriptural statement" (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdādanāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*), there is no occasion whatsoever for the meditation upon the attributeless Brahman.

This is indeed acceptable to you, since it would entail the consequence of [the object] being false by virtue of being an object of meditation; furthermore, no fruit can be postulated for the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa).

If that fruit were of the nature of Brahman, it would be non-fruit at all because it is established as beginningless. Therefore, the attainment of the fruit results only from the meditation upon [Brahman] with attributes (*saguṇa*), and it is thus established that such a fruit consists precisely of those attributes. If it is argued: "Let there be no meditation on the attribute-less Brahman (*nirguṇa*) in the scriptures, and let there be no such fruit; nevertheless, this has been postulated through the succession of our own tradition," the author provides the reply: "Not that which is outside the scriptures" (*nocchāstram*). Let these other objections stand aside; this alone is the "Brahma-missile" (*brahmāstra*).

This chapter is indeed well-known by the name "The Chapter on the Collection of Qualities" (Guṇopasaṃhārapāda). Regarding this chapter, he states that the statements concerning the negation of qualities are merely the confused prattle of those who are intoxicated with pride: "Because of the restriction of qualities."

In this section, having raised an objection regarding the emergence of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he begins the refutation with the words "pratyekam" (individually), and so forth. By the passage beginning "apahatāpāpmā" (free from evil), there is a meditation on each [attribute] individually; by the passage beginning "vrajantyetāṃśca satyān kāmān" (they go to these true desires), there is a meditation on them collectively. Be that as it may, even in both modes of meditation, since there can be no meditation on qualities without a possessor of qualities, the meditation on Brahman itself is established.

The intention of the objector is as follows: "How can it even be suspected here that there is no consideration of the possessor of qualities (guṇin)? And in the absence of such a suspicion, how can it be resolved? He rejects this with the words "no. He explains the manner of this rejection with the words "of the qualities" (guṇānām). The meaning is this: when the qualities ascend into the intellect, the form of the possessor of qualities—consisting of reality, knowledge, infinity, and so forth—is "arthyam," which means not departing from the actual fact (artha), i.e., inseparable from it. That [form] is established by its very nature.

That which is other than this is that which consists exclusively of knowledge (*vidyaikānta*), having the form of the abode (*sthāna*) and so forth. "In the repetition of that" means the engagement in the reflection on the repetition of Brahman together with that abode and so forth; such is the meaning of the words. The sense is this: the repetition pertains to Brahman precisely as accompanied by the specific qualifications—such as the particular abodes and so forth—belonging to each specific meditation (*vidyā*), which are distinct from the general qualities common to all meditations.

In this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the connection (*saṅgati*) is stated by expressing the sequence for raising the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Is it the case that, by virtue of being a single vidyā with the previously discussed one, the determination of the specific object of worship (*upāsya-viśeṣa*) is made by this [text]? The inquiry into its meaning, however, is as follows: Is Nārāyaṇa alone the object of worship in all higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), or is Nārāyaṇa the object of worship only in the Dahara-vidyā?

To that end, it is investigated whether, in the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka, the determination of the specific object of worship for all vidyās is made, or whether it is the determination of the specific object of worship for the Dahara-vidyā.

In this regard, is the status of Nārāyaṇa enjoined here with reference to the *dahara* (the small space) that is the object of meditation in the *Daharavidyā*, as indicated by such passages as "the heart, resembling a lotus bud, facing downwards," and so forth; or rather, is the object of meditation—which is pointed out in all meditations by terms such as *akṣara*, *Śiva*, *Śambhu*, *Parabrahman*, *Parajyotis*, and *Paratattva*—referred to here by those very same terms, and its status as Nārāyaṇa then enjoined?

Is it proper to enjoin [Nārāyaṇa] as the subject of the *dahara* (small) section in accordance with the scriptural hearing that the heart is the abode—beginning with the words "resembling the calyx of a lotus"? Or is it proper to enjoin Nārāyaṇahood as the object of all meditations on the basis of the abundance of indicative marks (*liṅga*), in accordance with the fact that Nārāyaṇahood is what is being enjoined? Regarding this, he presents the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) containing the connection [to the context] with the words "prakrānta" (already commenced): "In this section beginning with 'Smaller than the small,' the *dahara-vidyā* has been commenced."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position arises that the section beginning with "Sahasraśīrṣam" is intended for the determination of the object of knowledge in the previously mentioned Dahara-vidyā. He refutes this, saying, "Not so. He reveals the manner of rejecting the prima facie view with the words "tat-tat" (each of those). Since it is established by logic that among the means of proof—such as direct scriptural statement (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), and syntactical connection (vākya)—each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding, the syntactical connection (vākya) is stronger than the context (prakaraṇa). A "sentence" (vākya) consists of the co-occurrence of other words, such as: "Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman."

And that statement—in the form of "Tattvam nārāyaṇaḥ paraḥ" (Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality), "nārāyaṇaḥ paro jyotiḥ" (Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light), and so forth—establishes [Nārāyaṇa] as the object to be known by all vidyās. You, however, assert that it pertains exclusively to the Dahara-vidyā based solely on the context (prakaraṇa). Therefore, one should abandon the status of pertaining exclusively to the Dahara-vidyā—which is established by a weak means of proof—and instead accept its status of being subsidiary to all vidyās, which is established by a stronger means of proof. Thus he says: "For a sentence has greater force than context."

One might object: "Is it not the case that we do not rely on the context alone? Rather, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) supporting its status as a supplement to the *dahara-vidyā* is also seen in this passage. Therefore, since the indicative mark is stronger than the sentence when there is a conflict between them, one must accept that it is indeed a supplement to the *dahara-vidyā*. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "by sentences" (*vākyaiḥ*). The meaning is this: if there were only a single sentence, then it might be possible to claim the superiority of the indicative mark. However, [in our case, the situation is different].

In this context, however, there exist many scriptural passages (*vākya*); therefore, it is precisely these that possess greater force. Nor are they contradicted by the indicative mark (*liṅga*). For it is the status of being a supplement to all meditations (*sarvavidyāśeṣatva*) that is established by the passages. Here, by the principle of illustration (*upalakṣaṇanyāya*), only a few are mentioned; thus, once the status of being a supplement to all meditations is established, the Dahara-vidyā is included within all meditations, and consequently, the fact that the passages are intended as supplements to that [Dahara] meditation is indeed accepted. Therefore, the indicative mark of being a supplement to the Dahara-vidyā remains within its own passage without contradiction, as the opposition has been pacified.

The context (*prakaraṇa*) as well, which establishes [the mantra] as a supplement to the Dahara-vidyā, is satisfied by obtaining that status as its supplement; therefore, it is not contradicted by the more powerful statements that establish it as a supplement to all vidyās. Furthermore, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the recognition of Puruṣa-Nārāyaṇa in the forms "the thousand-headed god" and "the thousand-headed Puruṣa" is seen to be extremely powerful because it occurs at the beginning (*upakrama*). Therefore, on account of this *liṅga*, the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) does not establish that [the mantra] is a supplement to the Dahara-vidyā alone.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: once it has been established by means of sentences that [the *dahara*] possesses all meanings, the worship of the *dahara* also participates in this; thus, the meaning of "partaking" (*bhāgin*) in this sense is "possessing the fulfillment of purpose" (*kṛtārthatāvān*). In this sentence, there is a portion endowed with indicative marks (*liṅga*) that establishes its status as a supplement to the *dahara-vidyā*. Precisely because of that fulfillment of purpose, there is no contradiction whatsoever on the part of the indicative mark. Since there is an absence of contradiction due to the attainment of the intended meaning, the indicative mark remains entirely neutral.

Thus, since its purpose has been fulfilled by this [preceding argument], the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is unable to contend with many other statements devoted to that [other conclusion]. This being the case, the context (*prakaraṇa*) as well is itself indifferent; for it is inherently weak and, having already achieved its purpose through the attainment of being a subordinate part of the *dahara-vidyā*, it does not assist this single indicative mark.

Indeed, when many contradictory and powerful [indications] are present, the context—which is itself weak, being effortless and lacking its own inherent power—cannot assist it, as it is itself satisfied and lacks exertion. Furthermore, once the meaning of a sentence has been determined through the consideration of the sixfold marks of purport (tātparya-liṅga), such as the beginning and conclusion, any other subsequently perceived meaning must simply be abandoned; such is the path of logic.

Furthermore, since this passage serves as the basis for all forms of knowledge (*sarvavidyopajīvyatva*), it is clearly understood that it establishes Nārāyaṇa alone as the supreme goal to be attained. Therefore, one must not abandon its unqualified meaning and attempt to establish it as pertaining solely to the *dahara-vidyā*; rather, it is proven that this statement is a supplement to all forms of knowledge (*sarvavidyāśeṣatva*). This is the sense: this statement, however, is not...

It establishes its status as being solely a subordinate element [of ritual action]. This is because, in the *Samanvaya* section, it was demonstrated that the authority of scriptural statements is possible even without being subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*). Nevertheless, it is indeed beneficial to all forms of knowledge (*vidyā*), since meditation upon that [Brahman] cannot be performed without a thorough understanding of the Supreme Reality. Therefore, since its status as the foundation of everything is established by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the attempt to discard it is utterly futile.

Having previously established the supremacy of Nārāyaṇa alone by refuting various opposing positions and demonstrating specific accepted means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the author] now establishes it through the doctrine of the identity of the Self (*ātmaikya*). Those who follow the systems of Bhāskara, Yādavaprakāśa, and Śaṅkara assert that all selves are indeed one and the same. Those who are like common folk, having only a superficial recitation of a few Vedic passages, claim the identity of all deities. And the proponents of the doctrine of that which transcends the void (*vyomātītavādinaḥ*) maintain that there exists some reality beyond the three forms (*trimūrti*).

Those who are satisfied merely with the recitation of the Purāṇas, being devoid of specialized knowledge, have asserted the equality of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Others of that same sort, however, maintain the identity of the three. Still others, imagining things incorrectly according to their own preconceptions, describe one among Bhāskara and the rest as the supreme over all. These people are indeed unskilled; because they contradict the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and the Sāttvika Purāṇas, those who know the truth do not respect their utterances.

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what is your authority?", he establishes the determination of the supreme reality by first presenting the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the words "by the final Vedas" (*trayyantaiḥ*). By the phrase "with one voice" (*ekakaṇṭhaiḥ*), he declares the absence of contradiction among all the Śrutis. By the term "conformable to that" (*tadanuguṇā*), he indicates that [the Smṛti] is supported by the *Upabṛṃhaṇas* (the Purāṇas). By the word "Śrīmān" ("the Glorious One"), he shows the indicative mark of the restriction stated in the Uttara-Nārāyaṇa: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives. By the name "Nārāyaṇa," he cites the very Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka.

The term *patiḥ* (Lord) serves to manifest the relationship between the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and the principal (*śeṣin*), as established by various scriptural passages such as "the Lord of the universe" (*patiṃ viśvasya*). For He alone is the meaning of the *praṇava*. Indeed, the *praṇava* itself is the essence of all the Vedas, as shown by the concluding statement beginning with "That goal which all the Vedas proclaim" (*sarve vedā yatpadamāmananti*) and ending with "I shall tell you that goal in brief: it is 'Om'. By the use of the plural form "our Lord" (*naḥ patiḥ*), the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) established by the scripture "the eternal among the eternals" (*nityo nityānām*) is justified.

The phrase "possessing an entire body" refers to the state of being the body of all, which is established in such texts as the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa and constitutes the essence of the adhyātma-śāstra. The phrases "bestower of liberation" and "enjoyed by the liberated" express the essential meaning taught in the third and fourth chapters respectively; the distinction between these two meanings is that the bestowal of liberation is treated in the third chapter, while being attained by the liberated is treated in the fourth.

By means of a sentence more powerful than context, it was stated that the Nārāyaṇānuvāka is common to all meditations (vidyās). Here, however, since there is no sublater of the context, the connection is to be questioned as to whether the "mind-altars" (manaścita) and so forth enter into a sacrifice consisting of ritual action (kriyāmaya-kratu).

Regarding the investigation of that meaning, in the Vājasaneyaka it is recorded: "The fire built of mind, the fire built of speech, the fire built of breath, the fire built of sight, the fire built of hearing, the fire built of action, and the fire built of fire. Concerning these fires beginning with the "fire built of mind," the question arises: do they consist of action through their connection with a ritual consisting of action, or do they consist of knowledge through their connection with a ritual consisting of knowledge? For that purpose, it is deliberated whether or not there is an application of these fires to a ritual consisting of action—which is proximate by virtue of their proximity to the fire built of bricks—by means of that [proximity].

Is it that by means of knowledge alone these [fires] become built for one who knows thus, and that all beings always build them for one who knows thus—thus, through the indicative marks (*liṅga*) and sentences (*vākya*) of the Śruti, is the application (*viniyoga*) of this knowledge understood as being part of the ritual act (*kratu*), or not? Is it that "the cups were drawn with the mind, they praised with the mind"?

The question arises whether an injunction for knowledge (*vidyā-vidhi*) is to be inferred—on the grounds that there is a connection with the sequence of hymns and recitations (*stotra-śastra*), an extension (*atideśa*) stating "for each one of these, it is as great as the former," and the possibility of a connection with a fruit—or whether it is not to be so inferred because no injunctive suffix is heard and no [independent] act of knowing (*vedana*) is mentioned. Since the collection of meanings stated by the author of the Sūtras has been very clearly explained by the Commentator (Śaṅkara) himself in this section, he himself provides only a brief supplement by setting forth the nature of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Therefore, the students must contemplate the meaning of the section with extreme care from beginning to end, as it is stated in the Bhāṣya itself. For here, there is an inquiry as to whether the fires consisting of mind (*manaścitādi*) and so forth—previously connected with the fire built of bricks—are of the nature of action by entering into the previously relevant sacrifice consisting of action, or whether they are of the nature of knowledge by entering into a postulated sacrifice consisting of knowledge. In this regard, [the author] restates the intention of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "an auxiliary" (*aṅgam*). The fires consisting of mind and so forth should indeed be an auxiliary to that very sacrifice which was previously presented by means of the fire built of bricks.

The meaning is this: although a sacrifice consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) was not previously heard of [in this context], it is nevertheless postulated by the force of the scriptural mention of the fire-altar built with bricks (*iṣṭakacitāgni*), which is invariably connected to a sacrifice. Since that very sacrifice is proximate here due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), let the "mind-built" (*manaścita*) altar and so forth also be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that sacrifice through the principle of option (*vikalpa*). This is what he says with the word "intellect" (*buddhi*): the meaning is that the "mind-built" and subsequent altars, though themselves of the nature of intellect (*buddhyātmaka*), must be auxiliaries to the very sacrifice consisting of ritual action—which was previously relevant and presented by the context—because they require a principal (*aṅgin*) to which they belong.

Now, one might object: "How can that which is itself of the nature of knowledge be a constituent part (*aṅga*) of a sacrifice consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*)? Anticipating this doubt, he provides an illustration with the word "just as" (*yathā*). Just as in the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice the *mānasa-graha* (mental cup-offering) is a constituent part of the ritual action-based sacrifice, so too here, even though they are in their essential nature of the form of knowledge (*vidyā-rūpa*), the *manaścita* and others may be constituent parts of the ritual action-based sacrifice; this is the meaning. He states that there is also another reason for this with the words "of its power" (*tadvīryasya*). The power (*vīrya*) of the brick-built altar (*iṣṭakacita*) and others is surpassed by that of the *manaścita* and others.

The meaning is this: just as the brick-built altar and the like possess the capacity to assist a ritual consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*), so too do the mind-built altars (*manaścita*) and others possess that same capacity; therefore, they enter into the ritual consisting of action. [The author] refutes this with the words "not so" (*na sat*). He establishes this point with the words "it has been stated" (*udita*). The sense is this: for if there were no ritual consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) within its own sentence, then the mind-built altars and the like would be dependent upon entering into the ritual consisting of action imagined in the preceding sentence.

It may be so. For within its own sentence, there exists a sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*), which is established by the very adjuncts heard therein. Therefore, one should not assume that the *manaścita* and other meditations are connected with a ritual consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) imagined from a preceding sentence, while abandoning the sacrifice consisting of knowledge situated in its own sentence. By the phrase "by direct statement and so forth" (*śrutyādyaiḥ*), the meaning is that the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) itself establishes that the sacrifice consisting of knowledge exists within its own sentence.

Anticipating the objection that—"In that case, since the capacity [of the fires] is extended by implication to those built of bricks which have entered into the ritual consisting of action, one must necessarily admit here too that the *manaścita* and other fires enter into the ritual consisting of action"—and that this has already been stated by me, he says "upakṛti" (the assistance).

This is the meaning: for an extension (atideśa) occurs on the basis of similarity; therefore, whatever capacity the fire-altars built of bricks and so forth possess by virtue of entering into the ritual (kratu) consisting of action which is their own principal, that same capacity belongs to the fire-altars built of mind and so forth precisely by virtue of entering into the ritual consisting of knowledge (vidyā) which is their own principal—thus there is no contradiction with the extension.

"Now, you claim that the mind-made [sacrifices] and so forth enter into a sacrifice consisting of imagined ignorance; therefore, it would be better for them to enter into a previously established sacrifice consisting of ritual action. To this objection from some dull-witted person, he replies with the word "kalpya" (imagined).

In this context, it is not only a ritual consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) that is postulated; rather, a ritual consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) must also be postulated first. Therefore, by drawing in the previously postulated ritual of action, the connection with the rituals consisting of knowledge—such as the "mind-altar" (*manaścita*) and others—is established here through their non-separation from that [action-based ritual]. This is the syntactical connection (*śabdānvaya*) here: even a ritual whose nature is action must indeed be postulated, and that postulation is performed precisely by means of the power of its constituent parts (*aṅga*) already acquired previously.

Regarding this, he states the disparity between the ritual consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*) and the ritual to be postulated [in other contexts] with the words "by those residing in the sentence" (*vākyasthaiḥ*). Here, the ritual consisting of knowledge shines forth—that is, it is revealed—by means of the very adjuncts (*anubandha*) residing within its own sentence. Therefore, this ritual consisting of knowledge, which is postulated by means of the adjuncts residing in its own sentence, is indeed superior to the ritual consisting of action (*kriyāmaya-kratu*) postulated by means of adjuncts residing in another sentence; thus, the meaning is that the mental fires (*manaścita*) and so forth are connected to this [knowledge-ritual] alone. He clearly demonstrates the support of reasoning for this point with the words "of that which is remote" (*dūrasthasya*).

Furthermore, the connection with that which is drawn by those situated at a distance is indeed more firmly established than the connection with that which is drawn by what is recited from one's own words; for resorting to the light alternative (laghu-pakṣa) is what is obtained by logic. Anticipating the objection that there is no injunctive suffix (*vidhi-pratyaya*) here for the sacrifice consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*), and that the word "knowing" (*veda-na*) does not appear directly, [the author] states, "When the matter is not otherwise established," to show that even in the absence of an explicit hearing of an injunction, the postulation of an injunction is accepted precisely within the section on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*).

The implication is that once it has been established by means of valid authority (*pramāṇa*) that [the Upanishads] enter into the sacrifice as a form of knowledge (*vidyārūpa-kratvanupraveśa*), the absence of the word "knowing" (*vedana*) is not a defect. The remainder of this matter, in its entirety, should be seen clearly in the Bhāṣya itself.

In this context, the preceding section has been introduced by way of incidental discussion; its connection with that prior section was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* as follows: "In all the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*), it has been stated that just as the nature of the object of meditation and the meditation itself must be known, so too must the nature of the meditator be known," as in the passage, "And thus there is the presentation and the question regarding these three alone. Furthermore, he will later state that this inner self (*pratyagātman*) is to be meditated upon as being identical in essence with the supreme self (*paramātman*), in the sūtra: "But they approach [the Self] as the Self, and they cause [it] to be grasped as such."

Is this the transmigrating individual self (*pratyag-ātman*)—the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer who moves between this world and the next and must be kept in mind—or rather is it the nature described in the *Prajāpati* dialogue as being free from sin and so forth? This is the underlying intention here: in the section concerning the "abundance of indicatory marks" (*liṅga-bhūyastva*), the determination was made regarding Nārāyaṇa as the object of meditation in all meditations; now, the nature of the individual self (*jīva*) is determined, who is to be kept in mind by the meditator himself as a qualifying attribute of the object of meditation in all meditations.
