The investigation into that meaning is as follows: the inner self (pratyagātman) is to be meditated upon as having the Supreme Self as its body, in the form "I am Brahman. Should it be meditated upon in the form of being a knower, an agent, an enjoyer, and so forth, or rather in the form of being free from sin and other qualities as stated in the Prajāpati discourse? To that end, it is deliberated whether the statement, "According to one's resolve in this world," which declares that attainment is in accordance with one's meditation, refers exclusively to the Supreme Self, or whether it also refers to the inner self.

Does the reference by the word "that" in the statement, "In whatever way one meditates upon it, so does one become," indicate that the teaching regarding attainment according to the mode of meditation refers to the Supreme Self, or not? What is the meaning of the word "that" here?

Does this refer to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), or does it refer to the supreme self alone? Here, the author sets forth the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "tatkālākāriṇa" (belonging to that time and form). In passages such as "O venerable deity, I am indeed you," worship of the Lord is described through the "I-grasp" (*ahaṃgraha*). However, the cognition "I" occurs only in respect to the self as endowed with the form of that particular time. Therefore, in the devotion to the supreme self expressed as "I," the intellect of the individual soul—which serves as a covering—would belong to that soul as it is joined with the form of that particular time.

Therefore, it is the very nature of the individual self (jīvātman), as characterized by agency, enjoyership, and so forth, that should be meditated upon during the state of worship. This is what he expresses with the words "on account of proximity" (āsatter iti). The meaning is: because of its immediate presence during the state of worship. He provides an illustration for this: "like [the case] when it was said, 'Worship me'. Just as in the Pratardana-vidyā, when Indra said, "Worship me," that which was to be worshipped was Indra as he was at that moment—endowed with a thousand eyes and other such attributes—and not as he would be in a future state of liberation; so it is here as well. He refutes this with the word "no" (na).

Regarding this, he states the reason with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means that [the meditation] would exist through a different mode of contact (*sannikarṣa*). He demonstrates that very alternative mode with the word "pure" (*śuddha*). For there are two aspects of the individual soul (*jīva*): the pure and the impure. That which is pure is alone to be accepted (*upādeya*). That which is to be accepted is precisely what should be focused upon during the state of meditation (*upāsanā*), because it is the fruits corresponding to the meditation that are proclaimed by the scriptures.

In order to demonstrate that only the pure form is present in the intellect (*buddhi*), he first states that the pure form alone is the fruit: "For the Self is to be realized as pure. Now, granted that the pure is the fruit, how is it present in the intellect? To this, he says: "The fruit is cognition."

In such injunctions as, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," activity for the sake of heaven indeed occurs through the mental apprehension of heaven as the fruit; likewise here too, the engagement in meditation occurs only in conjunction with the mental apprehension of the pure nature as the fruit. Thus, the fact that the pure form alone is present to the intellect is established. He states that the maxim of "the fruit according to one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*) also clearly supports this very point by saying, "when the pure nature is proximate to the intellect," meaning when it is internalized within the intellect.

The establishment of the principle of "that-kratu" (the intentionality of the ritual) is thus restricted by authoritative means; therefore, the meaning is that the pure essential nature alone is what should be intended.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is said that the agent's true nature as it exists must be contemplated, then in the Karma-kāṇḍa, the very same nature would have to be contemplated for the agent of ritual action as well; and thus, once the identity with the nature of the individual soul (jīva) has been established therein, the extensive exposition on the nature of the soul in the Vedānta-śāstra would be entirely redundant. To resolve this doubt, the author clearly demonstrates the distinction between the contemplation of the soul's nature as the agent of worldly and Vedic performances and so forth, by stating: "Of the agent... [kartuḥ].

For there are indeed three kinds of agents: one performs worldly actions such as lying down, sitting, eating, and agriculture; another performs Vedic actions such as sacrifice, giving, and oblation; and the third, moreover, performs the meditation on the Supreme Brahman, which is the cause for attaining the supreme human goal. In all three types of qualified agents, there certainly exists the mental conception of agency. Regarding these, he first speaks of the "perceived" [agent]: in the effort directed toward the attainment of perceived enjoyment, it is appropriate to consider only this much—that there is some enjoyer.

Furthermore, let there be no specific determination as to whether that body is [the self] or something distinct from the body, for such a distinction is useless. Indeed, even among common folk who lack the thorough knowledge of a self distinct from the body, hundreds and thousands of activities are observed which serve as the means for attaining their own desired ends. Now, he elucidates the second [alternative] with the words "heaven and so forth."

This is the meaning of the word here: in the case of ritual action performed for the sake of heaven and so forth, it is appropriate to reckon that the self undergoes transition into another body, accompanied by its own specific qualification such as being a Brahmin, and connected with a fruit related to a future time. This much, however, does not establish the meaning of the Vedānta texts. He states the third position as well: "for the sake of liberation."

Furthermore, regarding meditation for the sake of liberation, the state of attainment is indicated by the discussion of the *praṇidhi* (aspirational prayer); and by the statement of what is to be contemplated during the stage of meditation—namely, through the expression of the principle of "that which one intends" (*tatkratu-nyāya*)—it is made known and signified that whatever is contemplated is precisely what is attained. Thus, there is no possibility of the objection regarding over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the underlying meaning here: the *tatkratu-nyāya* is indeed specifically proclaimed in the Vedānta alone, and not in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*); therefore, during the stage of meditation, the contemplation of the state of attainment must necessarily be performed.

In the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), however, at the commencement of a rite, one need only contemplate a degree of stability corresponding to the capacity for experiencing results such as heaven, which manifest after a period of time.

Here someone objects: since the forms of the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) differ according to the various branches of knowledge (*vidyā*), one should contemplate only that which is specifically stated [in each], otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of mutual confusion. Furthermore, Brahman is to be attained as distinguished by both types of manifestations (*vibhūti*); therefore, even that which has the form of the bound (*baddha-rūpa*) is indeed an object of attainment, because it is included within "all" and is thus a particular aspect of Brahman. So how can a prohibition be made stating that this form is not to be contemplated on the grounds that it is not to be attained?

Therefore, let there be reflection upon that which is proximate and possesses a bound form. This is what he states with the word "knowledge" (vidyā). As for the meaning of the words: since the forms of the objects of knowledge differ in specific instances of knowledge such as the Sadvidyā and the Daharavidyā, one should reflect only upon exactly what has been stated [in each case].

In this regard, because of the meditation involving the appropriation of the self (*ahaṅgraha-upāsanā*) through the qualification of Brahman—namely, "I was Manu and Sūrya"—there is indeed the necessity of contemplating the individual soul (*jīva*) as well; however, the Brahman to be attained is qualified by all attributes. Since the bound soul is also included within the meaning of the word "all," even the bound form of the soul should be meditated upon as a qualification of Brahman, for it is impossible to abandon what is proximate. He refutes this with the words "No" (*na*), and explains that very rejection with the words "defiled" (*kaluṣita*).

The meaning is this: in the meditation on the grasping of the "I" (ahaṅgrahopāsana), the primary referent of the word "I" alone is to be meditated upon as a qualification of Brahman; and that [referent] is indeed the pure form. Therefore, because it would contradict the scriptural hearing of the word "I," the defiled form is not to be meditated upon, since it is secondary. Furthermore:

For in the discourse of Prajāpati, the nature of the individual self (jīvātman) is described as something to be contemplated as a subordinate element of the knowledge of Brahman; moreover, that nature is described as being purely pure, characterized by the eight qualities. Therefore, since it is precisely this contemplation of purity that is enjoined for the individual self even in the Vedāntas during the stage of meditative worship (upāsanā), there is no occasion for the contemplation of an impure form.

For this very reason, in the *Yogidhyeyārthanirṇaya*, the venerable Parāśara, beginning with "The Lord Hiraṇyagarbha," states that all those beginning with the gods, who have their origin in karma, are impure, thereby declaring that the impure are not to be meditated upon. This is what he expresses by the words "from the state of Prajāpati" (*prājāpatyāt*).

In the preceding section, it was stated that wherever Brahman is the object of meditation, there—in all such cases—the pure individual soul (jīva) is also the object of meditation. Now, however, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt as to whether, in every branch (śākhā) where there is an entry into the Udgītha, there is also an entry into the meditations on the Udgītha and so forth, or not. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: regarding the meditations on the Udgītha and other elements based on the limbs of the sacrifice, such as "One should meditate on this syllable 'Om' as the Udgītha," do these meditations remain restricted to each respective branch?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether the word *udgītha* in the injunction "one should meditate on the *udgītha*" refers to the *udgītha* in general, or to the *udgītha* as distinguished by its specific musical notes (*svara*). Does the proximity belong only to the individual instance of the *udgītha* distinguished by its notes due to the connection with the particular sub-division of the Vedic school (*śākhā*), or does the proximity belong to all individual instances of the *udgītha* by way of the unity of the sacrifice (*kratu*)—which serves as the primary referent (*śeṣin*)—across all Vedic schools?

Previously, an investigation was conducted regarding the difference between the two meditations on the *udgītha*. Immediately thereafter, as a corollary, it was considered how that very meditation on the *udgītha*—by virtue of being based upon a ritual action (*karma*)—possesses a fruit distinct from the fruit of the ritual, and thus serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Now, however, it is established that the meditation on the *udgītha*, though mentioned in one place, is subordinate to the *udgītha* alone wherever it may be mentioned. Because there is this distinction in meaning, there is no tautology. Here, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "of the *udgītha*, etc. (*udgīthādeḥ*).

"This rite of worship (bhajanavidhi) must be a specific form of the *udgītha* within the song of his own presence"—this is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). He rejects this with the words "not so" (*maivam*). He demonstrates the manner of this rejection with the words "the song of all limbs" (*sarvāṅgīti*).

For you assert that the connection of the meditation (*upāsana*) occurs in that very [context] solely by virtue of proximity (*sannidhi*); yet, proximity is indeed the same for all *udgītha*s, since—according to the principle of the "cognition of all branches" (*sarva-śākhā-pratyaya-nyāya*)—the proximity of the sacrifice which constitutes the whole is established, and thus the proximity of all *udgītha*s is established in this very place. Now, it may be argued that a universal (*sāmānya*) is not fit for performance without a particular instance (*vyakti-viśeṣa*).

Therefore, what is stated generally as "the udgītha" requires the manifestation of its specific form found therein, and consequently, the connection with the meditation (*upāsana*) would pertain only to that specific udgītha. This need not be so; for just as when it is said, "One should sacrifice with rice," the sacrifice is performed with rice in general, so too here let the meditation be performed by connecting it with the udgītha in general. However, as for the meaning of the words:

Even though the performance [of a ritual] depends upon an individual instance (*vyakti*), in the absence of a restrictive authority (*niyāmakapramāṇa*), as in the case of "one should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), one may proceed by taking up any particular instance whatsoever, just like the generic nature of rice (*vrīhitva*). If that is so, how could there be a restriction to the goat alone in the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*)? It would be thus: for in that case, since the word *paśu* (animal) requires a specific instance to complete its meaning, the word *chāga* (goat) is heard in the wording of the mantra (*mantravarṇa*) which presents that specific instance. However, in the present case, no such specific word exists.

Therefore, it is established that the meditation has as its object the *udgītha* in general, and not the specific *udgītha* mentioned in proximity; thus he says, "And the word [indicates this]. It denotes the generality of the *udgītha*, not a distinction, nor again a particular *udgītha*.

In the preceding section, the Udgītha and so forth were introduced; it was already stated there that the meditation upon the Udgītha and other parts of the Sāman—both collectively and individually—is established by scripture. Thus, the connection [of the present discussion] arises from the doubt: in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, should the meditation be performed on the whole, or on the parts individually, or on both?

The investigation into that matter is as follows: In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, is the Vaiśvānara, whose limbs consist of the earth and so forth, to be meditated upon only in his distributed (vyasta) form; or both in his distributed and his integrated (samasta) forms; or only in his integrated form? Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "Uddālaka, indeed, sirs," is the injunction for meditation intended for the distributed form alone, or for both the distributed and the integrated forms, or for the integrated form alone?

Is it that, because the designation "Vaiśvānara" applies to each individual limb and because the connection with fruits is heard for each limb, there is a plurality of injunctions for meditation upon the limbs—such that the passage "But he who thus [meditates] on this one, the span-long, the all-measuring" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.18.1) is a restatement of the whole—or rather, because the hearing of fruits is mentioned for the meditation on the parts separately in the passage "He eats food, sees what is dear, and becomes beloved," and because of the passage: "But he who thus meditates on this self as Vaiśvānara, the span-long, the all-measuring, he eats food in all worlds, in all beings, and in all selves"?

Since the hearing of results is mentioned for both [the whole and the parts], is it logical that there is an injunction for both? Or, in accordance with the unity of the sentence, is there an injunction for the meditation on the whole alone in the passage "But he who [meditates on] this," while the meditation on the parts is merely a detached restatement (*avayutyānuvāda*)? On this point, someone says: because the mention of results occurs in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā regarding the meditation on the parts, the deity should be meditated upon only as divided; the mention of results regarding the meditation on the whole, however, is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).

Alternatively, just as in the case of meditating on [the parts] individually, since a result is also specified for the meditation on the whole, one should contemplate it individually, and likewise, one must also contemplate it as a whole. He restates this position with the words "individually" (*vyasta*). He refutes this with "not so" (*maivam*). He states the reasoning for that: "in the case of the individual [parts]" (*vyasteṣu*). For here, a fault is declared regarding the meditations on the individual parts; therefore, one must conclude that the mention of a result in the case of meditations on the individual parts is merely an *arthavāda* (a commendatory statement). He reiterates this very point:

He confirms this with the example of the Vaiśvānareṣṭi passage, stating: "It is seen. Just as in the sentence, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara," it is the offering on twelve potsherds alone that is the object of the injunction; and by the words "he indeed becomes purified," etc., the declaration of its fruit is stated for that very act. The conclusion of the ritualistic schools (tāntrika-goṣṭhā) is that there is no injunction regarding the eight-potsherd cakes and so forth, and the mention of their fruits is merely an isolated restatement (avayutyānuvāda).

Similarly here as well, the worship of the whole alone is enjoined, and not that of the parts separately; even in the mention of the fruit there, it is merely a praise by way of a partial restatement (avayutyānuvāda).

In this regard, when someone asks, "Since both collective meditation (*samastopāsana*) and individual meditation (*vyastopāsana*) appear to be enjoined here, and since the declaration of results exists for both, and likewise in the *Bhūmavidyā* where a lesser meditation is first mentioned followed by progressively greater meditations—therein accepting small results for the former meditations and not even imagining them to be mere restatements (*avayutyānuvāda*)—how can this discrepancy (*vaiṣamya*) be asserted? the author begins his response by demonstrating two types of discrepancies.

Regarding the phrase "of the totality": the syntactical connection (*śabdānvaya*) here is as follows. When there is a firm consistency (*samanvaya*) in this sentence through the conjunction of the entire [text] by virtue of the purport (*tātparya*) of the great sentence, then, regarding the meditations on the individual parts—as in the case of the Vaiśvānara-śāṇḍilya and others—the mention of the fruit must, according to the established principle that praise is restricted to what is being restated, be understood as having the purpose of praise alone. However, in the Bhūma-vidyā (the knowledge of the Great), it is appropriate to state that the subsequent [knowledge] is a means to a superior fruit compared to the preceding one, because [there] there is no such lack of syntactical connection (*ananvitatvāt*).

Rather, "abundance" (bhūmatva) must be stated as consisting in the superiority of a greater fruit over a lesser fruit. Consequently, since it is not a mandatory injunction (*avidhi*), the connection with the fruits of the preceding [meditations] must also be stated; thus, the difference between them is established. On this point, he states another reason: "Nor is it so. In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, a transgression is heard of in the case of meditating on the parts separately; however, in the Bhūma-vidyā, no transgression is heard of in the case of meditating on each preceding stage. Therefore, this too constitutes a certain difference.

Therefore, the citation of a dissimilar example does not lead to the establishment of the intended meaning; indeed, it cannot establish the intended meaning, which consists in the uniformity of character between both [the subject and the example].

In the preceding section, an inquiry was made concerning specific types of knowledge (*vidyā*); now, an inquiry is being made concerning all forms of knowledge—this is the connection (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, since in the Vaiśvānara-vidyā it was established that only the meditation on the whole is valid and thus meditations on the parts are absent, the plurality of distinct knowledges was refuted; now, however, the plurality [of distinct knowledges] in the Sad-vidyā, Dahara-vidyā, Upakośala-vidyā, and others is being established in accordance with the evidence for their differentiation—this is the connection.

The inquiry into that matter concerns whether all the meditations (*vidyā*) enjoined in the Vedānta are indeed identical, or whether they are distinct. To that end, it is deliberated: is it reasonable to maintain their identity because the meditation—the meaning of the verbal root *vid* consisting in the repetition of cognition—has everywhere Brahman as its object and thus lacks difference in form, and because there is no difference in the fruit, which consists in non-return? Or, even though the Brahman to be meditated upon is one, is there still the possibility of a difference in meditation due to the fact that it is to be meditated upon as qualified by attributes such as being "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmatva*) and so forth?

Since the sentences are independent in their presentation of such meditations, it is logical to resort to a distinction between them. Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) establishes the unity of the knowledge (vidyaikya) along with supporting arguments, beginning with the words "In all [meditations]. In this first section (adhikaraṇa), the unity of knowledge was stated on the basis of specific factors such as connection, form, and injunction; that same principle applies here as well. In all these meditations, the form is undifferentiated, in that Brahman alone is the object to be known.

He says, "The result also," because conjunction is likewise non-distinct. Similarly, the designation is also non-distinct, namely "the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmavidyā*). Let this triad be non-distinct; nevertheless, the injunction (*codanā*) varies: in some places it is "one should know" (*vidyāt*), in others "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*), in others "it is to be contemplated" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), and in others, by means of a verbal root synonymous with "seeing," the means for crossing over death is stated as "having perceived Him, one is released from the jaws of death" (*nicāyya taṃ mṛtyumukhāt pramucyate*).

In the *Bhagavadgītā* and other texts, the means to liberation (*apavarga*) is enjoined through the repeated use of the very word "devotion" (*bhakti*). Therefore, how can there be a suspicion of the identity of knowledge (*vidyaikya*) when there is such an injunction? Not so. For in the *Bhāṣya* itself, the venerable author of the *Bhāṣya* has established that all these injunctions have a single purpose (*ekārthya*) according to the logic of the goat and the animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*). By this, their unity of purpose is proven. Indeed, the experts in the system (*tāntrika*) maintain that a difference in injunction (*codanābheda*) occurs only upon the use of words that are not synonymous, such as "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations."

Furthermore, because there is rest in one and the same place here, there is no difference in the injunction; this he shows by the words "meditation and so forth. The meaning is that the injunction (*vidhi*) is likewise without distinction. Therefore, the unity of the knowledge (*vidyaikya*) alone [follows]. He refutes this with the words "that is not so" (*tan na*). Here, he states four reasons consisting of the difference in name and so forth, beginning with the word "name" (*ākhyā*). First, the difference in name is such as "the Knowledge of Being" (*sadvidyā*), "the Knowledge of the Day" (*aharavidyā*), "the Knowledge of the Earth" (*bhūmavidyā*), and so on.

Furthermore, the mere identity of a general name, when employed alongside specific names, does not preclude a difference in knowledge; just as the general term "sacrifice" (yāga) and so forth, common to all [rites], does not preclude the difference occasioned by specific names such as, "Now this is the Jyotis," "Now this is the Viśvajyotis," and "Now this is the Sarvajyotis. Similarly here too, the mere general name "Brahmavidyā" cannot preclude a difference in knowledge. Moreover, a difference in form (rūpa) is clearly perceived in all these meditations.

The commonality of form as "Brahman" does not act as an obstacle to the distinction of forms produced by specific, particular attributes fixed in their respective vidyās, because the distinction of the qualified [entities] is unavoidable due to the difference in their qualifiers. For in this very way, there is a restriction regarding performance even in the Karmakāṇḍa. Having thus established the difference in form and the difference in designation, he establishes the difference in injunction as well, with the words "tadupahita... (qualified by that).

The two knowledges (*vidyā*)—characterized by the specific qualities common to each respective [meditation]—have their distinction established solely through their respective objects, according to the principle that "the distinction between cognitions, being formless, is indeed by means of the object itself. Thus, it has been very clearly demonstrated by the Commentator himself that the injunctions are indeed non-synonymous (*aparyāya*), since the differentiation of those respective knowledges is established by the object alone. Here, he states "mixed" (*miśra*) because there is also a difference in conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for in the Madhu-vidyā, the fruit is the attainment of the Supreme Self preceded by the attainment of the state of the Vasus, and thus in some cases the fruit is mixed, whereas in other knowledges it is not.

Since the attainment of the absolute Supreme Self alone is the fruit, the fruit is indeed unmixed; thus, there is also a distinction in the conjunction [of means]. In this way, having explained the distinction among the various knowledges taught in the Vedānta sections by means of the logic stated for the knowledge of Brahman, he says "kāmya" (desirable) and so forth to show that the distinction must likewise be determined for those optional knowledges.

In this context, indeed, while stating the distinction between the sciences (vidyā-bheda) by means of the aphorism "On account of the difference in words and so forth," the author of the Sūtras prioritizes the very difference in words; for "difference in words" means a difference in injunctions (codanā-bheda), and a difference in injunctions refers to an injunction regarding the meaning of an action (bhāvārtha-vidhi) through non-synonymous verbal forms such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*. Here, however, the Commentator himself has established the synonymy of words such as "knowing" (*vedana*) and "meditating" (*upāsana*).

Someone objects: "Since there is identity of word (*śabdasāmya*) here, how can the author of the Sūtras say, 'Because of the difference of various words and so forth' (*nānā śabdādibhedāt*)? [The author] anticipates the opponent's intention—that this refers to the difference between the verbal roots *vidyāt*, *upāsīta*, and *dhyāyīta*—and provides the answer: "No" (*na hi*). For verbal roots attain the status of being different words merely through a difference in their own forms; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even words such as *asti*, *vidyate*, and *bhavati* would be considered different words. Therefore, it must be stated that a difference of words consists only in the use of non-synonymous (*aparyāya*) terms.

It has already been established that *vidyā*, *āditya*, and so forth are synonyms. He refutes this with partial acceptance by saying "True. Although there is no primary difference between words as stated in the *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*, nevertheless, a difference between words is figuratively attributed based on a difference in form (*rūpa*). To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "To strengthen the distinction of forms. This is the meaning: here, it is the difference in form itself that is the direct differentiator.

However, since that difference in form qualifies the meaning of the verbal root, it also differentiates the meaning of the root itself; thus, because they express distinct meanings, a difference between the words is also established. This statement regarding the difference between the words is therefore figurative (*aupacārikī*). Regarding the purpose for stating this figurative usage, he says: "Knowledge" (*jñānam*). For those who propound falsehoods indeed claim that knowledge which is not subject to injunction is the means to liberation. To refute that and establish that knowledge is indeed subject to injunction, it is stated that there exists a difference in the injunctions concerning the object of knowledge (*vidyā*).

This is the underlying intention: whether the terms such as *veda*, *dhyāna*, and *upāsana*, occurring in their respective contexts, are synonyms; or whether they terminate in a specific meaning according to the "goat-sacrifice" (*chāgapaśu*) maxim; or whether, following the sequence stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), they are not synonyms because they establish different types of knowledge based on the difference in the objects of knowledge (*vedya*) within distinct contexts—in every case, knowledge is indeed that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

The statement regarding the difference in injunctions (*codanābheda*) is intended to demonstrate this point: that the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*) results precisely from knowledge that is enjoined.

Having thus stated the difference in words according to the manner described by the author of the Bhāṣya, he establishes that very primary difference in words intended by the Bhāṣyakāra with the words "Or else" (*yadvā*). This is the meaning: the author of the Sūtras first mentions the difference in words in the phrase "due to the difference in various words and so forth. That difference in words consists in the mention of non-synonymous terms, and this exists directly in the case of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), because one observes a difference in injunctions regarding devotion (*bhakti*) and surrender (*prapatti*), which are prescribed as means to liberation.

The injunction for devotion is seen in the words, "Having reached this transient world, O [Name], worship me"; the injunction for surrender (*prapatti*) is in the words, "Come to me alone as your refuge. For surrender itself is indeed taking refuge (*śaraṇāgati*).

In this statement defining *prapatti*, "ananyasādhye," the term *prapatti* is taught as a synonym for *śaraṇāgati*. Therefore, a direct difference in the injunctions (*vidhi*) between *bhakti* and *prapatti* is perceived; thus, this distinction of words is primary and resides in the intention of the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*). This is because, like the distinction between words such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*, this distinction of words also possesses the characteristic of a direct verbal differentiation. Here, the syntactical connection of the words is as follows: he introduces an alternative view with the phrase "yadvā" (or else).

By stating "due to the difference in words and so forth," the author of the Sūtras has correctly distinguished between ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*upāsana*). He provides an illustration for this: "like sacrificing and offering. Therein, he shows the reason for the distinction: "because of the difference in words. By saying "not figurative" (*abhāktāt*), he states that it is primary. Thus, a different method is established from the previously mentioned method. Having thus stated the difference in injunctions (*codanā*), [he now states] the difference in the names of those Vedas.

He says "designation" (*ākhyā*) because there is also a difference in the nature of the means (*rūpa-bheda*) corresponding to a difference in the type of union (*saṃyoga-bheda*). For in *bhakti*, there are designations such as "the knowledge of the small" (*dahara-vidyā*), and so forth; whereas in *prapatti*, there are [designations] such as "entrustment" (*nikṣepa*), "renunciation" (*nyāsa*), and "taking refuge" (*śaraṇāgati*). Furthermore, in *bhakti*, the form [of the Lord] consists of qualities such as being free from sin (*apahata-pāpmatva*) and so on, as found in the "knowledge of the small" and other meditations. Here, however, the form of the Lord is the assumption of the status of another means; that very thing is designated by those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*) as "being the independent means" (*nirapekṣopāyatva*).

For those established in the yoga of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*), the Supreme Person grants the fruit [of liberation] in dependence upon such knowledge as the Sadvidyā and Aharavidyā. Here, however, being Himself present in the place of other means, He grants that very fruit which is liberation. This is precisely what is stated: "Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone. The detailed exposition of this meaning is to be sought in the works of the Teacher, such as the *Nyāsaviṃśati* and others.

"Equal to others" means that just as a difference among the *sadvidyā* and other meditations is established through differences in name, form, and association, so too is there a difference in *prapatti*. Although the primary fruit of all Brahma-vidyās is liberation (*mokṣa*), the intention is that at the time of contemplation, there exists a disparity in the fruits consisting of the experience of the Lord as qualified by His respective forms. Furthermore, he states that there is a difference in form due to a difference in qualification: "Moreover, the qualification is distinct on account of swift attainment and so forth."

For one who is steadfast in *bhaktiyoga*, liberation occurs indeed at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma; however, for one steadfast in *prapatti*, *prapatti* itself is capable of exhausting even *prārabdha* karma. This is because of the scriptural statement: "Devotion as a means (*upāyabhakti*) destroys all sins except for *prārabdha*; but devotion as the goal (*sādhyabhakti*) is more powerful, being the destroyer even of *prārabdha*," from which it is heard that *prapatti* bestows its fruit swiftly.

As for the meaning of the words: devotion in the form of a means (*upāya-bhakti*) does not destroy even *prārabdha* karma, but rather destroys only that which is distinct from it; whereas devotion as the goal (*sādhya-bhakti*, i.e., *prapatti*) destroys even *prārabdha*. For this very reason, *prapatti* is superior to devotion because of its greater fruit. Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), all fifteen specific qualifications mentioned in the Teacher’s text—beginning with "the absence of capacity regarding devotion and so forth"—are intended.

Capacity, knowledge, birth, and the capacity for delay—these together constitute the qualification for devotion (*bhakti*). This applies whether there is the absence of one or another, the absence of pairs, the absence of triads, or the absence of all of them.

They become entitled to the attainment [of the goal], and thus the number fifteen is established. Now, one might object: "The fruit of the Brahma-vidyās is indeed the attainment of Brahman, and that is one and the same. To address this doubt of a person of immature intellect, he shows another distinction in the fruits as an illustration by saying, "They sang. For in the Madhu-vidyā, the fruit is the attainment of the lower Self in the form of reaching the status of the Vasus; however, in the Dahara-vidyā and others, he points out the attainment of the supreme Self alone as the fruit. Therefore, due to the difference in connection (*saṃyoga-bheda*), the distinction between the meditation on the Nyāsa and the other is indeed established.

In this regard, the *Bhāṣya* itself clearly states the connection: "The diversity of the various knowledges (*vidyās*)—such as the Knowledge of Being (*sadvidyā*), the Knowledge of the Day (*aharavidyā*), and so forth—which have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit, has been explained. Now, there arises a doubt: is it possible for these knowledges to be combined (*samuccaya*) within a single person because they serve a purpose, or is there only an option (*vikalpa*) due to a lack of such a purpose? The inquiry into that matter is as follows: is there a combination of all [the knowledges] within one person because their purposes can coexist, or is there an option?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether the attainment of Brahman, which is the fruit of all the sciences (*vidyās*), is uniform in nature, or whether it is diverse like the attainment of heaven and other such results. On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains: "In the world, indeed, sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and Agnihotra, which are enjoined for the sake of heaven and so forth, are performed through a combination (*samuccaya*) by a single qualified person (*adhikārin*) for the sake of a superior result; and by the increased performance of those respective rites, a superior fruit is obtained. In the same way, it should be here with regard to the various knowledges of Brahman."

"For the sake of attaining the Supreme Brahman, let [the practices] be performed in combination; and let the fruit also be obtained in varying degrees according to the excellence of place, time, and other factors. This is what he expresses with the words "jyotiṣṭoma" etc. Furthermore, there is no rule that a single meditation belongs to only one qualified person; thus he says "na ca" (nor is it...). According to the maxim, "Nor is it taught for only one," every injunction regarding worship is indeed enjoined for all. Therefore, their combination is certainly possible.

Raising the objection that because one particular meditation must be practiced for a long duration, there would be no time for another meditation, he refutes this with the words "to perform. The meaning is that one should not be deluded into thinking that there is no combination [of meditations] due to a lack of time for performance, on the grounds that here—as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, Agnihotra, and so forth—it is possible to perform them in succession. He rejects this position with the word "no," and states the reason for that with the word "mutually."

The meaning is as follows: "He, indeed, conducting himself thus for as long as life lasts"—thus the scripture declares that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is to be practiced until the fall of the body. And this applies equally to all forms of the knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, since the entirety of one's time is occupied by a single instance of the knowledge of Brahman, there is no opportunity to practice another form of the knowledge of Brahman; consequently, there can be no combination (samuccaya) of them. He concludes the point thus established with the word "sampūrṇa" (complete).

In this context, only one single fruit is seen: the attainment of the complete Brahman. For the sake of achieving that, the meditations (*upāsanā*) are to be practiced separately, and they are enjoined as distinct. He states the reason for this: "At the end of life, in meditative absorption" (*samādhi*). The meaning is this: each individual meditation—such as the *sadvidyā* or the *aharavidyā*—is enjoined to last until the moment of death. Therefore, because it is impossible to perform all the enjoined meditations simultaneously, and in order to allow for their practice individually, they must be regarded as separate means; thus, an option (*vikalpa*) between them must be accepted.

"Now, you have asserted that because the fruits of the various knowledges of Brahman (brahmavidyās) are one and the same, there must be an option (vikalpa) among them; however, a matter is not established by mere assertion alone. Indeed, we do not accept that the fruit is one, for when there is a difference in causes, a difference in effects necessarily follows. Furthermore, the meditations upon Brahman (brahmopāsanās), which are the causes, are indeed distinct due to differences in form and other attributes; therefore, a difference in fruit must also necessarily be admitted. Consequently, if the fruits are different, how can there be an option?"—this prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) he restates with the words "rūpādīnām" (of form, etc.).

The verbal connection of form and the other [sensory objects] with their specific qualities is not of a single uniform nature, as it is differentiated. The phrase "not of a single uniform nature" (*naikarūpam*) is not a compound, just like words such as *naga-naika* (not one mountain). Having established the difference in causes, he states the resulting difference in effects with the words "due to the difference in the causal complex" (*sāmagrībhedataḥ*). By the phrase "it is accepted according to reason" (*nyāyataḥ sammatam*), he means that the difference in effects arising from a difference in causes is indeed accepted by the world. He refutes this [objection] with the words "it would not be so" (*na syāt*). He provides the reason for this with the words "in all [cases]" (*sarvāsu*).

And because of the indicative mark of equality in enjoyment alone—the equality of enjoyment established by the scriptural text, "The stainless one attains supreme equality"—is here declared as the fruit.

Therefore, the identity of the fruit is established. Now, one might object: "Since all four—sālokya and the others—are designated as fruits, how can there be an identity of the fruit? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The identity of what is attained" (*prāpyaikyam*). By the statement, "Others say it is *sāyujya*; that indeed is declared to be liberation," it is determined that liberation is precisely *sāyujya* with Brahman. The sense is that *sālokya* and the others are merely restated as fruits because they are included within that [state of *sāyujya*]. By this, the suspicion that different means must have different fruits is also dispelled.

Because even when there is a difference in means, the oneness of the fruit is observed both in the world and in the Veda. For in the world, people reach the same single village by many different paths; likewise in the Veda, practitioners of ritual action attain the very same single fruit through various rites such as sacrifice, charity, and oblation prescribed here and there. Similarly, it is well known from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources that those who know the supreme self also attain their desired fruit by propitiating the Supreme Person through praise, salutation, and glorification.

Thus, since it is established by scripture that those devoted to various branches of knowledge attain the Supreme Person through the practice of their respective sciences according to their own specific qualifications, this is perfectly consistent.

In the preceding section (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*), having raised the doubt regarding a gradation in the fruits of various Brahma-vidyās and having refuted it, the present section—arising from the context of that fruit—raises the fruit of the previously mentioned *udgītha*-vidyā itself through many arguments and then resolves it; this is the connection (*saṅgati*). Alternatively, the connection is stated in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) itself by the phrase "according to one's desire" (*yathākāmam*). For it was stated previously that there may be either option (*vikalpa*) or combination (*samuccaya*) according to one's desire. Likewise, [the question here is] whether the *udgītha* and other such vidyās are to be adopted according to one's desire or not.

The doubt concerns their connection. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: Are meditations such as that on the *udgītha*, which have the constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) as their basis, to be undertaken as a rule within the sacrifices; or, like the *godohana* vessel and so forth, are they optional? Do these meditations serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by way of being based on the *udgītha* and other sacrificial elements—just like the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood [which makes the ladle effective for the sacrifice]—or do they serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*), being based on the sacrificial elements yet having human welfare as their goal because of the scriptural mention of results, such as: "Whatever one performs with knowledge"?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether the *godohana* vessel and the like serve the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatva*) because their connection with a fruit is heard within their own sentences, or whether they are connected to a fruit distinct from the fruit of the sacrifice because such a connection is heard [elsewhere]. Here, having stated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) preceded by an explanation of the connection [of this topic], he begins to resolve it by means of the reasons held by the proponent of the prima facie view in their proper order, starting with the words "tattad" (each of those). In the preceding section, after setting aside any gradation in the fruits of various Brahma-knowledges, it was stated that they have the same fruit as their means; and following from that discussion on the means to the fruit, by means of this present section—

In the sūtra "tannirdhāraṇāniyamaḥ," the fruit of the Udgītha-vidyā, which was already discussed previously, is now challenged again by means of numerous arguments and then reaffirmed through the refutation of those arguments. By this, the redundancy between these two sections concerning the Udgītha is avoided; for this present section achieves a superior purpose by way of resolving the objections raised in the previous one.

Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks as follows: Previously, by the analogy of the *godohana* vessel, it was stated that the knowledge of the *udgītha* serves the purpose of human life (*puruṣārtha*); however, that is not tenable. In the case of the *godohana* injunction, the mention of a fruit is seen within its own sentence itself: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] with the *godohana*. But in the sentence concerning the knowledge of the *udgītha*, there is no mention of a fruit; rather, only the fact that the meditation has the *udgītha* as its object is perceived in the statement, "One should meditate upon the *udgītha*."

In another very passage, namely "Whatever one performs with knowledge," the mention of the fruit is seen. This is one point of difference. There is also another difference: in the Godohana passage itself, there is an injunctive hearing, "One desiring cattle should fetch [water]"; however, in the sentence "Whatever one performs with knowledge," there is only a reference to the present tense in the word "performs" (karoti), and not an injunctive hearing.

Therefore, just like the statement regarding the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood—"He whose *juhū* ladle is made of *parṇa* wood hears no evil report"—which contains a reference to the present tense, there is no establishment of its being a means for achieving a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, even the mention of the result consisting of "greater vigor" is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), just like the mention of the result consisting of hearing no evil report.

Just as the quality of being made of *parṇa* wood is a subsidiary element of the sacrifice by way of the *juhū* ladle—which is invariably connected to the sacrifice—so too the meditation on the *udgītha* is a subsidiary element of the sacrifice by way of the *udgītha*, which is invariably connected to the sacrifice. This is another point of distinction between this sentence and the sentence concerning the *godohana* vessel. A third distinction is also seen precisely in the Sūtra itself: by the accusative case-ending in the phrase "one should meditate on the *udgītha*," meditation is enjoined as being directly a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *udgītha*; and the *udgītha* is a subordinate part of the ritual action (*karma*).

Therefore, meditation by means of that [syllable] is also an auxiliary part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*); for, as in the case of the injunction, "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel," since another qualification is heard in the injunctive sentence, it is understood that the status of being an auxiliary to the *udgītha* alone is what is to be enjoined. Furthermore, another reason is seen in the statement "from the seat of the Hotṛ priest he indeed rectifies even a poorly performed *udgītha*," where the rectification (*anusamāhāra*) of the meditation is specifically stated as a rule. For instance, an *udgītha* lacking the proper recitation is called a "poorly performed *udgītha*" (*durudgītha*).

Since there is a mention of "restoring" from the Hotṛ’s seat, it is stated that the meditation on the Udgītha must be performed as a mandatory duty; for when there is a transgression of what is necessarily to be done, a restoration must be prescribed. Thus, because this meditation is a necessary duty, its status as an auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅga*) is established. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of qualities (*guṇasādhāraṇya*) here also serves as a reason for its being an auxiliary to the ritual action.

This has also been stated in the Bhāṣya itself: "Because of the common scriptural statement—'By this [Oṃ] the threefold knowledge proceeds; one causes [the Adhvaryu] to announce with 'Oṃ', one recites the Śastra with 'Oṃ', and one chants the Udgītha with 'Oṃ'—it is understood that there is a combination of meditations on the Praṇava, which is the substratum of meditation and possesses the qualities of meditation. Thus, he refutes the reasons for the objection in their respective order so that they may not stand. Let it be that no fruit is mentioned in its own sentence.

Furthermore, the principle [established] regarding the nature of being made of *parṇa* wood and so forth would not apply here, because there exists a much clearer reason for establishing that [meditation] has human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). In the sentence concerning the *parṇamayī* [ladle], there is a statement in the present tense; and in the sentence, "Whatever one performs with knowledge," there is likewise a statement in the present tense. On the basis of such similarity, it is not established that the meditation on the *udgītha* lacks human purpose like the [nature of] being made of *parṇa* wood.
This is because, by the use of the instrumental case in the phrase, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," its status as a means to a result is indicated.

Because it is more clearly expressed, the meditation on the *udgītha* has human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) as its very aim; however, because there is an absence of a specific case-ending that establishes the status of being a means to a result for the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood, it has only the status of being a subsidiary part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*). This is what he states with the word "clearly" (*spaṣṭa*). Here, in the sentence "Whatever one performs with knowledge," knowledge is seen to be clearly a means to the result. Therefore, there is a difference from the passage concerning the *parṇa*-wood ladle.

Previously, it was stated that because of the accusative case-ending in the scriptural text "One should meditate on the Udgītha," meditation is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the Udgītha; he refutes that with the words "tādarthyam" (being for the sake of that). Here, the scriptural mention of the ritual action does not convey subordination in the sense of being for the sake of that [action]. He states the reason for this: "because it merely takes that as its locus and support. The meaning is that here the scriptural mention of the ritual action merely takes the Udgītha as the locus or support for the meditation, which is itself for the sake of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); it does not state that the meditation is a subordinate part of the ritual action.

You have stated that the mention of a remedy for the failure of knowledge—on account of a poorly performed *udgītha*—is a reason for its being an auxiliary to ritual action; however, he says that even this reason is established otherwise: "In the case of the failure of knowledge. That statement of a remedy following the mention of the poor performance of the *udgītha* due to the failure of knowledge is indeed appropriate only in connection with one who desires the fruit of that [knowledge].

The meaning is this: for that qualified person who, having desired the fruit of knowledge—such as vigor and so forth—in the *udgītha* which is a subsidiary part of the ritual (*karma*), begins the knowledge but does not perform it correctly, it is for that very qualified person alone that the "retrieval from the Hotṛ’s seat" is prescribed; it is not, however, for every qualified person who performs the *udgītha* as a subsidiary part of the ritual. Therefore, it is not [the case that it applies to all].

The status of the *udgītha* meditation as a subsidiary part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*) is established. Here, the syntactical connection of the words is as follows: in the context of one who desires such qualities as greater vigor (*vīryavattara*) which constitute the fruit of the meditation, it is indeed appropriate that there is a statement regarding the bringing together [of the priests] when the knowledge is lost at the seat of the Hotṛ priest. As for what was said—that the meditation is a subsidiary part of the *praṇava* because the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the *praṇava* accompanied by the meditation, and because of the statement regarding its following along with the three Vedas (*trayī*)—he says "the Savior" (*tāra*) to show that this too is not the case.

The name "Tārā" (the Savior) is to be used in the *sopāsana* (contemplative) context because it follows [from the root] and because it recurs throughout all three Vedas. Nevertheless, it is not a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the contemplation; for although contemplation serves a human purpose as a means to achieve results such as greater efficacy (*vīryavattara*), it can still be appropriately applied as a hymn of praise (*stotra*). This is the meaning.

One might object: "Was not all this collection of matters already required to be stated previously in the context of the Udgītha-vidyā? For what purpose is it being stated here, having left its proper place? Anticipating this doubt, the author says: "Of that which was to be stated before. The underlying intention here is as follows: the exposition of the limbs (aṅgas) of the knowledge of Brahman will be carried out in the subsequent section (pāda); for the sake of that connection, the consideration of the relationship between the limb and the principal (aṅga-aṅgitva) has now been performed at the end of the section. Thus, there is no fault of being misplaced.

Having stated the topics, he now sets forth the distinctions among their primary meanings by declaring "the unity of knowledge" (*vidyaikya*). In the first topic, there is the unity of knowledge; following this, there is the division of the two *udgītha* knowledges. Thus, in due order, there is the oneness of the *prāṇa* knowledge. In all these knowledges, bliss and so forth—which are attributes defining the essential nature—follow along with that nature itself. There is the vision of the reality of the abode of *prāṇa*. There is the unity of the *Śāṇḍilya* knowledge. And there is the distinct placement of the word "day" (*ahaḥ*) and the word "I" (*aham*).

The restriction of the location for those possessing qualities such as the *sambhṛti* [meditations]; the distinction between the *puruṣavidyā* [meditations]; and the status of the mantras beginning with "śannaḥ" as being subsidiary to the study [of the Veda].

The mutual connection between abandonment (*hāna*) and the means thereto (*upāya*), as well as the appropriate time for those two; likewise, the commonality of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) across all meditations (*vidyā*); the association of qualities such as "not gross" (*asthūlatā*) and so forth in all meditations; the mutual transposition of attributes heard in various texts concerning different disciples; the unity of the *dahara-vidyā*s; the injunction regarding the fruit of qualities in a meditation based on a vision of the *udgītha*; the recurrence of the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) in all meditations on qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*); and the conclusion that Nārāyaṇa is the one to be known through all the higher meditations.

The *manaścit* and other such [altars] consist of knowledge (*vidyā*) and enter into the sacrifice composed of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-kratu*). The Knower (*kṣetrajña*), however, is to be meditated upon as pure alone. There is an injunction for meditation regarding all the *udgītha* and other elements that have become auxiliary parts of ritual action. In the Vaiśvānara-vidyā, there is worship of the whole [body] as a single unit. Now, concerning the diversity of knowledges: there is an option (*vikalpa*) among those knowledges whose purpose is liberation. It was stated with firm reasoning that even for one who has already attained full liberation, the meditation on the *udgītha* remains an unrestricted duty.
Thus ends the third quarter of the third chapter.

In the *Guṇopasaṃhārapāda*, the exposition of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)—which serves as the means to liberation—was completed; now, the exposition of ritual action (*karman*), which constitutes an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of that knowledge of Brahman, is undertaken. This is the logical connection (*saṅgati*). An objection is raised: "In the previous section (*pūrva-kāṇḍa*), rituals were expounded as means for attaining worldly fruits such as heaven and self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); how, then, can they be auxiliary limbs of the knowledge of Brahman? Furthermore, how does the exposition of them constitute a reconciliation (*samanvaya*) with the Vedānta within this section on the auxiliaries of knowledge? Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the following resolution: "Karma... [and so forth].

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: having first considered ritual action (*karman*), it was stated immediately after the inquiry into action that Brahman is the object of inquiry, in the sūtra: "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*). In this *pāda*, the statement that ritual actions are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*) is redundant because it is a repetition. Furthermore, it is contradictory because ritual actions are means for achieving results that are opposed [to liberation]. This is what he says: "Because of the statement that they are to be abandoned in many ways."

"Neither by action nor by progeny," and "For these forms of sacrifice are but frail rafts"—thus it is stated that actions are indeed to be abandoned. To refute this raised objection, he says, "Not so. He demonstrates the manner of refutation by dividing it into two parts, beginning with "It is action itself. Indeed, those very actions which are enjoined for other results are themselves enjoined as auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*) through a different application; thus, their status as auxiliaries is established.

Likewise, there exist many other actions—such as meditation upon, worship of, and prostration before the pair of feet of the Supreme Person—which, although not specifically enjoined for the attainment of heaven and the like, are established by the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇa, the authoritative Āgamas rich in *sattva*, and the conduct of the virtuous; the purpose of commencing this chapter is to establish its meaningfulness by investigating the manner in which these constitute auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) of knowledge (*vidyā*).

Here too, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: action alone—such as sacrifice and the like—is that very action endowed with qualities such as the renunciation of attachment to fruits and agency; being distinguished by the distinct applications established by authoritative sources such as the *Bhagavadgītā*, it is differentiated from desire-driven action (*kāmyakarman*). Thus, it becomes the cause for the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, what is described under the alternative name "the dharma of cessation" (*nivṛttidharma*) would indeed be a meritorious deed (*sukṛta*).

Likewise, since acts such as salutation—which are well-known from the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other sources as causes for the accomplishment of knowledge—are also the dharma of cessation (nivṛttidharma), this is perfectly consistent: the entire collection of logical principles concerning the limbs of knowledge is established by demonstrating the specific distinctions between these two types [of dharma].

In this context, for the disciple who does not know which things are to be abandoned and which are to be accepted, the Lord explains the distinction by demonstrating the specific modes of what is to be relinquished and what is to be adopted, beginning with the word "tyāga" (renunciation). For one established in the knowledge of Brahman, the renunciation of desire-driven actions (*kāmya-kriyā*) must indeed be performed; that is to say, of all unworthy actions that are of the nature of sin. Having stated the abandonment of prohibited and desire-driven acts by their very nature, He now speaks of the abandonment of attachment to results and the sense of agency even regarding obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, using the phrase "of the notion of being dependent solely on oneself."

This is the renunciation of agency, because of the abandonment within oneself of the notion of being an agent independent of God. He also states the renunciation of possession with the words "unconditioned" (*anupādhika*). The notion of one's own interest as subservient to the Supreme Self is not contradictory; however, the notion of one's own interest as independent is contradictory—this is what he specifies by the term "unconditioned."

The idea is this: just as the maintenance of royal servants and others is for the sake of the king and not for their own sake, so too, for those who know the inner self (adhyātmavid), the accomplishment of the knowledge of reality and so forth is not for their own sake, but rather solely for the sake of the excellence of the Supreme Self, who is their own subordinate (śeṣin). For the talk of those who know the truth is that the ornament of a devoted wife is indeed for the sake of her husband and not for her own sake. Therefore, by virtue of being subordinate to the Supreme Self—as described in the phrase "the Lord of the Self of the universe"—those who know the truth bring about their own excellence as well.

By the phrase "here [in] the Gītā," it is stated that this is what is propounded by the Bhagavadgītā. Having thus described what is to be abandoned, he now shows, by distinguishing it, what is to be adopted even for the wise: "here. He declares in this section (the fourth chapter) that non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and so forth—which are of the nature of observances (*niyama*), causes for the destruction of sin, common to all classes of people, as well as those specifically prescribed for particular castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*)—constitute the state of being ancillaries to meditation (*upāsti*).

Regarding this, the connection between the sections is stated in the Commentary: "In the preceding section, an inquiry was conducted concerning the unity or diversity of meditations, with the result being whether there is a combination or non-combination of their qualities. Now, it is considered whether the human goal arises from the meditation itself, or from the ritual action that is an auxiliary to the meditation. By this, the distinction is shown that the inquiry into meditation was in the previous section, while the inquiry into the auxiliaries of meditation is in this section.

In this first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the status of knowledge as the primary element (*aṅgin*) is established for the purpose of proving that ritual actions are subordinate elements (*aṅga*); thus, the primacy of this first section within this chapter (*pāda*) is established. Furthermore, in the final section concerning the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*), it was stated that the Udgītha-knowledge serves the human goal by virtue of having its own distinct fruit; now, the fact that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) serves the human goal by virtue of possessing a fruit is being established—this constitutes the logical connection of the section.

The investigation into that matter is as follows: does the human goal [arise] from knowledge itself, or from ritual action that is an auxiliary to knowledge? For that purpose, it is deliberated whether knowledge—by way of being a refinement of the self who is the performer of the sacrifice—is for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), or whether it is for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of being a means to non-return. Are such Vedāntic passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and "Having known Him thus, one transcends death" injunctions regarding results, or are they commendatory statements (*arthavāda*) regarding results?

Is the Self perceived as an object of action in the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) the individual soul (*jīvātman*), or is it the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) distinct from that? Is [the former view] supported by signs such as the observation of ritual conduct, namely, "O venerable ones, I am indeed about to perform a sacrifice"?

It is not the case that grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in statements such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) makes known that the object of meditation is the individual self (*jīvātman*). Is this indicative mark (*liṅga*) inconclusive? To this, he restates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*): "The agent," etc. There is no Brahman whatsoever that is superior to the individual self who is the agent of actions; therefore, in sacrifices and the like, the Upanishads are employed through that very cognition [of the self] and benefit [the practitioner] solely by means of the thorough knowledge of the nature of the individual self.

Thus, having restated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) expressed by the Mimamsakas in the phrase "itijñamīmāṃsakoktau," he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "jīvānyeti" (other than the individual soul). In the injunction for devotion consisting of contemplation upon Brahman as distinct from the individual soul, he declares that ritual actions (*karman*) serve as subordinate members (*aṅga*). Now, one might ask: "If the individual soul is the referent [of the Upanishads] according to valid means of knowledge, how can the Upanishads have Brahman as their referent? To this, he replies: "kṣiptānyaliṅga" (having rejected other marks). This means: "having rejected the marks of the individual soul. Those marks of the individual soul which appear—[these are what is rejected].

The meaning is that they are not [inherently] real entities because they are established as mere appearances. Anticipating the question, "In what way do such actions constitute auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)?", he says: "of those that increase *sattva*. To the question, "By what means?", he says: "by the pacification of impurity (*kaluṣa*)."

The logical connection here is as follows: rites that increase *sattva*—such as those involving injunctions regarding the attachment to fruits and the like—serve as auxiliaries (*aṅga*) to the knowledge of Brahman by increasing *sattva* through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) via the pacification of impurities. Since liberation is attained through the very knowledge of Brahman by those whose minds have been rendered stainless by the performance of pure actions, it is precisely this knowledge that constitutes the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Here, someone raises an objection: "In this manner, by means of the eleven quarters (pādas), it has been established that the Supreme Brahman alone is the ultimate reality (paratattva); how then can there be a doubt in this section regarding the individual soul (jīva) being the subject to be propounded by the Upaniṣads? To this he says: "By the quarters" (pādaiḥ). The syntactical connection here is as follows: "In this [work], by means of the eleven quarters, the Supreme Brahman alone is well-established and renowned as the object of knowledge."

Furthermore, how can the Brahma-vidyā—the cause of the manifestation [of reality]—be disturbed by insignificant sectarian marks (liṅgas) that are like letters in the sky, resembling characters written in space? To this, he gives an answer by partial acceptance, saying "It is true. This signifies acceptance of the stated point as being true; however, there is a remainder of what must be said for the sake of protecting those of immature intellect who have been agitated by arrogant scholars, so there is non-acceptance from the other half.

The meaning is this: first of all, the utterances of Dhūrta must indeed be refuted in their entirety; furthermore, it is implied that Jaimini—the preeminent disciple of Bādarāyaṇa—would find the rejection of Brahman utterly unacceptable.

In this context, he refutes, one by one, the indicative marks (*liṅga*) intended by the proponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) regarding the status of knowledge as a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*), beginning with the words "kurvanneva" and so forth. The meaning is as follows: the statement, "Only performing actions here, let him desire to live a hundred years," declares the primacy of ritual action; thus, the objection that "therefore, the knowledge of Brahman is a subsidiary part of ritual action" is already refuted as being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).

That statement of the knower of Brahman means that action must indeed be performed; it does not, however, imply that knowledge is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of action, because there is no specific indicative mark (*liṅga*) to prove that. Therefore, this sentence is merely a declaration of the obligatory conduct for the knower of Brahman. He refutes another reason as well by citing the phrase "anvārambha": "Knowledge and action follow him together" (*taṃ vidyākarmaṇī samanvārabhete*). Since this declares a necessary connection between knowledge and action for the knower of Brahman, [the opponent argues] that the knowledge of Brahman is a subordinate part of action.

Even that does not state merely the coexistence of knowledge and action; nor does it imply that knowledge is a subordinate member (*aṅga*) of action, nor that action is a subordinate member of knowledge. While such coexistence would allow either knowledge or action to attain the status of the principal member (*aṅgin*) according to the authority of the texts, here—following thousands of millions of scriptural authorities such as "by sacrifice and charity," "for by action alone one attains perfection," and "he too performed many sacrifices"—it is action alone that is the subordinate member of knowledge, and not knowledge that is the subordinate member of action.

The syntactical connection of the words is as follows: the simultaneous undertaking (*anvārambha*) along with both wisdom (*dhī*) and action (*kriyā*) would not restrict knowledge and action to either being subordinate (*aṅga*) or principal (*aṅgin*). He refutes the third reason also held by the opponent [the Mīmāṃsakas] with the phrase "preceded by knowledge" (*vidyāpūrvam*). Having rejected action devoid of knowledge by the passage, "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable," and having referred to action preceded by knowledge by the passage, "he who knows it," the text teaches the attainment of the state of a *brāhmaṇa* as the fruit in the words, "he is a *brāhmaṇa*"; therefore, knowledge is a subordinate factor of action.

And this statement declares that the ritual action which is an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman must be performed only after the prior attainment of the knowledge of Brahman; it does not, however, declare that the knowledge of Brahman is an auxiliary to ritual action, as has been stated in various places. He explains that very point with the words, "For this is not...": in the passage, "O Gārgī, having known this very Imperishable," it is precisely the knowledge produced by the Vedānta texts that is mentioned as being useful for practice; therefore, the meaning is that this sentence does not refer back to a knowledge consisting of the meditation on Brahman.

Therefore, the knowledge of Brahman is not a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Alternatively, having raised the objection that the knowledge [of Brahman] is a subsidiary part of ritual action based on the passage, "Having studied the Veda in the house of a teacher," it is stated that even this refers merely to the study of the Veda and so forth, and not to the knowledge of Brahman; thus, "Not indeed this" [is said]. Even if the knowledge of Brahman were not a subsidiary part of ritual action for these reasons, one might still object: "Let it be a subsidiary part of ritual action, since the *udgītha* knowledge is enjoined as such. Anticipating this, he says "And not... to show that this too has already been refuted.
Thus, by refuting the collection of reasons intended by the opponent, the meaning is that action alone is a constituent part of knowledge.

Having analyzed the position of the opponent who asserts that knowledge (*vidyā*) is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karma-aṅga*), [the author] refutes it with the words "svādhyāya... (regarding Vedic study). The alternative options are as follows: Is it the mere study of the Veda that you designate as "knowledge"? Or is it the grasping of the mass of syllables produced by that study? Or is it the hearing of the *Śārīraka-mīmāṃsā* (Vedānta) produced by that? Or is it the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedāntic passages augmented by that? Or is it the meditation on Brahman produced by that, through the process of continuous reflection (*manana*)? Among these, he demonstrates the refutation of the first position with the words "svādhyāya...": "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*).

Thus, study is enjoined solely for the purpose of acquiring the mass of syllables; it is not enjoined as a subsequent limb for the sake of performing subsequent rites. Regarding this, he provides an example accepted by the Karma-kāṇḍa: "like the establishment of the sacred fires" (ādhānavat). For the establishment of the fires is enjoined for the sake of accomplishing the fires themselves, and not for the sake of performing subsequent rites. Even in the second alternative—that it is for the purpose of acquiring the mass of syllables—since that is well-established as being subordinate to the act of hearing [the Veda], there remains nothing further to be said regarding it.

The fourth position—that it is the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedānta texts—remains; regarding that, he states the answer: "It is a subsidiary part of knowledge" (*vidyāṅgam*). Let the thorough comprehension of the meaning of the Vedānta texts be a subsidiary part of the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*) alone, because they share the same object and because [the former] is dependent [on the latter]. It is not, however, a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karman*), due to the absence of mutual dependence between them. Anticipating the objection that "knowledge produced by the [Vedānta] sentence is itself the knowledge of Brahman, so it is inconsistent to say that the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman comes from the knowledge of Brahman, as this would involve the fallacy of self-dependence" (*ātmāśraya*), he refutes it with the words: "That which exceeds... (*yadadhika*).

Knowledge consisting of meditation (*upāsanā*) is indeed superior to the knowledge produced by the [Vedic] sentence. For the knowledge produced by the sentence is indirect (*parokṣa*) and occurs only once, serving as a cause for reflection (*manana*). Meditation, however, through daily practice, acquires excellence, continues until death, culminates in direct perception (*aparokṣajñāna*), and leads directly to the attainment of Brahman. How then could the performance of ritual action be established by that [meditation], such that the knowledge of Brahman would become a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of ritual action? He says "no," adding: "merely the knowledge of the eternal Self. This refers to the rituals being performed by those well-versed in the dharma of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*).

For it is precisely the knowledge of an eternal self distinct from the body that is required; and that is already established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* (the section on ritual action). However, the knowledge of Brahman—which is to be accomplished by the *Brahmakāṇḍa* (the section on Brahman)—is indeed contrary to those intent upon the duties of active engagement (*pravṛttidharma*), because it is the cause for their renunciation. Therefore, the fifth position remains as the only alternative. Yet even that is not tenable, because there is no possibility of the meditation on the Supreme Brahman—which is to be practiced solely by those free from passion—becoming a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the rituals that lead to results such as heaven. Consequently, the status of knowledge (*vidyā*) as a subordinate part of ritual action is not established.

Furthermore, if you say out of delusion that the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmavidyā*) is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), then that is merely the prattle of a madman. If the knowledge of Brahman were an auxiliary part of optional rites, how then is the renunciation of optional rites heard of everywhere among those who know the Self (*adhyātma*) for one established in the knowledge of Brahman?
