For if one abandons the rite that is to be performed as an auxiliary to knowledge, there would be a loss of the primary element (*pradhānalopa*); yet if it is not abandoned, there is a contradiction with the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establish its necessity to be relinquished.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: if even this knowledge of the Supreme Brahman were an auxiliary (aṅga) to those optional rites (kāmyakarman) propounded in the earlier section [of the Veda], then how could there be a renunciation of optional rites when the qualified person (adhikārī) is one who is proficient in the knowledge of Brahman along with that [auxiliary] knowledge?

He states the refutation of the view that knowledge (*vidyā*) is a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karma-aṅgatva*) with the words "not a subsidiary part" (*nāṅgam*). This is the meaning: Is the status of knowledge as a subsidiary part of ritual action established by one of the means of proof such as direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth? Or is it without any such means of proof? In the latter case, everything would be a subsidiary part of everything. In the former case as well, this is not so; for no scriptural statement is observed that establishes knowledge as a subsidiary part of ritual action. Nor is it established by an indicative mark (*liṅga*), since such a mark is also not observed. Nor is it established by syntactical connection (*vākya*), position (*sthāna*), or name (*samākhyā*), because these too are not perceived.

Only one point remains to be addressed, and he says "not so" (*na hi*) to show that even that does not exist. If the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) were enjoined with reference to an agent qualified for ritual action, then its status as a subsidiary part of ritual action (*karmaśeṣatva*) would have to be admitted; but since that is not the case, how could the knowledge be a limb of ritual action? Now, one might object that because austerity, visiting sacred fords, and other such practices are enjoined specifically for those established in the knowledge of Brahman, this knowledge must be a subsidiary part of those respective duties. Anticipating this doubt, he says "it may be," indicating that such a view is a contrary assumption.

It should not be said that knowledge is merely an auxiliary (aṅga) to those various ritual actions, for such a conception would be contrary to fact. For Vyāsa, Parāśara, and others who were devoted to austerity, pilgrimage, and so forth, it is evident that knowledge alone was primary and ritual action was secondary; thus all of them attained their goals. Accordingly, it is revealed in scripture: "By sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting, the Brāhmaṇas seek to know [Brahman]."

"This man is an actor, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman"; "For by action alone did Janaka and others attain perfection"; "When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, then knowledge arises"—such a collection of statements exists by the thousands. Therefore, the conclusion of the wise is that action alone is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of knowledge. Furthermore, if knowledge were an auxiliary limb of sacrifices and other rituals, then knowledge would surely perish in the case of those who have sublimated their vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), due to the absence of sacrifices and other such rituals.

If there is no status as a subordinate member (*aṅga*), what is the use of this fruitless status? Or, if it does possess fruitfulness, how can its status as a subordinate member be postulated? In that case, we shall simply abandon the stage of life (*āśrama*) of those whose vital seed is drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*); and for those established in that stage, we shall consider even their knowledge to be merely imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). Anticipating this objection, he provides the answer with the words "by the Jābālas. The rule regarding those whose vital seed is drawn upward is recited by the Jābālas. Likewise, the stage of life of those whose vital seed is drawn upward is mentioned here and there by other readers of the Śruti, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.

The stage of life (āśrama) of the forest-dwellers must also be accepted, as must their knowledge of Brahman in accordance with authoritative sources; furthermore, because they lack rituals such as sacrifices, the notion that knowledge is merely a supplement to ritual action must also be set aside. Now, one might object: "All of this is merely a restatement (anuvāda), not an injunction (vidhi). Therefore, the stage of life for those of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) lacks a foundation in authoritative proof. Anticipating this doubt, the author provides the rebuttal: "Therefore, there is attainment [of authority]."

The meaning is this: since the collection of means of knowledge currently perceived cannot be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) without a preceding statement (*purovāda*) to support it, a preceding statement must be postulated through the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*); thus, the scriptural authority (*prāmāṇikatva*) of that *āśrama* is established. Alternatively, even if these were not restatements, they would still be authoritative because their subject matter is not already established by other means.

This is the meaning of the words here: if these were restatements, the "attainment" (*prāpti*)—that is, the expression of a preceding statement—would have to be accepted; however, since their subject matter is unestablished, these very sentences are themselves the authorities.

[Objection: Surely, an attainment [of a stage of life] can only be postulated in the absence of a subverting authority (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). However, a subverting authority does indeed exist: "He who causes the fire to be removed is indeed a deserter from the gods. Therefore, one might suspect that there is no stage of life for those of perpetual chastity (*ūrdhvaretas*). Anticipating this, he states the refutation: "The prohibition of that [refers to one who has passions]. The prohibition against abandoning the sacred fires applies only to one who possesses passion (*sarāga*). For it is well known in all the *Smṛtis*, *Itihāsas*, and *Purāṇas* that one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) may abandon the stages of life such as studentship and adopt the final stage of life. Moreover, this is seen to be entirely beyond dispute in the *Śrutis* recited by Jābāla and others.

Previously, having taken as the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) the fact that the state of being "established in Brahman" was merely restated for the sake of praise, it was established that there is indeed an injunction regarding the two stages of life (āśramas). In this same manner, now, on the occasion of praise, a doubt arises as to whether the passages establishing the state of being the "highest essence" (rasatama) are intended for praise or not; from this doubt, the prima facie view is raised—this constitutes the incidental connection (prāsaṅgikī saṅgatiḥ) of this section.

One might object: "Has this context concerning the *udgītha* not already been established previously? For what purpose is it stated again? Anticipating this doubt, the Commentator himself has explained the difference between the two sections dealing with the *udgītha* based on the distinction in their purposes: "Having accepted that the subject matter established here is intent upon meditation (*upāsana*), it was stated [previously] that there is no rule regarding the employment of meditation within rituals, because meditation serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). The meaning is this: here the purport is on meditation itself, whereas previously the purport was on the lack of a rule for employing [meditation] within rituals.

The investigation into that matter concerns such passages as: "This eighth [syllable], which is the Udgītha, is the most flavorful of flavors, the highest, the supreme, the most excellent. Are these sentences intended merely for the purpose of praising the Udgītha and other parts of the Sāman, or do they intend to enjoin the meditation (dṛṣṭi) upon the Udgītha and others as being the "most flavorful"? For that purpose, it is deliberated whether it is more reasonable to rely on these words as being explanatory praises (arthavāda), or to regard them as having the nature of injunctions (vidhi). In this regard, does the quality of "novelty" (apūrvatva) lead one to understand the presence of an injunction, or not?

Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "juhvādi" (beginning with the *juhū* ladle). [The opponent argues: "This very *juhū* is the heavenly world, and the *āhavanīya* fire," and so forth; thus, even the description of the *rasatama* (the most flavorful) and other such qualities should be regarded merely as praise for the *udgītha* and other elements that are constituent parts of the sacrifice, just like the praise of the *juhū* and other implements. He refutes the prima facie view with "maivam" (not so). He explains the refutation itself as follows:

Regarding the phrase "tattat" (this and that): if this sentence were situated within the very context of the injunctions for the *udgītha* and so forth, then it would take the form of an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) intended to glorify what has already been enjoined. Consequently, by virtue of not being separated from that context, it would not be considered an *arthavāda*. Furthermore, in the immediate vicinity of this sentence, the injunctions for those respective meditations (*dṛṣṭi*) are observed; this is not the case with sentences concerning the *juhū* ladle and so on, because they are studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*) injunctions.

Therefore, in a case where something has been enjoined for its own sake and is not prescribed as a subordinate element (aṅga) to anything else—as in the case of the meditation on the Udgītha which yields a fruit, expressed by the text, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful"—it is appropriate that it be understood as an injunction (vidhi), and not as a mere explanatory passage (arthavāda). On the other hand, the quality of being made of *parṇa*-wood and so forth has been enjoined for another purpose; furthermore, because it lacks a verbal suffix indicating its status as a means to a result, it is devoid of a fruit. Thus, it was already stated previously that in such cases there can be no injunction—this is the intended meaning.

He establishes, through arguments, that the texts are indeed intent upon injunctions (*vidhiparatva*), for the sake of clear understanding, beginning with the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*). The meaning is as follows: by one who asserts that there is no intent toward injunction, is it meant here that these passages are merely restatements (*anuvāda*), or that they are intent upon praising what is to be enjoined? Neither case is possible, because there is no prior attainment [of the object]. For a restatement could only be assumed here if the injunction of something already qualified by attributes such as being the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) had already occurred previously.

In that same way, one might also imagine it to be a mere eulogy; however, since there is no attainment [of the fruit] here, neither of the two can be imagined. For neither can a superimposition be established, nor can there be a eulogy of something else—such as "the most flavorful" (*rasatamatva*)—that is being superimposed upon another. Anticipating the objection, "But in various other instances, both are indeed seen to be imagined; why then is this not accepted here?", he says: "It is logical" (*yuktā*).

"In accordance with the principle that 'because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction, [passages] must serve the purpose of praising the injunctions,' this interpretation is appropriate only when it is established that they constitute a single syntactical unit with an injunction; since such a necessity does not exist here, this particular interpretation is not tenable. The meaning is that in this case—concerning the passages enjoining the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) on being the 'most flavorful' (*rasatama*) and so forth—there is no such interpretation, because there is an absence of attachment to an injunction, that is, an absence of the contingency of forming a single syntactical unit with an injunction."

If it is argued that even though there is no injunction here, this sentence should be extracted and interpreted as being for the purpose of praise in another place where an injunction exists, [the author] says "no" to that as well: "In a case where there is no other way, that must be accepted by force. For the assumption of extraction (utkarṣa) is indeed to be accepted by force only in a subject matter devoid of any other recourse; but here there is a recourse, because the injunction of the meditation (dṛṣṭi) on [the Self] as the "most flavorful" (rasatama) and so forth—which has an unprecedented (apūrva) object—is established. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, this sentence is recited in the midst of many injunctions for the purpose of establishing the meditative vision (dṛṣṭi) of being the "most flavorful" (rasatama) and so forth; therefore, by the force of its association with them, it is logical that this sentence has the nature of an injunction itself—thus he says, "in the midst."

In this regard, having restated the argument intended by the opponent, he refutes it with the words "vidyārthatve" (if it were for the sake of knowledge). You have indeed asserted that the statement beginning with "This is the essence of essences" is solely for the purpose of knowledge and not for the purpose of praise; however, that is not tenable. Even if it were for the sake of knowledge, its purpose as praise is perfectly appropriate, because qualities such as being the "essence of essences," which do not actually exist [in the object], are mentioned here for the sake of visualization (*dṛṣṭi*).

The opponent's position is that this sentence is solely for the purpose of praise, because it describes something non-existent. To show that this is incorrect, he says, "It is improper. He states the reason for this: "Because of deviation in the case of injunctions regarding meditative visions (*dṛṣṭi*). This means there is an inconsistency in the injunctions regarding meditative visions. In injunctions such as "One should know oneself as Garuḍa," there is indeed the mention of something non-existent, yet they are accepted as being intent on injunction (*vidhipara*). Therefore, since there is no rule that the mention of something non-existent cannot be intent on an injunction, this [argument of the opponent] is indeed inconsistent.

[The opponent objects: "But surely, even if there is a deviation in the reasoning 'because of the mention of what is non-existent,' there would still be doubt; for when there is a deviation, it brings about doubt precisely because it fails to establish the intended meaning. Therefore, regarding the passage concerning 'being the essence of aesthetic flavor' (rasatamatva) and so forth, there would indeed be doubt as to whether it is an injunction or a praise. To this, [the author] says, "Now, moreover" (*atha ca*), asserting that this is merely the talk of a child. He makes manifest the childish nature of that talk with the words, "eternal" (*nitya*).

In this regard, there is this dilemma: do you mean that doubt would be eternal, or rather that it persists as long as no specific determining factor is perceived? Regarding the first case, he says "eternal," because if doubt were eternal, there would be a total lack of authority for the Vedas. Even when a determining factor is perceived, an eternal doubt remains easily established. Regarding the second position—that let there be doubt, and that such doubt is removed by the perception of specific characteristics—he states the fault with the word "reasoning."

"When the mode of being [of a thing] is to be known, the mode of being of the authoritative statement consists precisely in the critical investigation of the method (*nyāya*)," according to the statement: "Mīmāṃsā will fulfill the portion concerning the 'how-to' (*itikartavyatā*). Thus, when the method that supports the statement is intended to be determined here, the words become fruitful; for instance, the passage "Whatever one knows through knowledge" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10), which is understood to be purposeful, serves solely as an injunction for the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of being the essence of all (*rasatama*), and is not merely a eulogy.

This is the meaning: one should not offer a reply to those who are incapable of reflecting upon statements supported by reasoning (*nyāya*). However, for those capable of such reflection, it is established that statements such as "the state of being the essence of aesthetic flavor" (*rasatamatva*) are intended solely for the purpose of enjoining a meditative vision (*dṛṣṭi*) of that state. Herein lies the syntactical connection: the claim that, even if [a passage] is for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārthatva*), praise alone is appropriate because it proclaims something non-existent, is incorrect. For there is no deviation from the fact that such passages constitute mere praise when they enjoin a meditative vision, such as "the Hotṛ priest should know himself as Garuḍa."

If it is argued that there would then be a doubt as to whether this is a praise (stuti) or an injunction (vidhi), that is the talk of a child; for if one were to accept perpetual doubt regarding the meaning of the Veda, the Veda itself would lose its authority. However, if one accepts that doubt is removed by the perception of specific distinguishing features (viśeṣadarśana), then such a perception exists here as well, because many logical reasons (yukti) that determine the meaning of a sentence—serving as the procedural means (itikartavyatā) for deciding the sense—are present here. Therefore, the meaning is that it is indeed an injunction, and not merely a praise.

Here too, the connection is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). For in the preceding section, having raised as the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that passages such as "the most savory" (*rasatama*) are intended for mere praise, it was established that they are instead intended for meditation (*upāsanā*). Similarly, a doubt arises as to whether narrative accounts (*ākhyāna*) such as those concerning Pratardana and others are to be understood as being for the sake of praise, or rather for the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the ritual recitation during the horse sacrifice). To that end, the inquiry proceeds with the following texts: "Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, indeed approached the beloved abode of Indra," and "Śvetaketu, the son of Āruṇi, existed [as a youth]..."

Regarding such narratives situated within the Vedānta texts, the question arises whether they are intended for the *pāriplava* recitation or for the purpose of enjoining meditative knowledge (*vidyā*). To that end, it is investigated whether all narratives are to be employed in the *pāriplava*, or only those such as the accounts of Manu and others. Is the term "narratives" (*ākhyāna*) in the phrase "they recite the narratives" (*ākhyānāni śaṃsanti*) intended to refer to all narratives, or is it intended to refer specifically to the narratives of Manu and others?

Does the mention of a specific detail—namely, "King Manu Vaivasvata"—in that very context lead one to understand that the word *ākhyāna* (narrative) refers specifically to that [particular narrative], or not? Here, the opponent raises the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that all narratives have the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the ritual recitation for the horse-sacrifice), on the strength of the injunction: "They recite the narratives" (*ākhyānāni śaṃsanti*). This is expressed by the words "vidyāsu" (regarding the knowledges).

The various specific narratives (ākhyāna-bhedas) such as "Pratardana, indeed... and so forth, which occur in all the *vidyās*, might—by virtue of the injunction "they recite the narratives"—be intended solely for the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the daily recitation at the horse sacrifice). This [view] he refutes with the words "they should not be. He states the reason for this: "by the injunctions of the *vidyās*. The meaning is that, because those narratives are seen to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*) with the respective injunctions of the *vidyās* read within their own specific contexts, they do not have the purpose of the *pāriplava*.

For in this case, unlike the second Śruti passage—"One should meditate on the Udgītha"—which establishes a connection between meditation and the Udgītha in general, there is no Śruti that establishes a connection with the *pāriplava* (the ritual recitation of legends) for all the narrative accounts (*ākhyānas*). There exists only the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, that context restricts the narrative account under discussion to the purpose of the *pāriplava*. Anticipating the objection, "In that case, what is the subject matter of the injunction to recite the narrative for the sake of the *pāriplava*?", he says: "Manu and so forth."

In that regard, it has been stated that let the mere narration of Manu and others serve the purpose of the *pāriplava*; thus, there is no contingency of violating the injunction due to its being purposeless. Now, one might object: "Granted that the narration of Manu and others is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) [of the rite] by virtue of the context, yet other narratives as well should become subsidiaries of the *pāriplava*. Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "by that" (*tena*).

The meaning is this: since the *pāriplava* [section] has its requirements satisfied by the narratives of Manu and others recited within its own context, and since the narratives of Pratardana and others have their requirements satisfied by their connection with the respective Brahma-vidyās recited in their own passages, the assignment of all these narratives to the *pāriplava* is without any basis of proof. As for the literal sense of the words: because the requirement [of the *pāriplava*] is already satisfied by the reason stated above, there would be no justification for assigning the narratives of Pratardana and others—which exceed those of Manu and the rest—to the purpose of the *pāriplava*.

Regarding the incidental nature of these two explained sections, it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya itself: "Two matters have been considered due to the context of praise, by way of a specific intermediate connection. Furthermore, the connection of this section with the first section is also set forth in the Bhāṣya: "It has been stated that there are celibate (ūrdhvaretas) ascetics who possess knowledge," as expressed in the sūtras beginning with "And because of the word [indicating them] among those whose vital seed is drawn up" (sūtra 3.4.17).

Now, raising the objection that since those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas) lack sacrifices and other such rites, knowledge that has them as its constituent parts cannot possibly exist for them, [the author] says: "Thus. The investigation into the meaning of this is as follows: Do wandering mendicants (parivrājakas) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman or not? And is it the case that, according to passages such as "they desire to know," knowledge has sacrifices and the like as its constituent parts, or rather that it has the duties enjoined by the [specific] stage of life (āśrama) as its constituent parts?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether such statements as, "Established in Brahman, he attains immortality," "And those who in the forest worship with faith and austerity," and "Desiring this world alone, mendicants go forth into the homeless state," establish a connection between knowledge (vidyā) and those whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), thereby making it understood that knowledge has the duties prescribed for the [specific] stages of life (āśrama) as its constituent parts—or not. Furthermore, is it possible for ritual action (karman) to produce knowledge, or not? In this regard, the author restates the doubt of the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words, "of sacrifice and so forth."

Because of the instruction that sacrifice, charity, austerity, and fasting are limbs (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman—namely, "by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, by fasting"—there would be no eligibility for the primary meditation (*upāsana*), which is the principal (*aṅgin*), among those who have renounced sexual intercourse (*ūrdhvaretas*) and are thus ineligible for sacrifice and the like. This is because, due to the deficiency of the limbs, there is an absence of excellence in the principal, which results in the failure of its capacity as a means to the fruit. He rejects this position with the word "no" (*na*). He states the reason for this in the phrase "of many kinds" (*bahuvidhā*).

The meaning is this: because it is stated that various general duties, such as truthful speech and the like, as well as specific duties pertaining exclusively to one's own stage of life (*āśrama*), are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, the application of knowledge (*vidyā-yoga*) for all four stages of life, as well as the injunctions (*vidhi*) that establish it, are heard in the scriptures; the sense is that they are set forth by the Śruti itself. He says, "And it is also recorded in Smṛti," to show that it is not only the Śruti [that supports this], but there is also Smṛti. For the primary purpose of the Smṛtis is generally the prescription of duties for the four stages of life.

Therefore, all four stages of life (āśramas) possess the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman through the performance of their respective duties. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, how is the specific renown of the renunciate stage (saṃnyāsāśrama) as the 'liberation stage' (mokṣāśrama) to be justified?"—the author provides the answer with the word "generally" (prāyeṇa). The meaning is this: for householders who are overwhelmed by many disturbances such as sons and grandsons, one-pointed concentration on the knowledge of Brahman is generally destroyed; however, for some, by the power of their fortune, such one-pointedness is indeed achieved.

In this way, for those who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*) and forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) may or may not be fulfilled, because, like renunciants (*saṃnyāsin*), they lack absolute one-pointedness. However, for the renunciant, because he has abandoned all possessions, the qualification for the knowledge of Brahman will generally be fully perfected; therefore, it is precisely in him that the well-known status of being in the stage of liberation (*mokṣāśrama*) is appropriately applied.

Previously, it was stated that for those who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas), there is no dependence on the kindling of fires and so forth; now, however, it is stated that for householders, there is dependence on rituals such as sacrifice. Since this connection is evident, it is not explicitly mentioned in the Commentary (Bhāṣya). The inquiry into its meaning, however, is as follows: Does a householder who performs sacrifices and other rites possess qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, or is it one devoid of such rites? To determine this, it is investigated whether ritual acts such as sacrifice are auxiliary parts (aṅga) of knowledge or not. Specifically, does the scriptural text "by sacrifice" enjoin ritual acts like sacrifice as being auxiliary to knowledge, or not?

Is it possible for action to produce knowledge, or not? Here, the author sets forth the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view with the words "abandoned. [The opponent argues: Since the practice of worshipping the Supreme (parabhajana) is observed even among those of perpetual celibacy (ūrdhvaretas) who have abandoned duties such as sacrifice, knowledge might exist even in a householder without depending on sacrifices and other rites. He refutes this with the words "this is an unconsidered statement. He demonstrates the method of refutation with the words "by sacrifice" (yajñena). For this householder, that knowledge is understood through such scriptural texts as "by sacrifice" to be accomplished by that—namely, accomplished precisely by sacrifice and the like. Now, one might object: by the texts beginning with "by sacrifice"...

In the phrase "they desire to know" (*vividiṣanti*), it is stated that sacrifices and the like are merely means for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), and not direct means for knowledge (*vidyā*). To the question, "How then can it be said that actions are means for realization? he provides the answer with the word "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*). Just as in the expression "he wishes to go by horse," the horse is a means for the act of going—which is the primary factor relative to the desire to go—so too, sacrifices and the like are means for knowledge, which is the primary factor relative to the desire to know; this is a conclusion established by logic.

Therefore, the meaning is that [the objection] must indeed be set aside in the theory that the suffix denotes the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). This is the underlying point: in the rule "after a verbal root denoting an action having the same agent, *san* is used in the sense of desire" (*dhātoḥ karmaṇassamānakartṛkādicchāyāṃ vā*), the suffix *san* is prescribed in the sense of a desire where the meaning of the verbal root itself is primary. Thus, the suffix *san* itself declares the primacy of the root-meaning; consequently, there is no contradiction in the use of *san* if one accepts that knowledge alone is the object to be accomplished through sacrifice and other means. Likewise, another example should be cited, such as "he wishes to kill with a sword" (*asinā jighāṃsati*). In the verse, the example of the foot was stated as "he wishes to go on foot" (*padbhyāṃ jigamiṣati*).

Now, in cases such as "he desires to go on foot" (*pādena jigamiṣati*), since there is no actual going, the use of the desiderative suffix (*san*) must refer solely to the root-meaning; and this absence of going is evident from perception, for the foot is not a means for the desire to go, but rather a means for the act of going itself. Therefore, due to a contradiction in meaning, let there indeed be a reversal of the application in the example; however, in instances such as "they desire to know through sacrifices and so forth" (*yajñādibhir vividiṣanti*), there is no such contradiction in meaning whatsoever.

Anticipating the opponent's intention, he refutes it with the passage beginning with "nanu" and ending with "asad. He demonstrates that the absence of a means of transition (gatyabhāva) cited by the opponent in the illustrative example applies equally to the subject under discussion (pakṣa) by stating "gatyabhāva"; thus he makes the equality explicit with the word "icchet. For instance, you claim that for one who desires to attain the inquiry into Brahman (brahmajijñāsā), the performance of ritual action (karmānuṣṭhāna) is required; however, that is not so, because desire cannot be accomplished through rituals without first knowing the distinction between the objects [of worldly action and spiritual inquiry].

If it is argued that ritual action (*karman*) is for the purpose of knowing the distinction between objects (*viṣaya*), then it would follow that action is merely for the sake of knowledge; and thus there would be a contradiction with one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) as well as a self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*), because this would undermine the very point you yourself have stated—that action is the cause of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). Alternatively, there is a logical inconsistency (*vaighaṭya*): namely, that from the performance of action arises the desire, and from the desire arises the performance of action. He explains this very inconsistency by saying "the desire to know" (*jijñāsām*).

For a person who performs ritual action with the desire to attain *jijñāsā*, knowledge is not something that was not previously desired; rather, it is indeed already desired. Therefore, the claim that *jijñāsā* is simply the desire for knowledge—that [desire] being already established beforehand—and that one who wishes to attain it performs ritual action and thereby attains it again, is inconsistent.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: for a person desiring to attain the inquiry (*jijñāsā*), knowledge is already desired; it is not that it is not so, for it is precisely for the sake of knowledge that the inquiry is sought. When it is said "for the sake of knowledge," the fact that knowledge is desired is already established. Indeed, the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is nothing other than the longing for knowledge; that [longing] is already established.

Now, it was previously argued that there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) such that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) exists only when ritual action (*karma*) has been performed, and ritual action can only be performed once the desire to know exists; however, that is not possible because knowledge differs according to its specific object. To explain: first there is knowledge in a general sense, from which arises the desire; from the desire comes the performance of ritual action; from the performance of ritual action arises a particularized desire; and from that, there follows a successive sequence of desires and knowledges. Thus, there is no fault. Having thus restated the opponent’s position, the author refutes it:

Regarding the word "nanu": this is the meaning of the term here; the action prescribed should be applied in accordance with the current desire, and not in accordance with a prior desire. To the question "What follows from that?", the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies:

The intention is as follows: if the performance of ritual action were required for the sake of following one's desires throughout one's entire life, then—since action for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) would be a constant requirement—the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*) itself would necessarily be established as the prerequisite for understanding the nature of what is to be performed; this would contradict your own established doctrine. Furthermore, since it was already stated that the production of specific forms of cognition (*dhīviśeṣa*) is necessary for the sake of establishing each subsequent desire, that [requirement] would not have been refuted by your argument. Thus he says: "not for the sake of desire" (*necchārtham*).

The meaning is this: one must admit that the existence of a specific knowledge of Brahman exists even prior to the desire [to know it]; thus, the existence of that knowledge is established by action, which proves that the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*) has already occurred. Alternatively, even if this injunction is for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), he says "for the sake of knowledge" to show that there is also an injunction regarding action for the sake of [actual] knowledge.

Granted that the performance of ritual action may be for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), nevertheless, one cannot deny that action is also for the sake of knowledge, based on such statements as: "This man who performs action is the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman"; "When the impurity has been cooked away by actions, then knowledge arises"; "Indeed, Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone"; and "He too performed many sacrifices. Therefore, it is established that the inquiry into the scriptures is preceded by the inquiry into ritual action.

Then, raising the objection as to what the status of the suffix *san* in the word "vividiṣanti" (they desire to know) might be, he extends the same principle [to this case] by saying, "by the logic of 'nididhyāsitavyaḥ'.

This is the meaning: just as in the phrase "nididhyāsitavyaḥ" (it is to be meditated upon), the use of the suffix *san* with respect to meditation expresses that the meditation is something desired, but does not mean that the desire itself is the object of injunction; likewise here too, in "vividiṣanti," the desire is not the object of injunction. Rather, it is stated that knowledge is the goal to be attained as the object of that desire. Thus, this is perfectly consistent.

The connection [of this section] is stated very clearly in the Bhāṣya itself: "In the inquiry as to whether tranquility (*śama*), self-restraint (*dama*), and so forth are also to be practiced by a householder or not. The investigation into its meaning, however, is as follows: Are tranquility and self-restraint to be adopted by a householder established in knowledge (*vidyā*) or not? Is there a contradiction between sacrifices and the like on one hand, and tranquility and self-restraint on the other, or not? And in this context, is the "tranquility" enjoined here the cessation of activity in the form of abstaining from actions other than sacrifice and the like, or is it the cessation of all activity whatsoever? Here, having set forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with the words "sacrifices and the like," etc.

This, indeed, is the summary of the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) and the established conclusion (siddhānta). The prima facie position is as follows: since ritual acts such as sacrifice consist of active engagement (*karaṇa-vyāpāra-rūpa*), whereas tranquility (*śama*) and the like consist of cessation from those acts, tranquility, self-control (*dama*), and so forth are absent in the householder. [Objection:

In that case, even for those devoted to renunciation (*pravrajyā*) and other stages of life, there would likewise be no tranquility, self-control, and so forth, because of the abundance of specific activities prescribed for each respective stage (*āśrama*). [Reply: If it is argued that tranquility, self-control, and the like are defined as cessation from activities other than those specifically enjoined [for one's stage], then such cessation exists in the householder as well, insofar as he desists from activities other than those enjoined for him.

Thus, "the complete pacification of the mind" is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). However, it has been stated that because householders are occupied with activities such as sacrifices and rituals, their faculties remain unsteady at all times; therefore, qualities such as tranquility (*śānti*) are [more difficult to attain] for them. This is also the case for those situated in the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-āśrama*), since they are engaged in the manifold duties appropriate to their respective stages of life.

If you accept all that—even though it consists of the activity of the instruments of action—on the strength of scriptural injunctions, then by the same logic, you must also endure the actions prescribed for the householder’s stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*) and so forth. If you argue that those devoted to renunciation (*pravrajyā*) and the like perform their actions only by abandoning attachment to results and the sense of agency, that is equally true for the householder;
thus, no difference is established.

It is said that [the Lord] inspires confidence in his disciples through the process observed in the world: that those qualified persons who have previously incurred offenses against the Lord attain the fruit by propitiating the Lord through the performance of rituals in the form of appropriate expiations. For in the world, servants who have committed known offenses, when repentance arises, worship their master with world-renowned means suited to their own status; thus, having gradually appeased his anger, they obtain the fruit of service.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even for us, the grace of Śrīdhara—the friend without conditions—is attained without obstacle by those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*), who are devoted to Him and whose actions, divided according to their respective duties, consist of "this must be done" and "this must not be done."

It has been stated that for those who know Brahman, tranquility and other such qualities are to be practiced. In this regard, the connection [of the present discussion] is as follows: it is now considered whether there is a specific rule regarding food as a particular form of tranquility, or not. The inquiry into that matter is as follows: Is the permission to eat all kinds of food for one who knows the Prāṇa valid at all times, or only when a threat to life arises? Does the observation of Uṣasti, the knower of Brahman, eating the leavings of another when his life was in danger indicate that the permission for a knower of the Prāṇa to eat all food is restricted to times of distress, or does it not?

Here the opponent says: "Action proceeds from scriptural injunction and cessation proceeds from scriptural injunction"—this is indeed a world-established principle that cannot be transgressed by anyone. For it is stated that one established in the knowledge of Prāṇa is fit for all food; therefore, the prohibition against eating forbidden things applies only to those other than those established in the knowledge of Prāṇa. Just as in such cases as "one should not kill," a general prohibition is determined to apply to everything except what is specifically enjoined by "one should sacrifice," so it is here as well.

He states this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words beginning "of food" (āhārasya), etc. Having restated it, he refutes it with "it is improper" (ayuktam). He establishes its impropriety with the words "as a constituent part" (aṅgatvena). Since the statement regarding the eating of all kinds of food in the Prāṇavidyā is not an injunction made as a constituent part of that knowledge, it is merely a statement of permission in cases where there is a threat to life. This very point the author of the Sūtras has explicitly stated: "And the permission for all food [is only in times of distress]. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.2.1; Brahma Sūtra 3.4.28).

In order to establish that the statement permitting all food for one established in the knowledge of Prāṇa refers specifically to the occasion of life-threatening danger (prāṇātyaya), the author employs the logic of "how much more so" (kaimutya) by showing that even for Uṣasta—who was established in Brahman and thus possessed a greatness greater than that of one established in Prāṇa—this permission was granted only in the context of life-threatening danger; this is indicated by the word "paśya" (see). As for the syntactical connection: there is no fixed restriction regarding food for the one who is the subject of the discourse on the knowledge of Prāṇa, because of the scriptural statement.

It is incorrect to argue that a prohibition against eating forbidden food, which applies generally, must necessarily be restricted upon seeing a powerful injunction; for there is no injunction [to eat such food] as a constituent part of the knowledge of the vital breath (prāṇavidyā). Furthermore, even in the case of Uṣasti, who possessed a superior majesty as a knower of the vital breath, we observe the consumption of forbidden food when there was a threat to his life—that is, in a situation where his life was at stake. Therefore, it is established by the logic of *kaimutya* (how much more so) that the statement permitting the consumption of all kinds of food within the context of the knowledge of the vital breath refers only to times of distress (*āpad*).

Regarding this, the connection [of the topic] is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It has been said that the knowledge of Brahman has sacrifices and other rites as its auxiliaries. Now, in the inquiry whether those rites—sacrifices and the like—must be performed even by one who belongs to a [particular] stage of life (āśrama) alone and is not seeking liberation, or not... The investigation into that purpose is as follows: must the duties of the stages of life, which serve as auxiliaries to knowledge, be performed even by one belonging to a stage of life alone, or not? And if these are auxiliaries to knowledge, is it possible for them to be auxiliaries to the stage of life alone, or not?

Does the contradiction between the obligatory and the non-obligatory (nitya-anitya-saṃyoga-virodha) necessarily follow if [the ritual acts] are merely auxiliary to the stage of life (āśrama), or not? Here, the author restates the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "of caste and so forth" (varṇādeḥ). By the passage beginning with "by sacrifice" (yajñena), the status of rituals such as those pertaining to caste as auxiliaries to the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) is asserted. Therefore, since there is an absence of the knowledge of Brahman in one who does not abide in Brahman, and consequently no pursuit of the rituals that are auxiliaries to that knowledge, let there simply be freedom of action (svairitva). To this, the reply is: "Not so. He states the reason for this: "Because of its obligatory nature" (nityatvasya).

Such indeed is the Tantric rule: those ritual acts which are enjoined in one place, if they are also enjoined by a specific injunction in another, their application in both places is established precisely because of the distinctness of the injunctions; this follows from the principle that an act is determined by the nature of its various injunctions.

The meaning is "due to another application" (*viniyuktyantarāt*). In this case, the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) is indeed *tantra* (simultaneous). For where, due to the identity of place, time, and so forth, separate performance is impossible, there the performance is by way of *tantra*; such is the Tantric method. To provide an example accepted for the stated point, he says "kāmya" (desirable). For it is the established rule that the *agnihotra* performed for a specific desire also effects the fulfillment of the obligatory (*nitya*) requirement. And he says "here" (*iha*), indicating that this should also be applied to the category of the obligatory among those who know the Supreme.
The meaning is that the daily practice of those who know the Self, by virtue of being an auxiliary to the knowledge of Brahman, also effects its accomplishment through a single application.

In this commentary (*bhāṣya*), the connection (*saṅgati*) has been stated: "The four orders of life (*āśramins*) possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and it has also been said that the duties of the orders are auxiliaries to that knowledge. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether those who exist outside the orders—such as widowers (*vidhura*) and others—possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman or not," the investigation into its meaning is as follows: Do widowers and others possess eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman or not? Do they have the capacity to integrate the knowledge of Brahman along with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) or not? Is it possible for the knowledge to occur even when the common duties of the orders are not observed or not? [As it is said: "By austerity... (*tapasā*).

The observation that Raikva and others were devoted to knowledge—as reinforced by scriptural injunctions such as "by means of celibacy" (*brahmacaryeṇa*)—indicates whether or not knowledge has common duties (*sādhāraṇadharma*) as its constituent parts. Here, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "In the absence of obtaining a wife. This means: one who stands in between, being devoid of an [ascetic] order (*āśrama*), in the sense of being without the renunciation appropriate for entering the stage of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka-āśrama*) due to the absence of having obtained a wife.

An objection is raised: "Since there is an absence of entitlement (*adhikāra*) in that person who is devoid of the performance of all ritual duties (*niḥśeṣakarmānuṣṭhāna*), how can there be an entitlement to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*)? He refutes this with the word "no" (*na*). Let it be that the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) are absent; nevertheless, through the general duties of the castes (*varṇadharma*) alone—endowed with the qualities of renouncing attachment to fruits, agency, and so forth, as well as self-restraint—that knowledge of Brahman indeed becomes complete with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅgā*) for that qualified person. This is not merely our own fabrication; rather, he states "in Bhīṣma and others" to show that this has been observed in cases such as Bhīṣma.

One might then ask: "In that case, why should there not be eligibility even for a Śūdra? Anticipating this, [the author] notes that since the exclusion of the Śūdra from eligibility has been observed in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, he indeed lacks eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Furthermore, while widowers and others do possess eligibility because they are seen to have many duties conducive to the practice of knowledge—such as the study of the Vedas—the Śūdra does not have such duties, as they are prohibited by numerous authorities; this is the intended meaning.

In this regard, the connection [of the topic] has been shown in the Bhāṣya itself according to the sequence of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In the inquiry as to whether or not there is eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman even for those who have fallen away from the stages of life (*āśrama*) of the perpetual student (*naiṣṭhika*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the initial position is reached that there is eligibility, because—just as in the case of the widower (*vidhura*) and others—the knowledge may be assisted by acts such as charity, which are not restricted to a specific stage of life; then it is said [in response]. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: Is there eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman for those who have fallen from the stages of life of the perpetual student and so forth, or not?

Do these [ascetics] possess the capacity to acquire the knowledge along with its constituent limbs (sāṅgavidyā), or not? Is it possible for them to attain purity through expiation (prāyaścitta), or not? Does the prescribed expiation—"If a religious student (brahmacārī) should approach a woman"—apply to all religious students, or only to those other than the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika)? Does the statement, "I see no expiation," indicate that the rule regarding expiation applies to religious students other than the lifelong student, or not?

Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "one who has ascended" (*ārūḍha*). One who has ascended to the three stages beginning with the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*), and subsequently falls from them—that in him too, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) certainly exists; the meaning is that it is assisted by his own duties (*svadharma*) which are worthy of that state, because of being so assisted. He refutes the prima facie view with "not so" (*maivam*). He establishes the reason for the refutation with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth. Even though the fallen state of a lifelong student is included among secondary sins (*upapātaka*), it is not, however, a major sin (*mahāpātaka*).

In the world, it is well known from the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and other sources that the chanting, praising, and bowing to Hari serve as the cause for the destruction of all sins, up to and including the great mortal transgressions (*mahāpātaka*). Nevertheless, one who has fallen from the state of a perpetual student (*naiṣṭhika*) and so forth has no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman, because a direct prohibition of atonement is clearly perceived in the statement: "I see no expiation. Indeed, when there is a contradiction with a scriptural statement, logic has no power.

Therefore, whether this be a minor offense (*upapātaka*) or a major sin (*mahāpātaka*), even so, there is no qualification for the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). This is what [the author] expresses by the words "that too. He states the reason for this with the phrase "because of such a prohibition" (*tādṛṅniṣedhāt*); the meaning is: by the force of the prohibitory statements that establish the lack of qualification. Although there are purifying acts such as the chanting of Hari’s names and so forth, the point is that even those only render him fit for conversation and the like, but do not grant qualification for the knowledge of Brahman.

One might object: "Is it not said that 'for one who beholds Puruṣottama from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, even great sins perish instantly, let alone minor offenses'? Thus, it is taught in various scriptures that the very act of beholding the Blessed One destroys both major and minor sins, and that Yoga itself removes the sins of one who has fallen from Yoga. Therefore, how can there be an absence of expiation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The expiation... [prāyaścittam].

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: the sages declare that for both minor offenses (*upapātaka*) and major sins (*mahāpātaka*), the contemplation of Brahman alone is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Furthermore, they declare that when a fall occurs due to the negligence of yogis, yoga itself is again the expiation. Therefore, it should not be said that even when a fall has occurred, there remains eligibility for the knowledge of Brahman through expiation. The reason for this is: "For the scripture is not to be questioned. Indeed, the course of the scripture is beyond questioning.

Whatever is stated in the scriptures must be accepted exactly as it is. Now, one might object: "The statement that the contemplation of the Lord removes all sins is itself a scripture; for one scripture does not depend upon another. Indeed, we see that even those like Ajāmila, who were engaged in many sinful acts, attained liberation. So how can it be said that there is no atonement? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "As long as one lives" (*yāvajjīvam*). The intention of the author of the Sūtras and others is that, just as in the case of Ajāmila and others, the contemplation of the Lord throughout one's entire life is the expiation even for such sins. For it is said: [The text continues with a citation: "One who remembers Kṛṣṇa even once, even if he be a slayer of a cow, a drinker of liquor, a thief of gold, or a violator of his teacher’s bed—he is liberated from all sins. Thus, the meaning is that for one who has committed great sins, there is no other means of purification than the constant remembrance of the Lord throughout one's life. Therefore, the statement that there is no atonement is made with reference to those who do not perform such lifelong remembrance. Hence, there is no contradiction. Thus it is established. End of section. 10.2.28. *Note: The final sentence provided in the source text appears to be a concluding remark by the commentator regarding the consistency of the doctrine.*
"By constant remembrance one becomes pure; by chanting one becomes as if bathed;
by prostrating oneself before him, the self becomes purified—these are the great virtues of Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, the meaning is that for such sins, the means of atonement (prāyaścitta) is the contemplation of the Blessed Lord until the end of life.

He establishes the same point through another illustration with the verse beginning "He who kills a child," and so forth: "He who kills a child, he who kills a woman, he who kills one who has come for refuge, and he who is ungrateful—even these, though purified by penances, are declared by the wise to be unworthy of association with the virtuous. For it is recorded in the Smṛtis:
'In the scriptures, expiation is seen even for those who have committed the great sins;
but for the slayer of one who has sought refuge, no expiation is seen anywhere.'"

Likewise, one should recite such statements as "there is no atonement for an ungrateful person," as well as words censuring the killing of children and women. Thus, by the force of these words and because such individuals who follow wrong paths are not accepted by those who know the inner self (adhyātmavid), the Sūtra-writers have demonstrated this. Anticipating the objection—"For what purpose does this scripture speak such harsh words that establish the absence of atonement?"—he says: "The scripture... [and so forth].

If the scripture were subject to instruction, then there would be dependence on the scripture regarding those inclined toward evil, and thus the bridge of dharma would be submerged; there would be an absence of rules governing what ought and ought not to be done. Enough with this elaboration.

Anticipating the objection—"The distinction between what is to be avoided and what is not has already been established in accordance with the limits of the scriptures; for what purpose is this being established again by the author of the Sūtras?"—he provides a reply by demonstrating a specific purpose, beginning with the words "brahmāṃśatve" (because of being a portion of Brahman).

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: according to the Śruti, "Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this that has been declared is the threefold Brahman"—although the status of being a portion of Brahman is equal for both the conscious and the unconscious, it has already been stated by the authors of the Sūtras that, due to the inequality of the qualities (guṇas) and the resulting natures of purity and impurity, there occurs the permission or prohibition of beholding, touching, and so forth, based on association with bodies such as those of Brāhmaṇas or Caṇḍālas.

Nevertheless, here again, for the sake of pacifying the agitation caused by various types of smearing (attachment), there are those who, relying on the very side of the "smearless" liars, live without belonging to any stage of life (*āśrama*); they proceed without any rules regarding what is to be done and what is not to be done, bearing only the name of "knowers of Brahman," performing what should not be done and failing to do what should be done. The use of the word "various" (*vividha*) here is intended to include such practices when they are concealed. Others, however, rely on the drama of devotion to Viṣṇu and proceed precisely with the practice of being "smearless."

Thus, for the sake of pacifying the agitation caused by various types of ointments, it was taught that even one who has correctly known the Self must observe the permissions and prohibitions regarding looking at, touching, and so forth. The meaning is this: since the Self is correctly known as being subservient to the Lord, one must simply follow His commands. And the command of the Lord consists of the Śruti and Smṛti, because the Lord Himself has said, "The Śruti and Smṛti are My very command. Therefore, especially for those who know the Truth, the performance of action according to their own specific qualification must be carried out.

This section is incidental. The connection (*saṅgati*) is that, in the context of distinguishing between those who perform meditations and those who do not, an inquiry is now made regarding the distinction between performers and non-performers of meditations such as that on the *udgītha*. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: Are meditations based on parts of the sacrifice, such as the *udgītha*, to be performed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), or are they to be performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*)? Is it logical that these have the same performer as their fruit—as is the case with meditations like that on the "small ether" (*dahara*)—or rather, that they have the priest as their performer, like the *godohana* vessel?

Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks: according to the principle that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer," it must be accepted that whoever is the enjoyer of the fruit is himself the agent. Thus, even in the meditation on the *udgītha*, the agency must be attributed to the sacrificer who is the enjoyer of the fruit, just as in meditations such as that of the "small [space]" (*dahara*), the agency of meditation belongs only to the enjoyer of the fruit. This is what he says with the words "in the case of the *udgītha* and so forth": the meditation on the *udgītha* is performed by the sacrificer alone, who is the enjoyer of the fruit.

An objection is raised: "Granted that [the *godohana* vessel] serves a fruit-bearing purpose, why is it not employed by the sacrificer (*yajamāna*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "It is possible" (*śakya*). In the case of the *godohana* and similar implements used in the act of fetching water (*praṇayana*) performed by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer is simply unable to employ the *godohana*; therefore, its use by the priest is established there. However, in the present case of the meditation on the *udgītha*, because meditation consists of the nature of the intellect (*buddhi-rūpa*), it is possible to perform the meditation even upon the *udgītha* which is performed by the priest; thus, the illustrative example is dissimilar.

Thus, because it is appropriate for the fruit to have the [Udgātṛ] as its agent, and because of the disparity with the illustrative example, he states "therefore" that the agency belongs to the sacrificer alone. He refutes the stated position with "no," providing the reason there: "because it rests upon an action performed by one who has been hired. For the Udgītha performance is that very action performed by one who has been hired through the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and the meditation (upāsana) rests upon that action.

The meaning is this: for the sake of establishing that the sacrifice, together with its auxiliary parts (*sāṅga*), becomes a cause for its fruit through performance free from obstacles, one must indeed hire a priest (*parikrīta*). In that context, without the performance of that meditation (*upāsanā*) by which the removal of obstacles occurs, the fruit of the ritual action will not be accomplished even if free from hindrances. Therefore, even in the meditation performed there for the purpose of pacifying obstacles, the agency must belong to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) alone. Regarding the point thus asserted, he provides an illustration with the words "just as others," referring to the performance [of the rule]: "One desiring cattle should fetch water in a *godohana* vessel."

The performance of all rituals at that time belongs to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) alone. Nor do we postulate this merely on the basis of reasoning; rather, we speak by relying upon scripture. For this very knowledge is restated in the passage: "Whatever one performs with knowledge" (*yadeva vidyayā karoti*). Since the agency in the *udgītha* chant belongs to the officiating priest alone, his agency as the performer of the knowledge mentioned in conjunction with the phrase "with knowledge" is likewise understood to belong to him alone. Indeed, when it is said, "Devadatta sees with his eye," the impelling of the eye does not belong to anyone other than Devadatta.
Thus, the agency in the performance of knowledge belongs to the officiating priest alone. [Objection: But...

In the case of the *godohana* vessel, since the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is capable of performing it while the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) lacks the capacity to do so, the sacrificer does not act as the agent. If it is argued that in this instance, however, the sacrificer possesses the capacity for meditation (*upāsana*), [the author] says "no," stating "possibility" (*śakyatva*). There is no rule that whatever a person has the capacity to perform must necessarily be performed by him. For if that were so, it would follow that all officiating priests, possessing the capacity to perform every rite, would be bound to perform them all. Rather, scripture itself restricts who the agent shall be.

For this is the path of logic: that he whom the scripture declares to be the agent in a particular action is alone fit to perform it. In this context, however, the scripture—in the passage, "Whatever one performs with knowledge"—shows that the agency in both the application of the *udgītha* chant and its meditation belongs solely to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Through the agency of the priest, the agency of the fruit-bearer (the patron) will also be established, because the priests have been purchased by the patron through the payment of sacrificial fees for the purpose of performing his own work. Regarding this, he also provides a worldly illustration based on the relationship between master and servant.

Indeed, the king’s servants, being supported by the king, carry out the king’s business according to the king’s command. It is a well-established path that they alone perform whatever tasks are to be done, whether they pertain to the inner circle or the outer circle. By this, it is proven that the meditations on the *udgītha* and so forth have the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) as their performers.
Previously, the status of sacrifices and the like, as well as tranquility and the like, as auxiliaries to knowledge was stated; now, however, another auxiliary is being considered.

This is the connection (*saṅgati*). Here, however, the mention of the *udgītha* and so forth is obtained through a specific connection; thus, there is no contradiction. In this context, since reflection (*manana*) has as its object a virtuous support that serves as the basis for meditation (*dhyāna*), it is distinct from sacrifices and the like, as well as from tranquility (*śama*) and the like, which do not have that as their object. Therefore, by virtue of this commonality of not having that as their object, reflection is defined subsequently after mentioning sacrifices and tranquility. The inquiry regarding its purpose is: is "silence" (*mauna*) enjoined in this sentence, or is it merely restated (*anūdyate*)?

Is "mauna" merely silence of the hands, or is it something else in the form of reflection (*manana*)? Is reflection capable of being enjoined, or not? Is there a contradiction between reflection and the scriptural injunctions for sacrifices and other rites, or not? Does reflection exclude the performance of ritual actions, or not? And does the fact that certain duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) are not mentioned in its own context or in other contexts strengthen the view that reflection excludes the performance of rituals, or not?

Does the mention of only a few [reasons] imply disregard for those not mentioned, or does it serve to indicate that there are others? In this regard, he restates the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "the state of being an object of reflection" (mantavyatve).

This, indeed, is the method of practice for those who know reality: the performance of rituals such as sacrifices is enjoined as an auxiliary to knowledge by the passage beginning with "by sacrifice," and likewise, tranquility, self-control, and so forth are enjoined by the passage beginning with "tranquil and self-controlled. Therefore, both of these are indeed auxiliaries to knowledge. Although hearing and reflection are restated by the sentence "it is to be heard and reflected upon" because they are already prompted by natural inclination (*rāga*), nevertheless, since knowledge cannot be accomplished without hearing and reflection, both of them [are required].

It is indeed a limb of that [knowledge]. Thus, the passage, "Therefore, having become disillusioned with scholarship, a Brāhmaṇa should remain in a state of childlike simplicity; and having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he then becomes a sage," prescribes that the triad beginning with scholarship is indeed a limb of the knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, it is stated by the Śruti in the words "he is a Brāhmaṇa" that one should become established in the knowledge of Brahman through these limbs, ending with sagehood, by which the knowledge of Brahman is attained.

Regarding this, someone says: "In the phrase 'then a sage' (*atha muniḥ*), meditation (*manana*) is not enjoined as something new, because meditation has already been established previously. First, there is meditation for the sake of stabilizing what was heard; immediately after that, there is another form, namely scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). Indeed, it is well-known in all the world that scholarship is an intellect capable of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*); one who has attained such an intellect is called a scholar (*paṇḍita*). Therefore, since meditation is already established and since there is no hearing of an injunction in the phrase 'then a sage,' silence (*mauna*) is not being enjoined."

This is the meaning of the words here: since the capacity for reflection (*manana*) has already been heard [in the previous section], let the statement "then a sage" (*atha muniḥ*) be a restatement (*anuvāda*) of that reflection already established previously. The meaning of "its restatement" is that it is a restatement of something already extremely well-known. He states the reason for its being a restatement with the words "some [think]": for no injunction (*vidhi*) such as "one should be a sage" is observed here; the meaning is, in the absence of an injunctive word, how can it be accepted as an injunction? Having thus restated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he refutes it with "no."

He states the reason for this rejection in the word "previously" (*pura*). This is because the state of being a scholar (*paṇḍitatva*) was already attained prior to the mention of his being a sage (*munitva*). The meaning is as follows: what is called "reflection" (*manana*) is merely the process of contemplating through logical reasoning for the sake of stabilizing what has been heard (*śravaṇa*). And that [reflection] was already accomplished even before [the attainment of] scholarship. Scholarship, moreover, is defined here as possessing an intellectual intuition (*pratibhā*) capable of extremely superior deliberation and exclusion (*ūhāpoha*), which is said to exist prior to sagehood.

Therefore, it must be accepted that this silence (*mauna*), which is described hereafter as attainable through various specific auxiliary factors and is distinct from [mere scholarship], is prescribed as another internal limb (*antaraṅga*) of knowledge. The word "ūha" (inference/reflection) clearly demonstrates that scholarship is something other than hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*). Furthermore, he states another reason for the distinctness of silence: "maunakhyātiḥ" (the renown of silence). This refers to the well-known status of silence in the scriptures of spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) as being for the purpose of reflection, which serves to stabilize what has been heard.

It does not exist; rather, it refers to excellent reflection (*manana*) occurring immediately after scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), meaning uninterrupted contemplation. Then, anticipating the question "What is this *mauna*?", he clearly demonstrates the nature of *mauna* with the words "the concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon the All-pervading One. This is the meaning: in the eightfold yoga, *samādhi* alone is the direct knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*); that which precedes it, such as *dhāraṇā* and so forth, is called *mauna*.

In the passage, "Therefore, a Brahmin, having desisted from scholarship, should remain [as a child]," the state of childhood is heard of as something to be adopted by the wise man. Regarding the doubt as to whether everything characteristic of a child—such as acting according to one's own whims—is to be adopted by the wise man, or only the state of being free from hypocrisy and the like, the connection is made explicit in the Commentary (Bhāṣya).

The investigation into that meaning is as follows: regarding the adoption of "childlikeness" (*bālya*), should things such as the practice of *kāca* (or *kācāra*) also be adopted, or is it only the non-manifestation of greatness? Does the word "childlikeness" refer to all the activities of a child, or does it refer to a specific nature of a child consisting in the non-manifestation of greatness? Does the scriptural passage beginning with "Not one who has not ceased [from evil]" (*nāvirataḥ*) lead us to understand that the word "childlikeness" has the sense of non-manifestation?

"No. Here the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) thinks: "In the scripture [it is said], 'One should remain in a state of childhood' (*bālyena tiṣṭhāset*). The 'childhood' taught for the knower must refer simply to the behavior of a child—namely, acting, speaking, and eating according to one's own will—and not to the actual absence of childhood. For it is not possible for the existence of one thing to be maintained by another, because qualities such as childhood and so forth are fixed in their nature. Therefore, let 'childhood' mean simply freedom of action. He restates this with the word 'taught' (*śiṣṭam*). He rejects the stated meaning with the word 'no' (*na*)."

He clarifies the manner of refutation with the words "from misconduct" (*duścāritrāt*). The statement you cited, "Not one who has not desisted from misconduct," negates this very point. Alternatively, it excludes this self-willed person as being qualified [for knowledge]. Anticipating the doubt, "In that case, what is the determination regarding childhood? he explains the meaning of the word "childhood" by providing a definitive conclusion with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Indeed, the concealment of one's own greatness is enjoined by the sages for those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*); therefore, the intended meaning of the word *bālya* (childhood) would be this concealment of one's own greatness when so enjoined. For this very reason, even in the case of Bharata—who was devoted to right conduct—it is said that his acting like a confused person was due to his being known for "not defiling the path of the virtuous," which implies a failure to conceal his greatness. Likewise, here too, it is precisely the concealment of one's own greatness that is meant by "acting like a child. And this concealment of one's own greatness is for the purpose of turning away from worldly honor and the like; for those who know the inner self, honor and such things are indeed to be abandoned.

For it is recorded in tradition that public honor should be renounced: "From lack of honor, ascetic power increases; but from honor, ascetic power wanes. A Brahmin who is honored and worshipped departs like a cow that has been milked."

Thus the consideration of the constituent parts has been completed; now, the consideration of the time of the accomplishment of that which possesses those parts is undertaken—this is the connection. The investigation into its meaning is as follows: does meditation, which is the means for attaining results in this life, arise immediately after the meritorious actions that are its own means, or is there no fixed rule, such that it may arise either immediately or at a later time? Furthermore, is an obstacle to its arising possible or not?

Thus, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that meditations performed for the sake of enjoyment—meditations whose fruits are experienced in this life—should arise at that very moment through their own generative merits, that is, the merits that produce them. Now, one might object: "Since the arising of knowledge is a fruit of ritual action (*karman*), its production should occur at a later time, just like [the attainment of] heaven and so forth. Anticipating this doubt, [the author replies]: Since heaven and the like are to be experienced in another body, they cannot arise in this present body; however, the arising of knowledge is indeed possible in this very body by means of the purification of the heart and other such factors.

Therefore, in this case, there must be a rule regarding purification through bathing. Just as for a person who has bathed, purification—that is, the state of being purified—occurs at that very moment and not in another body, so too the attainment of knowledge through one's own actions would necessarily occur at that very time. He restates this with the words "for the sake of enjoyment" (*bhogārtha*). He rejects the unstated position with "no" (*na*). There is simply no fixed rule; [the attainment] might occur at that very time, or it might occur at another time.

Now, one might ask: "How can the accomplishment of the fruit occur at another time in the case of a rite performed with attributes? To this he replies: "By those [obstacles] suited to that. Even in a rite performed with attributes, there may indeed sometimes be an obstacle due to extremely powerful karmas capable of obstructing it.

Previously, it was stated that there is no fixed rule regarding the time of attainment for those sciences whose fruits are experienced in this life; in the same way, it is extended [to the present case] that there is likewise no fixed rule for the times of attainment of those sciences which are the means for reaching Brahman—this is the introductory connection (*saṅgati*). The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is the meditation whose fruit is liberation produced immediately after its own instrumental karma, or is there no fixed rule, such that it may occur either immediately or at a later time? Furthermore, is another karma more powerful than the karma that serves as a means for the higher knowledge possible, or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects by stating a specific distinction: "Let it be so" for those who do not know Brahman.

Granted that there may be a lapse in the rites for the accomplishment of knowledge (*vidyā*), because the rites of those who do not know Brahman are weak. It has been stated that the rite called *nivṛtti* (renunciation), which is joined with the abandonment of attachment to results and the sense of agency, is most powerful. Therefore, because this rite is stronger than all others, it should—having set aside its entire opposing class—immediately bestow or produce the knowledge of Brahman. He refutes this, saying, "Not so. The meaning here is as follows:
"There is a fish named Timi, a hundred yojanas long;
there is also the Timiṅgilagila, and there is even one that swallows that in the ocean."

According to this principle, for those dwelling in the ocean of saṃsāra, an increasing severity of actions is observed through the law of the fishes (*mātsyanyāya*). Likewise, even among the actions against a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), there is another action that is even more severe than those: namely, this offense committed against a knower of Brahman; by such great offenses as these against a knower of Brahman, [the consequences are even greater].
