Since it is possible for sins to obstruct even that dharma called *nivṛtti* which produces the knowledge of Brahman, the following is established: in the absence of such great evils, the dharma of cessation (*nivṛtti*) generates the knowledge of Brahman immediately; however, when they are present, it generates it at a later time. Thus, the production of the knowledge of Brahman is indeed not fixed.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: if there should be an offense against a devotee of the Supreme Brahman, which is even more powerful than the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti-dharma), then for the pacification of that [offense], there is the arising of that [knowledge]; that is to say, upon the pacification of such an offense, there is the arising of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā). This implies that if such an offense were absent, the attainment of the knowledge of Brahman would occur instantaneously.

In this context, he clearly demonstrates the specific purpose of the two sections (adhikaraṇas) located at the conclusion of the "Limb of Knowledge" (vidyāṅga-pāda), which concern the matter of non-restriction (aniyama), by stating: "the state of being for the sake of knowledge" (vidyārthatvam). In these two sections, the doubt of one who might say that ritual actions do not invariably serve the purpose of knowledge is dispelled; likewise, it is established that the pacification of the four obstacles (prayūhas) is always appropriate, and it is made known to the virtuous that the fruit of the dharma called "cessation" (nivṛtti), when free from obstacles, is immediate.

Satisfaction is obtained. Therefore, at the end of this section (pāda), the author of the treatise has established two authorities regarding the scope of non-restriction; that is to say, he has composed them as authoritative topics. ||649||

Here someone objects regarding the term "obstacle" (*pratyūha*). [The objection is: "In this context, there is the possibility of an obstacle to the actions of one who knows the supreme (*paravid*) as well as to the actions of one who knows the inner self (*adhyātmavid*); therefore, for the sake of shaking that off—that is, for the removal of the obstacle—it is only appropriate that there be a discussion of obstacles concerning those ritual acts which are the means for the purpose of enjoyment (*bhoga*). Why, then, has this been mentioned in vain? He refutes this with the word "no" (*na*). He shows the manner of this refutation with the word "kāmya" (desirable).

Indeed, in the case of a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmya-karma), some person of dull intellect may have the notion that it will be free from obstacles. By that notion, their mind becomes attached to that very rite. Consequently, in order to achieve an excellence of detachment (vairāgyātiśaya) regarding that rite of desire through the cultivation of great detachment, the occurrence of obstacles to it necessarily becomes fruitful.

The meaning is this: the notion that optional (kāmya) action is free from obstacles is not authoritative; rather, even optional action is indeed accompanied by obstacles, and for that reason it is included within the category of things to be abandoned. To establish this point, the text states, "the occurrence of obstacles even in the case of optional action. Alternatively, what is intended here may be optional action performed for the sake of knowledge (vidyā); the meaning is that even optional action is enjoined as being subordinate to knowledge through a distinct application (viniyoga-pṛthaktva). Since that is what is being considered here, such reflection is entirely appropriate.

In these two verses beginning with "Vidyā" (knowledge), he enumerates the principal subjects of the fifteen sections (*adhikaraṇa*) propounded in this chapter (*pāda*). In the first section, the understanding is established that knowledge is an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma-aṅga*). In the second, however, because [the state of] being the "most flavorful" (*rasatamatva*) and so forth has not been previously attained, it is indeed enjoined. In the third, moreover, the narratives (*ākhyāna*) read within the context of knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*) are themselves specific forms of knowledge.

Thus, in the subsequent sections as well, for those of the *ūrdhvaretas* (celibate) orders, knowledge with its constituent parts (*sāṅgā vidyā*) arises precisely from the duties fixed to their respective stages of life (*āśrama*). However, for the householder, that same knowledge depends upon sacrifice, charity, and so forth; yet even the householder must be worthy of tranquility and other such virtues. Even for the learned man, when not in times of distress, the perfection of yoga is attained through the purity of food alone.

The meaning is that there is indeed one and the same action for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*) and for the sake of the stages of life (*āśrama*); they say it is "separate" (*vidhura*) yet "not separate" (*aviyuta*), being conjoined with knowledge. Alternatively, there is the reading *vidhuram api yutam*, which means even though it is separate, it is still connected with knowledge. The syntactical connection is: they do not say that one who has fallen away (*cyuta*)—that is, one who has strayed from the lifelong student stage (*naiṣṭhika*) and so forth—is conjoined with knowledge. The perception of the Soma as the "most flavorful" (*rasatama*) and so on within a subsidiary part of a sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*) is the duty of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). Now, "sagehood" (*munitā*) is silence (*mauna*).

The meaning is: "for the sake of accomplishing the meditation that has been enjoined," which is to say, for the sake of accomplishing the meditation on Brahman that has been prescribed. Alternatively, there is a word-division as *dhyānasiddhayai coditā* (enjoined for the sake of accomplishing meditation). *Bālya* (childlike state) means the concealment of one's own capacities and so forth. The meaning is that other knowledges—that is, knowledges other than the knowledge of Brahman—do not fail to arise because they are obstructed by powerful opposing factors or hindered by powerful impediments [in the form of past] actions (*karma*).

Similarly, the author of the Sūtras declares in this section that even the knowledge of Brahman intended for liberation does not arise due to its generative actions being obstructed by powerful impediments such as the transgressions of those who possess the knowledge of Brahman. This is the syntactical connection.

In this quarter, the refutation of the four opposing views is intended as the primary subject; thus he says, "Regarding the meaning of the sentence. Here, [the author addresses] the proponents of falsity (*mṛṣāvādinaḥ*).

The followers of Yādavaprakāśa’s doctrine declare that the mere knowledge of the meaning of the Vedic sentences is the means to liberation. Others, however, maintain that both knowledge and ritual action combined constitute the instrument for liberation, thus regarding their conjunction as the cause of final release (*apavarga*). Yet others, the atheistic Mīmāṃsakas, have declared that knowledge is merely an auxiliary to ritual action, and that ritual action alone is the cause for achieving the human goal. Still others, such as the Sāṃkhyas, hold that since the individual soul (*jīva*) is eternally liberated, liberation is indeed unattainable; this is the meaning of what they say. All these disputants [hold these views] here.
In this quarter [of the verse], those [objections] are refuted by the statement establishing the injunction for worship as a means to liberation that has ritual action as its constituent part.

On this point, someone has objected: "Liberation (mokṣa) is indeed defined by the knowers of the inner self as the cessation of all suffering pertaining to transmigratory existence, and it is held that this liberation is accomplished through a method that takes ritual action (karman) as its constituent part. This, however, is entirely untenable. Is liberation said to be the cessation of existing suffering, the cessation of past suffering, or the cessation of future suffering? None of these three is possible. Since that which is present is momentary, it ceases of its own accord; therefore [liberation cannot be the cessation of existing suffering]."

[The opponent argues: "There is a dependence upon a cause. Likewise, the second position is also entirely incoherent; for since past sufferings have already been discarded, there is no need for the practice of meditation which serves as the cause for their removal. Furthermore, because future suffering has not yet come into being, the cultivation of meditation as a means to remove it is useless. Refuting this by restating it, [the author] says: "As for that which is suffering... The grammatical connection here is as follows: That suffering which exists here [in the present], because of its momentariness, cannot be obstructed by one's own effort. As for the cessation of past suffering, that too has already [been dealt with].

Since it is already accomplished, no effort need even be made for its sake. Consequently, future suffering remains; and that is not easily avoided. Furthermore, it cannot be avoided. Why? To this he says: "When the cause is complete. Since many sins established from beginningless time exist, how will that future suffering be easily avoided? Moreover, the word "future" (*bhāvi*) itself indicates the connection of suffering with a subsequent time. Its elimination cannot be achieved at all. If that were so, everything—

[If that were so,] it would be false everywhere and at all times; therefore, the injunction for the meditation on Brahman as the absolute cessation of all suffering would be a mere empty statement. He refutes this by saying, "partially acceptable" (*ardharamyam*). The meaning is this: we do not say there is a cessation of present suffering, nor do we say there is a cessation of past suffering, nor is it said that there is the production of the destruction of future suffering. Rather, it is the obstruction of the causal complex of that suffering which, given the presence of its causes, was otherwise certain to arise.

It is performed; that is to say, the destruction of those karmas existing as causes for future suffering is effected. For it is indeed possible to destroy existing causes of suffering through the practice of Brahman-meditation in the form of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*) for the removal of sin. This, which is well-known to all the world, cannot be refuted by the base disputations imagined by those of false views. For in the world, suffering such as death, which is produced by the provocation of causes like wind, bile, and phlegm, [is removed] by the application of medicines established through the instructions of physicians.

It is obstructed by means of the prevention of its causes; likewise here as well, because previously committed sins are destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman, and because future sins do not commence due to that very knowledge of Brahman, the continuation of saṃsāra is blocked by the obstruction of its causal totality.

Thus, everything has been established. This very point is shown by the words "by means of expiation" (*prāyaścittyā*). Because of the performance of expiation for past misdeeds and because of the non-commission of further ones, there will be no arising of suffering due to the removal of the causal complex of suffering; for as the saying goes, "in the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect"—a principle known even to cowherds and parrots.

In the world, activity for the sake of avoiding future misfortune is frequently observed; thus, here too, one should apply oneself to the meditation on Brahman in order to eliminate the causes of suspected future misfortune. This is shown by the phrase "from what is disliked by the king," and so forth. You avoid transgressing the king’s commands and other unfavorable causes such as snakes, and that avoidance is solely for the purpose of warding off future suffering. Indeed, you carry an umbrella and the like beforehand precisely to ward off the deluges of rain and other such things that may occur in the future. It is the same in this case as well.

In the absence of the worship of the Blessed One, which constitutes the expiation for all sins, every suffering pertaining to saṃsāra will arise. However, by performing that worship, because the causal conditions are severed, what was previously attached will not occur in the future; therefore, apply yourself to the practice of Brahman-worship. Furthermore, what is the use of this other laborious illustration? Now you should strive solely for the removal of impending calamities. For instance, if I were to remain silent, then my defeat would be certain.

Thinking, "It shall come to pass," and desiring the fruitfulness of your own words by pacifying the impending defeat that has taken root in your imagination, you should remain silent—meaning, "remain thus in silence"—while observing the movement of everyone from children to animals as they proceed with steps agitated by fear. Even children and animals move only with steps agitated by fear; and fear arises from the apprehension of future misfortune, for it is precisely to avoid that very misfortune that they flee. Therefore, one should not dispute a matter so well known even to cowherds and children.

Thus, it has been stated that through the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) which has ritual action as its constituent part, there is the attainment of Brahman preceded by the cessation of all suffering. Here, someone objects: "Since the very nature of the relationship between cause and effect is difficult to define, knowledge cannot be the means [to liberation], nor can ritual action be an auxiliary to knowledge, nor can liberation be something to be accomplished through the meditation on Brahman assisted by ritual action; for every such alternative fails to withstand scrutiny."

For what reason is the effect either different or non-different from the cause? If it were different, it could not be its effect; for a cloth is not the effect of a jar. If it were non-different, it likewise could not be an effect; for a jar is not itself the effect of a jar. The state of being both different and non-different is simply inexpressible due to contradiction. Furthermore, does the cause produce [the effect] or not produce it? In either case, it cannot truly be a cause. As they say:
"Whether it produces the effect or does not produce it, how can anything whatsoever be a cause?"
"If it acts, there is an infinite regress; if it does not act, its status as a cause is not established.

Thus, does the cause perform its function by reaching the effect or without reaching it? In either case, causality is impossible. A refutation based on the parity of reaching and not reaching (*prāptyaprāptisama*) should also be stated. Furthermore, the very meaning of the word "cause" cannot be defined. If it is defined as "that which invariably precedes," is it that which invariably precedes everything? No, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is said to be that which invariably precedes the effect, that too is not possible, because the meaning of the word "effect" itself is difficult to define.

If it is argued that the effect exists subsequent to the cause, then if this is meant in relation to everything, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); if it is meant in relation to its own cause, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*), because the cause and effect would be mutually defining. Thus, being vitiated by these various types of faults, the very relationship of cause and effect is not tenable.

"How could there be an injunction for the meditation on Brahman as a cause with respect to liberation, since an instrument is a specific type of cause?"—because the causal relationship is thus difficult to establish, those injunctions for meditation which designate [the soul] as an instrument when life is at the throat find their only refuge in death itself. To refute the opponent who speaks thus, [the author] says: "Or else, that which is to be accomplished... and so forth.

When you claim that either the effect or the cause is indefinable because it is undermined by self-contradiction on the path of fallacious reasoning, with what purpose have you engaged in this debate? This is the point: Is your engagement in this debate purposeless or purposeful? If it is purposeless, then engagement itself is not possible; for even a fool does not act without aiming at a purpose. If, however, it is purposeful, then that very relationship of cause and effect must exist.

Because this very engagement in debate is the cause, and the defeat of the opposing debater—the result—is the effect. If you then say, "In that case, since the defeat of the opposing debater is established, we are victorious," [the author] replies: "This is like fashioning a bracelet with gold obtained in a dream," by the words "by the wrong paths prescribed by yourself. You are merely prattling that neither the probandum nor the proof can be properly defined; yet the establishment of the opposing debater's defeat does not follow from this, because this statement is undermined by its own internal contradiction.

The meaning is this: if one accepts the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), there is no defeat of the opponent; if one does not accept it, there is no defeat of the opponent because the reason for such defeat is absent. Therefore, this "path" imagined by you is merely empty chatter (*pralāpa*). By the phrase "what is the engagement in that doctrine? we have stated the collection of self-contradictions (*svyāghāta*) that has been expressed. If it is asked: "In this way, having obstructed the very engagement in debate, why do you also obstruct worldly activity (*lokavṛtti*)? [the answer follows].
In the absence of the engagement in debate, you would be disregarded; in the absence of worldly activity, you would lack the means for your own livelihood, food, and so forth.

Having stated the connection between the preceding and following chapters by means of the first half [of this verse], he states the sequence of the two pairs of quarters (pādas) within the fourth chapter by means of the second half; thus, according to the order of origination (*utpatti-krama*): since in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" it is observed that the consideration of the means (*sādhana*) is preceded by the consideration of the end (*sādhya*), this same order of consideration applies here as well—first the reflection upon Brahman-knowledge in accordance with its order of origination, and subsequently the reflection upon the attainment of Brahman; this is the order of origination.

Thus, the meaning of the third chapter is that [the soul] is accompanied by the means consisting of the order of origination (*utpatti-krama*). Now, he states the meaning of the fourth chapter with the words "that which is to be accomplished" (*tatsādhyam*). The author of the Sūtras elucidates the fruit, which consists of the attainment of Brahman and is to be accomplished by the means, through its various stages (*parva-bheda*). The meaning is that he elucidates it through the distinct stages of the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman: the dissolution of the connection with the previously mentioned substrate, departure from the body, the journey via the path of light (*arcir-ādi*), and the final attainment of Brahman. Having thus stated the distinction between the meanings of the chapters, [he proceeds].

He shows the division even of the meaning of the quarters [of the verse]. He says "the gross" (*sthūla*) to indicate that he states, by means of the first two quarters, the fruit for one who has not yet departed from the gross body. He shows that he states, by means of the latter two quarters, the fruit for one who has departed from the gross body with the words "having departed" (*niṣkrāntasya*).

This is the meaning: the destruction of all impurities and so forth, as well as the act of departing, occurs only for one remaining in the gross body; whereas traveling by the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) and the attainment of the Supreme Brahman occur for one who has departed from the gross body—such is the distinction.

Fearing that the restatement of knowledge (*vidyā*) here in the chapter on results (*phalādhyāya*) might be afflicted by the fault of incoherence, [the author] demonstrates its consistency by stating a specific purpose, beginning with the words "sūkta" (well-stated). The objection here is as follows: since the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) has already been well-stated previously, for what purpose does he state this same knowledge of Brahman again here, in an inappropriate place?

The author of the Sūtras [responds]: "But surely there remains something yet to be said regarding the knowledge of Brahman. Anticipating this objection, the author of the Sūtras has already stated that very point earlier in the third chapter, as it was its proper place. Furthermore, anticipating the question, "Even so, what fault is there in stating it here?", he says: "Not so" (na hi). This is the meaning: if the knowledge of Brahman were stated here under the section on the fruit, it would not be a fruit. Even if it were stated here despite not being a fruit, because it would be irrelevant, it would only produce a sense of distaste for the subject. Therefore, he rejects this [objection] by saying "not so."

I shall now describe the manner of its refutation, beginning with the words "from liberation" (*mukteḥ*). Here, four points must be specifically clarified; these are indeed included within the [four] fruits (*phala*). For the purpose of stating them:

Because of its connection with that [liberation], the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is also mentioned here. One meaning is that liberation is not established by other means; for it is well known from the text, "There is no other path for going," that liberation cannot be achieved through anything else. Another meaning is its inseparable connection with what is under discussion; that is, the inseparable connection of the practice of meditating on Brahman—which is the subject at hand—with liberation, as it is said: "They, being of great majesty, attain the heavenly world. Yet another meaning is the proximity of its accomplishment: "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here."

It is heard in scripture that immediately after the knowledge of the Blessed One, one attains a state equal to the state of liberation through non-attachment. Furthermore, the flavor (*rasa*) of steady devotion is equal to the state of liberation; this is another point. Regarding the worship of the Blessed One, its nature as a flavor exceeding even the state of liberation is established. While the means for achieving heaven and other goals are themselves of the nature of suffering and yield fruits mixed with suffering—consisting of only partial happiness—the very nature of the fruit of the worship of Brahman consists of happiness equal to that [liberation]. To illuminate these matters, the worship of Brahman, though it is a means, is indicated at the beginning of the Chapter on the Fruit (*Phalādhyāya*).

The meaning is that because [the knowledge] is connected with this [text], it is intended here as a compendium of the science of Brahman (brahmavidyā), in order to establish its inclusion within the category of results by virtue of the equality of its fruit (*phala*).

Regarding the connection of this section, the *Bhāṣya* states at the beginning of the third chapter: "Having considered knowledge along with its means, there arises the doubt: regarding the realization enjoined in the Vedānta texts as the attainment of Brahman, is the purpose of the scripture fulfilled by performing it only once, or must it be repeated? Thus it is expressed.

The inquiry into that meaning, however, is as follows: Is the purpose of the scripture the knowledge (*vedana*) enjoined by the Vedānta performed only once, or is it that which is repeated? Does [the text] "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" and so forth enjoin mere knowledge, or does it enjoin meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*)? In this context, does the word *vidi* refer to knowledge in general?

"He is intent on meditation. It is understood from the introduction and the conclusion, as well as from other scriptural passages, that the word *vidi* (knowing) has meditation as its primary meaning. Here, stating the connection of this section with the final section of the third chapter, he also states the specific subject matter to be established by saying "by the pure ones" (*śuddhaiḥ*). In the preceding section, it was stated that when one conducts oneself properly through the practice of qualities such as tranquility (*śama*), which are free from defects like attachment to fruits and the sense of agency, and which are highly exalted, there will be no failure in the knower of Brahman, and thus the knowledge of Brahman will come to pass.

In this section, he deliberates upon the true nature of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). One might raise the objection: "Has not the nature of the knowledge of Brahman already been described here and there previously? Would this not then result in redundancy? Anticipating this, he demonstrates that there is no redundancy by showing that a specific form of the knowledge of Brahman exists which was not previously described, and thus establishes it through the exposition of that specific form, beginning with the words "It is directly perceived" (*pratyakṣam*), etc.

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: It was not previously stated whether the meditation on Brahman—which serves as the means to liberation—is of the nature of direct perception or of the nature of recollection; nor was it previously stated whether it is performed once, according to the maxim "the meaning of the scripture is accomplished by performing it once," or according to the authority of the rule "recollection must be constant" (dhruvānusmṛti), which implies repetition. Furthermore, it was not previously stated that one should continue this practice throughout one's entire life, as expressed in the passage beginning with "he who lives thus for as long as he lives. Therefore, there is no possibility of even a scent of redundancy.

Having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) here by means of the notion of "once," he demonstrates the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) while reminding us of the method for establishing "repetition" as stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts, beginning with the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Here, this is the prima facie position: in such passages as "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and so forth, it is stated that the mere knowledge of Brahman alone is the means to liberation. However, the number of that knowledge—whether it is one or many—is not mentioned; nor is it stated whether it is to be repeated or not repeated. This is the meaning.

Furthermore, there would be simplicity itself in the case of performing [the practice] once; for the meaning is that by accepting the "lighter" (laghu) alternative, one follows the principle of logical consistency (*nyāyānusāra*). Likewise, by the maxim that "the purpose of a scriptural injunction is fulfilled once performed," the injunctions would have achieved their objective.

Now, raising the objection that the term "constant recollection" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) refers to the constancy of the meditation on Brahman, he states that even this is established otherwise: "Because of its perfection" (*samyaktvāt*).

Here he refutes [the opponent's view] by stating "it is essence-less" (*asāram*). He demonstrates its essence-lessness through reasoning with the words "by means of the universal" (*sāmānyena*). When there exists another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that presents a particular (*viśeṣa*) for a universal discourse that requires further specification, its final resting place (*viśrānti*) is established in the particular alone, according to the maxim of the goat and the sacrificial animal (*chāgapaśunyāya*). Since this point has been explained in detail in the introductory portion of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*), which establishes that the terms "knowing," "meditating," "worshipping," "constant remembrance," and "vision" find their rest in devotion (*bhakti*), he has here set forth that same meaning in brief.

Having set forth another reasoning for that very feeling being meditation (*dhyāna*), and establishing that this same feeling is also worship (*upāsana*) by virtue of its being service, the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) demonstrates that the opening and concluding statements of the *Vidya* and *Upāsya* are interchangeable; then, concluding that devotion (*bhakti*) alone is the means to liberation, it states "furthermore" (*kiñca*) that the use of the word "devotion" elsewhere than in "constant remembrance" (*dhruvānusmṛti*) is merely figurative. Here is the distinction of words: in the passage "one worships the Āgnīdhra with an *Āgneyī* [verse]," the word *Āgneyī* refers specifically to the *Āgneyī* verse under discussion. Likewise, "he knows Brahman, he becomes Brahman itself."

In such passages, the word *vedanā* indicates precisely that meditation (*dhyāna*) which is presented within the same context. Now, one might object: "Practitioners of the inner science (*adhyātmavid*) state that worship (*upāsana*) is the means to liberation; how then can meditation be the means to liberation? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] shows that the term *upāsana* culminates in meditation itself by stating: "meditation" (*dhyāna*). Meditation...

The meaning is that this mention of *upāsana* (meditative worship) expresses a specific quality consisting of service, insofar as it takes the form of supreme devotion (*parabhajana*). *Dhyāna* (meditation), on the other hand, is merely reflection; in that regard, even the meditation upon objects such as snakes or thieves is simply *dhyāna*. Therefore, the intention is that the term *upāsana* here denotes the contemplation of a favorable object in order to exclude those [unfavorable] ones. The proof for the identity of meaning between *vid* (to know) and *upāsi* (to worship) is the very usage heard in the scripture where they are used interchangeably: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; for this Self is incomplete; one should worship [the Self] as 'I am indeed this'. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.10).

Now, one might object: "In passages such as 'Hearing, chanting,' etc., ninefold devotion (navavidhā bhakti) is taught, and among those, meditative worship (upāsana) is also mentioned; how then can it be said that constant remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti) alone constitutes the nature of devotion? Anticipating this doubt, the author concludes that the application of the word "devotion" to both the previously mentioned [ninefold] and the yet-to-be-described [constant remembrance] is merely figurative (aupacārika), stating "the effect" (kārya). Sometimes there is a figurative usage of the cause for the effect, and sometimes a figurative usage of the effect for the cause; thus, there is no difficulty whatsoever. The phrase "the doctrine of being a variety of devotion" means the doctrine of being a specific type of devotion.

Now, one might raise the objection: "But [the Smṛti] states, 'By unswerving devotion alone He can be attained,' thus teaching that devotion itself is the means for liberation in the form of attaining the Supreme Brahman; yet this is contradicted by such Śruti passages as 'He is attainable only by whomsoever He chooses. Therefore, due to this conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, there can be no comprehension of a specific meaning. Dispelling this doubt, [the author] demonstrates the mutual consistency of Śruti and Smṛti with the words: "Yoga is for those who are intent upon it. Here, the syntactical connection of the words is as follows: "Among those qualified persons who are intent upon Yoga..."

The Supreme Self is attainable only by one who has become the object of the Lord’s choice; and that person’s being chosen by the Supreme Self occurs solely because of their being dear to Him. Furthermore, that state of being dear arises from the very quality of devotion consisting of steadfastness in Him. This being the case, it is devotion itself that is directly sought after.
For this devotion, when described as a quality of steadfastness, is in certain instances an intellect whose nature is supreme love. Therefore, [the scripture] is a propounder of devotion.

This is because there is no contradiction with the Smṛti. Since Śruti and Smṛti are in mutual agreement, the Smṛti indeed states that devotion (bhakti) is [the means]. Śruti also, by way of its result, shows that very same devotion—which consists of love directed toward the Lord—in the passage: "He is to be attained by whomsoever He chooses. If it is asked:

"In that case, how is there no contradiction when you state that constant remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti) is devotion, while Śruti speaks of it as such?"—anticipating this doubt, he shows that this very [remembrance] is called devotion, and because it is uninterrupted like a stream of oil, it is called constant remembrance; thus he says, "It has been stated," meaning because it flows continuously or is woven through [the mind].

Now, an objection may be raised: since it is stated that "one must meditate" (*nididhyāsitavyaḥ*), you claim that meditation alone is the means to liberation and thus constitutes an injunction; yet the hearing of injunctions is observed in four matters—namely, "it is to be seen," "it is to be heard," "it is to be reflected upon," and "it is to be meditated upon. How is this so? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] explains by way of the distinction between their respective objects.

He demonstrates the distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*) with the words "from desire" (*rāgāt*). This is the meaning: since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) concern objects already established [by other means], activity toward them arises solely from desire (*rāga*); therefore, because it is not otherwise established, *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) alone is what is to be enjoined. Now, one might object: "How can it be said that meditation alone is to be enjoined while the word 'it is to be seen' (*draṣṭavya*) is present? Anticipating this doubt, he refutes it with the words "therein" (*tatra*). The very word "it is to be seen" indicates that for meditation, its similarity in form to [actual] perception is merely a subordinate quality (*guṇabhūta*).

It demonstrates this; the meaning is that it does not, however, demonstrate that anything other than meditation (dhyāna) is a means to liberation (mokṣa) denoted by the word "vision" (darśana). This is the underlying intention here: in one place, it is stated that constant mindfulness (dhruvānusmṛti) is the means for the release from the knots, as in, "Upon the attainment of mindfulness, there is the loosening of all knots. In another place, it is said: "The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away, and his karmas are exhausted—when that which is both high and low is seen."

Thus, it has been stated that vision (*darśana*) is the means for the loosening of the knot (*granthi-vimokṣa*). Here, a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of recollection (*smaraṇa*) and vision is not possible as two independent means to liberation prescribed separately, precisely because of the scriptural hearing of their independence. Nor is there an option (*vikalpa*), because an option between a heavy and a light [means] is untenable. Therefore, having brought recollection to its culmination in vision, the status of both together as a single means for the loosening of the knot must be asserted. In this regard—

Because it "shows" (darśayati) what is to be seen (darśana), it is said to be in grammatical apposition with "vision" (*darśana*). This, however, is the clarity of memory, which possesses the nature of direct perception once again; for the two universals of "memory-ness" and "vision-ness," being contradictory genera, cannot coexist in a single locus. When the meaning of the scripture has been thus determined, in such passages as "it is to be seen, it is to be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*), the term "vision" is used figuratively due to the excellence of the clarity of that meditation (*nididhyāsana*). For a word denoting a superior state is applied figuratively when the primary sense is set aside, just as the word "king" is applied to a king's servant. Thus it is here as well, in this meditation—which consists of memory and lacks the form of immediate intuition.

The term "vision" (*darśana*) is used figuratively to denote direct perception (*sākṣātkāratva*). This is because a scriptural meaning determined in one instance is to be accepted elsewhere as well. Here, some maintain that—following the word *draṣṭavya* (to be seen)—the object of knowledge is the domain of a perception produced by words, citing examples such as "You are the tenth. Having restated their position, the author refutes it with the words "arising from words" (*śabdottham*). By the phrase "contradiction and excessive prolixity," what is included is self-contradiction, opposition to the consensus of all the world, contradiction with the definitions and classifications of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth. The very statement that "perception is produced by words" is itself contradictory.

In this way, other cases should also be understood. If that is so, how can there be the arising of perception in the case of the statement "you are the tenth"? There is no arising of perception there; rather, when a mediate (parokṣa) cognition has arisen from the sentence, it itself—like the raising of the causal complex for perception consisting of reflective awareness (parāmarśa)—gives rise to a mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa) regarding the state of being the tenth within oneself. Thus, there is no contingency of a mutual confusion of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-saṅkara). He demonstrates this very point:

Regarding the word "amiṣām" (of these): he says "nipuṇaiḥ" (by the skillful) to indicate that this must be investigated subtly by discerning disciples. Here, "skillfulness" consists in proficiency in discerning the divisions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

When the opponent objects, "In your position, since you speak of [the state] as being merely identical in form to perception (*darśana*), the term 'that which is to be seen' (*draṣṭavya*) would be figurative," [the author] accepts that point and refutes it by way of a counter-argument, stating "in meditation" (*dhyāne*). The meaning is this: we admit that the application of the word "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) to meditation occurs figuratively due to mere clarity (*vaiśadya*). However, he says that such figurative usage is equally applicable in your own position as well.

"It is equal," he says; he explains that very point with the words, "he speaks. For the word 'vision' (*dṛṣṭi*) denotes only visual cognition. However, in the case of Brahman, there is no visual vision, but rather mental [vision]. The meaning is that for you as well, the word 'vision' is not primary (*mukhya*) in regard to that metaphorical vision; it is equal [to our position]. He demonstrates this very equality with an example: "as in the case of the 'smeller' (*ghrātṛ*)," etc. Just as the words 'smeller,' 'toucher,' and so forth, in reference to Brahman, [do not denote] that which is produced by those respective sense organs...

Just as [the word "seer"] cannot be applied to that which is devoid of the functions of the nose and so forth, likewise, the word "seer" (draṣṭṛ) cannot be applied in its primary sense to one who possesses the knowledge of Brahman—which is the object of the knowledge produced by the eye. Thus, the figurative nature of the term "that which is to be seen" (draṣṭavya) is equal for you as well. If that is so, then according to the maxim "where the fault is equal for both," since the two positions are equivalent, what is the reason for the determining factor that your position alone should be accepted and not ours?

Anticipating this objection, he states the distinction with the word "tat" (that). This means that when those two—your position and our position—are equal; or alternatively, "tat" is a reference to the reason:
"because of such an establishment. Our position possesses a multitude of systems and is endowed with many logical arguments, whereas your position is rooted in fallacious reasoning.
The word "tu" (but) serves precisely to demonstrate this distinction.

One might object: "In this context, let there be a relationship of door and doorkeeper—namely, from realization (vedanā) comes meditation (dhyāna), from meditation comes constant remembrance (dhruvānusmṛti), from constant remembrance comes vision (darśana), and from vision comes devotion (bhakti). Anticipating this, [the author] says "not by way of a door" (na dvārataḥ), meaning that since resting in one [directly] is possible, such a conceptualization is improper due to its complexity. Here is the grammatical connection of the words: if the rest is in the specific [direct object], then the arrangement of door and doorkeeper cannot be established in any way. Therefore, [there is no need for] realization and the others, up to and including devotion.

Anticipating the objection that there might be an option (*vikalpa*) [between the two], he says "because they are of the nature of a universal" (*sāmānyātmatvāt*), meaning that logicians do not accept an option between a universal and a particular, as in the case of a "beast" and a "goat. Rather, it is accepted that one of them must terminate in the other. Furthermore, he says "light" (*laghu*) because an option between what is heavy and what is light is simply impossible; for logicians do not accept an option between bathing and sprinkling with water regarding a single qualified person (*adhikārin*). If it is argued that an option may be postulated here just as it is in those cases based on the distinction between the capable and the incapable, that too is not so; for in the case of an option...

First, there is the defect of being corrupted by the eight flaws [of contradiction]. Now, furthermore, in the acceptance of an alternative based on a fixed distinction, the postulation of a restriction regarding the qualified aspirant (*adhikārī*) is an even greater defect.

For in all scriptural statements, it is *mumukṣutva* (the state of desiring liberation) alone that is heard as the qualification of the aspirant; the meaning is that one does not hear each individual qualification as being something different from another. Nor can there be an option here based on the distinction between the capable and the incapable, because such is not heard in the texts. If it is argued that what is not heard may still be postulated, then the very act of postulation is itself a defect.

This is what he means by saying, "because of the identity of the agent. For a fixed alternative (*vyavasthitavikalpa*) would indeed be appropriate if it were determined that there are different qualifications (*adhikāritva*) for the two; however, the meaning here is that no such difference in qualification has been established. If one objects: "In that case, you have stated that 'vision' is metaphorically applied (*upacarita*) to the constant remembrance (*dhruvānusmṛti*); why could it not be the reverse—that 'constant remembrance' is metaphorically applied to vision?"—anticipating this doubt, he says: "because of the identity of the object" (*arthaikye*). For a metaphorical application consists in treating something as secondary by designating it with a term that primarily denotes a superior object elsewhere. That [superiority] is appropriate when meditation (*dhyāna*) designates an object superior to that [of constant remembrance], as in the expression, "Devadatta is a lion."

As in such cases, the statement that remembrance possesses direct perception (*sākṣātkāratva*) would be a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Conversely, to designate direct perception as remembrance would indeed be a misapplication (*apacāra*), like calling a servant a king. Therefore, the only logical path is that direct perception is metaphorically attributed to meditation (*dhyāna*). The syntactical connection here is as follows: since the meaning is identical, it is appropriate to employ the term "remembrance" as a metaphor for the sake of establishing clarity through the use of the word "vision" (*darśana*).

The figurative application of the term "seeing" (*darśana*) to [meditation] on the basis of the word "recollection" (*smṛti*) is both baseless and improper. Anticipating the objection that the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) refers only to the fruit—the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*)—and not to the means, he says: "something else. That, however, is the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of others alone; for us, however, because of the hearing of the injunction "it is to be seen," the established doctrine is that meditation itself is what is enjoined, which is expressed by the term "seeing" due to its similarity in form to seeing. This is the meaning.

For one who has become thus established in this yoga of recollecting the Blessed One—which is declared by authoritative scripture to be the expiation for all [sins] without exception—two courses are indeed described by those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*). One course is that, in the event of inability to perform the specific *kṛcchra* penances constituting those various expiations, this very yoga stands as an alternative in their place. The other course, however, is that the contemplation of the Blessed One excels all those expiations by bringing about their perfect efficacy (*sādguṇya*).

"Superior to all penances (prāyaścitta)" means that this alone is declared here as the universal expiation for every single sin that has been active since beginningless time. Regarding this, he says: "In the case of kṛcchra and other [penances].

This is the meaning of the verse beginning with "all penances without exception": when kṛcchra and other such rites prescribed as expiations for specific sins are performed, one who is incapable [of them], who possesses firm austerity (dṛḍhaparitapana), who is endowed with firm repentance (dṛḍhānutāpa), and who is fit for self-restraint and fit for the practice of yoga, should himself perform the remembrance of Keśava, which serves as the substitute for all penances.

In this context, "supremacy" (paratva) means that even among all penances, a single one is established as an alternative; its application as an alternative is according to what is appropriate. Among those various numerous penances that are seen, in place of whichever one is sufficient to produce the primary fruit—as far as the recollection of Keśava [is maintained]—to that extent it applies in each respective case.

"It must be done. He states another meaning, beginning with "from the commonality" (*sāmānyāt*). Since all defects are equally applicable, for all those who possess various specific remedies, the remembrance of Keśava serves as a primary auxiliary. In this view, "supremacy" (*paratvam*) consists in being the helper of all and being superior to everything else. Having thus explained the two meanings of the verse beginning with "expiations" (*prāyaścittāni*), he states the other meaning intended by the author of the Sūtras, which is the most important of all, beginning with "in liberation" (*muktau*).

The intention of the author of the Sūtras is this: the remembrance of Keśava does not stand merely in the place of a single expiation, nor does it stand merely as an auxiliary to all expiations taken together; rather, it stands by itself alone as the expiation for the infinite, beginningless misdeeds. Furthermore, it is the very root of liberation here—not only of the cessation of the undesirable, but the meaning is that it is the primary root of liberation in the form of the attainment of the desirable preceded by the cessation of the undesirable.

Regarding the verse, "Those who have come to You for refuge here," an objection is raised: since it is prescribed that *śaraṇāgati* (taking refuge) alone is the means for all atonement (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) and the cause for attaining the supreme state, how can yoga, which consists of meditation (*upāsanā*), also be considered a universal atonement? Anticipating this doubt, the author confirms that both are universal atonements by distinguishing between qualified aspirants who are capable and those who are incapable, stating: "But is it not so... The meaning is as follows: "Those who have approached Mukunda for refuge, even if they are devoid of the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*), they too, having transcended death, go to the supreme abode just like the self-controlled ones, the yogis. Thus, [the text says] "to You, the refuge... [and so forth].

"Those who have taken refuge, even if they are devoid of the yoga of meditation, they too, having transcended death, go to that very abode of Viṣṇu. It is thus stated; how then can the yoga of meditation be considered a means? To this, he gives an answer by partial acceptance, saying "True. Let it be granted that taking refuge is a means to liberation; nevertheless, the yoga of meditation is also stated here itself to be a means to liberation, by the force of the word "even" (api) in the phrase "they too, having transcended death. For it is not the case that only those [who take refuge] transcend death.

This is stated with emphasis; for by the connection with the word "also" in the phrase "but even they," the intended meaning of the sentence would be that those who have sought refuge go to the Vaiṣṇava state, as do those established in yoga. Therefore, this very statement, having first described the attainment of the Vaiṣṇava state by those established in yoga—

In the same way, since [the scripture] declares that even those who have come for refuge attain the state of the Vaiṣṇavas, it does not reject the attainment of the fruit of liberation (apavarga) for those established in yoga; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Regarding the phrase "of those with restricted domains," this means that for one who is capable, there is the performance of the weightier [practice], while for one who is incapable, there is the performance of the lighter [practice]; thus, despite the difference in weightiness, the status of being for the capable or the incapable is fixed for those two respective domains. The meaning is that the masters of yoga, through their meditative concentration, regard the treatise on meditation as having its purpose already attained. It has been stated that only those who are capable should perform the more weighty treatise on meditation.

Just as the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) serve as a means for spiritual practice (*upāsana*) by way of producing purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇanairmalya*), so too does surrender (*aṅgaprapatti*) serve as a means for spiritual practice through that very same door. He states this with supporting evidence: "Dharma. The syntactical connection is as follows: just as the duty appropriate for one's caste and so forth assists devotion (*bhakti*) by pacifying the turbidity of the heart and thereby increasing the quality of goodness (*sattva*), in the same way, surrender also removes obstacles during times when there is no other recourse—that is, during times when [the goal] cannot be accomplished by any other means.

This, indeed, is the nature of *prapatti*: when a person who is compassionate, endowed with mercy, and capable takes refuge, it accomplishes everything desired by all means. Consequently, in the event of incapacity for the path of worship (*upāsanā*) which is the means to liberation, one attains liberation itself by abiding in the place of *prapatti*. However, in the event of incapacity for the yoga of action (*karmayoga*) and other limbs of worship, one accomplishes that very worship by abiding in the place of *karmayoga* and so forth.

With the intention that both of these are intended by the Śruti, he says, "one who desires liberation. It is heard in a certain mantra: "I, desiring liberation, indeed take refuge [in Him]. The meaning is that this can be applied as one pleases, either as referring to the auxiliary *prapatti* (limb-prapatti) or as referring to independent *prapatti*.

It was previously stated that the meditation on the Supreme Brahman (parabrahma) must be performed repeatedly. Now, however, this is considered: Is the Brahman to be meditated upon as distinct from the meditator, or as the very self of the meditator? This constitutes the connection [of the present discussion] through such a doubt. This very inquiry is the commencement of the investigation into its meaning: Does the meditation on [Brahman] as one's own self involve a contradiction with the injunction "meditating on oneself as distinct," or not? In this regard, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with the words "from the individual soul" (*jīvāt*).

That Supreme Person is designated as "the All-pervading" (Vibhu) because He is absolutely distinct from the individual soul (jīva) by means of characteristics—such as the means of proof and their conclusions—which define His nature. Therefore, the meaning is that it is impossible to truly conceive of Him as being atomic in size, like the individual soul.

Now, one might raise the objection that, according to the maxim "one should know oneself to be Garuḍa," the vision of the Supreme Self may be applied to one's own self; anticipating this, he says "mukhyārtheti" (regarding the primary sense), thereby refuting even that.

The meaning is this: for while the application of ritual injunctions (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is useful for attaining minor fruits, here, however, in the practice aimed at liberation where darkness has been dispelled and all ignorance has ceased, there can be no "other-worldly vision" (*anyadṛṣṭi*) consisting of erroneous knowledge. Therefore, he concludes his intended point with the words, "one who knows reality" (*tattvajña*).

In one who knows reality, who possesses knowledge of things as they truly are, and who is free from passion, there can be no meditation based on the conceit "I am He" when that person is devoid of the attainment of any other fruit. This [objection] he refutes with the words "That is not so. The meaning is this: if the identity of the nature of one's own self and the Supreme Self were taught here, then because it would be an error, it could not be a cause of liberation; and if the vision of the Supreme Self in one's own self were taught, then, like the meditation on the *udgītha* and so forth, it would be a means to liberation because it is an injunction of a [spiritual] vision (*dṛṣṭi-vidhi*).

It would not be so. This is not taught here as both [the individual soul and the Supreme Lord]; rather, it is the contemplation of the Lord in His capacity as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of one's own self. Anticipating the objection that such [contemplation] would not constitute a primary application (*mukhyavṛtti*) because it concerns the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he refutes it with the words "of primary application. The meaning is this: just as words denoting bodies, such as "god" or "human," apply primarily even to the individual soul (*jīva*) who presides over the body, so too the word "I," which denotes the individual soul, applies primarily to the Supreme Self who is the inner ruler of the soul.

Regarding the phrase "it proceeds": if words such as *brāhmaṇa* and *kṣatriya* were not used in their primary sense even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), then injunctions (*vidhi*) which proceed by taking specific qualified persons—distinguished by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of *brāhmaṇa*-hood, *kṣatriya*-hood, and so forth—as their subjects would become non-primary (*amukhya*) for those who are not liberated. Consequently, since even the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras proceed by referring to persons characterized by those various adventitious forms, they too would be non-primary. Thus, to abandon the primary sense in every sentence of the entire Veda is sheer audacity.
Regarding this, someone who asserts that there is no purpose for the meditation on the "I-grasp" (*ahaṅgraha-upāsanā*) demonstrates its specific purpose by saying, "of Vasu, Indra, and so forth.

Here, the intention of the objector is as follows: "What is the specific purpose in teaching this meditation on the 'I-grasp'? If it is the meditation on the Supreme Self as qualified by one's own self, which is in turn qualified by the insentient [body], then that has already been stated in the context of the worship of Vasu, Indra, and the rest. Furthermore, the pure self must be meditated upon somewhere—indeed, the pure self, free from contact with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), must certainly be contemplated at some point; however, in this case, by means of the pure [self]..."

The all-pervading Supreme Self (paramātman) is indeed to be contemplated by one who is endowed with such purity; that is, by one who is pure. This very contemplation of the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme is precisely what is meant, because they are designated as distinct from one another in the expressions "I" and "you. Furthermore, if there were no distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, then manifestation (vyakti)—that is, the act of being made manifest—would not occur through words situated in different substrata (vyadhikaraṇapada).

Furthermore, regarding the contemplation by means of words in grammatical apposition, one might ask: "What, then, is the fruit of the meditation involving the grasping of the self (ahaṅgrahopāsana)? To this it is said: "Even so" (tathāpi). Although what you have stated is indeed logical, nevertheless, the extreme firmness of the cognition of the essential nature of Brahman—which is dependent on another [the individual soul]—arises only from the meditation involving the grasping of the self;
for that purpose, the mention of the grasping of the self is truly fruitful.

Having stated that the meditation on identity (*ahaṅgraha-upāsanā*) regarding the opposing view is contrary to reason, he now demonstrates that his own position is endowed with reason, beginning with the words "In the case of identity... Therein, he first states the refutation of the position of the proponents of illusion (*mṛṣāvādin*), beginning with "In the case of the attributeless (*nirviśeṣa*). How could there be a grammatical co-referential cognition (*samānādhikaraṇa-buddhi*) in the form of "Thou art I" or "I am Thou"—expressed as "O Venerable One, I am indeed You, the Deity; You are indeed I"—with respect to an attributeless reality, wherein the referents of the words "Thou" and "I" would have to exist? If so, [how could it be possible?]

If it is argued that we speak of "identity-in-difference" (*bhedābheda*) according to the view of Bhāskara, even that is not primary; for while there is indeed difference between the hand and the water-jar, there is only non-difference in the ether (*ākāśa*), and since neither difference nor non-difference exists in a single locus, the designation "identity-in-difference" is not primary. Then another says that by the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), only similarity is expressed; regarding that position as well, he says "equal to the previous" (*pūrvavat tulyaḥ*), meaning that the usage of the term "I" is not primary even in that case.

Regarding the statement, "I am indeed you, O Blessed One; O Divinity, you are indeed I," for those who claim that equality is the literal meaning of the words, only a figurative usage (*upacāra*) would be accepted, but that is certainly not tenable. Having thus refuted the opposing view, he concludes his own position, which is consistent with the *Soma* and *Pakti* [sections], by saying "Therefore. The phrase "the inner Self of all" is stated as the basis for the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

For it is precisely the identity between the body and the self that is the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Just as words such as "human" are used in coreferential construction with the embodied being by referring to the body, so too the word "living being" (*jīva*) is used in coreferential construction with the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); thus, everything is perfectly consistent.

Regarding this, he refutes the false claimant who says that in the concluding formula (*anuvākya*), "Thou indeed art I, O Blessed One, O Divinity," there is no possibility of duality at all because duality is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatva*), and thus only non-duality (*advaita*) is being taught, by stating: "Non-duality... Here, the following dilemma (*vikalpa*) arises:

By the word "non-duality" (*advaita*), is the opposition to duality (*dvaita*) denoted, or something other than duality, or the state of being devoid of duality, or is nothing at all denoted? In all three of these alternatives, the three meanings are unestablished due to the absence of their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*); for if the counter-correlate exists, that very thing is established. In the case of the position that "nothing is denoted," the statement would be entirely meaningless. Therefore, you who speak of "non-duality" must necessarily admit duality. This is the meaning of the word here.

The statement that "non-duality [arises] upon the abandonment of duality" is not easily maintained, because non-duality is the very opposite of duality. Likewise, upon the abandonment of non-duality, duality also cannot be easily maintained; thus, he states by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "duality contains non-duality within it. For if non-duality were absent, duality would also not exist. Indeed, duality exists only as the state of two things being one; for the oneness of those two is precisely what constitutes non-duality. He explains this very point with the word "duality": each individual thing, which serves as the substratum of duality, is non-different from its own essential nature.

The meaning is that by this, non-duality (*advaita*) is established therein. Another says: "Let there be neither duality nor non-duality; rather, let us accept only both duality and non-duality (*dvaitādvaita*). To that he replies: "Not even that, [namely] 'duality-and-non-duality'. Does the word *dvaitādvaita* denote the collection (*samāhāra*) of duality and non-duality, or some other appearance of an object? If it denotes their collection, then one must speak while having accepted the characteristics of both duality and non-duality. And thus, because those two restrictions are not abandoned, when that [collection] is spoken of, both duality and non-duality are established. If they were abandoned—

Both [positions] are indeed well-established. There is no harm whatsoever to those who hear the statement of any such appearance (ābhāsa). Anticipating the objection—"In that case, what reality (*tattva*) would be accepted by you who establish everything such as duality (*dvaita*) and so forth?"—the author concludes with "all is unreal" (*sarvam asat*), summarizing that for those who do not follow valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), everything is indeed unreal.

In the preceding verse, it was stated that duality possesses reality by virtue of being the object of negation within the term "non-duality" (advaita). The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) rejects this with the words "But surely" (nanu). The underlying intention here is as follows: just as in the statement "there is no sky-flower," the very sky-flower established through delusion is what is to be negated, so too in this case, it would be only duality established through delusion that is negated. Consequently, the ultimate reality of non-duality is not established; therefore, non-duality alone is the supreme truth.

He refutes this with the words "Not so" (*maivam*). Here, he refutes it by means of a dilemma (*vikalpya*): "Because [it would follow that] the real [would be unreal]" (*satyāt*). The dilemma is as follows: is that difference non-different from Brahman, which is real, or is it different?

If it is different, is that difference ultimately real (*pāramārtha*) or not ultimately real (*apāramārtha*)? Regarding the first position, he states the refutation: "Certainly not" (*na khalu*). The meaning is this: if that difference, which is non-different from the real, were established through illusion (*bhrānti*), then the real itself would also have to be established through illusion.

If that [oneness] were established through non-delusion, then difference would also have to be established through non-delusion. Having thus stated the refutation of the position that [the world] is non-different from Reality, he states the refutation of the position of difference in both ways with the words "And if there is difference. If that difference here were false—meaning, if the difference consisting of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is unreal, from the Real were false—then [it follows that] for the phenomenal world...

"Brahman might be real, or it might be unreal. To this he says: "The answer has already been given. If the world, which is unreal, and its difference from Brahman—which is real—were real, it would follow that one must accept a difference within reality; thus, running away from that [consequence] at a distance would be entirely useless. He says: "If [Brahman] were real... If it is argued that while the difference of the world from Brahman is false, there nevertheless exists a difference within the world itself, we say no, because of contradiction; for it is a self-contradictory statement to say, "Difference is false, yet difference exists. In that case, the difference of a rabbit’s horn from reality would be real...

If you say, "We too shall inquire whether it is real," we shall give the answer: "It is indeed real. But surely, how can that distinction of reality reside in the unreal horn of a rabbit? It does not reside there. Then where does it reside? Listen attentively:

what is called the falsity of the rabbit's horn is the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the rabbit's horn. And for those who maintain that non-existence has a cognized counter-correlative (*pramita-pratiyogika-abhāva*), that [non-existence] resides in the rabbit.

For those who maintain that non-existence has an immeasurable counter-correlative (aprāmāṇika-pratiyogin), the rabbit’s horn is "false" because it serves as the counter-correlative for an absolute non-existence residing in the entire universe; thus, the venerable one should be satisfied with the fact that the rabbit’s horn functions as a qualifier of that universal absolute non-existence, just as in the case of expressions such as "the pot is destroyed."

Thus, it has been stated that meditation on Brahman should be performed as one's own self (*svātmatayā*). A doubt may arise: since there is no difference in these being meditations on Brahman, even in the case of symbolic meditations (*pratīkopāsana*) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" (*mano brahmety upāsīta*), meditation should likewise be performed as one's own self. To address this, the following connection [is made]: [The text continues: ...[the following connection is made]. (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "asaṅgatiḥ". The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument leading into the resolution of the doubt.)

The investigation into that matter concerns whether, in meditations on symbols (pratīkopāsana) such as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," one must contemplate [the symbol] as being the Self, or not; whether in those cases the object of meditation is the Self of the meditator or not; and whether the name is a qualification of the vision [applied to the symbol], or whether the vision of Brahman is a qualification of the symbol. Regarding this, he states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa):
"Not the name. He states the reason for the rejection: "Indeed, not... The meaning is as follows:

In meditations on Brahman directly, it is indeed appropriate to contemplate [the object] as being identical with Brahman because Brahman is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) and possesses the nature of Brahman; however, in meditations on names and so forth, since names and so forth lack the status of being the inner ruler, it is not appropriate to contemplate them as being identical with names and so forth. Now, one might raise the objection: "Could there not be the perception of something else in Brahman? And thus, even in an injunction for a perception where Brahman is primary, there would still be a contemplation of its identity with Brahman? Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words: "Not in Brahman."

He states the reason for the absence of the view of [the inferior] in Brahman with the word "tasya" (of that). The underlying idea is this: in such passages as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman," it is taught that the injunction of meditation consists precisely in viewing the superior in the inferior; and likewise, when there is the view of something other than Brahman in [what is actually] the superior...

It might be argued that if [the meditation were] on a degraded object, it would not possess the defining characteristic of a "vidhi of vision" (dṛṣṭividhi). To this he says, "In another," meaning that when Brahman is viewed as superimposed upon another, it certainly does possess the defining characteristic of a vidhi of vision. The meaning is that when Brahman is viewed in other things such as names and so forth, the apprehension of those respective objects remains consistent with the true nature of Brahman (arthādanapeta), by means of the defining characteristics of Brahman—such as being the cause of the world—which are presented in their entirety.

Just as the perception of a king in a king’s servant—being of the nature of perceiving a superior object in an inferior subject—becomes a cause for a fruit, so too the perception of the supreme Brahman in inferior objects becomes the cause for the desired fruit in each respective case; this is the meaning.

Here, the proponent of falsehood thinks: "Just as in the case of the practice of [wrong] views one sees the result desired by oneself, so too will the contemplation of Brahman alone lead to our desired liberation. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words beginning "ātmani" and so forth.

The meaning is this: although the contemplation of Brahman upon the Self—which is not actually Brahman—may indeed be fruitful, nevertheless, the established nature of reality cannot be denied. Just as in the case of the instruction "one should know oneself to be Garuḍa," one does not thereby actually attain the state of being Garuḍa; rather, due to the unimpeded power of the injunction, the mere cessation of the poison of snakes and the like will be achieved through meditation on Garuḍa. This is all that occurs.

By merely citing this example, he says "etāvanmātre" (by this much alone): the deceiver, out of delusion establishing the meaning "I am Brahman" as his supreme goal by relying on the identity of essential nature, will certainly fall from his station and reach a degraded state, according to the maxim of Nahuṣa—who, though exalted by the thought that he was the slayer of Namuci, fell from his position. This popular saying is a joke: that one who has set out for the sake of liberation (apavarga) attains equality with serpents of crooked gait.

In the preceding section, it was stated that it is logical to view the inferior as the superior. Now, a doubt arises regarding the connection: since the *udgītha* and other such elements are superior by virtue of being means to the fruit, should one instead perform the meditation (*dṛṣṭi*) upon the sun and so forth as being the *udgītha*? The inquiry into this matter is as follows: among meditations based on the constituent parts of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅga*), is the meditation on the *udgītha* to be applied to the sun and so forth, or is the meditation on the sun and so forth to be applied to the *udgītha* and so forth? Is the superiority [of the object] due to its being a means to the fruit, and if so, does it belong to the sun and so forth, or to the *udgītha* and so forth? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "Because of the nature of that" (*tādrūpyāt*). This is because the deities are subordinate to the ritual action.

The meaning is that because the ritual action (*karman*) is enjoined as the means for accomplishing the fruit, one should view the inferior self—such as the Sun and so forth—as a limb of the superior ritual action by way of its being a means to the fruit. He refutes the unstated position with "Not so" (*maivam*). He explains the manner of this rejection with "The ritual action" (*karma*): the sense is this—that although the ritual action is indeed prescribed as primary and thus possesses primacy according to the literal expression (*śābda-prādhānyam*), nevertheless, primacy according to the actual purpose (*ārtha-prādhānyam*) belongs to the deities alone.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because its propitiation is that [the goal]. In all instances such as "yaj" (to sacrifice) meaning "worship of a deity," the object is subordinate because it consists of the propitiation of a deity. Here too, it is the same; since the Adityas and others—who are the primary objects—are viewed through the lens of being limbs of the sacrifice, they are subordinate. Therefore, it is logical to view the subordinate elements, such as the *udgītha*, through the lens of the exalted forms of the Adityas and so forth. Thus, he establishes the very primacy of the deity by stating: "By pleasing that [deity]. Every performance of ritual action is solely for the sake of a result; it is the deity alone, propitiated by the rites, who bestows the fruit.
Therefore, the deity alone is primary; consequently, the contemplation of the deity alone should be performed in other instances as well.
On this point, someone raises an objection: "In another [case]... According to some, the limit of your own school's doctrine is that there is indeed error (*bhrānti*).

According to others, the limit is that there is merely a non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) between perception and memory, and no error exists; for you are proponents of the theory of the manifestation of reality (*yathārthakhyāti-vādin*). This being so, how can those of your school, who assert the absence of error, accept the injunction regarding the vision [of Brahman], since the vision of something other [than what is seen] is of the nature of error?

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: first of all, if one accepts the position of anyathākhyāti (the theory of misapprehension), then the prescription of seeing one thing in another is indeed possible.

"The view of the knowers of the Vedas is that all cognition is in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*). Regarding this position, the meaning is that neither the perception of something as other (*anyadṛṣṭi*) nor the injunction of such a perception (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is tenable. He rejects this with the words "That is not so" (*tan na*). He demonstrates the reason for this rejection by analyzing the first part [of the argument]: "In the first case," etc. Otherwise, there would be no disagreement in your own theory of "cognition as it is" (*yathārthakhyāti*), because you yourself have accepted the tenability of the injunction of perception in that very position. This is the sense: for those who maintain the theory of "cognition as it is," even they must, from the perspective of worldly experience, provide some way to account for the occurrence of delusion and bondage; and that accounting must be provided by you as well.

Regarding the statement "it should be stated in the section on [wrong] views," he shows the refutation here with the words "tādṛg" (such). This is the sense: those who maintain the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) assert that in cases such as "this is shell-silver," there is an apprehension of identity (*tādātmya*) between the shell and the silver. However, the Prābhākaras, who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), assert that error consists in the non-apprehension of the difference between the perception of the shell and the recollection of the silver, as well as the non-apprehension of the non-identity between the shell and the silver. But for those who maintain that all cognition is consistent with reality (*yathārtha*), both the shell and the silver exist; according to the principle of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), they both reside in what stands before one.

They say that [the cognition] refers to the object itself; therein, they maintain that it is the apprehension of silver accompanied by the grasping of the predominance of the mother-of-pearl. Therefore, the activity [toward the silver] is sublated here because of the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is the conclusion: if there is an error, then there is no contradiction with the injunction for vision;

if there is none, then even so, by accepting two cognitions accompanied by the non-apprehension of difference—just as in the view of the Prābhākaras—there is no conflict for us either regarding the prescription of the injunction for vision.

In this section on the method of viewing, he concludes his own intended position through two modes with the words "it is to be seen. Here, some say: "Just as by the maxim of the thief and the post, the state of being a thief is sublated through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and that [state] is indeed false, so too here in the case of 'I am Brahman,' there is a negation of the object to be seen. To the second mode—where the object to be seen here consists of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—he states the fault in the negation of the soul with the word "no" (*na*).

For one who wanders [in saṃsāra], even the very vision [of reality] would not be established. Regarding the denial of Brahman (*brahmāpahnava*), he states the fault as "the delusion of non-duality" (*advaitamoha*). Here, by the word *advaita*, Brahman is denoted; by the word *moha*, the vision regarding Brahman is meant. In this context, when there is a statement denying the object of vision (*draṣṭavyāpahnava*), the offense would belong to Brahman itself, which is the object of vision; thus there is grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*). What greater offense could there be than the offense of Brahman’s falsity? Therefore, [the injunctions] such as "I am Brahman" (*brahmāhamasmi*) and so forth are prescribed.
