He says "tataḥ" (therefore) to indicate the notion of equality with Brahman. Some believe that in this view the previously mentioned defect does not exist; he expresses this with the words "katicit" (some). Here, he shows the view of perceiving one thing in another in two ways by means of an alternative position with the word "dvedhā" (in two ways). In passages such as "one should know [them] as having the nature of Garuḍa," is it not the case that the twofold perception has been understood? Or rather, the meaning is that it has been understood in those others. He demonstrates that very twofold nature starting from "vyaktitaḥ" (from the manifest).

Regarding the phrase "and by way of genus" (*jātitaśca*): if one is made to understand "I am Garuḍa himself," then it is by way of individual (*vyaktitaḥ*); but if one is made to understand "I belong to the genus Garuḍa," then it is by way of genus. Therefore, both these positions are accepted; and by the word "also" (*ca*), the aforementioned apprehension of similarity is likewise accepted. However, the previously mentioned position is not to be accepted because it contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is the meaning.

Regarding the inquiry as to how those who possess the realization that "Brahman alone is one" can have the perception of Brahman in other things, he provides the following reply according to the view of others, beginning with the words "mukhyam ityādinā. The syntactical connection here is as follows: the question is, "How can there be the perception of Brahman in other things for those whose minds are fixed on the thought that 'Brahman alone is the primary [reality]'? In this regard, some followers of the school of Bhāskara say: "By way of oneness (*ekatvena*)."

Since all this, divided into the states of the enjoyer, fortune, and so forth, is indeed Brahman, one is therefore able to perform the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of Brahman upon it. Anticipating the objection as to how this can be said when there is a contradiction, he says: "The injunction is powerful" (*balinī*). For an injunction (*vidhi*) is the most powerful of all means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, by the force of such injunctions as "One should meditate on the mind as Brahman" and "One should meditate on name as Brahman," the identity with Brahman must be accepted in its entirety. Indeed, [it cannot be rejected].

The view of some others is that when a matter is established by scripture (*śruti*), one must suspect some transgression or defect [in the reasoning]. Others, however, say that just as there is a conceptualization of duality and so forth regarding the moon despite its oneness due to the pressure of the finger and other factors, so too is there a perception of multiplicity in Brahman even though its oneness is fully known.

It is conceptualized as follows: regarding this matter, he provides an illustration according to the worldly perspective by saying, "they wander about. Although Brahman is in reality one, the ignorant—or those who are like children—understand the state of Brahman as being manifold in various instances such as the three forms (Trimūrti) and so forth, based on their superficial perception through the Vedas, Smṛtis, and other sources.

All of this is merely a restatement of the opposing view; in reality, however, in each respective case, the similarity to Brahman, the belonging to its class, or the identity with it in respect to names and so forth is merely imagined through a figurative perspective (*dṛṣṭi*). This method of the injunction of perspectives (*dṛṣṭividhiprakriyā*) must be accepted exactly as it is, because it alone is not contradicted by any worldly or Vedic examples.

The connection here is well-established in the Bhāṣya itself: "It has been stated that the knowledge enjoined by the Vedānta scriptures as the means to liberation—expressed by such terms as 'meditation' (*dhyāna*) and 'worship' (*upāsanā*)—is of the nature of continuous recollection (*santata-smṛti*) when repeated many times. One performing this [practice] might perform it without restriction, whether sitting, lying down, standing, or walking, since there is no difference [in these states]. This is the doubt to be raised. Since the two immediately preceding sections were incidental, the meaning is that only the primary connection (*pradhāna-saṅgati*) must now be stated. The inquiry into its purpose is as follows: "Should one contemplate while sitting, or while sitting, lying down, standing, or walking? Is there any [restriction] regarding walking and so forth?
Whether meditation (*dhyāna*) is possible or not—here the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as "of one who is seated" (*āsīnasya*). This is the meaning of the words here:

first of all, there is no scriptural statement (*śrutivākya*) to the effect that "yoga belongs only to one who is seated," nor is there any presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) of such a scriptural meaning, [as seen in passages like] "He, indeed, living thus for the duration of his life... and "In the cognition of that form, and in one... [and so forth].

And by such statements as "the continuity [of the mind] being free from desire for anything else," we also understand that meditation (*dhyāna*) is constant. Now, one might object: "Is it not heard in tradition that yogins prepare a seat with cloth, antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass? Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it with the word "renunciation" (*nyāsa*). The meaning is this: the preparation of a seat is not mandatory; rather, it occurs only occasionally during the state of sitting. In that regard, [regarding] "cloth, antelope skin... [and so forth].

The rule of discipline (*niyamavidhi*) is established as follows: "By this [rule], one should practice meditation whether walking, sitting, or lying down. To this he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). In this regard, it might be possible for a person whose senses have not yet been mastered to practice meditation while standing, walking, or lying down. He refutes this with the words, "This is unattained" (*aprāptam*). He clarifies the very fact that it is unattained with the words, "In effort" (*yatne*). For in walking, there is indeed effort; and in lying down, due to the presence of sleep, a greater lack of wakefulness arises. Therefore, by virtue of what is appropriate (*aucityāt*), the meditation on Brahman should be undertaken only while sitting; such is the meaning.

In this context, the constant practice of meditation alone is prescribed; nevertheless, even when other unavoidable activities exist, meditation performed even with interruptions does not contradict the prescribed constant meditation—this is what he states with the words beginning "cittaikāgrye" (for one-pointedness of mind). Here is the syntactical connection: the great sages prescribe the regulation of place, time, posture, and so forth, for the sake of achieving one-pointedness of mind during the state of yoga. Since meditation with interruptions can be performed even when there is a deficiency in place, time, and so forth, [it is performed] when there is excellence of place, time, and so forth.

They remember that one must constantly practice contemplation without distraction. Now, fearing that one intent on uninterrupted meditation might neglect other duties, [the author] states that since it is impossible to abandon those actions that are mandatory, all actions—including the maintenance of the body and so forth—which are subordinate to the goal, must certainly be performed for the sake of attaining yoga, provided they are carried out according to authoritative means and preceded by the realization that they are impelled by the Lord. However, those actions which are prohibited must not be performed at all.

Furthermore, those rites performed for the sake of specific desires (kāmya) should likewise not be performed [if they conflict with yoga]. However, if those very same rites are prescribed for the attainment of yoga through the distinct application (viniyoga-pṛthaktva) of removing sins, then they certainly must not be abandoned. This does not, however, constitute a contradiction to the attainment of yoga; for it has been stated that "the performance of actions for the sake of yoga is prescribed according to one's inclination," following the principle of non-interference (vyāsakta-nīti). The meaning is that just as in the world, while engaged in some primary action, one may simultaneously attend to its incidental duties without mutual contradiction, so it is here as well.

In order to strengthen the very point already stated, [the author], having restated the primacy of yoga, demonstrates that the application of time must be conceived for its subsidiary (aṅga) in accordance with the primary (pradhāna). Thus, concluding that even all ritual action (karman) must be performed at the proper time because it serves the purpose of accomplishing the nature of yoga—which is the primary element—he says: "karma" and so forth. Here is the syntactical connection (*śabdānvaya*) of this passage: that which was explained in the section on the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga-pāda*) as being an auxiliary to ritual action and meditation—namely, "But this is the supreme dharma... [is now concluded].

"Self-realization is attained through yoga"—since this has been stated by the authoritative great seers (*maharṣi*), the preeminence of yoga is established; therefore, all other ritual action (*karman*) must be applied as being subordinate to it. This is the meaning: when there is a conflict between a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and its principal (*aṅgin*), the performance of the other must be carried out in such a way that it does not obstruct the performance of the subsidiary. This being the case, for a person who has commenced yoga, because of a lack of proficiency due to the sluggishness of his practice, he must accept the application of time regarding rituals in order to achieve proficiency in that yoga.

The intention is that as proficiency arises through gradual practice, one should nevertheless perform one's duties as appropriate even at that time. This point is expressed by the statement, "He, indeed, living thus for the duration of his life," which applies equally to knowledge as the primary element and to the rituals that remain subordinate as its auxiliaries.

Here, someone, suspecting redundancy, says that the consideration of the limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅga*) should not be undertaken here, stating "the limb of knowledge. This is the meaning of the words here: since the limb of knowledge was already stated in the previous section (*pūrva-pāda*), why is this consideration of the limbs of sitting and so forth (*āsana-ādi*) being undertaken again? Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*), having raised the opponent's objection, refutes it with the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). In that [previous] case, a consideration of limbs for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) was made; but here, on the other hand, a consideration of limbs such as sitting for a seen purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*) is being made—thus there is no need to state a distinction. He states the reason for this with the word "previously" (*prāk*). [He refers to] the prima facie view.

The sense is that this distinction does not hold for those who have seen the truth (dṛṣṭārtha), because they are already liberated through tranquility and the other means. He refutes the stated point by accepting it with the word "True" (satyam). The meaning is as follows: although one may admit that what is taught in the section on the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga) applies to both visible and invisible purposes, nevertheless, the uninterrupted flow called meditation (dhyāna) must be practiced daily by the worshippers; the meaning is that it must be cultivated with increasing attentiveness throughout one's entire life.

And since that state will be accomplished only when there is an absence of all other efforts directed toward other objects through the preeminence of the mind, the author of the Sūtras, in order to illuminate this meaning specifically, repeatedly brings to light the instruction being imparted to the disciple by means of a special favor.

Regarding this, the *Saṅgati-bhāṣya* states: "In this matter of doubt—whether this aforementioned meditation (*upāsana*), which is the means to liberation, is to be accomplished in a single day alone, or whether it is to be continued every day until death—the inquiry into its purpose is as follows: Is the meditation characterized as described to be performed on a single day, or until death? Is the purpose of the scripture fulfilled by performance for one day, or not? In this context, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) after refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words: "On a single [day]. The syntactical connection here is as follows: "If, however, devotion consisting of supreme meditation were to take place on a single day alone..."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is that the injunction rests there alone [in the stage of the householder], whereas any further reflection on Brahman would be fruitless. He refutes this, saying "that is incorrect. He states the reason for this: for in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, good conduct (*sucarita*) is enjoined for the duration of one's life in such passages as, "He who conducts himself thus, indeed, for as long as he lives," and so forth. Since good conduct is a subsidiary aid (*sannipatyopakāraka*) to meditation—which is the cause for attaining the world of Brahman—it must be performed throughout one's life; otherwise, its very production of its own nature would be impossible, as it would be untenable for the knowledge of Brahman to be practiced for the duration of one's life without such lifelong performance of good conduct.

The fact that the knowledge of Brahman must be maintained until death is understood through the implication of what is heard (śrutārthāpatti); its establishment is not achieved by śrutārthāpatti alone, but rather because that very meditation on Brahman is enjoined in some scriptural passage to last until the moment of departure, as in: "One should meditate upon the syllable Om until the end of life."

"The commentary states: 'Having thus distinguished the nature of knowledge (*vidyā-svarūpa*), he begins to contemplate the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā-phala*). This, however, is the connection between the sections (*peṭikā-saṅgati*). The underlying intention (*āśaya*) is as follows: since the nature of the knowledge of Brahman consists of unsurpassed bliss, it is incapable of being relegated to the category of a mere fruit; therefore, the purification of its own nature is also appropriately connected to the determination of the fruit. The inquiry into that matter, however, concerns whether there is indeed a contradiction between the scriptures on non-adherence and destruction [of karma] and the scripture stating that unexperienced karma is not exhausted."

Furthermore, regarding the possibility of non-obstruction: can the scripture concerning the destruction of accumulated karma (*aśleṣavināśa*)—situated as a supplementary portion of the statements that teach the knowledge which is the means to liberation—be interpreted as being intended solely for the purpose of praising that knowledge, or not? Here, the author establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) after first stating the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). "Karma is not destroyed without being experienced, even in hundreds of millions of aeons"—thus have the lords of sages proclaimed that karma cannot be easily dispelled without the experience of its fruit.

Therefore, from that very reason, there is the scriptural teaching regarding the non-destruction of sin and the scriptural teaching regarding its destruction; and for that same reason, the majesty of those who know Brahman is proclaimed. He refutes the stated position with the words, "Not so. He establishes that very point by saying, "Not [destroyed] until experienced," and so forth. Anticipating the objection that actions will bear fruit because no atonement has been performed, he provides a rebuttal with the phrase, "by means of the sequence of atonement. This is the meaning: indeed, atonement (*prāyaścitta*) is taught to be of two kinds.

And there is also the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). Specifically, when the particular cause [of the transgression] is known, the corresponding expiatory rite (*pratipādika-prāyaścitta*) should be performed; when it is known only in a general sense, [the universal expiation is required].

However, one must perform that which is prescribed by the authoritative sources as the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*). "The remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is supreme"—thus, because it serves as the locus for the entire expiation, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa alone is enjoined by the authorities. In this regard, one should cite thousands of scriptural statements—historical, puranic, traditional, and based on the Smṛtis—such as, "By remembering Him, one becomes pure. Indeed, when many [authoritative texts] coincide, a single statement like "there is no lack of devotion" does not stand independently in opposition to the Śruti that proclaims its excellence.
Indeed, a cat does not become a rival to a hundred elephants.

Having stated that the meditation on the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahmopāsana*) constitutes an expiation for all sins, [the author] now clarifies its scope regarding the taint of sin by demonstrating it through its very definition, saying: "The expiation" (*niṣkṛti*). For this meditation on Brahman to be of the nature of an expiation is entirely appropriate, because it consists in the total uprooting of accumulated evil. This indeed is the defining characteristic of an expiation; such is the meaning. Now, let it be granted that meditation on Brahman is an expiation; nevertheless—

Fearing that, just as one must practice other means for the sake of attaining human goals such as heaven, so too another means would have to be practiced for the sake of expanding the knowledge that consists in the unconditioned experience of Brahman, he rejects this with the words "not here. He establishes that very point with the words "the removal of obstacles. This is the intended meaning: the experience of heaven and the like...

For [the state of being a transmigrating soul] is non-intrinsic (asvābhāvika), because it is manifested by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of karma and form; therefore, it requires the performance of spiritual means (sādhana). However, the attainment of Brahman is intrinsic to all selves. Nevertheless, for some, it remains obscured by beginningless obstacles due to the force of a beginningless stream of sin. Upon the removal of these obstacles, it manifests spontaneously. Therefore it is said: "Just as the luster of a gem is not produced but revealed by the washing away of its impurities, so too the knowledge of the Self is not produced but revealed by the removal of defects."

And thus, there is a difference between the attainment of the supreme Brahman and [attainments] such as heaven; for the meaning is that nothing is to be doubted which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

As for the appearance of individuality (*vyaktyābhāsa*), however, it is not to be respected in debate because it contradicts valid means of knowledge. Here, the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates well-known fact. Just as the expansion of light occurs spontaneously when the covering of a lamp or the like—such as a jar—is removed, so too, in the case of the Self, upon the absence of obstacles, there is the expansion of the knowledge that constitutes its nature. This is the meaning here.

Someone objects: "If there is no clinging to sin for those who know Brahman, then they would simply engage in wrong paths. To this, he says: "There is no clinging to sin" (*pāpālepa*). What we mean by the absence of clinging to sin for those who know Brahman is only the non-clinging to sins committed through negligence (*pramāda*), and not the non-clinging to sins committed intentionally (*buddhipūrvaka*). If one asks, "For what purpose [is this]? he says: "By following the command" (*ājñānuvṛttyā*). The meaning is that even for those who know the supreme self, the Lord has himself stated that the non-transgression of the Śruti and Smṛti—which are His very commands—is essential, as in: "The Śruti and Smṛti are My commands."

Thus, if there were no admission [of the existence of such a path], there would be no basis for the statement that "one does not deviate from misconduct. Furthermore, there would be no basis for the movement of yogins who invariably proceed according to the performance of their own specific domain. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. Even Bharata, while manifesting a state of delusion, is said to "follow the path of the virtuous" without defiling the way of the good; for he is described as one who abides on the true path.

Having indicated here the specific meanings of the words "non-adhesion" (*aśleṣa*) and "destruction" (*vināśa*), and having raised an objection regarding the status of the knowledge of Brahman as an expiation even for future [sins], he provides the resolution with the word "non-adhesion. Here, "non-adhesion" is the non-arising of the potency of karma; "destruction" is the cessation of that [potency] once it has arisen. In this context, the potency of karma also belongs to the Lord, the leader of all, who acts as a restrainer by producing fruits appropriate to each respective action; therefore, there is no contradiction with the established doctrine. This is what he states with the words beginning "the potency," and so forth.

In this context, he dispels the doubt raised by someone regarding the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) with the words "it is not to be questioned. The objector's intention is as follows: "In the state of performing the means for the destruction of subsequent sins, there is no arising at all of that which was not preceded by intentional thought; how then can knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) be an expiation for a sin that has not arisen? He rejects this objection with the words "it is not to be questioned," and demonstrates its unobjectionable nature with the words "for it is not a duty (*dharma*)."

The meaning is that this expresses the intention of those who state that the knowledge of Brahman is an expiation for all sins, asserting that for one established in the knowledge of Brahman, no sin whatsoever could possibly exist, even if committed unintentionally.

Having thus stated the previous position regarding unintentional [offenses], he establishes that for those who know the inner self, there is non-arising of [sin] for what is done intentionally; for others, even when it has arisen, there is atonement; and for yet others, even in the absence of atonement, there is swift enjoyment [of the fruit]. Thus, in every respect, even for a devotee of the Lord who has committed an offense, [there is purification] gradually.

He shows the exception by saying "intentionally" (*dhīpūrvam*). A knower of Brahman who is always virtuous never commits a transgression intentionally. However, a knower of Brahman of middling capacity casts away the sin that has arisen through expiatory rites; thus he says "arisen" (*jātam*). Furthermore, another knower of Brahman certainly does not go to the domain of Yama, the lord of the dead.

In this very world, some of these [beings] undergo afflictions; they become one-eyed, they become lame, and so forth—in the manner described by the Śruti, when there is no cause for a specific penance for each step, one should undergo a light punishment. This is indeed seen in the case of Vṛtrāsura and others. Vṛtra was indeed a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata), yet through some transgression he attained an asura body; even there, due to the innate nature of his birth, [he possessed] the characteristics of the gods.

It is a well-known tradition of the ancients that even one committing an offense, having experienced a retribution corresponding to that offense at the end, attains the desired fruit by meditating solely upon the Blessed One. Now, one might object: "Even so, how could the king of Cedi—who committed a hundred offenses and had not performed any expiation—have attained Brahman? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states therein [in the *Kṛṣṇacarita*]: "He whose nature was now governed by his previously performed merit, whose enmity had dissolved, stood for a moment with his bowstring slackened, beholding the wondrous form of Kṛṣṇa."

Thus [it is said]. This very point is expressed by the phrase "by the power of destiny" (*niyativibhavataḥ*). Having granted that [the result] is established, one might still wonder whether its accomplishment occurs this very day or at some other time; anticipating this doubt, the venerable Bādarāyaṇa maintains that the attainment of the fruit is non-deterministic, occurring in accordance with the Lord’s will which conforms to past karma. He expresses this with the words "this very day" (*adyaiva*).

The connection [of this section] is by way of extension (*atideśa*): previously, the non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*vināśa*) of evil were stated; now, the non-clinging and destruction of merit (*sukṛta*) are also stated. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: is the non-clinging and destruction of both future and past merit possible, or not? Do these two statements—"evil action does not cling" and "all evils are burnt away"—refer to the non-clinging and destruction of both merit and demerit, or do they refer to the non-clinging and destruction of demerit alone? Furthermore, in this context, does the term "evil action" (*pāpakarma*) refer to what is prohibited?

[The opponent asks: Does the statement, "All evils (sarve pāpmānaḥ)," make it understood that the word *pāpman* refers to actions that result in opposition to knowledge (*vidyāvirodhaphalakarma*), or not? Here, he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words, "Of merit" (*dharmasya*). For both the destruction and the attainment [of the self] are possible through the grace of merit (*dharma*) which favors supreme devotion. He states the reason for the impossibility [of the opposite view] with the words, "Of that" (*tasya*). Indeed, it is not tenable for merit (*dharma*), which is well-known to all the world, to possess the nature of evil (*pāpa*).

For in that case, it would follow that the distinction between merit and demerit is untenable. Furthermore, the Śruti also says that one who knows the Self, having experienced the entire fruit of merit, shall afterwards attain liberation. This is what is meant by the words "by parts. He refutes this with the word "no. Therein he states the reason with the word "since":

for this knower of the Self, even that which is performed out of desire is indeed demerit. Now, [an objection may be raised]: surely the statement that meritorious action performed out of desire is demerit is merely figurative, for even one performing such action—

The wise say that those intent on ritual action (*karmaṭha*) are sinners; therefore, one might suspect that it is an extreme rashness to claim that desirable action (*kāmya-karman*) is sinful. Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "In that... For in the world everywhere, whatever characteristic is observed in something, by that very [characteristic] it is designated by its corresponding word. Words such as "cow" and words such as "jar" are employed by the learned in accordance with their respective characteristics. Here too, among desirable actions, depending on the difference in the qualified agent (*adhikārin*), the difference in time, and the difference in state, even what is sinful becomes meritorious.

Since the rule that "merit itself is indeed evil" is well-known throughout all the worlds, for those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*), even action performed with desire (*kāmya-karma*) is nothing but evil. Indeed, liberation alone is what is desired by those who know the supreme self; for the enjoyment of heaven and such is contrary to that [liberation]. For this very reason, heaven and the like are called "hell" by those devoted to Nārāyaṇa. In this regard, the following statements serve as authoritative evidence: "O dear one, these are indeed to be cast aside by you who abide in the Supreme Self; you are intent on wealth and pleasure, whereas we are intent on Nārāyaṇa," and so forth.

We do not merely state that actions performed for desire (kāmyakarman) are sinful on the basis of their definition alone; rather, scriptural passages such as "Neither what has been done nor what has been left undone—all sins turn away from him" also explicitly reveal and demonstrate the sinfulness of desire-driven action by stating it directly in words such as "neither what has been done."

In this context, he says "merit" (puṇyam), because like sin, merit is also to be discarded since it accomplishes results that are opposed [to liberation]; for, according to the maxim of the two fetters—one of gold and one of iron—placed upon a king’s servant by his restrainer, everything must be broken when the state of attaining the human goal is reached. Indeed, merit is of two kinds: that which is conducive to knowledge and that which is for the sake of mere enjoyment. Among these, action conducive to knowledge has fulfilled its purpose through the predominance of knowledge. He says "in that [knowledge]" regarding that action which is not employed in knowledge—that is, optional (kāmya) action—which, like sin, must be warded off. Sin...

For that which is a cause of suffering may sometimes also become a cause of detachment. Since desirable action (*kāmya-karma*), by virtue of being a cause of pleasure, brings about the very increase of saṃsāra through the expansion of hope for it, the sense is that even sinful desirable action must be especially abandoned. He establishes the necessity of avoiding both merit and sin by means of a worldly analogy: "as in a prison... This, however, is for the sake of making it understood even by common people.

Here, having raised the objection that for one who knows the self (*adhyātmavid*), meritorious action (*sukṛta*) cannot pertain to the sphere of non-attachment (*amalepa*), the author establishes by means of a distinction of types that it is indeed possible, stating: "That which is performed with desire" (*kāmyam*). The intention of the objector here is as follows: because the knower of the self is dispassionate (*virakta*), he would not desire action performed for the sake of rewards; therefore, he does not perform it. Consequently, it cannot be said that there is non-attachment simply because the action was not performed. Now, one might suspect that even a detached person might occasionally perform an action for reward due to the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*);

anticipating this, [the author] states that if he were to perform such an action, that action would certainly yield its fruit, and because of being destroyed by that fruit, [non-attachment would not occur].

He says "yadi kila" (if indeed) to show that one cannot say there is no stain even by that action. Anticipating the objection that "there is desire [for results] even without prior conscious intent, and therefore one is said to be unstained," he refutes that as well with "nidhīpūrvam" (not preceded by knowledge). Since desire is necessarily preceded by conscious intent—because desire is produced by a specific state of consciousness—if it were not preceded by conscious intent, it would not be a "desire" at all. Anticipating the further objection that "there are both known and unknown meritorious deeds, and it is by means of those unknown meritorious deeds alone that one is said to be unstained," he refutes that as well...

"And it does not ward off [evil] either. For a duty that is unknown does not bestow a desired fruit, because there is no performance of it with a specific fruit in view. If it is argued that the non-tainting is said to be by those very duties performed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārtha*), he says "no" to that as well with the words "by those for the sake of knowledge. Because they are rendered obsolete by the completion of knowledge, the actions performed for the sake of knowledge have already yielded their fruit through the very completion of knowledge. Therefore, no other action remains; by what, then, could tainting be spoken of? To this he replies with "therefore" and provides the answer: "No."

The meaning is this: actions performed for the sake of knowledge remain even after they have not yet yielded their fruit, because of the persistence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even when one has become free from passion; or, certain actions performed with delusion for other purposes—being obstructed by intervening factors—remain even though they have not yet given their fruit. Furthermore, many meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*) performed by relatives on behalf of a knower of the Self (*adhyātmavit*) remain; those very meritorious deeds become, for him, as if they were evil deeds (*duṣkṛta*). Therefore, for that knower of the Self who feels remorse, the statement "he is said to be smeared with oil" provides an occasion for the declaration that he is untainted (*alepa*).

The connection here is stated in the Commentary: "In the [preceding] section, the non-clinging and destruction of good and evil deeds occurring before and after the arising of the knowledge of Brahman were declared. Therefore, regarding the doubt as to whether there is destruction without distinction of the good and evil deeds occurring prior to that, or only of those whose effects have not yet begun," the investigation into its meaning is as follows: do the previous good and evil deeds perish without distinction, or only those whose fruits have not yet commenced?

Is it more reasonable to follow the word "all" in the phrase "all evils," or to follow the scriptural statement regarding the delay in the phrase "for him [it lasts] so long"? Furthermore, is the maintenance of the body through residual impressions (saṃskāra) possible even after the destruction of karma—like the continued spinning of a potter's wheel—or is it not?

Is there any authority for postulating the destruction of impressions (*saṃskāra*) apart from the pleasure or displeasure of the Lord? Or is there not? Here, he restates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "But it perishes. Even that evil deed whose effects have already begun (*ārabdhakārya*) surely perishes, just like that whose effects have not yet begun (*anārabdhakārya*), because there is no distinction between them; this is the reason he gives with the words "for not. The meaning is that no distinction has been taught—that only that which has not begun its effects perishes while that which has begun its effects does not perish.
Having raised the doubt as to how this is not taught, he states the teaching in a general sense with the words "all."

Since it was stated in general terms that "all evils [perish]," one might argue that both [the body and the subtle body] perish. He rejects this prima facie view with the word "no" (*na*). He states the reason for this: "because of perception and so forth" (*upalambhādīti*). This means because of sublation by direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*), and sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*). For the persistence of pleasure and pain is indeed perceived even among those who know Brahman; otherwise, there would be no such things as activity toward what is favorable or cessation from it—this constitutes sublation by inference.

There is also sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*), namely, sublation by such scriptural statements as "For him, there is delay only so long" and "He, indeed, living thus. He specifically clarifies this sublation by scripture with the words "those who know the True Knowledge" (*sadvidya*). Being knowers of scripture, Parāśara, Pārāśarya (Vyāsa), and others—recollecting through thousands of statements such as "A human being attains perfection by worshipping Him with his own duty"—remembered that even for those who possess knowledge of Brahman, the performance of rituals as auxiliary limbs of knowledge (*vidyāṅgakarman*) in the form of worship of the Lord is mandatory.

Then, raising the objection as to how the statement regarding liberation while living—namely, “One who knows him thus becomes immortal here”—can be justified, he says, “Regarding liberation while living. The meaning is that the mention of immortality here is figurative (*aupacārika*), because it is merely similar to immortality. To a certain disciple who follows others blindly and asks, “In that case, why do those who speak falsehoods establish the doctrine of liberation while living with such great care? he replies, “They are deluded.
The meaning is that dull-witted people, not understanding the intended sense of the Vedic statement, prattle on about the doctrine of liberation while living out of sheer ignorance.

Here someone objects: "Surely you state that merit and demerit whose effects have already begun are destroyed through experience; however, that is not tenable, because there is no experience [of the results] for those who have performed expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). To this he says: "Sickness, etc. For in the world, the destruction even of sins whose effects have begun is observed without experience [of their results], as it is said: "Sin committed in another birth afflicts one in the form of disease; its pacification occurs through medicines, gifts, recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth."

Furthermore, [it is said]: "O Arjuna, he who knows in truth my divine birth and action, having abandoned the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me. Thus, for those who know the secret of the Incarnation, it is stated that liberation is attained through the experiencing of the remainder of *prārabdha* (commenced karma). How then can there be the experience of *prārabdha*? To this he says: "In order that they may believe" (*pratyetum*). The grammatical connection is: "so that they may believe in his own incarnation and so forth. Therefore, the statement regarding the necessity of the fruit in the case of karma whose effects have already commenced appears difficult to reconcile—this is the syntactical meaning.

To this, he states the reply: "It is not so. He explains that very point with the words, "of those [karmas] abandoned by expiation" (*prāyaścittojjhitānām*). The intended meaning of the author of the Sūtras is that the fruit of actions necessarily follows for those whose expiation has not been performed, but not for those whose expiation has been performed; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever—this is the sense.

In this commentary, by the statement "so too for the other, there is non-attachment," it is stated that even good deeds (*sukṛta*) do not adhere [to the soul] due to the power of knowledge (*vidyā*). A connection is appropriately established by raising the doubt: "Is there non-adherence of the fruit even for the obligatory and occasional rites such as the *agnihotra*, as well as for the duties of one's own stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*), because they share the common nature of being 'good deeds,' should they not be performed? The inquiry into the meaning of that [passage] is as follows: Are the duties of the stages of life, such as the *agnihotra*, to be performed by the knower (*vidvān*)—or rather, are they not to be performed because of the non-adherence of their results? Is the statement regarding non-adherence intended to apply to all good deeds, or...

This concerns the subject of meritorious deeds distinct from the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) that are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā*). Is the fruit of the duties of the stages of life related to a knower (*vidvat-sambandhin*) also something distinct from knowledge, or is it knowledge itself? Here, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the word "śleṣa" (conjunction).

If there were no connection [between action and its result], then the higher knowledge (*paravidyā*) and the merit consisting of the *agnihotra* sacrifice and so forth would be fruitless. For that reason, even *dharma* (righteous action) would have to be abandoned in the same manner as *adharma* (unrighteous action). He refutes this by saying, "That is improper. He states the reason for that: "It would not be so. If the *agnihotra* and other such acts led to bondage, then indeed it would be improper; however, they do not lead to bondage, but rather assist toward liberation. Thus he says, "[They are] the sprout of knowledge (*vidyāṅkura*)."

The meaning is that the dharma of the Agnihotra and other rites nourishes the purity of the internal organ, which is the sprout of the knowledge of Brahman; thus, you should have the notion that these are supportive, not contrary, to it, so that your sin may be removed.

Anticipating the objection that there is tautology here, he refutes it with the words, "All [requirements]. In the sūtra "dependence on all," he stated that ritual action (*karman*) has no obstructive power regarding the attainment of the Supreme; now, by the phrase "the Agnihotra and so forth," that very same point is being expressed. Therefore, one of the two would be redundant. He refutes this with the words, "Not so. Here, he avoids the charge of tautology by stating the specific purpose of each through the words, "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*). For in that [previous] case, by stating the independence of knowledge, its dependence [on action] was implied.

The statement that knowledge is devoid of accessories (*niraṅga*) because it lacks such equipment was previously introduced in a general sense. Now, however, in the context of the connection with merit (*sukṛta*), a doubt is raised that because there is no distinction in their being "merit," rites such as the *agnihotra* should be abandoned; thus, that very point is refuted once again. Therefore, there is no charge of redundancy, as this serves to establish a difference in the underlying principle (*nīti*). This is the meaning.

The connection [of this section] with the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is evident from the following reflection: "Is there a fixed rule that merit and demeritorious actions whose effects have begun terminate upon the completion of knowledge, the source [of the body], or the body itself; or rather, is there no such rule, [the termination occurring] either at the end of that body or at the end of another body? This lack of a fixed rule—that it may be at the end of that body or at the end of another body—indicates that the termination occurs upon the exhaustion of the experience of the fruits of those commenced actions. Here, having stated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its supporting arguments, [the author] refutes it by demonstrating its alternative establishment, beginning with the words "nirdiṣṭe" (when it has been specified). Thus, indeed, the proponent of the prima facie view thinks: "This..."

In this very passage, "The serene one, having risen up from this body and having reached the highest light... it is indeed said "from this body"; therefore, the attainment of Brahman occurs precisely at the conclusion of the body that began with the undertaking of knowledge. Consequently, the statement "until I am released" refers only to the karma that has already begun its effects; nevertheless, for the knower, that karma lasts only until the end of his current body. Thus, there is no contradiction even in that statement. He refutes this, saying, "Not so," and provides the reason for this.

Regarding the phrase "in the case of *prārabdha*": the statement beginning with "as long as I am not liberated" (*yāvanna vimokṣye*) refers to the karma that has begun its fruition (*prārabdhakārya*). Even so, for the knower (*vidvān*), that karma lasts only until the end of that body; therefore, there is no contradiction in that statement either. He refutes this, saying "not so. He states the reason for this: "because of the variety of *prārabdha* karmas. Due to the diversity of *prārabdha* karmas, liberation does not necessarily occur at the conclusion of that particular body. It should be understood that the expression "from this body" (*asmāccharīrāt*) refers to the termination of the final body present in the mind.

Anticipating the objection—"Why do you assume the unintended meaning 'either there [in the sun] or elsewhere,' thereby abandoning the straightforward sense of the scriptural statement *nanvasmāccharīrāt*?"—he says: "Furthermore. This refers to the meaning of the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*), namely: "And the conceptions of the sun and so forth [are of the Self], because that is logical. (BS 4.1.6)

The *praṇidhi* (meditative application) should also be performed while seated; indeed, worship (*upāsana*) must be carried out in a manner conducive to sitting. This is the meaning of the fifth section (*adhikaraṇa*), beginning with the sūtra: "Because it is possible for one who is seated" (*āsīnaḥ sambhavāt*). Furthermore, this *praṇidhi* should occur daily; thus, this very worship is to be performed every day until the moment of death. This is the meaning of the sixth section, beginning with the sūtra: "Until death, for that too is seen [in scripture]" (*āprāyaṇāttatrāpi hi dṛṣṭam*).

Regarding sin and merit, there is destruction and so forth when knowledge has been practiced previously and subsequently; furthermore, regarding merit, there is both destruction and non-clinging. These two points are to be understood respectively from the seventh section beginning with "Upon the attainment of that [Brahman], of the subsequent and prior sins... and from the eighth section beginning with "The same applies to the other [merit]...". However, in the ninth section following that, beginning with "But only those whose effects have not yet begun...", [the matter is treated differently].

Regarding those two, merit and demerit: with respect to the *ārabdhakārya* (commenced action)—that is, karma that has begun to yield its fruit—its state of being experienced (*bhogyatā*) means its destruction through the very experience of the fruit. The purpose of the [textual] mention of "karma" is to indicate that it must be performed according to its own appropriate course. Furthermore, regarding the cessation of the commenced [action], liberation is attained upon the termination of the *prārabdha-karman*, which occurs according to the varying degrees dependent on the specific differences between individuals. This is the meaning of the eleventh section (adhikaraṇa) beginning with "But by experience, the others" (*bhogena tvitare*). Such is the collection of topics stated in this sequence here, in the first quarter (pāda) of this fourth chapter.
"Expounded" means explained; "by the authors of the Sūtras," is the ellipsis to be supplied.

In the introduction to the second quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter, the author states the connection (*saṅgati*) by way of restating the subject matter of the two preceding chapters, beginning with the words "In the case of eternity" (*nityatve*). In the first chapter, the Supreme Reality was expounded; in the second chapter, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), preceded by its eternity and omniscience, was also explained in detail; and in the third chapter, the section on dispassion (*vairāgyapāda*), the suffering of the individual soul—who is like a great traveler in the forest of the world—was also described.

Furthermore, regarding the remaining portion of the teaching, after beginning with the commencement of knowledge (*vidyārambha*) and extending up to its conclusion (*vidyāvasāna*), everything that was to be stated in the interim has already been explained. Hereafter, [the author] introduces the chapter on departure (*utkrāntipāda*) in order to describe the manner of the soul’s (*jīva*) movement and departure when it abandons the gross body at the end of the *prārabdha* [karma], stating: "Of the *prārabdha*... and so forth.

One might object: "Since death was already to be considered in the chapter on detachment (*vairāgyapāda*) in connection with waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fainting, why is death being considered here out of place? Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes that this too is a consideration of the state (*sthānacintana*) by means of the verse beginning with *varṇya*. The syntactical connection of the word *ayam* (this) here is as follows: although [death] was [discussed] in the chapter on detachment...

In this very context, the agitation of the body and the senses at the time of death must also be mentioned. Nevertheless, it is included as a subsidiary topic (*anubandha*) in the Chapter on Fruition (*phalādhyāya*) in order to make known that even for one who knows Brahman, death occurs when its time has arrived. Some of immature intellect think that because the knower of Brahman possesses great majesty, there is no death for him at all; it is to ward off such a misconception that this subsidiary topic is presented here. Furthermore, he states "of that" (*tasya*) to indicate that there is another reason for this connection.

In order to describe the specific departure through the *mūrdhan-nāḍī* (the channel at the crown of the head) for one who knows Brahman at the time of death, [it must be shown that] there is no contradiction with the general departure and liberation [that applies to others]. This is what you have previously accepted. If there were "non-attachment" (*aśleṣa*) for the knower of the Supreme (*paravid*), meaning a lack of connection in the form of an incapacity to experience the fruits together with the *agnihotra* and other rites—if such non-attachment were to occur—then subsequently, the merits would be fruitless; that is, the performance of duties such as the *agnihotra* in a later time would indeed be useless. Therefore, even dharma possesses the aforementioned justification.

Even duties such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, though they appear to be similar to non-duty (*adharma*) due to their sequential nature, must indeed be abandoned—that is, not performed—in this context of one who knows Brahman. To raise the objection that this is improper is itself improper. Such duties as the *agnihotra* would not lead to bondage; they would not become a cause of bondage. For the *agnihotra* and other duties pertaining to caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) nourish the sprout of knowledge; indeed, they foster the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-śuddhi*), which stands as the very sprout of knowledge. Their performance is solely for the sake of the accomplishment of knowledge, and their fruit is the attainment of that knowledge.
The meaning is that [this knowledge] is not a mere cause for bondage, but rather a direct cause for liberation; therefore, there is no inconsistency with what was stated previously.

Anticipating the objection that this involves redundancy, he refutes it with the words "all" (*sarve*). In the sūtra "dependence on all" (*sarvāpekṣā*), he stated that ritual actions serve as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) for the supreme goal; now, by the phrase "the Agnihotra and so forth," that very same point is being restated. Therefore, one of the two would be useless. He refutes this with the word "no. Here, he avoids the charge of redundancy by stating the specific purpose of each: with the words "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*). For in that [previous] case, its dependence was mentioned by way of stating that knowledge is independent [of action].

The claim that knowledge (*vidyā*) is devoid of accessories (*niraṅga*) because it lacks such equipment was already refuted in general terms previously. Now, however, in the context of the connection with merit (*sukṛta*), a doubt is raised that rites such as the *agnihotra* should be abandoned since there is no distinction in their being "well-done" (*sukṛta*); thus, that very point is refuted once more. Therefore, there is no charge of tautology, because a difference in the application of logic is established—that is to say, a difference in the manner in which the reasoning proceeds is established.

The connection [of this section] with the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is evident from the consideration: "Regarding merit and demerit whose effects have already begun, is there no fixed rule as to whether they perish at the conclusion of knowledge, the source [of the body], or the body itself, or rather at the conclusion of that body or at the conclusion of another body? The investigation into that meaning, however, is precisely the first inquiry already mentioned; for its sake, it is investigated once more.

Does the phrase "What then of him? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.12) indicate that [liberation] terminates with the body born of knowledge (*vidyā-yoni-śarīra*), or does it indicate that, setting aside that body, [liberation] terminates with the exhaustion of the enjoyment of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma? Having stated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) along with its supporting arguments here, [the author] points out its refutation by demonstrating that [the prima facie view] is established otherwise.

Thus, indeed, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks: "In this sentence, 'This serene being (*samprasāda*), having risen from this body and having attained the supreme light...', it is said 'from this body'; therefore, the attainment of Brahman occurs precisely at the conclusion of the body that began with the commencement of knowledge. Consequently, the passage beginning with 'until I am released' merely describes the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma; nevertheless, for the knower, that karma lasts only until the end of that body. Therefore, there is no contradiction even with that scriptural statement."

He refutes this with the words "not so. He states the reason for this as "because of the commenced [karma]": because of the diversity of commenced karmas, as indicated by such scriptural statements as "until I am released," liberation does not occur at the end of that particular body. It should be understood that the expression "from this body" refers to the end of the final body that has entered the stream of consciousness.

Anticipating the objection—“Why is an unintended meaning (*asvarasārtha*) such as ‘either there or elsewhere’ (*tatra vā anyatra vā*) postulated, when it would be better to follow the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the scripture which says, ‘from this very body’?”—the author replies with the word “furthermore” (*bhūyaḥ*). This is because the Mahārṣis have established in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts that for great sages devoted to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), there occurs a succession of births over many lifetimes. Vidura, for instance, was an incarnation of the deity Dharma. Thus, for those established in the knowledge of Brahman, after they have experienced the fruits of their commenced karma until the end of their final body, liberation (*mokṣa*) occurs at its conclusion.

Having raised the objection, "Is it not the case that you have already correctly stated the utility of the phrase 'from this body' (asmāccharīrāt)? he begins the resolution by stating that this phrase possesses ultimate utility: "But not [so]," etc. The objection is that the word "from" (asmāt), employed as a qualifier of the body, is redundant; the response is that it is not so. He states that the word "from," used as a qualifier of the body, is purposeful because its intent is to reveal the immediate state of wretchedness.

It is indeed so. Dwelling again in this body—which is impure and unfit for the experience of the Lord, unlike the mouths of Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and others—is like dwelling in a prison. To show that the Lord Himself has directly stated this very point, he says: "Regarding the fact that it must be abandoned. For it was said by the Lord Himself: "This world is impermanent and full of suffering. That the body must be abandoned is not only sung by the Lord; the great seers have also said so, as he states: "The abode of beings."

"One should abandon this abode of the elements, which has bones for its pillars, sinews for its bindings, flesh and blood for its plaster, and skin for its covering; which is foul-smelling and filled with urine and feces; which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. Thus it was said by the Blessed Manu.

Here, someone might raise an objection: "This is not tenable; since the Blessed One exists with equanimity toward all and is supremely compassionate, how can it be that for some there is liberation now, for others tomorrow, or for others the day after? If that were the case, either everyone would be liberated at once, or perhaps no one would ever be liberated at all. To this he says: "All [are equal]. All living beings are indeed equal; their various karmas are also equal insofar as they are beginningless.
Even though their karma is equal, it is impossible even to suggest that the Blessed One possesses defects such as partiality.

If there were a subversion of the scriptures that prevents [the charge of] partiality, cruelty, and so forth, then there would certainly be no partiality such as one person being liberated first and another later. This objection is extremely trivial. To mock this—asking "What kind of objection is this from you, whose mind has been refined by hearing various kinds of logic for such a long time?"—he says it is "trivial" (*alpasāra*). He clarifies its triviality with the word "extraordinary" (*citra*).

Since the flow of karma is diverse, the division of the timing of its fruits is accepted by all Tantrikas: that one person attains the station of the four-faced Brahmā now, another had already attained it previously, and yet another will attain it after a long time. By what cause is this division [determined]? This same question may be raised regarding the attainment of heaven, hell, and so forth. If it is argued that this diversity in the beginningless flow of karma is not to be questioned because it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then [the same applies] to the difference in time.

Even when the state of desiring liberation (mumukṣutva) has been established, that very state is to be employed as something not subject to further questioning; therefore, let your honor remain silent.

He enumerates the primary distinctions in meaning among the topics beginning with the fourth [adhikaraṇa] in the phrase "āvartya" (to be repeated). The meaning of the first topic is that the knowledge of Brahman is to be repeated many times; the subsequent topic has determined that the contemplation "I am [Brahman]" must be performed. In the third, however, it was stated that in the meditation on symbols (*pratīkopāsana*), the notion "I am [that]" is not to be formed. In the fourth, the meditation on the Sun and other deities as being limbs of ritual action (*karmāṅga*) is to be performed. In the fifth, however, there is the meditation on the *praṇava* together with its seat (*āsana*).

In the sixth [section], there is the daily contemplation. In the seventh and eighth, there is the non-clinging and destruction, respectively, of future merit and demerit. In the ninth, however, it is stated that those commenced merits and demerits are to be experienced only as they have begun. In the tenth, the necessity of performing the duties of one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) is established. In the final section, it is declared that liberation occurs at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma; this is the summary of the meaning.

At the beginning of the second quarter of the fourth chapter, he states the connection by way of restating the meaning of the two preceding chapters, saying "In the case of eternity," etc. In the first chapter, the exposition of the Supreme Reality was carried out; likewise, the nature of the individual soul—including its eternity, consciousness, and so forth—was also precisely explained in the second chapter.

In the third chapter, in the section on detachment (*vairāgyapāda*), the suffering of the individual soul (*jīva*)—who is like a great traveler in the forest of the world—was described. Furthermore, in the remaining portion of the scripture, beginning from the commencement of knowledge (*vidyārambha*) and ending with the latent impressions of knowledge (*vidyāvāsana*), whatever was to be stated in the interim has also been explained. Henceforth, they introduce the section on departure (*utkrāntipāda*) by stating "of one whose *prārabdha* karma remains," as it describes the manner of the soul's transition when casting off the gross body at the conclusion of *prārabdha*.

One might object: "Since death was already to be contemplated in the very section on detachment (*vairāgyapāda*) in connection with waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and fainting, why is death being considered here out of place? Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes that this too is a contemplation of the state [of the self] by means of the words beginning with "varṇye" (in what is being described). The syntactical connection here is as follows: although...

Such a form of death, characterized by the agitation of the collection of the body and the organs, should indeed be described in this very section on detachment (*vairāgyapāda*). Nevertheless, it is included as a supplementary topic (*anubandha*) in the chapter on the fruits (*phalādhyāya*) so that it may be understood that even for one who knows Brahman, death occurs when its time has arrived. Furthermore, some of childish intellect might think that because of the great majesty of Brahman, there is no death at all; to dispel that notion, this supplementary topic is provided here. Moreover, he states "of that" (*tasya*) to indicate that there is another reason for this connection.

In order to explain the specific departure through the cranial channel (*mūrdhanyanāḍī*) for one who knows Brahman during the process of exiting the body (*utkrānti*), there is first a description of the departure common to all. Now, one might object: "Is it not true that in the section on the fruits [of knowledge], death—which is essentially painful—should not even be mentioned? Anticipating this doubt, the author states "in the middle" (*madhye*) to show that for those who know Brahman, that very death is essentially blissful.

By mentioning death even among the fruits of knowledge—namely, the destruction of the remaining sins of the prior and subsequent [lives], the departure via the path beginning with light (*arciḥ*), and the attainment of Brahman—the author of the Sūtras implies that for one who knows Brahman, death is indeed of the nature of bliss, because it is included within the category of its results.

In this quarter [of the verse], you yourself have stated elsewhere regarding the fixed manner of departure: "Quickly uniting the group of organs in the mind, the mind in the vital breath (prāṇa), that [prāṇa] in the person, and him in the elements, and those elements in the Supreme, and that Supreme in the Self—the Lord leads both the knower of his own nature and the ignorant alike toward the common entrance of the path beyond, through the various channels as is appropriate. Anticipating the objection—namely, "What is the use of this restriction or such reflection? Even for one who departs in any manner whatsoever, by the majesty of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), there shall be entry into a specific channel and travel by the path beginning with light (arcirādi-mārga)"—the author says "vṛttiḥ" (the function) to show that this is not so.

The meaning is as follows: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) stated that it is the functioning of speech and the other organs; the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntin*) stated that it is speech and the others themselves. Likewise, the proponent of the prima facie view stated that the merging (*sampatti*) occurs in a different sequence; the proponent of the established conclusion stated that the merging occurs according to the specific manner and fixed rule [given] in the passage, "the collection of instruments [is merged] in the mind."

"What is the use of this restriction regarding a specific mode? Departure may occur by any means whatsoever. Anticipating the opponent's view—that by contemplating a specific mode of departure, a specific result will be achieved—he says "no" to that as well. He rejects this prima facie position with the words "not so. He establishes this rejection itself with the words "in the case of the attainment [of Brahman]. For scripture alone is our authority regarding the true nature of reality, and it is scripture alone that must be followed regarding the specific details to be contemplated.

Likewise, there is authority [for this]. Furthermore, the sequence is prescribed by rule, and it is not appropriate to claim that it is purposeless. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding the purposelessness of what is established by scripture, everything must be accepted exactly as it is heard; likewise, it must be contemplated in that very same way, and thus the investigation of the path (gati-cintana) and so forth must be performed.

"These two paths, O Pārtha, one who knows"—thus it was said by the Blessed Lord himself. The mention of reflecting upon that path is also an indication for reflecting upon the departure (*utkrānti*), since departure is the commencement of the journey. It is not proper to say that the scriptural teaching on the attainment [of Brahman], which is endowed with such a fixed order of sequence, is purposeless; this is the syntactical connection. He concludes the stated point with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). That reflection refers to the reflection on departure. It assists the knowledge (*vidyā*) insofar as it is established according to its nature and according to the authority of the scriptures.

Thus, he shows that the specific purpose of the statement regarding "departure" (*utkramaṇa*) and so forth is the refutation of the activity of those who propound falsehood, by means of the word "jīva. Both the Sāṅkhyas and the proponents of falsehood assert, "The *jīva* is not liberated [until death]. Among them, the proponents of falsehood also assert "liberation while living" (*jīvanmukti*), meaning that liberation occurs even while one is still alive once the knowledge of reality has been attained. For the sake of refuting both of these two positions, [the text] serves as a fortress for the village of the Vedas (*nigama-grāma*), which has been besieged by the collective incitements of their various sophistries.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: Having stated that for the sake of pacifying disturbances, the actions already commenced by the knower bear fruit, and that both the departure and the exit from the body are the same for both types of knowers of Brahman, the author of the Sūtras will later declare that for the attainment of Brahman—that is, for reaching Brahman—the process beginning with the entry into the *brahmanāḍī* (the channel to Brahman) is superior for the knower of Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that a practitioner (*yogin*) must contemplate future events, and that even matters such as the restraint of sons and others should be contemplated because they are destined to occur, [the author] states "Life-span" (*āyuḥ*), asserting that nothing whatsoever destined to occur need be contemplated; rather, only that which has been declared in the *Bhagavadgītā* as being worthy of contemplation should be contemplated.

The meaning is this: having perceived through many undesirable specific signs the limit of his own lifespan—that is, death—the yogi should perform in the interim whatever action is appropriate for that time; and as for the regulation of what ought to be done or not done regarding his sons and others that will arise in the future, that is not to be deliberated upon, for it is not to be thought about. Thus, there is simply no mention of it here. For there is no authoritative basis for the claim that a yogi must contemplate every future task, whether visible or invisible.

Anticipating the question, "What then is to be contemplated?", he states the specific object of contemplation with the words "in the Bhagavadgītā and so forth. Even that contemplation which is reckoned as a duty to be performed at the time of death in the Bhagavadgītā and other texts is necessarily restricted to the previously established method of yoga, corresponding to the state one has attained; thus, "steadfastness as before" (yathāpūrvadhī) is to be understood here. The meaning is that the uninterrupted continuation of the yoga already commenced is what must be cultivated here. All that is to be contemplated at the time of death is to be seen in detail precisely in the Bhagavadgītā and similar works.

The connection between the chapters (*pāda*) is as follows: that which is the fruit of knowledge during the time the gross body persists has already been stated; now, the fruit to be attained at the commencement of the journey during the state of its dissolution is being considered. Furthermore, because the commencement of the departure (*utkrānti*) is discussed here, there is also a connection with the first section (*adhikaraṇa*). The inquiry into its meaning begins with this first consideration: does this "attainment" (*sampatti*) concern the function of speech (*vāgvṛtti*), or does it concern the essential nature of speech (*vāksvarūpa*) itself?

For that purpose, it is investigated whether it is appropriate to accept the primary meaning of the word "vāk" (speech), and whether this "attainment" (*sampatti*) consists of dissolution (*laya*) or of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) preceded by the cessation of activity. Furthermore, does the mention of the attainment of the other organs apply even to the sense of dissolution, or does it apply to the sense of conjunction? Here, the author restates the position of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*): "The organs of action also [do not dissolve]. This is the meaning: the group of organs of action and the group of organs of knowledge do not undergo dissolution into the organ of mind (*manas*).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "because they do not originate from that" (*atatsambhavatvāt*). For the sense organs do not originate from the mind, such that their dissolution could be said to occur in the mind. Then, one might ask: "Of what, then, is 'merging' (*sampatti*) said? Anticipating this doubt, he says "of its function" (*tadvṛtteḥ*), meaning that because the function of the senses is dependent upon the mind, their dissolution can be said to occur in the mind. Therefore, it should be understood that the word "merging" refers only to the cessation of the function of speech. He rejects this [interpretation] with the words "this [is not so]. Here, he provides the reason: "because of both of those" (*tadubhaya-*).

The objection regarding the dissolution of the function of speech (*vāgvṛtti*) and the dissolution of the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) is the same, and the resolution is likewise the same. Thus, the meaning is that this falls under the scope of the maxim: "Where the fault is equal for both sides. Just as the merging (*sampatti*) cannot be asserted because speech does not have the mind (*manas*) as its material cause (*prakṛti*), so too the statement of merging is not tenable for the function of speech, as it also lacks the mind as its material cause; any kind of reconciliation applicable in one case applies equally to both.

Now, raising the objection that since the merits and defects are equal in both positions, why is one position accepted, or how is the term *sampatti* (attainment/perfection) appropriate in that position, he says: "It is attainment (*sampatti*). The word *sampatti*, through its root and prefix, expresses precisely a connection (*sambandha*). And such a connection is indeed possible between the organ of speech (*vāgindriya*) and the mind-organ (*manaindriya*).

Regarding this position, he states the specific reason [for preferring it] with the words "by the instrument" (karaṇa). The word "speech" (vāk) refers primarily to the organ of speech; its application to that function is figurative, because [the function] possesses the attributes of that [organ]. Therefore, the sense is that our own position alone must be accepted in order to establish the primary status of the word "speech."

The connection [of the topic] is clear through reflection according to the sequence of the scripture: "Speech merges into the mind; the mind into the breath. However, an inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is it here stated that there is a dissolution (*laya*) of the mind, or rather a conjunction (*saṃyoga*)? Furthermore, in this context, does the term "breath" (*prāṇa*) refer to water (*āpaḥ*), or to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) itself? And in the sentence "Consisting of water" (*āpomayaḥ*), does it intend to express a relationship between material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*), or does it intend to express nourishment (*āpyāyana*)? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains that it refers to food (*anna*).

In the statement "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of water," since a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikṛti-bhāva*) is possible between two things that are not themselves the vital breath, let it be that the dissolution of the mind occurs in the water which is the material cause of the vital breath—water being its material cause and food being the material cause of the mind, according to the scriptural statement, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food. Therefore, it might be argued that the dissolution of the mind in the water—the material cause of the vital breath—is what is expressed by the phrase "the mind [is merged] in the vital breath. He rejects this position with the words "Not so. He states the reason for this as follows: "Because of each respective... (*tattaditi*).

In the passage, “For the mind, my dear, consists of food” (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*), it is not stated that the mind has food as its material cause (*prakṛti*), but rather that it is nourished by food. Consequently, since there is no possibility of a relationship between material cause and effect, the word “merging” (*sampatti*) does not denote dissolution (*pralaya*). This is what [the author] expresses with the words “that and that. If one then asks, “What is being said then? he replies, “as before” (*prāgvat*). Previously, in the statement “Speech merges into the mind” (*vāṅmanasi sampadyate*), mere conjunction was expressed by means of the locative case; here too, it is the same. To the question, “How is that so? he says, “for from that... here” (*tata iha hi*).

Just as previously, in the passage "speech [merges] into the mind," there was an indication of conjunction by means of the locative case, so too here, in the phrase "the mind [merges] into breath," conjunction itself is indicated by the locative case; for it is improper to abandon the introductory principle (upakrama).

Because of the sequential statement, "The mind [merges] in breath, breath in heat," the connection is clear according to the order of the Śruti. However, the investigation of its meaning is as follows: Does the breath merge into heat, or into the individual soul (jīva)? Is the sentence "breath in heat" intended to mean merging into heat preceded by merging into the individual soul, or is it intended to mean merging into heat alone? If it is intended to mean merging into heat preceded by merging into the individual soul...

Does the natural sense of the statement, "The vital breath [merges] in heat," suffer any loss? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks as follows: since the direct merging of the vital breath—along with its eleven organs—into heat is explicitly stated by scripture, there is no intermediate merging into the self (*ātman*). He expresses this in the words, "the vital breath. That vital breath, together with its eleven organs, enters into heat immediately thereafter. He states the reason for this: "because it is heard thus. For it is the established rule of those who know the principles of interpretation that one must accept exactly what is heard in scripture.

Furthermore, regarding the assumption that the self (ātman) reaches [the heart] in the middle stage, he says "in the middle" to indicate that this would entail the abandonment of what is heard in scripture. To this, the reply is "no. He states the reason for this: "because the conjunction with the self has also been stated. If only the conjunction with light were heard in scripture, then the process you have described might be accepted; however, the conjunction with the self in the middle stage is also directly declared by scripture itself in the passage: "In this very way, at the time of death, all the vital breaths (prāṇas) gather together into this self.
Therefore, since both effects are equally heard in scripture, one must provide a consistent interpretation that reconciles them without contradiction.

To the question, "How is there no contradiction?", he says: "Of the vital breath" (*prāṇasya*). When the soul in sleep—that is, the soul connected with itself—merges with the subtle elements extracted from its own body, the vital breath's attainment of fire occurs through a succession, according to the analogy of the Yamunā reaching the ocean after having fallen into the Gaṅgā; it is not a direct attainment, according to the analogy of the Gaṅgā reaching the ocean directly. This is the meaning: that the vital breath, together with all the senses, reaches the soul and, along with the soul, merges into fire; this must be accepted in order to avoid the contradiction between the two authorities.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: in the passage, "His vital breath (*prāṇa*) merges into heat (*tejas*)," the merging of the vital breath into heat is stated; the question is whether that merging is into heat alone or into all the elements (*bhūta*). To that end, the inquiry is: does the merging consist in conjunction with heat conjoined with other elements, or conjunction with heat alone? Is the word "heat" intended to denote heat alone, or is it intended to denote [heat] as conjoined [with others]? Does the statement, "consisting of earth," "consisting of water," and so forth, show a simultaneous conjunction with multiple elements, or not?

Do the scriptural statement on tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and the traditional teaching on quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) together demonstrate that only combined elements possess the capacity for causal efficacy, or not? Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says, "In fire," arguing that since the text "he attains fire" mentions only fire as the material cause, the attainment must occur in fire alone. [The word] *yukta* refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the embodied soul (*tanubhṛt*), because prefixes illuminate the meaning already contained within the verbal root.
