The sense is: let the vital breath—the soul residing therein—be connected to fire alone. He states the reason for this with the words "in fire."

Anticipating the objection that, according to the "logic of the umbrella-bearer" (*chatrinyāya*), there might be an inclusion of even those things distinct from fire, he says "no" with the words "the logic of the umbrella-bearer.

For in that case, since the movement of even those without umbrellas is perceived through direct observation, all are included by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, in this present case, as for the existence of things distinct from fire—

"How can that be logical, given the absence of authoritative evidence?"—to this objection, he rejects the position with the word "no. He states the reason for this: "so elsewhere," meaning that there is scriptural authority for the soul's consisting of all elements as it migrates, such as: "It consists of earth, it consists of water, it consists of fire. Furthermore, he cites the scripture regarding the tripartition of elements—"I shall make each of these threefold"—as proof for the commencement of the universe. He shows that the author of the Sūtras has declared this very point by stating: "on account of abundance."

The meaning is that this is according to the sūtra: "But [it is so] because of the triadic nature and the predominance [of fire]. Therefore, since a single element lacks the capacity to produce an effect on its own, it should be understood that the vital breath (prāṇa) merges into light (tejas) as it is conjoined with the other elements. Here, the mention of the fivefold compounding (pañcīkaraṇa) serves as an illustration for the five gross elements (pañcīkṛta-pañcabhūta) derived from them. For in the world, the commencement of the body and so forth is clearly perceived not merely by means of the five gross elements alone, but rather by means of the material cause consisting of the five gross elements.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is considered whether this departure (utkrānti) is common to both the knower and the ignorant, or belongs to the ignorant alone. The inquiry into that matter is: does the scriptural text, "Going upwards by that," convey the departure of the knower or not?

Does this scriptural statement conflict here with the texts concerning immortality and the denial of departure? Is "immortality" of the nature of the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, or is it of the nature of liberation from all bonds? And is the departure being denied one that has the body as its point of departure, or one that has the self as its point of departure? Here, he sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "In this regard," etc. Based on the scripture, "One who knows Him thus becomes immortal here," the one established in Brahman becomes immortal in this world; therefore, his departure is not logical.

He refutes this with the word "non-existent" (*asad*). He states the reason for its non-existence with the words "possessing qualities" (*saguṇa*). The meaning is as follows: only if liberation were twofold could it be said that the scriptural passages concerning the "going" (*gati*) and so forth have another purpose; but there is no such twofold nature. This is because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for a Brahman distinct from the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahman*), nor for the attainment thereof. Therefore, if liberation exists, it must be qualified alone. The common assertion that "liberation is devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇā muktiḥ*) is merely a rumor among those who hold such views. [As the scripture says: "He enjoys all desires together."

Thus, [the qualified Brahman] is indicated as that which is to be attained. However, since the unqualified [Brahman] is neither heard of in scripture, nor meditated upon, nor attained, the construction of liberation through the unqualified is declared to be laughable due to its lack of scriptural authority. This very point is stated by the words "suguṇa" (endowed with qualities). He concludes the established meaning with the words "tasmāt" (therefore): by the phrase "he becomes immortal here," a certain state of liberation similar to such [liberation] has been described—namely, a state of liberation resembling direct liberation, characterized by the non-clinging and destruction of past and future karmas, as stated in the passage concerning the fire.

Here, someone raises an objection: "Since everything without exception has dissolved at the end of the gross body, movement due to the embrace of the subtle elements is indeed purposeless, as there is an absence of experience. One should not object by asking how movement could occur in the absence of a body; for it is entirely logical that the soul, whose nature is atomic, can move even in the absence of a body. To this he replies: "Of that which is determined to be atomic. Because the atomic soul is by its very nature possessed of activity, movement is indeed possible even without the persistence of a subtle body.

If it is then objected: "The meeting with the Moon is heard of on the path; how can that be for one who is devoid of a body?", [the author] states the following to show that this too is unestablished: "On the path," etc. The sense is this: having gone to the world of the Moon in one's own form, one might assume some new body there and converse with the Moon. To such an inquiry, the answer must be stated as follows: "Upon reaching the Supreme Light, immediately thereafter [a new state] arises," and so forth, which implies the cessation of all ignorance. This is the meaning: for one who has departed from the body...

For one who has attained the supreme light, the cessation of all ignorance occurs only afterwards; therefore, a journey is required. And that journey—by means of a specific path, after having engaged in dialogues and so forth along the way—is clearly seen to belong to one possessing a physical body (*vigraha*), because this is explicitly stated by the Śruti itself. Nor can it be said that one assumes a body midway and then engages in dialogues; for if one were to postulate a new body at each successive stage, it would result in the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Therefore...

It is more appropriate to say that the soul proceeds toward the attainment of a specific destination with the very constituent parts of its former body still attached. Therefore, it travels enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), for the body consists precisely of the envelopment of these subtle elements. It is only for one who possesses such a body that all the following is logical: the journey along the path beginning with the Rays (*arciḥ*); the intermediate discourse; the traveling to the respective deities presiding over the Rays and so forth; and being carried across by them. This is not the case otherwise.
Going is not said to be mere vibration, but rather a specific kind of action; for it is described as the attainment of a specific location by one possessing a body, by means of a specific path.

In response to the student's inquiry, "What is meant here by the 'subtle body'?", [the author] restates the Sāṅkhya system and, because that system lacks a foundation in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), reveals his own intended meaning starting with the words "At the beginning of the kalpa. This is indeed the Sāṅkhya procedure: at the beginning of a *kalpa*, a body is formed from the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) and so forth, which is destroyed at the end of the *kalpa*. Furthermore, each such body is restricted to a specific individual living being and follows its respective gross body, which is not so restricted.

The gross bodies of gods, animals, humans, and so forth, are indefinite, varying according to one's karma. The subtle body, however, persists and follows along through all gross bodies from the beginning of a kalpa until its end; thus it is called "the follower" (*anuyāyin*). It is also called the "liṅga-śarīra" (the subtle body). Its nature is shown by way of an illustration: "like a doll inside a puppet-maker's box. For the Sāṅkhyas maintain that it exists like an artificial doll placed within a puppet-maker's box.

This Sāṅkhya position, however, is accepted as a mere conceptual construction because no specific means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is observed for it. He states his own preferred view, which is consistent with all means of valid cognition, beginning with the words "subtle constituents" (sūkṣmāṃśa). That which has departed from the previous body for the sake of assuming a subsequent body is specifically a particular collection of the subtle constituents of the five elements; this alone is called the "subtle body" (sūkṣmaśarīra).

Here, the proponent of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-vādī*), unable to tolerate the report of further departure (*utkramaṇa*), objects: "By the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*)—that is, by the realization of 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*) and other such statements—the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) dissolves even beforehand; it does not dissolve through departure. Therefore, the mention of departure for those who know reality is indeed purposeless. He states that this [objection] is without substance:

"Insubstantial" (*asāra*)—he establishes this very insubstantiality with the words "O Mother" (*māta*). The phrase "while living" refers to the bondage of *saṃsāra*. To say that both [liberation and living] reside in one and the same thing at once is entirely incoherent, like saying, "My mother is barren. He demonstrates this contradiction by showing the undesirable consequence: "If he were liberated" (*muktaścediti*). If the one you call "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) were truly liberated through the mere knowledge of reality, then he would not experience suffering thereafter; in subsequent time, that person would not suffer. Yet, [such a person] is seen [to suffer].

If it is argued that the suffering rooted in hunger, thirst, anger, and so forth—which is associated with the bodies of those whom you yourself designate as "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta)—is therefore false for them, we reply: no, because their suffering was already false previously. Thus, there is no difference between the earlier and later states; this is what he means by saying "it should be told. For it is your own established doctrine that suffering is always false, and you yourself state that this very suffering, being false, constitutes saṃsāra. Consequently, there is no liberation from saṃsāra.

Now, as for the claim that there is equality regarding departure [from the body], that is not so; for the Blessed One has specifically described a distinction in the departure of the knower and the ignorant: "Remembering whatever state [of being] he leaves the body at the end. Therefore, how can it be said that the departure is the same? To this he says: "Whichever... This is the construction: "Whatever state the embodied beings remember while leaving this body, to that very state they go"—thus the departure is said to be unequal. Therefore, the equality of departure does not hold.

He refutes this with the words "that is not so. He states the reason for that: "because there is equality in respect to that alone" (*tanmātrasāmyāt*). The meaning is this: let it be granted that there is a specific difference in the departure [of the soul] according to one's karma; nevertheless, we have stated that the mere fact of departing from the body is common to all. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, you have admitted a disparity in the final cognition (*antima-pratyaya*); how is that so?"—he refutes it by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandhī*) with the word "knowledge" (*vidyā*). In the *Sadvidyā*, the *Daharavidyā*, and others, there is indeed a distinction due to the difference in the forms of the objects of knowledge (*vedya-ākāra-bheda*).

Moreover, because they are both called "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavidyā), there is also an identity of the vidyās; likewise, here too, the departure (utkramaṇa) is one and the same. Nevertheless, it is not the case that there is no distinction due to the particularity of the respective meditations (bhāvanā).

There is no contradiction. The phrase "something" establishes the stated meaning through a method observed in common worldly usage. The sense is that in the doctrine of partial similarity (*ekadeśasādharmya*), the establishment of total identity is neither necessary nor established; for similarity and dissimilarity are well-known in both the world and the Veda according to the authority of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is because similarity and dissimilarity are well-established in both the world and the Veda in accordance with the means of valid cognition.

This is the intended meaning: since the *Vājasaneyaka* states, "His vital breaths do not depart," thereby prohibiting the departure of the breaths for one who knows the self (*adhyātma-vid*), it has been said that such departure pertains to the subject of the ignorant; this is stated in another passage of that very same text.

It has already been clearly stated and demonstrated in the Bhāṣya itself that this [objection] has been answered by the denial of the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the individual soul (*jīva*), as in the passage: "The vital breaths do not depart from him. Therefore, nothing remains for us to say here. Disciples must strictly engage in the contemplation of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*). Consequently, the definitive conclusion of the Śārīraka-śāstra is this: whether accompanied by the vital breaths or not, the soul departs through the cranial artery and proceeds by the path beginning with light (*arcis*).

In this regard, the internal connection (*avāntarasaṅgati*) is very clear in the Commentary: "It was stated that at the time of departure, the inner self—the presiding lord of the organs—along with the collection of organs and the vital breaths, merges into the subtle elements beginning with fire. Fearing that this merging does not occur for the one who knows (*vidvas*), [the author] has refuted that objection. Now, regarding the doubt as to whether those subtle elements, enveloped by the living self (*jīva*), proceed toward their own effects according to one's karma and knowledge, or whether they merge into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)."

The investigation into that matter, however, is as follows: do the elements designated by the word "light" proceed according to their respective actions and knowledge, or do they merge into the Supreme Self? Is the term "Supreme Deity" here intended to refer to the Supreme Self in its state as the destination, or to the Supreme Self not in that state? Is there a purpose possible for this merging, or not? Now, one might ask: why is the resolution regarding the denial of the departure of the knower not stated immediately after the departure of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the subsequent departure of the elements, rather than here? To this, he says: "Of the soul... [and so forth].

The meaning is this: having spoken of the departure of the living being (jīva) in general, there is a great appropriateness in the connection [of the next section], which addresses the doubt that for those who are wise—being a specific kind of living being—there is no departure, and asserts that even for them there is indeed departure. If one were to speak of the departure of the wise only after first stating the departure of the elements immediately following the departure of the living being, the connection would be somewhat forced.

Therefore, for this reason, this connection with the heart (*hārdayoga*), although common to both the knower and the ignorant, is placed above that; it is placed above the establishment of the departure of the knower. The word "api" (even/although) is used to clarify this meaning: that the connection with the heart, like the statement "speech merges into the mind" (*vāṅ manasi saṃpadyate*) and so forth, is indeed common to both the knower and the ignorant, yet it is mentioned immediately after the establishment of the knower’s departure due to a specific point of connection.

Now, raising the objection that if the connection with the heart (*hṛdayayoga*) is equal, then the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) must also be equal, he says "not so" by stating "unequal. He states the reason for this inequality as "having reached," and the reason for the equality of the connection with the heart as "by way of the opening of the path. The meaning is this: the connection with the heart is the opening of the path, and that is indeed the same for both the knower and the ignorant; however, the paths beyond that—the channels—are divided.

Just as many people who have departed through a single gate travel to various places by way of different paths, even so, from the single location of the heart, there occurs the departure to those various places according to one's own karma by way of the paths of the various channels (nāḍīs).

Here, one might raise the objection: "Since there is no purpose in reaching the heart (*hārda*), let there simply be departure according to one's karma and according to one's knowledge; what is the use of this pointless attainment of the heart? Anticipating this, he states the specific purpose for that attainment with the words "to attain" (*prāptum*). The connection [of the verse] is as follows: In order to attain both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), when the embodied soul (*tanubhṛt*)—having attained its subtle body—is departing, what fruit could there be from merging (*sampatti*) into the Supreme Deity who resides in the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*)? Therefore, such a merging does not even exist.

Therefore, for this reason, the statement "fire [is merged] in the highest deity" is merely a restatement of what is already established regarding the Supreme Self—which is eternally uncomposed and never subject to composition; there is no new act of composition here at all, because such would be fruitless. He refutes this with the words "it is not so. He provides the justification for this refutation with the words "in accordance with the means of knowledge" (*mānānusārāt*). For when an object is established by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is precisely in accordance with that means of knowledge that the purpose (*prayojana*) is to be conceived.

It is the established rule for those who know political ethics (*nīti*) that an object proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must not be abandoned merely because its purpose is not immediately apparent. Anticipating the question, "What then is the purpose here?", he says: "Supreme" (*parama*).

Fatigue arises from the process of departing from the body during the transition into the Supreme Self; the cessation of that fatigue results from such a transition into the Supreme Self. Therefore, the meaning is that one proceeds by way of each respective path after resting in the heart (*hārda*), for the sake of ceasing the fatigue produced by departure and for the attainment of the desired fruit.

"In the commentary (*bhāṣya*), the connection [of the topic] is as follows: 'Is this merging into the Supreme Self of the nature of an absorption into the cause, like the dissolution of the material world (*prākṛta-laya*), or is it of the nature of non-distinction (*avibhāga*), as in the case of the passage beginning with "Speech [is merged] in the mind"? The investigation into its meaning is: Is this merging of the nature of dissolution, or is it of the nature of non-distinction?"

Is it reasonable that the statement, "Heat [reaches] the highest," intends to express the attainment of the state of being a cause (*kāraṇāpatti*), or does it intend merely non-distinction (*avibhāga*)? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) thinks as follows: the "attainment" (*sampatti*) mentioned here with respect to the deity must indeed be dissolution (*laya*). He states this with the words, "attainment. He provides the reason for this with the words, "for she... The meaning is that because that deity is the cause of all things, it is not logical to speak of anything other than dissolution.

"In that case, the deity is capable of creating [the next body]; let it go by means of what has been given by her"—this is the meaning. He states that this is improper with the word "unreal" (asat). He establishes that very point with the phrase "it follows" (anuṣajyate): for here, the word "sampadyate" (is merged/attains), which is first introduced in the passage "Speech is merged in the mind," is supplied throughout all subsequent instances.

A lack of uniformity (vaiṣamya) would result for that which is continuously connected; moreover, when a consistent (avaipūpya) explanation is possible, inconsistency is indeed improper. Furthermore, what is called "destruction" would have to be merely a separation from the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma); but that is not tenable, because such a separation from the subtle elements is incompatible with the continued connection to activities such as movement and so forth. Now, one might object: "The Supreme Deity, who is omnipotent, could simply initiate another body for him whose body has perished. Anticipating this, the meaning is that there would be the fault of the excessive complexity (kalpanā-gaurava) of such an assumption.

Furthermore, for the knower of Brahman traveling by the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*), travel is simply not possible without being enveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*). In contrast, the travel of the individual soul (*jīva*) proceeding by the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādi*) is clearly stated in the Pañcāgni-vidyā and other texts to occur through envelopment by the subtle elements. Therefore, in this case as well, it occurs precisely through envelopment by the subtle elements, and not by its own nature (*svarūpa*). For this very reason, the claim that travel occurs by its own nature because of its atomic dimension (*aṇutva*) is refuted, as it contradicts numerous authoritative proofs.

"In this way, the mode of departure has been described as being identical in form for both the wise and the ignorant, up to the point of the commencement of the journey. Now, the specific distinction regarding the wise is stated"—thus the connection (*saṅgati*) was stated in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*). The investigation into its meaning is as follows: Is it possible that there is a restrictive rule that the wise must travel solely through the cranial aperture (*mūrdhanya-nāḍī*), or not? Is the passage, "Going upwards by those two," a restatement of an accidental departure, or is it an injunction prescribing a restrictive rule for traveling via a specific channel? And are the channels difficult to discern, or easy to discern?

Here he restates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "the network of channels" (*nāḍījāla*). In an extremely subtle network of channels, it is not easy for a person who has departed from the body to discern the specific channel of liberation. Therefore, the statement beginning with "going upwards by that" (*tayordhvamāyan*) refers to a meaning that is possible only occasionally, and not to a fixed or necessary meaning. He states this very point with the words "therefore, indeed. The movement through the channel at the crown of the head for a person being liberated occurs only occasionally and is not mandatory.

The meaning is that there might be a departure for a person even through the *mūrdhan* (cranial) channel at some time. Therefore, let such passages as "going upwards from those two" (*tad ūrdhvam āyan*) be possible for one who goes upward [through the cranial channel] and attains immortality. He refutes this prima facie view with the words "Not so. He states the reason for that: "By knowledge" (*vidyā*). For one who is delighted by the knowledge of Brahman, a clear understanding of his own appropriate channel arises through the radiance of the heart; by means of that, he enters his own channel and proceeds toward the human goal he desires. This is the meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with *svādhīna*, it describes how one who has attained full knowledge through the grace of the Blessed One travels instantly, like an arrow, to the end of the Brahma-world via the central channel (*mūrdhan-āḍī*) solely by the impulsion of the Blessed One. The term *svatantra* refers to the Blessed One known as the "Heart" (*hārda*). Along with his own unimpaired prosperity (*sampad*), he is accompanied by *Lakṣmī*, who is called his "consort in dharma" (*sahadharmacāriṇī*) because she bestows all sovereignty; for they say, "Hṛṣīkeśa is with Lakṣmī. Alternatively, it may refer to the sovereignty of the Blessed One himself.

The word *eka* signifies preeminence. Abiding in the center of the heart-lotus, he has his own form concealed from non-devotees—that is, he does not manifest his own form to those who are not devotees. Alternatively, it may mean that his own form is not fixed [in one place] for non-devotees, while it is manifested to devotees; for they say, "He is exceedingly far away for non-devotees, yet stands before the devotees. The statement that he is the "householder of the seven worlds" demonstrates his role as the protector and father of all.

The meaning is this: although there are many channels within the wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), [the yogi] pierces the Suṣumnā channel—which extends from the navel to the crown of the head, sustains everything, and brings all satisfaction—and having opened its mouth, he hurls the individual soul (jīva) through the central aperture like an arrow discharged by an archer, leading the seeker of liberation as far as the supreme state.

The connection [of this section] is that the departure of the knower, having emerged from the heart through the suṣumnā channel—which is superior to the śaṅku—and following the rays of the sun, is being considered. The inquiry into its meaning, however, is as follows: Is it possible for the knower to have a restriction regarding the path by following the rays, or not? Does the statement, "He ascends upwards by means of the rays," merely restate an optional course of departure, or does it intend to enjoin a restrictive rule? And is it possible for one who dies at night to proceed by following the rays, or not?

"Do the rays exist by night or not? Here, he restates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "by these. In the statement, "By these very rays he ascends upwards," that upward journey of the yogi which was described as having the sun's rays as its support is restricted to daytime. He states the reason for this with the words "because it is untenable at night. The meaning is that because the sun's rays are absent during the night, [the journey] is illogical. He rejects this with the word "no," and establishes that very point with the words "during the day."

Just as during the day the existence of the sun’s rays is established by the mark of heat in the shadow, so too at night the existence of the sun’s rays is indeed present due to the very same mark of heat. Anticipating the objection, "Why then is it not clearly perceived?", he says, "They are subtler. In this case as well, the shadow during the day serves as the illustrative example. To the objection, "In the rainy season and so forth, there is no heat at night; how can the existence of the sun’s rays be established there?", he replies, "According to the logic of winter days. The meaning is: if even during the day in the winter season there is no heat, does that mean the existence of the sun’s rays is thereby non-existent? No.

Granted that the presence of sunbeams may exist for one who dies at night; nevertheless, since the death of those who know the Self at night is prohibited by the scripture itself, it is impossible for them to die at night—thus there is no connection [to the present topic] to be doubted. However, the investigation into its meaning is as follows: is the attainment of Brahman possible for a knower who dies at night, or not?

Does the statement that dying at night is a cause for falling into a lower state indicate that one who dies at night fails to attain Brahman? Or does it not? Is this censure of dying at night intended for both the wise and the ignorant, or is it restricted to the ignorant? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated as "of all": dying during the night is unpraiseworthy for everyone, both the wise and the ignorant; therefore, a yogin should die by day alone. If this yogin were to depart [from the body] at night, he would die, but that death would not be his final death. He refutes this prima facie view:

"It is improper"—this is what he explains by the word "karman" (action). The meaning is this: it has been determined that liberation occurs at the conclusion of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma; and that conclusion of commenced karma is indeed at an indefinite time, occurring either by night or by day. Regarding this point, he says "tāvat" (only for so long), indicating that the scripture itself—"For him, there is delay only for so long"—is the authority. This means that the delay in liberation is stated to last only until the end of karma; and that end of karma the knower of Brahman attains.

Having stated that the final body is preceded by the means of knowledge that manifest it as the final body, he demonstrates therein the absence of any restriction regarding day or night, place or time, or other instrumental causes for the departure from the body; and [he shows] that even for those who practice the rites performed upon the funeral pyre, the knowers of the supreme self go by the path beginning with the Rays (arcir-ādi) to the Supreme Person.

He also makes known the attainment [of liberation] by the words "wherein" (*yatra*). That final body (*antyam śarīram*) would be that one in which the liberation of a certain qualified person is reckoned as being fixed by those who know the birth-records (*jātaka-jña*). However, it cannot be determined by that much alone that there is no other body, because another birth is still possible due to the potential occurrence of specific sins in the interim; thus he says "but not" (*na tu*). Here, by the words beginning with "for not" (*na hi*), he shows that there is no distinction such as day and night, nor distinctions of place and so forth.

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), he shows that what was previously stated—the absence of distinction between day and night—is taken here as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The meaning is: just as there is no distinction between day and night, so too in this state there is no death in this place, nor death by this cause, and so forth; it is exactly like that. Thus [is described] the performance of rituals related to the corpse.

He says, "The corpse (śavyam)," to show that even ritual observance (*niyama*) is not required for those who know the supreme self (*adhyātmavid*) in order to attain liberation (*apavarga*). The scriptural passage beginning with, "Whether they perform the funeral rites (*śavya*) for him here or not, they proceed to the light (*arciḥ*) itself," is heard. Thus it should be understood; such is the unique [rule] concerning those who know the supreme self.

The meaning is that the statement must be considered in its proper context. Now, an objection may be raised: if it is true that a knower of the Self (*adhyātmavid*) has no duty to perform funeral rites (*śrāddha*), then upon his death, his sons and disciples might not perform the collection of rites associated with his passing; and if that were so, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the doctrine of non-attachment (*alepaka*). This is not a valid consequence, because for those very sons who follow the Vedic path, the entire range of ritual acts is to be performed specifically for the sake of the deceased.

If those [rites] were not performed, there would be transgression due to the abandonment of prescribed duties; therefore, the entire collection of ritual acts must necessarily be performed by sons and others for the sake of their fathers and ancestors. Consequently, the objection that [the liberated soul] is "untainted" (alepaka) does not apply. Just as a rite performed by Kuśa, Lava, and others with respect to Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and so forth, serves solely for their own welfare, so too a rite performed by sons and others with respect to a liberated soul becomes a cause for one's own prosperity; thus, it is faultless.

By the same reason for which it was stated that there is no distinction between day and night at the death of the wise man (*vidvan*), it is stated by that very reason that there is also no distinction between the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). This constitutes an analogical connection (*atideśikī saṅgatiḥ*). The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Is the attainment of Brahman possible for the wise man who dies during the southern course, or not? Does the statement, "Now, he who dies during the southern course,"—which speaks of the deceased reaching the moon—imply the absence of attainment of Brahman, or not?

Regarding the statement about the return of those who have reached the moon: does it apply equally to both the wise and the ignorant, or is it restricted to the ignorant? Is it more reasonable to adopt its general application—conforming to the general scriptural text supported by the traditional rules regarding the timing of death for Bhīṣma and others, who waited for the proper time—or is it more reasonable to adopt its restriction to the ignorant, in accordance with the supplementary passage, "the majesty of Brahman"?

Regarding this, the author restates the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—that for one who has reached the moon, a return is indeed certain—by saying "the body. Even a master of yoga, if he casts off the body at the time of the southern course [of the sun], then he attains union with the moon; but after that union with the moon, he is born here again. Why? To this he says: "because of the scriptural statement to that effect" (tacchruteḥ). This refers to the scriptural declaration of the return of those who have reached the moon. Likewise, there is the scriptural statement of return in the Smṛti: "Then they return again by that very same path. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.5)
Regarding this, there is the Smṛti passage: "Having reached the lunar light there, the yogins return. This [view] he now refutes.

"Not so," he says. He establishes that very point by means of the principle previously stated: at the conclusion of *prārabdha* karma, liberation is indeed certain in every respect. "Whether one reaches the moon or the sun"—this is the general rule. If it is asked, "Then for what purpose does the knower of Brahman reach the moon?", [the answer is: for what purpose does he reach the sun? If it is argued that they do so "for the sake of rest" (*viśrānti*), he replies that this is equal in both cases. Then, raising the objection as to why Bhīṣma, who was desirous of liberation, waited for the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), [the author] addresses this by showing it to be established otherwise.

"He protects the world"—this is the meaning. For Bhīṣma, as the promoter of Dharma, is a benefactor of the universe. Thus, in order to demonstrate the excellence of death during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa) for those of meritorious deeds, he waited for the northern course. Just as the Blessed Lord performs every action for the sake of the welfare of the world (lokasaṅgraha), so too Bhīṣma’s waiting for the northern course was for the sake of the welfare of the world; therefore, there is no contradiction.

Regarding this, he states another way of resolving the objection with the words "kiñcit" (something). This is the meaning: in the world, it cannot be asserted that because a certain practice is observed for one specific person, that same practice belongs to everyone; for example, among the five Pāṇḍavas, there was but one wife, yet Karṇa was Kānīna (born of a maiden) and Vyāsa was also Kānīna. Therefore, the rule or dharma pertaining to a particular case remains restricted to that very case.

Thus, it cannot be inferred that because Bhīṣma had the expectation of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*), this must be the rule for all knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*). This is the grammatical connection of the words here: for the son of Jahnavī, the battle, dying in battle, the waiting for the time of the northern solstice, and so forth—these were by his own will, determined by the specific karma remaining from his *prārabdha* (commenced) actions. This is not common to all knowers of Brahman.

And that Bhīṣma became a Vasu, yet he was not liberated directly; thus [the author] says "sa ca" (and he). Therefore, this is not an illustration for the point that one who desires liberation must wait for a specific time.

He concludes the stated point with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). For men, night is the dark fortnight; for the ancestors, night is the dark fortnight; for the gods, night is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). Even during these times, a yogi who casts off the body may attain liberation. Anticipating the objection—"In that case, why is the excellence of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) and the censure of the southern solstice expressed in the Purāṇas and other texts?"—he says: "They may be [so] regarding others. This means: regarding those other than the knower of the Self (*adhyātmavid-yati*).

Furthermore, in the Bhagavad Gītā, what are expressed by the words "day" and so forth, as well as the words "night" and so forth, are indeed two paths and not specific divisions of time; therefore, the meaning is that for those who know Brahman, there is no such restriction regarding day and night.

He summarizes the principal meanings of the topics (adhikaraṇas) already discussed by stating, "they merge" (*sampadyante*). The meaning of the first topic—that speech and the other organs merge into the mind—is as follows: likewise, in the subsequent topics as well, he explains the meanings in sequence: that mind, conjoined with the sense organs such as speech, merges into the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and that vital air, accompanied by them, merges into the presiding soul (*jīva*); and that soul, possessing all those aforementioned things, merges into the subtle group of elements.

This departure is the same for both the knower of Brahman and the non-knower of Brahman. "Union" refers to immediate conjunction; "attainment" refers to merging into the Supreme Brahman, which is merely a union with the Supreme Self. It involves exiting through the *brahmanāḍī* (the channel of Brahman) and traveling by means of the rays of the sun. The meaning is that liberation occurs immediately thereafter, even during the night, during the night of the gods, or during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
The third quarter of the fourth chapter.

Now, summarizing the meaning of the section to be explained, he shows it with the words "having emerged" (nirgatya). This is the meaning: having emerged from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) and having taken hold of the sun’s ray connected to the channels (nāḍī), the yogi goes by whatever path he travels, while offerings are sent to him by the hosts of gods who come forth to meet him, in accordance with the scriptural authority: "All the gods bring tribute to him. Thus, the yogi is one to whom offerings have been sent—that is, to whom oblations have been presented.

This path, which leads to Mukunda—that is, the means for attaining Mukunda—is established by the sage Pārāśarya (Vyāsa) through five distinct logical sections (*adhikaraṇas*). What does it do? It causes us to reach the supreme abode, the city on the far shore of the ocean of delusion. It is the "highway to liberation," meaning the path beginning with the *arcis* (the flame).

The connection here is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Having described the commencement of the journey for the knower who has departed by means of the specific channel (nāḍī) through the favor of light and so forth, the path of that one as he travels is now determined. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Does the knower travel only by the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi), or is there no fixed rule, such that he may go either by that path or by another? Furthermore, is a single path taught in all the meditations (vidyās), or are there various paths?

Is it proper to resort to various paths because of the mention of different sequences and different constituent elements, or is it proper to resort to the unity of the path through the recognition of the Sun and other [deities] as being the same? Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is stated: "In the case of the differences among the branches (*śākhābheda*). In the *Chāndogya*, the *Vājasaneyaka*, and the *Kauṣītaki-brāhmaṇa*, as well as in various other differences among the branches, the Upanishads teach the goal of those who know Brahman as if it were distinct.

In this regard, the fact that there are different types [of paths] has been very clearly stated in the Bhāṣya itself. Consequently, for one seeking liberation, even the contemplation of the path is diverse, according to the principle of the diversity of the knowledge of Brahman. Therefore, there is no uniformity or fixed rule regarding the path beginning with the light (*arcis*) and so forth. He refutes this [objection] with the words "Not so" (*naitat*).

Since it is established everywhere through recognition that the path of the gods is indeed that very same one—consisting of fire, wind, sun, moon, lightning, and so forth—all instances of deficiency, excess, or the description of these elements in a reversed order must be understood as being contrary to logic (nyāya-viruddha).

Thus, you have stated that for those who know Brahman, there is a fixed rule of travel toward the attainment of the Blessed Lord via the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi). However, one might raise the objection: "In the authoritative scriptures, various modes of travel are observed for those going to the supreme abode; how is this so? Anticipating this, [the author] says, "Of Caidya and others," meaning that since it is improper to discard a matter established by authoritative means of knowledge, those possessed of discernment should consider that the diversity of modes is appropriate in each respective case.

The point here is this: while it is a general principle that those who know Brahman depart through the *brahmanāḍī* and proceed by the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), one must not deny the difference in their destinations—which is established by equal authority for specific types of knowers of Brahman—merely because of this. Nor should the "Great Path" (the *mahāmārga*) by which knowers of Brahman travel via light and so forth be denied on such grounds. Furthermore, Caidya attained the state of Vāsudeva at that very moment.

The departure of all beings, both mobile and immobile, of Ayodhyā, along with the blessed Rāmabhadra, to the world of Brahmā; the attainment of liberation by specific individuals such as Puṇḍarīka and others, according to the manner described in their respective dialogues; the attainment of the supreme state by Bhīṣma and others, preceded by their attainment of the status of Vasus and other deities; and the attainment of fruits at the time desired by those residing in the worlds of the various manifestations of the Blessed Lord, through the sequence of their meditative worship.

The attainment of the supreme state from their own worlds by the creators, such as the Four-faced One (Brahmā) and others, should likewise be contemplated by the wise in other cases as well. Thus, it is stated that one must not deny the specific departure appropriate to each case merely on the basis of a general instruction regarding departure.

The connection [of this section] is as follows: Since it has been established that the path beginning with light (*arcis*) is one and the same despite being taught in different locations, the question now arises regarding the consideration of the sequence therein. Specifically, between the year (*saṃvatsara*) and the sun (*āditya*), there are the wind (*vāyu*) and the world of the gods (*devaloka*) obtained from the *Śruti*; the inquiry is whether one must accept a difference between these two and thus establish a different order, or whether, by accepting their identity on the strength of authoritative evidence, they occupy a single position within a unified whole. The investigation for that purpose is as follows: When the wind and the world of the gods are introduced between the year and the sun, are they to be placed in an indefinite order? Or... [text continues].

Should [the two] be established as one or not? Or rather, do the words "Vāyu" and "world of the gods" (devaloka) refer to different things or not? Is it logical that the word "world of the gods" refers to the abode of the gods, or—given the scriptural mention of Vāyu as the dwelling-place of the gods—is it appropriate for it to refer to Vāyu? Since these two cannot be said to be identical, as distinct conventional usages are observed in the world, there would necessarily be an option (vikalpa) between them, as both are established by equal authority regarding a single location.

"That which blows here is the abode of the gods"—thus, Vāyu’s status as the abode of the gods is well-known from the Śruti. Anticipating the question of how it can be the world of the gods (devaloka), he says: "because of its supporting nature. It is well-known in the Purāṇas and other texts that the heavenly world is supported by Vāyu alone. Having thus established this point, he concludes it logically with the word "therefore. The qualification "beyond conceptual construction" (nirvikalpam) was stated to show that this alternative (vikalpa) is indeed miserable, as it is afflicted by eight defects. This is the meaning: for the sake of avoiding the defects caused by conceptual construction, one must accept the identity of Vāyu and the world of the gods.

Here too, the connection [of the discussion] is that the very consideration of a specific order is being undertaken. The inquiry into its meaning is as follows: Should Varuṇa and the others be placed according to the order of the text, or after lightning? Is it logical for Varuṇa to follow in accordance with his connection to lightning, or not? On this point, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) says: In the Kauṣītaki passage, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati are taught as "conveyors" (ātivāhika). Since these teachings must not be rendered meaningless, they must be placed somewhere. Their placement, however, is not established by direct scriptural statement (śruti) in every instance.

It is contradicted. Or rather, even by overriding the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) in accordance with the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*), Varuṇa should be placed above Vāyu. This being so, since it is better to override a single scriptural statement than to override multiple scriptural statements, one should follow this principle and place Indra and Prajāpati immediately after Varuṇa for the sake of making that very instruction not purposeless; furthermore, their respective order of recitation exists there. This is what is stated in the Kauṣītaki [Upaniṣad]. Thus, here the syntactical connection of the words is as declared in the Kauṣītaki Āgama.

Varuṇa, Indra (Śatamakha), and Prajāpati must be placed somewhere even if it contradicts the Vedic text (śruti). He states the reason for this: "because [the text] would be fruitless" (viphalā). If they were not placed somewhere, their mention in the scripture would be purposeless. Thus, once it is established that they must be placed somewhere, they should be inserted after the world of Vāyu, following the order of the recitation (pāṭhakrama). He refutes this with the words "that is improper" (ayuktam). Then, raising the question of where they should be placed, he says: "Because of the connection" (saṃbandhāt). On the basis of the sense (artha), Varuṇa should be placed above lightning (vidyut).
But Indra and Prajāpati, by the very fact of their recitation, come after Varuṇa; the meaning is that they follow immediately after Varuṇa.

Anticipating the objection that "let there be no direct attainment of Brahman by the non-human (āmānava) being; rather, let it occur through Indra and Prajāpati," [the author] establishes—by following the natural force of the sentence—that it is appropriate for the non-human being alone, acting in conjunction with Indra and Prajāpati who stand as auxiliaries, to be the one who brings about the attainment of Brahman. As for the meaning of the words "yattu asya": although the capacity of this non-human being to bring about the attainment of Brahman, as heard in scripture, remains uncontradicted even when Indra and Prajāpati serve as intermediaries, [it is still the case that...]

Nevertheless, there is a great degree of appropriateness in the Śruti for these non-human beings (amānava), Indra, and Prajāpati, acting together as the means for attaining Brahman. There is also a great degree of appropriateness for understanding the attainment of Brahman—heard in the text as "He leads them to Brahman"—as being performed by a non-human agent. The meaning is this: the non-human being alone leads to Brahman primarily; as for Indra and Prajāpati, they belong to the mental realm (mānasa). Anticipating the question of how this is so, it is replied that the non-human being itself is designated by the word "mental" (mānasa); therefore, there is merely a difference in name.

Regarding the statement, "He who says 'it was said'": the connection with the word [is as follows]. That which was mentioned above as the cause for attaining the world of Brahman (brahmaloka)—namely, that which is called the "mental" (mānasa)—therefore, the leader is the mental one; it is not another, a non-mental one. He states the reason for this: "The wise say. The non-mental is a specific person associated with lightning, and the mental is likewise so; therefore, they say that the carrying across is performed by one and the same person associated with lightning.

Regarding this, the connection [of the topic] is stated in the Bhāṣya: "Are the *arciḥ* (flame) and others signs of the path, or are they places of enjoyment, or are they the bearers who carry the wise who desire to reach Brahman? The investigation into that purpose, however, is as follows: in the inquiry as to whether the *arciḥ* and others are signs of the path, it is further considered once again—what?

Is it reasonable to follow the sequence of worldly instruction? Or is it reasonable to follow the statement, "These indeed are the worlds: namely, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years"? Or is it appropriate to follow the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being a "conveyor" (*gamayitṛ*)? Having presented the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) in both these ways, [the author] establishes the view that they are "places of enjoyment" (*bhogasthāna*), because those two modes are contrary to authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*).

The syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: these [places] beginning with the "blazing day" (jvalana-dina) must either be places of enjoyment (bhoga-sthāna) or they must be signs of the path (mārga-cihna). To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of worldly sayings" (lokokti). The manner of these worldly sayings has been very clearly explained in the Commentary itself. This very point is what is being countered by the word "no" (na).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "because it is impossible. For it is not possible for a word denoting time to denote a signpost on a path or a land of enjoyment. To the question, "In that case, what is the restrictive factor in your own position? he replies: "Because it is explicit. Since in certain passages—such as "A non-human *puruṣa* leads them to Brahman" and "A *puruṣa* born of mind comes from the lightning and leads them to the world of Brahman"—the leadership and masculinity of the non-human being are explicit, others likewise must perform the leading in exactly that manner. In this sense...

He demonstrates this very point according to logic with the words "but when there is doubt. For those who know the principles of reasoning have said: "But when there is doubt, the determination comes from the remainder of the sentence. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can words such as 'Agni' and so forth denote specific *ativāhika* persons? Anticipating this objection, he says "Agni and so forth," because it is well-established that these words denote specific presiding deities (*adhiṣṭhātṛ-devatā*), and by extension, they denote the persons [presided over]. Here too, the phrase "so they say" (*jaguḥ*) is to be supplied. Furthermore, even in common worldly usage, the fact that words like 'Agni' denote the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*) is recited by the authors of lexicons (*abhidhānakośa*).

Having shown the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga) as distinct from the other two paths of merit and demerit, [the author] now confirms that the words "day," "fortnight," "month," and so forth, refer specifically to particular deities, by means of the verse beginning with "yām. For the son of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), having heard of the path to hell, fell down in distress; whereas the flood of tamasic beings—that multitude of tamasic persons—would themselves rush toward it and enter it.

The class of those devoted to the three aims of life (*traivargika*), who accept the triad alone as the human goal and perform actions for the sake of desired rewards (*kāmya-karma*), shall whirl again on the wheel of the water-wheel (*ghaṭī-yantra*) along the path of smoke and so forth. The performer of optional rites, having ascended with his face upward like a jar in a water-wheel, shall fall back down in the very same manner at the conclusion of the experience of the fruits of that karma.

Furthermore, this path of those who do not return is established as being indeed shared by the sacred scriptures (Śrutis). Now, one might object: "In this context, since there is the possibility of [the soul] passing over [the worlds], words such as 'day,' 'fortnight,' and 'month' would be inappropriate, because they lack the capacity to denote specific persons. Anticipating this doubt, he says "Therein," meaning that once it is determined that certain words denote specific persons, then by that same principle, one must accept that all such words denote specific persons.

Regarding the doubt as to whether this attainment of the moon (*candraprāpti*) mentioned here is one or many, he says "the former" (*pūrvam*) to show that after demonstrating the differences among the three attainments of the moon mentioned in various places, students of subtle intellect should themselves discern the distinctions in every case of doubt. One particular attainment of the moon is described as the state of union (*sāyujya*) with the moon on the path of smoke and so forth, and that is different from this [other] one, which belongs to those who die during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*) or the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*).

It is stated that for all knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) without distinction, there is the attainment of the eighth moon by means of the *ativāhika* (conveying) deities. This [attainment] is also something distinct from those two aforementioned attainments of Indra, which is taught without distinction for all those proceeding toward liberation in the Pañcāgni-vidyā. He expresses this with the words "other than these" (*anyatra*). Having thus clarified the implicit meaning through favor toward his disciples, he concludes with the words "when [the mind] is focused" (*praṇihite*), implying that since such matters to be explained are numerous, students of subtle intellect should themselves achieve the full understanding of every particular detail.

In this context, for a certain disciple who harbors the doubt as to whether the previously mentioned *ātivāhika* (conveying) deities are of the nature of worldly deities such as Agni and so forth, or rather, are of the nature of primordial (*prākṛta*) deities who carry out the commands of the Supreme Person, [the author] shows both positions by distinguishing them according to different types of perceivers, and concludes that only the latter position is supported by authoritative evidence with the words: "In the world of the Lord of the Earth. Regarding the passage "Earth, intermediate space, heaven," followed by "Agni, Vāyu, Āditya," there is a sequential enumeration of the three deities beginning with Agni.

Because of the designation of these as deities (*devatātva*), the "Lord of the Earth" (*bhūlokeśa*) is the well-known fire; likewise, [the lords] of the intermediate space and the sky are Vāyu and Āditya. Some people consider these to be specific conducting deities (*ativāhika-devatā*) who are transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*), preceded by the well-known fires and so forth. Regarding this, he states the reason: "because of the identity of the word" (*śabdaikya*). The sense is that when there is identity of the words "fire" and so on, it is an overly complex assumption to posit a difference in meaning—namely, that some fires and so forth are transmigrating beings while others are non-transmigrating. It is more logical that the word simply recurs to denote the same object.

The view of those [others] is that the formulation of the mantras for those non-material deities, such as Agni and others—who are distinct from the worldly deities like Agni and so forth—is cumbersome. However, other teachers, following logical reasoning, state another method; he shows that very method with the words "Others [say]. The meaning is this: for it is the non-human [guide] who leads one to the Lord residing in Vaikuṇṭha; therefore, the non-human does not lead [one elsewhere].

Therefore, the non-human (amānava) is not of the material nature (aprākṛta). Since Indra and Prajāpati, who convey [the soul] along with him, are associated with him, they too are not of the material nature. This being the case, to conceive of those conducting deities (ātivāhika) as being of the material nature is an extreme rashness due to its inconsistency. Therefore, we conclude that all these conducting deities are indeed divine persons.

As for the positive concomitance (anvaya), other teachers—whose intellects are intent on determining the principles of logic—establish their eternality because, by virtue of the non-human deity’s role as the conveyor to the Supreme Person residing in Vaikuṇṭha, they are among the eternal beings.

In the same way, they declared that the others—the eternal servants of Vaikuṇṭha, such as Arci and the rest—are [the primary ones]; therefore, those very beings beginning with Arcis are the principal ones. As for the well-known Agni and the others, they merely bear those names and are followers of his command; thus, everything is perfectly consistent.

Regarding this, the connection [of the present topic] with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is as follows: "It has been stated that the wise go by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*) alone; that the group beginning with light and ending with the non-human (*amānava*) acts as the guide, leading the wise to Brahman. Now, the following is considered: Does this group beginning with light lead those who meditate upon the *kārya* (the effected) Hiraṇyagarbha, or only those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman, or both those who meditate upon the supreme Brahman and those who meditate upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*) as being identical with Brahman? Such is the doubt. Thus ends the previous [section].

By means of three sections (*adhikaraṇas*), the inclusion of attributes (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) for the path beginning with Light (*arcir-ādi*) was stated as being one and the same; now, by means of two sections, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is determined—thus there is a division of the sub-section (*peṭikā*). Among these, it was previously stated that those named Light and so forth are "conveyors" (*ativāhika*); now, a specific inquiry is made as to what the object of their status as conveyors is—thereby establishing that these two belong to a single sub-section. To that end, the investigation is as follows: Is the group of conveyors beginning with Light one who leads only those meditating upon the effect (*kārya*), namely Hiraṇyagarbha?

[The question is: Do these [passages] refer only to those who meditate on the Supreme Brahman, or do they refer to those who meditate on the inner self (pratyagātman) as being identical with Brahman? Are the terms "attainment" and "the world of Brahman" (brahmaloka) applicable when the Supreme Brahman is the goal to be reached, or not? If the one who leads them there is the one who leads only those who meditate on Brahman, then [it contradicts the scripture]: "Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest... and so forth.

There is a general agreement regarding such statements as these. Here, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "In the place of Vaikuṇṭha. Indeed, Bādari is the proponent of the prima facie view here; he thinks as follows: Bādari declared that these are the *ātivāhika* (conveying) beings who lead one to the station of Vaikuṇṭha—such beings being fit for the station of the Ordainer (*vidhātṛ*). He states the reason for this as "appropriateness of the destination" (*gatyaucityam*).

Regarding the attainment of the world of Brahmā as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), there is appropriateness for going; however, regarding the attainment of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is no appropriateness for going—thus he says, "Indeed not" (*na khalu*). This is the meaning: for the worshippers of the all-pervading Lord, what fruit could not be obtained right here? For the attainment of the very nature of the Lord is the fruit, and that is obtained right here; so what is the use of this useless instruction to go? [Objection: But if the attainment of the four-faced Brahmā is intended, [as in the passage] "He leads them to Brahmā... *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument as presented.*

Regarding the objection that the neuter gender of the word *brahma* in the phrase "he causes [him] to go" (*gamayati*) is untenable because one ought to say "he causes Brahmā to go" (*brahmāṇaṃ gamayati*), he replies: "On account of proximity" (*sāmīpyāt*). In the passage "He who [causes him to go] to Brahmā," the name *brahma* in the neuter gender also refers to him (the Creator) because of his proximity to the Supreme Brahman, who is born from the Supreme Brahman; thus there is no contradiction. Here, in the phrase "having approached the mental [world], he causes [them] to go to the worlds of Brahmā" (*brahmalokān*), the plural number in "worlds of Brahmā" (*brahmalokān*) is explained according to the principle of the section on the *pāśas* (the rope-section).

It must be understood that, by applying the *niṣādasthapati* maxim, the term "world" (*loka*) refers to Brahman itself—thus, "the world of Brahman" (*brahmaloka*) means Brahman who is the world—and therefore there is not even a scent of inconsistency. Nor should it be thought that there is an impossibility regarding the instruction on liberation here; thus he says, "by that. This is the meaning: having first reached the abode of the lotus-born (Brahmā), one shall attain liberation along with him. All of this has been clearly restated in the commentary itself, so we do not elaborate upon it here. He refutes this [objection] with the words "this is not so," and states the reason for that.

Regarding the word "nānā" (various): since the journey to the supreme station, as recited in the scripture [Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.12.7] as "That highest step of Viṣṇu," is established by various scriptural passages, it is not logical that the scriptures should be sublated. The rest is in the Bhāṣya.
Having restated the position of Jaimini, who rejected the view of Bādari, [the author] explains what remains to be said there for the sake of the disciples’ clear understanding: "The path.

This path beginning with the *arcis* leads to the supreme abode—the supreme abode known as Vaikuṇṭha, established by scripture in the words, "That highest step of Viṣṇu. Alternatively, it leads to the Supreme Person Himself—who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha and resides in the divine world according to the text, "Now, that light which shines beyond this heaven"—and who is denoted by the word "abode" (*dhāma*) due to His possession of unsurpassed splendor.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of going, etc. This is because it is possible for that [attainment] to be reached by the movement of the divine one who dwells in that place, as well as by the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). He shows that this matter is established not only by its suitability, but also because the word *brahman* ending in the neuter gender is used in its primary sense, with the words: "because of the mention of Brahman. The venerable Jaimini determined that this path belongs only to those who attain the Supreme Brahman. Having accepted the stated point, [the author] speaks of a certain specific detail therein, saying: "Satya..."

The Teacher has employed the word "yuktaḥ" (joined/fitting); he expresses that very point by saying "vaktavyam" (it must be stated). He clarifies what was already promised by stating "nayati" (he leads). This is the meaning: there are indeed two kinds of those established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*). Some are worshippers of the Supreme Self whose body is their own self; others are established in their own self which is the body of the Supreme Self. It is Jaimini’s intended meaning that the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) leads both these types of knowers of the Supreme (*paravidaḥ*), who are established in Brahman through different approaches. But then—

Anticipating the objection as to how both [the individual souls] associated with Viṣṇu and Upāsaka can possess complete absorption in Brahman, he says, "And these... Here, only a reversal of the relationship between the qualifier and the qualified is being taught. In both cases, the primacy of Brahman and the soul's status as its qualifier remain identical; thus, the unity of meaning is established. This is just as in expressions such as "Rāma’s younger brother and Lakṣmaṇa’s elder brother," where despite the reversal in instruction, the reality of the matter remains the same. Having all this in mind, the authors of the Sūtras stated: "Bādarāyaṇa holds that [the Lord] leads [the souls] because they have the Imperishable as their support."

Anticipating the doubt as to whose view it is that "they are worshippers with symbols" (*pratikopāsakāḥ*) and whose it is that "they are worshippers without symbols" (*apratikopāsakāḥ*), [the author] shows their distinction and then demonstrates that for those very worshippers without symbols, liberation by way of the path beginning with light (*arcirādi-mārga*) is certain. The phrase "those who should meditate" (*dhyāyeyuḥ*) refers to those who meditate upon the individual souls (*jīvas*)—whether as qualified by *prakṛti* or as isolated—as being none other than Brahman through the vision of Brahman; or likewise, those who meditate upon the aggregate of insentient matter (*jaḍanivaha*) either in its own form or [as Brahman].

They might meditate upon something else [than Brahman]. All of them, being divided into six classes, have their minds fixed on symbols (*pratīka*). Being thus divided into six classes, none of them are fit for the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-adhvā*). For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras stated: "He leads those who do not rely on symbols" (*apratīkālambanān nayati*). Anticipating the objection, "Is this a royal decree? he shows that it is we who speak in accordance with the approval of the author of the Sūtras by saying "Brahma," etc. This is the meaning: previously...

In the section defining the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), having raised the doubt as to whether this is a knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) or a knowledge of the individual soul (*jīvavidyā*), its status as a knowledge of Brahman is established by the sūtra: "And because the path consisting of the Śruti and the Parāvidyā is declared" (*śrutiparāvidyākagatyabhidhānācca*). This is the intended meaning of the sūtra here: if this were not a knowledge of Brahman, the journey via the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*) would not be taught, for the journey via the path of light is common to all knowledges of Brahman. Yet, the journey via the path of light is indeed taught here; therefore, the knowledge of the five fires is a knowledge of Brahman.

Regarding the term *brahmavidyā*: in the world, smoke and the like are indeed unerring signs (*liṅga*). Therefore, since it is logical that those who know Brahman alone proceed by the path beginning with light (*arcirādi*), it is logical that everyone should follow this path. But is it not the case that it was stated that only those who meditate upon Brahman proceed by the path of light and so forth? This is untenable, because in the Pañcāgni-vidyā, the path of light and so forth is also taught for those who "know thus" (*tadya itthaṃ viduḥ*). And they are meditators upon the nature of the Self as dissociated from primordial matter (*prakṛti*). For them...

It is claimed that there is also a liberation called *kaivalya*, which consists of the experience of bliss in one’s own self. This very liberation is described in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "The immortal state of the yogis who find contentment in the Self. Therefore, [the opponent argues] that even they, having gone to the supreme abode by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), remain in some region possessing the experience of their own self while devoid of the experience of the Lord. This, however, is without substance, because the *Pañcāgni-vidyā* is devoted to the meditation on one’s own self as being the body of the Supreme Self, as established by the indications of the purport found in the introduction and other parts of the text.

Because it has already been established; however, the detailed exposition should be seen in the Bhāṣya and other works. As for what was stated, "the immortal abode of the yogins," there too there is a contradiction with authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the Lord Parāśara, having stated, "The station of Prajāpati is ordained for householders, and that of Brahmā for renunciants," subsequently spoke of the attainment of a specific abode denoted by the word "immortal" for those who contemplate the individual soul (*jīvātman*)—namely, "for the yogins who are single-mindedly devoted and always meditate upon Brahman."

"That which is their supreme station, which indeed the wise perceive"—thus [the text] declares that only those who worship Brahman attain the supreme state. Here, if the word "immortal" (*amṛta*) in the phrase "the immortal station of the yogis" refers to the essential nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*), its designation by the word "immortal" is justified because of its eternity. If, however, the word "station" (*sthāna*) is taken in its primary sense as a specific location, then the word "immortal" is used figuratively, as in such passages as "We have drunk Soma, we have become immortal. For they say: "Immortality is indeed spoken of as that state which lasts until the dissolution of all beings."

"But those three classes of disciples who are devoted [to the path] are considered seekers of results; they are all subject to the law of falling away (*cyavana-dharman*), whereas the awakened one (*pratibuddha*) partakes in liberation. This is the statement that determines the permanent and the impermanent. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate the contradiction with reason regarding the status of the "Supreme Abode" (*paramapada*). Is the meditator on the individual soul (*jīva-upāsaka*), designated as the "imagined" (*parikalpita*) and "mere" (*kevala*), even after attaining the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), free from all karma—having abandoned the experience of that [attainment]—or does he still possess residual karma, like Divākīrti?

If one were liberated from all karma, there would be no cessation of the experience of Brahman; for the experience of Brahman is innate (*svābhāvika*), whereas its cessation is adventitious (*aupādhika*). If even for one liberated from all karma there were a cessation of the experience of Brahman, then that cessation itself would have to be admitted as innate. And in that case, there would be a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). If it is argued: "Let karma not be the cause; there may be some other cause altogether for the non-experience of Brahman," [the response follows].

Therefore, tell me specifically: O Blessed One, what is this "restraint"? Is it with cause or without cause? If it is without cause, then having stated your doctrine that favor is without cause, you who speak of restraint as being without cause are indeed laughable. If it is with cause, then the cause must be stated. If it is karma, this has already been answered. If it is the will of the Blessed One, then since the Blessed One is supremely compassionate, your own desire—that He should wish for restraint toward one who is entirely free from all karma—is simply your own desire. In that case—

If it is argued that we say the individual soul (*jīva*) exists by its own will apart from the Blessed Lord, that is incorrect. For a soul liberated from all karma, to claim that it—having been released from the Supreme Self, who is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss according to the text, "He is indeed essence; for having obtained this essence, he becomes blissful"—experiences its own self as something comparable to a firefly is simply an impossibility. If it is argued that this occurs due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then that very [impression], being difficult to restrain, would itself be a sin, and such a one would remain a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).

The discussion regarding the entry into the supreme state (*paramapada*) is hereby concluded. In this regard, the traditional doctrine (*satyampradāya*) must also be examined. On this point, some maintain: "There is a path consisting of light and so forth (*arcirādigati*) for those who meditate upon the individual soul (*jīva*). For the Commentator himself, having spoken of the meditator on the individual soul as distinct from the meditator on Brahman, has clearly stated in the Commentary that both [types of meditators] proceed by way of light and so forth. Therefore, having traveled by that path of light and reached the Blessed Lord, they experience the fruit according to their meditation; yet, by the logic that [the result is temporary], they abandon the direct experience of the Blessed Lord."

"Remaining in some corner of the supreme abode, she enjoys only herself like a cow suckling her own calf; she does not, however, necessarily attain the enjoyment of the Supreme Person. On this basis, they claim that because she lacks the enjoyment of the Supreme Person—of whom it is said, "the Lord of the universe"—she shares the characteristics of a woman abandoned by her husband. This is worthless, because it contradicts the Sūtra, contradicts the statements of the Bhāṣya, contradicts authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), contradicts reason, and contradicts tradition. For instance, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā: ... [The text continues with a description of the path of the gods and the attainment of the Supreme. ... Thus, having reached the world of Brahman, he becomes one with Brahman. Therefore, there is no lack of enjoyment for him. Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "And because of the non-difference [of the individual soul] from Him" (Brahmasūtra 4.4.22). The Bhāṣya explains: "Because of the non-difference of the individual soul from the Supreme Self, as stated in the Śruti: 'Having attained the Supreme Self, he is no longer conscious of anything else' and so forth. Moreover, it contradicts the *pramāṇas*, such as the Śruti: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman. It contradicts reason, for how could one who has attained the nature of the Supreme Reality be subject to the state of being abandoned? And it contradicts tradition, as the lineage of teachers has always taught that upon attaining the Supreme, there is no separation. Thus, the claim is baseless. Furthermore, in the Pañcāgni-vidyā: ... [The text concludes with the final verses of the Pañcāgni-vidyā. ... "Those who know this and those who, in the forest, meditate on faith and austerity—they, passing through the world of fire, reach the world of wind... and so on, until: "...having reached the world of Brahman, they become one with Brahman. Therefore, there is no lack of enjoyment for the liberated soul. ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt ||| End of excerpt
