By the sūtra, "And because the path of one who has heard the Upaniṣads is declared," it is established that the Pañcāgni-vidyā is a knowledge of Brahman rather than a mere knowledge of the individual soul (jīva), on account of the instruction regarding the path beginning with light (arcirādi). The meaning is this: since the path beginning with light is exclusively for those possessing the knowledge of Brahman, this Pañcāgni-vidyā is therefore a knowledge of Brahman. Consequently, in the case of a knowledge of the individual soul, there is no [attainment] by way of the path beginning with light.

[This is] the fragrance of going to the supreme state. The contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* regarding that subject matter should also be seen in that very place. For this very reason, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* have stated that in the Prajāpati passage, there is a mention of the fruit consisting of the attainment of Brahman, and the conclusion is made by means of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman. Here too, in the context of the *ātivāhika* [guides], it is clearly stated by the authors of the *Bhāṣya* themselves that only those who know Brahman proceed by way of the *arciḥ* and other paths. In this regard, through the specific euphonic combination (*sandhi*) of the words "kevalaṃ vā cidvastu," depending on whether the vowel *a* is elided or not elided, [the meaning differs].

There is the inclusion of both consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). The meaning here is this: meditation on the Supreme Self as having one's own self as its body, and meditation on one's own self as being the body of the Supreme Self—both of these are, in effect, one and the same. Therefore, since even one who meditates on their own self as the body of the Supreme Self is a meditator on Brahman, the instruction regarding the journey by way of the *arciḥ* (flames) and so forth is not contradicted. However, a meditator on pure consciousness alone has already been refuted, because such a person is a meditator on a mere symbol (*pratīka*). A symbol is a single part [of the whole], whereas Brahman possesses both consciousness and the unconscious as its body.

Because the conscious and the unconscious occupy the same locus, even one who worships the individual soul (jīva) is a worshiper of a mere symbol (pratīkopāsaka). Thus, since this point has been stated by the Commentator himself two or three times in this section, and because the worshiper of the individual soul alone has been refuted as being a worshiper of a symbol, it is established that the worshiper of one's own self—which is the body of the Supreme Self—is not a worshiper of a symbol; therefore, being a knower of Brahman, such a person attains Brahman via the path beginning with light (arciḥ), etc. Enough of this elaboration.

In this matter, even for those who argue that "everything is false" and are thus proponents of falsehood, all things established by the Śruti must indeed be accepted according to the authority of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nevertheless, they merely engage in despicable chatter, such as claiming that this [world] is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) or that it concerns Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahma*). Their claim of "conventionality" is already destroyed because it cannot withstand logical analysis. Furthermore, Brahman is only with attributes and not without attributes (*nirguṇa*), because the latter lacks any basis in authoritative evidence. Therefore, even their attempt to delineate the scope of these categories is untenable.

This is as discarded as the claim that [the world] is merely conventional; this alone is the truth for those who investigate logic. Nevertheless, since the collection of points we are stating is accepted by others in some manner or another, he says "pratyāpatti" (recovery/return) to indicate that it is not to be transgressed, as it is already established. The manner of recovery is the engagement of the transmigrating soul, who has been wandering since beginningless time, in the path to liberation due to its connection with unknown merit (*sukṛta*) and so forth.

The rules governing eligibility for specific branches of knowledge—such as Karma-yoga, Dīpa-vidyā, Madhu-vidyā, Nyāsa-vidyā, and others—consist precisely in steadfast devotion to action, knowledge, and bhakti. Through devotion to the Lord alone, the cessation of the impurities that obstruct liberation occurs. Regarding the determination of the final state: some are liberated at the conclusion of the body initiated by past karma (prārabdha), while others, according to their remaining karma, attain liberation after taking on another body following that one.

The attainment of rest in various destinations—whether on the path beginning with smoke (*dhūmādimārga*) or the path beginning with light (*arcirādimārga*), or at specific locations such as the regions of the moon and the sun—is, for some, direct liberation (*sākṣānmukti*) for those established in the *Sadvidyā* and *Daharavidyā*, while for others it is gradual [liberation] for those established in the *Madhuvidyā*. All such a variety of differentiated effects, well-known from the Upaniṣadic texts, must certainly not be rejected even by those who maintain the doctrine of non-duality (*nirviśeṣavāda*), for the sake of upholding the scriptural passages that establish those respective meanings;
there remains only the designation of these as being "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*).

Having thus departed by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), he gradually reaches the vicinity of the divine throne of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva; this is what the author states with the words "the path" (*panthānam*). Having reached this path called the "way of the gods" (*devayāna*) upon the final fall of the body, he traverses the series of principles (*tattva-stoma*) beginning with earth and ending with darkness (*tamaḥ*). He also crosses the divine river named Virajā. Immediately thereafter, having obtained a divine body and so forth, he reaches that which is devoid of birth and abode, meaning free from origination and destruction.

"He goes to the station of Viṣṇu," according to the Śruti: "Having perfected the self, I shall attain the world of Brahman. But this [other] one, blessed by the dialogue with Brahmā, receives great honor culminating in his being seated upon the couch.

Regarding this, someone who does not accept a divine location and so forth consisting of the five powers (*pañcaśaktimaya*) says: "It is a composite" (*saṅghāta*). Indeed, you describe a divine location as consisting of the five powers. Here, by the word "power," the five divine elements are denoted. Are those divine elements of the nature of a composite (*saṅghātātmaka*) or of the nature of a non-composite (*asaṅghātātmaka*)? If they are of the nature of a composite, there can be no permanence at all, because every object that is a composite is observed to be perishable. Thus, since it would be impermanent, he says "no," meaning that the state of being eternal earth and so forth would not exist.

The meaning is this: you maintain that the eternal elements, such as earth and the rest, constitute the abode of Vaikuṇṭha; however, if these exist in the form of atoms, there would be no perception of them as divided into the forms of earth and so forth. If, on the other hand, they consist of composite aggregates, their eternity would not be possible. Furthermore, according to your own tenet, the Lord possesses a couch and other such furnishings; yet you claim that these serve no purpose. To this he says, "by means of couches and the like. He provides the reason for this by stating, "because His power is full and limitless. [Thus,] the arrangement of couches and so forth for the sake of the queens and others— [Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a verse concerning the nature of the divine abode and the logical inconsistencies in certain Vaiṣṇava positions regarding its composition.]

The purpose of providing a bed and seat is to avoid fatigue and other causes of physical lethargy; however, for the Blessed One, whose power is perfect and limitless, what need is there for such arrangements as a couch? Furthermore, for the Blessed One who pervades all space, even the act of rising upward to reach [a place] would be futile. Thus, the Śruti itself has silenced the trivial, drunken ravings of those logicians who employ such fallacious arguments—those most base and intoxicated prattle. Regarding a matter established by the Śruti, there should be no groundless doubt.

The claim that [the soul] is born from those of good intellect or those of evil intellect is indeed to be disregarded by those who know the authority of the Śruti. Anticipating the objection as to how the Śruti possesses such power, he provides the answer with the word "adbhuta" (wondrous). To express a previously unknown matter is the ornament of the Śruti; therein, expressing a wondrous matter is its supreme ornament. For "wonderfulness" consists in being of a nature entirely different from what is commonly perceived. Therefore, in the absence of sublation, the true meaning should be determined exactly as heard by those who follow right principles; however, the arguments put forward by opponents—

The meaning is that subverting inferences (*bādhakānumāna*) themselves attain the status of non-validity because they contradict scripture (*āgama*). For in the world, even sentences of ordinary people that convey mundane matters are accepted as valid with respect to unprecedented subjects when they come from those who have traveled to other continents and so forth. This being the case, why are Vedic sentences, which convey extraordinary matters, not accepted as such? Because the presence of defects in the cause [of their composition] is not to be suspected, and because no subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been observed. For if there were groundless suspicion of invalidity, it would lead to the collapse of all knowledge.

One might object: "If there is no contradiction even when there is a contradiction with observed reality (*dṛṣṭavirodha*), then there would be no contradiction anywhere. Anticipating this doubt, the author states the word "existence" (*bhāva*) to provide an example of where contradiction actually exists. In that case, existence and non-existence are not seen to be contradictory when they are taught through the distinction of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as place and time; however, if those two were expressed without the distinction of limiting conditions, then there would indeed be a contradiction. For example, a jar exists in its own place and does not exist in another place, and likewise it exists at its own time and does not exist at another time. So it is here.

This is an example of non-contradiction: [the statement] "it exists as its own self, but does not exist as another self. An example of contradiction, however, is: "A jar exists in some place, but does not exist in any [other] place; it exists at its own time, but never exists [at another time]; it exists as its own self, but does not exist as every self"; or alternatively, "The jar exists, the jar does not exist," where one designates "exists" and "does not exist" without the delimitation of distinctions such as place and time. Such examples as these are contradictory. Therefore, it is not the case that there is no example of contradiction.

The meaning is that it must be reflected upon. Having thus stated examples of mutual contradiction, he now states an example of the contradiction of one weak [element] by another strong one, in accordance with the present subject, beginning with the words "prajñāte" (when known).

The statement "one should not harm any living beings" has a universal scope; yet, even though the meaning of this sentence is all-pervasive, its own inherent force—when restricted to a specific domain despite being obstructed by the injunction to "sacrifice" (*ālabheta*) in certain cases of ritual slaughter—ensures the very establishment of its own purpose. Similarly, the universal rule that "whatever is a composite is perishable," though based on observation, is sublated by the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the eternity of the divine manifestations (*vibhūti*). This is just as [the inference] regarding the purity of a human head [is sublated].

The universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) regarding [the impurity] being a part of a living being is sublated by the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the impurity of the skull. Therefore, the means of valid cognition that establish the eternity of divine manifestations (*vibhūti*) are indeed purposeful. He shows that this is observed in the world and is accepted even by all proponents of philosophical systems (*siddhāntin*) with the word "observed" (*dṛṣṭam*). He states the fault in not accepting it in such a manner with the words "if not" (*na yadi*). If one accepts only the observed procedure and does not accept that a specific scripture (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) can sublate [general rules], then scripture would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all.

The general statement "other than through perception" (*adhyakṣato 'nyat*) is intended as an illustration for inference (*anumāna*) as well. The meaning is that even when an object is being perceived, scholars of logic (*nyāyavidbhiḥ*) declare that sublation (*bādha*) occurs there and there through reasoning (*yukti*) by means of specific examples. Regarding this, he states another fault: "sublation. If, in the case of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) concerning a general and a particular, the general were not subject to sublation by the particular, then even in the case of two perceptions (*pratyakṣa*) concerning a general and a particular, the sublation of the general by the perception of the particular would not occur.

There may be a perception of generality based on a superficial observation, whereas a perception of particularity is preceded by careful and skillful investigation. Now, one might object: "To say that this entire universe exists within the belly of the Lord as a child lying on a banyan leaf is to state something utterly contradictory; how then can it be accepted as established by scripture? Anticipating this doubt, he says, "On the banyan leaf. The meaning is that intelligent persons should reconcile this in an appropriate manner so that it does not remain an absolute contradiction.

In this chapter, he shows the sequence of the subjects to be established in each section with the words "unity" (*ekatvam*). He states the meaning of the first section: that there is unity of the "good path," the *supatha*, which is studied in the assembly of those who know Brahman. Immediately following, Vāyu—designated by the term "world of Vāyu"—is referred to by the scriptural expression "world of the gods. In the third section, Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati follow after lightning. In the fourth section, however, those ending with the "non-human" (*amānava*) are the guides for proceeding to the Supreme State.

Thus it is stated. He states the meaning of the fifth [chapter] as follows: "This is the path of those who know Brahman. Having summarized the meaning of the quarters (pādas), he says "having gone through four. In the third quarter of the fourth chapter, the path—the route beginning with light—is thus described by means of five topical sections (adhikaraṇas).
The Fourth Pāda of the Fourth Adhyāya.

Here, having analyzed and restated the distinctions in meaning of the Pādas contained within this Fourth Adhyāya, [the author] demonstrates the specific meaning of the Fourth Pāda, as well as the specific meanings of the two sections (*peṭikā*) divided into three parts that are included therein, beginning with the words "It has been stated" (*uktam iti*). First, the distinction in the meaning of the [first] three Pādas is demonstrated by the words "by the Pādas. In this manner, the abandonment of works—both in their gross and subtle forms—has been established in due order. Having thus analyzed the meaning of the Fourth Pāda...

He shows that [the soul] is "shaken off" (nirdhūta). The limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consists of the connection with the body and the connection with its attributes; however, that is shaken off in the state of the stainless boat (*virajā-taraṇa*). Thus, he speaks of the cessation of the entire collection of shaken-off adjuncts through the final quarter-verse characterized by supreme bliss. Here, he shows the division of the sections (*peṭikā-vibhāga*) by saying "by three": the manifestation of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is to be considered through three topics (*adhikaraṇa*); furthermore, the enjoyment of voluntary service (*svacchanda-kaṅkarya*) is described through another three topics.

In this very manner, there are two *peṭikās* (sections). This dyad—consisting of the manifestation of one's own nature (*svarūpa*), service (*aiṅkarya*), and enjoyment (*bhoga*)—occurs spontaneously and is not dependent on karma. Then, raising the objection as to how an effect can exist in the absence of a cause, he places the Supreme Self, the cause of all, at the forefront here, saying "by the grace of the Lord" (*nāthanighnam*). The meaning is this: when all obstacles without exception have been completely removed, the Blessed Lord Himself brings about for the individual soul (*jīva*) the manifestation of the eight qualities and so forth; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

In this regard, the connection between the quarters (*pādasaṅgati*) and the connection with the subject matter (*adhikaraṇasaṅgati*) are shown separately in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "For those who meditate upon the Supreme Brahman, and for those who meditate upon the Self as being of the nature of Brahman when separated from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), a path characterized by non-return has been described via the route beginning with light (*arcis*). Now, he begins to consider the manner of the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) of the liberated. This is the connection between the quarters. [The question is: "Does one who, having risen from this body, has attained the Supreme Light, become connected with a form to be accomplished—such as that of a god or other beings—as described here?"

The connection with the section (*adhikaraṇasaṅgati*) is as follows: Is it by means of the statement that the liberated soul's connection with a form to be attained is taught, or is it the manifestation of its own natural essential nature? The investigation into that meaning is as follows: Does the scripture on liberation, if it were intended to teach the manifestation of the natural essential nature, fail to communicate a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), or not? And does the essential nature possess, by itself, the quality of being unlimited bliss?

"Is it possible or not?"—that is, is the concealment of the nature of bliss possible or not? "If the intent is manifestation, is there futility in the designation of 'accomplishment' or not?"—here, the proponent (pūrvapakṣin), asserting that the attainment of a previously non-existent form is the result, demonstrates the objections against the view that the natural form is manifested, beginning with the words "aśrānte."

The nature of the Self is eternally self-luminous; since its manifestation is already established from the very beginning, there could be no result whatsoever that is unprecedented. This is because that which is eternally manifest has no need for a further manifestation. Furthermore, if liberation were established eternally merely by the manifestation of one's own nature, then even one in deep sleep would be liberated, since the manifestation of one's own nature exists for him as well. He demonstrates this with the words, "because it is not different from deep sleep. Having thus refuted the opponent's position, [he sets forth] his own intended view...

He shows the manner [of this] with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the meaning: just as the eternally liberated Lord (*īśvara*) assumes forms such as those of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, so too must it be said that the liberated one (*mukta*) also assumes a distinct form. He states the reason for this with the words "because of the word 'form'" (*rūpaśabdāt*).

The meaning is that the word *rūpa* (form), because it denotes the body, indicates this very sense; he rejects this with the words "not indeed so. He states the reason for this rejection with the words "by its own" (*svena*). This is the meaning: it is not said that he "manifests by form alone," but rather that he manifests "by his own form. For the word "own" (*sva*) is employed here as a qualification; therefore, the meaning must be stated in such a way that the word does not become purposeless. Anticipating the objection, "How can it be purposeless? he says "in the case of form," [meaning] regarding the attainment of a form not previously possessed.

One need only say, "he is manifested with form. By this, through the force of the word *sva* (own), the meaning is that the manifestation of his natural form is expressed. For it is the intention that the word *sva* achieves its purpose only when there is the manifestation of what is natural.

In this context, showing that the statement of the proponents of falsity (mṛṣāvādins) regarding the manifestation of their own nature is incoherent, [the author] establishes its perfect consistency within his own position in the verse beginning with "nitye. The underlying meaning here is as follows: Do the proponents of falsity claim that the "attainment" (abhinirvṛtti) is simply the persistence of an eternal self, or is it the acquisition of a previously non-existent form? In the latter case, there would be the undesirable consequence of falling into dualism; therefore, only the former alternative remains. Yet even that does not hold together, for they claim that this "attainment" is the persistence of the nature of an eternal self.

They do not understand that the mere *tanmātra* is not the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā*). This is because the *tanmātra* is established from beginningless time, whereas the fruit of knowledge is something yet to come as its result. Indeed, it is impossible to assert an identity between that which is yet to come and that which is already established from before, due to the contradiction involved.

This is what he means by saying, "eternally established" (*nityasiddham*). Now, one might object: "If it cannot be said that there is a 'coming into being' (*abhiniṣpatti*) according to our position, then how can it be said so according to your position? To this he replies: "established" (*siddham*). Even though something is established by its own nature in the world, it assumes the state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through association with qualifying attributes that themselves are to be accomplished. For example, a person who is impure due to a particular touch is said to be "accomplished" (purified) by his own pure nature through the act of bathing, which is itself something to be accomplished; in the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*), being impure due to [past] actions, [is purified].

What contradiction is there in the statement that [the result] is accomplished in a form entirely free from connection with action? This is what he says: "because of the permeation by the goal" (*sādhyānuvedhāt*). Even an established entity is said to be "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) because of its permeation by the goal. Thus, for example, rice and other grains are accomplished through sprinkling and so forth in their state of purity. He shows the very nature of the result here; the use of the feminine gender in the word *sā* is intended to express the sense of "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*). Having thus explained that the word "attainment" (*abhiniṣpatti*) signifies the acquisition of another state, [he proceeds].

The phrase "or rather" (*yadvā*) indicates that he explains even the attainment of realization as being the object itself. For in common worldly usage, those who communicate various meanings say: "This meaning is thus accomplished," or "It is thus determined. Likewise, here too, the expression "he is manifested in his own form" means that he is known in his own essential nature. Therefore, since the word "liberated" (*mukta*) is meaningful in our position, he concludes that the Sūtra passage beginning with "Because of the declaration of the liberated one" (*muktaḥ pratijñānāt*) is indeed meaningful. "That" (*tat*) refers to this conclusion.

This is the meaning: in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses qualities (*saguṇa*), there exists the possibility of contraction and expansion of those qualities; furthermore, since the acquisition of a previously non-existent form is adventitious (*āgantuka*), the application of the term "liberation" (*mukti*) is perfectly consistent. In your position, however, because the Self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) and is eternally self-luminous, there is no acquisition of a previously non-existent form; thus, the statement that "one was previously unliberated and later becomes liberated" would be entirely meaningless. If it is argued that the cessation of ignorance (*avidyānivṛtti*) constitutes this unprecedented state, we ask: is that [cessation] the very nature of Brahman, or is it something distinct from it?

Even if it were distinct from that [consciousness], the same objection remains whether its nature is ultimate (paramārtha) or non-ultimate (aparamārtha). Even if it were distinct, if it were non-ultimate, it would be infinite because it would consist of a series of subsequent absences by destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva). If one admits the cessation of that [non-ultimate absence] as well, there would be an infinite regress due to a succession of cessations. And thus, by admitting such a succession of its cessation, the consequence of eternal saṃsāra remains exactly as it was. On the other hand, in the case of its being ultimate, the consequence of duality has already been stated previously.

Now, if liberation is the manifestation of the soul’s true nature (*svarūpa*), then since that nature is already manifested even during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), what is the distinction in the state of liberation? To this, he gives the answer: "Because of its own form" (*svākārāt*). For in the world, when one sees the very same object before oneself appearing more and more agreeable as time goes on—

Subsequently, it is perceived with a greater degree of conformity; thus, although the true nature of the self is eternally manifest, it is first cognized through partial conformity, whereas in the state of liberation, it is cognized through absolute conformity. Here, the syntactical connection of the words is as follows: "At that time, in the state of liberation, the individual soul (jīva) shines forth with a happiness greater than its own eternally manifest form. Nor should it be thought that there is no inherent force in the word *abhiniṣpatti* (manifestation/perfection); for it is said: "In the case of an established fact (*siddhe*), usage alone is the authority for determining the meaning of a word."

It has already been stated that the term *abhiniṣpatti* (manifestation/perfection) is frequently used even in the sense of mere appearance. Now, raising the objection: "The word *abhiniṣpatti* indeed expresses some adventitious (*āgantuka*) meaning; what is this adventitious meaning?"—the author says: "of contraction" (*saṅkoca*). The meaning is "the absolute cessation of contraction," which is "expansion. Previously, it was stated that [the nature] is conditioned by its own essence (*svarūpopādhika*); now, since the word *abhiniṣpatti* denotes the absolute cessation of contraction, the meaning is that the word *svena* (by itself) unimpededly declares the form as being conditioned by its own essence.

Regarding this, someone objects: "It is universally accepted that for those who know the Vedānta, liberation is the manifestation of the Self. Thus, for those who assert that the manifestation of the nature of Brahman as pure consciousness is the human goal (puruṣārtha), the absence of a human goal remains the same [for you as well]. Even though you accept a Supreme Self distinct from the individual soul (jīva) as the object to be seen, that too is indeed seen during the state of yoga; therefore, since there is no specific object to be seen in the state of liberation, the absence of a human goal is common to both positions."

Thus [it is said]. He refutes this with the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*). The meaning is as follows: the general nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) as "I" is well-known to all the world. Nevertheless, that soul—whether it be all-pervading (*vibhu*) or atomic (*aṇu*); whether it be subordinate to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavat*) or subordinate to another; whether independent (*svatantra*) or dependent (*paratantra*); whether of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-rūpa*) or of the nature of insentience (*jaḍa-rūpa*); whether possessing the quality of knowledge (*jñāna-guṇaka*) or devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*); whether its essence is bliss (*ānanda-ātmaka*) or its very form is bliss (*ānanda-svarūpa*); and whether it be merely a momentary continuum (*kṣaṇika-santāna-mātra*) or stable (*sthira*); and if stable, whether it persists until liberation (*āmokṣa-sthāyī*) or otherwise.

Furthermore, because it is described in various ways—such as having neither rising nor setting, being conceptualized or non-conceptualized, distinct or non-distinct, or both distinct and non-distinct—by disputants who wander in many directions, its true nature remains undetermined. Thus, its true nature is perceived specifically only in the state of liberation through its being subordinate to the Blessed Lord and so forth. Let this nature of the individual soul (jīva) rest; for even in the state of liberation, it is not that which is to be manifested to us, but rather the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who dwells within it. This is what he says:

[The Lord is] the one who yields His own [bliss]. He is to be understood as the body of all, as declared by hundreds of Vedic texts such as, "Whose self is the body," and "He has entered within as the ruler of people. Furthermore, that which is understood during the stage of hearing (*śravaṇa*) is not the full extent of what is understood during the stage of reflection (*manana*); and that which is understood even during the stage of reflection is not merely that much which is understood during the stage of meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). As it is said: "In that [space], there is a vast, sorrowless sky; that which is within it is to be sought."

Even here, although there is the manifestation of the eightfold qualities such as freedom from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), all the bliss to be relied upon in the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) becomes like a mere drop in the ocean of experience of the Blessed Lord—who is characterized by all specific attributes such as the Vaikuṇṭha abode, the lotus, the Goddess, ornaments, weapons, attendants, and retinue; who is supreme in every respect; and who is determined to be the sovereign of the two-fold manifestations according to the text: "All beings are one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven. This is the syntactical connection of the words with respect to Himself.

Whatever is perceived during *samādhi*—the state of yoga—within one’s own self, which is a treasure-house of faultless qualities and the bestower of its own bliss, or within the Supreme Self, or in His two manifestations (either the eternal manifestation or the playful manifestation), that becomes like something seen only after one has already attained liberation. The point is that because this experience of the Supreme Brahman, characterized by both manifestations, occurs subsequent [to liberation], it is appropriately considered the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). [Objection: But if something was previously perceived as being of the nature of suffering, how can it be seen later in the same way? How could that [be a human goal]?

Anticipating the objection that this [manifestation] serves a human purpose (*puruṣārthatva*), he says "entire" (*kṛtsnam*). There is nothing whatsoever within the Lord’s manifestation (*vibhūti*) that is inherently disagreeable; rather, it was this very manifestation that appeared as disagreeable for so long due to the persistence of karma—just as milk appears so to one afflicted by bile. However, for one who has attained the Supreme Light (*parañjyotis*), even the manifestation of the eternal realm (*nityavibhūti*) did not previously exist [in its true nature]. But now, through the emergence of the realization of the Lord's supremacy (*śeṣatva*), both of these manifestations [the eternal and the material] [are experienced as agreeable].

It shines as being of the nature of unsurpassed bliss. Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the words "like sugar. Here, the two manifestations are the ocean of nectar and the heap of sugar; furthermore, the Lord is distinguished by the eight qualities such as being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*). Alternatively, the Lord himself is the ocean of nectar, while the eight qualities beginning with freedom from sin, as well as the non-material (aprākṛta) goddess, ornaments, weapons, retinue, specific locations, and so forth, occupy the place of the sugar. Thus, [it refers to] the Blessed Lord Śrīnivāsa, who is endowed with all these attributes.

The Teachers mock us, saying we are like "tortoises in the belly of a well," because we dwell in an utterly unknown land and, due to our total lack of perception [of the truth], we claim that there is no human goal (puruṣārtha) for us who are eternally devoted to service—those of us who are incessantly served by the inner circle of attendants such as Ananta, Garuḍa, and Viṣvaksena, while the Lord dwells in Vaikuṇṭha. Therefore, we are most worthy of compassion and fit for mercy; indeed, those people who are inclined toward what is harmful must be favored by the knowers of the Self. For it is remembered in the Smṛti: "One should feel even greater compassion for the self-betrayer, the transgressor of bounds, the fool who has abandoned the true path—he who is fuel for the flames of hell."

When it is established that the innate nature (*svābhāvika-svarūpa*), which is established from beginningless time, undergoes a transformation due to the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and when it is subsequently established that upon the removal of those adjuncts it returns to its former state, then that form would persist eternally at a later time. To illustrate this point, he provides the example of the *mallī* flower: indeed, due to the influence of an adjunct in the form of the entry of a hollow tube made of *kiṃśuka* wood and so forth into its center, the *mallī*—which by nature produces pure blossoms—produces red blossoms; yet, when the occasion for the removal of the coloring adjunct arises, it produces only pure blossoms once again.

In this way, just like Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and others, the individual soul (jīva), though pure by nature, undergoes the concealment of its innate form due to the power of beginningless karma; subsequently, upon liberation from limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it attains the expansion of knowledge. This is what is expressed by the phrase "just like that."

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the compassion of the Lord produces a fruit equal to that of a *sūri* (spiritual master). Herein lies this distinction: although souls are eternally capable of experiencing the Lord just like a *sūri*, there is a lack of experience due to beginningless obstructions; upon the cessation of those obstructions, the attainment of an experience equal to that of a *sūri* is established. In the case of the *mallī* flower and others, there is purity even before [the fragrance appears], then in the interim the acquisition of a specific form conditioned by external factors, and finally the connection with its own natural essence. Regarding this, the direct illustration is: "Just as it is not made..."

The "moonlight" and so forth mentioned [in the verse] refer precisely to the jewel. Indeed, luminosity is inherent in the very nature of a jewel; however, that luminosity may become obscured by impurity from the time of its birth for some jewels. For others, there has been no connection with impurity from the beginning; they are like that [luminous jewel], eternal. Transmigrating beings, on the other hand, are like jewels possessed of a connection with impurity from the very beginning. Yet, through the polishing of the whetstone—just as in the case of a jewel—their natural luminosity becomes manifest through the polishing of the whetstone consisting of the worship of the Lord.

It occurs. He concludes the stated point with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since it is observed in the world that once there is an absence of obstruction, the manifestation of one's innate nature remains permanently because there is no further impediment to it—even though such an expansion of wisdom may be adventitious—the attainment of the Self is established; thus, the sequence for the inner self (*pratyagātman*) who has attained the fruit and has realized its own nature is described here.

The meaning is as follows: suppose the paternal wealth of a certain son is naturally his by right, but it is obstructed by some other powerful and wicked person; later, when that obstruction is removed, the son regains his own wealth which was naturally his. In the same way, because the experience of the Blessed One is naturally attained by all souls, once the karma that obstructs it has ceased—and since there is no possibility of another obstacle arising—it persists eternally; thus, this [attainment] is free from all thorns.

The path of ethics: however, the inference of impermanence based on the fact of being produced is like the inference of the purity of a human head and so forth; because it is sublated by the authoritative testimony of the scripture stating, "And he does not return," it receives only the name of "friendship" [i.e., it is merely a semblance of reasoning].

On this point, some say: "There is a certain kind of liberation consisting in the attainment of the mere individual soul (jīvātman); however, to demonstrate that this is not liberation itself, he restates their position with the words 'arvāñcam' (downward). Thus, certain thinkers, disregarding the experience of one's own Self alone as a specific form of liberation, [hold such a view].

To this, he provides the following answer: "In that regard" (*tatra*). Here, one must state the refutation of both alternatives in the dilemma: whether the interruption of the experience of Brahman is natural or rooted in karma. When asked, "What is the refutation?", he states that "the defects previously mentioned by us exist here. Anticipating the objection that "historians and those versed in the Purāṇas declare that liberation is isolation (*kaivalya*)," and that not only they but some followers of your own school have also said so, he says "from that" (*tataḥ*) to show that all such conventional usage is merely figurative. Let it be so.

Although liberation (*kaivalya*) is figurative, you yourself describe specific types of liberation in the forms of *sālokya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sārūpya*; anticipating the question of how this can be so, he says: "sālokya... and so forth.

The meaning is that even in those cases, the word "liberation" (mukti) is used figuratively. There is indeed scriptural authority for this: "Some dwell in the worlds of Viṣṇu; others attain his proximity; still others assume a form similar to his; and others attain union (sāyujya)—that [last] is said to be liberation. This is the sense: liberation is not merely residence in the same world (sālokya) and so forth; rather, in those cases, the word "liberation" is figurative. However, as for one who has attained union (sāyujya), even the triad beginning with residence in the same world is included within that state of union.

It acquires the status of being denoted by the word "liberation" (mukti). Therefore, by distinguishing between what has been attained and what has not yet been attained, *sāyujya* (union) alone is the meaning of the word "mokṣa. As for other [states], let them acquire the status of being denoted by the word "liberation" precisely through their connection with *sāyujya*. What loss is there to us? Moreover, *sāyujya* is itself defined by the Śruti: "He enjoys all desires together [with Him]. The author of the Sūtras as well, in the aphorism "And because of the indicative mark of equality in enjoyment alone," states that *sāyujya* is indeed equality in experience. As for the specific distinction some mention regarding the state of liberation, namely "being equal to the Lord" (*sāṣṭitā*), [it is not the primary meaning].

This has also been clearly demonstrated elsewhere by the Teachers themselves: "In this state of union (*sāyujya*), there is no distinction between the two enjoyers; therein lies 'equality' (*sāṣṭatā*), which is the absence of any gradation in enjoyment. For in the world, even when the object of enjoyment is the same, there exists inequality in the desire of the enjoyers; the virtuous explain that such a thing does not exist here, and thus they mention "equality"—which is inherent within union—in order to demonstrate this point. However, for those who propound falsehood, the very possibility of union does not exist, because of the prefix [in *sāyujya*].

To that extent, the contradiction with their own doctrine is indeed well-established, as if the word "saha" (together) were a synonym for identity. Furthermore, it is undisputed among all disputants that the verbal root *yuj* (to join), meaning "union," possesses the sense of difference. The derivative term *sāyujyam*—meaning "the state of being joined" (*sayuja-bhāva*)—also clearly expresses difference through its very formation. Therefore, the claim that "sāyujya is liberation" is merely the talk of those who lack analytical understanding. If you argue: "In that case, we maintain that 'sāyujya' denotes oneness by virtue of conventional usage (*rūḍhi-śakti*)," even that is not so.

This is because there is no evidence establishing that the word *sāyujya* has the conventional power (*rūḍhi-śakti*) to mean identity; on the contrary, in Vedic usages such as "two birds, companions, united" (*dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā*) and "union with the Sun" (*ādityasya sāyujyam*), it is expressed precisely as being preceded by difference. Furthermore, even common folk do not claim in the world that *sāyujya* means identity, so how much less could poets? If those like you were to say so, they would be either monkeys or apes.

In the *Bhāṣya*, the connection [of the topic] is stated as follows: "In this doubt—whether this inner self, having reached the supreme light and being liberated from all bonds, experiences itself as distinct from the Supreme Self, or rather as non-different from it by being a mode (*prakāra*) of that [Self]?"—the investigation into its meaning is as follows: "Does the self [experience itself] as distinct from the Supreme Self..."

Does one experience [the Self] as distinct, or as non-distinct from it by way of being its mode (*tad-prakāratayā*)? Do the expressions of "conjunction," "similarity," and "common characteristics" contradict an experience that is non-distinct, or not? Is conjunction and so forth possible only for that which is distinct, or not? In this regard, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) states the specific reasons for the perception of difference alone in the state of liberation: "The individual soul and the Lord... The meaning is this: the scripture itself, in the verse "Two birds...," declares the difference between the individual soul and the Supreme. He also states another reason:

Regarding the scriptural authority (*śruti*): that very scripture, in the passage "He enjoys all desires together" (*so'śnute sarvān kāmān saha*), speaks of the enjoyment of the liberated one preceded by the word "together" (*saha*). For the word "together" (*saha*) is applicable only where there is distinction; people say, "The father has come with his son," but they do not say, "The father has come with the father," nor do they say, "The son has come with the son. He states a third reason as well: "on account of equality" (*sāmya*). Equality, for its part, presupposes distinction; here, moreover, supreme equality refers to absolute distinction. [This is so] when there is equality through some particular qualification.

It is appropriate to speak of "equality" (*sāmya*); for even through many qualifications, it is indeed "supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam*) that is established. Therefore, that too is intended to emphasize difference. And this is established by Smṛti, because the Lord himself is seen to use the word "conformity" (*sādharmya*) as a synonym for "equality" in the passage: "Having attained conformity with Me" (*mama sādharmyam āgatāḥ*). Thus, he says "He [is distinct]" so that the individual soul (*jīva*) may appear as separate from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). He rejects this very point with "Not so," and states the reason for that: "The reality... at the stage of liberation.

Only reality (tattva) appears, not unreality (atattva). "Unreality," however, means a difference that is independent [of Brahman], that is to say, a difference whose nature is non-Brahman; the meaning is: "by that [realization], may the faultless difference between these two—the individual soul and the Supreme—shine forth. If one then asks, "What kind of difference is being negated?", he says: "established" (siddha). Indeed, difference is perceived in two ways: difference whose nature is Brahman and difference whose nature is non-Brahman. Of these, the former difference is [expressed by such texts as] "Two birds, inseparable companions... ("dvā suparṇā sayujā"), "The eternal among eternals... ("nityo nityānām"), and "the enjoyer... ("bhoktā").

Because this is well-known from such scriptural passages as "the object of enjoyment," it is indeed a point accepted by those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*). However, any distinction consisting of a non-Brahman nature must be disregarded, for it contradicts the contemplation of the identity with Brahman established by such authorities as: "He has entered within, the ruler of people, the Self of all," and "Because of the omnipresence of the Infinite, He alone abides as I. Therefore, the meaning is that for those who know the inner self, the contemplation of inseparability—that is, the contemplation of the relationship between body and self—is established by their very birth. This is the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here.

The meaning is that once the identification of the self with the body is established, the vision of that living being as being self-sufficient does not indeed occur; that is to say, the failure to perceive its dependence on the Supreme Self is not possible [to maintain].

On this point, the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) maintains: "You state that the contemplation of the Lord without distinction occurs at the stage of liberation; however, this is directly contrary to scripture. For in the mantra beginning with 'Truth, Knowledge,' etc., it is precisely difference (*bheda*) that is explicitly stated regarding the stage of the fruit. To illustrate: 'He enjoys all desires together'—this is the indication of the fruit. Here, one must discern whether the word 'together' (*saha*) denotes association with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-sāhitya*) or association with the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-sāhitya*). If it denotes association with the enjoyer, [it would fall under the rule] *sahayukte'pradhāne*..."

"Because of the connection with the word 'together' in the phrase 'together with Brahman,' Brahman might appear to be subordinate to the individual soul (jīva) as its enjoyer; and that is improper, because it is illogical for Brahman—the Lord of all—to be subordinate to the individual soul, who is entirely subservient to Him. Thus [it is said].

This is what he means by saying, "stated in the mantra. Since it is inappropriate to speak of the association with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) in this manner, he states that it is proper to speak only of the association with the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya*), beginning with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He provides another reason for this propriety with the word "Brāhmaṇa": the Brāhmaṇa passage is "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*); its explanation is the mantra "Truth, Knowledge... (*satyaṃ jñānam*). Therein, the term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*) was explained previously; regarding the portion "attains the Supreme" (*param āpnoti*), [the mantra says] "He enjoys all desires together with Brahman" (*sa aśnute sarvān kāmān saha brahmaṇā*).

The grammatical analysis is performed as "vipaścitā. By this, the meaning is that it is appropriate to speak of the association with the objects of enjoyment (*bhogya-sāhitya*). The syntactical construction "he enjoys together with Brahman" expresses association with the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-sāhitya*); the syntactical construction "he enjoys all desires together with Brahman" expresses association with the objects of enjoyment. For a master does not lack primacy toward his servants, nor should that [lack of primacy] be asserted, as it contradicts common worldly experience.

"Or let there be here an intended association with the enjoyer; even in both cases, the individual soul (jīva) is perceived as distinct from the reality of Brahman. Thus, [the opponent] raises the objection that non-differentiated contemplation (*avibhāgānusandhāna*) is not tenable, using the words 'even in both ways' (*dvedhāpi*). He refutes this with the word 'nonsense' (*vārtam*). The meaning is this: here, the difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) between the individual soul and the Supreme is not being denied, for that difference in essential nature is already established; rather, what is being rejected is their existence in independence (*svātantryeṇāvasthānam*), which is what the Sūtra seeks to establish."

The meaning is that this is the intention of the author of the Sūtras; for a word is an authoritative means of knowledge only with respect to its intended purport (tātparya). Therefore, setting aside the superficial meaning, it is the intended purport alone that should be thoroughly examined by those who are leaders in inquiry.

He concludes the meaning of the statement, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," by reflecting upon the purport of the scripture, saying: "Supremacy. Here, by the phrase "supreme equality," it is not meant that there is equality in every respect; rather, the meaning is that one must accept as much equality as is consistent with the means of valid knowledge and remains uncontradicted. To illustrate this point, he provides a worldly example: "Of the stone and gold. When a stone and gold are held on an equal balance—that is, when they are placed on a scale with equal weights—there would be a statement of their equality.

By this much alone, there would not even be equality of color; rather, equality exists in the form of being a *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, and so forth. Similarly here as well, there is only equality of enjoyment (*bhoga*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), but not equality in lordship (*svāmitva*) and other attributes, because those [attributes] are established by authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) as having distinct functions. If that is so, how is it that the common grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) seen in the statement, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," is observed? Coordination indeed refers to identity, while the particle *eva* (itself) negates difference; therefore—

The answer here is that there is indeed identity between the essential nature of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; this is the logical connection (anvaya), because of the abundance of various scriptural authorities (āmnāya) that establish the relationship of the body and the self for the individual soul.

When it is determined that the Blessed One, while remaining in the state of a physical body, becomes Brahman itself, this exclusive designation (*sāvadhāraṇa-nirdeśa*) merely confirms their similarity. Just as in the verse: "Just as the various seasonal signs appear in their recurring cycle according to the seasons, so do these very same phenomena appear at the beginnings of the Yugas,"—here the term of exclusive grammatical coreferentiality (*sāvadhāraṇa-sāmānādhikaraṇya-śabda*), namely "those very same ones," expresses only that they belong to the same class (*tajjātīyatvam*), and not that they are the identical entities themselves, since those produced in the preceding and succeeding seasons are distinct.

Because they are distinct by virtue of arising at different times, the statement "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed" expresses only a state of similarity to Brahman, and not identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*). For Brahman is eternally stainless, whereas the knower of Brahman becomes stainless only now through meditation upon It; how then can it be said that there is identity of their essential natures? Therefore, the meaning is that by virtue of being of the same nature as Brahman, the term "becomes Brahman" is used in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Thus, the meaning established by this reasoning—

He establishes this by means of a scriptural authority (*pramāṇa*): "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly the same, so too, O Gautama, does the self of the sage who possesses true knowledge become. Thus, even the state of being "the same" (*tāddagbhāva*) regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) in relation to Brahman is stated; it is not, however, identity (*tattva*). Therefore, the meaning is that one should understand that wherever identity is mentioned, in all such cases it is actually the state of being "the same" that is being expressed.

It has been stated that for the inner self (pratyagātman), upon attaining the supreme light, there occurs the manifestation of its own true nature once all obstructions have ceased. Regarding this, the connection [of the topic] in the Commentary is as follows: "That true nature by which it manifests is now investigated due to the diversity of scriptural statements. The investigation into its meaning, however, concerns whether its true nature consists solely of the eight qualities, or whether it is pure consciousness alone, or whether both constitute its true nature.

Is the distinction between the strength and weakness of the two types of scriptural texts—one concerning the mere nature of the Self as consciousness and the other concerning its distinction from the eightfold qualities—justified or not? Is a contradiction between them possible or not? Having presented here each of the two positions favored by Jaimini and Auḍulomi respectively, [the author] begins to establish his own desired synthesis of both views with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). This, indeed, is the intention of Jaimini: "In the teaching that the Self consists of the nature of knowledge alone, of that..."

Because it is incapable of grasping its own objects, it is indeed fruitless; therefore, by that [absence of fruitfulness], identity with Brahman is intended through the qualities. However, this is the view of Auḍulomi: "What is the purpose of qualities mentioned as distinct from the essential nature? Let there be only the manifestation of the essential nature as pure consciousness. Having thus set forth these two prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the author] concludes that since both positions are supported by scripture and are therefore not contradictory, his own desired essential nature consists of the synthesis of both.

He brought about the manifestation [of the Lord]. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "because of the contradiction arising from both kinds of scriptural passages, and because of the revelation of the established reality. This is the underlying meaning (*bhāva*) here: if, accepting the view of Jaimini, we were to maintain only that [the Self] has knowledge as its quality (*jñāna-guṇakatva*) and so forth, then there would be a contradiction with those scriptural passages that establish the nature of the Self as being consciousness itself (*jñāna-svarūpatva*). And if, following those scriptures, we were to abandon qualities such as having knowledge as an attribute and instead realize only the nature of being consciousness itself, then [there would be a contradiction] regarding qualities such as having knowledge as an attribute.

There would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts that establish [the soul as having knowledge], and there would also be a contradiction with perception in both cases. Therefore, for the sake of avoiding all contradictions, we accept the nature of being knowledge and the possession of the quality of knowledge in combination; thus, we maintain that in the state of liberation, it manifests in both forms, and so there is no contradiction whatsoever.

Anticipating an objection regarding a contradiction between the meaning of this present section and that of the preceding one, [the author] explains that there is not even a scent of contradiction by stating, "They are synonyms. Herein lies the intention of the opponent (pūrvapakṣin): "In such passages as 'liberation is isolation (kaivalya) and nirvāṇa,' the terms 'mokṣa' and 'kaivalya' are listed as synonyms. Among them, the word 'kaivalya' indicates precisely the non-existence of any other entity. Therefore, how can the vision of the individual soul (jīva) as non-different from Brahman, as stated in the preceding section, be possible?"

And in this context, how can the designation of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and [the Self] as quality and qualified—by virtue of the soul's possession of the eight qualities such as freedom from sin (apahatapāpmatva) and so forth—be consistent? For by that [designation], liberation (kaivalya), which consists in the absence of everything else, [would be undermined].

"How could there be a concomitance between the subject (dharmin) and its property (dharma)? How could there be a concomitance between the qualifier and the qualified?"—he rejects this objection with the words "Not so" (maivam). Here, he demonstrates the existence of the meaning of the term *kaivalya* by analyzing it as "Brahman. In the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), it was stated that nothing distinct from the nature of Brahman possesses independent existence; that itself is its *kaivalya*. In this section, it is stated that no substance exists devoid of qualities; here too, that very same [absence of independence] is *kaivalya*.

Because of the teaching that [the Self] is devoid of being without qualities (nirguṇatva-rāhitya), he says "the pair of topics" (adhikaraṇayugam) to show that in both cases there is the presentation of the intended meaning in the respective sections, and thus it is entirely free from blemish.

The connection here is stated in the Bhāṣya: "It has been said that the liberated one, having attained the Supreme Brahman, manifests as the very nature of knowledge, possessing attributes beginning with freedom from sin and ending with the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). With reference to him, scriptural accounts of his activities prompted by that power of true resolve are heard: 'There he moves about, laughing, playing, and delighting, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen. Regarding this, the inquiry is: does his attainment of kinsmen and so forth depend upon some other effort, or [is it spontaneous]?

[The world] has its root solely in volition (saṅkalpa). Does his possession of true volition (satya-saṅkalpatva) belong to him as it does to kings and others, or rather like that of the Supreme Person? Is the restrictive emphasis "from volition alone" capable of excluding similarity with kings and others, or not?

Is it possible for the resolve of a liberated soul (*muktātman*) to be free from delusion in the same way as the resolve of the Lord (*īśvara*), or not? Do its activities, such as eating and so forth, become causes of bondage by taking the form of merit and demerit, or not? Here, one might raise the objection that the liberated one must perform those various actions only by means of instruments (*upakaraṇa*); and if there is a dependence on instruments, he would necessarily remain a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*). Anticipating this, the author refutes it with the verse beginning "of Dhātṛ and others" (*dhātrādeḥ*). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: even for Dhātṛ and others, whose activity consists of true resolve, there is a dependence on instruments.

Thus, even for one who is liberated, there would be a dependence upon the collection of subtle instruments (liṅga-deha) for the performance of actions; and consequently, he would be no different from one who is not liberated. This very point, which has been raised as a doubt, [is refuted] by its inability to withstand logical alternatives.

"He corrupts [the doctrine] with falsehood"—regarding this, there is the following dilemma: do you mean by "dependence" (sāpekṣatva) merely the dependence upon substances and so forth, or rather dependence upon merit (*puṇya*) and demerit (*pāpa*)? It cannot be the first, because that would result in proving what is already established; thus he says, "In the desired [view]. Nor can it be the latter; thus he says, "In regard to good deeds. For one who is liberated is indeed free from merit and demerit; it is impossible even to say that such a person has dependence upon merit and demerit. Just as, in the view of those learned in Nyāya, there is dependence upon karma when the agency belongs to a conscious being, but not when the agency belongs to God.

Thus, here too, it is indeed contradictory to claim that liberated souls require karma for their agency. However, while it is because of His very nature as the Lord (*īśvara*) that the Lord has no dependence on karma, the same would apply to the liberated soul because of His very state of liberation (*muktatva*). This is because both are established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being beyond the control of karma—this is the intended meaning. Now, one might object: "Since the liberated soul possesses agency, could there not occasionally be an obstruction of his will? [The author replies: "It could not be so; by what karma could such an obstruction possibly occur? Then, perhaps one might suspect that it could be obstructed by the will of the Lord (*īśvara*). Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of the Divine," etc. Indeed, the liberated soul...

The passage, "Wandering through these worlds, eating what he desires, and assuming whatever form he desires," is heard [in scripture] precisely as being due to his following the Lord; therefore, the meaning is that it is not even possible to suspect any obstruction of his will by the desire of the Lord.

Having cited the Lord himself as the very example for the liberated one’s direct perception of all things and the performance of all actions, he convinces those of weak intellect that [the liberated] possesses such power. This is the logical connection (*anvaya*) here: just as the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this universe proceed from the Lord, the creator of the universe, so too must there be a necessity (*niyati*) even for the activities of those eternally liberated ones, due to the distinctions within the continuum of their wills. Now, an objection may be raised: since the continuum of will is an effect, it must be subject to cessation, just like the continuum of a lamp's flame; and if that were so—

Fearing that even the continuum of liberated activities—described in such passages as "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—might be cut off, he offers a rebuttal with the words "of that. Indeed, the non-interruption of the continuum of will cannot be denied, as it is established by such scriptural texts as "and he does not return again"; otherwise, if one asserts that for whatever has a prior limit there must necessarily be a subsequent limit, then just like that, the continuum of karma for whatever has a subsequent limit would also have a prior limit. And in that case, the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra* itself would not exist.

It is established because it is proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it is impossible even to suggest that it is abandoned—this is the consistent resolution. Now, is the cognition of the liberated one indirect (*pārokṣya*) or direct (*āparokṣya*)? If it were indirect, there would indeed be bondage. Nor is directness possible; for directness belongs to knowledge produced by the senses, yet the liberated one possesses no body, senses, or the like. If they did exist, then the karma which is their root would also exist, and thus there would be rebirth once again. And so...

To the objection that even direct perception (*aparokṣya*) is not possible for one whose knowledge has been liberated, he says "tadbuddheḥ" and so forth. Just as the direct perception of the Lord’s intellect exists, so too must the direct perception of the individual soul’s (*jīva*) intellect be admitted. That [perception] has been contracted by karma for all this time; now, once the obstacle has ceased, it shall become natural.

In this world, even though one possesses the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), obstruction is observed when powerful counteracting forces exist; likewise, one might suspect that for the liberated (*mukta*) as well, there could be obstruction due to the presence of powerful counteracting forces. Anticipating this, [the author] states that the capacity to obstruct belongs only to merit and demerit (*puṇya-pāpa*); since those two do not exist in that state, the very suspicion of obstruction cannot arise. There is indeed some gradation in the activity of the liberated; let it be so, yet by that much, the equality of their enjoyment (*bhoga-sāmya*) is not contradicted. This is because for all liberated ones—

He shows that [the Lord] possesses uncontracted knowledge because of the absence of any obstructing factors by saying "capable of obstacles. As for the connection with the words: even though He possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*), those who possess limited merit or merit at a particular time are "capable of obstacles. By the maxim "one thing was begun, another has occurred," he uses the phrase "in the undertaking of mortals" (*martyārambhe*) to show that for those who act with one intention, something entirely different results.

"Mortal" refers to sons and the like. The meaning is that when one performs actions out of a desire to initiate [benefit for] sons and so forth, one observes only the initiation of enemies due to defects in the agent, the instrument, and other factors. Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: "because, in the case of a mortal’s desire for initiation and so forth, one perceives the creation of various living beings that are opposed to it. Having raised the objection that if there were thought of one thing while another was being initiated, the activity would be purposeless due to the absence of a regulating cause, he shows that very regulating cause with the words "by that" (tena).

For these transmigrating souls engaged in worldly activity, success, failure, and contrary results occur solely due to past merit and demerit. However, for the liberated soul, merit and demerit do not exist. His desire is invariably successful; as the Śruti also declares, God extends his uninterrupted activity in accordance with that very desire—this is what is meant by "of the liberated. Now, one might object: even in the absence of an obstruction to the desire of the liberated soul, there certainly exists a gradation in their activities, and through that, a gradation in experience would also exist.

Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "the gradation" (*tāratamyam*). It is not the gradation of activity itself that constitutes a defect in liberation; rather, a defect would exist only if there were a gradation in enjoyment. For the performance of an actor does not produce satisfaction for the actor alone, but also for other spectators; likewise, the activities of all liberated beings, such as following after the Lord, are causes of satisfaction for everyone equally. Thus, equality of enjoyment is indeed established. Indeed, those residing in royal households [enjoy] individually...
The virtuous serve the king through activities corresponding to their respective offices; however, that satisfaction is common to all—this is as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand.

Regarding this, someone raises an objection: "In the two sūtras, 'Because he obtains that merely by will' and 'And for this very reason, he has no other lord,' it is stated that the liberated one has no other lord. Therefore, he cannot have a subordinate (śeṣin). Furthermore, by the scripture itself, 'He becomes self-ruling,' the liberated one [is described]."

[If it were] independent, it would not have been mentioned [there]. Therefore, there would be a contradiction of all the meanings previously established, such as the Lord’s being the sovereign and the soul’s state of dependence upon Him. To this, the reply is: "Not so. He states the manner of refutation with the word "na" (not). In this section, the status of the soul as a subordinate (*śeṣa*) to anyone other than the Blessed Lord—which would imply sin—is refuted, and likewise His dependence upon them is also refuted. This is because of the one described in the text, "the Lord of the universe, the Master of the Self," who is the Lord of the universe.

It is simply not subject to sublation; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the liberated soul’s state of being subservient to the Lord and its dependence on Him. Regarding this, the connection (*saṅgati*) in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) is as follows: "In the matter of whether the liberated one possesses a body and senses, or does not possess them, or whether they exist or do not exist according to his will. The inquiry into that purpose begins with the first investigation: "Whether the liberated one... and so forth. For the sake of that [inquiry], it is deliberated upon: [The text continues: "Is the liberated one devoid of body and senses, or does he possess them? Or rather, are they present or absent according to his own resolve? This doubt arises because there are conflicting scriptural statements. Some texts declare that the liberated one is 'without body' (*videha*), while others state that he is 'possessed of a body' (*sadeha*). Furthermore, some passages describe him as being 'without senses' (*vīta-indriya*), whereas other texts speak of him as having 'all the senses' (*sarvendriya-yukta*). [The text continues: "Moreover, some passages teach that the liberated one is 'without activity' (*niṣkriya*), while others teach that he is 'capable of all actions' (*sarvakarmakṣama*). Likewise, some texts declare that he is 'devoid of qualities' (*nirguṇa*), while others teach that he is 'possessed of all qualities' (*sarvaguṇopeta*). And finally, some passages state that he is 'without form' (*amūrta*), while others state that he is 'possessed of form' (*mūrtimant*). [The text continues: "Therefore, the doubt arises: 'Does the liberated one have a body and senses, or does he not? To resolve this, the following must be considered: Is the liberated one naturally devoid of body and senses, or is he endowed with them by nature? Or is it that he is without them by nature, but possesses them through his own resolve? Or is it that he is without them by nature, yet possesses them through the resolve of the Lord? Or is it that he is without them by nature, but possesses them through the resolve of both himself and the Lord? Or is it that he is without them by nature, but possesses them through the resolve of the Lord alone? Or is it that he is without them by nature, but possesses them through the resolve of the Lord and the grace of the Lord? Or is it that he is without them by nature, but possesses them through the resolve of the Lord and the grace of the Lord and the resolve of himself?
