Can the scriptural passage beginning with "He becomes onefold," and so forth, restrict the scriptural teaching regarding bodilessness? Or not? Does the statement "He becomes onefold," and so forth, have the power to establish that the liberated soul possesses a body, or not? Even if it does establish it, does it establish mere possession of a body, or does it convey that this is *this* specific body? To determine that, is becoming onefold, becoming threefold, and so on, possible for the liberated soul without a body, or not? In this regard:

He restates the prima facie position according to the views of Bādari and Jaimini with the words "the liberated one. In a certain scriptural passage, it is stated: "Verily, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless"; thus, the liberated one is described as being bodiless.

Furthermore, regarding that very same liberated one, the possibility of manifold existence is heard in scriptural passages such as, "He becomes singlefold; he becomes threefold. Moreover, in certain instances, activities accomplished by means of the body and senses, such as singing and playing, are set forth in passages like, "Singing this Sāman... Anticipating the refutation of the two pairs of views held by the Ṛṣis—namely, the view of Bādarāyaṇa which maintains the rule of bodilessness, and the view of Jaimini which maintains the rule of having a body—the author of the Sūtras demonstrates his own position exactly as it is.

Regarding the phrase *svacchandasya* ("of one who is independent"): whether possessing a body or being bodiless, both states are equal according to his will. This is the intended meaning: in the human goal consisting of the experience of the undifferentiated Brahman, there is no dependence on a body; however, for the service (*kaiṅkarya*) to the Lord—which is appropriate in all places, at all times, and in all conditions, as stated in such scriptural passages as "these worlds" and "eating, playing, and rejoicing"—there is a dependence on a body. Now, if possessing a body is indeed accepted, [one might object] that it contradicts the statement, "For one who is embodied, there is truly no freedom from pleasure and pain."

Fearing that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) might recur because there could still be "being joined with what is dear," he says: "It would be so. This is the meaning: if mere possession of a body were *saṃsāra*, then even the Lord (*īśvara*) would be subject to *saṃsāra*. However, *saṃsāra* is actually the state of having a body dependent upon karma. Thus, even though the liberated one—like the Lord—possesses a body dependent solely on his own independent will (*saṅkalpa*), there is no room for even a scent of *saṃsāra*; this is a beautiful conclusion.

Now, one might object: "Is not the position of Bādari also his own preferred view, and likewise the position of Jaimini? This being the case, when the author of the Sūtras refutes those positions, what is this specific position he establishes as his own? In response to this objection, for the sake of awakening the understanding of his disciples, he demonstrates his own position once again with particular clarity by stating, "Liberation. The grammatical connection here is as follows: since merit and demerit do not exist in liberation, Bādari’s statement that the body conditioned by them is abandoned is not to be refuted; likewise, [the soul] is devoid of a body subject to suffering.

When that [objection] has been refuted, even the position regarding the existence of an auspicious body and its constituent elements (sattva) as stated by Jaimini cannot be dismissed. If this were so, one might ask: what kind of state for the liberated one would have been indicated by the sage Bādarāyaṇa here? To this, he provides the answer: "Not so" (maivam). He reveals his own intended view with the words "svacchande" (at will). By stating that there is a body at will, Bādarī, who claimed that connection with a body does not exist as a rule, is refuted. Therefore, the established conclusion is that the liberated one becomes both embodied and bodiless according to the circumstances, solely through his own volition, which is rooted in the volition of the Lord.

On this point, someone objects, saying "no" (*na*). It is well known that the *jīva* is atomic (*aṇu*). Now, it is further stated here that for one who has attained equality with Brahman, that *jīva* simultaneously possesses multiple bodies. If this is so, then it is appropriate that those bodies, arising in different locations, should possess the nature of the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, and not the nature of the atomic *jīva*. Consequently, the doctrine of the atom-sized *jīva* would be undermined in the state of liberation. If, on the other hand, the *jīva* were all-pervasive at that time, then the distinction between the *jīva* and the Lord (*īśvara*) would not exist.

It might be argued: "Your established doctrine is that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic and possesses cognition, while the Lord (īśvara) is different [from it]. He refutes this with the words, "This is not so. He states the reason for this here: "Because the pervasion of cognition is established."

The meaning is that even though there is no pervasion by the soul's own essential form (*svarūpa*), the pervasion by its attribute-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) is established during the state of liberation. He states "And it occurs... to show that this point was clearly expressed by the author of the Sūtras when he said, "The entry [of the soul] is like that of a lamp. The meaning is that although the soul is atomic, statements regarding its entry into the universe—such as "And it is capable of infinity" and "It becomes one-fold"—are based on the pervasion of its attribute-knowledge. Now, regarding the soul in the state of liberation, it is said: "It attains supreme equality."

Anticipating the objection that "by virtue of the scriptural statement, why could the assumption of multiple bodies not simply be an exercise of sovereign power (*vibhutva*)," he says, "In the case of Saubhari and others," and so forth. The meaning is this: in the case of Saubhari and others, the assumption of multiple bodies was established precisely through the pervasion of knowledge as a quality (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), even without [the soul's] being omnipresent (*vibhu*). And thus, rather than postulating omnipresence for the liberated soul and then describing the assumption of multiple bodies, it is better to describe the assumption of multiple bodies through the pervasion of knowledge alone, according to the very principle established in the case of Saubhari and others.

When there is a conflict between what is already established (*klṛpta*) and what is merely conceivable (*kalpya*), it is the settled conclusion of those who know the principles of logic that the acceptance of what is already established is indeed more reasonable. Furthermore, the author of the Sūtras himself determined that supreme equality consists only in respect to experience, in the words, "And because of the indicative mark of equality in experience alone" (*bhogamātrasāmyaliṅgācca*); it does not, however, mean equality in essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the definition of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) remains firmly established.

Having stated that it is impossible for the atomic individual soul (*jīva*) to simultaneously occupy multiple bodies, he provides the resolution with the words "of the bodies" (*dehānām*). The syntactical connection here is as follows: if there were simultaneity of bodies, how could the atomic soul, once liberated, itself be the sustainer of many bodies? Here, the mention of being a "sustainer" (*dhāraka*) is also indicative of being a controller (*niyāmaka*) and so forth.

If it is argued that the maintenance of the body occurs through the medium of consciousness—that is, by means of knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*)—then one must consider that since the liberated knowledge pervades all objects, the liberated soul would also possess the power to sustain everything. Consequently, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) would be untenable. To this he says: "Even all... The answer here is: "Not so. For the capacity to sustain everything does not follow from mere pervasion; if it did, it would follow that time (*kāla*) also sustains everything, since time too is pervasive. Rather, [the power to sustain] arises only from a specific capacity (*śaktiviśeṣa*).

[The capacity for] sustaining [the world]. For one who is liberated, there is no power conducive to sustaining [the world] in its manifold forms; rather, the power of the liberated one has a restricted scope, because the author of the Sūtras restricted that power to specific instances by stating, "except for the activity of the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*). Even where the power of the intellect of the liberated one exists, it is governed solely by the will of the omnipotent Lord; thus he says, "by the will of the omnipotent one. How then...

Anticipating the objection that Saubhari and others, though not yet liberated, possess the power to assume multiple bodies, he says "prāk" (previously). The meaning is: "by the power of yoga associated with that," i.e., by the power of yoga granted by the Lord. He states "karmabandha" (the bondage of karma) to show that it is not only the power of yoga, but also the ripening of karma established from time immemorial, that is the cause here. The meaning is that such a power, which is the perfection of yoga, is called "yogasiddhi" because it arises from the ripening of knowledge assisted by karma.

Here, someone objects: "You claim that there is an expansion of contracted knowledge during the state of liberation after its contraction during the state of bondage; however, that contraction and expansion belong to the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) itself, which is enveloped by karma. Once it is freed from karma, that same soul undergoes expansion. What is the purpose of this postulation of contraction and expansion regarding *dharma-bhūta-jñāna* (knowledge as an attribute), which contradicts the evidence?"

This is what he says with the words "power" (*śakti*). Now, one might object: "Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is partless, how can there be an expansion [of its knowledge]? Anticipating this doubt, he states "of the person" (*puṃsaḥ*), showing that the same partlessness applies to the knowledge that constitutes its attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*) as well. Just as the intellect (*buddhi*) of a person, though partless, possesses various modifications such as memory and direct experience through its different states, so too the individual soul may be atomic in its bound state, yet all-pervading in its liberated state. This difference in dimension exists within the partless [soul] according to the distinction between the bound and the liberated.

The meaning is that you yourself must also admit that this [nature] exists even in your own doctrine of consciousness as a property of the self (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*). He concludes this point with the words "Therefore, this... (*tad idam*). He refutes this with the words "It would not be so" (*na syāt*). He states the reason for the refutation in the phrase "in the refutation of the Jaina and others" (*jainādibhaṅge*). For the Jainas indeed maintain that the soul (*jīva*) is of the same dimension as the body and undergoes transformation from time to time. However, because the soul is devoid of modification (*vikāra*), that view has been refuted in the *Jainādhikaraṇa* (the section on the Jainas). The syntactical connection here is as follows: in the refutation of the Jaina and other views, since the soul is free from modification, its uniformity (*ekarūpya*) remains unimpaired.

"Because there is no departure from the absence of reaching a state ending in *diti* (destruction). This is the meaning: the changelessness of the self is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the infinity of that very same atom in its state of liberation during its state of bondage is also established by that same valid means of knowledge.

The non-contradiction of both types of authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa) must be asserted. That non-contradiction is established through a difference in their respective objects: because there is no modification of its essential nature, and because the infinity established by scripture is accepted as pertaining to knowledge in its manifested state (dharmabhūtajñāna). However, there is no direct scriptural statement declaring that knowledge is devoid of modification; on the contrary, statements describing it as possessing modifications are indeed heard, due to the abundance of scriptural, traditional, historical, and Puranic declarations establishing the contraction and expansion of knowledge. As for the mention of concealment in the Self, it occurs through the medium of knowledge, just as the sun's rays are concealed by a thick mass of clouds.

Here, however, an objection is raised: "Of the living soul (jīva). The living soul, existing by pervading all branches of a tree, abandons some branches while remaining in others; where there is abandonment, that part of the tree withers, whereas where there is no abandonment, further growth of branches is observed. Therefore, since the abandoning and non-abandoning of its own nature are observed, it must be understood that there is a transformation of the soul's own nature.

He concludes this with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Because it has been established in this manner, when there is an absence of obscuration in the individual soul (*jīva*), the infinity taught in the passage, "And he becomes fit for infinity," is not mediated by the knowledge that constitutes its attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), but rather is non-mediated. He says "not so" (*maivam*) to reject this, and he establishes that very point with the words "in the branches" (*śākhāsu*). For the abandonment [of the soul] in the various branches does not mean the abandonment of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather simply the cessation of merit and demerit which produce its status as the locus of enjoyment in those respective branches; therefore, there is no [abandonment] of the soul itself.

This is a modification of its own nature (*svarūpa-vikāra*). Regarding this point, he provides an illustration by saying "according to the analogy of the field, etc. Just as in the case of "one acquires or abandons a field," the acquisition of the field by the individual soul (*jīva*) is not a pervasion of its own nature, nor is its abandonment a release from it by way of that nature; rather, the acquisition of the field consists in the acquisition of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which establish its status as a means for the soul's experience, and the abandonment of that [field] is the abandonment of the field itself.

The meaning is: "due to the absence of specific conceits caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of [false] identification. This is the sense: in passages such as "Just as one casts off worn-out garments," the abandonment and acquisition of the body that are mentioned refer merely to specific conceits dependent upon karma; they do not, however, denote the attainment of a new essential nature nor the loss of the essential nature. Therefore, no suspicion arises regarding a modification of the soul's essential nature.

He says "one" (eka) to show that those who maintain both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) in the state of liberation must abandon their contradictory position—due to self-contradiction and contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—and instead follow the true path which is free from the fault of contradiction, just like the Jaina doctrine. This is the meaning: since our own position is free from the suspicion of contradiction or conflict with valid means of knowledge, it alone is the true path, while others are false paths. As for the grammatical construction of the words: the liberated soul is one, yet not one; it is both different and non-different from the Supreme, and also separate and non-separate.

Those who, like children or madmen, wander about thinking that one becomes oneself the enjoyer of all desired objects by means of one's own nature as well as through a nature of separateness or non-separateness from the Supreme Self, face the following: their own statement is contradicted; there is a self-contradiction in saying "one is both one and many, and separate from the other"; there is a violation of hundreds of scriptural texts such as "He [sees] himself as distinct from the Impeller"; there is a subversion of the intended meaning of those respective statements; and there is the fact that the scriptures teaching difference and non-difference have another purpose.

The demonstration of the mutual identity of individual souls (*jīva*) is based on their commonality (*sājātya*); however, the demonstration of the mutual identity between the individual soul and Brahman is based on their commonality in the form of consciousness, bliss, and so forth, as well as the intention to show that [the soul] has Brahman as its self by means of establishing the relationship of body and self. Considering that the demonstration of the identity of consciousness and Brahman is due to the identity of the qualified (*viśiṣṭaikya*), and having thus abandoned the quarrel of sectarian views by relying on the Jaina perspective so that people may follow the true path alone—this is the meaning: those who maintain the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vāda*) are the followers of the Karma-Mīmāṃsā.

Furthermore, those Brahma-mīmāṃsakas who follow that [Advaita] doctrine and rely upon both difference and non-difference—namely, both the Jainas and the Gāndhi-mīmāṃsakas—should therefore abandon the Jaina doctrine and instead resort to the true path. By accepting the distinction in the essential nature of the triad of principles—"the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the impeller"—the contemplation of their qualified unity, expressed as "all this has been declared to be the threefold Brahman," is indeed the true path; let them embrace that very path.

Anticipating the objection that this involves tautology, he refutes it with the words "all this. That which was stated in the Śruti—"If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition (saṅkalpa) the fathers arise for him"—has already been established by the author of the Sūtras as well in the aphorism, "Because of [the Lord's] mere volition, that [is accomplished]. Now, however, it is stated again that there is no restriction regarding the assumption of a body and so forth according to His own will; thus, the opponent’s intention is that this would be like "grinding what has already been ground. To this, he says: "That is not so. Here, the maxim of grinding what is already ground does not apply.

Thus [the author] establishes that very point with the words "anyonya" (mutually). This is the meaning: if what was stated previously were stated here as well, then it would be like the maxim of grinding what has already been ground. For previously, in the passage "Because of its being obtained from mere resolve alone," it was stated only this much: that the body, senses, and so forth arise from one's own resolve alone, independent of effort. Now, however, someone says: "In the absence of a body dependent on karma... [and so on].

Another, however, says that the existence of the body is not dependent on karma. But we state the restriction of the scope of the scriptural passages concerning "having a body" and "being bodiless"; this is the additional point. He states another further point with the words "at will" (*kāmataḥ*). When accepting various parts [of a body] by mere volition (*saṅkalpa*), sometimes there is the assumption of a body fashioned by oneself, and sometimes the assumption of a body fashioned by the Supreme Person; such is the intention of the author of the Sūtras in explaining the non-restriction regarding the assumption of a body.

Since there is no contradiction because [the former] does not exist [in the latter], there is no risk of tautology regarding the teaching of a superior meaning. Here, the statement concerning the description of non-restriction (*aniyati*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the description of restriction (*niyati*) mentioned immediately prior.

Regarding this, the connection [of the topic] is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The doubt is whether the sovereignty of the liberated one consists in being the Lord of all—which is the power of creation, maintenance, and so forth, unique to the Supreme Person—or whether it is devoid of that and has as its object only the experience of the Supreme Person. The inquiry into that, however, is: does the sovereignty of the liberated one concern the activity of the world, or not?

Is the scriptural definition of Brahman, beginning with "From which indeed these [beings arise]," contradicted by the inclusion of the governance of the world within the sovereignty of the liberated one? Or is it not? Is it reasonable to accept the governance of the world as a defining characteristic of Brahman because the context of creation is absent for the liberated one; or is it unreasonable to accept the governance of the world as a defining characteristic of Brahman because scripture mentions that the liberated one wanders through the worlds of transformation? And is the wandering of the liberated one through the worlds of transformation for the purpose of governance?

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of mere enjoyment": here, the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) raises the objection with the words "even though," suggesting that based on the prima facie understanding of the scriptural statement, "He attains the highest equality," the liberated soul (mukta) might also possess the activity of governing the world, just like the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa). This is the meaning: although it was previously stated that the body of the Supreme Self consists of the liberated soul due to its being an attribute (ādheyatva) and so forth characterized by corporeality, nevertheless, the "highest equality" heard in scripture concerning the aspect of activity must not be disturbed. Therefore, [it is said] "merely by his will, that [body] comes into being."

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣin) objection—that because it is stated in the Sūtra that "all [creation] arises from mere volition," the activity of the world-creation must also belong [to the individual soul]—is cut down and dispelled at the end of the treatise. By not establishing equality of agency for the two others, he shows that there is only equality of enjoyment; that is, while the one is the agent of the world (*kṛtimān*) and the other is the individual soul (*itara*), only equality of enjoyment is possible between them, but never equality of world-activity. For if there were such equality, it would entail the disappearance of the distinction characterized as the difference between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśvara*).
Here, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) raises an objection regarding the absence of equality in the world-activity.

Regarding the term *sāyujya*: this is the sequence of the meaning of the words here. Indeed, from the sequence of the words and their meanings, it was determined that *sāyujya* is simply the equality of enjoyment (*bhogasāmya*) with those who are devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). And that has already been explained by us previously. He states the reason for this: "because there is no sublation of the power of the word and so forth. We have already demonstrated the power of the word. Here, the mention of "by the experts" (*nipuṇaiḥ*) is for the purpose of refuting the Advaitins who assert that *sāyujya* is identity (*aikya*). Having raised the objection—"Let the meaning of the word *sāyujya* be as you say; what does that have to do with the subject at hand?"—he says: *tacca...* (And that...)

Thus: if there were equality of activity, then indeed there would also be identity of being (*sāyujya*). For when there is equality of eating, equality of enjoyment is also possible. He strengthens the stated point by means of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "if [it] were non-existent" (*asati*). He establishes that very point with the words "in its own action" (*svakriye*): since the Lord always possesses the relish of His own actions, if the individual soul (*jīva*) lacks the activity of the world, it would lack the relish of its own actions; how, then, could the establishment of total equality occur? He concludes the stated point along with its supporting reasoning with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is what has been said.

He rejects [the opponent's view] with the words "not so" (*maivam*). He establishes that very point with the phrase "that which has its characteristic" (*tallakṣaṇam*). The meaning is as follows: whatever is the characteristic of a thing, it must belong to that thing alone and not to another. Therefore, how could the activity of the world, being the characteristic of God, belong to someone other than Him through concomitance (*anugama*) or persistence (*anuvṛtti*)? For those who know the definition of a characteristic state that what persists in both the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the non-characterized (*alakṣya*) cannot be the characteristic of the characterized.

Now, one might ask: "In the absence of activity, how can there be equality of enjoyment? To this, the author explains that even in its absence, equality of enjoyment is established by means of a process observed in the world, stating: "It is said. Here is the grammatical connection (*śabdānvaya*): In any statement regarding creation, liberated souls are never described as being the cause of the world. Then, raising the objection—"If that is so, how could there be such statements of acting according to desire (*kāmacāra*) as 'having enjoyed these worlds and desires'?"—the author replies: "Let that [acting according to desire] indeed exist; nevertheless, the status of being the originator of the world is not established," saying: "The primary [cause]," and so forth. In this context:

It remains to be asked: "In the absence of equality of activity, how can there be equality of enjoyment? To this he says, "All [enjoy]," meaning that equality of enjoyment arises precisely from the equality of the objects of enjoyment, not from the equality of activity. For in the world, in activities such as acting or dancing, we observe that the audience leader, the actors, and others experience an equality of enjoyment through the equality of the objects to be experienced; it is not the actor alone who has the enjoyment. Just as among those serving a king, the joy of the king’s intimate attendants is equal to that of the king himself. It is only...

Ownership and independence reside in the king, and not in Ānanda; this, however, is the method observed in the world. This is not the only instance; even the Śruti, stating, "That is one [measure of] the bliss of Brahman, and of the learned Śrotriya who is untouched by desire," establishes that there is equality of enjoyment despite the difference in essential nature and the difference in activity between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśvara), due to their relationship as the subordinate and the superior. Thus, the equality of enjoyment, established by both visible and invisible means of knowledge, is desired by those who possess right vision and are distinguished; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

On this point, some say: "Having described the gradations of bliss starting from human bliss up to the bliss of the Four-faced One (Brahmā), it is stated [in the text], 'And of the Śrotriya who is untouched by desire'; thus, even for one who is a Śrotriya free from desire, that same bliss is indicated as increasing in sequence. Therefore, it must be admitted that even those residing in the supreme state who are Śrotriyas free from desire possess a bliss equal to human bliss and the rest. This [objection] he restates with the words, "niṣkāme... (in the case of one free from desire).

He refutes what has been stated as follows: the meaning is that because each successive enjoyment of the transmigrating soul is a hundredth part less than the preceding enjoyment previously mentioned, it is miserable. Indeed, among the assemblies of the orthodox (āstikas), there is no discussion asserting that the state of one who has gone to the supreme abode is infinitely inferior to the well-known enjoyments of Indra and others. Nor does the Supreme Person consider even the description of one who has gone to the supreme abode as being inferior to the well-known Indra and others to be acceptable for those who are exclusively devoted to Him (paramaikāntins). Nor do His intimate servants [accept such a thing].

Even serpents, the lord of birds, and others accept his word. Regarding the statement, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," the Śruti declares that for all knowers of Brahman, upon the cessation of all obstructions, the fruit is common and uniform: "He enjoys all desires together. Indeed, it is not logical here to restrict the meaning of the word "all" to some [desires] alone, as that would result in a contradiction of the word's meaning. Therefore, [the state of] "being stainless and attaining supreme equality" applies to all without exception.

The fruit for those who know Brahman is indeed of one and the same form. If so, one might ask: "How then is there a description of distinct fruits? Anticipating this doubt, I say: "He is liberated. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) here is as follows: Mukunda’s beloved people—the eternal class consisting of Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and others—exist in that same eternal bliss; therefore, the mention of specific [fruits] for various qualified aspirants is an *avayutyanuvāda* (a partial restatement). This is the tradition of those learned in the principles of interpretation (*nīti*). Just as in the Vaiśvānara passage, the mention of specific fruits in the supplementary statements regarding the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*) and so forth is an *avayutyanuvāda*.

The meaning is that this [matter] is likewise described by the Tantrikas. Having previously stated the infinity and uniformity of the bliss of the liberated (muktānanda), he now establishes that very point clearly and cites an authoritative text of the true tradition (satsampradāya) as proof therein, saying: "The infinity of bliss. The scriptural passage beginning with "from which words turn back" declares the very infinity of the bliss of the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), which is to be experienced by the liberated. Anticipating the objection—"How can there be such infinity for that which is known through the Vedas?"—he says: "Because it consists of mere cessation of exhaustion" (śrāntimātratvāt).

In the verse beginning with “*yadvā śramāvadhi*,” the teacher Yamunācārya states that the bliss of the Lord cannot be known in its entirety even by the Vedas; the Veda itself describes the bliss of the Lord only up to the point of exhaustion. He further remarks that, likewise, it is appropriate for me as well to describe the bliss of the Lord only up to the point of my own exhaustion. Now, one might object: just as in the case of human bliss and so forth, it is possible to describe the bliss of the Lord in its entirety through a progressive method of conceptualization (*vidhiṣatakalpanā*). Anticipating this doubt:

To this he replies, "No, even that," by saying "the statement of a hundred injunctions. Even an injunction is indeed very small; for even when one conceives of a hundredfold number of increasingly smaller [units], their smallness does not cease. Therefore, a complete description of the bliss of Brahman is never possible.

Because both the opening and the conclusion proceed in an identical manner, he says "And that [is stated]" to show that this very point has been clearly expressed in the words of Yāmunācārya: "Even beyond the Puruṣas who are higher than the Lotus-born [Brahmā]. Indeed, the Śruti reflects as follows: "Taking one Lotus-born as a limit, I conceive of another born from that Lotus-born who possesses an bliss a hundred times greater; then yet another beyond him, and still another beyond him. Even when such a conception is continued indefinitely, by the statement of their equality...
The immeasurability of the Blessed One’s bliss is already established; therefore, what is the use of this exertion? It could have been established from the very beginning by some other means.

I shall describe the infinity of the Blessed Lord’s bliss. This very same approach is that of describing infinity by way of negation (*vyatireka-mukhena*). With the statement, "From which words [turn back]," she has described it by way of negation. Here, for the sake of easy comprehension, she provides two examples intended by Yāmunācārya and clearly stated: "As with a staff," and so forth. For just as space cannot be measured by a staff, even so the bliss of the Supreme Brahman cannot be measured by the limited mind; this is the first example.

This is the illustration. As for the other [example], he says "And that," because it has been stated quite explicitly: "What difference is there between the two Aruna mountains submerged in the ocean?"

In this context, for the sake of a clear understanding of the meaning of what was stated as "excluding the activity of the world," the exclusion of the activity of the world follows from the fact that the liberated one lacks the status of being the material cause of the world. Even in the absence of such activity, the previously mentioned equality regarding experience is now clearly established by the verse beginning with "viśvam. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: first of all, the universe does not even constitute the body of the liberated one.

Since the absence of non-separation from the liberated soul (*muktāpṛthaksiddhyabhāva*) is clearly perceived throughout the universe, it is not appropriate to say that [the Lord] is its material cause (*upādāna*), because He lacks omnipotence (*sarvaśaktitva*). Now, an objection might be raised: "Surely you yourself have established with great effort that for the liberated there is no obstruction of their will; yet now you say that there is generally an obstruction of will because the state of being a material cause and so forth is impossible. How can this be? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not the Self" (*nātma*). This is the meaning: for the liberated one is a knower of reality, and by that [knowledge], it is indeed possible.

One should desire to do what is possible; therefore, for one who is liberated, there is no frustration of desire regarding what is impossible. As for that which is possible, he surely desires to do it; in that regard, there is no frustration of his desire—this is what is meant by the phrase "with respect to other objects. This is the intended meaning: the Blessed Lord indeed does not frustrate the desire of the liberated soul regarding the desired tasks such as service (*kaiṅkarya*), nor regarding the creation of the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*) and so forth according to his wish. Consequently, there is an absence of frustration of desire for the liberated one; for the liberated soul does not even long for the swallowing of space.

[Otherwise,] there would be the undesirable consequence of [the liberated soul] being ignorant. For what else could ignorance be, if not the inability to express? Now, one might object: "In that case, when the activity [of the soul] is restricted, there would also be a restriction of the aesthetic flavor (rasa) for the liberated one. Anticipating this, he repeats the very answer already stated many times before, out of favor toward the questioner who has asked again and again: "The activity... For we have stated many times that there is no disparity in bliss among those who have entered the royal assembly, even though there are differences in their respective offices.

He confirms the aforementioned point for the sake of ultimate clarity for his disciples by means of the analogy of the Emperor’s favor, beginning with the words "tattad" (that and that). Just as the Emperor’s favor, when it has reached a state of firm transformation through appropriate specific service according to one's qualification, produces equality among the servants; even there, in order to ward off improper requests, he qualifies that very equality with the word "svayam" (himself). For a servant does not himself desire the insignia of the master, such as the parasol and chowries, nor the ascending onto the throne.

In this very way, the state of friendship—whose essence is unsurpassed bliss, which is free from the limiting conditions of space, time, and so forth, and whose potential for recurrence has been utterly dispelled by the scripture itself through such passages as "He does not return again"—is attained by those who know the inner self and have sought refuge in the compassionate Lord. It is to be attained only by those qualified persons described as "by unswerving devotion," and not by other types of qualified persons; it is a state characterized by the absence of the Lord’s extraordinary attributes, such as His being the Lord of Śrī or His reclining upon Śeṣa.
The meaning of "state" (avasthā) is the state of obtaining every kind of service that is appropriate for all places, all times, and all circumstances.

In this quarter (pāda), six sections (adhikaraṇas) have been stated due to the difference in their subject matter; others, however, say that there is also a seventh section consisting of a single topic and a single aphorism: "There is no return, on account of the scriptural statement; there is no return, on account of the scriptural statement. That [view] is generally not favored by the author of the Bhāṣya, and he states that it does not even serve the purpose of a formal section (adhikaraṇa-prayojana). Regarding this, he says: "Here they say... The syntactical connection here is as follows: "In this context, some say that the final aphorism, which establishes non-return, constitutes a separate section. They also state the reason for this: because of the attainment of directness (āñjasya-lābhāt)."

The meaning is that this is because the natural sense (*svārasya*) of the Sūtra is obtained. The intention is that since a new section (*adhikaraṇa*) is commenced after the previous section has concluded, there must be a suspicion of repeated recurrence; thus, the natural sense of the Sūtra exists. He states "there is" to show that there is another supporting reason here. This is the underlying point: in the sentence "They do not return to this human whirlpool," the word "this" (*imam*) is observed; by that, it is indicated that while there is a recurrence, it is not merely the attainment of this world.

"Therefore, because there is a suspicion of return (*āvṛtti*), the commencement of this section (*adhikaraṇa*) is justified; thus it is begun as a separate section. To this, he states the answer at the beginning of the *Bhāṣya*: "That is not seen. Then, raising the objection: "In that case, if the sūtra 'Non-return [is established] from the word' (*anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt*) does not constitute a separate section, its status as a supplement to the preceding section must be asserted; yet such a supplementary status is not observed," he says: "It exists. Raising the objection again: "How is it a supplement to the preceding? he says: "It may be so. The intention here is as follows: regarding the return of a living being (*jīva*) who possesses true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*).

Since the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) stated in the preceding section—that because the Supreme Person also possesses true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpa*), there exists some similarity between Him and this liberated soul in terms of their absolute equality regarding the activity of the universe—could be suspected, it is precisely for the purpose of removing this doubt that the liberated soul's engagement in such activity is denied. It is established as a supplement to the preceding section that he remains solely engaged in serving the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.

Regarding the phrase "of the Sūtra," the following is the determination: In the passage, "They do not return to this human whirlpool," the word "this" (*imam*) is intended as an indicator for the entire human cycle of existence (*mānavāvarta*). Since there is no possibility of a liberated soul—who is entirely freed from all karma—returning anywhere under the influence of karma, even the voluntary return mentioned in the context of "these worlds" as a subordinate part of the service consisting of spontaneous attendance is the same everywhere; that is, within this very world referred to by "these worlds."

[The opponent objects: "Because of the mention of returning again. Now, one might suspect that just as the explanatory passage (arthavāda) stating, "The merit of the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible," is satisfied by the mere fact of lasting for a long time, so too the statement "and he does not return again" and similar passages would be satisfied by the mere fact of abiding for a long duration. Anticipating this, [the author] shows that since there is no possibility of returning again for one who is completely liberated from all karma, these passages eternally negate the return of those who have performed ritual actions; thus he says, "at the beginning of creation," etc. The syntactical connection here is as follows: [the cycle of] creation, maintenance, dissolution, and return...

Having seen the individual soul (jīva) engaged in the revolutions of worldly existence—which are for the most part like the *daṇḍarāsa* dance accompanied by the flavor of divine play—the Lord, with a satisfied mind, bestows upon it the bliss of attaining liberation from saṃsāra as if it were a reward; then, granting union (*sāyujya*), He enjoys—that is, He protects—that very same fortunate one. This is the meaning.

Since the Blessed One has declared through the very statement, "And he does not return," that there is the absolute cessation of all actions for the liberated one such that he is no longer made to return, this cessation [of doubt] may arise from the removal of any suspicion prompted by the description of imperishable fruits, such as in the passage, "The Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed yield imperishable results. This is the meaning: for if there were no complete liberation from all karma, the statement "And he does not return" would have to be interpreted in some other way; however, once the complete liberation from all karma is established, [the text stands as it is].
The statement regarding non-return is more effective when taken according to the literal sense, [showing] that "this path is indeed excellent."

Here, he explains the specific meanings of the six previously mentioned sections (adhikaraṇas) by dividing them, beginning with "svāvirbhāva" (the manifestation of one's own nature). In liberation (apavarga), the manifestation of one’s own essential nature is the meaning of the first section. Thus, five meanings are established through the [remaining] five sections. In the second [section], there is the vision extending up to one’s own body as the constant locus, free from all limiting adjuncts (nirupadhi). And in the third, there is the perception of the conscious self (jīva) together with its own attributes, as known from the crest-jewels of the Vedas (śruti-śikhara).

Furthermore, in the fourth [state], there is the accomplishment of one's own desired objects through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*); in the fifth, however, there is the unrestricted assumption of various bodies; and in the sixth, upon attaining equality with the Supreme Brahman, there is the relinquishing of the attributes of Brahman—such as being the creator of the world, the bestower of liberation, and the Lord of Śrī. These are the essential points of the six topics in the fourth section of the fourth chapter.

And here, by means of a complete compilation of the arguments of the proponents of falsity (mṛṣāvādins) regarding the subject matter of the fourth chapter, he says "meditation and so forth" to show that [their position] does not exist.

"Meditation" refers to the meditation of the Blessed Lord. By the word "and so forth," there are included its constituent parts, such as ritual action, tranquility, self-control, and the like. Its "power" consists in the non-clinging and destruction of future and past sins, respectively. The "departure" is the exit of the individual soul (the bearer of the instruments) from the small hut of the body, as described in the section on departure (*utkrānti-pāda*). The "path" is the journey through the artery of Brahman (*brahmanāḍī*) by way of the auspicious path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*). "Attaining the supreme light which is self-luminous" means becoming manifest in one's own true nature. "Creation according to one's own will" means the manifestation of whatever is desired solely through one's own volition. "Even the supreme [state]" refers to equality with the Supreme Brahman in respect to mere enjoyment.

How could one who stands within the doctrine of Māyā possibly reconcile this entire collection of topics described here, which constitutes the essence of the final chapter? The meaning is that he could not reconcile it in any way; for all these matters pertain to Brahman with attributes (*saguṇa-brahman*) and lack any connection to Brahman without attributes (*nirguṇa-brahman*), and furthermore, that attribute-less Brahman is not mentioned anywhere in the chapter concerning the fruits [of action].

Having previously stated that the claims of the Mṛṣāvādins contradict the meaning of the final chapter, [the author] says "mānāmāne" to show that there is no conformity with logic (*nyāya*) anywhere in the *Trikāṇḍī* Mīmāṃsā. First, in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, we observe a systematic sequence dedicated to establishing the various means of knowledge (*māna*), the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), their application (*prayukti*), the order of performance (*krama*), the agent (*kartṛ*), and so forth.

Therefore, the first section (Pūrva-mīmāṃsā) is exclusively concerned with distinctions. Likewise, in the middle section as well, through the collection of sūtras beginning with "The deities are indeed diverse" (*nānā vā devatā*), the diversity of deities and so forth is established; this too is certainly contradictory to those who maintain that all is false. Furthermore, in this very section concerning Brahman, the refutation of the Buddhists and others—who seek to subvert the distinction between attributes and the substratum of attributes—is seen everywhere through the logical demonstration of their respective points. Thus, for these reasons, there is no scope whatsoever for a proponent of falsehood who follows the views of the Buddhists and others within the three-sectioned Mīmāṃsā.

Having thus explained the entire subject matter without any doubt, if some doubt should remain in certain places, even that will be pacified by the course of time; and if it is not entirely pacified here, let it be pacified in the state of liberation (*muktadaśā*). There is no contradiction whatsoever regarding the meaning clearly understood. Indeed, this is the established rule (*maryādā*), which is to be followed not only in the context of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātmaśāstra*) but also in ritual practices (*anuṣṭhāna*) well-known from the *Kalpasūtras*. Thus he shows [this] with the words "at the end of the three Vedas" (*trayyante*).

The path [leading] to the end of the three Vedas is indeed difficult; this path is described by most teachers as having its course within that [Vedic realm]. It is well known in the world that a path instructed by a teacher leads one to the further shore. Likewise, this path—the way—pointed out by teachers who know reality leads to the further shore of knowledge. Whatever remains unknown here should be understood as pertaining to liberation alone. For even those in the world who employ the investigation of valid means of knowledge do not know everything; how many points of doubt remain?

Even for those who have attained transcendent vision (*krāntadarśin*), this is the limit regarding the inner self (*adhyātma*). He shows that this same method applies to practice as well by stating, "it must be done. Even the authors of the ritual manuals (*kalpakāra*) announce certain matters regarding what is to be done while remaining in doubt, yet they are not thereby released from what is enjoined in the manuals. Likewise, even in the exposition of the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*), the knowers of the Self should be content by grasping the meaning that has been understood without doubt; the remainder, however, will be revealed by time, even if it is not yet understood.

Upon attaining the supreme light, in the state of manifesting in one's own true form, this will be perceived with perfect clarity; nevertheless, the realization of the portions pertaining to oneself is by no means false in any respect.

Thus, having purified the meaning determined in the four chapters, he describes them in four sections (*pādas*) within the *Śrutyanta* [text]. Indeed, the topics of reconciliation (*samanvaya*), non-contradiction (*avirodha*), means (*sādhana*), and fruit (*phala*) are described as the subject matter of the four chapters. Having stated each one individually, he concludes: in the first chapter, reasoning consistent with the scriptural statements was established; and in establishing the weightiness of that reasoning, even all the mountains become like cotton. In the second chapter, however, there is the refutation of opposing views.

This is what he says: "Because that is established" (*tatsiddheḥ*). Since the thorough knowledge of Brahman is established in the first chapter, the disputants' chatter—which is like a mass of darkness in the absence of light—is refuted; by this, it is stated that the second definition has as its primary purpose the rejection of the opposing position. He also shows the subject matter of the third chapter by dividing it: "In the means to liberation" (*mokṣopāye*).

The means to liberation are *sadvidyā* and the like; in their sole sovereignty, other methods—namely, the injunctions for rites that are ancillary to knowledge (*vidyāṅga-karma-vidhi*) and the injunctions for tranquility, self-control, and so forth (*śama-dama-ādi-vidhi*)—assume the status of servants; the meaning is that they assume a subordinate role. By this, the subject matter of the third chapter has been reviewed. He also states the subject matter of the fourth chapter, beginning with the word "mukteḥ."

The meaning is that the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*)—such as the happiness of one's own kingdom, heaven, and so forth—which compete with a mere drop from the great ocean whose form is the nectar of liberated bliss, attain the state of being drops within the great ocean of the bliss of experiencing the Supreme Person. By this, it is stated that for those who know the supreme self, liberation characterized by non-return alone is to be pursued, through the complete renunciation of other goals of human existence.

Having thus correctly understood the meaning of the four chapters, the text shows the result—beginning with prosperity and culminating in liberation—for the qualified seeker in due order, by means of the phrase "the state of being on this side and that side" (pārāvaryam).

First, having discerned the beginning and end of the category of reality through the unerring scriptures, a person develops intense fear regarding saṃsāra according to the sequence set forth in the first chapter on detachment (*vairāgya-pāda*). Then, according to the sequence set forth in the second chapter on the two-fold characteristics (*ubhaya-liṅga-pāda*), that person becomes one whose passion has reached its culmination in the attainment of the lotus feet of the Supreme Person. By this, the subject matter described across the ten chapters ending with the chapter on the two-fold characteristics has been stated. Hereafter, he summarizes and demonstrates the meaning of the six subsequent chapters, beginning with the words "Someone... (*kañcit*) in the section on true knowledge (*sad-vidyā*).

Having mastered a certain specific knowledge along with its ancillaries, being one whose obstacles have been stilled and who is established in the knowledge of Brahman, he attains Brahman; then, among the denizens of Vaikuṇṭha who travel in celestial chariots, he himself assumes one of their forms and becomes an unconditioned attendant at the lotus feet of Paravāsudeva. Regarding him, the author states two qualifications: "without return," which refers to the scriptural passage, "And he does not return again."

Thus, "one who has heard the meaning" means one who has learned the entire subject matter from the mouth of the teacher, according to the passage: "He who knows the imperishable, true Person—[he] has declared that knowledge of Brahman in its true essence."

Demonstrating the weight of his own work as the cause for ascending to liberation (*apavarga*), he composes this verse in the form of a benediction for his disciples: "Sāsā...," meaning that this work is well-known. It is "the uprooter of those various wicked doctrines accompanied by envy" (*sāsūya-tattat-kumati-mata-samunmūlanī*).

[The Brahmasūtra] is like a ladder for the series of fundamental principles (*mūlanītiśreṇī*), resembling a staircase leading to the path of logic concerning the cause of the universe (*jagatkāraṇaviṣayanyāyanīthīniśśreṇisaddaśī*). It is the charioteer (*sārathi*) for mounting the chariot on the path to the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣaprāptimārgarathārohaṇe*), acting as the driver for those ascending the chariot of the three paths of the Yugas (*triyugapatharathārohasūtam*). "O virtuous ones" (*santaḥ*) is an address to the wise. May the virtuous ones (*santaḥ*) attain contentment (*santoṣam*)—which is accompanied by innate knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānena sahajena*) that is capable of pacifying the three types of suffering (*tāpatrayapraśamanapaṭunā*)—through this *Sūtrādhikaraṇacaraṇādhyāyasāravali*, [a work consisting of] the essence of the Sūtras, Adhikaraṇas, Pādas, and Adhyāyas.

The meaning is "the tradition of collecting the essence" of all four [Vedas]. By this, it is stated that the purpose of composing this unprecedented work is the satisfaction of the students who desire to understand the reality of the inner self (adhyātmatattva).

Now, in order to ensure that the previously mentioned topics are understood without confusion, we shall specify their particular number. Having thus stated our position, we address those who know the science of words, sentences, and logic: "What can others do—those intoxicated ones who reject everything?"; and having thus disparaged those of a mad disposition, we disregard them. Setting aside only the grace of the Blessed One, we do not even offer a jest toward those ill-behaved ones; by this, we manifest our own discernment.

"Five thousand six hundred"—this is the indication of the number of topics (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, by means of these groups of topics, the boundaries have been clearly defined in this division of the Brahma-kāṇḍa. Furthermore, we have stated that only a few who possess discernment understand this; as for others—those whose intellects are ruined, who are satisfied merely by rejecting everything and are wretched—what more need be said of them? We, however, perceive this entire universe as being under the control of minds bound by the machinery of the three qualities (*guṇa*).

Seeing that their own minds are constrained by the repetition of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—that is, bound by the accumulation of these qualities—and are thus subservient and dependent upon them; for in this world, those who are ill-disciplined are seen to be single-mindedly intent on perceiving the faults of others.

While our Lord Śrī Raṅganātha—the witness to the excellence of the compositions we have fashioned—is our protector, we do not engage even in the playful jest of mocking such wicked people. The meaning is this: according to the maxim "when you are pleased," we seek only the grace of the Blessed One as our human goal. As for other men, let them view us otherwise or not at all based on their own qualities; what is the use of conforming to their futile intellects?

[Objection: "But surely you yourselves stated at the very beginning [of your work] that you were giving meaning to the name 'Vedāntācārya' by receiving the command of the Lord of Śrīraṅga and others. In this treatise, however, we do not see you elucidating the body of the *Śārīraka* (the *Brahma-sūtras*) alone, nor do we see the extensive refutation of opposing views, nor even the formulation of the specific modes of reality intended for your own position—though these ought to have been stated by those who have ascended to the throne of the Teacher. How is this so? Anticipating this doubt, he provides the answer with the verse beginning "viśvam. This is the meaning:

Hundreds of treatises (*nibandhana*) concerning the subject matter of Vedānta have been composed by us; among them, this pair of treatises provides mutual support and establishes every point of meaning. First is the *Tattvamuktākalāpa*, and this is the specific treatise named *Adhikaraṇasārāvalī*, which bears a name true to its content. Both of these should be understood as being mutually beneficial. For those who possess a thorough knowledge of this pair, there remains nothing further to be understood—unless, indeed, there is something yet to be known through the *Mīmāṃsāpādukā*.

Thus, by this [work], everything is established; therefore, these three treatises must be understood in their entirety by diligent students. Furthermore, whatever remains should be sought in our other treatises at the various relevant places. As for the grammatical connection of the words, it has been clearly explained in the *Tattvamuktākalāpa* starting with the verse: "By the division into substance and non-substance," and so forth.

In this treatise, the nature of the *Śārīraka* is firmly established and arranged through mutual connection, either by way of distinction or as a continuous whole from beginning to end; such is the meaning. By means of the analogy of nectar (*amṛta*), he demonstrates that these two treatises are to be accepted by students, stating "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This pair of compositions is described as being like nectar vomited forth from his own ocean of heard scripture (*śruta*). They are "giving hand to one another," meaning they are mutually supportive.

It should be held in the mind by those of the highest qualification—those who possess unflagging and firmly bound faith, who are endowed with teachers, and who are humble through devotion to their guru as prescribed in the scripture, "A person who has a teacher knows"—and whose minds have been purified by his grace.

Establishing the similarity of these aforementioned *sragdharā* verses to divine apsarases who create ornaments for Brahmā, he demonstrates that the Person (Puruṣa) residing on the far shore of the ocean of illusion—who is adorned with the artistic crafts of the intent of the Sūtras—is worthy of being honored by all those of superior being (*sattva*). He does so with the words "In this way" (*ittham*).

The connection [of the verses] is as follows: the *sragdharā* verses, having arrived by the path described in the *Śārīraka*, adorn this man—who is full of faith and endowed with devotion—once he has been led by the wise (*sūri*) who face him with pure dispositions along the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*). Here, the term "by the wise" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who know the inner self (*adhyātma-vid*). This is the meaning: just as divine nymphs adorn a man brought by beloved learned men, so do these *sragdharā* verses adorn him once he has been led by the path of light and the rest.

He states with what they adorn [the person]: "by the crafts of the purport of the Sūtras and Upaniṣads. This word *śilpa* denotes a particular kind of ornament. The meaning is that these *Sragdharās*, having adorned the person by revealing the purport made manifest in the Sūtras, honor him by crossing over the passionless state (*viraja*) as far as the supreme abode (*paramapada*).

Since the composition of this work was obtained through the special divine command of Śrī Raṅgarāja, the Lord has thus made his very self resonant, like the conch Pāñcajanya; so he says: "O Wisdom! (prajñe).

"Prājñā" refers to a certain noble lady; her service to the teachers known as the "prājñas"—who possess the fragrance of the *dhampilla* and *mallī* jasmine—is intended. Likewise, "samudyat" means "risen," signifying the pure light that is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Here, the term "śruti" denotes both the portion of the Veda that establishes the inner self (*adhyātma*) and the hearing by the wise, expressed through a double entendre (*tantra*). By these verses, which are dear to one's own heart and agreeable to oneself, [the greatness of the *praṇava*] is [described] according to the sequence of the *pāñcajanya*, meaning like the *pāñcajanya* [conch].

For the Pāñcajanya conch possesses the greatness of the *praṇava* by way of its form; and it possesses the greatness of the *praṇava* because of the high pitch of its sound. The Pāñcajanya resounds through the blowing of the Lord; likewise, I too have composed these verses only as impelled by the Lord. Thus, the meaning is that [the Lord], having made me speak at inappropriate places as if impelled by Himself, rejoiced—that is, was satisfied. Therefore, the meaning is that, just as in the phrase "Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya," He has repeatedly caused me to speak even on matters consisting of the refutation of opposing views.

Thus, first reiterating that his own composed work was obtained through the grace of Pārāśarya, and setting aside the conceit of non-authorship which constitutes his very essence, he proclaims that it was actually composed by the Lord Hayagrīva himself—who is distinguished as his own teacher and the originator of all sciences—by stating "Pārāśarya.
This is the syntactical connection here:

The Lord of Sages, the Blessed One Pārāśarya, whose name signifies one who has gone the unerring path, churned the vast ocean of the nectar of the Upaniṣads with the Vedānta-sūtras and extracted its essence. This very nectar, thus extracted by us and established in the heart of the Commentator, was spoken by my own teachers—who are like clouds raining upon the swans that are great disputants—and it is Hayagrīva himself who is its speaker; he alone is its speaker.

The word *vaktṛ* ends in the suffix *tṛn*; therefore, the accusative case is used here. In this context, the meaning of the verse—“Having churned the churning-stick of his intellect, by him the moon of the Mahābhārata was produced from the great ocean of the Veda for the welfare of the world”—is to be contemplated.
Victorious is the speech of the King of Ascetics— a sword that severs the tenets of opposing schools,
a braid of the young maidens of the Vedas, and a noble ladder for ascending to the divine state.
In order to establish the true meaning of the verses composed by the teachers— which are in harmony with all the works of the venerable gurus and possess a splendor rivaling the fierce sun—
this Varadaguru, a knower of the Vedānta, has provided a diverse commentary.
The son of Vedāntācārya, a lion who effects the destruction of the opposing views of those holding divergent opinions.

Thus concludes the *Śārīrakādhikaraṇacintāmaṇi*, composed by Kumāravedāntācārya— the crest-jewel of all logicians, independent in all philosophical systems, and known by the alternative name of Śrīmad Varadārya.
The fourth quarter of the fourth chapter.
